the north-west of the Peloponnesus. Subsequently it was applied
by the Romans to the whole Peloponnesus, now called the Morea,
and the south of Greece. It was then one of the two provinces
(Macedonia being the other) into which they divided the country
when it fell under their dominion. It is in this latter enlarged

meaning that the name is always used in the New Testament (<scripRef passage="Acts 18:12" id="a-p120.1" parsed="|Acts|18|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.12">Acts 18:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 18:27" id="a-p120.2" parsed="|Acts|18|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.27">27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 19:21" id="a-p120.3" parsed="|Acts|19|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.21">19:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 15" id="a-p120.4" parsed="|Rom|15|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.15">Rom. 15</scripRef>: 26; 16:5, etc.). It was at the time
when Luke wrote the Acts of the Apostles under the proconsular
form of government; hence the appropriate title given to Gallio
as the “deputy,” i.e., proconsul, of Achaia (Acts 18:12).
</def>
<term id="a-p120.6">Achaichus</term>
(1 Cor. 16:17), one of the members of the church of Corinth who,
with Fortunatus and Stephanas, visited Paul while he was at
Ephesus, for the purpose of consulting him on the affairs of the
church. These three probably were the bearers of the letter from
Corinth to the apostle to which he alludes in 1 Cor. 7:1.
</def>
<term id="a-p121.3">Achan</term>
Called also Achar, i.e., one who troubles (1 Chr. 2:7), in
commemoration of his crime, which brought upon him an awful
destruction (<scripRef passage="Josh. 7:1" id="a-p122.2" parsed="|Josh|7|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.7.1">Josh. 7:1</scripRef>). On the occasion of the fall of Jericho,
he seized, contrary to the divine command, an ingot of gold, a
quantity of silver, and a costly Babylonish garment, which he
hid in his tent. Joshua was convinced that the defeat which the
Israelites afterwards sustained before Ai was a proof of the
divine displeasure on account of some crime, and he at once
adopted means by the use of the lot for discovering the
criminal. It was then found that Achan was guilty, and he was
stoned to death in the valley of Achor. He and all that belonged
to him were then consumed by fire, and a heap of stones was
raised over the ashes.
</def>
<term id="a-p122.3">Achbor</term>
Gnawing = mouse. (1.) An Edomitish king (Gen. 36:38; 1 Chr. 1:49).
(2.) One of Josiah’s officers sent to the prophetess Huldah to
inquire regarding the newly-discovered book of the law (2 Kings 22:12, 14). He is also called Abdon (2 Chr. 34:20).
</def>
<term id="a-p124.4">Achish</term>
Angry, perhaps only a general title of royalty applicable to the
Philistine kings. (1.) The king with whom David sought refuge
when he fled from Saul (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 21:10-15" id="a-p125.1" parsed="|1Sam|21|10|21|15" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.21.10-1Sam.21.15">1 Sam. 21:10-15</scripRef>). He is called Abimelech
in the superscription of <scripRef passage="Ps. 34" id="a-p125.2" parsed="|Ps|34|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.34">Ps. 34</scripRef>. It was probably this same king
to whom David a second time repaired at the head of a band of
600 warriors, and who assigned him Ziklag, whence he carried on
war against the surrounding tribes (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 27:5-12" id="a-p125.3" parsed="|1Sam|27|5|27|12" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.27.5-1Sam.27.12">1 Sam. 27:5-12</scripRef>). Achish had

great confidence in the valour and fidelity of David (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 28:1" id="a-p125.4" parsed="|1Sam|28|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.28.1">1 Sam. 28:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 28:2" id="a-p125.5" parsed="|1Sam|28|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.28.2">2</scripRef>), but at the instigation of his courtiers did not permit

him to go up to battle along with the Philistine hosts (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 29:2-11" id="a-p125.6" parsed="|1Sam|29|2|29|11" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.29.2-1Sam.29.11">1 Sam. 29:2-11</scripRef>). David remained with Achish a year and four months.
(2.) Another king of Gath, probably grandson of the foregoing,
to whom the two servants of Shimei fled. This led Shimei to go
to Gath in pursuit of them, and the consequence was that Solomon
put him to death (1 Kings 2:39-46).
</def>
<term id="a-p125.8">Achmetha</term>
(Ezra 6:2), called Ecbatana by classical writers, the capital of
northern Media. Here was the palace which was the residence of
the old Median monarchs, and of Cyrus and Cambyses. In the time
of Ezra, the Persian kings resided usually at Susa of Babylon.
But Cyrus held his court at Achmetha; and Ezra, writing a
century after, correctly mentions the place where the decree of
Cyrus was found.
</def>
<term id="a-p126.2">Achor</term>
Trouble, a valley near Jericho, so called in consequence of the

trouble which the sin of Achan caused Israel (<scripRef passage="Josh. 7:24" id="a-p127.1" parsed="|Josh|7|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.7.24">Josh. 7:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 7:26" id="a-p127.2" parsed="|Josh|7|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.7.26">26</scripRef>).
The expression “valley of Achor” probably became proverbial for
that which caused trouble, and when Isaiah (<scripRef passage="Isa. 65:10" id="a-p127.3" parsed="|Isa|65|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.65.10">Isa. 65:10</scripRef>) refers
to it he uses it in this sense: “The valley of Achor, a place
for herds to lie down in;” i.e., that which had been a source of

calamity would become a source of blessing. Hosea also (<scripRef passage="Hos. 2:15" id="a-p127.4" parsed="|Hos|2|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.2.15">Hos. 2:15</scripRef>) uses the expression in the same sense: “The valley of
Achor for a door of hope;” i.e., trouble would be turned into
joy, despair into hope. This valley has been identified with the
Wady Kelt.
</def>
<term id="a-p127.5">Achsah</term>
Anklet, Caleb’s only daughter (1 Chr. 2:49). She was offered in
marriage to the man who would lead an attack on the city of
Debir, or Kirjath-sepher. This was done by Othniel (q.v.), who
accordingly obtained her as his wife (Josh. 15:16-19; Judg. 1:9-15).
</def>
<term id="a-p128.4">Achshaph</term>
Fascination, a royal city of the Canaanites, in the north of

Palestine (<scripRef passage="Josh. 11:1" id="a-p129.1" parsed="|Josh|11|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.1">Josh. 11:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 12:20" id="a-p129.2" parsed="|Josh|12|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.12.20">12:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 19:25" id="a-p129.3" parsed="|Josh|19|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.25">19:25</scripRef>). It was in the eastern
boundary of the tribe of Asher, and is identified with the
modern ruined village of Kesaf or Yasif, N.E. of Accho.
</def>
<term id="a-p129.4">Achzib</term>
Falsehood. (1.) A town in the Shephelah, or plain country of

Judah (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:44" id="a-p130.1" parsed="|Josh|15|44|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.44">Josh. 15:44</scripRef>); probably the same as Chezib of <scripRef passage="Gen. 38:5" id="a-p130.2" parsed="|Gen|38|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.38.5">Gen. 38:5</scripRef> =
Ain Kezbeh.
(2.) A Phoenician city (the Gr. Ecdippa), always retained in

their possession though assigned to the tribe of Asher (<scripRef passage="Josh. 19:29" id="a-p131.1" parsed="|Josh|19|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.29">Josh. 19:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 1:31" id="a-p131.2" parsed="|Judg|1|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.31">Judg. 1:31</scripRef>). It is identified with the modern es-Zib, on
the Mediterranean, about 8 miles north of Accho.
</def>
<term id="a-p131.3">Acre</term>
Is the translation of a word (tse’med), which properly means a
yoke, and denotes a space of ground that may be ploughed by a
yoke of oxen in a day. It is about an acre of our measure (Isa. 5:10; 1 Sam. 14:14).
</def>
<term id="a-p132.3">Acts of the Apostles</term>
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=Acts%20of%20the%20Apostles" id="a-p132.5" />
The title now given to the fifth and last of the historical
books of the New Testament. The author styles it a “treatise”
(1:1). It was early called “The Acts,” “The Gospel of the Holy
Ghost,” and “The Gospel of the Resurrection.” It contains
properly no account of any of the apostles except Peter and
Paul. John is noticed only three times; and all that is recorded
of James, the son of Zebedee, is his execution by Herod. It is
properly therefore not the history of the “Acts of the
Apostles,” a title which was given to the book at a later date,
but of “Acts of Apostles,” or more correctly, of “Some Acts of
Certain Apostles.”
As regards its authorship, it was certainly the work of Luke,

the “beloved physician” (comp. <scripRef passage="Luke 1:1-4" id="a-p134.1" parsed="|Luke|1|1|1|4" osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.1-Luke.1.4">Luke 1:1-4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 1:1" id="a-p134.2" parsed="|Acts|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.1">Acts 1:1</scripRef>). This is
the uniform tradition of antiquity, although the writer nowhere
makes mention of himself by name. The style and idiom of the
Gospel of Luke and of the Acts, and the usage of words and
phrases common to both, strengthen this opinion. The writer
first appears in the narrative in 16:11, and then disappears
till Paul’s return to Philippi two years afterwards, when he and
Paul left that place together (20:6), and the two seem
henceforth to have been constant companions to the end. He was
certainly with Paul at Rome (28; <scripRef passage="Col. 4:14" id="a-p134.3" parsed="|Col|4|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.4.14">Col. 4:14</scripRef>). Thus he wrote a
great portion of that history from personal observation. For
what lay beyond his own experience he had the instruction of
Paul. If, as is very probable, 2 Tim. was written during Paul’s
second imprisonment at Rome, Luke was with him then as his
faithful companion to the last (<scripRef passage="2 Tim. 4:11" id="a-p134.4" parsed="|2Tim|4|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.4.11">2 Tim. 4:11</scripRef>). Of his subsequent
history we have no certain information.
The design of Luke’s Gospel was to give an exhibition of the
character and work of Christ as seen in his history till he was
taken up from his disciples into heaven; and of the Acts, as its
sequel, to give an illustration of the power and working of the
gospel when preached among all nations, “beginning at
Jerusalem.” The opening sentences of the Acts are just an
expansion and an explanation of the closing words of the Gospel.
In this book we have just a continuation of the history of the
church after Christ’s ascension. Luke here carries on the
history in the same spirit in which he had commenced it. It is
only a book of beginnings, a history of the founding of
churches, the initial steps in the formation of the Christian
society in the different places visited by the apostles. It
records a cycle of “representative events.”
All through the narrative we see the ever-present,
all-controlling power of the ever-living Saviour. He worketh all
and in all in spreading abroad his truth among men by his Spirit
and through the instrumentality of his apostles.
The time of the writing of this history may be gathered from
the fact that the narrative extends down to the close of the
second year of Paul’s first imprisonment at Rome. It could not
therefore have been written earlier than A.D. 61 or 62, nor
later than about the end of A.D. 63. Paul was probably put to
death during his second imprisonment, about A.D. 64, or, as some
think, 66.
The place where the book was written was probably Rome, to
which Luke accompanied Paul.
The key to the contents of the book is in 1:8, “Ye shall be
witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judea, and in
Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.” After
referring to what had been recorded in a “former treatise” of
the sayings and doings of Jesus Christ before his ascension, the
author proceeds to give an account of the circumstances
connected with that event, and then records the leading facts
with reference to the spread and triumphs of Christianity over
the world during a period of about thirty years. The record
begins with Pentecost (A.D. 33) and ends with Paul’s first
imprisonment (A.D. 63 or 64). The whole contents of the book may
be divided into these three parts:
(1.) Chaps. 1-12, describing the first twelve years of the
Christian church. This section has been entitled “From Jerusalem
to Antioch.” It contains the history of the planting and
extension of the church among the Jews by the ministry of Peter.
(2.) Chaps. 13-21, Paul’s missionary journeys, giving the
history of the extension and planting of the church among the
Gentiles.
(3.) Chaps. 21-28, Paul at Rome, and the events which led to
this. Chaps. 13-28 have been entitled “From Antioch to Rome.”
In this book it is worthy of note that no mention is made of
the writing by Paul of any of his epistles. This may be
accounted for by the fact that the writer confined himself to a
history of the planting of the church, and not to that of its
training or edification. The relation, however, between this
history and the epistles of Paul is of such a kind, i.e., brings
to light so many undesigned coincidences, as to prove the
genuineness and authenticity of both, as is so ably shown by
Paley in his Horae Paulinae. “No ancient work affords so many
tests of veracity; for no other has such numerous points of
contact in all directions with contemporary history, politics,
and topography, whether Jewish, or Greek, or Roman.” Lightfoot.
(See PAUL.)
</def>
<term id="a-p143.2">Adah</term>
Ornament. (1.) The first of Lamech’s two wives, and the mother
of Jabal and Jubal (Gen. 4:19, 20, 23).
(2.) The first of Esau’s three wives, the daughter of Elon the
Hittite (Gen. 36:2, 4), called also Bashemath (26:34).
</def>
<term id="a-p145.3">Adam</term>
Red, a Babylonian word, the generic name for man, having the
same meaning in the Hebrew and the Assyrian languages. It was
the name given to the first man, whose creation, fall, and
subsequent history and that of his descendants are detailed in
the first book of Moses (<scripRef passage="Gen. 1:27" id="a-p146.1" parsed="|Gen|1|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.1.27">Gen. 1:27</scripRef>-ch. 5). “God created man
[Heb., Adam] in his own image, in the image of God created he
him; male and female created he them.”
Adam was absolutely the first man whom God created. He was
formed out of the dust of the earth (and hence his name), and
God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and gave him

dominion over all the lower creatures (<scripRef passage="Gen. 1:26" id="a-p147.1" parsed="|Gen|1|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.1.26">Gen. 1:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 2:7" id="a-p147.2" parsed="|Gen|2|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.2.7">2:7</scripRef>). He was
placed after his creation in the Garden of Eden, to cultivate
it, and to enjoy its fruits under this one prohibition: “Of the
tree of the knowledge of good and evil thou shalt not eat of it;
for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.”
The first recorded act of Adam was his giving names to the
beasts of the field and the fowls of the air, which God brought
to him for this end. Thereafter the Lord caused a deep sleep to
fall upon him, and while in an unconscious state took one of his
ribs, and closed up his flesh again; and of this rib he made a
woman, whom he presented to him when he awoke. Adam received her
as his wife, and said, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh
of my flesh: she shall be called Woman, because she was taken
out of Man.” He called her Eve, because she was the mother of
all living.
Being induced by the tempter in the form of a serpent to eat
the forbidden fruit, Eve persuaded Adam, and he also did eat.
Thus man fell, and brought upon himself and his posterity all
the sad consequences of his transgression. The narrative of the

Fall comprehends in it the great promise of a Deliverer (<scripRef passage="Gen. 3:15" id="a-p149.1" parsed="|Gen|3|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.3.15">Gen. 3:15</scripRef>), the “first gospel” message to man. They were expelled
from Eden, and at the east of the garden God placed a flame,
which turned every way, to prevent access to the tree of life
(<scripRef passage="Gen. 3" id="a-p149.2" parsed="|Gen|3|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.3">Gen. 3</scripRef>). How long they were in Paradise is matter of mere
conjecture.
Shortly after their expulsion Eve brought forth her
first-born, and called him Cain. Although we have the names of
only three of Adam’s sons, viz., Cain, Abel, and Seth, yet it is
obvious that he had several sons and daughters (<scripRef passage="Gen. 5:4" id="a-p150.1" parsed="|Gen|5|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.5.4">Gen. 5:4</scripRef>). He
died aged 930 years.
Adam and Eve were the progenitors of the whole human race.
Evidences of varied kinds are abundant in proving the unity of
the human race. The investigations of science, altogether
independent of historical evidence, lead to the conclusion that
God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on
all the face of the earth” (Acts 17:26. Comp. Rom. 5:12-12; 1 Cor. 15:22-49).
</def>
<term id="a-p151.4">Adamah</term>
Red earth, a fortified city of Naphtali, probably the modern
Damieh, on the west side of the sea of Tiberias (Josh. 19:33, 36).
</def>
<term id="a-p152.3">Adamant</term>
(Heb. shamir), Ezek. 3:9. The Greek word adamas means diamond.
This stone is not referred to, but corundum or some kind of hard
steel. It is an emblem of firmness in resisting adversaries of
the truth (<scripRef passage="Zech. 7:12" id="a-p153.2" parsed="|Zech|7|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.7.12">Zech. 7:12</scripRef>), and of hard-heartedness against the
truth (Jer. 17:1).
</def>
<term id="a-p153.4">Adam, a type</term>
The apostle Paul speaks of Adam as “the figure of him who was to
come.” On this account our Lord is sometimes called the second
Adam. This typical relation is described in Rom. 5:14-19.
</def>
<term id="a-p154.2">Adam, the city of</term>
Is referred to in Josh. 3:16. It stood “beside Zarethan,” on the
west bank of Jordan (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:12" id="a-p155.2" parsed="|1Kgs|4|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.12">1 Kings 4:12</scripRef>). At this city the flow of the
water was arrested and rose up “upon an heap” at the time of the
Israelites’ passing over (Josh. 3:16).
</def>
<term id="a-p155.4">Adar</term>
Large, the sixth month of the civil and the twelfth of the

ecclesiastical year of the Jews (<scripRef passage="Esther 3:7" id="a-p156.1" parsed="|Esth|3|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.3.7">Esther 3:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Esther 3:13" id="a-p156.2" parsed="|Esth|3|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.3.13">13</scripRef>; 8:12; 9:1, 15,
17, 19, 21). It included the days extending from the new moon of
our March to the new moon of April. The name was first used
after the Captivity. When the season was backward, and the lambs
not yet of a paschal size, or the barley not forward enough for
abib, then a month called Veadar, i.e., a second Adar, was
intercalated.
</def>
<term id="a-p156.3">Adbeel</term>
Miracle of God, the third of the twelve sons of Ishmael, and
head of an Arabian tribe (Gen. 25:13; 1 Chr. 1:29).
</def>
<term id="a-p157.3">Addar</term>
Ample, splendid, son of Bela (1 Chr. 8:3); called also “Ard”
(Gen. 46:21)
</def>
<term id="a-p158.3">Adder</term>
(Ps. 140:3; Rom. 3:13, “asp”) is the rendering of, (1.) Akshub
(“coiling” or “lying in wait”), properly an asp or viper, found
only in this passage. (2.) Pethen (“twisting”), a viper or

venomous serpent identified with the cobra (Naja haje) (<scripRef passage="Ps. 58:4" id="a-p159.3" parsed="|Ps|58|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.58.4">Ps. 58:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 91:13" id="a-p159.4" parsed="|Ps|91|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.91.13">91:13</scripRef>); elsewhere “asp.” (3.) Tziphoni (“hissing”) (<scripRef passage="Prov. 23:32" id="a-p159.5" parsed="|Prov|23|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.23.32">Prov. 23:32</scripRef>); elsewhere rendered “cockatrice,” <scripRef passage="Isa. 11:8" id="a-p159.6" parsed="|Isa|11|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.11.8">Isa. 11:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 14:29" id="a-p159.7" parsed="|Isa|14|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.14.29">14:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 59:5" id="a-p159.8" parsed="|Isa|59|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.59.5">59:5</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Jer. 8:17" id="a-p159.9" parsed="|Jer|8|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.8.17">Jer. 8:17</scripRef>, as it is here in the margin of the Authorized
Version. The Revised Version has “basilisk.” This may have been
the yellow viper, the Daboia xanthina, the largest and most
dangerous of the vipers of Palestine. (4.) Shephiphon
(“creeping”), occurring only in <scripRef passage="Gen. 49:17" id="a-p159.10" parsed="|Gen|49|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.17">Gen. 49:17</scripRef>, the small speckled
venomous snake, the “horned snake,” or cerastes. Dan is compared
to this serpent, which springs from its hiding-place on the
passer-by.
</def>
<term id="a-p159.11">Addi</term>
Ornament, (Luke 3:28), the son of Cosam, and father of Melchi,
one of the progenitors of Christ.
</def>
<term id="a-p160.2">Addon</term>
Low, one of the persons named in Neh. 7:61 who could not “shew
their father’s house” on the return from captivity. This, with
similar instances (ver. 63), indicates the importance the Jews
attached to their genealogies.
</def>
<term id="a-p161.2">Adiel</term>
Ornament of God. (1.) The father of Azmaveth, who was treasurer
under David and Solomon (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 27:25" id="a-p162.1" parsed="|1Chr|27|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.27.25">1 Chr. 27:25</scripRef>). (2.) A family head of
the tribe of Simeon (1 Chr. 4:36). (3.) A priest (1 Chr. 9:12).
</def>
<term id="a-p162.4">Adin</term>
Effeminate. (1.) Ezra 8:6. (2.) Neh. 10:16.
</def>
<term id="a-p163.3">Adina</term>
Slender, one of David’s warriors (1 Chr. 11:42), a Reubenite.
</def>
<term id="a-p164.2">Adino</term>
The Eznite, one of David’s mighty men (2 Sam. 23:8). (See JASHOBEAM.)
</def>
<term id="a-p165.3">Adjuration</term>
A solemn appeal whereby one person imposes on another the
obligation of speaking or acting as if under an oath (1 Sam. 14:24; Josh. 6:26; 1 Kings 22:16).
We have in the New Testament a striking example of this (Matt. 26:63; Mark 5:7), where the high priest calls upon Christ to
avow his true character. It would seem that in such a case the
person so adjured could not refuse to give an answer.
The word “adjure”, i.e., cause to swear is used with reference
to the casting out of demons (Acts 19:13).
</def>
<term id="a-p168.2">Admah</term>
Earth, one of the five cities of the vale of Siddim (Gen. 10:19). It was destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah (19:24;
<scripRef passage="Deut. 29:23" id="a-p169.2" parsed="|Deut|29|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.29.23">Deut. 29:23</scripRef>). It is supposed by some to be the same as the Adam
of <scripRef passage="Josh. 3:16" id="a-p169.3" parsed="|Josh|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.3.16">Josh. 3:16</scripRef>, the name of which still lingers in Damieh, the
ford of Jordan. (See ZEBOIM.)
</def>
<term id="a-p169.5">Adnah</term>
Delight. (1.) A chief of the tribe of Manasseh who joined David
at Ziklag (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 12:20" id="a-p170.1" parsed="|1Chr|12|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.12.20">1 Chr. 12:20</scripRef>). (2.) A general under Jehoshaphat,
chief over 300,000 men (2 Chr. 17:14).
</def>
<term id="a-p170.3">Adonibezek</term>
Lord of Bezek, a Canaanitish king who, having subdued seventy of
the chiefs that were around him, made an attack against the
armies of Judah and Simeon, but was defeated and brought as a
captive to Jerusalem, where his thumbs and great toes were cut
off. He confessed that God had requited him for his like cruelty
to the seventy kings whom he had subdued (Judg. 1:4-7; comp. 1 Sam. 15:33).
</def>
<term id="a-p171.3">Adonijah</term>
My Lord is Jehovah. (1.) The fourth son of David (2 Sam. 3:4).
After the death of his elder brothers, Amnon and Absalom, he
became heir-apparent to the throne. But Solomon, a younger
brother, was preferred to him. Adonijah, however, when his
father was dying, caused himself to be proclaimed king. But
Nathan and Bathsheba induced David to give orders that Solomon
should at once be proclaimed and admitted to the throne.
Adonijah fled and took refuge at the altar, and received pardon
for his conduct from Solomon on the condition that he showed
himself “a worthy man” (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 1:5-53" id="a-p172.2" parsed="|1Kgs|1|5|1|53" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.1.5-1Kgs.1.53">1 Kings 1:5-53</scripRef>). He afterwards made a
second attempt to gain the throne, but was seized and put to
death (1 Kings 2:13-25).
(2.) A Levite sent with the princes to teach the book of the
law to the inhabitants of Judah (2 Chr. 17:8).
(3.) One of the “chiefs of the people” after the Captivity
(Neh. 10:16).
</def>
<term id="a-p174.2">Adonikam</term>
Whom the Lord sets up, one of those “which came with Zerubbabel”
(<scripRef passage="Ezra 2:13" id="a-p175.1" parsed="|Ezra|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2.13">Ezra 2:13</scripRef>). His “children,” or retainers, to the number of 666,
came up to Jerusalem (8:13).
</def>
<term id="a-p175.2">Adoniram</term>
(Adoram, 1 Kings 12:18), the son of Abda, was “over the
tribute,” i.e., the levy or forced labour. He was stoned to
death by the people of Israel (1 Kings 4:6; 5:14)
</def>
<term id="a-p176.4">Adoni-zedec</term>
Lord of justice or righteousness, was king in Jerusalem at the

time when the Israelites invaded Palestine (<scripRef passage="Josh. 10:1" id="a-p177.1" parsed="|Josh|10|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.1">Josh. 10:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 10:3" id="a-p177.2" parsed="|Josh|10|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.3">3</scripRef>). He
formed a confederacy with the other Canaanitish kings against
the Israelites, but was utterly routed by Joshua when he was
engaged in besieging the Gibeonites. The history of this victory
and of the treatment of the five confederated kings is recorded

in <scripRef passage="Josh. 10:1-27" id="a-p177.3" parsed="|Josh|10|1|10|27" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.1-Josh.10.27">Josh. 10:1-27</scripRef>. (Comp. <scripRef passage="Deut. 21:23" id="a-p177.4" parsed="|Deut|21|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.21.23">Deut. 21:23</scripRef>). Among the Tell Amarna
tablets (see EGYPT) are some very interesting letters
from Adoni-zedec to the King of Egypt. These illustrate in a
very remarkable manner the history recorded in <scripRef passage="Josh. 10" id="a-p177.6" parsed="|Josh|10|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10">Josh. 10</scripRef>, and
indeed throw light on the wars of conquest generally, so that
they may be read as a kind of commentary on the book of Joshua.
Here the conquering career of the Abiri (i.e., Hebrews) is
graphically described: “Behold, I say that the land of the king
my lord is ruined”, “The wars are mighty against me”, “The
Hebrew chiefs plunder all the king’s lands”, “Behold, I the
chief of the Amorites am breaking to pieces.” Then he implores
the king of Egypt to send soldiers to help him, directing that
the army should come by sea to Ascalon or Gaza, and thence march
to Wru-sa-lim (Jerusalem) by the valley of Elah.
</def>
<term id="a-p177.7">Adoption</term>
The giving to any one the name and place and privileges of a son
who is not a son by birth.
(1.) Natural. Thus Pharaoh’s daughter adopted Moses (Ex. 2:10), and Mordecai Esther (Esther 2:7).
(2.) National. God adopted Israel (Ex. 4:22; Deut. 7:6; Hos. 11:1; Rom. 9:4).
(3.) Spiritual. An act of God’s grace by which he brings men
into the number of his redeemed family, and makes them partakers
of all the blessings he has provided for them. Adoption
represents the new relations into which the believer is
introduced by justification, and the privileges connected
therewith, viz., an interest in God’s peculiar love (<scripRef passage="John 17:23" id="a-p181.1" parsed="|John|17|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.17.23">John 17:23</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Rom. 5:5-8" id="a-p181.2" parsed="|Rom|5|5|5|8" osisRef="Bible:Rom.5.5-Rom.5.8">Rom. 5:5-8</scripRef>), a spiritual nature (2 Pet. 1:4; <scripRef passage="John 1:13" id="a-p181.3" parsed="|John|1|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.1.13">John 1:13</scripRef>), the

possession of a spirit becoming children of God (<scripRef passage="1 Pet. 1:14" id="a-p181.4" parsed="|1Pet|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.1.14">1 Pet. 1:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 John 4" id="a-p181.5" parsed="|2John|1|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2John.1.4">2 John 4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 8:15-21" id="a-p181.6" parsed="|Rom|8|15|8|21" osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.15-Rom.8.21">Rom. 8:15-21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal. 5:1" id="a-p181.7" parsed="|Gal|5|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.5.1">Gal. 5:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 2:15" id="a-p181.8" parsed="|Heb|2|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.2.15">Heb. 2:15</scripRef>), present protection,

consolation, supplies (<scripRef passage="Luke 12:27-32" id="a-p181.9" parsed="|Luke|12|27|12|32" osisRef="Bible:Luke.12.27-Luke.12.32">Luke 12:27-32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 14:18" id="a-p181.10" parsed="|John|14|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.14.18">John 14:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 3:21-23" id="a-p181.11" parsed="|1Cor|3|21|3|23" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.3.21-1Cor.3.23">1 Cor. 3:21-23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 1:4" id="a-p181.12" parsed="|2Cor|1|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.1.4">2 Cor. 1:4</scripRef>), fatherly chastisements (<scripRef passage="Heb. 12:5-11" id="a-p181.13" parsed="|Heb|12|5|12|11" osisRef="Bible:Heb.12.5-Heb.12.11">Heb. 12:5-11</scripRef>), and
a future glorious inheritance (Rom. 8:17, 23; James 2:5; Phil. 3:21).
</def>
<term id="a-p181.18">Adoram</term>
See ADONIRAM.
</def>
<term id="a-p182.2">Adore</term>
To worship; to express reverence and homage. The forms of
adoration among the Jews were putting off the shoes (<scripRef passage="Ex. 3:5" id="a-p183.1" parsed="|Exod|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.3.5">Ex. 3:5</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Josh. 5:15" id="a-p183.2" parsed="|Josh|5|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.5.15">Josh. 5:15</scripRef>), and prostration (<scripRef passage="Gen. 17:3" id="a-p183.3" parsed="|Gen|17|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.17.3">Gen. 17:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 95:6" id="a-p183.4" parsed="|Ps|95|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.95.6">Ps. 95:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 44:15" id="a-p183.5" parsed="|Isa|44|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.44.15">Isa. 44:15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa 44:17" id="a-p183.6" parsed="|Isa|44|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.44.17">17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa 44:19" id="a-p183.7" parsed="|Isa|44|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.44.19">19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 46:6" id="a-p183.8" parsed="|Isa|46|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.46.6">46:6</scripRef>). To “kiss the Son” in <scripRef passage="Ps. 2:12" id="a-p183.9" parsed="|Ps|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.2.12">Ps. 2:12</scripRef> is to adore and

worship him. (See <scripRef passage="Dan. 3:5" id="a-p183.10" parsed="|Dan|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.3.5">Dan. 3:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan. 3:6" id="a-p183.11" parsed="|Dan|3|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.3.6">6</scripRef>.) The word itself does not occur
in Scripture.
</def>
<term id="a-p183.12">Adrammelech</term>
Adar the king. (1.) An idol; a form of the sun-god worshipped by
the inhabitants of Sepharvaim (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:31" id="a-p184.1" parsed="|2Kgs|17|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.31">2 Kings 17:31</scripRef>), and brought by
the Sepharvite colonists into Samaria. (2.) A son of
Sennacherib, king of Assyria (2 Kings 19:37; Isa. 37:38).
</def>
<term id="a-p184.4">Adramyttium</term>
A city of Asia Minor on the coast of Mysia, which in early times
was called AEolis. The ship in which Paul embarked at Caesarea
belonged to this city (<scripRef passage="Acts 27:2" id="a-p185.1" parsed="|Acts|27|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.27.2">Acts 27:2</scripRef>). He was conveyed in it only to
Myra, in Lycia, whence he sailed in an Alexandrian ship to
Italy. It was a rare thing for a ship to sail from any port of
Palestine direct for Italy. It still bears the name Adramyti,
and is a place of some traffic.
</def>
<term id="a-p185.2">Adria</term>
(Acts 27:27; R.V., “the sea of Adria”), the Adriatic Sea,
including in Paul’s time the whole of the Mediterranean lying
between Crete and Sicily. It is the modern Gulf of Venice, the
Mare Superum_ of the Romans, as distinguished from the Mare
Inferum_ or Tyrrhenian Sea.
</def>
<term id="a-p186.2">Adriel</term>
Flock of God, the son of Barzillai, the Meholathite, to whom
Saul gave in marriage his daughter Merab (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 18:19" id="a-p187.1" parsed="|1Sam|18|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.18.19">1 Sam. 18:19</scripRef>). The
five sons that sprang from this union were put to death by the

Gibeonites (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:8" id="a-p187.2" parsed="|2Sam|21|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.8">2 Sam. 21:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:9" id="a-p187.3" parsed="|2Sam|21|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.9">9</scripRef>. Here it is said that Michal “brought
up” [R.V., “bare”] these five sons, either that she treated them
as if she had been their own mother, or that for “Michal” we
should read “Merab,” as in 1 Sam. 18:19).
</def>
<term id="a-p187.5">Adullam</term>
One of the royal cities of the Canaanites, now ‘Aid-el-ma (Josh. 12:15; 15:35). It stood on the old Roman road in the valley of
Elah (q.v.), which was the scene of David’s memorable victory
over Goliath (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:2" id="a-p188.3" parsed="|1Sam|17|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.2">1 Sam. 17:2</scripRef>), and not far from Gath. It was one of
the towns which Rehoboam fortified against Egypt (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 11:7" id="a-p188.4" parsed="|2Chr|11|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.11.7">2 Chr. 11:7</scripRef>).
It was called “the glory of Israel” (Micah 1:15).
The Cave of Adullam has been discovered about 2 miles south of
the scene of David’s triumph, and about 13 miles west from
Bethlehem. At this place is a hill some 500 feet high pierced
with numerous caverns, in one of which David gathered together
“every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt,
and every one that was discontented” (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 22:2" id="a-p189.1" parsed="|1Sam|22|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.22.2">1 Sam. 22:2</scripRef>). Some of
these caverns are large enough to hold 200 or 300 men. According
to tradition this cave was at Wady Khureitun, between Bethlehem
and the Dead Sea, but this view cannot be well maintained.
</def>
<term id="a-p189.2">Adullamite</term>
An inhabitant of the city of Adullam (Gen. 38:1, 12, 20).
</def>
<term id="a-p190.4">Adultery</term>
Conjugal infidelity. An adulterer was a man who had illicit
intercourse with a married or a betrothed woman, and such a
woman was an adulteress. Intercourse between a married man and
an unmarried woman was fornication. Adultery was regarded as a
great social wrong, as well as a great sin.
The Mosaic law (Num. 5:11-31) prescribed that the suspected
wife should be tried by the ordeal of the “water of jealousy.”
There is, however, no recorded instance of the application of
this law. In subsequent times the Rabbis made various
regulations with the view of discovering the guilty party, and

of bringing about a divorce. It has been inferred from <scripRef passage="John 8:1-11" id="a-p192.2" parsed="|John|8|1|8|11" osisRef="Bible:John.8.1-John.8.11">John 8:1-11</scripRef> that this sin became very common during the age preceding
the destruction of Jerusalem.
Idolatry, covetousness, and apostasy are spoken of as adultery

spiritually (<scripRef passage="Jer. 3:6" id="a-p193.1" parsed="|Jer|3|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.3.6">Jer. 3:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer. 3:8" id="a-p193.2" parsed="|Jer|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.3.8">8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer. 3:9" id="a-p193.3" parsed="|Jer|3|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.3.9">9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 16:32" id="a-p193.4" parsed="|Ezek|16|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.16.32">Ezek. 16:32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos. 1:2" id="a-p193.5" parsed="|Hos|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.1.2">Hos. 1:2</scripRef>:3; <scripRef passage="Rev. 2:22" id="a-p193.6" parsed="|Rev|2|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.2.22">Rev. 2:22</scripRef>). An apostate church is an adulteress (<scripRef passage="Isa. 1:21" id="a-p193.7" parsed="|Isa|1|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.21">Isa. 1:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 23:4" id="a-p193.8" parsed="|Ezek|23|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.23.4">Ezek. 23:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek 23:7" id="a-p193.9" parsed="|Ezek|23|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.23.7">7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek 23:37" id="a-p193.10" parsed="|Ezek|23|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.23.37">37</scripRef>), and the Jews are styled “an adulterous generation”
(Matt. 12:39). (Comp. Rev. 12.)
</def>
<term id="a-p193.13">Adummim</term>
The red ones, a place apparently on the road between Jericho and
Jerusalem, “on the south side of the torrent” Wady Kelt, looking

toward Gilgal, mentioned <scripRef passage="Josh. 15:7" id="a-p194.1" parsed="|Josh|15|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.7">Josh. 15:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 18:17" id="a-p194.2" parsed="|Josh|18|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.18.17">18:17</scripRef>. It was nearly
half-way between Jerusalem and Jericho, and now bears the name
of Tal-at-ed-Dumm. It is supposed to have been the place

referred to in the parable of the Good Samaritan (<scripRef passage="Luke 10:30-37" id="a-p194.3" parsed="|Luke|10|30|10|37" osisRef="Bible:Luke.10.30-Luke.10.37">Luke 10:30-37</scripRef>). Recently a new carriage-road has been completed, and
carriages for the first time have come along this road from
Jerusalem.
</def>
<term id="a-p194.4">Adversary</term>
(Heb. satan), an opponent or foe (1 Kings 5:4; 11:14, 23, 25;
<scripRef passage="Luke 13:17" id="a-p195.5" parsed="|Luke|13|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.13.17">Luke 13:17</scripRef>); one that speaks against another, a complainant

(<scripRef passage="Matt. 5:25" id="a-p195.6" parsed="|Matt|5|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.25">Matt. 5:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 12:58" id="a-p195.7" parsed="|Luke|12|58|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.12.58">Luke 12:58</scripRef>); an enemy (<scripRef passage="Luke 18:3" id="a-p195.8" parsed="|Luke|18|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.18.3">Luke 18:3</scripRef>), and specially
the devil (1 Pet. 5:8).
</def>
<term id="a-p195.10">Advocate</term>
(Gr. parakletos), one who pleads another’s cause, who helps
another by defending or comforting him. It is a name given by

Christ three times to the Holy Ghost (<scripRef passage="John 14:16" id="a-p196.1" parsed="|John|14|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.14.16">John 14:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 15:26" id="a-p196.2" parsed="|John|15|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.15.26">15:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 16:7" id="a-p196.3" parsed="|John|16|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.16.7">16:7</scripRef>,
where the Greek word is rendered “Comforter,” q.v.). It is
applied to Christ in <scripRef passage="1 John 2:1" id="a-p196.4" parsed="|1John|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.2.1">1 John 2:1</scripRef>, where the same Greek word is
rendered “Advocate,” the rendering which it should have in all
the places where it occurs. Tertullus “the orator” (<scripRef passage="Acts 24:1" id="a-p196.5" parsed="|Acts|24|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.24.1">Acts 24:1</scripRef>)
was a Roman advocate whom the Jews employed to accuse Paul
before Felix.
</def>
<term id="a-p196.6">AEnon</term>
Springs, a place near Salim where John baptized (John 3:23). It
was probably near the upper source of the Wady Far’ah, an open
valley extending from Mount Ebal to the Jordan. It is full of
springs. A place has been found called ‘Ainun, four miles north
of the springs.
</def>
<term id="a-p197.2">Affection</term>
Feeling or emotion. Mention is made of “vile affections” (Rom. 1:26) and “inordinate affection” (Col. 3:5). Christians are
exhorted to set their affections on things above (<scripRef passage="Col. 3:2" id="a-p198.3" parsed="|Col|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.3.2">Col. 3:2</scripRef>).
There is a distinction between natural and spiritual or gracious
affections (Ezek. 33:32).
</def>
<term id="a-p198.5">Affinity</term>
Relationship by alliance (2 Chr. 18:1) or by marriage (1 Kings 3:1). Marriages are prohibited within certain degrees of
affinity, enumerated <scripRef passage="Lev. 18:6-17" id="a-p199.3" parsed="|Lev|18|6|18|17" osisRef="Bible:Lev.18.6-Lev.18.17">Lev. 18:6-17</scripRef>. Consanguinity is relationship
by blood.
</def>
<term id="a-p199.4">Afflictions</term>
Common to all (Job 5:7; 14:1; Ps. 34:19); are for the good of

men (<scripRef passage="James 1:2" id="a-p200.4" parsed="|Jas|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jas.1.2">James 1:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="James 1:3" id="a-p200.5" parsed="|Jas|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jas.1.3">3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="James 1:12" id="a-p200.6" parsed="|Jas|1|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jas.1.12">12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 12:7" id="a-p200.7" parsed="|2Cor|12|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.12.7">2 Cor. 12:7</scripRef>) and the glory of God (<scripRef passage="2 Cor. 12:7-10" id="a-p200.8" parsed="|2Cor|12|7|12|10" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.12.7-2Cor.12.10">2 Cor. 12:7-10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Pet. 4:14" id="a-p200.9" parsed="|1Pet|4|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.4.14">1 Pet. 4:14</scripRef>), and are to be borne with patience by the

Lord’s people (<scripRef passage="Ps. 94:12" id="a-p200.10" parsed="|Ps|94|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.94.12">Ps. 94:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 3:12" id="a-p200.11" parsed="|Prov|3|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.3.12">Prov. 3:12</scripRef>). They are all directed by
God (<scripRef passage="Lam. 3:33" id="a-p200.12" parsed="|Lam|3|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lam.3.33">Lam. 3:33</scripRef>), and will result in the everlasting good of his
people (2 Cor. 4:16-18) in Christ Jesus (Rom. 8:35-39).
</def>
<term id="a-p200.15">Agabus</term>
A “prophet,” probably one of the seventy disciples of Christ. He

prophesied at Antioch of an approaching famine (<scripRef passage="Acts 11:27" id="a-p201.1" parsed="|Acts|11|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.27">Acts 11:27</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 11:28" id="a-p201.2" parsed="|Acts|11|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.28">28</scripRef>).
Many years afterwards he met Paul at Caesarea, and warned him of
the bonds and affliction that awaited him at Jerusalem should he
persist in going thither (Acts 21:10-12).
</def>
<term id="a-p201.4">Agag</term>
Flame, the usual title of the Amalekite kings, as “Pharaoh” was
of the Egyptian. (1.) A king of the Amalekites referred to by
Balaam (Num. 24:7). He lived at the time of the Exodus.
(2.) Another king of the Amalekites whom Saul spared
unlawfully, but whom Samuel on his arrival in the camp of Saul
ordered, in retributive justice (<scripRef passage="Judg. 1" id="a-p203.1" parsed="|Judg|1|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1">Judg. 1</scripRef>), to be brought out and
cut in pieces (1 Sam. 15:8-33. Comp. Ex. 17:11; Num. 14:45).
</def>
<term id="a-p203.5">Agagite</term>
A name applied to Haman and also to his father (Esther 3:1, 10;
8:3, 5). Probably it was equivalent to Amalekite.
</def>
<term id="a-p204.3">Agate</term>
(Heb. shebo), a precious stone in the breast-plate of the high

priest (<scripRef passage="Ex. 28:19" id="a-p205.1" parsed="|Exod|28|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.19">Ex. 28:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 39:12" id="a-p205.2" parsed="|Exod|39|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.39.12">39:12</scripRef>), the second in the third row. This may
be the agate properly so called, a semi-transparent crystallized

quartz, probably brought from Sheba, whence its name. In <scripRef passage="Isa. 54:12" id="a-p205.3" parsed="|Isa|54|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.54.12">Isa. 54:12</scripRef> and <scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:16" id="a-p205.4" parsed="|Ezek|27|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.16">Ezek. 27:16</scripRef>, this word is the rendering of the Hebrew
cadcod, which means “ruddy,” and denotes a variety of minutely
crystalline silica more or less in bands of different tints.
This word is from the Greek name of a stone found in the river
Achates in Sicily.
</def>
<term id="a-p206.1">Age</term>
Used to denote the period of a man’s life (Gen. 47:28), the

maturity of life (<scripRef passage="John 9:21" id="a-p207.2" parsed="|John|9|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.9.21">John 9:21</scripRef>), the latter end of life (<scripRef passage="Job 11:17" id="a-p207.3" parsed="|Job|11|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.11.17">Job 11:17</scripRef>), a generation of the human race (<scripRef passage="Job 8:8" id="a-p207.4" parsed="|Job|8|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.8.8">Job 8:8</scripRef>), and an

indefinite period (<scripRef passage="Eph. 2:7" id="a-p207.5" parsed="|Eph|2|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.7">Eph. 2:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph 3:5" id="a-p207.6" parsed="|Eph|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.3.5">3:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Eph 3:21" id="a-p207.7" parsed="|Eph|3|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.3.21">21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Col. 1:26" id="a-p207.8" parsed="|Col|1|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.1.26">Col. 1:26</scripRef>). Respect to be
shown to the aged (<scripRef passage="Lev. 19:32" id="a-p207.9" parsed="|Lev|19|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.32">Lev. 19:32</scripRef>). It is a blessing to communities

when they have old men among them (<scripRef passage="Isa. 65:20" id="a-p207.10" parsed="|Isa|65|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.65.20">Isa. 65:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 8:4" id="a-p207.11" parsed="|Zech|8|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.8.4">Zech. 8:4</scripRef>). The

aged supposed to excel in understanding (<scripRef passage="Job 12:20" id="a-p207.12" parsed="|Job|12|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.12.20">Job 12:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 15:10" id="a-p207.13" parsed="|Job|15|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.15.10">15:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 32:4" id="a-p207.14" parsed="|Job|32|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.32.4">32:4</scripRef>,

<scripRef passage="Job 32:9" id="a-p207.15" parsed="|Job|32|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.32.9">9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 12:6" id="a-p207.16" parsed="|1Kgs|12|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.12.6">1 Kings 12:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 12:8" id="a-p207.17" parsed="|1Kgs|12|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.12.8">8</scripRef>). A full age the reward of piety (<scripRef passage="Job 5:26" id="a-p207.18" parsed="|Job|5|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.5.26">Job 5:26</scripRef>;
Gen. 15:15).
</def>
<term id="a-p207.20">Agee</term>
Fugitive, the father of Shammah, who was one of David’s mighty
men (2 Sam. 23:11)
</def>
<term id="a-p208.2">Agony</term>
Contest; wrestling; severe struggling with pain and suffering.
Anguish is the reflection on evil that is already past, while
agony is a struggle with evil at the time present. It is only
used in the New Testament by Luke (22:44) to describe our Lord’s
fearful struggle in Gethsemane.
The verb from which the noun “agony” is derived is used to
denote an earnest endeavour or striving, as “Strive [agonize] to
enter” (<scripRef passage="Luke 13:24" id="a-p210.1" parsed="|Luke|13|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.13.24">Luke 13:24</scripRef>); “Then would my servants fight” [agonize]

(<scripRef passage="John 18:36" id="a-p210.2" parsed="|John|18|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.18.36">John 18:36</scripRef>). Comp. <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 9:25" id="a-p210.3" parsed="|1Cor|9|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.9.25">1 Cor. 9:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Col. 1:29" id="a-p210.4" parsed="|Col|1|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.1.29">Col. 1:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Col 4:12" id="a-p210.5" parsed="|Col|4|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.4.12">4:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Tim. 6:12" id="a-p210.6" parsed="|1Tim|6|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.6.12">1 Tim. 6:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Tim. 4:7" id="a-p210.7" parsed="|2Tim|4|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.4.7">2 Tim. 4:7</scripRef>, where the words “striveth,” “labour,” “conflict,”
“fight,” are the renderings of the same Greek verb.
</def>
<term id="a-p210.8">Agriculture</term>
Tilling the ground (Gen. 2:15; 4:2, 3, 12) and rearing cattle
were the chief employments in ancient times. The Egyptians
excelled in agriculture. And after the Israelites entered into
the possession of the Promised Land, their circumstances
favoured in the highest degree a remarkable development of this
art. Agriculture became indeed the basis of the Mosaic
commonwealth.
The year in Palestine was divided into six agricultural
periods:-
I. SOWING TIME.
Tisri, latter half
(beginning about the autumnal equinox.)
Marchesvan.
Kisleu, former half.
Early rain due = first showers of autumn.
II. UNRIPE TIME.
Kisleu, latter half.
Tebet.
Sebat, former half.
III. COLD SEASON.
Sebat, latter half.
Adar.
[Veadar.]
Nisan, former half.

Latter rain due (<scripRef passage="Deut. 11:14" id="a-p215.1" parsed="|Deut|11|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.11.14">Deut. 11:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 5:24" id="a-p215.2" parsed="|Jer|5|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.5.24">Jer. 5:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos. 6:3" id="a-p215.3" parsed="|Hos|6|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.6.3">Hos. 6:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 10:1" id="a-p215.4" parsed="|Zech|10|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.10.1">Zech. 10:1</scripRef>;
James 5:7; Job 29:23).
IV. HARVEST TIME.
Nisan, latter half.
(Beginning about vernal equinox. Barley green. Passover.)
Ijar.
Sivan, former half., Wheat ripe. Pentecost.
V. SUMMER (total absence of rain)
Sivan, latter half.
Tammuz.
Ab, former half.
VI. SULTRY SEASON
Ab, latter half.
Elul.
Tisri, former half., Ingathering of fruits.
The six months from the middle of Tisri to the middle of Nisan
were occupied with the work of cultivation, and the rest of the
year mainly with the gathering in of the fruits. The extensive
and easily-arranged system of irrigation from the rills and
streams from the mountains made the soil in every part of

Palestine richly productive (<scripRef passage="Ps. 1:3" id="a-p219.1" parsed="|Ps|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.1.3">Ps. 1:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 65:10" id="a-p219.2" parsed="|Ps|65|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.65.10">65:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 21:1" id="a-p219.3" parsed="|Prov|21|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.21.1">Prov. 21:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 30:25" id="a-p219.4" parsed="|Isa|30|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.30.25">Isa. 30:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 32:2" id="a-p219.5" parsed="|Isa|32|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.32.2">32:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa 32:20" id="a-p219.6" parsed="|Isa|32|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.32.20">20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos. 12:11" id="a-p219.7" parsed="|Hos|12|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.12.11">Hos. 12:11</scripRef>), and the appliances of careful
cultivation and of manure increased its fertility to such an
extent that in the days of Solomon, when there was an abundant
population, “20,000 measures of wheat year by year” were sent to
Hiram in exchange for timber (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 5:11" id="a-p219.8" parsed="|1Kgs|5|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.5.11">1 Kings 5:11</scripRef>), and in large
quantities also wheat was sent to the Tyrians for the
merchandise in which they traded (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:17" id="a-p219.9" parsed="|Ezek|27|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.17">Ezek. 27:17</scripRef>). The wheat

sometimes produced an hundredfold (<scripRef passage="Gen. 26:12" id="a-p219.10" parsed="|Gen|26|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.26.12">Gen. 26:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 13:23" id="a-p219.11" parsed="|Matt|13|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.13.23">Matt. 13:23</scripRef>).
Figs and pomegranates were very plentiful (<scripRef passage="Num. 13:23" id="a-p219.12" parsed="|Num|13|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.13.23">Num. 13:23</scripRef>), and the
vine and the olive grew luxuriantly and produced abundant fruit
(Deut. 33:24).
Lest the productiveness of the soil should be exhausted, it
was enjoined that the whole land should rest every seventh year,
when all agricultural labour would entirely cease (<scripRef passage="Lev. 25:1-7" id="a-p220.1" parsed="|Lev|25|1|25|7" osisRef="Bible:Lev.25.1-Lev.25.7">Lev. 25:1-7</scripRef>;
Deut. 15:1-10).
It was forbidden to sow a field with divers seeds (Deut. 22:9). A passer-by was at liberty to eat any quantity of corn or

grapes, but he was not permitted to carry away any (<scripRef passage="Deut. 23:24" id="a-p221.2" parsed="|Deut|23|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.23.24">Deut. 23:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut 23:25" id="a-p221.3" parsed="|Deut|23|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.23.25">25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 12:1" id="a-p221.4" parsed="|Matt|12|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.12.1">Matt. 12:1</scripRef>). The poor were permitted to claim the corners of
the fields and the gleanings. A forgotten sheaf in the field was
to be left also for the poor. (See Lev. 19:9, 10; Deut. 24:19.)
Agricultural implements and operations.
The sculptured monuments and painted tombs of Egypt and
Assyria throw much light on this subject, and on the general
operations of agriculture. Ploughs of a simple construction were

known in the time of Moses (<scripRef passage="Deut. 22:10" id="a-p223.1" parsed="|Deut|22|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.22.10">Deut. 22:10</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Job 1:14" id="a-p223.2" parsed="|Job|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.1.14">Job 1:14</scripRef>). They
were very light, and required great attention to keep them in

the ground (<scripRef passage="Luke 9:62" id="a-p223.3" parsed="|Luke|9|62|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.9.62">Luke 9:62</scripRef>). They were drawn by oxen (<scripRef passage="Job 1:14" id="a-p223.4" parsed="|Job|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.1.14">Job 1:14</scripRef>), cows

(<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 6:7" id="a-p223.5" parsed="|1Sam|6|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.6.7">1 Sam. 6:7</scripRef>), and asses (<scripRef passage="Isa. 30:24" id="a-p223.6" parsed="|Isa|30|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.30.24">Isa. 30:24</scripRef>); but an ox and an ass must
not be yoked together in the same plough (<scripRef passage="Deut. 22:10" id="a-p223.7" parsed="|Deut|22|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.22.10">Deut. 22:10</scripRef>). Men
sometimes followed the plough with a hoe to break the clods
(<scripRef passage="Isa. 28:24" id="a-p223.8" parsed="|Isa|28|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.28.24">Isa. 28:24</scripRef>). The oxen were urged on by a “goad,” or long staff
pointed at the end, so that if occasion arose it could be used
as a spear also (Judg. 3:31; 1 Sam. 13:21).
When the soil was prepared, the seed was sown broadcast over

the field (<scripRef passage="Matt. 13:3-8" id="a-p224.1" parsed="|Matt|13|3|13|8" osisRef="Bible:Matt.13.3-Matt.13.8">Matt. 13:3-8</scripRef>). The “harrow” mentioned in <scripRef passage="Job 39:10" id="a-p224.2" parsed="|Job|39|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.39.10">Job 39:10</scripRef>
was not used to cover the seeds, but to break the clods, being
little more than a thick block of wood. In highly irrigated
spots the seed was trampled in by cattle (<scripRef passage="Isa. 32:20" id="a-p224.3" parsed="|Isa|32|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.32.20">Isa. 32:20</scripRef>); but
doubtless there was some kind of harrow also for covering in the
seed scattered in the furrows of the field.
The reaping of the corn was performed either by pulling it up
by the roots, or cutting it with a species of sickle, according
to circumstances. The corn when cut was generally put up in

sheaves (<scripRef passage="Gen. 37:7" id="a-p225.1" parsed="|Gen|37|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.7">Gen. 37:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 23:10-15" id="a-p225.2" parsed="|Lev|23|10|23|15" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.10-Lev.23.15">Lev. 23:10-15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ruth 2:7" id="a-p225.3" parsed="|Ruth|2|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.2.7">Ruth 2:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ruth 2:15" id="a-p225.4" parsed="|Ruth|2|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.2.15">15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 24:10" id="a-p225.5" parsed="|Job|24|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.24.10">Job 24:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 9:22" id="a-p225.6" parsed="|Jer|9|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.9.22">Jer. 9:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Micah 4:12" id="a-p225.7" parsed="|Mic|4|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.4.12">Micah 4:12</scripRef>), which were afterwards gathered to the
threshing-floor or stored in barns (Matt. 6:26).
The process of threshing was performed generally by spreading
the sheaves on the threshing-floor and causing oxen and cattle

to tread repeatedly over them (<scripRef passage="Deut. 25:4" id="a-p226.1" parsed="|Deut|25|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.25.4">Deut. 25:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 28:28" id="a-p226.2" parsed="|Isa|28|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.28.28">Isa. 28:28</scripRef>). On

occasions flails or sticks were used for this purpose (<scripRef passage="Ruth 2:17" id="a-p226.3" parsed="|Ruth|2|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.2.17">Ruth 2:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 28:27" id="a-p226.4" parsed="|Isa|28|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.28.27">Isa. 28:27</scripRef>). There was also a “threshing instrument” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 41:15" id="a-p226.5" parsed="|Isa|41|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.41.15">Isa. 41:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Amos 1:3" id="a-p226.6" parsed="|Amos|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.1.3">Amos 1:3</scripRef>) which was drawn over the corn. It was called by
the Hebrews a moreg, a threshing roller or sledge (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 24:22" id="a-p226.7" parsed="|2Sam|24|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.24.22">2 Sam. 24:22</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 21:23" id="a-p226.8" parsed="|1Chr|21|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.21.23">1 Chr. 21:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 3:15" id="a-p226.9" parsed="|Isa|3|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.15">Isa. 3:15</scripRef>). It was somewhat like the Roman
tribulum, or threshing instrument.
When the grain was threshed, it was winnowed by being thrown
up against the wind (<scripRef passage="Jer. 4:11" id="a-p227.1" parsed="|Jer|4|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.4.11">Jer. 4:11</scripRef>), and afterwards tossed with
wooden scoops (<scripRef passage="Isa. 30:24" id="a-p227.2" parsed="|Isa|30|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.30.24">Isa. 30:24</scripRef>). The shovel and the fan for winnowing

are mentioned in <scripRef passage="Ps. 35:5" id="a-p227.3" parsed="|Ps|35|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.35.5">Ps. 35:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Job 21:18" id="a-p227.4" parsed="|Job|21|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.21.18">Job 21:18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 17:13" id="a-p227.5" parsed="|Isa|17|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.17.13">Isa. 17:13</scripRef>. The refuse of
straw and chaff was burned (<scripRef passage="Isa. 5:24" id="a-p227.6" parsed="|Isa|5|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.5.24">Isa. 5:24</scripRef>). Freed from impurities,
the grain was then laid up in granaries till used (<scripRef passage="Deut. 28:8" id="a-p227.7" parsed="|Deut|28|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.8">Deut. 28:8</scripRef>;
Prov. 3:10; Matt. 6:26; 13:30; Luke 12:18).
</def>
<term id="a-p227.12">Agrippa I.</term>
The grandson of Herod the Great, and son of Aristobulus and
Bernice. The Roman emperor Caligula made him governor first of
the territories of Philip, then of the tetrarchy of Lysanias,
with the title of king (“king Herod”), and finally of that of
Antipas, who was banished, and of Samaria and Judea. Thus he
became ruler over the whole of Palestine. He was a persecutor of
the early Christians. He slew James, and imprisoned Peter (Acts 12:1-4). He died at Caesarea, being “eaten of worms” (Acts 12:23), A.D. 44. (Comp. Josephus, Ant. xix. 8.)
</def>
<term id="a-p228.3">Agrippa II.</term>
Son of the foregoing, was born at Rome, A.D. 27. He was the
brother of Bernice and Drusilla. The Emperor Claudius (A.D. 48)
invested him with the office of superintendent of the Temple of
Jerusalem, and made him governor (A.D. 50) of Chalcis. He was
afterwards raised to the rank of king, and made governor over

the tetrarchy of Philip and Lysanias (<scripRef passage="Acts 25:13" id="a-p229.1" parsed="|Acts|25|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.25.13">Acts 25:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 26:2" id="a-p229.2" parsed="|Acts|26|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.26.2">26:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 26:7" id="a-p229.3" parsed="|Acts|26|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.26.7">7</scripRef>). It
was before him that Paul delivered (A.D. 59) his speech recorded
in <scripRef passage="Acts 26" id="a-p229.4" parsed="|Acts|26|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.26">Acts 26</scripRef>. His private life was very profligate. He died (the
last of his race) at Rome, at the age of about seventy years,
</def>
<term id="a-p229.5">Ague</term>
The translation in Lev. 26:16 (R.V., “fever”) of the Hebrew word
kaddah’ath, meaning “kindling”, i.e., an inflammatory or burning
fever. In Deut. 28:22 the word is rendered “fever.”
</def>
<term id="a-p230.3">Agur</term>
Gatherer; the collector, mentioned as author of the sayings in
Prov. 30. Nothing is known of him beyond what is there recorded.
</def>
<term id="a-p231.2">Ah!</term>
An exclamation of sorrow or regret (Ps. 35:25; Isa. 1:4, 24;
Jer. 1:6; 22:18; Mark 15:29).
</def>
<term id="a-p232.7">Aha!</term>
An exclamation of ridicule (Ps. 35:21; 40:15; 70:3). In Isa. 44:16 it signifies joyful surprise, as also in Job 39:25, R.V.
</def>
<term id="a-p233.6">Ahab</term>
Father’s brother. (1.) The son of Omri, whom he succeeded as the

seventh king of Israel. His history is recorded in <scripRef passage="1 Kings 16" id="a-p234.1" parsed="|1Kgs|16|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.16">1 Kings 16</scripRef>-22. His wife was Jezebel (q.v.), who exercised a very evil
influence over him. To the calf-worship introduced by Jeroboam
he added the worship of Baal. He was severely admonished by
Elijah (q.v.) for his wickedness. His anger was on this account
kindled against the prophet, and he sought to kill him. He
undertook three campaigns against Ben-hadad II., king of
Damascus. In the first two, which were defensive, he gained a
complete victory over Ben-hadad, who fell into his hands, and
was afterwards released on the condition of his restoring all
the cities of Israel he then held, and granting certain other
concessions to Ahab. After three years of peace, for some cause
Ahab renewed war (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 22:3" id="a-p234.2" parsed="|1Kgs|22|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.22.3">1 Kings 22:3</scripRef>) with Ben-hadad by assaulting the
city of Ramoth-gilead, although the prophet Micaiah warned him
that he would not succeed, and that the 400 false prophets who
encouraged him were only leading him to his ruin. Micaiah was
imprisoned for thus venturing to dissuade Ahab from his purpose.
Ahab went into the battle disguised, that he might if possible
escape the notice of his enemies; but an arrow from a bow “drawn
at a venture” pierced him, and though stayed up in his chariot

for a time he died towards evening, and Elijah’s prophecy (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 21:19" id="a-p234.3" parsed="|1Kgs|21|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.21.19">1 Kings 21:19</scripRef>) was fulfilled. He reigned twenty-three years.
Because of his idolatry, lust, and covetousness, Ahab is
referred to as pre-eminently the type of a wicked king (2 Kings 8:18; 2 Chr. 22:3; Micah 6:16).
(2.) A false prophet referred to by Jeremiah (Jer. 29:21), of
whom nothing further is known.
</def>
<term id="a-p235.2">Ahasuerus</term>
There are three kings designated by this name in Scripture. (1.)
The father of Darius the Mede, mentioned in <scripRef passage="Dan. 9:1" id="a-p236.1" parsed="|Dan|9|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.9.1">Dan. 9:1</scripRef>. This was
probably the Cyaxares I. known by this name in profane history,
the king of Media and the conqueror of Nineveh.
(2.) The king mentioned in Ezra 4:6, probably the Cambyses of
profane history, the son and successor of Cyrus (B.C. 529).
(3.) The son of Darius Hystaspes, the king named in the Book
of Esther. He ruled over the kingdoms of Persia, Media, and
Babylonia, “from India to Ethiopia.” This was in all probability
the Xerxes of profane history, who succeeded his father Darius
(B.C. 485). In the LXX. version of the Book of Esther the name
Artaxerxes occurs for Ahasuerus. He reigned for twenty-one years
(B.C. 486-465). He invaded Greece with an army, it is said, of
more than 2,000,000 soldiers, only 5,000 of whom returned with
him. Leonidas, with his famous 300, arrested his progress at the
Pass of Thermopylae, and then he was defeated disastrously by
Themistocles at Salamis. It was after his return from this
invasion that Esther was chosen as his queen.
</def>
<term id="a-p238.1">Ahava</term>
Water, the river (Ezra 8:21) by the banks of which the Jewish
exiles assembled under Ezra when about to return to Jerusalem
from Babylon. In all probability this was one of the streams of
Mesopotamia which flowed into the Euphrates somewhere in the
north-west of Babylonia. It has, however, been supposed to be
the name of a place (<scripRef passage="Ezra 8:15" id="a-p239.2" parsed="|Ezra|8|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.8.15">Ezra 8:15</scripRef>) now called Hit, on the
Euphrates, east of Damascus.
</def>
<term id="a-p239.3">Ahaz</term>
Possessor. (1.) A grandson of Jonathan (1 Chr. 8:35; 9:42).
(2.) The son and successor of Jotham, king of Judah (2 Kings 16; Isa. 7-9; 2 Chr. 28). He gave himself up to a life of
wickedness and idolatry. Notwithstanding the remonstrances and
warnings of Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah, he appealed for help
against Rezin, king of Damascus, and Pekah, king of Israel, who
threatened Jerusalem, to Tiglath-pileser, the king of Assyria,
to the great injury of his kingdom and his own humilating

subjection to the Assyrians (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 16:7" id="a-p241.4" parsed="|2Kgs|16|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.16.7">2 Kings 16:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 16:9" id="a-p241.5" parsed="|2Kgs|16|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.16.9">9</scripRef>; 15:29). He also
introduced among his people many heathen and idolatrous customs

(<scripRef passage="Isa. 8:19" id="a-p241.6" parsed="|Isa|8|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.8.19">Isa. 8:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 38:8" id="a-p241.7" parsed="|Isa|38|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.38.8">38:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 23:12" id="a-p241.8" parsed="|2Kgs|23|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.12">2 Kings 23:12</scripRef>). He died at the age of
thirty-five years, after reigning sixteen years (B.C. 740-724),
and was succeeded by his son Hezekiah. Because of his wickedness
he was “not brought into the sepulchre of the kings.”
</def>
<term id="a-p241.9">Ahaziah</term>
Held by Jehovah. (1.) The son and successor of Ahab. He followed
the counsels of his mother Jezebel, and imitated in wickedness
the ways of his father. In his reign the Moabites revolted from
under his authority (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 3:5-7" id="a-p242.1" parsed="|2Kgs|3|5|3|7" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.3.5-2Kgs.3.7">2 Kings 3:5-7</scripRef>). He united with Jehoshaphat
in an attempt to revive maritime trade by the Red Sea, which
proved a failure (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 20:35-37" id="a-p242.2" parsed="|2Chr|20|35|20|37" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.20.35-2Chr.20.37">2 Chr. 20:35-37</scripRef>). His messengers, sent to
consult the god of Ekron regarding his recovery from the effects
of a fall from the roof-gallery of his palace, were met on the
way by Elijah, who sent them back to tell the king that he would
never rise from his bed (1 Kings 22:51; 2 Kings 1:18).
(2.) The son of Joram, or Jehoram, and sixth king of Judah.

Called Jehoahaz (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 21:17" id="a-p243.1" parsed="|2Chr|21|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.21.17">2 Chr. 21:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 25:23" id="a-p243.2" parsed="|2Chr|25|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.25.23">25:23</scripRef>), and Azariah (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 22:6" id="a-p243.3" parsed="|2Chr|22|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.22.6">2 Chr. 22:6</scripRef>). Guided by his idolatrous mother Athaliah, his reign was

disastrous (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 8:24-29" id="a-p243.4" parsed="|2Kgs|8|24|8|29" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.8.24-2Kgs.8.29">2 Kings 8:24-29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 9:29" id="a-p243.5" parsed="|2Kgs|9|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.9.29">9:29</scripRef>). He joined his uncle Jehoram,
king of Israel, in an expedition against Hazael, king of
Damascus; but was wounded at the pass of Gur when attempting to
escape, and had strength only to reach Megiddo, where he died (2 Kings 9:22-28). He reigned only one year.
</def>
<term id="a-p243.7">Ahiam</term>
Mother’s brother, one of David’s thirty heroes (2 Sam. 23:33; 1 Chr. 11:35).
</def>
<term id="a-p244.3">Ahiezer</term>
Brother of help; i.e., “helpful.” (1.) The chief of the tribe of
Dan at the time of the Exodus (Num. 1:12; 2:25; 10:25).
(2.) The chief of the Benjamite slingers that repaired to
David at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:3).
</def>
<term id="a-p246.2">Ahihud</term>
Brother (i.e., “friend”) of union. (1.) A son of Bela, the son
of Benjamin (1 Chr. 8:7).
(2.) Name different in Hebrew, meaning brother of Judah. Chief
of the tribe of Asher; one of those appointed by Moses to
superintend the division of Canaan among the tribe (Num. 34:27).
</def>
<term id="a-p248.2">Ahijah</term>
Brother (i.e., “friend”) of Jehovah. (1.) One of the sons of
Bela (1 Chr. 8:7, R.V.). In A.V. called “Ahiah.”
(2.) One of the five sons of Jerahmeel, who was great-grandson
of Judah (1 Chr. 2:25).
(3.) Son of Ahitub (1 Sam. 14:3, 18), Ichabod’s brother; the
same probably as Ahimelech, who was high priest at Nob in the
reign of Saul (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 22:11" id="a-p251.3" parsed="|1Sam|22|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.22.11">1 Sam. 22:11</scripRef>). Some, however, suppose that
Ahimelech was the brother of Ahijah, and that they both
officiated as high priests, Ahijah at Gibeah or Kirjath-jearim,
and Ahimelech at Nob.
(4.) A Pelonite, one of David’s heroes (1 Chr. 11:36); called
also Eliam (2 Sam. 23:34).
(5.) A Levite having charge of the sacred treasury in the
temple (1 Chr. 26:20).
(6.) One of Solomon’s secretaries (1 Kings 4:3).
(7.) A prophet of Shiloh (1 Kings 11:29; 14:2), called the
“Shilonite,” in the days of Rehoboam. We have on record two of
his remarkable prophecies, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 11:31-39" id="a-p255.3" parsed="|1Kgs|11|31|11|39" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.11.31-1Kgs.11.39">1 Kings 11:31-39</scripRef>, announcing the
rending of the ten tribes from Solomon; and <scripRef passage="1 Kings 14:6-16" id="a-p255.4" parsed="|1Kgs|14|6|14|16" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.14.6-1Kgs.14.16">1 Kings 14:6-16</scripRef>,
delivered to Jeroboam’s wife, foretelling the death of Abijah
the king’s son, the destruction of Jeroboam’s house, and the
captivity of Israel “beyond the river.” Jeroboam bears testimony
to the high esteem in which he was held as a prophet of God (1 Kings 14:2, 3).
</def>
<term id="a-p255.7">Ahikam</term>
Brother of support = helper, one of the five whom Josiah sent to
consult the prophetess Huldah in connection with the discovery

of the book of the law (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 22:12-14" id="a-p256.1" parsed="|2Kgs|22|12|22|14" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.22.12-2Kgs.22.14">2 Kings 22:12-14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 34:20" id="a-p256.2" parsed="|2Chr|34|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.34.20">2 Chr. 34:20</scripRef>). He was
the son of Shaphan, the royal secretary, and the father of
Gedaliah, governor of Judea after the destruction of Jerusalem

by the Babylonians (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 25:22" id="a-p256.3" parsed="|2Kgs|25|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.25.22">2 Kings 25:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 40:5-16" id="a-p256.4" parsed="|Jer|40|5|40|16" osisRef="Bible:Jer.40.5-Jer.40.16">Jer. 40:5-16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 43:6" id="a-p256.5" parsed="|Jer|43|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.43.6">43:6</scripRef>). On one
occasion he protected Jeremiah against the fury of Jehoiakim
(<scripRef passage="Jer. 26:24" id="a-p256.6" parsed="|Jer|26|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.26.24">Jer. 26:24</scripRef>). It was in the chamber of another son (Germariah)
of Shaphan that Baruch read in the ears of all the people
Jeremiah’s roll.
</def>
<term id="a-p256.7">Ahimaaz</term>
Brother of anger = irascible. (1.) The father Ahinoam, the wife
of Saul (1 Sam. 14:50).
(2.) The son and successor of Zadok in the office of high

priest (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 6:8" id="a-p258.1" parsed="|1Chr|6|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.6.8">1 Chr. 6:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 6:53" id="a-p258.2" parsed="|1Chr|6|53|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.6.53">53</scripRef>). On the occasion of the revolt of
Absalom he remained faithful to David, and was of service to him
in conveying to him tidings of the proceedings of Absalom in

Jerusalem (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 15:24-37" id="a-p258.3" parsed="|2Sam|15|24|15|37" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.15.24-2Sam.15.37">2 Sam. 15:24-37</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 17:15-21" id="a-p258.4" parsed="|2Sam|17|15|17|21" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.17.15-2Sam.17.21">17:15-21</scripRef>). He was swift of foot, and
was the first to carry to David tidings of the defeat of
Absalom, although he refrained, from delicacy of feeling, from
telling him of his death (2 Sam. 18:19-33).
</def>
<term id="a-p258.6">Ahiman</term>
Brother of a gift = liberal. (1.) One of the three giant Anakim

brothers whom Caleb and the spies saw in Mount Hebron (<scripRef passage="Num. 13:22" id="a-p259.1" parsed="|Num|13|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.13.22">Num. 13:22</scripRef>) when they went in to explore the land. They were
afterwards driven out and slain (Josh. 15:14; Judg. 1:10).
(2.) One of the guardians of the temple after the Exile (1 Chr. 9:17).
</def>
<term id="a-p260.2">Ahimelech</term>
Brother of the king, the son of Ahitub and father of Abiathar (1 Sam. 22:20-23). He descended from Eli in the line of Ithamar. In
<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 18:16" id="a-p261.2" parsed="|1Chr|18|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.18.16">1 Chr. 18:16</scripRef> he is called Abimelech, and is probably the same as

Ahiah (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 14:3" id="a-p261.3" parsed="|1Sam|14|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.14.3">1 Sam. 14:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 14:18" id="a-p261.4" parsed="|1Sam|14|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.14.18">18</scripRef>). He was the twelfth high priest, and
officiated at Nob, where he was visited by David (to whom and
his companions he gave five loaves of the showbread) when he
fled from Saul (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 21:1-9" id="a-p261.5" parsed="|1Sam|21|1|21|9" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.21.1-1Sam.21.9">1 Sam. 21:1-9</scripRef>). He was summoned into Saul’s
presence, and accused, on the information of Doeg the Edomite,
of disloyalty because of his kindness to David; whereupon the
king commanded that he, with the other priests who stood beside
him (86 in all), should be put to death. This sentence was

carried into execution by Doeg in the most cruel manner (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 22:9-23" id="a-p261.6" parsed="|1Sam|22|9|22|23" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.22.9-1Sam.22.23">1 Sam. 22:9-23</scripRef>). Possibly Abiathar had a son also called Ahimelech, or
the two names, as some think, may have been accidentally
transposed in 2 Sam. 8:17; 1 Chr. 18:16, marg.; 24:3, 6, 31.
</def>
<term id="a-p261.9">Ahinadab</term>
Brother of liberality = liberal, one of the twelve commissariat
officers appointed by Solomon in so many districts of his
kingdom to raise supplies by monthly rotation for his household.
He was appointed to the district of Mahanaim (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:14" id="a-p262.1" parsed="|1Kgs|4|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.14">1 Kings 4:14</scripRef>),
east of Jordan.
</def>
<term id="a-p262.2">Ahinoam</term>
Brother of pleasantness = pleasant. (1.) The daughter of
Ahimaaz, and wife of Saul (1 Sam. 14:50).
(2.) A Jezreelitess, the first wife of David (1 Sam. 25:43;
27:3). She was the mother of Amnon (2 Sam. 3:2). (See 1 Sam. 30:5, 18; 2 Sam. 2:2.)
</def>
<term id="a-p264.7">Ahio</term>
Brotherly. (1.) One of the sons of Beriah (1 Chr. 8:14).
(2.) One of the sons of Jehiel the Gibeonite (1 Chr. 8:31;
9:37).
(3.) One of the sons of Abinadab the Levite. While Uzzah went
by the side of the ark, he walked before it guiding the oxen
which drew the cart on which it was carried, after having
brought it from his father’s house in Gibeah (1 Chr. 13:7; 2 Sam. 6:3, 4).
</def>
<term id="a-p267.4">Ahira</term>
Brother of evil = unlucky, or my brother is friend, chief of the
tribe of Naphtali at the Exodus (Num. 1:15; 2:29).
</def>
<term id="a-p268.3">Ahishar</term>
Brother of song = singer, the officer who was “over the
household” of Solomon (1 Kings 4:6).
</def>
<term id="a-p269.2">Ahithophel</term>
Brother of insipidity or impiety, a man greatly renowned for his
sagacity among the Jews. At the time of Absalom’s revolt he

deserted David (<scripRef passage="Ps. 41:9" id="a-p270.1" parsed="|Ps|41|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.41.9">Ps. 41:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 55:12-14" id="a-p270.2" parsed="|Ps|55|12|55|14" osisRef="Bible:Ps.55.12-Ps.55.14">55:12-14</scripRef>) and espoused the cause of
Absalom (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 15:12" id="a-p270.3" parsed="|2Sam|15|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.15.12">2 Sam. 15:12</scripRef>). David sent his old friend Hushai back to
Absalom, in order that he might counteract the counsel of
Ahithophel (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 15:31-37" id="a-p270.4" parsed="|2Sam|15|31|15|37" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.15.31-2Sam.15.37">2 Sam. 15:31-37</scripRef>). This end was so far gained that
Ahithophel saw he had no longer any influence, and accordingly
he at once left the camp of Absalom and returned to Giloh, his
native place, where, after arranging his wordly affairs, he
hanged himself, and was buried in the sepulchre of his fathers
(2 Sam. 17:1-23). He was the type of Judas (Ps. 41:9).
</def>
<term id="a-p270.7">Ahitub</term>
Brother of goodness = good. (1.) The son of Phinehas. On the
death of his grandfather Eli he succeeded to the office of high
priest, and was himself succeeded by his son Ahijah (1 Sam. 14:3; 22:9, 11, 12, 20).
(2.) The father of Zadok, who was made high priest by Saul
after the extermination of the family of Ahimelech (1 Chr. 6:7, 8; 2 Sam. 8:17).
</def>
<term id="a-p272.4">Ahlab</term>
Fatness, a town of Asher lying within the unconquered Phoenician
border (<scripRef passage="Judg. 1:31" id="a-p273.1" parsed="|Judg|1|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.31">Judg. 1:31</scripRef>), north-west of the Sea of Galilee; commonly
identified with Giscala, now el-Jish.
</def>
<term id="a-p273.2">Ahoah</term>
Brotherly, one of the sons of Bela, the son of Benjamin (1 Chr. 8:4). He is also called Ahiah (ver. 7) and Iri (1 Chr. 7:7). His
descendants were called Ahohites (2 Sam. 23:9, 28).
</def>
<term id="a-p274.5">Ahohite</term>
An epithet applied to Dodo, one of Solomon’s captains (1 Chr. 27:4); to his son Eleazar, one of David’s three mightiest heroes
(2 Sam. 23:9; 1 Chr. 11:12); and to Zalmon, one of the thirty (2 Sam. 23:28; 1 Chr. 11:29), from their descent from Ahoah.
</def>
<term id="a-p275.6">Aholah</term>
She has her own tent, a name used by Ezekiel (23:4, 5, 36, 44)
as a symbol of the idolatry of the kingdom of Israel. This
kingdom is described as a lewdwoman, an adulteress, given up to
the abominations and idolatries of the Egyptians and Assyrians.
Because of her crimes, she was carried away captive, and ceased
to be a kingdom. (Comp. Ps. 78:67-69; 1 Kings 12:25-33; 2 Chr. 11:13-16.)
</def>
<term id="a-p276.4">Aholiab</term>
Tent of the father, an artist of the tribe of Dan, appointed to
the work of preparing materials for the tabernacle (<scripRef passage="Ex. 31:6" id="a-p277.1" parsed="|Exod|31|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.31.6">Ex. 31:6</scripRef>;
35:34; 36:1, 2; 38:23).
</def>
<term id="a-p277.6">Aholibah</term>
My tent is in her, the name of an imaginary harlot, applied
