symbolically to Jerusalem, because she had abandoned the worship
of the true God and given herself up to the idolatries of
foreign nations. (Ezek. 23:4, 11, 22, 36, 44).
</def>
<term id="a-p278.6">Aholibamah</term>
Tent of the height, the name given to Judith, the daughter of

Beeri = Anah (<scripRef passage="Gen. 26:34" id="a-p279.1" parsed="|Gen|26|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.26.34">Gen. 26:34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 36:2" id="a-p279.2" parsed="|Gen|36|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36.2">36:2</scripRef>), when she became the wife of
Esau. A district among the mountains of Edom, probably near
Mount Hor, was called after her name, or it may be that she
received her name from the district. From her descended three
tribes of Edomites, founded by her three sons.
</def>
<term id="a-p279.3">Ai</term>
Ruins. (1.) One of the royal cities of the Canaanites (Josh. 10:1; Gen. 12:8; 13:3). It was the scene of Joshua’s defeat, and
afterwards of his victory. It was the second Canaanite city

taken by Israel (<scripRef passage="Josh. 7:2-5" id="a-p280.4" parsed="|Josh|7|2|7|5" osisRef="Bible:Josh.7.2-Josh.7.5">Josh. 7:2-5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 8:1-29" id="a-p280.5" parsed="|Josh|8|1|8|29" osisRef="Bible:Josh.8.1-Josh.8.29">8:1-29</scripRef>). It lay rebuilt and

inhibited by the Benjamites (<scripRef passage="Ezra 2:28" id="a-p280.6" parsed="|Ezra|2|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2.28">Ezra 2:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh. 7:32" id="a-p280.7" parsed="|Neh|7|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.7.32">Neh. 7:32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh 11:31" id="a-p280.8" parsed="|Neh|11|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.11.31">11:31</scripRef>). It
lay to the east of Bethel, “beside Beth-aven.” The spot which is
most probably the site of this ancient city is Haiyan, 2 miles
east from Bethel. It lay up the Wady Suweinit, a steep, rugged
valley, extending from the Jordan valley to Bethel.
(2.) A city in the Ammonite territory (Jer. 49:3). Some have
thought that the proper reading of the word is Ar (Isa. 15:1).
</def>
<term id="a-p281.3">Aijeleth Shahar</term>
Hind of the dawn, a name found in the title of Ps. 22. It is
probably the name of some song or tune to the measure of which
the psalm was to be chanted. Some, however, understand by the
name some instrument of music, or an allegorical allusion to the
subject of the psalm.
</def>
<term id="a-p282.2">Air</term>
The atmosphere, as opposed to the higher regions of the sky (1 Thess. 4:17; Rev. 9:2; 16:17). This word occurs once as the
rendering of the Hebrew ruah (Job 41:16); elsewhere it is the
rendering of shamaiyim, usually translated “heavens.”
The expression “to speak into the air” (1 Cor. 14:9) is a
proverb denoting to speak in vain, as to “beat the air” (1 Cor. 9:26) denotes to labour in vain.
</def>
<term id="a-p284.3">Ajalon</term>
And Aij’alon, place of deer. (1.) A town and valley originally
assigned to the tribe of Dan, from which, however, they could
not drive the Amorites (<scripRef passage="Judg. 1:35" id="a-p285.1" parsed="|Judg|1|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.35">Judg. 1:35</scripRef>). It was one of the Levitical
cities given to the Kohathites (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 6:69" id="a-p285.2" parsed="|1Chr|6|69|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.6.69">1 Chr. 6:69</scripRef>). It was not far
from Beth-shemesh (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 28:18" id="a-p285.3" parsed="|2Chr|28|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.28.18">2 Chr. 28:18</scripRef>). It was the boundary between
the kingdoms of Judah and Israel, and is frequently mentioned in

Jewish history (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 11:10" id="a-p285.4" parsed="|2Chr|11|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.11.10">2 Chr. 11:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 14:31" id="a-p285.5" parsed="|1Sam|14|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.14.31">1 Sam. 14:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 8:13" id="a-p285.6" parsed="|1Chr|8|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.8.13">1 Chr. 8:13</scripRef>). With
reference to the valley named after the town, Joshua uttered the
celebrated command, “Sun, stand thou still on Gibeon; and thou,
Moon, in the valley of Ajalon” (<scripRef passage="Josh. 10:12" id="a-p285.7" parsed="|Josh|10|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.12">Josh. 10:12</scripRef>). It has been
identified as the modern Yalo, at the foot of the Beth-horon
pass (q.v.). In the Tell Amarna letters Adoni-zedek (q.v.)
speaks of the destruction of the “city of Ajalon” by the
invaders, and describes himself as “afflicted, greatly
afflicted” by the calamities that had come on the land, urging
the king of Egypt to hasten to his help.
(2.) A city in the tribe of Zebulun (Judg. 12:12), the modern
Jalun, three miles north of Cabul.
</def>
<term id="a-p286.2">Akkub</term>
(another form of Jacob). (1.) The head of one of the families of
Nethinim (Ezra 2:45).
(2.) A Levite who kept the gate of the temple after the return
from Babylon (1 Chr. 9:17; Ezra 2:42; Neh. 7:45).
(3.) A descendant of David (1 Chr. 3:24).
</def>
<term id="a-p289.2">Akrabbim</term>
Scorpions, probably the general name given to the ridge
containing the pass between the south of the Dead Sea and Zin,
es-Sufah, by which there is an ascent to the level of the land
of Palestine. Scorpions are said to abound in this whole
district, and hence the name (<scripRef passage="Num. 34:4" id="a-p290.1" parsed="|Num|34|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.34.4">Num. 34:4</scripRef>). It is called
“Maaleh-acrabbim” in <scripRef passage="Josh. 15:3" id="a-p290.2" parsed="|Josh|15|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.3">Josh. 15:3</scripRef>, and “the ascent of Akrabbim” in
Num. 34:4.
</def>
<term id="a-p290.4">Alabaster</term>
Occurs only in the New Testament in connection with the box of
“ointment of spikenard very precious,” with the contents of
which a woman anointed the head of Jesus as he sat at supper in

the house of Simon the leper (<scripRef passage="Matt. 26:7" id="a-p291.1" parsed="|Matt|26|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.7">Matt. 26:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 14:3" id="a-p291.2" parsed="|Mark|14|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.14.3">Mark 14:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 7:37" id="a-p291.3" parsed="|Luke|7|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.7.37">Luke 7:37</scripRef>).
These boxes were made from a stone found near Alabastron in
Egypt, and from this circumstance the Greeks gave them the name
of the city where they were made. The name was then given to the
stone of which they were made; and finally to all perfume
vessels, of whatever material they were formed. The woman
“broke” the vessel; i.e., she broke off, as was usually done,
the long and narrow neck so as to reach the contents. This stone
resembles marble, but is softer in its texture, and hence very
easily wrought into boxes. Mark says (14:5) that this box of
ointment was worth more than 300 pence, i.e., denarii, each of
the value of sevenpence halfpenny of our money, and therefore
worth about 10 pounds. But if we take the denarius as the day’s
wage of a labourer (<scripRef passage="Matt. 20:2" id="a-p291.4" parsed="|Matt|20|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.20.2">Matt. 20:2</scripRef>), say two shillings of our money,
then the whole would be worth about 30 pounds, so costly was
Mary’s offering.
</def>
<term id="a-p291.5">Alamoth</term>
Virgins, a musical term (1 Chr. 15:20), denoting that the psalm
which bears this inscription (<scripRef passage="Ps. 46" id="a-p292.2" parsed="|Ps|46|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.46">Ps. 46</scripRef>) was to be sung by soprano
or female voices.
</def>
<term id="a-p292.3">Alarm</term>
A particular quivering sound of the silver trumpets to give
warning to the Hebrews on their journey through the wilderness

(<scripRef passage="Num. 10:5" id="a-p293.1" parsed="|Num|10|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.10.5">Num. 10:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 10:6" id="a-p293.2" parsed="|Num|10|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.10.6">6</scripRef>), a call to arms, or a war-note (<scripRef passage="Jer. 4:19" id="a-p293.3" parsed="|Jer|4|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.4.19">Jer. 4:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 49:2" id="a-p293.4" parsed="|Jer|49|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.49.2">49:2</scripRef>;
Zeph. 1:16).
</def>
<term id="a-p293.6">Alemeth</term>
Covering. (1.) One of the nine sons of Becher, the son of
Benjamin (1 Chr. 7:8).
(2.) One of the sons of Jehoadah, or Jarah, son of Ahaz (1 Chr. 8:36).
(3.) A sacerdotal city of Benjamin (1 Chr. 6:60), called also
Almon (<scripRef passage="Josh. 21:18" id="a-p296.2" parsed="|Josh|21|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.21.18">Josh. 21:18</scripRef>), now Almit, a mile north-east of the ancient
Anathoth.
</def>
<term id="a-p296.3">Alexander</term>
Man-defender. (1.) A relative of Annas the high priest, present
when Peter and John were examined before the Sanhedrim (Acts 4:6).
(2.) A man whose father, Simon the Cyrenian, bore the cross of
Christ (Mark 15:21).
(3.) A Jew of Ephesus who took a prominent part in the uproar
raised there by the preaching of Paul (<scripRef passage="Acts 19:33" id="a-p299.1" parsed="|Acts|19|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.33">Acts 19:33</scripRef>). The Jews put
him forward to plead their cause before the mob. It was probably
intended that he should show that he and the other Jews had no
sympathy with Paul any more than the Ephesians had. It is
possible that this man was the same as the following.
(4.) A coppersmith who, with Hymenaeus and others, promulgated

certain heresies regarding the resurrection (<scripRef passage="1 Tim. 1:19" id="a-p300.1" parsed="|1Tim|1|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.1.19">1 Tim. 1:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Tim. 4:14" id="a-p300.2" parsed="|2Tim|4|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.4.14">2 Tim. 4:14</scripRef>), and made shipwreck of faith and of a good conscience.
Paul excommunicated him (1 Tim. 1:20; comp. 1 Cor. 5:5).
</def>
<term id="a-p300.5">Alexander the Great</term>
The king of Macedonia, the great conqueror; probably represented
in Daniel by the “belly of brass” (<scripRef passage="Dan. 2:32" id="a-p301.1" parsed="|Dan|2|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.2.32">Dan. 2:32</scripRef>), and the leopard
and the he-goat (7:6; 11:3, 4). He succeeded his father Philip,
and died at the age of thirty-two from the effects of
intemperance, B.C. 323. His empire was divided among his four
generals.
</def>
<term id="a-p301.2">Alexandria</term>
The ancient metropolis of Lower Egypt, so called from its
founder, Alexander the Great (about B.C. 333). It was for a long
period the greatest of existing cities, for both Nineveh and
Babylon had been destroyed, and Rome had not yet risen to
greatness. It was the residence of the kings of Egypt for 200
years. It is not mentioned in the Old Testament, and only
incidentally in the New. Apollos, eloquent and mighty in the
Scriptures, was a native of this city (<scripRef passage="Acts 18:24" id="a-p302.1" parsed="|Acts|18|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.24">Acts 18:24</scripRef>). Many Jews
from Alexandria were in Jerusalem, where they had a synagogue
(<scripRef passage="Acts 6:9" id="a-p302.2" parsed="|Acts|6|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.6.9">Acts 6:9</scripRef>), at the time of Stephen’s martyrdom. At one time it
is said that as many as 10,000 Jews resided in this city. It
possessed a famous library of 700,000 volumes, which was burned
by the Saracens (A.D. 642). It was here that the Hebrew Bible
was translated into Greek. This is called the Septuagint
version, from the tradition that seventy learned men were
engaged in executing it. It was, however, not all translated at
one time. It was begun B.C. 280, and finished about B.C. 200 or
150. (See VERSION.)
</def>
<term id="a-p302.4">Algum</term>
(2 Chr. 2:8; 9:10, 11), the same as almug (1 Kings 10:11).
</def>
<term id="a-p303.5">Alien</term>
A foreigner, or person born in another country, and therefore
not entitled to the rights and privileges of the country where
he resides. Among the Hebrews there were two classes of aliens.
(1.) Those who were strangers generally, and who owned no
landed property.
(2.) Strangers dwelling in another country without being
naturalized (Lev. 22:10; Ps. 39:12).
Both of these classes were to enjoy, under certain conditions,

the same rights as other citizens (<scripRef passage="Lev. 19:33" id="a-p307.1" parsed="|Lev|19|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.33">Lev. 19:33</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 19:34" id="a-p307.2" parsed="|Lev|19|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.34">34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 10:19" id="a-p307.3" parsed="|Deut|10|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.10.19">Deut. 10:19</scripRef>).
They might be naturalized and permitted to enter into the
congregation of the Lord by submitting to circumcision and
abandoning idolatry (Deut. 23:3-8).
This term is used (Eph. 2:12) to denote persons who have no
interest in Christ.
</def>
<term id="a-p308.2">Allegory</term>
Used only in Gal. 4:24, where the apostle refers to the history
of Isaac the free-born, and Ishmael the slave-born, and makes
use of it allegorically.
Every parable is an allegory. Nathan (2 Sam. 12:1-4) addresses
David in an allegorical narrative. In the eightieth Psalm there
is a beautiful allegory: “Thou broughtest a vine out of Egypt,”
etc. In <scripRef passage="Eccl. 12:2-6" id="a-p310.2" parsed="|Eccl|12|2|12|6" osisRef="Bible:Eccl.12.2-Eccl.12.6">Eccl. 12:2-6</scripRef>, there is a striking allegorical
description of old age.
</def>
<term id="a-p310.3">Alleluia</term>
The Greek form (Rev. 19:1, 3, 4, 6) of the Hebrew Hallelujah =
Praise ye Jehovah, which begins or ends several of the psalms
</def>
<term id="a-p311.5">Alliance</term>
A treaty between nations, or between individuals, for their
mutual advantage.
Abraham formed an alliance with some of the Canaanitish
princes (<scripRef passage="Gen. 14:13" id="a-p313.1" parsed="|Gen|14|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.13">Gen. 14:13</scripRef>), also with Abimelech (21:22-32). Joshua and
the elders of Israel entered into an alliance with the
Gibeonites (<scripRef passage="Josh. 9:3-27" id="a-p313.2" parsed="|Josh|9|3|9|27" osisRef="Bible:Josh.9.3-Josh.9.27">Josh. 9:3-27</scripRef>). When the Israelites entered Palestine
they were forbidden to enter into alliances with the inhabitants
of the country (Lev. 18:3, 4; 20:22, 23).
Solomon formed a league with Hiram (1 Kings 5:12). This

“brotherly covenant” is referred to 250 years afterwards (<scripRef passage="Amos 1:9" id="a-p314.2" parsed="|Amos|1|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.1.9">Amos 1:9</scripRef>). He also appears to have entered into an alliance with
Pharaoh (1 Kings 10:28, 29).
In the subsequent history of the kingdoms of Judah and Israel
various alliances were formed between them and also with
neighbouring nations at different times.
From patriarchal times a covenant of alliance was sealed by
the blood of some sacrificial victim. The animal sacrificed was
cut in two (except birds), and between these two parts the
persons contracting the alliance passed (<scripRef passage="Gen. 15:10" id="a-p316.1" parsed="|Gen|15|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.10">Gen. 15:10</scripRef>). There are
frequent allusions to this practice (<scripRef passage="Jer. 34:18" id="a-p316.2" parsed="|Jer|34|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.34.18">Jer. 34:18</scripRef>). Such alliances

were called “covenants of salt” (<scripRef passage="Num. 18:19" id="a-p316.3" parsed="|Num|18|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.18.19">Num. 18:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 13:5" id="a-p316.4" parsed="|2Chr|13|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.13.5">2 Chr. 13:5</scripRef>), salt
being the symbol of perpetuity. A pillar was set up as a
memorial of the alliance between Laban and Jacob (<scripRef passage="Gen. 31:52" id="a-p316.5" parsed="|Gen|31|52|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.52">Gen. 31:52</scripRef>).
The Jews throughout their whole history attached great
importance to fidelity to their engagements. Divine wrath fell
upon the violators of them (Josh. 9:18; 2 Sam. 21:1, 2; Ezek. 17:16).
</def>
<term id="a-p316.10">Allon</term>
Oak. (1.) The expression in the Authorized Version of Josh. 19:33, “from Allon to Zaanannim,” is more correctly rendered in
the Revised Version, “from the oak in Zaanannim.” The word
denotes some remarkable tree which stood near Zaanannim, and
which served as a landmark.
(2.) The son of Jedaiah, of the family of the Simeonites, who
expelled the Hamites from the valley of Gedor (1 Chr. 4:37).
</def>
<term id="a-p318.2">Allon-bachuth</term>
Oak of weeping, a tree near Bethel, at the spot where Deborah,
Rebekah’s nurse, was buried (<scripRef passage="Gen. 35:8" id="a-p319.1" parsed="|Gen|35|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.35.8">Gen. 35:8</scripRef>). Large trees, from their
rarity in the plains of Palestine, were frequently designated as
landmarks. This particular tree was probably the same as the
“palm tree of Deborah” (Judg. 4:5).
</def>
<term id="a-p319.3">Almodad</term>
Immeasurable, the first named of the sons of Joktan (Gen. 10:26), the founder of an Arabian tribe.
</def>
<term id="a-p320.2">Almon</term>
Hidden, one of the sacerdotal cities of Benjamin (Josh. 21:18),
called also Alemeth (1 Chr. 6:60).
</def>
<term id="a-p321.3">Almond</term>
A native of Syria and Palestine. In form, blossoms, and fruit it
resembles the peach tree. Its blossoms are of a very pale pink
colour, and appear before its leaves. Its Hebrew name, shaked,
signifying “wakeful, hastening,” is given to it on account of
its putting forth its blossoms so early, generally in February,
and sometimes even in January. In <scripRef passage="Eccl. 12:5" id="a-p322.1" parsed="|Eccl|12|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eccl.12.5">Eccl. 12:5</scripRef>, it is referred to
as illustrative, probably, of the haste with which old age
comes. There are others, however, who still contend for the old
interpretation here. “The almond tree bears its blossoms in the
midst of winter, on a naked, leafless stem, and these blossoms
(reddish or flesh-coloured in the beginning) seem at the time of
their fall exactly like white snow-flakes. In this way the
almond blossom is a very fitting symbol of old age, with its
silvery hair and its wintry, dry, barren, unfruitful condition.”
In <scripRef passage="Jer. 1:11" id="a-p322.2" parsed="|Jer|1|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.1.11">Jer. 1:11</scripRef> “I see a rod of an almond tree [shaked]...for I
will hasten [shaked] my word to perform it” the word is used as
an emblem of promptitude. Jacob desired his sons (<scripRef passage="Gen. 43:11" id="a-p322.3" parsed="|Gen|43|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.43.11">Gen. 43:11</scripRef>) to
take with them into Egypt of the best fruits of the land,
almonds, etc., as a present to Joseph, probably because this
tree was not a native of Egypt. Aaron’s rod yielded almonds

(<scripRef passage="Num. 17:8" id="a-p322.4" parsed="|Num|17|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.17.8">Num. 17:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 9:4" id="a-p322.5" parsed="|Heb|9|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.4">Heb. 9:4</scripRef>). Moses was directed to make certain parts
of the candlestick for the ark of carved work “like unto
almonds” (Ex. 25:33, 34). The Hebrew word luz, translated
“hazel” in the Authorized Version (<scripRef passage="Gen. 30:37" id="a-p322.8" parsed="|Gen|30|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.30.37">Gen. 30:37</scripRef>), is rendered in
the Revised Version “almond.” It is probable that luz denotes
the wild almond, while shaked denotes the cultivated variety.
</def>
<term id="a-p322.9">Alms</term>
Not found in the Old Testament, but repeatedly in the New. The

Mosaic legislation (<scripRef passage="Lev. 25:35" id="a-p323.1" parsed="|Lev|25|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.25.35">Lev. 25:35</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 15:7" id="a-p323.2" parsed="|Deut|15|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.15.7">Deut. 15:7</scripRef>) tended to promote a
spirit of charity, and to prevent the occurrence of destitution

among the people. Such passages as these, <scripRef passage="Ps. 41:1" id="a-p323.3" parsed="|Ps|41|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.41.1">Ps. 41:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 112:9" id="a-p323.4" parsed="|Ps|112|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.112.9">112:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 14:31" id="a-p323.5" parsed="|Prov|14|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.14.31">Prov. 14:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 10:2" id="a-p323.6" parsed="|Isa|10|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.2">Isa. 10:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Amos 2:7" id="a-p323.7" parsed="|Amos|2|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.2.7">Amos 2:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 5:28" id="a-p323.8" parsed="|Jer|5|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.5.28">Jer. 5:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 22:29" id="a-p323.9" parsed="|Ezek|22|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.22.29">Ezek. 22:29</scripRef>, would also
naturally foster the same benevolent spirit.
In the time of our Lord begging was common (Mark 10:46; Acts 3:2). The Pharisees were very ostentatious in their almsgivings
(<scripRef passage="Matt. 6:2" id="a-p324.3" parsed="|Matt|6|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.2">Matt. 6:2</scripRef>). The spirit by which the Christian ought to be
actuated in this duty is set forth in <scripRef passage="1 John 3:17" id="a-p324.4" parsed="|1John|3|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.3.17">1 John 3:17</scripRef>. A regard to
the state of the poor and needy is enjoined as a Christian duty

(<scripRef passage="Luke 3:11" id="a-p324.5" parsed="|Luke|3|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.11">Luke 3:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 6:30" id="a-p324.6" parsed="|Luke|6|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.6.30">6:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 6:1" id="a-p324.7" parsed="|Matt|6|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.1">Matt. 6:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 9:36" id="a-p324.8" parsed="|Acts|9|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.9.36">Acts 9:36</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 10:2" id="a-p324.9" parsed="|Acts|10|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.10.2">10:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 10:4" id="a-p324.10" parsed="|Acts|10|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.10.4">4</scripRef>), a duty which

was not neglected by the early Christians (<scripRef passage="Luke 14:13" id="a-p324.11" parsed="|Luke|14|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.14.13">Luke 14:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 20:35" id="a-p324.12" parsed="|Acts|20|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.35">Acts 20:35</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal. 2:10" id="a-p324.13" parsed="|Gal|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.2.10">Gal. 2:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 15:25-27" id="a-p324.14" parsed="|Rom|15|25|15|27" osisRef="Bible:Rom.15.25-Rom.15.27">Rom. 15:25-27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 16:1-4" id="a-p324.15" parsed="|1Cor|16|1|16|4" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.16.1-1Cor.16.4">1 Cor. 16:1-4</scripRef>). They cared not
only for the poor among themselves, but contributed also to the

necessities of those at a distance (<scripRef passage="Acts 11:29" id="a-p324.16" parsed="|Acts|11|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.29">Acts 11:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 24:17" id="a-p324.17" parsed="|Acts|24|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.24.17">24:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 9:12" id="a-p324.18" parsed="|2Cor|9|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.9.12">2 Cor. 9:12</scripRef>). Our Lord and his attendants showed an example also in
this (John 13:29).
In modern times the “poor-laws” have introduced an element
which modifies considerably the form in which we may discharge
this Christian duty.
</def>
<term id="a-p325.1">Almug</term>
(1 Kings 10:11, 12) = algum (2 Chr. 2:8; 9:10, 11), in the
Hebrew occurring only in the plural almuggim (indicating that
the wood was brought in planks), the name of a wood brought from
Ophir to be used in the building of the temple, and for other
purposes. Some suppose it to have been the white sandal-wood of
India, the Santalum album of botanists, a native of the
mountainous parts of the Malabar coasts. It is a fragrant wood,
and is used in China for incense in idol-worship. Others, with
some probability, think that it was the Indian red sandal-wood,
the pterocarpus santalinus, a heavy, fine-grained wood, the
Sanscrit name of which is valguka. It is found on the Coromandel
coast and in Ceylon.
</def>
<term id="a-p326.6">Aloes</term>
(Heb. ‘ahalim), a fragrant wood (Num. 24:6; Ps. 45:8; Prov. 7:17; Cant. 4:14), the Aquilaria agallochum of botanists, or, as
some suppose, the costly gum or perfume extracted from the wood.
It is found in China, Siam, and Northern India, and grows to the
height sometimes of 120 feet. This species is of great rarity
even in India. There is another and more common species, called
by Indians aghil, whence Europeans have given it the name of
Lignum aquile, or eagle-wood. Aloewood was used by the Egyptians
for embalming dead bodies. Nicodemus brought it (pounded
aloe-wood) to embalm the body of Christ (<scripRef passage="John 19:39" id="a-p327.5" parsed="|John|19|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.39">John 19:39</scripRef>); but
whether this was the same as that mentioned elsewhere is
uncertain.
The bitter aloes of the apothecary is the dried juice of the
leaves Aloe vulgaris.
</def>
<term id="a-p328.1">Alphaeus</term>
(1.) The father of James the Less, the apostle and writer of the

epistle (<scripRef passage="Matt. 10:3" id="a-p329.1" parsed="|Matt|10|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.10.3">Matt. 10:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 3:18" id="a-p329.2" parsed="|Mark|3|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.3.18">Mark 3:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 6:15" id="a-p329.3" parsed="|Luke|6|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.6.15">Luke 6:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 1:13" id="a-p329.4" parsed="|Acts|1|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.13">Acts 1:13</scripRef>), and the
husband of Mary (<scripRef passage="John 19:25" id="a-p329.5" parsed="|John|19|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.25">John 19:25</scripRef>). The Hebrew form of this name is
Cleopas, or Clopas (q.v.).
(2.) The father of Levi, or Matthew (Mark 2:14).
</def>
<term id="a-p330.2">Altar</term>
(Heb. mizbe’ah, from a word meaning “to slay”), any structure of
earth (<scripRef passage="Ex. 20:24" id="a-p331.1" parsed="|Exod|20|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.20.24">Ex. 20:24</scripRef>) or unwrought stone (20:25) on which sacrifices
were offered. Altars were generally erected in conspicuous

places (<scripRef passage="Gen. 22:9" id="a-p331.2" parsed="|Gen|22|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.22.9">Gen. 22:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 6:3" id="a-p331.3" parsed="|Ezek|6|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.6.3">Ezek. 6:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 23:12" id="a-p331.4" parsed="|2Kgs|23|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.12">2 Kings 23:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 16:4" id="a-p331.5" parsed="|2Kgs|16|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.16.4">16:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 23:8" id="a-p331.6" parsed="|2Kgs|23|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.8">23:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 14:13" id="a-p331.7" parsed="|Acts|14|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.14.13">Acts 14:13</scripRef>). The word is used in <scripRef passage="Heb. 13:10" id="a-p331.8" parsed="|Heb|13|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.13.10">Heb. 13:10</scripRef> for the sacrifice offered
upon it—the sacrifice Christ offered.
Paul found among the many altars erected in Athens one bearing
the inscription, “To the unknown God” (<scripRef passage="Acts 17:23" id="a-p332.1" parsed="|Acts|17|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.17.23">Acts 17:23</scripRef>), or rather
“to an [i.e., some] unknown God.” The reason for this
inscription cannot now be accurately determined. It afforded the
apostle the occasion of proclaiming the gospel to the “men of
Athens.”
The first altar we read of is that erected by Noah (Gen. 8:20). Altars were erected by Abraham (Gen. 12:7; 13:4; 22:9),
by Isaac (<scripRef passage="Gen. 26:25" id="a-p333.5" parsed="|Gen|26|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.26.25">Gen. 26:25</scripRef>), by Jacob (33:20; 35:1, 3), and by Moses
(Ex. 17:15, “Jehovah-nissi”).
In the tabernacle, and afterwards in the temple, two altars
were erected.
(1.) The altar of burnt offering (Ex. 30:28), called also the
“brasen altar” (Ex. 39:39) and “the table of the Lord” (Mal. 1:7).
This altar, as erected in the tabernacle, is described in Ex. 27:1-8. It was a hollow square, 5 cubits in length and in
breadth, and 3 cubits in height. It was made of shittim wood,
and was overlaid with plates of brass. Its corners were
ornamented with “horns” (Ex. 29:12; Lev. 4:18).
In Ex. 27:3 the various utensils appertaining to the altar are

enumerated. They were made of brass. (Comp. <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 2:13" id="a-p337.2" parsed="|1Sam|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.2.13">1 Sam. 2:13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 2:14" id="a-p337.3" parsed="|1Sam|2|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.2.14">14</scripRef>;
Lev. 16:12; Num. 16:6, 7.)
In Solomon’s temple the altar was of larger dimensions (2 Chr. 4:1. Comp. 1 Kings 8:22, 64; 9:25), and was made wholly of
brass, covering a structure of stone or earth. This altar was

renewed by Asa (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 15:8" id="a-p338.4" parsed="|2Chr|15|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.15.8">2 Chr. 15:8</scripRef>). It was removed by Ahaz (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 16:14" id="a-p338.5" parsed="|2Kgs|16|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.16.14">2 Kings 16:14</scripRef>), and “cleansed” by Hezekiah, in the latter part of whose
reign it was rebuilt. It was finally broken up and carried away
by the Babylonians (Jer. 52:17).
After the return from captivity it was re-erected (Ezra 3:3, 6) on the same place where it had formerly stood. (Comp. 1 Macc. 4:47.) When Antiochus Epiphanes pillaged Jerusalem the altar of
burnt offering was taken away.
Again the altar was erected by Herod, and remained in its
place till the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans (70 A.D.).
The fire on the altar was not permitted to go out (Lev. 6:9).
In the Mosque of Omar, immediately underneath the great dome,
which occupies the site of the old temple, there is a rough
projection of the natural rock, of about 60 feet in its extreme
length, and 50 in its greatest breadth, and in its highest part
about 4 feet above the general pavement. This rock seems to have
been left intact when Solomon’s temple was built. It was in all
probability the site of the altar of burnt offering. Underneath
this rock is a cave, which may probably have been the granary of
Araunah’s threshing-floor (1 Chr. 21:22).
(2.) The altar of incense (Ex. 30:1-10), called also “the
golden altar” (39:38; <scripRef passage="Num. 4:11" id="a-p343.2" parsed="|Num|4|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.4.11">Num. 4:11</scripRef>), stood in the holy place
“before the vail that is by the ark of the testimony.” On this
altar sweet spices were continually burned with fire taken from
the brazen altar. The morning and the evening services were
commenced by the high priest offering incense on this altar. The
burning of the incense was a type of prayer (Ps. 141:2; Rev. 5:8; 8:3, 4).
This altar was a small movable table, made of acacia wood

overlaid with gold (<scripRef passage="Ex. 37:25" id="a-p344.1" parsed="|Exod|37|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.37.25">Ex. 37:25</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 37:26" id="a-p344.2" parsed="|Exod|37|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.37.26">26</scripRef>). It was 1 cubit in length and
breadth, and 2 cubits in height.
In Solomon’s temple the altar was similar in size, but was

made of cedar-wood (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 6:20" id="a-p345.1" parsed="|1Kgs|6|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.6.20">1 Kings 6:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 7:48" id="a-p345.2" parsed="|1Kgs|7|48|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.7.48">7:48</scripRef>) overlaid with gold. In
Ezek. 41:22 it is called “the altar of wood.” (Comp. Ex. 30:1-6.)
In the temple built after the Exile the altar was restored.
Antiochus Epiphanes took it away, but it was afterwards restored

by Judas Maccabaeus (<scripRef passage="1 Macc. 1:23" id="a-p346.1" parsed="|1Macc|1|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Macc.1.23">1 Macc. 1:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Macc. 4:49" id="a-p346.2" parsed="|1Macc|4|49|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Macc.4.49">4:49</scripRef>). Among the trophies
carried away by Titus on the destruction of Jerusalem the altar

of incense is not found, nor is any mention made of it in <scripRef passage="Heb. 9" id="a-p346.3" parsed="|Heb|9|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9">Heb. 9</scripRef>. It was at this altar Zacharias ministered when an angel
appeared to him (<scripRef passage="Luke 1:11" id="a-p346.4" parsed="|Luke|1|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.11">Luke 1:11</scripRef>). It is the only altar which appears
in the heavenly temple (Isa. 6:6; Rev. 8:3, 4).
</def>
<term id="a-p346.8">Altaschith</term>
Destroy not, the title of Ps. 57, 58, 59, and 75. It was
probably the name of some song to the melody of which these
psalms were to be chanted.
</def>
<term id="a-p347.4">Alush</term>
One of the places, the last before Rephidim, at which the

Hebrews rested on their way to Sinai (<scripRef passage="Num. 33:13" id="a-p348.1" parsed="|Num|33|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.13">Num. 33:13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 33:14" id="a-p348.2" parsed="|Num|33|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.14">14</scripRef>). It was
probably situated on the shore of the Red Sea.
</def>
<term id="a-p348.3">Amalek</term>
Dweller in a valley, the son of Eliphaz and grandson of Esau

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 36:12" id="a-p349.1" parsed="|Gen|36|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36.12">Gen. 36:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 1:36" id="a-p349.2" parsed="|1Chr|1|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.1.36">1 Chr. 1:36</scripRef>); the chief of an Idumean tribe (<scripRef passage="Gen. 36:16" id="a-p349.3" parsed="|Gen|36|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36.16">Gen. 36:16</scripRef>). His mother was a Horite, a tribe whose territory the
descendants of Esau had seized.
</def>
<term id="a-p349.4">Amalekite</term>
A tribe that dwelt in Arabia Petraea, between the Dead Sea and
the Red Sea. They were not the descendants of Amalek, the son of
Eliphaz, for they existed in the days of Abraham (<scripRef passage="Gen. 14:7" id="a-p350.1" parsed="|Gen|14|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.7">Gen. 14:7</scripRef>).
They were probably a tribe that migrated from the shores of the
Persian Gulf and settled in Arabia. “They dwelt in the land of
the south...from Havilah until thou comest to Shur” (<scripRef passage="Num. 13:29" id="a-p350.2" parsed="|Num|13|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.13.29">Num. 13:29</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 15:7" id="a-p350.3" parsed="|1Sam|15|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.15.7">1 Sam. 15:7</scripRef>). They were a pastoral, and hence a nomadic race.

Their kings bore the hereditary name of Agag (<scripRef passage="Num. 24:7" id="a-p350.4" parsed="|Num|24|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.24.7">Num. 24:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 15:8" id="a-p350.5" parsed="|1Sam|15|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.15.8">1 Sam. 15:8</scripRef>). They attempted to stop the Israelites when they marched
through their territory (<scripRef passage="Deut. 25:18" id="a-p350.6" parsed="|Deut|25|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.25.18">Deut. 25:18</scripRef>), attacking them at

Rephidim (<scripRef passage="Ex. 17:8-13" id="a-p350.7" parsed="|Exod|17|8|17|13" osisRef="Bible:Exod.17.8-Exod.17.13">Ex. 17:8-13</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Deut. 25:17" id="a-p350.8" parsed="|Deut|25|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.25.17">Deut. 25:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 15:2" id="a-p350.9" parsed="|1Sam|15|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.15.2">1 Sam. 15:2</scripRef>). They
afterwards attacked the Israelites at Hormah (<scripRef passage="Num. 14:45" id="a-p350.10" parsed="|Num|14|45|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.14.45">Num. 14:45</scripRef>). We

read of them subsequently as in league with the Moabites (<scripRef passage="Judg. 3:13" id="a-p350.11" parsed="|Judg|3|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.3.13">Judg. 3:13</scripRef>) and the Midianites (<scripRef passage="Judg. 6:3" id="a-p350.12" parsed="|Judg|6|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.6.3">Judg. 6:3</scripRef>). Saul finally desolated

their territory and destroyed their power (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 14:48" id="a-p350.13" parsed="|1Sam|14|48|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.14.48">1 Sam. 14:48</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 15:3" id="a-p350.14" parsed="|1Sam|15|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.15.3">15:3</scripRef>),
and David recovered booty from them (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 30:18-20" id="a-p350.15" parsed="|1Sam|30|18|30|20" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.30.18-1Sam.30.20">1 Sam. 30:18-20</scripRef>). In the
Babylonian inscriptions they are called Sute, in those of Egypt
Sittiu, and the Amarna tablets include them under the general
name of Khabbati, or “plunderers.”
</def>
<term id="a-p350.16">Amana</term>
Perennial. (1.) The Hebrew margin of 2 Kings 5:12 gives this as
another reading of Abana (q.v.), a stream near Damascus.
(2.) A mountain (Cant. 4:8), probably the southern summit of
Anti-Libanus, at the base of which are the sources of the Abana.
</def>
<term id="a-p352.2">Amariah</term>
Said by Jehovah. (1.) One of the descendants of Aaron by Eleazar

(<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 6:7" id="a-p353.1" parsed="|1Chr|6|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.6.7">1 Chr. 6:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 6:52" id="a-p353.2" parsed="|1Chr|6|52|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.6.52">52</scripRef>). He was probably the last of the high priests of
Eleazar’s line prior to the transfer of that office to Eli, of
the line of Ithamar.
(2.) A Levite, son of Hebron, of the lineage of Moses (1 Chr. 23:19; 24:23).
(3.) A “chief priest” who took an active part in the
reformation under Jehoshaphat (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 19:11" id="a-p355.1" parsed="|2Chr|19|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.19.11">2 Chr. 19:11</scripRef>); probably the same
as mentioned in 1 Chr. 6:9.
(4.) 1 Chr. 6:11; Ezra 7:3. (5.) One of the high priests in
the time of Hezekiah (2 Chr. 31:15). (6.) Zeph. 1:1. (7.) Neh. 11:4. (8.) Neh. 10:3. (9.) Ezra 10:42.
</def>
<term id="a-p356.8">Amasa</term>
Burden. (1.) The son of Abigail, a sister of king David (1 Chr. 2:17; 2 Sam. 17:25). He was appointed by David to command the
army in room of his cousin Joab (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 19:13" id="a-p357.3" parsed="|2Sam|19|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.19.13">2 Sam. 19:13</scripRef>), who afterwards
treacherously put him to death as a dangerous rival (2 Sam. 20:4-12).
(2.) A son of Hadlai, and chief of Ephraim (2 Chr. 28:12) in
the reign of Ahaz.
</def>
<term id="a-p358.2">Amasai</term>
Burdensome. (1.) A Levite, son of Elkanah, of the ancestry of
Samuel (1 Chr. 6:25, 35).
(2.) The leader of a body of men who joined David in the
“stronghold,” probably of Adullam (1 Chr. 12:18).
(3.) One of the priests appointed to precede the ark with
blowing of trumpets on its removal from the house of Obed-edom
(1 Chr. 15:24).
(4.) The father of a Levite, one of the two Kohathites who
took a prominent part at the instance of Hezekiah in the
cleansing of the temple (2 Chr. 29:12).
</def>
<term id="a-p362.2">Amashai</term>
The son of Azareel, appointed by Nehemiah to reside at Jerusalem
and do the work of the temple (Neh. 11:13).
</def>
<term id="a-p363.2">Amasiah</term>
Burden of (i.e., “sustained by”) Jehovah, the “son of Zichri,
who willingly offered himself unto the Lord,” a captain over
thousands under Jehoshaphat (2 Chr. 17:16; comp. Judg. 5:9).
</def>
<term id="a-p364.3">Amaziah</term>
Strengthened by Jehovah. (1.) A Levite, son of Hilkiah, of the
descendants of Ethan the Merarite (1 Chr. 6:45).
(2.) The son and successor of Joash, and eighth king of the
separate kingdom of Judah (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 14:1-4" id="a-p366.1" parsed="|2Kgs|14|1|14|4" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.14.1-2Kgs.14.4">2 Kings 14:1-4</scripRef>). He began his reign
by punishing the murderers of his father (5-7; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 25:3-5" id="a-p366.2" parsed="|2Chr|25|3|25|5" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.25.3-2Chr.25.5">2 Chr. 25:3-5</scripRef>).
He was the first to employ a mercenary army of 100,000 Israelite
soldiers, which he did in his attempt to bring the Edomites

again under the yoke of Judah (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 25:5" id="a-p366.3" parsed="|2Chr|25|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.25.5">2 Chr. 25:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 25:6" id="a-p366.4" parsed="|2Chr|25|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.25.6">6</scripRef>). He was commanded
by a prophet of the Lord to send back the mercenaries, which he

did (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 25:7-10" id="a-p366.5" parsed="|2Chr|25|7|25|10" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.25.7-2Chr.25.10">2 Chr. 25:7-10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 25:13" id="a-p366.6" parsed="|2Chr|25|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.25.13">13</scripRef>), much to their annoyance. His obedience
to this command was followed by a decisive victory over the
Edomites (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 25:14-16" id="a-p366.7" parsed="|2Chr|25|14|25|16" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.25.14-2Chr.25.16">2 Chr. 25:14-16</scripRef>). Amaziah began to worship some of the
idols he took from the Edomites, and this was his ruin, for he
was vanquished by Joash, king of Israel, whom he challenged to
battle. The disaster he thus brought upon Judah by his
infatuation in proclaiming war against Israel probably

occasioned the conspiracy by which he lost his life (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 14:8-14" id="a-p366.8" parsed="|2Kgs|14|8|14|14" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.14.8-2Kgs.14.14">2 Kings 14:8-14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 14:19" id="a-p366.9" parsed="|2Kgs|14|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.14.19">19</scripRef>). He was slain at Lachish, whither he had fled, and
his body was brought upon horses to Jerusalem, where it was
buried in the royal sepulchre (2 Kings 14:19, 20; 2 Chr. 25:27, 28).
(3.) A priest of the golden calves at Bethel (Amos 7:10-17).
(4.) The father of Joshah, one of the Simeonite chiefs in the
time of Hezekiah (1 Chr. 4:34).
</def>
<term id="a-p368.2">Ambassador</term>
In the Old Testament the Hebrew word tsir, meaning “one who

goes on an errand,” is rendered thus (<scripRef passage="Josh. 9:4" id="a-p369.1" parsed="|Josh|9|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.9.4">Josh. 9:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 13:17" id="a-p369.2" parsed="|Prov|13|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.13.17">Prov. 13:17</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Isa. 18:2" id="a-p369.3" parsed="|Isa|18|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.18.2">Isa. 18:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 49:14" id="a-p369.4" parsed="|Jer|49|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.49.14">Jer. 49:14</scripRef>; Obad. 1:1). This is also the rendering of
melits, meaning “an interpreter,” in 2 Chr. 32:31; and of
malak, a “messenger,” in 2 Chr. 35:21; Isa. 30:4; 33:7; Ezek. 17:15. This is the name used by the apostle as designating those
who are appointed by God to declare his will (2 Cor. 5:20; Eph. 6:20).
The Hebrews on various occasions and for various purposes had
recourse to the services of ambassadors, e.g., to contract

alliances (<scripRef passage="Josh. 9:4" id="a-p370.1" parsed="|Josh|9|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.9.4">Josh. 9:4</scripRef>), to solicit favours (<scripRef passage="Num. 20:14" id="a-p370.2" parsed="|Num|20|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.20.14">Num. 20:14</scripRef>), to
remonstrate when wrong was done (<scripRef passage="Judg. 11:12" id="a-p370.3" parsed="|Judg|11|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.11.12">Judg. 11:12</scripRef>), to condole with a
young king on the death of his father (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 10:2" id="a-p370.4" parsed="|2Sam|10|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.10.2">2 Sam. 10:2</scripRef>), and to
congratulate a king on his accession to the throne (1 Kings 5:1).
To do injury to an ambassador was to insult the king who sent
him (2 Sam. 10:5).
</def>
<term id="a-p371.2">Amber</term>
(Ezek. 1:4, 27; 8:2. Heb., hashmal, rendered by the LXX.
elektron, and by the Vulgate electrum), a metal compounded of
silver and gold. Some translate the word by “polished brass,”

others “fine brass,” as in <scripRef passage="Rev. 1:15" id="a-p372.3" parsed="|Rev|1|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.1.15">Rev. 1:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev 2:18" id="a-p372.4" parsed="|Rev|2|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.2.18">2:18</scripRef>. It was probably the
mixture now called electrum. The word has no connection,
however, with what is now called amber, which is a gummy
substance, reckoned as belonging to the mineral kingdom though
of vegetable origin, a fossil resin.
</def>
<term id="a-p372.5">Ambush</term>
Joshua at the capture of Ai lay in ambush, and so deceived the
inhabitants that he gained an easy victory (<scripRef passage="Josh. 8:4-26" id="a-p373.1" parsed="|Josh|8|4|8|26" osisRef="Bible:Josh.8.4-Josh.8.26">Josh. 8:4-26</scripRef>).
Shechem was taken in this manner (Judg. 9:30-45. Comp. Jer. 51:12).
</def>
<term id="a-p373.4">Amen</term>
This Hebrew word means firm, and hence also faithful (Rev. 3:14). In Isa. 65:16, the Authorized Version has “the God of
truth,” which in Hebrew is “the God of Amen.” It is frequently
used by our Saviour to give emphasis to his words, where it is
translated “verily.” Sometimes, only, however, in John’s Gospel,
it is repeated, “Verily, verily.” It is used as an epithet of
the Lord Jesus Christ (Rev. 3:14).
It is found singly and sometimes doubly at the end of prayers

(<scripRef passage="Ps. 41:13" id="a-p375.1" parsed="|Ps|41|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.41.13">Ps. 41:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 72:19" id="a-p375.2" parsed="|Ps|72|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.72.19">72:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 89:52" id="a-p375.3" parsed="|Ps|89|52|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.89.52">89:52</scripRef>), to confirm the words and invoke the
fulfilment of them. It is used in token of being bound by an

oath (<scripRef passage="Num. 5:22" id="a-p375.4" parsed="|Num|5|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.5.22">Num. 5:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 27:15-26" id="a-p375.5" parsed="|Deut|27|15|27|26" osisRef="Bible:Deut.27.15-Deut.27.26">Deut. 27:15-26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh. 5:13" id="a-p375.6" parsed="|Neh|5|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.5.13">Neh. 5:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh 8:6" id="a-p375.7" parsed="|Neh|8|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.8.6">8:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 16:36" id="a-p375.8" parsed="|1Chr|16|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.16.36">1 Chr. 16:36</scripRef>).
In the primitive churches it was common for the general audience
to say “Amen” at the close of the prayer (1 Cor. 14:16).
The promises of God are Amen; i.e., they are all true and sure
(2 Cor. 1:20).
</def>
<term id="a-p376.2">Amethyst</term>
One of the precious stones in the breastplate of the high priest

(<scripRef passage="Ex. 28:19" id="a-p377.1" parsed="|Exod|28|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.19">Ex. 28:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 39:12" id="a-p377.2" parsed="|Exod|39|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.39.12">39:12</scripRef>), and in the foundation of the New Jerusalem
(<scripRef passage="Rev. 21:20" id="a-p377.3" parsed="|Rev|21|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.21.20">Rev. 21:20</scripRef>). The ancients thought that this stone had the power
of dispelling drunkenness in all who wore or touched it, and
hence its Greek name formed from a_, “privative,” and _methuo,
“to get drunk.” Its Jewish name, ahlamah’, was derived by the
rabbins from the Hebrew word halam, “to dream,” from its
supposed power of causing the wearer to dream.
It is a pale-blue crystallized quartz, varying to a dark
purple blue. It is found in Persia and India, also in different
parts of Europe.
</def>
<term id="a-p378.1">Amittai</term>
True, the father of Jonah the prophet, a native of Gath-hepher
(2 Kings 14:25; Jonah 1:1).
</def>
<term id="a-p379.3">Ammah</term>
A cubit, the name of a hill which Joab and Abishai reached as
the sun went down, when they were in pursuit of Abner (2 Sam. 2:24). It lay to the east of Gibeon.
</def>
<term id="a-p380.2">Ammi</term>
My people, a name given by Jehovah to the people of Israel (Hos. 2:1, 23. Comp. 1:9; Ezek. 16:8; Rom. 9:25, 26; 1 Pet. 2:10).
</def>
<term id="a-p381.7">Ammiel</term>
People of God. (1.) One of the twelve spies sent by Moses to
search the land of Canaan (<scripRef passage="Num. 13:12" id="a-p382.1" parsed="|Num|13|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.13.12">Num. 13:12</scripRef>). He was one of the ten
who perished by the plague for their unfavourable report (Num. 14:37).
(2.) The father of Machir of Lo-debar, in whose house
Mephibosheth resided (2 Sam. 9:4, 5; 17:27).
(3.) The father of Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah, and
afterwards of David (1 Chr. 3:5). He is called Eliam in 2 Sam. 11:3.
(4.) One of the sons of Obed-edom the Levite (1 Chr. 26:5).
</def>
<term id="a-p385.2">Ammihud</term>
People of glory; i.e., “renowned.” (1.) The father of the
Ephraimite chief Elishama, at the time of the Exodus (<scripRef passage="Num. 1:10" id="a-p386.1" parsed="|Num|1|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.1.10">Num. 1:10</scripRef>;
2:18; 7:48, 53).
(2.) Num. 34:20. (3.) Num. 34:28.
(4.) The father of Talmai, king of Geshur, to whom Absalom
fled after the murder of Amnon (2 Sam. 13:37).
(5.) The son of Omri, and the father of Uthai (1 Chr. 9:4).
</def>
<term id="a-p389.2">Amminadab</term>
Kindred of the prince. (1.) The father of Nahshon, who was chief

of the tribe of Judah (<scripRef passage="Num. 1:7" id="a-p390.1" parsed="|Num|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.1.7">Num. 1:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 2:3" id="a-p390.2" parsed="|Num|2|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.2.3">2:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 7:12" id="a-p390.3" parsed="|Num|7|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.7.12">7:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num 7:17" id="a-p390.4" parsed="|Num|7|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.7.17">17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 10:14" id="a-p390.5" parsed="|Num|10|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.10.14">10:14</scripRef>). His
daughter Elisheba was married to Aaron (Ex. 6:23).
(2.) A son of Kohath, the second son of Levi (1 Chr. 6:22),
called also Izhar (2, 18).
(3.) Chief of the 112 descendants of Uzziel the Levite (1 Chr. 15:10, 11).
</def>
<term id="a-p392.3">Amminadib</term>
A person mentioned in Cant. 6:12, whose chariots were famed for
their swiftness. It is rendered in the margin “my willing
people,” and in the Revised Version “my princely people.”
</def>
<term id="a-p393.2">Ammishaddai</term>
People of the Almighty, the father of Ahiezer, who was chief of

the Danites at the time of the Exodus (<scripRef passage="Num. 1:12" id="a-p394.1" parsed="|Num|1|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.1.12">Num. 1:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 2:25" id="a-p394.2" parsed="|Num|2|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.2.25">2:25</scripRef>). This is
one of the few names compounded with the name of God, Shaddai,
“Almighty.”
</def>
<term id="a-p394.3">Ammizabad</term>
People of the giver, the son of Benaiah, who was the third and
chief captain of the host under David (1 Chr. 27:6).
</def>
<term id="a-p395.2">Ammon</term>
Another form of the name Ben-ammi, the son of Lot (Gen. 19:38).
This name is also used for his posterity (Ps. 83:7).
</def>
<term id="a-p396.3">Ammonite</term>
The usual name of the descendants of Ammon, the son of Lot (Gen. 19:38). From the very beginning (Deut. 2:16-20) of their history
till they are lost sight of (<scripRef passage="Judg. 5:2" id="a-p397.3" parsed="|Judg|5|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.5.2">Judg. 5:2</scripRef>), this tribe is closely

associated with the Moabites (<scripRef passage="Judg. 10:11" id="a-p397.4" parsed="|Judg|10|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.10.11">Judg. 10:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 20:1" id="a-p397.5" parsed="|2Chr|20|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.20.1">2 Chr. 20:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zeph. 2:8" id="a-p397.6" parsed="|Zeph|2|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zeph.2.8">Zeph. 2:8</scripRef>). Both of these tribes hired Balaam to curse Israel (<scripRef passage="Deut. 23:4" id="a-p397.7" parsed="|Deut|23|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.23.4">Deut. 23:4</scripRef>). The Ammonites were probably more of a predatory tribe,
moving from place to place, while the Moabites were more
settled. They inhabited the country east of the Jordan and north
of Moab and the Dead Sea, from which they had expelled the

Zamzummims or Zuzims (<scripRef passage="Deut. 2:20" id="a-p397.8" parsed="|Deut|2|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.2.20">Deut. 2:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen. 14:5" id="a-p397.9" parsed="|Gen|14|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.5">Gen. 14:5</scripRef>). They are known as
the Beni-ammi (<scripRef passage="Gen. 19:38" id="a-p397.10" parsed="|Gen|19|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.19.38">Gen. 19:38</scripRef>), Ammi or Ammon being worshipped as
their chief god. They were of Semitic origin, and closely
related to the Hebrews in blood and language. They showed no
kindness to the Israelites when passing through their territory,
and therefore they were prohibited from “entering the
congregation of the Lord to the tenth generation” (<scripRef passage="Deut. 23:3" id="a-p397.11" parsed="|Deut|23|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.23.3">Deut. 23:3</scripRef>).
They afterwards became hostile to Israel (<scripRef passage="Judg. 3:13" id="a-p397.12" parsed="|Judg|3|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.3.13">Judg. 3:13</scripRef>). Jephthah
waged war against them, and “took twenty cities with a very
great slaughter” (<scripRef passage="Judg. 11:33" id="a-p397.13" parsed="|Judg|11|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.11.33">Judg. 11:33</scripRef>). They were again signally
defeated by Saul (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 11:11" id="a-p397.14" parsed="|1Sam|11|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.11.11">1 Sam. 11:11</scripRef>). David also defeated them and
their allies the Syrians (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 10:6-14" id="a-p397.15" parsed="|2Sam|10|6|10|14" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.10.6-2Sam.10.14">2 Sam. 10:6-14</scripRef>), and took their chief

city, Rabbah, with much spoil (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 10:14" id="a-p397.16" parsed="|2Sam|10|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.10.14">2 Sam. 10:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 12:26-31" id="a-p397.17" parsed="|2Sam|12|26|12|31" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.12.26-2Sam.12.31">12:26-31</scripRef>). The
subsequent events of their history are noted in <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 20:25" id="a-p397.18" parsed="|2Chr|20|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.20.25">2 Chr. 20:25</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 26:8" id="a-p397.19" parsed="|2Chr|26|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.26.8">26:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 49:1" id="a-p397.20" parsed="|Jer|49|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.49.1">Jer. 49:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 25:3" id="a-p397.21" parsed="|Ezek|25|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.25.3">Ezek. 25:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 25:6" id="a-p397.22" parsed="|Ezek|25|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.25.6">6</scripRef>. One of Solomon’s wives was
Naamah, an Ammonite. She was the mother of Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:31; 2 Chr. 12:13).
The prophets predicted fearful judgments against the Ammonites

because of their hostility to Israel (<scripRef passage="Zeph. 2:8" id="a-p398.1" parsed="|Zeph|2|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zeph.2.8">Zeph. 2:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 49:1-6" id="a-p398.2" parsed="|Jer|49|1|49|6" osisRef="Bible:Jer.49.1-Jer.49.6">Jer. 49:1-6</scripRef>;
Ezek. 25:1-5, 10; Amos 1:13-15).
The national idol worshipped by this people was Molech or

Milcom, at whose altar they offered human sacrifices (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 11:5" id="a-p399.1" parsed="|1Kgs|11|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.11.5">1 Kings 11:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 11:7" id="a-p399.2" parsed="|1Kgs|11|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.11.7">7</scripRef>). The high places built for this idol by Solomon, at the
instigation of his Ammonitish wives, were not destroyed till the
time of Josiah (2 Kings 23:13).
</def>
<term id="a-p399.4">Amnon</term>
Faithful. (1.) One of the sons of Shammai, of the children of
Ezra (1 Chr. 4:20; comp. 17).
(2.) The eldest son of David, by Ahinoam of Jezreel (1 Chr. 3:1; 2 Sam. 3:2). Absalom caused him to be put to death for his
great crime in the matter of Tamar (2 Sam. 13:28, 29).
</def>
<term id="a-p401.5">Amon</term>
Builder. (1.) The governor of Samaria in the time of Ahab. The
prophet Micaiah was committed to his custody (1 Kings 22:26; 2 Chr. 18:25).
(2.) The son of Manasseh, and fourteenth king of Judah. He
restored idolatry, and set up the images which his father had
cast down. Zephaniah (1:4; 3:4, 11) refers to the moral
depravity prevailing in this king’s reign.
He was assassinated (2 Kings 21:18-26: 2 Chr. 33:20-25) by his
own servants, who conspired against him.
(3.) An Egyptian god, usually depicted with a human body and
the head of a ram, referred to in <scripRef passage="Jer. 46:25" id="a-p405.1" parsed="|Jer|46|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.46.25">Jer. 46:25</scripRef>, where the word
“multitudes” in the Authorized Version is more appropriately
rendered “Amon” in the Revised Version. In <scripRef passage="Nah. 3:8" id="a-p405.2" parsed="|Nah|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Nah.3.8">Nah. 3:8</scripRef> the
expression “populous No” of the Authorized version is rendered
in the Revised Version “No-amon.” Amon is identified with Ra,
the sun-god of Heliopolis.
(4.) Neh. 7:59.
</def>
<term id="a-p406.2">Amorites</term>
Highlanders, or hillmen, the name given to the descendants of
one of the sons of Canaan (<scripRef passage="Gen. 14:7" id="a-p407.1" parsed="|Gen|14|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.7">Gen. 14:7</scripRef>), called Amurra or Amurri
in the Assyrian and Egyptian inscriptions. On the early
Babylonian monuments all Syria, including Palestine, is known as
“the land of the Amorites.” The southern slopes of the mountains

of Judea are called the “mount of the Amorites” (<scripRef passage="Deut. 1:7" id="a-p407.2" parsed="|Deut|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.1.7">Deut. 1:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut 1:19" id="a-p407.3" parsed="|Deut|1|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.1.19">19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut 1:20" id="a-p407.4" parsed="|Deut|1|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.1.20">20</scripRef>). They seem to have originally occupied the land stretching
from the heights west of the Dead Sea (<scripRef passage="Gen. 14:7" id="a-p407.5" parsed="|Gen|14|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.7">Gen. 14:7</scripRef>) to Hebron (13.

Comp. 13:8; <scripRef passage="Deut. 3:8" id="a-p407.6" parsed="|Deut|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.8">Deut. 3:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut 4:46-48" id="a-p407.7" parsed="|Deut|4|46|4|48" osisRef="Bible:Deut.4.46-Deut.4.48">4:46-48</scripRef>), embracing “all Gilead and all
Bashan” (<scripRef passage="Deut. 3:10" id="a-p407.8" parsed="|Deut|3|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.10">Deut. 3:10</scripRef>), with the Jordan valley on the east of the
river (4:49), the land of the “two kings of the Amorites,” Sihon

and Og (<scripRef passage="Deut. 31:4" id="a-p407.9" parsed="|Deut|31|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.31.4">Deut. 31:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 2:10" id="a-p407.10" parsed="|Josh|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.2.10">Josh. 2:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 9:10" id="a-p407.11" parsed="|Josh|9|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.9.10">9:10</scripRef>). The five kings of the
Amorites were defeated with great slaughter by Joshua (10:10).
They were again defeated at the waters of Merom by Joshua, who
smote them till there were none remaining (<scripRef passage="Josh. 11:8" id="a-p407.12" parsed="|Josh|11|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.8">Josh. 11:8</scripRef>). It is
mentioned as a surprising circumstance that in the days of

Samuel there was peace between them and the Israelites (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 7:14" id="a-p407.13" parsed="|1Sam|7|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.7.14">1 Sam. 7:14</scripRef>). The discrepancy supposed to exist between <scripRef passage="Deut. 1:44" id="a-p407.14" parsed="|Deut|1|44|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.1.44">Deut. 1:44</scripRef> and
<scripRef passage="Num. 14:45" id="a-p407.15" parsed="|Num|14|45|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.14.45">Num. 14:45</scripRef> is explained by the circumstance that the terms
“Amorites” and “Amalekites” are used synonymously for the
“Canaanites.” In the same way we explain the fact that the

“Hivites” of <scripRef passage="Gen. 34:2" id="a-p407.16" parsed="|Gen|34|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.34.2">Gen. 34:2</scripRef> are the “Amorites” of 48:22. Comp. <scripRef passage="Josh. 10:6" id="a-p407.17" parsed="|Josh|10|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.6">Josh. 10:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 11:19" id="a-p407.18" parsed="|Josh|11|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.19">11:19</scripRef> with <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:2" id="a-p407.19" parsed="|2Sam|21|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.2">2 Sam. 21:2</scripRef>; also <scripRef passage="Num. 14:45" id="a-p407.20" parsed="|Num|14|45|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.14.45">Num. 14:45</scripRef> with <scripRef passage="Deut. 1:44" id="a-p407.21" parsed="|Deut|1|44|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.1.44">Deut. 1:44</scripRef>.
The Amorites were warlike mountaineers. They are represented on
the Egyptian monuments with fair skins, light hair, blue eyes,
aquiline noses, and pointed beards. They are supposed to have
been men of great stature; their king, Og, is described by Moses
as the last “of the remnant of the giants” (<scripRef passage="Deut. 3:11" id="a-p407.22" parsed="|Deut|3|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.11">Deut. 3:11</scripRef>). Both
Sihon and Og were independent kings. Only one word of the
Amorite language survives, “Shenir,” the name they gave to Mount
Hermon (Deut. 3:9).
</def>
<term id="a-p407.24">Amos</term>
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=Amos" id="a-p407.26" />
Borne; a burden, one of the twelve minor prophets. He was a
native of Tekota, the modern Tekua, a town about 12 miles
south-east of Bethlehem. He was a man of humble birth, neither a
“prophet nor a prophet’s son,” but “an herdman and a dresser of
sycomore trees,” R.V. He prophesied in the days of Uzziah, king
of Judah, and was contemporary with Isaiah and Hosea (<scripRef passage="Amos 1:1" id="a-p408.1" parsed="|Amos|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.1.1">Amos 1:1</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Amos 7:14" id="a-p408.2" parsed="|Amos|7|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.7.14">7:14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Amos 7:15" id="a-p408.3" parsed="|Amos|7|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.7.15">15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 14:5" id="a-p408.4" parsed="|Zech|14|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.14.5">Zech. 14:5</scripRef>), who survived him a few years. Under
Jeroboam II. the kingdom of Israel rose to the zenith of its
prosperity; but that was followed by the prevalence of luxury
and vice and idolatry. At this period Amos was called from his
obscurity to remind the people of the law of God’s retributive
justice, and to call them to repentance.
The Book of Amos consists of three parts:
(1.) The nations around are summoned to judgment because of
their sins (1:1-2:3). He quotes Joel 3:16.
(2.) The spiritual condition of Judah, and especially of
Israel, is described (2:4-6:14).
(3.) In 7:1-9:10 are recorded five prophetic visions. (a) The
first two (7:1-6) refer to judgments against the guilty people.
(b) The next two (7:7-9; 8:1-3) point out the ripeness of the
people for the threatened judgements. 7:10-17 consists of a
conversation between the prophet and the priest of Bethel. (c)
The fifth describes the overthrow and ruin of Israel (9:1-10);
to which is added the promise of the restoration of the kingdom
and its final glory in the Messiah’s kingdom.
The style is peculiar in the number of the allusions made to
natural objects and to agricultural occupations. Other allusions
show also that Amos was a student of the law as well as a “child
of nature.” These phrases are peculiar to him: “Cleanness of
teeth” [i.e., want of bread] (4:6); “The excellency of Jacob”
(6:8; 8:7); “The high places of Isaac” (7:9); “The house of
Isaac” (7:16); “He that createth the wind” (4:13). Quoted, Acts 7:42.
</def>
<term id="a-p413.2">Amoz</term>
Strong, the father of the prophet Isaiah (2 Kings 19:2, 20;

20:1; <scripRef passage="Isa. 1:1" id="a-p414.3" parsed="|Isa|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.1">Isa. 1:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 2:1" id="a-p414.4" parsed="|Isa|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.2.1">2:1</scripRef>). As to his personal history little is
positively known. He is supposed by some to have been the “man
of God” spoken of in 2 Chr. 25:7, 8.
</def>
<term id="a-p414.7">Amphipolis</term>
City on both sides, a Macedonian city, a great Roman military
station, through which Paul and Silas passed on their way from
Philippi to Thessalonica, a distance of 33 Roman miles from
Philippi (Acts 17:1).
</def>
<term id="a-p415.2">Amplias</term>
A Roman Christian saluted by Paul (Rom. 16:8).
</def>
<term id="a-p416.2">Amram</term>
Kindred of the High; i.e., “friend of Jehovah.” (1.) The son of
Kohath, the son of Levi. He married Jochebed, “his father’s

sister,” and was the father of Aaron, Miriam, and Moses (<scripRef passage="Ex. 6:18" id="a-p417.1" parsed="|Exod|6|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.6.18">Ex. 6:18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex 6:20" id="a-p417.2" parsed="|Exod|6|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.6.20">20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 3:19" id="a-p417.3" parsed="|Num|3|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.3.19">Num. 3:19</scripRef>). He died in Egypt at the age of 137 years
(Ex. 6:20). His descendants were called Amramites (Num. 3:27; 1 Chr. 26:23). (2.) Ezra 10:34.
</def>
<term id="a-p417.8">Amraphel</term>
King of Shinar, southern Chaldea, one of the confederates of
Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, in a war against Sodom and cities of

the plain (<scripRef passage="Gen. 14:1" id="a-p418.1" parsed="|Gen|14|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.1">Gen. 14:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 14:4" id="a-p418.2" parsed="|Gen|14|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.4">4</scripRef>). It is now found that Amraphel (or
Ammirapaltu) is the Khammu-rabi whose name appears on
recently-discovered monuments. (See CHEDORLAOMER).
After defeating Arioch (q.v.) he united Babylonia under one
rule, and made Babylon his capital.
</def>
<term id="a-p418.4">Anab</term>
Grape-town, one of the cities in the mountains of Judah, from

which Joshua expelled the Anakim (<scripRef passage="Josh. 11:21" id="a-p419.1" parsed="|Josh|11|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.21">Josh. 11:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 15:50" id="a-p419.2" parsed="|Josh|15|50|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.50">15:50</scripRef>). It still
retains its ancient name. It lies among the hills, 10 miles
south-south-west of Hebron.
</def>
<term id="a-p419.3">Anah</term>
Speech. (1.) One of the sons of Seir, and head of an Idumean
tribe, called a Horite, as in course of time all the branches of
this tribe were called from their dwelling in caves in Mount
Seir (Gen. 36:20, 29; 1 Chr. 1:38).
(2.) One of the two sons of Zibeon the Horite, and father of
Esau’s wife Aholibamah (Gen. 36:18, 24).
</def>
<term id="a-p421.3">Anak</term>
Long-necked, the son of Arba, father of the Anakim (Josh. 15:13;
21:11, Heb. Anok).
</def>
<term id="a-p422.3">Anakim</term>
The descendants of Anak (Josh. 11:21; Num. 13:33; Deut. 9:2).
They dwelt in the south of Palestine, in the neighbourhood of

Hebron (<scripRef passage="Gen. 23:2" id="a-p423.4" parsed="|Gen|23|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.23.2">Gen. 23:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 15:13" id="a-p423.5" parsed="|Josh|15|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.13">Josh. 15:13</scripRef>). In the days of Abraham (<scripRef passage="Gen. 14:5" id="a-p423.6" parsed="|Gen|14|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.5">Gen. 14:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 14:6" id="a-p423.7" parsed="|Gen|14|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.6">6</scripRef>) they inhabited the region afterwards known as Edom and
Moab, east of the Jordan. They were probably a remnant of the
original inhabitants of Palestine before the Canaanites, a
Cushite tribe from Babel, and of the same race as the
Phoenicians and the Egyptian shepherd kings. Their formidable
warlike appearance, as described by the spies sent to search the
land, filled the Israelites with terror. They seem to have

identified them with the Nephilim, the “giants” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 6:4" id="a-p423.8" parsed="|Gen|6|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.6.4">Gen. 6:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 13:33" id="a-p423.9" parsed="|Num|13|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.13.33">Num. 13:33</scripRef>) of the antediluvian age. There were various tribes of
Anakim (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:14" id="a-p423.10" parsed="|Josh|15|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.14">Josh. 15:14</scripRef>). Joshua finally expelled them from the
land, except a remnant that found a refuge in the cities of
Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod (<scripRef passage="Josh. 11:22" id="a-p423.11" parsed="|Josh|11|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.22">Josh. 11:22</scripRef>). The Philistine giants whom
David encountered (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:15-22" id="a-p423.12" parsed="|2Sam|21|15|21|22" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.15-2Sam.21.22">2 Sam. 21:15-22</scripRef>) were descendants of the
Anakim. (See GIANTS.)
</def>
<term id="a-p423.14">Anamim</term>
The name of an Egyptian tribe descended from Mizraim (Gen. 10:13; 1 Chr. 1:11).
</def>
<term id="a-p424.3">Anammelech</term>
One of the gods worshipped by the people of Sepharvaim, who
colonized Samaria (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:31" id="a-p425.1" parsed="|2Kgs|17|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.31">2 Kings 17:31</scripRef>). The name means “Anu is king.”
It was a female deity representing the moon, as Adrammelech
(q.v.) was the male representing the sun.
</def>
<term id="a-p425.2">Anan</term>
Cloud, one of the Israelites who sealed the covenant after the
return from Babylon (Neh. 10:26).
</def>
<term id="a-p426.2">Ananiah</term>
Protected by Jehovah, the name of a town in the tribe of
Benjamin between Nob and Hazor (<scripRef passage="Neh. 11:32" id="a-p427.1" parsed="|Neh|11|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.11.32">Neh. 11:32</scripRef>). It is probably the
modern Beit Hanina, a small village 3 miles north of Jerusalem.
</def>
<term id="a-p427.2">Ananias</term>
A common Jewish name, the same as Hananiah. (1.) One of the
members of the church at Jerusalem, who conspired with his wife
Sapphira to deceive the brethren, and who fell down and

immediately expired after he had uttered the falsehood (<scripRef passage="Acts 5:5" id="a-p428.1" parsed="|Acts|5|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.5.5">Acts 5:5</scripRef>). By common agreement the members of the early Christian
community devoted their property to the work of furthering the
gospel and of assisting the poor and needy. The proceeds of the
possessions they sold were placed at the disposal of the

apostles (<scripRef passage="Acts 4:36" id="a-p428.2" parsed="|Acts|4|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.4.36">Acts 4:36</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 4:37" id="a-p428.3" parsed="|Acts|4|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.4.37">37</scripRef>). Ananias might have kept his property
had he so chosen; but he professed agreement with the brethren
in the common purpose, and had of his own accord devoted it all,
as he said, to these sacred ends. Yet he retained a part of it
for his own ends, and thus lied in declaring that he had given
it all. “The offence of Ananias and Sapphira showed contempt of
God, vanity and ambition in the offenders, and utter disregard
of the corruption which they were bringing into the society.
Such sin, committed in despite of the light which they
possessed, called for a special mark of divine indignation.”
(2.) A Christian at Damascus (Acts 9:10). He became Paul’s
instructor; but when or by what means he himself became a
Christian we have no information. He was “a devout man according
to the law, having a good report of all the Jews which dwelt” at
Damascus (22:12).
(3.) The high priest before whom Paul was brought in the

procuratorship of Felix (<scripRef passage="Acts 23:2" id="a-p430.1" parsed="|Acts|23|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.23.2">Acts 23:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 23:5" id="a-p430.2" parsed="|Acts|23|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.23.5">5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 23:24" id="a-p430.3" parsed="|Acts|23|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.23.24">24</scripRef>). He was so enraged at
Paul’s noble declaration, “I have lived in all good conscience
before God until this day,” that he commanded one of his
attendants to smite him on the mouth. Smarting under this
unprovoked insult, Paul quickly replied, “God shall smite thee,
thou whited wall.” Being reminded that Ananias was the high
priest, to whose office all respect was to be paid, he answered,
“I wist not, brethren, that he was the high priest” (<scripRef passage="Acts 23:5" id="a-p430.4" parsed="|Acts|23|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.23.5">Acts 23:5</scripRef>).
This expression has occasioned some difficulty, as it is
scarcely probable that Paul should have been ignorant of so
public a fact. The expression may mean (a) that Paul had at the
moment overlooked the honour due to the high priest; or (b), as
others think, that Paul spoke ironically, as if he had said,
“The high priest breaking the law! God’s high priest a tyrant
and a lawbreaker! I see a man in white robes, and have heard his
voice, but surely it cannot, it ought not to be, the voice of
the high priest.” (See Dr. Lindsay on Acts, in loco.) (c)
Others think that from defect of sight Paul could not observe
that the speaker was the high priest. In all this, however, it
may be explained, Paul, with all his excellency, comes short of
the example of his divine Master, who, when he was reviled,
reviled not again.
</def>
<term id="a-p430.5">Anath</term>
An answer; i.e., to “prayer”, the father of Shamgar, who was one
of the judges of Israel (Judg. 3:31).
</def>
<term id="a-p431.2">Anathema</term>
Anything laid up or suspended; hence anything laid up in a
temple or set apart as sacred. In this sense the form of the
word is anath(ee)ma, once in plural used in the Greek New
Testament, in <scripRef passage="Luke 21:5" id="a-p432.1" parsed="|Luke|21|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.21.5">Luke 21:5</scripRef>, where it is rendered “gifts.” In the
LXX. the form anathema is generally used as the rendering of
the Hebrew word herem, derived from a verb which means (1) to
consecrate or devote; and (2) to exterminate. Any object so

devoted to the Lord could not be redeemed (<scripRef passage="Num. 18:14" id="a-p432.2" parsed="|Num|18|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.18.14">Num. 18:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 27:28" id="a-p432.3" parsed="|Lev|27|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.27.28">Lev. 27:28</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev 27:29" id="a-p432.4" parsed="|Lev|27|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.27.29">29</scripRef>); and hence the idea of exterminating connected with
the word. The Hebrew verb (haram) is frequently used of the
extermination of idolatrous nations. It had a wide range of
application. The anathema_ or _herem was a person or thing

irrevocably devoted to God (<scripRef passage="Lev. 27:21" id="a-p432.5" parsed="|Lev|27|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.27.21">Lev. 27:21</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 27:28" id="a-p432.6" parsed="|Lev|27|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.27.28">28</scripRef>); and “none devoted
shall be ransomed. He shall surely be put to death” (27:29). The

word therefore carried the idea of devoted to destruction (<scripRef passage="Num. 21:2" id="a-p432.7" parsed="|Num|21|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.21.2">Num. 21:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num 21:3" id="a-p432.8" parsed="|Num|21|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.21.3">3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 6:17" id="a-p432.9" parsed="|Josh|6|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.6.17">Josh. 6:17</scripRef>); and hence generally it meant a thing
accursed. In Deut. 7:26 an idol is called a herem =
anathema, a thing accursed.
In the New Testament this word always implies execration. In
some cases an individual denounces an anathema on himself unless

certain conditions are fulfilled (<scripRef passage="Acts 23:12" id="a-p433.1" parsed="|Acts|23|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.23.12">Acts 23:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 23:14" id="a-p433.2" parsed="|Acts|23|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.23.14">14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 23:21" id="a-p433.3" parsed="|Acts|23|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.23.21">21</scripRef>). “To call
Jesus accursed” [anathema] (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 12:3" id="a-p433.4" parsed="|1Cor|12|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.12.3">1 Cor. 12:3</scripRef>) is to pronounce him
execrated or accursed. If any one preached another gospel, the

apostle says, “let him be accursed” (<scripRef passage="Gal. 1:8" id="a-p433.5" parsed="|Gal|1|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.1.8">Gal. 1:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gal. 1:9" id="a-p433.6" parsed="|Gal|1|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.1.9">9</scripRef>); i.e., let his
conduct in so doing be accounted accursed.
In Rom. 9:3, the expression “accursed” (anathema) from Christ,
i.e., excluded from fellowship or alliance with Christ, has
occasioned much difficulty. The apostle here does not speak of
his wish as a possible thing. It is simply a vehement expression
of feeling, showing how strong was his desire for the salvation
of his people.
The anathema in 1 Cor. 16:22 denotes simply that they who love
not the Lord are rightly objects of loathing and execration to
all holy beings; they are guilty of a crime that merits the
severest condemnation; they are exposed to the just sentence of
“everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord.”
</def>
<term id="a-p435.2">Anathoth</term>
The name of one of the cities of refuge, in the tribe of
Benjamin (<scripRef passage="Josh. 21:18" id="a-p436.1" parsed="|Josh|21|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.21.18">Josh. 21:18</scripRef>). The Jews, as a rule, did not change the
names of the towns they found in Palestine; hence this town may
be regarded as deriving its name from the goddess Anat. It was

the native place of Abiezer, one of David’s “thirty” (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 23:27" id="a-p436.2" parsed="|2Sam|23|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.23.27">2 Sam. 23:27</scripRef>), and of Jehu, another of his mighty men (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 12:3" id="a-p436.3" parsed="|1Chr|12|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.12.3">1 Chr. 12:3</scripRef>). It
is chiefly notable, however, as the birth-place and usual

residence of Jeremiah (<scripRef passage="Jer. 1:1" id="a-p436.4" parsed="|Jer|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.1.1">Jer. 1:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 11:21-23" id="a-p436.5" parsed="|Jer|11|21|11|23" osisRef="Bible:Jer.11.21-Jer.11.23">11:21-23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 29:27" id="a-p436.6" parsed="|Jer|29|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.29.27">29:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 32:7-9" id="a-p436.7" parsed="|Jer|32|7|32|9" osisRef="Bible:Jer.32.7-Jer.32.9">32:7-9</scripRef>). It
suffered greatly from the army of Sennacherib, and only 128 men

returned to it from the Exile (<scripRef passage="Neh. 7:27" id="a-p436.8" parsed="|Neh|7|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.7.27">Neh. 7:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezra 2:23" id="a-p436.9" parsed="|Ezra|2|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2.23">Ezra 2:23</scripRef>). It lay
about 3 miles north of Jerusalem. It has been identified with
the small and poor village of ‘Anata, containing about 100
inhabitants.
</def>
<term id="a-p436.10">Anchor</term>
From Acts 27:29, 30, 40, it would appear that the Roman vessels
carried several anchors, which were attached to the stern as
well as to the prow. The Roman anchor, like the modern one, had
two teeth or flukes. In <scripRef passage="Heb. 6:19" id="a-p437.4" parsed="|Heb|6|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.6.19">Heb. 6:19</scripRef> the word is used
metaphorically for that which supports or keeps one steadfast in
the time of trial or of doubt. It is an emblem of hope.
“If you fear,
Put all your trust in God: that anchor holds.”
</def>
<term id="a-p438.1">Ancient of Days</term>
An expression applied to Jehovah three times in the vision of
Daniel (7:9, 13, 22) in the sense of eternal. In contrast with
all earthly kings, his days are past reckoning.
</def>
<term id="a-p439.1">Andrew</term>
Manliness, a Greek name; one of the apostles of our Lord. He was
of Bethsaida in Galilee (<scripRef passage="John 1:44" id="a-p440.1" parsed="|John|1|44|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.1.44">John 1:44</scripRef>), and was the brother of

Simon Peter (<scripRef passage="Matt. 4:18" id="a-p440.2" parsed="|Matt|4|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.4.18">Matt. 4:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 10:2" id="a-p440.3" parsed="|Matt|10|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.10.2">10:2</scripRef>). On one occasion John the
