Baptist, whose disciple he then was, pointing to Jesus, said,
“Behold the Lamb of God” (<scripRef passage="John 1:40" id="a-p440.4" parsed="|John|1|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.1.40">John 1:40</scripRef>); and Andrew, hearing him,
immediately became a follower of Jesus, the first of his
disciples. After he had been led to recognize Jesus as the
Messiah, his first care was to bring also his brother Simon to
Jesus. The two brothers seem to have after this pursued for a
while their usual calling as fishermen, and did not become the
stated attendants of the Lord till after John’s imprisonment

(<scripRef passage="Matt. 4:18" id="a-p440.5" parsed="|Matt|4|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.4.18">Matt. 4:18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 4:19" id="a-p440.6" parsed="|Matt|4|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.4.19">19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 1:16" id="a-p440.7" parsed="|Mark|1|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.16">Mark 1:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Mark 1:17" id="a-p440.8" parsed="|Mark|1|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.17">17</scripRef>). Very little is related of
Andrew. He was one of the confidential disciples (<scripRef passage="John 6:8" id="a-p440.9" parsed="|John|6|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.6.8">John 6:8</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="John 12:22" id="a-p440.10" parsed="|John|12|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.12.22">12:22</scripRef>), and with Peter, James, and John inquired of our Lord
privately regarding his future coming (<scripRef passage="Mark 13:3" id="a-p440.11" parsed="|Mark|13|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.13.3">Mark 13:3</scripRef>). He was
present at the feeding of the five thousand (<scripRef passage="John 6:9" id="a-p440.12" parsed="|John|6|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.6.9">John 6:9</scripRef>), and he
introduced the Greeks who desired to see Jesus (<scripRef passage="John 12:22" id="a-p440.13" parsed="|John|12|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.12.22">John 12:22</scripRef>); but
of his subsequent history little is known. It is noteworthy that
Andrew thrice brings others to Christ, (1) Peter; (2) the lad
with the loaves; and (3) certain Greeks. These incidents may be
regarded as a key to his character.
</def>
<term id="a-p440.14">Andronicus</term>
Man-conquering, a Jewish Christian, the kinsman and
fellowprisoner of Paul (<scripRef passage="Rom. 16:7" id="a-p441.1" parsed="|Rom|16|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.16.7">Rom. 16:7</scripRef>); “of note among the
apostles.”
</def>
<term id="a-p441.2">Anem</term>
Two fountains, a Levitical city in the tribe of Issachar (1 Chr. 6:73). It is also called En-gannim (q.v.) in Josh. 19:21; the
modern Jenin.
</def>
<term id="a-p442.3">Aner</term>
A boy. (1.) A Canaanitish chief who joined his forces with those
of Abraham in pursuit of Chedorlaomer (Gen. 14:13, 24).
(2.) A city of Manasseh given to the Levites of Kohath’s
family (1 Chr. 6:70).
</def>
<term id="a-p444.2">Angel</term>
A word signifying, both in the Hebrew and Greek, a “messenger,”
and hence employed to denote any agent God sends forth to

execute his purposes. It is used of an ordinary messenger (<scripRef passage="Job 1:14" id="a-p445.1" parsed="|Job|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.1.14">Job 1:14</scripRef>: <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 11:3" id="a-p445.2" parsed="|1Sam|11|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.11.3">1 Sam. 11:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 7:24" id="a-p445.3" parsed="|Luke|7|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.7.24">Luke 7:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 9:52" id="a-p445.4" parsed="|Luke|9|52|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.9.52">9:52</scripRef>), of prophets (<scripRef passage="Isa. 42:19" id="a-p445.5" parsed="|Isa|42|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.42.19">Isa. 42:19</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Hag. 1:13" id="a-p445.6" parsed="|Hag|1|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hag.1.13">Hag. 1:13</scripRef>), of priests (<scripRef passage="Mal. 2:7" id="a-p445.7" parsed="|Mal|2|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mal.2.7">Mal. 2:7</scripRef>), and ministers of the New
Testament (Rev. 1:20).
It is also applied to such impersonal agents as the pestilence
(2 Sam. 24:16, 17; 2 Kings 19:35), the wind (Ps. 104:4).
But its distinctive application is to certain heavenly
intelligences whom God employs in carrying on his government of
the world. The name does not denote their nature but their

office as messengers. The appearances to Abraham at Mamre (<scripRef passage="Gen. 18:2" id="a-p447.1" parsed="|Gen|18|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.18.2">Gen. 18:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 18:22" id="a-p447.2" parsed="|Gen|18|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.18.22">22</scripRef>. Comp. 19:1), to Jacob at Peniel (<scripRef passage="Gen. 32:24" id="a-p447.3" parsed="|Gen|32|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.32.24">Gen. 32:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 32:30" id="a-p447.4" parsed="|Gen|32|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.32.30">30</scripRef>), to

Joshua at Gilgal (<scripRef passage="Josh. 5:13" id="a-p447.5" parsed="|Josh|5|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.5.13">Josh. 5:13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 5:15" id="a-p447.6" parsed="|Josh|5|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.5.15">15</scripRef>), of the Angel of the Lord,
were doubtless manifestations of the Divine presence,
“foreshadowings of the incarnation,” revelations before the
“fulness of the time” of the Son of God.
(1.) The existence and orders of angelic beings can only be
discovered from the Scriptures. Although the Bible does not
treat of this subject specially, yet there are numerous
incidental details that furnish us with ample information. Their
personal existence is plainly implied in such passages as Gen. 16:7, 10, 11; Judg. 13:1-21; Matt. 28:2-5; Heb. 1:4, etc.
These superior beings are very numerous. “Thousand thousands,”

etc. (<scripRef passage="Dan. 7:10" id="a-p449.1" parsed="|Dan|7|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.7.10">Dan. 7:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 26:53" id="a-p449.2" parsed="|Matt|26|53|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.53">Matt. 26:53</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 2:13" id="a-p449.3" parsed="|Luke|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.13">Luke 2:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 12:22" id="a-p449.4" parsed="|Heb|12|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.12.22">Heb. 12:22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Heb. 12:23" id="a-p449.5" parsed="|Heb|12|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.12.23">23</scripRef>). They
are also spoken of as of different ranks in dignity and power
(Zech. 1:9, 11; Dan. 10:13; 12:1; 1 Thess. 4:16; Jude 1:9; Eph. 1:21; Col. 1:16).
(2.) As to their nature, they are spirits (Heb. 1:14), like
the soul of man, but not incorporeal. Such expressions as “like
the angels” (<scripRef passage="Luke 20:36" id="a-p450.2" parsed="|Luke|20|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.20.36">Luke 20:36</scripRef>), and the fact that whenever angels

appeared to man it was always in a human form (<scripRef passage="Gen. 18:2" id="a-p450.3" parsed="|Gen|18|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.18.2">Gen. 18:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 19:1" id="a-p450.4" parsed="|Gen|19|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.19.1">19:1</scripRef>,

<scripRef passage="Gen 19:10" id="a-p450.5" parsed="|Gen|19|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.19.10">10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 24:4" id="a-p450.6" parsed="|Luke|24|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.24.4">Luke 24:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 1:10" id="a-p450.7" parsed="|Acts|1|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.10">Acts 1:10</scripRef>), and the titles that are applied to

them (“sons of God,” <scripRef passage="Job 1:6" id="a-p450.8" parsed="|Job|1|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.1.6">Job 1:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 38:7" id="a-p450.9" parsed="|Job|38|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.38.7">38:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Dan. 3:25" id="a-p450.10" parsed="|Dan|3|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.3.25">Dan. 3:25</scripRef>; comp. 28) and to
men (<scripRef passage="Luke 3:38" id="a-p450.11" parsed="|Luke|3|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.38">Luke 3:38</scripRef>), seem all to indicate some resemblance between
them and the human race. Imperfection is ascribed to them as

creatures (<scripRef passage="Job 4:18" id="a-p450.12" parsed="|Job|4|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.4.18">Job 4:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 24:36" id="a-p450.13" parsed="|Matt|24|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.24.36">Matt. 24:36</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Pet. 1:12" id="a-p450.14" parsed="|1Pet|1|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.1.12">1 Pet. 1:12</scripRef>). As finite
creatures they may fall under temptation; and accordingly we
read of “fallen angels.” Of the cause and manner of their “fall”
we are wholly ignorant. We know only that “they left their first

estate” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 25:41" id="a-p450.15" parsed="|Matt|25|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.25.41">Matt. 25:41</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 12:7" id="a-p450.16" parsed="|Rev|12|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.12.7">Rev. 12:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Rev. 12:9" id="a-p450.17" parsed="|Rev|12|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.12.9">9</scripRef>), and that they are “reserved
unto judgement” (2 Pet. 2:4). When the manna is called “angels’
food,” this is merely to denote its excellence (<scripRef passage="Ps. 78:25" id="a-p450.18" parsed="|Ps|78|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.78.25">Ps. 78:25</scripRef>).
Angels never die (<scripRef passage="Luke 20:36" id="a-p450.19" parsed="|Luke|20|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.20.36">Luke 20:36</scripRef>). They are possessed of superhuman

intelligence and power (<scripRef passage="Mark 13:32" id="a-p450.20" parsed="|Mark|13|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.13.32">Mark 13:32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Thess. 1:7" id="a-p450.21" parsed="|2Thess|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Thess.1.7">2 Thess. 1:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 103:20" id="a-p450.22" parsed="|Ps|103|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.103.20">Ps. 103:20</scripRef>).

They are called “holy” (<scripRef passage="Luke 9:26" id="a-p450.23" parsed="|Luke|9|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.9.26">Luke 9:26</scripRef>), “elect” (<scripRef passage="1 Tim. 5:21" id="a-p450.24" parsed="|1Tim|5|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.5.21">1 Tim. 5:21</scripRef>). The
redeemed in glory are “like unto the angels” (<scripRef passage="Luke 20:36" id="a-p450.25" parsed="|Luke|20|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.20.36">Luke 20:36</scripRef>). They
are not to be worshipped (Col. 2:18; Rev. 19:10).
(3.) Their functions are manifold. (a) In the widest sense

they are agents of God’s providence (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:23" id="a-p451.1" parsed="|Exod|12|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.23">Ex. 12:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 104:4" id="a-p451.2" parsed="|Ps|104|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.104.4">Ps. 104:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 11:28" id="a-p451.3" parsed="|Heb|11|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.11.28">Heb. 11:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 10:10" id="a-p451.4" parsed="|1Cor|10|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.10.10">1 Cor. 10:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 24:16" id="a-p451.5" parsed="|2Sam|24|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.24.16">2 Sam. 24:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 21:16" id="a-p451.6" parsed="|1Chr|21|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.21.16">1 Chr. 21:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 19:35" id="a-p451.7" parsed="|2Kgs|19|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.19.35">2 Kings 19:35</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Acts 12:23" id="a-p451.8" parsed="|Acts|12|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.12.23">Acts 12:23</scripRef>). (b) They are specially God’s agents in carrying on
his great work of redemption. There is no notice of angelic
appearances to man till after the call of Abraham. From that
time onward there are frequent references to their ministry on

earth (<scripRef passage="Gen. 18" id="a-p451.9" parsed="|Gen|18|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.18">Gen. 18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 19" id="a-p451.10" parsed="|Gen|19|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.19">19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 24:7" id="a-p451.11" parsed="|Gen|24|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.7">24:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 24:40" id="a-p451.12" parsed="|Gen|24|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.40">40</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 28:12" id="a-p451.13" parsed="|Gen|28|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.28.12">28:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 32:1" id="a-p451.14" parsed="|Gen|32|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.32.1">32:1</scripRef>). They appear to

rebuke idolatry (<scripRef passage="Judg. 2:1-4" id="a-p451.15" parsed="|Judg|2|1|2|4" osisRef="Bible:Judg.2.1-Judg.2.4">Judg. 2:1-4</scripRef>), to call Gideon (<scripRef passage="Judg. 6:11" id="a-p451.16" parsed="|Judg|6|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.6.11">Judg. 6:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Judg. 6:12" id="a-p451.17" parsed="|Judg|6|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.6.12">12</scripRef>),
and to consecrate Samson (13:3). In the days of the prophets,

from Samuel downward, the angels appear only in their behalf (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 19:5" id="a-p451.18" parsed="|1Kgs|19|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.19.5">1 Kings 19:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 6:17" id="a-p451.19" parsed="|2Kgs|6|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.6.17">2 Kings 6:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 1" id="a-p451.20" parsed="|Zech|1|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.1">Zech. 1</scripRef>-6; <scripRef passage="Dan. 4:13" id="a-p451.21" parsed="|Dan|4|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.4.13">Dan. 4:13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan. 4:23" id="a-p451.22" parsed="|Dan|4|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.4.23">23</scripRef>; 10:10, 13,
The Incarnation introduces a new era in the ministrations of
angels. They come with their Lord to earth to do him service

while here. They predict his advent (<scripRef passage="Matt. 1:20" id="a-p452.1" parsed="|Matt|1|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.1.20">Matt. 1:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 1:26-38" id="a-p452.2" parsed="|Luke|1|26|1|38" osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.26-Luke.1.38">Luke 1:26-38</scripRef>),

minister to him after his temptation and agony (<scripRef passage="Matt. 4:11" id="a-p452.3" parsed="|Matt|4|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.4.11">Matt. 4:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 22:43" id="a-p452.4" parsed="|Luke|22|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.22.43">Luke 22:43</scripRef>), and declare his resurrection and ascension (<scripRef passage="Matt. 28:2-8" id="a-p452.5" parsed="|Matt|28|2|28|8" osisRef="Bible:Matt.28.2-Matt.28.8">Matt. 28:2-8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 20:12" id="a-p452.6" parsed="|John|20|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.20.12">John 20:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="John 20:13" id="a-p452.7" parsed="|John|20|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.20.13">13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 1:10" id="a-p452.8" parsed="|Acts|1|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.10">Acts 1:10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 1:11" id="a-p452.9" parsed="|Acts|1|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.11">11</scripRef>). They are now ministering

spirits to the people of God (<scripRef passage="Heb. 1:14" id="a-p452.10" parsed="|Heb|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.1.14">Heb. 1:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 34:7" id="a-p452.11" parsed="|Ps|34|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.34.7">Ps. 34:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 91:11" id="a-p452.12" parsed="|Ps|91|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.91.11">91:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 18:10" id="a-p452.13" parsed="|Matt|18|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.18.10">Matt. 18:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 5:19" id="a-p452.14" parsed="|Acts|5|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.5.19">Acts 5:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 8:26" id="a-p452.15" parsed="|Acts|8|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.8.26">8:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 10:3" id="a-p452.16" parsed="|Acts|10|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.10.3">10:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 12:7" id="a-p452.17" parsed="|Acts|12|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.12.7">12:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 27:23" id="a-p452.18" parsed="|Acts|27|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.27.23">27:23</scripRef>). They rejoice over a
penitent sinner (<scripRef passage="Luke 15:10" id="a-p452.19" parsed="|Luke|15|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.15.10">Luke 15:10</scripRef>). They bear the souls of the
redeemed to paradise (<scripRef passage="Luke 16:22" id="a-p452.20" parsed="|Luke|16|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.16.22">Luke 16:22</scripRef>); and they will be the

ministers of judgement hereafter on the great day (<scripRef passage="Matt. 13:39" id="a-p452.21" parsed="|Matt|13|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.13.39">Matt. 13:39</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt 13:41" id="a-p452.22" parsed="|Matt|13|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.13.41">41</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt 13:49" id="a-p452.23" parsed="|Matt|13|49|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.13.49">49</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 16:27" id="a-p452.24" parsed="|Matt|16|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.16.27">16:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 24:31" id="a-p452.25" parsed="|Matt|24|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.24.31">24:31</scripRef>). The passages (<scripRef passage="Ps. 34:7" id="a-p452.26" parsed="|Ps|34|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.34.7">Ps. 34:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 18:10" id="a-p452.27" parsed="|Matt|18|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.18.10">Matt. 18:10</scripRef>)
usually referred to in support of the idea that every individual
has a particular guardian angel have no such meaning. They
merely indicate that God employs the ministry of angels to
deliver his people from affliction and danger, and that the
angels do not think it below their dignity to minister even to
children and to the least among Christ’s disciples.
The “angel of his presence” (Isa. 63:9. Comp. Ex. 23:20, 21;
32:34; 33:2; <scripRef passage="Num. 20:16" id="a-p453.4" parsed="|Num|20|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.20.16">Num. 20:16</scripRef>) is probably rightly interpreted of the
Messiah as the guide of his people. Others have supposed the
expression to refer to Gabriel (Luke 1:19).
</def>
<term id="a-p453.6">Anger</term>
The emotion of instant displeasure on account of something evil
that presents itself to our view. In itself it is an original
susceptibility of our nature, just as love is, and is not
necessarily sinful. It may, however, become sinful when

causeless, or excessive, or protracted (<scripRef passage="Matt. 5:22" id="a-p454.1" parsed="|Matt|5|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.22">Matt. 5:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 4:26" id="a-p454.2" parsed="|Eph|4|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.4.26">Eph. 4:26</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Col. 3:8" id="a-p454.3" parsed="|Col|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.3.8">Col. 3:8</scripRef>). As ascribed to God, it merely denotes his displeasure
with sin and with sinners (Ps. 7:11).
</def>
<term id="a-p454.5">Anim</term>
Fountains, a city in the mountains of Judah (Josh. 15:50), now
el-Ghuwein, near Eshtemoh, about 10 miles south-west of Hebron.
</def>
<term id="a-p455.2">Animal</term>
An organized living creature endowed with sensation. The
Levitical law divided animals into clean and unclean, although

the distinction seems to have existed before the Flood (<scripRef passage="Gen. 7:2" id="a-p456.1" parsed="|Gen|7|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.7.2">Gen. 7:2</scripRef>). The clean could be offered in sacrifice and eaten. All
animals that had not cloven hoofs and did not chew the cud were
unclean. The list of clean and unclean quadrupeds is set forth
in the Levitical law (Deut. 14:3-20; Lev. 11).
</def>
<term id="a-p456.4">Anise</term>
This word is found only in Matt. 23:23. It is the plant commonly
known by the name of dill, the Peucedanum graveolens of the
botanist. This name dill is derived from a Norse word which
means to soothe, the plant having the carminative property of
allaying pain. The common dill, the Anethum graveolens, is an
annual growing wild in the cornfields of Spain and Portugal and
the south of Europe generally. There is also a species of dill
cultivated in Eastern countries known by the name of shubit. It
was this species of garden plant of which the Pharisees were in
the habit of paying tithes. The Talmud requires that the seeds,
leaves, and stem of dill shall pay tithes. It is an
umbelliferous plant, very like the caraway, its leaves, which
are aromatic, being used in soups and pickles. The proper anise
is the Pimpinella anisum.
</def>
<term id="a-p457.2">Anna</term>
Grace, an aged widow, the daughter of Phanuel. She was a
“prophetess,” like Miriam, Deborah, and Huldah (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 34:22" id="a-p458.1" parsed="|2Chr|34|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.34.22">2 Chr. 34:22</scripRef>).
After seven years of married life her husband died, and during
her long widowhood she daily attended the temple services. When
she was eighty-four years old, she entered the temple at the
moment when the aged Simeon uttered his memorable words of
praise and thanks to God that he had fulfilled his ancient
promise in sending his Son into the world (Luke 2:36, 37).
</def>
<term id="a-p458.4">Annas</term>
Was high priest A.D. 7-14. In A.D. 25 Caiaphas, who had married
the daughter of Annas (<scripRef passage="John 18:13" id="a-p459.1" parsed="|John|18|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.18.13">John 18:13</scripRef>), was raised to that office,
and probably Annas was now made president of the Sanhedrim, or
deputy or coadjutor of the high priest, and thus was also called
high priest along with Caiaphas (<scripRef passage="Luke 3:2" id="a-p459.2" parsed="|Luke|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.2">Luke 3:2</scripRef>). By the Mosaic law
the high-priesthood was held for life (<scripRef passage="Num. 3:10" id="a-p459.3" parsed="|Num|3|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.3.10">Num. 3:10</scripRef>); and although
Annas had been deposed by the Roman procurator, the Jews may
still have regarded him as legally the high priest. Our Lord was
first brought before Annas, and after a brief questioning of him
(<scripRef passage="John 18:19-23" id="a-p459.4" parsed="|John|18|19|18|23" osisRef="Bible:John.18.19-John.18.23">John 18:19-23</scripRef>) was sent to Caiaphas, when some members of the
Sanhedrim had met, and the first trial of Jesus took place
(<scripRef passage="Matt. 26:57-68" id="a-p459.5" parsed="|Matt|26|57|26|68" osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.57-Matt.26.68">Matt. 26:57-68</scripRef>). This examination of our Lord before Annas is
recorded only by John. Annas was president of the Sanhedrim
before which Peter and John were brought (Acts 4:6).
</def>
<term id="a-p459.7">Anoint</term>
The practice of anointing with perfumed oil was common among the
Hebrews. (1.) The act of anointing was significant of
consecration to a holy or sacred use; hence the anointing of the

high priest (<scripRef passage="Ex. 29:29" id="a-p460.1" parsed="|Exod|29|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.29">Ex. 29:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 4:3" id="a-p460.2" parsed="|Lev|4|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.4.3">Lev. 4:3</scripRef>) and of the sacred vessels (<scripRef passage="Ex. 30:26" id="a-p460.3" parsed="|Exod|30|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.30.26">Ex. 30:26</scripRef>). The high priest and the king are thus called “the

anointed” (<scripRef passage="Lev. 4:3" id="a-p460.4" parsed="|Lev|4|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.4.3">Lev. 4:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 4:5" id="a-p460.5" parsed="|Lev|4|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.4.5">5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 4:16" id="a-p460.6" parsed="|Lev|4|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.4.16">16</scripRef>; 6:20; <scripRef passage="Ps. 132:10" id="a-p460.7" parsed="|Ps|132|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.132.10">Ps. 132:10</scripRef>). Anointing a king

was equivalent to crowning him (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 16:13" id="a-p460.8" parsed="|1Sam|16|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.16.13">1 Sam. 16:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 2:4" id="a-p460.9" parsed="|2Sam|2|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.2.4">2 Sam. 2:4</scripRef>, etc.).

Prophets were also anointed (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 19:16" id="a-p460.10" parsed="|1Kgs|19|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.19.16">1 Kings 19:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 16:22" id="a-p460.11" parsed="|1Chr|16|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.16.22">1 Chr. 16:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 105:15" id="a-p460.12" parsed="|Ps|105|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.105.15">Ps. 105:15</scripRef>). The expression, “anoint the shield” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 21:5" id="a-p460.13" parsed="|Isa|21|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.21.5">Isa. 21:5</scripRef>), refers
to the custom of rubbing oil on the leather of the shield so as
to make it supple and fit for use in war.
(2.) Anointing was also an act of hospitality (Luke 7:38, 46).
It was the custom of the Jews in like manner to anoint
themselves with oil, as a means of refreshing or invigorating

their bodies (<scripRef passage="Deut. 28:40" id="a-p461.3" parsed="|Deut|28|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.40">Deut. 28:40</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ruth 3:3" id="a-p461.4" parsed="|Ruth|3|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.3.3">Ruth 3:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 14:2" id="a-p461.5" parsed="|2Sam|14|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.14.2">2 Sam. 14:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 104:15" id="a-p461.6" parsed="|Ps|104|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.104.15">Ps. 104:15</scripRef>,
etc.). This custom is continued among the Arabians to the
present day.
(3.) Oil was used also for medicinal purposes. It was applied
to the sick, and also to wounds (Ps. 109:18; Isa. 1:6; Mark 6:13; James 5:14).
(4.) The bodies of the dead were sometimes anointed (Mark 14:8; Luke 23:56).
(5.) The promised Deliverer is twice called the “Anointed” or

Messiah (<scripRef passage="Ps. 2:2" id="a-p464.1" parsed="|Ps|2|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.2.2">Ps. 2:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Dan. 9:25" id="a-p464.2" parsed="|Dan|9|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.9.25">Dan. 9:25</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan. 9:26" id="a-p464.3" parsed="|Dan|9|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.9.26">26</scripRef>), because he was anointed with
the Holy Ghost (<scripRef passage="Isa. 61:1" id="a-p464.4" parsed="|Isa|61|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.61.1">Isa. 61:1</scripRef>), figuratively styled the “oil of

gladness” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 45:7" id="a-p464.5" parsed="|Ps|45|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.45.7">Ps. 45:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 1:9" id="a-p464.6" parsed="|Heb|1|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.1.9">Heb. 1:9</scripRef>). Jesus of Nazareth is this

anointed One (<scripRef passage="John 1:41" id="a-p464.7" parsed="|John|1|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.1.41">John 1:41</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 9:22" id="a-p464.8" parsed="|Acts|9|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.9.22">Acts 9:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 17:2" id="a-p464.9" parsed="|Acts|17|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.17.2">17:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 17:3" id="a-p464.10" parsed="|Acts|17|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.17.3">3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 18:5" id="a-p464.11" parsed="|Acts|18|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.5">18:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 18:28" id="a-p464.12" parsed="|Acts|18|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.28">28</scripRef>), the
Messiah of the Old Testament.
</def>
<term id="a-p464.13">Ant</term>
(Heb. nemalah, from a word meaning to creep, cut off, destroy),

referred to in <scripRef passage="Prov. 6:6" id="a-p465.1" parsed="|Prov|6|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.6.6">Prov. 6:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov 30:25" id="a-p465.2" parsed="|Prov|30|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.30.25">30:25</scripRef>, as distinguished for its
prudent habits. Many ants in Palestine feed on animal
substances, but others draw their nourishment partly or
exclusively from vegetables. To the latter class belongs the ant
to which Solomon refers. This ant gathers the seeds in the
season of ripening, and stores them for future use; a habit that
has been observed in ants in Texas, India, and Italy.
</def>
<term id="a-p465.3">Antichrist</term>
Against Christ, or an opposition Christ, a rival Christ. The
word is used only by the apostle John. Referring to false

teachers, he says (<scripRef passage="1 John 2:18" id="a-p466.1" parsed="|1John|2|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.2.18">1 John 2:18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 John 2:22" id="a-p466.2" parsed="|1John|2|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.2.22">22</scripRef>; 4:3; <scripRef passage="2 John 1" id="a-p466.3" parsed="|2John|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2John.1.1">2 John 1</scripRef>:7), “Even now
are there many antichrists.”
(1.) This name has been applied to the “little horn” of the
“king of fierce countenance” (Dan. 7:24, 25; 8:23-25).
(2.) It has been applied also to the “false Christs” spoken of
by our Lord (Matt. 24:5, 23, 24).
(3.) To the “man of sin” described by Paul (2 Thess. 2:3, 4, 8-10).
(4.) And to the “beast from the sea” (Rev. 13:1; 17:1-18).
</def>
<term id="a-p470.3">Antioch</term>
(1.) In Syria, on the river Orontes, about 16 miles from the
Mediterranean, and some 300 miles north of Jerusalem. It was the
metropolis of Syria, and afterwards became the capital of the
Roman province in Asia. It ranked third, after Rome and
Alexandria, in point of importance, of the cities of the Roman
empire. It was called the “first city of the East.” Christianity

was early introduced into it (<scripRef passage="Acts 11:19" id="a-p471.1" parsed="|Acts|11|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.19">Acts 11:19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 11:21" id="a-p471.2" parsed="|Acts|11|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.21">21</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 11:24" id="a-p471.3" parsed="|Acts|11|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.24">24</scripRef>), and the name

“Christian” was first applied here to its professors (<scripRef passage="Acts 11:26" id="a-p471.4" parsed="|Acts|11|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.26">Acts 11:26</scripRef>). It is intimately connected with the early history of the

gospel (<scripRef passage="Acts 6:5" id="a-p471.5" parsed="|Acts|6|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.6.5">Acts 6:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 11:19" id="a-p471.6" parsed="|Acts|11|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.19">11:19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 11:27" id="a-p471.7" parsed="|Acts|11|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.27">27</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 11:28" id="a-p471.8" parsed="|Acts|11|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.28">28</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 11:30" id="a-p471.9" parsed="|Acts|11|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.30">30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 12:25" id="a-p471.10" parsed="|Acts|12|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.12.25">12:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 15:22-35" id="a-p471.11" parsed="|Acts|15|22|15|35" osisRef="Bible:Acts.15.22-Acts.15.35">15:22-35</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal. 2:11" id="a-p471.12" parsed="|Gal|2|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.2.11">Gal. 2:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gal 2:12" id="a-p471.13" parsed="|Gal|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.2.12">12</scripRef>). It was the great central point whence missionaries to the
Gentiles were sent forth. It was the birth-place of the famous
Christian father Chrysostom, who died A.D. 407. It bears the
modern name of Antakia, and is now a miserable, decaying Turkish
town. Like Philippi, it was raised to the rank of a Roman
colony. Such colonies were ruled by “praetors” (R.V. marg., Acts 16:20, 21).
(2.) In the extreme north of Pisidia; was visited by Paul and
Barnabas on the first missionary journey (<scripRef passage="Acts 13:14" id="a-p472.1" parsed="|Acts|13|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.13.14">Acts 13:14</scripRef>). Here they
found a synagogue and many proselytes. They met with great
success in preaching the gospel, but the Jews stirred up a
violent opposition against them, and they were obliged to leave
the place. On his return, Paul again visited Antioch for the
purpose of confirming the disciples (<scripRef passage="Acts 14:21" id="a-p472.2" parsed="|Acts|14|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.14.21">Acts 14:21</scripRef>). It has been
identified with the modern Yalobatch, lying to the east of
Ephesus.
</def>
<term id="a-p472.3">Antiochus</term>
The name of several Syrian kings from B.C. 280 to B.C. 65. The
most notable of these were, (1.) Antiochus the Great, who
ascended the throne B.C. 223. He is regarded as the “king of the
north” referred to in <scripRef passage="Dan. 11:13-19" id="a-p473.1" parsed="|Dan|11|13|11|19" osisRef="Bible:Dan.11.13-Dan.11.19">Dan. 11:13-19</scripRef>. He was succeeded (B.C. 187)
by his son, Seleucus Philopater, spoken of by Daniel (11:20) as
“a raiser of taxes”, in the Revised Version, “one that shall
cause an exactor to pass through the glory of the kingdom.”
(2.) Antiochus IV., surnamed “Epiphanes” i.e., the
Illustrious, succeeded his brother Seleucus (B.C. 175). His
career and character are prophetically described by Daniel
(11:21-32). He was a “vile person.” In a spirit of revenge he
organized an expedition against Jerusalem, which he destroyed,
putting vast multitudes of its inhabitants to death in the most
cruel manner. From this time the Jews began the great war of
independence under their heroic Maccabean leaders with marked
success, defeating the armies of Antiochus that were sent
against them. Enraged at this, Antiochus marched against them in
person, threatening utterly to exterminate the nation; but on
the way he was suddenly arrested by the hand of death (B.C.
</def>
<term id="a-p474.1">Antipas</term>
(1.) Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great by his Samaritan
wife Malthace. He was tetrarch of Galilee and Peraea during the
whole period of our Lord’s life on earth (<scripRef passage="Luke 23:7" id="a-p475.1" parsed="|Luke|23|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.23.7">Luke 23:7</scripRef>). He was a
frivolous and vain prince, and was chargeable with many infamous

crimes (<scripRef passage="Mark 8:15" id="a-p475.2" parsed="|Mark|8|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.8.15">Mark 8:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 3:19" id="a-p475.3" parsed="|Luke|3|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.19">Luke 3:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 13:31" id="a-p475.4" parsed="|Luke|13|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.13.31">13:31</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Luke 13:32" id="a-p475.5" parsed="|Luke|13|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.13.32">32</scripRef>). He beheaded John the
Baptist (<scripRef passage="Matt. 14:1-12" id="a-p475.6" parsed="|Matt|14|1|14|12" osisRef="Bible:Matt.14.1-Matt.14.12">Matt. 14:1-12</scripRef>) at the instigation of Herodias, the wife
of his half-brother Herod-Philip, whom he had married. Pilate
sent Christ to him when he was at Jerusalem at the Passover
(<scripRef passage="Luke 23:7" id="a-p475.7" parsed="|Luke|23|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.23.7">Luke 23:7</scripRef>). He asked some idle questions of him, and after
causing him to be mocked, sent him back again to Pilate. The
wife of Chuza, his house-steward, was one of our Lord’s
disciples (Luke 8:3).
(2.) A “faithful martyr” (Rev. 2:13), of whom nothing more is
certainly known.
</def>
<term id="a-p476.2">Antipatris</term>
A city built by Herod the Great, and called by this name in
honour of his father, Antipater. It lay between Caesarea and
Lydda, two miles inland, on the great Roman road from Caesarea

to Jerusalem. To this place Paul was brought by night (<scripRef passage="Acts 23:31" id="a-p477.1" parsed="|Acts|23|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.23.31">Acts 23:31</scripRef>) on his way to Caesarea, from which it was distant 28
miles. It is identified with the modern, Ras-el-Ain, where rise
the springs of Aujeh, the largest springs in Palestine.
</def>
<term id="a-p477.2">Antonia</term>
A fortress in Jerusalem, at the north-west corner of the temple

area. It is called “the castle” (<scripRef passage="Acts 21:34" id="a-p478.1" parsed="|Acts|21|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.21.34">Acts 21:34</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 21:37" id="a-p478.2" parsed="|Acts|21|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.21.37">37</scripRef>). From the
stairs of this castle Paul delivered his famous speech to the
multitude in the area below (<scripRef passage="Acts 22:1-21" id="a-p478.3" parsed="|Acts|22|1|22|21" osisRef="Bible:Acts.22.1-Acts.22.21">Acts 22:1-21</scripRef>). It was originally a
place in which were kept the vestments of the high priest. Herod
fortified it, and called it Antonia in honour of his friend Mark
Antony. It was of great size, and commanded the temple. It was
built on a plateau of rock, separated on the north from the hill
Bezetha by a ditch about 30 feet deep and 165 feet wide.
</def>
<term id="a-p478.4">Antothite</term>
An inhabitant of Anathoth, found only in 1 Chr. 11:28; 12:3. In

<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 23:27" id="a-p479.3" parsed="|2Sam|23|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.23.27">2 Sam. 23:27</scripRef> it is Anethothite; in <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 27:12" id="a-p479.4" parsed="|1Chr|27|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.27.12">1 Chr. 27:12</scripRef>, Anetothite.
(R.V., “Anathothite.”)
</def>
<term id="a-p479.5">Anvil</term>
The rendering of the Hebrew word , “beaten,” found only in Isa. 41:7.
</def>
<term id="a-p480.2">Ape</term>
An animal of the monkey tribe (1 Kings 10:22; 2 Chr. 9:21). It
was brought from India by the fleets of Solomon and Hiram, and
was called by the Hebrews koph_, and by the Greeks _kepos,
both words being just the Indian Tamil name of the monkey, kapi,
i.e., swift, nimble, active. No species of ape has ever been
found in Palestine or the adjacent regions.
</def>
<term id="a-p481.3">Apelles</term>
A Christian at Rome whom Paul salutes (Rom. 16:10), and styles
“approved in Christ.”
</def>
<term id="a-p482.2">Apharsachites</term>
A company of the colonists whom the Assyrian king planted in
Samaria (Ezra 5:6; 6:6).
</def>
<term id="a-p483.3">Apharsites</term>
Another of the tribes removed to Samaria (Ezra 4:9), or perhaps
the same as the preceding.
</def>
<term id="a-p484.2">Aphik</term>
(Judg. 1:31); Aphek (Josh. 13:4; 19:30), stronghold. (1.) A city
of the tribe of Asher. It was the scene of the licentious
worship of the Syrian Aphrodite. The ruins of the temple,
“magnificent ruins” in a “spot of strange wildness and beauty”,
are still seen at Afka, on the north-west slopes of Lebanon,
near the source of the river Adonis (now Nahr Ibrahim), 12 miles
east of Gebal.
(2.) A city of the tribe of Issachar, near to Jezreel (1 Sam. 4:1; 29:1; comp. 28:4).
(3.) A town on the road from Damascus to Palestine, in the
level plain east of Jordan, near which Benhadad was defeated by

the Israelites (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 20:26" id="a-p487.1" parsed="|1Kgs|20|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.20.26">1 Kings 20:26</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 20:30" id="a-p487.2" parsed="|1Kgs|20|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.20.30">30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 13:17" id="a-p487.3" parsed="|2Kgs|13|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.13.17">2 Kings 13:17</scripRef>). It has been
identified with the modern Fik, 6 miles east of the Sea of
Galilee, opposite Tiberias.
</def>
<term id="a-p487.4">Apocalypse</term>
The Greek name of the Book of Revelation (q.v.).
</def>
<term id="a-p488.1">Apocrypha</term>
Hidden, spurious, the name given to certain ancient books which
found a place in the LXX. and Latin Vulgate versions of the Old
Testament, and were appended to all the great translations made
from them in the sixteenth century, but which have no claim to
be regarded as in any sense parts of the inspired Word.
(1.) They are not once quoted by the New Testament writers,
who frequently quote from the LXX. Our Lord and his apostles
confirmed by their authority the ordinary Jewish canon, which
was the same in all respects as we now have it.
(2.) These books were written not in Hebrew but in Greek, and
during the “period of silence,” from the time of Malachi, after
which oracles and direct revelations from God ceased till the
Christian era.
(3.) The contents of the books themselves show that they were
no part of Scripture. The Old Testament Apocrypha consists of
fourteen books, the chief of which are the Books of the
Maccabees (q.v.), the Books of Esdras, the Book of Wisdom, the
Book of Baruch, the Book of Esther, Ecclesiasticus, Tobit,
Judith, etc.
The New Testament Apocrypha consists of a very extensive
literature, which bears distinct evidences of its non-apostolic
origin, and is utterly unworthy of regard.
</def>
<term id="a-p493.1">Apollonia</term>
A city of Macedonia between Amphipolis and Thessalonica, from
which it was distant about 36 miles. Paul and Silas passed
through it on their way to Thessalonica (Acts 17:1).
</def>
<term id="a-p494.2">Apollos</term>
A Jew “born at Alexandria,” a man well versed in the Scriptures
and eloquent (<scripRef passage="Acts 18:24" id="a-p495.1" parsed="|Acts|18|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.24">Acts 18:24</scripRef>; R.V., “learned”). He came to Ephesus
(about A.D. 49), where he spake “boldly” in the synagogue
(18:26), although he did not know as yet that Jesus of Nazareth
was the Messiah. Aquila and Priscilla instructed him more
perfectly in “the way of God”, i.e., in the knowledge of Christ.
He then proceeded to Corinth, where he met Paul (<scripRef passage="Acts 18:27" id="a-p495.2" parsed="|Acts|18|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.27">Acts 18:27</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Acts 19:1" id="a-p495.3" parsed="|Acts|19|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.1">19:1</scripRef>). He was there very useful in watering the good seed Paul
had sown (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 1:12" id="a-p495.4" parsed="|1Cor|1|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.1.12">1 Cor. 1:12</scripRef>), and in gaining many to Christ. His

disciples were much attached to him (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 3:4-7" id="a-p495.5" parsed="|1Cor|3|4|3|7" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.3.4-1Cor.3.7">1 Cor. 3:4-7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 3:22" id="a-p495.6" parsed="|1Cor|3|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.3.22">22</scripRef>). He was
with Paul at Ephesus when he wrote the First Epistle to the
Corinthians; and Paul makes kindly reference to him in his
letter to Titus (3:13). Some have supposed, although without
sufficient ground, that he was the author of the Epistle to the
Hebrews.
</def>
<term id="a-p495.7">Apollyon</term>
Destroyer, the name given to the king of the hosts represented
by the locusts (<scripRef passage="Rev. 9:11" id="a-p496.1" parsed="|Rev|9|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.9.11">Rev. 9:11</scripRef>). It is the Greek translation of the
Hebrew Abaddon (q.v.).
</def>
<term id="a-p496.2">Apostle</term>
A person sent by another; a messenger; envoy. This word is once
used as a descriptive designation of Jesus Christ, the Sent of

the Father (<scripRef passage="Heb. 3:1" id="a-p497.1" parsed="|Heb|3|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.3.1">Heb. 3:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 20:21" id="a-p497.2" parsed="|John|20|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.20.21">John 20:21</scripRef>). It is, however, generally
used as designating the body of disciples to whom he intrusted
the organization of his church and the dissemination of his

gospel, “the twelve,” as they are called (<scripRef passage="Matt. 10:1-5" id="a-p497.3" parsed="|Matt|10|1|10|5" osisRef="Bible:Matt.10.1-Matt.10.5">Matt. 10:1-5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 3:14" id="a-p497.4" parsed="|Mark|3|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.3.14">Mark 3:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 6:7" id="a-p497.5" parsed="|Mark|6|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.6.7">6:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 6:13" id="a-p497.6" parsed="|Luke|6|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.6.13">Luke 6:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 9:1" id="a-p497.7" parsed="|Luke|9|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.9.1">9:1</scripRef>). We have four lists of the apostles,

one by each of the synoptic evangelists (<scripRef passage="Matt. 10:2-4" id="a-p497.8" parsed="|Matt|10|2|10|4" osisRef="Bible:Matt.10.2-Matt.10.4">Matt. 10:2-4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 3:16" id="a-p497.9" parsed="|Mark|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.3.16">Mark 3:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 6:14" id="a-p497.10" parsed="|Luke|6|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.6.14">Luke 6:14</scripRef>), and one in the Acts (1:13). No two of these
lists, however, perfectly coincide.
Our Lord gave them the “keys of the kingdom,” and by the gift
of his Spirit fitted them to be the founders and governors of

his church (<scripRef passage="John 14:16" id="a-p498.1" parsed="|John|14|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.14.16">John 14:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="John 14:17" id="a-p498.2" parsed="|John|14|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.14.17">17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="John 14:26" id="a-p498.3" parsed="|John|14|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.14.26">26</scripRef>; 15:26, 27; 16:7-15). To them, as
representing his church, he gave the commission to “preach the
gospel to every creature” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 28:18-20" id="a-p498.4" parsed="|Matt|28|18|28|20" osisRef="Bible:Matt.28.18-Matt.28.20">Matt. 28:18-20</scripRef>). After his ascension
he communicated to them, according to his promise, supernatural

gifts to qualify them for the discharge of their duties (<scripRef passage="Acts 2:4" id="a-p498.5" parsed="|Acts|2|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.2.4">Acts 2:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 2:16" id="a-p498.6" parsed="|1Cor|2|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.2.16">1 Cor. 2:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 2:7" id="a-p498.7" parsed="|1Cor|2|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.2.7">2:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 2:10" id="a-p498.8" parsed="|1Cor|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.2.10">10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 2:13" id="a-p498.9" parsed="|1Cor|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.2.13">13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 5:20" id="a-p498.10" parsed="|2Cor|5|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.5.20">2 Cor. 5:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 11:2" id="a-p498.11" parsed="|1Cor|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.11.2">1 Cor. 11:2</scripRef>). Judas
Iscariot, one of “the twelve,” fell by transgression, and
Matthias was substituted in his place (<scripRef passage="Acts 1:21" id="a-p498.12" parsed="|Acts|1|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.21">Acts 1:21</scripRef>). Saul of

Tarsus was afterwards added to their number (<scripRef passage="Acts 9:3-20" id="a-p498.13" parsed="|Acts|9|3|9|20" osisRef="Bible:Acts.9.3-Acts.9.20">Acts 9:3-20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 20:4" id="a-p498.14" parsed="|Acts|20|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.4">20:4</scripRef>;
26:15-18; 1 Tim. 1:12; 2:7; 2 Tim. 1:11).
Luke has given some account of Peter, John, and the two

Jameses (<scripRef passage="Acts 12:2" id="a-p499.1" parsed="|Acts|12|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.12.2">Acts 12:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 12:17" id="a-p499.2" parsed="|Acts|12|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.12.17">17</scripRef>; 15:13; 21:18), but beyond this we know
nothing from authentic history of the rest of the original
twelve. After the martyrdom of James the Greater (<scripRef passage="Acts 12:2" id="a-p499.3" parsed="|Acts|12|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.12.2">Acts 12:2</scripRef>),
James the Less usually resided at Jerusalem, while Paul, “the
apostle of the uncircumcision,” usually travelled as a
missionary among the Gentiles (<scripRef passage="Gal. 2:8" id="a-p499.4" parsed="|Gal|2|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.2.8">Gal. 2:8</scripRef>). It was characteristic
of the apostles and necessary (1) that they should have seen the
Lord, and been able to testify of him and of his resurrection

from personal knowledge (<scripRef passage="John 15:27" id="a-p499.5" parsed="|John|15|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.15.27">John 15:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 1:21" id="a-p499.6" parsed="|Acts|1|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.21">Acts 1:21</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 1:22" id="a-p499.7" parsed="|Acts|1|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.22">22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 9:1" id="a-p499.8" parsed="|1Cor|9|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.9.1">1 Cor. 9:1</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Acts 22:14" id="a-p499.9" parsed="|Acts|22|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.22.14">Acts 22:14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 22:15" id="a-p499.10" parsed="|Acts|22|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.22.15">15</scripRef>). (2.) They must have been immediately called to

that office by Christ (<scripRef passage="Luke 6:13" id="a-p499.11" parsed="|Luke|6|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.6.13">Luke 6:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal. 1:1" id="a-p499.12" parsed="|Gal|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.1.1">Gal. 1:1</scripRef>). (3.) It was
essential that they should be infallibly inspired, and thus
secured against all error and mistake in their public teaching,
whether by word or by writing (John 14:26; 16:13; 1 Thess. 2:13).
(4.) Another qualification was the power of working miracles

(<scripRef passage="Mark 16:20" id="a-p500.1" parsed="|Mark|16|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.16.20">Mark 16:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 2:43" id="a-p500.2" parsed="|Acts|2|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.2.43">Acts 2:43</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 12:8-11" id="a-p500.3" parsed="|1Cor|12|8|12|11" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.12.8-1Cor.12.11">1 Cor. 12:8-11</scripRef>). The apostles therefore
could have had no successors. They are the only authoritative
teachers of the Christian doctrines. The office of an apostle
ceased with its first holders.
In 2 Cor. 8:23 and Phil. 2:25 the word “messenger” is the
rendering of the same Greek word, elsewhere rendered “apostle.”
</def>
<term id="a-p501.3">Apothecary</term>
Rendered in the margin and the Revised Version “perfumer,” in

<scripRef passage="Ex. 30:25" id="a-p502.1" parsed="|Exod|30|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.30.25">Ex. 30:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 37:29" id="a-p502.2" parsed="|Exod|37|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.37.29">37:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eccl. 10:1" id="a-p502.3" parsed="|Eccl|10|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eccl.10.1">Eccl. 10:1</scripRef>. The holy oils and ointments were
prepared by priests properly qualified for this office. The
feminine plural form of the Hebrew word is rendered
“confectionaries” in 1 Sam. 8:13.
</def>
<term id="a-p502.5">Apparel</term>
In Old Testament times the distinction between male and female
attire was not very marked. The statute forbidding men to wear
female apparel (<scripRef passage="Deut. 22:5" id="a-p503.1" parsed="|Deut|22|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.22.5">Deut. 22:5</scripRef>) referred especially to ornaments and
head-dresses. Both men and women wore (1) an under garment or
tunic, which was bound by a girdle. One who had only this tunic

on was spoken of as “naked” (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 19:24" id="a-p503.2" parsed="|1Sam|19|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.19.24">1 Sam. 19:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 24:10" id="a-p503.3" parsed="|Job|24|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.24.10">Job 24:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 20:2" id="a-p503.4" parsed="|Isa|20|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.20.2">Isa. 20:2</scripRef>). Those in high stations sometimes wore two tunics, the

outer being called the “upper garment” (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 15:27" id="a-p503.5" parsed="|1Sam|15|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.15.27">1 Sam. 15:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 18:4" id="a-p503.6" parsed="|1Sam|18|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.18.4">18:4</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 24:5" id="a-p503.7" parsed="|1Sam|24|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.24.5">24:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 1:20" id="a-p503.8" parsed="|Job|1|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.1.20">Job 1:20</scripRef>). (2.) They wore in common an over-garment

(“mantle,” <scripRef passage="Isa. 3:22" id="a-p503.9" parsed="|Isa|3|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.22">Isa. 3:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 19:13" id="a-p503.10" parsed="|1Kgs|19|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.19.13">1 Kings 19:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 2:13" id="a-p503.11" parsed="|2Kgs|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.2.13">2 Kings 2:13</scripRef>), a loose and
flowing robe. The folds of this upper garment could be formed

into a lap (<scripRef passage="Ruth 3:15" id="a-p503.12" parsed="|Ruth|3|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.3.15">Ruth 3:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 79:12" id="a-p503.13" parsed="|Ps|79|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.79.12">Ps. 79:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 17:23" id="a-p503.14" parsed="|Prov|17|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.17.23">Prov. 17:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 6:38" id="a-p503.15" parsed="|Luke|6|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.6.38">Luke 6:38</scripRef>).

Generals of armies usually wore scarlet robes (<scripRef passage="Judg. 8:26" id="a-p503.16" parsed="|Judg|8|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.8.26">Judg. 8:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Nah. 2:3" id="a-p503.17" parsed="|Nah|2|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Nah.2.3">Nah. 2:3</scripRef>). A form of conspicuous raiment is mentioned in <scripRef passage="Luke 20:46" id="a-p503.18" parsed="|Luke|20|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.20.46">Luke 20:46</scripRef>;
comp. Matt. 23:5.
Priests alone wore trousers. Both men and women wore turbans.
Kings and nobles usually had a store of costly garments for

festive occasions (<scripRef passage="Isa. 3:22" id="a-p504.1" parsed="|Isa|3|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.22">Isa. 3:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 3:4" id="a-p504.2" parsed="|Zech|3|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.3.4">Zech. 3:4</scripRef>) and for presents (<scripRef passage="Gen. 45:22" id="a-p504.3" parsed="|Gen|45|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.45.22">Gen. 45:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Esther 4:4" id="a-p504.4" parsed="|Esth|4|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.4.4">Esther 4:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Esther 6:8" id="a-p504.5" parsed="|Esth|6|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.6.8">6:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Esther 6:11" id="a-p504.6" parsed="|Esth|6|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.6.11">11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 18:4" id="a-p504.7" parsed="|1Sam|18|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.18.4">1 Sam. 18:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 5:5" id="a-p504.8" parsed="|2Kgs|5|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.5.5">2 Kings 5:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 10:22" id="a-p504.9" parsed="|2Kgs|10|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.10.22">10:22</scripRef>).
Prophets and ascetics wore coarse garments (Isa. 20:2; Zech. 13:4; Matt. 3:4).
</def>
<term id="a-p504.13">Appeal</term>
A reference of any case from an inferior to a superior court.
Moses established in the wilderness a series of judicatories
such that appeals could be made from a lower to a higher (Ex. 18:13-26.)
Under the Roman law the most remarkable case of appeal is that
of Paul from the tribunal of Festus at Caesarea to that of the

emperor at Rome (<scripRef passage="Acts 25:11" id="a-p506.1" parsed="|Acts|25|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.25.11">Acts 25:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 25:12" id="a-p506.2" parsed="|Acts|25|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.25.12">12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 25:21" id="a-p506.3" parsed="|Acts|25|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.25.21">21</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 25:25" id="a-p506.4" parsed="|Acts|25|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.25.25">25</scripRef>). Paul availed himself
of the privilege of a Roman citizen in this matter.
</def>
<term id="a-p506.5">Apphia</term>
Increasing, a female Christian at Colosse (Philemon 1:2),
supposed by some to have been the wife of Philemon.
</def>
<term id="a-p507.2">Appii Forum</term>
I.e., “the market of Appius” (Acts 28:15, R.V.), a town on the
road, the “Appian Way,” from Rome to Brundusium. It was 43 miles
from Rome. Here Paul was met by some Roman Christians on his way
to the capital. It was natural that they should halt here and
wait for him, because from this place there were two ways by
which travellers might journey to Rome.
</def>
<term id="a-p508.2">Apple</term>
(Heb. tappuah, meaning “fragrance”). Probably the apricot or
quince is intended by the word, as Palestine was too hot for the
growth of apples proper. It is enumerated among the most
valuable trees of Palestine (<scripRef passage="Joel 1:12" id="a-p509.1" parsed="|Joel|1|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Joel.1.12">Joel 1:12</scripRef>), and frequently referred
to in Canticles, and noted for its beauty (2:3, 5; 8:5). There
is nothing to show that it was the “tree of the knowledge of
good and evil.” Dr. Tristram has suggested that the apricot has
better claims than any other fruit-tree to be the apple of
Scripture. It grows to a height of 30 feet, has a roundish mass
of glossy leaves, and bears an orange coloured fruit that gives
out a delicious perfume. The “apple of the eye” is the Heb.
ishon, meaning manikin, i.e., the pupil of the eye (Prov. 7:2). (Comp. the promise, Zech. 2:8; the prayer, Ps. 17:8; and
its fulfilment, Deut. 32:10.)
The so-called “apple of Sodom” some have supposed to be the

Solanum sanctum (Heb. hedek), rendered “brier” (q.v.) in <scripRef passage="Micah 7:4" id="a-p510.1" parsed="|Mic|7|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.7.4">Micah 7:4</scripRef>, a thorny plant bearing fruit like the potato-apple. This
shrub abounds in the Jordan valley. (See ENGEDI.)
</def>
<term id="a-p510.3">Apron</term>
Found in the Authorized Version in Gen. 3:7, of the bands of
fig-leaves made by our first parents. In <scripRef passage="Acts 19:12" id="a-p511.2" parsed="|Acts|19|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.12">Acts 19:12</scripRef>, it denotes
the belt or half-girdle worn by artisans and servants round the
waist for the purpose of preserving the clothing from injury. In
marg. of Authorized Version, <scripRef passage="Ruth 3:15" id="a-p511.3" parsed="|Ruth|3|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.3.15">Ruth 3:15</scripRef>, correctly rendered
instead of “vail.” (R.V., “mantle.”)
</def>
<term id="a-p511.4">Aquila</term>
Eagle, a native of Pontus, by occupation a tent-maker, whom Paul
met on his first visit to Corinth (<scripRef passage="Acts 18:2" id="a-p512.1" parsed="|Acts|18|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.2">Acts 18:2</scripRef>). Along with his
wife Priscilla he had fled from Rome in consequence of a decree
(A.D. 50) by Claudius commanding all Jews to leave the city.
Paul sojourned with him at Corinth, and they wrought together at
their common trade, making Cilician hair-cloth for tents. On
Paul’s departure from Corinth after eighteen months, Aquila and
his wife accompanied him to Ephesus, where they remained, while

he proceeded to Syria (<scripRef passage="Acts 18:18" id="a-p512.2" parsed="|Acts|18|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.18">Acts 18:18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 18:26" id="a-p512.3" parsed="|Acts|18|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.26">26</scripRef>). When they became

Christians we are not informed, but in Ephesus they were (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 16:19" id="a-p512.4" parsed="|1Cor|16|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.16.19">1 Cor. 16:19</scripRef>) Paul’s “helpers in Christ Jesus.” We find them afterwards
at Rome (<scripRef passage="Rom. 16:3" id="a-p512.5" parsed="|Rom|16|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.16.3">Rom. 16:3</scripRef>), interesting themselves still in the cause
of Christ. They are referred to some years after this as being
at Ephesus (<scripRef passage="2 Tim. 4:19" id="a-p512.6" parsed="|2Tim|4|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.4.19">2 Tim. 4:19</scripRef>). This is the last notice we have of
them.
</def>
<term id="a-p512.7">Arab</term>
Ambush, a city in the mountains of Judah (Josh. 15:52), now
Er-Rabiyeh.
</def>
<term id="a-p513.2">Arabah</term>
Plain, in the Revised Version of 2 Kings 14:25; Josh. 3:16;

<scripRef passage="Josh 8:14" id="a-p514.3" parsed="|Josh|8|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.8.14">8:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 2:29" id="a-p514.4" parsed="|2Sam|2|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.2.29">2 Sam. 2:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 4:7" id="a-p514.5" parsed="|2Sam|4|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.4.7">4:7</scripRef> (in all these passages the A.V. has
“plain”); <scripRef passage="Amos 6:14" id="a-p514.6" parsed="|Amos|6|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.6.14">Amos 6:14</scripRef> (A.V. “wilderness”). This word is found in
the Authorized Version only in <scripRef passage="Josh. 18:18" id="a-p514.7" parsed="|Josh|18|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.18.18">Josh. 18:18</scripRef>. It denotes the
hollow depression through which the Jordan flows from the Lake
of Galilee to the Dead Sea. It is now called by the Arabs
el-Ghor. But the Ghor is sometimes spoken of as extending 10
miles south of the Dead Sea, and thence to the Gulf of Akabah on
the Red Sea is called the Wady el-Arabah.
</def>
<term id="a-p514.8">Arabia</term>
Arid, an extensive region in the south-west of Asia. It is
bounded on the west by the Isthmus of Suez and the Red Sea, on
the south by the Indian Ocean, and on the east by the Persian
Gulf and the Euphrates. It extends far into the north in barren
deserts, meeting those of Syria and Mesopotamia. It is one of
the few countries of the world from which the original
inhabitants have never been expelled.
It was anciently divided into three parts:, (1.) Arabia Felix
(Happy Arabia), so called from its fertility. It embraced a
large portion of the country now known by the name of Arabia.
The Arabs call it Yemen. It lies between the Red Sea and the
Persian Gulf. (2.) Arabia Deserta, the el-Badieh or “Great
Wilderness” of the Arabs. From this name is derived that which
is usually given to the nomadic tribes which wander over this
region, the “Bedaween,” or, more generally, “Bedouin,” (3.)
Arabia Petraea, i.e., the Rocky Arabia, so called from its rocky
mountains and stony plains. It comprehended all the north-west
portion of the country, and is much better known to travellers
than any other portion. This country is, however, divided by
modern geographers into (1) Arabia Proper, or the Arabian
Peninsula; (2) Northern Arabia, or the Arabian Desert; and (3)
Western Arabia, which includes the peninsula of Sinai and the
Desert of Petra, originally inhabited by the Horites (<scripRef passage="Gen. 14:6" id="a-p516.1" parsed="|Gen|14|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.6">Gen. 14:6</scripRef>,
etc.), but in later times by the descendants of Esau, and known
as the Land of Edom or Idumea, also as the Desert of Seir or
Mount Seir.
The whole land appears (Gen. 10) to have been inhabited by a
variety of tribes of different lineage, Ishmaelites, Arabians,
Idumeans, Horites, and Edomites; but at length becoming
amalgamated, they came to be known by the general designation of
Arabs. The modern nation of Arabs is predominantly Ishmaelite.
Their language is the most developed and the richest of all the
Semitic languages, and is of great value to the student of
Hebrew.
The Israelites wandered for forty years in Arabia. In the days
of Solomon, and subsequently, commercial intercourse was to a

considerable extent kept up with this country (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:15" id="a-p518.1" parsed="|1Kgs|10|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.15">1 Kings 10:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 9:14" id="a-p518.2" parsed="|2Chr|9|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.9.14">2 Chr. 9:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 17:11" id="a-p518.3" parsed="|2Chr|17|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.17.11">17:11</scripRef>). Arabians were present in Jerusalem at
Pentecost (<scripRef passage="Acts 2:11" id="a-p518.4" parsed="|Acts|2|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.2.11">Acts 2:11</scripRef>). Paul retired for a season into Arabia
after his conversion (<scripRef passage="Gal. 1:17" id="a-p518.5" parsed="|Gal|1|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.1.17">Gal. 1:17</scripRef>). This country is frequently

referred to by the prophets (<scripRef passage="Isa. 21:11" id="a-p518.6" parsed="|Isa|21|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.21.11">Isa. 21:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 42:11" id="a-p518.7" parsed="|Isa|42|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.42.11">42:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 25:24" id="a-p518.8" parsed="|Jer|25|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.25.24">Jer. 25:24</scripRef>,
etc.)
</def>
<term id="a-p518.9">Arad</term>
(1.) Now Tell Arad, a Canaanite city, about 20 miles south of
Hebron. The king of Arad “fought against Israel and took of them
prisoners” when they were retreating from the confines of Edom

(<scripRef passage="Num. 21:1" id="a-p519.1" parsed="|Num|21|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.21.1">Num. 21:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 33:40" id="a-p519.2" parsed="|Num|33|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.40">33:40</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 1:16" id="a-p519.3" parsed="|Judg|1|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.16">Judg. 1:16</scripRef>). It was finally subdued by Joshua
(2.) One of the sons of Beriah (1 Chr. 8:15).
</def>
<term id="a-p520.2">Aram</term>
The son of Shem (Gen. 10:22); according to Gen. 22:21, a

grandson of Nahor. In <scripRef passage="Matt. 1:3" id="a-p521.3" parsed="|Matt|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.1.3">Matt. 1:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 1:4" id="a-p521.4" parsed="|Matt|1|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.1.4">4</scripRef>, and <scripRef passage="Luke 3:33" id="a-p521.5" parsed="|Luke|3|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.33">Luke 3:33</scripRef>, this word is
the Greek form of Ram, the father of Amminadab (1 Chr. 2:10).
The word means high, or highlands, and as the name of a
country denotes that elevated region extending from the
northeast of Palestine to the Euphrates. It corresponded
generally with the Syria and Mesopotamia of the Greeks and

Romans. In <scripRef passage="Gen. 25:20" id="a-p522.1" parsed="|Gen|25|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.20">Gen. 25:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 31:20" id="a-p522.2" parsed="|Gen|31|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.20">31:20</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 31:24" id="a-p522.3" parsed="|Gen|31|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.24">24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 26:5" id="a-p522.4" parsed="|Deut|26|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.26.5">Deut. 26:5</scripRef>, the word “Syrian”
is properly “Aramean” (R.V., marg.). Damascus became at length
the capital of the several smaller kingdoms comprehended under
the designation “Aram” or “Syria.”
</def>
<term id="a-p522.5">Aram-naharaim</term>
Aram of the two rivers, is Mesopotamia (as it is rendered in
<scripRef passage="Gen. 24:10" id="a-p523.1" parsed="|Gen|24|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.10">Gen. 24:10</scripRef>), the country enclosed between the Tigris on the east
and the Euphrates on the west (<scripRef passage="Ps. 60" id="a-p523.2" parsed="|Ps|60|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.60">Ps. 60</scripRef>, title); called also the
“field of Aram” (<scripRef passage="Hos. 12:12" id="a-p523.3" parsed="|Hos|12|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.12.12">Hos. 12:12</scripRef>, R.V.) i.e., the open country of
Aram; in the Authorized Version, “country of Syria.” Padan-aram
(q.v.) was a portion of this country.
</def>
<term id="a-p523.4">Aram-zobah</term>
(Ps. 60, title), probably the region between the Euphrates and
the Orontes.
</def>
<term id="a-p524.2">Aran</term>
Wild goat, a descendant of Seir the Horite (Gen. 36:28).
</def>
<term id="a-p525.2">Ararat</term>
Sacred land or high land, the name of a country on one of the

mountains of which the ark rested after the Flood subsided (<scripRef passage="Gen. 8:4" id="a-p526.1" parsed="|Gen|8|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.8.4">Gen. 8:4</scripRef>). The “mountains” mentioned were probably the Kurdish range

of South Armenia. In <scripRef passage="2 Kings 19:37" id="a-p526.2" parsed="|2Kgs|19|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.19.37">2 Kings 19:37</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 37:38" id="a-p526.3" parsed="|Isa|37|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.37.38">Isa. 37:38</scripRef>, the word is
rendered “Armenia” in the Authorized Version, but in the Revised
Version, “Land of Ararat.” In <scripRef passage="Jer. 51:27" id="a-p526.4" parsed="|Jer|51|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.51.27">Jer. 51:27</scripRef>, the name denotes the
central or southern portion of Armenia. It is, however,
generally applied to a high and almost inaccessible mountain
which rises majestically from the plain of the Araxes. It has
two conical peaks, about 7 miles apart, the one 14,300 feet and
the other 10,300 feet above the level of the plain. Three
thousand feet of the summit of the higher of these peaks is
covered with perpetual snow. It is called Kuh-i-nuh, i.e.,
“Noah’s mountain”, by the Persians. This part of Armenia was
inhabited by a people who spoke a language unlike any other now
known, though it may have been related to the modern Georgian.
About B.C. 900 they borrowed the cuneiform characters of
Nineveh, and from this time we have inscriptions of a line of
kings who at times contended with Assyria. At the close of the
seventh century B.C. the kingdom of Ararat came to an end, and
the country was occupied by a people who are ancestors of the
Armenians of the present day.
</def>
<term id="a-p526.5">Araunah</term>
Agile; also called Ornan 1 Chr. 21:15, a Jebusite who dwelt in
Jerusalem before it was taken by the Israelites. The destroying
angel, sent to punish David for his vanity in taking a census of
the people, was stayed in his work of destruction near a
threshing-floor belonging to Araunah which was situated on Mount
Moriah. Araunah offered it to David as a free gift, together
with the oxen and the threshing instruments; but the king

insisted on purchasing it at its full price (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 24:24" id="a-p527.2" parsed="|2Sam|24|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.24.24">2 Sam. 24:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 21:24" id="a-p527.3" parsed="|1Chr|21|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.21.24">1 Chr. 21:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 21:25" id="a-p527.4" parsed="|1Chr|21|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.21.25">25</scripRef>), for, according to the law of sacrifices, he
could not offer to God what cost him nothing. On the same place
Solomon afterwards erected the temple (2 Sam. 24:16; 2 Chr. 3:1). (See ALTAR.)
</def>
<term id="a-p527.8">Arba</term>
Four, a giant, father of Anak. From him the city of Hebron
derived its name of Kirjath-arba, i.e., the city of Araba (Josh. 14:15; 15:13; 21:11; Gen. 13:18; 23:2). (See HEBRON.)
</def>
<term id="a-p528.7">Arbathite</term>
A name given to Abi-albon, or, as elsewhere called, Abiel, one

of David’s warriors (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 23:31" id="a-p529.1" parsed="|2Sam|23|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.23.31">2 Sam. 23:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 11:32" id="a-p529.2" parsed="|1Chr|11|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.11.32">1 Chr. 11:32</scripRef>), probably as
being an inhabitant of Arabah (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:61" id="a-p529.3" parsed="|Josh|15|61|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.61">Josh. 15:61</scripRef>), a town in the
wilderness of Judah.
</def>
<term id="a-p529.4">Arch</term>
An architectural term found only in Ezek. 40:16, 21, 22, 26, 29.
There is no absolute proof that the Israelites employed arches
in their buildings. The arch was employed in the building of the
pyramids of Egypt. The oldest existing arch is at Thebes, and
bears the date B.C. 1350. There are also still found the remains
of an arch, known as Robinson’s Arch, of the bridge connecting
Zion and Moriah. (See TYROPOEON VALLEY.)
</def>
<term id="a-p530.7">Archangel</term>
(1Thess. 4:16; Jude 1:9), the prince of the angels.
</def>
<term id="a-p531.3">Archelaus</term>
Ruler of the people, son of Herod the Great, by Malthace, a
Samaritan woman. He was educated along with his brother Antipas
at Rome. He inherited from his father a third part of his
kingdom viz., Idumea, Judea, and Samaria, and hence is called
“king” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 2:22" id="a-p532.1" parsed="|Matt|2|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.2.22">Matt. 2:22</scripRef>). It was for fear of him that Joseph and Mary
turned aside on their way back from Egypt. Till a few days
before his death Herod had named Antipas as his successor, but
in his last moments he named Archelaus.
</def>
<term id="a-p532.2">Archer</term>
A shooter with the bow (1 Chr. 10:3). This art was of high

antiquity (<scripRef passage="Gen. 21:20" id="a-p533.2" parsed="|Gen|21|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.20">Gen. 21:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 27:3" id="a-p533.3" parsed="|Gen|27|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.3">27:3</scripRef>). Saul was wounded by the Philistine

archers (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 31:3" id="a-p533.4" parsed="|1Sam|31|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.31.3">1 Sam. 31:3</scripRef>). The phrase “breaking the bow” (<scripRef passage="Hos. 1:5" id="a-p533.5" parsed="|Hos|1|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.1.5">Hos. 1:5</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Jer. 49:35" id="a-p533.6" parsed="|Jer|49|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.49.35">Jer. 49:35</scripRef>) is equivalent to taking away one’s power, while
“strengthening the bow” is a symbol of its increase (Gen. 49:24). The Persian archers were famous among the ancients (Isa. 13:18; Jer. 49:35; 50:9, 14, 29, 42. (See BOW).
</def>
<term id="a-p533.15">Archevite</term>
One of the nations planted by the Assyrians in Samaria (Ezra 4:9); the men of Erech.
</def>
<term id="a-p534.2">Archi</term>
A city on the boundary of Ephraim and Benjamin (Josh. 16:2),
between Bethel and Beth-horon the nether.
</def>
<term id="a-p535.2">Archippus</term>
Master of the horse, a “fellow-soldier” of Paul’s (Philemon 1:2), whom he exhorts to renewed activity (Col. 4:17). He was a
member of Philemon’s family, probably his son.
</def>
<term id="a-p536.3">Archite</term>
The usual designation of Hushai (2 Sam. 15:32; 17:5, 14; 1 Chr. 27:33), who was a native of Archi. He was “the king’s friend”,
i.e., he held office under David similar to that of our modern
privy councillor.
</def>
<term id="a-p537.5">Arcturus</term>
Bear-keeper, the name given by the ancients to the brightest
star in the constellation Bootes. In the Authorized Version (Job 9:9; 38:32) it is the rendering of the Hebrew word ’ash, which
probably designates the constellation the Great Bear. This word
(‘ash) is supposed to be derived from an Arabic word meaning
night-watcher, because the Great Bear always revolves about the
pole, and to our nothern hemisphere never sets.
</def>
<term id="a-p538.3">Ard</term>
Descent, a grandson of Benjamin (Num. 26:38-40). In 1 Chr. 8:3
he is called Addar. His descendants are mentioned in Num. 26:40.
</def>
<term id="a-p539.4">Ardon</term>
Descendant, the last of the three sons of Caleb by his first
wife Azubah (1 Chr. 2:18).
</def>
<term id="a-p540.2">Areopagite</term>
A member of the court of Areopagus (Acts 17:34).
</def>
<term id="a-p541.2">Areopagus</term>
The Latin form of the Greek word rendered “Mars’ hill.” But it
denotes also the council or court of justice which met in the
open air on the hill. It was a rocky height to the west of the
Acropolis at Athens, on the south-east summit of which the
council was held which was constituted by Solon, and consisted
of nine archons or chief magistrates who were then in office,
and the ex-archons of blameless life.
On this hill of Mars (Gr. Ares) Paul delivered his memorable
address to the “men of Athens” (Acts 17:22-31).
</def>
<term id="a-p543.2">Aretas</term>
The father-in-law of Herod Antipas, and king of Arabia Petraea.
His daughter returned to him on the occasion of her husband’s
entering into an adulterous alliance with Herodias, the wife of

Herod-Philip, his half-brother (<scripRef passage="Luke 3:19" id="a-p544.1" parsed="|Luke|3|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.19">Luke 3:19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Luke 3:20" id="a-p544.2" parsed="|Luke|3|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.20">20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 6:17" id="a-p544.3" parsed="|Mark|6|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.6.17">Mark 6:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 14:3" id="a-p544.4" parsed="|Matt|14|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.14.3">Matt. 14:3</scripRef>). This led to a war between Aretas and Herod Antipas.
Herod’s army was wholly destroyed (A.D. 36). Aretas, taking
advantage of the complications of the times on account of the
death of the Emperor Tiberius (A.D. 37), took possession of

Damascus (<scripRef passage="2 Cor. 11:32" id="a-p544.5" parsed="|2Cor|11|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.11.32">2 Cor. 11:32</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Acts 9:25" id="a-p544.6" parsed="|Acts|9|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.9.25">Acts 9:25</scripRef>). At this time Paul
returned to Damascus from Arabia.
</def>
<term id="a-p544.7">Argob</term>
Stony heap, an “island,” as it has been called, of rock about 30
miles by 20, rising 20 or 30 feet above the table-land of
Bashan; a region of crags and chasms wild and rugged in the
extreme. On this “island” stood sixty walled cities, ruled over
by Og. It is called Trachonitis (“the rugged region”) in the New
Testament (<scripRef passage="Luke 3:1" id="a-p545.1" parsed="|Luke|3|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.1">Luke 3:1</scripRef>). These cities were conquered by the

Israelites (<scripRef passage="Deut. 3:4" id="a-p545.2" parsed="|Deut|3|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.4">Deut. 3:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:13" id="a-p545.3" parsed="|1Kgs|4|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.13">1 Kings 4:13</scripRef>). It is now called the
Lejah. Here “sixty walled cities are still traceable in a space
of 308 square miles. The architecture is ponderous and massive.
Solid walls 4 feet thick, and stones on one another without
cement; the roofs enormous slabs of basaltic rock, like iron;
the doors and gates are of stone 18 inches thick, secured by
ponderous bars. The land bears still the appearance of having
been called the ‘land of giants’ under the giant Og.” “I have
more than once entered a deserted city in the evening, taken
possession of a comfortable house, and spent the night in peace.
Many of the houses in the ancient cities of Bashan are perfect,
as if only finished yesterday. The walls are sound, the roofs
unbroken, and even the window-shutters in their places. These
ancient cities of Bashan probably contain the very oldest
specimens of domestic architecture in the world” (Porter’s Giant
Cities). (See BASHAN.)
</def>
<term id="a-p545.5">Arieh</term>
The lion, the name of one of the body-guard slain with Pekahiah
at Samaria (2 Kings 15:25) by the conspirator Pekah.
</def>
<term id="a-p546.2">Ariel</term>
The lion of God. (1.) One of the chief men sent by Ezra to
procure Levites for the sanctuary (Ezra 8:16).
(2.) A symbolic name for Jerusalem (Isa. 29:1, 2, 7) as

“victorious under God,” and in <scripRef passage="Ezek. 43:15" id="a-p548.4" parsed="|Ezek|43|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.43.15">Ezek. 43:15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 43:16" id="a-p548.5" parsed="|Ezek|43|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.43.16">16</scripRef>, for the altar
(marg., Heb. ‘ariel) of burnt offerings, the secret of Israel’s
lion-like strength.
</def>
<term id="a-p548.6">Arimathea</term>
A “city of the Jews” (Luke 23:51), the birth-place of Joseph in

whose sepulchre our Lord was laid (<scripRef passage="Matt. 27:57" id="a-p549.2" parsed="|Matt|27|57|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.57">Matt. 27:57</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 27:60" id="a-p549.3" parsed="|Matt|27|60|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.60">60</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 19:38" id="a-p549.4" parsed="|John|19|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.38">John 19:38</scripRef>).
It is probably the same place as Ramathaim in Ephraim, and the

birth-place of Samuel (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 1:1" id="a-p549.5" parsed="|1Sam|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.1.1">1 Sam. 1:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 1:19" id="a-p549.6" parsed="|1Sam|1|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.1.19">19</scripRef>). Others identify it with
Ramleh in Dan, or Rama (q.v.) in Benjamin (Matt. 2:18).
</def>
<term id="a-p549.8">Arioch</term>
Lion-like, venerable. (1.) A king of Ellasar who was confederate

with Chedorlamer (<scripRef passage="Gen. 14:1" id="a-p550.1" parsed="|Gen|14|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.1">Gen. 14:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 14:9" id="a-p550.2" parsed="|Gen|14|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.9">9</scripRef>). The tablets recently discovered
by Mr. Pinches (see CHALDEA) show the true reading is
Eri-Aku of Larsa. This Elamite name meant “servant of the
moon-god.” It was afterwards changed into Rimsin, “Have mercy, O
moon-god.” (2.) Dan. 2:14.
</def>
<term id="a-p550.5">Aristarchus</term>
Best ruler, native of Thessalonica (Acts 20:4), a companion of

Paul (<scripRef passage="Acts 19:29" id="a-p551.2" parsed="|Acts|19|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.29">Acts 19:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 27:2" id="a-p551.3" parsed="|Acts|27|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.27.2">27:2</scripRef>). He was Paul’s “fellow-prisoner” at Rome
(Col. 4:10; Philemon 1:24).
</def>
<term id="a-p551.6">Aristobulus</term>
A Roman mentioned in Paul’s Epistle to the Romans (16:10), whose
“household” is saluated.
</def>
<term id="a-p552.1">Ark</term>
Noah’s ark, a building of gopher-wood, and covered with pitch,
