300 cubits long, 50 cubits broad, and 30 cubits high (<scripRef passage="Gen. 6:14-16" id="a-p553.1" parsed="|Gen|6|14|6|16" osisRef="Bible:Gen.6.14-Gen.6.16">Gen. 6:14-16</scripRef>); an oblong floating house of three stories, with a door
in the side and a window in the roof. It was 100 years in

building (<scripRef passage="Gen. 5:32" id="a-p553.2" parsed="|Gen|5|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.5.32">Gen. 5:32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 7:6" id="a-p553.3" parsed="|Gen|7|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.7.6">7:6</scripRef>). It was intended to preserve certain
persons and animals from the deluge which God was about to bring

over the earth. It contained eight persons (<scripRef passage="Gen. 7:13" id="a-p553.4" parsed="|Gen|7|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.7.13">Gen. 7:13</scripRef>; 2 Pet. 2:5), and of all “clean” animals seven pairs, and of “unclean”

one pair, and of birds seven pairs of each sort (<scripRef passage="Gen. 7:2" id="a-p553.5" parsed="|Gen|7|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.7.2">Gen. 7:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 7:3" id="a-p553.6" parsed="|Gen|7|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.7.3">3</scripRef>).
It was in the form of an oblong square, with flat bottom and
sloping roof. Traditions of the Deluge, by which the race of man
was swept from the earth, and of the ark of Noah have been found
existing among all nations.
The ark of bulrushes in which the infant Moses was laid (Ex. 2:3) is called in the Hebrew teebah, a word derived from the
Egyptian teb, meaning “a chest.” It was daubed with slime and
with pitch. The bulrushes of which it was made were the papyrus
reed.
The sacred ark is designated by a different Hebrew word,
’aron’, which is the common name for a chest or coffer used

for any purpose (<scripRef passage="Gen. 50:26" id="a-p555.1" parsed="|Gen|50|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.50.26">Gen. 50:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 12:9" id="a-p555.2" parsed="|2Kgs|12|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.12.9">2 Kings 12:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 12:10" id="a-p555.3" parsed="|2Kgs|12|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.12.10">10</scripRef>). It is
distinguished from all others by such titles as the “ark of God”

(<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 3:3" id="a-p555.4" parsed="|1Sam|3|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.3.3">1 Sam. 3:3</scripRef>), “ark of the covenant” (<scripRef passage="Josh. 3:6" id="a-p555.5" parsed="|Josh|3|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.3.6">Josh. 3:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 9:4" id="a-p555.6" parsed="|Heb|9|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.4">Heb. 9:4</scripRef>), “ark
of the testimony” (<scripRef passage="Ex. 25:22" id="a-p555.7" parsed="|Exod|25|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.25.22">Ex. 25:22</scripRef>). It was made of acacia or shittim
wood, a cubit and a half broad and high and two cubits long, and
covered all over with the purest gold. Its upper surface or lid,
the mercy-seat, was surrounded with a rim of gold; and on each
of the two sides were two gold rings, in which were placed two
gold-covered poles by which the ark could be carried (<scripRef passage="Num. 7:9" id="a-p555.8" parsed="|Num|7|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.7.9">Num. 7:9</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Num 10:21" id="a-p555.9" parsed="|Num|10|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.10.21">10:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 4:5" id="a-p555.10" parsed="|Num|4|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.4.5">4:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num 4:19" id="a-p555.11" parsed="|Num|4|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.4.19">19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num 4:20" id="a-p555.12" parsed="|Num|4|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.4.20">20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 8:3" id="a-p555.13" parsed="|1Kgs|8|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.8.3">1 Kings 8:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 8:6" id="a-p555.14" parsed="|1Kgs|8|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.8.6">6</scripRef>). Over the ark, at the two
extremities, were two cherubim, with their faces turned toward

each other (<scripRef passage="Lev. 16:2" id="a-p555.15" parsed="|Lev|16|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.16.2">Lev. 16:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 7:89" id="a-p555.16" parsed="|Num|7|89|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.7.89">Num. 7:89</scripRef>). Their outspread wings over
the top of the ark formed the throne of God, while the ark

itself was his footstool (<scripRef passage="Ex. 25:10-22" id="a-p555.17" parsed="|Exod|25|10|25|22" osisRef="Bible:Exod.25.10-Exod.25.22">Ex. 25:10-22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 37:1-9" id="a-p555.18" parsed="|Exod|37|1|37|9" osisRef="Bible:Exod.37.1-Exod.37.9">37:1-9</scripRef>). The ark was
deposited in the “holy of holies,” and was so placed that one
end of the poles by which it was carried touched the veil which
separated the two apartments of the tabernacle (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 8:8" id="a-p555.19" parsed="|1Kgs|8|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.8.8">1 Kings 8:8</scripRef>).
The two tables of stone which constituted the “testimony” or
evidence of God’s covenant with the people (<scripRef passage="Deut. 31:26" id="a-p555.20" parsed="|Deut|31|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.31.26">Deut. 31:26</scripRef>), the

“pot of manna” (<scripRef passage="Ex. 16:33" id="a-p555.21" parsed="|Exod|16|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.16.33">Ex. 16:33</scripRef>), and “Aaron’s rod that budded” (<scripRef passage="Num. 17:10" id="a-p555.22" parsed="|Num|17|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.17.10">Num. 17:10</scripRef>), were laid up in the ark (<scripRef passage="Heb. 9:4" id="a-p555.23" parsed="|Heb|9|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.4">Heb. 9:4</scripRef>). (See
TABERNACLE)
The ark and the sanctuary were “the beauty of Israel”
(<scripRef passage="Lam. 2:1" id="a-p555.25" parsed="|Lam|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lam.2.1">Lam. 2:1</scripRef>). During the journeys of the Israelites the ark was

carried by the priests in advance of the host (<scripRef passage="Num. 4:5" id="a-p555.26" parsed="|Num|4|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.4.5">Num. 4:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 4:6" id="a-p555.27" parsed="|Num|4|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.4.6">6</scripRef>;

10:33-36; <scripRef passage="Ps. 68:1" id="a-p555.28" parsed="|Ps|68|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.68.1">Ps. 68:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 132:8" id="a-p555.29" parsed="|Ps|132|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.132.8">132:8</scripRef>). It was borne by the priests into the
bed of the Jordan, which separated, opening a pathway for the

whole of the host to pass over (<scripRef passage="Josh. 3:15" id="a-p555.30" parsed="|Josh|3|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.3.15">Josh. 3:15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 3:16" id="a-p555.31" parsed="|Josh|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.3.16">16</scripRef>; 4:7, 10, 11, 17,

18). It was borne in the procession round Jericho (<scripRef passage="Josh. 6:4" id="a-p555.32" parsed="|Josh|6|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.6.4">Josh. 6:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh 6:6" id="a-p555.33" parsed="|Josh|6|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.6.6">6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh 6:8" id="a-p555.34" parsed="|Josh|6|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.6.8">8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh 6:11" id="a-p555.35" parsed="|Josh|6|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.6.11">11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh 6:12" id="a-p555.36" parsed="|Josh|6|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.6.12">12</scripRef>). When carried it was always wrapped in the veil, the
badgers’ skins, and blue cloth, and carefully concealed even
from the eyes of the Levites who carried it. After the
settlement of Israel in Palestine the ark remained in the
tabernacle at Gilgal for a season, and was then removed to

Shiloh till the time of Eli, between 300 and 400 years (<scripRef passage="Jer. 7:12" id="a-p555.37" parsed="|Jer|7|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.7.12">Jer. 7:12</scripRef>), when it was carried into the field of battle so as to
secure, as they supposed, victory to the Hebrews, and was taken
by the Philistines (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 4:3-11" id="a-p555.38" parsed="|1Sam|4|3|4|11" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.4.3-1Sam.4.11">1 Sam. 4:3-11</scripRef>), who sent it back after

retaining it seven months (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 5:7" id="a-p555.39" parsed="|1Sam|5|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.5.7">1 Sam. 5:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 5:8" id="a-p555.40" parsed="|1Sam|5|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.5.8">8</scripRef>). It remained then at
Kirjath-jearim (7:1, 2) till the time of David (twenty years),
who wished to remove it to Jerusalem; but the proper mode of
removing it having been neglected, Uzzah was smitten with death
for putting “forth his hand to the ark of God,” and in
consequence of this it was left in the house of Obed-edom in
Gath-rimmon for three months (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 6:1-11" id="a-p555.41" parsed="|2Sam|6|1|6|11" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.6.1-2Sam.6.11">2 Sam. 6:1-11</scripRef>), at the end of
which time David removed it in a grand procession to Jerusalem,
where it was kept till a place was prepared for it (12-19). It

was afterwards deposited by Solomon in the temple (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 8:6-9" id="a-p555.42" parsed="|1Kgs|8|6|8|9" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.8.6-1Kgs.8.9">1 Kings 8:6-9</scripRef>). When the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem and plundered
the temple, the ark was probably taken away by Nebuchadnezzar
and destroyed, as no trace of it is afterwards to be found. The
absence of the ark from the second temple was one of the points
in which it was inferior to the first temple.
</def>
<term id="a-p555.43">Arkite</term>
(Gen. 10:17; 1 Chr. 1:15), a designation of certain descendants
from the Phoenicians or Sidonians, the inhabitants of Arka, 12
miles north of Tripoli, opposite the northern extremity of
Lebanon.
</def>
<term id="a-p556.3">Arm</term>
Used to denote power (Ps. 10:15; Ezek. 30:21; Jer. 48:25). It is

also used of the omnipotence of God (<scripRef passage="Ex. 15:16" id="a-p557.4" parsed="|Exod|15|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.15.16">Ex. 15:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 89:13" id="a-p557.5" parsed="|Ps|89|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.89.13">Ps. 89:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 98:1" id="a-p557.6" parsed="|Ps|98|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.98.1">98:1</scripRef>;
77:15; Isa. 53:1; John 12:38; Acts 13:17)
</def>
<term id="a-p557.11">Armageddon</term>
Occurs only in Rev. 16:16 (R.V., “Har-Magedon”), as symbolically
designating the place where the “battle of that great day of God
Almighty” (ver. 14) shall be fought. The word properly means the
“mount of Megiddo.” It is the scene of the final conflict
between Christ and Antichrist. The idea of such a scene was
suggested by the Old Testament great battle-field, the plain of
Esdraelon (q.v.).
</def>
<term id="a-p558.2">Armenia</term>
High land, occurs only in Authorized Version, 2 Kings 19:37; in
Revised Version, “Ararat,” which is the Hebrew word. A country
in western Asia lying between the Caspian and the Black Sea.
Here the ark of Noah rested after the Deluge (<scripRef passage="Gen. 8:4" id="a-p559.2" parsed="|Gen|8|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.8.4">Gen. 8:4</scripRef>). It is
for the most part high table-land, and is watered by the Aras,
the Kur, the Euphrates, and the Tigris. Ararat was properly the
name of a part of ancient Armenia. Three provinces of Armenia
are mentioned in <scripRef passage="Jer. 51:27" id="a-p559.3" parsed="|Jer|51|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.51.27">Jer. 51:27</scripRef>, Ararat, Minni, and Ashchenaz. Some,
however, think Minni a contraction for Armenia. (See ARARAT.)
</def>
<term id="a-p559.5">Armoni</term>
Inhabitant of a fortress, the first-named of the two sons of
Saul and Rizpah. He was delivered up to the Gibeonites by David,
and hanged by them (2 Sam. 21:8, 9).
</def>
<term id="a-p560.3">Armour</term>
Is employed in the English Bible to denote military equipment,
both offensive and defensive.
(1.) The offensive weapons were different at different periods
of history. The “rod of iron” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 2:9" id="a-p562.1" parsed="|Ps|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.2.9">Ps. 2:9</scripRef>) is supposed to mean a
mace or crowbar, an instrument of great power when used by a
strong arm. The “maul” (<scripRef passage="Prov. 25:18" id="a-p562.2" parsed="|Prov|25|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.25.18">Prov. 25:18</scripRef>; cognate Hebrew word
rendered “battle-axe” in <scripRef passage="Jer. 51:20" id="a-p562.3" parsed="|Jer|51|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.51.20">Jer. 51:20</scripRef>, and “slaughter weapon” in
<scripRef passage="Ezek. 9:2" id="a-p562.4" parsed="|Ezek|9|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.9.2">Ezek. 9:2</scripRef>) was a war-hammer or martel. The “sword” is the usual
translation of hereb, which properly means “poniard.” The real
sword, as well as the dirk-sword (which was always

double-edged), was also used (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:39" id="a-p562.5" parsed="|1Sam|17|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.39">1 Sam. 17:39</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 20:8" id="a-p562.6" parsed="|2Sam|20|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.20.8">2 Sam. 20:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 20:11" id="a-p562.7" parsed="|1Kgs|20|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.20.11">1 Kings 20:11</scripRef>). The spear was another offensive weapon (<scripRef passage="Josh. 8:18" id="a-p562.8" parsed="|Josh|8|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.8.18">Josh. 8:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:7" id="a-p562.9" parsed="|1Sam|17|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.7">1 Sam. 17:7</scripRef>). The javelin was used by light troops (<scripRef passage="Num. 25:7" id="a-p562.10" parsed="|Num|25|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.25.7">Num. 25:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 25:8" id="a-p562.11" parsed="|Num|25|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.25.8">8</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 13:22" id="a-p562.12" parsed="|1Sam|13|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.13.22">1 Sam. 13:22</scripRef>). Saul threw a javelin at David (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 19:9" id="a-p562.13" parsed="|1Sam|19|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.19.9">1 Sam. 19:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 19:10" id="a-p562.14" parsed="|1Sam|19|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.19.10">10</scripRef>),
and so virtually absolved him from his allegiance. The bow was,
however, the chief weapon of offence. The arrows were carried in
a quiver, the bow being always unbent till the moment of action

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 27:3" id="a-p562.15" parsed="|Gen|27|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.3">Gen. 27:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 48:22" id="a-p562.16" parsed="|Gen|48|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.48.22">48:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 18:34" id="a-p562.17" parsed="|Ps|18|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.18.34">Ps. 18:34</scripRef>). The sling was a favourite weapon
of the Benjamites (1 Sam. 17:40; 1 Chr. 12:2. Comp. 1 Sam. 25:29).
(2.) Of the defensive armour a chief place is assigned to the
shield or buckler. There were the great shield or target (the
tzinnah), for the protection of the whole person (Gen. 15:1;

<scripRef passage="Ps. 47:9" id="a-p563.2" parsed="|Ps|47|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.47.9">Ps. 47:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:7" id="a-p563.3" parsed="|1Sam|17|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.7">1 Sam. 17:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 30:5" id="a-p563.4" parsed="|Prov|30|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.30.5">Prov. 30:5</scripRef>), and the buckler (Heb.
mageen) or small shield (1 Kings 10:17; Ezek. 26:8). In Ps. 91:4 “buckler” is properly a roundel appropriated to archers or

slingers. The helmet (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:10" id="a-p563.8" parsed="|Ezek|27|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.10">Ezek. 27:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:38" id="a-p563.9" parsed="|1Sam|17|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.38">1 Sam. 17:38</scripRef>), a covering for
the head; the coat of mail or corselet (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:5" id="a-p563.10" parsed="|1Sam|17|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.5">1 Sam. 17:5</scripRef>), or

habergeon (<scripRef passage="Neh. 4" id="a-p563.11" parsed="|Neh|4|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.4">Neh. 4</scripRef>;<scripRef passage="Neh 16" id="a-p563.12" parsed="|Neh|16|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.16">16</scripRef>), harness or breat-plate (<scripRef passage="Rev. 9:9" id="a-p563.13" parsed="|Rev|9|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.9.9">Rev. 9:9</scripRef>), for

the covering of the back and breast and both upper arms (<scripRef passage="Isa. 59:17" id="a-p563.14" parsed="|Isa|59|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.59.17">Isa. 59:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 6:14" id="a-p563.15" parsed="|Eph|6|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.6.14">Eph. 6:14</scripRef>). The cuirass and corselet, composed of leather
or quilted cloth, were also for the covering of the body.
Greaves, for the covering of the legs, were worn in the time of

David (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:6" id="a-p563.16" parsed="|1Sam|17|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.6">1 Sam. 17:6</scripRef>). Reference is made by Paul (<scripRef passage="Eph. 6:14-17" id="a-p563.17" parsed="|Eph|6|14|6|17" osisRef="Bible:Eph.6.14-Eph.6.17">Eph. 6:14-17</scripRef>) to
the panoply of a Roman soldier. The shield here is the thureon,
a door-like oblong shield above all, i.e., covering the whole
person, not the small round shield. There is no armour for the
back, but only for the front.
</def>
<term id="a-p563.18">Armour-bearer</term>
An officer selected by kings and generals because of his
bravery, not only to bear their armour, but also to stand by
them in the time of danger. They were the adjutants of our
modern armies (Judg. 9:54; 1 Sam. 14:7; 16:21; 31:6).
</def>
<term id="a-p564.5">Armoury</term>
The place in which armour was deposited when not used (Neh. 3:19; Jer. 50:25). At first each man of the Hebrews had his own
arms, because all went to war. There were no arsenals or
magazines for arms till the time of David, who had a large
collection of arms, which he consecrated to the Lord in his
tabernacle (1 Sa,. 21:9; 2 Sam. 8:7-12; 1 Chr. 26:26, 27).
</def>
<term id="a-p565.6">Army</term>
The Israelites marched out of Egypt in military order (Ex. 13:18, “harnessed;” marg., “five in a rank”). Each tribe formed

a battalion, with its own banner and leader (<scripRef passage="Num. 2:2" id="a-p566.2" parsed="|Num|2|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.2.2">Num. 2:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 10:14" id="a-p566.3" parsed="|Num|10|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.10.14">10:14</scripRef>).
In war the army was divided into thousands and hundreds under
their several captains (<scripRef passage="Num. 31:14" id="a-p566.4" parsed="|Num|31|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.31.14">Num. 31:14</scripRef>), and also into families

(<scripRef passage="Num. 2:34" id="a-p566.5" parsed="|Num|2|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.2.34">Num. 2:34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 25:5" id="a-p566.6" parsed="|2Chr|25|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.25.5">2 Chr. 25:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 26:12" id="a-p566.7" parsed="|2Chr|26|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.26.12">26:12</scripRef>). From the time of their entering
the land of Canaan to the time of the kings, the Israelites made
little progress in military affairs, although often engaged in
warfare. The kings introduced the custom of maintaining a
bodyguard (the Gibborim; i.e., “heroes”), and thus the nucleus
of a standing army was formed. Saul had an army of 3,000 select

warriors (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 13:2" id="a-p566.8" parsed="|1Sam|13|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.13.2">1 Sam. 13:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 14:52" id="a-p566.9" parsed="|1Sam|14|52|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.14.52">14:52</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 24:2" id="a-p566.10" parsed="|1Sam|24|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.24.2">24:2</scripRef>). David also had a band of

soldiers around him (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 23:13" id="a-p566.11" parsed="|1Sam|23|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.23.13">1 Sam. 23:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 25:13" id="a-p566.12" parsed="|1Sam|25|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.25.13">25:13</scripRef>). To this band he

afterwards added the Cherethites and the Pelethites (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 15:18" id="a-p566.13" parsed="|2Sam|15|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.15.18">2 Sam. 15:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 20:7" id="a-p566.14" parsed="|2Sam|20|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.20.7">20:7</scripRef>). At first the army consisted only of infantry (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 4:10" id="a-p566.15" parsed="|1Sam|4|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.4.10">1 Sam. 4:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 15:4" id="a-p566.16" parsed="|1Sam|15|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.15.4">15:4</scripRef>), as the use of horses was prohibited (<scripRef passage="Deut. 17:16" id="a-p566.17" parsed="|Deut|17|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.17.16">Deut. 17:16</scripRef>); but chariots and horses were afterwards added (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 8:4" id="a-p566.18" parsed="|2Sam|8|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.8.4">2 Sam. 8:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:26" id="a-p566.19" parsed="|1Kgs|10|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.26">1 Kings 10:26</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:28" id="a-p566.20" parsed="|1Kgs|10|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.28">28</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:29" id="a-p566.21" parsed="|1Kgs|10|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.29">29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 9:19" id="a-p566.22" parsed="|1Kgs|9|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.9.19">1 Kings 9:19</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="1 Kings 9:22" id="a-p566.23" parsed="|1Kgs|9|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.9.22">1 Kings 9:22</scripRef> there
is given a list of the various gradations of rank held by those
who composed the army. The equipment and maintenance of the army

were at the public expense (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 17:28" id="a-p566.24" parsed="|2Sam|17|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.17.28">2 Sam. 17:28</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 17:29" id="a-p566.25" parsed="|2Sam|17|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.17.29">29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:27" id="a-p566.26" parsed="|1Kgs|4|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.27">1 Kings 4:27</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:16" id="a-p566.27" parsed="|1Kgs|10|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.16">10:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:17" id="a-p566.28" parsed="|1Kgs|10|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.17">17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 20:10" id="a-p566.29" parsed="|Judg|20|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.20.10">Judg. 20:10</scripRef>). At the Exodus the number of males above
twenty years capable of bearing arms was 600,000 (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:37" id="a-p566.30" parsed="|Exod|12|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.37">Ex. 12:37</scripRef>). In
David’s time it mounted to the number of 1,300,000 (2 Sam. 24:9).
</def>
<term id="a-p566.32">Arnon</term>
Swift, the southern boundary of the territory of Israel beyond

Jordan, separating it from the land of Moab (<scripRef passage="Deut. 3:8" id="a-p567.1" parsed="|Deut|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.8">Deut. 3:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 3:16" id="a-p567.2" parsed="|Deut|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.16">16</scripRef>).
This river (referred to twenty-four times in the Bible) rises in
the mountains of Gilead, and after a circuitous course of about
80 miles through a deep ravine it falls into the Dead Sea nearly
opposite Engedi. The stream is almost dry in summer. It is now
called el-Mujeb. The territory of the Amorites extended from the
Arnon to the Jabbok.
</def>
<term id="a-p567.3">Aroer</term>
Ruins. (1.) A town on the north bank of the Arnon (Deut. 4:48;

<scripRef passage="Judg. 11:26" id="a-p568.2" parsed="|Judg|11|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.11.26">Judg. 11:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 10:33" id="a-p568.3" parsed="|2Kgs|10|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.10.33">2 Kings 10:33</scripRef>), the southern boundary of the
kingdom of Sihon (<scripRef passage="Josh. 12:2" id="a-p568.4" parsed="|Josh|12|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.12.2">Josh. 12:2</scripRef>). It is now called Arair, 13 miles
west of the Dead Sea.
(2.) One of the towns built by the tribe of Gad (Num. 32:34)
“before Rabbah” (<scripRef passage="Josh. 13:25" id="a-p569.2" parsed="|Josh|13|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.25">Josh. 13:25</scripRef>), the Ammonite capital. It was
famous in the history of Jephthah (Judg. 11:33) and of David (2 Sam. 24:5). (Comp. Isa. 17:2; 2 Kings 15:29.)
(3.) A city in the south of Judah, 12 miles south-east of
Beersheba, to which David sent presents after recovering the

spoil from the Amalekites at Ziklag (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 30:26" id="a-p570.1" parsed="|1Sam|30|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.30.26">1 Sam. 30:26</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 30:28" id="a-p570.2" parsed="|1Sam|30|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.30.28">28</scripRef>). It was
the native city of two of David’s warriors (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 11:44" id="a-p570.3" parsed="|1Chr|11|44|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.11.44">1 Chr. 11:44</scripRef>). It is
now called Ar’arah.
</def>
<term id="a-p570.4">Arpad</term>
(Isa. 10:9; 36:19; 37:13), also Arphad, support, a Syrian city

near Hamath, along with which it is invariably mentioned (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 19:13" id="a-p571.4" parsed="|2Kgs|19|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.19.13">2 Kings 19:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:34" id="a-p571.5" parsed="|2Kgs|18|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.34">18:34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 10:9" id="a-p571.6" parsed="|Isa|10|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.9">Isa. 10:9</scripRef>), and Damascus (<scripRef passage="Jer. 49:23" id="a-p571.7" parsed="|Jer|49|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.49.23">Jer. 49:23</scripRef>). After
a siege of three years it fell (B.C. 742) before the Assyrian
king Tiglath-pileser II. Now Tell Erfud.
</def>
<term id="a-p571.8">Arphaxad</term>
Son of Shem, born the year after the Deluge. He died at the age

of 438 years (<scripRef passage="Gen. 11:10-13" id="a-p572.1" parsed="|Gen|11|10|11|13" osisRef="Bible:Gen.11.10-Gen.11.13">Gen. 11:10-13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 1:17" id="a-p572.2" parsed="|1Chr|1|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.1.17">1 Chr. 1:17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 1:18" id="a-p572.3" parsed="|1Chr|1|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.1.18">18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 3:36" id="a-p572.4" parsed="|Luke|3|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.36">Luke 3:36</scripRef>). He
dwelt in Mesopotamia, and became, according to the Jewish
historian Josephus, the progenitor of the Chaldeans. The
tendency is to recognize in the word the name of the country
nearest the ancient domain of the Chaldeans. Some regard the
word as an Egypticized form of the territorial name of Ur
Kasdim, or Ur of the Chaldees.
</def>
<term id="a-p572.5">Arrows</term>
At first made of reeds, and then of wood tipped with iron.

Arrows are sometimes figuratively put for lightning (<scripRef passage="Deut. 32:23" id="a-p573.1" parsed="|Deut|32|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.23">Deut. 32:23</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut 32:42" id="a-p573.2" parsed="|Deut|32|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.42">42</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 7:13" id="a-p573.3" parsed="|Ps|7|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.7.13">Ps. 7:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 18:14" id="a-p573.4" parsed="|Ps|18|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.18.14">18:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 144:6" id="a-p573.5" parsed="|Ps|144|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.144.6">144:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 9:14" id="a-p573.6" parsed="|Zech|9|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.9.14">Zech. 9:14</scripRef>). They were used

in war as well as in the chase (<scripRef passage="Gen. 27:3" id="a-p573.7" parsed="|Gen|27|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.3">Gen. 27:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 49:23" id="a-p573.8" parsed="|Gen|49|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.23">49:23</scripRef>). They were
also used in divination (Ezek. 21:21).
The word is frequently employed as a symbol of calamity or

disease inflicted by God (<scripRef passage="Job 6:4" id="a-p574.1" parsed="|Job|6|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.6.4">Job 6:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 34:6" id="a-p574.2" parsed="|Job|34|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.34.6">34:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 38:2" id="a-p574.3" parsed="|Ps|38|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.38.2">Ps. 38:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 32:23" id="a-p574.4" parsed="|Deut|32|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.23">Deut. 32:23</scripRef>.

Comp. <scripRef passage="Ezek. 5:16" id="a-p574.5" parsed="|Ezek|5|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.5.16">Ezek. 5:16</scripRef>), or of some sudden danger (<scripRef passage="Ps. 91:5" id="a-p574.6" parsed="|Ps|91|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.91.5">Ps. 91:5</scripRef>), or
bitter words (Ps. 64:3), or false testimony (Prov. 25:18).
</def>
<term id="a-p574.9">Artaxerxes</term>
The Greek form of the name of several Persian kings. (1.) The
king who obstructed the rebuilding of the temple (<scripRef passage="Ezra 4:7" id="a-p575.1" parsed="|Ezra|4|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.4.7">Ezra 4:7</scripRef>). He
was probably the Smerdis of profane history.
(2.) The king mentioned in Ezra 7:1, in the seventh year (B.C.
458) of whose reign Ezra led a second colony of Jews back to
Jerusalem, was probably Longimanus, who reigned for forty years
(B.C. 464-425); the grandson of Darius, who, fourteen years
later, permitted Nehemiah to return and rebuild Jerusalem.
</def>
<term id="a-p576.2">Artificer</term>
A person engaged in any kind of manual occupation (Gen. 4:22;
Isa. 3:3).
</def>
<term id="a-p577.3">Artillery</term>
1 Sam. 20:40, (Heb. keli, meaning “apparatus;” here meaning
collectively any missile weapons, as arrows and lances. In
Revised Version, “weapons”). This word is derived from the Latin
artillaria = equipment of war.
</def>
<term id="a-p578.2">Arvad</term>
Wandering, (Ezek. 27:8), a small island and city on the coast of
Syria, mentioned as furnishing mariners and soldiers for Tyre.
The inhabitants were called Arvadites. The name is written
Aruada or Arada in the Tell-el-Amarna tablets.
</def>
<term id="a-p579.2">Asa</term>
Physician, son of Abijah and grandson of Rehoboam, was the third
king of Judah. He was zealous in maintaining the true worship of
God, and in rooting all idolatry, with its accompanying
immoralities, out of the land (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 15:8-14" id="a-p580.1" parsed="|1Kgs|15|8|15|14" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.15.8-1Kgs.15.14">1 Kings 15:8-14</scripRef>). The Lord gave
him and his land rest and prosperity. It is recorded of him,
however, that in his old age, when afflicted, he “sought not to
the Lord, but to the physicians” (comp. <scripRef passage="Jer. 17:5" id="a-p580.2" parsed="|Jer|17|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.17.5">Jer. 17:5</scripRef>). He died in
the forty-first year of his reign, greatly honoured by his
people (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 16:1-13" id="a-p580.3" parsed="|2Chr|16|1|16|13" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.16.1-2Chr.16.13">2 Chr. 16:1-13</scripRef>), and was succeeded by his son
Jehoshaphat.
</def>
<term id="a-p580.4">Asahel</term>
Made by God, the youngest son of Zeruiah, David’s sister. He was
celebrated for his swiftness of foot. When fighting against
Ish-bosheth at Gibeon, in the army of his brother Joab, he was
put to death by Abner, whom he pursued from the field of battle

(<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 2:18" id="a-p581.1" parsed="|2Sam|2|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.2.18">2 Sam. 2:18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 2:19" id="a-p581.2" parsed="|2Sam|2|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.2.19">19</scripRef>). He is mentioned among David’s thirty mighty

men (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 23:24" id="a-p581.3" parsed="|2Sam|23|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.23.24">2 Sam. 23:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 11:26" id="a-p581.4" parsed="|1Chr|11|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.11.26">1 Chr. 11:26</scripRef>). Others of the same name are
mentioned (2 Chr. 17:8; 31:13; Ezra 10:15).
</def>
<term id="a-p581.8">Asaph</term>
Convener, or collector. (1.) A Levite; one of the leaders of

David’s choir (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 6:39" id="a-p582.1" parsed="|1Chr|6|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.6.39">1 Chr. 6:39</scripRef>). <scripRef passage="Psalms 50" id="a-p582.2" parsed="|Ps|50|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.50">Psalms 50</scripRef> and 73-83 inclusive are
attributed to him. He is mentioned along with David as skilled
in music, and a “seer” (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 29:30" id="a-p582.3" parsed="|2Chr|29|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.29.30">2 Chr. 29:30</scripRef>). The “sons of Asaph,”

mentioned in <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 25:1" id="a-p582.4" parsed="|1Chr|25|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.25.1">1 Chr. 25:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 25:2" id="a-p582.5" parsed="|1Chr|25|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.25.2">2</scripRef> Chr. 20:14, and <scripRef passage="Ezra 2:41" id="a-p582.6" parsed="|Ezra|2|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2.41">Ezra 2:41</scripRef>, were his
descendants, or more probably a class of poets or singers who
recognized him as their master.
(2.) The “recorder” in the time of Hezekiah (2 Kings 18:18, 37).
(3.) The “keeper of the king’s forest,” to whom Nehemiah
requested from Artaxerxes a “letter” that he might give him
timber for the temple at Jerusalem (Neh. 2:8).
</def>
<term id="a-p584.2">Ascension</term>
See CHRIST.
</def>
<term id="a-p585.2">Asenath</term>
An Egyptian name, meaning “gift of the sun-god”, daughter of

Potipherah, priest of On or Heliopolis, wife of Joseph (<scripRef passage="Gen. 41:45" id="a-p586.1" parsed="|Gen|41|45|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.41.45">Gen. 41:45</scripRef>). She was the mother of Manasseh and Ephraim (50-52;
</def>
<term id="a-p586.2">Ash</term>
(Heb. o’ren, “tremulous”), mentioned only Isa. 44:14 (R.V., “fir
tree”). It is rendered “pine tree” both in the LXX. and Vulgate
versions. There is a tree called by the Arabs aran, found
still in the valleys of Arabia Petraea, whose leaf resembles
that of the mountain ash. This may be the tree meant. Our ash
tree is not known in Syria.
</def>
<term id="a-p587.2">Ashdod</term>
Stronghold, a Philistine city (Josh. 15:47), about midway
between Gaza and Joppa, and 3 miles from the Mediterranean. It
was one of the chief seats of the worship of Dagon (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 5:5" id="a-p588.2" parsed="|1Sam|5|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.5.5">1 Sam. 5:5</scripRef>).
It belonged to the tribe of Judah (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:47" id="a-p588.3" parsed="|Josh|15|47|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.47">Josh. 15:47</scripRef>), but it never
came into their actual possession. It was an important city, as
it stood on the highroad from Egypt to Palestine, and hence was

strongly fortified (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 26:6" id="a-p588.4" parsed="|2Chr|26|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.26.6">2 Chr. 26:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 20:1" id="a-p588.5" parsed="|Isa|20|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.20.1">Isa. 20:1</scripRef>). Uzziah took it, but
fifty years after his death it was taken by the Assyrians (B.C.
758). According to Sargon’s record, it was captured by him in
B.C. 711. The only reference to it in the New Testament, where
it is called Azotus, is in the account of Philip’s return from
Gaza (Acts 8:40). It is now called Eshdud.
</def>
<term id="a-p588.7">Ashdoth-pisgah</term>
(Deut. 3:17; Josh. 12:3; 13:20) in Authorized Version, but in
Revised Version translated “slopes of Pisgah.” In <scripRef passage="Deut. 4:49" id="a-p589.4" parsed="|Deut|4|49|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.4.49">Deut. 4:49</scripRef> it
is translated in the Authorized Version “springs of Pisgah.” The
name Ashdoth is translated “springs” in the Authorized Version,
but “slopes” in the Revised Version, of <scripRef passage="Josh. 10:40" id="a-p589.5" parsed="|Josh|10|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.40">Josh. 10:40</scripRef> and 12:8. It
has been identified with the springs under Mount Nebo, now
called ‘Ayun Musa.
</def>
<term id="a-p589.6">Asher</term>
Happy, Jacob’s eigth son; his mother was Zilpah, Leah’s handmaid
(<scripRef passage="Gen. 30:13" id="a-p590.1" parsed="|Gen|30|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.30.13">Gen. 30:13</scripRef>). Of the tribe founded by him nothing is recorded
beyond its holding a place in the list of the tribes (35:26;
46:17; <scripRef passage="Ex. 1:4" id="a-p590.2" parsed="|Exod|1|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.1.4">Ex. 1:4</scripRef>, etc.) It increased in numbers twenty-nine
percent, during the thirty-eight years’ wanderings. The place of
this tribe during the march through the desert was between Dan
and Naphtali (<scripRef passage="Num. 2:27" id="a-p590.3" parsed="|Num|2|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.2.27">Num. 2:27</scripRef>). The boundaries of the inheritance
given to it, which contained some of the richest soil in

Palestine, and the names of its towns, are recorded in <scripRef passage="Josh. 19:24-31" id="a-p590.4" parsed="|Josh|19|24|19|31" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.24-Josh.19.31">Josh. 19:24-31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 1:31" id="a-p590.5" parsed="|Judg|1|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.31">Judg. 1:31</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Judg. 1:32" id="a-p590.6" parsed="|Judg|1|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.32">32</scripRef>. Asher and Simeon were the only tribes
west of the Jordan which furnished no hero or judge for the
nation. Anna the prophetess was of this tribe (Luke 2:36).
</def>
<term id="a-p590.8">Asherah</term>
And pl. Asherim in Revised Version, instead of “grove” and
“groves” of the Authorized Version. This was the name of a
sensual Canaanitish goddess Astarte, the feminine of the
Assyrian Ishtar. Its symbol was the stem of a tree deprived of
its boughs, and rudely shaped into an image, and planted in the
ground. Such religious symbols (“groves”) are frequently alluded

to in Scripture (<scripRef passage="Ex. 34:13" id="a-p591.1" parsed="|Exod|34|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.34.13">Ex. 34:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 6:25" id="a-p591.2" parsed="|Judg|6|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.6.25">Judg. 6:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 23:6" id="a-p591.3" parsed="|2Kgs|23|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.6">2 Kings 23:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 16:33" id="a-p591.4" parsed="|1Kgs|16|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.16.33">1 Kings 16:33</scripRef>, etc.). These images were also sometimes made of silver or
of carved stone (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 21:7" id="a-p591.5" parsed="|2Kgs|21|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.21.7">2 Kings 21:7</scripRef>; “the graven image of Asherah,”
R.V.). (See GROVE [1].).
</def>
<term id="a-p591.7">Ashes</term>
The ashes of a red heifer burned entire (Num. 19:5) when
sprinkled on the unclean made them ceremonially clean (Heb. 9:13).
To cover the head with ashes was a token of self-abhorrence
and humiliation (2 Sam. 13:19; Esther 4:3; Jer. 6:26, etc.).
To feed on ashes (Isa. 44:20), means to seek that which will
prove to be vain and unsatisfactory, and hence it denotes the
unsatisfactory nature of idol-worship. (Comp. Hos. 12:1).
</def>
<term id="a-p594.3">Ashkelon</term>
=Askelon=Ascalon, was one of the five cities of the Philistines

(<scripRef passage="Josh. 13:3" id="a-p595.1" parsed="|Josh|13|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.3">Josh. 13:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 6:17" id="a-p595.2" parsed="|1Sam|6|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.6.17">1 Sam. 6:17</scripRef>). It stood on the shore of the
Mediterranean, 12 miles north of Gaza. It is mentioned on an
inscription at Karnak in Egypt as having been taken by king
Rameses II., the oppressor of the Hebrews. In the time of the
judges (<scripRef passage="Judg. 1:18" id="a-p595.3" parsed="|Judg|1|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.18">Judg. 1:18</scripRef>) it fell into the possession of the tribe of

Judah; but it was soon after retaken by the Philistines (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 1:20" id="a-p595.4" parsed="|2Sam|1|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.1.20">2 Sam. 1:20</scripRef>), who were not finally dispossessed till the time of
Alexander the Great. Samson went down to this place from
Timnath, and slew thirty men and took their spoil. The prophets

foretold its destruction (<scripRef passage="Jer. 25:20" id="a-p595.5" parsed="|Jer|25|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.25.20">Jer. 25:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 47:5" id="a-p595.6" parsed="|Jer|47|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.47.5">47:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer 47:7" id="a-p595.7" parsed="|Jer|47|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.47.7">7</scripRef>). It became a
noted place in the Middle Ages, having been the scene of many a
bloody battle between the Saracens and the Crusaders. It was
beseiged and taken by Richard the Lion-hearted, and “within its
walls and towers now standing he held his court.” Among the Tell
Amarna tablets (see EGYPT) are found letters or
official despatches from Yadaya, “captain of horse and dust of
the king’s feet,” to the “great king” of Egypt, dated from
Ascalon. It is now called ‘Askalan.
</def>
<term id="a-p595.9">Ashkenaz</term>
One of the three sons of Gomer (Gen. 10:3), and founder of one
of the tribes of the Japhetic race. They are mentioned in
connection with Minni and Ararat, and hence their original seat
must have been in Armenia (<scripRef passage="Jer. 51:27" id="a-p596.2" parsed="|Jer|51|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.51.27">Jer. 51:27</scripRef>), probably near the Black
Sea, which, from their founder, was first called Axenus, and
afterwards the Euxine.
</def>
<term id="a-p596.3">Ashpenaz</term>
The master of the eunuchs of Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. 1:3), the
“Rabsaris” of the court. His position was similar to that of the
Kislar-aga of the modern Turkish sultans.
</def>
<term id="a-p597.2">Ashtaroth</term>
A city of Bashan, in the kingdom of Og (Deut. 1:4; Josh. 12:4;

<scripRef passage="Josh 13:12" id="a-p598.3" parsed="|Josh|13|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.12">13:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 9:10" id="a-p598.4" parsed="|Josh|9|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.9.10">9:10</scripRef>). It was in the half-tribe of Manasseh (<scripRef passage="Josh. 13:12" id="a-p598.5" parsed="|Josh|13|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.12">Josh. 13:12</scripRef>), and as a Levitical city was given to the Gershonites (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 6:71" id="a-p598.6" parsed="|1Chr|6|71|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.6.71">1 Chr. 6:71</scripRef>). Uzzia, one of David’s valiant men (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 11:44" id="a-p598.7" parsed="|1Chr|11|44|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.11.44">1 Chr. 11:44</scripRef>), is
named as of this city. It is identified with Tell Ashterah, in
the Hauran, and is noticed on monuments B.C. 1700-1500. The name
Beesh-terah (<scripRef passage="Josh. 21:27" id="a-p598.8" parsed="|Josh|21|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.21.27">Josh. 21:27</scripRef>) is a contraction for Beth-eshterah,
i.e., “the house of Ashtaroth.”
</def>
<term id="a-p598.9">Ashteroth Karnaim</term>
Ashteroth of the two horns, the abode of the Rephaim (Gen. 14:5). It may be identified with Ashtaroth preceding; called
“Karnaim”, i.e., the “two-horned” (the crescent moon). The
Samaritan version renders the word by “Sunamein,” the present
es-Sunamein, 28 miles south of Damascus.
</def>
<term id="a-p599.2">Ashtoreth</term>
The moon goddess of the Phoenicians, representing the passive
principle in nature, their principal female deity; frequently
associated with the name of Baal, the sun-god, their chief male

deity (<scripRef passage="Judg. 10:6" id="a-p600.1" parsed="|Judg|10|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.10.6">Judg. 10:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 7:4" id="a-p600.2" parsed="|1Sam|7|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.7.4">1 Sam. 7:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 12:10" id="a-p600.3" parsed="|1Sam|12|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.12.10">12:10</scripRef>). These names often occur
in the plural (Ashtaroth, Baalim), probably as indicating either
different statues or different modifications of the deities.
This deity is spoken of as Ashtoreth of the Zidonians. She was

the Ishtar of the Accadians and the Astarte of the Greeks (<scripRef passage="Jer. 44:17" id="a-p600.4" parsed="|Jer|44|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.44.17">Jer. 44:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 11:5" id="a-p600.5" parsed="|1Kgs|11|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.11.5">1 Kings 11:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 11:33" id="a-p600.6" parsed="|1Kgs|11|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.11.33">33</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 23:13" id="a-p600.7" parsed="|2Kgs|23|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.13">2 Kings 23:13</scripRef>). There was a temple of

this goddess among the Philistines in the time of Saul (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 31:10" id="a-p600.8" parsed="|1Sam|31|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.31.10">1 Sam. 31:10</scripRef>). Under the name of Ishtar, she was one of the great
deities of the Assyrians. The Phoenicians called her Astarte.
Solomon introduced the worship of this idol (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 11:33" id="a-p600.9" parsed="|1Kgs|11|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.11.33">1 Kings 11:33</scripRef>).
Jezebel’s 400 priests were probably employed in its service (1 Kings 18:19). It was called the “queen of heaven” (Jer. 44:25).
</def>
<term id="a-p600.12">Ashurites</term>
Mentioned among those over whom Ish-bosheth was made king (2 Sam. 2:9).
</def>
<term id="a-p601.2">Asia</term>
Is used to denote Proconsular Asia, a Roman province which
embraced the western parts of Asia Minor, and of which Ephesus

was the capital, in <scripRef passage="Acts 2:9" id="a-p602.1" parsed="|Acts|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.2.9">Acts 2:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 6:9" id="a-p602.2" parsed="|Acts|6|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.6.9">6:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 16:6" id="a-p602.3" parsed="|Acts|16|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.16.6">16:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 19:10" id="a-p602.4" parsed="|Acts|19|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.10">19:10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 19:22" id="a-p602.5" parsed="|Acts|19|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.22">22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 20:4" id="a-p602.6" parsed="|Acts|20|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.4">20:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 20:16" id="a-p602.7" parsed="|Acts|20|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.16">16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 20:18" id="a-p602.8" parsed="|Acts|20|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.18">18</scripRef>,

etc., and probably Asia Minor in <scripRef passage="Acts 19:26" id="a-p602.9" parsed="|Acts|19|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.26">Acts 19:26</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 19:27" id="a-p602.10" parsed="|Acts|19|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.27">27</scripRef>; 21:27; 24:18;
27:2. Proconsular Asia contained the seven churches of the

Apocalypse (<scripRef passage="Rev. 1:11" id="a-p602.11" parsed="|Rev|1|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.1.11">Rev. 1:11</scripRef>). The “chiefs of Asia” (<scripRef passage="Acts 19:31" id="a-p602.12" parsed="|Acts|19|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.31">Acts 19:31</scripRef>) were
certain wealthy citizens who were annually elected to preside
over the games and religious festivals of the several cities to
which they belonged. Some of these “Asiarchs” were Paul’s
friends.
</def>
<term id="a-p602.13">Asnapper</term>
Probably the same as Assur-bani-pal (Sardanapalos of the
Greeks), styled the “great and noble” (<scripRef passage="Ezra 4:10" id="a-p603.1" parsed="|Ezra|4|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.4.10">Ezra 4:10</scripRef>), was the son
and successor (B.C. 668) of Esar-haddon (q.v.). He was
“luxurious, ambitious, and cruel, but a magnificent patron of
literature.” He formed at Nineveh a library of clay tablets,
numbering about 10,000. These are now mostly in the British
Museum. They throw much light on the history and antiquities of
Assyria.
Assur-bani-pal was a munificent patron of literature, and the
conqueror of Elam. Towards the middle of his reign his empire
was shaken by a great rebellion headed by his brother in
Babylon. The rebellion was finally put down, but Egypt was lost,
and the military power of Assyria was so exhausted that it could
with difficulty resist the hordes of Kimmerians who poured over
Western Asia. (See NINEVEH.)
</def>
<term id="a-p604.2">Asp</term>
(Heb. pethen), Deut. 32:33; Job 20:14, 16; Isa. 11:8. It was
probably the Egyptian cobra (Naja haje), which was very
poisonous (<scripRef passage="Rom. 3:13" id="a-p605.5" parsed="|Rom|3|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.3.13">Rom. 3:13</scripRef>; Gr. aspis). The Egyptians worshipped it as
the uraeus, and it was found in the desert and in the fields.
The peace and security of Messiah’s reign is represented by the
figure of a child playing on the hole of the asp. (See ADDER.)
</def>
<term id="a-p605.7">Ass</term>
Frequently mentioned throughout Scripture. Of the domesticated
species we read of, (1.) The she ass (Heb. ‘athon), so named

from its slowness (<scripRef passage="Gen. 12:16" id="a-p606.1" parsed="|Gen|12|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.12.16">Gen. 12:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 45:23" id="a-p606.2" parsed="|Gen|45|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.45.23">45:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 22:23" id="a-p606.3" parsed="|Num|22|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.22.23">Num. 22:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 9:3" id="a-p606.4" parsed="|1Sam|9|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.9.3">1 Sam. 9:3</scripRef>).
(2.) The male ass (Heb. hamor), the common working ass of
Western Asia, so called from its red colour. Issachar is
compared to a strong ass (<scripRef passage="Gen. 49:14" id="a-p606.5" parsed="|Gen|49|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.14">Gen. 49:14</scripRef>). It was forbidden to yoke
together an ass and an ox in the plough (<scripRef passage="Deut. 22:10" id="a-p606.6" parsed="|Deut|22|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.22.10">Deut. 22:10</scripRef>). (3.) The

ass’s colt (Heb. ‘air), mentioned <scripRef passage="Judg. 10:4" id="a-p606.7" parsed="|Judg|10|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.10.4">Judg. 10:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg 12:14" id="a-p606.8" parsed="|Judg|12|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.12.14">12:14</scripRef>. It is

rendered “foal” in <scripRef passage="Gen. 32:15" id="a-p606.9" parsed="|Gen|32|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.32.15">Gen. 32:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 49:11" id="a-p606.10" parsed="|Gen|49|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.11">49:11</scripRef>. (Comp. <scripRef passage="Job 11:12" id="a-p606.11" parsed="|Job|11|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.11.12">Job 11:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 30:6" id="a-p606.12" parsed="|Isa|30|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.30.6">Isa. 30:6</scripRef>.) The ass is an unclean animal, because it does not chew

the cud (<scripRef passage="Lev. 11:26" id="a-p606.13" parsed="|Lev|11|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.11.26">Lev. 11:26</scripRef>. Comp. <scripRef passage="2 Kings 6:25" id="a-p606.14" parsed="|2Kgs|6|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.6.25">2 Kings 6:25</scripRef>). Asses constituted a
considerable portion of wealth in ancient times (<scripRef passage="Gen. 12:16" id="a-p606.15" parsed="|Gen|12|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.12.16">Gen. 12:16</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Gen 30:43" id="a-p606.16" parsed="|Gen|30|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.30.43">30:43</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 27:30" id="a-p606.17" parsed="|1Chr|27|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.27.30">1 Chr. 27:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 1:3" id="a-p606.18" parsed="|Job|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.1.3">Job 1:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 42:12" id="a-p606.19" parsed="|Job|42|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.42.12">42:12</scripRef>). They were noted for their
spirit and their attachment to their master (<scripRef passage="Isa. 1:3" id="a-p606.20" parsed="|Isa|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.3">Isa. 1:3</scripRef>). They are
frequently spoken of as having been ridden upon, as by Abraham

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 22:3" id="a-p606.21" parsed="|Gen|22|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.22.3">Gen. 22:3</scripRef>), Balaam (<scripRef passage="Num. 22:21" id="a-p606.22" parsed="|Num|22|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.22.21">Num. 22:21</scripRef>), the disobedient prophet (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 13:23" id="a-p606.23" parsed="|1Kgs|13|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.13.23">1 Kings 13:23</scripRef>), the family of Abdon the judge, seventy in number

(<scripRef passage="Judg. 12:14" id="a-p606.24" parsed="|Judg|12|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.12.14">Judg. 12:14</scripRef>), Zipporah (<scripRef passage="Ex. 4:20" id="a-p606.25" parsed="|Exod|4|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.4.20">Ex. 4:20</scripRef>), the Shunammite (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 25:30" id="a-p606.26" parsed="|1Sam|25|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.25.30">1 Sam. 25:30</scripRef>), etc. Zechariah (9:9) predicted our Lord’s triumphal
entrance into Jerusalem, “riding upon an ass, and upon a colt,”
etc. (Matt. 21:5, R.V.).
Of wild asses two species are noticed, (1) that called in
Hebrew ’arod, mentioned Job 39:5 and Dan. 5:21, noted for its
swiftness; and (2) that called pe’re, the wild ass of Asia

(<scripRef passage="Job 39:6-8" id="a-p607.3" parsed="|Job|39|6|39|8" osisRef="Bible:Job.39.6-Job.39.8">Job 39:6-8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 6:5" id="a-p607.4" parsed="|Job|6|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.6.5">6:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 11:12" id="a-p607.5" parsed="|Job|11|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.11.12">11:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 32:14" id="a-p607.6" parsed="|Isa|32|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.32.14">Isa. 32:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 2:24" id="a-p607.7" parsed="|Jer|2|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.2.24">Jer. 2:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 14:6" id="a-p607.8" parsed="|Jer|14|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.14.6">14:6</scripRef>, etc.). The
wild ass was distinguished for its fleetness and its extreme
shyness. In allusion to his mode of life, Ishmael is likened to
a wild ass (<scripRef passage="Gen. 16:12" id="a-p607.9" parsed="|Gen|16|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.16.12">Gen. 16:12</scripRef>. Here the word is simply rendered “wild”
in the Authorized Version, but in the Revised Version, “wild-ass
among men”).
</def>
<term id="a-p607.10">Asshur</term>
Second son of Shem (Gen. 10:22; 1 Chr. 1:17). He went from the

land of Shinar and built Nineveh, etc. (<scripRef passage="Gen. 10:11" id="a-p608.3" parsed="|Gen|10|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.11">Gen. 10:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 10:12" id="a-p608.4" parsed="|Gen|10|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.12">12</scripRef>). He
probably gave his name to Assyria, which is the usual
translation of the word, although the form Asshur is sometimes

retained (<scripRef passage="Num. 24:22" id="a-p608.5" parsed="|Num|24|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.24.22">Num. 24:22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 24:24" id="a-p608.6" parsed="|Num|24|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.24.24">24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:23" id="a-p608.7" parsed="|Ezek|27|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.23">Ezek. 27:23</scripRef>, etc.). In <scripRef passage="Gen. 2:14" id="a-p608.8" parsed="|Gen|2|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.2.14">Gen. 2:14</scripRef>
“Assyria” ought to be “Asshur,” which was the original capital
of Assyria, a city represented by the mounds of Kalah Sherghat,
on the west bank of the Tigris. This city was founded by
Bel-kap-kapu about B.C. 1700. At a later date the capital was
shifted to Ninua, or Nineveh, now Koyunjik, on the eastern bank
of the river. (See CALAH; NINEVEH.)
</def>
<term id="a-p608.11">Assos</term>
A sea-port town of Proconsular Asia, in the district of Mysia,
on the north shore of the Gulf of Adramyttium. Paul came hither

on foot along the Roman road from Troas (<scripRef passage="Acts 20:13" id="a-p609.1" parsed="|Acts|20|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.13">Acts 20:13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 20:14" id="a-p609.2" parsed="|Acts|20|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.14">14</scripRef>), a
distance of 20 miles. It was about 30 miles distant from Troas
by sea. The island of Lesbos lay opposite it, about 7 miles
distant.
</def>
<term id="a-p609.3">Assurance</term>
The resurrection of Jesus (Acts 17:31) is the “assurance” (Gr.
pistis, generally rendered “faith”) or pledge God has given that
his revelation is true and worthy of acceptance. The “full

assurance [Gr. plerophoria, ‘full bearing’] of faith” (<scripRef passage="Heb. 10:22" id="a-p610.2" parsed="|Heb|10|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.10.22">Heb. 10:22</scripRef>) is a fulness of faith in God which leaves no room for
doubt. The “full assurance of understanding” (<scripRef passage="Col. 2:2" id="a-p610.3" parsed="|Col|2|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.2.2">Col. 2:2</scripRef>) is an
entire unwavering conviction of the truth of the declarations of
Scripture, a joyful steadfastness on the part of any one of
conviction that he has grasped the very truth. The “full
assurance of hope” (<scripRef passage="Heb. 6:11" id="a-p610.4" parsed="|Heb|6|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.6.11">Heb. 6:11</scripRef>) is a sure and well-grounded

expectation of eternal glory (<scripRef passage="2 Tim. 4:7" id="a-p610.5" parsed="|2Tim|4|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.4.7">2 Tim. 4:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Tim. 4:8" id="a-p610.6" parsed="|2Tim|4|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.4.8">8</scripRef>). This assurance of
hope is the assurance of a man’s own particular salvation.
This infallible assurance, which believers may attain unto as
to their own personal salvation, is founded on the truth of the
promises (<scripRef passage="Heb. 6:18" id="a-p611.1" parsed="|Heb|6|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.6.18">Heb. 6:18</scripRef>), on the inward evidence of Christian

graces, and on the testimony of the Spirit of adoption (<scripRef passage="Rom. 8:16" id="a-p611.2" parsed="|Rom|8|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.16">Rom. 8:16</scripRef>). That such a certainty may be attained appears from the

testimony of Scripture (<scripRef passage="Rom. 8:16" id="a-p611.3" parsed="|Rom|8|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.16">Rom. 8:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 John 2:3" id="a-p611.4" parsed="|1John|2|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.2.3">1 John 2:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 John 3:14" id="a-p611.5" parsed="|1John|3|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.3.14">3:14</scripRef>), from the
command to seek after it (<scripRef passage="Heb. 6:11" id="a-p611.6" parsed="|Heb|6|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.6.11">Heb. 6:11</scripRef>; 2 Pet. 1:10), and from the

fact that it has been attained (<scripRef passage="2 Tim. 1:12" id="a-p611.7" parsed="|2Tim|1|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.1.12">2 Tim. 1:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Tim. 4:7" id="a-p611.8" parsed="|2Tim|4|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.4.7">4:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Tim. 4:8" id="a-p611.9" parsed="|2Tim|4|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.4.8">8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 John 2:3" id="a-p611.10" parsed="|1John|2|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.2.3">1 John 2:3</scripRef>;
4:16).
This full assurance is not of the essence of saving faith. It
is the result of faith, and posterior to it in the order of
nature, and so frequently also in the order of time. True
believers may be destitute of it. Trust itself is something
different from the evidence that we do trust. Believers,
moreover, are exhorted to go on to something beyond what they at
present have when they are exhorted to seek the grace of full
assurance (<scripRef passage="Heb. 10:22" id="a-p612.1" parsed="|Heb|10|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.10.22">Heb. 10:22</scripRef>; 2 Pet. 1:5-10). The attainment of this
grace is a duty, and is to be diligently sought.
“Genuine assurance naturally leads to a legitimate and abiding
peace and joy, and to love and thankfulness to God; and these
from the very laws of our being to greater buoyancy, strength,
and cheerfulness in the practice of obedience in every
department of duty.”
This assurance may in various ways be shaken, diminished, and
intermitted, but the principle out of which it springs can never
be lost. (See FAITH.)
</def>
<term id="a-p614.2">Assyria</term>
The name derived from the city Asshur on the Tigris, the
original capital of the country, was originally a colony from
Babylonia, and was ruled by viceroys from that kingdom. It was a
mountainous region lying to the north of Babylonia, extending
along the Tigris as far as to the high mountain range of
Armenia, the Gordiaean or Carduchian mountains. It was founded
in B.C. 1700 under Bel-kap-kapu, and became an independent and a
conquering power, and shook off the yoke of its Babylonian
masters. It subdued the whole of Northern Asia. The Assyrians
were Semites (<scripRef passage="Gen. 10:22" id="a-p615.1" parsed="|Gen|10|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.22">Gen. 10:22</scripRef>), but in process of time non-Semite
tribes mingled with the inhabitants. They were a military
people, the “Romans of the East.”
Of the early history of the kingdom of Assyria little is
positively known. In B.C. 1120 Tiglath-pileser I., the greatest
of the Assyrian kings, “crossed the Euphrates, defeated the
kings of the Hittites, captured the city of Carchemish, and
advanced as far as the shores of the Mediterranean.” He may be
regarded as the founder of the first Assyrian empire. After this
the Assyrians gradually extended their power, subjugating the
states of Northern Syria. In the reign of Ahab, king of Israel,
Shalmaneser II. marched an army against the Syrian states, whose
allied army he encountered and vanquished at Karkar. This led to
Ahab’s casting off the yoke of Damascus and allying himself with
Judah. Some years after this the Assyrian king marched an army
against Hazael, king of Damascus. He besieged and took that
city. He also brought under tribute Jehu, and the cities of Tyre
and Sidon.
About a hundred years after this (B.C. 745) the crown was
seized by a military adventurer called Pul, who assumed the name
of Tiglath-pileser III. He directed his armies into Syria, which
had by this time regained its independence, and took (B.C. 740)
Arpad, near Aleppo, after a siege of three years, and reduced
Hamath. Azariah (Uzziah) was an ally of the king of Hamath, and
thus was compelled by Tiglath-pileser to do him homage and pay a
yearly tribute.
In B.C. 738, in the reign of Menahem, king of Israel, Pul

invaded Israel, and imposed on it a heavy tribute (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 15:19" id="a-p618.1" parsed="|2Kgs|15|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.19">2 Kings 15:19</scripRef>). Ahaz, the king of Judah, when engaged in a war against
Israel and Syria, appealed for help to this Assyrian king by
means of a present of gold and silver (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 16:8" id="a-p618.2" parsed="|2Kgs|16|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.16.8">2 Kings 16:8</scripRef>); who
accordingly “marched against Damascus, defeated and put Rezin to
death, and besieged the city itself.” Leaving a portion of his
army to continue the siege, “he advanced through the province
east of Jordan, spreading fire and sword,” and became master of
Philistia, and took Samaria and Damascus. He died B.C. 727, and
was succeeded by Shalmanezer IV., who ruled till B.C. 722. He
also invaded Syria (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:5" id="a-p618.3" parsed="|2Kgs|17|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.5">2 Kings 17:5</scripRef>), but was deposed in favour of
Sargon (q.v.) the Tartan, or commander-in-chief of the army, who
took Samaria (q.v.) after a siege of three years, and so put an
end to the kingdom of Israel, carrying the people away into

captivity, B.C. 722 (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:1-6" id="a-p618.4" parsed="|2Kgs|17|1|17|6" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.1-2Kgs.17.6">2 Kings 17:1-6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:24" id="a-p618.5" parsed="|2Kgs|17|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.24">24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:7" id="a-p618.6" parsed="|2Kgs|18|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.7">18:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:9" id="a-p618.7" parsed="|2Kgs|18|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.9">9</scripRef>). He also

overran the land of Judah, and took the city of Jerusalem (<scripRef passage="Isa. 10:6" id="a-p618.8" parsed="|Isa|10|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.6">Isa. 10:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa 10:12" id="a-p618.9" parsed="|Isa|10|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.12">12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa 10:22" id="a-p618.10" parsed="|Isa|10|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.22">22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa 10:24" id="a-p618.11" parsed="|Isa|10|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.24">24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa 10:34" id="a-p618.12" parsed="|Isa|10|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.34">34</scripRef>). Mention is next made of Sennacherib (B.C.

705), the son and successor of Sargon (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:13" id="a-p618.13" parsed="|2Kgs|18|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.13">2 Kings 18:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 19:37" id="a-p618.14" parsed="|2Kgs|19|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.19.37">19:37</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Isa. 7:17" id="a-p618.15" parsed="|Isa|7|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.7.17">Isa. 7:17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 7:18" id="a-p618.16" parsed="|Isa|7|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.7.18">18</scripRef>); and then of Esar-haddon, his son and successor,
who took Manasseh, king of Judah, captive, and kept him for some
time a prisoner at Babylon, which he alone of all the Assyrian
kings made the seat of his government (2 Kings 19:37; Isa. 37:38).
Assur-bani-pal, the son of Esarhaddon, became king, and in
<scripRef passage="Ezra 4:10" id="a-p619.1" parsed="|Ezra|4|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.4.10">Ezra 4:10</scripRef> is referred to as Asnapper. From an early period
Assyria had entered on a conquering career, and having absorbed
Babylon, the kingdoms of Hamath, Damascus, and Samaria, it
conquered Phoenicia, and made Judea feudatory, and subjected
Philistia and Idumea. At length, however, its power declined. In
B.C. 727 the Babylonians threw off the rule of the Assyrians,
under the leadership of the powerful Chaldean prince
Merodach-baladan (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 20:12" id="a-p619.2" parsed="|2Kgs|20|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.20.12">2 Kings 20:12</scripRef>), who, after twelve years, was
subdued by Sargon, who now reunited the kingdom, and ruled over
a vast empire. But on his death the smouldering flames of
rebellion again burst forth, and the Babylonians and Medes
successfully asserted their independence (B.C. 625), and Assyria
fell according to the prophecies of Isaiah (10:5-19), Nahum
(3:19), and Zephaniah (3:13), and the many separate kingdoms of

which it was composed ceased to recognize the “great king” (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:19" id="a-p619.3" parsed="|2Kgs|18|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.19">2 Kings 18:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 36:4" id="a-p619.4" parsed="|Isa|36|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.36.4">Isa. 36:4</scripRef>). Ezekiel (31) attests (about B.C. 586)
how completely Assyria was overthrown. It ceases to be a nation.
(See NINEVEH; BABYLON.)
</def>
<term id="a-p619.7">Astrologer</term>
(Dan. 1:20; 2:2, 10, 27, etc.) Heb. ‘ashshaph’, an enchanter,
one who professes to divine future events by the appearance of
the stars. This science flourished among the Chaldeans. It was
positively forbidden to the Jews (Deut. 4:19; 18:10; Isa. 47:13).
</def>
<term id="a-p620.8">Astronomy</term>
The Hebrews were devout students of the wonders of the starry

firmanent (<scripRef passage="Amos 5:8" id="a-p621.1" parsed="|Amos|5|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.5.8">Amos 5:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 19" id="a-p621.2" parsed="|Ps|19|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.19">Ps. 19</scripRef>). In the Book of Job, which is the
oldest book of the Bible in all probability, the constellations
are distinguished and named. Mention is made of the “morning

star” (<scripRef passage="Rev. 2:28" id="a-p621.3" parsed="|Rev|2|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.2.28">Rev. 2:28</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Isa. 14:12" id="a-p621.4" parsed="|Isa|14|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.14.12">Isa. 14:12</scripRef>), the “seven stars” and

“Pleiades,” “Orion,” “Arcturus,” the “Great Bear” (<scripRef passage="Amos 5:8" id="a-p621.5" parsed="|Amos|5|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.5.8">Amos 5:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 9:9" id="a-p621.6" parsed="|Job|9|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.9.9">Job 9:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 38:31" id="a-p621.7" parsed="|Job|38|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.38.31">38:31</scripRef>), “the crooked serpent,” Draco (<scripRef passage="Job 26:13" id="a-p621.8" parsed="|Job|26|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.26.13">Job 26:13</scripRef>), the
Dioscuri, or Gemini, “Castor and Pollux” (<scripRef passage="Acts 28:11" id="a-p621.9" parsed="|Acts|28|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.28.11">Acts 28:11</scripRef>). The stars
were called “the host of heaven” (Isa. 40:26; Jer. 33:22).
The oldest divisions of time were mainly based on the
observation of the movements of the heavenly bodies, the

“ordinances of heaven” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 1:14-18" id="a-p622.1" parsed="|Gen|1|14|1|18" osisRef="Bible:Gen.1.14-Gen.1.18">Gen. 1:14-18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 38:33" id="a-p622.2" parsed="|Job|38|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.38.33">Job 38:33</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 31:35" id="a-p622.3" parsed="|Jer|31|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.31.35">Jer. 31:35</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Jer 33:25" id="a-p622.4" parsed="|Jer|33|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.33.25">33:25</scripRef>). Such observations led to the division of the year into
months and the mapping out of the appearances of the stars into
twelve portions, which received from the Greeks the name of the
“zodiac.” The word “Mazzaroth” (<scripRef passage="Job 38:32" id="a-p622.5" parsed="|Job|38|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.38.32">Job 38:32</scripRef>) means, as the margin
notes, “the twelve signs” of the zodiac. Astronomical
observations were also necessary among the Jews in order to the
fixing of the proper time for sacred ceremonies, the “new
moons,” the “passover,” etc. Many allusions are found to the
display of God’s wisdom and power as seen in the starry heavens
(Ps. 8; 19:1-6; Isa. 51:6, etc.)
</def>
<term id="a-p622.9">Asuppim</term>
(1 Chr. 26:15, 17, Authorized Version; but in Revised Version,
“storehouse”), properly the house of stores for the priests. In
<scripRef passage="Neh. 12:25" id="a-p623.3" parsed="|Neh|12|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.12.25">Neh. 12:25</scripRef> the Authorized Version has “thresholds,” marg.
“treasuries” or “assemblies;” Revised Version, “storehouses.”
</def>
<term id="a-p623.4">Atad</term>
Buckthorn, a place where Joseph and his brethren, when on their
way from Egypt to Hebron with the remains of their father Jacob,
made for seven days a “great and very sore lamentation.” On this

account the Canaanites called it “Abel-mizraim” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 50:10" id="a-p624.1" parsed="|Gen|50|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.50.10">Gen. 50:10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 50:11" id="a-p624.2" parsed="|Gen|50|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.50.11">11</scripRef>). It was probably near Hebron. The word is rendered “bramble”
in Judg. 9:14, 15, and “thorns” in Ps. 58:9.
</def>
<term id="a-p624.6">Ataroth</term>
Crowns. (1.) A city east of Jordan, not far from Gilead (Num. 32:3).
(2.) A town on the border of Ephraim and Benjamin (Josh. 16:2, 7), called also Ataroth-adar (16:5). Now ed-Da’rieh.
(3.) “Ataroth, the house of Joab” (1 Chr. 2:54), a town of
Judah inhabited by the descendants of Caleb.
</def>
<term id="a-p627.2">Ater</term>
Shut; lame. (1.) Ezra 2:16. (2.) Neh. 10:17. (3.) Ezra 2:42.
</def>
<term id="a-p628.4">Athaliah</term>
Whom God afflicts. (1.) The daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, and
the wife of Jehoram, king of Judah (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 8:18" id="a-p629.1" parsed="|2Kgs|8|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.8.18">2 Kings 8:18</scripRef>), who “walked
in the ways of the house of Ahab” (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 21:6" id="a-p629.2" parsed="|2Chr|21|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.21.6">2 Chr. 21:6</scripRef>), called
“daughter” of Omri (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 8:26" id="a-p629.3" parsed="|2Kgs|8|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.8.26">2 Kings 8:26</scripRef>). On the death of her husband
and of her son Ahaziah, she resolved to seat herself on the
vacant throne. She slew all Ahaziah’s children except Joash, the

youngest (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 11:1" id="a-p629.4" parsed="|2Kgs|11|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.11.1">2 Kings 11:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 11:2" id="a-p629.5" parsed="|2Kgs|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.11.2">2</scripRef>). After a reign of six years she was

put to death in an insurrection (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 11:20" id="a-p629.6" parsed="|2Kgs|11|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.11.20">2 Kings 11:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 21:6" id="a-p629.7" parsed="|2Chr|21|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.21.6">2 Chr. 21:6</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 22:10-12" id="a-p629.8" parsed="|2Chr|22|10|22|12" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.22.10-2Chr.22.12">22:10-12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 23:15" id="a-p629.9" parsed="|2Chr|23|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.23.15">23:15</scripRef>), stirred up among the people in connection with
Josiah’s being crowned as king.
(2.) Ezra 8:7. (3.) 1 Chr. 8:26.
</def>
<term id="a-p630.3">Athens</term>
The capital of Attica, the most celebrated city of the ancient
world, the seat of Greek literature and art during the golden
period of Grecian history. Its inhabitants were fond of novelty
(<scripRef passage="Acts 17:21" id="a-p631.1" parsed="|Acts|17|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.17.21">Acts 17:21</scripRef>), and were remarkable for their zeal in the worship
of the gods. It was a sarcastic saying of the Roman satirist
that it was “easier to find a god at Athens than a man.”
On his second missionary journey Paul visited this city (Acts 17:15; comp. 1 Thess. 3:1), and delivered in the Areopagus his
famous speech (17:22-31). The altar of which Paul there speaks
as dedicated “to the [properly “an”] unknown God” (23) was
probably one of several which bore the same inscription. It is
supposed that they originated in the practice of letting loose a
flock of sheep and goats in the streets of Athens on the
occasion of a plague, and of offering them up in sacrifice, at
the spot where they lay down, “to the god concerned.”
</def>
<term id="a-p632.3">Atonement</term>
This word does not occur in the Authorized Version of the New
Testament except in <scripRef passage="Rom. 5:11" id="a-p633.1" parsed="|Rom|5|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.5.11">Rom. 5:11</scripRef>, where in the Revised Version the
word “reconciliation” is used. In the Old Testament it is of
frequent occurrence.
The meaning of the word is simply at-one-ment, i.e., the state
of being at one or being reconciled, so that atonement is
reconciliation. Thus it is used to denote the effect which flows
from the death of Christ.
But the word is also used to denote that by which this
reconciliation is brought about, viz., the death of Christ
itself; and when so used it means satisfaction, and in this
sense to make an atonement for one is to make satisfaction for

his offences (<scripRef passage="Ex. 32:30" id="a-p635.1" parsed="|Exod|32|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.32.30">Ex. 32:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 4:26" id="a-p635.2" parsed="|Lev|4|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.4.26">Lev. 4:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 5:16" id="a-p635.3" parsed="|Lev|5|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.5.16">5:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 6:11" id="a-p635.4" parsed="|Num|6|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.6.11">Num. 6:11</scripRef>), and, as
regards the person, to reconcile, to propitiate God in his
behalf.
By the atonement of Christ we generally mean his work by which
he expiated our sins. But in Scripture usage the word denotes
the reconciliation itself, and not the means by which it is
effected. When speaking of Christ’s saving work, the word
“satisfaction,” the word used by the theologians of the
Reformation, is to be preferred to the word “atonement.”
Christ’s satisfaction is all he did in the room and in behalf of
sinners to satisfy the demands of the law and justice of God.
Christ’s work consisted of suffering and obedience, and these
were vicarious, i.e., were not merely for our benefit, but were
in our stead, as the suffering and obedience of our vicar, or
substitute. Our guilt is expiated by the punishment which our
vicar bore, and thus God is rendered propitious, i.e., it is now
consistent with his justice to manifest his love to
transgressors. Expiation has been made for sin, i.e., it is
covered. The means by which it is covered is vicarious
satisfaction, and the result of its being covered is atonement
or reconciliation. To make atonement is to do that by virtue of
which alienation ceases and reconciliation is brought about.
Christ’s mediatorial work and sufferings are the ground or
efficient cause of reconciliation with God. They rectify the
disturbed relations between God and man, taking away the
obstacles interposed by sin to their fellowship and concord. The
reconciliation is mutual, i.e., it is not only that of sinners
toward God, but also and pre-eminently that of God toward
sinners, effected by the sin-offering he himself provided, so
that consistently with the other attributes of his character his
love might flow forth in all its fulness of blessing to men. The
primary idea presented to us in different forms throughout the
Scripture is that the death of Christ is a satisfaction of
infinite worth rendered to the law and justice of God (q.v.),
and accepted by him in room of the very penalty man had
incurred. It must also be constantly kept in mind that the
atonement is not the cause but the consequence of God’s love to

guilty men (<scripRef passage="John 3:16" id="a-p636.1" parsed="|John|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.3.16">John 3:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 3:24" id="a-p636.2" parsed="|Rom|3|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.3.24">Rom. 3:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Rom. 3:25" id="a-p636.3" parsed="|Rom|3|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.3.25">25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 1:7" id="a-p636.4" parsed="|Eph|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.1.7">Eph. 1:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 John 1:9" id="a-p636.5" parsed="|1John|1|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.1.9">1 John 1:9</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="1 John 4:9" id="a-p636.6" parsed="|1John|4|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.4.9">4:9</scripRef>). The atonement may also be regarded as necessary, not in an
absolute but in a relative sense, i.e., if man is to be saved,
there is no other way than this which God has devised and

carried out (<scripRef passage="Ex. 34:7" id="a-p636.7" parsed="|Exod|34|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.34.7">Ex. 34:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 24:19" id="a-p636.8" parsed="|Josh|24|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.24.19">Josh. 24:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 5:4" id="a-p636.9" parsed="|Ps|5|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.5.4">Ps. 5:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 7:11" id="a-p636.10" parsed="|Ps|7|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.7.11">7:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Nahum 1:2" id="a-p636.11" parsed="|Nah|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Nah.1.2">Nahum 1:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Nahum 1:6" id="a-p636.12" parsed="|Nah|1|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Nah.1.6">6</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Rom. 3:5" id="a-p636.13" parsed="|Rom|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.3.5">Rom. 3:5</scripRef>). This is God’s plan, clearly revealed; and that is
enough for us to know.
</def>
<term id="a-p636.14">Atonement, Day of</term>
The great annual day of humiliation and expiation for the sins
of the nation, “the fast” (<scripRef passage="Acts 27:9" id="a-p637.1" parsed="|Acts|27|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.27.9">Acts 27:9</scripRef>), and the only one
commanded in the law of Moses. The mode of its observance is
described in Lev. 16:3-10; 23:26-32; and Num. 29:7-11.
It was kept on the tenth day of the month Tisri, i.e., five
days before the feast of Tabernacles, and lasted from sunset to
sunset. (See AZAZEL.)
</def>
<term id="a-p638.2">Augustus</term>
The cognomen of the first Roman emperor, C. Julius Caesar
Octavianus, during whose reign Christ was born (<scripRef passage="Luke 2:1" id="a-p639.1" parsed="|Luke|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.1">Luke 2:1</scripRef>). His
decree that “all the world should be taxed” was the divinely
ordered occasion of Jesus’ being born, according to prophecy
(<scripRef passage="Micah 5:2" id="a-p639.2" parsed="|Mic|5|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.5.2">Micah 5:2</scripRef>), in Bethlehem. This name being simply a title
meaning “majesty” or “venerable,” first given to him by the
senate (B.C. 27), was borne by succeeding emperors. Before his
death (A.D. 14) he associated Tiberius with him in the empire
(Luke 3:1), by whom he was succeeded.
</def>
<term id="a-p639.4">Augustus band</term>
(Acts 27:1.: literally, of Sebaste, the Greek form of Augusta,
the name given to Caesarea in honour of Augustus Caesar).
