The inhabitants of Malta are so called (<scripRef passage="Acts 28:1" id="b-p112.4" parsed="|Acts|28|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.28.1">Acts 28:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 28:2" id="b-p112.5" parsed="|Acts|28|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.28.2">2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 28:4" id="b-p112.6" parsed="|Acts|28|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.28.4">4</scripRef>). They were originally a Carthaginian colony. This
word nowhere in Scripture bears the meaning it does in modern
times.
</def>
<term id="b-p112.7">Barber</term>
Found only once, in Ezek. 5:1, where reference is made to the
Jewish custom of shaving the head as a sign of mourning. The
Nazarites were untouched by the razor from their birth (Num. 6:5). Comp. Judg. 16:19.
</def>
<term id="b-p113.4">Barefoot</term>
To go barefoot was a sign of great distress (Isa. 20:2, 3, 4),
or of some great calamity having fallen on a person (2 Sam. 15:30).
</def>
<term id="b-p114.5">Bariah</term>
Fugitive, one of Shemaiah’s five sons. Their father is counted
along with them in 1 Chr. 3:22.
</def>
<term id="b-p115.2">Bar-jesus</term>
Son of Joshua, the patronymic of Elymas the sorcerer (Acts 13:6), who met Paul and Barnabas at Paphos. Elymas is a word of
Arabic origin meaning “wise.”
</def>
<term id="b-p116.2">Bar-jona</term>
Son of Jonah, the patronymic of Peter (Matt. 16:17; John 1:42),
because his father’s name was Jonas. (See PETER.)
</def>
<term id="b-p117.4">Barkos</term>
Painter, (Ezra 2:53; Neh. 7:55). The father of some of the
Nethinim.
</def>
<term id="b-p118.3">Barley</term>
A grain much cultivated in Egypt (Ex. 9:31) and in Palestine

(<scripRef passage="Lev. 27:16" id="b-p119.2" parsed="|Lev|27|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.27.16">Lev. 27:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 8:8" id="b-p119.3" parsed="|Deut|8|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.8.8">Deut. 8:8</scripRef>). It was usually the food of horses (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:28" id="b-p119.4" parsed="|1Kgs|4|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.28">1 Kings 4:28</scripRef>). Barley bread was used by the poorer people (<scripRef passage="Judg. 7:13" id="b-p119.5" parsed="|Judg|7|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.7.13">Judg. 7:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 4:42" id="b-p119.6" parsed="|2Kgs|4|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.4.42">2 Kings 4:42</scripRef>). Barley of the first crop was ready for the
harvest by the time of the Passover, in the middle of April

(<scripRef passage="Ruth 1:22" id="b-p119.7" parsed="|Ruth|1|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.1.22">Ruth 1:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:9" id="b-p119.8" parsed="|2Sam|21|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.9">2 Sam. 21:9</scripRef>). Mention is made of barley-meal (<scripRef passage="Num. 5:15" id="b-p119.9" parsed="|Num|5|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.5.15">Num. 5:15</scripRef>). Our Lord fed five thousand with “five barley loaves and
two small fishes” (John 6:9).
</def>
<term id="b-p119.11">Barn</term>
A storehouse (Deut. 28:8; Job 39:12; Hag. 2:19) for grain, which
was usually under ground, although also sometimes above ground
(Luke 12:18).
</def>
<term id="b-p120.5">Barnabas</term>
Son of consolation, the surname of Joses, a Levite (Acts 4:36).
His name stands first on the list of prophets and teachers of
the church at Antioch (13:1). Luke speaks of him as a “good man”
(11:24). He was born of Jewish parents of the tribe of Levi. He

was a native of Cyprus, where he had a possession of land (<scripRef passage="Acts 4:36" id="b-p121.2" parsed="|Acts|4|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.4.36">Acts 4:36</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 4:37" id="b-p121.3" parsed="|Acts|4|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.4.37">37</scripRef>), which he sold. His personal appearance is supposed to

have been dignified and commanding (<scripRef passage="Acts 14:11" id="b-p121.4" parsed="|Acts|14|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.14.11">Acts 14:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 14:12" id="b-p121.5" parsed="|Acts|14|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.14.12">12</scripRef>). When Paul
returned to Jerusalem after his conversion, Barnabas took him
and introduced him to the apostles (9:27). They had probably
been companions as students in the school of Gamaliel.
The prosperity of the church at Antioch led the apostles and
brethren at Jerusalem to send Barnabas thither to superintend
the movement. He found the work so extensive and weighty that he
went to Tarsus in search of Saul to assist him. Saul returned

with him to Antioch and laboured with him for a whole year (<scripRef passage="Acts 11:25" id="b-p122.1" parsed="|Acts|11|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.25">Acts 11:25</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 11:26" id="b-p122.2" parsed="|Acts|11|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.26">26</scripRef>). The two were at the end of this period sent up to
Jerusalem with the contributions the church at Antioch had made
for the poorer brethren there (11:28-30). Shortly after they
returned, bringing John Mark with them, they were appointed as
missionaries to the heathen world, and in this capacity visited

Cyprus and some of the principal cities of Asia Minor (<scripRef passage="Acts 13:14" id="b-p122.3" parsed="|Acts|13|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.13.14">Acts 13:14</scripRef>). Returning from this first missionary journey to Antioch,
they were again sent up to Jerusalem to consult with the church

there regarding the relation of Gentiles to the church (<scripRef passage="Acts 15:2" id="b-p122.4" parsed="|Acts|15|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.15.2">Acts 15:2</scripRef>: <scripRef passage="Gal. 2:1" id="b-p122.5" parsed="|Gal|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.2.1">Gal. 2:1</scripRef>). This matter having been settled, they returned
again to Antioch, bringing the decree of the council as the rule
by which Gentiles were to be admitted into the church.
When about to set forth on a second missionary journey, a
dispute arose between Saul and Barnabas as to the propriety of
taking John Mark with them again. The dispute ended by Saul and
Barnabas taking separate routes. Saul took Silas as his
companion, and journeyed through Syria and Cilicia; while
Barnabas took his nephew John Mark, and visited Cyprus (Acts 15:36-41). Barnabas is not again mentioned by Luke in the Acts.
</def>
<term id="b-p123.2">Barrel</term>
A vessel used for keeping flour (1 Kings 17:12, 14, 16). The
same word (cad) so rendered is also translated “pitcher,” a
vessel for carrying water (Gen. 24:14; Judg. 7:16).
</def>
<term id="b-p124.6">Barren</term>
For a woman to be barren was accounted a severe punishment among

the Jews (<scripRef passage="Gen. 16:2" id="b-p125.1" parsed="|Gen|16|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.16.2">Gen. 16:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 30:1-23" id="b-p125.2" parsed="|Gen|30|1|30|23" osisRef="Bible:Gen.30.1-Gen.30.23">30:1-23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 1:6" id="b-p125.3" parsed="|1Sam|1|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.1.6">1 Sam. 1:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 1:27" id="b-p125.4" parsed="|1Sam|1|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.1.27">27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 47:9" id="b-p125.5" parsed="|Isa|47|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.47.9">Isa. 47:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 49:21" id="b-p125.6" parsed="|Isa|49|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.49.21">49:21</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Luke 1:25" id="b-p125.7" parsed="|Luke|1|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.25">Luke 1:25</scripRef>). Instances of barrenness are noticed (<scripRef passage="Gen. 11:30" id="b-p125.8" parsed="|Gen|11|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.11.30">Gen. 11:30</scripRef>;
25:21; 29:31; Judg. 13:2, 3; Luke 1:7, 36).
</def>
<term id="b-p125.15">Barsabas</term>
Son of Saba, the surname (1) of Joseph, also called Justus (Acts 1:23), some identify him with Barnabas; (2) of Judas, who was a
“prophet.” Nothing more is known of him than what is mentioned
in Acts 15:32.
</def>
<term id="b-p126.3">Bartholomew</term>
Son of Tolmai, one of the twelve apostles (Matt. 10:3; Acts 1:13); generally supposed to have been the same as Nathanael. In
the synoptic gospels Philip and Bartholomew are always mentioned
together, while Nathanael is never mentioned; in the fourth
gospel, on the other hand, Philip and Nathanael are similarly
mentioned together, but nothing is said of Bartholomew. He was
one of the disciples to whom our Lord appeared at the Sea of
Tiberias after his resurrection (<scripRef passage="John 21:2" id="b-p127.3" parsed="|John|21|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.21.2">John 21:2</scripRef>). He was also a

witness of the Ascension (<scripRef passage="Acts 1:4" id="b-p127.4" parsed="|Acts|1|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.4">Acts 1:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 1:12" id="b-p127.5" parsed="|Acts|1|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.12">12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 1:13" id="b-p127.6" parsed="|Acts|1|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.13">13</scripRef>). He was an
“Israelite indeed” (John 1:47).
</def>
<term id="b-p127.8">Bartimaeus</term>
Son of Timaeus, one of the two blind beggars of Jericho (Mark 10:46; Matt. 20:30). His blindness was miraculously cured on the
ground of his faith.
</def>
<term id="b-p128.3">Baruch</term>
Blessed. (1.) The secretary of the prophet Jeremiah (32:12;
36:4). He was of the tribe of Judah (51:59). To him Jeremiah
dictated his prophecies regarding the invasion of the
Babylonians and the Captivity. These he read to the people from
a window in the temple in the fourth year of the reign of
Jehoiakim, king of Judah (<scripRef passage="Jer. 36" id="b-p129.1" parsed="|Jer|36|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.36">Jer. 36</scripRef>). He afterwards read them
before the counsellors of the king at a private interview; and
then to the king himself, who, after hearing a part of the roll,
cut it with a penknife, and threw it into the fire of his winter
parlour, where he was sitting.
During the siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar, he was the
keeper of the deed of purchase Jeremiah had made of the
territory of Hanameel (<scripRef passage="Jer. 32:12" id="b-p130.1" parsed="|Jer|32|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.32.12">Jer. 32:12</scripRef>). Being accused by his enemies
of favouring the Chaldeans, he was cast, with Jeremiah, into
prison, where he remained till the capture of Jerusalem (B.C.
586). He probably died in Babylon.
(2.) Neh. 3:20; 10:6; 11:5.
</def>
<term id="b-p131.4">Barzillai</term>
Of iron. (1.) A Meholathite, the father of Adriel (2 Sam. 21:8).
(2.) A Gileadite of Rogelim who was distinguished for his
loyalty to David. He liberally provided for the king’s followers
(<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 17:27" id="b-p133.1" parsed="|2Sam|17|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.17.27">2 Sam. 17:27</scripRef>). David on his death-bed, remembering his
kindness, commended Barzillai’s children to the care of Solomon
(1 Kings 2:7).
(3.) A priest who married a daughter of the preceding (Ezra 2:61).
</def>
<term id="b-p134.2">Bashan</term>
Light soil, first mentioned in Gen. 14:5, where it is said that
Chedorlaomer and his confederates “smote the Rephaim in
Ashteroth,” where Og the king of Bashan had his residence. At
the time of Israel’s entrance into the Promised Land, Og came

out against them, but was utterly routed (<scripRef passage="Num. 21:33-35" id="b-p135.2" parsed="|Num|21|33|21|35" osisRef="Bible:Num.21.33-Num.21.35">Num. 21:33-35</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 3:1-7" id="b-p135.3" parsed="|Deut|3|1|3|7" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.1-Deut.3.7">Deut. 3:1-7</scripRef>). This country extended from Gilead in the south to Hermon
in the north, and from the Jordan on the west to Salcah on the
east. Along with the half of Gilead it was given to the
half-tribe of Manasseh (<scripRef passage="Josh. 13:29-31" id="b-p135.4" parsed="|Josh|13|29|13|31" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.29-Josh.13.31">Josh. 13:29-31</scripRef>). Golan, one of its
cities, became a “city of refuge” (<scripRef passage="Josh. 21:27" id="b-p135.5" parsed="|Josh|21|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.21.27">Josh. 21:27</scripRef>). Argob, in

Bashan, was one of Solomon’s commissariat districts (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:13" id="b-p135.6" parsed="|1Kgs|4|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.13">1 Kings 4:13</scripRef>). The cities of Bashan were taken by Hazael (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 10:33" id="b-p135.7" parsed="|2Kgs|10|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.10.33">2 Kings 10:33</scripRef>), but were soon after reconquered by Jehoash (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 13:25" id="b-p135.8" parsed="|2Kgs|13|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.13.25">2 Kings 13:25</scripRef>), who overcame the Syrians in three battles, according to
the word of Elisha (19). From this time Bashan almost disappears
from history, although we read of the wild cattle of its rich

pastures (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 39:18" id="b-p135.9" parsed="|Ezek|39|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.39.18">Ezek. 39:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 22:12" id="b-p135.10" parsed="|Ps|22|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.22.12">Ps. 22:12</scripRef>), the oaks of its forests (<scripRef passage="Isa. 2:13" id="b-p135.11" parsed="|Isa|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.2.13">Isa. 2:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:6" id="b-p135.12" parsed="|Ezek|27|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.6">Ezek. 27:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 11:2" id="b-p135.13" parsed="|Zech|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.11.2">Zech. 11:2</scripRef>), and the beauty of its extensive

plains (<scripRef passage="Amos 4:1" id="b-p135.14" parsed="|Amos|4|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.4.1">Amos 4:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 50:19" id="b-p135.15" parsed="|Jer|50|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.50.19">Jer. 50:19</scripRef>). Soon after the conquest, the name
“Gilead” was given to the whole country beyond Jordan. After the
Exile, Bashan was divided into four districts, (1.) Gaulonitis,

or Jaulan, the most western; (2.) Auranitis, the Hauran (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 47:16" id="b-p135.16" parsed="|Ezek|47|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.47.16">Ezek. 47:16</scripRef>); (3.) Argob or Trachonitis, now the Lejah; and (4.)
Batanaea, now Ard-el-Bathanyeh, on the east of the Lejah, with
many deserted towns almost as perfect as when they were
inhabited. (See HAURAN.)
</def>
<term id="b-p135.18">Bashan-havoth-jair</term>
The Bashan of the villages of Jair, the general name given to
Argob by Jair, the son of Manasseh (<scripRef passage="Deut. 3:14" id="b-p136.1" parsed="|Deut|3|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.14">Deut. 3:14</scripRef>), containing
sixty cities with walls and brazen gates (Josh. 13:30; 1 Kings 4:13). (See ARGOB.)
</def>
<term id="b-p136.5">Bashan, Hill of</term>
(Ps. 68:15), probably another name for Hermon, which lies to the
north of Bashan.
</def>
<term id="b-p137.2">Bashemath</term>
Sweet-smelling. (1.) The daughter of Ishmael, the last of Esau’s

three wives (<scripRef passage="Gen. 36:3" id="b-p138.1" parsed="|Gen|36|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36.3">Gen. 36:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 36:4" id="b-p138.2" parsed="|Gen|36|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36.4">4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 36:13" id="b-p138.3" parsed="|Gen|36|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36.13">13</scripRef>), from whose son Reuel four tribes
of the Edomites sprung. She is also called Mahalath (<scripRef passage="Gen. 28:9" id="b-p138.4" parsed="|Gen|28|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.28.9">Gen. 28:9</scripRef>).
It is noticeable that Esau’s three wives receive different names
in the genealogical table of the Edomites (<scripRef passage="Gen. 36" id="b-p138.5" parsed="|Gen|36|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36">Gen. 36</scripRef>) from those
given to them in the history (Gen. 26:34; 28:9).
(2.) A daughter of Solomon, and wife of Ahimaaz, one of his
officers (1 Kings 4:15).
</def>
<term id="b-p139.2">Basilisk</term>
(in R.V., Isa. 11:8; 14:29; 59:5; Jer. 8:17), the “king
serpent,” as the name imports; a fabulous serpent said to be
three spans long, with a spot on its head like a crown. Probably
the yellow snake is intended. (See COCKATRICE.)
</def>
<term id="b-p140.6">Basin</term>
Or Bason. (1.) A trough or laver (Heb. aggan’) for washing (Ex. 24:6); rendered also “goblet” (Cant. 7:2) and “cups” (Isa. 22:24).
(2.) A covered dish or urn (Heb. k’for) among the vessels of
the temple (1 Chr. 28:17; Ezra 1:10; 8:27).
(3.) A vase (Heb. mizrak) from which to sprinkle anything. A

metallic vessel; sometimes rendered “bowl” (<scripRef passage="Amos 6:6" id="b-p143.1" parsed="|Amos|6|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.6.6">Amos 6:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 9:15" id="b-p143.2" parsed="|Zech|9|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.9.15">Zech. 9:15</scripRef>). The vessels of the tabernacle were of brass (<scripRef passage="Ex. 27:3" id="b-p143.3" parsed="|Exod|27|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.27.3">Ex. 27:3</scripRef>),
while those of the temple were of gold (2 Chr. 4:8).
(4.) A utensil (Heb. saph) for holding the blood of the
victims (Ex. 12:22); also a basin for domestic purposes (2 Sam. 17:28).
The various vessels spoken of by the names “basin, bowl,
charger, cup, and dish,” cannot now be accurately distinguished.
The basin in which our Lord washed the disciples’ feet (John 13:5) must have been larger and deeper than the hand-basin.
</def>
<term id="b-p146.2">Basket</term>
There are five different Hebrew words so rendered in the
Authorized Version: (1.) A basket (Heb. sal, a twig or osier)

for holding bread (<scripRef passage="Gen. 40:16" id="b-p147.1" parsed="|Gen|40|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.40.16">Gen. 40:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex. 29:3" id="b-p147.2" parsed="|Exod|29|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.3">Ex. 29:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 29:23" id="b-p147.3" parsed="|Exod|29|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.23">23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 8:2" id="b-p147.4" parsed="|Lev|8|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.8.2">Lev. 8:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 8:26" id="b-p147.5" parsed="|Lev|8|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.8.26">26</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 8:31" id="b-p147.6" parsed="|Lev|8|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.8.31">31</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Num. 6:15" id="b-p147.7" parsed="|Num|6|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.6.15">Num. 6:15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 6:17" id="b-p147.8" parsed="|Num|6|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.6.17">17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 6:19" id="b-p147.9" parsed="|Num|6|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.6.19">19</scripRef>). Sometimes baskets were made of twigs peeled;
their manufacture was a recognized trade among the Hebrews.
(2.) That used (Heb. salsilloth’) in gathering grapes (Jer. 6:9).
(3.) That in which the first fruits of the harvest were

presented, Heb. tene, (<scripRef passage="Deut. 26:2" id="b-p149.1" parsed="|Deut|26|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.26.2">Deut. 26:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 26:4" id="b-p149.2" parsed="|Deut|26|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.26.4">4</scripRef>). It was also used for
household purposes. In form it tapered downwards like that
called corbis by the Romans.
(4.) A basket (Heb. kelub) having a lid, resembling a
bird-cage. It was made of leaves or rushes. The name is also
applied to fruit-baskets (Amos 8:1, 2).
(5.) A basket (Heb. dud) for carrying figs (Jer. 24:2), also

clay to the brick-yard (R.V., <scripRef passage="Ps. 81:6" id="b-p151.2" parsed="|Ps|81|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.81.6">Ps. 81:6</scripRef>), and bulky articles (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 10:7" id="b-p151.3" parsed="|2Kgs|10|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.10.7">2 Kings 10:7</scripRef>). This word is also rendered in the Authorized

Version “kettle” (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 2:14" id="b-p151.4" parsed="|1Sam|2|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.2.14">1 Sam. 2:14</scripRef>), “caldron” (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 35:13" id="b-p151.5" parsed="|2Chr|35|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.35.13">2 Chr. 35:13</scripRef>),
“seething-pot” (Job 41:20).
In the New Testament mention is made of the basket (Gr.
kophinos, small “wicker-basket”) for the “fragments” in the

miracle recorded <scripRef passage="Mark 6:43" id="b-p152.1" parsed="|Mark|6|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.6.43">Mark 6:43</scripRef>, and in that recorded <scripRef passage="Matt. 15:37" id="b-p152.2" parsed="|Matt|15|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.15.37">Matt. 15:37</scripRef>
(Gr. spuris, large “rope-basket”); also of the basket in which

Paul escaped (<scripRef passage="Acts 9:25" id="b-p152.3" parsed="|Acts|9|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.9.25">Acts 9:25</scripRef>, Gr. spuris; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 11" id="b-p152.4" parsed="|2Cor|11|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.11">2 Cor. 11</scripRef>: 33, Gr. sargane,
“basket of plaited cords”).
</def>
<term id="b-p152.5">Bastard</term>
In the Old Testament the rendering of the Hebrew word mamzer’,
which means “polluted.” In <scripRef passage="Deut. 23:2" id="b-p153.1" parsed="|Deut|23|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.23.2">Deut. 23:2</scripRef>, it occurs in the ordinary
sense of illegitimate offspring. In <scripRef passage="Zech. 9:6" id="b-p153.2" parsed="|Zech|9|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.9.6">Zech. 9:6</scripRef>, the word is used
in the sense of foreigner. From the history of Jephthah we learn
that there were bastard offspring among the Jews (<scripRef passage="Judg. 11:1-7" id="b-p153.3" parsed="|Judg|11|1|11|7" osisRef="Bible:Judg.11.1-Judg.11.7">Judg. 11:1-7</scripRef>).
In <scripRef passage="Heb. 12:8" id="b-p153.4" parsed="|Heb|12|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.12.8">Heb. 12:8</scripRef>, the word (Gr. nothoi) is used in its ordinary
sense, and denotes those who do not share the privileges of
God’s children.
</def>
<term id="b-p153.5">Bastinado</term>
Beating, a mode of punishment common in the East. It is referred

to by “the rod of correction” (<scripRef passage="Prov. 22:15" id="b-p154.1" parsed="|Prov|22|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.22.15">Prov. 22:15</scripRef>), “scourging” (<scripRef passage="Lev. 19:20" id="b-p154.2" parsed="|Lev|19|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.20">Lev. 19:20</scripRef>), “chastising” (<scripRef passage="Deut. 22:18" id="b-p154.3" parsed="|Deut|22|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.22.18">Deut. 22:18</scripRef>). The number of blows could
not exceed forty (Deut. 25:2, 3).
</def>
<term id="b-p154.6">Bat</term>
The Hebrew word (atalleph’) so rendered (Lev. 11:19; Deut. 14:18) implies “flying in the dark.” The bat is reckoned among
the birds in the list of unclean animals. To cast idols to the
“moles and to the bats” means to carry them into dark caverns or
desolate places to which these animals resort (<scripRef passage="Isa. 2:20" id="b-p155.3" parsed="|Isa|2|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.2.20">Isa. 2:20</scripRef>), i.e.,
to consign them to desolation or ruin.
</def>
<term id="b-p155.4">Bath</term>
A Hebrew liquid measure, the tenth part of an homer (1 Kings 7:26, 38; Ezek. 45:10, 14). It contained 8 gallons 3 quarts of
our measure. “Ten acres of vineyard shall yield one bath” (Isa. 5:10) denotes great unproductiveness.
</def>
<term id="b-p156.6">Bath-rabbim</term>
Daughter of many, the name of one of the gates of the city of
Heshbon, near which were pools (Cant. 7:4).
</def>
<term id="b-p157.2">Baths</term>
The use of the bath was very frequent among the Hebrews (Lev. 14:8; Num. 19:19, ect.). The high priest at his inauguration
(<scripRef passage="Lev. 8:6" id="b-p158.3" parsed="|Lev|8|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.8.6">Lev. 8:6</scripRef>), and on the day of atonement, was required to bathe

himself (16:4, 24). The “pools” mentioned in <scripRef passage="Neh. 3:15" id="b-p158.4" parsed="|Neh|3|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.3.15">Neh. 3:15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Neh. 3:16" id="b-p158.5" parsed="|Neh|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.3.16">16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Neh. 3:2" id="b-p158.6" parsed="|Neh|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.3.2">2</scripRef>
Kings 20:20, Isa. 22:11, John 9:7, were public bathing-places.
</def>
<term id="b-p158.9">Bath-sheba</term>
Daughter of the oath, or of seven, called also Bath-shu’a (1 Chr. 3:5), was the daughter of Eliam (2 Sam. 11:3) or Ammiel (1 Chr. 3:5), and wife of Uriah the Hittite. David committed

adultery with her (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 11:4" id="b-p159.4" parsed="|2Sam|11|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.11.4">2 Sam. 11:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 11:5" id="b-p159.5" parsed="|2Sam|11|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.11.5">5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 51:1" id="b-p159.6" parsed="|Ps|51|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.51.1">Ps. 51:1</scripRef>). The child born in
adultery died (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 12:15-19" id="b-p159.7" parsed="|2Sam|12|15|12|19" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.12.15-2Sam.12.19">2 Sam. 12:15-19</scripRef>). After her husband was slain
(11:15) she was married to David (11:27), and became the mother

of Solomon (12:24; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 1:11" id="b-p159.8" parsed="|1Kgs|1|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.1.11">1 Kings 1:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 2:13" id="b-p159.9" parsed="|1Kgs|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.2.13">2:13</scripRef>). She took a prominent
part in securing the succession of Solomon to the throne (1 Kings 1:11, 16-21).
</def>
<term id="b-p159.12">Battering-ram</term>
(Ezek. 4:2; 21:22), a military engine, consisting of a long beam
of wood hung upon a frame, for making breaches in walls. The end
of it which was brought against the wall was shaped like a ram’s
head.
</def>
<term id="b-p160.3">Battle-axe</term>
A mallet or heavy war-club. Applied metaphorically (Jer. 51:20)
to Cyrus, God’s instrument in destroying Babylon.
</def>
<term id="b-p161.2">Battle-bow</term>
The war-bow used in fighting (Zech. 9:10; 10:4). “Thy bow was
made quite naked” (<scripRef passage="Hab. 3:9" id="b-p162.3" parsed="|Hab|3|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hab.3.9">Hab. 3:9</scripRef>) means that it was made ready for
use. By David’s order (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 1:18" id="b-p162.4" parsed="|2Sam|1|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.1.18">2 Sam. 1:18</scripRef>) the young men were taught
the use, or rather the song of the bow. (See ARMOUR, BOW.)
</def>
<term id="b-p162.7">Battlement</term>
A parapet wall or balustrade surrounding the flat roofs of the
houses, required to be built by a special law (<scripRef passage="Deut. 22:8" id="b-p163.1" parsed="|Deut|22|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.22.8">Deut. 22:8</scripRef>). In
Jer. 5:10, it denotes the parapet of a city wall.
</def>
<term id="b-p163.3">Bay</term>
Denotes the estuary of the Dead Sea at the mouth of the Jordan

(<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:5" id="b-p164.1" parsed="|Josh|15|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.5">Josh. 15:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 18:19" id="b-p164.2" parsed="|Josh|18|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.18.19">18:19</scripRef>), also the southern extremity of the same sea
(15:2). The same Hebrew word is rendered “tongue” in <scripRef passage="Isa. 11:15" id="b-p164.3" parsed="|Isa|11|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.11.15">Isa. 11:15</scripRef>,
where it is used with reference to the forked mouths of the
Nile.
Bay in Zech. 6:3, 7 denotes the colour of horses, but the
original Hebrew means strong, and is here used rather to
describe the horses as fleet or spirited.
</def>
<term id="b-p165.3">Bay tree</term>
Named only in Ps. 37:35, Authorized Version. The Hebrew word so
rendered is ereh, which simply means “native born”, i.e., a
tree not transplanted, but growing on its native soil, and
therefore luxuriantly. If the psalmist intended by this word to
denote any particular tree, it may have been the evergreen bay
laurel (Laurus nobilis), which is a native of Palestine. Instead
of “like a green bay tree” in the Authorized Version, the
Revised Version has, “like a green tree in its native soil.”
</def>
<term id="b-p166.2">Bdellium</term>
Occurs only in Gen. 2:12, where it designates a product of the
land of Havilah; and in <scripRef passage="Num. 11:7" id="b-p167.2" parsed="|Num|11|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.11.7">Num. 11:7</scripRef>, where the manna is likened to
it in colour. It was probably an aromatic gum like balsam which
exuded from a particular tree (Borassus flabelliformis) still
found in Arabia, Media, and India. It bears a resemblance in
colour to myrrh. Others think the word denotes “pearls,” or some
precious stone.
</def>
<term id="b-p167.3">Beacon</term>
A pole (Heb. to’ren) used as a standard or ensign set on the
tops of mountains as a call to the people to assemble themselves

for some great national purpose (<scripRef passage="Isa. 30:17" id="b-p168.1" parsed="|Isa|30|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.30.17">Isa. 30:17</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="Isa. 33:23" id="b-p168.2" parsed="|Isa|33|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.33.23">Isa. 33:23</scripRef> and
Ezek. 27:5, the same word is rendered “mast.” (See Banner.)
</def>
<term id="b-p168.5">Bealiah</term>
Whose Lord is Jehovah, a Benjamite, one of David’s thirty heroes
of the sling and bow (1 Chr. 12:5).
</def>
<term id="b-p169.2">Bealoth</term>
Citizens, a town in the extreme south of Judah (Josh. 15:24);
probably the same as Baalath-beer (19:8). In <scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:16" id="b-p170.2" parsed="|1Kgs|4|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.16">1 Kings 4:16</scripRef>, the
Authorized Version has “in Aloth,” the Revised Version
“Bealoth.”
</def>
<term id="b-p170.3">Beam</term>
Occurs in the Authorized Version as the rendering of various
Hebrew words. In <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:7" id="b-p171.1" parsed="|1Sam|17|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.7">1 Sam. 17:7</scripRef>, it means a weaver’s frame or

principal beam; in <scripRef passage="Hab. 2:11" id="b-p171.2" parsed="|Hab|2|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hab.2.11">Hab. 2:11</scripRef>, a crossbeam or girder; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 6:2" id="b-p171.3" parsed="|2Kgs|6|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.6.2">2 Kings 6:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 6:5" id="b-p171.4" parsed="|2Kgs|6|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.6.5">5</scripRef>, a cross-piece or rafter of a house; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 7:6" id="b-p171.5" parsed="|1Kgs|7|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.7.6">1 Kings 7:6</scripRef>, an

architectural ornament as a projecting step or moulding; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 41:25" id="b-p171.6" parsed="|Ezek|41|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.41.25">Ezek. 41:25</scripRef>, a thick plank. In the New Testament the word occurs only

in <scripRef passage="Matt. 7:3" id="b-p171.7" parsed="|Matt|7|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.7.3">Matt. 7:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 7:4" id="b-p171.8" parsed="|Matt|7|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.7.4">4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 7:5" id="b-p171.9" parsed="|Matt|7|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.7.5">5</scripRef>, and <scripRef passage="Luke 6:41" id="b-p171.10" parsed="|Luke|6|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.6.41">Luke 6:41</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Luke 6:42" id="b-p171.11" parsed="|Luke|6|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.6.42">42</scripRef>, where it means (Gr.
dokos) a large piece of wood used for building purposes, as
contrasted with “mote” (Gr. karphos), a small piece or mere
splinter. “Mote” and “beam” became proverbial for little and
great faults.
</def>
<term id="b-p171.12">Beans</term>
Mentioned in 2 Sam. 17:28 as having been brought to David when
flying from Absalom. They formed a constituent in the bread
Ezekiel (4:9) was commanded to make, as they were in general
much used as an article of diet. They are extensively cultivated
in Egypt and Arabia and Syria.
</def>
<term id="b-p172.2">Bear</term>
A native of the mountain regions of Western Asia, frequently
mentioned in Scripture. David defended his flocks against the
attacks of a bear (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:34-37" id="b-p173.1" parsed="|1Sam|17|34|17|37" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.34-1Sam.17.37">1 Sam. 17:34-37</scripRef>). Bears came out of the wood

and destroyed the children who mocked the prophet Elisha (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 2:24" id="b-p173.2" parsed="|2Kgs|2|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.2.24">2 Kings 2:24</scripRef>). Their habits are referred to in <scripRef passage="Isa. 59:11" id="b-p173.3" parsed="|Isa|59|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.59.11">Isa. 59:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 28:15" id="b-p173.4" parsed="|Prov|28|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.28.15">Prov. 28:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lam. 3:10" id="b-p173.5" parsed="|Lam|3|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lam.3.10">Lam. 3:10</scripRef>. The fury of the female bear when robbed of her

young is spoken of (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 17:8" id="b-p173.6" parsed="|2Sam|17|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.17.8">2 Sam. 17:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 17:12" id="b-p173.7" parsed="|Prov|17|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.17.12">Prov. 17:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos. 13:8" id="b-p173.8" parsed="|Hos|13|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.13.8">Hos. 13:8</scripRef>). In
Daniel’s vision of the four great monarchies, the Medo-Persian
empire is represented by a bear (7:5).
</def>
<term id="b-p173.9">Beard</term>
The mode of wearing it was definitely prescribed to the Jews

(<scripRef passage="Lev. 19:27" id="b-p174.1" parsed="|Lev|19|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.27">Lev. 19:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 21:5" id="b-p174.2" parsed="|Lev|21|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.21.5">21:5</scripRef>). Hence the import of Ezekiel’s (5:1-4)
description of the “razor” i.e., the agents of an angry
providence being used against the guilty nation of the Jews. It
was a part of a Jew’s daily toilet to anoint his beard with oil
and perfume (<scripRef passage="Ps. 133:2" id="b-p174.3" parsed="|Ps|133|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.133.2">Ps. 133:2</scripRef>). Beards were trimmed with the most
fastidious care (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 19:24" id="b-p174.4" parsed="|2Sam|19|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.19.24">2 Sam. 19:24</scripRef>), and their neglet was an

indication of deep sorrow (<scripRef passage="Isa. 15:2" id="b-p174.5" parsed="|Isa|15|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.15.2">Isa. 15:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 41:5" id="b-p174.6" parsed="|Jer|41|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.41.5">Jer. 41:5</scripRef>). The custom was
to shave or pluck off the hair as a sign of mourning (<scripRef passage="Isa. 50:6" id="b-p174.7" parsed="|Isa|50|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.50.6">Isa. 50:6</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Jer. 48:37" id="b-p174.8" parsed="|Jer|48|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.37">Jer. 48:37</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezra 9:3" id="b-p174.9" parsed="|Ezra|9|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.9.3">Ezra 9:3</scripRef>). The beards of David’s ambassadors were
cut off by hanun (2 Sam. 10:4) as a mark of indignity.
On the other hand, the Egyptians carefully shaved the hair off
their faces, and they compelled their slaves to do so also (Gen. 41:14).
</def>
<term id="b-p175.2">Beast</term>
This word is used of flocks or herds of grazing animals (Ex. 22:5; Num. 20:4, 8, 11; Ps. 78:48); of beasts of burden (Gen. 45:17); of eatable beasts (Prov. 9:2); and of swift beasts or
dromedaries (<scripRef passage="Isa. 60:6" id="b-p176.8" parsed="|Isa|60|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.60.6">Isa. 60:6</scripRef>). In the New Testament it is used of a

domestic animal as property (<scripRef passage="Rev. 18:13" id="b-p176.9" parsed="|Rev|18|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.18.13">Rev. 18:13</scripRef>); as used for food (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 15:39" id="b-p176.10" parsed="|1Cor|15|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.15.39">1 Cor. 15:39</scripRef>), for service (<scripRef passage="Luke 10:34" id="b-p176.11" parsed="|Luke|10|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.10.34">Luke 10:34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 23:24" id="b-p176.12" parsed="|Acts|23|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.23.24">Acts 23:24</scripRef>), and for
sacrifice (Acts 7:42).
When used in contradistinction to man (Ps. 36:6), it denotes a
brute creature generally, and when in contradistinction to
creeping things (Lev. 11:2-7; 27:26), a four-footed animal.
The Mosaic law required that beasts of labour should have rest

on the Sabbath (<scripRef passage="Ex. 20:10" id="b-p178.1" parsed="|Exod|20|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.20.10">Ex. 20:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 23:12" id="b-p178.2" parsed="|Exod|23|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.12">23:12</scripRef>), and in the Sabbatical year
all cattle were allowed to roam about freely, and eat whatever

grew in the fields (<scripRef passage="Ex. 23:11" id="b-p178.3" parsed="|Exod|23|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.11">Ex. 23:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 25:7" id="b-p178.4" parsed="|Lev|25|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.25.7">Lev. 25:7</scripRef>). No animal could be
castrated (<scripRef passage="Lev. 22:24" id="b-p178.5" parsed="|Lev|22|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.22.24">Lev. 22:24</scripRef>). Animals of different kinds were to be

always kept separate (<scripRef passage="Lev. 19:19" id="b-p178.6" parsed="|Lev|19|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.19">Lev. 19:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 22:10" id="b-p178.7" parsed="|Deut|22|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.22.10">Deut. 22:10</scripRef>). Oxen when used
in threshing were not to be prevented from eating what was
within their reach (Deut. 25:4; 1 Cor. 9:9).
This word is used figuratively of an infuriated multitude (1 Cor. 15:32; Acts 19:29; comp. Ps. 22:12, 16; Eccl. 3:18; Isa. 11:6-8), and of wicked men (2 Pet. 2:12). The four beasts of
Daniel 7:3, 17, 23 represent four kingdoms or kings.
</def>
<term id="b-p179.10">Beaten gold</term>
In Num. 8:4, means “turned” or rounded work in gold. The Greek
Version, however, renders the word “solid gold;” the Revised

Version, “beaten work of gold.” In <scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:16" id="b-p180.2" parsed="|1Kgs|10|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.16">1 Kings 10:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:17" id="b-p180.3" parsed="|1Kgs|10|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.17">17</scripRef>, it
probably means “mixed” gold, as the word ought to be rendered,
i.e., not pure gold. Others render the word in these places
“thin plates of gold.”
</def>
<term id="b-p180.4">Beaten oil</term>
(Ex. 27:20; 29:40), obtained by pounding olives in a mortar, not
by crushing them in a mill. It was reckoned the best. (See OLIVE.)
</def>
<term id="b-p181.4">Beautiful gate</term>
The name of one of the gates of the temple (Acts 3:2). It is
supposed to have been the door which led from the court of the
Gentiles to the court of the women. It was of massive structure,
and covered with plates of Corinthian brass.
</def>
<term id="b-p182.2">Becher</term>
First-born; a youth, the second son of Benjamin (Gen. 46:21),
who came down to Egypt with Jacob. It is probable that he
married an Ephraimitish heiress, and that his descendants were

consequently reckoned among the tribe of Ephraim (<scripRef passage="Num. 26:35" id="b-p183.2" parsed="|Num|26|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.26.35">Num. 26:35</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 7:20" id="b-p183.3" parsed="|1Chr|7|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.7.20">1 Chr. 7:20</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 7:21" id="b-p183.4" parsed="|1Chr|7|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.7.21">21</scripRef>). They are not reckoned among the descendants of
Benjamin (Num. 26:38).
</def>
<term id="b-p183.6">Bed</term>
(Heb. mittah), for rest at night (Ex. 8:3; 1 Sam. 19:13, 15, 16,

etc.); during sickness (<scripRef passage="Gen. 47:31" id="b-p184.5" parsed="|Gen|47|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.47.31">Gen. 47:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 48:2" id="b-p184.6" parsed="|Gen|48|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.48.2">48:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 49:33" id="b-p184.7" parsed="|Gen|49|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.33">49:33</scripRef>, etc.); as a

sofa for rest (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 28:23" id="b-p184.8" parsed="|1Sam|28|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.28.23">1 Sam. 28:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Amos 3:12" id="b-p184.9" parsed="|Amos|3|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.3.12">Amos 3:12</scripRef>). Another Hebrew word
(er’es) so rendered denotes a canopied bed, or a bed with
curtains (Deut. 3:11; Ps. 132:3), for sickness (Ps. 6:6; 41:3).
In the New Testament it denotes sometimes a litter with a
coverlet (Matt. 9:2, 6; Luke 5:18; Acts 5:15).
The Jewish bedstead was frequently merely the divan or
platform along the sides of the house, sometimes a very slight
portable frame, sometimes only a mat or one or more quilts. The
only material for bed-clothes is mentioned in <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 19:13" id="b-p186.1" parsed="|1Sam|19|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.19.13">1 Sam. 19:13</scripRef>.
Sleeping in the open air was not uncommon, the sleeper wrapping
himself in his outer garment (Ex. 22:26, 27; Deut. 24:12, 13).
</def>
<term id="b-p186.6">Bedan</term>
One of the judges of Israel (1 Sam. 12:11). It is uncertain who
he was. Some suppose that Barak is meant, others Samson, but
most probably this is a contracted form of Abdon (Judg. 12:13).
</def>
<term id="b-p187.3">Bed-chamber</term>
An apartment in Eastern houses, furnished with a slightly
elevated platform at the upper end and sometimes along the
sides, on which were laid mattresses. This was the general
arrangement of the public sleeping-room for the males of the
family and for guests, but there were usually besides distinct

bed-chambers of a more private character (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 4:10" id="b-p188.1" parsed="|2Kgs|4|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.4.10">2 Kings 4:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex. 8:3" id="b-p188.2" parsed="|Exod|8|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.8.3">Ex. 8:3</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="2 Kings 6:12" id="b-p188.3" parsed="|2Kgs|6|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.6.12">2 Kings 6:12</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="2 Kings 11:2" id="b-p188.4" parsed="|2Kgs|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.11.2">2 Kings 11:2</scripRef> this word denotes, as in the
margin of the Revised Version, a store-room in which mattresses
were kept.
</def>
<term id="b-p188.5">Bedstead</term>
Used in Deut. 3:11, but elsewhere rendered “couch,” “bed.” In 2 Kings 1:4; 16:2; Ps. 132:3; Amos 3:12, the divan is meant by
this word.
</def>
<term id="b-p189.6">Bee</term>
First mentioned in Deut. 1:44. Swarms of bees, and the danger of
their attacks, are mentioned in <scripRef passage="Ps. 118:12" id="b-p190.2" parsed="|Ps|118|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.118.12">Ps. 118:12</scripRef>. Samson found a

“swarm of bees” in the carcass of a lion he had slain (<scripRef passage="Judg. 14:8" id="b-p190.3" parsed="|Judg|14|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.14.8">Judg. 14:8</scripRef>). Wild bees are described as laying up honey in woods and

in clefts of rocks (<scripRef passage="Deut. 32:13" id="b-p190.4" parsed="|Deut|32|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.13">Deut. 32:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 81:16" id="b-p190.5" parsed="|Ps|81|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.81.16">Ps. 81:16</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="Isa. 7:18" id="b-p190.6" parsed="|Isa|7|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.7.18">Isa. 7:18</scripRef> the
“fly” and the “bee” are personifications of the Egyptians and
Assyrians, the inveterate enemies of Israel.
</def>
<term id="b-p190.7">Beelzebub</term>
(Gr. form Beel’zebul), the name given to Satan, and found only

in the New Testament (<scripRef passage="Matt. 10:25" id="b-p191.1" parsed="|Matt|10|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.10.25">Matt. 10:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 12:24" id="b-p191.2" parsed="|Matt|12|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.12.24">12:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt 12:27" id="b-p191.3" parsed="|Matt|12|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.12.27">27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 3:22" id="b-p191.4" parsed="|Mark|3|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.3.22">Mark 3:22</scripRef>). It is
probably the same as Baalzebub (q.v.), the god of Ekron, meaning
“the lord of flies,” or, as others think, “the lord of dung,” or
“the dung-god.”
</def>
<term id="b-p191.5">Beer</term>
Well. (1.) A place where a well was dug by the direction of
Moses, at the forty-fourth station of the Hebrews in their
wanderings (Num. 21:16-18) in the wilderness of Moab. (See WELL.)
(2.) A town in the tribe of Judah to which Jotham fled for
fear of Abimelech (<scripRef passage="Judg. 9:21" id="b-p193.1" parsed="|Judg|9|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.9.21">Judg. 9:21</scripRef>). Some have identified this place
with Beeroth.
</def>
<term id="b-p193.2">Beer-elim</term>
Well of heroes, probably the name given to Beer, the place where
the chiefs of Israel dug a well (Num. 21:16; Isa. 15:8).
</def>
<term id="b-p194.3">Beeri</term>
Illustrious, or the well-man. (1.) The father of Judith, one of

the wives of Esau (<scripRef passage="Gen. 26:34" id="b-p195.1" parsed="|Gen|26|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.26.34">Gen. 26:34</scripRef>), the same as Adah (<scripRef passage="Gen. 36:2" id="b-p195.2" parsed="|Gen|36|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36.2">Gen. 36:2</scripRef>).
(2.) The father of the prophet Hosea (1:1).
</def>
<term id="b-p195.3">Beer-lahai-roi</term>
I.e., “the well of him that liveth and seeth me,” or, as some
render it, “the well of the vision of life”, the well where the
Lord met with Hagar (<scripRef passage="Gen. 16:7-14" id="b-p196.1" parsed="|Gen|16|7|16|14" osisRef="Bible:Gen.16.7-Gen.16.14">Gen. 16:7-14</scripRef>). Isaac dwelt beside this well
(24:62; 25:11). It has been identified with ‘Ain Muweileh, or
Moilahhi, south-west of Beersheba, and about 12 miles W. from
Kadesh-barnea.
</def>
<term id="b-p196.2">Beeroth</term>
Wells, one of the four cities of the Hivites which entered by

fraud into a league with Joshua. It belonged to Benjamin (<scripRef passage="Josh. 18:25" id="b-p197.1" parsed="|Josh|18|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.18.25">Josh. 18:25</scripRef>). It has by some been identified with el-Bireh on the way
to Nablus, 10 miles north of Jerusalem.
</def>
<term id="b-p197.2">Beeroth of the children of Jaakan</term>
(Deut. 10:6). The same as Bene-jaakan (Num. 33:31).
</def>
<term id="b-p198.3">Beersheba</term>
Well of the oath, or well of seven, a well dug by Abraham, and
so named because he and Abimelech here entered into a compact
(<scripRef passage="Gen. 21:31" id="b-p199.1" parsed="|Gen|21|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.31">Gen. 21:31</scripRef>). On re-opening it, Isaac gave it the same name
(<scripRef passage="Gen. 26:31-33" id="b-p199.2" parsed="|Gen|26|31|26|33" osisRef="Bible:Gen.26.31-Gen.26.33">Gen. 26:31-33</scripRef>). It was a favourite place of abode of both of
these patriarchs (21:33-22:1, 19; 26:33; 28:10). It is mentioned

among the “cities” given to the tribe of Simeon (<scripRef passage="Josh. 19:2" id="b-p199.3" parsed="|Josh|19|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.2">Josh. 19:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 4:28" id="b-p199.4" parsed="|1Chr|4|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.4.28">1 Chr. 4:28</scripRef>). From Dan to Beersheba, a distance of about 144 miles

(<scripRef passage="Judg. 20:1" id="b-p199.5" parsed="|Judg|20|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.20.1">Judg. 20:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 21:2" id="b-p199.6" parsed="|1Chr|21|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.21.2">1 Chr. 21:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 24:2" id="b-p199.7" parsed="|2Sam|24|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.24.2">2 Sam. 24:2</scripRef>), became the usual way of
designating the whole Promised Land, and passed into a proverb.
After the return from the Captivity the phrase is narrowed into
“from Beersheba unto the valley of Hinnom” (<scripRef passage="Neh. 11:30" id="b-p199.8" parsed="|Neh|11|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.11.30">Neh. 11:30</scripRef>). The
kingdom of the ten tribes extended from Beersheba to Mount
Ephraim (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 19:4" id="b-p199.9" parsed="|2Chr|19|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.19.4">2 Chr. 19:4</scripRef>). The name is not found in the New
Testament. It is still called by the Arabs Bir es-Seba, i.e.,
“well of the seven”, where there are to the present day two
principal wells and five smaller ones. It is nearly midway
between the southern end of the Dead Sea and the Mediterranean.
</def>
<term id="b-p199.10">Beetle</term>
(Heb. hargol, meaning “leaper”). Mention of it is made only in
<scripRef passage="Lev. 11:22" id="b-p200.1" parsed="|Lev|11|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.11.22">Lev. 11:22</scripRef>, where it is obvious the word cannot mean properly
the beetle. It denotes some winged creeper with at least four
feet, “which has legs above its feet, to leap withal.” The
description plainly points to the locust (q.v.). This has been
an article of food from the earliest times in the East to the
present day. The word is rendered “cricket” in the Revised
Version.
</def>
<term id="b-p200.2">Beeves</term>
(an old English plural of the word beef), a name applicable to
all ruminating animals except camels, and especially to the
Bovidce, or horned cattle (Lev. 22:19, 21; Num. 31:28, 30, 33, 38, 44).
</def>
<term id="b-p201.8">Beg</term>
That the poor existed among the Hebrews we have abundant

evidence (<scripRef passage="Ex. 23:11" id="b-p202.1" parsed="|Exod|23|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.11">Ex. 23:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 15:11" id="b-p202.2" parsed="|Deut|15|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.15.11">Deut. 15:11</scripRef>), but there is no mention of
beggars properly so called in the Old Testament. The poor were

provided for by the law of Moses (<scripRef passage="Lev. 19:10" id="b-p202.3" parsed="|Lev|19|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.10">Lev. 19:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 12:12" id="b-p202.4" parsed="|Deut|12|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.12.12">Deut. 12:12</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Deut 14:29" id="b-p202.5" parsed="|Deut|14|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.14.29">14:29</scripRef>). It is predicted of the seed of the wicked that they
shall be beggars (Ps. 37:25; 109:10).
In the New Testament we find not seldom mention made of

beggars (<scripRef passage="Mark 10:46" id="b-p203.1" parsed="|Mark|10|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.10.46">Mark 10:46</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 16:20" id="b-p203.2" parsed="|Luke|16|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.16.20">Luke 16:20</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Luke 16:21" id="b-p203.3" parsed="|Luke|16|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.16.21">21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 3:2" id="b-p203.4" parsed="|Acts|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.3.2">Acts 3:2</scripRef>), yet there is no
mention of such a class as vagrant beggars, so numerous in the
East. “Beggarly,” in Gal. 4:9, means worthless.
</def>
<term id="b-p203.6">Behead</term>
A method of taking away life practised among the Egyptians (Gen. 40:17-19). There are instances of this mode of punishment also

among the Hebrews (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 4:8" id="b-p204.2" parsed="|2Sam|4|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.4.8">2 Sam. 4:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 20:21" id="b-p204.3" parsed="|2Sam|20|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.20.21">20:21</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 20:22" id="b-p204.4" parsed="|2Sam|20|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.20.22">22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 10:6-8" id="b-p204.5" parsed="|2Kgs|10|6|10|8" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.10.6-2Kgs.10.8">2 Kings 10:6-8</scripRef>). It is
also mentioned in the New Testament (Matt. 14:8-12; Acts 12:2).
</def>
<term id="b-p204.8">Behemoth</term>
(Job 40:15-24). Some have supposed this to be an Egyptian word
meaning a “water-ox.” The Revised Version has here in the margin
“hippopotamus,” which is probably the correct rendering of the
word. The word occurs frequently in Scripture, but, except here,
always as a common name, and translated “beast” or “cattle.”
</def>
<term id="b-p205.2">Bekah</term>
Both the name and its explanation, “a half shekel,” are given in
<scripRef passage="Ex. 38:26" id="b-p206.1" parsed="|Exod|38|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.38.26">Ex. 38:26</scripRef>. The word properly means a “division,” a “part.”
</def>
<term id="b-p206.2">Bel</term>
The Aramaic form of Baal, the national god of the Babylonians
(Isa. 46:1; Jer. 50:2; 51:44). It signifies “lord.” (See BAAL.)
</def>
<term id="b-p207.5">Bela</term>
A thing swallowed. (1.) A city on the shore of the Dead Sea, not
far from Sodom, called also Zoar. It was the only one of the
five cities that was spared at Lot’s intercession (Gen. 19:20, 23). It is first mentioned in Gen. 14:2, 8.
(2.) The eldest son of Benjamin (Num. 26:38; “Belah,” Gen. 46:21).
(3.) The son of Beor, and a king of Edom (Gen. 36:32, 33; 1 Chr. 1:43).
(4.) A son of Azaz (1 Chr. 5:8).
</def>
<term id="b-p211.2">Belial</term>
Worthlessness, frequently used in the Old Testament as a proper
name. It is first used in <scripRef passage="Deut. 13:13" id="b-p212.1" parsed="|Deut|13|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.13.13">Deut. 13:13</scripRef>. In the New Testament it
is found only in <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 6:15" id="b-p212.2" parsed="|2Cor|6|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.6.15">2 Cor. 6:15</scripRef>, where it is used as a name of
Satan, the personification of all that is evil. It is translated

“wicked” in <scripRef passage="Deut. 15:9" id="b-p212.3" parsed="|Deut|15|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.15.9">Deut. 15:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 41:8" id="b-p212.4" parsed="|Ps|41|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.41.8">Ps. 41:8</scripRef> (R.V. marg.); 101:3; <scripRef passage="Prov. 6:12" id="b-p212.5" parsed="|Prov|6|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.6.12">Prov. 6:12</scripRef>, etc. The expression “son” or “man of Belial” means simply

a worthless, lawless person (<scripRef passage="Judg. 19:22" id="b-p212.6" parsed="|Judg|19|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.19.22">Judg. 19:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg 20:13" id="b-p212.7" parsed="|Judg|20|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.20.13">20:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 1:16" id="b-p212.8" parsed="|1Sam|1|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.1.16">1 Sam. 1:16</scripRef>;
2:12).
</def>
<term id="b-p212.10">Bell</term>
The bells first mentioned in Scripture are the small golden

bells attached to the hem of the high priest’s ephod (<scripRef passage="Ex. 28:33" id="b-p213.1" parsed="|Exod|28|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.33">Ex. 28:33</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex 28:34" id="b-p213.2" parsed="|Exod|28|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.34">34</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex 28:35" id="b-p213.3" parsed="|Exod|28|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.35">35</scripRef>). The “bells of the horses” mentioned by Zechariah
(14:20) were attached to the bridles or belts round the necks of
horses trained for war, so as to accustom them to noise and
tumult.
</def>
<term id="b-p213.4">Bellows</term>
Occurs only in Jer. 6:29, in relation to the casting of metal.
Probably they consisted of leather bags similar to those common
in Egypt.
</def>
<term id="b-p214.2">Belly</term>
The seat of the carnal affections (Titus 1:12; Phil. 3:19; Rom. 16:18). The word is used symbolically for the heart (Prov. 18:8;

<scripRef passage="Prov 20:27" id="b-p215.5" parsed="|Prov|20|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.20.27">20:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov 22:18" id="b-p215.6" parsed="|Prov|22|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.22.18">22:18</scripRef>, marg.). The “belly of hell” signifies the grave or
underworld (Jonah 2:2).
</def>
<term id="b-p215.8">Belshazzar</term>
Bel protect the king!, the last of the kings of Babylon (Dan. 5:1). He was the son of Nabonidus by Nitocris, who was the
daughter of Nebuchadnezzar and the widow of Nergal-sharezer.
When still young he made a great feast to a thousand of his
lords, and when heated with wine sent for the sacred vessels his
“father” (<scripRef passage="Dan. 5:2" id="b-p216.2" parsed="|Dan|5|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.5.2">Dan. 5:2</scripRef>), or grandfather, Nebuchadnezzar had carried
away from the temple in Jerusalem, and he and his princes drank
out of them. In the midst of their mad revelry a hand was seen
by the king tracing on the wall the announcement of God’s
judgment, which that night fell upon him. At the instance of the
queen (i.e., his mother) Daniel was brought in, and he
interpreted the writing. That night the kingdom of the Chaldeans
came to an end, and the king was slain (<scripRef passage="Dan. 5:30" id="b-p216.3" parsed="|Dan|5|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.5.30">Dan. 5:30</scripRef>). (See
NERGAL-SHAREZER.)
The absence of the name of Belshazzar on the monuments was
long regarded as an argument against the genuineness of the Book
of Daniel. In 1854 Sir Henry Rawlinson found an inscription of
Nabonidus which referred to his eldest son. Quite recently,
however, the side of a ravine undermined by heavy rains fell at
Hillah, a suburb of Babylon. A number of huge, coarse
earthenware vases were laid bare. These were filled with
tablets, the receipts and contracts of a firm of Babylonian
bankers, which showed that Belshazzar had a household, with
secretaries and stewards. One was dated in the third year of the
king Marduk-sar-uzur. As Marduk-sar-uzar was another name for
Baal, this Marduk-sar-uzur was found to be the Belshazzar of
Scripture. In one of these contract tablets, dated in the July
after the defeat of the army of Nabonidus, we find him paying
tithes for his sister to the temple of the sun-god at Sippara.
</def>
<term id="b-p217.1">Belteshazzar</term>
Beltis protect the king!, the Chaldee name given to Daniel by
Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. 1:7).
</def>
<term id="b-p218.2">Benaiah</term>
Built up by Jehovah. (1.) The son of Jehoiada, chief priest (1 Chr. 27:5). He was set by David over his body-guard of

Cherethites and Pelethites (2 Sam. 8:18; 1 Kings 1:32; 1 Chr. 18:17). His exploits are enumerated in 2 Sam. 23:20, 21, 22; 1 Chr. 11:22. He remained faithful to Solomon (1 Kings 1:8, 10, 26), by whom he was raised to the rank of commander-in-chief (1 Kings 2:25, 29, 30, 34, 35; 4:4).
(2.) 2 Sam. 23:30; 1 Chr. 11:31.
(3.) A musical Levite (1 Chr. 15:18, 20).
(4.) A priest (1 Chr. 15:24; 16:6).
(5.) The son of Jeiel (2 Chr. 20:14).
</def>
<term id="b-p223.2">Ben-ammi</term>
Son of my kindred; i.e., “born of incest”, the son of Lot by his
youngest daughter (Gen. 19:38).
</def>
<term id="b-p224.2">Bench</term>
Deck of a Tyrian ship, described by Ezekiel (27:6) as overlaid
with box-wood.
</def>
<term id="b-p225.1">Bene-jaakan</term>
Children of Jaakan (Num. 33:31, 32), the same as Beeroth.
</def>
<term id="b-p226.3">Ben-hadad</term>
The standing title of the Syrian kings, meaning “the son of
Hadad.” (See HADADEZER.)
(1.) The king of Syria whom Asa, king of Judah, employed to
invade Israel (1 Kings 15:18).
(2.) Son of the preceding, also king of Syria. He was long
engaged in war against Israel. He was murdered probably by
Hazael, by whom he was succeeded (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 8:7-15" id="b-p229.1" parsed="|2Kgs|8|7|8|15" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.8.7-2Kgs.8.15">2 Kings 8:7-15</scripRef>), after a reign
of some thirty years.
(3.) King of Damascus, and successor of his father Hazael on

the throne of Syria (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 13:3" id="b-p230.1" parsed="|2Kgs|13|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.13.3">2 Kings 13:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 13:4" id="b-p230.2" parsed="|2Kgs|13|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.13.4">4</scripRef>). His misfortunes in war
are noticed by Amos (1:4).
</def>
<term id="b-p230.3">Benjamin</term>
Son of my right hand. (1.) The younger son of Jacob by Rachel
(<scripRef passage="Gen. 35:18" id="b-p231.1" parsed="|Gen|35|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.35.18">Gen. 35:18</scripRef>). His birth took place at Ephrath, on the road
between Bethel and Bethlehem, at a short distance from the
latter place. His mother died in giving him birth, and with her
last breath named him Ben-oni, son of my pain, a name which was
changed by his father into Benjamin. His posterity are called
Benjamites (Gen. 49:27; Deut. 33:12; Josh. 18:21).
The tribe of Benjamin at the Exodus was the smallest but one

(<scripRef passage="Num. 1:36" id="b-p232.1" parsed="|Num|1|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.1.36">Num. 1:36</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 1:37" id="b-p232.2" parsed="|Num|1|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.1.37">37</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 68:27" id="b-p232.3" parsed="|Ps|68|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.68.27">Ps. 68:27</scripRef>). During the march its place was along
with Manasseh and Ephraim on the west of the tabernacle. At the
entrance into Canaan it counted 45,600 warriors. It has been
inferred by some from the words of Jacob (<scripRef passage="Gen. 49:27" id="b-p232.4" parsed="|Gen|49|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.27">Gen. 49:27</scripRef>) that the
figure of a wolf was on the tribal standard. This tribe is
mentioned in Rom. 11:1; Phil. 3:5.
The inheritance of this tribe lay immediately to the south of
that of Ephraim, and was about 26 miles in length and 12 in
breadth. Its eastern boundary was the Jordan. Dan intervened
between it and the Philistines. Its chief towns are named in
Josh. 18:21-28.
The history of the tribe contains a sad record of a desolating
civil war in which they were engaged with the other eleven

tribes. By it they were almost exterminated (<scripRef passage="Judg. 20:20" id="b-p234.1" parsed="|Judg|20|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.20.20">Judg. 20:20</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Judg. 20:21" id="b-p234.2" parsed="|Judg|20|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.20.21">21</scripRef>;
21:10). (See GIBEAH.)
The first king of the Jews was Saul, a Benjamite. A close
alliance was formed between this tribe and that of Judah in the

time of David (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 19:16" id="b-p235.1" parsed="|2Sam|19|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.19.16">2 Sam. 19:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 19:17" id="b-p235.2" parsed="|2Sam|19|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.19.17">17</scripRef>), which continued after his

death (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 11:13" id="b-p235.3" parsed="|1Kgs|11|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.11.13">1 Kings 11:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 12:20" id="b-p235.4" parsed="|1Kgs|12|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.12.20">12:20</scripRef>). After the Exile these two tribes
formed the great body of the Jewish nation (Ezra 1:5; 10:9).
The tribe of Benjamin was famous for its archers (1 Sam. 20:20, 36; 2 Sam. 1:22; 1 Chr. 8:40; 12:2) and slingers (Judge.
The gate of Benjamin, on the north side of Jerusalem (Jer. 37:13; 38:7; Zech. 14:10), was so called because it led in the
direction of the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. It is
called by Jeremiah (20:2) “the high gate of Benjamin;” also “the
gate of the children of the people” (17:19). (Comp. 2 Kings 14:13.)
</def>
<term id="b-p237.5">Beor</term>
A torch. (1.) The father of Bela, one of the kings of Edom (Gen. 36:32).
(2.) The father of Balaam (Num. 22:5; 24:3, 15; 31:8). In 2 Pet. 2:15 he is called Bosor.
</def>
<term id="b-p239.5">Bera</term>
Gift, or son of evil, king of Sodom at the time of the invasion
of the four kings under Chedorlaomer (Gen. 14:2, 8, 17, 21).
</def>
<term id="b-p240.5">Berachah</term>
Blessing. (1.) A valley not far from Engedi, where Jehoshaphat
overthrew the Moabites and Ammonites (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 20:26" id="b-p241.1" parsed="|2Chr|20|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.20.26">2 Chr. 20:26</scripRef>). It has been
identified with the valley of Bereikut. (R.V., “Beracah.”)
(2.) One of the Benjamite warriors, Saul’s brethren, who
joined David when at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:3).
</def>
<term id="b-p242.2">Berea</term>
A city of Macedonia to which Paul with Silas and Timotheus went

when persecuted at Thessalonica (<scripRef passage="Acts 17:10" id="b-p243.1" parsed="|Acts|17|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.17.10">Acts 17:10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 17:13" id="b-p243.2" parsed="|Acts|17|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.17.13">13</scripRef>), and from which
also he was compelled to withdraw, when he fled to the sea-coast
and thence sailed to Athens (14, 15). Sopater, one of Paul’s
companions belonged to this city, and his conversion probably
took place at this time (Acts 20:4). It is now called Verria.
</def>
<term id="b-p243.4">Berechiah</term>
Blessed by Jehovah. (1.) Son of Shimea, and father of Asaph the
musician (1 Chr. 6:39; 15:17).
(2.) One of the seven Ephraimite chieftains, son of
Meshillemoth (2 Chr. 28:12).
(3.) The fourth of the five sons of Zerubbabel, of the royal
family of Judah (1 Chr. 3:20).
(4.) The father of the prophet Zechariah (1:1, 7).
</def>
<term id="b-p247.1">Bered</term>
Hail. (1.) A town in the south of Palestine (Gen. 16:14), in the
desert of Shur, near Lahai-roi.
(2.) A son of Shuthelah, and grandson of Ephraim (1 Chr. 7:20).
</def>
<term id="b-p249.2">Beriah</term>
A gift, or in evil. (1.) One of Asher’s four sons, and father of
Heber (Gen. 46:17).
(2.) A son of Ephraim (1 Chr. 7:20-23), born after the
slaughter of his brothers, and so called by his father “because
it went evil with his house” at that time.
(3.) A Benjamite who with his brother Shema founded Ajalon and
expelled the Gittites (1 Chr. 8:13).
</def>
<term id="b-p252.2">Bernice</term>
Bearer of victory, the eldest daughter of Agrippa I., the Herod
Agrippa of <scripRef passage="Acts 12:20" id="b-p253.1" parsed="|Acts|12|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.12.20">Acts 12:20</scripRef>. After the early death of her first
husband she was married to her uncle Herod, king of Chalcis.
After his death (A.D. 40) she lived in incestuous connection

with her brother Agrippa II. (<scripRef passage="Acts 25:13" id="b-p253.2" parsed="|Acts|25|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.25.13">Acts 25:13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 25:23" id="b-p253.3" parsed="|Acts|25|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.25.23">23</scripRef>; 26:30). They
joined the Romans at the outbreak of the final war between them
and the Jews, and lived afterwards at Rome.
</def>
<term id="b-p253.4">Berodach-baladan</term>
The king of Babylon who sent a friendly deputation to Hezekiah

(<scripRef passage="2 Kings 20:12" id="b-p254.1" parsed="|2Kgs|20|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.20.12">2 Kings 20:12</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="Isa. 39:1" id="b-p254.2" parsed="|Isa|39|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.39.1">Isa. 39:1</scripRef> he is called Merodach-baladan
</def>
<term id="b-p254.3">Beryl</term>
The rendering in the Authorized Version of the Hebrew word
tarshish, a precious stone; probably so called as being
brought from Tarshish. It was one of the stones on the
breastplate of the high priest (<scripRef passage="Ex. 28:20" id="b-p255.1" parsed="|Exod|28|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.20">Ex. 28:20</scripRef>; R.V. marg.,
“chalcedony;” 39:13). The colour of the wheels in Ezekiel’s
vision was as the colour of a beryl stone (1:16; 10:9; R.V.,

“stone of Tarshish”). It is mentioned in <scripRef passage="Cant. 5:14" id="b-p255.2" parsed="|Song|5|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.5.14">Cant. 5:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Dan. 10:6" id="b-p255.3" parsed="|Dan|10|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.10.6">Dan. 10:6</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Rev. 21:20" id="b-p255.4" parsed="|Rev|21|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.21.20">Rev. 21:20</scripRef>. In <scripRef passage="Ezek. 28:13" id="b-p255.5" parsed="|Ezek|28|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.28.13">Ezek. 28:13</scripRef> the LXX. render the word by
“chrysolite,” which the Jewish historian Josephus regards as its
proper translation. This also is the rendering given in the
Authorized Version in the margin. That was a gold-coloured gem,
the topaz of ancient authors.
</def>
<term id="b-p255.6">Besom</term>
The rendering of a Hebrew word meaning sweeper, occurs only in
Isa. 14:23, of the sweeping away, the utter ruin, of Babylon.
</def>
<term id="b-p256.2">Besor</term>
Cold, a ravine or brook in the extreme south-west of Judah,
where 200 of David’s men stayed behind because they were faint,
while the other 400 pursued the Amalekites (1 Sam. 30:9, 10, 21). Probably the Wadyes Sheriah, south of Gaza.
</def>
<term id="b-p257.4">Bestead</term>
The rendering in Isa. 8:21, where alone it occurs, of a Hebrew
word meaning to oppress, or be in circumstances of hardship.
</def>
<term id="b-p258.2">Betah</term>
Confidence, a city belonging to Hadadezer, king of Zobah, which
yielded much spoil of brass to David (2 Sam. 8:8). In 1 Chr. 18:8 it is called Tibhath.
</def>
<term id="b-p259.3">Beth</term>
Occurs frequently as the appellation for a house, or
dwelling-place, in such compounds as the words immediately
following:
</def>
<term id="b-p260.1">Bethabara</term>
House of the ford, a place on the east bank of the Jordan, where
John was baptizing (<scripRef passage="John 1:28" id="b-p261.1" parsed="|John|1|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.1.28">John 1:28</scripRef>). It may be identical with
Bethbarah, the ancient ford of Jordan of which the men of
Ephraim took possession (<scripRef passage="Judg. 7:24" id="b-p261.2" parsed="|Judg|7|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.7.24">Judg. 7:24</scripRef>). The Revised Version reads
“Bethany beyond Jordan.” It was the great ford, and still bears
the name of “the ford,” Makhadhet ‘Abarah, “the ford of crossing
over,” about 25 miles from Nazareth. (See BETHBARAH.)
</def>
<term id="b-p261.4">Beth-anath</term>
House of response, one of the fenced cities of Naphtali (Josh. 19:38). It is perhaps identical with the modern village ‘Ainata,
6 miles west of Kedesh.
</def>
<term id="b-p262.2">Beth-anoth</term>
House of answers, a city in the mountainous district of Judah
(<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:59" id="b-p263.1" parsed="|Josh|15|59|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.59">Josh. 15:59</scripRef>). It has been identified with the modern
Beit-‘Anun, about 3 miles northeast of Hebron.
</def>
<term id="b-p263.2">Bethany</term>
House of dates. (1.) The Revised Version in John 1:28 has this
word instead of Bethabara, on the authority of the oldest
manuscripts. It appears to have been the name of a place on the
east of Jordan.
(2.) A village on the south-eastern slope of the Mount of
Olives (<scripRef passage="Mark 11:1" id="b-p265.1" parsed="|Mark|11|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.11.1">Mark 11:1</scripRef>), about 2 miles east of Jerusalem, on the road
to Jericho. It derived its name from the number of palm-trees
which grew there. It was the residence of Lazarus and his
sisters. It is frequently mentioned in connection with memorable

incidents in the life of our Lord (<scripRef passage="Matt. 21:17" id="b-p265.2" parsed="|Matt|21|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.21.17">Matt. 21:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 26:6" id="b-p265.3" parsed="|Matt|26|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.6">26:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 11:11" id="b-p265.4" parsed="|Mark|11|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.11.11">Mark 11:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Mark 11:12" id="b-p265.5" parsed="|Mark|11|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.11.12">12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 14:3" id="b-p265.6" parsed="|Mark|14|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.14.3">14:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 24:50" id="b-p265.7" parsed="|Luke|24|50|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.24.50">Luke 24:50</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 11:1" id="b-p265.8" parsed="|John|11|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.11.1">John 11:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 12:1" id="b-p265.9" parsed="|John|12|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.12.1">12:1</scripRef>). It is now known
by the name of el-Azariyeh, i.e., “place of Lazarus,” or simply
Lazariyeh. Seen from a distance, the village has been described
as “remarkably beautiful, the perfection of retirement and
repose, of seclusion and lovely peace.” Now a mean village,
containing about twenty families.
</def>
<term id="b-p265.10">Beth-arabah</term>
House of the desert, one of the six cities of Judah, situated in
the sunk valley of the Jordan and Dead Sea (<scripRef passage="Josh. 18:22" id="b-p266.1" parsed="|Josh|18|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.18.22">Josh. 18:22</scripRef>). In
<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:61" id="b-p266.2" parsed="|Josh|15|61|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.61">Josh. 15:61</scripRef> it is said to have been “in the wilderness.” It was
afterwards included in the towns of Benjamin. It is called
Arabah (Josh. 18:18).
</def>
<term id="b-p266.4">Beth-aram</term>
House of the height; i.e., “mountain-house”, one of the towns of
Gad, 3 miles east of Jordan, opposite Jericho (<scripRef passage="Josh. 13:27" id="b-p267.1" parsed="|Josh|13|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.27">Josh. 13:27</scripRef>).
Probably the same as Beth-haran in <scripRef passage="Num. 32:36" id="b-p267.2" parsed="|Num|32|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.32.36">Num. 32:36</scripRef>. It was called by
king Herod, Julias, or Livias, after Livia, the wife of
Augustus. It is now called Beit-haran.
</def>
<term id="b-p267.3">Beth-arbel</term>
House of God’s court, a place alluded to by Hosea (10:14) as the
scene of some great military exploit, but not otherwise
mentioned in Scripture. The Shalman here named was probably
Shalmaneser, the king of Assyria (2 Kings 17:3).
</def>
<term id="b-p268.2">Beth-aven</term>
House of nothingness; i.e., “of idols”, a place in the mountains

of Benjamin, east of Bethel (<scripRef passage="Josh. 7:2" id="b-p269.1" parsed="|Josh|7|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.7.2">Josh. 7:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 18:12" id="b-p269.2" parsed="|Josh|18|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.18.12">18:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 13:5" id="b-p269.3" parsed="|1Sam|13|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.13.5">1 Sam. 13:5</scripRef>). In

<scripRef passage="Hos. 4:15" id="b-p269.4" parsed="|Hos|4|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.4.15">Hos. 4:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos 5:8" id="b-p269.5" parsed="|Hos|5|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.5.8">5:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos 10:5" id="b-p269.6" parsed="|Hos|10|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.10.5">10:5</scripRef> it stands for “Bethel” (q.v.), and it is so
called because it was no longer the “house of God,” but “the
house of idols,” referring to the calves there worshipped.
</def>
<term id="b-p269.7">Beth-barah</term>
House of crossing, a place south of the scene of Gideon’s
victory (<scripRef passage="Judg. 7:24" id="b-p270.1" parsed="|Judg|7|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.7.24">Judg. 7:24</scripRef>). It was probably the chief ford of the
Jordan in that district, and may have been that by which Jacob

crossed when he returned from Mesopotamia, near the Jabbok (<scripRef passage="Gen. 32:22" id="b-p270.2" parsed="|Gen|32|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.32.22">Gen. 32:22</scripRef>), and at which Jephthah slew the Ephraimites (<scripRef passage="Judg. 12:4" id="b-p270.3" parsed="|Judg|12|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.12.4">Judg. 12:4</scripRef>).
Nothing, however, is certainly known of it. (See BETHABARA.)
</def>
<term id="b-p270.5">Beth-car</term>
Sheep-house, a place to which the Israelites pursued the
Philistines west from Mizpeh (1 Sam. 7:11).
</def>
<term id="b-p271.2">Beth-dagon</term>
House of Dagon. (1.) A city in the low country or plain of
Judah, near Philistia (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:41" id="b-p272.1" parsed="|Josh|15|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.41">Josh. 15:41</scripRef>); the modern Beit Degan,
about 5 miles from Lydda.
(2.) A city near the south-east border of Asher (Josh. 19:27).
It was a Philistine colony. It is identical with the modern
ruined village of Tell D’auk.
</def>
<term id="b-p273.2">Beth-diblathaim</term>
House of two cakes of figs, a city of Moab, upon which Jeremiah
(48:22) denounced destruction. It is called also

Almon-diblathaim (<scripRef passage="Num. 33:46" id="b-p274.1" parsed="|Num|33|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.46">Num. 33:46</scripRef>) and Diblath (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 6:14" id="b-p274.2" parsed="|Ezek|6|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.6.14">Ezek. 6:14</scripRef>). (R.V.,
“Diblah.”)
</def>
<term id="b-p274.3">Bethel</term>
House of God. (1.) A place in Central Palestine, about 10 miles
north of Jerusalem, at the head of the pass of Michmash and Ai.
It was originally the royal Canaanite city of Luz (<scripRef passage="Gen. 28:19" id="b-p275.1" parsed="|Gen|28|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.28.19">Gen. 28:19</scripRef>).
The name Bethel was at first apparently given to the sanctuary
in the neighbourhood of Luz, and was not given to the city
itself till after its conquest by the tribe of Ephraim. When
Abram entered Canaan he formed his second encampment between
Bethel and Hai (<scripRef passage="Gen. 12:8" id="b-p275.2" parsed="|Gen|12|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.12.8">Gen. 12:8</scripRef>); and on his return from Egypt he came
back to it, and again “called upon the name of the Lord” (13:4).
Here Jacob, on his way from Beersheba to Haran, had a vision of
the angels of God ascending and descending on the ladder whose
top reached unto heaven (28:10, 19); and on his return he again
visited this place, “where God talked with him” (35:1-15), and
there he “built an altar, and called the place El-beth-el”
(q.v.). To this second occasion of God’s speaking with Jacob at
Bethel, Hosea (12:4, 5) makes reference.
In troublous times the people went to Bethel to ask counsel of

God (<scripRef passage="Judg. 20:18" id="b-p276.1" parsed="|Judg|20|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.20.18">Judg. 20:18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Judg. 20:31" id="b-p276.2" parsed="|Judg|20|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.20.31">31</scripRef>; 21:2). Here the ark of the covenant was
kept for a long time under the care of Phinehas, the grandson of
Aaron (20:26-28). Here also Samuel held in rotation his court of
justice (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 7:16" id="b-p276.3" parsed="|1Sam|7|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.7.16">1 Sam. 7:16</scripRef>). It was included in Israel after the
kingdom was divided, and it became one of the seats of the

worship of the golden calf (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 12:28-33" id="b-p276.4" parsed="|1Kgs|12|28|12|33" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.12.28-1Kgs.12.33">1 Kings 12:28-33</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 13:1" id="b-p276.5" parsed="|1Kgs|13|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.13.1">13:1</scripRef>). Hence the

prophet Hosea (<scripRef passage="Hos. 4:15" id="b-p276.6" parsed="|Hos|4|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.4.15">Hos. 4:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos 5:8" id="b-p276.7" parsed="|Hos|5|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.5.8">5:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos 10:5" id="b-p276.8" parsed="|Hos|10|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.10.5">10:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Hos 10:8" id="b-p276.9" parsed="|Hos|10|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.10.8">8</scripRef>) calls it in contempt
Beth-aven, i.e., “house of idols.” Bethel remained an abode of
priests even after the kingdom of Israel was desolated by the

king of Assyria (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:28" id="b-p276.10" parsed="|2Kgs|17|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.28">2 Kings 17:28</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:29" id="b-p276.11" parsed="|2Kgs|17|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.29">29</scripRef>). At length all traces of the

idolatries were extirpated by Josiah, king of Judah (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 23:15-18" id="b-p276.12" parsed="|2Kgs|23|15|23|18" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.15-2Kgs.23.18">2 Kings 23:15-18</scripRef>); and the place was still in existence after the

Captivity (<scripRef passage="Ezra 2:28" id="b-p276.13" parsed="|Ezra|2|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2.28">Ezra 2:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh. 7:32" id="b-p276.14" parsed="|Neh|7|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.7.32">Neh. 7:32</scripRef>). It has been identified with
the ruins of Beitin, a small village amid extensive ruins some 9
miles south of Shiloh.
(2.) Mount Bethel was a hilly district near Bethel (Josh. 16:1; 1 Sam. 13:2).
(3.) A town in the south of Judah (Josh. 8:17; 12:16).
</def>
<term id="b-p278.3">Bethelite</term>
A designation of Hiel (q.v.), who rebuilt Jericho and
experienced the curse pronounced long before (1 Kings 16:34).
</def>
<term id="b-p279.2">Bether</term>
Dissection or separation, certain mountains mentioned in Cant. 2:17; probably near Lebanon.
</def>
<term id="b-p280.2">Bethesda</term>
House of mercy, a reservoir (Gr. kolumbethra, “a swimming bath”)
with five porches, close to the sheep-gate or market (<scripRef passage="Neh. 3:1" id="b-p281.1" parsed="|Neh|3|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.3.1">Neh. 3:1</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="John 5:2" id="b-p281.2" parsed="|John|5|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.5.2">John 5:2</scripRef>). Eusebius the historian (A.D. 330) calls it “the
sheep-pool.” It is also called “Bethsaida” and “Beth-zatha”
(<scripRef passage="John 5:2" id="b-p281.3" parsed="|John|5|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.5.2">John 5:2</scripRef>, R.V. marg.). Under these “porches” or colonnades were
usually a large number of infirm people waiting for the
“troubling of the water.” It is usually identified with the
modern so-called Fountain of the Virgin, in the valley of the
Kidron, and not far from the Pool of Siloam (q.v.); and also
with the Birket Israel, a pool near the mouth of the valley
which runs into the Kidron south of “St. Stephen’s Gate.” Others
again identify it with the twin pools called the “Souterrains,”
under the convent of the Sisters of Zion, situated in what must
have been the rock-hewn ditch between Bezetha and the fortress
