of Antonia. But quite recently Schick has discovered a large
tank, as sketched here, situated about 100 feet north-west of
St. Anne’s Church, which is, as he contends, very probably the
Pool of Bethesda. No certainty as to its identification,
however, has as yet been arrived at. (See FOUNTAIN; GIHON.)
</def>
<term id="b-p281.6">Beth-gamul</term>
Camel-house, a city in the “plain country” of Moab denounced by
the prophet (<scripRef passage="Jer. 48:23" id="b-p282.1" parsed="|Jer|48|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.23">Jer. 48:23</scripRef>); probably the modern Um-el-Jemal, near
Bozrah, one of the deserted cities of the Hauran.
</def>
<term id="b-p282.2">Beth-gilgal</term>
House of Gilgal, a place from which the inhabitants gathered for
the purpose of celebrating the rebuilding of the walls on the
return exile (Neh. 12:29). (See GILGAL.)
</def>
<term id="b-p283.3">Beth-haccerem</term>
House of a vineyard, a place in the tribe of Judah (Neh. 3:14)
where the Benjamites were to set up a beacon when they heard the
trumpet against the invading army of the Babylonians (<scripRef passage="Jer. 6:1" id="b-p284.2" parsed="|Jer|6|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.6.1">Jer. 6:1</scripRef>).
It is probable that this place is the modern ‘Ain Karim, or
“well of the vineyards,” near which there is a ridge on which
are cairns which may have served as beacons of old, one of which
is 40 feet high and 130 in diameter.
</def>
<term id="b-p284.3">Beth-horon</term>
House of the hollow, or of the cavern, the name of two towns or

villages (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 8:5" id="b-p285.1" parsed="|2Chr|8|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.8.5">2 Chr. 8:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 7:24" id="b-p285.2" parsed="|1Chr|7|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.7.24">1 Chr. 7:24</scripRef>) in the territory of Ephraim,
on the way from Jerusalem to Joppa. They are distinguished as
Beth-horon “the upper” and Beth-horon “the nether.” They are
about 2 miles apart, the former being about 10 miles north-west
of Jerusalem. Between the two places was the ascent and descent
of Beth-horon, leading from Gibeon down to the western plain

(<scripRef passage="Josh. 10:10" id="b-p285.3" parsed="|Josh|10|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.10">Josh. 10:10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 10:11" id="b-p285.4" parsed="|Josh|10|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.11">11</scripRef>; 18:13, 14), down which the five kings of the
Amorites were driven by Joshua in that great battle, the most
important in which the Hebrews had been as yet engaged, being
their first conflict with their enemies in the open field.
Jehovah interposed in behalf of Israel by a terrific hailstorm,
which caused more deaths among the Canaanites than did the
swords of the Israelites. Beth-horon is mentioned as having been
taken by Shishak, B.C. 945, in the list of his conquests, and
the pass was the scene of a victory of Judas Maccabeus. (Comp.

<scripRef passage="Ex. 9:19" id="b-p285.5" parsed="|Exod|9|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.9.19">Ex. 9:19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 9:25" id="b-p285.6" parsed="|Exod|9|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.9.25">25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 38:22" id="b-p285.7" parsed="|Job|38|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.38.22">Job 38:22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Job 38:23" id="b-p285.8" parsed="|Job|38|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.38.23">23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 18:12-14" id="b-p285.9" parsed="|Ps|18|12|18|14" osisRef="Bible:Ps.18.12-Ps.18.14">Ps. 18:12-14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 30:30" id="b-p285.10" parsed="|Isa|30|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.30.30">Isa. 30:30</scripRef>.) The
modern name of these places is Beit-ur, distinguished by
el-Foka, “the upper,” and el-Tahta, “the nether.” The lower was
at the foot of the pass, and the upper, 500 feet higher, at the
top, west of Gibeon. (See GIBEON.)
</def>
<term id="b-p285.12">Beth-jeshimoth</term>
House of wastes, or deserts, a town near Abel-shittim, east of
Jordan, in the desert of Moab, where the Israelites encamped not
long before crossing the Jordan (<scripRef passage="Num. 33:49" id="b-p286.1" parsed="|Num|33|49|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.49">Num. 33:49</scripRef>; A.V.,
“Bethjesimoth”). It was within the territory of Sihon, king of
the Amorites (Josh. 12:3).
</def>
<term id="b-p286.3">Beth-le-Aphrah</term>
(R.V. Micah 1:10), house of dust. The Authorized Version reads
“in the house of Aphrah.” This is probably the name of a town in
the Shephelah, or “low country,” between Joppa and Gaza.
</def>
<term id="b-p287.2">Bethlehem</term>
House of bread. (1.) A city in the “hill country” of Judah. It

was originally called Ephrath (<scripRef passage="Gen. 35:16" id="b-p288.1" parsed="|Gen|35|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.35.16">Gen. 35:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 35:19" id="b-p288.2" parsed="|Gen|35|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.35.19">19</scripRef>; 48:7; <scripRef passage="Ruth 4:11" id="b-p288.3" parsed="|Ruth|4|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.4.11">Ruth 4:11</scripRef>).
It was also called Beth-lehem Ephratah (<scripRef passage="Micah 5:2" id="b-p288.4" parsed="|Mic|5|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.5.2">Micah 5:2</scripRef>),

Beth-lehem-judah (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:12" id="b-p288.5" parsed="|1Sam|17|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.12">1 Sam. 17:12</scripRef>), and “the city of David” (<scripRef passage="Luke 2:4" id="b-p288.6" parsed="|Luke|2|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.4">Luke 2:4</scripRef>). It is first noticed in Scripture as the place where Rachel
died and was buried “by the wayside,” directly to the north of
the city (<scripRef passage="Gen. 48:7" id="b-p288.7" parsed="|Gen|48|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.48.7">Gen. 48:7</scripRef>). The valley to the east was the scene of
the story of Ruth the Moabitess. There are the fields in which
she gleaned, and the path by which she and Naomi returned to the
town. Here was David’s birth-place, and here also, in after
years, he was anointed as king by Samuel (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 16:4-13" id="b-p288.8" parsed="|1Sam|16|4|16|13" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.16.4-1Sam.16.13">1 Sam. 16:4-13</scripRef>); and
it was from the well of Bethlehem that three of his heroes
brought water for him at the risk of their lives when he was in
the cave of Adullam (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 23:13-17" id="b-p288.9" parsed="|2Sam|23|13|23|17" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.23.13-2Sam.23.17">2 Sam. 23:13-17</scripRef>). But it was distinguished
above every other city as the birth-place of “Him whose goings

forth have been of old” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 2:6" id="b-p288.10" parsed="|Matt|2|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.2.6">Matt. 2:6</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Micah 5:2" id="b-p288.11" parsed="|Mic|5|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.5.2">Micah 5:2</scripRef>). Afterwards
Herod, “when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men,” sent
and slew “all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all
the coasts thereof, from two years old and under” (Matt. 2:16, 18; Jer. 31:15).
Bethlehem bears the modern name of Beit-Lahm, i.e., “house of
flesh.” It is about 5 miles south of Jerusalem, standing at an
elevation of about 2,550 feet above the sea, thus 100 feet
higher than Jerusalem.
There is a church still existing, built by Constantine the
Great (A.D. 330), called the “Church of the Nativity,” over a
grotto or cave called the “holy crypt,” and said to be the
“stable” in which Jesus was born. This is perhaps the oldest
existing Christian church in the world. Close to it is another
grotto, where Jerome the Latin father is said to have spent
thirty years of his life in translating the Scriptures into
Latin. (See VERSION.)
(2.) A city of Zebulun, mentioned only in Josh. 19:15. Now
Beit-Lahm, a ruined village about 6 miles west-north-west of
Nazareth.
</def>
<term id="b-p291.2">Beth-peor</term>
House of Peor; i.e., “temple of Baal-peor”, a place in Moab, on
the east of Jordan, opposite Jericho. It was in the tribe of

Reuben (<scripRef passage="Josh. 13:20" id="b-p292.1" parsed="|Josh|13|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.20">Josh. 13:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 3:29" id="b-p292.2" parsed="|Deut|3|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.29">Deut. 3:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut 4:46" id="b-p292.3" parsed="|Deut|4|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.4.46">4:46</scripRef>). In the “ravine” or
valley over against Beth-peor Moses was probably buried (Deut. 34:6).
</def>
<term id="b-p292.5">Beth-phage</term>
House of the unripe fig, a village on the Mount of Olives, on

the road from Jerusalem to Jericho (<scripRef passage="Matt. 21:1" id="b-p293.1" parsed="|Matt|21|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.21.1">Matt. 21:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 11:1" id="b-p293.2" parsed="|Mark|11|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.11.1">Mark 11:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 19:29" id="b-p293.3" parsed="|Luke|19|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.19.29">Luke 19:29</scripRef>), and very close to Bethany. It was the limit of a
Sabbath-day’s journey from Jerusalem, i.e., 2,000 cubits. It has
been identified with the modern Kefr-et-Tur.
</def>
<term id="b-p293.4">Bethsaida</term>
House of fish. (1.) A town in Galilee, on the west side of the
sea of Tiberias, in the “land of Gennesaret.” It was the native
place of Peter, Andrew, and Philip, and was frequently resorted

to by Jesus (<scripRef passage="Mark 6:45" id="b-p294.1" parsed="|Mark|6|45|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.6.45">Mark 6:45</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 1:44" id="b-p294.2" parsed="|John|1|44|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.1.44">John 1:44</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 12:21" id="b-p294.3" parsed="|John|12|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.12.21">12:21</scripRef>). It is supposed to
have been at the modern ‘Ain Tabighah, a bay to the north of
Gennesaret.
(2.) A city near which Christ fed 5,000 (Luke 9:10; comp. John 6:17; Matt. 14:15-21), and where the blind man had his sight
restored (<scripRef passage="Mark 8:22" id="b-p295.4" parsed="|Mark|8|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.8.22">Mark 8:22</scripRef>), on the east side of the lake, two miles up
the Jordan. It stood within the region of Gaulonitis, and was
enlarged by Philip the tetrarch, who called it “Julias,” after
the emperor’s daughter. Or, as some have supposed, there may
have been but one Bethsaida built on both sides of the lake,
near where the Jordan enters it. Now the ruins et-Tel.
</def>
<term id="b-p295.5">Beth-shean</term>
House of security or rest, a city which belonged to Manasseh (1 Chr. 7:29), on the west of Jordan. The bodies of Saul and his
sons were fastened to its walls. In Solomon’s time it gave its
name to a district (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:12" id="b-p296.2" parsed="|1Kgs|4|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.12">1 Kings 4:12</scripRef>). The name is found in an

abridged form, Bethshan, in <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 31:10" id="b-p296.3" parsed="|1Sam|31|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.31.10">1 Sam. 31:10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 31:12" id="b-p296.4" parsed="|1Sam|31|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.31.12">12</scripRef> and <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:12" id="b-p296.5" parsed="|2Sam|21|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.12">2 Sam. 21:12</scripRef>.
It is on the road from Jerusalem to Damascus, about 5 miles from
the Jordan, and 14 from the south end of the Lake of Gennesaret.
After the Captivity it was called Scythopolis, i.e., “the city
of the Scythians,” who about B.C. 640 came down from the steppes
of Southern Russia and settled in different places in Syria. It
is now called Beisan.
</def>
<term id="b-p296.6">Beth-shemesh</term>
House of the sun. (1.) A sacerdotal city in the tribe of Dan

(<scripRef passage="Josh. 21:16" id="b-p297.1" parsed="|Josh|21|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.21.16">Josh. 21:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 6:15" id="b-p297.2" parsed="|1Sam|6|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.6.15">1 Sam. 6:15</scripRef>), on the north border of Judah (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:10" id="b-p297.3" parsed="|Josh|15|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.10">Josh. 15:10</scripRef>). It was the scene of an encounter between Jehoash, king
of Israel, and Amaziah, king of Judah, in which the latter was

made prisoner (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 14:11" id="b-p297.4" parsed="|2Kgs|14|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.14.11">2 Kings 14:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 14:13" id="b-p297.5" parsed="|2Kgs|14|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.14.13">13</scripRef>). It was afterwards taken by
the Philistines (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 28:18" id="b-p297.6" parsed="|2Chr|28|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.28.18">2 Chr. 28:18</scripRef>). It is the modern ruined Arabic
village ‘Ain-shems, on the north-west slopes of the mountains of
Judah, 14 miles west of Jerusalem.
(2.) A city between Dothan and the Jordan, near the southern
border of Issachar (<scripRef passage="Josh. 19:22" id="b-p298.1" parsed="|Josh|19|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.22">Josh. 19:22</scripRef>), 7 1/2 miles south of
Beth-shean. It is the modern Ain-esh-Shemsiyeh.
(3.) One of the fenced cities of Naphtali (Josh. 19:38),
between Mount Tabor and the Jordan. Now Khurbet Shema, 3 miles
west of Safed. But perhaps the same as No. 2.
(4.) An idol sanctuary in Egypt (Jer. 43:13); called by the
Greeks Heliopolis, and by the Egyptians On (q.v.), Gen. 41:45.
</def>
<term id="b-p300.3">Beth-tappuah</term>
House of apples, a town of Judah, now Tuffuh, 5 miles west of
Hebron (Josh. 15:53).
</def>
<term id="b-p301.2">Bethuel</term>
Man of God, or virgin of God, or house of God. (1.) The son of

Nahor by Milcah; nephew of Abraham, and father of Rebekah (<scripRef passage="Gen. 22:22" id="b-p302.1" parsed="|Gen|22|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.22.22">Gen. 22:22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 22:23" id="b-p302.2" parsed="|Gen|22|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.22.23">23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 24:15" id="b-p302.3" parsed="|Gen|24|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.15">24:15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 24:24" id="b-p302.4" parsed="|Gen|24|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.24">24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 24:47" id="b-p302.5" parsed="|Gen|24|47|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.47">47</scripRef>). He appears in person only once
(2.) A southern city of Judah (1 Chr. 4:30); called also
Bethul (Josh. 19:4) and Bethel (12:16; 1 Sam. 30:27).
</def>
<term id="b-p303.4">Bethzur</term>
House of rock, a town in the mountains of Judah (Josh. 15:58),
about 4 miles to the north of Hebron. It was built by Rehoboam
for the defence of his kingdom (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 11:7" id="b-p304.2" parsed="|2Chr|11|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.11.7">2 Chr. 11:7</scripRef>). It stood near the
modern ed-Dirweh. Its ruins are still seen on a hill which bears
the name of Beit-Sur, and which commands the road from
Beer-sheba and Hebron to Jerusalem from the south.
</def>
<term id="b-p304.3">Betroth</term>
To promise “by one’s truth.” Men and women were betrothed when
they were engaged to be married. This usually took place a year
or more before marriage. From the time of betrothal the woman
was regarded as the lawful wife of the man to whom she was

betrothed (<scripRef passage="Deut. 28:30" id="b-p305.1" parsed="|Deut|28|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.30">Deut. 28:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 14:2" id="b-p305.2" parsed="|Judg|14|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.14.2">Judg. 14:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Judg. 14:8" id="b-p305.3" parsed="|Judg|14|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.14.8">8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 1:18-21" id="b-p305.4" parsed="|Matt|1|18|1|21" osisRef="Bible:Matt.1.18-Matt.1.21">Matt. 1:18-21</scripRef>). The term
is figuratively employed of the spiritual connection between God
and his people (Hos. 2:19, 20).
</def>
<term id="b-p305.7">Beulah</term>
Married, is used in Isa. 62:4 metaphorically as the name of
Judea: “Thy land shall be married,” i.e., favoured and blessed
of the Lord.
</def>
<term id="b-p306.2">Bewray</term>
To reveal or disclose; an old English word equivalent to
“betray” (Prov. 27:16; 29:24, R.V., “uttereth;” Isa. 16:3; Matt. 26:73).
</def>
<term id="b-p307.5">Beyond</term>
When used with reference to Jordan, signifies in the writings of
Moses the west side of the river, as he wrote on the east bank

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 50:10" id="b-p308.1" parsed="|Gen|50|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.50.10">Gen. 50:10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 50:11" id="b-p308.2" parsed="|Gen|50|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.50.11">11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 1:1" id="b-p308.3" parsed="|Deut|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.1.1">Deut. 1:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 1:5" id="b-p308.4" parsed="|Deut|1|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.1.5">5</scripRef>; 3:8, 20; 4:46); but in the
writings of Joshua, after he had crossed the river, it means the
east side (Josh. 5:1; 12:7; 22:7).
</def>
<term id="b-p308.8">Bezaleel</term>
In the shadow of God; i.e., “under his protection”, the
artificer who executed the work of art in connection with the

tabernacle in the wilderness (<scripRef passage="Ex. 31:2" id="b-p309.1" parsed="|Exod|31|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.31.2">Ex. 31:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 35:30" id="b-p309.2" parsed="|Exod|35|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.35.30">35:30</scripRef>). He was engaged
principally in works of metal, wood, and stone; while Aholiab,
who was associated with him and subordinate to him, had the
charge of the textile fabrics (36:1, 2; 38:22). He was of the
tribe of Judah, the son of Uri, and grandson of Hur (31:2).
Mention is made in Ezra 10:30 of another of the same name.
</def>
<term id="b-p309.4">Bezek</term>
Lightning. (1.) The residence of Adoni-bezek, in the lot of
Judah (<scripRef passage="Judg. 1:5" id="b-p310.1" parsed="|Judg|1|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.5">Judg. 1:5</scripRef>). It was in the mountains, not far from
Jerusalem. Probably the modern Bezkah, 6 miles south-east of
Lydda.
(2.) The place where Saul numbered the forces of Israel and
Judah (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 11:8" id="b-p311.1" parsed="|1Sam|11|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.11.8">1 Sam. 11:8</scripRef>); somewhere in the centre of the country,
near the Jordan valley. Probably the modern Ibzik, 13 miles
north-east of Shechem.
</def>
<term id="b-p311.2">Bezer</term>
Ore of gold or silver. (1.) A city of the Reubenites; one of the

three cities of refuge on the east of Jordan (<scripRef passage="Deut. 4" id="b-p312.1" parsed="|Deut|4|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.4">Deut. 4</scripRef>: 43; <scripRef passage="Josh. 20:8" id="b-p312.2" parsed="|Josh|20|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.20.8">Josh. 20:8</scripRef>). It has been identified with the modern ruined village of
Burazin, some 12 miles north of Heshbon; also with
Kasur-el-Besheir, 2 miles south-west of Dibon.
(2.) A descendant of Asher (1 Chr. 7:37).
</def>
<term id="b-p313.2">Bible</term>
Bible, the English form of the Greek name Biblia, meaning
“books,” the name which in the fifth century began to be given
to the entire collection of sacred books, the “Library of Divine
Revelation.” The name Bible was adopted by Wickliffe, and came
gradually into use in our English language. The Bible consists
of sixty-six different books, composed by many different
writers, in three different languages, under different
circumstances; writers of almost every social rank, statesmen
and peasants, kings, herdsmen, fishermen, priests,
tax-gatherers, tentmakers; educated and uneducated, Jews and
Gentiles; most of them unknown to each other, and writing at
various periods during the space of about 1600 years: and yet,
after all, it is only one book dealing with only one subject in
its numberless aspects and relations, the subject of man’s
redemption.
It is divided into the Old Testament, containing thirty-nine
books, and the New Testament, containing twenty-seven books. The
names given to the Old in the writings of the New are “the
scriptures” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 21:42" id="b-p315.1" parsed="|Matt|21|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.21.42">Matt. 21:42</scripRef>), “scripture” (2 Pet. 1:20), “the holy

scriptures” (<scripRef passage="Rom. 1:2" id="b-p315.2" parsed="|Rom|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.2">Rom. 1:2</scripRef>), “the law” (<scripRef passage="John 12:34" id="b-p315.3" parsed="|John|12|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.12.34">John 12:34</scripRef>), “the law of
Moses, the prophets, and the psalms” (<scripRef passage="Luke 24:44" id="b-p315.4" parsed="|Luke|24|44|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.24.44">Luke 24:44</scripRef>), “the law and

the prophets” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 5:17" id="b-p315.5" parsed="|Matt|5|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.17">Matt. 5:17</scripRef>), “the old covenant” (<scripRef passage="2 Cor. 3:14" id="b-p315.6" parsed="|2Cor|3|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.3.14">2 Cor. 3:14</scripRef>,
R.V.). There is a break of 400 years between the Old Testament
and the New. (See APOCRYPHA.)
The Old Testament is divided into three parts:, 1. The Law
(Torah), consisting of the Pentateuch, or five books of Moses.
2. The Prophets, consisting of (1) the former, namely, Joshua,
Judges, the Books of Samuel, and the Books of Kings; (2) the
latter, namely, the greater prophets, Isaiah, Jeremiah, and
Ezekiel, and the twelve minor prophets. 3. The Hagiographa, or
holy writings, including the rest of the books. These were
ranked in three divisions:, (1) The Psalms, Proverbs, and Job,
distinguished by the Hebrew name, a word formed of the initial
letters of these books, emeth, meaning truth. (2) Canticles,
Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, and Esther, called the five
rolls, as being written for the synagogue use on five separate
rolls. (3) Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, and 1 and 2 Chronicles.
Between the Old and the New Testament no addition was made to
the revelation God had already given. The period of New
Testament revelation, extending over a century, began with the
appearance of John the Baptist.
The New Testament consists of (1) the historical books, viz.,
the Gospels, and the Acts of the Apostles; (2) the Epistles; and
(3) the book of prophecy, the Revelation.
The division of the Bible into chapters and verses is
altogether of human invention, designed to facilitate reference
to it. The ancient Jews divided the Old Testament into certain
sections for use in the synagogue service, and then at a later
period, in the ninth century A.D., into verses. Our modern
system of chapters for all the books of the Bible was introduced
by Cardinal Hugo about the middle of the thirteenth century (he
died 1263). The system of verses for the New Testament was
introduced by Stephens in 1551, and generally adopted, although
neither Tyndale’s nor Coverdale’s English translation of the
Bible has verses. The division is not always wisely made, yet it
is very useful. (See VERSION.)
</def>
<term id="b-p318.2">Bier</term>
The frame on which dead bodies were conveyed to the grave (Luke 7:14).
</def>
<term id="b-p319.2">Bigtha</term>
Garden, or gift of fortune, one of the seven eunuchs or
chamberlains who had charge of the harem of Ahasuerus (Esther 1:10).
</def>
<term id="b-p320.2">Bigthan</term>
One of the eunuchs who “kept the door” in the court of
Ahasuerus. With Teresh he conspired against the king’s life.
Mordecai detected the conspiracy, and the culprits were hanged
(Esther 2:21-23; 6:1-3).
</def>
<term id="b-p321.3">Bildad</term>
Son of contention, one of Job’s friends. He is called “the
Shuhite,” probably as belonging to Shuah, a district in Arabia,
in which Shuah, the sixth son of Abraham by Keturah, settled
(<scripRef passage="Gen. 25:2" id="b-p322.1" parsed="|Gen|25|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.2">Gen. 25:2</scripRef>). He took part in each of the three controversies

into which Job’s friends entered with him (<scripRef passage="Job 8:1" id="b-p322.2" parsed="|Job|8|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.8.1">Job 8:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 18:1" id="b-p322.3" parsed="|Job|18|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.18.1">18:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 25:1" id="b-p322.4" parsed="|Job|25|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.25.1">25:1</scripRef>),
and delivered three speeches, very severe and stern in their
tone, although less violent than those of Zophar, but more so
than those of Eliphaz.
</def>
<term id="b-p322.5">Bilgah</term>
Cheerful. (1.) The head of the fifteenth sacerdotal course for
the temple service (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 24:14" id="b-p323.1" parsed="|1Chr|24|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.24.14">1 Chr. 24:14</scripRef>). (2.) A priest who returned
from Babylon with Zerubbabel (Neh. 12:5, 18).
</def>
<term id="b-p323.4">Bilhah</term>
Faltering; bashful, Rachel’s handmaid, whom she gave to Jacob

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 29:29" id="b-p324.1" parsed="|Gen|29|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.29.29">Gen. 29:29</scripRef>). She was the mother of Dan and Naphtali (<scripRef passage="Gen. 30:3-8" id="b-p324.2" parsed="|Gen|30|3|30|8" osisRef="Bible:Gen.30.3-Gen.30.8">Gen. 30:3-8</scripRef>). Reuben was cursed by his father for committing adultry
with her (35:22; 49:4). He was deprived of the birth-right,
which was given to the sons of Joseph.
</def>
<term id="b-p324.3">Bilshan</term>
Son of the tongue; i.e., “eloquent”, a man of some note who
returned from the Captivity with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:2; Neh. 7:7).
</def>
<term id="b-p325.3">Bird</term>
Birds are divided in the Mosaic law into two classes, (1) the

clean (<scripRef passage="Lev. 1:14-17" id="b-p326.1" parsed="|Lev|1|14|1|17" osisRef="Bible:Lev.1.14-Lev.1.17">Lev. 1:14-17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 5:7-10" id="b-p326.2" parsed="|Lev|5|7|5|10" osisRef="Bible:Lev.5.7-Lev.5.10">5:7-10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 14:4-7" id="b-p326.3" parsed="|Lev|14|4|14|7" osisRef="Bible:Lev.14.4-Lev.14.7">14:4-7</scripRef>), which were offered in
sacrifice; and (2) the unclean (<scripRef passage="Lev. 11:13-20" id="b-p326.4" parsed="|Lev|11|13|11|20" osisRef="Bible:Lev.11.13-Lev.11.20">Lev. 11:13-20</scripRef>). When offered in

sacrifice, they were not divided as other victims were (<scripRef passage="Gen. 15:10" id="b-p326.5" parsed="|Gen|15|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.10">Gen. 15:10</scripRef>). They are mentioned also as an article of food (<scripRef passage="Deut. 14:11" id="b-p326.6" parsed="|Deut|14|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.14.11">Deut. 14:11</scripRef>). The art of snaring wild birds is referred to (<scripRef passage="Ps. 124:7" id="b-p326.7" parsed="|Ps|124|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.124.7">Ps. 124:7</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Prov. 1:17" id="b-p326.8" parsed="|Prov|1|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.1.17">Prov. 1:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov 7:23" id="b-p326.9" parsed="|Prov|7|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.7.23">7:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 5:27" id="b-p326.10" parsed="|Jer|5|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.5.27">Jer. 5:27</scripRef>). Singing birds are mentioned in <scripRef passage="Ps. 104:12" id="b-p326.11" parsed="|Ps|104|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.104.12">Ps. 104:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eccl. 12:4" id="b-p326.12" parsed="|Eccl|12|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eccl.12.4">Eccl. 12:4</scripRef>. Their timidity is alluded to (<scripRef passage="Hos. 11:11" id="b-p326.13" parsed="|Hos|11|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.11.11">Hos. 11:11</scripRef>).
The reference in <scripRef passage="Ps. 84:3" id="b-p326.14" parsed="|Ps|84|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.84.3">Ps. 84:3</scripRef> to the swallow and the sparrow may be
only a comparison equivalent to, “What her house is to the
sparrow, and her nest to the swallow, that thine altars are to
my soul.”
</def>
<term id="b-p326.15">Birsha</term>
Son of wickedness, a king of Gomorrah whom Abraham succoured in
the invasion of Chedorlaomer (Gen. 14:2).
</def>
<term id="b-p327.2">Birth</term>
As soon as a child was born it was washed, and rubbed with salt

(<scripRef passage="Ezek. 16:4" id="b-p328.1" parsed="|Ezek|16|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.16.4">Ezek. 16:4</scripRef>), and then swathed with bandages (<scripRef passage="Job 38:9" id="b-p328.2" parsed="|Job|38|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.38.9">Job 38:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 2:7" id="b-p328.3" parsed="|Luke|2|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.7">Luke 2:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Luke 2:12" id="b-p328.4" parsed="|Luke|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.12">12</scripRef>). A Hebrew mother remained forty days in seclusion after
the birth of a son, and after the birth of a daughter double
that number of days. At the close of that period she entered
into the tabernacle or temple and offered up a sacrifice of

purification (<scripRef passage="Lev. 12:1-8" id="b-p328.5" parsed="|Lev|12|1|12|8" osisRef="Bible:Lev.12.1-Lev.12.8">Lev. 12:1-8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 2:22" id="b-p328.6" parsed="|Luke|2|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.22">Luke 2:22</scripRef>). A son was circumcised on
the eighth day after his birth, being thereby consecrated to God

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 17:10-12" id="b-p328.7" parsed="|Gen|17|10|17|12" osisRef="Bible:Gen.17.10-Gen.17.12">Gen. 17:10-12</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Rom. 4:11" id="b-p328.8" parsed="|Rom|4|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.4.11">Rom. 4:11</scripRef>). Seasons of misfortune are
likened to the pains of a woman in travail, and seasons of

prosperity to the joy that succeeds child-birth (<scripRef passage="Isa. 13:8" id="b-p328.9" parsed="|Isa|13|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.13.8">Isa. 13:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 4:31" id="b-p328.10" parsed="|Jer|4|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.4.31">Jer. 4:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 16:21" id="b-p328.11" parsed="|John|16|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.16.21">John 16:21</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="John 16:22" id="b-p328.12" parsed="|John|16|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.16.22">22</scripRef>). The natural birth is referred to as the

emblem of the new birth (<scripRef passage="John 3:3-8" id="b-p328.13" parsed="|John|3|3|3|8" osisRef="Bible:John.3.3-John.3.8">John 3:3-8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal. 6:15" id="b-p328.14" parsed="|Gal|6|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.6.15">Gal. 6:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Titus 3:5" id="b-p328.15" parsed="|Titus|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Titus.3.5">Titus 3:5</scripRef>,
etc.).
</def>
<term id="b-p328.16">Birth-day</term>
The observance of birth-days was common in early times (Job 1:4, 13, 18). They were specially celebrated in the land of Egypt
(<scripRef passage="Gen. 40:20" id="b-p329.4" parsed="|Gen|40|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.40.20">Gen. 40:20</scripRef>). There is no recorded instance in Scripture of the
celebration of birth-days among the Jews. On the occasion of
Herod’s birth-day John the Baptist was beheaded (Matt. 14:6).
</def>
<term id="b-p329.6">Birthright</term>
(1.) This word denotes the special privileges and advantages
belonging to the first-born son among the Jews. He became the
priest of the family. Thus Reuben was the first-born of the
patriarchs, and so the priesthood of the tribes belonged to him.
That honour was, however, transferred by God from Reuben to Levi
(Num. 3:12, 13; 8:18).
(2.) The first-born son had allotted to him also a double
portion of the paternal inheritance (<scripRef passage="Deut. 21:15-17" id="b-p331.1" parsed="|Deut|21|15|21|17" osisRef="Bible:Deut.21.15-Deut.21.17">Deut. 21:15-17</scripRef>). Reuben
was, because of his undutiful conduct, deprived of his

birth-right (<scripRef passage="Gen. 49:4" id="b-p331.2" parsed="|Gen|49|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.4">Gen. 49:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 5:1" id="b-p331.3" parsed="|1Chr|5|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5.1">1 Chr. 5:1</scripRef>). Esau transferred his
birth-right to Jacob (Gen. 25:33).
(3.) The first-born inherited the judicial authority of his
father, whatever it might be (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 21:3" id="b-p332.1" parsed="|2Chr|21|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.21.3">2 Chr. 21:3</scripRef>). By divine
appointment, however, David excluded Adonijah in favour of
Solomon.
(4.) The Jews attached a sacred importance to the rank of
“first-born” and “first-begotten” as applied to the Messiah

(<scripRef passage="Rom. 8:29" id="b-p333.1" parsed="|Rom|8|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.29">Rom. 8:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Col. 1:18" id="b-p333.2" parsed="|Col|1|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.1.18">Col. 1:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 1:4-6" id="b-p333.3" parsed="|Heb|1|4|1|6" osisRef="Bible:Heb.1.4-Heb.1.6">Heb. 1:4-6</scripRef>). As first-born he has an
inheritance superior to his brethren, and is the alone true
priest.
</def>
<term id="b-p333.4">Bishop</term>
An overseer. In apostolic times, it is quite manifest that there
was no difference as to order between bishops and elders or

presbyters (<scripRef passage="Acts 20:17-28" id="b-p334.1" parsed="|Acts|20|17|20|28" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.17-Acts.20.28">Acts 20:17-28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Pet. 5:1" id="b-p334.2" parsed="|1Pet|5|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.5.1">1 Pet. 5:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Pet. 5:2" id="b-p334.3" parsed="|1Pet|5|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.5.2">2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Phil. 1:1" id="b-p334.4" parsed="|Phil|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Phil.1.1">Phil. 1:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Tim. 3" id="b-p334.5" parsed="|1Tim|3|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.3">1 Tim. 3</scripRef>).
The term bishop is never once used to denote a different office
from that of elder or presbyter. These different names are
simply titles of the same office, “bishop” designating the
function, namely, that of oversight, and “presbyter” the dignity
appertaining to the office. Christ is figuratively called “the
bishop [episcopos] of souls” (1 Pet. 2:25).
</def>
<term id="b-p334.7">Bit</term>
The curb put into the mouths of horses to restrain them. The
Hebrew word (metheg) so rendered in <scripRef passage="Ps. 32:9" id="b-p335.1" parsed="|Ps|32|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.32.9">Ps. 32:9</scripRef> is elsewhere

translated “bridle” (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 19:28" id="b-p335.2" parsed="|2Kgs|19|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.19.28">2 Kings 19:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 26:3" id="b-p335.3" parsed="|Prov|26|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.26.3">Prov. 26:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 37:29" id="b-p335.4" parsed="|Isa|37|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.37.29">Isa. 37:29</scripRef>).
Bits were generally made of bronze or iron, but sometimes also
of gold or silver. In <scripRef passage="James 3:3" id="b-p335.5" parsed="|Jas|3|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jas.3.3">James 3:3</scripRef> the Authorized Version
translates the Greek word by “bits,” but the Revised Version by
“bridles.”
</def>
<term id="b-p335.6">Bith-ron</term>
The broken or divided place, a district in the Arabah or Jordan
valley, on the east of the river (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 2:29" id="b-p336.1" parsed="|2Sam|2|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.2.29">2 Sam. 2:29</scripRef>). It was probably
the designation of the region in general, which is broken and
intersected by ravines.
</def>
<term id="b-p336.2">Bithynia</term>
A province in Asia Minor, to the south of the Euxine and
Propontis. Christian congregations were here formed at an early
time (<scripRef passage="1 Pet. 1:1" id="b-p337.1" parsed="|1Pet|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.1.1">1 Pet. 1:1</scripRef>). Paul was prevented by the Spirit from
entering this province (<scripRef passage="Acts 16:7" id="b-p337.2" parsed="|Acts|16|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.16.7">Acts 16:7</scripRef>). It is noted in church
history as the province ruled over by Pliny as Roman proconsul,
who was perplexed as to the course he should take with the
numerous Christians brought before his tribunal on account of
their profession of Christianity and their conduct, and wrote to
Trajan, the emperor, for instructions (A.D. 107).
</def>
<term id="b-p337.3">Bitter</term>
Bitterness is symbolical of affliction, misery, and servitude

(<scripRef passage="Ex. 1:14" id="b-p338.1" parsed="|Exod|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.1.14">Ex. 1:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ruth 1:20" id="b-p338.2" parsed="|Ruth|1|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.1.20">Ruth 1:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 9:15" id="b-p338.3" parsed="|Jer|9|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.9.15">Jer. 9:15</scripRef>). The Chaldeans are called the
“bitter and hasty nation” (<scripRef passage="Hab. 1:6" id="b-p338.4" parsed="|Hab|1|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hab.1.6">Hab. 1:6</scripRef>). The “gall of bitterness”
expresses a state of great wickedness (<scripRef passage="Acts 8:23" id="b-p338.5" parsed="|Acts|8|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.8.23">Acts 8:23</scripRef>). A “root of
bitterness” is a wicked person or a dangerous sin (Heb. 12:15).
The Passover was to be eaten with “bitter herbs” (Ex. 12:8;
<scripRef passage="Num. 9:11" id="b-p339.2" parsed="|Num|9|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.9.11">Num. 9:11</scripRef>). The kind of herbs so designated is not known.
Probably they were any bitter herbs obtainable at the place and
time when the Passover was celebrated. They represented the
severity of the servitude under which the people groaned; and
have been regarded also as typical of the sufferings of Christ.
</def>
<term id="b-p339.3">Bittern</term>
Is found three times in connection with the desolations to come

upon Babylon, Idumea, and Nineveh (<scripRef passage="Isa. 14:23" id="b-p340.1" parsed="|Isa|14|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.14.23">Isa. 14:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 34:11" id="b-p340.2" parsed="|Isa|34|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.34.11">34:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zeph. 2:14" id="b-p340.3" parsed="|Zeph|2|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zeph.2.14">Zeph. 2:14</scripRef>). This bird belongs to the class of cranes. Its scientific
name is Botaurus stellaris. It is a solitary bird, frequenting
marshy ground. The Hebrew word (kippod) thus rendered in the
Authorized Version is rendered “porcupine” in the Revised
Version. But in the passages noted the kippod is associated with
birds, with pools of water, and with solitude and desolation.
This favours the idea that not the “porcupine” but the “bittern”
is really intended by the word.
</def>
<term id="b-p340.4">Bitumen</term>
Gen. 11:3, R.V., margin, rendered in the A.V. “slime”), a
mineral pitch. With this the ark was pitched (6:14. See also Ex. 2:3.) (See SLIME.)
</def>
<term id="b-p341.4">Black</term>
Properly the absence of all colour. In Prov. 7:9 the Hebrew word
means, as in the margin of the Revised Version, “the pupil of
the eye.” It is translated “apple” of the eye in <scripRef passage="Deut. 32:10" id="b-p342.2" parsed="|Deut|32|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.10">Deut. 32:10</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Ps. 17:8" id="b-p342.3" parsed="|Ps|17|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.17.8">Ps. 17:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 7:2" id="b-p342.4" parsed="|Prov|7|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.7.2">Prov. 7:2</scripRef>. It is a different word which is rendered

“black” in <scripRef passage="Lev. 13:31" id="b-p342.5" parsed="|Lev|13|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.13.31">Lev. 13:31</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 13:37" id="b-p342.6" parsed="|Lev|13|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.13.37">37</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Cant. 1:5" id="b-p342.7" parsed="|Song|1|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.1.5">Cant. 1:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Cant 5:11" id="b-p342.8" parsed="|Song|5|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.5.11">5:11</scripRef>; and <scripRef passage="Zech. 6:2" id="b-p342.9" parsed="|Zech|6|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.6.2">Zech. 6:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Zech. 6:6" id="b-p342.10" parsed="|Zech|6|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.6.6">6</scripRef>. It
is uncertain what the “black marble” of <scripRef passage="Esther 1:6" id="b-p342.11" parsed="|Esth|1|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.1.6">Esther 1:6</scripRef> was which
formed a part of the mosaic pavement.
</def>
<term id="b-p342.12">Blade</term>
Applied to the glittering point of a spear (Job 39:23) or sword

(<scripRef passage="Nah. 3:3" id="b-p343.2" parsed="|Nah|3|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Nah.3.3">Nah. 3:3</scripRef>), the blade of a dagger (<scripRef passage="Judg. 3:22" id="b-p343.3" parsed="|Judg|3|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.3.22">Judg. 3:22</scripRef>); the “shoulder
blade” (Job 31:22); the “blade” of cereals (Matt. 13:26).
</def>
<term id="b-p343.6">Blains</term>
Occurs only in connection with the sixth plague of Egypt (Ex. 9:9, 10). In Deut. 28:27, 35, it is called “the botch of Egypt.”
It seems to have been the fearful disease of black leprosy, a
kind of elephantiasis, producing burning ulcers.
</def>
<term id="b-p344.5">Blasphemy</term>
In the sense of speaking evil of God this word is found in Ps. 74:18; Isa. 52:5; Rom. 2:24; Rev. 13:1, 6; 16:9, 11, 21. It

denotes also any kind of calumny, or evil-speaking, or abuse (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 21:10" id="b-p345.6" parsed="|1Kgs|21|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.21.10">1 Kings 21:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 13:45" id="b-p345.7" parsed="|Acts|13|45|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.13.45">Acts 13:45</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 18:6" id="b-p345.8" parsed="|Acts|18|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.6">18:6</scripRef>, etc.). Our Lord was accused of
blasphemy when he claimed to be the Son of God (<scripRef passage="Matt. 26:65" id="b-p345.9" parsed="|Matt|26|65|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.65">Matt. 26:65</scripRef>;

comp. <scripRef passage="Matt. 9:3" id="b-p345.10" parsed="|Matt|9|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.9.3">Matt. 9:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 2:7" id="b-p345.11" parsed="|Mark|2|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.2.7">Mark 2:7</scripRef>). They who deny his Messiahship
blaspheme Jesus (Luke 22:65; John 10:36).
Blasphemy against the Holy Ghost (Matt. 12:31, 32; Mark 3:28, 29; Luke 12:10) is regarded by some as a continued and obstinate
rejection of the gospel, and hence is an unpardonable sin,
simply because as long as a sinner remains in unbelief he
voluntarily excludes himself from pardon. Others regard the
expression as designating the sin of attributing to the power of
Satan those miracles which Christ performed, or generally those
works which are the result of the Spirit’s agency.
</def>
<term id="b-p346.6">Blastus</term>
Chamberlain to king Herod Agrippa I. (Acts 12:20). Such persons
generally had great influence with their masters.
</def>
<term id="b-p347.2">Blemish</term>
Imperfection or bodily deformity excluding men from the
priesthood, and rendering animals unfit to be offered in

sacrifice (<scripRef passage="Lev. 21:17-23" id="b-p348.1" parsed="|Lev|21|17|21|23" osisRef="Bible:Lev.21.17-Lev.21.23">Lev. 21:17-23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 22:19-25" id="b-p348.2" parsed="|Lev|22|19|22|25" osisRef="Bible:Lev.22.19-Lev.22.25">22:19-25</scripRef>). The Christian church, as
justified in Christ, is “without blemish” (<scripRef passage="Eph. 5:27" id="b-p348.3" parsed="|Eph|5|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.5.27">Eph. 5:27</scripRef>). Christ
offered himself a sacrifice “without blemish,” acceptable to God
(1 Pet. 1:19).
</def>
<term id="b-p348.5">Bless</term>
(1.) God blesses his people when he bestows on them some gift

temporal or spiritual (<scripRef passage="Gen. 1:22" id="b-p349.1" parsed="|Gen|1|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.1.22">Gen. 1:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 24:35" id="b-p349.2" parsed="|Gen|24|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.35">24:35</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 42:12" id="b-p349.3" parsed="|Job|42|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.42.12">Job 42:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 45:2" id="b-p349.4" parsed="|Ps|45|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.45.2">Ps. 45:2</scripRef>;
104:24, 35).
(2.) We bless God when we thank him for his mercies (Ps. 103:1, 2; 145:1, 2).
(3.) A man blesses himself when he invokes God’s blessing

(<scripRef passage="Isa. 65:16" id="b-p351.1" parsed="|Isa|65|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.65.16">Isa. 65:16</scripRef>), or rejoices in God’s goodness to him (<scripRef passage="Deut. 29:19" id="b-p351.2" parsed="|Deut|29|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.29.19">Deut. 29:19</scripRef>;
Ps. 49:18).
(4.) One blesses another when he expresses good wishes or

offers prayer to God for his welfare (<scripRef passage="Gen. 24:60" id="b-p352.1" parsed="|Gen|24|60|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.60">Gen. 24:60</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 31:55" id="b-p352.2" parsed="|Gen|31|55|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.55">31:55</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 2:20" id="b-p352.3" parsed="|1Sam|2|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.2.20">1 Sam. 2:20</scripRef>). Sometimes blessings were uttered under divine
inspiration, as in the case of Noah, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 9:26" id="b-p352.4" parsed="|Gen|9|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.9.26">Gen. 9:26</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 9:27" id="b-p352.5" parsed="|Gen|9|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.9.27">27</scripRef>; 27:28, 29, 40; 48:15-20; 49:1-28; <scripRef passage="Deut. 33" id="b-p352.6" parsed="|Deut|33|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.33">Deut. 33</scripRef>). The

priests were divinely authorized to bless the people (<scripRef passage="Deut. 10:8" id="b-p352.7" parsed="|Deut|10|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.10.8">Deut. 10:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 6:22-27" id="b-p352.8" parsed="|Num|6|22|6|27" osisRef="Bible:Num.6.22-Num.6.27">Num. 6:22-27</scripRef>). We have many examples of apostolic

benediction (<scripRef passage="2 Cor. 13:14" id="b-p352.9" parsed="|2Cor|13|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.13.14">2 Cor. 13:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 6:23" id="b-p352.10" parsed="|Eph|6|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.6.23">Eph. 6:23</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Eph. 6:24" id="b-p352.11" parsed="|Eph|6|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.6.24">24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Thess. 3:16" id="b-p352.12" parsed="|2Thess|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Thess.3.16">2 Thess. 3:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Thess. 3:18" id="b-p352.13" parsed="|2Thess|3|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Thess.3.18">18</scripRef>;
Heb. 13:20, 21; 1 Pet. 5:10, 11).
(5.) Among the Jews in their thank-offerings the master of the
feast took a cup of wine in his hand, and after having blessed
God for it and for other mercies then enjoyed, handed it to his
guests, who all partook of it. <scripRef passage="Ps. 116:13" id="b-p353.1" parsed="|Ps|116|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.116.13">Ps. 116:13</scripRef> refers to this custom.
It is also alluded to in <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 10:16" id="b-p353.2" parsed="|1Cor|10|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.10.16">1 Cor. 10:16</scripRef>, where the apostle speaks
of the “cup of blessing.”
</def>
<term id="b-p353.3">Blind</term>
Blind beggars are frequently mentioned (Matt. 9:27; 12:22;

<scripRef passage="Matt 20:30" id="b-p354.3" parsed="|Matt|20|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.20.30">20:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 5:3" id="b-p354.4" parsed="|John|5|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.5.3">John 5:3</scripRef>). The blind are to be treated with compassion

(<scripRef passage="Lev. 19:14" id="b-p354.5" parsed="|Lev|19|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.14">Lev. 19:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 27:18" id="b-p354.6" parsed="|Deut|27|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.27.18">Deut. 27:18</scripRef>). Blindness was sometimes a punishment

for disobedience (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 11:2" id="b-p354.7" parsed="|1Sam|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.11.2">1 Sam. 11:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 39:7" id="b-p354.8" parsed="|Jer|39|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.39.7">Jer. 39:7</scripRef>), sometimes the effect

of old age (<scripRef passage="Gen. 27:1" id="b-p354.9" parsed="|Gen|27|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.1">Gen. 27:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 14:4" id="b-p354.10" parsed="|1Kgs|14|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.14.4">1 Kings 14:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 4:15" id="b-p354.11" parsed="|1Sam|4|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.4.15">1 Sam. 4:15</scripRef>). Conquerors

sometimes blinded their captives (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 25:7" id="b-p354.12" parsed="|2Kgs|25|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.25.7">2 Kings 25:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 11:2" id="b-p354.13" parsed="|1Sam|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.11.2">1 Sam. 11:2</scripRef>).
Blindness denotes ignorance as to spiritual things (<scripRef passage="Isa. 6:10" id="b-p354.14" parsed="|Isa|6|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.6.10">Isa. 6:10</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Isa 42:18" id="b-p354.15" parsed="|Isa|42|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.42.18">42:18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa 42:19" id="b-p354.16" parsed="|Isa|42|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.42.19">19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 15:14" id="b-p354.17" parsed="|Matt|15|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.15.14">Matt. 15:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 4:18" id="b-p354.18" parsed="|Eph|4|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.4.18">Eph. 4:18</scripRef>). The opening of the eyes of
the blind is peculiar to the Messiah (<scripRef passage="Isa. 29:18" id="b-p354.19" parsed="|Isa|29|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.29.18">Isa. 29:18</scripRef>). Elymas was
smitten with blindness at Paul’s word (Acts 13:11).
</def>
<term id="b-p354.21">Blood</term>
(1.) As food, prohibited in Gen. 9:4, where the use of animal

food is first allowed. Comp. <scripRef passage="Deut. 12:23" id="b-p355.2" parsed="|Deut|12|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.12.23">Deut. 12:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 3:17" id="b-p355.3" parsed="|Lev|3|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.3.17">Lev. 3:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 7:26" id="b-p355.4" parsed="|Lev|7|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.7.26">7:26</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Lev 17:10-14" id="b-p355.5" parsed="|Lev|17|10|17|14" osisRef="Bible:Lev.17.10-Lev.17.14">17:10-14</scripRef>. The injunction to abstain from blood is renewed in the
decree of the council of Jerusalem (<scripRef passage="Acts 15:29" id="b-p355.6" parsed="|Acts|15|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.15.29">Acts 15:29</scripRef>). It has been
held by some, and we think correctly, that this law of
prohibition was only ceremonial and temporary; while others
regard it as still binding on all. Blood was eaten by the
Israelites after the battle of Gilboa (1 Sam. 14:32-34).
(2.) The blood of sacrifices was caught by the priest in a
basin, and then sprinkled seven times on the altar; that of the
passover on the doorposts and lintels of the houses (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12" id="b-p356.1" parsed="|Exod|12|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12">Ex. 12</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Lev. 4:5-7" id="b-p356.2" parsed="|Lev|4|5|4|7" osisRef="Bible:Lev.4.5-Lev.4.7">Lev. 4:5-7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 16:14-19" id="b-p356.3" parsed="|Lev|16|14|16|19" osisRef="Bible:Lev.16.14-Lev.16.19">16:14-19</scripRef>). At the giving of the law (<scripRef passage="Ex. 24:8" id="b-p356.4" parsed="|Exod|24|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.24.8">Ex. 24:8</scripRef>) the
blood of the sacrifices was sprinkled on the people as well as
on the altar, and thus the people were consecrated to God, or
entered into covenant with him, hence the blood of the covenant
(Matt. 26:28; Heb. 9:19, 20; 10:29; 13:20).
(3.) Human blood. The murderer was to be punished (Gen. 9:5).
The blood of the murdered “crieth for vengeance” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 4:10" id="b-p357.2" parsed="|Gen|4|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.4.10">Gen. 4:10</scripRef>).
The “avenger of blood” was the nearest relative of the murdered,

and he was required to avenge his death (<scripRef passage="Num. 35:24" id="b-p357.3" parsed="|Num|35|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.35.24">Num. 35:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 35:27" id="b-p357.4" parsed="|Num|35|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.35.27">27</scripRef>). No
satisfaction could be made for the guilt of murder (Num. 35:31).
(4.) Blood used metaphorically to denote race (Acts 17:26),
and as a symbol of slaughter (<scripRef passage="Isa. 34:3" id="b-p358.2" parsed="|Isa|34|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.34.3">Isa. 34:3</scripRef>). To “wash the feet in
blood” means to gain a great victory (<scripRef passage="Ps. 58:10" id="b-p358.3" parsed="|Ps|58|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.58.10">Ps. 58:10</scripRef>). Wine, from its
red colour, is called “the blood of the grape” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 49:11" id="b-p358.4" parsed="|Gen|49|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.11">Gen. 49:11</scripRef>).
Blood and water issued from our Saviour’s side when it was
pierced by the Roman soldier (<scripRef passage="John 19:34" id="b-p358.5" parsed="|John|19|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.34">John 19:34</scripRef>). This has led
pathologists to the conclusion that the proper cause of Christ’s
death was rupture of the heart. (Comp. Ps. 69:20.)
</def>
<term id="b-p358.7">Bloody sweat</term>
The sign and token of our Lord’s great agony (Luke 22:44).
</def>
<term id="b-p359.2">Blot</term>
A stain or reproach (Job 31:7; Prov. 9:7). To blot out sin is to

forgive it (<scripRef passage="Ps. 51:1" id="b-p360.3" parsed="|Ps|51|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.51.1">Ps. 51:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps. 51:9" id="b-p360.4" parsed="|Ps|51|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.51.9">9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 44:22" id="b-p360.5" parsed="|Isa|44|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.44.22">Isa. 44:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 3:19" id="b-p360.6" parsed="|Acts|3|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.3.19">Acts 3:19</scripRef>). Christ’s
blotting out the handwriting of ordinances was his fulfilling
the law in our behalf (Col. 2:14).
</def>
<term id="b-p360.8">Blue</term>
Generally associated with purple (Ex. 25:4; 26:1, 31, 36, etc.).
It is supposed to have been obtained from a shellfish of the
Mediterranean, the Helix ianthina of Linnaeus. The robe of the
high priest’s ephod was to be all of this colour (<scripRef passage="Ex. 28:31" id="b-p361.5" parsed="|Exod|28|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.31">Ex. 28:31</scripRef>),
also the loops of the curtains (26:4) and the ribbon of the
breastplate (28:28). Blue cloths were also made for various
sacred purposes (Num. 4:6, 7, 9, 11, 12). (See COLOUR.)
</def>
<term id="b-p361.12">Boanerges</term>
Sons of thunder, a surname given by our Lord to James and John
(<scripRef passage="Mark 3:17" id="b-p362.1" parsed="|Mark|3|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.3.17">Mark 3:17</scripRef>) on account of their fervid and impetuous temper
(Luke 9:54).
</def>
<term id="b-p362.3">Boar</term>
Occurs only in Ps. 80:13. The same Hebrew word is elsewhere

rendered “swine” (<scripRef passage="Lev. 11:7" id="b-p363.2" parsed="|Lev|11|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.11.7">Lev. 11:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 14:8" id="b-p363.3" parsed="|Deut|14|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.14.8">Deut. 14:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 11:22" id="b-p363.4" parsed="|Prov|11|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.11.22">Prov. 11:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 65:4" id="b-p363.5" parsed="|Isa|65|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.65.4">Isa. 65:4</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Isa 66:3" id="b-p363.6" parsed="|Isa|66|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.66.3">66:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa 66:17" id="b-p363.7" parsed="|Isa|66|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.66.17">17</scripRef>). The Hebrews abhorred swine’s flesh, and accordingly
none of these animals were reared, except in the district beyond
the Sea of Galilee. In the psalm quoted above the powers that
destroyed the Jewish nation are compared to wild boars and wild
beasts of the field.
</def>
<term id="b-p363.8">Boaz</term>
Alacrity. (1.) The husband of Ruth, a wealthy Bethlehemite. By
the “levirate law” the duty devolved on him of marrying Ruth the
Moabitess (<scripRef passage="Ruth 4:1-13" id="b-p364.1" parsed="|Ruth|4|1|4|13" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.4.1-Ruth.4.13">Ruth 4:1-13</scripRef>). He was a kinsman of Mahlon, her first
husband.
(2.) The name given (for what reason is unknown) to one of the
two (the other was called Jachin) brazen pillars which Solomon

erected in the court of the temple (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 7:21" id="b-p365.1" parsed="|1Kgs|7|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.7.21">1 Kings 7:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 3:17" id="b-p365.2" parsed="|2Chr|3|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.3.17">2 Chr. 3:17</scripRef>).
These pillars were broken up and carried to Babylon by
Nebuchadnezzar.
</def>
<term id="b-p365.3">Bochim</term>
Weepers, a place where the angel of the Lord reproved the
Israelites for entering into a league with the people of the
land. This caused them bitterly to weep, and hence the name of

the place (<scripRef passage="Judg. 2:1" id="b-p366.1" parsed="|Judg|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.2.1">Judg. 2:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Judg. 2:5" id="b-p366.2" parsed="|Judg|2|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.2.5">5</scripRef>). It lay probably at the head of one of
the valleys between Gilgal and Shiloh.
</def>
<term id="b-p366.3">Boil</term>
(rendered “botch” in Deut. 28:27, 35), an aggravated ulcer, as

in the case of Hezekiah (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 20:7" id="b-p367.3" parsed="|2Kgs|20|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.20.7">2 Kings 20:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 38:21" id="b-p367.4" parsed="|Isa|38|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.38.21">Isa. 38:21</scripRef>) or of the

Egyptians (<scripRef passage="Ex. 9:9" id="b-p367.5" parsed="|Exod|9|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.9.9">Ex. 9:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 9:10" id="b-p367.6" parsed="|Exod|9|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.9.10">10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 9:11" id="b-p367.7" parsed="|Exod|9|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.9.11">11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 28:27" id="b-p367.8" parsed="|Deut|28|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.27">Deut. 28:27</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 28:35" id="b-p367.9" parsed="|Deut|28|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.35">35</scripRef>). It designates the
disease of Job (2:7), which was probably the black leprosy.
</def>
<term id="b-p367.10">Bolled</term>
(Ex. 9:31), meaning “swollen or podded for seed,” was adopted in
the Authorized Version from the version of Coverdale (1535). The
Revised Version has in the margin “was in bloom,” which is the
more probable rendering of the Hebrew word. It is the fact that
in Egypt when barley is in ear (about February) flax is
blossoming.
</def>
<term id="b-p368.2">Bolster</term>
The Hebrew word kebir, rendered “pillow” in 1 Sam. 19:13, 16,
but in Revised Version marg. “quilt” or “network,” probably
means some counterpane or veil intended to protect the head of
the sleeper. A different Hebrew word (meraashoth’) is used for

“bolster” (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 26:7" id="b-p369.3" parsed="|1Sam|26|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.26.7">1 Sam. 26:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 26:11" id="b-p369.4" parsed="|1Sam|26|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.26.11">11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 26:16" id="b-p369.5" parsed="|1Sam|26|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.26.16">16</scripRef>). It is rightly rendered in

Revised Version “at his head.” In <scripRef passage="Gen. 28:11" id="b-p369.6" parsed="|Gen|28|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.28.11">Gen. 28:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 28:18" id="b-p369.7" parsed="|Gen|28|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.28.18">18</scripRef> the Authorized
Version renders it “for his pillows,” and the Revised Version

“under his head.” In <scripRef passage="Ezek. 13:18" id="b-p369.8" parsed="|Ezek|13|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.13.18">Ezek. 13:18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 13:20" id="b-p369.9" parsed="|Ezek|13|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.13.20">20</scripRef> another Hebrew word
(kesathoth) is used, properly denoting “cushions” or “pillows,”
as so rendered both in the Authorized and the Revised Version.
</def>
<term id="b-p369.10">Bond</term>
An obligation of any kind (Num. 30:2, 4, 12). The word means

also oppression or affliction (<scripRef passage="Ps. 116:16" id="b-p370.4" parsed="|Ps|116|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.116.16">Ps. 116:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Phil. 1:7" id="b-p370.5" parsed="|Phil|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Phil.1.7">Phil. 1:7</scripRef>). Christian
love is the “bond of perfectness” (<scripRef passage="Col. 3:14" id="b-p370.6" parsed="|Col|3|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.3.14">Col. 3:14</scripRef>), and the
influences of the Spirit are the “bond of peace” (Eph. 4:3).
</def>
<term id="b-p370.8">Bondage</term>
Of Israel in Egypt (Ex. 2:23, 25; 5), which is called the “house
of bondage” (13:3; 20:2). This word is used also with reference
to the captivity in Babylon (<scripRef passage="Isa. 14:3" id="b-p371.3" parsed="|Isa|14|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.14.3">Isa. 14:3</scripRef>), and the oppression of
the Persian king (Ezra 9:8, 9).
</def>
<term id="b-p371.6">Bonnet</term>
(Heb. peer), Ex. 39:28 (R.V., “head-tires”); Ezek. 44:18 (R.V.,

“tires”), denotes properly a turban worn by priests, and in <scripRef passage="Isa. 3:20" id="b-p372.3" parsed="|Isa|3|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.20">Isa. 3:20</scripRef> (R.V., “head-tires”) a head-dress or tiara worn by females.
The Hebrew word so rendered literally means an ornament, as in

<scripRef passage="Isa. 61:10" id="b-p372.4" parsed="|Isa|61|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.61.10">Isa. 61:10</scripRef> (R.V., “garland”), and in <scripRef passage="Ezek. 24:17" id="b-p372.5" parsed="|Ezek|24|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.24.17">Ezek. 24:17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 24:23" id="b-p372.6" parsed="|Ezek|24|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.24.23">23</scripRef> “tire”
(R.V., “head-tire”). It consisted of a piece of cloth twisted

about the head. In <scripRef passage="Ex. 28:40" id="b-p372.7" parsed="|Exod|28|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.40">Ex. 28:40</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 29:9" id="b-p372.8" parsed="|Exod|29|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.9">29:9</scripRef> it is the translation of a
different Hebrew word (migba’ah), which denotes the turban
(R.V., “head-tire”) of the common priest as distinguished from
the mitre of the high priest. (See MITRE.)
</def>
<term id="b-p372.10">Book</term>
This word has a comprehensive meaning in Scripture. In the Old
Testament it is the rendering of the Hebrew word sepher, which
properly means a “writing,” and then a “volume” (<scripRef passage="Ex. 17:14" id="b-p373.1" parsed="|Exod|17|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.17.14">Ex. 17:14</scripRef>;
Deut. 28:58; 29:20; Job 19:23) or “roll of a book” (Jer. 36:2, 4).
Books were originally written on skins, on linen or cotton
cloth, and on Egyptian papyrus, whence our word “paper.” The
leaves of the book were generally written in columns, designated
by a Hebrew word properly meaning “doors” and “valves” (Jer. 36:23, R.V., marg. “columns”).
Among the Hebrews books were generally rolled up like our
maps, or if very long they were rolled from both ends, forming
two rolls (<scripRef passage="Luke 4:17-20" id="b-p375.1" parsed="|Luke|4|17|4|20" osisRef="Bible:Luke.4.17-Luke.4.20">Luke 4:17-20</scripRef>). Thus they were arranged when the
writing was on flexible materials; but if the writing was on
tablets of wood or brass or lead, then the several tablets were
bound together by rings through which a rod was passed.
A sealed book is one whose contents are secret (Isa. 29:11;

<scripRef passage="Rev. 5:1-3" id="b-p376.2" parsed="|Rev|5|1|5|3" osisRef="Bible:Rev.5.1-Rev.5.3">Rev. 5:1-3</scripRef>). To “eat” a book (<scripRef passage="Jer. 15:16" id="b-p376.3" parsed="|Jer|15|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.15.16">Jer. 15:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 2:8-10" id="b-p376.4" parsed="|Ezek|2|8|2|10" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.2.8-Ezek.2.10">Ezek. 2:8-10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek 3:1-3" id="b-p376.5" parsed="|Ezek|3|1|3|3" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.3.1-Ezek.3.3">3:1-3</scripRef>;
Rev. 10:9) is to study its contents carefully.
The book of judgment (Dan. 7:10) refers to the method of human
courts of justice as illustrating the proceedings which will
take place at the day of God’s final judgment.
The book of the wars of the Lord (Num. 21:14), the book of
Jasher (<scripRef passage="Josh. 10:13" id="b-p378.2" parsed="|Josh|10|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.13">Josh. 10:13</scripRef>), and the book of the chronicles of the
kings of Judah and Israel (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 25:26" id="b-p378.3" parsed="|2Chr|25|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.25.26">2 Chr. 25:26</scripRef>), were probably ancient
documents known to the Hebrews, but not forming a part of the
canon.
The book of life (Ps. 69:28) suggests the idea that as the

redeemed form a community or citizenship (<scripRef passage="Phil. 3:20" id="b-p379.2" parsed="|Phil|3|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Phil.3.20">Phil. 3:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Phil 4:3" id="b-p379.3" parsed="|Phil|4|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Phil.4.3">4:3</scripRef>), a
catalogue of the citizens’ names is preserved (Luke 10:20; Rev. 20:15). Their names are registered in heaven (Luke 10:20; Rev. 3:5).
The book of the covenant (Ex. 24:7), containing Ex. 20:22-23:33, is the first book actually mentioned as a part of
the written word. It contains a series of laws, civil, social,
and religious, given to Moses at Sinai immediately after the
delivery of the decalogue. These were written in this “book.”
</def>
<term id="b-p380.3">Booth</term>
A hut made of the branches of a tree. In such tabernacles Jacob
sojourned for a season at a place named from this circumstance
Succoth (<scripRef passage="Gen. 33:17" id="b-p381.1" parsed="|Gen|33|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.33.17">Gen. 33:17</scripRef>). Booths were erected also at the feast of

Tabernacles (q.v.), <scripRef passage="Lev. 23:42" id="b-p381.2" parsed="|Lev|23|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.42">Lev. 23:42</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 23:43" id="b-p381.3" parsed="|Lev|23|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.43">43</scripRef>, which commemorated the abode
of the Israelites in the wilderness.
</def>
<term id="b-p381.4">Booty</term>
Captives or cattle or objects of value taken in war. In Canaan
all that breathed were to be destroyed (<scripRef passage="Deut. 20" id="b-p382.1" parsed="|Deut|20|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.20">Deut. 20</scripRef>: 16). The
“pictures and images” of the Canaanites were to be destroyed
also (<scripRef passage="Num. 33:52" id="b-p382.2" parsed="|Num|33|52|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.52">Num. 33:52</scripRef>). The law of booty as to its division is laid
down in <scripRef passage="Num. 31:26-47" id="b-p382.3" parsed="|Num|31|26|31|47" osisRef="Bible:Num.31.26-Num.31.47">Num. 31:26-47</scripRef>. David afterwards introduced a regulation
that the baggage-guard should share the booty equally with the
soldiers engaged in battle. He also devoted of the spoils of war
for the temple (1 Sam. 30:24-26; 2 Sam. 8:11; 1 Chr. 26:27).
</def>
<term id="b-p382.7">Borrow</term>
The Israelites “borrowed” from the Egyptians (Ex. 12:35, R.V.,
“asked”) in accordance with a divine command (3:22; 11:2). But
the word (sha’al) so rendered here means simply and always to
“request” or “demand.” The Hebrew had another word which is

properly translated “borrow” in <scripRef passage="Deut. 28:12" id="b-p383.2" parsed="|Deut|28|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.12">Deut. 28:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 37:21" id="b-p383.3" parsed="|Ps|37|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.37.21">Ps. 37:21</scripRef>. It was
well known that the parting was final. The Egyptians were so
anxious to get the Israelites away out of their land that “they
let them have what they asked” (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:36" id="b-p383.4" parsed="|Exod|12|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.36">Ex. 12:36</scripRef>, R.V.), or literally
“made them to ask,” urged them to take whatever they desired and
depart. (See LOAN.)
</def>
<term id="b-p383.6">Bosom</term>
In the East objects are carried in the bosom which Europeans
carry in the pocket. To have in one’s bosom indicates kindness,

secrecy, or intimacy (<scripRef passage="Gen. 16:5" id="b-p384.1" parsed="|Gen|16|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.16.5">Gen. 16:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 12:8" id="b-p384.2" parsed="|2Sam|12|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.12.8">2 Sam. 12:8</scripRef>). Christ is said to
have been in “the bosom of the Father,” i.e., he had the most
perfect knowledge of the Father, had the closest intimacy with
him (<scripRef passage="John 1:18" id="b-p384.3" parsed="|John|1|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.1.18">John 1:18</scripRef>). John (13:23) was “leaning on Jesus’ bosom” at
the last supper. Our Lord carries his lambs in his bosom, i.e.,
has a tender, watchful care over them (Isa. 40:11).
</def>
<term id="b-p384.5">Bosor</term>
The Chaldee or Aramaic form of the name Beor, the father of
Balaam (2 Pet. 2:15).
</def>
<term id="b-p385.1">Bosses</term>
The projecting parts of a shield (Job 15:26). The Hebrew word
thus rendered means anything convex or arched, and hence the
back, as of animals.
</def>
<term id="b-p386.2">Botch</term>
The name given in Deut. 28:27, 35 to one of the Egyptian plagues
(<scripRef passage="Ex. 9:9" id="b-p387.3" parsed="|Exod|9|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.9.9">Ex. 9:9</scripRef>). The word so translated is usually rendered “boil”
</def>
<term id="b-p387.4">Bottle</term>
A vessel made of skins for holding wine (Josh. 9:4. 13; 1 Sam. 16:20; Matt. 9:17; Mark 2:22; Luke 5:37, 38), or milk (Judg. 4:19), or water (Gen. 21:14, 15, 19), or strong drink (Hab. 2:15).
Earthenware vessels were also similarly used (Jer. 19:1-10; 1 Kings 14:3; Isa. 30:14). In Job 32:19 (comp. Matt. 9:17; Luke 5:37, 38; Mark 2:22) the reference is to a wine-skin ready to
burst through the fermentation of the wine. “Bottles of wine” in
the Authorized Version of <scripRef passage="Hos. 7:5" id="b-p389.9" parsed="|Hos|7|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.7.5">Hos. 7:5</scripRef> is properly rendered in the
Revised Version by “the heat of wine,” i.e., the fever of wine,
its intoxicating strength.
The clouds are figuratively called the “bottles of heaven”
(<scripRef passage="Job 38:37" id="b-p390.1" parsed="|Job|38|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.38.37">Job 38:37</scripRef>). A bottle blackened or shrivelled by smoke is
referred to in <scripRef passage="Ps. 119:83" id="b-p390.2" parsed="|Ps|119|83|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.119.83">Ps. 119:83</scripRef> as an image to which the psalmist
likens himself.
</def>
<term id="b-p390.3">Bow</term>
The bow was in use in early times both in war and in the chase

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 21:20" id="b-p391.1" parsed="|Gen|21|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.20">Gen. 21:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 27:3" id="b-p391.2" parsed="|Gen|27|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.3">27:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 48:22" id="b-p391.3" parsed="|Gen|48|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.48.22">48:22</scripRef>). The tribe of Benjamin were famous for

the use of the bow (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 8:40" id="b-p391.4" parsed="|1Chr|8|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.8.40">1 Chr. 8:40</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 12:2" id="b-p391.5" parsed="|1Chr|12|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.12.2">12:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 14:8" id="b-p391.6" parsed="|2Chr|14|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.14.8">2 Chr. 14:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 17:17" id="b-p391.7" parsed="|2Chr|17|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.17.17">17:17</scripRef>); so

also were the Elamites (<scripRef passage="Isa. 22:6" id="b-p391.8" parsed="|Isa|22|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.22.6">Isa. 22:6</scripRef>) and the Lydians (<scripRef passage="Jer. 46:9" id="b-p391.9" parsed="|Jer|46|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.46.9">Jer. 46:9</scripRef>).

The Hebrew word commonly used for bow means properly to tread (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 5:18" id="b-p391.10" parsed="|1Chr|5|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5.18">1 Chr. 5:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 8:40" id="b-p391.11" parsed="|1Chr|8|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.8.40">8:40</scripRef>), and hence it is concluded that the foot was
employed in bending the bow. Bows of steel (correctly “copper”)
are mentioned (2 Sam. 22:35; Ps. 18:34).
The arrows were carried in a quiver (Gen. 27:3; Isa. 22:6;

<scripRef passage="Isa 49:2" id="b-p392.3" parsed="|Isa|49|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.49.2">49:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 127:5" id="b-p392.4" parsed="|Ps|127|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.127.5">Ps. 127:5</scripRef>). They were apparently sometimes shot with some
burning material attached to them (Ps. 120:4).
The bow is a symbol of victory (Ps. 7:12). It denotes also
falsehood, deceit (Ps. 64:3, 4; Hos. 7:16; Jer. 9:3).
“The use of the bow” in 2 Sam. 1:18 (A.V.) ought to be “the
song of the bow,” as in the Revised Version.
</def>
<term id="b-p394.2">Bowels</term>
(Phil. 1:8; 2:1; Col. 3:12), compassionate feelings; R.V.,
“tender mercies.”
</def>
<term id="b-p395.4">Bowing</term>
A mode of showing respect. Abraham “bowed himself to the people

of the land” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 23:7" id="b-p396.1" parsed="|Gen|23|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.23.7">Gen. 23:7</scripRef>); so Jacob to Esau (<scripRef passage="Gen. 33:3" id="b-p396.2" parsed="|Gen|33|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.33.3">Gen. 33:3</scripRef>); and the

brethren of Joseph before him as the governor of the land (<scripRef passage="Gen. 43:28" id="b-p396.3" parsed="|Gen|43|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.43.28">Gen. 43:28</scripRef>). Bowing is also frequently mentioned as an act of
adoration to idols (Josh. 23:7; 2 Kings 5:18; Judg. 2:19; Isa. 44:15), and to God (Josh. 5:14; Ps. 22:29; 72:9; Micah 6:6; Ps. 95:6; Eph. 3:14).
</def>
<term id="b-p396.14">Bowl</term>
The sockets of the lamps of the golden candlestick of the

tabernacle are called bowls (<scripRef passage="Ex. 25:31" id="b-p397.1" parsed="|Exod|25|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.25.31">Ex. 25:31</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 25:33" id="b-p397.2" parsed="|Exod|25|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.25.33">33</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 25:34" id="b-p397.3" parsed="|Exod|25|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.25.34">34</scripRef>; 37:17, 19, 20);

the same word so rendered being elsewhere rendered “cup” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 44:2" id="b-p397.4" parsed="|Gen|44|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.44.2">Gen. 44:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 44:12" id="b-p397.5" parsed="|Gen|44|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.44.12">12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 44:16" id="b-p397.6" parsed="|Gen|44|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.44.16">16</scripRef>), and wine “pot” (<scripRef passage="Jer. 35:5" id="b-p397.7" parsed="|Jer|35|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.35.5">Jer. 35:5</scripRef>). The reservoir for
oil, from which pipes led to each lamp in Zechariah’s vision of

the candlestick, is called also by this name (<scripRef passage="Zech. 4:2" id="b-p397.8" parsed="|Zech|4|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.4.2">Zech. 4:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Zech. 4:3" id="b-p397.9" parsed="|Zech|4|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.4.3">3</scripRef>); so
also are the vessels used for libations (Ex. 25:29; 37:16).
</def>
<term id="b-p397.12">Box</term>
For holding oil or perfumery (Mark 14:3). It was of the form of
a flask or bottle. The Hebrew word (pak) used for it is more
appropriately rendered “vial” in <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 10:1" id="b-p398.2" parsed="|1Sam|10|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.10.1">1 Sam. 10:1</scripRef>, and should also be
so rendered in 2 Kings 9:1, where alone else it occurs.
</def>
<term id="b-p398.4">Box-tree</term>
(Heb. teashshur), mentioned in Isa. 60:13; 41:19, was, according
to some, a species of cedar growing in Lebanon. The words of
<scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:6" id="b-p399.3" parsed="|Ezek|27|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.6">Ezek. 27:6</scripRef> literally translated are, “Thy benches they have made
of ivory, the daughter of the ashur tree,” i.e., inlaid with
ashur wood. The ashur is the box-tree, and accordingly the
Revised Version rightly reads “inlaid in box wood.” This is the
Buxus sempervirens of botanists. It is remarkable for the beauty
of its evergreen foliage and for the utility of its hard and
durable wood.
</def>
<term id="b-p399.4">Bozrah</term>
Enclosure; fortress. (1.) The city of Jobab, one of the early
Edomite kings (<scripRef passage="Gen. 36:33" id="b-p400.1" parsed="|Gen|36|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36.33">Gen. 36:33</scripRef>). This place is mentioned by the

prophets in later times (<scripRef passage="Isa. 34:6" id="b-p400.2" parsed="|Isa|34|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.34.6">Isa. 34:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 49:13" id="b-p400.3" parsed="|Jer|49|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.49.13">Jer. 49:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Amos 1:12" id="b-p400.4" parsed="|Amos|1|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.1.12">Amos 1:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Micah 2:12" id="b-p400.5" parsed="|Mic|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.2.12">Micah 2:12</scripRef>). Its modern representative is el-Busseireh. It lies in the
mountain district of Petra, 20 miles to the south-east of the
Dead Sea.
(2.) A Moabite city in the “plain country” (Jer. 48:24), i.e.,
on the high level down on the east of the Dead Sea. It is
probably the modern Buzrah.
</def>
<term id="b-p401.2">Bracelet</term>
(1.) Anklets (Num. 31:50; 2 Sam. 1:10), and with reference to
men.
(2.) The rendering of a Hebrew word meaning fasteners, found
in Gen. 24:22, 30, 47.
(3.) In Isa. 3:19, the rendering of a Hebrew word meaning
chains, i.e., twisted or chain-like bracelets.
(4.) In Ex. 35:22 it designates properly a clasp for fastening
the dress of females. Some interpret it as a nose-ring.
(5.) In Gen. 38:18, 25, the rendering of a Hebrew word meaning
“thread,” and may denote the ornamental cord with which the
signet was suspended from the neck of the wearer.
Bracelets were worn by men as well as by women (Cant. 5:14,
R.V.). They were of many various forms. The weight of those
presented by Eliezer to Rebekah was ten shekels (Gen. 24:22).
</def>
<term id="b-p407.3">Bramble</term>
(1.) Hebrew atad, Judg. 9:14; rendered “thorn,” Ps. 58:9. The
LXX. and Vulgate render by rhamnus, a thorny shrub common in
Palestine, resembling the hawthorn.
(2.) Hebrew hoah, Isa. 34:13 (R.V. “thistles”); “thickets”

in <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 13:6" id="b-p409.2" parsed="|1Sam|13|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.13.6">1 Sam. 13:6</scripRef>; “thistles” in <scripRef passage="2 Kings 14:9" id="b-p409.3" parsed="|2Kgs|14|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.14.9">2 Kings 14:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 14:2" id="b-p409.4" parsed="|2Kgs|14|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.14.2">2</scripRef> Chr. 25:18, <scripRef passage="Job 31:40" id="b-p409.5" parsed="|Job|31|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.31.40">Job 31:40</scripRef>; “thorns” in <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 33:11" id="b-p409.6" parsed="|2Chr|33|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.33.11">2 Chr. 33:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Cant. 2:2" id="b-p409.7" parsed="|Song|2|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.2.2">Cant. 2:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Hos. 9:6" id="b-p409.8" parsed="|Hos|9|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.9.6">Hos. 9:6</scripRef>. The word
may be regarded as denoting the common thistle, of which there
are many species which encumber the corn-fields of Palestine.
(See THORNS.)
</def>
<term id="b-p409.10">Branch</term>
A symbol of kings descended from royal ancestors (Ezek. 17:3, 10; Dan. 11:7); of prosperity (Job 8:16); of the Messiah, a
branch out of the root of the stem of Jesse (<scripRef passage="Isa. 11:1" id="b-p410.5" parsed="|Isa|11|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.11.1">Isa. 11:1</scripRef>), the
“beautiful branch” (4:2), a “righteous branch” (<scripRef passage="Jer. 23:5" id="b-p410.6" parsed="|Jer|23|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.23.5">Jer. 23:5</scripRef>), “the
Branch” (Zech. 3:8; 6:12).
Disciples are branches of the true vine (John 15:5, 6). “The
branch of the terrible ones” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 25:5" id="b-p411.3" parsed="|Isa|25|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.25.5">Isa. 25:5</scripRef>) is rightly translated
in the Revised Version “the song of the terrible ones,” i.e.,
the song of victory shall be brought low by the destruction of
Babylon and the return of the Jews from captivity.
The “abominable branch” is a tree on which a malefactor has

been hanged (<scripRef passage="Isa. 14:19" id="b-p412.1" parsed="|Isa|14|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.14.19">Isa. 14:19</scripRef>). The “highest branch” in <scripRef passage="Ezek. 17:3" id="b-p412.2" parsed="|Ezek|17|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.17.3">Ezek. 17:3</scripRef>
represents Jehoiakim the king.
</def>
<term id="b-p412.3">Brass</term>
Which is an alloy of copper and zinc, was not known till the
thirteenth century. What is designated by this word in Scripture

is properly copper (<scripRef passage="Deut. 8:9" id="b-p413.1" parsed="|Deut|8|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.8.9">Deut. 8:9</scripRef>).
