It was used for fetters (<scripRef passage="Judg. 16:21" id="b-p413.2" parsed="|Judg|16|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.16.21">Judg. 16:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 25:7" id="b-p413.3" parsed="|2Kgs|25|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.25.7">2 Kings 25:7</scripRef>), for pieces of armour (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:5" id="b-p413.4" parsed="|1Sam|17|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.5">1 Sam. 17:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:6" id="b-p413.5" parsed="|1Sam|17|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.6">6</scripRef>), for

musical instruments (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 15:19" id="b-p413.6" parsed="|1Chr|15|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.15.19">1 Chr. 15:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 13:1" id="b-p413.7" parsed="|1Cor|13|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.13.1">1 Cor. 13:1</scripRef>), and for money
(Matt. 10:9).
It is a symbol of insensibility and obstinacy in sin (Isa. 48:4; Jer. 6:28; Ezek. 22:18), and of strength (Ps. 107:16;
Micah 4:13).
The Macedonian empire is described as a kingdom of brass (Dan. 2:39). The “mountains of brass” Zechariah (6:1) speaks of have
been supposed to represent the immutable decrees of God.
The serpent of brass was made by Moses at the command of God
(<scripRef passage="Num. 21:4-9" id="b-p416.1" parsed="|Num|21|4|21|9" osisRef="Bible:Num.21.4-Num.21.9">Num. 21:4-9</scripRef>), and elevated on a pole, so that it might be seen
by all the people when wounded by the bite of the serpents that
were sent to them as a punishment for their murmurings against
God and against Moses. It was afterwards carried by the Jews
into Canaan, and preserved by them till the time of Hezekiah,
who caused it to be at length destroyed because it began to be
viewed by the people with superstitious reverence (2 Kings 18:4). (See NEHUSHTAN.)
The brazen serpent is alluded to by our Lord in John 3:14, 15.
(See SERPENT.)
</def>
<term id="b-p417.4">Bravery</term>
(Isa. 3:18), an old English word meaning comeliness or beauty.
</def>
<term id="b-p418.2">Breach</term>
An opening in a wall (1 Kings 11:27; 2 Kings 12:5); the fracture
of a limb (<scripRef passage="Lev. 24:20" id="b-p419.3" parsed="|Lev|24|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.24.20">Lev. 24:20</scripRef>), and hence the expression, “Heal, etc.”
(Ps. 60:2). Judg. 5:17, a bay or harbour; R.V., “by his creeks.”
</def>
<term id="b-p419.6">Bread</term>
Among the Jews was generally made of wheat (Ex. 29:2; Judg. 6:19), though also sometimes of other grains (Gen. 14:18; Judg. 7:13). Parched grain was sometimes used for food without any
other preparation (Ruth 2:14).
Bread was prepared by kneading in wooden bowls or “kneading

troughs” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 18:6" id="b-p421.1" parsed="|Gen|18|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.18.6">Gen. 18:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex. 12:34" id="b-p421.2" parsed="|Exod|12|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.34">Ex. 12:34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 7:18" id="b-p421.3" parsed="|Jer|7|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.7.18">Jer. 7:18</scripRef>). The dough was mixed
with leaven and made into thin cakes, round or oval, and then
baked. The bread eaten at the Passover was always unleavened

(<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:15-20" id="b-p421.4" parsed="|Exod|12|15|12|20" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.15-Exod.12.20">Ex. 12:15-20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 16:3" id="b-p421.5" parsed="|Deut|16|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.16.3">Deut. 16:3</scripRef>). In the towns there were public
ovens, which were much made use of for baking bread; there were

also bakers by trade (<scripRef passage="Hos. 7:4" id="b-p421.6" parsed="|Hos|7|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.7.4">Hos. 7:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 37:21" id="b-p421.7" parsed="|Jer|37|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.37.21">Jer. 37:21</scripRef>). Their ovens were
not unlike those of modern times. But sometimes the bread was
baked by being placed on the ground that had been heated by a
fire, and by covering it with the embers (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 19:6" id="b-p421.8" parsed="|1Kgs|19|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.19.6">1 Kings 19:6</scripRef>). This
was probably the mode in which Sarah prepared bread on the
occasion referred to in Gen. 18:6.
In Lev. 2 there is an account of the different kinds of bread
and cakes used by the Jews. (See BAKE.)
The shew-bread (q.v.) consisted of twelve loaves of unleavened
bread prepared and presented hot on the golden table every
Sabbath. They were square or oblong, and represented the twelve
tribes of Israel. The old loaves were removed every Sabbath, and
were to be eaten only by the priests in the court of the
sanctuary (Ex. 25:30; Lev. 24:8; 1 Sam. 21:1-6; Matt. 12:4).
The word bread is used figuratively in such expressions as
“bread of sorrows” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 127:2" id="b-p424.1" parsed="|Ps|127|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.127.2">Ps. 127:2</scripRef>), “bread of tears” (80:5), i.e.,
sorrow and tears are like one’s daily bread, they form so great
a part in life. The bread of “wickedness” (<scripRef passage="Prov. 4:17" id="b-p424.2" parsed="|Prov|4|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.4.17">Prov. 4:17</scripRef>) and “of
deceit” (20:17) denote in like manner that wickedness and deceit
are a part of the daily life.
</def>
<term id="b-p424.3">Breastplate</term>
(1.) That piece of ancient armour that protected the breast.
This word is used figuratively in Eph. 6:14 and Isa. 59:17. (See ARMOUR.)
(2.) An ornament covering the breast of the high priest, first
mentioned in <scripRef passage="Ex. 25:7" id="b-p426.1" parsed="|Exod|25|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.25.7">Ex. 25:7</scripRef>. It was made of embroidered cloth, set
with four rows of precious stones, three in each row. On each

stone was engraved the name of one of the twelve tribes (<scripRef passage="Ex. 28:15-29" id="b-p426.2" parsed="|Exod|28|15|28|29" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.15-Exod.28.29">Ex. 28:15-29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 39:8-21" id="b-p426.3" parsed="|Exod|39|8|39|21" osisRef="Bible:Exod.39.8-Exod.39.21">39:8-21</scripRef>). It was in size about ten inches square. The
two upper corners were fastened to the ephod by blue ribbons. It
was not to be “loosed from the ephod” (<scripRef passage="Ex. 28:28" id="b-p426.4" parsed="|Exod|28|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.28">Ex. 28:28</scripRef>). The lower
corners were fastened to the girdle of the priest. As it
reminded the priest of his representative character, it was
called the memorial (28:29). It was also called the breastplate
of judgment (28:15). (See PRIEST.)
</def>
<term id="b-p426.6">Breeches</term>
(Ex. 28:42), rather linen drawers, reaching from the waist to a
little above the knee, worn by the priests (Ezek. 44:17, 18).
</def>
<term id="b-p427.4">Bribe</term>
None to be taken; “for the gift maketh open eyes blind, and
perverteth the cause of the righteous” (<scripRef passage="Ex. 23:8" id="b-p428.1" parsed="|Exod|23|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.8">Ex. 23:8</scripRef>, literally
rendered).
</def>
<term id="b-p428.2">Bricks</term>
The making of, formed the chief labour of the Israelites in

Egypt (<scripRef passage="Ex. 1:13" id="b-p429.1" parsed="|Exod|1|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.1.13">Ex. 1:13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 1:14" id="b-p429.2" parsed="|Exod|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.1.14">14</scripRef>). Those found among the ruins of Babylon and
Nineveh are about a foot square and four inches thick. They were
usually dried in the sun, though also sometimes in kilns (2 Sam. 12:31; Jer. 43:9; Nah. 3:14). (See NEBUCHADNEZZAR.)
The bricks used in the tower of Babel were burnt bricks,
cemented in the building by bitumen (Gen. 11:3).
</def>
<term id="b-p430.2">Bride</term>
Frequently used in the ordinary sense (Isa. 49:18; 61:10, etc.).
The relation between Christ and his church is set forth under
the figure of that between a bridegroom and bride (<scripRef passage="John 3:29" id="b-p431.3" parsed="|John|3|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.3.29">John 3:29</scripRef>).

The church is called “the bride” (<scripRef passage="Rev. 21:9" id="b-p431.4" parsed="|Rev|21|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.21.9">Rev. 21:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev 22:17" id="b-p431.5" parsed="|Rev|22|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.22.17">22:17</scripRef>). Compare
parable of the Ten Virgins (Matt. 25:1-13).
</def>
<term id="b-p431.7">Bridle</term>
Three Hebrew words are thus rendered in the Authorized Version.
(1.) Heb. mahsom’ signifies a muzzle or halter or bridle, by
which the rider governs his horse (Ps. 39:1).
(2.) Me’theg, rendered also “bit” in Ps. 32:9, which is its
proper meaning. Found in <scripRef passage="2 Kings 19:28" id="b-p433.2" parsed="|2Kgs|19|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.19.28">2 Kings 19:28</scripRef>, where the restraints of
God’s providence are metaphorically styled his “bridle” and

“hook.” God’s placing a “bridle in the jaws of the people” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 30:28" id="b-p433.3" parsed="|Isa|30|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.30.28">Isa. 30:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 37:29" id="b-p433.4" parsed="|Isa|37|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.37.29">37:29</scripRef>) signifies his preventing the Assyrians from
carrying out their purpose against Jerusalem.
(3.) Another word, re’sen, was employed to represent a
halter or bridle-rein, as used Ps. 32:9; Isa. 30:28. In Job 30:11 the restraints of law and humanity are called a bridle.
</def>
<term id="b-p434.4">Brier</term>
This word occurs frequently, and is the translation of several
different terms. (1.) <scripRef passage="Micah 7:4" id="b-p435.1" parsed="|Mic|7|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.7.4">Micah 7:4</scripRef>, it denotes a species of thorn
shrub used for hedges. In <scripRef passage="Prov. 15:19" id="b-p435.2" parsed="|Prov|15|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.15.19">Prov. 15:19</scripRef> the word is rendered
“thorn” (Heb. hedek, “stinging”), supposed by some to be what
is called the “apple of Sodom” (q.v.).
(2.) Ezek. 28:24, sallon’, properly a “prickle,” such as is
found on the shoots of the palm tree.
(3.) Isa. 55:13, probably simply a thorny bush. Some,
following the Vulgate Version, regard it as the “nettle.”
(4.) Isa. 5:6; 7:23-25, etc., frequently used to denote thorny
shrubs in general. In 10:17; 27:4, it means troublesome men.
(5.) In Heb. 6:8 the Greek word (tribolos) so rendered means
“three-pronged,” and denotes the land caltrop, a low throny
shrub resembling in its spikes the military “crow-foot.” Comp.
Matt. 7:16, “thistle.”
</def>
<term id="b-p439.3">Brigandine</term>
(Jer. 46:4; 51:3), an obsolete English word denoting a scale
coat of armour, or habergeon, worn by light-armed “brigands.”
The Revised Version has “coat of mail.”
</def>
<term id="b-p440.3">Brimstone</term>
An inflammable mineral substance found in quantities on the
shores of the Dead Sea. The cities of the plain were destroyed

by a rain of fire and brimstone (<scripRef passage="Gen. 19:24" id="b-p441.1" parsed="|Gen|19|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.19.24">Gen. 19:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 19:25" id="b-p441.2" parsed="|Gen|19|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.19.25">25</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="Isa. 34:9" id="b-p441.3" parsed="|Isa|34|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.34.9">Isa. 34:9</scripRef>
allusion is made to the destruction of these cities. This word

figuratively denotes destruction or punishment (<scripRef passage="Job 18:15" id="b-p441.4" parsed="|Job|18|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.18.15">Job 18:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 30:33" id="b-p441.5" parsed="|Isa|30|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.30.33">Isa. 30:33</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 34:9" id="b-p441.6" parsed="|Isa|34|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.34.9">34:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 11:6" id="b-p441.7" parsed="|Ps|11|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.11.6">Ps. 11:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 38:22" id="b-p441.8" parsed="|Ezek|38|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.38.22">Ezek. 38:22</scripRef>). It is used to express the
idea of excruciating torment in Rev. 14:10; 19:20; 20:10.
</def>
<term id="b-p441.12">Brook</term>
A torrent. (1.) Applied to small streams, as the Arnon, Jabbok,
etc. Isaiah (15:7) speaks of the “book of the willows,” probably
the Wady-el-Asha. (2.) It is also applied to winter torrents

(<scripRef passage="Job 6:15" id="b-p442.1" parsed="|Job|6|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.6.15">Job 6:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 34:5" id="b-p442.2" parsed="|Num|34|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.34.5">Num. 34:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 15:4" id="b-p442.3" parsed="|Josh|15|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.4">Josh. 15:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 15:47" id="b-p442.4" parsed="|Josh|15|47|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.47">47</scripRef>), and to the torrent-bed or

wady as well as to the torrent itself (<scripRef passage="Num. 13:23" id="b-p442.5" parsed="|Num|13|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.13.23">Num. 13:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 17:3" id="b-p442.6" parsed="|1Kgs|17|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.17.3">1 Kings 17:3</scripRef>). (3.) In <scripRef passage="Isa. 19:7" id="b-p442.7" parsed="|Isa|19|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.19.7">Isa. 19:7</scripRef> the river Nile is meant, as rendered in
the Revised Version.
</def>
<term id="b-p442.8">Brother</term>
(1.) In the natural and common sense (Matt. 1:2; Luke 3:1, 19).
(2.) A near relation, a cousin (Gen. 13:8; 14:16; Matt. 12:46;
John 7:3; Acts 1:14; Gal. 1:19).
(3.) Simply a fellow-countryman (Matt. 5:47; Acts 3:22; Heb. 7:5).
(4.) A disciple or follower (Matt. 25:40; Heb. 2:11, 12).
(5.) One of the same faith (Amos 1:9; Acts 9:30; 11:29; 1 Cor. 5:11); whence the early disciples of our Lord were known to each
other as brethren.
(6.) A colleague in office (Ezra 3:2; 1 Cor. 1:1; 2 Cor. 1:1).
(7.) A fellow-man (Gen. 9:5; 19:7; Matt. 5:22, 23, 24; 7:5;
Heb. 2:17).
(8.) One beloved or closely united with another in affection

(<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 1:26" id="b-p450.1" parsed="|2Sam|1|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.1.26">2 Sam. 1:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 6:3" id="b-p450.2" parsed="|Acts|6|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.6.3">Acts 6:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Thess. 5:1" id="b-p450.3" parsed="|1Thess|5|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Thess.5.1">1 Thess. 5:1</scripRef>). Brethren of Jesus (<scripRef passage="Matt. 1:25" id="b-p450.4" parsed="|Matt|1|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.1.25">Matt. 1:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 12:46" id="b-p450.5" parsed="|Matt|12|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.12.46">12:46</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt 12:50" id="b-p450.6" parsed="|Matt|12|50|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.12.50">50</scripRef>: <scripRef passage="Mark 3:31" id="b-p450.7" parsed="|Mark|3|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.3.31">Mark 3:31</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Mark 3:32" id="b-p450.8" parsed="|Mark|3|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.3.32">32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal. 1:19" id="b-p450.9" parsed="|Gal|1|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.1.19">Gal. 1:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 9:5" id="b-p450.10" parsed="|1Cor|9|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.9.5">1 Cor. 9:5</scripRef>, etc.)
were probably the younger children of Joseph and Mary. Some have
supposed that they may have been the children of Joseph by a
former marriage, and others that they were the children of Mary,
the Virgin’s sister, and wife of Cleophas. The first
interpretation, however, is the most natural.
</def>
<term id="b-p450.11">Bruit</term>
A rumour or report (Jer. 10:22, R.V. “rumour;” Nah. 3:19).
</def>
<term id="b-p451.3">Bucket</term>
A vessel to draw water with (Isa. 40:15); used figuratively,
probably, of a numerous issue (Num. 24:7).
</def>
<term id="b-p452.3">Buckler</term>
(1.) A portable shield (2 Sam. 22:31; 1 Chr. 5:18).
(2.) A shield surrounding the person; the targe or round form;
used once figuratively (Ps. 91:4).
(3.) A large shield protecting the whole body (Ps. 35:2; Ezek. 23:24; 26:8).
(4.) A lance or spear; improperly rendered “buckler” in the
Authorized Version (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 12:8" id="b-p456.1" parsed="|1Chr|12|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.12.8">1 Chr. 12:8</scripRef>), but correctly in the Revised
Version “spear.”
The leather of shields required oiling (2 Sam. 1:21; Isa. 21:5), so as to prevent its being injured by moisture. Copper (=

“brass”) shields were also in use (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:6" id="b-p457.3" parsed="|1Sam|17|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.6">1 Sam. 17:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 14:27" id="b-p457.4" parsed="|1Kgs|14|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.14.27">1 Kings 14:27</scripRef>).
Those spoken of in <scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:16" id="b-p457.5" parsed="|1Kgs|10|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.16">1 Kings 10:16</scripRef>, etc.; 14:26, were probably of
massive metal.
The shields David had taken from his enemies were suspended in
the temple as mementoes (2 Kings 11:10). (See ARMOUR, SHIELD.)
</def>
<term id="b-p458.4">Building</term>
Among the Jews was suited to the climate and conditions of the
country. They probably adopted the kind of architecture for
their dwellings which they found already existing when they

entered Canaan (<scripRef passage="Deut. 6:10" id="b-p459.1" parsed="|Deut|6|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.6.10">Deut. 6:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 13:19" id="b-p459.2" parsed="|Num|13|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.13.19">Num. 13:19</scripRef>). Phoenician artists (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 5:11" id="b-p459.3" parsed="|2Sam|5|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.5.11">2 Sam. 5:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 5:6" id="b-p459.4" parsed="|1Kgs|5|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.5.6">1 Kings 5:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 5:18" id="b-p459.5" parsed="|1Kgs|5|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.5.18">18</scripRef>) assisted at the erection of the
royal palace and the temple at Jerusalem. Foreigners also
assisted at the restoration of the temple after the Exile (Ezra 3:7).
In Gen. 11:3, 9, we have the first recorded instance of the
erection of buildings. The cities of the plain of Shinar were
founded by the descendants of Shem (10:11, 12, 22).
The Israelites were by occupation shepherds and dwellers in
tents (<scripRef passage="Gen. 47:3" id="b-p461.1" parsed="|Gen|47|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.47.3">Gen. 47:3</scripRef>); but from the time of their entering Canaan
they became dwellers in towns, and in houses built of the native
limestone of Palestine. Much building was carried on in
Solomon’s time. Besides the buildings he completed at Jerusalem,

he also built Baalath and Tadmor (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 9:15" id="b-p461.2" parsed="|1Kgs|9|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.9.15">1 Kings 9:15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 9:24" id="b-p461.3" parsed="|1Kgs|9|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.9.24">24</scripRef>). Many of the
kings of Israel and Judah were engaged in erecting various
buildings.
Herod and his sons and successors restored the temple, and
built fortifications and other structures of great magnificence
in Jerusalem (Luke 21:5).
The instruments used in building are mentioned as the

plumb-line (<scripRef passage="Amos 7:7" id="b-p463.1" parsed="|Amos|7|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.7.7">Amos 7:7</scripRef>), the measuring-reed (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 40:3" id="b-p463.2" parsed="|Ezek|40|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.40.3">Ezek. 40:3</scripRef>), and the
saw (1 Kings 7:9).
Believers are “God’s building” (1 Cor. 3:9); and heaven is
called “a building of God” (<scripRef passage="2 Cor. 5:1" id="b-p464.2" parsed="|2Cor|5|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.5.1">2 Cor. 5:1</scripRef>). Christ is the only
foundation of his church (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 3:10-12" id="b-p464.3" parsed="|1Cor|3|10|3|12" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.3.10-1Cor.3.12">1 Cor. 3:10-12</scripRef>), of which he also is
the builder (Matt. 16:18).
</def>
<term id="b-p464.5">Bul</term>
Rainy, the eighth ecclesiastical month of the year (1 Kings 6:38), and the second month of the civil year; later called
Marchesvan (q.v.). (See MONTH.)
</def>
<term id="b-p465.3">Bullock</term>
(1.) The translation of a word which is a generic name for
horned cattle (Isa. 65:25). It is also rendered “cow” (Ezek. 4:15), “ox” (Gen. 12:16).
(2.) The translation of a word always meaning an animal of the
ox kind, without distinction of age or sex (<scripRef passage="Hos. 12:11" id="b-p467.1" parsed="|Hos|12|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.12.11">Hos. 12:11</scripRef>). It is
rendered “cow” (Num. 18:17) and “ox” (Lev. 17:3).
(3.) Another word is rendered in the same way (Jer. 31:18). It

is also translated “calf” (<scripRef passage="Lev. 9:3" id="b-p468.2" parsed="|Lev|9|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.9.3">Lev. 9:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Micah 6:6" id="b-p468.3" parsed="|Mic|6|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.6.6">Micah 6:6</scripRef>). It is the same

word used of the “molten calf” (<scripRef passage="Ex. 32:4" id="b-p468.4" parsed="|Exod|32|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.32.4">Ex. 32:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex 32:8" id="b-p468.5" parsed="|Exod|32|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.32.8">8</scripRef>) and “the golden
calf” (1 Kings 12:28).
(4.) In Judg. 6:25; Isa. 34:7, the Hebrew word is different.

It is the customary word for bulls offered in sacrifice. In <scripRef passage="Hos. 14:2" id="b-p469.3" parsed="|Hos|14|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.14.2">Hos. 14:2</scripRef>, the Authorized Version has “calves,” the Revised Version
“bullocks.”
</def>
<term id="b-p469.4">Bulrush</term>
(1.) In Isa. 58:5 the rendering of a word which denotes
“belonging to a marsh,” from the nature of the soil in which it
grows (Isa. 18:2). It was sometimes platted into ropes (Job. 41:2; A.V., “hook,” R.V., “rope,” lit. “cord of rushes”).
(2.) In Ex. 2:3, Isa. 18:2 (R.V., “papyrus”) this word is the
translation of the Hebrew gome, which designates the plant as

absorbing moisture. In <scripRef passage="Isa. 35:7" id="b-p471.3" parsed="|Isa|35|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.35.7">Isa. 35:7</scripRef> and <scripRef passage="Job 8:11" id="b-p471.4" parsed="|Job|8|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.8.11">Job 8:11</scripRef> it is rendered
“rush.” This was the Egyptian papyrus (papyrus Nilotica). It was
anciently very abundant in Egypt. The Egyptians made garments
and shoes and various utensils of it. It was used for the

construction of the ark of Moses (<scripRef passage="Ex. 2:3" id="b-p471.5" parsed="|Exod|2|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.2.3">Ex. 2:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 2:5" id="b-p471.6" parsed="|Exod|2|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.2.5">5</scripRef>). The root portions
of the stem were used for food. The inside bark was cut into
strips, which were sewed together and dried in the sun, forming
the papyrus used for writing. It is no longer found in Egypt,
but grows luxuriantly in Palestine, in the marshes of the Huleh,
and in the swamps at the north end of the Lake of Gennesaret.
(See CANE.)
</def>
<term id="b-p471.8">Bulwarks</term>
Mural towers, bastions, were introduced by king Uzziah (2 Chr. 26:15; Zeph. 1:16; Ps. 48:13; Isa. 26:1). There are five Hebrew
words so rendered in the Authorized Version, but the same word
is also variously rendered.
</def>
<term id="b-p472.5">Bunch</term>
(1.) A bundle of twigs (Ex. 12:22). (2.) Bunch or cake of
raisins (2 Sam. 16:1). (3.) The “bunch of a camel” (Isa. 30:6).
</def>
<term id="b-p473.4">Burden</term>
(1.) A load of any kind (Ex. 23:5). (2.) A severe task (Ex. 2:11). (3.) A difficult duty, requiring effort (Ex. 18:22). (4.)
A prophecy of a calamitous or disastrous nature (<scripRef passage="Isa. 13:1" id="b-p474.4" parsed="|Isa|13|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.13.1">Isa. 13:1</scripRef>;
17:1; Hab. 1:1, etc.).
</def>
<term id="b-p474.7">Burial</term>
The first burial we have an account of is that of Sarah (Gen. 23). The first commercial transaction recorded is that of the
purchase of a burial-place, for which Abraham weighed to Ephron
“four hundred shekels of silver current money with the
merchants.” Thus the patriarch became the owner of a part of the
land of Canaan, the only part he ever possessed. When he himself
died, “his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the cave of
Machpelah,” beside Sarah his wife (Gen. 25:9).
Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, was buried under Allon-bachuth, “the
oak of weeping” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 35:8" id="b-p476.1" parsed="|Gen|35|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.35.8">Gen. 35:8</scripRef>), near to Bethel. Rachel died, and
was buried near Ephrath; “and Jacob set a pillar upon her grave”
(16-20). Isaac was buried at Hebron, where he had died (27, 29).
Jacob, when charging his sons to bury him in the cave of
Machpelah, said, “There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife;
there they buried Isaac and Rebekah his wife; and there I buried
Leah” (49:31). In compliance with the oath which he made him
swear unto him (47:29-31), Joseph, assisted by his brethren,
buried Jacob in the cave of Machpelah (50:2, 13). At the Exodus,
Moses “took the bones of Joseph with him,” and they were buried
in the “parcel of ground” which Jacob had bought of the sons of

Hamor (<scripRef passage="Josh. 24:32" id="b-p476.2" parsed="|Josh|24|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.24.32">Josh. 24:32</scripRef>), which became Joseph’s inheritance (<scripRef passage="Gen. 48:22" id="b-p476.3" parsed="|Gen|48|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.48.22">Gen. 48:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 5:1" id="b-p476.4" parsed="|1Chr|5|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5.1">1 Chr. 5:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 4:5" id="b-p476.5" parsed="|John|4|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.4.5">John 4:5</scripRef>). Two burials are mentioned as

having taken place in the wilderness. That of Miriam (<scripRef passage="Num. 20:1" id="b-p476.6" parsed="|Num|20|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.20.1">Num. 20:1</scripRef>), and that of Moses, “in the land of Moab” (<scripRef passage="Deut. 34:5" id="b-p476.7" parsed="|Deut|34|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.34.5">Deut. 34:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut 34:6" id="b-p476.8" parsed="|Deut|34|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.34.6">6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut 34:8" id="b-p476.9" parsed="|Deut|34|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.34.8">8</scripRef>). There is no account of the actual burial of Aaron, which
probably, however, took place on the summit of Mount Hor (Num. 20:28, 29).
Joshua was buried “in the border of his inheritance in
Timnath-serah” (Josh. 24: 30).
In Job we find a reference to burying-places, which were
probably the Pyramids (3:14, 15). The Hebrew word for “waste
places” here resembles in sound the Egyptian word for
“pyramids.”
Samuel, like Moses, was honoured with a national burial (1 Sam. 25:1). Joab (1 Kings 2:34) “was buried in his own house in
the wilderness.”
In connection with the burial of Saul and his three sons we

meet for the first time with the practice of burning the dead (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 31:11-13" id="b-p480.1" parsed="|1Sam|31|11|31|13" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.31.11-1Sam.31.13">1 Sam. 31:11-13</scripRef>). The same practice is again referred to by Amos
Absalom was buried “in the wood” where he was slain (2 Sam. 18:17, 18). The raising of the heap of stones over his grave was

intended to mark abhorrence of the person buried (comp. <scripRef passage="Josh. 7:26" id="b-p481.3" parsed="|Josh|7|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.7.26">Josh. 7:26</scripRef> and 8:29). There was no fixed royal burying-place for the
Hebrew kings. We find several royal burials taking place,

however, “in the city of David” (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 2:10" id="b-p481.4" parsed="|1Kgs|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.2.10">1 Kings 2:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 11:43" id="b-p481.5" parsed="|1Kgs|11|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.11.43">11:43</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 15:8" id="b-p481.6" parsed="|1Kgs|15|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.15.8">15:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 14:19" id="b-p481.7" parsed="|2Kgs|14|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.14.19">2 Kings 14:19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 14:20" id="b-p481.8" parsed="|2Kgs|14|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.14.20">20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 15:38" id="b-p481.9" parsed="|2Kgs|15|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.38">15:38</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 14:31" id="b-p481.10" parsed="|1Kgs|14|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.14.31">1 Kings 14:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 22:50" id="b-p481.11" parsed="|1Kgs|22|50|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.22.50">22:50</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 21:19" id="b-p481.12" parsed="|2Chr|21|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.21.19">2 Chr. 21:19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 21:20" id="b-p481.13" parsed="|2Chr|21|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.21.20">20</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 24:25" id="b-p481.14" parsed="|2Chr|24|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.24.25">2 Chr. 24:25</scripRef>, etc.). Hezekiah was buried in the mount of the
sepulchres of the sons of David; “and all Judah and the
inhabitants of Jerusalem did him honour at his death” (2 Chr. 32:33).
Little is said regarding the burial of the kings of Israel.
Some of them were buried in Samaria, the capital of their
kingdom (2 Kings 10:35; 13:9; 14:16).
Our Lord was buried in a new tomb, hewn out of the rock, which
Joseph of Arimathea had prepared for himself (<scripRef passage="Matt. 27:57-60" id="b-p483.1" parsed="|Matt|27|57|27|60" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.57-Matt.27.60">Matt. 27:57-60</scripRef>;
Mark 15:46; John 19:41, 42).
The grave of Lazarus was “a cave, and a stone lay on it” (John 11:38). Graves were frequently either natural caverns or
artificial excavations formed in the sides of rocks (<scripRef passage="Gen. 23:9" id="b-p484.2" parsed="|Gen|23|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.23.9">Gen. 23:9</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Matt. 27:60" id="b-p484.3" parsed="|Matt|27|60|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.60">Matt. 27:60</scripRef>); and coffins were seldom used, unless when the body
was brought from a distance.
</def>
<term id="b-p484.4">Burnt offering</term>
Hebrew olah; i.e., “ascending,” the whole being consumed by
fire, and regarded as ascending to God while being consumed.
Part of every offering was burnt in the sacred fire, but this
was wholly burnt, a “whole burnt offering.” It was the most
frequent form of sacrifice, and apparently the only one
mentioned in the book of Genesis. Such were the sacrifices
offered by Abel (Gen. 4:3, 4, here called minhah; i.e., “a

gift”), Noah (<scripRef passage="Gen. 8:20" id="b-p485.3" parsed="|Gen|8|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.8.20">Gen. 8:20</scripRef>), Abraham (<scripRef passage="Gen. 22:2" id="b-p485.4" parsed="|Gen|22|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.22.2">Gen. 22:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 22:7" id="b-p485.5" parsed="|Gen|22|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.22.7">7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 22:8" id="b-p485.6" parsed="|Gen|22|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.22.8">8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 22:13" id="b-p485.7" parsed="|Gen|22|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.22.13">13</scripRef>), and by
the Hebrews in Egypt (Ex. 10:25).
The law of Moses afterwards prescribed the occasions and the
manner in which burnt sacrifices were to be offered. There were

“the continual burnt offering” (<scripRef passage="Ex. 29:38-42" id="b-p486.1" parsed="|Exod|29|38|29|42" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.38-Exod.29.42">Ex. 29:38-42</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 6:9-13" id="b-p486.2" parsed="|Lev|6|9|6|13" osisRef="Bible:Lev.6.9-Lev.6.13">Lev. 6:9-13</scripRef>), “the
burnt offering of every sabbath,” which was double the daily one

(<scripRef passage="Num. 28:9" id="b-p486.3" parsed="|Num|28|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.28.9">Num. 28:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 28:10" id="b-p486.4" parsed="|Num|28|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.28.10">10</scripRef>), “the burnt offering of every month” (28:11-15),

the offerings at the Passover (19-23), at Pentecost (<scripRef passage="Lev. 23:16" id="b-p486.5" parsed="|Lev|23|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.16">Lev. 23:16</scripRef>), the feast of Trumpets (23:23-25), and on the day of
Atonement (Lev. 16).
On other occasions special sacrifices were offered, as at the
consecration of Aaron (<scripRef passage="Ex. 29" id="b-p487.1" parsed="|Exod|29|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29">Ex. 29</scripRef>) and the dedication of the temple
(1 Kings 8:5, 62-64).
Free-will burnt offerings were also permitted (Lev. 1:13), and
were offered at the accession of Solomon to the throne (1 Chr. 29:21), and at the reformation brought about by Hezekiah (2 Chr. 29: 31-35).
These offerings signified the complete dedication of the
offerers unto God. This is referred to in <scripRef passage="Rom. 12:1" id="b-p489.1" parsed="|Rom|12|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.12.1">Rom. 12:1</scripRef>. (See
ALTAR,
SACRIFICE.)
</def>
<term id="b-p489.4">Bush</term>
In which Jehovah appeared to Moses in the wilderness (Ex. 3:2;
<scripRef passage="Acts 7:30" id="b-p490.2" parsed="|Acts|7|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.7.30">Acts 7:30</scripRef>). It is difficult to say what particular kind of plant
or bush is here meant. Probably it was the mimosa or acacia. The

words “in the bush” in <scripRef passage="Mark 12:26" id="b-p490.3" parsed="|Mark|12|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.12.26">Mark 12:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 20:37" id="b-p490.4" parsed="|Luke|20|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.20.37">Luke 20:37</scripRef>, mean “in the
passage or paragraph on the bush;” i.e., in Ex. 3.
</def>
<term id="b-p490.6">Butler</term>
Properly a servant in charge of the wine (Gen. 40:1-13; 41:9).
The Hebrew word, mashkeh, thus translated is rendered also

(plural) “cup-bearers” (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:5" id="b-p491.3" parsed="|1Kgs|10|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.5">1 Kings 10:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 9:4" id="b-p491.4" parsed="|2Chr|9|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.9.4">2 Chr. 9:4</scripRef>). Nehemiah
(1:11) was cup-bearer to king Artaxerxes. It was a position of
great responsibility and honour in royal households.
</def>
<term id="b-p491.5">Butter</term>
(Heb. hemah), curdled milk (Gen. 18:8; Judg. 5:25; 2 Sam. 17:29), or butter in the form of the skim of hot milk or cream,

called by the Arabs kaimak, a semi-fluid (<scripRef passage="Job 20:17" id="b-p492.4" parsed="|Job|20|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.20.17">Job 20:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 29:6" id="b-p492.5" parsed="|Job|29|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.29.6">29:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 32:14" id="b-p492.6" parsed="|Deut|32|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.14">Deut. 32:14</scripRef>). The words of <scripRef passage="Prov. 30:33" id="b-p492.7" parsed="|Prov|30|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.30.33">Prov. 30:33</scripRef> have been rendered by some “the
pressure [not churning] of milk bringeth forth cheese.”
</def>
<term id="b-p492.8">Buz</term>
Contempt. (1.) The second son of Nahor and Milcah, and brother
of Huz (Gen. 22:21). Elihu was one of his descendants (Job 32:2).
(2.) One of the chiefs of the tribe of Gad (1 Chr. 5:14).
(3.) A district in Arabia Petrea (Jer. 25:23).
</def>
<term id="b-p495.2">Buzi</term>
The father of the prophet Ezekiel (1:3).
</def>
<term id="b-p496.1">By</term>
In the expression “by myself” (A.V., 1 Cor. 4:4), means, as
rendered in the Revised Version, “against myself.”
</def>
<term id="b-p497.2">By and by</term>
Immediately (Matt. 13:21; R.V., “straightway;” Luke 21:9).
</def>
<term id="b-p498.3">By-ways</term>
Only in Judg. 5:6 and Ps. 125:5; literally “winding or twisted
roads.” The margin has “crooked ways.”
</def>
<term id="b-p499.3">By-word</term>
Hebrew millah (Job 30:9), a word or speech, and hence object
of talk; Hebrew mashal (Ps. 44:14), a proverb or parable. When

it denotes a sharp word of derision, as in <scripRef passage="Deut. 28:37" id="b-p500.3" parsed="|Deut|28|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.37">Deut. 28:37</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 28:1" id="b-p500.4" parsed="|Deut|28|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.1">1</scripRef> Kings
9:7, 2 Chr. 7:20, the Hebrew sheninah is used. In Jer. 24:9 it
is rendered “taunt.”
</def>
</glossary>
</div2>
<div2 title="C" prev="b" next="d" id="c">
<glossary id="c-p0.1">
<term id="c-p0.2">Cab</term>
<def id="c-p0.3">
Hollow (R.V., “kab”), occurs only in 2 Kings 6:25; a dry
measure, the sixth part of a seah, and the eighteenth part of an
ephah, equal to about two English quarts.
</def>
<term id="c-p1.2">Cabins</term>
<def id="c-p1.3">
Only in Jer. 37:16 (R.V., “cells”), arched vaults or recesses
off a passage or room; cells for the closer confinement of
prisoners.
</def>
<term id="c-p2.2">Cabul</term>
<def id="c-p2.3">
How little! as nothing. (1.) A town on the eastern border of
Asher (<scripRef passage="Josh. 19:27" id="c-p3.1" parsed="|Josh|19|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.27">Josh. 19:27</scripRef>), probably one of the towns given by Solomon
to Hiram; the modern Kabul, some 8 miles east of Accho, on the
very borders of Galilee.
(2.) A district in the north-west of Galilee, near to Tyre,
containing twenty cities given to Hiram by Solomon as a reward

for various services rendered to him in building the temple (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 9:13" id="c-p4.1" parsed="|1Kgs|9|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.9.13">1 Kings 9:13</scripRef>), and as payment of the six score talents of gold he
had borrowed from him. Hiram gave the cities this name because
he was not pleased with the gift, the name signifying “good for
nothing.” Hiram seems afterwards to have restored these cities
to Solomon (2 Chr. 8:2).
</def>
<term id="c-p4.3">Caesar</term>
<def id="c-p4.4">
The title assumed by the Roman emperors after Julius Caesar. In
the New Testament this title is given to various emperors as
sovereigns of Judaea without their accompanying distinctive

proper names (<scripRef passage="John 19:15" id="c-p5.1" parsed="|John|19|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.15">John 19:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 17:7" id="c-p5.2" parsed="|Acts|17|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.17.7">Acts 17:7</scripRef>). The Jews paid tribute to
Caesar (<scripRef passage="Matt. 22:17" id="c-p5.3" parsed="|Matt|22|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.22.17">Matt. 22:17</scripRef>), and all Roman citizens had the right of
appeal to him (<scripRef passage="Acts 25:11" id="c-p5.4" parsed="|Acts|25|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.25.11">Acts 25:11</scripRef>). The Caesars referred to in the New
Testament are Augustus (<scripRef passage="Luke 2:1" id="c-p5.5" parsed="|Luke|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.1">Luke 2:1</scripRef>), Tiberius (3:1; 20:22),
Claudius (Acts 11:28), and Nero (Acts 25:8; Phil. 4:22).
</def>
<term id="c-p5.9">Caesara Philippi</term>
<def id="c-p5.10">
A city on the northeast of the marshy plain of el-Huleh, 120
miles north of Jerusalem, and 20 miles north of the Sea of
Galilee, at the “upper source” of the Jordan, and near the base

of Mount Hermon. It is mentioned in <scripRef passage="Matt. 16:13" id="c-p6.1" parsed="|Matt|16|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.16.13">Matt. 16:13</scripRef> and <scripRef passage="Mark 8:27" id="c-p6.2" parsed="|Mark|8|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.8.27">Mark 8:27</scripRef> as
the northern limit of our Lord’s public ministry. According to
some its original name was Baal-Gad (<scripRef passage="Josh. 11:17" id="c-p6.3" parsed="|Josh|11|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.17">Josh. 11:17</scripRef>), or

Baal-Hermon (<scripRef passage="Judg. 3:3" id="c-p6.4" parsed="|Judg|3|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.3.3">Judg. 3:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 5:23" id="c-p6.5" parsed="|1Chr|5|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5.23">1 Chr. 5:23</scripRef>), when it was a Canaanite
sanctuary of Baal. It was afterwards called Panium or Paneas,
from a deep cavern full of water near the town. This name was
given to the cavern by the Greeks of the Macedonian kingdom of
Antioch because of its likeness to the grottos of Greece, which
were always associated with the worship of their god Pan. Its
modern name is Banias. Here Herod built a temple, which he
dedicated to Augustus Caesar. This town was afterwards enlarged
and embellished by Herod Philip, the tetrarch of Trachonitis, of
whose territory it formed a part, and was called by him Caesarea
Philippi, partly after his own name, and partly after that of
the emperor Tiberius Caesar. It is thus distinguished from the
Caesarea of Palestine. (See JORDAN.)
</def>
<term id="c-p6.7">Caesarea</term>
<def id="c-p6.8">
(Palestinae), a city on the shore of the Mediterranean, on the
great road from Tyre to Egypt, about 70 miles northwest of
Jerusalem, at the northern extremity of the plain of Sharon. It
was built by Herod the Great (B.C. 10), who named it after
Caesar Augustus, hence called Caesarea Sebaste (Gr. Sebastos =
“Augustus”), on the site of an old town called “Strato’s Tower.”
It was the capital of the Roman province of Judaea, the seat of
the governors or procurators, and the headquarters of the Roman
troops. It was the great Gentile city of Palestine, with a
spacious artificial harbour. It was adorned with many buildings
of great splendour, after the manner of the Roman cities of the
West. Here Cornelius the centurion was converted through the

instrumentality of Peter (<scripRef passage="Acts 10:1" id="c-p7.1" parsed="|Acts|10|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.10.1">Acts 10:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 10:24" id="c-p7.2" parsed="|Acts|10|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.10.24">24</scripRef>), and thus for the first
time the door of faith was opened to the Gentiles. Philip the
evangelist resided here with his four daughters (21:8). From
this place Saul sailed for his native Tarsus when forced to flee
from Jerusalem (9:30), and here he landed when returning from
his second missionary journey (18:22). He remained as a prisoner

here for two years before his voyage to Rome (<scripRef passage="Acts 24:27" id="c-p7.3" parsed="|Acts|24|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.24.27">Acts 24:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 25:1" id="c-p7.4" parsed="|Acts|25|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.25.1">25:1</scripRef>,

<scripRef passage="Acts 25:4" id="c-p7.5" parsed="|Acts|25|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.25.4">4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 25:6" id="c-p7.6" parsed="|Acts|25|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.25.6">6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 25:13" id="c-p7.7" parsed="|Acts|25|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.25.13">13</scripRef>). Here on a “set day,” when games were celebrated in
the theatre in honour of the emperor Claudius, Herod Agrippa I.
appeared among the people in great pomp, and in the midst of the
idolatrous homage paid to him was suddenly smitten by an angel,
and carried out a dying man. He was “eaten of worms” (12:19-23),
thus perishing by the same loathsome disease as his granfather,
Herod the Great. It still retains its ancient name Kaiseriyeh,
but is now desolate. “The present inhabitants of the ruins are
snakes, scorpions, lizards, wild boars, and jackals.” It is
described as the most desolate city of all Palestine.
</def>
<term id="c-p7.8">Cage</term>
<def id="c-p7.9">
(Heb. kelub’, Jer. 5:27, marg. “coop;” rendered “basket” in Amos 8:1), a basket of wicker-work in which birds were placed after
being caught. In <scripRef passage="Rev. 18:2" id="c-p8.3" parsed="|Rev|18|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.18.2">Rev. 18:2</scripRef> it is the rendering of the Greek
phulake, properly a prison or place of confinement.
</def>
<term id="c-p8.4">Caiaphas</term>
<def id="c-p8.5">
The Jewish high priest (A.D. 27-36) at the beginning of our
Lord’s public ministry, in the reign of Tiberius (<scripRef passage="Luke 3:2" id="c-p9.1" parsed="|Luke|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.2">Luke 3:2</scripRef>), and

also at the time of his condemnation and crucifixion (<scripRef passage="Matt. 26:3" id="c-p9.2" parsed="|Matt|26|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.3">Matt. 26:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt 26:57" id="c-p9.3" parsed="|Matt|26|57|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.57">57</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 11:49" id="c-p9.4" parsed="|John|11|49|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.11.49">John 11:49</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 18:13" id="c-p9.5" parsed="|John|18|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.18.13">18:13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="John 18:14" id="c-p9.6" parsed="|John|18|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.18.14">14</scripRef>). He held this office during the
whole of Pilate’s administration. His wife was the daughter of
Annas, who had formerly been high priest, and was probably the
vicar or deputy (Heb. sagan) of Caiaphas. He was of the sect of
the Sadducees (<scripRef passage="Acts 5:17" id="c-p9.7" parsed="|Acts|5|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.5.17">Acts 5:17</scripRef>), and was a member of the council when
he gave his opinion that Jesus should be put to death “for the
people, and that the whole nation perish not” (<scripRef passage="John 11:50" id="c-p9.8" parsed="|John|11|50|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.11.50">John 11:50</scripRef>). In
these words he unconsciously uttered a prophecy. “Like Saul, he
was a prophet in spite of himself.” Caiaphas had no power to
inflict the punishment of death, and therefore Jesus was sent to
Pilate, the Roman governor, that he might duly pronounce the

sentence against him (<scripRef passage="Matt. 27:2" id="c-p9.9" parsed="|Matt|27|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.2">Matt. 27:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 18:28" id="c-p9.10" parsed="|John|18|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.18.28">John 18:28</scripRef>). At a later period
his hostility to the gospel is still manifest (Acts 4:6). (See ANNAS.)
</def>
<term id="c-p9.13">Cain</term>
<def id="c-p9.14">
A possession; a spear. (1.) The first-born son of Adam and Eve
(<scripRef passage="Gen. 4" id="c-p10.1" parsed="|Gen|4|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.4">Gen. 4</scripRef>). He became a tiller of the ground, as his brother Abel
followed the pursuits of pastoral life. He was “a sullen,
self-willed, haughty, vindictive man; wanting the religious
element in his character, and defiant even in his attitude
towards God.” It came to pass “in process of time” (marg. “at
the end of days”), i.e., probably on the Sabbath, that the two
brothers presented their offerings to the Lord. Abel’s offering
was of the “firstlings of his flock and of the fat,” while
Cain’s was “of the fruit of the ground.” Abel’s sacrifice was
“more excellent” (<scripRef passage="Heb. 11:4" id="c-p10.2" parsed="|Heb|11|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.11.4">Heb. 11:4</scripRef>) than Cain’s, and was accepted by
God. On this account Cain was “very wroth,” and cherished
feelings of murderous hatred against his brother, and was at
length guilty of the desperate outrage of putting him to death
(<scripRef passage="1 John 3:12" id="c-p10.3" parsed="|1John|3|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.3.12">1 John 3:12</scripRef>). For this crime he was expelled from Eden, and
henceforth led the life of an exile, bearing upon him some mark
which God had set upon him in answer to his own cry for mercy,
so that thereby he might be protected from the wrath of his
fellow-men; or it may be that God only gave him some sign to
assure him that he would not be slain (<scripRef passage="Gen. 4:15" id="c-p10.4" parsed="|Gen|4|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.4.15">Gen. 4:15</scripRef>). Doomed to be
a wanderer and a fugitive in the earth, he went forth into the
“land of Nod”, i.e., the land of “exile”, which is said to have
been in the “east of Eden,” and there he built a city, the first
we read of, and called it after his son’s name, Enoch. His
descendants are enumerated to the sixth generation. They
gradually degenerated in their moral and spiritual condition
till they became wholly corrupt before God. This corruption
prevailed, and at length the Deluge was sent by God to prevent
the final triumph of evil. (See ABEL.)
(2.) A town of the Kenites, a branch of the Midianites (Josh. 15:57), on the east edge of the mountain above Engedi; probably
the “nest in a rock” mentioned by Balaam (<scripRef passage="Num. 24:21" id="c-p11.2" parsed="|Num|24|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.24.21">Num. 24:21</scripRef>). It is
identified with the modern Yekin, 3 miles south-east of Hebron.
</def>
<term id="c-p11.3">Cainan</term>
<def id="c-p11.4">
Possession; smith. (1.) The fourth antediluvian patriarch, the
eldest son of Enos. He was 70 years old at the birth of his

eldest son Mahalaleel, after which he lived 840 years (<scripRef passage="Gen. 5:9-14" id="c-p12.1" parsed="|Gen|5|9|5|14" osisRef="Bible:Gen.5.9-Gen.5.14">Gen. 5:9-14</scripRef>), and was 910 years old when he died. He is also called
Kenan (1 Chr. 1:2).
(2.) The son of Arphaxad (Luke 3:36). He is nowhere named in
the Old Testament. He is usually called the “second Cainan.”
</def>
<term id="c-p13.2">Cake</term>
<def id="c-p13.3">
Cakes made of wheat or barley were offered in the temple. They

were salted, but unleavened (<scripRef passage="Ex. 29:2" id="c-p14.1" parsed="|Exod|29|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.2">Ex. 29:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 2:4" id="c-p14.2" parsed="|Lev|2|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.2.4">Lev. 2:4</scripRef>). In idolatrous
worship thin cakes or wafers were offered “to the queen of
heaven” (Jer. 7:18; 44:19).
Pancakes are described in 2 Sam. 13:8, 9. Cakes mingled with
oil and baked in the oven are mentioned in <scripRef passage="Lev. 2:4" id="c-p15.3" parsed="|Lev|2|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.2.4">Lev. 2:4</scripRef>, and “wafers

unleavened anointed with oil,” in <scripRef passage="Ex. 29:2" id="c-p15.4" parsed="|Exod|29|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.2">Ex. 29:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 8:26" id="c-p15.5" parsed="|Lev|8|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.8.26">Lev. 8:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 23:29" id="c-p15.6" parsed="|1Chr|23|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.23.29">1 Chr. 23:29</scripRef>. “Cracknels,” a kind of crisp cakes, were among the things
Jeroboam directed his wife to take with her when she went to
consult Ahijah the prophet at Shiloh (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 14:3" id="c-p15.7" parsed="|1Kgs|14|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.14.3">1 Kings 14:3</scripRef>). Such hard
cakes were carried by the Gibeonites when they came to Joshua
(9:5, 12). They described their bread as “mouldy;” but the
Hebrew word nikuddim, here used, ought rather to be rendered
“hard as biscuit.” It is rendered “cracknels” in <scripRef passage="1 Kings 14:3" id="c-p15.8" parsed="|1Kgs|14|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.14.3">1 Kings 14:3</scripRef>.
The ordinary bread, when kept for a few days, became dry and
excessively hard. The Gibeonites pointed to this hardness of
their bread as an evidence that they had come a long journey.
We read also of honey-cakes (Ex. 16:31), “cakes of figs” (1 Sam. 25:18), “cake” as denoting a whole piece of bread (1 Kings 17:12), and “a [round] cake of barley bread” (Judg. 7:13). In
<scripRef passage="Lev. 2" id="c-p16.5" parsed="|Lev|2|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.2">Lev. 2</scripRef> is a list of the different kinds of bread and cakes which
were fit for offerings.
</def>
<term id="c-p16.6">Calah</term>
<def id="c-p16.7">
One of the most ancient cities of Assyria. “Out of that land he
[i.e., Nimrod] went forth into Assyria, and built Nineveh,
Rehoboth-Ir, and Calah, and Resen” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 10:11" id="c-p17.1" parsed="|Gen|10|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.11">Gen. 10:11</scripRef>, R.V.). Its site
is now marked probably by the Nimrud ruins on the left bank of
the Tigris. These cover an area of about 1,000 acres, and are
second only in size and importance to the mass of ruins opposite
Mosul. This city was at one time the capital of the empire, and
was the residence of Sardanapalus and his successors down to the
time of Sargon, who built a new capital, the modern Khorsabad.

It has been conjectured that these four cities mentioned in <scripRef passage="Gen. 10:11" id="c-p17.2" parsed="|Gen|10|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.11">Gen. 10:11</scripRef> were afterwards all united into one and called Nineveh
</def>
<term id="c-p17.3">Calamus</term>
<def id="c-p17.4">
The Latin for cane, Hebrew Kaneh, mentioned (Ex. 30:23) as one
of the ingredients in the holy anointing oil, one of the sweet
scents (<scripRef passage="Cant. 4:14" id="c-p18.2" parsed="|Song|4|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.4.14">Cant. 4:14</scripRef>), and among the articles sold in the markets
of Tyre (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:19" id="c-p18.3" parsed="|Ezek|27|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.19">Ezek. 27:19</scripRef>). The word designates an Oriental plant
called the “sweet flag,” the Acorus calamus of Linnaeus. It is

elsewhere called “sweet cane” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 43:24" id="c-p18.4" parsed="|Isa|43|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.43.24">Isa. 43:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 6:20" id="c-p18.5" parsed="|Jer|6|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.6.20">Jer. 6:20</scripRef>). It has an
aromatic smell, and when its knotted stalk is cut and dried and
reduced to powder, it forms an ingredient in the most precious
perfumes. It was not a native of Palestine, but was imported
from Arabia Felix or from India. It was probably that which is
now known in India by the name of “lemon grass” or “ginger
grass,” the Andropogon schoenanthus. (See CANE.)
</def>
<term id="c-p18.7">Calcol</term>
<def id="c-p18.8">
(1 Chr. 2:6), sustenance, the same probably as Chalcol (1 Kings 4:31), one of the four sages whom Solomon excelled in wisdom;
for “he was wiser than all men.”
</def>
<term id="c-p19.3">Caleb</term>
<def id="c-p19.4">
A dog. (1.) One of the three sons of Hezron of the tribe of
Judah. He is also called Chelubai (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 2:9" id="c-p20.1" parsed="|1Chr|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.2.9">1 Chr. 2:9</scripRef>). His descendants
are enumerated (18-20, 42-49).
(2.) A “son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah” (1 Chr. 2:50).
Some would read the whole passage thus: “These [i.e., the list
in ver. 42-49] were the sons of Caleb. The sons of Hur, the
firstborn of Ephratah, were Shobal, etc.” Thus Hur would be the
name of the son and not the father of Caleb (ver. 19).
(3.) The son of Jephunneh (Num. 13:6; 32:12; Josh. 14:6, 14).
He was one of those whom Moses sent to search the land in the
second year after the Exodus. He was one of the family chiefs of
the tribe of Judah. He and Joshua the son of Nun were the only
two of the whole number who encouraged the people to go up and
possess the land, and they alone were spared when a plague broke

out in which the other ten spies perished (<scripRef passage="Num. 13" id="c-p22.5" parsed="|Num|13|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.13">Num. 13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 14" id="c-p22.6" parsed="|Num|14|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.14">14</scripRef>). All the
people that had been numbered, from twenty years old and upward,
perished in the wilderness except these two. The last notice we
have of Caleb is when (being then eighty-five years of age) he
came to Joshua at the camp at Gilgal, after the people had
gained possession of the land, and reminded him of the promise
Moses had made to him, by virtue of which he claimed a certain

portion of the land of Kirjath-arba as his inheritance (<scripRef passage="Josh. 14:6-15" id="c-p22.7" parsed="|Josh|14|6|14|15" osisRef="Bible:Josh.14.6-Josh.14.15">Josh. 14:6-15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 15:13-15" id="c-p22.8" parsed="|Josh|15|13|15|15" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.13-Josh.15.15">15:13-15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 21:10-12" id="c-p22.9" parsed="|Josh|21|10|21|12" osisRef="Bible:Josh.21.10-Josh.21.12">21:10-12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 25:2" id="c-p22.10" parsed="|1Sam|25|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.25.2">1 Sam. 25:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 25:3" id="c-p22.11" parsed="|1Sam|25|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.25.3">3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 30:14" id="c-p22.12" parsed="|1Sam|30|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.30.14">30:14</scripRef>). He is called

a “Kenezite” in <scripRef passage="Josh. 14:6" id="c-p22.13" parsed="|Josh|14|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.14.6">Josh. 14:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 14:14" id="c-p22.14" parsed="|Josh|14|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.14.14">14</scripRef>. This may simply mean “son of
Kenez” (<scripRef passage="Num. 32:12" id="c-p22.15" parsed="|Num|32|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.32.12">Num. 32:12</scripRef>). Some, however, read “Jephunneh, the son of
Kenez,” who was a descendant of Hezron, the son of Pharez, a
grandson of Judah (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 2:5" id="c-p22.16" parsed="|1Chr|2|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.2.5">1 Chr. 2:5</scripRef>). This Caleb may possibly be
identical with (2).
(4.) Caleb gave his name apparently to a part of the south
country (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 30:14" id="c-p23.1" parsed="|1Sam|30|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.30.14">1 Sam. 30:14</scripRef>) of Judah, the district between Hebron and
Carmel, which had been assigned to him. When he gave up the city
of Hebron to the priests as a city of refuge, he retained
possession of the surrounding country (Josh. 21:11, 12; comp. 1 Sam. 25:3).
</def>
<term id="c-p23.5">Calf</term>
<def id="c-p23.6">
Calves were commonly made use of in sacrifices, and are
therefore frequently mentioned in Scripture. The “fatted calf”
was regarded as the choicest of animal food; it was frequently

also offered as a special sacrifice (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 28:24" id="c-p24.1" parsed="|1Sam|28|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.28.24">1 Sam. 28:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Amos 6:4" id="c-p24.2" parsed="|Amos|6|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.6.4">Amos 6:4</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Luke 15:23" id="c-p24.3" parsed="|Luke|15|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.15.23">Luke 15:23</scripRef>). The words used in <scripRef passage="Jer. 34:18" id="c-p24.4" parsed="|Jer|34|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.34.18">Jer. 34:18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer. 34:19" id="c-p24.5" parsed="|Jer|34|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.34.19">19</scripRef>, “cut the calf in
twain,” allude to the custom of dividing a sacrifice into two
parts, between which the parties ratifying a covenant passed

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 15:9" id="c-p24.6" parsed="|Gen|15|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.9">Gen. 15:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 15:10" id="c-p24.7" parsed="|Gen|15|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.10">10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 15:17" id="c-p24.8" parsed="|Gen|15|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.17">17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 15:18" id="c-p24.9" parsed="|Gen|15|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.18">18</scripRef>). The sacrifice of the lips, i.e.,
priase, is called “the calves of our lips” (<scripRef passage="Hos. 14:2" id="c-p24.10" parsed="|Hos|14|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.14.2">Hos. 14:2</scripRef>, R.V., “as

bullocks the offering of our lips.” Comp. <scripRef passage="Heb. 13:15" id="c-p24.11" parsed="|Heb|13|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.13.15">Heb. 13:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 116:7" id="c-p24.12" parsed="|Ps|116|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.116.7">Ps. 116:7</scripRef>;
Jer. 33:11).
The golden calf which Aaron made (Ex. 32:4) was probably a
copy of the god Moloch rather than of the god Apis, the sacred
ox or calf of Egypt. The Jews showed all through their history a
tendency toward the Babylonian and Canaanitish idolatry rather
than toward that of Egypt.
Ages after this, Jeroboam, king of Israel, set up two idol
calves, one at Dan, and the other at Bethel, that he might thus
prevent the ten tribes from resorting to Jerusalem for worship
(<scripRef passage="1 Kings 12:28" id="c-p26.1" parsed="|1Kgs|12|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.12.28">1 Kings 12:28</scripRef>). These calves continued to be a snare to the
people till the time of their captivity. The calf at Dan was
carried away in the reign of Pekah by Tiglath-pileser, and that
at Bethel ten years later, in the reign of Hoshea, by

Shalmaneser (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 15:29" id="c-p26.2" parsed="|2Kgs|15|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.29">2 Kings 15:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:33" id="c-p26.3" parsed="|2Kgs|17|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.33">17:33</scripRef>). This sin of Jeroboam is
almost always mentioned along with his name (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 15:28" id="c-p26.4" parsed="|2Kgs|15|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.28">2 Kings 15:28</scripRef>
etc.).
</def>
<term id="c-p26.5">Calkers</term>
<def id="c-p26.6">
Workmen skilled in stopping the seams of the deck or sides of
vessels. The inhabitants of Gebel were employed in such work on

Tyrian vessels (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:9" id="c-p27.1" parsed="|Ezek|27|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.9">Ezek. 27:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:27" id="c-p27.2" parsed="|Ezek|27|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.27">27</scripRef>; marg., “strengtheners” or
“stoppers of chinks”).
</def>
<term id="c-p27.3">Call</term>
<def id="c-p27.4">
(1.) To cry for help, hence to pray (Gen. 4:26). Thus men are

said to “call upon the name of the Lord” (<scripRef passage="Acts 2:21" id="c-p28.2" parsed="|Acts|2|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.2.21">Acts 2:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 7:59" id="c-p28.3" parsed="|Acts|7|59|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.7.59">7:59</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 9:14" id="c-p28.4" parsed="|Acts|9|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.9.14">9:14</scripRef>;
Rom. 10:12; 1 Cor. 1:2).
(2.) God calls with respect to men when he designates them to

some special office (<scripRef passage="Ex. 31:2" id="c-p29.1" parsed="|Exod|31|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.31.2">Ex. 31:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 22:20" id="c-p29.2" parsed="|Isa|22|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.22.20">Isa. 22:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 13:2" id="c-p29.3" parsed="|Acts|13|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.13.2">Acts 13:2</scripRef>), and when

he invites them to accept his offered grace (<scripRef passage="Matt. 9:13" id="c-p29.4" parsed="|Matt|9|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.9.13">Matt. 9:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 11:28" id="c-p29.5" parsed="|Matt|11|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.11.28">11:28</scripRef>;
22:4).
In the message of the gospel his call is addressed to all men,

to Jews and Gentiles alike (<scripRef passage="Matt. 28:19" id="c-p30.1" parsed="|Matt|28|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.28.19">Matt. 28:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 16:15" id="c-p30.2" parsed="|Mark|16|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.16.15">Mark 16:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 9:24" id="c-p30.3" parsed="|Rom|9|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.9.24">Rom. 9:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Rom 9:25" id="c-p30.4" parsed="|Rom|9|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.9.25">25</scripRef>). But this universal call is not inseparably connected with
salvation, although it leaves all to whom it comes inexcusable
if they reject it (John 3:14-19; Matt. 22:14).
An effectual call is something more than the outward message
of the Word of God to men. It is internal, and is the result of
the enlightening and sanctifying influence of the Holy Spirit

(<scripRef passage="John 16:14" id="c-p31.1" parsed="|John|16|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.16.14">John 16:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 26" id="c-p31.2" parsed="|Acts|26|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.26">Acts 26</scripRef>: 18; <scripRef passage="John 6:44" id="c-p31.3" parsed="|John|6|44|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.6.44">John 6:44</scripRef>), effectually drawing men to
Christ, and disposing and enabling them to receive the truth
(John 6:45; Acts 16:14; Eph. 1:17).
</def>
<term id="c-p31.7">Calling</term>
<def id="c-p31.8">
A profession, or as we usually say, a vocation (1 Cor. 7:20).
The “hope of your calling” in <scripRef passage="Eph. 4:4" id="c-p32.2" parsed="|Eph|4|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.4.4">Eph. 4:4</scripRef> is the hope resulting
from your being called into the kingdom of God.
</def>
<term id="c-p32.3">Calneh</term>
<def id="c-p32.4">
Fort, one of the four cities founded by Nimrod (Gen. 10:10). It
is the modern Niffer, a lofty mound of earth and rubbish
situated in the marshes on the left, i.e., the east, bank of the
Euphrates, but 30 miles distant from its present course, and
about 60 miles south-south-east from Babylon. It is mentioned as
one of the towns with which Tyre carried on trade. It was
finally taken and probably destroyed by one of the Assyrian

kings (<scripRef passage="Amos 6:2" id="c-p33.2" parsed="|Amos|6|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.6.2">Amos 6:2</scripRef>). It is called Calno (<scripRef passage="Isa. 10:9" id="c-p33.3" parsed="|Isa|10|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.9">Isa. 10:9</scripRef>) and Canneh
(Ezek. 27:23).
</def>
<term id="c-p33.5">Calvary</term>
<def id="c-p33.6">
Only in Luke 23:33, the Latin name Calvaria, which was used as a
translation of the Greek word Kranion, by which the Hebrew
word Gulgoleth was interpreted, “the place of a skull.” It
probably took this name from its shape, being a hillock or low,
rounded, bare elevation somewhat in the form of a human skull.
It is nowhere in Scripture called a “hill.” The crucifixion of
our Lord took place outside the city walls (<scripRef passage="Heb. 13:11-13" id="c-p34.2" parsed="|Heb|13|11|13|13" osisRef="Bible:Heb.13.11-Heb.13.13">Heb. 13:11-13</scripRef>) and
near the public thoroughfare. “This thing was not done in a
corner.” (See GOLGOTHA.)
</def>
<term id="c-p34.4">Camel</term>
<def id="c-p34.5">
From the Hebrew gamal, “to repay” or “requite,” as the camel
does the care of its master. There are two distinct species of
camels, having, however, the common characteristics of being
“ruminants without horns, without muzzle, with nostrils forming
oblique slits, the upper lip divided and separately movable and
extensile, the soles of the feet horny, with two toes covered by
claws, the limbs long, the abdomen drawn up, while the neck,
long and slender, is bent up and down, the reverse of that of a
horse, which is arched.”
(1.) The Bactrian camel is distinguished by two humps. It is a
native of the high table-lands of Central Asia.
(2.) The Arabian camel or dromedary, from the Greek dromos,

“a runner” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 60:6" id="c-p37.1" parsed="|Isa|60|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.60.6">Isa. 60:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 2:23" id="c-p37.2" parsed="|Jer|2|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.2.23">Jer. 2:23</scripRef>), has but one hump, and is a
native of Western Asia or Africa.
The camel was early used both for riding and as a beast of

burden (<scripRef passage="Gen. 24:64" id="c-p38.1" parsed="|Gen|24|64|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.64">Gen. 24:64</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 37:25" id="c-p38.2" parsed="|Gen|37|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.25">37:25</scripRef>), and in war (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 30:17" id="c-p38.3" parsed="|1Sam|30|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.30.17">1 Sam. 30:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 21:7" id="c-p38.4" parsed="|Isa|21|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.21.7">Isa. 21:7</scripRef>). Mention is made of the camel among the cattle given by
Pharaoh to Abraham (<scripRef passage="Gen. 12:16" id="c-p38.5" parsed="|Gen|12|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.12.16">Gen. 12:16</scripRef>). Its flesh was not to be eaten,

as it was ranked among unclean animals (<scripRef passage="Lev. 11:4" id="c-p38.6" parsed="|Lev|11|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.11.4">Lev. 11:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 14:7" id="c-p38.7" parsed="|Deut|14|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.14.7">Deut. 14:7</scripRef>).
Abraham’s servant rode on a camel when he went to fetch a wife

for Isaac (<scripRef passage="Gen. 24:10" id="c-p38.8" parsed="|Gen|24|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.10">Gen. 24:10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 24:11" id="c-p38.9" parsed="|Gen|24|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.11">11</scripRef>). Jacob had camels as a portion of his
wealth (30:43), as Abraham also had (24:35). He sent a present
of thirty milch camels to his brother Esau (32:15). It appears
to have been little in use among the Jews after the conquest. It
is, however, mentioned in the history of David (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 27:30" id="c-p38.10" parsed="|1Chr|27|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.27.30">1 Chr. 27:30</scripRef>),

and after the Exile (<scripRef passage="Ezra 2:67" id="c-p38.11" parsed="|Ezra|2|67|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2.67">Ezra 2:67</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh. 7:69" id="c-p38.12" parsed="|Neh|7|69|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.7.69">Neh. 7:69</scripRef>). Camels were much in
use among other nations in the East. The queen of Sheba came
with a caravan of camels when she came to see the wisdom of

Solomon (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:2" id="c-p38.13" parsed="|1Kgs|10|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.2">1 Kings 10:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 9:1" id="c-p38.14" parsed="|2Chr|9|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.9.1">2 Chr. 9:1</scripRef>). Benhadad of Damascus also
sent a present to Elisha, “forty camels’ burden” (2 Kings 8:9).
To show the difficulty in the way of a rich man’s entering
into the kingdom, our Lord uses the proverbial expression that
it was easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle
(Matt. 19:24).
To strain at (rather, out) a gnat and swallow a camel was also
a proverbial expression (<scripRef passage="Matt. 23:24" id="c-p40.1" parsed="|Matt|23|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.23.24">Matt. 23:24</scripRef>), used with reference to
those who were careful to avoid small faults, and yet did not
hesitate to commit the greatest sins. The Jews carefully
filtered their wine before drinking it, for fear of swallowing
along with it some insect forbidden in the law as unclean, and
yet they omitted openly the “weightier matters” of the law.
The raiment worn by John the Baptist was made of camel’s hair

(<scripRef passage="Matt. 3:4" id="c-p41.1" parsed="|Matt|3|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.4">Matt. 3:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 1:6" id="c-p41.2" parsed="|Mark|1|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.6">Mark 1:6</scripRef>), by which he was distinguished from those
who resided in royal palaces and wore soft raiment. This was
also the case with Elijah (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 1:8" id="c-p41.3" parsed="|2Kgs|1|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.1.8">2 Kings 1:8</scripRef>), who is called “a hairy
man,” from his wearing such raiment. “This is one of the most
admirable materials for clothing; it keeps out the heat, cold,
and rain.” The “sackcloth” so often alluded to (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 1:8" id="c-p41.4" parsed="|2Kgs|1|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.1.8">2 Kings 1:8</scripRef>;
Isa. 15:3; Zech. 13:4, etc.) was probably made of camel’s hair.
</def>
<term id="c-p41.7">Camon</term>
<def id="c-p41.8">
Full of stalks, a place (Judg. 10:5) where Jair was buried. It
has usually been supposed to have been a city of Gilead, on the
east of Jordan. It is probably, however, the modern
Tell-el-Kaimun, on the southern slopes of Carmel, the Jokneam of

Carmel (<scripRef passage="Josh. 12:22" id="c-p42.2" parsed="|Josh|12|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.12.22">Josh. 12:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:12" id="c-p42.3" parsed="|1Kgs|4|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.12">1 Kings 4:12</scripRef>), since it is not at all
unlikely that after he became judge, Jair might find it more
convenient to live on the west side of Jordan; and that he was
buried where he had lived.
</def>
<term id="c-p42.4">Camp</term>
<def id="c-p42.5">
During their journeys across the wilderness, the twelve tribes
formed encampments at the different places where they halted

(<scripRef passage="Ex. 16:13" id="c-p43.1" parsed="|Exod|16|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.16.13">Ex. 16:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 2:3" id="c-p43.2" parsed="|Num|2|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.2.3">Num. 2:3</scripRef>). The diagram here given shows the position
of the different tribes and the form of the encampment during

the wanderings, according to <scripRef passage="Num. 1:53" id="c-p43.3" parsed="|Num|1|53|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.1.53">Num. 1:53</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 2:2-31" id="c-p43.4" parsed="|Num|2|2|2|31" osisRef="Bible:Num.2.2-Num.2.31">2:2-31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 3:29" id="c-p43.5" parsed="|Num|3|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.3.29">3:29</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num 3:35" id="c-p43.6" parsed="|Num|3|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.3.35">35</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num 3:38" id="c-p43.7" parsed="|Num|3|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.3.38">38</scripRef>;
10:13-28.
The area of the camp would be in all about 3 square miles.
After the Hebrews entered Palestine, the camps then spoken of
were exclusively warlike (Josh. 11:5, 7; Judg. 5:19, 21; 7:1; 1 Sam. 29:1; 30:9, etc.).
</def>
<term id="c-p44.7">Camphire</term>
<def id="c-p44.8">
(Heb. copher), mentioned in Cant. 1:14 (R.V., “henna-flowers”);
4:13 (R.V., “henna”), is the al-henna of the Arabs, a native of
Egypt, producing clusters of small white and yellow odoriferous
flowers, whence is made the Oleum Cyprineum. From its leaves is
made the peculiar auburn dye with which Eastern women stain
their nails and the palms of their hands. It is found only at
Engedi, on the shore of the Dead Sea. It is known to botanists
by the name Lawsonia alba or inermis, a kind of privet, which
grows 6 or 8 feet high. The margin of the Authorized Version of
the passages above referred to has “or cypress,” not with
reference to the conifer so called, but to the circumstance that
one of the most highly appreciated species of this plant grew in
the island of Cyprus.
</def>
<term id="c-p45.2">Cana</term>
<def id="c-p45.3">
Reedy, a town of Galilee, near Capernaum. Here our Lord wrought
his first miracle, the turning of water into wine (<scripRef passage="John 2:1-11" id="c-p46.1" parsed="|John|2|1|2|11" osisRef="Bible:John.2.1-John.2.11">John 2:1-11</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="John 4:46" id="c-p46.2" parsed="|John|4|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.4.46">4:46</scripRef>). It is also mentioned as the birth-place of Nathanael
(21:2). It is not mentioned in the Old Testament. It has been
identified with the modern Kana el-Jelil, also called Khurbet
Kana, a place 8 or 9 miles north of Nazareth. Others have
identified it with Kefr Kenna, which lies on the direct road to
the Sea of Galilee, about 5 miles north-east of Nazareth, and 12
in a direct course from Tiberias. It is called “Cana of
Galilee,” to distinguish it from Cana of Asher (Josh. 19:28).
</def>
<term id="c-p46.4">Canaan</term>
<def id="c-p46.5">
(1.) The fourth son of Ham (Gen. 10:6). His descendants were
under a curse in consequence of the transgression of his father
(9:22-27). His eldest son, Zidon, was the father of the
Sidonians and Phoenicians. He had eleven sons, who were the
founders of as many tribes (10:15-18).
(2.) The country which derived its name from the preceding.
The name as first used by the Phoenicians denoted only the
maritime plain on which Sidon was built. But in the time of
Moses and Joshua it denoted the whole country to the west of the

Jordan and the Dead Sea (<scripRef passage="Deut. 11:30" id="c-p48.1" parsed="|Deut|11|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.11.30">Deut. 11:30</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="Josh. 5:12" id="c-p48.2" parsed="|Josh|5|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.5.12">Josh. 5:12</scripRef> the LXX.
read, “land of the Phoenicians,” instead of “land of Canaan.”
The name signifies “the lowlands,” as distinguished from the
land of Gilead on the east of Jordan, which was a mountainous
district. The extent and boundaries of Canaan are fully set
forth in different parts of Scripture (Gen. 10:19; 17:8; Num. 13:29; 34:8). (See CANAANITES, PALESTINE.)
</def>
<term id="c-p49.7">Canaanite</term>
<def id="c-p49.8">
A name given to the apostle Simon (Matt. 10:4; Mark 3:18). The
word here does not, however, mean a descendant of Canaan, but is
a translation, or rather almost a transliteration, of the Syriac
word Kanenyeh (R.V. rendered “Cananaen”), which designates the

Jewish sect of the Zealots. Hence he is called elsewhere (<scripRef passage="Luke 6:15" id="c-p50.3" parsed="|Luke|6|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.6.15">Luke 6:15</scripRef>) “Simon Zelotes;” i.e., Simon of the sect of the Zealots.
(See SIMON.)
</def>
<term id="c-p50.5">Canaanites</term>
<def id="c-p50.6">
The descendants of Canaan, the son of Ham. Migrating from their
original home, they seem to have reached the Persian Gulf, and
to have there sojourned for some time. They thence “spread to
the west, across the mountain chain of Lebanon to the very edge
of the Mediterranean Sea, occupying all the land which later
became Palestine, also to the north-west as far as the mountain
chain of Taurus. This group was very numerous, and broken up
into a great many peoples, as we can judge from the list of
nations (<scripRef passage="Gen. 10" id="c-p51.1" parsed="|Gen|10|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10">Gen. 10</scripRef>), the ‘sons of Canaan.’” Six different tribes

are mentioned in <scripRef passage="Ex. 3:8" id="c-p51.2" parsed="|Exod|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.3.8">Ex. 3:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 3:17" id="c-p51.3" parsed="|Exod|3|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.3.17">17</scripRef>; 23:23; 33:2; 34:11. In <scripRef passage="Ex. 13:5" id="c-p51.4" parsed="|Exod|13|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.13.5">Ex. 13:5</scripRef>
the “Perizzites” are omitted. The “Girgashites” are mentioned in
addition to the foregoing in Deut. 7:1; Josh. 3:10.
The “Canaanites,” as distinguished from the Amalekites, the

Anakim, and the Rephaim, were “dwellers in the lowlands” (<scripRef passage="Num. 13:29" id="c-p52.1" parsed="|Num|13|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.13.29">Num. 13:29</scripRef>), the great plains and valleys, the richest and most
important parts of Palestine. Tyre and Sidon, their famous
cities, were the centres of great commercial activity; and hence
the name “Canaanite” came to signify a “trader” or “merchant”

(<scripRef passage="Job 41:6" id="c-p52.2" parsed="|Job|41|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.41.6">Job 41:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 31:24" id="c-p52.3" parsed="|Prov|31|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.31.24">Prov. 31:24</scripRef>, lit. “Canaanites;” comp. <scripRef passage="Zeph. 1:11" id="c-p52.4" parsed="|Zeph|1|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zeph.1.11">Zeph. 1:11</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Ezek. 17:4" id="c-p52.5" parsed="|Ezek|17|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.17.4">Ezek. 17:4</scripRef>). The name “Canaanite” is also sometimes used to
designate the non-Israelite inhabitants of the land in general
(Gen. 12:6; Num. 21:3; Judg. 1:10).
The Israelites, when they were led to the Promised Land, were
commanded utterly to destroy the descendants of Canaan then

possessing it (<scripRef passage="Ex. 23:23" id="c-p53.1" parsed="|Exod|23|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.23">Ex. 23:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 33:52" id="c-p53.2" parsed="|Num|33|52|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.52">Num. 33:52</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 33:53" id="c-p53.3" parsed="|Num|33|53|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.53">53</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 20:16" id="c-p53.4" parsed="|Deut|20|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.20.16">Deut. 20:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 20:17" id="c-p53.5" parsed="|Deut|20|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.20.17">17</scripRef>). This
was to be done “by little and little,” lest the beasts of the

field should increase (<scripRef passage="Ex. 23:29" id="c-p53.6" parsed="|Exod|23|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.29">Ex. 23:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 7:22" id="c-p53.7" parsed="|Deut|7|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.7.22">Deut. 7:22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 7:23" id="c-p53.8" parsed="|Deut|7|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.7.23">23</scripRef>). The history
of these wars of conquest is given in the Book of Joshua. The
extermination of these tribes, however, was never fully carried

out. Jerusalem was not taken till the time of David (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 5:6" id="c-p53.9" parsed="|2Sam|5|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.5.6">2 Sam. 5:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 5:7" id="c-p53.10" parsed="|2Sam|5|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.5.7">7</scripRef>). In the days of Solomon bond-service was exacted from the

fragments of the tribes still remaining in the land (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 9:20" id="c-p53.11" parsed="|1Kgs|9|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.9.20">1 Kings 9:20</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 9:21" id="c-p53.12" parsed="|1Kgs|9|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.9.21">21</scripRef>). Even after the return from captivity survivors of
five of the Canaanitish tribes were still found in the land.
In the Tell-el-Amarna tablets Canaan is found under the forms
of Kinakhna and Kinakhkhi. Under the name of Kanana the
Canaanites appear on Egyptian monuments, wearing a coat of mail
and helmet, and distinguished by the use of spear and javelin
and the battle-axe. They were called Phoenicians by the Greeks
and Poeni by the Romans. By race the Canaanites were Semitic.
