They were famous as merchants and seamen, as well as for their
artistic skill. The chief object of their worship was the
sun-god, who was addressed by the general name of Baal, “lord.”
Each locality had its special Baal, and the various local Baals
were summed up under the name of Baalim, “lords.”
</def>
<term id="c-p54.1">Canaan, the language of</term>
<def id="c-p54.2">
Mentioned in Isa. 19:18, denotes the language spoken by the Jews
resident in Palestine. The language of the Canaanites and of the
Hebrews was substantially the same. This is seen from the
fragments of the Phoenician language which still survive, which
show the closest analogy to the Hebrew. Yet the subject of the
language of the “Canaanites” is very obscure. The cuneiform
writing of Babylon, as well as the Babylonian language, was
taught in the Canaanitish schools, and the clay tablets of
Babylonian literature were stored in the Canaanitish libraries.
Even the Babylonian divinities were borrowed by the Canaanites.
</def>
<term id="c-p55.2">Candace</term>
<def id="c-p55.3">
The queen of the Ethiopians whose “eunuch” or chamberlain was
converted to Christianity by the instrumentality of Philip the
evangelist (<scripRef passage="Acts 8:27" id="c-p56.1" parsed="|Acts|8|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.8.27">Acts 8:27</scripRef>). The country which she ruled was called
by the Greeks Meroe, in Upper Nubia. It was long the centre of
commercial intercourse between Africa and the south of Asia, and
hence became famous for its wealth (Isa. 45:14).
It is somewhat singular that female sovereignty seems to have
prevailed in Ethiopia, the name Candace (compare “Pharaoh,”
“Ptolemy,” “Caesar”) being a title common to several successive
queens. It is probable that Judaism had taken root in Ethiopia
at this time, and hence the visit of the queen’s treasurer to
Jerusalem to keep the feast. There is a tradition that Candace
was herself converted to Christianity by her treasurer on his
return, and that he became the apostle of Christianity in that
whole region, carrying it also into Abyssinia. It is said that
he also preached the gospel in Arabia Felix and in Ceylon, where
he suffered martyrdom. (See PHILIP.)
</def>
<term id="c-p57.2">Candle</term>
<def id="c-p57.3">
Heb. ner, Job 18:6; 29:3; Ps. 18:28; Prov. 24:20, in all which
places the Revised Version and margin of Authorized Version have
“lamp,” by which the word is elsewhere frequently rendered. The
Hebrew word denotes properly any kind of candle or lamp or
torch. It is used as a figure of conscience (<scripRef passage="Prov. 20:27" id="c-p58.5" parsed="|Prov|20|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.20.27">Prov. 20:27</scripRef>), of a
Christian example (Matt. 5:14, 15), and of prosperity (Job 21:17; Prov. 13:9).
</def>
<term id="c-p58.10">Candlestick</term>
The lamp-stand, “candelabrum,” which Moses was commanded to make
for the tabernacle, according to the pattern shown him. Its form

is described in <scripRef passage="Ex. 25:31-40" id="c-p59.1" parsed="|Exod|25|31|25|40" osisRef="Bible:Exod.25.31-Exod.25.40">Ex. 25:31-40</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 37:17-24" id="c-p59.2" parsed="|Exod|37|17|37|24" osisRef="Bible:Exod.37.17-Exod.37.24">37:17-24</scripRef>, and may be seen
represented on the Arch of Titus at Rome. It was among the
spoils taken by the Romans from the temple of Jerusalem (A.D.
70). It was made of fine gold, and with the utensils belonging
to it was a talent in weight.
The tabernacle was a tent without windows, and thus artificial
light was needed. This was supplied by the candlestick, which,
however, served also as a symbol of the church or people of God,
who are “the light of the world.” The light which “symbolizes
the knowledge of God is not the sun or any natural light, but an
artificial light supplied with a specially prepared oil; for the
knowledge of God is in truth not natural nor common to all men,
but furnished over and above nature.”
This candlestick was placed on the south side of the Holy

Place, opposite the table of shewbread (<scripRef passage="Ex. 27:21" id="c-p61.1" parsed="|Exod|27|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.27.21">Ex. 27:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 30:7" id="c-p61.2" parsed="|Exod|30|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.30.7">30:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex 30:8" id="c-p61.3" parsed="|Exod|30|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.30.8">8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 24:3" id="c-p61.4" parsed="|Lev|24|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.24.3">Lev. 24:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 3:3" id="c-p61.5" parsed="|1Sam|3|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.3.3">1 Sam. 3:3</scripRef>). It was lighted every evening, and was
extinguished in the morning. In the morning the priests trimmed
the seven lamps, borne by the seven branches, with golden
snuffers, carrying away the ashes in golden dishes (<scripRef passage="Ex. 25:38" id="c-p61.6" parsed="|Exod|25|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.25.38">Ex. 25:38</scripRef>),
and supplying the lamps at the same time with fresh oil. What
ultimately became of the candlestick is unknown.
In Solomon’s temple there were ten separate candlesticks of
pure gold, five on the right and five on the left of the Holy

Place (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 7:49" id="c-p62.1" parsed="|1Kgs|7|49|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.7.49">1 Kings 7:49</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 4:7" id="c-p62.2" parsed="|2Chr|4|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.4.7">2 Chr. 4:7</scripRef>). Their structure is not
mentioned. They were carried away to Babylon (Jer. 52:19).
In the temple erected after the Exile there was again but one
candlestick, and like the first, with seven branches. It was
this which was afterwards carried away by Titus to Rome, where
it was deposited in the Temple of Peace. When Genseric plundered
Rome, he is said to have carried it to Carthage (A.D. 455). It
was recaptured by Belisarius (A.D. 533), and carried to
Constantinople and thence to Jerusalem, where it finally
disappeared.
</def>
<term id="c-p63.1">Cane</term>
<def id="c-p63.2">
A tall sedgy plant with a hollow stem, growing in moist places.
In Isa. 43:24; Jer. 6:20, the Hebrew word kaneh is thus
rendered, giving its name to the plant. It is rendered “reed” in

<scripRef passage="1 Kings 14:15" id="c-p64.3" parsed="|1Kgs|14|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.14.15">1 Kings 14:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 40:21" id="c-p64.4" parsed="|Job|40|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.40.21">Job 40:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 19:6" id="c-p64.5" parsed="|Isa|19|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.19.6">Isa. 19:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 35:7" id="c-p64.6" parsed="|Isa|35|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.35.7">35:7</scripRef>. In <scripRef passage="Ps. 68:30" id="c-p64.7" parsed="|Ps|68|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.68.30">Ps. 68:30</scripRef> the
expression “company of spearmen” is in the margin and the
Revised Version “beasts of the reeds,” referring probably to the

crocodile or the hippopotamus as a symbol of Egypt. In <scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:21" id="c-p64.8" parsed="|2Kgs|18|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.21">2 Kings 18:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 36:6" id="c-p64.9" parsed="|Isa|36|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.36.6">Isa. 36:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 29:6" id="c-p64.10" parsed="|Ezek|29|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.29.6">Ezek. 29:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 29:7" id="c-p64.11" parsed="|Ezek|29|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.29.7">7</scripRef>, the reference is to the weak,
fragile nature of the reed. (See CALAMUS.)
</def>
<term id="c-p64.13">Canker</term>
A gangrene or mortification which gradually spreads over the

whole body (<scripRef passage="2 Tim. 2:17" id="c-p65.1" parsed="|2Tim|2|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.2.17">2 Tim. 2:17</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="James 5:3" id="c-p65.2" parsed="|Jas|5|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jas.5.3">James 5:3</scripRef> “cankered” means “rusted”
(R.V.) or tarnished.
</def>
<term id="c-p65.3">Cankerworm</term>
<def id="c-p65.4">
(Heb. yelek), “the licking locust,” which licks up the grass of
the field; probably the locust at a certain stage of its growth,

just as it emerges from the caterpillar state (<scripRef passage="Joel 1:4" id="c-p66.1" parsed="|Joel|1|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Joel.1.4">Joel 1:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Joel 2:25" id="c-p66.2" parsed="|Joel|2|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Joel.2.25">2:25</scripRef>).

The word is rendered “caterpillar” in <scripRef passage="Ps. 105:34" id="c-p66.3" parsed="|Ps|105|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.105.34">Ps. 105:34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 51:14" id="c-p66.4" parsed="|Jer|51|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.51.14">Jer. 51:14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer. 51:17" id="c-p66.5" parsed="|Jer|51|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.51.17">17</scripRef>

(but R.V. “canker-worm”). “It spoileth and fleeth away” (<scripRef passage="Nah. 3:16" id="c-p66.6" parsed="|Nah|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Nah.3.16">Nah. 3:16</scripRef>), or as some read the passage, “The cankerworm putteth off
[i.e., the envelope of its wings], and fleeth away.”
</def>
<term id="c-p66.7">Canneh</term>
<def id="c-p66.8">
Mentioned only in Ezek. 27:23. (See CALNEH.)
</def>
<term id="c-p67.3">Canon</term>
<def id="c-p67.4">
This word is derived from a Hebrew and Greek word denoting a
reed or cane. Hence it means something straight, or something to
keep straight; and hence also a rule, or something ruled or
measured. It came to be applied to the Scriptures, to denote
that they contained the authoritative rule of faith and
practice, the standard of doctrine and duty. A book is said to
be of canonical authority when it has a right to take a place
with the other books which contain a revelation of the Divine
will. Such a right does not arise from any ecclesiastical
authority, but from the evidence of the inspired authorship of
the book. The canonical (i.e., the inspired) books of the Old
and New Testaments, are a complete rule, and the only rule, of
faith and practice. They contain the whole supernatural
revelation of God to men. The New Testament Canon was formed
gradually under divine guidance. The different books as they
were written came into the possession of the Christian
associations which began to be formed soon after the day of
Pentecost; and thus slowly the canon increased till all the
books were gathered together into one collection containing the
whole of the twenty-seven New Testament inspired books.
Historical evidence shows that from about the middle of the
second century this New Testament collection was substantially
such as we now possess. Each book contained in it is proved to
have, on its own ground, a right to its place; and thus the
whole is of divine authority.
The Old Testament Canon is witnessed to by the New Testament
writers. Their evidence is conclusive. The quotations in the New
from the Old are very numerous, and the references are much more
numerous. These quotations and references by our Lord and the
apostles most clearly imply the existence at that time of a
well-known and publicly acknowledged collection of Hebrew
writings under the designation of “The Scriptures;” “The Law and
the Prophets and the Psalms;” “Moses and the Prophets,” etc. The
appeals to these books, moreover, show that they were regarded
as of divine authority, finally deciding all questions of which
they treat; and that the whole collection so recognized
consisted only of the thirty-nine books which we now posses.
Thus they endorse as genuine and authentic the canon of the
Jewish Scriptures. The Septuagint Version (q.v.) also contained
every book we now have in the Old Testament Scriptures. As to
the time at which the Old Testament canon was closed, there are
many considerations which point to that of Ezra and Nehemiah,
immediately after the return from Babylonian exile. (See
BIBLE,
EZRA,
QUOTATIONS.)
</def>
<term id="c-p69.4">Capernaum</term>
<def id="c-p69.5">
Nahum’s town, a Galilean city frequently mentioned in the
history of our Lord. It is not mentioned in the Old Testament.

After our Lord’s expulsion from Nazareth (<scripRef passage="Matt. 4:13-16" id="c-p70.1" parsed="|Matt|4|13|4|16" osisRef="Bible:Matt.4.13-Matt.4.16">Matt. 4:13-16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 4:16-31" id="c-p70.2" parsed="|Luke|4|16|4|31" osisRef="Bible:Luke.4.16-Luke.4.31">Luke 4:16-31</scripRef>), Capernaum became his “own city.” It was the scene of

many acts and incidents of his life (<scripRef passage="Matt. 8:5" id="c-p70.3" parsed="|Matt|8|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.8.5">Matt. 8:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 8:14" id="c-p70.4" parsed="|Matt|8|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.8.14">14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 8:15" id="c-p70.5" parsed="|Matt|8|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.8.15">15</scripRef>; 9:2-6,
10-17; 15:1-20; <scripRef passage="Mark 1:32-34" id="c-p70.6" parsed="|Mark|1|32|1|34" osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.32-Mark.1.34">Mark 1:32-34</scripRef>, etc.). The impenitence and
unbelief of its inhabitants after the many evidences our Lord
gave among them of the truth of his mission, brought down upon
them a heavy denunciation of judgement (Matt. 11:23).
It stood on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee. The “land
of Gennesaret,” near, if not in, which it was situated, was one
of the most prosperous and crowded districts of Palestine. This
city lay on the great highway from Damascus to Acco and Tyre. It
has been identified with Tell Hum, about two miles south-west of
where the Jordan flows into the lake. Here are extensive ruins
of walls and foundations, and also the remains of what must have
been a beautiful synagogue, which it is conjectured may have
been the one built by the centurion (<scripRef passage="Luke 7:5" id="c-p71.1" parsed="|Luke|7|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.7.5">Luke 7:5</scripRef>), in which our

Lord frequently taught (<scripRef passage="John 6:59" id="c-p71.2" parsed="|John|6|59|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.6.59">John 6:59</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 1:21" id="c-p71.3" parsed="|Mark|1|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.21">Mark 1:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 4:33" id="c-p71.4" parsed="|Luke|4|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.4.33">Luke 4:33</scripRef>). Others
have conjectured that the ruins of the city are to be found at
Khan Minyeh, some three miles further to the south on the shore
of the lake. “If Tell Hum be Capernaum, the remains spoken of
are without doubt the ruins of the synagogue built by the Roman
centurion, and one of the most sacred places on earth. It was in
this building that our Lord gave the well-known discourse in
<scripRef passage="John 6" id="c-p71.5" parsed="|John|6|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.6">John 6</scripRef>; and it was not without a certain strange feeling that on
turning over a large block we found the pot of manna engraved on
its face, and remembered the words, ‘I am that bread of life:
your fathers did eat manna in the wilderness, and are dead.’”,
(The Recovery of Jerusalem.)
</def>
<term id="c-p71.6">Caphtor</term>
<def id="c-p71.7">
A chaplet, the original seat of the Philistines (Deut. 2:23;

<scripRef passage="Jer. 47:4" id="c-p72.2" parsed="|Jer|47|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.47.4">Jer. 47:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Amos 9:7" id="c-p72.3" parsed="|Amos|9|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.9.7">Amos 9:7</scripRef>). The name is found written in hieroglyphics
in the temple of Kom Ombos in Upper Egypt. But the exact
situation of Caphtor is unknown, though it is supposed to be
Crete, since the Philistines seem to be meant by the

“Cherethites” in <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 30:14" id="c-p72.4" parsed="|1Sam|30|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.30.14">1 Sam. 30:14</scripRef> (see also <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 8:18" id="c-p72.5" parsed="|2Sam|8|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.8.18">2 Sam. 8:18</scripRef>). It may,
however, have been a part of Egypt, the Caphtur in the north
Delta, since the Caphtorim were of the same race as the Mizraite
people (Gen. 10:14; 1 Chr. 1:12).
</def>
<term id="c-p72.8">Cappadocia</term>
<def id="c-p72.9">
The easternmost and the largest province of Asia Minor.

Christianity very early penetrated into this country (<scripRef passage="1 Pet. 1:1" id="c-p73.1" parsed="|1Pet|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.1.1">1 Pet. 1:1</scripRef>). On the day of Pentecost there were Cappadocians at
Jerusalem (Acts 2:9).
</def>
<term id="c-p73.3">Captain</term>
<def id="c-p73.4">
(1.) Heb. sar (1 Sam. 22:2; 2 Sam. 23:19). Rendered “chief,”

<scripRef passage="Gen. 40:2" id="c-p74.3" parsed="|Gen|40|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.40.2">Gen. 40:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 41:9" id="c-p74.4" parsed="|Gen|41|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.41.9">41:9</scripRef>; rendered also “prince,” <scripRef passage="Dan. 1:7" id="c-p74.5" parsed="|Dan|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.1.7">Dan. 1:7</scripRef>; “ruler,”

<scripRef passage="Judg. 9:30" id="c-p74.6" parsed="|Judg|9|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.9.30">Judg. 9:30</scripRef>; “governor,’ <scripRef passage="1 Kings 22:26" id="c-p74.7" parsed="|1Kgs|22|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.22.26">1 Kings 22:26</scripRef>. This same Hebrew word

denotes a military captain (<scripRef passage="Ex. 18:21" id="c-p74.8" parsed="|Exod|18|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.18.21">Ex. 18:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 1:9" id="c-p74.9" parsed="|2Kgs|1|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.1.9">2 Kings 1:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 1:15" id="c-p74.10" parsed="|Deut|1|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.1.15">Deut. 1:15</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 18:13" id="c-p74.11" parsed="|1Sam|18|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.18.13">1 Sam. 18:13</scripRef>, etc.), the “captain of the body-guard” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 37:36" id="c-p74.12" parsed="|Gen|37|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.36">Gen. 37:36</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 39:1" id="c-p74.13" parsed="|Gen|39|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.39.1">39:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 41:10" id="c-p74.14" parsed="|Gen|41|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.41.10">41:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 40:1" id="c-p74.15" parsed="|Jer|40|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.40.1">Jer. 40:1</scripRef>), or, as the word may be rendered,
“chief of the executioners” (marg.). The officers of the king’s
body-guard frequently acted as executioners. Nebuzar-adan (Jer. 39:13) and Arioch (Dan. 2:14) held this office in Babylon.
The “captain of the guard” mentioned in Acts 28:16 was the
Praetorian prefect, the commander of the Praetorian troops.
(2.) Another word (Heb. katsin) so translated denotes

sometimes a military (<scripRef passage="Josh. 10:24" id="c-p76.1" parsed="|Josh|10|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.24">Josh. 10:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 11:6" id="c-p76.2" parsed="|Judg|11|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.11.6">Judg. 11:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Judg. 11:11" id="c-p76.3" parsed="|Judg|11|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.11.11">11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 22:3" id="c-p76.4" parsed="|Isa|22|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.22.3">Isa. 22:3</scripRef>
“rulers;” <scripRef passage="Dan. 11:18" id="c-p76.5" parsed="|Dan|11|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.11.18">Dan. 11:18</scripRef>) and sometimes a civil command, a judge,
magistrate, Arab. kady, (Isa. 1:10; 3:6; Micah 3:1, 9).
(3.) It is also the rendering of a Hebrew word (shalish)
meaning “a third man,” or “one of three.” The LXX. render in
plural by tristatai; i.e., “soldiers fighting from chariots,”
so called because each war-chariot contained three men, one of
whom acted as charioteer while the other two fought (<scripRef passage="Ex. 14:7" id="c-p77.1" parsed="|Exod|14|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.14.7">Ex. 14:7</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Ex 15:4" id="c-p77.2" parsed="|Exod|15|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.15.4">15:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 9:22" id="c-p77.3" parsed="|1Kgs|9|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.9.22">1 Kings 9:22</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="2 Kings 9:25" id="c-p77.4" parsed="|2Kgs|9|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.9.25">2 Kings 9:25</scripRef>). This word is used also
to denote the king’s body-guard (2 Kings 10:25; 1 Chr. 12:18; 2 Chr. 11:11) or aides-de-camp.
(4.) The “captain of the temple” mentioned in Acts 4:1 and
5:24 was not a military officer, but superintendent of the guard
of priests and Levites who kept watch in the temple by night.
(Comp. “the ruler of the house of God,” 1 Chr. 9:11; 2 Chr. 31:13; Neh. 11:11.)
(5.) The Captain of our salvation is a name given to our Lord
(<scripRef passage="Heb. 2:10" id="c-p79.1" parsed="|Heb|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.2.10">Heb. 2:10</scripRef>), because he is the author and source of our
salvation, the head of his people, whom he is conducting to

glory. The “captain of the Lord’s host” (<scripRef passage="Josh. 5:14" id="c-p79.2" parsed="|Josh|5|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.5.14">Josh. 5:14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 5:15" id="c-p79.3" parsed="|Josh|5|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.5.15">15</scripRef>) is the
name given to that mysterious person who manifested himself to

Abraham (<scripRef passage="Gen. 12:7" id="c-p79.4" parsed="|Gen|12|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.12.7">Gen. 12:7</scripRef>), and to Moses in the bush (<scripRef passage="Ex. 3:2" id="c-p79.5" parsed="|Exod|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.3.2">Ex. 3:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 3:6" id="c-p79.6" parsed="|Exod|3|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.3.6">6</scripRef>, etc.)
the Angel of the covenant. (See ANGEL.)
</def>
<term id="c-p79.8">Captive</term>
<def id="c-p79.9">
One taken in war. Captives were often treated with great cruelty

and indignity (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 20:32" id="c-p80.1" parsed="|1Kgs|20|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.20.32">1 Kings 20:32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 10:24" id="c-p80.2" parsed="|Josh|10|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.24">Josh. 10:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 1:7" id="c-p80.3" parsed="|Judg|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.7">Judg. 1:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 4:12" id="c-p80.4" parsed="|2Sam|4|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.4.12">2 Sam. 4:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 8:7" id="c-p80.5" parsed="|Judg|8|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.8.7">Judg. 8:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 12:31" id="c-p80.6" parsed="|2Sam|12|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.12.31">2 Sam. 12:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 20:3" id="c-p80.7" parsed="|1Chr|20|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.20.3">1 Chr. 20:3</scripRef>). When a city was
taken by assault, all the men were slain, and the women and

children carried away captive and sold as slaves (<scripRef passage="Isa. 20" id="c-p80.8" parsed="|Isa|20|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.20">Isa. 20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 47:3" id="c-p80.9" parsed="|Isa|47|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.47.3">47:3</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 28:9-15" id="c-p80.10" parsed="|2Chr|28|9|28|15" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.28.9-2Chr.28.15">2 Chr. 28:9-15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 44:12" id="c-p80.11" parsed="|Ps|44|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.44.12">Ps. 44:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Joel 3:3" id="c-p80.12" parsed="|Joel|3|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Joel.3.3">Joel 3:3</scripRef>), and exposed to the most

cruel treatment (<scripRef passage="Nah. 3:10" id="c-p80.13" parsed="|Nah|3|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Nah.3.10">Nah. 3:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 14:2" id="c-p80.14" parsed="|Zech|14|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.14.2">Zech. 14:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Esther 3:13" id="c-p80.15" parsed="|Esth|3|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.3.13">Esther 3:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 8:12" id="c-p80.16" parsed="|2Kgs|8|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.8.12">2 Kings 8:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 13:16" id="c-p80.17" parsed="|Isa|13|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.13.16">Isa. 13:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 13:18" id="c-p80.18" parsed="|Isa|13|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.13.18">18</scripRef>). Captives were sometimes carried away into
foreign countries, as was the case with the Jews (<scripRef passage="Jer. 20:5" id="c-p80.19" parsed="|Jer|20|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.20.5">Jer. 20:5</scripRef>;
39:9, 10; 40:7).
</def>
<term id="c-p80.23">Captivity</term>
(1.) Of Israel. The kingdom of the ten tribes was successively
invaded by several Assyrian kings. Pul (q.v.) imposed a tribute

on Menahem of a thousand talents of silver (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 15:19" id="c-p81.1" parsed="|2Kgs|15|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.19">2 Kings 15:19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 15:20" id="c-p81.2" parsed="|2Kgs|15|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.20">20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 5:26" id="c-p81.3" parsed="|1Chr|5|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5.26">1 Chr. 5:26</scripRef>) (B.C. 762), and Tiglath-pileser, in the days of Pekah
(B.C. 738), carried away the trans-Jordanic tribes and the

inhabitants of Galilee into Assyria (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 15:29" id="c-p81.4" parsed="|2Kgs|15|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.29">2 Kings 15:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 9:1" id="c-p81.5" parsed="|Isa|9|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.9.1">Isa. 9:1</scripRef>).
Subsequently Shalmaneser invaded Israel and laid siege to
Samaria, the capital of the kingdom. During the siege he died,
and was succeeded by Sargon, who took the city, and transported
the great mass of the people into Assyria (B.C. 721), placing

them in Halah and in Habor, and in the cities of the Medes (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:3" id="c-p81.6" parsed="|2Kgs|17|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.3">2 Kings 17:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:5" id="c-p81.7" parsed="|2Kgs|17|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.5">5</scripRef>). Samaria was never again inhabited by the
Israelites. The families thus removed were carried to distant
cities, many of them not far from the Caspian Sea, and their

place was supplied by colonists from Babylon and Cuthah, etc. (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:24" id="c-p81.8" parsed="|2Kgs|17|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.24">2 Kings 17:24</scripRef>). Thus terminated the kingdom of the ten tribes,
after a separate duration of two hundred and fifty-five years
Many speculations have been indulged in with reference to
these ten tribes. But we believe that all, except the number
that probably allied themselves with Judah and shared in their
restoration under Cyrus, are finally lost.
“Like the dew on the mountain, Like the
foam on the river,
Like the bubble on the fountain,
They are gone, and for ever.”
(2.) Of Judah. In the third year of Jehoiachim, the eighteenth
king of Judah (B.C. 605), Nebuchadnezzar having overcome the
Egyptians at Carchemish, advanced to Jerusalem with a great
army. After a brief siege he took that city, and carried away
the vessels of the sanctuary to Babylon, and dedicated them in

the Temple of Belus (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 24:1" id="c-p84.1" parsed="|2Kgs|24|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.24.1">2 Kings 24:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 36:6" id="c-p84.2" parsed="|2Chr|36|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.36.6">2 Chr. 36:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 36:7" id="c-p84.3" parsed="|2Chr|36|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.36.7">7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Dan. 1:1" id="c-p84.4" parsed="|Dan|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.1.1">Dan. 1:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan 1:2" id="c-p84.5" parsed="|Dan|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.1.2">2</scripRef>).
He also carried away the treasures of the king, whom he made his
vassal. At this time, from which is dated the “seventy years” of

captivity (<scripRef passage="Jer. 25" id="c-p84.6" parsed="|Jer|25|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.25">Jer. 25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Dan. 9:1" id="c-p84.7" parsed="|Dan|9|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.9.1">Dan. 9:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan 9:2" id="c-p84.8" parsed="|Dan|9|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.9.2">2</scripRef>), Daniel and his companions were
carried to Babylon, there to be brought up at the court and
trained in all the learning of the Chaldeans. After this, in the
fifth year of Jehoiakim, a great national fast was appointed
(<scripRef passage="Jer. 36:9" id="c-p84.9" parsed="|Jer|36|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.36.9">Jer. 36:9</scripRef>), during which the king, to show his defiance, cut up
the leaves of the book of Jeremiah’s prophecies as they were
read to him in his winter palace, and threw them into the fire.

In the same spirit he rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 24:1" id="c-p84.10" parsed="|2Kgs|24|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.24.1">2 Kings 24:1</scripRef>), who again a second time (B.C. 598) marched against
Jerusalem, and put Jehoiachim to death, placing his son
Jehoiachin on the throne in his stead. But Jehoiachin’s
counsellors displeasing Nebuchadnezzar, he again a third time
turned his army against Jerusalem, and carried away to Babylon a
second detachment of Jews as captives, to the number of 10,000

(<scripRef passage="2 Kings 24:13" id="c-p84.11" parsed="|2Kgs|24|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.24.13">2 Kings 24:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 24:1" id="c-p84.12" parsed="|Jer|24|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.24.1">Jer. 24:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 36:10" id="c-p84.13" parsed="|2Chr|36|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.36.10">2 Chr. 36:10</scripRef>), among whom were the
king, with his mother and all his princes and officers, also
Ezekiel, who with many of his companions were settled on the
banks of the river Chebar (q.v.). He also carried away all the
remaining treasures of the temple and the palace, and the golden
vessels of the sanctuary.
Mattaniah, the uncle of Jehoiachin, was now made king over
what remained of the kingdom of Judah, under the name of

Zedekiah (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 24:17" id="c-p85.1" parsed="|2Kgs|24|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.24.17">2 Kings 24:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 36:10" id="c-p85.2" parsed="|2Chr|36|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.36.10">2 Chr. 36:10</scripRef>). After a troubled reign
of eleven years his kingdom came to an end (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 36:11" id="c-p85.3" parsed="|2Chr|36|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.36.11">2 Chr. 36:11</scripRef>).
Nebuchadnezzar, with a powerful army, besieged Jerusalem, and
Zedekiah became a prisoner in Babylon. His eyes were put out,

and he was kept in close confinement till his death (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 25:7" id="c-p85.4" parsed="|2Kgs|25|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.25.7">2 Kings 25:7</scripRef>). The city was spoiled of all that was of value, and then
given up to the flames. The temple and palaces were consumed,
and the walls of the city were levelled with the ground (B.C.
586), and all that remained of the people, except a number of
the poorest class who were left to till the ground and dress the
vineyards, were carried away captives to Babylon. This was the
third and last deportation of Jewish captives. The land was now
utterly desolate, and was abondoned to anarchy.
In the first year of his reign as king of Babylon (B.C. 536),
Cyrus issued a decree liberating the Jewish captives, and
permitting them to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the city and

the temple (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 36:22" id="c-p86.1" parsed="|2Chr|36|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.36.22">2 Chr. 36:22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 36:23" id="c-p86.2" parsed="|2Chr|36|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.36.23">23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezra 1" id="c-p86.3" parsed="|Ezra|1|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.1">Ezra 1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezra 2" id="c-p86.4" parsed="|Ezra|2|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2">2</scripRef>). The number of the
people forming the first caravan, under Zerubbabel, amounted in

all to 42,360 (<scripRef passage="Ezra 2:64" id="c-p86.5" parsed="|Ezra|2|64|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2.64">Ezra 2:64</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezra 2:65" id="c-p86.6" parsed="|Ezra|2|65|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2.65">65</scripRef>), besides 7,337 men-servants and
maid-servants. A considerable number, 12,000 probably, from the
ten tribes who had been carried away into Assyria no doubt
combined with this band of liberated captives.
At a later period other bands of the Jews returned (1) under
Ezra (7:7) (B.C. 458), and (2) Nehemiah (7:66) (B.C. 445). But
the great mass of the people remained still in the land to which
they had been carried, and became a portion of the Jews of the

“dispersion” (<scripRef passage="John 7:35" id="c-p87.1" parsed="|John|7|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.7.35">John 7:35</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Pet. 1:1" id="c-p87.2" parsed="|1Pet|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.1.1">1 Pet. 1:1</scripRef>). The whole number of the
exiles that chose to remain was probably about six times the
number of those who returned.
</def>
<term id="c-p87.3">Carbuncle</term>
<def id="c-p87.4">
(Ex. 28:17; 39:10; Ezek. 28:13). Heb. barkath; LXX. smaragdos;
Vulgate, smaragdus; Revised Version, marg., “emerald.” The
Hebrew word is from a root meaning “to glitter,” “lighten,”
“flash.” When held up to the sun, this gem shines like a burning
coal, a dark-red glowing coal, and hence is called
“carbunculus”, i.e., a little coal. It was one of the jewels in
the first row of the high priest’s breastplate. It has been
conjectured by some that the garnet is meant. In <scripRef passage="Isa. 54:12" id="c-p88.4" parsed="|Isa|54|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.54.12">Isa. 54:12</scripRef> the
Hebrew word is ’ekdah, used in the prophetic description of
the glory and beauty of the mansions above. Next to the diamond
it is the hardest and most costly of all precious stones.
</def>
<term id="c-p88.5">Carcase</term>
<def id="c-p88.6">
Contact with a, made an Israelite ceremonially unclean, and made
whatever he touched also unclean, according to the Mosaic law
(Hag. 2:13; comp. Num. 19:16, 22; Lev. 11:39).
</def>
<term id="c-p89.5">Carchemish</term>
<def id="c-p89.6">
Fortress of Chemosh, a city on the west bank of the Euphrates

(<scripRef passage="Jer. 46:2" id="c-p90.1" parsed="|Jer|46|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.46.2">Jer. 46:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 35:20" id="c-p90.2" parsed="|2Chr|35|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.35.20">2 Chr. 35:20</scripRef>), not, as was once supposed, the
Circesium at the confluence of the Chebar and the Euphrates, but
a city considerably higher up the river, and commanding the
ordinary passage of the Euphrates; probably identical with
Hierapolis. It was the capital of the kingdom of the northern
Hittites. The Babylonian army, under Nebuchadnezzar, the son of
Nabopolassar, here met and conquered the army of Pharaoh-necho,
king of Egypt (B.C. 607). It is mentioned in monuments in B.C.
1600 and down to B.C. 717.
</def>
<term id="c-p90.3">Carmel</term>
<def id="c-p90.4">
A park; generally with the article, “the park.” (1.) A prominent
headland of Central Palestine, consisting of several connected
hills extending from the plain of Esdraelon to the sea, a
distance of some 12 miles or more. At the east end, in its
highest part, it is 1,728 feet high, and at the west end it
forms a promontory to the bay of Acre about 600 feet above the
sea. It lay within the tribe of Asher. It was here, at the east
end of the ridge, at a place called el-Mukhrakah (i.e., the
place of burning), that Elijah brought back the people to their
allegiance to God, and slew the prophets of Baal (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 18" id="c-p91.1" parsed="|1Kgs|18|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.18">1 Kings 18</scripRef>).
Here were consumed the “fifties” of the royal guard; and here
also Elisha received the visit of the bereaved mother whose son
was restored by him to life (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 4:25-37" id="c-p91.2" parsed="|2Kgs|4|25|4|37" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.4.25-2Kgs.4.37">2 Kings 4:25-37</scripRef>). “No mountain in
or around Palestine retains its ancient beauty so much as
Carmel. Two or three villages and some scattered cottages are
found on it; its groves are few but luxuriant; it is no place
for crags and precipices or rocks of wild goats; but its surface
is covered with a rich and constant verdure.” “The whole
mountain-side is dressed with blossom, and flowering shrubs, and
fragrant herbs.” The western extremity of the ridge is, however,
more rocky and bleak than the eastern. The head of the bride in
<scripRef passage="Cant. 7:5" id="c-p91.3" parsed="|Song|7|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.7.5">Cant. 7:5</scripRef> is compared to Carmel. It is ranked with Bashan on

account of its rich pastures (<scripRef passage="Isa. 33:9" id="c-p91.4" parsed="|Isa|33|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.33.9">Isa. 33:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 50:19" id="c-p91.5" parsed="|Jer|50|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.50.19">Jer. 50:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Amos 1:2" id="c-p91.6" parsed="|Amos|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.1.2">Amos 1:2</scripRef>).
The whole ridge is deeply furrowed with rocky ravines filled
with dense jungle. There are many caves in its sides, which at
one time were inhabited by swarms of monks. These caves are
referred to in <scripRef passage="Amos 9:3" id="c-p91.7" parsed="|Amos|9|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.9.3">Amos 9:3</scripRef>. To them Elijah and Elisha often

resorted (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 18:19" id="c-p91.8" parsed="|1Kgs|18|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.18.19">1 Kings 18:19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 18:42" id="c-p91.9" parsed="|1Kgs|18|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.18.42">42</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 2:25" id="c-p91.10" parsed="|2Kgs|2|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.2.25">2 Kings 2:25</scripRef>). On its north-west
summit there is an ancient establishment of Carmelite monks.
Vineyards have recently been planted on the mount by the German
colonists of Haifa. The modern Arabic name of the mount is
Kurmul, but more commonly Jebel Mar Elyas, i.e., Mount St.
Elias, from the Convent of Elias.
(2.) A town in the hill country of Judah (Josh. 15:55), the

residence of Nabal (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 25:2" id="c-p92.2" parsed="|1Sam|25|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.25.2">1 Sam. 25:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 25:5" id="c-p92.3" parsed="|1Sam|25|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.25.5">5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 25:7" id="c-p92.4" parsed="|1Sam|25|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.25.7">7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 25:40" id="c-p92.5" parsed="|1Sam|25|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.25.40">40</scripRef>), and the native place
of Abigail, who became David’s wife (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 27:3" id="c-p92.6" parsed="|1Sam|27|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.27.3">1 Sam. 27:3</scripRef>). Here king
Uzziah had his vineyards (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 26:10" id="c-p92.7" parsed="|2Chr|26|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.26.10">2 Chr. 26:10</scripRef>). The ruins of this town
still remain under the name of Kurmul, about 10 miles
south-south-east of Hebron, close to those of Maon.
</def>
<term id="c-p92.8">Carmi</term>
<def id="c-p92.9">
Vine-dresser. (1.) The last named of the four sons of Reuben
(Gen. 46:9).
(2.) A descendant of Judah (1 Chr. 4:1). He is elsewhere
(2:18) called Caleb (q.v.).
(3.) The son of Zimri, and the father of Achan (Josh. 7:1),
“the troubler of Israel.”
</def>
<term id="c-p95.2">Carnal</term>
<def id="c-p95.3">
Unconverted men are so called (1 Cor. 3:3). They are represented

as of a “carnal mind, which is enmity against God” (<scripRef passage="Rom. 8:6" id="c-p96.2" parsed="|Rom|8|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.6">Rom. 8:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Rom 8:7" id="c-p96.3" parsed="|Rom|8|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.7">7</scripRef>). Enjoyments that minister to the wants and desires of man’s

animal nature are so called (<scripRef passage="Rom. 15:27" id="c-p96.4" parsed="|Rom|15|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.15.27">Rom. 15:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 9:11" id="c-p96.5" parsed="|1Cor|9|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.9.11">1 Cor. 9:11</scripRef>). The
ceremonial of the Mosaic law is spoken of as “carnal,” because
it related to things outward, the bodies of men and of animals,

and the purification of the flesh (<scripRef passage="Heb. 7:16" id="c-p96.6" parsed="|Heb|7|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.7.16">Heb. 7:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb 9:10" id="c-p96.7" parsed="|Heb|9|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.10">9:10</scripRef>). The weapons
of Christian warfare are “not carnal”, that is, they are not of
man’s device, nor are wielded by human power (2 Cor. 10:4).
</def>
<term id="c-p96.9">Carpenter</term>
An artificer in stone, iron, and copper, as well as in wood (2 Sam. 5:11; 1 Chr. 14:1; Mark 6:3). The tools used by carpenters

are mentioned in <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 13:19" id="c-p97.4" parsed="|1Sam|13|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.13.19">1 Sam. 13:19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 13:20" id="c-p97.5" parsed="|1Sam|13|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.13.20">20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 4:21" id="c-p97.6" parsed="|Judg|4|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.4.21">Judg. 4:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 10:15" id="c-p97.7" parsed="|Isa|10|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.15">Isa. 10:15</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Isa 44:13" id="c-p97.8" parsed="|Isa|44|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.44.13">44:13</scripRef>. It was said of our Lord, “Is not this the carpenter’s

son?” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 13:55" id="c-p97.9" parsed="|Matt|13|55|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.13.55">Matt. 13:55</scripRef>); also, “Is not this the carpenter?” (<scripRef passage="Mark 6:3" id="c-p97.10" parsed="|Mark|6|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.6.3">Mark 6:3</scripRef>). Every Jew, even the rabbis, learned some handicraft: Paul
was a tentmaker. “In the cities the carpenters would be Greeks,
and skilled workmen; the carpenter of a provincial village could
only have held a very humble position, and secured a very
moderate competence.”
</def>
<term id="c-p97.11">Carriage</term>
In the Authorized Version this word is found as the rendering of
many different words. In <scripRef passage="Judg. 18:21" id="c-p98.1" parsed="|Judg|18|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.18.21">Judg. 18:21</scripRef> it means valuables, wealth,
or booty. In <scripRef passage="Isa. 46:1" id="c-p98.2" parsed="|Isa|46|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.46.1">Isa. 46:1</scripRef> (R.V., “the things that ye carried

about”) the word means a load for a beast of burden. In <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:22" id="c-p98.3" parsed="|1Sam|17|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.22">1 Sam. 17:22</scripRef> and <scripRef passage="Isa. 10:28" id="c-p98.4" parsed="|Isa|10|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.28">Isa. 10:28</scripRef> it is the rendering of a word (“stuff” in <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 10:22" id="c-p98.5" parsed="|1Sam|10|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.10.22">1 Sam. 10:22</scripRef>) meaning implements, equipments, baggage. The phrase
in <scripRef passage="Acts 21:15" id="c-p98.6" parsed="|Acts|21|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.21.15">Acts 21:15</scripRef>, “We took up our carriages,” means properly, “We
packed up our baggage,” as in the Revised Version.
</def>
<term id="c-p98.7">Cart</term>
<def id="c-p98.8">
A vehicle moving on wheels, and usually drawn by oxen (2 Sam. 6:3). The Hebrew word thus rendered, ’agalah (1 Sam. 6:7, 8),
is also rendered “wagon” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 45:19" id="c-p99.4" parsed="|Gen|45|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.45.19">Gen. 45:19</scripRef>). It is used also to denote
a war-chariot (<scripRef passage="Ps. 46:9" id="c-p99.5" parsed="|Ps|46|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.46.9">Ps. 46:9</scripRef>). Carts were used for the removal of the

ark and its sacred utensils (<scripRef passage="Num. 7:3" id="c-p99.6" parsed="|Num|7|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.7.3">Num. 7:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 7:6" id="c-p99.7" parsed="|Num|7|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.7.6">6</scripRef>). After retaining the
ark amongst them for seven months, the Philistines sent it back
to the Israelites. On this occasion they set it in a new cart,
probably a rude construction, with solid wooden wheels like that
still used in Western Asia, which was drawn by two milch cows,
which conveyed it straight to Beth-shemesh.
A “cart rope,” for the purpose of fastening loads on carts, is
used (<scripRef passage="Isa. 5:18" id="c-p100.1" parsed="|Isa|5|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.5.18">Isa. 5:18</scripRef>) as a symbol of the power of sinful pleasures or
habits over him who indulges them. (See CORD.) In
Syria and Palestine wheel-carriages for any other purpose than
the conveyance of agricultural produce are almost unknown.
</def>
<term id="c-p100.3">Carve</term>
The arts of engraving and carving were much practised among the
Jews. They were practised in connection with the construction of

the tabernacle and the temple (<scripRef passage="Ex. 31:2" id="c-p101.1" parsed="|Exod|31|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.31.2">Ex. 31:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 31:5" id="c-p101.2" parsed="|Exod|31|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.31.5">5</scripRef>; 35:33; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 6:18" id="c-p101.3" parsed="|1Kgs|6|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.6.18">1 Kings 6:18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 6:35" id="c-p101.4" parsed="|1Kgs|6|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.6.35">35</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 74:6" id="c-p101.5" parsed="|Ps|74|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.74.6">Ps. 74:6</scripRef>), as well as in the ornamentation of the priestly

dresses (<scripRef passage="Ex. 28:9-36" id="c-p101.6" parsed="|Exod|28|9|28|36" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.9-Exod.28.36">Ex. 28:9-36</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 3:9" id="c-p101.7" parsed="|Zech|3|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.3.9">Zech. 3:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 2:7" id="c-p101.8" parsed="|2Chr|2|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.2.7">2 Chr. 2:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 2:14" id="c-p101.9" parsed="|2Chr|2|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.2.14">14</scripRef>). Isaiah
(44:13-17) gives a minute description of the process of carving
idols of wood.
</def>
<term id="c-p101.10">Casement</term>
A barrier of open-work placed before windows (Prov. 7:6). In
<scripRef passage="Judg. 5:28" id="c-p102.2" parsed="|Judg|5|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.5.28">Judg. 5:28</scripRef> the Hebrew word is rendered “lattice,” in the LXX.
“network,” an opening through which cool air is admitted.
</def>
<term id="c-p102.3">Casiphia</term>
Silver, a place between Babylon and Jerusalem, where Iddo
resided (Ezra 8:17); otherwise unknown.
</def>
<term id="c-p103.2">Casluhim</term>
Fortified, a people descended from Mizraim (Gen. 10:14; 1 Chr. 1:12). Their original seat was probably somewhere in Lower
Egypt, along the sea-coast to the south border of Palestine.
</def>
<term id="c-p104.3">Cassia</term>
(1.) Hebrew kiddah’, i.e., “split.” One of the principal
spices of the holy anointing oil (<scripRef passage="Ex. 30:24" id="c-p105.1" parsed="|Exod|30|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.30.24">Ex. 30:24</scripRef>), and an article of
commerce (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:19" id="c-p105.2" parsed="|Ezek|27|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.19">Ezek. 27:19</scripRef>). It is the inner bark of a tree
resembling the cinnamon (q.v.), the Cinnamomum cassia of
botanists, and was probably imported from India.
(2.) Hebrew pl. ketzi’oth (Ps. 45:8). Mentioned in
connection with myrrh and aloes as being used to scent garments.
It was probably prepared from the peeled bark, as the Hebrew
word suggests, of some kind of cinnamon.
</def>
<term id="c-p106.2">Castaway</term>
Gr. adokimos, (1 Cor. 9:27), one regarded as unworthy (R.V.,
“rejected”); elsewhere rendered “reprobate” (<scripRef passage="2 Tim. 3:8" id="c-p107.2" parsed="|2Tim|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.3.8">2 Tim. 3:8</scripRef>, etc.);
“rejected” (Heb. 6:8, etc.).
</def>
<term id="c-p107.4">Castle</term>
A military fortress (1 Chr. 11:7), also probably a kind of tower
used by the priests for making known anything discovered at a

distance (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 6:54" id="c-p108.2" parsed="|1Chr|6|54|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.6.54">1 Chr. 6:54</scripRef>). Castles are also mentioned (<scripRef passage="Gen. 25:16" id="c-p108.3" parsed="|Gen|25|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.16">Gen. 25:16</scripRef>)
as a kind of watch-tower, from which shepherds kept watch over
their flocks by night. The “castle” into which the chief captain
commanded Paul to be brought was the quarters of the Roman
soldiers in the fortress of Antonia (so called by Herod after
his patron Mark Antony), which was close to the north-west
corner of the temple (Acts 21:34), which it commanded.
</def>
<term id="c-p108.5">Castor and Pollux</term>
The “Dioscuri”, two heroes of Greek and Roman mythology. Their
figures were probably painted or sculptured on the prow of the
ship which Luke refers to (<scripRef passage="Acts 28:11" id="c-p109.1" parsed="|Acts|28|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.28.11">Acts 28:11</scripRef>). They were regarded as
the tutelary divinities of sailors. They appeared in the heavens
as the constellation Gemini.
</def>
<term id="c-p109.2">Caterpillar</term>
The consumer. Used in the Old Testament (1 Kings 8:37; 2 Chr. 6:28; Ps. 78:46; Isa. 33:4) as the translation of a word (hasil)
the root of which means “to devour” or “consume,” and which is
used also with reference to the locust in <scripRef passage="Deut. 28:38" id="c-p110.5" parsed="|Deut|28|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.38">Deut. 28:38</scripRef>. It may
have been a species of locust, or the name of one of the
transformations through which the locust passes, locust-grub. It

is also found (<scripRef passage="Ps. 105:34" id="c-p110.6" parsed="|Ps|105|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.105.34">Ps. 105:34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 51:14" id="c-p110.7" parsed="|Jer|51|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.51.14">Jer. 51:14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer. 51:27" id="c-p110.8" parsed="|Jer|51|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.51.27">27</scripRef>; R.V., “cankerworm”)
as the rendering of a different Hebrew word, yelek, a word
elsewhere rendered “cankerworm” (q.v.), Joel 1:4; 2:25. (See LOCUST.)
</def>
<term id="c-p110.12">Catholic epistles</term>
The epistles of James, Peter, John, and Jude; so called because
they are addressed to Christians in general, and not to any
church or person in particular.
</def>
<term id="c-p111.1">Cattle</term>
Abounded in the Holy Land. To the rearing and management of them

the inhabitants chiefly devoted themselves (<scripRef passage="Deut. 8:13" id="c-p112.1" parsed="|Deut|8|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.8.13">Deut. 8:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut 12:21" id="c-p112.2" parsed="|Deut|12|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.12.21">12:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 11:5" id="c-p112.3" parsed="|1Sam|11|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.11.5">1 Sam. 11:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 12:3" id="c-p112.4" parsed="|1Sam|12|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.12.3">12:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 144:14" id="c-p112.5" parsed="|Ps|144|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.144.14">Ps. 144:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 3:24" id="c-p112.6" parsed="|Jer|3|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.3.24">Jer. 3:24</scripRef>). They may be classified
as,
(1.) Neat cattle. Many hundreds of these were yearly consumed
in sacrifices or used for food. The finest herds were found in
Bashan, beyond Jordan (<scripRef passage="Num. 32:4" id="c-p113.1" parsed="|Num|32|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.32.4">Num. 32:4</scripRef>). Large herds also pastured on
the wide fertile plains of Sharon. They were yoked to the plough

(<scripRef passage="1 Kings 19:19" id="c-p113.2" parsed="|1Kgs|19|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.19.19">1 Kings 19:19</scripRef>), and were employed for carrying burdens (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 12:40" id="c-p113.3" parsed="|1Chr|12|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.12.40">1 Chr. 12:40</scripRef>). They were driven with a pointed rod (<scripRef passage="Judg. 3:31" id="c-p113.4" parsed="|Judg|3|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.3.31">Judg. 3:31</scripRef>) or goad
According to the Mosaic law, the mouths of cattle employed for
the threshing-floor were not to be muzzled, so as to prevent
them from eating of the provender over which they trampled
(<scripRef passage="Deut. 25:4" id="c-p114.1" parsed="|Deut|25|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.25.4">Deut. 25:4</scripRef>). Whosoever stole and sold or slaughtered an ox must
give five in satisfaction (<scripRef passage="Ex. 22:1" id="c-p114.2" parsed="|Exod|22|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.22.1">Ex. 22:1</scripRef>); but if it was found alive
in the possession of him who stole it, he was required to make
double restitution only (22:4). If an ox went astray, whoever

found it was required to bring it back to its owner (23:4; <scripRef passage="Deut. 22:1" id="c-p114.3" parsed="|Deut|22|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.22.1">Deut. 22:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut 22:4" id="c-p114.4" parsed="|Deut|22|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.22.4">4</scripRef>). An ox and an ass could not be yoked together in the
plough (Deut. 22:10).
(2.) Small cattle. Next to herds of neat cattle, sheep formed
the most important of the possessions of the inhabitants of

Palestine (<scripRef passage="Gen. 12:16" id="c-p115.1" parsed="|Gen|12|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.12.16">Gen. 12:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 13:5" id="c-p115.2" parsed="|Gen|13|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.13.5">13:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 26:14" id="c-p115.3" parsed="|Gen|26|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.26.14">26:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 21:27" id="c-p115.4" parsed="|Gen|21|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.27">21:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 29:2" id="c-p115.5" parsed="|Gen|29|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.29.2">29:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 29:3" id="c-p115.6" parsed="|Gen|29|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.29.3">3</scripRef>). They are
frequently mentioned among the booty taken in war (<scripRef passage="Num. 31:32" id="c-p115.7" parsed="|Num|31|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.31.32">Num. 31:32</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Josh. 6:21" id="c-p115.8" parsed="|Josh|6|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.6.21">Josh. 6:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 14:32" id="c-p115.9" parsed="|1Sam|14|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.14.32">1 Sam. 14:32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 15:3" id="c-p115.10" parsed="|1Sam|15|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.15.3">15:3</scripRef>). There were many who were owners

of large flocks (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 25:2" id="c-p115.11" parsed="|1Sam|25|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.25.2">1 Sam. 25:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 12:2" id="c-p115.12" parsed="|2Sam|12|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.12.2">2 Sam. 12:2</scripRef>, comp. <scripRef passage="Job 1:3" id="c-p115.13" parsed="|Job|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.1.3">Job 1:3</scripRef>). Kings
also had shepherds “over their flocks” (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 27:31" id="c-p115.14" parsed="|1Chr|27|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.27.31">1 Chr. 27:31</scripRef>), from

which they derived a large portion of their revenue (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 17:29" id="c-p115.15" parsed="|2Sam|17|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.17.29">2 Sam. 17:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 12:40" id="c-p115.16" parsed="|1Chr|12|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.12.40">1 Chr. 12:40</scripRef>). The districts most famous for their flocks
of sheep were the plain of Sharon (<scripRef passage="Isa. 65" id="c-p115.17" parsed="|Isa|65|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.65">Isa. 65</scripRef>: 10), Mount Carmel

(<scripRef passage="Micah 7:14" id="c-p115.18" parsed="|Mic|7|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.7.14">Micah 7:14</scripRef>), Bashan and Gilead (<scripRef passage="Micah 7:14" id="c-p115.19" parsed="|Mic|7|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.7.14">Micah 7:14</scripRef>). In patriarchal
times the flocks of sheep were sometimes tended by the daughters
of the owners. Thus Rachel, the daughter of Laban, kept her
father’s sheep (<scripRef passage="Gen. 29:9" id="c-p115.20" parsed="|Gen|29|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.29.9">Gen. 29:9</scripRef>); as also Zipporah and her six sisters
had charge of their father Jethro’s flocks (<scripRef passage="Ex. 2:16" id="c-p115.21" parsed="|Exod|2|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.2.16">Ex. 2:16</scripRef>). Sometimes
they were kept by hired shepherds (<scripRef passage="John 10:12" id="c-p115.22" parsed="|John|10|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.10.12">John 10:12</scripRef>), and sometimes by

the sons of the family (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 16:11" id="c-p115.23" parsed="|1Sam|16|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.16.11">1 Sam. 16:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:15" id="c-p115.24" parsed="|1Sam|17|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.15">17:15</scripRef>). The keepers so
familiarized their sheep with their voices that they knew them,
and followed them at their call. Sheep, but more especially rams
and lambs, were frequently offered in sacrifice. The shearing of

sheep was a great festive occasion (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 25:4" id="c-p115.25" parsed="|1Sam|25|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.25.4">1 Sam. 25:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 13:23" id="c-p115.26" parsed="|2Sam|13|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.13.23">2 Sam. 13:23</scripRef>).
They were folded at night, and guarded by their keepers against

the attacks of the lion (<scripRef passage="Micah 5:8" id="c-p115.27" parsed="|Mic|5|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.5.8">Micah 5:8</scripRef>), the bear (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:34" id="c-p115.28" parsed="|1Sam|17|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.34">1 Sam. 17:34</scripRef>),

and the wolf (<scripRef passage="Matt. 10:16" id="c-p115.29" parsed="|Matt|10|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.10.16">Matt. 10:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 10:12" id="c-p115.30" parsed="|John|10|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.10.12">John 10:12</scripRef>). They were liable to
wander over the wide pastures and go astray (Ps. 119:176; Isa. 53:6; Hos. 4:16; Matt. 18:12).
Goats also formed a part of the pastoral wealth of Palestine

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 15:9" id="c-p116.1" parsed="|Gen|15|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.9">Gen. 15:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 32:14" id="c-p116.2" parsed="|Gen|32|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.32.14">32:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 37:31" id="c-p116.3" parsed="|Gen|37|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.31">37:31</scripRef>). They were used both for sacrifice and

for food (<scripRef passage="Deut. 14:4" id="c-p116.4" parsed="|Deut|14|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.14.4">Deut. 14:4</scripRef>), especially the young males (<scripRef passage="Gen. 27:9" id="c-p116.5" parsed="|Gen|27|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.9">Gen. 27:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 27:14" id="c-p116.6" parsed="|Gen|27|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.14">14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 27:17" id="c-p116.7" parsed="|Gen|27|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.17">17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 6:19" id="c-p116.8" parsed="|Judg|6|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.6.19">Judg. 6:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg 13:15" id="c-p116.9" parsed="|Judg|13|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.13.15">13:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 16:20" id="c-p116.10" parsed="|1Sam|16|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.16.20">1 Sam. 16:20</scripRef>). Goat’s hair was used

for making tent cloth (<scripRef passage="Ex. 26:7" id="c-p116.11" parsed="|Exod|26|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.26.7">Ex. 26:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 36:14" id="c-p116.12" parsed="|Exod|36|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.36.14">36:14</scripRef>), and for mattresses and
bedding (1 Sam. 19:13, 16). (See GOAT.)
</def>
<term id="c-p116.16">Caul</term>
(Heb. yothe’reth; i.e., “something redundant”), the membrane

which covers the upper part of the liver (<scripRef passage="Ex. 29:13" id="c-p117.1" parsed="|Exod|29|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.13">Ex. 29:13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 29:22" id="c-p117.2" parsed="|Exod|29|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.22">22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 3:4" id="c-p117.3" parsed="|Lev|3|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.3.4">Lev. 3:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev 3:10" id="c-p117.4" parsed="|Lev|3|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.3.10">10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev 3:15" id="c-p117.5" parsed="|Lev|3|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.3.15">15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 4:9" id="c-p117.6" parsed="|Lev|4|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.4.9">4:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 7:4" id="c-p117.7" parsed="|Lev|7|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.7.4">7:4</scripRef>; marg., “midriff”). In <scripRef passage="Hos. 13:8" id="c-p117.8" parsed="|Hos|13|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.13.8">Hos. 13:8</scripRef> (Heb.
seghor; i.e., “an enclosure”) the pericardium, or parts about
the heart, is meant.
</def>
<term id="c-p117.9">Cauls</term>
In Isa. 3:18 this word (Heb. shebisim), in the marg. “networks,”
denotes network caps to contain the hair, worn by females.
Others explain it as meaning “wreaths worn round the forehead,
reaching from one ear to the other.”
</def>
<term id="c-p118.2">Causeway</term>
A raised way, an ascent by steps, or a raised slope between Zion

and the temple (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 26:16" id="c-p119.1" parsed="|1Chr|26|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.26.16">1 Chr. 26:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 26:18" id="c-p119.2" parsed="|1Chr|26|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.26.18">18</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 9:11" id="c-p119.3" parsed="|2Chr|9|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.9.11">2 Chr. 9:11</scripRef> the same word
is translated “terrace.”
</def>
<term id="c-p119.4">Cave</term>
There are numerous natural caves among the limestone rocks of
Syria, many of which have been artificially enlarged for various
purposes.
The first notice of a cave occurs in the history of Lot (Gen. 19:30).
The next we read of is the cave of Machpelah (q.v.), which

Abraham purchased from the sons of Heth (<scripRef passage="Gen. 25:9" id="c-p122.1" parsed="|Gen|25|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.9">Gen. 25:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 25:10" id="c-p122.2" parsed="|Gen|25|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.10">10</scripRef>). It was
the burying-place of Sarah and of Abraham himself, also of
Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob (Gen. 49:31; 50:13).
The cave of Makkedah, into which the five Amorite kings
retired after their defeat by Joshua (10:16, 27).
The cave of Adullam (q.v.), an immense natural cavern, where
David hid himself from Saul (1 Sam. 22:1, 2).
The cave of Engedi (q.v.), now called ‘Ain Jidy, i.e., the
“Fountain of the Kid”, where David cut off the skirt of Saul’s
robe (24:4). Here he also found a shelter for himself and his
followers to the number of 600 (23:29; 24:1). “On all sides the
country is full of caverns which might serve as lurking-places
for David and his men, as they do for outlaws at the present
day.”
The cave in which Obadiah hid the prophets (1 Kings 18:4) was
probably in the north, but it cannot be identified.
The cave of Elijah (1 Kings 19:9), and the “cleft” of Moses on
Horeb (Ex. 33:22), cannot be determined.
In the time of Gideon the Israelites took refuge from the
Midianites in dens and caves, such as abounded in the mountain
regions of Manasseh (Judg. 6:2).
Caves were frequently used as dwelling-places (Num. 24:21;

<scripRef passage="Cant. 2:14" id="c-p129.2" parsed="|Song|2|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.2.14">Cant. 2:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 49:16" id="c-p129.3" parsed="|Jer|49|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.49.16">Jer. 49:16</scripRef>; Obad. 1:3). “The excavations at Deir
Dubban, on the south side of the wady leading to Santa Hanneh,
are probably the dwellings of the Horites,” the ancient
inhabitants of Idumea Proper. The pits or cavities in rocks were

also sometimes used as prisons (<scripRef passage="Isa. 24:22" id="c-p129.4" parsed="|Isa|24|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.24.22">Isa. 24:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 51:14" id="c-p129.5" parsed="|Isa|51|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.51.14">51:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 9:11" id="c-p129.6" parsed="|Zech|9|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.9.11">Zech. 9:11</scripRef>).
Those which had niches in their sides were occupied as
burying-places (Ezek. 32:23; John 11:38).
</def>
<term id="c-p129.9">Cedar</term>
(Heb. e’rez, Gr. kedros, Lat. cedrus), a tree very frequently
mentioned in Scripture. It was stately (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 31:3-5" id="c-p130.1" parsed="|Ezek|31|3|31|5" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.31.3-Ezek.31.5">Ezek. 31:3-5</scripRef>),

long-branched (<scripRef passage="Ps. 80:10" id="c-p130.2" parsed="|Ps|80|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.80.10">Ps. 80:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 92:12" id="c-p130.3" parsed="|Ps|92|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.92.12">92:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 31:6-9" id="c-p130.4" parsed="|Ezek|31|6|31|9" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.31.6-Ezek.31.9">Ezek. 31:6-9</scripRef>), odoriferous

(<scripRef passage="Cant. 4:11" id="c-p130.5" parsed="|Song|4|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.4.11">Cant. 4:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos. 14:6" id="c-p130.6" parsed="|Hos|14|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.14.6">Hos. 14:6</scripRef>), durable, and therefore much used for
boards, pillars, and ceilings (1 Kings 6:9, 10; 7:2; Jer. 22:14), for masts (Ezek. 27:5), and for carved images (Isa. 44:14).
It grew very abundantly in Palestine, and particularly on

Lebanon, of which it was “the glory” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 35:2" id="c-p131.1" parsed="|Isa|35|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.35.2">Isa. 35:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 60:13" id="c-p131.2" parsed="|Isa|60|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.60.13">60:13</scripRef>). Hiram
supplied Solomon with cedar trees from Lebanon for various
purposes connected with the construction of the temple and the

king’s palace (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 5:11" id="c-p131.3" parsed="|2Sam|5|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.5.11">2 Sam. 5:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 7:2" id="c-p131.4" parsed="|2Sam|7|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.7.2">7:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 7:7" id="c-p131.5" parsed="|2Sam|7|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.7.7">7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 5:6" id="c-p131.6" parsed="|1Kgs|5|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.5.6">1 Kings 5:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 5:8" id="c-p131.7" parsed="|1Kgs|5|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.5.8">8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 5:10" id="c-p131.8" parsed="|1Kgs|5|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.5.10">10</scripRef>; 6:9, 10,
also in the building of the second temple under Zerubbabel (Ezra 3:7).
Of the ancient cedars of Lebanon there remain now only some
seven or eight. They are not standing together. But beside them
there are found between three hundred and four hundred of
younger growth. They stand in an amphitheatre fronting the west,
about 6,400 feet above the level of the sea.
The cedar is often figuratively alluded to in the sacred
Scriptures. “The mighty conquerors of olden days, the despots of
Assyria and the Pharaohs of Egypt, the proud and idolatrous
monarchs of Judah, the Hebrew commonwealth itself, the war-like
Ammonites of patriarchal times, and the moral majesty of the
Messianic age, are all compared to the towering cedar, in its

royal loftiness and supremacy (<scripRef passage="Isa. 2:13" id="c-p133.1" parsed="|Isa|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.2.13">Isa. 2:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 17:3" id="c-p133.2" parsed="|Ezek|17|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.17.3">Ezek. 17:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek 17:22" id="c-p133.3" parsed="|Ezek|17|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.17.22">22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek 17:23" id="c-p133.4" parsed="|Ezek|17|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.17.23">23</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek 17:31" id="c-p133.5" parsed="|Ezek|17|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.17.31">31</scripRef>:3-9; <scripRef passage="Amos 2:9" id="c-p133.6" parsed="|Amos|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.2.9">Amos 2:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 11:1" id="c-p133.7" parsed="|Zech|11|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.11.1">Zech. 11:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Zech 11:2" id="c-p133.8" parsed="|Zech|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.11.2">2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 40:17" id="c-p133.9" parsed="|Job|40|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.40.17">Job 40:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 29:5" id="c-p133.10" parsed="|Ps|29|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.29.5">Ps. 29:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 80:10" id="c-p133.11" parsed="|Ps|80|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.80.10">80:10</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Ps 92:12" id="c-p133.12" parsed="|Ps|92|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.92.12">92:12</scripRef>, etc).”, Groser’s Scrip. Nat. Hist. (See
BOX-TREE.)
</def>
<term id="c-p133.14">Cedron</term>
The black torrent, the brook flowing through the ravine below
the eastern wall of Jerusalem (John 18:1). (See KIDRON.)
</def>
<term id="c-p134.3">Ceiling</term>
The covering (1 Kings 7:3, 7) of the inside roof and walls of a

house with planks of wood (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 3:5" id="c-p135.3" parsed="|2Chr|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.3.5">2 Chr. 3:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 22:14" id="c-p135.4" parsed="|Jer|22|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.22.14">Jer. 22:14</scripRef>). Ceilings
were sometimes adorned with various ornaments in stucco, gold,
silver, gems, and ivory. The ceilings of the temple and of
Solomon’s palace are described 1 Kings 6:9, 15; 7:3; 2 Chr. 3:5, 9.
</def>
<term id="c-p135.9">Cellar</term>
A subterranean vault (1 Chr. 27:28), a storehouse. The word is
also used to denote the treasury of the temple (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 7:51" id="c-p136.2" parsed="|1Kgs|7|51|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.7.51">1 Kings 7:51</scripRef>)
and of the king (14:26). The Hebrew word is rendered “garner” in
Joel 1:17, and “armoury” in Jer. 50:25.
</def>
<term id="c-p136.5">Cenchrea</term>
Millet, the eastern harbour of Corinth, from which it was
distant about 9 miles east, and the outlet for its trade with
the Asiatic shores of the Mediterranean. When Paul returned from
his second missionary journey to Syria, he sailed from this port

(<scripRef passage="Acts 18:18" id="c-p137.1" parsed="|Acts|18|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.18">Acts 18:18</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="Rom. 16:1" id="c-p137.2" parsed="|Rom|16|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.16.1">Rom. 16:1</scripRef> he speaks as if there were at the
time of his writing that epistle an organized church there. The
western harbour of Corinth was Lechaeum, about a mile and a half
from the city. It was the channel of its trade with Italy and
the west.
</def>
<term id="c-p137.3">Censer</term>
The vessel in which incense was presented on “the golden altar”
before the Lord in the temple (<scripRef passage="Ex. 30:1-9" id="c-p138.1" parsed="|Exod|30|1|30|9" osisRef="Bible:Exod.30.1-Exod.30.9">Ex. 30:1-9</scripRef>). The priest filled
the censer with live coal from the sacred fire on the altar of
burnt-offering, and having carried it into the sanctuary, there

threw upon the burning coals the sweet incense (<scripRef passage="Lev. 16:12" id="c-p138.2" parsed="|Lev|16|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.16.12">Lev. 16:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 16:13" id="c-p138.3" parsed="|Lev|16|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.16.13">13</scripRef>),
which sent up a cloud of smoke, filling the apartment with
fragrance. The censers in daily use were of brass (<scripRef passage="Num. 16:39" id="c-p138.4" parsed="|Num|16|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.16.39">Num. 16:39</scripRef>),
and were designated by a different Hebrew name, miktereth (2 Chr. 26:19; Ezek. 8:11): while those used on the day of
Atonement were of gold, and were denoted by a word (mahtah)
meaning “something to take fire with;” LXX. pureion = a
fire-pan. Solomon prepared for the temple censers of pure gold

(<scripRef passage="1 Kings 7:50" id="c-p138.7" parsed="|1Kgs|7|50|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.7.50">1 Kings 7:50</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 4:22" id="c-p138.8" parsed="|2Chr|4|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.4.22">2 Chr. 4:22</scripRef>). The angel in the Apocalypse is

represented with a golden censer (<scripRef passage="Rev. 8:3" id="c-p138.9" parsed="|Rev|8|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.8.3">Rev. 8:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Rev. 8:5" id="c-p138.10" parsed="|Rev|8|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.8.5">5</scripRef>). Paul speaks of
the golden censer as belonging to the tabernacle (<scripRef passage="Heb. 9:4" id="c-p138.11" parsed="|Heb|9|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.4">Heb. 9:4</scripRef>). The
Greek word thumiaterion, here rendered “censer,” may more
appropriately denote, as in the margin of Revised Version, “the
altar of incense.” Paul does not here say that the thumiaterion
was in the holiest, for it was in the holy place, but that the

holiest had it, i.e., that it belonged to the holiest (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 6:22" id="c-p138.12" parsed="|1Kgs|6|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.6.22">1 Kings 6:22</scripRef>). It was intimately connected with the high priest’s
service in the holiest.
The manner in which the censer is to be used is described in
Num. 4:14; Lev. 16:12.
</def>
<term id="c-p139.3">Census</term>
There are five instances of a census of the Jewish people having
been taken. (1.) In the fourth month after the Exodus, when the
people were encamped at Sinai. The number of men from twenty
years old and upward was then 603,550 (<scripRef passage="Ex. 38:26" id="c-p140.1" parsed="|Exod|38|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.38.26">Ex. 38:26</scripRef>). (2.) Another
census was made just before the entrance into Canaan, when the
number was found to be 601,730, showing thus a small decrease
(<scripRef passage="Num. 26:51" id="c-p140.2" parsed="|Num|26|51|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.26.51">Num. 26:51</scripRef>). (3.) The next census was in the time of David,
when the number, exclusive of the tribes of Levi and Benjamin,

was found to be 1,300,000 (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 24:9" id="c-p140.3" parsed="|2Sam|24|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.24.9">2 Sam. 24:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 21:5" id="c-p140.4" parsed="|1Chr|21|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.21.5">1 Chr. 21:5</scripRef>). (4.)
Solomon made a census of the foreigners in the land, and found

153,600 able-bodied workmen (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 2:17" id="c-p140.5" parsed="|2Chr|2|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.2.17">2 Chr. 2:17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 2:18" id="c-p140.6" parsed="|2Chr|2|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.2.18">18</scripRef>). (5.) After the
return from Exile the whole congregation of Israel was numbered,
and found to amount to 42,360 (<scripRef passage="Ezra 2:64" id="c-p140.7" parsed="|Ezra|2|64|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2.64">Ezra 2:64</scripRef>). A census was made by
the Roman government in the time of our Lord (Luke 2:1). (See TAXING.)
</def>
<term id="c-p140.10">Centurion</term>
A Roman officer in command of a hundred men (Mark 15:39, 44, 45). Cornelius, the first Gentile convert, was a centurion (Acts 10:1, 22). Other centurions are mentioned in Matt. 8:5, 8, 13;

<scripRef passage="Luke 7:2" id="c-p141.9" parsed="|Luke|7|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.7.2">Luke 7:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Luke 7:6" id="c-p141.10" parsed="|Luke|7|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.7.6">6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 21:32" id="c-p141.11" parsed="|Acts|21|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.21.32">Acts 21:32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 22:25" id="c-p141.12" parsed="|Acts|22|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.22.25">22:25</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 22:26" id="c-p141.13" parsed="|Acts|22|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.22.26">26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 23:17" id="c-p141.14" parsed="|Acts|23|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.23.17">23:17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 23:23" id="c-p141.15" parsed="|Acts|23|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.23.23">23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 24:23" id="c-p141.16" parsed="|Acts|24|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.24.23">24:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 27:1" id="c-p141.17" parsed="|Acts|27|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.27.1">27:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 27:6" id="c-p141.18" parsed="|Acts|27|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.27.6">6</scripRef>,

<scripRef passage="Acts 27:11" id="c-p141.19" parsed="|Acts|27|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.27.11">11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 27:31" id="c-p141.20" parsed="|Acts|27|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.27.31">31</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 27:43" id="c-p141.21" parsed="|Acts|27|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.27.43">43</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 28:16" id="c-p141.22" parsed="|Acts|28|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.28.16">28:16</scripRef>. A centurion watched the crucifixion of our

Lord (<scripRef passage="Matt. 27:54" id="c-p141.23" parsed="|Matt|27|54|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.54">Matt. 27:54</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 23:47" id="c-p141.24" parsed="|Luke|23|47|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.23.47">Luke 23:47</scripRef>), and when he saw the wonders
attending it, exclaimed, “Truly this man was the Son of God.”
“The centurions mentioned in the New Testament are uniformly
spoken of in terms of praise, whether in the Gospels or in the
Acts. It is interesting to compare this with the statement of
Polybius (vi. 24), that the centurions were chosen by merit, and
so were men remarkable not so much for their daring courage as
for their deliberation, constancy, and strength of mind.”, Dr.
Maclear’s N. T. Hist.
</def>
<term id="c-p141.25">Cephas</term>
A Syriac surname given by Christ to Simon (John 1:42), meaning
“rock.” The Greeks translated it by Petros, and the Latins by
Petrus.
</def>
<term id="c-p142.2">Cesarea</term>
See CAESAREA.
</def>
<term id="c-p143.2">Chaff</term>
The refuse of winnowed corn. It was usually burned (Ex. 15:7;

<scripRef passage="Isa. 5:24" id="c-p144.2" parsed="|Isa|5|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.5.24">Isa. 5:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 3:12" id="c-p144.3" parsed="|Matt|3|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.12">Matt. 3:12</scripRef>). This word sometimes, however, means

dried grass or hay (<scripRef passage="Isa. 5:24" id="c-p144.4" parsed="|Isa|5|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.5.24">Isa. 5:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 33:11" id="c-p144.5" parsed="|Isa|33|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.33.11">33:11</scripRef>). Chaff is used as a figure

of abortive wickedness (<scripRef passage="Ps. 1:4" id="c-p144.6" parsed="|Ps|1|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.1.4">Ps. 1:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 3:12" id="c-p144.7" parsed="|Matt|3|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.12">Matt. 3:12</scripRef>). False doctrines
are also called chaff (<scripRef passage="Jer. 23:28" id="c-p144.8" parsed="|Jer|23|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.23.28">Jer. 23:28</scripRef>), or more correctly rendered
“chopped straw.” The destruction of the wicked, and their
powerlessness, are likened to the carrying away of chaff by the
wind (Isa. 17:13; Hos. 13:3; Zeph. 2:2).
</def>
<term id="c-p144.12">Chain</term>
(1.) A part of the insignia of office. A chain of gold was
placed about Joseph’s neck (<scripRef passage="Gen. 41:42" id="c-p145.1" parsed="|Gen|41|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.41.42">Gen. 41:42</scripRef>); and one was promised to

Daniel (5:7). It is used as a symbol of sovereignty (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 16:11" id="c-p145.2" parsed="|Ezek|16|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.16.11">Ezek. 16:11</scripRef>). The breast-plate of the high-priest was fastened to the
ephod by golden chains (Ex. 39:17, 21).
(2.) It was used as an ornament (Prov. 1:9; Cant. 1:10). The
Midianites adorned the necks of their camels with chains (Judg. 8:21, 26).
(3.) Chains were also used as fetters wherewith prisoners were

bound (<scripRef passage="Judg. 16:21" id="c-p147.1" parsed="|Judg|16|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.16.21">Judg. 16:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 3:34" id="c-p147.2" parsed="|2Sam|3|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.3.34">2 Sam. 3:34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 25:7" id="c-p147.3" parsed="|2Kgs|25|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.25.7">2 Kings 25:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 39:7" id="c-p147.4" parsed="|Jer|39|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.39.7">Jer. 39:7</scripRef>). Paul

was in this manner bound to a Roman soldier (<scripRef passage="Acts 28:20" id="c-p147.5" parsed="|Acts|28|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.28.20">Acts 28:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 6:20" id="c-p147.6" parsed="|Eph|6|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.6.20">Eph. 6:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Tim. 1:16" id="c-p147.7" parsed="|2Tim|1|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.1.16">2 Tim. 1:16</scripRef>). Sometimes, for the sake of greater security,
the prisoner was attached by two chains to two soldiers, as in
the case of Peter (Acts 12:6).
</def>
<term id="c-p147.9">Chalcedony</term>
Mentioned only in Rev. 21:19, as one of the precious stones in
the foundation of the New Jerusalem. The name of this stone is
derived from Chalcedon, where it is said to have been first
discovered. In modern mineralogy this is the name of an
