agate-like quartz of a bluish colour. Pliny so names the Indian
ruby. The mineral intended in Revelation is probably the Hebrew
nophekh, translated “emerald” (Ex. 28:18; 39:11; Ezek. 27:16;
<scripRef passage="Ezek 28:13" id="c-p148.5" parsed="|Ezek|28|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.28.13">28:13</scripRef>). It is rendered “anthrax” in the LXX., and “carbunculus”
in the Vulgate. (See CARBUNCLE.)
</def>
<term id="c-p148.7">Chaldea</term>
The southern portion of Babylonia, Lower Mesopotamia, lying
chiefly on the right bank of the Euphrates, but commonly used of
the whole of the Mesopotamian plain. The Hebrew name is Kasdim,
which is usually rendered “Chaldeans” (Jer. 50:10; 51:24, 35).
The country so named is a vast plain formed by the deposits of
the Euphrates and the Tigris, extending to about 400 miles along
the course of these rivers, and about 100 miles in average
breadth. “In former days the vast plains of Babylon were
nourished by a complicated system of canals and water-courses,
which spread over the surface of the country like a network. The
wants of a teeming population were supplied by a rich soil, not
less bountiful than that on the banks of the Egyptian Nile. Like
islands rising from a golden sea of waving corn stood frequent
groves of palm-trees and pleasant gardens, affording to the
idler or traveller their grateful and highly-valued shade.
Crowds of passengers hurried along the dusty roads to and from
the busy city. The land was rich in corn and wine.”
Recent discoveries, more especially in Babylonia, have thrown
much light on the history of the Hebrew patriarchs, and have
illustrated or confirmed the Biblical narrative in many points.
The ancestor of the Hebrew people, Abram, was, we are told, born
at “Ur of the Chaldees.” “Chaldees” is a mistranslation of the
Hebrew Kasdim, Kasdim being the Old Testament name of the
Babylonians, while the Chaldees were a tribe who lived on the
shores of the Persian Gulf, and did not become a part of the
Babylonian population till the time of Hezekiah. Ur was one of
the oldest and most famous of the Babylonian cities. Its site is
now called Mugheir, or Mugayyar, on the western bank of the
Euphrates, in Southern Babylonia. About a century before the
birth of Abram it was ruled by a powerful dynasty of kings.
Their conquests extended to Elam on the one side, and to the
Lebanon on the other. They were followed by a dynasty of princes
whose capital was Babylon, and who seem to have been of South
Arabian origin. The founder of the dynasty was Sumu-abi (“Shem
is my father”). But soon afterwards Babylonia fell under Elamite
dominion. The kings of Babylon were compelled to acknowledge the
supremacy of Elam, and a rival kingdom to that of Babylon, and
governed by Elamites, sprang up at Larsa, not far from Ur, but
on the opposite bank of the river. In the time of Abram the king
of Larsa was Eri-Aku, the son of an Elamite prince, and Eri-Aku,
as has long been recognized, is the Biblical “Arioch king of
Ellasar” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 14:1" id="c-p151.1" parsed="|Gen|14|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.1">Gen. 14:1</scripRef>). The contemporaneous king of Babylon in the
north, in the country termed Shinar in Scripture, was
Khammu-rabi. (See
BABYLON;
ABRAHAM;
AMRAPHEL.)
</def>
<term id="c-p151.5">Chaldee language</term>
Employed by the sacred writers in certain portions of the Old

Testament, viz., <scripRef passage="Dan. 2:4-7" id="c-p152.1" parsed="|Dan|2|4|2|7" osisRef="Bible:Dan.2.4-Dan.2.7">Dan. 2:4-7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan 2:28" id="c-p152.2" parsed="|Dan|2|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.2.28">28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezra 4:8-6:18" id="c-p152.3" parsed="|Ezra|4|8|6|18" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.4.8-Ezra.6.18">Ezra 4:8-6:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezra 7:12-26" id="c-p152.4" parsed="|Ezra|7|12|7|26" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.7.12-Ezra.7.26">7:12-26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen. 31:46" id="c-p152.5" parsed="|Gen|31|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.46">Gen. 31:46</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 10:11" id="c-p152.6" parsed="|Jer|10|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.10.11">Jer. 10:11</scripRef>. It is the Aramaic dialect, as it is sometimes
called, as distinguished from the Hebrew dialect. It was the
language of commerce and of social intercourse in Western Asia,
and after the Exile gradually came to be the popular language of
Palestine. It is called “Syrian” in <scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:26" id="c-p152.7" parsed="|2Kgs|18|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.26">2 Kings 18:26</scripRef>. Some isolated

words in this language are preserved in the New Testament (<scripRef passage="Matt. 5:22" id="c-p152.8" parsed="|Matt|5|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.22">Matt. 5:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 6:24" id="c-p152.9" parsed="|Matt|6|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.24">6:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 16:17" id="c-p152.10" parsed="|Matt|16|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.16.17">16:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 27:46" id="c-p152.11" parsed="|Matt|27|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.46">27:46</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 3:17" id="c-p152.12" parsed="|Mark|3|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.3.17">Mark 3:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 5:41" id="c-p152.13" parsed="|Mark|5|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.5.41">5:41</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 7:34" id="c-p152.14" parsed="|Mark|7|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.7.34">7:34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 14:36" id="c-p152.15" parsed="|Mark|14|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.14.36">14:36</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 1:19" id="c-p152.16" parsed="|Acts|1|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.19">Acts 1:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 16:22" id="c-p152.17" parsed="|1Cor|16|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.16.22">1 Cor. 16:22</scripRef>). These are specimens of the vernacular
language of Palestine at that period. The term “Hebrew” was also
sometimes applied to the Chaldee because it had become the
language of the Hebrews (John 5:2; 19:20).
</def>
<term id="c-p152.20">Chaldees</term>
Or Chaldeans, the inhabitants of the country of which Babylon
was the capital. They were so called till the time of the

Captivity (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 25" id="c-p153.1" parsed="|2Kgs|25|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.25">2 Kings 25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 13:19" id="c-p153.2" parsed="|Isa|13|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.13.19">Isa. 13:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 23:13" id="c-p153.3" parsed="|Isa|23|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.23.13">23:13</scripRef>), when, particularly in
the Book of Daniel (5:30; 9:1), the name began to be used with
special reference to a class of learned men ranked with the
magicians and astronomers. These men cultivated the ancient
Cushite language of the original inhabitants of the land, for
they had a “learning” and a “tongue” (1:4) of their own. The
common language of the country at that time had become
assimilated to the Semitic dialect, especially through the
influence of the Assyrians, and was the language that was used
for all civil purposes. The Chaldeans were the learned class,
interesting themselves in science and religion, which consisted,
like that of the ancient Arabians and Syrians, in the worship of
the heavenly bodies. There are representations of this priestly
class, of magi and diviners, on the walls of the Assyrian
palaces.
</def>
<term id="c-p153.4">Chamber</term>
“on the wall,” which the Shunammite prepared for the prophet
Elisha (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 4:10" id="c-p154.1" parsed="|2Kgs|4|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.4.10">2 Kings 4:10</scripRef>), was an upper chamber over the porch
through the hall toward the street. This was the “guest chamber”
where entertainments were prepared (<scripRef passage="Mark 14:14" id="c-p154.2" parsed="|Mark|14|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.14.14">Mark 14:14</scripRef>). There were also

“chambers within chambers” (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 22:25" id="c-p154.3" parsed="|1Kgs|22|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.22.25">1 Kings 22:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 9:2" id="c-p154.4" parsed="|2Kgs|9|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.9.2">2 Kings 9:2</scripRef>). To
enter into a chamber is used metaphorically of prayer and
communion with God (<scripRef passage="Isa. 26:20" id="c-p154.5" parsed="|Isa|26|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.26.20">Isa. 26:20</scripRef>). The “chambers of the south”
(<scripRef passage="Job 9:9" id="c-p154.6" parsed="|Job|9|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.9.9">Job 9:9</scripRef>) are probably the constelations of the southern
hemisphere. The “chambers of imagery”, i.e., chambers painted
with images, as used by Ezekiel (8:12), is an expression
denoting the vision the prophet had of the abominations
practised by the Jews in Jerusalem.
</def>
<term id="c-p154.7">Chambering</term>
(Rom. 13:13), wantonness, impurity.
</def>
<term id="c-p155.2">Chamberlain</term>
A confidential servant of the king (Gen. 37:36; 39:1). In Rom. 16:23 mention is made of “Erastus the chamberlain.” Here the
word denotes the treasurer of the city, or the quaestor, as the
Romans styled him. He is almost the only convert from the higher
ranks of whom mention is made (comp. <scripRef passage="Acts 17:34" id="c-p156.4" parsed="|Acts|17|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.17.34">Acts 17:34</scripRef>). Blastus,
Herod’s “chamberlain” (<scripRef passage="Acts 12:20" id="c-p156.5" parsed="|Acts|12|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.12.20">Acts 12:20</scripRef>), was his personal attendant
or valet-de-chambre. The Hebrew word saris, thus translated in

<scripRef passage="Esther 1:10" id="c-p156.6" parsed="|Esth|1|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.1.10">Esther 1:10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Esther 1:15" id="c-p156.7" parsed="|Esth|1|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.1.15">15</scripRef>; 2:3, 14, 21, etc., properly means an eunuch (as
in the marg.), as it is rendered in Isa. 39:7; 56:3.
</def>
<term id="c-p156.10">Chameleon</term>
A species of lizard which has the faculty of changing the colour
of its skin. It is ranked among the unclean animals in Lev. 11:30, where the Hebrew word so translated is coah (R.V.,
“land crocodile”). In the same verse the Hebrew tanshemeth,
rendered in Authorized Version “mole,” is in Revised Version
“chameleon,” which is the correct rendering. This animal is very
common in Egypt and in the Holy Land, especially in the Jordan
valley.
</def>
<term id="c-p157.2">Chamois</term>
Only in Deut. 14:5 (Heb. zemer), an animal of the deer or
gazelle species. It bears this Hebrew name from its leaping or
springing. The animal intended is probably the wild sheep (Ovis
tragelephus), which is still found in Sinai and in the broken
ridges of Stony Arabia. The LXX. and Vulgate render the word by
camelopardus, i.e., the giraffe; but this is an animal of
Central Africa, and is not at all known in Syria.
</def>
<term id="c-p158.2">Champion</term>
(1 Sam. 17:4, 23), properly “the man between the two,” denoting
the position of Goliath between the two camps. Single combats of
this kind at the head of armies were common in ancient times. In
ver. 51 this word is the rendering of a different Hebrew word,
and properly denotes “a mighty man.”
</def>
<term id="c-p159.3">Chance</term>
(Luke 10:31). “It was not by chance that the priest came down by
that road at that time, but by a specific arrangement and in
exact fulfilment of a plan; not the plan of the priest, nor the
plan of the wounded traveller, but the plan of God. By
coincidence (Gr. sungkuria) the priest came down, that is, by
the conjunction of two things, in fact, which were previously
constituted a pair in the providence of God. In the result they
fell together according to the omniscient Designer’s plan. This
is the true theory of the divine government.” Compare the

meeting of Philip with the Ethiopian (<scripRef passage="Acts 8:26" id="c-p160.2" parsed="|Acts|8|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.8.26">Acts 8:26</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 8:27" id="c-p160.3" parsed="|Acts|8|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.8.27">27</scripRef>). There is
no “chance” in God’s empire. “Chance” is only another word for
our want of knowledge as to the way in which one event falls in
with another (1 Sam. 6:9; Eccl. 9:11).
</def>
<term id="c-p160.6">Chancellor</term>
One who has judicial authority, literally, a “lord of
judgement;” a title given to the Persian governor of Samaria
(Ezra 4:8, 9, 17).
</def>
<term id="c-p161.4">Changes of raiment</term>
Were reckoned among the treasures of rich men (Gen. 45:22; Judg. 14:12, 13; 2 Kings 5:22, 23).
</def>
<term id="c-p162.6">Channel</term>
(1.) The bed of the sea or of a river (Ps. 18:15; Isa. 8:7).
(2.) The “chanelbone” (Job 31:22 marg.), properly “tube” or
“shaft,” an old term for the collar-bone.
</def>
<term id="c-p164.2">Chapel</term>
A holy place or sanctuary, occurs only in Amos 7:13, where one
of the idol priests calls Bethel “the king’s chapel.”
</def>
<term id="c-p165.2">Chapiter</term>
The ornamental head or capital of a pillar. Three Hebrew words
are so rendered. (1.) Cothereth (1 Kings 7:16; 2 Kings 25:17;
2 Chr. 4:12), meaning a “diadem” or “crown.” (2.) Tzepheth (2 Chr. 3:15). (3.) Rosh (Ex. 36:38; 38:17, 19, 28), properly a
“head” or “top.”
</def>
<term id="c-p166.9">Chapter</term>
The several books of the Old and New Testaments were from an
early time divided into chapters. The Pentateuch was divided by
the ancient Hebrews into 54 parshioth or sections, one of
which was read in the synagogue every Sabbath day (<scripRef passage="Acts. 13:15" id="c-p167.1" parsed="|Acts|13|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.13.15">Acts. 13:15</scripRef>).
These sections were afterwards divided into 669 sidrim or
orders of unequal length. The Prophets were divided in somewhat
the same manner into haphtaroth or passages.
In the early Latin and Greek versions of the Bible, similar
divisions of the several books were made. The New Testament
books were also divided into portions of various lengths under
different names, such as titles and heads or chapters.
In modern times this ancient example was imitated, and many
attempts of the kind were made before the existing division into
chapters was fixed. The Latin Bible published by Cardinal Hugo
of St. Cher in A.D. 1240 is generally regarded as the first
Bible that was divided into our present chapters, although it
appears that some of the chapters were fixed as early as A.D.
1059. This division into chapters came gradually to be adopted
in the published editions of the Hebrew, with some few
variations, and of the Greek Scriptures, and hence of other
versions.
</def>
<term id="c-p169.1">Charashim</term>
Craftsmen, a valley named in 1 Chr. 4:14. In Neh. 11:35 the
Hebrew word is rendered “valley of craftsmen” (R.V. marg.,
Geha-rashim). Nothing is known of it.
</def>
<term id="c-p170.3">Charger</term>
A bowl or deep dish. The silver vessels given by the heads of

the tribes for the services of the tabernacle are so named (<scripRef passage="Num. 7:13" id="c-p171.1" parsed="|Num|7|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.7.13">Num. 7:13</scripRef>, etc.). The “charger” in which the Baptist’s head was

presented was a platter or flat wooden trencher (<scripRef passage="Matt. 14:8" id="c-p171.2" parsed="|Matt|14|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.14.8">Matt. 14:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 14:11" id="c-p171.3" parsed="|Matt|14|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.14.11">11</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Mark 6:25" id="c-p171.4" parsed="|Mark|6|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.6.25">Mark 6:25</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Mark 6:28" id="c-p171.5" parsed="|Mark|6|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.6.28">28</scripRef>). The chargers of gold and silver of <scripRef passage="Ezra 1:9" id="c-p171.6" parsed="|Ezra|1|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.1.9">Ezra 1:9</scripRef> were
probably basins for receiving the blood of sacrifices.
</def>
<term id="c-p171.7">Chariot</term>
A vehicle generally used for warlike purposes. Sometimes, though
but rarely, it is spoken of as used for peaceful purposes.
The first mention of the chariot is when Joseph, as a mark of

distinction, was placed in Pharaoh’s second state chariot (<scripRef passage="Gen. 41:43" id="c-p173.1" parsed="|Gen|41|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.41.43">Gen. 41:43</scripRef>); and the next, when he went out in his own chariot to
meet his father Jacob (46:29). Chariots formed part of the
funeral procession of Jacob (50:9). When Pharaoh pursued the
Israelites he took 600 war-chariots with him (<scripRef passage="Ex. 14:7" id="c-p173.2" parsed="|Exod|14|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.14.7">Ex. 14:7</scripRef>). The
Canaanites in the valleys of Palestine had chariots of iron

(<scripRef passage="Josh. 17:18" id="c-p173.3" parsed="|Josh|17|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.17.18">Josh. 17:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 1:19" id="c-p173.4" parsed="|Judg|1|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.19">Judg. 1:19</scripRef>). Jabin, the king of Canaan, had 900
chariots (<scripRef passage="Judg. 4:3" id="c-p173.5" parsed="|Judg|4|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.4.3">Judg. 4:3</scripRef>); and in Saul’s time the Philistines had
30,000. In his wars with the king of Zobah and with the Syrians,

David took many chariots among the spoils (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 8:4" id="c-p173.6" parsed="|2Sam|8|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.8.4">2 Sam. 8:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 10:18" id="c-p173.7" parsed="|2Sam|10|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.10.18">10:18</scripRef>).

Solomon maintained as part of his army 1,400 chariots (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:26" id="c-p173.8" parsed="|1Kgs|10|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.26">1 Kings 10:26</scripRef>), which were chiefly imported from Egypt (29). From this
time forward they formed part of the armies of Israel (1 Kings 22:34; 2 Kings 9:16, 21; 13:7, 14; 18:24; 23:30).
In the New Testament we have only one historical reference to
the use of chariots, in the case of the Ethiopian eunuch (Acts. 8:28, 29, 38).
This word is sometimes used figuratively for hosts (Ps. 68:17;
<scripRef passage="2 Kings 6:17" id="c-p175.2" parsed="|2Kgs|6|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.6.17">2 Kings 6:17</scripRef>). Elijah, by his prayers and his counsel, was “the
chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof.” The rapid agency
of God in the phenomena of nature is also spoken of under the
similitude of a chariot (Ps. 104:3; Isa. 66:15; Hab. 3:8).
Chariot of the cherubim (1 Chr. 28:18), the chariot formed by
the two cherubs on the mercy-seat on which the Lord rides.
Chariot cities were set apart for storing the war-chariots in
time of peace (2 Chr. 1:14).
Chariot horses were such as were peculiarly fitted for service
in chariots (2 Kings 7:14).
Chariots of war are described in Ex. 14:7; 1 Sam. 13:5; 2 Sam. 8:4; 1 Chr. 18:4; Josh. 11:4; Judg. 4:3, 13. They were not used
by the Israelites till the time of David. Elijah was translated

in a “chariot of fire” (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 2:11" id="c-p179.8" parsed="|2Kgs|2|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.2.11">2 Kings 2:11</scripRef>). Comp. <scripRef passage="2 Kings 6:17" id="c-p179.9" parsed="|2Kgs|6|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.6.17">2 Kings 6:17</scripRef>. This
vision would be to Elisha a source of strength and
encouragement, for now he could say, “They that be with us are
more than they that be with them.”
</def>
<term id="c-p179.10">Charity</term>
(1 Cor. 13), the rendering in the Authorized Version of the word
which properly denotes love, and is frequently so rendered
(always so in the Revised Version). It is spoken of as the
greatest of the three Christian graces (1 Cor. 12:31-13:13).
</def>
<term id="c-p180.3">Charmer</term>
One who practises serpent-charming (Ps. 58:5; Jer. 8:17; Eccl. 10:11). It was an early and universal opinion that the most
venomous reptiles could be made harmless by certain charms or by
sweet sounds. It is well known that there are jugglers in India
and in other Eastern lands who practise this art at the present
day.
In Isa. 19:3 the word “charmers” is the rendering of the
Hebrew ’ittim, meaning, properly, necromancers (R.V. marg.,
“whisperers”). In <scripRef passage="Deut. 18:11" id="c-p182.2" parsed="|Deut|18|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.18.11">Deut. 18:11</scripRef> the word “charmer” means a dealer
in spells, especially one who, by binding certain knots, was
supposed thereby to bind a curse or a blessing on its object. In
<scripRef passage="Isa. 3:3" id="c-p182.3" parsed="|Isa|3|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.3">Isa. 3:3</scripRef> the words “eloquent orator” should be, as in the
Revised Version, “skilful enchanter.”
</def>
<term id="c-p182.4">Charran</term>
Another form (Acts 7:2, 4) of Haran (q.v.).
</def>
<term id="c-p183.3">Chebar</term>
Length, a river in the “land of the Chaldeans” (Ezek. 1:3), on
the banks of which were located some of the Jews of the

Captivity (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 1:1" id="c-p184.2" parsed="|Ezek|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.1.1">Ezek. 1:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek 3:15" id="c-p184.3" parsed="|Ezek|3|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.3.15">3:15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek 3:23" id="c-p184.4" parsed="|Ezek|3|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.3.23">23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek 10:15" id="c-p184.5" parsed="|Ezek|10|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.10.15">10:15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek 10:20" id="c-p184.6" parsed="|Ezek|10|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.10.20">20</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek 10:22" id="c-p184.7" parsed="|Ezek|10|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.10.22">22</scripRef>). It has been
supposed to be identical with the river Habor, the Chaboras, or
modern Khabour, which falls into the Euphrates at Circesium. To
the banks of this river some of the Israelites were removed by
the Assyrians (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:6" id="c-p184.8" parsed="|2Kgs|17|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.6">2 Kings 17:6</scripRef>). An opinion that has much to
support it is that the “Chebar” was the royal canal of
Nebuchadnezzar, the Nahr Malcha, the greatest in Mesopotamia,
which connected the Tigris with the Euphrates, in the excavation
of which the Jewish captives were probably employed.
</def>
<term id="c-p184.9">Chedorlaomer</term>
(= Khudur-Lagamar of the inscriptions), king of Elam. Many
centuries before the age of Abraham, Canaan and even the
Sinaitic peninsula had been conquered by Babylonian kings, and
in the time of Abraham himself Babylonia was ruled by a dynasty
which claimed sovereignity over Syria and Palestine. The kings
of the dynasty bore names which were not Babylonian, but at once
South Arabic and Hebrew. The most famous king of the dynasty was
Khammu-rabi, who united Babylonia under one rule, and made
Babylon its capital. When he ascended the throne, the country
was under the suzerainty of the Elamites, and was divided into
two kingdoms, that of Babylon (the Biblical Shinar) and that of
Larsa (the Biblical Ellasar). The king of Larsa was Eri-Aku
(“the servant of the moon-god”), the son of an Elamite prince,
Kudur-Mabug, who is entitled “the father of the land of the
Amorites.” A recently discovered tablet enumerates among the
enemies of Khammu-rabi, Kudur-Lagamar (“the servant of the
goddess Lagamar”) or Chedorlaomer, Eri-Aku or Arioch, and
Tudkhula or Tidal. Khammu-rabi, whose name is also read
Ammi-rapaltu or Amraphel by some scholars, succeeded in
overcoming Eri-Aku and driving the Elamites out of Babylonia.
Assur-bani-pal, the last of the Assyrian conquerors, mentions in
two inscriptions that he took Susa 1635 years after
Kedor-nakhunta, king of Elam, had conquered Babylonia. It was in
the year B.C. 660 that Assur-bani-pal took Susa.
</def>
<term id="c-p185.1">Cheek</term>
Smiting on the cheek was accounted a grievous injury and insult

(<scripRef passage="Job 16:10" id="c-p186.1" parsed="|Job|16|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.16.10">Job 16:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lam. 3:30" id="c-p186.2" parsed="|Lam|3|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lam.3.30">Lam. 3:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Micah 5:1" id="c-p186.3" parsed="|Mic|5|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.5.1">Micah 5:1</scripRef>). The admonition (<scripRef passage="Luke 6:29" id="c-p186.4" parsed="|Luke|6|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.6.29">Luke 6:29</scripRef>),
“Unto him that smiteth thee on the one cheek offer also the

other,” means simply, “Resist not evil” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 5:39" id="c-p186.5" parsed="|Matt|5|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.39">Matt. 5:39</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Pet. 2:19-23" id="c-p186.6" parsed="|1Pet|2|19|2|23" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.2.19-1Pet.2.23">1 Pet. 2:19-23</scripRef>). <scripRef passage="Ps. 3:7" id="c-p186.7" parsed="|Ps|3|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.3.7">Ps. 3:7</scripRef> = that God had deprived his enemies of the
power of doing him injury.
</def>
<term id="c-p186.8">Cheese</term>
(A.S. cese). This word occurs three times in the Authorized
Version as the translation of three different Hebrew words: (1.)

<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:18" id="c-p187.1" parsed="|1Sam|17|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.18">1 Sam. 17:18</scripRef>, “ten cheeses;” i.e., ten sections of curd. (2.) <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 17:29" id="c-p187.2" parsed="|2Sam|17|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.17.29">2 Sam. 17:29</scripRef>, “cheese of kine” = perhaps curdled milk of kine. The
Vulgate version reads “fat calves.” (3.) <scripRef passage="Job 10:10" id="c-p187.3" parsed="|Job|10|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.10.10">Job 10:10</scripRef>, curdled milk
is meant by the word.
</def>
<term id="c-p187.4">Chemarim</term>
Black, (Zeph. 1:4; rendered “idolatrous priests” in 2 Kings 23:5, and “priests” in Hos. 10:5). Some derive this word from
the Assyrian Kamaru, meaning “to throw down,” and interpret it
as describing the idolatrous priests who prostrate themselves
before the idols. Others regard it as meaning “those who go
about in black,” or “ascetics.”
</def>
<term id="c-p188.4">Chemosh</term>
The destroyer, subduer, or fish-god, the god of the Moabites

(<scripRef passage="Num. 21:29" id="c-p189.1" parsed="|Num|21|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.21.29">Num. 21:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 48:7" id="c-p189.2" parsed="|Jer|48|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.7">Jer. 48:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer. 48:13" id="c-p189.3" parsed="|Jer|48|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.13">13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer. 48:46" id="c-p189.4" parsed="|Jer|48|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.46">46</scripRef>). The worship of this god, “the

abomination of Moab,” was introduced at Jerusalem by Solomon (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 11:7" id="c-p189.5" parsed="|1Kgs|11|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.11.7">1 Kings 11:7</scripRef>), but was abolished by Josiah (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 23:13" id="c-p189.6" parsed="|2Kgs|23|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.13">2 Kings 23:13</scripRef>). On the
“Moabite Stone” (q.v.), Mesha (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 3:5" id="c-p189.7" parsed="|2Kgs|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.3.5">2 Kings 3:5</scripRef>) ascribes his
victories over the king of Israel to this god, “And Chemosh
drove him before my sight.”
</def>
<term id="c-p189.8">Chenaanah</term>
Merchant. (1.) A Benjamite (1 Chr. 7:10). (2.) The father of
Zedekiah (1 Kings 22:11, 24).
</def>
<term id="c-p190.4">Chenaiah</term>
Whom Jehovah hath made. “Chief of the Levites,” probably a
Kohathite (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 15:22" id="c-p191.1" parsed="|1Chr|15|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.15.22">1 Chr. 15:22</scripRef>), and therefore not the same as
mentioned in 26:29.
</def>
<term id="c-p191.2">Chephirah</term>
Village, one of the four cities of the Gibeonitish Hivites with
whom Joshua made a league (9:17). It belonged to Benjamin. It
has been identified with the modern Kefireh, on the west
confines of Benjamin, about 2 miles west of Ajalon and 11 from
Jerusalem.
</def>
<term id="c-p192.1">Cherethim</term>
(Ezek. 25:16), more frequently Cherethites, the inhabitants of
Southern Philistia, the Philistines (<scripRef passage="Zeph. 2:5" id="c-p193.2" parsed="|Zeph|2|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zeph.2.5">Zeph. 2:5</scripRef>). The Cherethites

and the Pelethites were David’s life-guards (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 30:14" id="c-p193.3" parsed="|1Sam|30|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.30.14">1 Sam. 30:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 8:18" id="c-p193.4" parsed="|2Sam|8|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.8.18">2 Sam. 8:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 20:7" id="c-p193.5" parsed="|2Sam|20|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.20.7">20:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 20:23" id="c-p193.6" parsed="|2Sam|20|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.20.23">23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 23:23" id="c-p193.7" parsed="|2Sam|23|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.23.23">23:23</scripRef>). This name is by some interpreted as
meaning “Cretans,” and by others “executioners,” who were ready
to execute the king’s sentence of death (Gen. 37:36, marg.; 1 Kings 2:25).
</def>
<term id="c-p193.10">Cherith</term>
A cutting; separation; a gorge, a torrent-bed or winter-stream,
a “brook,” in whose banks the prophet Elijah hid himself during

the early part of the three years’ drought (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 17:3" id="c-p194.1" parsed="|1Kgs|17|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.17.3">1 Kings 17:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 17:5" id="c-p194.2" parsed="|1Kgs|17|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.17.5">5</scripRef>). It
has by some been identified as the Wady el-Kelt behind Jericho,
which is formed by the junction of many streams flowing from the
mountains west of Jericho. It is dry in summer. Travellers have
described it as one of the wildest ravines of this wild region,
and peculiarly fitted to afford a secure asylum to the
persecuted. But if the prophet’s interview with Ahab was in
Samaria, and he thence journeyed toward the east, it is probable
that he crossed Jordan and found refuge in some of the ravines
of Gilead. The “brook” is said to have been “before Jordan,”
which probably means that it opened toward that river, into
which it flowed. This description would apply to the east as
well as to the west of Jordan. Thus Elijah’s hiding-place may
have been the Jermuk, in the territory of the half-tribe of
Manasseh.
</def>
<term id="c-p194.3">Cherub</term>
Plural cherubim, the name of certain symbolical figures
frequently mentioned in Scripture. They are first mentioned in
connection with the expulsion of our first parents from Eden
(<scripRef passage="Gen. 3:24" id="c-p195.1" parsed="|Gen|3|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.3.24">Gen. 3:24</scripRef>). There is no intimation given of their shape or
form. They are next mentioned when Moses was commanded to

provide furniture for the tabernacle (<scripRef passage="Ex. 25:17-20" id="c-p195.2" parsed="|Exod|25|17|25|20" osisRef="Bible:Exod.25.17-Exod.25.20">Ex. 25:17-20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 26:1" id="c-p195.3" parsed="|Exod|26|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.26.1">26:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex 26:31" id="c-p195.4" parsed="|Exod|26|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.26.31">31</scripRef>).
God promised to commune with Moses “from between the cherubim”
(25:22). This expression was afterwards used to denote the

Divine abode and presence (<scripRef passage="Num. 7:89" id="c-p195.5" parsed="|Num|7|89|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.7.89">Num. 7:89</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 4:4" id="c-p195.6" parsed="|1Sam|4|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.4.4">1 Sam. 4:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 37:16" id="c-p195.7" parsed="|Isa|37|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.37.16">Isa. 37:16</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Ps. 80:1" id="c-p195.8" parsed="|Ps|80|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.80.1">Ps. 80:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 99:1" id="c-p195.9" parsed="|Ps|99|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.99.1">99:1</scripRef>). In Ezekiel’s vision (10:1-20) they appear as
living creatures supporting the throne of God. From Ezekiel’s
description of them (1;10; 41:18, 19), they appear to have been
compound figures, unlike any real object in nature; artificial
images possessing the features and properties of several
animals. Two cherubim were placed on the mercy-seat of the ark;
two of colossal size overshadowed it in Solomon’s temple.
Ezekiel (1:4-14) speaks of four; and this number of “living
creatures” is mentioned in <scripRef passage="Rev. 4:6" id="c-p195.10" parsed="|Rev|4|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.4.6">Rev. 4:6</scripRef>. Those on the ark are called
the “cherubim of glory” (<scripRef passage="Heb. 9:5" id="c-p195.11" parsed="|Heb|9|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.5">Heb. 9:5</scripRef>), i.e., of the Shechinah, or
cloud of glory, for on them the visible glory of God rested.
They were placed one at each end of the mercy-seat, with wings
stretched upward, and their faces “toward each other and toward
the mercy-seat.” They were anointed with holy oil, like the ark
itself and the other sacred furniture.
The cherubim were symbolical. They were intended to represent
spiritual existences in immediate contact with Jehovah. Some
have regarded them as symbolical of the chief ruling power by
which God carries on his operations in providence (<scripRef passage="Ps. 18:10" id="c-p196.1" parsed="|Ps|18|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.18.10">Ps. 18:10</scripRef>).
Others interpret them as having reference to the redemption of
men, and as symbolizing the great rulers or ministers of the
church. Many other opinions have been held regarding them which
need not be referred to here. On the whole, it seems to be most
satisfactory to regard the interpretation of the symbol to be
variable, as is the symbol itself.
Their office was, (1) on the expulsion of our first parents
from Eden, to prevent all access to the tree of life; and (2) to
form the throne and chariot of Jehovah in his manifestation of
himself on earth. He dwelleth between and sitteth on the
cherubim (1 Sam. 4:4; Ps. 80:1; Ezek. 1:26, 28).
</def>
<term id="c-p197.5">Chesalon</term>
Strength; confidence, a place on the border of Judah, on the
side of Mount Jearim (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:10" id="c-p198.1" parsed="|Josh|15|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.10">Josh. 15:10</scripRef>); probably identified with the
modern village of Kesla, on the western mountains of Judah.
</def>
<term id="c-p198.2">Chesed</term>
Gain, the son of Nahor (Gen. 22:22).
</def>
<term id="c-p199.2">Chesil</term>
Ungodly, a town in the south of Judah (Josh. 15:30); probably
the same as Bethul (19:4) and Bethuel (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 4:30" id="c-p200.2" parsed="|1Chr|4|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.4.30">1 Chr. 4:30</scripRef>); now
Khelasa.
</def>
<term id="c-p200.3">Chest</term>
(Heb. ’aron, generally rendered “ark”), the coffer into which

the contributions for the repair of the temple were put (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 12:9" id="c-p201.1" parsed="|2Kgs|12|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.12.9">2 Kings 12:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 12:10" id="c-p201.2" parsed="|2Kgs|12|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.12.10">10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 24:8" id="c-p201.3" parsed="|2Chr|24|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.24.8">2 Chr. 24:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 24:10" id="c-p201.4" parsed="|2Chr|24|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.24.10">10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 24:11" id="c-p201.5" parsed="|2Chr|24|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.24.11">11</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="Gen. 50:26" id="c-p201.6" parsed="|Gen|50|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.50.26">Gen. 50:26</scripRef> it is rendered
“coffin.” In Ezek. 27:24 a different Hebrew word, genazim
(plur.), is used. It there means “treasure-chests.”
</def>
<term id="c-p201.8">Chestnut tree</term>
(Heb. ’armon; i.e., “naked”), mentioned in connection with
Jacob’s artifice regarding the cattle (<scripRef passage="Gen. 30:37" id="c-p202.1" parsed="|Gen|30|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.30.37">Gen. 30:37</scripRef>). It is one of
the trees of which, because of its strength and beauty, the
Assyrian empire is likened (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 31:8" id="c-p202.2" parsed="|Ezek|31|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.31.8">Ezek. 31:8</scripRef>; R.V., “plane trees”). It
is probably the Oriental plane tree (Platanus orientalis) that
is intended. It is a characteristic of this tree that it
annually sheds its outer bark, becomes “naked.” The chestnut
tree proper is not a native of Palestine.
</def>
<term id="c-p202.3">Chesulloth</term>
Fertile places; the loins, a town of Issachar, on the slopes of
some mountain between Jezreel and Shunem (<scripRef passage="Josh. 19:18" id="c-p203.1" parsed="|Josh|19|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.18">Josh. 19:18</scripRef>). It has
been identified with Chisloth-tabor, 2 1/2 miles to the west of
Mount Tabor, and north of Jezreel; now Iksal.
</def>
<term id="c-p203.2">Chezib</term>
Deceitful, a town where Shelah, the son of Judah, was born (Gen. 38:5). Probably the same as Achzib (q.v.).
</def>
<term id="c-p204.2">Chidon</term>
Dart, the name of the threshing-floor at which the death of
Uzzah took place (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 13:9" id="c-p205.1" parsed="|1Chr|13|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.13.9">1 Chr. 13:9</scripRef>). In the parallel passage in
Samuel (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 6:6" id="c-p205.2" parsed="|2Sam|6|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.6.6">2 Sam. 6:6</scripRef>) it is called “Nachon’s threshing-floor.” It
was a place not far north-west from Jerusalem.
</def>
<term id="c-p205.3">Chief of the three</term>
A title given to Adino the Eznite, one of David’s greatest
heroes (2 Sam. 23:8); also called Jashobeam (1 Chr. 11:11).
</def>
<term id="c-p206.3">Chief priest</term>
See PRIEST.
</def>
<term id="c-p207.2">Chiefs of Asia</term>
“Asiarchs,” the title given to certain wealthy persons annually
appointed to preside over the religious festivals and games in
the various cities of proconsular Asia (<scripRef passage="Acts 19:31" id="c-p208.1" parsed="|Acts|19|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.31">Acts 19:31</scripRef>). Some of
these officials appear to have been Paul’s friends.
</def>
<term id="c-p208.2">Child</term>
This word has considerable latitude of meaning in Scripture.
Thus Joseph is called a child at the time when he was probably
about sixteen years of age (<scripRef passage="Gen. 37:3" id="c-p209.1" parsed="|Gen|37|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.3">Gen. 37:3</scripRef>); and Benjamin is so
called when he was above thirty years (44:20). Solomon called
himself a little child when he came to the kingdom (1 Kings 3:7).
The descendants of a man, however remote, are called his
children; as, “the children of Edom,” “the children of Moab,”
“the children of Israel.”
In the earliest times mothers did not wean their children till
they were from thirty months to three years old; and the day on
which they were weaned was kept as a festival day (<scripRef passage="Gen. 21:8" id="c-p211.1" parsed="|Gen|21|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.8">Gen. 21:8</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Ex. 2:7" id="c-p211.2" parsed="|Exod|2|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.2.7">Ex. 2:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 2:9" id="c-p211.3" parsed="|Exod|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.2.9">9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 1:22-24" id="c-p211.4" parsed="|1Sam|1|22|1|24" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.1.22-1Sam.1.24">1 Sam. 1:22-24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 21:16" id="c-p211.5" parsed="|Matt|21|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.21.16">Matt. 21:16</scripRef>). At the age of five,
children began to learn the arts and duties of life under the
care of their fathers (Deut. 6:20-25; 11:19).
To have a numerous family was regarded as a mark of divine

favour (<scripRef passage="Gen. 11:30" id="c-p212.1" parsed="|Gen|11|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.11.30">Gen. 11:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 30:1" id="c-p212.2" parsed="|Gen|30|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.30.1">30:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 2:5" id="c-p212.3" parsed="|1Sam|2|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.2.5">1 Sam. 2:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 6:23" id="c-p212.4" parsed="|2Sam|6|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.6.23">2 Sam. 6:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 127:3" id="c-p212.5" parsed="|Ps|127|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.127.3">Ps. 127:3</scripRef>;
128:3).
Figuratively the name is used for those who are ignorant or

narrow-minded (<scripRef passage="Matt. 11:16" id="c-p213.1" parsed="|Matt|11|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.11.16">Matt. 11:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 7:32" id="c-p213.2" parsed="|Luke|7|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.7.32">Luke 7:32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 13:11" id="c-p213.3" parsed="|1Cor|13|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.13.11">1 Cor. 13:11</scripRef>). “When I
was a child, I spake as a child.” “Brethren, be not children in
understanding” (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 14:20" id="c-p213.4" parsed="|1Cor|14|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.14.20">1 Cor. 14:20</scripRef>). “That we henceforth be no more
children, tossed to and fro” (Eph. 4:14).
Children are also spoken of as representing simplicity and

humility (<scripRef passage="Matt. 19:13-15" id="c-p214.1" parsed="|Matt|19|13|19|15" osisRef="Bible:Matt.19.13-Matt.19.15">Matt. 19:13-15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 10:13-16" id="c-p214.2" parsed="|Mark|10|13|10|16" osisRef="Bible:Mark.10.13-Mark.10.16">Mark 10:13-16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 18:15-17" id="c-p214.3" parsed="|Luke|18|15|18|17" osisRef="Bible:Luke.18.15-Luke.18.17">Luke 18:15-17</scripRef>).

Believers are “children of light” (<scripRef passage="Luke 16:8" id="c-p214.4" parsed="|Luke|16|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.16.8">Luke 16:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Thess. 5:5" id="c-p214.5" parsed="|1Thess|5|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Thess.5.5">1 Thess. 5:5</scripRef>) and
“children of obedience” (1 Pet. 1:14).
</def>
<term id="c-p214.7">Chileab</term>
Protected by the father, David’s second son by Abigail (2 Sam. 3:3); called also Daniel (1 Chr. 3:1). He seems to have died
when young.
</def>
<term id="c-p215.3">Chilion</term>
The pining one, the younger son of Elimelech and Naomi, and
husband of Orpah, Ruth’s sister (Ruth 1:2; 4:9).
</def>
<term id="c-p216.3">Chilmad</term>
A place or country unknown which, along with Sheba and Asshur,
traded with Tyre (Ezek. 27:23).
</def>
<term id="c-p217.2">Chimham</term>
Pining, probably the youngest son of Barzillai the Gileadite (2 Sam. 19:37-40). The “habitation of Chimham” (Jer. 41:17) was
probably an inn or khan, which is the proper meaning of the
Hebrew geruth, rendered “habitation”, established in later
times in his possession at Bethlehem, which David gave to him as
a reward for his loyalty in accompanying him to Jerusalem after
the defeat of Absalom (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 2:7" id="c-p218.3" parsed="|1Kgs|2|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.2.7">1 Kings 2:7</scripRef>). It has been supposed that,
considering the stationary character of Eastern institutions, it
was in the stable of this inn or caravanserai that our Saviour
was born (Luke 2:7).
</def>
<term id="c-p218.5">Chinnereth</term>
Lyre, the singular form of the word (Deut. 3:17; Josh. 19:35),
which is also used in the plural form, Chinneroth, the name of a
fenced city which stood near the shore of the lake of Galilee, a
little to the south of Tiberias. The town seems to have given
its name to a district, as appears from <scripRef passage="1 Kings 15:20" id="c-p219.3" parsed="|1Kgs|15|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.15.20">1 Kings 15:20</scripRef>, where the
plural form of the word is used.
The Sea of Chinnereth (Num. 34:11; Josh. 13:27), or of
Chinneroth (<scripRef passage="Josh. 12" id="c-p220.3" parsed="|Josh|12|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.12">Josh. 12</scripRef>: 3), was the “lake of Gennesaret” or “sea

of Tiberias” (<scripRef passage="Deut. 3:17" id="c-p220.4" parsed="|Deut|3|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.17">Deut. 3:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 11:2" id="c-p220.5" parsed="|Josh|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.2">Josh. 11:2</scripRef>). Chinnereth was probably
an ancient Canaanitish name adopted by the Israelites into their
language.
</def>
<term id="c-p220.6">Chios</term>
Mentioned in Acts 20:15, an island in the Aegean Sea, about 5
miles distant from the mainland, having a roadstead, in the
shelter of which Paul and his companions anchored for a night
when on his third missionary return journey. It is now called
Scio.
</def>
<term id="c-p221.2">Chisleu</term>
The name adopted from the Babylonians by the Jews after the
Captivity for the third civil, or ninth ecclesiastical, month

(<scripRef passage="Neh. 1:1" id="c-p222.1" parsed="|Neh|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.1.1">Neh. 1:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 7:1" id="c-p222.2" parsed="|Zech|7|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.7.1">Zech. 7:1</scripRef>). It corresponds nearly with the moon in
November.
</def>
<term id="c-p222.3">Chittim</term>
Or Kittim, a plural form (Gen. 10:4), the name of a branch of
the descendants of Javan, the “son” of Japheth. Balaam foretold
(<scripRef passage="Num. 24:24" id="c-p223.2" parsed="|Num|24|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.24.24">Num. 24:24</scripRef>) “that ships shall come from the coast of Chittim,
and afflict Eber.” Daniel prophesied (11:30) that the ships of
Chittim would come against the king of the north. It probably
denotes Cyprus, whose ancient capital was called Kition by the
Greeks.
The references elsewhere made to Chittim (Isa. 23:1, 12; Jer. 2:10; Ezek. 27:6) are to be explained on the ground that while
the name originally designated the Phoenicians only, it came
latterly to be used of all the islands and various settlements
on the sea-coasts which they had occupied, and then of the
people who succeeded them when the Phoenician power decayed.
Hence it designates generally the islands and coasts of the
Mediterranean and the races that inhabit them.
</def>
<term id="c-p224.5">Chiun</term>
Occurs only in Amos 5:26 (R.V. marg., “shrine”). The LXX.
translated the word by Rhephan, which became corrupted into
Remphan, as used by Stephen (<scripRef passage="Acts 7:43" id="c-p225.2" parsed="|Acts|7|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.7.43">Acts 7:43</scripRef>; but R.V., “Rephan”).
Probably the planet Saturn is intended by the name. Astrologers
represented this planet as baleful in its influences, and hence
the Phoenicians offered to it human sacrifices, especially
children.
</def>
<term id="c-p225.3">Chloe</term>
Verdure, a female Christian (1 Cor. 1:11), some of whose
household had informed Paul of the divided state of the
Corinthian church. Nothing is known of her.
</def>
<term id="c-p226.2">Chor-ashan</term>
Smoking furnace, one of the places where “David himself and his

men were wont to haunt” (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 30:30" id="c-p227.1" parsed="|1Sam|30|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.30.30">1 Sam. 30:30</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 30:31" id="c-p227.2" parsed="|1Sam|30|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.30.31">31</scripRef>). It is probably

identical with Ashan (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:42" id="c-p227.3" parsed="|Josh|15|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.42">Josh. 15:42</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 19:7" id="c-p227.4" parsed="|Josh|19|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.7">19:7</scripRef>), a Simeonite city in
the Negeb, i.e., the south, belonging to Judah. The word ought,
according to another reading, to be “Bor-ashan.”
</def>
<term id="c-p227.5">Chorazin</term>
Named along with Bethsaida and Capernaum as one of the cities in
which our Lord’s “mighty works” were done, and which was doomed

to woe because of signal privileges neglected (<scripRef passage="Matt. 11:21" id="c-p228.1" parsed="|Matt|11|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.11.21">Matt. 11:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 10:13" id="c-p228.2" parsed="|Luke|10|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.10.13">Luke 10:13</scripRef>). It has been identified by general consent with the
modern Kerazeh, about 2 1/2 miles up the Wady Kerazeh from
Capernaum; i.e., Tell Hum.
</def>
<term id="c-p228.3">Chosen</term>
Spoken of warriors (Ex. 15:4; Judg. 20:16), of the Hebrew nation

(<scripRef passage="Ps. 105:43" id="c-p229.3" parsed="|Ps|105|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.105.43">Ps. 105:43</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 7:7" id="c-p229.4" parsed="|Deut|7|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.7.7">Deut. 7:7</scripRef>), of Jerusalem as the seat of the temple

(<scripRef passage="1 Kings 11:13" id="c-p229.5" parsed="|1Kgs|11|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.11.13">1 Kings 11:13</scripRef>). Christ is the “chosen” of God (<scripRef passage="Isa. 42:1" id="c-p229.6" parsed="|Isa|42|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.42.1">Isa. 42:1</scripRef>); and
the apostles are “chosen” for their work (<scripRef passage="Acts 10:41" id="c-p229.7" parsed="|Acts|10|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.10.41">Acts 10:41</scripRef>). It is
said with regard to those who do not profit by their
opportunities that “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16). (See ELECTION.)
</def>
<term id="c-p229.10">Chozeba</term>
(1 Chr. 4:22), the same as Chezib and Achzib, a place in the
lowlands of Judah (Gen. 38:5; Josh. 15:44).
</def>
<term id="c-p230.4">Christ</term>
Anointed, the Greek translation of the Hebrew word rendered
“Messiah” (q.v.), the official title of our Lord, occurring five
hundred and fourteen times in the New Testament. It denotes that
he was anointed or consecrated to his great redemptive work as
Prophet, Priest, and King of his people. He is Jesus the Christ

(<scripRef passage="Acts 17:3" id="c-p231.1" parsed="|Acts|17|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.17.3">Acts 17:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 18:5" id="c-p231.2" parsed="|Acts|18|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.5">18:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 22:42" id="c-p231.3" parsed="|Matt|22|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.22.42">Matt. 22:42</scripRef>), the Anointed One. He is thus
spoken of by Isaiah (61:1), and by Daniel (9:24-26), who styles
him “Messiah the Prince.”
The Messiah is the same person as “the seed of the woman”

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 3:15" id="c-p232.1" parsed="|Gen|3|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.3.15">Gen. 3:15</scripRef>), “the seed of Abraham” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 22:18" id="c-p232.2" parsed="|Gen|22|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.22.18">Gen. 22:18</scripRef>), the “Prophet
like unto Moses” (<scripRef passage="Deut. 18:15" id="c-p232.3" parsed="|Deut|18|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.18.15">Deut. 18:15</scripRef>), “the priest after the order of
Melchizedek” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 110:4" id="c-p232.4" parsed="|Ps|110|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.110.4">Ps. 110:4</scripRef>), “the rod out of the stem of Jesse”

(<scripRef passage="Isa. 11:1" id="c-p232.5" parsed="|Isa|11|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.11.1">Isa. 11:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 11:10" id="c-p232.6" parsed="|Isa|11|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.11.10">10</scripRef>), the “Immanuel,” the virgin’s son (<scripRef passage="Isa. 7:14" id="c-p232.7" parsed="|Isa|7|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.7.14">Isa. 7:14</scripRef>),
“the branch of Jehovah” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 4:2" id="c-p232.8" parsed="|Isa|4|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.4.2">Isa. 4:2</scripRef>), and “the messenger of the
covenant” (<scripRef passage="Mal. 3:1" id="c-p232.9" parsed="|Mal|3|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mal.3.1">Mal. 3:1</scripRef>). This is he “of whom Moses in the law and
the prophets did write.” The Old Testament Scripture is full of
prophetic declarations regarding the Great Deliverer and the
work he was to accomplish. Jesus the Christ is Jesus the Great
Deliverer, the Anointed One, the Saviour of men. This name
denotes that Jesus was divinely appointed, commissioned, and

accredited as the Saviour of men (<scripRef passage="Heb. 5:4" id="c-p232.10" parsed="|Heb|5|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.5.4">Heb. 5:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 11:2-4" id="c-p232.11" parsed="|Isa|11|2|11|4" osisRef="Bible:Isa.11.2-Isa.11.4">Isa. 11:2-4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 49:6" id="c-p232.12" parsed="|Isa|49|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.49.6">49:6</scripRef>;
John 5:37; Acts 2:22).
To believe that “Jesus is the Christ” is to believe that he is
the Anointed, the Messiah of the prophets, the Saviour sent of
God, that he was, in a word, what he claimed to be. This is to
believe the gospel, by the faith of which alone men can be
brought unto God. That Jesus is the Christ is the testimony of
God, and the faith of this constitutes a Christian (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 12:3" id="c-p233.1" parsed="|1Cor|12|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.12.3">1 Cor. 12:3</scripRef>;
1 John 5:1).
</def>
<term id="c-p233.3">Christian</term>
The name given by the Greeks or Romans, probably in reproach, to
the followers of Jesus. It was first used at Antioch. The names
by which the disciples were known among themselves were
“brethren,” “the faithful,” “elect,” “saints,” “believers.” But
as distinguishing them from the multitude without, the name
“Christian” came into use, and was universally accepted. This
name occurs but three times in the New Testament (<scripRef passage="Acts 11:26" id="c-p234.1" parsed="|Acts|11|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.26">Acts 11:26</scripRef>;
26:28; 1 Pet. 4:16).
</def>
<term id="c-p234.4">Christs, False</term>
Our Lord warned his disciples that they would arise (Matt. 24:24). It is said that no fewer than twenty-four persons have
at different times appeared (the last in 1682) pretending to be
the Messiah of the prophets.
</def>
<term id="c-p235.2">Chronicles</term>
The words of the days, (1 Kings 14:19; 1 Chr. 27:24), the daily
or yearly records of the transactions of the kingdom; events
recorded in the order of time.
</def>
<term id="c-p236.3">Chronicles, Books of</term>
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=Chronicles,%20Books%20of" id="c-p236.5" />
The two books were originally one. They bore the title in the
Massoretic Hebrew Dibre hayyamim, i.e., “Acts of the Days.”
This title was rendered by Jerome in his Latin version
“Chronicon,” and hence “Chronicles.” In the Septuagint version
the book is divided into two, and bears the title Paraleipomena,
i.e., “things omitted,” or “supplements”, because containing
many things omitted in the Books of Kings.
The contents of these books are comprehended under four heads.
(1.) The first nine chapters of Book I. contain little more than
a list of genealogies in the line of Israel down to the time of
David. (2.) The remainder of the first book contains a history
of the reign of David. (3.) The first nine chapters of Book II.
contain the history of the reign of Solomon. (4.) The remaining
chapters of the second book contain the history of the separate
kingdom of Judah to the time of the return from Babylonian
Exile.
The time of the composition of the Chronicles was, there is
every ground to conclude, subsequent to the Babylonian Exile,
probably between 450 and 435 B.C. The contents of this twofold
book, both as to matter and form, correspond closely with this
idea. The close of the book records the proclamation of Cyrus
permitting the Jews to return to their own land, and this forms
the opening passage of the Book of Ezra, which must be viewed as
a continuation of the Chronicles. The peculiar form of the
language, being Aramaean in its general character, harmonizes
also with that of the books which were written after the Exile.
The author was certainly contemporary with Zerubbabel, details
of whose family history are given (1 Chr. 3:19).
The time of the composition being determined, the question of
the authorship may be more easily decided. According to Jewish
tradition, which was universally received down to the middle of
the seventeenth century, Ezra was regarded as the author of the
Chronicles. There are many points of resemblance and of contact
between the Chronicles and the Book of Ezra which seem to
confirm this opinion. The conclusion of the one and the
beginning of the other are almost identical in expression. In
their spirit and characteristics they are the same, showing thus
also an identity of authorship.
In their general scope and design these books are not so much
historical as didactic. The principal aim of the writer appears
to be to present moral and religious truth. He does not give
prominence to political occurences, as is done in Samuel and
Kings, but to ecclesiastical institutions. “The genealogies, so
uninteresting to most modern readers, were really an important
part of the public records of the Hebrew state. They were the
basis on which not only the land was distributed and held, but
the public services of the temple were arranged and conducted,
the Levites and their descendants alone, as is well known, being
entitled and first fruits set apart for that purpose.” The
“Chronicles” are an epitome of the sacred history from the days
of Adam down to the return from Babylonian Exile, a period of
about 3,500 years. The writer gathers up “the threads of the old
national life broken by the Captivity.”
The sources whence the chronicler compiled his work were
public records, registers, and genealogical tables belonging to

the Jews. These are referred to in the course of the book (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 27:24" id="c-p242.1" parsed="|1Chr|27|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.27.24">1 Chr. 27:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 29:29" id="c-p242.2" parsed="|1Chr|29|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.29.29">29:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 9:29" id="c-p242.3" parsed="|2Chr|9|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.9.29">2 Chr. 9:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 12:15" id="c-p242.4" parsed="|2Chr|12|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.12.15">12:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 13:22" id="c-p242.5" parsed="|2Chr|13|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.13.22">13:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 20:34" id="c-p242.6" parsed="|2Chr|20|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.20.34">20:34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 24:27" id="c-p242.7" parsed="|2Chr|24|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.24.27">24:27</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 26:22" id="c-p242.8" parsed="|2Chr|26|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.26.22">26:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 32:32" id="c-p242.9" parsed="|2Chr|32|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.32.32">32:32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 33:18" id="c-p242.10" parsed="|2Chr|33|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.33.18">33:18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 33:19" id="c-p242.11" parsed="|2Chr|33|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.33.19">19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 27:7" id="c-p242.12" parsed="|2Chr|27|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.27.7">27:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 35:25" id="c-p242.13" parsed="|2Chr|35|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.35.25">35:25</scripRef>). There are in Chronicles,
and the books of Samuel and Kings, forty parallels, often
verbal, proving that the writer both knew and used these records

(<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 17:18" id="c-p242.14" parsed="|1Chr|17|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.17.18">1 Chr. 17:18</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 7:18-20" id="c-p242.15" parsed="|2Sam|7|18|7|20" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.7.18-2Sam.7.20">2 Sam. 7:18-20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 19" id="c-p242.16" parsed="|1Chr|19|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.19">1 Chr. 19</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 10" id="c-p242.17" parsed="|2Sam|10|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.10">2 Sam. 10</scripRef>,
etc.).
As compared with Samuel and Kings, the Book of Chronicles

omits many particulars there recorded (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 6:20-23" id="c-p243.1" parsed="|2Sam|6|20|6|23" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.6.20-2Sam.6.23">2 Sam. 6:20-23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 9" id="c-p243.2" parsed="|2Sam|9|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.9">9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 11" id="c-p243.3" parsed="|2Sam|11|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.11">11</scripRef>;

14-19, etc.), and includes many things peculiar to itself (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 12" id="c-p243.4" parsed="|1Chr|12|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.12">1 Chr. 12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 22" id="c-p243.5" parsed="|1Chr|22|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.22">22</scripRef>; 23-26; 27; 28; 29, etc.). Twenty whole chapters,
and twenty-four parts of chapters, are occupied with matter not
found elsewhere. It also records many things in fuller detail,
as (e.g.) the list of David’s heroes (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 12:1-37" id="c-p243.6" parsed="|1Chr|12|1|12|37" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.12.1-1Chr.12.37">1 Chr. 12:1-37</scripRef>), the
removal of the ark from Kirjath-jearim to Mount Zion (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 13" id="c-p243.7" parsed="|1Chr|13|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.13">1 Chr. 13</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 15:2-24" id="c-p243.8" parsed="|1Chr|15|2|15|24" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.15.2-1Chr.15.24">15:2-24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 16:4-43" id="c-p243.9" parsed="|1Chr|16|4|16|43" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.16.4-1Chr.16.43">16:4-43</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 6" id="c-p243.10" parsed="|2Sam|6|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.6">2 Sam. 6</scripRef>), Uzziah’s leprosy and its
cause (2 Chr. 26:16-21; comp. 2 Kings 15:5), etc.
It has also been observed that another peculiarity of the book
is that it substitutes modern and more common expressions for
those that had then become unusual or obsolete. This is seen
particularly in the substitution of modern names of places, such
as were in use in the writer’s day, for the old names; thus
Gezer (1 Chr. 20:4) is used instead of Gob (2 Sam. 21:18), etc.
The Books of Chronicles are ranked among the khethubim or
hagiographa. They are alluded to, though not directly quoted, in

the New Testament (<scripRef passage="Heb. 5:4" id="c-p245.1" parsed="|Heb|5|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.5.4">Heb. 5:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 12:42" id="c-p245.2" parsed="|Matt|12|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.12.42">Matt. 12:42</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 23:35" id="c-p245.3" parsed="|Matt|23|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.23.35">23:35</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 1:5" id="c-p245.4" parsed="|Luke|1|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.5">Luke 1:5</scripRef>;
11:31, 51).
</def>
<term id="c-p245.7">Chronicles of king David</term>
(1 Chr. 27:24) were statistical state records; one of the public
sources from which the compiler of the Books of Chronicles
derived information on various public matters.
</def>
<term id="c-p246.2">Chronology</term>
Is the arrangement of facts and events in the order of time. The
writers of the Bible themselves do not adopt any standard era
according to which they date events. Sometimes the years are

reckoned, e.g., from the time of the Exodus (<scripRef passage="Num. 1:1" id="c-p247.1" parsed="|Num|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.1.1">Num. 1:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 33:38" id="c-p247.2" parsed="|Num|33|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.38">33:38</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 6:1" id="c-p247.3" parsed="|1Kgs|6|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.6.1">1 Kings 6:1</scripRef>), and sometimes from the accession of kings (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 15:1" id="c-p247.4" parsed="|1Kgs|15|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.15.1">1 Kings 15:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 15:9" id="c-p247.5" parsed="|1Kgs|15|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.15.9">9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 15:25" id="c-p247.6" parsed="|1Kgs|15|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.15.25">25</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 15:33" id="c-p247.7" parsed="|1Kgs|15|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.15.33">33</scripRef>, etc.), and sometimes again from the return from
Exile (Ezra 3:8).
Hence in constructing a system of Biblecal chronology, the
plan has been adopted of reckoning the years from the ages of
the patriarchs before the birth of their first-born sons for the
period from the Creation to Abraham. After this period other
data are to be taken into account in determining the relative
sequence of events.
As to the patriarchal period, there are three principal
systems of chronology: (1) that of the Hebrew text, (2) that of
the Septuagint version, and (3) that of the Samaritan
Pentateuch, as seen in the scheme on the opposite page.
The Samaritan and the Septuagint have considerably modified
the Hebrew chronology. This modification some regard as having
been wilfully made, and to be rejected. The same system of
variations is observed in the chronology of the period between
the Flood and Abraham. Thus:
| Hebrew Septuigant Samaritan
| From the birth of
|  Arphaxad, 2 years
|  after the Flood, to
|  the birth of Terah.   220   1000    870
| From the birth of
|  Terah to the birth
| of Abraham. 130 70 72
The Septuagint fixes on seventy years as the age of Terah at

the birth of Abraham, from <scripRef passage="Gen. 11:26" id="c-p252.1" parsed="|Gen|11|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.11.26">Gen. 11:26</scripRef>; but a comparison of <scripRef passage="Gen. 11:32" id="c-p252.2" parsed="|Gen|11|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.11.32">Gen. 11:32</scripRef> and <scripRef passage="Acts 7:4" id="c-p252.3" parsed="|Acts|7|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.7.4">Acts 7:4</scripRef> with <scripRef passage="Gen. 12:4" id="c-p252.4" parsed="|Gen|12|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.12.4">Gen. 12:4</scripRef> shows that when Terah died, at
the age of two hundred and five years, Abraham was seventy-five
years, and hence Terah must have been one hundred and thirty
years when Abraham was born. Thus, including the two years from
the Flood to the birth of Arphaxad, the period from the Flood to
the birth of Abraham was three hundred and fifty-two years.
The next period is from the birth of Abraham to the Exodus.
This, according to the Hebrew, extends to five hundred and five
years. The difficulty here is as to the four hundred and thirty

years mentioned <scripRef passage="Ex. 12:40" id="c-p253.1" parsed="|Exod|12|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.40">Ex. 12:40</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 12:41" id="c-p253.2" parsed="|Exod|12|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.41">41</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal. 3:17" id="c-p253.3" parsed="|Gal|3|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.3.17">Gal. 3:17</scripRef>. These years are

regarded by some as dating from the covenant with Abraham (<scripRef passage="Gen. 15" id="c-p253.4" parsed="|Gen|15|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.15">Gen. 15</scripRef>), which was entered into soon after his sojourn in Egypt;
others, with more probability, reckon these years from Jacob’s
going down into Egypt. (See EXODUS.)
In modern times the systems of Biblical chronology that have
been adopted are chiefly those of Ussher and Hales. The former
follows the Hebrew, and the latter the Septuagint mainly.
Archbishop Ussher’s (died 1656) system is called the short
chronology. It is that given on the margin of the Authorized
Version, but is really of no authority, and is quite uncertain.

| Abram leaves Haran    1921   2078

<term id="c-p257.1">Chrysoprasus</term>
Golden leek, a precious stone of the colour of leek’s juice, a
greenish-golden colour (Rev. 21:20).
</def>
<term id="c-p258.2">Chub</term>
The name of a people in alliance with Egypt in the time of
Nebuchadnezzar. The word is found only in <scripRef passage="Ezek. 30:5" id="c-p259.1" parsed="|Ezek|30|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.30.5">Ezek. 30:5</scripRef>. They were
probably a people of Northern Africa, or of the lands near Egypt
in the south.
</def>
<term id="c-p259.2">Chun</term>
One of the cities of Hadarezer, king of Syria. David procured

brass (i.e., bronze or copper) from it for the temple (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 18:8" id="c-p260.1" parsed="|1Chr|18|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.18.8">1 Chr. 18:8</scripRef>). It is called Berothai in <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 8:8" id="c-p260.2" parsed="|2Sam|8|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.8.8">2 Sam. 8:8</scripRef>; probably the same as
Berothah in Ezek. 47:16.
</def>
<term id="c-p260.4">Church</term>
Derived probably from the Greek kuriakon (i.e., “the Lord’s
house”), which was used by ancient authors for the place of
worship.
In the New Testament it is the translation of the Greek word
ecclesia, which is synonymous with the Hebrew kahal of the Old
Testament, both words meaning simply an assembly, the character
of which can only be known from the connection in which the word
is found. There is no clear instance of its being used for a
place of meeting or of worship, although in post-apostolic times
it early received this meaning. Nor is this word ever used to
denote the inhabitants of a country united in the same
profession, as when we say the “Church of England,” the “Church
of Scotland,” etc.
We find the word ecclesia used in the following senses in the
New Testament: (1.) It is translated “assembly” in the ordinary
classical sense (Acts 19:32, 39, 41).
(2.) It denotes the whole body of the redeemed, all those whom
the Father has given to Christ, the invisible catholic church
(Eph. 5:23, 25, 27, 29; Heb. 12:23).
(3.) A few Christians associated together in observing the
ordinances of the gospel are an ecclesia (Rom. 16:5; Col. 4:15).
(4.) All the Christians in a particular city, whether they
assembled together in one place or in several places for
religious worship, were an ecclesia. Thus all the disciples in

Antioch, forming several congregations, were one church (<scripRef passage="Acts 13:1" id="c-p266.1" parsed="|Acts|13|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.13.1">Acts 13:1</scripRef>); so also we read of the “church of God at Corinth” (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 1:2" id="c-p266.2" parsed="|1Cor|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.1.2">1 Cor. 1:2</scripRef>), “the church at Jerusalem” (<scripRef passage="Acts 8:1" id="c-p266.3" parsed="|Acts|8|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.8.1">Acts 8:1</scripRef>), “the church of
Ephesus” (Rev. 2:1), etc.
(5.) The whole body of professing Christians throughout the

world (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 15:9" id="c-p267.1" parsed="|1Cor|15|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.15.9">1 Cor. 15:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal. 1:13" id="c-p267.2" parsed="|Gal|1|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.1.13">Gal. 1:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 16:18" id="c-p267.3" parsed="|Matt|16|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.16.18">Matt. 16:18</scripRef>) are the church of
Christ.
The church visible “consists of all those throughout the world
that profess the true religion, together with their children.”
It is called “visible” because its members are known and its
assemblies are public. Here there is a mixture of “wheat and
chaff,” of saints and sinners. “God has commanded his people to
organize themselves into distinct visible ecclesiastical
communities, with constitutions, laws, and officers, badges,
ordinances, and discipline, for the great purpose of giving
visibility to his kingdom, of making known the gospel of that
kingdom, and of gathering in all its elect subjects. Each one of
these distinct organized communities which is faithful to the
great King is an integral part of the visible church, and all
together constitute the catholic or universal visible church.” A
credible profession of the true religion constitutes a person a
member of this church. This is “the kingdom of heaven,” whose
character and progress are set forth in the parables recorded in
Matt. 13.
The children of all who thus profess the true religion are
members of the visible church along with their parents. Children
are included in every covenant God ever made with man. They go

along with their parents (<scripRef passage="Gen. 9:9-17" id="c-p269.1" parsed="|Gen|9|9|9|17" osisRef="Bible:Gen.9.9-Gen.9.17">Gen. 9:9-17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 12:1-3" id="c-p269.2" parsed="|Gen|12|1|12|3" osisRef="Bible:Gen.12.1-Gen.12.3">12:1-3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 17:7" id="c-p269.3" parsed="|Gen|17|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.17.7">17:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex. 20:5" id="c-p269.4" parsed="|Exod|20|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.20.5">Ex. 20:5</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Deut. 29:10-13" id="c-p269.5" parsed="|Deut|29|10|29|13" osisRef="Bible:Deut.29.10-Deut.29.13">Deut. 29:10-13</scripRef>). Peter, on the day of Pentecost, at the
beginning of the New Testament dispensation, announces the same
great principle. “The promise [just as to Abraham and his seed

the promises were made] is unto you, and to your children” (<scripRef passage="Acts 2:38" id="c-p269.6" parsed="|Acts|2|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.2.38">Acts 2:38</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 2:39" id="c-p269.7" parsed="|Acts|2|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.2.39">39</scripRef>). The children of believing parents are “holy”, i.e.,
are “saints”, a title which designates the members of the
Christian church (1 Cor. 7:14). (See BAPTISM.)
The church invisible “consists of the whole number of the
elect that have been, are, or shall be gathered into one under
Christ, the head thereof.” This is a pure society, the church in
which Christ dwells. It is the body of Christ. it is called
“invisible” because the greater part of those who constitute it
are already in heaven or are yet unborn, and also because its
members still on earth cannot certainly be distinguished. The
qualifications of membership in it are internal and are hidden.
It is unseen except by Him who “searches the heart.” “The Lord
knoweth them that are his” (2 Tim. 2:19).
The church to which the attributes, prerogatives, and promises
appertaining to Christ’s kingdom belong, is a spiritual body
consisting of all true believers, i.e., the church invisible.
(1.) Its unity. God has ever had only one church on earth. We
sometimes speak of the Old Testament Church and of the New
Testament church, but they are one and the same. The Old

Testament church was not to be changed but enlarged (<scripRef passage="Isa. 49:13-23" id="c-p272.1" parsed="|Isa|49|13|49|23" osisRef="Bible:Isa.49.13-Isa.49.23">Isa. 49:13-23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 60:1-14" id="c-p272.2" parsed="|Isa|60|1|60|14" osisRef="Bible:Isa.60.1-Isa.60.14">60:1-14</scripRef>). When the Jews are at length restored, they
will not enter a new church, but will be grafted again into

“their own olive tree” (<scripRef passage="Rom. 11:18-24" id="c-p272.3" parsed="|Rom|11|18|11|24" osisRef="Bible:Rom.11.18-Rom.11.24">Rom. 11:18-24</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Eph. 2:11-22" id="c-p272.4" parsed="|Eph|2|11|2|22" osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.11-Eph.2.22">Eph. 2:11-22</scripRef>). The
apostles did not set up a new organization. Under their ministry
disciples were “added” to the “church” already existing (Acts 2:47).
(2.) Its universality. It is the “catholic” church; not
confined to any particular country or outward organization, but
comprehending all believers throughout the whole world.
(3.) Its perpetuity. It will continue through all ages to the
end of the world. It can never be destroyed. It is an
“everlasting kindgdom.”
</def>
<term id="c-p274.1">Churl</term>
In Isa. 32:5 (R.V. marg., “crafty”), means a deceiver. In 1 Sam. 25:3, the word churlish denotes a man that is coarse and
ill-natured, or, as the word literally means, “hard.” The same
Greek word as used by the LXX. here is found in <scripRef passage="Matt. 25:24" id="c-p275.3" parsed="|Matt|25|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.25.24">Matt. 25:24</scripRef>, and
there is rendered “hard.”
</def>
<term id="c-p275.4">Chushan-rishathaim</term>
Cush of double wickedness, or governor of two presidencies, the
king of Mesopotamia who oppressed Israel in the generation
immediately following Joshua (<scripRef passage="Judg. 3:8" id="c-p276.1" parsed="|Judg|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.3.8">Judg. 3:8</scripRef>). We learn from the
Tell-el-Amarna tablets that Palestine had been invaded by the
forces of Aram-naharaim (A.V., “Mesopotamia”) more than once,
long before the Exodus, and that at the time they were written
the king of Aram-naharaim was still intriguing in Canaan. It is
mentioned among the countries which took part in the attack upon
Egypt in the reign of Rameses III. (of the Twentieth Dynasty),
but as its king is not one of the princes stated to have been
conquered by the Pharaoh, it would seem that he did not actually
enter Egypt. As the reign of Rameses III. corresponds with the
Israelitish occupation of Canaan, it is probable that the
Egyptian monuments refer to the oppression of the Israelites by
Chushan-rishathaim. Canaan was still regarded as a province of
Egypt, so that, in attacking it Chushan-rishathaim would have
been considered to be attacking Egypt.
</def>
<term id="c-p276.2">Cilicia</term>
A maritime province in the south-east of Asia Minor. Tarsus, the
birth-place of Paul, was one of its chief towns, and the seat of
a celebrated school of philosophy. Its luxurious climate
attracted to it many Greek residents after its incorporation
with the Macedonian empire. It was formed into a Roman province,

B.C. 67. The Jews of Cilicia had a synagogue at Jerusalem (<scripRef passage="Acts 6:9" id="c-p277.1" parsed="|Acts|6|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.6.9">Acts 6:9</scripRef>). Paul visited it soon after his conversion (<scripRef passage="Gal. 1:21" id="c-p277.2" parsed="|Gal|1|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.1.21">Gal. 1:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 9:30" id="c-p277.3" parsed="|Acts|9|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.9.30">Acts 9:30</scripRef>), and again, on his second missionary journey (15:41), “he
went through Syria and Cilicia, confirming the churches.” It was
famous for its goat’s-hair cloth, called cilicium. Paul learned
in his youth the trade of making tents of this cloth.
</def>
<term id="c-p277.4">Cinnamon</term>
Heb. kinamon, the Cinnamomum zeylanicum of botanists, a tree of
the Laurel family, which grows only in India on the Malabar
coast, in Ceylon, and China. There is no trace of it in Egypt,
and it was unknown in Syria. The inner rind when dried and
rolled into cylinders forms the cinnamon of commerce. The fruit
and coarser pieces of bark when boiled yield a fragrant oil. It
was one of the principal ingredients in the holy anointing oil

(<scripRef passage="Ex. 30:23" id="c-p278.1" parsed="|Exod|30|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.30.23">Ex. 30:23</scripRef>). It is mentioned elsewhere only in <scripRef passage="Prov. 7:17" id="c-p278.2" parsed="|Prov|7|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.7.17">Prov. 7:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Cant. 4:14" id="c-p278.3" parsed="|Song|4|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.4.14">Cant. 4:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 18:13" id="c-p278.4" parsed="|Rev|18|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.18.13">Rev. 18:13</scripRef>. The mention of it indicates a very early and
extensive commerce carried on between Palestine and the East.
</def>
<term id="c-p278.5">Cinnereth</term>
A harp, one of the “fenced cities” of Naphtali (Josh. 19:35;
comp. <scripRef passage="Deut. 3:17" id="c-p279.2" parsed="|Deut|3|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.17">Deut. 3:17</scripRef>). It also denotes, apparently, a district which
may have taken its name from the adjacent city or lake of
Gennesaret, anciently called “the sea of Chinnereth” (q.v.), and
was probably that enclosed district north of Tiberias afterwards
called “the plain of Gennesaret.” Called Chinneroth (R.V.,
Chinnereth) <scripRef passage="Josh. 11:2" id="c-p279.3" parsed="|Josh|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.2">Josh. 11:2</scripRef>. The phrase “all Cinneroth, with all the
land of Naphtali” in <scripRef passage="1 Kings 15:20" id="c-p279.4" parsed="|1Kgs|15|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.15.20">1 Kings 15:20</scripRef> is parallel to “the
store-houses of the cities of Naphtali” (R.V. marg.) in 2 Chr. 16:4.
</def>
<term id="c-p279.6">Circuit</term>
The apparent diurnal revolution of the sun round the earth (Ps. 19:6), and the changes of the wind (Eccl. 1:6). In Job 22:14,
“in the circuit of heaven” (R.V. marg., “on the vault of
heaven”) means the “arch of heaven,” which seems to be bent over
our heads.
</def>
<term id="c-p280.4">Circumcision</term>
Cutting around. This rite, practised before, as some think, by
divers races, was appointed by God to be the special badge of
his chosen people, an abiding sign of their consecration to him.

It was established as a national ordinance (<scripRef passage="Gen. 17:10" id="c-p281.1" parsed="|Gen|17|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.17.10">Gen. 17:10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 17:11" id="c-p281.2" parsed="|Gen|17|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.17.11">11</scripRef>). In
compliance with the divine command, Abraham, though ninety-nine
years of age, was circumcised on the same day with Ishmael, who
was thirteen years old (17:24-27). Slaves, whether home-born or
purchased, were circumcised (17:12, 13); and all foreigners must
have their males circumcised before they could enjoy the
privileges of Jewish citizenship (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:48" id="c-p281.3" parsed="|Exod|12|48|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.48">Ex. 12:48</scripRef>). During the journey
