through the wilderness, the practice of circumcision fell into
disuse, but was resumed by the command of Joshua before they
entered the Promised Land (<scripRef passage="Josh. 5:2-9" id="c-p281.4" parsed="|Josh|5|2|5|9" osisRef="Bible:Josh.5.2-Josh.5.9">Josh. 5:2-9</scripRef>). It was observed always
afterwards among the tribes of israel, although it is not
expressly mentioned from the time of the settlement in Canaan
till the time of Christ, about 1,450 years. The Jews prided
themselves in the possession of this covenant distinction (Judg. 14:3; 15:18; 1 Sam. 14:6; 17:26; 2 Sam. 1:20; Ezek. 31:18).
As a rite of the church it ceased when the New Testament times

began (<scripRef passage="Gal. 6:15" id="c-p282.1" parsed="|Gal|6|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.6.15">Gal. 6:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Col. 3:11" id="c-p282.2" parsed="|Col|3|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.3.11">Col. 3:11</scripRef>). Some Jewish Christians sought to
impose it, however, on the Gentile converts; but this the

apostles resolutely resisted (<scripRef passage="Acts 15:1" id="c-p282.3" parsed="|Acts|15|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.15.1">Acts 15:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal. 6:12" id="c-p282.4" parsed="|Gal|6|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.6.12">Gal. 6:12</scripRef>). Our Lord
was circumcised, for it “became him to fulfil all
righteousness,” as of the seed of Abraham, according to the
flesh; and Paul “took and circumcised” Timothy (<scripRef passage="Acts 16:3" id="c-p282.5" parsed="|Acts|16|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.16.3">Acts 16:3</scripRef>), to
avoid giving offence to the Jews. It would render Timothy’s
labours more acceptable to the Jews. But Paul would by no means

consent to the demand that Titus should be circumcised (<scripRef passage="Gal. 2:3-5" id="c-p282.6" parsed="|Gal|2|3|2|5" osisRef="Bible:Gal.2.3-Gal.2.5">Gal. 2:3-5</scripRef>). The great point for which he contended was the free
admission of uncircumcised Gentiles into the church. He
contended successfully in behalf of Titus, even in Jerusalem.
In the Old Testament a spiritual idea is attached to
circumcision. It was the symbol of purity (<scripRef passage="Isa. 52:1" id="c-p283.1" parsed="|Isa|52|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.52.1">Isa. 52:1</scripRef>). We read

of uncircumcised lips (<scripRef passage="Ex. 6:12" id="c-p283.2" parsed="|Exod|6|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.6.12">Ex. 6:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 6:30" id="c-p283.3" parsed="|Exod|6|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.6.30">30</scripRef>), ears (<scripRef passage="Jer. 6:10" id="c-p283.4" parsed="|Jer|6|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.6.10">Jer. 6:10</scripRef>), hearts
(<scripRef passage="Lev. 26:41" id="c-p283.5" parsed="|Lev|26|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.26.41">Lev. 26:41</scripRef>). The fruit of a tree that is unclean is spoken of
as uncircumcised (Lev. 19:23).
It was a sign and seal of the covenant of grace as well as of
the national covenant between God and the Hebrews. (1.) It
sealed the promises made to Abraham, which related to the
commonwealth of Israel, national promises. (2.) But the promises
made to Abraham included the promise of redemption (<scripRef passage="Gal. 3:14" id="c-p284.1" parsed="|Gal|3|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.3.14">Gal. 3:14</scripRef>),
a promise which has come upon us. The covenant with Abraham was
a dispensation or a specific form of the covenant of grace, and
circumcision was a sign and seal of that covenant. It had a
spiritual meaning. It signified purification of the heart,

inward circumcision effected by the Spirit (<scripRef passage="Deut. 10:16" id="c-p284.2" parsed="|Deut|10|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.10.16">Deut. 10:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut 30:6" id="c-p284.3" parsed="|Deut|30|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.30.6">30:6</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Ezek. 44:7" id="c-p284.4" parsed="|Ezek|44|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.44.7">Ezek. 44:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 7:51" id="c-p284.5" parsed="|Acts|7|51|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.7.51">Acts 7:51</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 2:28" id="c-p284.6" parsed="|Rom|2|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.2.28">Rom. 2:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Col. 2:11" id="c-p284.7" parsed="|Col|2|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.2.11">Col. 2:11</scripRef>). Circumcision as a
symbol shadowing forth sanctification by the Holy Spirit has now
given way to the symbol of baptism (q.v.). But the truth
embodied in both ordinances is ever the same, the removal of
sin, the sanctifying effects of grace in the heart.
Under the Jewish dispensation, church and state were
identical. No one could be a member of the one without also
being a member of the other. Circumcision was a sign and seal of
membership in both. Every circumcised person bore thereby
evidence that he was one of the chosen people, a member of the
church of God as it then existed, and consequently also a member
of the Jewish commonwealth.
</def>
<term id="c-p285.1">Cistern</term>
The rendering of a Hebrew word bor, which means a receptacle
for water conveyed to it; distinguished from beer, which

denotes a place where water rises on the spot (<scripRef passage="Jer. 2:13" id="c-p286.1" parsed="|Jer|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.2.13">Jer. 2:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 5:15" id="c-p286.2" parsed="|Prov|5|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.5.15">Prov. 5:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 36:16" id="c-p286.3" parsed="|Isa|36|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.36.16">Isa. 36:16</scripRef>), a fountain. Cisterns are frequently mentioned
in Scripture. The scarcity of springs in Palestine made it
necessary to collect rain-water in reservoirs and cisterns (Num. 21:22). (See WELL.)
Empty cisterns were sometimes used as prisons (Jer. 38:6; Lam. 3:53; Ps. 40:2; 69:15). The “pit” into which Joseph was cast
(Gen. 37:24) was a beer or dry well. There are numerous
remains of ancient cisterns in all parts of Palestine.
</def>
<term id="c-p287.6">Citizenship</term>
The rights and privileges of a citizen in distinction from a

foreigner (<scripRef passage="Luke 15:15" id="c-p288.1" parsed="|Luke|15|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.15.15">Luke 15:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 19:14" id="c-p288.2" parsed="|Luke|19|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.19.14">19:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 21:39" id="c-p288.3" parsed="|Acts|21|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.21.39">Acts 21:39</scripRef>). Under the Mosaic law
non-Israelites, with the exception of the Moabites and the
Ammonites and others mentioned in <scripRef passage="Deut. 23:1-3" id="c-p288.4" parsed="|Deut|23|1|23|3" osisRef="Bible:Deut.23.1-Deut.23.3">Deut. 23:1-3</scripRef>, were admitted to
the general privileges of citizenship among the Jews (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:19" id="c-p288.5" parsed="|Exod|12|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.19">Ex. 12:19</scripRef>;
Lev. 24:22; Num. 15:15; 35:15; Deut. 10:18; 14:29; 16:10, 14).
The right of citizenship under the Roman government was
granted by the emperor to individuals, and sometimes to
provinces, as a favour or as a recompense for services rendered
to the state, or for a sum of money (<scripRef passage="Acts 22:28" id="c-p289.1" parsed="|Acts|22|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.22.28">Acts 22:28</scripRef>). This “freedom”
secured privileges equal to those enjoyed by natives of Rome.
Among the most notable of these was the provision that a man

could not be bound or imprisoned without a formal trial (<scripRef passage="Acts 22:25" id="c-p289.2" parsed="|Acts|22|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.22.25">Acts 22:25</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 22:26" id="c-p289.3" parsed="|Acts|22|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.22.26">26</scripRef>), or scourged (16:37). All Roman citizens had the
right of appeal to Caesar (25:11).
</def>
<term id="c-p289.4">City</term>
The earliest mention of city-building is that of Enoch, which
was built by Cain (<scripRef passage="Gen. 4:17" id="c-p290.1" parsed="|Gen|4|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.4.17">Gen. 4:17</scripRef>). After the confusion of tongues,
the descendants of Nimrod founded several cities (10:10-12).
Next, we have a record of the cities of the Canaanites, Sidon,
Gaza, Sodom, etc. (10:12, 19; 11:3, 9; 36:31-39). The earliest
description of a city is that of Sodom (19:1-22). Damascus is
said to be the oldest existing city in the world. Before the
time of Abraham there were cities in Egypt (<scripRef passage="Num. 13:22" id="c-p290.2" parsed="|Num|13|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.13.22">Num. 13:22</scripRef>). The
Israelites in Egypt were employed in building the “treasure
cities” of Pithom and Raamses (<scripRef passage="Ex. 1:11" id="c-p290.3" parsed="|Exod|1|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.1.11">Ex. 1:11</scripRef>); but it does not seem
that they had any cities of their own in Goshen (<scripRef passage="Gen. 46:34" id="c-p290.4" parsed="|Gen|46|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.46.34">Gen. 46:34</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Gen 47:1-11" id="c-p290.5" parsed="|Gen|47|1|47|11" osisRef="Bible:Gen.47.1-Gen.47.11">47:1-11</scripRef>). In the kingdom of Og in Bashan there were sixty “great
cities with walls,” and twenty-three cities in Gilead partly

rebuilt by the tribes on the east of Jordan (<scripRef passage="Num. 21:21" id="c-p290.6" parsed="|Num|21|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.21.21">Num. 21:21</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num 21:32" id="c-p290.7" parsed="|Num|21|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.21.32">32</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num 21:33" id="c-p290.8" parsed="|Num|21|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.21.33">33</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num 21:35" id="c-p290.9" parsed="|Num|21|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.21.35">35</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 32:1-3" id="c-p290.10" parsed="|Num|32|1|32|3" osisRef="Bible:Num.32.1-Num.32.3">32:1-3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num 32:34-42" id="c-p290.11" parsed="|Num|32|34|32|42" osisRef="Bible:Num.32.34-Num.32.42">34-42</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 3:4" id="c-p290.12" parsed="|Deut|3|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.4">Deut. 3:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 3:5" id="c-p290.13" parsed="|Deut|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.5">5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 3:14" id="c-p290.14" parsed="|Deut|3|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.14">14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:13" id="c-p290.15" parsed="|1Kgs|4|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.13">1 Kings 4:13</scripRef>). On the west
of Jordan were thirty-one “royal cities” (<scripRef passage="Josh. 12" id="c-p290.16" parsed="|Josh|12|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.12">Josh. 12</scripRef>), besides
many others spoken of in the history of Israel.
A fenced city was a city surrounded by fortifications and high

walls, with watch-towers upon them (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 11:11" id="c-p291.1" parsed="|2Chr|11|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.11.11">2 Chr. 11:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 3:5" id="c-p291.2" parsed="|Deut|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.5">Deut. 3:5</scripRef>).
There was also within the city generally a tower to which the
citizens might flee when danger threatened them (Judg. 9:46-52).
A city with suburbs was a city surrounded with open
pasture-grounds, such as the forty-eight cities which were given
to the Levites (<scripRef passage="Num. 35:2-7" id="c-p292.1" parsed="|Num|35|2|35|7" osisRef="Bible:Num.35.2-Num.35.7">Num. 35:2-7</scripRef>). There were six cities of refuge,
three on each side of Jordan, namely, Kadesh, Shechem, Hebron,
on the west of Jordan; and on the east, Bezer, Ramoth-gilead,
and Golan. The cities on each side of the river were nearly
opposite each other. The regulations concerning these cities are
given in Num. 35:9-34; Deut. 19:1-13; Ex. 21:12-14.
When David reduced the fortress of the Jebusites which stood
on Mount Zion, he built on the site of it a palace and a city,
which he called by his own name (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 11:5" id="c-p293.1" parsed="|1Chr|11|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.11.5">1 Chr. 11:5</scripRef>), the city of
David. Bethlehem is also so called as being David’s native town
(Luke 2:4).
Jerusalem is called the Holy City, the holiness of the temple
being regarded as extending in some measure over the whole city
(Neh. 11:1).
Pithom and Raamses, built by the Israelites as “treasure
cities,” were not places where royal treasures were kept, but
were fortified towns where merchants might store their goods and
transact their business in safety, or cities in which munitions
of war were stored. (See PITHOM.)
</def>
<term id="c-p295.2">Clauda</term>
A small island off the southwest coast of Crete, passed by Paul
on his voyage to Rome (<scripRef passage="Acts 27:16" id="c-p296.1" parsed="|Acts|27|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.27.16">Acts 27:16</scripRef>). It is about 7 miles long and
3 broad. It is now called Gozzo (R.V., “Cauda”).
</def>
<term id="c-p296.2">Claudia</term>
A female Christian mentioned in 2 Tim. 4:21. It is a conjecture
having some probability that she was a British maiden, the
daughter of king Cogidunus, who was an ally of Rome, and assumed
the name of the emperor, his patron, Tiberius Claudius, and that
she was the wife of Pudens.
</def>
<term id="c-p297.2">Claudius</term>
Lame. (1.) The fourth Roman emperor. He succeeded Caligula (A.D.
41). Though in general he treated the Jews, especially those in
Asia and Egypt, with great indulgence, yet about the middle of
his reign (A.D. 49) he banished them all from Rome (<scripRef passage="Acts 18:2" id="c-p298.1" parsed="|Acts|18|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.2">Acts 18:2</scripRef>).
In this edict the Christians were included, as being, as was
supposed, a sect of Jews. The Jews, however soon again returned
to Rome.
During the reign of this emperor, several persecutions of the
Christians by the Jews took place in the dominions of Herod
Agrippa, in one of which the apostle James was “killed” (12:2).
He died A.D. 54.
(2.) Claudius Lysias, a Greek who, having obtained by purchase
the privilege of Roman citizenship, took the name of Claudius
(Acts 21:31-40; 22:28; 23:26).
</def>
<term id="c-p300.4">Clay</term>
This word is used of sediment found in pits or in streets (Isa. 57:20; Jer. 38:60), of dust mixed with spittle (John 9:6), and

of potter’s clay (<scripRef passage="Isa. 41:25" id="c-p301.4" parsed="|Isa|41|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.41.25">Isa. 41:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Nah. 3:14" id="c-p301.5" parsed="|Nah|3|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Nah.3.14">Nah. 3:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 18:1-6" id="c-p301.6" parsed="|Jer|18|1|18|6" osisRef="Bible:Jer.18.1-Jer.18.6">Jer. 18:1-6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 9:21" id="c-p301.7" parsed="|Rom|9|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.9.21">Rom. 9:21</scripRef>). Clay was used for sealing (<scripRef passage="Job 38:14" id="c-p301.8" parsed="|Job|38|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.38.14">Job 38:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 32:14" id="c-p301.9" parsed="|Jer|32|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.32.14">Jer. 32:14</scripRef>). Our
Lord’s tomb may have been thus sealed (<scripRef passage="Matt. 27:66" id="c-p301.10" parsed="|Matt|27|66|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.66">Matt. 27:66</scripRef>). The
practice of sealing doors with clay is still common in the East.
Clay was also in primitive times used for mortar (<scripRef passage="Gen. 11:3" id="c-p301.11" parsed="|Gen|11|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.11.3">Gen. 11:3</scripRef>).
The “clay ground” in which the large vessels of the temple were

cast (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 7:46" id="c-p301.12" parsed="|1Kgs|7|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.7.46">1 Kings 7:46</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 4:17" id="c-p301.13" parsed="|2Chr|4|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.4.17">2 Chr. 4:17</scripRef>) was a compact loam fitted for
the purpose. The expression literally rendered is, “in the
thickness of the ground,”, meaning, “in stiff ground” or in
clay.
</def>
<term id="c-p301.14">Clean</term>
The various forms of uncleanness according to the Mosaic law are

enumerated in <scripRef passage="Lev. 11" id="c-p302.1" parsed="|Lev|11|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.11">Lev. 11</scripRef>-15; <scripRef passage="Num. 19" id="c-p302.2" parsed="|Num|19|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.19">Num. 19</scripRef>. The division of animals into
clean and unclean was probably founded on the practice of
sacrifice. It existed before the Flood (<scripRef passage="Gen. 7:2" id="c-p302.3" parsed="|Gen|7|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.7.2">Gen. 7:2</scripRef>). The
regulations regarding such animals are recorded in <scripRef passage="Lev. 11" id="c-p302.4" parsed="|Lev|11|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.11">Lev. 11</scripRef> and
Deut. 14:1-21.
The Hebrews were prohibited from using as food certain animal
substances, such as (1) blood; (2) the fat covering the
intestines, termed the caul; (3) the fat on the intestines,
called the mesentery; (4) the fat of the kidneys; and (5) the

fat tail of certain sheep (<scripRef passage="Ex. 29:13" id="c-p303.1" parsed="|Exod|29|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.13">Ex. 29:13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 29:22" id="c-p303.2" parsed="|Exod|29|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.22">22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 3:4-9" id="c-p303.3" parsed="|Lev|3|4|3|9" osisRef="Bible:Lev.3.4-Lev.3.9">Lev. 3:4-9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 9:19" id="c-p303.4" parsed="|Lev|9|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.9.19">9:19</scripRef>;
17:10; 19:26).
The chief design of these regulations seems to have been to
establish a system of regimen which would distinguish the Jews
from all other nations. Regarding the design and the abolition
of these regulations the reader will find all the details in
Lev. 20:24-26; Acts 10:9-16; 11:1-10; Heb. 9:9-14.
</def>
<term id="c-p304.5">Clement</term>
Mild, a Christian of Philippi, Paul’s “fellow-labourer,” whose
name he mentions as “in the book of life” (<scripRef passage="Phil. 4:3" id="c-p305.1" parsed="|Phil|4|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Phil.4.3">Phil. 4:3</scripRef>). It was an
opinion of ancient writers that he was the Clement of Rome whose
name is well known in church history, and that he was the author
of an Epistle to the Corinthians, the only known manuscript of
which is appended to the Alexandrian Codex, now in the British
Museum. It is of some historical interest, and has given rise to
much discussion among critics. It makes distinct reference to
Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians.
</def>
<term id="c-p305.2">Cleopas</term>
(abbreviation of Cleopatros), one of the two disciples with whom
Jesus conversed on the way to Emmaus on the day of the
resurrection (<scripRef passage="Luke 24:18" id="c-p306.1" parsed="|Luke|24|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.24.18">Luke 24:18</scripRef>). We know nothing definitely regarding
him. It is not certain that he was the Clopas of <scripRef passage="John 19:25" id="c-p306.2" parsed="|John|19|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.25">John 19:25</scripRef>, or
the Alphaeus of Matt. 10:3, although he may have been so.
</def>
<term id="c-p306.4">Cleophas</term>
(in the spelling of this word h is inserted by mistake from
Latin MSS.), rather Cleopas, which is the Greek form of the
word, while Clopas is the Aramaic form. In <scripRef passage="John 19:25" id="c-p307.1" parsed="|John|19|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.25">John 19:25</scripRef> the
Authorized Version reads, “Mary, the wife of Clopas.” The word
“wife” is conjecturally inserted here. If “wife” is rightly
inserted, then Mary was the mother of James the Less, and Clopas
is the same as Alphaeus (Matt. 10:3; 27:56).
</def>
<term id="c-p307.4">Cloak</term>
An upper garment, “an exterior tunic, wide and long, reaching to
the ankles, but without sleeves” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 59:17" id="c-p308.1" parsed="|Isa|59|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.59.17">Isa. 59:17</scripRef>). The word so
rendered is elsewhere rendered “robe” or “mantle.” It was worn
by the high priest under the ephod (<scripRef passage="Ex. 28:31" id="c-p308.2" parsed="|Exod|28|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.31">Ex. 28:31</scripRef>), by kings and
others of rank (1 Sam. 15:27; Job 1:20; 2:12), and by women (2 Sam. 13:18).
The word translated “cloke”, i.e., outer garment, in Matt. 5:40 is in its plural form used of garments in general (Matt. 17:2; 26:65). The cloak mentioned here and in Luke 6:29 was the
Greek himation, Latin pallium, and consisted of a large square
piece of wollen cloth fastened round the shoulders, like the
abba of the Arabs. This could be taken by a creditor (Ex. 22:26, 27), but the coat or tunic (Gr. chiton) mentioned in Matt. 5:40 could not.
The cloak which Paul “left at Troas” (2 Tim. 4:13) was the
Roman paenula, a thick upper garment used chiefly in travelling
as a protection from the weather. Some, however, have supposed
that what Paul meant was a travelling-bag. In the Syriac version
the word used means a bookcase. (See Dress.)
</def>
<term id="c-p310.3">Closet</term>
As used in the New Testament, signifies properly a storehouse
(<scripRef passage="Luke 12" id="c-p311.1" parsed="|Luke|12|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.12">Luke 12</scripRef>: 24), and hence a place of privacy and retirement
(Matt. 6:6; Luke 12:3).
</def>
<term id="c-p311.4">Cloud</term>
The Hebrew so rendered means “a covering,” because clouds cover
the sky. The word is used as a symbol of the Divine presence, as

indicating the splendour of that glory which it conceals (<scripRef passage="Ex. 16:10" id="c-p312.1" parsed="|Exod|16|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.16.10">Ex. 16:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 33:9" id="c-p312.2" parsed="|Exod|33|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.33.9">33:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 11:25" id="c-p312.3" parsed="|Num|11|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.11.25">Num. 11:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 12:5" id="c-p312.4" parsed="|Num|12|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.12.5">12:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 22:14" id="c-p312.5" parsed="|Job|22|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.22.14">Job 22:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 18:11" id="c-p312.6" parsed="|Ps|18|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.18.11">Ps. 18:11</scripRef>). A “cloud
without rain” is a proverbial saying, denoting a man who does

not keep his promise (<scripRef passage="Prov. 16:15" id="c-p312.7" parsed="|Prov|16|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.16.15">Prov. 16:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 18:4" id="c-p312.8" parsed="|Isa|18|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.18.4">Isa. 18:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 25:5" id="c-p312.9" parsed="|Isa|25|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.25.5">25:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jude 1" id="c-p312.10" parsed="|Jude|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jude.1.1">Jude 1</scripRef>:12).
A cloud is the figure of that which is transitory (<scripRef passage="Job 30:15" id="c-p312.11" parsed="|Job|30|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.30.15">Job 30:15</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Hos. 6:4" id="c-p312.12" parsed="|Hos|6|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.6.4">Hos. 6:4</scripRef>). A bright cloud is the symbolical seat of the Divine

presence (<scripRef passage="Ex. 29:42" id="c-p312.13" parsed="|Exod|29|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.42">Ex. 29:42</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex 29:43" id="c-p312.14" parsed="|Exod|29|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.43">43</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 8:10" id="c-p312.15" parsed="|1Kgs|8|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.8.10">1 Kings 8:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 5:14" id="c-p312.16" parsed="|2Chr|5|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.5.14">2 Chr. 5:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 43:4" id="c-p312.17" parsed="|Ezek|43|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.43.4">Ezek. 43:4</scripRef>),
and was called the Shechinah (q.v.). Jehovah came down upon
Sinai in a cloud (<scripRef passage="Ex. 19:9" id="c-p312.18" parsed="|Exod|19|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.19.9">Ex. 19:9</scripRef>); and the cloud filled the court
around the tabernacle in the wilderness so that Moses could not

enter it (<scripRef passage="Ex. 40:34" id="c-p312.19" parsed="|Exod|40|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.40.34">Ex. 40:34</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 40:35" id="c-p312.20" parsed="|Exod|40|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.40.35">35</scripRef>). At the dedication of the temple also
the cloud “filled the house of the Lord” (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 8:10" id="c-p312.21" parsed="|1Kgs|8|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.8.10">1 Kings 8:10</scripRef>). Thus in
like manner when Christ comes the second time he is described as

coming “in the clouds” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 17:5" id="c-p312.22" parsed="|Matt|17|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.17.5">Matt. 17:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 24:30" id="c-p312.23" parsed="|Matt|24|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.24.30">24:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 1:9" id="c-p312.24" parsed="|Acts|1|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.9">Acts 1:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 1:11" id="c-p312.25" parsed="|Acts|1|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.11">11</scripRef>). False
teachers are likened unto clouds carried about with a tempest (2 Pet. 2:17). The infirmities of old age, which come one after
another, are compared by Solomon to “clouds returning after the
rain” (<scripRef passage="Eccl. 12:2" id="c-p312.26" parsed="|Eccl|12|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eccl.12.2">Eccl. 12:2</scripRef>). The blotting out of sins is like the sudden
disappearance of threatening clouds from the sky (Isa. 44:22).
Cloud, the pillar of, was the glory-cloud which indicated
God’s presence leading the ransomed people through the

wilderness (<scripRef passage="Ex. 13:22" id="c-p313.1" parsed="|Exod|13|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.13.22">Ex. 13:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 33:9" id="c-p313.2" parsed="|Exod|33|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.33.9">33:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex 33:10" id="c-p313.3" parsed="|Exod|33|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.33.10">10</scripRef>). This pillar preceded the

people as they marched, resting on the ark (<scripRef passage="Ex. 13:21" id="c-p313.4" parsed="|Exod|13|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.13.21">Ex. 13:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 40:36" id="c-p313.5" parsed="|Exod|40|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.40.36">40:36</scripRef>).
By night it became a pillar of fire (Num. 9:17-23).
</def>
<term id="c-p313.7">Cnidus</term>
A town and harbour on the extreme south-west of the peninsula of
Doris in Asia Minor. Paul sailed past it on his voyage to Rome
after leaving Myra (Acts 27:7).
</def>
<term id="c-p314.2">Coal</term>
It is by no means certain that the Hebrews were acquainted with
mineral coal, although it is found in Syria. Their common fuel
was dried dung of animals and wood charcoal. Two different words

are found in Hebrew to denote coal, both occurring in <scripRef passage="Prov. 26:21" id="c-p315.1" parsed="|Prov|26|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.26.21">Prov. 26:21</scripRef>, “As coal [Heb. peham; i.e., “black coal”] is to burning

coal [Heb. gehalim].” The latter of these words is used in <scripRef passage="Job 41:21" id="c-p315.2" parsed="|Job|41|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.41.21">Job 41:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 6:28" id="c-p315.3" parsed="|Prov|6|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.6.28">Prov. 6:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 44:19" id="c-p315.4" parsed="|Isa|44|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.44.19">Isa. 44:19</scripRef>. The words “live coal” in <scripRef passage="Isa. 6:6" id="c-p315.5" parsed="|Isa|6|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.6.6">Isa. 6:6</scripRef>
are more correctly “glowing stone.” In <scripRef passage="Lam. 4:8" id="c-p315.6" parsed="|Lam|4|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lam.4.8">Lam. 4:8</scripRef> the expression
“blacker than a coal” is literally rendered in the margin of the

Revised Version “darker than blackness.” “Coals of fire” (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 22:9" id="c-p315.7" parsed="|2Sam|22|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.22.9">2 Sam. 22:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 22:13" id="c-p315.8" parsed="|2Sam|22|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.22.13">13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 18:8" id="c-p315.9" parsed="|Ps|18|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.18.8">Ps. 18:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps. 18:12" id="c-p315.10" parsed="|Ps|18|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.18.12">12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps. 18:13" id="c-p315.11" parsed="|Ps|18|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.18.13">13</scripRef>, etc.) is an expression used
metaphorically for lightnings proceeding from God. A false

tongue is compared to “coals of juniper” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 120:4" id="c-p315.12" parsed="|Ps|120|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.120.4">Ps. 120:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="James 3:6" id="c-p315.13" parsed="|Jas|3|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jas.3.6">James 3:6</scripRef>).
“Heaping coals of fire on the head” symbolizes overcoming evil
with good. The words of Paul (<scripRef passage="Rom. 12:20" id="c-p315.14" parsed="|Rom|12|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.12.20">Rom. 12:20</scripRef>) are equivalent to
saying, “By charity and kindness thou shalt soften down his
enmity as surely as heaping coals on the fire fuses the metal in
the crucible.”
</def>
<term id="c-p315.15">Coat</term>
The tunic worn like the shirt next the skin (Lev. 16:4; Cant. 5:3; 2 Sam. 15:32; Ex. 28:4; 29:5). The “coats of skins”
prepared by God for Adam and Eve were probably nothing more than
aprons (<scripRef passage="Gen. 3:21" id="c-p316.6" parsed="|Gen|3|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.3.21">Gen. 3:21</scripRef>). This tunic was sometimes woven entire
without a seam (<scripRef passage="John 19:23" id="c-p316.7" parsed="|John|19|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.23">John 19:23</scripRef>); it was also sometimes of “many
colours” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 37:3" id="c-p316.8" parsed="|Gen|37|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.3">Gen. 37:3</scripRef>; R.V. marg., “a long garment with sleeves”).
The “fisher’s coat” of <scripRef passage="John 21:7" id="c-p316.9" parsed="|John|21|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.21.7">John 21:7</scripRef> was obviously an outer garment
or cloak, as was also the “coat” made by Hannah for Samuel (1 Sam. 2:19). (See DRESS.)
</def>
<term id="c-p316.12">Coat of mail</term>
The rendering of a Hebrew word meaning “glittering” (1 Sam. 17:5, 38). The same word in the plural form is translated
“habergeons” in 2 Chr. 26:14 and Neh. 4:16. The “harness” (1 Kings 22:34), “breastplate” (Isa. 59:17), and “brigandine” (Jer. 46:4), were probably also corselets or coats of mail. (See ARMOUR.)
</def>
<term id="c-p317.9">Cockatrice</term>
The mediaeval name (a corruption of “crocodile”) of a fabulous
serpent supposed to be produced from a cock’s egg. It is
generally supposed to denote the cerastes, or “horned viper,” a
very poisonous serpent about a foot long. Others think it to be
the yellow viper (Daboia xanthina), one of the most dangerous
vipers, from its size and its nocturnal habits (<scripRef passage="Isa. 11:8" id="c-p318.1" parsed="|Isa|11|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.11.8">Isa. 11:8</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Isa 14:29" id="c-p318.2" parsed="|Isa|14|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.14.29">14:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 59:5" id="c-p318.3" parsed="|Isa|59|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.59.5">59:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 8:17" id="c-p318.4" parsed="|Jer|8|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.8.17">Jer. 8:17</scripRef>; in all which the Revised Version renders
the Hebrew tziph’oni by “basilisk”). In Prov. 23:32 the Hebrew
tzeph’a is rendered both in the Authorized Version and the
Revised Version by “adder;” margin of Revised Version
“basilisk,” and of Authorized Version “cockatrice.”
</def>
<term id="c-p318.6">Cock-crowing</term>
In our Lord’s time the Jews had adopted the Greek and Roman
division of the night into four watches, each consisting of
three hours, the first beginning at six o’clock in the evening

(<scripRef passage="Luke 12:38" id="c-p319.1" parsed="|Luke|12|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.12.38">Luke 12:38</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 14:25" id="c-p319.2" parsed="|Matt|14|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.14.25">Matt. 14:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 6:48" id="c-p319.3" parsed="|Mark|6|48|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.6.48">Mark 6:48</scripRef>). But the ancient division,
known as the first and second cock-crowing, was still retained.
The cock usually crows several times soon after midnight (this
is the first crowing), and again at the dawn of day (and this is
the second crowing). Mark mentions (14:30) the two
cock-crowings. Matthew (26:34) alludes to that only which was
emphatically the cock-crowing, viz, the second.
</def>
<term id="c-p319.4">Cockle</term>
Occurs only in Job 31:40 (marg., “noisome weeds”), where it is
the rendering of a Hebrew word (b’oshah) which means
“offensive,” “having a bad smell,” referring to some weed
perhaps which has an unpleasant odour. Or it may be regarded as
simply any noisome weed, such as the “tares” or darnel of Matt. 13:30. In Isa. 5:2, 4 the plural form is rendered “wild grapes.”
</def>
<term id="c-p320.5">Coele-Syria</term>
Hollow Syria, the name (not found in Scripture) given by the
Greeks to the extensive valley, about 100 miles long, between
the Lebanon and the Anti-Lebanon range of mountains.
</def>
<term id="c-p321.1">Coffer</term>
The receptacle or small box placed beside the ark by the
Philistines, in which they deposited the golden mice and the
emerods as their trespass-offering (1 Sam. 6:8, 11, 15).
</def>
<term id="c-p322.4">Coffin</term>
Used in Gen. 50:26 with reference to the burial of Joseph. Here,
it means a mummy-chest. The same Hebrew word is rendered “chest”
in 2 Kings 12:9, 10.
</def>
<term id="c-p323.4">Cogitations</term>
(or “thoughts,” as the Chaldee word in Dan. 7:28 literally
means), earnest meditation.
</def>
<term id="c-p324.2">Coin</term>
Before the Exile the Jews had no regularly stamped money. They
made use of uncoined shekels or talents of silver, which they

weighed out (<scripRef passage="Gen. 23:16" id="c-p325.1" parsed="|Gen|23|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.23.16">Gen. 23:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex. 38:24" id="c-p325.2" parsed="|Exod|38|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.38.24">Ex. 38:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 18:12" id="c-p325.3" parsed="|2Sam|18|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.18.12">2 Sam. 18:12</scripRef>). Probably the
silver ingots used in the time of Abraham may have been of a
fixed weight, which was in some way indicated on them. The
“pieces of silver” paid by Abimelech to Abraham (<scripRef passage="Gen. 20:16" id="c-p325.4" parsed="|Gen|20|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.20.16">Gen. 20:16</scripRef>),
and those also for which Joseph was sold (37:28), were proably
in the form of rings. The shekel was the common standard of
weight and value among the Hebrews down to the time of the

Captivity. Only once is a shekel of gold mentioned (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 21:25" id="c-p325.5" parsed="|1Chr|21|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.21.25">1 Chr. 21:25</scripRef>). The “six thousand of gold” mentioned in the transaction
between Naaman and Gehazi (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 5:5" id="c-p325.6" parsed="|2Kgs|5|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.5.5">2 Kings 5:5</scripRef>) were probably so many
shekels of gold. The “piece of money” mentioned in <scripRef passage="Job 42:11" id="c-p325.7" parsed="|Job|42|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.42.11">Job 42:11</scripRef>;
Gen. 33:19 (marg., “lambs”) was the Hebrew kesitah, probably
an uncoined piece of silver of a certain weight in the form of a
sheep or lamb, or perhaps having on it such an impression. The
same Hebrew word is used in <scripRef passage="Josh. 24:32" id="c-p325.9" parsed="|Josh|24|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.24.32">Josh. 24:32</scripRef>, which is rendered by
Wickliffe “an hundred yonge scheep.”
</def>
<term id="c-p325.10">Collar</term>
(Heb. peh), means in Job 30:18 the mouth or opening of the
garment that closes round the neck in the same way as a tunic
(<scripRef passage="Ex. 39:23" id="c-p326.2" parsed="|Exod|39|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.39.23">Ex. 39:23</scripRef>). The “collars” (Heb. netiphoth) among the spoils of
the Midianites (<scripRef passage="Judg. 8:26" id="c-p326.3" parsed="|Judg|8|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.8.26">Judg. 8:26</scripRef>; R.V., “pendants”) were ear-drops.
The same Hebrew word is rendered “chains” in Isa. 3:19.
</def>
<term id="c-p326.5">Collection</term>
The Christians in Palestine, from various causes, suffered from
poverty. Paul awakened an interest in them among the Gentile
churches, and made pecuniary collections in their behalf (Acts 24:17; Rom. 15:25, 26; 1 Cor. 16:1-3; 2 Cor. 8:9; Gal. 2:10).
</def>
<term id="c-p327.7">College</term>
Heb. mishneh (2 Kings 22:14; 2 Chr. 34:22), rendered in Revised
Version “second quarter”, the residence of the prophetess
Huldah. The Authorized Version followed the Jewish commentators,
who, following the Targum, gave the Hebrew word its
post-Biblical sense, as if it meant a place of instruction. It
properly means the “second,” and may therefore denote the lower
city (Acra), which was built after the portion of the city on
Mount Zion, and was enclosed by a second wall.
</def>
<term id="c-p328.3">Colony</term>
The city of Philippi was a Roman colony (Acts 16:12), i.e., a
military settlement of Roman soldiers and citizens, planted
there to keep in subjection a newly-conquered district. A colony
was Rome in miniature, under Roman municipal law, but governed
by military officers (praetors and lictors), not by proconsuls.
It had an independent internal government, the jus Italicum;
i.e., the privileges of Italian citizens.
</def>
<term id="c-p329.2">Colossae</term>
Or Colosse, a city of Phrygia, on the Lycus, which is a
tributary of the Maeander. It was about 12 miles above Laodicea,
and near the great road from Ephesus to the Euphrates, and was
consequently of some mercantile importance. It does not appear
that Paul had visited this city when he wrote his letter to the
church there (<scripRef passage="Col. 1:2" id="c-p330.1" parsed="|Col|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.1.2">Col. 1:2</scripRef>). He expresses in his letter to Philemon
(ver. 1:22) his hope to visit it on being delivered from his

imprisonment. From <scripRef passage="Col. 1:7" id="c-p330.2" parsed="|Col|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.1.7">Col. 1:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Col 4:12" id="c-p330.3" parsed="|Col|4|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.4.12">4:12</scripRef> it has been concluded that
Epaphras was the founder of the Colossian church. This town
afterwards fell into decay, and the modern town of Chonas or
Chonum occupies a site near its ruins.
</def>
<term id="c-p330.4">Colossians, Epistle to the</term>
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="c-p330.6" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="Col 0" id="c-p330.7" parsed="|Col|0|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col" />
Was written by Paul at Rome during his first imprisonment there

(<scripRef passage="Acts 28:16" id="c-p331.1" parsed="|Acts|28|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.28.16">Acts 28:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 28:30" id="c-p331.2" parsed="|Acts|28|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.28.30">30</scripRef>), probably in the spring of A.D. 57, or, as some
think, 62, and soon after he had written his Epistle to the
Ephesians. Like some of his other epistles (e.g., those to
Corinth), this seems to have been written in consequence of
information which had somehow been conveyed to him of the
internal state of the church there (<scripRef passage="Col. 1:4-8" id="c-p331.3" parsed="|Col|1|4|1|8" osisRef="Bible:Col.1.4-Col.1.8">Col. 1:4-8</scripRef>). Its object was
to counteract false teaching. A large part of it is directed
against certain speculatists who attempted to combine the
doctrines of Oriental mysticism and asceticism with
Christianity, thereby promising the disciples the enjoyment of a
higher spiritual life and a deeper insight into the world of
spirits. Paul argues against such teaching, showing that in
Christ Jesus they had all things. He sets forth the majesty of
his redemption. The mention of the “new moon” and “sabbath days”
(2:16) shows also that there were here Judaizing teachers who
sought to draw away the disciples from the simplicity of the
gospel.
Like most of Paul’s epistles, this consists of two parts, a
doctrinal and a practical.
(1.) The doctrinal part comprises the first two chapters. His
main theme is developed in chapter 2. He warns them against
being drawn away from Him in whom dwelt all the fulness of the
Godhead, and who was the head of all spiritual powers. Christ
was the head of the body of which they were members; and if they
were truly united to him, what needed they more?
(2.) The practical part of the epistle (3-4) enforces various
duties naturally flowing from the doctrines expounded. They are
exhorted to mind things that are above (3:1-4), to mortify every
evil principle of their nature, and to put on the new man
(3:5-14). Many special duties of the Christian life are also
insisted upon as the fitting evidence of the Christian
character. Tychicus was the bearer of the letter, as he was also
of that to the Ephesians and to Philemon, and he would tell them
of the state of the apostle (4:7-9). After friendly greetings
(10-14), he bids them interchange this letter with that he had
sent to the neighbouring church of Laodicea. He then closes this
brief but striking epistle with his usual autograph salutation.
There is a remarkable resemblance between this epistle and that
to the Ephesians (q.v.). The genuineness of this epistle has not
been called in question.
</def>
<term id="c-p334.1">Colour</term>
The subject of colours holds an important place in the
Scriptures.
White occurs as the translation of various Hebrew words. It is

applied to milk (<scripRef passage="Gen. 49:12" id="c-p336.1" parsed="|Gen|49|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.12">Gen. 49:12</scripRef>), manna (<scripRef passage="Ex. 16:31" id="c-p336.2" parsed="|Exod|16|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.16.31">Ex. 16:31</scripRef>), snow (<scripRef passage="Isa. 1:18" id="c-p336.3" parsed="|Isa|1|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.18">Isa. 1:18</scripRef>), horses (<scripRef passage="Zech. 1:8" id="c-p336.4" parsed="|Zech|1|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.1.8">Zech. 1:8</scripRef>), raiment (<scripRef passage="Eccl. 9:8" id="c-p336.5" parsed="|Eccl|9|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eccl.9.8">Eccl. 9:8</scripRef>). Another Hebrew
word so rendered is applied to marble (<scripRef passage="Esther 1:6" id="c-p336.6" parsed="|Esth|1|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.1.6">Esther 1:6</scripRef>), and a
cognate word to the lily (<scripRef passage="Cant. 2:16" id="c-p336.7" parsed="|Song|2|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.2.16">Cant. 2:16</scripRef>). A different term, meaning
“dazzling,” is applied to the countenance (Cant. 5:10).
This colour was an emblem of purity and innocence (Mark 16:5;

<scripRef passage="John 20:12" id="c-p337.2" parsed="|John|20|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.20.12">John 20:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 19:8" id="c-p337.3" parsed="|Rev|19|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.19.8">Rev. 19:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Rev. 19:14" id="c-p337.4" parsed="|Rev|19|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.19.14">14</scripRef>), of joy (<scripRef passage="Eccl. 9:8" id="c-p337.5" parsed="|Eccl|9|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eccl.9.8">Eccl. 9:8</scripRef>), and also of

victory (<scripRef passage="Zech. 6:3" id="c-p337.6" parsed="|Zech|6|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.6.3">Zech. 6:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 6:2" id="c-p337.7" parsed="|Rev|6|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.6.2">Rev. 6:2</scripRef>). The hangings of the tabernacle

court (<scripRef passage="Ex. 27:9" id="c-p337.8" parsed="|Exod|27|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.27.9">Ex. 27:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 38:9" id="c-p337.9" parsed="|Exod|38|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.38.9">38:9</scripRef>), the coats, mitres, bonnets, and breeches

of the priests (<scripRef passage="Ex. 39:27" id="c-p337.10" parsed="|Exod|39|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.39.27">Ex. 39:27</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 39:28" id="c-p337.11" parsed="|Exod|39|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.39.28">28</scripRef>), and the dress of the high priest
on the day of Atonement (Lev. 16:4, 32), were white.
Black, applied to the hair (Lev. 13:31; Cant. 5:11), the

complexion (<scripRef passage="Cant. 1:5" id="c-p338.3" parsed="|Song|1|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.1.5">Cant. 1:5</scripRef>), and to horses (<scripRef passage="Zech. 6:2" id="c-p338.4" parsed="|Zech|6|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.6.2">Zech. 6:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Zech. 6:6" id="c-p338.5" parsed="|Zech|6|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.6.6">6</scripRef>). The word
rendered “brown” in <scripRef passage="Gen. 30:32" id="c-p338.6" parsed="|Gen|30|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.30.32">Gen. 30:32</scripRef> (R.V., “black”) means properly
“scorched”, i.e., the colour produced by the influence of the
sun’s rays. “Black” in <scripRef passage="Job 30:30" id="c-p338.7" parsed="|Job|30|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.30.30">Job 30:30</scripRef> means dirty, blackened by
sorrow and disease. The word is applied to a mourner’s robes

(<scripRef passage="Jer. 8:21" id="c-p338.8" parsed="|Jer|8|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.8.21">Jer. 8:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 14:2" id="c-p338.9" parsed="|Jer|14|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.14.2">14:2</scripRef>), to a clouded sky (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 18:45" id="c-p338.10" parsed="|1Kgs|18|45|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.18.45">1 Kings 18:45</scripRef>), to night

(<scripRef passage="Micah 3:6" id="c-p338.11" parsed="|Mic|3|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.3.6">Micah 3:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 4:28" id="c-p338.12" parsed="|Jer|4|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.4.28">Jer. 4:28</scripRef>), and to a brook rendered turbid by melted

snow (<scripRef passage="Job 6:16" id="c-p338.13" parsed="|Job|6|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.6.16">Job 6:16</scripRef>). It is used as symbolical of evil in <scripRef passage="Zech. 6:2" id="c-p338.14" parsed="|Zech|6|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.6.2">Zech. 6:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Zech 6:6" id="c-p338.15" parsed="|Zech|6|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.6.6">6</scripRef> and <scripRef passage="Rev. 6:5" id="c-p338.16" parsed="|Rev|6|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.6.5">Rev. 6:5</scripRef>. It was the emblem of mourning, affliction,
calamity (Jer. 14:2; Lam. 4:8; 5:10).
Red, applied to blood (2 Kings 3;22), a heifer (Num. 19:2),

pottage of lentils (<scripRef passage="Gen. 25:30" id="c-p339.4" parsed="|Gen|25|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.30">Gen. 25:30</scripRef>), a horse (<scripRef passage="Zech. 1:8" id="c-p339.5" parsed="|Zech|1|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.1.8">Zech. 1:8</scripRef>), wine

(<scripRef passage="Prov. 23:31" id="c-p339.6" parsed="|Prov|23|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.23.31">Prov. 23:31</scripRef>), the complexion (<scripRef passage="Gen. 25:25" id="c-p339.7" parsed="|Gen|25|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.25">Gen. 25:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Cant. 5:10" id="c-p339.8" parsed="|Song|5|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.5.10">Cant. 5:10</scripRef>). This
colour is symbolical of bloodshed (Zech. 6:2; Rev. 6:4; 12:3).
Purple, a colour obtained from the secretion of a species of
shell-fish (the Murex trunculus) which was found in the
Mediterranean, and particularly on the coasts of Phoenicia and
Asia Minor. The colouring matter in each separate shell-fish
amounted to only a single drop, and hence the great value of
this dye. Robes of this colour were worn by kings (<scripRef passage="Judg. 8:26" id="c-p340.1" parsed="|Judg|8|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.8.26">Judg. 8:26</scripRef>)
and high officers (<scripRef passage="Esther 8:15" id="c-p340.2" parsed="|Esth|8|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.8.15">Esther 8:15</scripRef>). They were also worn by the

wealthy and luxurious (<scripRef passage="Jer. 10:9" id="c-p340.3" parsed="|Jer|10|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.10.9">Jer. 10:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:7" id="c-p340.4" parsed="|Ezek|27|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.7">Ezek. 27:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 16:19" id="c-p340.5" parsed="|Luke|16|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.16.19">Luke 16:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 17:4" id="c-p340.6" parsed="|Rev|17|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.17.4">Rev. 17:4</scripRef>). With this colour was associated the idea of royalty and
majesty (Judg. 8:26; Cant. 3:10; 7:5; Dan. 5:7, 16, 29).
Blue. This colour was also procured from a species of
shell-fish, the chelzon of the Hebrews, and the Helix ianthina
of modern naturalists. The tint was emblematic of the sky, the
deep dark hue of the Eastern sky. This colour was used in the
same way as purple. The ribbon and fringe of the Hebrew dress

were of this colour (<scripRef passage="Num. 15:38" id="c-p341.1" parsed="|Num|15|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.15.38">Num. 15:38</scripRef>). The loops of the curtains (<scripRef passage="Ex. 26:4" id="c-p341.2" parsed="|Exod|26|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.26.4">Ex. 26:4</scripRef>), the lace of the high priest’s breastplate, the robe of
the ephod, and the lace on his mitre, were blue (Ex. 28:28, 31, 37).
Scarlet, or Crimson. In Isa. 1:18 a Hebrew word is used which

denotes the worm or grub whence this dye was procured. In <scripRef passage="Gen. 38:28" id="c-p342.2" parsed="|Gen|38|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.38.28">Gen. 38:28</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 38:30" id="c-p342.3" parsed="|Gen|38|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.38.30">30</scripRef>, the word so rendered means “to shine,” and expresses
the brilliancy of the colour. The small parasitic insects from
which this dye was obtained somewhat resembled the cochineal
which is found in Eastern countries. It is called by naturalists
Coccus ilics. The dye was procured from the female grub alone.
The only natural object to which this colour is applied in
Scripture is the lips, which are likened to a scarlet thread
(<scripRef passage="Cant. 4:3" id="c-p342.4" parsed="|Song|4|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.4.3">Cant. 4:3</scripRef>). Scarlet robes were worn by the rich and luxurious

(<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 1:24" id="c-p342.5" parsed="|2Sam|1|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.1.24">2 Sam. 1:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 31:21" id="c-p342.6" parsed="|Prov|31|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.31.21">Prov. 31:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 4:30" id="c-p342.7" parsed="|Jer|4|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.4.30">Jer. 4:30</scripRef>. <scripRef passage="Rev. 17:4" id="c-p342.8" parsed="|Rev|17|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.17.4">Rev. 17:4</scripRef>). It was also

the hue of the warrior’s dress (<scripRef passage="Nah. 2:3" id="c-p342.9" parsed="|Nah|2|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Nah.2.3">Nah. 2:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 9:5" id="c-p342.10" parsed="|Isa|9|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.9.5">Isa. 9:5</scripRef>). The
Phoenicians excelled in the art of dyeing this colour (2 Chr. 2:7).
These four colours—white, purple, blue, and scarlet—were

used in the textures of the tabernacle curtains (<scripRef passage="Ex. 26:1" id="c-p343.1" parsed="|Exod|26|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.26.1">Ex. 26:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex 26:31" id="c-p343.2" parsed="|Exod|26|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.26.31">31</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex 26:36" id="c-p343.3" parsed="|Exod|26|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.26.36">36</scripRef>), and also in the high priest’s ephod, girdle, and

breastplate (<scripRef passage="Ex. 28:5" id="c-p343.4" parsed="|Exod|28|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.5">Ex. 28:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 28:6" id="c-p343.5" parsed="|Exod|28|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.6">6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 28:8" id="c-p343.6" parsed="|Exod|28|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.8">8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 28:15" id="c-p343.7" parsed="|Exod|28|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.15">15</scripRef>). Scarlet thread is mentioned in

connection with the rites of cleansing the leper (<scripRef passage="Lev. 14:4" id="c-p343.8" parsed="|Lev|14|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.14.4">Lev. 14:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev 14:6" id="c-p343.9" parsed="|Lev|14|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.14.6">6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev 14:51" id="c-p343.10" parsed="|Lev|14|51|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.14.51">51</scripRef>) and of burning the red heifer (<scripRef passage="Num. 19:6" id="c-p343.11" parsed="|Num|19|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.19.6">Num. 19:6</scripRef>). It was a crimson
thread that Rahab was to bind on her window as a sign that she

was to be saved alive (<scripRef passage="Josh. 2:18" id="c-p343.12" parsed="|Josh|2|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.2.18">Josh. 2:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 6:25" id="c-p343.13" parsed="|Josh|6|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.6.25">6:25</scripRef>) when the city of
Jericho was taken.
Vermilion, the red sulphuret of mercury, or cinnabar; a colour
used for drawing the figures of idols on the walls of temples
(<scripRef passage="Ezek. 23:14" id="c-p344.1" parsed="|Ezek|23|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.23.14">Ezek. 23:14</scripRef>), or for decorating the walls and beams of houses
(Jer. 22:14).
</def>
<term id="c-p344.3">Comforter</term>
The designation of the Holy Ghost (John 14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7;
R.V. marg., “or Advocate, or Helper; Gr. paracletos”). The same
Greek word thus rendered is translated “Advocate” in <scripRef passage="1 John 2:1" id="c-p345.3" parsed="|1John|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.2.1">1 John 2:1</scripRef>
as applicable to Christ. It means properly “one who is summoned
to the side of another” to help him in a court of justice by
defending him, “one who is summoned to plead a cause.”
“Advocate” is the proper rendering of the word in every case
where it occurs.
It is worthy of notice that although Paul nowhere uses the
word paracletos, he yet presents the idea it embodies when he
speaks of the “intercession” both of Christ and the Spirit (Rom. 8:27, 34).
</def>
<term id="c-p346.3">Coming of Christ</term>
(1) with reference to his first advent “in the fulness of the

time” (<scripRef passage="1 John 5:20" id="c-p347.1" parsed="|1John|5|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.5.20">1 John 5:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 John 1" id="c-p347.2" parsed="|2John|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2John.1.1">2 John 1</scripRef>:7), or (2) with reference to his

coming again the second time at the last day (<scripRef passage="Acts 1:11" id="c-p347.3" parsed="|Acts|1|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.11">Acts 1:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 3:20" id="c-p347.4" parsed="|Acts|3|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.3.20">3:20</scripRef>,
21; 1 Thess. 4:15; 2 Tim. 4:1; Heb. 9:28).
The expression is used metaphorically of the introduction of

the gospel into any place (<scripRef passage="John 15:22" id="c-p348.1" parsed="|John|15|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.15.22">John 15:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 2:17" id="c-p348.2" parsed="|Eph|2|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.17">Eph. 2:17</scripRef>), the visible
establishment of his kingdom in the world (<scripRef passage="Matt. 16:28" id="c-p348.3" parsed="|Matt|16|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.16.28">Matt. 16:28</scripRef>), the
conferring on his people of the peculiar tokens of his love

(<scripRef passage="John 14:18" id="c-p348.4" parsed="|John|14|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.14.18">John 14:18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="John 14:23" id="c-p348.5" parsed="|John|14|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.14.23">23</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="John 14:28" id="c-p348.6" parsed="|John|14|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.14.28">28</scripRef>), and his executing judgment on the wicked
(2 Thess. 2:8).
</def>
<term id="c-p348.8">Commandments, the Ten</term>
(Ex. 34:28; Deut. 10:4, marg. “ten words”) i.e., the Decalogue
(q.v.), is a summary of the immutable moral law. These
commandments were first given in their written form to the
people of Israel when they were encamped at Sinai, about fifty
days after they came out of Egypt (<scripRef passage="Ex. 19:10-25" id="c-p349.3" parsed="|Exod|19|10|19|25" osisRef="Bible:Exod.19.10-Exod.19.25">Ex. 19:10-25</scripRef>). They were
written by the finger of God on two tables of stone. The first
tables were broken by Moses when he brought them down from the
mount (32:19), being thrown by him on the ground. At the command
of God he took up into the mount two other tables, and God wrote
on them “the words that were on the first tables” (34:1). These

tables were afterwards placed in the ark of the covenant (<scripRef passage="Deut. 10:5" id="c-p349.4" parsed="|Deut|10|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.10.5">Deut. 10:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 8:9" id="c-p349.5" parsed="|1Kgs|8|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.8.9">1 Kings 8:9</scripRef>). Their subsequent history is unknown. They
are as a whole called “the covenant” (<scripRef passage="Deut. 4:13" id="c-p349.6" parsed="|Deut|4|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.4.13">Deut. 4:13</scripRef>), and “the
tables of the covenant” (9:9, 11; <scripRef passage="Heb. 9:4" id="c-p349.7" parsed="|Heb|9|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.4">Heb. 9:4</scripRef>), and “the
testimony.”
They are obviously “ten” in number, but their division is not
fixed, hence different methods of numbering them have been
adopted. The Jews make the “Preface” one of the commandments,
and then combine the first and second. The Roman Catholics and
Lutherans combine the first and second and divide the tenth into
two. The Jews and Josephus divide them equally. The Lutherans
and Roman Catholics refer three commandments to the first table
and seven to the second. The Greek and Reformed Churches refer
four to the first and six to the second table. The Samaritans
add to the second that Gerizim is the mount of worship. (See LAW.)
</def>
<term id="c-p350.2">Communion</term>
Fellowship with God (Gen. 18:17-33; Ex. 33:9-11; Num. 12:7, 8),

between Christ and his people (<scripRef passage="John 14:23" id="c-p351.5" parsed="|John|14|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.14.23">John 14:23</scripRef>), by the Spirit (<scripRef passage="2 Cor. 13:14" id="c-p351.6" parsed="|2Cor|13|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.13.14">2 Cor. 13:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Phil. 2:1" id="c-p351.7" parsed="|Phil|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Phil.2.1">Phil. 2:1</scripRef>), of believers with one another (<scripRef passage="Eph. 4:1-6" id="c-p351.8" parsed="|Eph|4|1|4|6" osisRef="Bible:Eph.4.1-Eph.4.6">Eph. 4:1-6</scripRef>). The Lord’s Supper is so called (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 10:16" id="c-p351.9" parsed="|1Cor|10|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.10.16">1 Cor. 10:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 10:17" id="c-p351.10" parsed="|1Cor|10|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.10.17">17</scripRef>),
because in it there is fellowship between Christ and his
disciples, and of the disciples with one another.
</def>
<term id="c-p351.11">Conaniah</term>
Whom Jehovah hath set, a Levite placed over the tithes brought
into the temple (2 Chr. 35:9).
</def>
<term id="c-p352.2">Concision</term>
(Gr. katatome; i.e., “mutilation”), a term used by Paul

contemptuously of those who were zealots for circumcision (<scripRef passage="Phil. 3:2" id="c-p353.1" parsed="|Phil|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Phil.3.2">Phil. 3:2</scripRef>). Instead of the warning, “Beware of the circumcision”
(peritome) i.e., of the party who pressed on Gentile converts
the necessity of still observing that ordinance, he says,
“Beware of the concision;” as much as to say, “This circumcision
which they vaunt of is in Christ only as the gashings and
mutilations of idolatrous heathen.”
</def>
<term id="c-p353.2">Concubine</term>
In the Bible denotes a female conjugally united to a man, but in
a relation inferior to that of a wife. Among the early Jews,
from various causes, the difference between a wife and a
concubine was less marked than it would be amongst us. The
concubine was a wife of secondary rank. There are various laws

recorded providing for their protection (<scripRef passage="Ex. 21:7" id="c-p354.1" parsed="|Exod|21|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.21.7">Ex. 21:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 21:10-14" id="c-p354.2" parsed="|Deut|21|10|21|14" osisRef="Bible:Deut.21.10-Deut.21.14">Deut. 21:10-14</scripRef>), and setting limits to the relation they sustained to

the household to which they belonged (<scripRef passage="Gen. 21:14" id="c-p354.3" parsed="|Gen|21|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.14">Gen. 21:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 25:6" id="c-p354.4" parsed="|Gen|25|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.6">25:6</scripRef>). They
had no authority in the family, nor could they share in the
household government.
The immediate cause of concubinage might be gathered from the

conjugal histories of Abraham and Jacob (<scripRef passage="Gen. 16" id="c-p355.1" parsed="|Gen|16|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.16">Gen. 16</scripRef>;<scripRef passage="Gen 30" id="c-p355.2" parsed="|Gen|30|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.30">30</scripRef>). But in
process of time the custom of concubinage degenerated, and laws
were made to restrain and regulate it (Ex. 21:7-9).
Christianity has restored the sacred institution of marriage
to its original character, and concubinage is ranked with the
sins of fornication and adultery (Matt. 19:5-9; 1 Cor. 7:2).
</def>
<term id="c-p356.3">Concupiscence</term>
Desire, Rom. 7:8 (R.V., “coveting”); Col. 3:5 (R.V., “desire”).
The “lust of concupiscence” (<scripRef passage="1 Thess. 4:5" id="c-p357.3" parsed="|1Thess|4|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Thess.4.5">1 Thess. 4:5</scripRef>; R.V., “passion of
lust”) denotes evil desire, indwelling sin.
</def>
<term id="c-p357.4">Conduit</term>
A water-course or channel (Job 38:25). The “conduit of the upper
pool” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 7:3" id="c-p358.2" parsed="|Isa|7|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.7.3">Isa. 7:3</scripRef>) was formed by Hezekiah for the purpose of
conveying the waters from the upper pool in the valley of Gihon

to the west side of the city of David (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:17" id="c-p358.3" parsed="|2Kgs|18|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.17">2 Kings 18:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 20:20" id="c-p358.4" parsed="|2Kgs|20|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.20.20">20:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 32:30" id="c-p358.5" parsed="|2Chr|32|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.32.30">2 Chr. 32:30</scripRef>). In carrying out this work he stopped “the waters of
the fountains which were without the city” i.e., “the upper
water-course of Gihon”, and conveyed it down from the west
through a canal into the city, so that in case of a siege the
inhabitants of the city might have a supply of water, which
would thus be withdrawn from the enemy. (See SILOAM.)
There are also the remains of a conduit which conducted water
from the so-called “Pools of Solomon,” beyond Bethlehem, into
the city. Water is still conveyed into the city from the
fountains which supplied these pools by a channel which crosses
the valley of Hinnom.
</def>
<term id="c-p359.1">Coney</term>
(Heb. shaphan; i.e., “the hider”), an animal which inhabits the
mountain gorges and the rocky districts of Arabia Petraea and
the Holy Land. “The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they

their houses in the rocks” (<scripRef passage="Prov. 30:26" id="c-p360.1" parsed="|Prov|30|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.30.26">Prov. 30:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 104:18" id="c-p360.2" parsed="|Ps|104|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.104.18">Ps. 104:18</scripRef>). They are
gregarious, and “exceeding wise” (<scripRef passage="Prov. 30:24" id="c-p360.3" parsed="|Prov|30|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.30.24">Prov. 30:24</scripRef>), and are
described as chewing the cud (Lev. 11:5; Deut. 14:7).
The animal intended by this name is known among naturalists as
the Hyrax Syriacus. It is neither a ruminant nor a rodent, but
is regarded as akin to the rhinoceros. When it is said to “chew
the cud,” the Hebrew word so used does not necessarily imply the
possession of a ruminant stomach. “The lawgiver speaks according
to appearances; and no one can watch the constant motion of the
little creature’s jaws, as it sits continually working its
teeth, without recognizing the naturalness of the expression”
(Tristram, Natural History of the Bible). It is about the size
and color of a rabbit, though clumsier in structure, and without
a tail. Its feet are not formed for digging, and therefore it
has its home not in burrows but in the clefts of the rocks.
“Coney” is an obsolete English word for “rabbit.”
</def>
<term id="c-p361.1">Confection</term>
(Ex. 30:35, “ointment” in ver. 25; R.V., “perfume”). The Hebrew
word so rendered is derived from a root meaning to compound oil
and perfume.
</def>
<term id="c-p362.2">Confectionaries</term>
Only in 1 Sam. 8:13, those who make confections, i.e.,
perfumers, who compound species and perfumes.
</def>
<term id="c-p363.2">Confession</term>
(1) An open profession of faith (Luke 12:8). (2.) An

acknowledment of sins to God (<scripRef passage="Lev. 16:21" id="c-p364.2" parsed="|Lev|16|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.16.21">Lev. 16:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezra 9:5-15" id="c-p364.3" parsed="|Ezra|9|5|9|15" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.9.5-Ezra.9.15">Ezra 9:5-15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Dan. 9:3-12" id="c-p364.4" parsed="|Dan|9|3|9|12" osisRef="Bible:Dan.9.3-Dan.9.12">Dan. 9:3-12</scripRef>), and to a neighbour whom we have wronged (<scripRef passage="James 5:16" id="c-p364.5" parsed="|Jas|5|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jas.5.16">James 5:16</scripRef>;
Matt. 18:15).
</def>
<term id="c-p364.7">Congregation</term>
(Heb. kahal), the Hebrew people collectively as a holy community
(<scripRef passage="Num. 15:15" id="c-p365.1" parsed="|Num|15|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.15.15">Num. 15:15</scripRef>). Every circumcised Hebrew from twenty years old and
upward was a member of the congregation. Strangers resident in

the land, if circumcised, were, with certain exceptions (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:19" id="c-p365.2" parsed="|Exod|12|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.19">Ex. 12:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 9:14" id="c-p365.3" parsed="|Num|9|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.9.14">Num. 9:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 23:1-3" id="c-p365.4" parsed="|Deut|23|1|23|3" osisRef="Bible:Deut.23.1-Deut.23.3">Deut. 23:1-3</scripRef>), admitted to the privileges of

citizenship, and spoken of as members of the congregation (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:19" id="c-p365.5" parsed="|Exod|12|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.19">Ex. 12:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 9:14" id="c-p365.6" parsed="|Num|9|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.9.14">Num. 9:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 15:15" id="c-p365.7" parsed="|Num|15|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.15.15">15:15</scripRef>). The congregation were summonded
together by the sound of two silver trumpets, and they met at
the door of the tabernacle (<scripRef passage="Num. 10:3" id="c-p365.8" parsed="|Num|10|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.10.3">Num. 10:3</scripRef>). These assemblies were
convened for the purpose of engaging in solemn religious

services (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:27" id="c-p365.9" parsed="|Exod|12|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.27">Ex. 12:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 25:6" id="c-p365.10" parsed="|Num|25|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.25.6">Num. 25:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Joel 2:15" id="c-p365.11" parsed="|Joel|2|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Joel.2.15">Joel 2:15</scripRef>), or of receiving new

commandments (<scripRef passage="Ex. 19:7" id="c-p365.12" parsed="|Exod|19|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.19.7">Ex. 19:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 19:8" id="c-p365.13" parsed="|Exod|19|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.19.8">8</scripRef>). The elders, who were summonded by
the sound of one trumpet (<scripRef passage="Num. 10:4" id="c-p365.14" parsed="|Num|10|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.10.4">Num. 10:4</scripRef>), represented on various
occasions the whole congregation (Ex. 3:16; 12:21; 17:5; 24:1).
After the conquest of Canaan, the people were assembled only

on occasions of the highest national importance (<scripRef passage="Judg. 20" id="c-p366.1" parsed="|Judg|20|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.20">Judg. 20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 30:5" id="c-p366.2" parsed="|2Chr|30|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.30.5">2 Chr. 30:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 34:29" id="c-p366.3" parsed="|2Chr|34|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.34.29">34:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 10:17" id="c-p366.4" parsed="|1Sam|10|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.10.17">1 Sam. 10:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 5:1-5" id="c-p366.5" parsed="|2Sam|5|1|5|5" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.5.1-2Sam.5.5">2 Sam. 5:1-5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 12:20" id="c-p366.6" parsed="|1Kgs|12|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.12.20">1 Kings 12:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 11:19" id="c-p366.7" parsed="|2Kgs|11|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.11.19">2 Kings 11:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 21:24" id="c-p366.8" parsed="|2Kgs|21|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.21.24">21:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 23:30" id="c-p366.9" parsed="|2Kgs|23|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.30">23:30</scripRef>). In subsequent times the congregation
was represented by the Sanhedrim; and the name synagogue,
applied in the Septuagint version exclusively to the
congregation, came to be used to denote the places of worship
established by the Jews. (See CHURCH.)
In Acts 13:43, where alone it occurs in the New Testament, it
is the same word as that rendered “synagogue” (q.v.) in ver. 42,
and is so rendered in ver. 43 in R.V.
</def>
<term id="c-p367.2">Congregation, mount of the</term>
(Isa. 14:13), has been supposed to refer to the place where God

promised to meet with his people (<scripRef passage="Ex. 25:22" id="c-p368.2" parsed="|Exod|25|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.25.22">Ex. 25:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 29:42" id="c-p368.3" parsed="|Exod|29|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.42">29:42</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex 29:43" id="c-p368.4" parsed="|Exod|29|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.43">43</scripRef>) i.e.,
the mount of the Divine presence, Mount Zion. But here the king
of Babylon must be taken as expressing himself according to his
own heathen notions, and not according to those of the Jews. The
“mount of the congregation” will therefore in this case mean the
northern mountain, supposed by the Babylonians to be the
meeting-place of their gods. In the Babylonian inscriptions
mention is made of a mountain which is described as “the mighty
mountain of Bel, whose head rivals heaven, whose root is the
holy deep.” This mountain was regarded in their mythology as the
place where the gods had their seat.
</def>
<term id="c-p368.5">Conscience</term>
That faculty of the mind, or inborn sense of right and wrong, by
which we judge of the moral character of human conduct. It is
common to all men. Like all our other faculties, it has been

perverted by the Fall (<scripRef passage="John 16:2" id="c-p369.1" parsed="|John|16|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.16.2">John 16:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 26:9" id="c-p369.2" parsed="|Acts|26|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.26.9">Acts 26:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 2:15" id="c-p369.3" parsed="|Rom|2|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.2.15">Rom. 2:15</scripRef>). It is

spoken of as “defiled” (<scripRef passage="Titus 1:15" id="c-p369.4" parsed="|Titus|1|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Titus.1.15">Titus 1:15</scripRef>), and “seared” (<scripRef passage="1 Tim. 4:2" id="c-p369.5" parsed="|1Tim|4|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.4.2">1 Tim. 4:2</scripRef>).
A “conscience void of offence” is to be sought and cultivated
(Acts 24:16; Rom. 9:1; 2 Cor. 1:12; 1 Tim. 1:5, 19; 1 Pet. 3:21).
</def>
<term id="c-p369.12">Consecration</term>
The devoting or setting apart of anything to the worship or
service of God. The race of Abraham and the tribe of Levi were

thus consecrated (<scripRef passage="Ex. 13:2" id="c-p370.1" parsed="|Exod|13|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.13.2">Ex. 13:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 13:12" id="c-p370.2" parsed="|Exod|13|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.13.12">12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 13:15" id="c-p370.3" parsed="|Exod|13|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.13.15">15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 3:12" id="c-p370.4" parsed="|Num|3|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.3.12">Num. 3:12</scripRef>). The Hebrews
devoted their fields and cattle, and sometimes the spoils of

war, to the Lord (<scripRef passage="Lev. 27:28" id="c-p370.5" parsed="|Lev|27|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.27.28">Lev. 27:28</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 27:29" id="c-p370.6" parsed="|Lev|27|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.27.29">29</scripRef>). According to the Mosaic law
the first-born both of man and beast were consecrated to God.
In the New Testament, Christians are regarded as consecrated
to the Lord (1 Pet. 2:9).
</def>
<term id="c-p371.2">Consolation of Israel</term>
A name for the Messiah in common use among the Jews, probably

suggested by <scripRef passage="Isa. 12:1" id="c-p372.1" parsed="|Isa|12|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.12.1">Isa. 12:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 49:13" id="c-p372.2" parsed="|Isa|49|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.49.13">49:13</scripRef>. The Greek word thus rendered
(<scripRef passage="Luke 2:25" id="c-p372.3" parsed="|Luke|2|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.25">Luke 2:25</scripRef>, paraklesis) is kindred to that translated
“Comforter” in John 14:16, etc., parakletos.
</def>
<term id="c-p372.5">Constellation</term>
A cluster of stars, or stars which appear to be near each other
in the heavens, and which astronomers have reduced to certain
figures (as the “Great Bear,” the “Bull,” etc.) for the sake of
classification and of memory. In <scripRef passage="Isa. 13:10" id="c-p373.1" parsed="|Isa|13|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.13.10">Isa. 13:10</scripRef>, where this word
only occurs, it is the rendering of the Hebrew kesil, i.e.,

“fool.” This was the Hebrew name of the constellation Orion (<scripRef passage="Job 9:9" id="c-p373.2" parsed="|Job|9|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.9.9">Job 9:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 38:31" id="c-p373.3" parsed="|Job|38|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.38.31">38:31</scripRef>), a constellation which represented Nimrod, the
symbol of folly and impiety. The word some interpret by “the
giant” in this place, “some heaven-daring rebel who was chained
to the sky for his impiety.”
</def>
<term id="c-p373.4">Contentment</term>
A state of mind in which one’s desires are confined to his lot

whatever it may be (<scripRef passage="1 Tim. 6:6" id="c-p374.1" parsed="|1Tim|6|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.6.6">1 Tim. 6:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 9:8" id="c-p374.2" parsed="|2Cor|9|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.9.8">2 Cor. 9:8</scripRef>). It is opposed to

envy (<scripRef passage="James 3:16" id="c-p374.3" parsed="|Jas|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jas.3.16">James 3:16</scripRef>), avarice (<scripRef passage="Heb. 13:5" id="c-p374.4" parsed="|Heb|13|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.13.5">Heb. 13:5</scripRef>), ambition (<scripRef passage="Prov. 13:10" id="c-p374.5" parsed="|Prov|13|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.13.10">Prov. 13:10</scripRef>),

anxiety (<scripRef passage="Matt. 6:25" id="c-p374.6" parsed="|Matt|6|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.25">Matt. 6:25</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 6:34" id="c-p374.7" parsed="|Matt|6|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.34">34</scripRef>), and repining (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 10:10" id="c-p374.8" parsed="|1Cor|10|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.10.10">1 Cor. 10:10</scripRef>). It arises
from the inward disposition, and is the offspring of humility,
and of an intelligent consideration of the rectitude and

benignity of divine providence (<scripRef passage="Ps. 96:1" id="c-p374.9" parsed="|Ps|96|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.96.1">Ps. 96:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps 96:2" id="c-p374.10" parsed="|Ps|96|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.96.2">2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 145" id="c-p374.11" parsed="|Ps|145|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.145">145</scripRef>), the greatness
of the divine promises (2 Pet. 1:4), and our own unworthiness
(<scripRef passage="Gen. 32:10" id="c-p374.12" parsed="|Gen|32|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.32.10">Gen. 32:10</scripRef>); as well as from the view the gospel opens up to us
of rest and peace hereafter (Rom. 5:2).
</def>
<term id="c-p374.14">Conversation</term>
Generally the goings out and in of social intercourse (Eph. 2:3;
<scripRef passage="Eph 4:22" id="c-p375.2" parsed="|Eph|4|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.4.22">4:22</scripRef>; R.V., “manner of life”); one’s deportment or course of
life. This word is never used in Scripture in the sense of

verbal communication from one to another (<scripRef passage="Ps. 50:23" id="c-p375.3" parsed="|Ps|50|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.50.23">Ps. 50:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 13:5" id="c-p375.4" parsed="|Heb|13|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.13.5">Heb. 13:5</scripRef>).
In <scripRef passage="Phil. 1:27" id="c-p375.5" parsed="|Phil|1|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Phil.1.27">Phil. 1:27</scripRef> and 3:20, a different Greek word is used. It there
means one’s relations to a community as a citizen, i.e.,
citizenship.
</def>
<term id="c-p375.6">Conversion</term>
The turning of a sinner to God (Acts 15:3). In a general sense
the heathen are said to be “converted” when they abandon
heathenism and embrace the Christian faith; and in a more
special sense men are converted when, by the influence of divine
grace in their souls, their whole life is changed, old things
pass away, and all things become new (<scripRef passage="Acts 26:18" id="c-p376.2" parsed="|Acts|26|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.26.18">Acts 26:18</scripRef>). Thus we speak
of the conversion of the Philippian jailer (16:19-34), of Paul
(9:1-22), of the Ethiopian treasurer (8:26-40), of Cornelius
(10), of Lydia (16:13-15), and others. (See REGENERATION.)
</def>
<term id="c-p376.4">Convocation</term>
A meeting of a religious character as distinguished from
congregation, which was more general, dealing with political and
legal matters. Hence it is called an “holy convocation.” Such

convocations were the Sabbaths (<scripRef passage="Lev. 23:2" id="c-p377.1" parsed="|Lev|23|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.2">Lev. 23:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 23:3" id="c-p377.2" parsed="|Lev|23|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.3">3</scripRef>), the Passover (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:16" id="c-p377.3" parsed="|Exod|12|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.16">Ex. 12:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 23:7" id="c-p377.4" parsed="|Lev|23|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.7">Lev. 23:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 23:8" id="c-p377.5" parsed="|Lev|23|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.8">8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 28:25" id="c-p377.6" parsed="|Num|28|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.28.25">Num. 28:25</scripRef>), Pentecost (<scripRef passage="Lev. 23:21" id="c-p377.7" parsed="|Lev|23|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.21">Lev. 23:21</scripRef>), the

feast of Trumpets (<scripRef passage="Lev. 23:24" id="c-p377.8" parsed="|Lev|23|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.24">Lev. 23:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 29:1" id="c-p377.9" parsed="|Num|29|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.29.1">Num. 29:1</scripRef>), the feast of Weeks

(<scripRef passage="Num. 28:26" id="c-p377.10" parsed="|Num|28|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.28.26">Num. 28:26</scripRef>), and the feast of Tabernacles (<scripRef passage="Lev. 23:35" id="c-p377.11" parsed="|Lev|23|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.35">Lev. 23:35</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 23:36" id="c-p377.12" parsed="|Lev|23|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.36">36</scripRef>). The
great fast, the annual day of atonement, was “the holy
convocation” (Lev. 23:27; Num. 29:7).
</def>
<term id="c-p377.15">Cook</term>
A person employed to perform culinary service. In early times
among the Hebrews cooking was performed by the mistress of the

household (<scripRef passage="Gen. 18:2-6" id="c-p378.1" parsed="|Gen|18|2|18|6" osisRef="Bible:Gen.18.2-Gen.18.6">Gen. 18:2-6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 6:19" id="c-p378.2" parsed="|Judg|6|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.6.19">Judg. 6:19</scripRef>), and the process was very

expeditiously performed (<scripRef passage="Gen. 27:3" id="c-p378.3" parsed="|Gen|27|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.3">Gen. 27:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 27:4" id="c-p378.4" parsed="|Gen|27|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.4">4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 27:9" id="c-p378.5" parsed="|Gen|27|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.9">9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 27:10" id="c-p378.6" parsed="|Gen|27|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.10">10</scripRef>). Professional

cooks were afterwards employed (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 8:13" id="c-p378.7" parsed="|1Sam|8|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.8.13">1 Sam. 8:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 9:23" id="c-p378.8" parsed="|1Sam|9|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.9.23">9:23</scripRef>). Few animals,
