as a rule, were slaughtered (other than sacrifices), except for

purposes of hospitality (<scripRef passage="Gen. 18:7" id="c-p378.9" parsed="|Gen|18|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.18.7">Gen. 18:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 15:23" id="c-p378.10" parsed="|Luke|15|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.15.23">Luke 15:23</scripRef>). The paschal

lamb was roasted over a fire (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:8" id="c-p378.11" parsed="|Exod|12|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.8">Ex. 12:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 12:9" id="c-p378.12" parsed="|Exod|12|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.9">9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2Chr. 35:13" id="c-p378.13" parsed="|2Chr|35|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.35.13">2Chr. 35:13</scripRef>). Cooking

by boiling was the usual method adopted (<scripRef passage="Lev. 8:31" id="c-p378.14" parsed="|Lev|8|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.8.31">Lev. 8:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex. 16:23" id="c-p378.15" parsed="|Exod|16|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.16.23">Ex. 16:23</scripRef>).
No cooking took place on the Sabbath day (Ex. 35:3).
</def>
<term id="c-p378.17">Coos</term>
(written Cos in the R.V.), a small island, one of the Sporades
in the Aegean Sea, in the north-west of Rhodes, off the coast of
Caria. Paul on his return from his third missionary journey,
passed the night here after sailing from Miletus (<scripRef passage="Acts 21:1" id="c-p379.1" parsed="|Acts|21|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.21.1">Acts 21:1</scripRef>). It
is now called Stanchio.
</def>
<term id="c-p379.2">Copper</term>
Derived from the Greek kupros (the island of Cyprus), called

“Cyprian brass,” occurs only in the Authorized Version in <scripRef passage="Ezra 8:27" id="c-p380.1" parsed="|Ezra|8|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.8.27">Ezra 8:27</scripRef>. Elsewhere the Hebrew word (nehosheth) is improperly

rendered “brass,” and sometimes “steel” (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 22:35" id="c-p380.2" parsed="|2Sam|22|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.22.35">2 Sam. 22:35</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 15:12" id="c-p380.3" parsed="|Jer|15|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.15.12">Jer. 15:12</scripRef>). The “bow of steel” (<scripRef passage="Job 20:24" id="c-p380.4" parsed="|Job|20|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.20.24">Job 20:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 18:34" id="c-p380.5" parsed="|Ps|18|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.18.34">Ps. 18:34</scripRef>) should have
been “bow of copper” (or “brass,” as in the R.V.). The vessels
of “fine copper” of <scripRef passage="Ezra 8:27" id="c-p380.6" parsed="|Ezra|8|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.8.27">Ezra 8:27</scripRef> were probably similar to those of
“bright brass” mentioned in 1 Kings 7:45; Dan. 10:6.
Tubal-cain was the first artificer in brass and iron (Gen. 4:22). Hiram was noted as a worker in brass (1 Kings 7:14).

Copper abounded in Palestine (<scripRef passage="Deut. 8:9" id="c-p381.3" parsed="|Deut|8|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.8.9">Deut. 8:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 60:17" id="c-p381.4" parsed="|Isa|60|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.60.17">Isa. 60:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 22:3" id="c-p381.5" parsed="|1Chr|22|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.22.3">1 Chr. 22:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 22:14" id="c-p381.6" parsed="|1Chr|22|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.22.14">14</scripRef>). All sorts of vessels in the tabernacle and the temple

were made of it (<scripRef passage="Lev. 6:28" id="c-p381.7" parsed="|Lev|6|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.6.28">Lev. 6:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 16:39" id="c-p381.8" parsed="|Num|16|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.16.39">Num. 16:39</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 4:16" id="c-p381.9" parsed="|2Chr|4|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.4.16">2 Chr. 4:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezra 8:27" id="c-p381.10" parsed="|Ezra|8|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.8.27">Ezra 8:27</scripRef>);

also weapons of war (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:5" id="c-p381.11" parsed="|1Sam|17|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.5">1 Sam. 17:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:6" id="c-p381.12" parsed="|1Sam|17|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.6">6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:38" id="c-p381.13" parsed="|1Sam|17|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.38">38</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:16" id="c-p381.14" parsed="|2Sam|21|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.16">2 Sam. 21:16</scripRef>). Iron is

mentioned only four times (<scripRef passage="Gen. 4:22" id="c-p381.15" parsed="|Gen|4|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.4.22">Gen. 4:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 26:19" id="c-p381.16" parsed="|Lev|26|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.26.19">Lev. 26:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 31:22" id="c-p381.17" parsed="|Num|31|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.31.22">Num. 31:22</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Num 35:16" id="c-p381.18" parsed="|Num|35|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.35.16">35:16</scripRef>) in the first four books of Moses, while copper (rendered
“brass”) is mentioned forty times. (See BRASS.)
We find mention of Alexander (q.v.), a “coppersmith” of
Ephesus (2 Tim. 4:14).
</def>
<term id="c-p382.2">Cor</term>
This Hebrew word, untranslated, denotes a round vessel used as a
measure both for liquids and solids. It was equal to one homer,
and contained ten ephahs in dry and ten baths in liquid measure
(<scripRef passage="Ezek. 45:14" id="c-p383.1" parsed="|Ezek|45|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.45.14">Ezek. 45:14</scripRef>). The Rabbins estimated the cor at forty-five

gallons, while Josephus estimated it at about eighty-seven. In <scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:22" id="c-p383.2" parsed="|1Kgs|4|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.22">1 Kings 4:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 5:11" id="c-p383.3" parsed="|1Kgs|5|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.5.11">5:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 2:10" id="c-p383.4" parsed="|2Chr|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.2.10">2 Chr. 2:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 27:5" id="c-p383.5" parsed="|2Chr|27|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.27.5">27:5</scripRef>, the original word is
rendered “measure.”
</def>
<term id="c-p383.6">Coral</term>
Heb. ramoth, meaning “heights;” i.e., “high-priced” or valuable
things, or, as some suppose, “that which grows high,” like a

tree (<scripRef passage="Job 28:18" id="c-p384.1" parsed="|Job|28|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.28.18">Job 28:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:16" id="c-p384.2" parsed="|Ezek|27|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.16">Ezek. 27:16</scripRef>), according to the Rabbins, red
coral, which was in use for ornaments.
The coral is a cretaceous marine product, the deposit by
minute polypous animals of calcareous matter in cells in which
the animal lives. It is of numberless shapes as it grows, but
usually is branched like a tree. Great coral reefs and coral
islands abound in the Red Sea, whence probably the Hebrews
derived their knowledge of it. It is found of different colours,
white, black, and red. The red, being esteemed the most
precious, was used, as noticed above, for ornamental purposes.
</def>
<term id="c-p385.1">Corban</term>
A Hebrew word adopted into the Greek of the New Testament and
left untranslated. It occurs only once (<scripRef passage="Mark 7:11" id="c-p386.1" parsed="|Mark|7|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.7.11">Mark 7:11</scripRef>). It means a
gift or offering consecrated to God. Anything over which this
word was once pronounced was irrevocably dedicated to the
temple. Land, however, so dedicated might be redeemed before the
year of jubilee (<scripRef passage="Lev. 27:16-24" id="c-p386.2" parsed="|Lev|27|16|27|24" osisRef="Bible:Lev.27.16-Lev.27.24">Lev. 27:16-24</scripRef>). Our Lord condemns the Pharisees
for their false doctrine, inasmuch as by their traditions they
had destroyed the commandment which requires children to honour
their father and mother, teaching them to find excuse from
helping their parents by the device of pronouncing “Corban” over
their goods, thus reserving them to their own selfish use.
</def>
<term id="c-p386.3">Cord</term>
Frequently used in its proper sense, for fastening a tent (Ex. 35:18; 39:40), yoking animals to a cart (Isa. 5:18), binding

prisoners (<scripRef passage="Judg. 15:13" id="c-p387.4" parsed="|Judg|15|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.15.13">Judg. 15:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 2:3" id="c-p387.5" parsed="|Ps|2|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.2.3">Ps. 2:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 129:4" id="c-p387.6" parsed="|Ps|129|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.129.4">129:4</scripRef>), and measuring ground (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 8" id="c-p387.7" parsed="|2Sam|8|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.8">2 Sam. 8</scripRef>;<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 2" id="c-p387.8" parsed="|2Sam|2|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.2">2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 78:55" id="c-p387.9" parsed="|Ps|78|55|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.78.55">Ps. 78:55</scripRef>). Figuratively, death is spoken of as the
giving way of the tent-cord (<scripRef passage="Job 4:21" id="c-p387.10" parsed="|Job|4|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.4.21">Job 4:21</scripRef>. “Is not their tent-cord
plucked up?” R.V.). To gird one’s self with a cord was a token
of sorrow and humiliation. To stretch a line over a city meant
to level it with the ground (<scripRef passage="Lam. 2:8" id="c-p387.11" parsed="|Lam|2|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lam.2.8">Lam. 2:8</scripRef>). The “cords of sin” are
the consequences or fruits of sin (<scripRef passage="Prov. 5:22" id="c-p387.12" parsed="|Prov|5|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.5.22">Prov. 5:22</scripRef>). A “threefold
cord” is a symbol of union (<scripRef passage="Eccl. 4:12" id="c-p387.13" parsed="|Eccl|4|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eccl.4.12">Eccl. 4:12</scripRef>). The “cords of a man”
(<scripRef passage="Hos. 11:4" id="c-p387.14" parsed="|Hos|11|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.11.4">Hos. 11:4</scripRef>) means that men employ, in inducing each other,
methods such as are suitable to men, and not “cords” such as
oxen are led by. Isaiah (5:18) says, “Woe unto them that draw
iniquity with cords of vanity, and sin as it were with a cart
rope.” This verse is thus given in the Chaldee paraphrase: “Woe
to those who begin to sin by little and little, drawing sin by
cords of vanity: these sins grow and increase till they are
strong and are like a cart rope.” This may be the true meaning.
The wicked at first draw sin with a slender cord; but by-and-by
their sins increase, and they are drawn after them by a cart
rope. Henderson in his commentary says: “The meaning is that the
persons described were not satisfied with ordinary modes of
provoking the Deity, and the consequent ordinary approach of his
vengeance, but, as it were, yoked themselves in the harness of
iniquity, and, putting forth all their strength, drew down upon
themselves, with accelerated speed, the load of punishment which
their sins deserved.”
</def>
<term id="c-p387.15">Coriander</term>
Heb. gad, (Ex. 16:31; Num. 11:7), seed to which the manna is
likened in its form and colour. It is the Coriandrum sativum of
botanists, an umbelliferous annual plant with a round stalk,
about two feet high. It is widely cultivated in Eastern
countries and in the south of Europe for the sake of its seeds,
which are in the form of a little ball of the size of a
peppercorn. They are used medicinally and as a spice. The Greek
name of this plant is korion or koriannon, whence the name
“coriander.”
</def>
<term id="c-p388.3">Corinth</term>
A Grecian city, on the isthmus which joins the Peloponnesus to
the mainland of Greece. It is about 48 miles west of Athens. The
ancient city was destroyed by the Romans (B.C. 146), and that
mentioned in the New Testament was quite a new city, having been
rebuilt about a century afterwards and peopled by a colony of
freedmen from Rome. It became under the Romans the seat of
government for Southern Greece or Achaia (<scripRef passage="Acts 18:12-16" id="c-p389.1" parsed="|Acts|18|12|18|16" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.12-Acts.18.16">Acts 18:12-16</scripRef>). It was
noted for its wealth, and for the luxurious and immoral and
vicious habits of the people. It had a large mixed population of
Romans, Greeks, and Jews. When Paul first visited the city (A.D.
51 or 52), Gallio, the brother of Seneca, was proconsul. Here
Paul resided for eighteen months (18:1-18). Here he first became
aquainted with Aquila and Priscilla, and soon after his
departure Apollos came to it from Ephesus. After an interval he
visited it a second time, and remained for three months (20:3).
During this second visit his Epistle to the Romans was written
(probably A.D. 55). Although there were many Jewish converts at
Corinth, yet the Gentile element prevailed in the church there.
Some have argued from 2 Cor. 12:14; 13:1, that Paul visited
Corinth a third time (i.e., that on some unrecorded occasion he
visited the city between what are usually called the first and
second visits). But the passages referred to only indicate
Paul’s intention to visit Corinth (comp. <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 16:5" id="c-p390.3" parsed="|1Cor|16|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.16.5">1 Cor. 16:5</scripRef>, where the
Greek present tense denotes an intention), an intention which
was in some way frustrated. We can hardly suppose that such a
visit could have been made by the apostle without more distinct
reference to it.
</def>
<term id="c-p390.4">Corinthians, First Epistle to the</term>
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="c-p390.6" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="1Cor 0" id="c-p390.7" parsed="|1Cor|0|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor" />
Was written from Ephesus (1 Cor. 16:8) about the time of the

Passover in the third year of the apostle’s sojourn there (<scripRef passage="Acts 19:10" id="c-p391.2" parsed="|Acts|19|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.10">Acts 19:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 20:31" id="c-p391.3" parsed="|Acts|20|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.31">20:31</scripRef>), and when he had formed the purpose to visit
Macedonia, and then return to Corinth (probably A.D. 57).
The news which had reached him, however, from Corinth
frustrated his plan. He had heard of the abuses and contentions
that had arisen among them, first from Apollos (<scripRef passage="Acts 19:1" id="c-p392.1" parsed="|Acts|19|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.1">Acts 19:1</scripRef>), and
then from a letter they had written him on the subject, and also
from some of the “household of Chloe,” and from Stephanas and

his two friends who had visited him (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 1:11" id="c-p392.2" parsed="|1Cor|1|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.1.11">1 Cor. 1:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 16:17" id="c-p392.3" parsed="|1Cor|16|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.16.17">16:17</scripRef>). Paul
thereupon wrote this letter, for the purpose of checking the
factious spirit and correcting the erroneous opinions that had
sprung up among them, and remedying the many abuses and
disorderly practices that prevailed. Titus and a brother whose
name is not given were probably the bearers of the letter (2 Cor. 2:13; 8:6, 16-18).
The epistle may be divided into four parts:
(1.) The apostle deals with the subject of the lamentable
divisions and party strifes that had arisen among them (1 Cor. 1-4).
(2.) He next treats of certain cases of immorality that had
become notorious among them. They had apparently set at nought
the very first principles of morality (5; 6).
(3.) In the third part he discusses various questions of
doctrine and of Christian ethics in reply to certain
communications they had made to him. He especially rectifies
certain flagrant abuses regarding the celebration of the Lord’s
supper (7-14).
(4.) The concluding part (15; 16) contains an elaborate
defense of the doctrine of the resurrection of the dead, which
had been called in question by some among them, followed by some
general instructions, intimations, and greetings.
This epistle “shows the powerful self-control of the apostle
in spite of his physical weakness, his distressed circumstances,
his incessant troubles, and his emotional nature. It was
written, he tells us, in bitter anguish, ‘out of much affliction
and pressure of heart...and with streaming eyes’ (<scripRef passage="2 Cor. 2:4" id="c-p398.1" parsed="|2Cor|2|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.2.4">2 Cor. 2:4</scripRef>);
yet he restrained the expression of his feelings, and wrote with
a dignity and holy calm which he thought most calculated to win
back his erring children. It gives a vivid picture of the early
church...It entirely dissipates the dream that the apostolic
church was in an exceptional condition of holiness of life or
purity of doctrine.” The apostle in this epistle unfolds and
applies great principles fitted to guide the church of all ages
in dealing with the same and kindred evils in whatever form they
may appear.
This is one of the epistles the authenticity of which has
never been called in question by critics of any school, so many
and so conclusive are the evidences of its Pauline origin.
The subscription to this epistle states erroneously in the
Authorized Version that it was written at Philippi. This error
arose from a mistranslation of <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 16:5" id="c-p400.1" parsed="|1Cor|16|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.16.5">1 Cor. 16:5</scripRef>, “For I do pass
through Macedonia,” which was interpreted as meaning, “I am
passing through Macedonia.” In 16:8 he declares his intention of
remaining some time longer in Ephesus. After that, his purpose
is to “pass through Macedonia.”
</def>
<term id="c-p400.2">Corinthians, Second Epistle to the</term>
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="c-p400.4" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="2Cor 0" id="c-p400.5" parsed="|2Cor|0|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor" />
Shortly after writing his first letter to the Corinthians, Paul
left Ephesus, where intense excitement had been aroused against
him, the evidence of his great success, and proceeded to
Macedonia. Pursuing the usual route, he reached Troas, the port
of departure for Europe. Here he expected to meet with Titus,
whom he had sent from Ephesus to Corinth, with tidings of the
effects produced on the church there by the first epistle; but

was disappointed (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 16:9" id="c-p401.1" parsed="|1Cor|16|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.16.9">1 Cor. 16:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 1:8" id="c-p401.2" parsed="|2Cor|1|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.1.8">2 Cor. 1:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 2:12" id="c-p401.3" parsed="|2Cor|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.2.12">2:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 2:13" id="c-p401.4" parsed="|2Cor|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.2.13">13</scripRef>). He then
left Troas and proceeded to Macedonia; and at Philippi, where he

tarried, he was soon joined by Titus (<scripRef passage="2 Cor. 7:6" id="c-p401.5" parsed="|2Cor|7|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.7.6">2 Cor. 7:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 7:7" id="c-p401.6" parsed="|2Cor|7|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.7.7">7</scripRef>), who
brought him good news from Corinth, and also by Timothy. Under
the influence of the feelings awakened in his mind by the
favourable report which Titus brought back from Corinth, this
second epistle was written. It was probably written at Philippi,
or, as some think, Thessalonica, early in the year A.D. 58, and
was sent to Corinth by Titus. This letter he addresses not only
to the church in Corinth, but also to the saints in all Achaia,
i.e., in Athens, Cenchrea, and other cities in Greece.
The contents of this epistle may be thus arranged:
(1.) Paul speaks of his spiritual labours and course of life,
and expresses his warm affection toward the Corinthians (2 Cor. 1-7).
(2.) He gives specific directions regarding the collection
that was to be made for their poor brethren in Judea (8; 9).
(3.) He defends his own apostolic claim (10-13), and justifies
himself from the charges and insinuations of the false teacher
and his adherents.
This epistle, it has been well said, shows the individuallity
of the apostle more than any other. “Human weakness, spiritual
strength, the deepest tenderness of affection, wounded feeling,
sternness, irony, rebuke, impassioned self-vindication,
humility, a just self-respect, zeal for the welfare of the weak
and suffering, as well as for the progress of the church of
Christ and for the spiritual advancement of its members, are all
displayed in turn in the course of his appeal.”—Lias, Second
Corinthians.
Of the effects produced on the Corinthian church by this
epistle we have no definite information. We know that Paul

visited Corinth after he had written it (<scripRef passage="Acts 20:2" id="c-p407.1" parsed="|Acts|20|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.2">Acts 20:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 20:3" id="c-p407.2" parsed="|Acts|20|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.3">3</scripRef>), and that
on that occasion he tarried there for three months. In his
letter to Rome, written at this time, he sent salutations from
some of the principal members of the church to the Romans.
</def>
<term id="c-p407.3">Cormorant</term>
(Lev. 11:17; Deut. 14:17), Heb. shalak, “plunging,” or “darting
down,” (the Phalacrocorax carbo), ranked among the “unclean”
birds; of the same family group as the pelican. It is a
“plunging” bird, and is common on the coasts and the island seas
of Palestine. Some think the Hebrew word should be rendered
“gannet” (Sula bassana, “the solan goose”); others that it is
the “tern” or “sea swallow,” which also frequents the coasts of
Palestine as well as the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan valley
during several months of the year. But there is no reason to
depart from the ordinary rendering.
In Isa. 34:11, Zeph. 2:14 (but in R.V., “pelican”) the Hebrew
word rendered by this name is ka’ath. It is translated
“pelican” (q.v.) in <scripRef passage="Ps. 102:6" id="c-p409.3" parsed="|Ps|102|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.102.6">Ps. 102:6</scripRef>. The word literally means the
“vomiter,” and the pelican is so called from its vomiting the
shells and other things which it has voraciously swallowed. (See PELICAN.)
</def>
<term id="c-p409.5">Corn</term>
The word so rendered (dagan) in Gen. 27:28, 37, Num. 18:27,

<scripRef passage="Deut. 28:51" id="c-p410.4" parsed="|Deut|28|51|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.51">Deut. 28:51</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lam. 2:12" id="c-p410.5" parsed="|Lam|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lam.2.12">Lam. 2:12</scripRef>, is a general term representing all the
commodities we usually describe by the words corn, grain, seeds,
peas, beans. With this corresponds the use of the word in John 12:24.
In Gen. 41:35, 49, Prov. 11:26, Joel 2:24 (“wheat”), the word
thus translated (bar; i.e., “winnowed”) means corn purified from
chaff. With this corresponds the use of the word in the New

Testament (<scripRef passage="Matt. 3:12" id="c-p411.5" parsed="|Matt|3|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.12">Matt. 3:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 3:17" id="c-p411.6" parsed="|Luke|3|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.17">Luke 3:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 7:12" id="c-p411.7" parsed="|Acts|7|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.7.12">Acts 7:12</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="Ps. 65:13" id="c-p411.8" parsed="|Ps|65|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.65.13">Ps. 65:13</scripRef> it
means “growing corn.”
In Gen. 42:1, 2, 19, Josh. 9:14, Neh. 10:31 (“victuals”), the
word (sheber; i.e., “broken,” i.e., grist) denotes generally
victuals, provisions, and corn as a principal article of food.
From the time of Solomon, corn began to be exported from

Palestine (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:17" id="c-p413.1" parsed="|Ezek|27|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.17">Ezek. 27:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Amos 8:5" id="c-p413.2" parsed="|Amos|8|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.8.5">Amos 8:5</scripRef>). “Plenty of corn” was a part
of Issac’s blessing conferred upon Jacob (Gen. 27:28; comp. Ps. 65:13).
</def>
<term id="c-p413.5">Cornelius</term>
A centurion whose history is narrated in Acts 10. He was a
“devout man,” and like the centurion of Capernaum, believed in
the God of Israel. His residence at Caesrea probably brought him
into contact with Jews who communicated to him their
expectations regarding the Messiah; and thus he was prepared to
welcome the message Peter brought him. He became the first fruit
of the Gentile world to Christ. He and his family were baptized
and admitted into the Christian church (Acts 10:1, 44-48). (See CENTURION.)
</def>
<term id="c-p414.5">Corner</term>
The angle of a house (Job 1:19) or a street (Prov. 7:8).
“Corners” in <scripRef passage="Neh. 9:22" id="c-p415.3" parsed="|Neh|9|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.9.22">Neh. 9:22</scripRef> denotes the various districts of the
promised land allotted to the Israelites. In <scripRef passage="Num. 24:17" id="c-p415.4" parsed="|Num|24|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.24.17">Num. 24:17</scripRef>, the
“corners of Moab” denotes the whole land of Moab. The “corner of

a field” (<scripRef passage="Lev. 19:9" id="c-p415.5" parsed="|Lev|19|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.9">Lev. 19:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 23:22" id="c-p415.6" parsed="|Lev|23|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.22">23:22</scripRef>) is its extreme part, which was not
to be reaped. The Jews were prohibited from cutting the
“corners,” i.e., the extremities, of the hair and whiskers

running round the ears (<scripRef passage="Lev. 19:27" id="c-p415.7" parsed="|Lev|19|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.27">Lev. 19:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 21:5" id="c-p415.8" parsed="|Lev|21|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.21.5">21:5</scripRef>). The “four corners of

the earth” in <scripRef passage="Isa. 11:12" id="c-p415.9" parsed="|Isa|11|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.11.12">Isa. 11:12</scripRef> and <scripRef passage="Ezek. 7:2" id="c-p415.10" parsed="|Ezek|7|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.7.2">Ezek. 7:2</scripRef> denotes the whole land.
The “corners of the streets” mentioned in <scripRef passage="Matt. 6:5" id="c-p415.11" parsed="|Matt|6|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.5">Matt. 6:5</scripRef> means the
angles where streets meet so as to form a square or place of
public resort.
The corner gate of Jerusalem (2 Kings 14:13; 2 Chr. 26:9) was
on the north-west side of the city.
Corner-stone (Job 38:6; Isa. 28:16), a block of great
importance in binding together the sides of a building. The

“head of the corner” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 118:22" id="c-p417.3" parsed="|Ps|118|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.118.22">Ps. 118:22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps. 118:23" id="c-p417.4" parsed="|Ps|118|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.118.23">23</scripRef>) denotes the coping, the
“coign of vantage”, i.e., the topstone of a building. But the
word “corner stone” is sometimes used to denote some person of
rank and importance (<scripRef passage="Isa. 28:16" id="c-p417.5" parsed="|Isa|28|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.28.16">Isa. 28:16</scripRef>). It is applied to our Lord, who
was set in highest honour (<scripRef passage="Matt. 21:42" id="c-p417.6" parsed="|Matt|21|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.21.42">Matt. 21:42</scripRef>). He is also styled “the

chief corner stone” (<scripRef passage="Eph. 2:20" id="c-p417.7" parsed="|Eph|2|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.20">Eph. 2:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Pet. 2:6-8" id="c-p417.8" parsed="|1Pet|2|6|2|8" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.2.6-1Pet.2.8">1 Pet. 2:6-8</scripRef>). When Zechariah
(10:4), speaking of Judah, says, “Out of him came forth the
corner,” he is probably to be understood as ultimately referring
to the Messiah as the “corner stone.” (See
TEMPLE, SOLOMON’S.)
</def>
<term id="c-p417.10">Cornet</term>
Heb. shophar, “brightness,” with reference to the clearness of

its sound (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 15:28" id="c-p418.1" parsed="|1Chr|15|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.15.28">1 Chr. 15:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 15:14" id="c-p418.2" parsed="|2Chr|15|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.15.14">2 Chr. 15:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 98:6" id="c-p418.3" parsed="|Ps|98|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.98.6">Ps. 98:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos. 5:8" id="c-p418.4" parsed="|Hos|5|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.5.8">Hos. 5:8</scripRef>). It
is usually rendered in the Authorized Version “trumpet.” It
denotes the long and straight horn, about eighteen inches long.
The words of Joel, “Blow the trumpet,” literally, “Sound the
cornet,” refer to the festival which was the preparation for the

day of Atonement. In <scripRef passage="Dan. 3:5" id="c-p418.5" parsed="|Dan|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.3.5">Dan. 3:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan. 3:7" id="c-p418.6" parsed="|Dan|3|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.3.7">7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan. 3:10" id="c-p418.7" parsed="|Dan|3|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.3.10">10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan. 3:15" id="c-p418.8" parsed="|Dan|3|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.3.15">15</scripRef>, the word (keren) so
rendered is a curved horn. The word “cornet” in <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 6:5" id="c-p418.9" parsed="|2Sam|6|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.6.5">2 Sam. 6:5</scripRef> (Heb.
mena’an’im, occurring only here) was some kind of instrument
played by being shaken like the Egyptian sistrum, consisting of
rings or bells hung loosely on iron rods.
</def>
<term id="c-p418.10">Cotes</term>
Pens or enclosures for flocks (2 Chr. 32:28, “cotes for flocks;”
R.V., “flocks in folds”).
</def>
<term id="c-p419.2">Cottage</term>
(1.) A booth in a vineyard (Isa. 1:8); a temporary shed covered
with leaves or straw to shelter the watchman that kept the
garden. These were slight fabrics, and were removed when no
longer needed, or were left to be blown down in winter (Job 27:18).
(2.) A lodging-place (rendered “lodge” in Isa. 1:8); a
slighter structure than the “booth,” as the cucumber patch is
more temporary than a vineyard (<scripRef passage="Isa. 24:20" id="c-p421.2" parsed="|Isa|24|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.24.20">Isa. 24:20</scripRef>). It denotes a frail
structure of boughs supported on a few poles, which is still in
use in the East, or a hammock suspended between trees, in which
the watchman was accustomed to sleep during summer.
(3.) In Zeph. 2:6 it is the rendering of the Hebrew keroth,
which some suppose to denote rather “pits” (R.V. marg., “caves”)
or “wells of water,” such as shepherds would sink.
</def>
<term id="c-p422.2">Couch</term>
(Gen. 49:4; 1 Chr. 5:1; Job 7:13; Ps. 6:6, etc.), a seat for
repose or rest. (See BED.)
</def>
<term id="c-p423.6">Coulter</term>
(1 Sam. 13:20, 21), an agricultural instrument, elsewhere called

“ploughshare” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 2:4" id="c-p424.3" parsed="|Isa|2|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.2.4">Isa. 2:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Micah 4:3" id="c-p424.4" parsed="|Mic|4|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.4.3">Micah 4:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Joel 3:10" id="c-p424.5" parsed="|Joel|3|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Joel.3.10">Joel 3:10</scripRef>). It was the
facing-piece of a plough, analogous to the modern coulter.
</def>
<term id="c-p424.6">Council</term>
Spoken of counsellors who sat in public trials with the governor
of a province (Acts 25:12).
The Jewish councils were the Sanhedrim, or supreme council of
the nation, which had subordinate to it smaller tribunals (the

“judgment,” perhaps, in <scripRef passage="Matt. 5:21" id="c-p426.1" parsed="|Matt|5|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.21">Matt. 5:21</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 5:22" id="c-p426.2" parsed="|Matt|5|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.22">22</scripRef>) in the cities of

Palestine (<scripRef passage="Matt. 10:17" id="c-p426.3" parsed="|Matt|10|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.10.17">Matt. 10:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 13:9" id="c-p426.4" parsed="|Mark|13|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.13.9">Mark 13:9</scripRef>). In the time of Christ the

functions of the Sanhedrim were limited (<scripRef passage="John 16:2" id="c-p426.5" parsed="|John|16|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.16.2">John 16:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 11:24" id="c-p426.6" parsed="|2Cor|11|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.11.24">2 Cor. 11:24</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="Ps. 68:27" id="c-p426.7" parsed="|Ps|68|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.68.27">Ps. 68:27</scripRef> the word “council” means simply a company
of persons. (R.V. marg., “company.”)
In ecclesiastical history the word is used to denote an
assembly of pastors or bishops for the discussion and regulation
of church affairs. The first of these councils was that of the
apostles and elders at Jerusalem, of which we have a detailed
account in Acts 15.
</def>
<term id="c-p427.2">Counsellor</term>
An adviser (Prov. 11:14; 15:22), a king’s state counsellor (2 Sam. 15:12). Used once of the Messiah (Isa. 9:6). In Mark 15:43,
<scripRef passage="Luke 23:50" id="c-p428.6" parsed="|Luke|23|50|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.23.50">Luke 23:50</scripRef>, the word probably means a member of the Jewish
Sanhedrim.
</def>
<term id="c-p428.7">Courses</term>
When David was not permitted to build the temple, he proceeded,
among the last acts of his life, with the assistance of Zadok
and Ahimelech, to organize the priestly and musical services to
be conducted in the house of God. (1.) He divided the priests
into twenty-four courses (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 24:1-19" id="c-p429.1" parsed="|1Chr|24|1|24|19" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.24.1-1Chr.24.19">1 Chr. 24:1-19</scripRef>), sixteen being of the
house of Eleazar and eight of that of Ithamar. Each course was
under a head or chief, and ministered for a week, the order
being determined by lot. (2.) The rest of the 38,000 Levites
(23:4) were divided also into twenty-four courses, each to
render some allotted service in public worship: 4,000 in
twenty-four courses were set apart as singers and musicians
under separate leaders (25); 4,000 as porters or keepers of the
doors and gates of the sanctuary (26:1-19); and 6,000 as
officers and judges to see to the administration of the law in
all civil and ecclesiastical matters (20-32).
This arrangement was re-established by Hezekiah (2 Chr. 31:2);
and afterwards the four sacerdotal courses which are said to
have returned from the Captivity were re-divided into the
original number of twenty-four by Ezra (6:18).
</def>
<term id="c-p430.2">Court</term>
The enclosure of the tabernacle (Ex. 27:9-19; 40:8), of the

temple (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 6:36" id="c-p431.3" parsed="|1Kgs|6|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.6.36">1 Kings 6:36</scripRef>), of a prison (<scripRef passage="Neh. 3:25" id="c-p431.4" parsed="|Neh|3|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.3.25">Neh. 3:25</scripRef>), of a private
house (2 Sam. 17:18), and of a king’s palace (2 Kings 20:4).
</def>
<term id="c-p431.7">Covenant</term>
A contract or agreement between two parties. In the Old
Testament the Hebrew word berith is always thus translated.
Berith is derived from a root which means “to cut,” and hence
a covenant is a “cutting,” with reference to the cutting or
dividing of animals into two parts, and the contracting parties
passing between them, in making a covenant (Gen. 15; Jer. 34:18, 19).
The corresponding word in the New Testament Greek is
diatheke, which is, however, rendered “testament” generally in
the Authorized Version. It ought to be rendered, just as the
word berith of the Old Testament, “covenant.”
This word is used (1) of a covenant or compact between man and

man (<scripRef passage="Gen. 21:32" id="c-p434.1" parsed="|Gen|21|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.32">Gen. 21:32</scripRef>), or between tribes or nations (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 11:1" id="c-p434.2" parsed="|1Sam|11|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.11.1">1 Sam. 11:1</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Josh. 9:6" id="c-p434.3" parsed="|Josh|9|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.9.6">Josh. 9:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 9:15" id="c-p434.4" parsed="|Josh|9|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.9.15">15</scripRef>). In entering into a convenant, Jehovah was
solemnly called on to witness the transaction (<scripRef passage="Gen. 31:50" id="c-p434.5" parsed="|Gen|31|50|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.50">Gen. 31:50</scripRef>), and
hence it was called a “covenant of the Lord” (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 20:8" id="c-p434.6" parsed="|1Sam|20|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.20.8">1 Sam. 20:8</scripRef>). The
marriage compact is called “the covenant of God” (<scripRef passage="Prov. 2:17" id="c-p434.7" parsed="|Prov|2|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.2.17">Prov. 2:17</scripRef>),
because the marriage was made in God’s name. Wicked men are
spoken of as acting as if they had made a “covenant with death”
not to destroy them, or with hell not to devour them (Isa. 28:15, 18).
(2.) The word is used with reference to God’s revelation of
himself in the way of promise or of favour to men. Thus God’s
promise to Noah after the Flood is called a covenant (<scripRef passage="Gen. 9" id="c-p435.1" parsed="|Gen|9|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.9">Gen. 9</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Jer. 33:20" id="c-p435.2" parsed="|Jer|33|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.33.20">Jer. 33:20</scripRef>, “my covenant”). We have an account of God’s

covernant with Abraham (<scripRef passage="Gen. 17" id="c-p435.3" parsed="|Gen|17|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.17">Gen. 17</scripRef>, comp. <scripRef passage="Lev. 26:42" id="c-p435.4" parsed="|Lev|26|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.26.42">Lev. 26:42</scripRef>), of the

covenant of the priesthood (<scripRef passage="Num. 25:12" id="c-p435.5" parsed="|Num|25|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.25.12">Num. 25:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 25:13" id="c-p435.6" parsed="|Num|25|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.25.13">13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 33:9" id="c-p435.7" parsed="|Deut|33|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.33.9">Deut. 33:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh. 13:29" id="c-p435.8" parsed="|Neh|13|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.13.29">Neh. 13:29</scripRef>), and of the covenant of Sinai (<scripRef passage="Ex. 34:27" id="c-p435.9" parsed="|Exod|34|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.34.27">Ex. 34:27</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 34:28" id="c-p435.10" parsed="|Exod|34|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.34.28">28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 26:15" id="c-p435.11" parsed="|Lev|26|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.26.15">Lev. 26:15</scripRef>), which was afterwards renewed at different times in the

history of Israel (<scripRef passage="Deut. 29" id="c-p435.12" parsed="|Deut|29|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.29">Deut. 29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 1:24" id="c-p435.13" parsed="|Josh|1|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.1.24">Josh. 1:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 15" id="c-p435.14" parsed="|2Chr|15|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.15">2 Chr. 15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 23" id="c-p435.15" parsed="|2Chr|23|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.23">23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 29" id="c-p435.16" parsed="|2Chr|29|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.29">29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 34" id="c-p435.17" parsed="|2Chr|34|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.34">34</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Ezra 10" id="c-p435.18" parsed="|Ezra|10|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.10">Ezra 10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh. 9" id="c-p435.19" parsed="|Neh|9|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.9">Neh. 9</scripRef>). In conformity with human custom, God’s

covenant is said to be confirmed with an oath (<scripRef passage="Deut. 4:31" id="c-p435.20" parsed="|Deut|4|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.4.31">Deut. 4:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 89:3" id="c-p435.21" parsed="|Ps|89|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.89.3">Ps. 89:3</scripRef>), and to be accompanied by a sign (<scripRef passage="Gen. 9" id="c-p435.22" parsed="|Gen|9|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.9">Gen. 9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 17" id="c-p435.23" parsed="|Gen|17|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.17">17</scripRef>). Hence the

covenant is called God’s “counsel,” “oath,” “promise” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 89:3" id="c-p435.24" parsed="|Ps|89|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.89.3">Ps. 89:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps 89:4" id="c-p435.25" parsed="|Ps|89|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.89.4">4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 105:8-11" id="c-p435.26" parsed="|Ps|105|8|105|11" osisRef="Bible:Ps.105.8-Ps.105.11">105:8-11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 6:13-20" id="c-p435.27" parsed="|Heb|6|13|6|20" osisRef="Bible:Heb.6.13-Heb.6.20">Heb. 6:13-20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 1:68-75" id="c-p435.28" parsed="|Luke|1|68|1|75" osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.68-Luke.1.75">Luke 1:68-75</scripRef>). God’s covenant
consists wholly in the bestowal of blessing (Isa. 59:21; Jer. 31:33, 34).
The term covenant is also used to designate the regular

succession of day and night (<scripRef passage="Jer. 33:20" id="c-p436.1" parsed="|Jer|33|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.33.20">Jer. 33:20</scripRef>), the Sabbath (<scripRef passage="Ex. 31:16" id="c-p436.2" parsed="|Exod|31|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.31.16">Ex. 31:16</scripRef>), circumcision (<scripRef passage="Gen. 17:9" id="c-p436.3" parsed="|Gen|17|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.17.9">Gen. 17:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 17:10" id="c-p436.4" parsed="|Gen|17|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.17.10">10</scripRef>), and in general any
ordinance of God (Jer. 34:13, 14).
A “covenant of salt” signifies an everlasting covenant, in the
sealing or ratifying of which salt, as an emblem of perpetuity,
is used (Num. 18:19; Lev. 2:13; 2 Chr. 13:5).
COVENANT OF WORKS, the constitution under which Adam was
placed at his creation. In this covenant, (1.) The contracting
parties were (a) God the moral Governor, and (b) Adam, a free
moral agent, and representative of all his natural posterity

(<scripRef passage="Rom. 5:12-19" id="c-p438.1" parsed="|Rom|5|12|5|19" osisRef="Bible:Rom.5.12-Rom.5.19">Rom. 5:12-19</scripRef>). (2.) The promise was “life” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 19:16" id="c-p438.2" parsed="|Matt|19|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.19.16">Matt. 19:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 19:17" id="c-p438.3" parsed="|Matt|19|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.19.17">17</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Gal. 3:12" id="c-p438.4" parsed="|Gal|3|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.3.12">Gal. 3:12</scripRef>). (3.) The condition was perfect obedience to the law,
the test in this case being abstaining from eating the fruit of
the “tree of knowledge,” etc. (4.) The penalty was death (Gen. 2:16, 17).
This covenant is also called a covenant of nature, as made
with man in his natural or unfallen state; a covenant of life,
because “life” was the promise attached to obedience; and a
legal covenant, because it demanded perfect obedience to the
law.
The “tree of life” was the outward sign and seal of that life
which was promised in the covenant, and hence it is usually
called the seal of that covenant.
This covenant is abrogated under the gospel, inasmuch as
Christ has fulfilled all its conditions in behalf of his people,
and now offers salvation on the condition of faith. It is still
in force, however, as it rests on the immutable justice of God,
and is binding on all who have not fled to Christ and accepted
his righteousness.
CONVENANT OF GRACE, the eternal plan of redemption entered
into by the three persons of the Godhead, and carried out by
them in its several parts. In it the Father represented the
Godhead in its indivisible sovereignty, and the Son his people
as their surety (John 17:4, 6, 9; Isa. 42:6; Ps. 89:3).
The conditions of this covenant were, (1.) On the part of the
Father (a) all needful preparation to the Son for the

accomplishment of his work (<scripRef passage="Heb. 10:5" id="c-p443.1" parsed="|Heb|10|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.10.5">Heb. 10:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 42:1-7" id="c-p443.2" parsed="|Isa|42|1|42|7" osisRef="Bible:Isa.42.1-Isa.42.7">Isa. 42:1-7</scripRef>); (b) support
in the work (<scripRef passage="Luke 22:43" id="c-p443.3" parsed="|Luke|22|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.22.43">Luke 22:43</scripRef>); and (c) a glorious reward in the
exaltation of Christ when his work was done (<scripRef passage="Phil. 2:6-11" id="c-p443.4" parsed="|Phil|2|6|2|11" osisRef="Bible:Phil.2.6-Phil.2.11">Phil. 2:6-11</scripRef>), his

investiture with universal dominion (<scripRef passage="John 5:22" id="c-p443.5" parsed="|John|5|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.5.22">John 5:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 110:1" id="c-p443.6" parsed="|Ps|110|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.110.1">Ps. 110:1</scripRef>), his
having the administration of the covenant committed into his

hands (<scripRef passage="Matt. 28:18" id="c-p443.7" parsed="|Matt|28|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.28.18">Matt. 28:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 1:12" id="c-p443.8" parsed="|John|1|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.1.12">John 1:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 17:2" id="c-p443.9" parsed="|John|17|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.17.2">17:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 2:33" id="c-p443.10" parsed="|Acts|2|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.2.33">Acts 2:33</scripRef>), and in the

final salvation of all his people (<scripRef passage="Isa. 35:10" id="c-p443.11" parsed="|Isa|35|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.35.10">Isa. 35:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 53:10" id="c-p443.12" parsed="|Isa|53|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.53.10">53:10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa 53:11" id="c-p443.13" parsed="|Isa|53|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.53.11">11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 31:33" id="c-p443.14" parsed="|Jer|31|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.31.33">Jer. 31:33</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Titus 1:2" id="c-p443.15" parsed="|Titus|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Titus.1.2">Titus 1:2</scripRef>). (2.) On the part of the Son the conditions

were (a) his becoming incarnate (<scripRef passage="Gal. 4:4" id="c-p443.16" parsed="|Gal|4|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.4.4">Gal. 4:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gal. 4:5" id="c-p443.17" parsed="|Gal|4|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.4.5">5</scripRef>); and (b) as the
second Adam his representing all his people, assuming their
place and undertaking all their obligations under the violated

covenant of works; (c) obeying the law (<scripRef passage="Ps. 40:8" id="c-p443.18" parsed="|Ps|40|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.40.8">Ps. 40:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 42:21" id="c-p443.19" parsed="|Isa|42|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.42.21">Isa. 42:21</scripRef>;
John 9:4, 5), and (d) suffering its penalty (Isa. 53; 2 Cor. 5:21; Gal. 3:13), in their stead.
Christ, the mediator of, fulfils all its conditions in behalf
of his people, and dispenses to them all its blessings. In Heb. 8:6; 9:15; 12:24, this title is given to Christ. (See DISPENSATION.)
</def>
<term id="c-p444.5">Covering of the eyes</term>
Occurs only in Gen. 20:16. In the Revised Version the rendering
is “it (i.e., Abimelech’s present of 1,000 pieces of silver to
Abraham) is for thee a covering of the eyes.” This has been
regarded as an implied advice to Sarah to conform to the custom
of married women, and wear a complete veil, covering the eyes as
well as the rest of the face.
</def>
<term id="c-p445.2">Covetousness</term>
A strong desire after the possession of worldly things (Col. 3:5; Eph. 5:5; Heb. 13:5; 1 Tim. 6:9, 10; Matt. 6:20). It
assumes sometimes the more aggravated form of avarice, which is
the mark of cold-hearted worldliness.
</def>
<term id="c-p446.7">Cow</term>
A cow and her calf were not to be killed on the same day (Lev. 22:28; Ex. 23:19; Deut. 22:6, 7). The reason for this enactment
is not given. A state of great poverty is described in the words
of <scripRef passage="Isa. 7:21-25" id="c-p447.5" parsed="|Isa|7|21|7|25" osisRef="Bible:Isa.7.21-Isa.7.25">Isa. 7:21-25</scripRef>, where, instead of possessing great resources, a
man shall depend for the subsistence of himself and his family
on what a single cow and two sheep could yield.
</def>
<term id="c-p447.6">Crane</term>
(Isa. 38:14; Jer. 8:7). In both of these passages the Authorized
Version has reversed the Hebrew order of the words. “Crane or
swallow” should be “swallow or crane,” as in the Revised
Version. The rendering is there correct. The Hebrew for crane is
’agur, the Grus cincerea, a bird well known in Palestine. It
is migratory, and is distinguished by its loud voice, its cry
being hoarse and melancholy.
</def>
<term id="c-p448.3">Creation</term>
“In the beginning” God created, i.e., called into being, all
things out of nothing. This creative act on the part of God was
absolutely free, and for infinitely wise reasons. The cause of
all things exists only in the will of God. The work of creation

is attributed (1) to the Godhead (<scripRef passage="Gen. 1:1" id="c-p449.1" parsed="|Gen|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.1.1">Gen. 1:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 1:26" id="c-p449.2" parsed="|Gen|1|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.1.26">26</scripRef>); (2) to the

Father (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 8:6" id="c-p449.3" parsed="|1Cor|8|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.8.6">1 Cor. 8:6</scripRef>); (3) to the Son (<scripRef passage="John 1:3" id="c-p449.4" parsed="|John|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.1.3">John 1:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Col. 1:16" id="c-p449.5" parsed="|Col|1|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.1.16">Col. 1:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Col. 1:17" id="c-p449.6" parsed="|Col|1|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.1.17">17</scripRef>);

(4) to the Holy Spirit (<scripRef passage="Gen. 1:2" id="c-p449.7" parsed="|Gen|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.1.2">Gen. 1:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 26:13" id="c-p449.8" parsed="|Job|26|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.26.13">Job 26:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 104:30" id="c-p449.9" parsed="|Ps|104|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.104.30">Ps. 104:30</scripRef>). The
fact that he is the Creator distinguishes Jehovah as the true

God (<scripRef passage="Isa. 37:16" id="c-p449.10" parsed="|Isa|37|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.37.16">Isa. 37:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 40:12" id="c-p449.11" parsed="|Isa|40|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.40.12">40:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa 40:13" id="c-p449.12" parsed="|Isa|40|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.40.13">13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 54:5" id="c-p449.13" parsed="|Isa|54|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.54.5">54:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 96:5" id="c-p449.14" parsed="|Ps|96|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.96.5">Ps. 96:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 10:11" id="c-p449.15" parsed="|Jer|10|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.10.11">Jer. 10:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer. 10:12" id="c-p449.16" parsed="|Jer|10|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.10.12">12</scripRef>). The
one great end in the work of creation is the manifestation of

the glory of the Creator (<scripRef passage="Col. 1:16" id="c-p449.17" parsed="|Col|1|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.1.16">Col. 1:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 4:11" id="c-p449.18" parsed="|Rev|4|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.4.11">Rev. 4:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 11:36" id="c-p449.19" parsed="|Rom|11|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.11.36">Rom. 11:36</scripRef>).
God’s works, equally with God’s word, are a revelation from him;
and between the teachings of the one and those of the other,
when rightly understood, there can be no contradiction.
Traditions of the creation, disfigured by corruptions, are
found among the records of ancient Eastern nations. (See ACCAD.) A peculiar interest belongs to the traditions of the
Accadians, the primitive inhabitants of the plains of Lower
Mesopotamia. These within the last few years have been brought
to light in the tablets and cylinders which have been rescued
from the long-buried palaces and temples of Assyria. They bear a
remarkable resemblance to the record of Genesis.
</def>
<term id="c-p450.2">Creature</term>
Denotes the whole creation in Rom. 8:39; Col. 1:15; Rev. 5:13;
the whole human race in Mark 16:15; Rom. 8:19-22.
The living creatures in Ezek. 10:15, 17, are imaginary beings,
symbols of the Divine attributes and operations.
</def>
<term id="c-p452.3">Crescens</term>
Increasing, probably one of the seventy disciples of Christ. He
was one of Paul’s assistants (<scripRef passage="2 Tim. 4:10" id="c-p453.1" parsed="|2Tim|4|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.4.10">2 Tim. 4:10</scripRef>), probably a Christian
of Rome.
</def>
<term id="c-p453.2">Crete</term>
Now called Candia, one of the largest islands in the
Meditterranean, about 140 miles long and 35 broad. It was at one
time a very prosperous and populous island, having a “hundred
cities.” The character of the people is described in Paul’s
quotation from “one of their own poets” (Epimenides) in his
epistle to Titus: “The Cretans are alway liars, evil beasts,
slow bellies” (<scripRef passage="Titus 1:12" id="c-p454.1" parsed="|Titus|1|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Titus.1.12">Titus 1:12</scripRef>). Jews from Crete were in Jerusalem on
the day of Pentecost (<scripRef passage="Acts 2:11" id="c-p454.2" parsed="|Acts|2|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.2.11">Acts 2:11</scripRef>). The island was visited by Paul
on his voyage to Rome (<scripRef passage="Acts 27" id="c-p454.3" parsed="|Acts|27|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.27">Acts 27</scripRef>). Here Paul subsequently left
Titus (1:5) “to ordain elders.” Some have supposed that it was
the original home of the Caphtorim (q.v.) or Philistines.
</def>
<term id="c-p454.4">Crimson</term>
See COLOUR.
</def>
<term id="c-p455.2">Crisping-pin</term>
(Isa. 3:22; R.V., “satchel”), some kind of female ornament,
probably like the modern reticule. The Hebrew word harit
properly signifies pouch or casket or purse. It is rendered
“bag” in 2 Kings 5:23.
</def>
<term id="c-p456.3">Crispus</term>
Curled, the chief of the synagogue at Corinth (Acts 18:8). He
was converted and, with his family, baptized by Paul (1 Cor. 1:14).
</def>
<term id="c-p457.3">Cross</term>
In the New Testament the instrument of crucifixion, and hence

used for the crucifixion of Christ itself (<scripRef passage="Eph. 2:16" id="c-p458.1" parsed="|Eph|2|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.16">Eph. 2:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 12:2" id="c-p458.2" parsed="|Heb|12|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.12.2">Heb. 12:2</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 1:17" id="c-p458.3" parsed="|1Cor|1|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.1.17">1 Cor. 1:17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 1:18" id="c-p458.4" parsed="|1Cor|1|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.1.18">18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal. 5:11" id="c-p458.5" parsed="|Gal|5|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.5.11">Gal. 5:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal 6:12" id="c-p458.6" parsed="|Gal|6|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.6.12">6:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gal 6:14" id="c-p458.7" parsed="|Gal|6|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.6.14">14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Phil. 3:18" id="c-p458.8" parsed="|Phil|3|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Phil.3.18">Phil. 3:18</scripRef>). The word is
also used to denote any severe affliction or trial (<scripRef passage="Matt. 10:38" id="c-p458.9" parsed="|Matt|10|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.10.38">Matt. 10:38</scripRef>;
16:24; Mark 8:34; 10:21).
The forms in which the cross is represented are these:
1. The crux simplex (I), a “single piece without transom.”
2. The crux decussata (X), or St. Andrew’s cross.
3. The crux commissa (T), or St. Anthony’s cross.
4. The crux immissa (t), or Latin cross, which was the kind of
cross on which our Saviour died. Above our Lord’s head, on the
projecting beam, was placed the “title.” (See CRUCIFIXION.)
After the conversion, so-called, of Constantine the Great
(B.C. 313), the cross first came into use as an emblem of
Christianity. He pretended at a critical moment that he saw a
flaming cross in the heavens bearing the inscription, “In hoc
signo vinces”, i.e., By this sign thou shalt conquer, and that
on the following night Christ himself appeared and ordered him
to take for his standard the sign of this cross. In this form a
new standard, called the Labarum, was accordingly made, and
borne by the Roman armies. It remained the standard of the Roman
army till the downfall of the Western empire. It bore the
embroidered monogram of Christ, i.e., the first two Greek
letters of his name, X and P (chi and rho), with the Alpha and
Omega. (See A.)
</def>
<term id="c-p464.2">Crown</term>
(1.) Denotes the plate of gold in the front of the high priest’s

mitre (<scripRef passage="Ex. 29:6" id="c-p465.1" parsed="|Exod|29|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.6">Ex. 29:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 39:30" id="c-p465.2" parsed="|Exod|39|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.39.30">39:30</scripRef>). The same Hebrew word so rendered

(ne’zer) denotes the diadem worn by Saul in battle (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 1:10" id="c-p465.3" parsed="|2Sam|1|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.1.10">2 Sam. 1:10</scripRef>), and also that which was used at the coronation of Joash
(2 Kings 11:12).
(2.) The more general name in Hebrew for a crown is ’atarah,
meaning a “circlet.” This is used of crowns and head ornaments
of divers kinds, including royal crowns. Such was the crown
taken from the king of Ammon by David (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 12:30" id="c-p466.1" parsed="|2Sam|12|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.12.30">2 Sam. 12:30</scripRef>). The crown
worn by the Assyrian kings was a high mitre, sometimes adorned
with flowers. There are sculptures also representing the crowns
worn by the early Egyptian and Persian kings. Sometimes a diadem
surrounded the royal head-dress of two or three fillets. This
probably signified that the wearer had dominion over two or

three countries. In <scripRef passage="Rev. 12:3" id="c-p466.2" parsed="|Rev|12|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.12.3">Rev. 12:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev 13:1" id="c-p466.3" parsed="|Rev|13|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.13.1">13:1</scripRef>, we read of “many crowns,” a
token of extended dominion.
(3.) The ancient Persian crown (Esther 1:11; 2:17; 6:8) was
called kether; i.e., “a chaplet,” a high cap or tiara. Crowns
were worn sometimes to represent honour and power (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 23:42" id="c-p467.4" parsed="|Ezek|23|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.23.42">Ezek. 23:42</scripRef>).

They were worn at marriages (<scripRef passage="Cant. 3:11" id="c-p467.5" parsed="|Song|3|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.3.11">Cant. 3:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 61:10" id="c-p467.6" parsed="|Isa|61|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.61.10">Isa. 61:10</scripRef>,
“ornaments;” R.V., “a garland”), and at feasts and public
festivals.
The crown was among the Romans and Greeks a symbol of victory
and reward. The crown or wreath worn by the victors in the
Olympic games was made of leaves of the wild olive; in the
Pythian games, of laurel; in the Nemean games, of parsley; and
in the Isthmian games, of the pine. The Romans bestowed the
“civic crown” on him who saved the life of a citizen. It was
made of the leaves of the oak. In opposition to all these fading
crowns the apostles speak of the incorruptible crown, the crown

of life (<scripRef passage="James 1:12" id="c-p468.1" parsed="|Jas|1|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jas.1.12">James 1:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 2:10" id="c-p468.2" parsed="|Rev|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.2.10">Rev. 2:10</scripRef>) “that fadeth not away” (<scripRef passage="1 Pet. 5:4" id="c-p468.3" parsed="|1Pet|5|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.5.4">1 Pet. 5:4</scripRef>, Gr. amarantinos; comp. 1:4). Probably the word “amaranth”
was applied to flowers we call “everlasting,” the “immortal
amaranth.”
</def>
<term id="c-p468.4">Crown of thorns</term>
Our Lord was crowned with a, in mockery by the Romans (Matt. 27:29). The object of Pilate’s guard in doing this was probably
to insult, and not specially to inflict pain. There is nothing
to show that the shrub thus used was, as has been supposed, the
spina Christi, which could have been easily woven into a wreath.
It was probably the thorny nabk, which grew abundantly round
about Jerusalem, and whose flexible, pliant, and round branches
could easily be platted into the form of a crown. (See
THORN, 3.)
</def>
<term id="c-p469.3">Crucifixion</term>
A common mode of punishment among heathen nations in early
times. It is not certain whether it was known among the ancient
Jews; probably it was not. The modes of capital punishment
according to the Mosaic law were, by the sword (<scripRef passage="Ex. 21" id="c-p470.1" parsed="|Exod|21|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.21">Ex. 21</scripRef>),
strangling, fire (Lev. 20), and stoning (Deut. 21).
This was regarded as the most horrible form of death, and to a
Jew it would acquire greater horror from the curse in Deut. 21:23.
This punishment began by subjecting the sufferer to scourging.
In the case of our Lord, however, his scourging was rather
before the sentence was passed upon him, and was inflicted by
Pilate for the purpose, probably, of exciting pity and procuring
his escape from further punishment (Luke 23:22; John 19:1).
The condemned one carried his own cross to the place of
execution, which was outside the city, in some conspicuous place
set apart for the purpose. Before the nailing to the cross took
place, a medicated cup of vinegar mixed with gall and myrrh (the
sopor) was given, for the purpose of deadening the pangs of the
sufferer. Our Lord refused this cup, that his senses might be
clear (<scripRef passage="Matt. 27:34" id="c-p473.1" parsed="|Matt|27|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.34">Matt. 27:34</scripRef>). The spongeful of vinegar, sour wine, posca,
the common drink of the Roman soldiers, which was put on a

hyssop stalk and offered to our Lord in contemptuous pity (<scripRef passage="Matt. 27:48" id="c-p473.2" parsed="|Matt|27|48|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.48">Matt. 27:48</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 23:36" id="c-p473.3" parsed="|Luke|23|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.23.36">Luke 23:36</scripRef>), he tasted to allay the agonies of his thirst
(<scripRef passage="John 19:29" id="c-p473.4" parsed="|John|19|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.29">John 19:29</scripRef>). The accounts given of the crucifixion of our Lord
are in entire agreement with the customs and practices of the
Roman in such cases. He was crucified between two “malefactors”

(<scripRef passage="Isa. 53:12" id="c-p473.5" parsed="|Isa|53|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.53.12">Isa. 53:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 23:32" id="c-p473.6" parsed="|Luke|23|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.23.32">Luke 23:32</scripRef>), and was watched by a party of four

soldiers (<scripRef passage="John 19:23" id="c-p473.7" parsed="|John|19|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.23">John 19:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 27:36" id="c-p473.8" parsed="|Matt|27|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.36">Matt. 27:36</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 27:54" id="c-p473.9" parsed="|Matt|27|54|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.54">54</scripRef>), with their centurion.
The “breaking of the legs” of the malefactors was intended to
hasten death, and put them out of misery (<scripRef passage="John 19:31" id="c-p473.10" parsed="|John|19|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.31">John 19:31</scripRef>); but the
unusual rapidity of our Lord’s death (19:33) was due to his
previous sufferings and his great mental anguish. The omission

of the breaking of his legs was the fulfilment of a type (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:46" id="c-p473.11" parsed="|Exod|12|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.46">Ex. 12:46</scripRef>). He literally died of a broken heart, a ruptured heart,
and hence the flowing of blood and water from the wound made by
the soldier’s spear (<scripRef passage="John 19:34" id="c-p473.12" parsed="|John|19|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.34">John 19:34</scripRef>). Our Lord uttered seven

memorable words from the cross, namely, (1) <scripRef passage="Luke 23:34" id="c-p473.13" parsed="|Luke|23|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.23.34">Luke 23:34</scripRef>; (<scripRef passage="Luke 2" id="c-p473.14" parsed="|Luke|2|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2">2</scripRef>)
23:43; (3) John 19:26; (4) Matt. 27:46, Mark 15:34; (5) John 19:28; (6) 19:30; (7) Luke 23:46.
</def>
<term id="c-p473.23">Cruse</term>
A utensil; a flask or cup for holding water (1 Sam. 26:11, 12, 16; 1 Kings 19:6) or oil (1 Kings 17:12, 14, 16). In 1 Kings 14:3 the word there so rendered means properly a bottle, as in

<scripRef passage="Jer. 19:1" id="c-p474.9" parsed="|Jer|19|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.19.1">Jer. 19:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer. 19:10" id="c-p474.10" parsed="|Jer|19|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.19.10">10</scripRef>, or pitcher. In <scripRef passage="2 Kings 2:20" id="c-p474.11" parsed="|2Kgs|2|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.2.20">2 Kings 2:20</scripRef>, a platter or flat
metal saucer is intended. The Hebrew word here used is
translated “dish” in 21:13; “pans,” in <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 35:13" id="c-p474.12" parsed="|2Chr|35|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.35.13">2 Chr. 35:13</scripRef>; and
“bosom,” in Prov. 19:24; 26:15 (R.V., “dish”).
</def>
<term id="c-p474.15">Crystal</term>
(Ezek. 1:22, with the epithet “terrible,” as dazzling the
spectators with its brightness). The word occurs in <scripRef passage="Rev. 4:6" id="c-p475.2" parsed="|Rev|4|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.4.6">Rev. 4:6</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Rev 21:11" id="c-p475.3" parsed="|Rev|21|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.21.11">21:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev 22:1" id="c-p475.4" parsed="|Rev|22|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.22.1">22:1</scripRef>. It is a stone of the flint order, the most refined
kind of quartz. The Greek word here used means also literally
“ice.” The ancients regarded the crystal as only pure water
congealed into extreme hardness by great length of time.
</def>
<term id="c-p475.5">Cubit</term>
Heb. ‘ammah; i.e., “mother of the arm,” the fore-arm, is a word
derived from the Latin cubitus, the lower arm. It is difficult
to determine the exact length of this measure, from the
uncertainty whether it included the entire length from the elbow
to the tip of the longest finger, or only from the elbow to the
root of the hand at the wrist. The probability is that the
longer was the original cubit. The common computation as to the
length of the cubit makes it 20.24 inches for the ordinary
cubit, and 21.888 inches for the sacred one. This is the same as
the Egyptian measurements.
A rod or staff the measure of a cubit is called in Judg. 3:16
gomed, which literally means a “cut,” something “cut off.” The
LXX. and Vulgate render it “span.”
</def>
<term id="c-p477.2">Cuckoo</term>
(Heb. shahaph), from a root meaning “to be lean; slender.” This

bird is mentioned only in <scripRef passage="Lev. 11:16" id="c-p478.1" parsed="|Lev|11|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.11.16">Lev. 11:16</scripRef> and <scripRef passage="Deut. 14:15" id="c-p478.2" parsed="|Deut|14|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.14.15">Deut. 14:15</scripRef> (R.V.,
“seamew”). Some have interpreted the Hebrew word by “petrel” or
“shearwater” (Puffinus cinereus), which is found on the coast of
Syria; others think it denotes the “sea-gull” or “seamew.” The
common cuckoo (Cuculus canorus) feeds on reptiles and large
insects. It is found in Asia and Africa as well as in Europe. It
only passes the winter in Palestine. The Arabs suppose it to
utter the cry Yakub_, and hence they call it _tir el-Yakub;
i.e., “Jacob’s bird.”
</def>
<term id="c-p478.3">Cucumbers</term>
(Heb. plur. kishshuim; i.e., “hard,” “difficult” of digestion,
only in <scripRef passage="Num. 11:5" id="c-p479.1" parsed="|Num|11|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.11.5">Num. 11:5</scripRef>). This vegetable is extensively cultivated in
the East at the present day, as it appears to have been in
earlier times among the Hebrews. It belongs to the gourd family
of plants. In the East its cooling pulp and juice are most
refreshing. “We need not altogether wonder that the Israelites,
wearily marching through the arid solitudes of the Sinaitic
peninsula, thought more of the cucumbers and watermelons of
which they had had no lack in Egypt, rather than of the cruel
bondage which was the price of these luxuries.” Groser’s
Scripture Natural History.
Isaiah speaks of a “lodge” (1:8; Heb. sukkah), i.e., a shed or
edifice more solid than a booth, for the protection throughout
the season from spring to autumn of the watchers in a “garden of
cucumbers.”
</def>
<term id="c-p480.1">Cummin</term>
(Heb. kammon; i.e., a “condiment”), the fruit or seed of an
umbelliferous plant, the Cuminum sativum, still extensively

cultivated in the East. Its fruit is mentioned in <scripRef passage="Isa. 28:25" id="c-p481.1" parsed="|Isa|28|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.28.25">Isa. 28:25</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa 28:27" id="c-p481.2" parsed="|Isa|28|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.28.27">27</scripRef>. In the New Testament it is mentioned in <scripRef passage="Matt. 23:23" id="c-p481.3" parsed="|Matt|23|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.23.23">Matt. 23:23</scripRef>, where
our Lord pronounces a “woe” on the scribes and Pharisees, who
were zealous in paying tithes of “mint and anise and cummin,”
while they omitted the weightier matters of the law.” “It is
used as a spice, both bruised, to mix with bread, and also
boiled, in the various messes and stews which compose an
Oriental banquet.” Tristram, Natural History.
</def>
<term id="c-p481.4">Cup</term>
A wine-cup (Gen. 40:11, 21), various forms of which are found on
Assyrian and Egyptian monuments. All Solomon’s drinking vessels
were of gold (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 10" id="c-p482.3" parsed="|1Kgs|10|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10">1 Kings 10</scripRef>: 21). The cups mentioned in the New
Testament were made after Roman and Greek models, and were
sometimes of gold (Rev. 17:4).
The art of divining by means of a cup was practiced in Egypt
(Gen. 44:2-17), and in the East generally.
The “cup of salvation” (Ps. 116:13) is the cup of thanksgiving
for the great salvation. The “cup of consolation” (<scripRef passage="Jer. 16:7" id="c-p484.2" parsed="|Jer|16|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.16.7">Jer. 16:7</scripRef>)
refers to the custom of friends sending viands and wine to

console relatives in mourning (<scripRef passage="Prov. 31:6" id="c-p484.3" parsed="|Prov|31|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.31.6">Prov. 31:6</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 10:16" id="c-p484.4" parsed="|1Cor|10|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.10.16">1 Cor. 10:16</scripRef>, the

“cup of blessing” is contrasted with the “cup of devils” (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 10:21" id="c-p484.5" parsed="|1Cor|10|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.10.21">1 Cor. 10:21</scripRef>). The sacramental cup is the “cup of blessing,” because of

blessing pronounced over it (<scripRef passage="Matt. 26:27" id="c-p484.6" parsed="|Matt|26|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.27">Matt. 26:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 22:17" id="c-p484.7" parsed="|Luke|22|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.22.17">Luke 22:17</scripRef>). The

“portion of the cup” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 11:6" id="c-p484.8" parsed="|Ps|11|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.11.6">Ps. 11:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 16:5" id="c-p484.9" parsed="|Ps|16|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.16.5">16:5</scripRef>) denotes one’s condition of
life, prosperous or adverse. A “cup” is also a type of sensual

allurement (<scripRef passage="Jer. 51:7" id="c-p484.10" parsed="|Jer|51|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.51.7">Jer. 51:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 23:31" id="c-p484.11" parsed="|Prov|23|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.23.31">Prov. 23:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 17:4" id="c-p484.12" parsed="|Rev|17|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.17.4">Rev. 17:4</scripRef>). We read also of
the “cup of astonishment,” the “cup of trembling,” and the “cup

of God’s wrath” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 75:8" id="c-p484.13" parsed="|Ps|75|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.75.8">Ps. 75:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 51:17" id="c-p484.14" parsed="|Isa|51|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.51.17">Isa. 51:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 25:15" id="c-p484.15" parsed="|Jer|25|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.25.15">Jer. 25:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lam. 4:21" id="c-p484.16" parsed="|Lam|4|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lam.4.21">Lam. 4:21</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Ezek. 23:32" id="c-p484.17" parsed="|Ezek|23|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.23.32">Ezek. 23:32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 16:19" id="c-p484.18" parsed="|Rev|16|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.16.19">Rev. 16:19</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Matt. 26:39" id="c-p484.19" parsed="|Matt|26|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.39">Matt. 26:39</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 26:42" id="c-p484.20" parsed="|Matt|26|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.42">42</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 18:11" id="c-p484.21" parsed="|John|18|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.18.11">John 18:11</scripRef>). The
cup is also the symbol of death (Matt. 16:28; Mark 9:1; Heb. 2:9).
</def>
<term id="c-p484.25">Cup-bearer</term>
An officer of high rank with Egyptian, Persian, Assyrian, and
Jewish monarchs. The cup-bearer of the king of Egypt is
mentioned in connection with Joseph’s history (<scripRef passage="Gen. 40:1-21" id="c-p485.1" parsed="|Gen|40|1|40|21" osisRef="Bible:Gen.40.1-Gen.40.21">Gen. 40:1-21</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Gen 41:9" id="c-p485.2" parsed="|Gen|41|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.41.9">41:9</scripRef>). Rabshakeh (q.v.) was cup-bearer in the Assyrian court (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:17" id="c-p485.3" parsed="|2Kgs|18|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.17">2 Kings 18:17</scripRef>). Nehemiah filled this office to the king of Persia
(Neh. 1:11). We read also of Solomon’s cup-bearers (1 Kings 10:5; 2 Chr. 9:4).
</def>
<term id="c-p485.7">Curious arts</term>
(Acts 19:19), magical arts; jugglery practised by the Ephesian
conjurers. Ephesus was noted for its wizard and the “Ephesian
spells;” i.e., charms or scraps of parchment written over with
certain formula, which were worn as a safeguard against all
manner of evils. The more important and powerful of these charms
were written out in books which circulated among the exorcists,
and were sold at a great price.
</def>
<term id="c-p486.2">Curse</term>
Denounced by God against the serpent (Gen. 3:14), and against
Cain (4:11). These divine maledictions carried their effect with
them. Prophetical curses were sometimes pronounced by holy men

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 9:25" id="c-p487.2" parsed="|Gen|9|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.9.25">Gen. 9:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 49:7" id="c-p487.3" parsed="|Gen|49|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.7">49:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 27:15" id="c-p487.4" parsed="|Deut|27|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.27.15">Deut. 27:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 6:26" id="c-p487.5" parsed="|Josh|6|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.6.26">Josh. 6:26</scripRef>). Such curses are not
the consequence of passion or revenge, they are predictions.

No one on pain of death shall curse father or mother (Ex. 21:17), nor the prince of his people (22:28), nor the deaf (Lev. 19:14). Cursing God or blaspheming was punishable by death (Lev. 24:10-16). The words “curse God and die” (R.V., “renounce God
and die”), used by Job’s wife (<scripRef passage="Job 2:9" id="c-p488.4" parsed="|Job|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.2.9">Job 2:9</scripRef>), have been variously
interpreted. Perhaps they simply mean that as nothing but death
was expected, God would by this cursing at once interpose and
destroy Job, and so put an end to his sufferings.
</def>
<term id="c-p488.5">Curtain</term>
(1.) Ten curtains, each twenty-eight cubits long and four wide,
made of fine linen, also eleven made of goat’s hair, covered the
tabernacle (Ex. 26:1-13; 36:8-17).
(2.) The sacred curtain, separating the holy of holies from
the sanctuary, is designated by a different Hebrew word
(peroketh). It is described as a “veil of blue, and purple, and
scarlet, and fine twined linen of cunning work” (Ex. 26:31; Lev. 16:2; Num. 18:7).
(3.) “Stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain” (Isa. 40:22),
is an expression used with reference to the veil or awning which
Orientals spread for a screen over their courts in summer.
According to the prophet, the heavens are spread over our heads
as such an awning. Similar expressions are found in <scripRef passage="Ps. 104:2" id="c-p491.2" parsed="|Ps|104|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.104.2">Ps. 104:2</scripRef>l;
comp. Isa. 44:24; Job 9:8.
</def>
<term id="c-p491.5">Cush</term>
Black. (1.) A son, probably the eldest, of Ham, and the father

of Nimrod (<scripRef passage="Gen. 10:8" id="c-p492.1" parsed="|Gen|10|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.8">Gen. 10:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 1:10" id="c-p492.2" parsed="|1Chr|1|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.1.10">1 Chr. 1:10</scripRef>). From him the land of Cush
seems to have derived its name. The question of the precise
locality of the land of Cush has given rise to not a little
controversy. The second river of Paradise surrounded the whole
land of Cush (<scripRef passage="Gen. 2:13" id="c-p492.3" parsed="|Gen|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.2.13">Gen. 2:13</scripRef>, R.V.). The term Cush is in the Old
Testament generally applied to the countries south of the
Israelites. It was the southern limit of Egypt (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 29:10" id="c-p492.4" parsed="|Ezek|29|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.29.10">Ezek. 29:10</scripRef>,
A.V. “Ethiopia,” Heb. Cush), with which it is generally

associated (<scripRef passage="Ps. 68:31" id="c-p492.5" parsed="|Ps|68|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.68.31">Ps. 68:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 18:1" id="c-p492.6" parsed="|Isa|18|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.18.1">Isa. 18:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 46:9" id="c-p492.7" parsed="|Jer|46|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.46.9">Jer. 46:9</scripRef>, etc.). It stands

also associated with Elam (<scripRef passage="Isa. 11:11" id="c-p492.8" parsed="|Isa|11|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.11.11">Isa. 11:11</scripRef>), with Persia (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 38:5" id="c-p492.9" parsed="|Ezek|38|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.38.5">Ezek. 38:5</scripRef>), and with the Sabeans (<scripRef passage="Isa. 45:14" id="c-p492.10" parsed="|Isa|45|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.45.14">Isa. 45:14</scripRef>). From these facts it
has been inferred that Cush included Arabia and the country on
the west coast of the Red Sea. Rawlinson takes it to be the
country still known as Khuzi-stan, on the east side of the Lower
Tigris. But there are intimations which warrant the conclusion
that there was also a Cush in Africa, the Ethiopia (so called by
the Greeks) of Africa. Ezekiel speaks (29:10; comp. 30:4-6) of
it as lying south of Egypt. It was the country now known to us

as Nubia and Abyssinia (<scripRef passage="Isa. 18:1" id="c-p492.11" parsed="|Isa|18|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.18.1">Isa. 18:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zeph. 3:10" id="c-p492.12" parsed="|Zeph|3|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zeph.3.10">Zeph. 3:10</scripRef>, Heb. Cush). In
ancient Egyptian inscriptions Ethiopia is termed Kesh. The
Cushites appear to have spread along extensive tracts,
stretching from the Upper Nile to the Euphrates and Tigris. At
an early period there was a stream of migration of Cushites
“from Ethiopia, properly so called, through Arabia, Babylonia,
and Persia, to Western India.” The Hamite races, soon after
their arrival in Africa, began to spread north, east, and west.
Three branches of the Cushite or Ethiopian stock, moving from
Western Asia, settled in the regions contiguous to the Persian
Gulf. One branch, called the Cossaeans, settled in the
mountainous district on the east of the Tigris, known afterwards
as Susiana; another occupied the lower regions of the Euphrates
and the Tigris; while a third colonized the southern shores and
islands of the gulf, whence they afterwards emigrated to the
Mediterranean and settled on the coast of Palestine as the
Phoenicians. Nimrod was a great Cushite chief. He conquered the
Accadians, a Tauranian race, already settled in Mesopotamia, and
founded his kingdom, the Cushites mingling with the Accads, and
so forming the Chaldean nation.
(2.) A Benjamite of this name is mentioned in the title of Ps. 7. “Cush was probably a follower of Saul, the head of his tribe,
and had sought the friendship of David for the purpose of
’rewarding evil to him that was at peace with him.’”
</def>
<term id="c-p493.2">Cushan</term>
Probably a poetic or prolonged name of the land of Cush, the
Arabian Cush (<scripRef passage="Hab. 3:7" id="c-p494.1" parsed="|Hab|3|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hab.3.7">Hab. 3:7</scripRef>). Some have, however, supposed this to be
