covers an area of about 300 square miles. Its depth varies from
1,310 to 11 feet. From various phenomena that have been
observed, its bottom appears to be still subsiding. It is about
53 miles long, and of an average breadth of 10 miles. It has no
outlet, the great heat of that region causing such rapid
evaporation that its average depth, notwithstanding the rivers
that run into it (see JORDAN), is maintained with
little variation. The Jordan alone discharges into it no less
than six million tons of water every twenty-four hours.
The waters of the Dead Sea contain 24.6 per cent. of mineral
salts, about seven times as much as in ordinary sea-water; thus
they are unusually buoyant. Chloride of magnesium is most
abundant; next to that chloride of sodium (common salt). But
terraces of alluvial deposits in the deep valley of the Jordan
show that formerly one great lake extended from the Waters of
Merom to the foot of the watershed in the Arabah. The waters
were then about 1,400 feet above the present level of the Dead
Sea, or slightly above that of the Mediterranean, and at that
time were much less salt.
Nothing living can exist in this sea. “The fish carried down
by the Jordan at once die, nor can even mussels or corals live
in it; but it is a fable that no bird can fly over it, or that
there are no living creatures on its banks. Dr. Tristram found
on the shores three kinds of kingfishers, gulls, ducks, and
grebes, which he says live on the fish which enter the sea in
shoals, and presently die. He collected one hundred and eighteen
species of birds, some new to science, on the shores, or
swimming or flying over the waters. The cane-brakes which fringe
it at some parts are the homes of about forty species of
mammalia, several of them animals unknown in England; and
innumerable tropical or semi-tropical plants perfume the
atmosphere wherever fresh water can reach. The climate is
perfect and most delicious, and indeed there is perhaps no place
in the world where a sanatorium could be established with so
much prospect of benefit as at Ain Jidi (Engedi).”, Geikie’s
Hours, etc.
</def>
<term id="d-p101.1">Deal, Tenth</term>
See OMER.
</def>
<term id="d-p102.2">Dearth</term>
A scarcity of provisions (1 Kings 17). There were frequent
dearths in Palestine. In the days of Abram there was a “famine
in the land” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 12:10" id="d-p103.2" parsed="|Gen|12|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.12.10">Gen. 12:10</scripRef>), so also in the days of Jacob (47:4,

13). We read also of dearths in the time of the judges (<scripRef passage="Ruth 1:1" id="d-p103.3" parsed="|Ruth|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.1.1">Ruth 1:1</scripRef>), and of the kings (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:1" id="d-p103.4" parsed="|2Sam|21|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.1">2 Sam. 21:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 18:2" id="d-p103.5" parsed="|1Kgs|18|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.18.2">1 Kings 18:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 4:38" id="d-p103.6" parsed="|2Kgs|4|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.4.38">2 Kings 4:38</scripRef>;
8:1).
In New Testament times there was an extensive famine in
Palestine (<scripRef passage="Acts 11:28" id="d-p104.1" parsed="|Acts|11|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.28">Acts 11:28</scripRef>) in the fourth year of the reign of the
emperor Claudius (A.D. 44 and 45).
</def>
<term id="d-p104.2">Death</term>
May be simply defined as the termination of life. It is
represented under a variety of aspects in Scripture: (1.) “The
dust shall return to the earth as it was” (Eccl. 12:7).
(2.) “Thou takest away their breath, they die” (Ps. 104:29).
(3.) It is the dissolution of “our earthly house of this
tabernacle” (2 Cor. 5:1); the “putting off this tabernacle” (2 Pet. 1:13, 14).
(4.) Being “unclothed” (2 Cor. 5:3, 4).
(5.) “Falling on sleep” (Ps. 76:5; Jer. 51:39; Acts 13:36; 2 Pet. 3:9.
(6.) “I go whence I shall not return” (Job 10:21); “Make me to
know mine end” (Ps. 39:4); “to depart” (Phil. 1:23).
The grave is represented as “the gates of death” (Job 38:17;

<scripRef passage="Ps. 9:13" id="d-p111.2" parsed="|Ps|9|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.9.13">Ps. 9:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 107:18" id="d-p111.3" parsed="|Ps|107|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.107.18">107:18</scripRef>). The gloomy silence of the grave is spoken of
under the figure of the “shadow of death” (Jer. 2:6).
Death is the effect of sin (Heb. 2:14), and not a “debt of
nature.” It is but once (9:27), universal (<scripRef passage="Gen. 3:19" id="d-p112.2" parsed="|Gen|3|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.3.19">Gen. 3:19</scripRef>), necessary
(<scripRef passage="Luke 2:28-30" id="d-p112.3" parsed="|Luke|2|28|2|30" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.28-Luke.2.30">Luke 2:28-30</scripRef>). Jesus has by his own death taken away its sting
for all his followers (1 Cor. 15:55-57).
There is a spiritual death in trespasses and sins, i.e., the

death of the soul under the power of sin (<scripRef passage="Rom. 8:6" id="d-p113.1" parsed="|Rom|8|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.6">Rom. 8:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 2:1" id="d-p113.2" parsed="|Eph|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.1">Eph. 2:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Eph. 2:3" id="d-p113.3" parsed="|Eph|2|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.3">3</scripRef>;
Col. 2:13).
The “second death” (Rev. 2:11) is the everlasting perdition of
the wicked (<scripRef passage="Rev. 21:8" id="d-p114.2" parsed="|Rev|21|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.21.8">Rev. 21:8</scripRef>), and “second” in respect to natural or
temporal death.
THE DEATH OF CHRIST is the procuring cause incidentally of all
the blessings men enjoy on earth. But specially it is the
procuring cause of the actual salvation of all his people,
together with all the means that lead thereto. It does not make
their salvation merely possible, but certain (Matt. 18:11; Rom. 5:10; 2 Cor. 5:21; Gal. 1:4; 3:13; Eph. 1:7; 2:16; Rom. 8:32-35).
</def>
<term id="d-p115.9">Debir</term>
Oracle town; sanctuary. (1.) One of the eleven cities to the

west of Hebron, in the highlands of Judah (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:49" id="d-p116.1" parsed="|Josh|15|49|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.49">Josh. 15:49</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 1:11-15" id="d-p116.2" parsed="|Judg|1|11|1|15" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.11-Judg.1.15">Judg. 1:11-15</scripRef>). It was originally one of the towns of the Anakim
(<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:15" id="d-p116.3" parsed="|Josh|15|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.15">Josh. 15:15</scripRef>), and was also called Kirjath-sepher (q.v.) and
Kirjath-sannah (49). Caleb, who had conquered and taken
possession of the town and district of Hebron (<scripRef passage="Josh. 14:6-15" id="d-p116.4" parsed="|Josh|14|6|14|15" osisRef="Bible:Josh.14.6-Josh.14.15">Josh. 14:6-15</scripRef>),
offered the hand of his daughter to any one who would
successfully lead a party against Debir. Othniel, his younger

brother (<scripRef passage="Judg. 1:13" id="d-p116.5" parsed="|Judg|1|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.13">Judg. 1:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg 3:9" id="d-p116.6" parsed="|Judg|3|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.3.9">3:9</scripRef>), achieved the conquest, and gained
Achsah as his wife. She was not satisfied with the portion her
father gave her, and as she was proceeding toward her new home,
she “lighted from off her ass” and said to him, “Give me a
blessing [i.e., a dowry]: for thou hast given me a south land”
(<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:19" id="d-p116.7" parsed="|Josh|15|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.19">Josh. 15:19</scripRef>, A.V.); or, as in the Revised Version, “Thou hast
set me in the land of the south”, i.e., in the Negeb, outside
the rich valley of Hebron, in the dry and barren land. “Give me
also springs of water. And he gave her the upper springs, and
the nether springs.”
Debir has been identified with the modern Edh-Dhaheriyeh,
i.e., “the well on the ridge”, to the south of Hebron.
(2.) A place near the “valley of Achor” (Josh. 15:7), on the
north boundary of Judah, between Jerusalem and Jericho.
(3.) The king of Eglon, one of the five Canaanitish kings who

were hanged by Joshua (<scripRef passage="Josh. 10:3" id="d-p119.1" parsed="|Josh|10|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.3">Josh. 10:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 10:23" id="d-p119.2" parsed="|Josh|10|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.23">23</scripRef>) after the victory at
Gibeon. These kings fled and took refuge in a cave at Makkedah.
Here they were kept confined till Joshua returned from the
pursuit of their discomfited armies, when he caused them to be
brought forth, and “Joshua smote them, and slew them, and hanged
them on five trees” (26).
</def>
<term id="d-p119.3">Deborah</term>
A bee. (1.) Rebekah’s nurse. She accompanied her mistress when
she left her father’s house in Padan-aram to become the wife of
Isaac (<scripRef passage="Gen. 24:59" id="d-p120.1" parsed="|Gen|24|59|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.59">Gen. 24:59</scripRef>). Many years afterwards she died at Bethel,
and was buried under the “oak of weeping”, Allon-bachuth (35:8).
(2.) A prophetess, “wife” (woman?) of Lapidoth. Jabin, the
king of Hazor, had for twenty years held Israel in degrading
subjection. The spirit of patriotism seemed crushed out of the
nation. In this emergency Deborah roused the people from their
lethargy. Her fame spread far and wide. She became a “mother in

Israel” (<scripRef passage="Judg. 4:6" id="d-p121.1" parsed="|Judg|4|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.4.6">Judg. 4:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Judg. 4:14" id="d-p121.2" parsed="|Judg|4|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.4.14">14</scripRef>; 5:7), and “the children of Israel came
up to her for judgment” as she sat in her tent under the palm
tree “between Ramah and Bethel.” Preparations were everywhere
made by her direction for the great effort to throw off the yoke
of bondage. She summoned Barak from Kadesh to take the command
of 10,000 men of Zebulun and Naphtali, and lead them to Mount
Tabor on the plain of Esdraelon at its north-east end. With his
aid she organized this army. She gave the signal for attack, and
the Hebrew host rushed down impetuously upon the army of Jabin,
which was commanded by Sisera, and gained a great and decisive
victory. The Canaanitish army almost wholly perished. That was a
great and ever-memorable day in Israel. In <scripRef passage="Judg. 5" id="d-p121.3" parsed="|Judg|5|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.5">Judg. 5</scripRef> is given the
grand triumphal ode, the “song of Deborah,” which she wrote in
grateful commemoration of that great deliverance. (See
LAPIDOTH,
JABIN [2].)
</def>
<term id="d-p121.6">Debt</term>
The Mosaic law encouraged the practice of lending (Deut. 15:7;

<scripRef passage="Ps. 37:26" id="d-p122.2" parsed="|Ps|37|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.37.26">Ps. 37:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 5:42" id="d-p122.3" parsed="|Matt|5|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.42">Matt. 5:42</scripRef>); but it forbade the exaction of interest

except from foreigners. Usury was strongly condemned (<scripRef passage="Prov. 28:8" id="d-p122.4" parsed="|Prov|28|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.28.8">Prov. 28:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 18:8" id="d-p122.5" parsed="|Ezek|18|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.18.8">Ezek. 18:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 18:13" id="d-p122.6" parsed="|Ezek|18|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.18.13">13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 18:17" id="d-p122.7" parsed="|Ezek|18|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.18.17">17</scripRef>; 22:12; <scripRef passage="Ps. 15:5" id="d-p122.8" parsed="|Ps|15|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.15.5">Ps. 15:5</scripRef>). On the Sabbatical
year all pecuniary obligations were cancelled (<scripRef passage="Deut. 15:1-11" id="d-p122.9" parsed="|Deut|15|1|15|11" osisRef="Bible:Deut.15.1-Deut.15.11">Deut. 15:1-11</scripRef>).
These regulations prevented the accumulation of debt.
</def>
<term id="d-p122.10">Debtor</term>
Various regulations as to the relation between debtor and
creditor are laid down in the Scriptures.
(1.) The debtor was to deliver up as a pledge to the creditor
what he could most easily dispense with (Deut. 24:10, 11).
(2.) A mill, or millstone, or upper garment, when given as a
pledge, could not be kept over night (Ex. 22:26, 27).
(3.) A debt could not be exacted during the Sabbatic year
(Deut. 15:1-15).
For other laws bearing on this relation see Lev. 25:14, 32, 39; Matt. 18:25, 34.
(4.) A surety was liable in the same way as the original
debtor (Prov. 11:15; 17:18).
</def>
<term id="d-p128.3">Decalogue</term>
The name given by the Greek fathers to the ten commandments;

“the ten words,” as the original is more literally rendered (<scripRef passage="Ex. 20:3-17" id="d-p129.1" parsed="|Exod|20|3|20|17" osisRef="Bible:Exod.20.3-Exod.20.17">Ex. 20:3-17</scripRef>). These commandments were at first written on two stone
slabs (31:18), which were broken by Moses throwing them down on
the ground (32:19). They were written by God a second time
(34:1). The decalogue is alluded to in the New Testament five

times (<scripRef passage="Matt. 5:17" id="d-p129.2" parsed="|Matt|5|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.17">Matt. 5:17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 5:18" id="d-p129.3" parsed="|Matt|5|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.18">18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 5:19" id="d-p129.4" parsed="|Matt|5|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.19">19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 10:19" id="d-p129.5" parsed="|Mark|10|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.10.19">Mark 10:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 18:20" id="d-p129.6" parsed="|Luke|18|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.18.20">Luke 18:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 7:7" id="d-p129.7" parsed="|Rom|7|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.7.7">Rom. 7:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Rom. 7:8" id="d-p129.8" parsed="|Rom|7|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.7.8">8</scripRef>;
13:9; 1 Tim. 1:9, 10).
These commandments have been divided since the days of Origen
the Greek father, as they stand in the Confession of all the
Reformed Churches except the Lutheran. The division adopted by
Luther, and which has ever since been received in the Lutheran
Church, makes the first two commandments one, and the third the
second, and so on to the last, which is divided into two. “Thou
shalt not covet thy neighbour’s house” being ranked as ninth,
and “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s wife,” etc., the
tenth. (See COMMANDMENTS.)
</def>
<term id="d-p130.2">Decapolis</term>
Ten cities=deka, ten, and polis, a city, a district on the east
and south-east of the Sea of Galilee containing “ten cities,”
which were chiefly inhabited by Greeks. It included a portion of
Bashan and Gilead, and is mentioned three times in the New

Testament (<scripRef passage="Matt. 4:25" id="d-p131.1" parsed="|Matt|4|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.4.25">Matt. 4:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 5:20" id="d-p131.2" parsed="|Mark|5|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.5.20">Mark 5:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 7:31" id="d-p131.3" parsed="|Mark|7|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.7.31">7:31</scripRef>). These cities were
Scythopolis, i.e., “city of the Scythians”, (ancient Bethshean,
the only one of the ten cities on the west of Jordan), Hippos,
Gadara, Pella (to which the Christians fled just before the
destruction of Jerusalem), Philadelphia (ancient Rabbath-ammon),
Gerasa, Dion, Canatha, Raphana, and Damascus. When the Romans
conquered Syria (B.C. 65) they rebuilt, and endowed with certain
privileges, these “ten cities,” and the province connected with
them they called “Decapolis.”
</def>
<term id="d-p131.4">Decision, Valley of</term>
A name given to the valley of Jehoshaphat (q.v.) as the vale of
the sentence. The scene of Jehovah’s signal inflictions on
Zion’s enemies (<scripRef passage="Joel 3:14" id="d-p132.1" parsed="|Joel|3|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Joel.3.14">Joel 3:14</scripRef>; marg., “valley of concision or
threshing”).
</def>
<term id="d-p132.2">Decrees of God</term>
“The decrees of God are his eternal, unchangeable, holy, wise,
and sovereign purpose, comprehending at once all things that
ever were or will be in their causes, conditions, successions,
and relations, and determining their certain futurition. The
several contents of this one eternal purpose are, because of the
limitation of our faculties, necessarily conceived of by us in
partial aspects, and in logical relations, and are therefore
styled Decrees.” The decree being the act of an infinite,
absolute, eternal, unchangeable, and sovereign Person,
comprehending a plan including all his works of all kinds, great
and small, from the beginning of creation to an unending
eternity; ends as well as means, causes as well as effects,
conditions and instrumentalities as well as the events which
depend upon them, must be incomprehensible by the finite

intellect of man. The decrees are eternal (<scripRef passage="Acts 15:18" id="d-p133.1" parsed="|Acts|15|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.15.18">Acts 15:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 1:4" id="d-p133.2" parsed="|Eph|1|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.1.4">Eph. 1:4</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="2 Thess. 2:13" id="d-p133.3" parsed="|2Thess|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Thess.2.13">2 Thess. 2:13</scripRef>), unchangeable (<scripRef passage="Ps. 33:11" id="d-p133.4" parsed="|Ps|33|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.33.11">Ps. 33:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 46:9" id="d-p133.5" parsed="|Isa|46|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.46.9">Isa. 46:9</scripRef>), and
comprehend all things that come to pass (Eph. 1:11; Matt. 10:29, 30; Eph. 2:10; Acts 2:23; 4:27, 28; Ps. 17:13, 14).
The decrees of God are (1) efficacious, as they respect those
events he has determined to bring about by his own immediate
agency; or (2) permissive, as they respect those events he has
determined that free agents shall be permitted by him to effect.
This doctrine ought to produce in our minds “humility, in view
of the infinite greatness and sovereignty of God, and of the
dependence of man; confidence and implicit reliance upon wisdom,
rightenousness, goodness, and immutability of God’s purpose.”
</def>
<term id="d-p135.1">Dedan</term>
Low ground. (1.) A son of Raamah (Gen. 10:7). His descendants

are mentioned in <scripRef passage="Isa. 21:13" id="d-p136.2" parsed="|Isa|21|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.21.13">Isa. 21:13</scripRef>, and <scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:15" id="d-p136.3" parsed="|Ezek|27|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.15">Ezek. 27:15</scripRef>. They probably
settled among the sons of Cush, on the north-west coast of the
Persian Gulf.
(2.) A son of Jokshan, Abraham’s son by Keturah (1 Chr. 1:32).
His descendants settled on the Syrian borders about the
territory of Edom. They probably led a pastoral life.
</def>
<term id="d-p137.2">Dedanim</term>
The descendants of Dedan, the son of Raamah. They are mentioned
in <scripRef passage="Isa. 21:13" id="d-p138.1" parsed="|Isa|21|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.21.13">Isa. 21:13</scripRef> as sending out “travelling companies” which lodged
“in the forest of Arabia.” They are enumerated also by Ezekiel
(27:20) among the merchants who supplied Tyre with precious
things.
</def>
<term id="d-p138.2">Dedication, Feast of the</term>
(John 10:22, 42), i.e., the feast of the renewing. It was
instituted B.C. 164 to commemorate the purging of the temple
after its pollution by Antiochus Epiphanes (B.C. 167), and the
rebuilding of the altar after the Syrian invaders had been
driven out by Judas Maccabaeus. It lasted for eight days,
beginning on the 25th of the month Chisleu (December), which was

often a period of heavy rains (<scripRef passage="Ezra 10:9" id="d-p139.3" parsed="|Ezra|10|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.10.9">Ezra 10:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezra 10:13" id="d-p139.4" parsed="|Ezra|10|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.10.13">13</scripRef>). It was an
occasion of much rejoicing and festivity.
But there were other dedications of the temple. (1) That of

Solomon’s temple (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 8:2" id="d-p140.1" parsed="|1Kgs|8|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.8.2">1 Kings 8:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 5:3" id="d-p140.2" parsed="|2Chr|5|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.5.3">2 Chr. 5:3</scripRef>); (2) the dedication
in the days of Hezekiah (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 29" id="d-p140.3" parsed="|2Chr|29|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.29">2 Chr. 29</scripRef>); and (3) the dedication of
the temple after the Captivity (Ezra 6:16).
</def>
<term id="d-p140.5">Deep</term>
Used to denote (1) the grave or the abyss (Rom. 10:7; Luke 8:31); (2) the deepest part of the sea (Ps. 69:15); (3) the
chaos mentioned in Gen. 1:2; (4) the bottomless pit, hell (Rev. 9:1, 2; 11:7; 20:13).
</def>
<term id="d-p141.10">Degrees, Song of</term>
Song of steps, a title given to each of these fifteen psalms,
120-134 inclusive. The probable origin of this name is the
circumstance that these psalms came to be sung by the people on
the ascents or goings up to Jerusalem to attend the three great
festivals (<scripRef passage="Deut. 16:16" id="d-p142.1" parsed="|Deut|16|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.16.16">Deut. 16:16</scripRef>). They were well fitted for being sung by
the way from their peculiar form, and from the sentiments they
express. “They are characterized by brevity, by a key-word, by
epanaphora [i.e, repetition], and by their epigrammatic
style...More than half of them are cheerful, and all of them
hopeful.” They are sometimes called “Pilgrim Songs.” Four of
them were written by David, one (127) by Solomon, and the rest
are anonymous.
</def>
<term id="d-p142.2">Dehavites</term>
Villagers, one of the Assyrian tribes which Asnapper sent to
repopulate Samaria (<scripRef passage="Ezra 4:9" id="d-p143.1" parsed="|Ezra|4|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.4.9">Ezra 4:9</scripRef>). They were probably a nomad
Persian tribe on the east of the Caspian Sea, and near the Sea
of Azof.
</def>
<term id="d-p143.2">Delaiah</term>
Freed by Jehovah. (1.) The head of the twenty-third division of
the priestly order (1 Chr. 24:18).
(2.) A son of Shemaiah, and one of the courtiers to whom
Jeremiah’s first roll of prophecy was read (Jer. 36:12).
(3.) The head of one of the bands of exiles that returned
under Zerubbabel to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:60; Neh. 7:62).
</def>
<term id="d-p146.3">Delilah</term>
Languishing, a Philistine woman who dwelt in the valley of Sorek
(<scripRef passage="Judg. 16:4-20" id="d-p147.1" parsed="|Judg|16|4|16|20" osisRef="Bible:Judg.16.4-Judg.16.20">Judg. 16:4-20</scripRef>). She was bribed by the “lords of the
Philistines” to obtain from Samson the secret of his strength
and the means of overcoming it (<scripRef passage="Judg. 16:4-18" id="d-p147.2" parsed="|Judg|16|4|16|18" osisRef="Bible:Judg.16.4-Judg.16.18">Judg. 16:4-18</scripRef>). She tried on
three occasions to obtain from him this secret in vain. On the
fourth occasion she wrung it from him. She made him sleep upon
her knees, and then called the man who was waiting to help her;
who “cut off the seven locks of his head,” and so his “strength
went from him.” (See SAMSON.)
</def>
<term id="d-p147.4">Deluge</term>
The name given to Noah’s flood, the history of which is recorded
in Gen. 7 and 8.
It began in the year 2516 B.C., and continued twelve lunar
months and ten days, or exactly one solar year.
The cause of this judgment was the corruption and violence
that filled the earth in the ninth generation from Adam. God in
righteous indignation determined to purge the earth of the
ungodly race. Amid a world of crime and guilt there was one
household that continued faithful and true to God, the household
of Noah. “Noah was a just man and perfect in his generations.”
At the command of God, Noah made an ark 300 cubits long, 50
broad, and 30 high. He slowly proceeded with this work during a
period of one hundred and twenty years (<scripRef passage="Gen. 6:3" id="d-p151.1" parsed="|Gen|6|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.6.3">Gen. 6:3</scripRef>). At length the
purpose of God began to be carried into effect. The following
table exhibits the order of events as they occurred:
In the six hundredth year of his life Noah is commanded by God
to enter the ark, taking with him his wife, and his three sons
with their wives (Gen. 7:1-10).
The rain begins on the seventeenth day of the second month
(Gen. 7:11-17).
The rain ceases, the waters prevail, fifteen cubits upward
(Gen. 7:18-24).
The ark grounds on one of the mountains of Ararat on the
seventeenth day of the seventh month, or one hundred and fifty
days after the Deluge began (Gen. 8:1-4).
Tops of the mountains visible on the first day of the tenth
month (Gen. 8:5).
Raven and dove sent out forty days after this (Gen. 8:6-9).
Dove again sent out seven days afterwards; and in the evening
she returns with an olive leaf in her mouth (Gen. 8:10, 11).
Dove sent out the third time after an interval of other seven
days, and returns no more (Gen. 8:12).
The ground becomes dry on the first day of the first month of
the new year (Gen. 8:13).
Noah leaves the ark on the twenty-seventh day of the second
month (Gen. 8:14-19).
The historical truth of the narrative of the Flood is

established by the references made to it by our Lord (<scripRef passage="Matt. 24:37" id="d-p162.1" parsed="|Matt|24|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.24.37">Matt. 24:37</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Luke 17:26" id="d-p162.2" parsed="|Luke|17|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.17.26">Luke 17:26</scripRef>). Peter speaks of it also (<scripRef passage="1 Pet. 3:20" id="d-p162.3" parsed="|1Pet|3|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.3.20">1 Pet. 3:20</scripRef>;
2 Pet. 2:5). In <scripRef passage="Isa. 54:9" id="d-p162.4" parsed="|Isa|54|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.54.9">Isa. 54:9</scripRef> the Flood is referred to as “the
waters of Noah.” The Biblical narrative clearly shows that so
far as the human race was concerned the Deluge was universal;
that it swept away all men living except Noah and his family,
who were preserved in the ark; and that the present human race
is descended from those who were thus preserved.
Traditions of the Deluge are found among all the great
divisions of the human family; and these traditions, taken as a
whole, wonderfully agree with the Biblical narrative, and agree
with it in such a way as to lead to the conclusion that the
Biblical is the authentic narrative, of which all these
traditions are more or less corrupted versions. The most
remarkable of these traditions is that recorded on tablets
prepared by order of Assur-bani-pal, the king of Assyria. These
were, however, copies of older records which belonged to
somewhere about B.C. 2000, and which formed part of the priestly
library at Erech (q.v.), “the ineradicable remembrance of a real
and terrible event.” (See NOAH; CHALDEA.)
</def>
<term id="d-p163.3">Demas</term>
A companion and fellow-labourer of Paul during his first

imprisonment at Rome (<scripRef passage="Philemon 1" id="d-p164.1" parsed="|Phlm|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Phlm.1.1">Philemon 1</scripRef>:24; <scripRef passage="Col. 4:14" id="d-p164.2" parsed="|Col|4|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.4.14">Col. 4:14</scripRef>). It appears,
however, that the love of the world afterwards mastered him, and
he deserted the apostle (2 Tim. 4:10).
</def>
<term id="d-p164.4">Demetrius</term>
(1.) A silversmith at Ephesus, whose chief occupation was to
make “silver shrines for Diana” (q.v.), <scripRef passage="Acts 19:24" id="d-p165.1" parsed="|Acts|19|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.24">Acts 19:24</scripRef>, i.e., models
either of the temple of Diana or of the statue of the goddess.
This trade brought to him and his fellow-craftsmen “no small
gain,” for these shrines found a ready sale among the countless
thousands who came to this temple from all parts of Asia Minor.
This traffic was greatly endangered by the progress of the
gospel, and hence Demetrius excited the tradesmen employed in
the manufacture of these shrines, and caused so great a tumult
that “the whole city was filled with confusion.”
(2.) A Christian who is spoken of as having “a good report of
all men, and of the truth itself” (3 John 1:12).
</def>
<term id="d-p166.2">Demon</term>
See DAEMON.
</def>
<term id="d-p167.2">Den</term>
A lair of wild beasts (Ps. 10:9; 104:22; Job 37:8); the hole of
a venomous reptile (<scripRef passage="Isa. 11:8" id="d-p168.4" parsed="|Isa|11|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.11.8">Isa. 11:8</scripRef>); a recess for secrecy “in dens

and caves of the earth” (<scripRef passage="Heb. 11:38" id="d-p168.5" parsed="|Heb|11|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.11.38">Heb. 11:38</scripRef>); a resort of thieves (<scripRef passage="Matt. 21:13" id="d-p168.6" parsed="|Matt|21|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.21.13">Matt. 21:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 11:17" id="d-p168.7" parsed="|Mark|11|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.11.17">Mark 11:17</scripRef>). Daniel was cast into “the den of lions”

(<scripRef passage="Dan. 6:16" id="d-p168.8" parsed="|Dan|6|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.6.16">Dan. 6:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan. 6:17" id="d-p168.9" parsed="|Dan|6|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.6.17">17</scripRef>). Some recent discoveries among the ruins of
Babylon have brought to light the fact that the practice of
punishing offenders against the law by throwing them into a den
of lions was common.
</def>
<term id="d-p168.10">Deputy</term>
In 1 Kings 22:47, means a prefect; one set over others. The same
Hebrew word is rendered “officer;” i.e., chief of the
commissariat appointed by Solomon (1 Kings 4:5, etc.).
In Esther 8:9; 9:3 (R.V., “governor”) it denotes a Persian
prefect “on this side” i.e., in the region west of the
Euphrates. It is the modern word pasha.
In Acts 13:7, 8, 12; 18:12, it denotes a proconsul; i.e., the
governor of a Roman province holding his appointment from the
senate. The Roman provinces were of two kinds, (1) senatorial
and (2) imperial. The appointment of a governor to the former
was in the hands of the senate, and he bore the title of
proconsul (Gr. anthupatos). The appointment of a governor to the
latter was in the hands of the emperor, and he bore the title of
propraetor (Gr. antistrategos).
</def>
<term id="d-p171.4">Derbe</term>
A small town on the eastern part of the upland plain of
Lycaonia, about 20 miles from Lystra. Paul passed through Derbe
on his route from Cilicia to Iconium, on his second missionary
journey (<scripRef passage="Acts 16:1" id="d-p172.1" parsed="|Acts|16|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.16.1">Acts 16:1</scripRef>), and probably also on his third journey
(18:23; 19:1). On his first journey (14:20, 21) he came to Derbe
from the other side; i.e., from Iconium. It was the native place
of Gaius, one of Paul’s companions (20:4). He did not here
suffer persecution (2 Tim. 3:11).
</def>
<term id="d-p172.3">Desert</term>
(1.) Heb. midbar, “pasture-ground;” an open tract for pasturage;

a common (<scripRef passage="Joel 2:22" id="d-p173.1" parsed="|Joel|2|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Joel.2.22">Joel 2:22</scripRef>). The “backside of the desert” (<scripRef passage="Ex. 3:1" id="d-p173.2" parsed="|Exod|3|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.3.1">Ex. 3:1</scripRef>) is
the west of the desert, the region behind a man, as the east is
the region in front. The same Hebrew word is rendered
“wildernes,” and is used of the country lying between Egypt and

Palestine (<scripRef passage="Gen. 21:14" id="d-p173.3" parsed="|Gen|21|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.14">Gen. 21:14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 21:21" id="d-p173.4" parsed="|Gen|21|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.21">21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex. 4:27" id="d-p173.5" parsed="|Exod|4|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.4.27">Ex. 4:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 19:2" id="d-p173.6" parsed="|Exod|19|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.19.2">19:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 1:4" id="d-p173.7" parsed="|Josh|1|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.1.4">Josh. 1:4</scripRef>), the
wilderness of the wanderings. It was a grazing tract, where the
flocks and herds of the Israelites found pasturage during the
whole of their journey to the Promised Land.
The same Hebrew word is used also to denote the wilderness of
Arabia, which in winter and early spring supplies good pasturage
to the flocks of the nomad tribes than roam over it (1 Kings 9:18).
The wilderness of Judah is the mountainous region along the
western shore of the Dead Sea, where David fed his father’s

flocks (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:28" id="d-p175.1" parsed="|1Sam|17|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.28">1 Sam. 17:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 26:2" id="d-p175.2" parsed="|1Sam|26|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.26.2">26:2</scripRef>). Thus in both of these instances the
word denotes a country without settled inhabitants and without
streams of water, but having good pasturage for cattle; a
country of wandering tribes, as distinguished from that of a

settled people (<scripRef passage="Isa. 35:1" id="d-p175.3" parsed="|Isa|35|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.35.1">Isa. 35:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 50:2" id="d-p175.4" parsed="|Isa|50|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.50.2">50:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 4:11" id="d-p175.5" parsed="|Jer|4|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.4.11">Jer. 4:11</scripRef>). Such, also, is the
meaning of the word “wilderness” in Matt. 3:3; 15:33; Luke 15:4.
(2.) The translation of the Hebrew Aribah’, “an arid tract”

(<scripRef passage="Isa. 35:1" id="d-p176.1" parsed="|Isa|35|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.35.1">Isa. 35:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 35:6" id="d-p176.2" parsed="|Isa|35|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.35.6">6</scripRef>; 40:3; 41:19; 51:3, etc.). The name Arabah is
specially applied to the deep valley of the Jordan (the Ghor of
the Arabs), which extends from the lake of Tiberias to the
Elanitic gulf. While midbar denotes properly a pastoral
region, arabah denotes a wilderness. It is also translated

“plains;” as “the plains of Jericho” (<scripRef passage="Josh. 5:10" id="d-p176.3" parsed="|Josh|5|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.5.10">Josh. 5:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 25:5" id="d-p176.4" parsed="|2Kgs|25|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.25.5">2 Kings 25:5</scripRef>),

“the plains of Moab” (<scripRef passage="Num. 22:1" id="d-p176.5" parsed="|Num|22|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.22.1">Num. 22:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 34:1" id="d-p176.6" parsed="|Deut|34|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.34.1">Deut. 34:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 34:8" id="d-p176.7" parsed="|Deut|34|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.34.8">8</scripRef>), “the plains of
the wilderness” (2 Sam. 17:16).
(3.) In the Revised Version of Num. 21:20 the Hebrew word
jeshimon is properly rendered “desert,” meaning the waste
tracts on both shores of the Dead Sea. This word is also

rendered “desert” in <scripRef passage="Ps. 78:40" id="d-p177.2" parsed="|Ps|78|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.78.40">Ps. 78:40</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 106:14" id="d-p177.3" parsed="|Ps|106|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.106.14">106:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 43:19" id="d-p177.4" parsed="|Isa|43|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.43.19">Isa. 43:19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 43:20" id="d-p177.5" parsed="|Isa|43|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.43.20">20</scripRef>. It
denotes a greater extent of uncultivated country than the other
words so rendered. It is especially applied to the desert of the

peninsula of Arabia (<scripRef passage="Num. 21:20" id="d-p177.6" parsed="|Num|21|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.21.20">Num. 21:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 23:28" id="d-p177.7" parsed="|Num|23|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.23.28">23:28</scripRef>), the most terrible of
all the deserts with which the Israelites were acquainted. It is
called “the desert” in Ex. 23:31; Deut. 11:24. (See JESHIMON.)
(4.) A dry place; hence a desolation (Ps. 9:6), desolate (Lev. 26:34); the rendering of the Hebrew word horbah’. It is

rendered “desert” only in <scripRef passage="Ps. 102:6" id="d-p178.3" parsed="|Ps|102|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.102.6">Ps. 102:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 48:21" id="d-p178.4" parsed="|Isa|48|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.48.21">Isa. 48:21</scripRef>, and <scripRef passage="Ezek. 13:4" id="d-p178.5" parsed="|Ezek|13|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.13.4">Ezek. 13:4</scripRef>,
where it means the wilderness of Sinai.
(5.) This word is the symbol of the Jewish church when they
had forsaken God (<scripRef passage="Isa. 40:3" id="d-p179.1" parsed="|Isa|40|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.40.3">Isa. 40:3</scripRef>). Nations destitute of the knowledge
of God are called a “wilderness” (32:15, midbar). It is a
symbol of temptation, solitude, and persecution (<scripRef passage="Isa. 27:10" id="d-p179.2" parsed="|Isa|27|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.27.10">Isa. 27:10</scripRef>,
midbar_; 33:9, _arabah).
</def>
<term id="d-p179.3">Desire of all nations</term>
(Hag. 2:7), usually interpreted as a title of the Messiah. The
Revised Version, however, more correctly renders “the desirable
things of all nations;” i.e., the choicest treasures of the
Gentiles shall be consecrated to the Lord.
</def>
<term id="d-p180.2">Desolation, Abomination of</term>
(Matt. 24:15; Mark 13:14; comp. Luke 21:20), is interpreted of
the eagles, the standards of the Roman army, which were an
abomination to the Jews. These standards, rising over the site
of the temple, were a sign that the holy place had fallen under
the idolatrous Romans. The references are to Dan. 9:27. (See ABOMINATION.)
</def>
<term id="d-p181.6">Destroyer</term>
(Ex. 12:23), the agent employed in the killing of the
first-born; the destroying angel or messenger of God. (Comp. 2 Kings 19:35; 2 Sam. 24:15, 16; Ps. 78:49; Acts 12:23.)
</def>
<term id="d-p182.7">Destruction</term>
In Job 26:6, 28:22 (Heb. abaddon) is sheol, the realm of the
dead.
</def>
<term id="d-p183.3">Destruction, City of</term>
(Isa. 19:18; Heb. Ir-ha-Heres, “city of overthrow,” because of
the evidence it would present of the overthrow of heathenism),
the ideal title of On or Heliopolis (q.v.).
</def>
<term id="d-p184.2">Deuteronomy</term>
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="d-p184.4" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="Deut 0" id="d-p184.5" parsed="|Deut|0|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut" />
In all the Hebrew manuscripts the Pentateuch (q.v.) forms one
roll or volume divided into larger and smaller sections called
parshioth_ and _sedarim. It is not easy to say when it was
divided into five books. This was probably first done by the
Greek translators of the book, whom the Vulgate follows. The
fifth of these books was called by the Greeks Deuteronomion,
i.e., the second law, hence our name Deuteronomy, or a second
statement of the laws already promulgated. The Jews designated
the book by the two first Hebrew words that occur, _’Elle
haddabharim_, i.e., “These are the words.” They divided it into
eleven parshioth. In the English Bible it contains thirty-four
chapters.
It consists chiefly of three discourses delivered by Moses a
short time before his death. They were spoken to all Israel in
the plains of Moab, in the eleventh month of the last year of
their wanderings.
The first discourse (1-4:40) recapitulates the chief events of
the last forty years in the wilderness, with earnest
exhortations to obedience to the divine ordinances, and warnings
against the danger of forsaking the God of their fathers.
The seond discourse (5-26:19) is in effect the body of the
whole book. The first address is introductory to it. It contains
practically a recapitulation of the law already given by God at
Mount Sinai, together with many admonitions and injunctions as
to the course of conduct they were to follow when they were
settled in Canaan.
The concluding discourse (ch. 27-30) relates almost wholly to
the solemn sanctions of the law, the blessings to the obedient,
and the curse that would fall on the rebellious. He solemnly
adjures them to adhere faithfully to the covenant God had made
with them, and so secure for themselves and their posterity the
promised blessings.
These addresses to the people are followed by what may be
called three appendices, namely (1), a song which God had
commanded Moses to write (32:1-47); (2) the blessings he
pronounced on the separate tribes (ch. 33); and (3) the story of
his death (32:48-52) and burial (ch. 34), written by some other
hand, probably that of Joshua.
These farewell addresses of Moses to the tribes of Israel he
had so long led in the wilderness “glow in each line with the
emotions of a great leader recounting to his contemporaries the
marvellous story of their common experience. The enthusiasm they
kindle, even to-day, though obscured by translation, reveals
their matchless adaptation to the circumstances under which they
were first spoken. Confidence for the future is evoked by
remembrance of the past. The same God who had done mighty works
for the tribes since the Exodus would cover their head in the
day of battle with the nations of Palestine, soon to be invaded.
Their great lawgiver stands before us, vigorous in his hoary
age, stern in his abhorrence of evil, earnest in his zeal for
God, but mellowed in all relations to earth by his nearness to
heaven. The commanding wisdom of his enactments, the dignity of
his position as the founder of the nation and the first of
prophets, enforce his utterances. But he touches our deepest
emotions by the human tenderness that breathes in all his words.
Standing on the verge of life, he speaks as a father giving his
parting counsels to those he loves; willing to depart and be
with God he has served so well, but fondly lengthening out his
last farewell to the dear ones of earth. No book can compare
with Deuteronomy in its mingled sublimity and tenderness.”
Geikie, Hours, etc.
The whole style and method of this book, its tone and its
peculiarities of conception and expression, show that it must
have come from one hand. That the author was none other than
Moses is established by the following considerations: (1.) The
uniform tradition both of the Jewish and the Christian Church
down to recent times. (2.) The book professes to have been
written by Moses (1:1; 29:1; 31:1, 9-11, etc.), and was
obviously intended to be accepted as his work. (3.) The

incontrovertible testimony of our Lord and his apostles (<scripRef passage="Matt. 19:7" id="d-p192.1" parsed="|Matt|19|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.19.7">Matt. 19:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt 19:8" id="d-p192.2" parsed="|Matt|19|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.19.8">8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 10:3" id="d-p192.3" parsed="|Mark|10|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.10.3">Mark 10:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Mark 10:4" id="d-p192.4" parsed="|Mark|10|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.10.4">4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 5:46" id="d-p192.5" parsed="|John|5|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.5.46">John 5:46</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="John 5:47" id="d-p192.6" parsed="|John|5|47|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.5.47">47</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 3:22" id="d-p192.7" parsed="|Acts|3|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.3.22">Acts 3:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 7:37" id="d-p192.8" parsed="|Acts|7|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.7.37">7:37</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 10:19" id="d-p192.9" parsed="|Rom|10|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.10.19">Rom. 10:19</scripRef>) establishes the same conclusion. (4.) The frequent

references to it in the later books of the canon (<scripRef passage="Josh. 8:31" id="d-p192.10" parsed="|Josh|8|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.8.31">Josh. 8:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 2:9" id="d-p192.11" parsed="|1Kgs|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.2.9">1 Kings 2:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 14:6" id="d-p192.12" parsed="|2Kgs|14|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.14.6">2 Kings 14:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 23:18" id="d-p192.13" parsed="|2Chr|23|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.23.18">2 Chr. 23:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 25:4" id="d-p192.14" parsed="|2Chr|25|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.25.4">25:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 34:14" id="d-p192.15" parsed="|2Chr|34|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.34.14">34:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezra 3:2" id="d-p192.16" parsed="|Ezra|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.3.2">Ezra 3:2</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Ezra 7:6" id="d-p192.17" parsed="|Ezra|7|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.7.6">7:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh. 8:1" id="d-p192.18" parsed="|Neh|8|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.8.1">Neh. 8:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Dan. 9:11" id="d-p192.19" parsed="|Dan|9|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.9.11">Dan. 9:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan. 9:13" id="d-p192.20" parsed="|Dan|9|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.9.13">13</scripRef>) prove its antiquity; and (5) the
archaisms found in it are in harmony with the age in which Moses
lived. (6.) Its style and allusions are also strikingly
consistent with the circumstances and position of Moses and of
the people at that time.
This body of positive evidence cannot be set aside by the
conjectures and reasonings of modern critics, who contended that
the book was somewhat like a forgery, introduced among the Jews
some seven or eight centuries after the Exodus.
</def>
<term id="d-p193.1">Devil</term>
(Gr. diabolos), a slanderer, the arch-enemy of man’s spiritual

interest (<scripRef passage="Job 1:6" id="d-p194.1" parsed="|Job|1|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.1.6">Job 1:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 2:10" id="d-p194.2" parsed="|Rev|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.2.10">Rev. 2:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 3:1" id="d-p194.3" parsed="|Zech|3|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.3.1">Zech. 3:1</scripRef>). He is called also “the
accuser of the brethen” (Rev. 12:10).
In Lev. 17:7 the word “devil” is the translation of the Hebrew
sair, meaning a “goat” or “satyr” (Isa. 13:21; 34:14),
alluding to the wood-daemons, the objects of idolatrous worship
among the heathen.
In Deut. 32:17 and Ps. 106:37 it is the translation of Hebrew
shed, meaning lord, and idol, regarded by the Jews as a
“demon,” as the word is rendered in the Revised Version.
In the narratives of the Gospels regarding the “casting out of
devils” a different Greek word (daimon) is used. In the time of
our Lord there were frequent cases of demoniacal possession
(Matt. 12:25-30; Mark 5:1-20; Luke 4:35; 10:18, etc.).
</def>
<term id="d-p197.5">Dew</term>
“There is no dew properly so called in Palestine, for there is
no moisture in the hot summer air to be chilled into dew-drops
by the coldness of the night. From May till October rain is
unknown, the sun shining with unclouded brightness day after
day. The heat becomes intense, the ground hard, and vegetation
would perish but for the moist west winds that come each night
from the sea. The bright skies cause the heat of the day to
radiate very quickly into space, so that the nights are as cold
as the day is the reverse, a peculiarity of climate from which
poor Jacob suffered thousands of years ago (<scripRef passage="Gen. 31:40" id="d-p198.1" parsed="|Gen|31|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.40">Gen. 31:40</scripRef>). To this
coldness of the night air the indispensable watering of all
plant-life is due. The winds, loaded with moisture, are robbed
of it as they pass over the land, the cold air condensing it
into drops of water, which fall in a gracious rain of mist on
every thirsty blade. In the morning the fog thus created rests
like a sea over the plains, and far up the sides of the hills,
which raise their heads above it like so many islands. At
sunrise, however, the scene speedily changes. By the kindling
light the mist is transformed into vast snow-white clouds, which
presently break into separate masses and rise up the
mountain-sides, to disappear in the blue above, dissipated by
the increasing heat. These are ‘the morning clouds and the early
dew that go away’ of which Hosea (6:4; 13:3) speaks so
touchingly” (Geikie’s The Holy Land, etc., i., p. 72). Dew is a

source of great fertility (<scripRef passage="Gen. 27:28" id="d-p198.2" parsed="|Gen|27|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.28">Gen. 27:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 33:13" id="d-p198.3" parsed="|Deut|33|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.33.13">Deut. 33:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 8:12" id="d-p198.4" parsed="|Zech|8|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.8.12">Zech. 8:12</scripRef>),
and its withdrawal is regarded as a curse from God (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 1:21" id="d-p198.5" parsed="|2Sam|1|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.1.21">2 Sam. 1:21</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="1 Kings 17:1" id="d-p198.6" parsed="|1Kgs|17|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.17.1">1 Kings 17:1</scripRef>). It is the symbol of a multitude (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 17:12" id="d-p198.7" parsed="|2Sam|17|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.17.12">2 Sam. 17:12</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Ps. 110:3" id="d-p198.8" parsed="|Ps|110|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.110.3">Ps. 110:3</scripRef>); and from its refreshing influence it is an emblem of
brotherly love and harmony (<scripRef passage="Ps. 133:3" id="d-p198.9" parsed="|Ps|133|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.133.3">Ps. 133:3</scripRef>), and of rich spiritual
blessings (Hos. 14:5).
</def>
<term id="d-p198.11">Diadem</term>
The tiara of a king (Ezek. 21:26; Isa. 28:5; 62:3); the turban
(<scripRef passage="Job 29:14" id="d-p199.4" parsed="|Job|29|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.29.14">Job 29:14</scripRef>). In the New Testament a careful distinction is drawn

between the diadem as a badge of royalty (<scripRef passage="Rev. 12:3" id="d-p199.5" parsed="|Rev|12|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.12.3">Rev. 12:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev 13:1" id="d-p199.6" parsed="|Rev|13|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.13.1">13:1</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Rev 19:12" id="d-p199.7" parsed="|Rev|19|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.19.12">19:12</scripRef>) and the crown as a mark of distinction in private life.
It is not known what the ancient Jewish “diadem” was. It was the
mark of Oriental sovereigns. (See CROWN.)
</def>
<term id="d-p199.9">Dial</term>
For the measurement of time, only once mentioned in the Bible,

erected by Ahaz (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 20:11" id="d-p200.1" parsed="|2Kgs|20|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.20.11">2 Kings 20:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 38:8" id="d-p200.2" parsed="|Isa|38|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.38.8">Isa. 38:8</scripRef>). The Hebrew word

(ma’aloth) is rendered “steps” in <scripRef passage="Ex. 20:26" id="d-p200.3" parsed="|Exod|20|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.20.26">Ex. 20:26</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 20:1" id="d-p200.4" parsed="|Exod|20|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.20.1">1</scripRef> Kings 10:19, and
“degrees” in 2 Kings 20:9, 10, 11. The ma’aloth was probably
stairs on which the shadow of a column or obelisk placed on the
top fell. The shadow would cover a greater or smaller number of
steps, according as the sun was low or high.
Probably the sun-dial was a Babylonian invention. Daniel at
Babylon (Dan. 3:6) is the first to make mention of the “hour.”
</def>
<term id="d-p201.2">Diamond</term>
(1.) A precious gem (Heb. yahalom’, in allusion to its
hardness), otherwise unknown, the sixth, i.e., the third in the
second row, in the breastplate of the high priest, with the name

of Naphtali engraven on it (<scripRef passage="Ex. 28:18" id="d-p202.1" parsed="|Exod|28|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.18">Ex. 28:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 39:11" id="d-p202.2" parsed="|Exod|39|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.39.11">39:11</scripRef>; R.V. marg.,
“sardonyx.”)
(2.) A precious stone (Heb. shamir’, a sharp point) mentioned
in <scripRef passage="Jer. 17:1" id="d-p203.1" parsed="|Jer|17|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.17.1">Jer. 17:1</scripRef>. From its hardness it was used for cutting and
perforating other minerals. It is rendered “adamant” (q.v.) in

<scripRef passage="Ezek. 3:9" id="d-p203.2" parsed="|Ezek|3|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.3.9">Ezek. 3:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Zech. 7:12" id="d-p203.3" parsed="|Zech|7|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.7.12">Zech. 7:12</scripRef>. It is the hardest and most valuable of
precious stones.
</def>
<term id="d-p203.4">Diana</term>
So called by the Romans; called Artemis by the Greeks, the
“great” goddess worshipped among heathen nations under various
modifications. Her most noted temple was that at Ephesus. It was
built outside the city walls, and was one of the seven wonders
of the ancient world. “First and last it was the work of 220
years; built of shining marble; 342 feet long by 164 feet broad;
supported by a forest of columns, each 56 feet high; a sacred
museum of masterpieces of sculpture and painting. At the centre,
hidden by curtains, within a gorgeous shrine, stood the very
ancient image of the goddess, on wood or ebony reputed to have
fallen from the sky. Behind the shrine was a treasury, where, as
in ‘the safest bank in Asia,’ nations and kings stored their
most precious things. The temple as St. Paul saw it subsisted
till A.D. 262, when it was ruined by the Goths” (Acts 19:23-41)., Moule on Ephesians: Introd.
</def>
<term id="d-p204.2">Diblaim</term>
Doubled cakes, the mother of Gomer, who was Hosea’s wife (Hos. 1:3).
</def>
<term id="d-p205.2">Diblathaim</term>
Two cakes, a city of Moab, on the east of the Dead Sea (Num. 33:46; Jer. 48:22).
</def>
<term id="d-p206.3">Dibon</term>
Pining; wasting. (1.) A city in Moab (Num. 21:30); called also

Dibon-gad (33:45), because it was built by Gad and Dimon (<scripRef passage="Isa. 15:9" id="d-p207.2" parsed="|Isa|15|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.15.9">Isa. 15:9</scripRef>). It has been identified with the modern Diban, about 3
miles north of the Arnon and 12 miles east of the Dead Sea. (See
Moabite Stone.)
(2.) A city of the tribe of Judah, inhabited after the

Captivity (<scripRef passage="Neh. 11:25" id="d-p208.1" parsed="|Neh|11|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.11.25">Neh. 11:25</scripRef>); called also Dimonah (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:22" id="d-p208.2" parsed="|Josh|15|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.22">Josh. 15:22</scripRef>). It is
probably the modern ed-Dheib.
</def>
<term id="d-p208.3">Didymus</term>
(Gr. twin = Heb. Thomas, q.v.), John 11:16; 20:24; 21:2.
</def>
<term id="d-p209.4">Dimnah</term>
Dunghill, a city of Zebulun given to the Merarite Levites (Josh. 21:35). In 1 Chr. 6:77 the name “Rimmon” is substituted.
</def>
<term id="d-p210.3">Dinah</term>
Judged; vindicated, daughter of Jacob by Leah, and sister of
Simeon and Levi (<scripRef passage="Gen. 30:21" id="d-p211.1" parsed="|Gen|30|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.30.21">Gen. 30:21</scripRef>). She was seduced by Shechem, the
son of Hamor, the Hivite chief, when Jacob’s camp was in the
neighbourhood of Shechem. This led to the terrible revenge of
Simeon and Levi in putting the Shechemites to death (<scripRef passage="Gen. 34" id="d-p211.2" parsed="|Gen|34|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.34">Gen. 34</scripRef>).
Jacob makes frequent reference to this deed of blood with

abhorrence and regret (<scripRef passage="Gen. 34:30" id="d-p211.3" parsed="|Gen|34|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.34.30">Gen. 34:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 49:5-7" id="d-p211.4" parsed="|Gen|49|5|49|7" osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.5-Gen.49.7">49:5-7</scripRef>). She is mentioned
among the rest of Jacob’s family that went down into Egypt (Gen. 46:8, 15).
</def>
<term id="d-p211.7">Dine</term>
(Gen. 43:16). It was the custom in Egypt to dine at noon. But it
is probable that the Egyptians took their principal meal in the
evening, as was the general custom in the East (Luke 14:12).
</def>
<term id="d-p212.3">Dinhabah</term>
Robbers’ den, an Edomitish city, the capital of king Bela (Gen. 36:32). It is probably the modern Dibdiba, a little north-east
of Petra.
</def>
<term id="d-p213.2">Dionysius</term>
The Areopagite, one of Paul’s converts at Athens (Acts 17:34).
</def>
<term id="d-p214.2">Diotrephes</term>
Jove-nourished, rebuked by John for his pride (3 John 1:9). He
was a Judaizer, prating against John and his fellow-labourers
“with malicious words” (7).
</def>
<term id="d-p215.2">Disciple</term>
A scholar, sometimes applied to the followers of John the
Baptist (<scripRef passage="Matt. 9:14" id="d-p216.1" parsed="|Matt|9|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.9.14">Matt. 9:14</scripRef>), and of the Pharisees (22:16), but
principally to the followers of Christ. A disciple of Christ is
one who (1) believes his doctrine, (2) rests on his sacrifice,
(3) imbibes his spirit, and (4) imitates his example (Matt. 10:24; Luke 14:26, 27, 33; John 6:69).
</def>
<term id="d-p216.7">Dish</term>
For eating from (2 Kings 21:13). Judas dipped his hand with a
“sop” or piece of bread in the same dish with our Lord, thereby
indicating friendly intimacy (<scripRef passage="Matt. 26:23" id="d-p217.2" parsed="|Matt|26|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.23">Matt. 26:23</scripRef>). The “lordly dish” in
<scripRef passage="Judg. 5:25" id="d-p217.3" parsed="|Judg|5|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.5.25">Judg. 5:25</scripRef> was probably the shallow drinking cup, usually of
brass. In Judg. 6:38 the same Hebrew word is rendered “bowl.”
The dishes of the tabernacle were made of pure gold (Ex. 25:29; 37:16).
</def>
<term id="d-p218.3">Dishan</term>
Antelope, the youngest son of Seir the Horite, head of one of
the tribes of Idumaea (Gen. 36:21, 28, 30).
</def>
<term id="d-p219.4">Dispensation</term>
(Gr. oikonomia, “management,” “economy”). (1.) The method or
scheme according to which God carries out his purposes towards
men is called a dispensation. There are usually reckoned three
dispensations, the Patriarchal, the Mosaic or Jewish, and the
Christian. (See COVENANT, Administration of.) These
were so many stages in God’s unfolding of his purpose of grace
toward men. The word is not found with this meaning in
Scripture.
(2.) A commission to preach the gospel (1 Cor. 9:17; Eph. 1:10; 3:2; Col. 1:25).
Dispensations of Providence are providential events which
affect men either in the way of mercy or of judgement.
</def>
<term id="d-p222.1">Dispersion</term>
(Gr. diaspora, “scattered,” James 1:1; 1 Pet. 1:1) of the Jews.
At various times, and from the operation of divers causes, the
Jews were separated and scattered into foreign countries “to the
outmost parts of heaven” (Deut. 30:4).
(1.) Many were dispersed over Assyria, Media, Babylonia, and
Persia, descendants of those who had been transported thither by
the Exile. The ten tribes, after existing as a separate kingdom
for two hundred and fifty-five years, were carried captive (B.C.
721) by Shalmaneser (or Sargon), king of Assyria. They never
returned to their own land as a distinct people, although many
individuals from among these tribes, there can be no doubt,
joined with the bands that returned from Babylon on the
proclamation of Cyrus.
(2.) Many Jews migrated to Egypt and took up their abode

there. This migration began in the days of Solomon (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:21" id="d-p225.1" parsed="|2Kgs|18|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.21">2 Kings 18:21</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:24" id="d-p225.2" parsed="|2Kgs|18|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.24">24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 30:7" id="d-p225.3" parsed="|Isa|30|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.30.7">Isa. 30:7</scripRef>). Alexander the Great placed a large number
of Jews in Alexandria, which he had founded, and conferred on
them equal rights with the Egyptians. Ptolemy Philadelphus, it
is said, caused the Jewish Scriptures to be translated into
Greek (the work began B.C. 284), for the use of the Alexandrian
Jews. The Jews in Egypt continued for many ages to exercise a
powerful influence on the public interests of that country. From
Egypt they spread along the coast of Africa to Cyrene (Acts 2:10) and to Ethiopia (8:27).
(3.) After the time of Seleucus Nicator (B.C. 280), one of the
captains of Alexander the Great, large numbers of Jews migrated
into Syria, where they enjoyed equal rights with the
Macedonians. From Syria they found their way into Asia Minor.
Antiochus the Great, king of Syria and Asia, removed 3,000
families of Jews from Mesopotamia and Babylonia, and planted
them in Phrygia and Lydia.
(4.) From Asia Minor many Jews moved into Greece and
Macedonia, chiefly for purposes of commerce. In the apostles’
time they were found in considerable numbers in all the
principal cities.
From the time of Pompey the Great (B.C. 63) numbers of Jews
from Palestine and Greece went to Rome, where they had a
separate quarter of the city assigned to them. Here they enjoyed
considerable freedom.
Thus were the Jews everywhere scattered abroad. This, in the
overruling providence of God, ultimately contributed in a great
degree toward opening the way for the spread of the gospel into
all lands.
Dispersion, from the plain of Shinar. This was occasioned by
the confusion of tongues at Babel (<scripRef passage="Gen. 11:9" id="d-p230.1" parsed="|Gen|11|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.11.9">Gen. 11:9</scripRef>). They were
scattered abroad “every one after his tongue, after their
families, in their nations” (Gen. 10:5, 20, 31).
The tenth chapter of Genesis gives us an account of the
principal nations of the earth in their migrations from the
plain of Shinar, which was their common residence after the
Flood. In general, it may be said that the descendants of
Japheth were scattered over the north, those of Shem over the
central regions, and those of Ham over the extreme south. The

<term id="d-p232.1">Distaff</term>
(Heb. pelek, a “circle”), the instrument used for twisting
threads by a whirl (Prov. 31:19).
</def>
<term id="d-p233.2">Divination</term>
Of false prophets (Deut. 18:10, 14; Micah 3:6, 7, 11), of
necromancers (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 28:8" id="d-p234.6" parsed="|1Sam|28|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.28.8">1 Sam. 28:8</scripRef>), of the Philistine priests and

diviners (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 6:2" id="d-p234.7" parsed="|1Sam|6|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.6.2">1 Sam. 6:2</scripRef>), of Balaam (<scripRef passage="Josh. 13:22" id="d-p234.8" parsed="|Josh|13|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.22">Josh. 13:22</scripRef>). Three kinds of
divination are mentioned in <scripRef passage="Ezek. 21:21" id="d-p234.9" parsed="|Ezek|21|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.21.21">Ezek. 21:21</scripRef>, by arrows, consulting
with images (the teraphim), and by examining the entrails of
animals sacrificed. The practice of this art seems to have been
encouraged in ancient Egypt. Diviners also abounded among the

aborigines of Canaan and the Philistines (<scripRef passage="Isa. 2:6" id="d-p234.10" parsed="|Isa|2|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.2.6">Isa. 2:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 28" id="d-p234.11" parsed="|1Sam|28|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.28">1 Sam. 28</scripRef>).
At a later period multitudes of magicians poured from Chaldea
and Arabia into the land of Israel, and pursued their

occupations (<scripRef passage="Isa. 8:19" id="d-p234.12" parsed="|Isa|8|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.8.19">Isa. 8:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 21:6" id="d-p234.13" parsed="|2Kgs|21|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.21.6">2 Kings 21:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 33:6" id="d-p234.14" parsed="|2Chr|33|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.33.6">2 Chr. 33:6</scripRef>). This
superstition widely spread, and in the time of the apostles
there were “vagabond Jews, exorcists” (<scripRef passage="Acts 19:13" id="d-p234.15" parsed="|Acts|19|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.13">Acts 19:13</scripRef>), and men like
Simon Magus (<scripRef passage="Acts 8:9" id="d-p234.16" parsed="|Acts|8|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.8.9">Acts 8:9</scripRef>), Bar-jesus (13:6, 8), and other jugglers
and impostors (19:19; <scripRef passage="2 Tim. 3:13" id="d-p234.17" parsed="|2Tim|3|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.3.13">2 Tim. 3:13</scripRef>). Every species and degree of
this superstition was strictly forbidden by the law of Moses
(Ex. 22:18; Lev. 19:26, 31; 20:27; Deut. 18:10, 11).
But beyond these various forms of superstition, there are
instances of divination on record in the Scriptures by which God
was pleased to make known his will.
(1.) There was divination by lot, by which, when resorted to
in matters of moment, and with solemnity, God intimated his will

(<scripRef passage="Josh. 7:13" id="d-p236.1" parsed="|Josh|7|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.7.13">Josh. 7:13</scripRef>). The land of Canaan was divided by lot (<scripRef passage="Num. 26:55" id="d-p236.2" parsed="|Num|26|55|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.26.55">Num. 26:55</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num 26:56" id="d-p236.3" parsed="|Num|26|56|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.26.56">56</scripRef>); Achan’s guilt was detected (<scripRef passage="Josh. 7:16-19" id="d-p236.4" parsed="|Josh|7|16|7|19" osisRef="Bible:Josh.7.16-Josh.7.19">Josh. 7:16-19</scripRef>), Saul was

elected king (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 10:20" id="d-p236.5" parsed="|1Sam|10|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.10.20">1 Sam. 10:20</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 10:21" id="d-p236.6" parsed="|1Sam|10|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.10.21">21</scripRef>), and Matthias chosen to the
apostleship, by the solem lot (<scripRef passage="Acts 1:26" id="d-p236.7" parsed="|Acts|1|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.26">Acts 1:26</scripRef>). It was thus also that
the scape-goat was determined (Lev. 16:8-10).
(2.) There was divination by dreams (Gen. 20:6; Deut. 13:1, 3;

<scripRef passage="Judg. 7:13" id="d-p237.4" parsed="|Judg|7|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.7.13">Judg. 7:13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Judg. 7:15" id="d-p237.5" parsed="|Judg|7|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.7.15">15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 1:20" id="d-p237.6" parsed="|Matt|1|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.1.20">Matt. 1:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 2:12" id="d-p237.7" parsed="|Matt|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.2.12">2:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt 2:13" id="d-p237.8" parsed="|Matt|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.2.13">13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt 2:19" id="d-p237.9" parsed="|Matt|2|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.2.19">19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt 2:22" id="d-p237.10" parsed="|Matt|2|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.2.22">22</scripRef>). This is
illustrated in the history of Joseph (<scripRef passage="Gen. 41:25-32" id="d-p237.11" parsed="|Gen|41|25|41|32" osisRef="Bible:Gen.41.25-Gen.41.32">Gen. 41:25-32</scripRef>) and of
(3.) By divine appointment there was also divination by the
Urim and Thummim (Num. 27:21), and by the ephod.
(4.) God was pleased sometimes to vouch-safe direct vocal

communications to men (<scripRef passage="Deut. 34:10" id="d-p239.1" parsed="|Deut|34|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.34.10">Deut. 34:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex. 3:4" id="d-p239.2" parsed="|Exod|3|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.3.4">Ex. 3:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 4:3" id="d-p239.3" parsed="|Exod|4|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.4.3">4:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 4:14" id="d-p239.4" parsed="|Deut|4|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.4.14">Deut. 4:14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut 4:15" id="d-p239.5" parsed="|Deut|4|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.4.15">15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 19:12" id="d-p239.6" parsed="|1Kgs|19|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.19.12">1 Kings 19:12</scripRef>). He also communed with men from above the
mercy-seat (Ex. 25:22), and at the door of the tabernacle (Ex. 29:42, 43).
(5.) Through his prophets God revealed himself, and gave
intimations of his will (2 Kings 13:17; Jer. 51:63, 64).
</def>
<term id="d-p240.4">Divorce</term>
The dissolution of the marriage tie was regulated by the Mosaic
law (<scripRef passage="Deut. 24:1-4" id="d-p241.1" parsed="|Deut|24|1|24|4" osisRef="Bible:Deut.24.1-Deut.24.4">Deut. 24:1-4</scripRef>). The Jews, after the Captivity, were reguired
to dismiss the foreign women they had married contrary to the
law (<scripRef passage="Ezra 10:11-19" id="d-p241.2" parsed="|Ezra|10|11|10|19" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.10.11-Ezra.10.19">Ezra 10:11-19</scripRef>). Christ limited the permission of divorce to
the single case of adultery. It seems that it was not uncommon
for the Jews at that time to dissolve the union on very slight

pretences (<scripRef passage="Matt. 5:31" id="d-p241.3" parsed="|Matt|5|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.31">Matt. 5:31</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 5:32" id="d-p241.4" parsed="|Matt|5|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.32">32</scripRef>; 19:1-9; <scripRef passage="Mark 10:2-12" id="d-p241.5" parsed="|Mark|10|2|10|12" osisRef="Bible:Mark.10.2-Mark.10.12">Mark 10:2-12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 16:18" id="d-p241.6" parsed="|Luke|16|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.16.18">Luke 16:18</scripRef>).
These precepts given by Christ regulate the law of divorce in
the Christian Church.
</def>
<term id="d-p241.7">Dizahab</term>
Region of gold, a place in the desert of Sinai, on the western
shore of the Elanitic gulf (Deut. 1:1). It is now called Dehab.
</def>
<term id="d-p242.2">Doctor</term>
(Luke 2:46; 5:17; Acts 5:34), a teacher. The Jewish doctors
taught and disputed in synagogues, or wherever they could find
an audience. Their disciples were allowed to propose to them
questions. They assumed the office without any appointment to
it. The doctors of the law were principally of the sect of the
Pharisees. Schools were established after the destruction of
Jerusalem at Babylon and Tiberias, in which academical degrees
were conferred on those who passed a certain examination. Those
of the school of Tiberias were called by the title “rabbi,” and
those of Babylon by that of “master.”
</def>
<term id="d-p243.4">Dodai</term>
Loving, one of David’s captains (1 Chr. 27:4). (See
DODO [2].)
</def>
<term id="d-p244.3">Dodanim</term>
Leaders, a race descended from Javan (Gen. 10:4). They are known
in profane history as the Dardani, originally inhabiting
Illyricum. They were a semi-Pelasgic race, and in the
ethnographical table (<scripRef passage="Gen. 10" id="d-p245.2" parsed="|Gen|10|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10">Gen. 10</scripRef>) they are grouped with the Chittim
(q.v.). In <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 1:7" id="d-p245.3" parsed="|1Chr|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.1.7">1 Chr. 1:7</scripRef>, they are called Rodanim. The LXX. and the
Samaritan Version also read Rhodii, whence some have concluded
that the Rhodians, the inhabitants of the island of Rhodes, are
meant.
</def>
<term id="d-p245.4">Dodo</term>
Amatory; loving. (1.) A descendant of Issachar (Judg. 10:1).
(2.) An Ahohite, father of Eleazar, who was one of David’s

three heroes (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 23:9" id="d-p247.1" parsed="|2Sam|23|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.23.9">2 Sam. 23:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 11:12" id="d-p247.2" parsed="|1Chr|11|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.11.12">1 Chr. 11:12</scripRef>). He was the same with
Dodai mentioned in 1 Chr. 27:4.
(3.) A Bethlehemite, and father of Elhanan, who was one of
David’s thirty heroes (2 Sam. 23:24).
</def>
<term id="d-p248.2">Doeg</term>
Fearful, an Edomite, the chief overseer of Saul’s flocks (1 Sam. 21:7). At the command of Saul he slew the high priest Ahimelech
(q.v.) at Nob, together with all the priests to the number of
eighty-five persons. (Comp. Ps. 52, title.)
</def>
<term id="d-p249.3">Dog</term>
Frequently mentioned both in the Old and New Testaments. Dogs

were used by the Hebrews as a watch for their houses (<scripRef passage="Isa. 56:10" id="d-p250.1" parsed="|Isa|56|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.56.10">Isa. 56:10</scripRef>), and for guarding their flocks (<scripRef passage="Job 30:1" id="d-p250.2" parsed="|Job|30|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.30.1">Job 30:1</scripRef>). There were
also then as now troops of semi-wild dogs that wandered about
devouring dead bodies and the offal of the streets (1 Kings 14:11; 16:4; 21:19, 23; 22:38; Ps. 59:6, 14).
As the dog was an unclean animal, the terms “dog,” “dog’s
head,” “dead dog,” were used as terms of reproach or of

humiliation (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 24:14" id="d-p251.1" parsed="|1Sam|24|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.24.14">1 Sam. 24:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 3:8" id="d-p251.2" parsed="|2Sam|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.3.8">2 Sam. 3:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 9:8" id="d-p251.3" parsed="|2Sam|9|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.9.8">9:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 16:9" id="d-p251.4" parsed="|2Sam|16|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.16.9">16:9</scripRef>). Paul calls
false apostles “dogs” (<scripRef passage="Phil. 3:2" id="d-p251.5" parsed="|Phil|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Phil.3.2">Phil. 3:2</scripRef>). Those who are shut out of the
kingdom of heaven are also so designated (<scripRef passage="Rev. 22:15" id="d-p251.6" parsed="|Rev|22|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.22.15">Rev. 22:15</scripRef>).
Persecutors are called “dogs” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 22:16" id="d-p251.7" parsed="|Ps|22|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.22.16">Ps. 22:16</scripRef>). Hazael’s words, “Thy
servant which is but a dog” (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 8:13" id="d-p251.8" parsed="|2Kgs|8|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.8.13">2 Kings 8:13</scripRef>), are spoken in mock
humility=impossible that one so contemptible as he should attain
to such power.
</def>
<term id="d-p251.9">Doleful creatures</term>
(occurring only Isa. 13:21. Heb. ochim, i.e., “shrieks;” hence
“howling animals”), a general name for screech owls (howlets),
which occupy the desolate palaces of Babylon. Some render the
word “hyaenas.”
</def>
<term id="d-p252.2">Door-keeper</term>
This word is used in Ps. 84:10 (R.V. marg., “stand at the
threshold of,” etc.), but there it signifies properly “sitting
at the threshold in the house of God.” The psalmist means that
he would rather stand at the door of God’s house and merely look
in, than dwell in houses where iniquity prevailed.
Persons were appointed to keep the street door leading into

the interior of the house (<scripRef passage="John 18:16" id="d-p254.1" parsed="|John|18|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.18.16">John 18:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="John 18:17" id="d-p254.2" parsed="|John|18|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.18.17">17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 12:13" id="d-p254.3" parsed="|Acts|12|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.12.13">Acts 12:13</scripRef>).
Sometimes females held this post.
</def>
<term id="d-p254.4">Door-posts</term>
The Jews were commanded to write the divine name on the posts
(mezuzoth’) of their doors (<scripRef passage="Deut. 6:9" id="d-p255.1" parsed="|Deut|6|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.6.9">Deut. 6:9</scripRef>). The Jews,
misunderstanding this injunction, adopted the custom of writing
on a slip of parchment these verses (<scripRef passage="Deut. 6:4-9" id="d-p255.2" parsed="|Deut|6|4|6|9" osisRef="Bible:Deut.6.4-Deut.6.9">Deut. 6:4-9</scripRef>, and 11:13-21),
which they enclosed in a reed or cylinder and fixed on the
right-hand door-post of every room in the house.
</def>
<term id="d-p255.3">Doors</term>
Moved on pivots of wood fastened in sockets above and below

(<scripRef passage="Prov. 26:14" id="d-p256.1" parsed="|Prov|26|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.26.14">Prov. 26:14</scripRef>). They were fastened by a lock (<scripRef passage="Judg. 3:23" id="d-p256.2" parsed="|Judg|3|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.3.23">Judg. 3:23</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Judg. 3:25" id="d-p256.3" parsed="|Judg|3|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.3.25">25</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Cant. 5:5" id="d-p256.4" parsed="|Song|5|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.5.5">Cant. 5:5</scripRef>) or by a bar (<scripRef passage="Judg. 16:3" id="d-p256.5" parsed="|Judg|16|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.16.3">Judg. 16:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 38:10" id="d-p256.6" parsed="|Job|38|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.38.10">Job 38:10</scripRef>). In the interior
of Oriental houses, curtains were frequently used instead of
doors.
The entrances of the tabernacle had curtains (Ex. 26:31-33,
<scripRef passage="Ex 26:36" id="d-p257.2" parsed="|Exod|26|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.26.36">36</scripRef>). The “valley of Achor” is called a “door of hope,” because
immediately after the execution of Achan the Lord said to
Joshua, “Fear not,” and from that time Joshua went forward in a
career of uninterrupted conquest. Paul speaks of a “door opened”

for the spread of the gospel (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 16:9" id="d-p257.3" parsed="|1Cor|16|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.16.9">1 Cor. 16:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 2:12" id="d-p257.4" parsed="|2Cor|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.2.12">2 Cor. 2:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Col. 4:3" id="d-p257.5" parsed="|Col|4|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.4.3">Col. 4:3</scripRef>). Our Lord says of himself, “I am the door” (<scripRef passage="John 10:9" id="d-p257.6" parsed="|John|10|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.10.9">John 10:9</scripRef>).
John (Rev. 4:1) speaks of a “door opened in heaven.”
</def>
<term id="d-p257.8">Dophkah</term>
Knocking, an encampment of the Israelites in the wilderness
(<scripRef passage="Num. 33:12" id="d-p258.1" parsed="|Num|33|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.12">Num. 33:12</scripRef>). It was in the desert of Sin, on the eastern shore
of the western arm of the Red Sea, somewhere in the Wady Feiran.
</def>
<term id="d-p258.2">Dor</term>
Dwelling, the Dora of the Romans, an ancient royal city of the

Canaanites (<scripRef passage="Josh. 11:1" id="d-p259.1" parsed="|Josh|11|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.1">Josh. 11:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh 11:2" id="d-p259.2" parsed="|Josh|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.2">2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 12:23" id="d-p259.3" parsed="|Josh|12|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.12.23">12:23</scripRef>). It was the most southern
settlement of the Phoenicians on the coast of Syria. The
original inhabitants seem never to have been expelled, although
they were made tributary by David. It was one of Solomon’s

commissariat districts (<scripRef passage="Judg. 1:27" id="d-p259.4" parsed="|Judg|1|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.27">Judg. 1:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:11" id="d-p259.5" parsed="|1Kgs|4|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.11">1 Kings 4:11</scripRef>). It has been
identified with Tantura (so named from the supposed resemblance
of its tower to a tantur, i.e., “a horn”). This tower fell in
1895, and nothing remains but debris and foundation walls, the
remains of an old Crusading fortress. It is about 8 miles north
of Caesarea, “a sad and sickly hamlet of wretched huts on a
naked sea-beach.”
</def>
<term id="d-p259.6">Dorcas</term>
A female antelope, or gazelle, a pious Christian widow at Joppa
whom Peter restored to life (<scripRef passage="Acts 9:36-41" id="d-p260.1" parsed="|Acts|9|36|9|41" osisRef="Bible:Acts.9.36-Acts.9.41">Acts 9:36-41</scripRef>). She was a
Hellenistic Jewess, called Tabitha by the Jews and Dorcas by the
Greeks.
</def>
<term id="d-p260.2">Dothan</term>
Two wells, a famous pasture-ground where Joseph found his
brethren watching their flocks. Here, at the suggestion of
Judah, they sold him to the Ishmaelite merchants (<scripRef passage="Gen. 37:17" id="d-p261.1" parsed="|Gen|37|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.17">Gen. 37:17</scripRef>).
It is mentioned on monuments in B.C. 1600.
It was the residence of Elisha (2 Kings 6:13), and the scene
of a remarkable vision of chariots and horses of fire
surrounding the mountain on which the city stood. It is
identified with the modern Tell-Dothan, on the south side of the
plain of Jezreel, about 12 miles north of Samaria, among the
hills of Gilboa. The “two wells” are still in existence, one of
which bears the name of the “pit of Joseph” (Jubb Yusuf).
</def>
<term id="d-p262.2">Dough</term>
(batsek, meaning “swelling,” i.e., in fermentation). The dough
the Israelites had prepared for baking was carried away by them

out of Egypt in their kneading-troughs (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:34" id="d-p263.1" parsed="|Exod|12|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.34">Ex. 12:34</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 12:39" id="d-p263.2" parsed="|Exod|12|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.39">39</scripRef>). In the
process of baking, the dough had to be turned (Hos. 7:8).
</def>
<term id="d-p263.4">Dove</term>
In their wild state doves generally build their nests in the
clefts of rocks, but when domesticated “dove-cots” are prepared
