for them (<scripRef passage="Cant. 2:14" id="d-p264.1" parsed="|Song|2|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.2.14">Cant. 2:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 48:28" id="d-p264.2" parsed="|Jer|48|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.28">Jer. 48:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 60:8" id="d-p264.3" parsed="|Isa|60|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.60.8">Isa. 60:8</scripRef>). The dove was
placed on the standards of the Assyrians and Babylonians in
honour, it is supposed, of Semiramis (<scripRef passage="Jer. 25:38" id="d-p264.4" parsed="|Jer|25|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.25.38">Jer. 25:38</scripRef>; Vulg.,

“fierceness of the dove;” comp. <scripRef passage="Jer. 46:16" id="d-p264.5" parsed="|Jer|46|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.46.16">Jer. 46:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 50:16" id="d-p264.6" parsed="|Jer|50|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.50.16">50:16</scripRef>). Doves and
turtle-doves were the only birds that could be offered in

sacrifice, as they were clean according to the Mosaic law (<scripRef passage="Ge. 15:9" id="d-p264.7" parsed="|Gen|15|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.9">Ge. 15:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 5:7" id="d-p264.8" parsed="|Lev|5|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.5.7">Lev. 5:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 12:6" id="d-p264.9" parsed="|Lev|12|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.12.6">12:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 2:24" id="d-p264.10" parsed="|Luke|2|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.24">Luke 2:24</scripRef>). The dove was the harbinger of

peace to Noah (<scripRef passage="Gen. 8:8" id="d-p264.11" parsed="|Gen|8|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.8.8">Gen. 8:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 8:10" id="d-p264.12" parsed="|Gen|8|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.8.10">10</scripRef>). It is often mentioned as the
emblem of purity (<scripRef passage="Ps. 68:13" id="d-p264.13" parsed="|Ps|68|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.68.13">Ps. 68:13</scripRef>). It is a symbol of the Holy Spirit

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 1:2" id="d-p264.14" parsed="|Gen|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.1.2">Gen. 1:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 3:16" id="d-p264.15" parsed="|Matt|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.16">Matt. 3:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 1:10" id="d-p264.16" parsed="|Mark|1|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.10">Mark 1:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 3:22" id="d-p264.17" parsed="|Luke|3|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.22">Luke 3:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 1:32" id="d-p264.18" parsed="|John|1|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.1.32">John 1:32</scripRef>); also of

tender and devoted affection (<scripRef passage="Cant. 1:15" id="d-p264.19" parsed="|Song|1|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.1.15">Cant. 1:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Cant 2:14" id="d-p264.20" parsed="|Song|2|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.2.14">2:14</scripRef>). David in his
distress wished that he had the wings of a dove, that he might
fly away and be at rest (<scripRef passage="Ps. 55:6-8" id="d-p264.21" parsed="|Ps|55|6|55|8" osisRef="Bible:Ps.55.6-Ps.55.8">Ps. 55:6-8</scripRef>). There is a species of dove
found at Damascus “whose feathers, all except the wings, are
literally as yellow as gold” (68:13).
</def>
<term id="d-p264.22">Dove’s dung</term>
(2 Kings 6:25) has been generally understood literally. There
are instances in history of the dung of pigeons being actually
used as food during a famine. Compare also the language of

Rabshakeh to the Jews (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:27" id="d-p265.2" parsed="|2Kgs|18|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.27">2 Kings 18:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 36:12" id="d-p265.3" parsed="|Isa|36|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.36.12">Isa. 36:12</scripRef>). This name,
however, is applied by the Arabs to different vegetable
substances, and there is room for the opinion of those who think
that some such substance is here referred to, as, e.g., the
seeds of a kind of millet, or a very inferior kind of pulse, or
the root of the ornithogalum, i.e., bird-milk, the
star-of-Bethlehem.
</def>
<term id="d-p265.4">Dowry</term>
(mohar; i.e., price paid for a wife, Gen. 34:12; Ex. 22:17; 1 Sam. 18:25), a nuptial present; some gift, as a sum of money,
which the bridegroom offers to the father of his bride as a
satisfaction before he can receive her. Jacob had no dowry to

give for his wife, but he gave his services (<scripRef passage="Gen. 29:18" id="d-p266.4" parsed="|Gen|29|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.29.18">Gen. 29:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 30:20" id="d-p266.5" parsed="|Gen|30|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.30.20">30:20</scripRef>;
34:12).
</def>
<term id="d-p266.7">Dragon</term>
(1.) Heb. tannim, plural of tan. The name of some unknown

creature inhabiting desert places and ruins (<scripRef passage="Job 30:29" id="d-p267.1" parsed="|Job|30|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.30.29">Job 30:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 44:19" id="d-p267.2" parsed="|Ps|44|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.44.19">Ps. 44:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 13:22" id="d-p267.3" parsed="|Isa|13|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.13.22">Isa. 13:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 34:13" id="d-p267.4" parsed="|Isa|34|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.34.13">34:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 43:20" id="d-p267.5" parsed="|Isa|43|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.43.20">43:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 10:22" id="d-p267.6" parsed="|Jer|10|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.10.22">Jer. 10:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Micah 1:8" id="d-p267.7" parsed="|Mic|1|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.1.8">Micah 1:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mal. 1:3" id="d-p267.8" parsed="|Mal|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mal.1.3">Mal. 1:3</scripRef>); probably, as translated in the Revised Version, the jackal
(2.) Heb. tannin. Some great sea monster (Jer. 51:34). In Isa. 51:9 it may denote the crocodile. In Gen. 1:21 (Heb. plural
tanninim) the Authorized Version renders “whales,” and the
Revised Version “sea monsters.” It is rendered “serpent” in Ex. 7:9. It is used figuratively in Ps. 74:13; Ezek. 29:3.
In the New Testament the word “dragon” is found only in Rev. 12:3, 4, 7, 9, 16, 17, etc., and is there used metaphorically of
“Satan.” (See WHALE.)
</def>
<term id="d-p269.8">Dragon well</term>
(Neh. 2:13), supposed by some to be identical with the Pool of
Gihon.
</def>
<term id="d-p270.2">Dram</term>
The Authorized Version understood the word ‘adarkonim (1 Chr. 29:7; Ezra 8:27), and the similar word darkomnim (Ezra 2:69;
<scripRef passage="Neh. 7:70" id="d-p271.4" parsed="|Neh|7|70|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.7.70">Neh. 7:70</scripRef>), as equivalent to the Greek silver coin the drachma.
But the Revised Version rightly regards it as the Greek
dareikos, a Persian gold coin (the daric) of the value of about
1 pound, 2s., which was first struck by Darius, the son of
Hystaspes, and was current in Western Asia long after the fall
of the Persian empire. (See DARIC.)
</def>
<term id="d-p271.6">Draught-house</term>
(2 Kings 10:27). Jehu ordered the temple of Baal to be
destroyed, and the place to be converted to the vile use of
receiving offal or ordure. (Comp. Matt. 15:17.)
</def>
<term id="d-p272.3">Drawer of water</term>
(Deut. 29:11; Josh. 9:21, 23), a servile employment to which the
Gibeonites were condemned.
</def>
<term id="d-p273.4">Dream</term>
God has frequently made use of dreams in communicating his will
to men. The most remarkable instances of this are recorded in

the history of Jacob (<scripRef passage="Gen. 28:12" id="d-p274.1" parsed="|Gen|28|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.28.12">Gen. 28:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 31:10" id="d-p274.2" parsed="|Gen|31|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.10">31:10</scripRef>), Laban (31:24), Joseph

(37:9-11), Gideon (<scripRef passage="Judg. 7" id="d-p274.3" parsed="|Judg|7|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.7">Judg. 7</scripRef>), and Solomon (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 3:5" id="d-p274.4" parsed="|1Kgs|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.3.5">1 Kings 3:5</scripRef>). Other
significant dreams are also recorded, such as those of Abimelech
(<scripRef passage="Gen. 20:3-7" id="d-p274.5" parsed="|Gen|20|3|20|7" osisRef="Bible:Gen.20.3-Gen.20.7">Gen. 20:3-7</scripRef>), Pharaoh’s chief butler and baker (40:5), Pharaoh

(41:1-8), the Midianites (<scripRef passage="Judg. 7:13" id="d-p274.6" parsed="|Judg|7|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.7.13">Judg. 7:13</scripRef>), Nebuchadnezzar (<scripRef passage="Dan. 2:1" id="d-p274.7" parsed="|Dan|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.2.1">Dan. 2:1</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Dan 4:10" id="d-p274.8" parsed="|Dan|4|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.4.10">4:10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan 4:18" id="d-p274.9" parsed="|Dan|4|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.4.18">18</scripRef>), the wise men from the east (<scripRef passage="Matt. 2:12" id="d-p274.10" parsed="|Matt|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.2.12">Matt. 2:12</scripRef>), and Pilate’s
To Joseph “the Lord appeared in a dream,” and gave him

instructions regarding the infant Jesus (<scripRef passage="Matt. 1:20" id="d-p275.1" parsed="|Matt|1|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.1.20">Matt. 1:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 2:12" id="d-p275.2" parsed="|Matt|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.2.12">2:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt 2:13" id="d-p275.3" parsed="|Matt|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.2.13">13</scripRef>,
<scripRef passage="Matt 2:19" id="d-p275.4" parsed="|Matt|2|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.2.19">19</scripRef>). In a vision of the night a “man of Macedonia” stood before
Paul and said, “Come over into Macedonia and help us” (Acts 16:9; see also 18:9; 27:23).
</def>
<term id="d-p275.6">Dredge</term>
(Job 24:6). See CORN.
</def>
<term id="d-p276.3">Dregs</term>
(Ps. 75:8; Isa. 51:17, 22), the lees of wine which settle at the
bottom of the vessel.
</def>
<term id="d-p277.4">Dress</term>
(1.) Materials used. The earliest and simplest an apron of
fig-leaves sewed together (<scripRef passage="Gen. 3:7" id="d-p278.1" parsed="|Gen|3|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.3.7">Gen. 3:7</scripRef>); then skins of animals

(3:21). Elijah’s dress was probably the skin of a sheep (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 1:8" id="d-p278.2" parsed="|2Kgs|1|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.1.8">2 Kings 1:8</scripRef>). The Hebrews were early acquainted with the art of weaving

hair into cloth (<scripRef passage="Ex. 26:7" id="d-p278.3" parsed="|Exod|26|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.26.7">Ex. 26:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 35:6" id="d-p278.4" parsed="|Exod|35|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.35.6">35:6</scripRef>), which formed the sackcloth of
mourners. This was the material of John the Baptist’s robe

(<scripRef passage="Matt. 3:4" id="d-p278.5" parsed="|Matt|3|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.4">Matt. 3:4</scripRef>). Wool was also woven into garments (<scripRef passage="Lev. 13:47" id="d-p278.6" parsed="|Lev|13|47|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.13.47">Lev. 13:47</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Deut. 22:11" id="d-p278.7" parsed="|Deut|22|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.22.11">Deut. 22:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 34:3" id="d-p278.8" parsed="|Ezek|34|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.34.3">Ezek. 34:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 31:20" id="d-p278.9" parsed="|Job|31|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.31.20">Job 31:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 27:26" id="d-p278.10" parsed="|Prov|27|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.27.26">Prov. 27:26</scripRef>). The Israelites
probably learned the art of weaving linen when they were in
Egypt (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 4:21" id="d-p278.11" parsed="|1Chr|4|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.4.21">1 Chr. 4:21</scripRef>). Fine linen was used in the vestments of the

high priest (<scripRef passage="Ex. 28:5" id="d-p278.12" parsed="|Exod|28|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.5">Ex. 28:5</scripRef>), as well as by the rich (<scripRef passage="Gen. 41:42" id="d-p278.13" parsed="|Gen|41|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.41.42">Gen. 41:42</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Prov. 31:22" id="d-p278.14" parsed="|Prov|31|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.31.22">Prov. 31:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 16:19" id="d-p278.15" parsed="|Luke|16|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.16.19">Luke 16:19</scripRef>). The use of mixed material, as wool and
flax, was forbidden (Lev. 19:19; Deut. 22:11).
(2.) Colour. The prevailing colour was the natural white of
the material used, which was sometimes rendered purer by the

fuller’s art (<scripRef passage="Ps. 104:1" id="d-p279.1" parsed="|Ps|104|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.104.1">Ps. 104:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps 104:2" id="d-p279.2" parsed="|Ps|104|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.104.2">2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 63:3" id="d-p279.3" parsed="|Isa|63|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.63.3">Isa. 63:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 9:3" id="d-p279.4" parsed="|Mark|9|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.9.3">Mark 9:3</scripRef>). The Hebrews

were acquainted with the art of dyeing (<scripRef passage="Gen. 37:3" id="d-p279.5" parsed="|Gen|37|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.3">Gen. 37:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 37:23" id="d-p279.6" parsed="|Gen|37|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.23">23</scripRef>). Various
modes of ornamentation were adopted in the process of weaving

(<scripRef passage="Ex. 28:6" id="d-p279.7" parsed="|Exod|28|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.6">Ex. 28:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 26:1" id="d-p279.8" parsed="|Exod|26|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.26.1">26:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex 26:31" id="d-p279.9" parsed="|Exod|26|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.26.31">31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 35:25" id="d-p279.10" parsed="|Exod|35|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.35.25">35:25</scripRef>), and by needle-work (<scripRef passage="Judg. 5:30" id="d-p279.11" parsed="|Judg|5|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.5.30">Judg. 5:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 45:13" id="d-p279.12" parsed="|Ps|45|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.45.13">Ps. 45:13</scripRef>). Dyed robes were imported from foreign countries,
particularly from Phoenicia (<scripRef passage="Zeph. 1:8" id="d-p279.13" parsed="|Zeph|1|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zeph.1.8">Zeph. 1:8</scripRef>). Purple and scarlet
robes were the marks of the wealthy (Luke 16:19; 2 Sam. 1:24).
(3.) Form. The robes of men and women were not very much
different in form from each other.
(a) The “coat” (kethoneth), of wool, cotton, or linen, was
worn by both sexes. It was a closely-fitting garment, resembling
in use and form our shirt (<scripRef passage="John 19:23" id="d-p281.1" parsed="|John|19|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.23">John 19:23</scripRef>). It was kept close to the
body by a girdle (<scripRef passage="John 21:7" id="d-p281.2" parsed="|John|21|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.21.7">John 21:7</scripRef>). A person wearing this “coat” alone

was described as naked (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 19:24" id="d-p281.3" parsed="|1Sam|19|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.19.24">1 Sam. 19:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 20:2" id="d-p281.4" parsed="|Isa|20|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.20.2">Isa. 20:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 6:30" id="d-p281.5" parsed="|2Kgs|6|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.6.30">2 Kings 6:30</scripRef>;
John 21:7); deprived of it he would be absolutely naked.
(b) A linen cloth or wrapper (sadin) of fine linen, used
somewhat as a night-shirt (Mark 14:51). It is mentioned in Judg. 14:12, 13, and rendered there “sheets.”
(c) An upper tunic (meil), longer than the “coat” (1 Sam. 2:19; 24:4; 28:14). In 1 Sam. 28:14 it is the mantle in which
Samuel was enveloped; in <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 24:4" id="d-p283.5" parsed="|1Sam|24|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.24.4">1 Sam. 24:4</scripRef> it is the “robe” under
which Saul slept. The disciples were forbidden to wear two
“coats” (Matt. 10:10; Luke 9:3).
(d) The usual outer garment consisted of a piece of woollen
cloth like a Scotch plaid, either wrapped round the body or
thrown over the shoulders like a shawl, with the ends hanging
down in front, or it might be thrown over the head so as to

conceal the face (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 15:30" id="d-p284.1" parsed="|2Sam|15|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.15.30">2 Sam. 15:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Esther 6:12" id="d-p284.2" parsed="|Esth|6|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.6.12">Esther 6:12</scripRef>). It was confined to
the waist by a girdle, and the fold formed by the overlapping of

the robe served as a pocket (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 4:39" id="d-p284.3" parsed="|2Kgs|4|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.4.39">2 Kings 4:39</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 79:12" id="d-p284.4" parsed="|Ps|79|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.79.12">Ps. 79:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hag. 2:12" id="d-p284.5" parsed="|Hag|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hag.2.12">Hag. 2:12</scripRef>;
Prov. 17:23; 21:14).
Female dress. The “coat” was common to both sexes (Cant. 5:3).
But peculiar to females were (1) the “veil” or “wimple,” a kind

of shawl (<scripRef passage="Ruth 3:15" id="d-p285.2" parsed="|Ruth|3|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.3.15">Ruth 3:15</scripRef>; rendered “mantle,” R.V., <scripRef passage="Isa. 3:22" id="d-p285.3" parsed="|Isa|3|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.22">Isa. 3:22</scripRef>); (2)
the “mantle,” also a species of shawl (<scripRef passage="Isa. 3:22" id="d-p285.4" parsed="|Isa|3|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.22">Isa. 3:22</scripRef>); (3) a “veil,”
probably a light summer dress (<scripRef passage="Gen. 24:65" id="d-p285.5" parsed="|Gen|24|65|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.65">Gen. 24:65</scripRef>); (4) a “stomacher,” a
holiday dress (<scripRef passage="Isa. 3:24" id="d-p285.6" parsed="|Isa|3|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.24">Isa. 3:24</scripRef>). The outer garment terminated in an
ample fringe or border, which concealed the feet (<scripRef passage="Isa. 47:2" id="d-p285.7" parsed="|Isa|47|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.47.2">Isa. 47:2</scripRef>;
Jer. 13:22).
The dress of the Persians is described in Dan. 3:21.
The reference to the art of sewing are few, inasmuch as the
garments generally came forth from the loom ready for being
worn, and all that was required in the making of clothes
devolved on the women of a family (Prov. 31:22; Acts 9:39).
Extravagance in dress is referred to in Jer. 4:30; Ezek. 16:10; Zeph. 1:8 (R.V., “foreign apparel”); 1 Tim. 2:9; 1 Pet. 3:3. Rending the robes was expressive of grief (Gen. 37:29, 34),

fear (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 21:27" id="d-p288.8" parsed="|1Kgs|21|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.21.27">1 Kings 21:27</scripRef>), indignation (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 5:7" id="d-p288.9" parsed="|2Kgs|5|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.5.7">2 Kings 5:7</scripRef>), or despair
(Judg. 11:35; Esther 4:1).
Shaking the garments, or shaking the dust from off them, was a
sign of renunciation (<scripRef passage="Acts 18:6" id="d-p289.1" parsed="|Acts|18|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.6">Acts 18:6</scripRef>); wrapping them round the head,

of awe (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 19:13" id="d-p289.2" parsed="|1Kgs|19|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.19.13">1 Kings 19:13</scripRef>) or grief (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 15:30" id="d-p289.3" parsed="|2Sam|15|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.15.30">2 Sam. 15:30</scripRef>; casting them off,
of excitement (<scripRef passage="Acts 22:23" id="d-p289.4" parsed="|Acts|22|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.22.23">Acts 22:23</scripRef>); laying hold of them, of supplication
(<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 15:27" id="d-p289.5" parsed="|1Sam|15|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.15.27">1 Sam. 15:27</scripRef>). In the case of travelling, the outer garments
were girded up (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 18:46" id="d-p289.6" parsed="|1Kgs|18|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.18.46">1 Kings 18:46</scripRef>). They were thrown aside also when
they would impede action (Mark 10:50; John 13:4; Acts 7:58).
</def>
<term id="d-p289.10">Drink</term>
The drinks of the Hebrews were water, wine, “strong drink,” and
vinegar. Their drinking vessels were the cup, goblet or “basin,”
the “cruse” or pitcher, and the saucer.
To drink water by measure (Ezek. 4:11), and to buy water to
drink (<scripRef passage="Lam. 5:4" id="d-p291.2" parsed="|Lam|5|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lam.5.4">Lam. 5:4</scripRef>), denote great scarcity. To drink blood means to
be satiated with slaughter.
The Jews carefully strained their drinks through a sieve,

through fear of violating the law of <scripRef passage="Lev. 11:20" id="d-p292.1" parsed="|Lev|11|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.11.20">Lev. 11:20</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 11:23" id="d-p292.2" parsed="|Lev|11|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.11.23">23</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 11:41" id="d-p292.3" parsed="|Lev|11|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.11.41">41</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 11:42" id="d-p292.4" parsed="|Lev|11|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.11.42">42</scripRef>.
(See Matt. 23:24. “Strain at” should be “strain out.”)
</def>
<term id="d-p292.6">Drink-offering</term>
Consisted of wine (Num. 15:5; Hos. 9:4) poured around the altar

(<scripRef passage="Ex. 30:9" id="d-p293.3" parsed="|Exod|30|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.30.9">Ex. 30:9</scripRef>). Joined with meat-offerings (<scripRef passage="Num. 6:15" id="d-p293.4" parsed="|Num|6|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.6.15">Num. 6:15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 6:17" id="d-p293.5" parsed="|Num|6|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.6.17">17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 16:13" id="d-p293.6" parsed="|2Kgs|16|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.16.13">2 Kings 16:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Joel 1:9" id="d-p293.7" parsed="|Joel|1|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Joel.1.9">Joel 1:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Joel 1:13" id="d-p293.8" parsed="|Joel|1|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Joel.1.13">13</scripRef>; 2:14), presented daily (<scripRef passage="Ex. 29:40" id="d-p293.9" parsed="|Exod|29|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.40">Ex. 29:40</scripRef>), on the
Sabbath (<scripRef passage="Num. 28:9" id="d-p293.10" parsed="|Num|28|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.28.9">Num. 28:9</scripRef>), and on feast-days (28:14). One-fourth of an
hin of wine was required for one lamb, one-third for a ram, and

one-half for a bullock (<scripRef passage="Num. 15:5" id="d-p293.11" parsed="|Num|15|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.15.5">Num. 15:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 28:7" id="d-p293.12" parsed="|Num|28|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.28.7">28:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num 28:14" id="d-p293.13" parsed="|Num|28|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.28.14">14</scripRef>). “Drink offerings
of blood” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 16:4" id="d-p293.14" parsed="|Ps|16|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.16.4">Ps. 16:4</scripRef>) is used in allusion to the heathen practice
of mingling the blood of animals sacrificed with wine or water,
and pouring out the mixture in the worship of the gods, and the
idea conveyed is that the psalmist would not partake of the
abominations of the heathen.
</def>
<term id="d-p293.15">Drink, strong</term>
(Heb. shekar’), an intoxicating liquor (Judg. 13:4; Luke 1:15;

<scripRef passage="Isa. 5:11" id="d-p294.3" parsed="|Isa|5|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.5.11">Isa. 5:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Micah 2:11" id="d-p294.4" parsed="|Mic|2|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.2.11">Micah 2:11</scripRef>) distilled from corn, honey, or dates. The
effects of the use of strong drink are referred to in Ps. 107:27; Isa. 24:20; 49:26; 51:17-22. Its use prohibited, Prov. 20:1. (See WINE.)
</def>
<term id="d-p294.11">Dromedary</term>
(Isa. 60:6), an African or Arabian species of camel having only
one hump, while the Bactrian camel has two. It is distinguished
from the camel only as a trained saddle-horse is distinguished
from a cart-horse. It is remarkable for its speed (<scripRef passage="Jer. 2:23" id="d-p295.2" parsed="|Jer|2|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.2.23">Jer. 2:23</scripRef>).

Camels are frequently spoken of in partriarchal times (<scripRef passage="Gen. 12:16" id="d-p295.3" parsed="|Gen|12|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.12.16">Gen. 12:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 24:10" id="d-p295.4" parsed="|Gen|24|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.10">24:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 30:43" id="d-p295.5" parsed="|Gen|30|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.30.43">30:43</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 31:17" id="d-p295.6" parsed="|Gen|31|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.17">31:17</scripRef>, etc.). They were used for carrying

burdens (<scripRef passage="Gen. 37:25" id="d-p295.7" parsed="|Gen|37|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.25">Gen. 37:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 6:5" id="d-p295.8" parsed="|Judg|6|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.6.5">Judg. 6:5</scripRef>), and for riding (<scripRef passage="Gen. 24:64" id="d-p295.9" parsed="|Gen|24|64|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.64">Gen. 24:64</scripRef>).
The hair of the camel falls off of itself in spring, and is
woven into coarse cloths and garments (Matt. 3:4). (See CAMEL.)
</def>
<term id="d-p295.12">Dropsy</term>
Mentioned only in Luke 14:2. The man afflicted with it was cured
by Christ on the Sabbath.
</def>
<term id="d-p296.2">Dross</term>
The impurities of silver separated from the one in the process

of melting (<scripRef passage="Prov. 25:4" id="d-p297.1" parsed="|Prov|25|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.25.4">Prov. 25:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov 26:23" id="d-p297.2" parsed="|Prov|26|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.26.23">26:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 119:119" id="d-p297.3" parsed="|Ps|119|119|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.119.119">Ps. 119:119</scripRef>). It is also used to
denote the base metal itself, probably before it is smelted, in
Isa. 1:22, 25.
</def>
<term id="d-p297.6">Drought</term>
From the middle of May to about the middle of August the land of

Palestine is dry. It is then the “drought of summer” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 31:40" id="d-p298.1" parsed="|Gen|31|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.40">Gen. 31:40</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 32:4" id="d-p298.2" parsed="|Ps|32|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.32.4">Ps. 32:4</scripRef>), and the land suffers (<scripRef passage="Deut. 28:23" id="d-p298.3" parsed="|Deut|28|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.23">Deut. 28:23</scripRef>: <scripRef passage="Ps. 102:4" id="d-p298.4" parsed="|Ps|102|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.102.4">Ps. 102:4</scripRef>),
vegetation being preserved only by the dews (Hag. 1:11). (See DEW.)
</def>
<term id="d-p298.7">Drown</term>
(Ex. 15:4; Amos 8:8; Heb. 11:29). Drowning was a mode of capital
punishment in use among the Syrians, and was known to the Jews
in the time of our Lord. To this he alludes in Matt. 18:6.
</def>
<term id="d-p299.5">Drunk</term>
The first case of intoxication on record is that of Noah (Gen. 9:21). The sin of drunkenness is frequently and strongly

condemned (<scripRef passage="Rom. 13:13" id="d-p300.2" parsed="|Rom|13|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.13.13">Rom. 13:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 6:9" id="d-p300.3" parsed="|1Cor|6|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.6.9">1 Cor. 6:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 6:10" id="d-p300.4" parsed="|1Cor|6|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.6.10">10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 5:18" id="d-p300.5" parsed="|Eph|5|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.5.18">Eph. 5:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Thess. 5:7" id="d-p300.6" parsed="|1Thess|5|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Thess.5.7">1 Thess. 5:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Thess. 5:8" id="d-p300.7" parsed="|1Thess|5|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Thess.5.8">8</scripRef>). The sin of drinking to excess seems to have been not
uncommon among the Israelites.
The word is used figuratively, when men are spoken of as being
drunk with sorrow, and with the wine of God’s wrath (<scripRef passage="Isa. 63:6" id="d-p301.1" parsed="|Isa|63|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.63.6">Isa. 63:6</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Jer. 51:57" id="d-p301.2" parsed="|Jer|51|57|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.51.57">Jer. 51:57</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 23:33" id="d-p301.3" parsed="|Ezek|23|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.23.33">Ezek. 23:33</scripRef>). To “add drunkenness to thirst” (<scripRef passage="Deut. 29:19" id="d-p301.4" parsed="|Deut|29|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.29.19">Deut. 29:19</scripRef>, A.V.) is a proverbial expression, rendered in the Revised
Version “to destroy the moist with the dry”, i.e., the
well-watered equally with the dry land, meaning that the effect
of such walking in the imagination of their own hearts would be
to destroy one and all.
</def>
<term id="d-p301.5">Drusilla</term>
Third and youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I. (Acts 12:1-4,
<scripRef passage="Acts 12:20-23" id="d-p302.2" parsed="|Acts|12|20|12|23" osisRef="Bible:Acts.12.20-Acts.12.23">20-23</scripRef>). Felix, the Roman procurator of Judea, induced her to
leave her husband, Azizus, the king of Emesa, and become his
wife. She was present with Felix when Paul reasoned of
“righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come” (<scripRef passage="Acts 24:24" id="d-p302.3" parsed="|Acts|24|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.24.24">Acts 24:24</scripRef>).
She and her son perished in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius, A.D.
</def>
<term id="d-p302.4">Duke</term>
Derived from the Latin dux, meaning “a leader;” Arabic, “a
sheik.” This word is used to denote the phylarch or chief of a
tribe (Gen. 36:15-43; Ex. 15:15; 1 Chr. 1:51-54).
</def>
<term id="d-p303.4">Dulcimer</term>
(Heb. sumphoniah), a musical instrument mentioned in Dan. 3:5, 15, along with other instruments there named, as sounded before
the golden image. It was not a Jewish instrument. In the margin
of the Revised Version it is styled the “bag-pipe.” Luther
translated it “lute,” and Grotius the “crooked trumpet.” It is
probable that it was introduced into Babylon by some Greek or
Western-Asiatic musician. Some Rabbinical commentators render it
by “organ,” the well-known instrument composed of a series of
pipes, others by “lyre.” The most probable interpretation is
that it was a bag-pipe similar to the zampagna of Southern
Europe.
</def>
<term id="d-p304.3">Dumah</term>
Silence, (comp. Ps. 94:17), the fourth son of Ishmael; also the
tribe descended from him; and hence also the region in Arabia
which they inhabited (Gen. 25:14; 1 Chr. 1:30).
There was also a town of this name in Judah (Josh. 15:52),
which has been identified with ed-Domeh, about 10 miles
southwest of Hebron. The place mentioned in the “burden” of the
prophet Isaiah (21:11) is Edom or Idumea.
</def>
<term id="d-p306.2">Dumb</term>
From natural infirmity (Ex. 4:11); not knowing what to say

(<scripRef passage="Prov. 31:8" id="d-p307.2" parsed="|Prov|31|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.31.8">Prov. 31:8</scripRef>); unwillingness to speak (<scripRef passage="Ps. 39:9" id="d-p307.3" parsed="|Ps|39|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.39.9">Ps. 39:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 10:3" id="d-p307.4" parsed="|Lev|10|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.10.3">Lev. 10:3</scripRef>).

Christ repeatedly restored the dumb (<scripRef passage="Matt. 9:32" id="d-p307.5" parsed="|Matt|9|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.9.32">Matt. 9:32</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 9:33" id="d-p307.6" parsed="|Matt|9|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.9.33">33</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 11:14" id="d-p307.7" parsed="|Luke|11|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.11.14">Luke 11:14</scripRef>;
Matt. 12:22) to the use of speech.
</def>
<term id="d-p307.9">Dung</term>
(1.) Used as manure (Luke 13:8); collected outside the city

walls (<scripRef passage="Neh. 2:13" id="d-p308.2" parsed="|Neh|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.2.13">Neh. 2:13</scripRef>). Of sacrifices, burned outside the camp (<scripRef passage="Ex. 29:14" id="d-p308.3" parsed="|Exod|29|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.14">Ex. 29:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 4:11" id="d-p308.4" parsed="|Lev|4|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.4.11">Lev. 4:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 8:17" id="d-p308.5" parsed="|Lev|8|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.8.17">8:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 19:5" id="d-p308.6" parsed="|Num|19|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.19.5">Num. 19:5</scripRef>). To be “cast out as dung,” a

figurative expression (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 14:10" id="d-p308.7" parsed="|1Kgs|14|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.14.10">1 Kings 14:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 9:37" id="d-p308.8" parsed="|2Kgs|9|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.9.37">2 Kings 9:37</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 8:2" id="d-p308.9" parsed="|Jer|8|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.8.2">Jer. 8:2</scripRef>;
Ps. 18:42), meaning to be rejected as unprofitable.
(2.) Used as fuel, a substitute for firewood, which was with
difficulty procured in Syria, Arabia, and Egypt (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 4:12-15" id="d-p309.1" parsed="|Ezek|4|12|4|15" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.4.12-Ezek.4.15">Ezek. 4:12-15</scripRef>),
where cows’ and camels’ dung is used to the present day for this
purpose.
</def>
<term id="d-p309.2">Dungeon</term>
Different from the ordinary prison in being more severe as a
place of punishment. Like the Roman inner prison (<scripRef passage="Acts 16:24" id="d-p310.1" parsed="|Acts|16|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.16.24">Acts 16:24</scripRef>),
it consisted of a deep cell or cistern (<scripRef passage="Jer. 38:6" id="d-p310.2" parsed="|Jer|38|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.38.6">Jer. 38:6</scripRef>). To be shut

up in, a punishment common in Egypt (<scripRef passage="Gen. 39:20" id="d-p310.3" parsed="|Gen|39|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.39.20">Gen. 39:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 40:3" id="d-p310.4" parsed="|Gen|40|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.40.3">40:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 41:10" id="d-p310.5" parsed="|Gen|41|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.41.10">41:10</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Gen 42:19" id="d-p310.6" parsed="|Gen|42|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.42.19">42:19</scripRef>). It is not mentioned, however, in the law of Moses as a
mode of punishment. Under the later kings imprisonment was

frequently used as a punishment (<scripRef passage="2 Chron. 16:10" id="d-p310.7" parsed="|2Chr|16|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.16.10">2 Chron. 16:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 20:2" id="d-p310.8" parsed="|Jer|20|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.20.2">Jer. 20:2</scripRef>;
32:2; 33:1; 37:15), and it was customary after the Exile (Matt. 11:2; Luke 3:20; Acts 5:18, 21; Matt. 18:30).
</def>
<term id="d-p310.17">Dung-gate</term>
(Neh. 2:13), a gate of ancient Jerusalem, on the south-west
quarter. “The gate outside of which lay the piles of sweepings
and offscourings of the streets,” in the valley of Tophet.
</def>
<term id="d-p311.2">Dung-hill</term>
To sit on a, was a sign of the deepest dejection (1 Sam. 2:8;
Ps. 113:7; Lam. 4:5).
</def>
<term id="d-p312.4">Dura</term>
The circle, the plain near Babylon in which Nebuchadnezzar set
up a golden image, mentioned in <scripRef passage="Dan. 3:1" id="d-p313.1" parsed="|Dan|3|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.3.1">Dan. 3:1</scripRef>. The place still
retains its ancient name. On one of its many mounds the pedestal
of what must have been a colossal statue has been found. It has
been supposed to be that of the golden image.
</def>
<term id="d-p313.2">Dust</term>
Storms of sand and dust sometimes overtake Eastern travellers.
They are very dreadful, many perishing under them. Jehovah
threatens to bring on the land of Israel, as a punishment for
forsaking him, a rain of “powder and dust” (Deut. 28:24).
To cast dust on the head was a sign of mourning (Josh. 7:6);
and to sit in dust, of extreme affliction (<scripRef passage="Isa. 47:1" id="d-p315.2" parsed="|Isa|47|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.47.1">Isa. 47:1</scripRef>). “Dust” is
used to denote the grave (<scripRef passage="Job 7:21" id="d-p315.3" parsed="|Job|7|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.7.21">Job 7:21</scripRef>). “To shake off the dust from
one’s feet” against another is to renounce all future

intercourse with him (<scripRef passage="Matt. 10:14" id="d-p315.4" parsed="|Matt|10|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.10.14">Matt. 10:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 13:51" id="d-p315.5" parsed="|Acts|13|51|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.13.51">Acts 13:51</scripRef>). To “lick the
dust” is a sign of abject submission (<scripRef passage="Ps. 72:9" id="d-p315.6" parsed="|Ps|72|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.72.9">Ps. 72:9</scripRef>); and to throw
dust at one is a sign of abhorrence (2 Sam. 16:13; comp. Acts 22:23).
</def>
<term id="d-p315.9">Dwarf</term>
A lean or emaciated person (Lev. 21:20).
</def>
<term id="d-p316.2">Dwell</term>
Tents were in primitive times the common dwellings of men.
Houses were afterwards built, the walls of which were frequently
of mud (Job 24:16; Matt. 6:19, 20) or of sun-dried bricks.
God “dwells in light” (1 Tim. 6:16; 1 John 1:7), in heaven

(<scripRef passage="Ps. 123:1" id="d-p318.3" parsed="|Ps|123|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.123.1">Ps. 123:1</scripRef>), in his church (<scripRef passage="Ps. 9:11" id="d-p318.4" parsed="|Ps|9|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.9.11">Ps. 9:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 John 4:12" id="d-p318.5" parsed="|1John|4|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.4.12">1 John 4:12</scripRef>). Christ dwelt
on earth in the days of his humiliation (<scripRef passage="John 1:14" id="d-p318.6" parsed="|John|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.1.14">John 1:14</scripRef>). He now
dwells in the hearts of his people (<scripRef passage="Eph. 3:17-19" id="d-p318.7" parsed="|Eph|3|17|3|19" osisRef="Bible:Eph.3.17-Eph.3.19">Eph. 3:17-19</scripRef>). The Holy

Spirit dwells in believers (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 3:16" id="d-p318.8" parsed="|1Cor|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.3.16">1 Cor. 3:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Tim. 1:14" id="d-p318.9" parsed="|2Tim|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.1.14">2 Tim. 1:14</scripRef>). We are
exhorted to “let the word of God dwell in us richly” (<scripRef passage="Col. 3:16" id="d-p318.10" parsed="|Col|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.3.16">Col. 3:16</scripRef>;
Ps. 119:11).
Dwell deep occurs only in Jer. 49:8, and refers to the custom
of seeking refuge from impending danger, in retiring to the
recesses of rocks and caverns, or to remote places in the
desert.
</def>
<term id="d-p319.2">Dwellings</term>
The materials used in buildings were commonly bricks, sometimes

also stones (<scripRef passage="Lev. 14:40" id="d-p320.1" parsed="|Lev|14|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.14.40">Lev. 14:40</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 14:42" id="d-p320.2" parsed="|Lev|14|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.14.42">42</scripRef>), which were held together by cement

(<scripRef passage="Jer. 43:9" id="d-p320.3" parsed="|Jer|43|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.43.9">Jer. 43:9</scripRef>) or bitumen (<scripRef passage="Gen. 11:3" id="d-p320.4" parsed="|Gen|11|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.11.3">Gen. 11:3</scripRef>). The exterior was usually

whitewashed (<scripRef passage="Lev. 14:41" id="d-p320.5" parsed="|Lev|14|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.14.41">Lev. 14:41</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 13:10" id="d-p320.6" parsed="|Ezek|13|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.13.10">Ezek. 13:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 23:27" id="d-p320.7" parsed="|Matt|23|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.23.27">Matt. 23:27</scripRef>). The beams
were of sycamore (Isa. 9:10), or olive-wood, or cedar (1 Kings 7:2; Isa. 9:10).
The form of Eastern dwellings differed in many respects from
that of dwellings in Western lands. The larger houses were built

in a quadrangle enclosing a court-yard (<scripRef passage="Luke 5:19" id="d-p321.1" parsed="|Luke|5|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.5.19">Luke 5:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 17:18" id="d-p321.2" parsed="|2Sam|17|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.17.18">2 Sam. 17:18</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Neh. 8:16" id="d-p321.3" parsed="|Neh|8|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.8.16">Neh. 8:16</scripRef>) surrounded by galleries, which formed the
guest-chamber or reception-room for visitors. The flat roof,
surrounded by a low parapet, was used for many domestic and
social purposes. It was reached by steps from the court. In
connection with it (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 23:12" id="d-p321.4" parsed="|2Kgs|23|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.12">2 Kings 23:12</scripRef>) was an upper room, used as a

private chamber (<scripRef passage="2 Sam 18:33" id="d-p321.5" parsed="|2Sam|18|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.18.33">2 Sam 18:33</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Dan. 6:11" id="d-p321.6" parsed="|Dan|6|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.6.11">Dan. 6:11</scripRef>), also as a bedroom (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 23:12" id="d-p321.7" parsed="|2Kgs|23|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.12">2 Kings 23:12</scripRef>), a sleeping apartment for guests (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 4:10" id="d-p321.8" parsed="|2Kgs|4|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.4.10">2 Kings 4:10</scripRef>),
and as a sick-chamber (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 17:19" id="d-p321.9" parsed="|1Kgs|17|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.17.19">1 Kings 17:19</scripRef>). The doors, sometimes of
stone, swung on morticed pivots, and were generally fastened by
wooden bolts. The houses of the more wealthy had a doorkeeper or

a female porter (<scripRef passage="John 18:16" id="d-p321.10" parsed="|John|18|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.18.16">John 18:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 12:13" id="d-p321.11" parsed="|Acts|12|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.12.13">Acts 12:13</scripRef>). The windows generally

opened into the courtyard, and were closed by a lattice (<scripRef passage="Judg. 5:28" id="d-p321.12" parsed="|Judg|5|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.5.28">Judg. 5:28</scripRef>). The interior rooms were set apart for the female portion
of the household.
The furniture of the room (2 Kings 4:10) consisted of a couch

furnished with pillows (<scripRef passage="Amos 6:4" id="d-p322.2" parsed="|Amos|6|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.6.4">Amos 6:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 13:20" id="d-p322.3" parsed="|Ezek|13|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.13.20">Ezek. 13:20</scripRef>); and besides
this, chairs, a table and lanterns or lamp-stands (2 Kings 4:10).
</def>
<term id="d-p322.5">Dye</term>
The art of dyeing is one of great antiquity, although no special
mention is made of it in the Old Testament. The Hebrews probably

learned it from the Egyptians (see <scripRef passage="Ex. 26:1" id="d-p323.1" parsed="|Exod|26|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.26.1">Ex. 26:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 28:5-8" id="d-p323.2" parsed="|Exod|28|5|28|8" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.5-Exod.28.8">28:5-8</scripRef>), who
brought it to great perfection. In New Testament times Thyatira
was famed for its dyers (Acts 16:14). (See COLOUR.)
</def>
</glossary>
</div2>
<div2 title="E" prev="d" next="f" id="e">
<glossary id="e-p0.1">
<term id="e-p0.2">Eagle</term>
<def id="e-p0.3">
(Herb. nesher; properly the griffon vulture or great vulture, so
called from its tearing its prey with its beak), referred to for

its swiftness of flight (<scripRef passage="Deut. 28:49" id="e-p1.1" parsed="|Deut|28|49|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.49">Deut. 28:49</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 1:23" id="e-p1.2" parsed="|2Sam|1|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.1.23">2 Sam. 1:23</scripRef>), its mounting

high in the air (<scripRef passage="Job 39:27" id="e-p1.3" parsed="|Job|39|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.39.27">Job 39:27</scripRef>), its strength (<scripRef passage="Ps. 103:5" id="e-p1.4" parsed="|Ps|103|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.103.5">Ps. 103:5</scripRef>), its
setting its nest in high places (<scripRef passage="Jer. 49:16" id="e-p1.5" parsed="|Jer|49|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.49.16">Jer. 49:16</scripRef>), and its power of
vision (Job 39:27-30).
This “ravenous bird” is a symbol of those nations whom God
employs and sends forth to do a work of destruction, sweeping

away whatever is decaying and putrescent (<scripRef passage="Matt. 24:28" id="e-p2.1" parsed="|Matt|24|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.24.28">Matt. 24:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 46:11" id="e-p2.2" parsed="|Isa|46|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.46.11">Isa. 46:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 39:4" id="e-p2.3" parsed="|Ezek|39|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.39.4">Ezek. 39:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 28:49" id="e-p2.4" parsed="|Deut|28|49|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.49">Deut. 28:49</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 4:13" id="e-p2.5" parsed="|Jer|4|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.4.13">Jer. 4:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 48:40" id="e-p2.6" parsed="|Jer|48|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.40">48:40</scripRef>). It is said
that the eagle sheds his feathers in the beginning of spring,
and with fresh plumage assumes the appearance of youth. To this,

allusion is made in <scripRef passage="Ps. 103:5" id="e-p2.7" parsed="|Ps|103|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.103.5">Ps. 103:5</scripRef> and <scripRef passage="Isa. 40:31" id="e-p2.8" parsed="|Isa|40|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.40.31">Isa. 40:31</scripRef>. God’s care over
his people is likened to that of the eagle in training its young

to fly (<scripRef passage="Ex. 19:4" id="e-p2.9" parsed="|Exod|19|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.19.4">Ex. 19:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 32:11" id="e-p2.10" parsed="|Deut|32|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.11">Deut. 32:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 32:12" id="e-p2.11" parsed="|Deut|32|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.12">12</scripRef>). An interesting illustration
is thus recorded by Sir Humphry Davy:, “I once saw a very
interesting sight above the crags of Ben Nevis. Two parent
eagles were teaching their offspring, two young birds, the
maneuvers of flight. They began by rising from the top of the
mountain in the eye of the sun. It was about mid-day, and bright
for the climate. They at first made small circles, and the young
birds imitated them. They paused on their wings, waiting till
they had made their flight, and then took a second and larger
gyration, always rising toward the sun, and enlarging their
circle of flight so as to make a gradually ascending spiral. The
young ones still and slowly followed, apparently flying better
as they mounted; and they continued this sublime exercise,
always rising till they became mere points in the air, and the
young ones were lost, and afterwards their parents, to our
aching sight.” (See Isa. 40:31.)
There have been observed in Palestine four distinct species of
eagles, (1) the golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos); (2) the
spotted eagle (Aquila naevia); (3) the common species, the
imperial eagle (Aquila heliaca); and (4) the Circaetos gallicus,
which preys on reptiles. The eagle was unclean by the Levitical
law (Lev. 11:13; Deut. 14:12).
</def>
<term id="e-p3.3">Ear</term>
<def id="e-p3.4">
Used frequently in a figurative sense (Ps. 34:15). To “uncover
the ear” is to show respect to a person (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 20:2" id="e-p4.2" parsed="|1Sam|20|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.20.2">1 Sam. 20:2</scripRef> marg.). To

have the “ear heavy”, or to have “uncircumcised ears” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 6:10" id="e-p4.3" parsed="|Isa|6|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.6.10">Isa. 6:10</scripRef>), is to be inattentive and disobedient. To have the ear
“bored” through with an awl was a sign of perpetual servitude
(Ex. 21:6).
</def>
<term id="e-p4.5">Earing</term>
<def id="e-p4.6">
An Old English word (from the Latin aro, I plough), meaning
“ploughing.” It is used in the Authorized Version in <scripRef passage="Gen. 45:6" id="e-p5.1" parsed="|Gen|45|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.45.6">Gen. 45:6</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Ex. 34:21" id="e-p5.2" parsed="|Exod|34|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.34.21">Ex. 34:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 8:12" id="e-p5.3" parsed="|1Sam|8|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.8.12">1 Sam. 8:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 21:4" id="e-p5.4" parsed="|Deut|21|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.21.4">Deut. 21:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 30:24" id="e-p5.5" parsed="|Isa|30|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.30.24">Isa. 30:24</scripRef>; but the Revised
Version has rendered the original in these places by the
ordinary word to plough or till.
</def>
<term id="e-p5.6">Earnest</term>
<def id="e-p5.7">
The Spirit is the earnest of the believer’s destined inheritance

(<scripRef passage="2 Cor. 1:22" id="e-p6.1" parsed="|2Cor|1|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.1.22">2 Cor. 1:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 5:5" id="e-p6.2" parsed="|2Cor|5|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.5.5">5:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 1:14" id="e-p6.3" parsed="|Eph|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.1.14">Eph. 1:14</scripRef>). The word thus rendered is the
same as that rendered “pledge” in <scripRef passage="Gen. 38:17-20" id="e-p6.4" parsed="|Gen|38|17|38|20" osisRef="Bible:Gen.38.17-Gen.38.20">Gen. 38:17-20</scripRef>; “indeed, the
Hebrew word has simply passed into the Greek and Latin
languages, probably through commercial dealings with the
Phoenicians, the great trading people of ancient days.
Originally it meant no more than a pledge; but in common usage
it came to denote that particular kind of pledge which is a part
of the full price of an article paid in advance; and as it is
joined with the figure of a seal when applied to the Spirit, it
seems to be used by Paul in this specific sense.” The Spirit’s
gracious presence and working in believers is a foretaste to
them of the blessedness of heaven. God is graciously pleased to
give not only pledges but foretastes of future blessedness.
</def>
<term id="e-p6.5">Earrings</term>
<def id="e-p6.6">
Rings properly for the ear (Gen. 35:4; Num. 31:50; Ezek. 16:12).
In <scripRef passage="Gen. 24:47" id="e-p7.4" parsed="|Gen|24|47|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.47">Gen. 24:47</scripRef> the word means a nose-jewel, and is so rendered in
the Revised Version. In <scripRef passage="Isa. 3:20" id="e-p7.5" parsed="|Isa|3|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.20">Isa. 3:20</scripRef> the Authorized Version has
“ear-rings,” and the Revised Version “amulets,” which more
correctly represents the original word (lehashim), which means
incantations; charms, thus remedies against enchantment, worn
either suspended from the neck or in the ears of females.
Ear-rings were ornaments used by both sexes (Ex. 32:2).
</def>
<term id="e-p7.7">Earth</term>
<def id="e-p7.8">
(1.) In the sense of soil or ground, the translation of the word
adamah’. In Gen. 9:20 “husbandman” is literally “man of the
ground or earth.” Altars were to be built of earth (<scripRef passage="Ex. 20:24" id="e-p8.2" parsed="|Exod|20|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.20.24">Ex. 20:24</scripRef>).
Naaman asked for two mules’ burden of earth (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 5:17" id="e-p8.3" parsed="|2Kgs|5|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.5.17">2 Kings 5:17</scripRef>),
under the superstitious notion that Jehovah, like the gods of
the heathen, could be acceptably worshipped only on his own
soil.
(2). As the rendering of ’erets, it means the whole world
(Gen. 1:2); the land as opposed to the sea (1:10). Erets also
denotes a country (21:32); a plot of ground (23:15); the ground
on which a man stands (33:3); the inhabitants of the earth (6:1;
11:1); all the world except Israel (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 13:9" id="e-p9.2" parsed="|2Chr|13|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.13.9">2 Chr. 13:9</scripRef>). In the New
Testament “the earth” denotes the land of Judea (<scripRef passage="Matt. 23:35" id="e-p9.3" parsed="|Matt|23|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.23.35">Matt. 23:35</scripRef>);
also things carnal in contrast with things heavenly (<scripRef passage="John 3:31" id="e-p9.4" parsed="|John|3|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.3.31">John 3:31</scripRef>;
Col. 3:1, 2).
</def>
<term id="e-p9.7">Earthquake</term>
<def id="e-p9.8">
Mentioned among the extraordinary phenomena of Palestine (Ps. 18:7; comp. Hab. 3:6; Nah. 1:5; Isa. 5:25).
The first earthquake in Palestine of which we have any record

happened in the reign of Ahab (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 19:11" id="e-p11.1" parsed="|1Kgs|19|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.19.11">1 Kings 19:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 19:12" id="e-p11.2" parsed="|1Kgs|19|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.19.12">12</scripRef>). Another took
place in the days of Uzziah, King of Judah (<scripRef passage="Zech. 14:5" id="e-p11.3" parsed="|Zech|14|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.14.5">Zech. 14:5</scripRef>). The
most memorable earthquake taking place in New Testament times
happened at the crucifixion of our Lord (<scripRef passage="Matt. 27:54" id="e-p11.4" parsed="|Matt|27|54|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.54">Matt. 27:54</scripRef>). An
earthquake at Philippi shook the prison in which Paul and Silas
were imprisoned (Act 16:26).
It is used figuratively as a token of the presence of the Lord
(Judg. 5:4; 2 Sam. 22:8; Ps. 77:18; 97:4; 104:32).
</def>
<term id="e-p12.6">East</term>
<def id="e-p12.7">
(1.) The orient (mizrah); the rising of the sun. Thus “the east
country” is the country lying to the east of Syria, the Elymais
(Zech. 8:7).
(2). Properly what is in front of one, or a country that is
before or in front of another; the rendering of the word
kedem. In pointing out the quarters, a Hebrew always looked
with his face toward the east. The word kedem is used when the

four quarters of the world are described (<scripRef passage="Gen. 13:14" id="e-p14.1" parsed="|Gen|13|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.13.14">Gen. 13:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 28:14" id="e-p14.2" parsed="|Gen|28|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.28.14">28:14</scripRef>);
and mizrah when the east only is distinguished from the west

(<scripRef passage="Josh. 11:3" id="e-p14.3" parsed="|Josh|11|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.3">Josh. 11:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 50:1" id="e-p14.4" parsed="|Ps|50|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.50.1">Ps. 50:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 103:12" id="e-p14.5" parsed="|Ps|103|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.103.12">103:12</scripRef>, etc.). In <scripRef passage="Gen. 25:6" id="e-p14.6" parsed="|Gen|25|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.6">Gen. 25:6</scripRef> “eastward” is
literally “unto the land of kedem;” i.e., the lands lying east
of Palestine, namely, Arabia, Mesopotamia, etc.
</def>
<term id="e-p14.7">East, Children of the</term>
<def id="e-p14.8">
The Arabs as a whole, known as the Nabateans or Kedarenes, nomad
tribes (Judg. 6:3, 33; 7:12; 8:10).
</def>
<term id="e-p15.3">Easter</term>
<def id="e-p15.4">
Originally a Saxon word (Eostre), denoting a goddess of the
Saxons, in honour of whom sacrifices were offered about the time
of the Passover. Hence the name came to be given to the festival
of the Resurrection of Christ, which occured at the time of the
Passover. In the early English versions this word was frequently
used as the translation of the Greek pascha (the Passover). When
the Authorized Version (1611) was formed, the word “passover”
was used in all passages in which this word pascha occurred,
except in <scripRef passage="Act 12:4" id="e-p16.1" parsed="|Acts|12|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.12.4">Act 12:4</scripRef>. In the Revised Version the proper word,
“passover,” is always used.
</def>
<term id="e-p16.2">East gate</term>
<def id="e-p16.3">
(Jer. 19:2), properly the Potter’s gate, the gate which led to
the potter’s field, in the valley of Hinnom.
</def>
<term id="e-p17.2">East sea</term>
<def id="e-p17.3">
(Joel 2:20; Ezek. 47:18), the Dead Sea, which lay on the east
side of the Holy Land. The Mediterranean, which lay on the west,
was hence called the “great sea for the west border” (Num. 34:6).
</def>
<term id="e-p18.4">East wind</term>
<def id="e-p18.5">
The wind coming from the east (Job 27:21; Isa. 27:8, etc.).
Blight caused by this wind, “thin ears” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 41:6" id="e-p19.3" parsed="|Gen|41|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.41.6">Gen. 41:6</scripRef>); the
withered “gourd” (<scripRef passage="Jonah 4" id="e-p19.4" parsed="|Jonah|4|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jonah.4">Jonah 4</scripRef>: 8). It was the cause and also the

emblem of evil (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 17:10" id="e-p19.5" parsed="|Ezek|17|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.17.10">Ezek. 17:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek 19:12" id="e-p19.6" parsed="|Ezek|19|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.19.12">19:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos. 13:15" id="e-p19.7" parsed="|Hos|13|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.13.15">Hos. 13:15</scripRef>). In Palestine
this wind blows from a burning desert, and hence is destitute of
moisture necessary for vegetation.
</def>
<term id="e-p19.8">Eating</term>
<def id="e-p19.9">
The ancient Hebrews would not eat with the Egyptians (Gen. 43:32). In the time of our Lord they would not eat with
Samaritans (<scripRef passage="John 4:9" id="e-p20.2" parsed="|John|4|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.4.9">John 4:9</scripRef>), and were astonished that he ate with
publicans and sinners (<scripRef passage="Matt. 9:11" id="e-p20.3" parsed="|Matt|9|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.9.11">Matt. 9:11</scripRef>). The Hebrews originally sat
at table, but afterwards adopted the Persian and Chaldean
practice of reclining (<scripRef passage="Luke 7:36-50" id="e-p20.4" parsed="|Luke|7|36|7|50" osisRef="Bible:Luke.7.36-Luke.7.50">Luke 7:36-50</scripRef>). Their principal meal was

at noon (<scripRef passage="Gen. 43:16" id="e-p20.5" parsed="|Gen|43|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.43.16">Gen. 43:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 20:16" id="e-p20.6" parsed="|1Kgs|20|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.20.16">1 Kings 20:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ruth 2:14" id="e-p20.7" parsed="|Ruth|2|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.2.14">Ruth 2:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 14:12" id="e-p20.8" parsed="|Luke|14|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.14.12">Luke 14:12</scripRef>). The

word “eat” is used metaphorically in <scripRef passage="Jer. 15:16" id="e-p20.9" parsed="|Jer|15|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.15.16">Jer. 15:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 3:1" id="e-p20.10" parsed="|Ezek|3|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.3.1">Ezek. 3:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 10:9" id="e-p20.11" parsed="|Rev|10|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.10.9">Rev. 10:9</scripRef>. In <scripRef passage="John 6:53-58" id="e-p20.12" parsed="|John|6|53|6|58" osisRef="Bible:John.6.53-John.6.58">John 6:53-58</scripRef>, “eating and drinking” means believing in
Christ. Women were never present as guests at meals (q.v.).
</def>
<term id="e-p20.13">Ebal</term>
Stony. (1.) A mountain 3,076 feet above the level of the sea,
and 1,200 feet above the level of the valley, on the north side
of which stood the city of Shechem (q.v.). On this mountain six

of the tribes (<scripRef passage="Deut. 27:12" id="e-p21.1" parsed="|Deut|27|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.27.12">Deut. 27:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 27:13" id="e-p21.2" parsed="|Deut|27|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.27.13">13</scripRef>) were appointed to take their
stand and respond according to a prescribed form to the
imprecations uttered in the valley, where the law was read by
the Levites (11:29; 29:4, 13). This mountain was also the site

of the first great altar erected to Jehovah (<scripRef passage="Deut. 27:5-8" id="e-p21.3" parsed="|Deut|27|5|27|8" osisRef="Bible:Deut.27.5-Deut.27.8">Deut. 27:5-8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 8:30-35" id="e-p21.4" parsed="|Josh|8|30|8|35" osisRef="Bible:Josh.8.30-Josh.8.35">Josh. 8:30-35</scripRef>). After this the name of Ebal does not again occur in
Jewish history. (See GERIZIM.)
(2.) A descendant of Eber (1 Chr. 1:22), called also Obal
(Gen. 10:28).
(3.) A descendant of Seir the Horite (Gen. 36:23).
</def>
<term id="e-p23.2">Ebed</term>
<def id="e-p23.3">
Slave, the father of Gaal, in whom the men of Shechem “put
confidence” in their conspiracy against Abimelech (Judg. 9:26, 26, 30, 31).
</def>
<term id="e-p24.5">Ebed-melech</term>
<def id="e-p24.6">
A servant of the king; probably an official title, an Ethiopian,
“one of the eunuchs which was in the king’s house;” i.e., in the
palace of Zedekiah, king of Judah. He interceded with the king
in Jeremiah’s behalf, and was the means of saving him from death
by famine (Jer. 38:7-13: comp. 39:15-18).
</def>
<term id="e-p25.2">Eben-ezer</term>
<def id="e-p25.3">
Stone of help, the memorial stone set up by Samuel to
commemorate the divine assistance to Israel in their great

battle against the Philistines, whom they totally routed (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 7:7-12" id="e-p26.1" parsed="|1Sam|7|7|7|12" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.7.7-1Sam.7.12">1 Sam. 7:7-12</scripRef>) at Aphek, in the neighbourhood of Mizpeh, in Benjamin,
near the western entrance of the pass of Beth-horon. On this
very battle-field, twenty years before, the Philistines routed
the Israelites, “and slew of the army in the field about four
thousand men” (4:1, 2; here, and at 5:1, called “Eben-ezer” by
anticipation). In this extremity the Israelites fetched the ark
out of Shiloh and carried it into their camp. The Philistines a
second time immediately attacked them, and smote them with a
very great slaughter, “for there fell of Israel thirty thousand
footmen. And the ark of God was taken” (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 4:10" id="e-p26.2" parsed="|1Sam|4|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.4.10">1 Sam. 4:10</scripRef>). And now in
the same place the Philistines are vanquished, and the memorial
stone is erected by Samuel (q.v.). The spot where the stone was
erected was somewhere “between Mizpeh and Shen.” Some have
identified it with the modern Beit Iksa, a conspicuous and
prominent position, apparently answering all the necessary
conditions; others with Dier Aban, 3 miles east of ‘Ain Shems.
</def>
<term id="e-p26.3">Eber</term>
<def id="e-p26.4">
Beyond. (1.). The third post-duluvian patriach after Shem (Gen. 10:24; 11:14). He is regarded as the founder of the Hebrew race
(10:21; Num. 24:24). In Luke 3:35 he is called Heber.
(2.) One of the seven heads of the families of the Gadites (1 Chr. 5:13).
(3.) The oldest of the three sons of Elpaal the Benjamite
(4.) One of the heads of the familes of Benjamites in
Jerusalem (22).
(5.) The head of the priestly family of Amok in the time of
Zerubbabel (Neh. 12:20).
</def>
<term id="e-p31.2">Ebony</term>
<def id="e-p31.3">
A black, hard wood, brought by the merchants from India to Tyre
(<scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:15" id="e-p32.1" parsed="|Ezek|27|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.15">Ezek. 27:15</scripRef>). It is the heart-wood, brought by Diospyros
ebenus, which grows in Ceylon and Southern India.
</def>
<term id="e-p32.2">Ebronah</term>
<def id="e-p32.3">
Passage, one of the stations of the Israelites in their
wanderings (Num. 33:34, 35). It was near Ezion-geber.
</def>
<term id="e-p33.3">Ecbatana</term>
<def id="e-p33.4">
(Ezra 6:2 marg.). (See ACHMETHA.)
</def>
<term id="e-p34.3">Ecclesiastes</term>
<def id="e-p34.4">
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="e-p34.5" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="Eccl 0" id="e-p34.6" parsed="|Eccl|0|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eccl" />
The Greek rendering of the Hebrew Koheleth, which means
“Preacher.” The old and traditional view of the authorship of
this book attributes it to Solomon. This view can be
satisfactorily maintained, though others date it from the
Captivity. The writer represents himself implicitly as Solomon
(1:12). It has been appropriately styled The Confession of King
Solomon. “The writer is a man who has sinned in giving way to
selfishness and sensuality, who has paid the penalty of that sin
in satiety and weariness of life, but who has through all this
been under the discipline of a divine education, and has learned
from it the lesson which God meant to teach him.” “The writer
concludes by pointing out that the secret of a true life is that
a man should consecrate the vigour of his youth to God.” The
key-note of the book is sounded in ch. 1:2,
“Vanity of vanities! saith the Preacher,
Vanity of vanities! all is vanity!”
i.e., all man’s efforts to find happiness apart from God are
without result.
</def>
<term id="e-p37.1">Eclipse</term>
<def id="e-p37.2">
Of the sun alluded to in Amos 8:9; Micah 3:6; Zech. 14:6; Joel 2:10. Eclipses were regarded as tokens of God’s anger (Joel 3:15; Job 9:7). The darkness at the crucifixion has been
ascribed to an eclipse (<scripRef passage="Matt. 27:45" id="e-p38.7" parsed="|Matt|27|45|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.45">Matt. 27:45</scripRef>); but on the other hand it
is argued that the great intensity of darkness caused by an
eclipse never lasts for more than six minutes, and this darkness
lasted for three hours. Moreover, at the time of the Passover
the moon was full, and therefore there could not be an eclipse
of the sun, which is caused by an interposition of the moon
between the sun and the earth.
</def>
<term id="e-p38.8">Ed</term>
<def id="e-p38.9">
Witness, a word not found in the original Hebrew, nor in the
LXX. and Vulgate, but added by the translators in the Authorized
Version, also in the Revised Version, of <scripRef passage="Josh. 22:34" id="e-p39.1" parsed="|Josh|22|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.22.34">Josh. 22:34</scripRef>. The words
are literally rendered: “And the children of Reuben and the
children of Gad named the altar. It is a witness between us that
Jehovah is God.” This great altar stood probably on the east
side of the Jordan, in the land of Gilead, “over against the
land of Canaan.” After the division of the Promised Land, the
tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, on

returning to their own settlements on the east of Jordan (<scripRef passage="Josh. 22:1-6" id="e-p39.2" parsed="|Josh|22|1|22|6" osisRef="Bible:Josh.22.1-Josh.22.6">Josh. 22:1-6</scripRef>), erected a great altar, which they affirmed, in answer
to the challenge of the other tribes, was not for sacrifice, but
only as a witness (‘Ed) or testimony to future generations that
they still retained the same interest in the nation as the other
tribes.
</def>
<term id="e-p39.3">Edar</term>
<def id="e-p39.4">
Tower of the flock, a tower between Bethlehem and Hebron, near
which Jacob first halted after leaving Bethlehem (<scripRef passage="Gen. 35:21" id="e-p40.1" parsed="|Gen|35|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.35.21">Gen. 35:21</scripRef>).
In <scripRef passage="Micah 4:8" id="e-p40.2" parsed="|Mic|4|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.4.8">Micah 4:8</scripRef> the word is rendered “tower of the flock” (marg.,
“Edar”), and is used as a designation of Bethlehem, which
figuratively represents the royal line of David as sprung from
Bethlehem.
</def>
<term id="e-p40.3">Eden</term>
<def id="e-p40.4">
Delight. (1.) The garden in which our first parents dewlt (Gen. 2:8-17). No geographical question has been so much discussed as
that bearing on its site. It has been placed in Armenia, in the
region west of the Caspian Sea, in Media, near Damascus, in
Palestine, in Southern Arabia, and in Babylonia. The site must
undoubtedly be sought for somewhere along the course of the
great streams the Tigris and the Euphrates of Western Asia, in
“the land of Shinar” or Babylonia. The region from about lat. 33
degrees 30’ to lat. 31 degrees, which is a very rich and fertile
tract, has been by the most competent authorities agreed on as
the probable site of Eden. “It is a region where streams abound,
where they divide and re-unite, where alone in the Mesopotamian
tract can be found the phenomenon of a single river parting into
four arms, each of which is or has been a river of consequence.”
Among almost all nations there are traditions of the primitive
innocence of our race in the garden of Eden. This was the
“golden age” to which the Greeks looked back. Men then lived a
“life free from care, and without labour and sorrow. Old age was
unknown; the body never lost its vigour; existence was a
perpetual feast without a taint of evil. The earth brought forth
spontaneously all things that were good in profuse abundance.”
(2.) One of the markets whence the merchants of Tyre obtained
richly embroidered stuffs (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:23" id="e-p43.1" parsed="|Ezek|27|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.23">Ezek. 27:23</scripRef>); the same, probably, as

that mentioned in <scripRef passage="2 Kings 19:12" id="e-p43.2" parsed="|2Kgs|19|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.19.12">2 Kings 19:12</scripRef>, and <scripRef passage="Isa. 37:12" id="e-p43.3" parsed="|Isa|37|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.37.12">Isa. 37:12</scripRef>, as the name of
a region conquered by the Assyrians.
(3.) Son of Joah, and one of the Levites who assisted in
reforming the public worship of the sanctuary in the time of
Hezekiah (2 Chr. 29:12).
</def>
<term id="e-p44.2">Eder</term>
<def id="e-p44.3">
Flock. (1.) A city in the south of Judah, on the border of
Idumea (Josh. 15:21).
(2.) The second of the three sons of Mushi, of the family of
Merari, appointed to the Levitical office (1 Chr. 23:23; 24:30).
</def>
<term id="e-p46.3">Edom</term>
<def id="e-p46.4">
(1.) The name of Esau (q.v.), Gen. 25:30, “Feed me, I pray thee,
with that same red pottage [Heb. haadom, haadom, i.e., ‘the red
pottage, the red pottage’] ...Therefore was his name called
Edom”, i.e., Red.
(2.) Idumea (Isa. 34:5, 6; Ezek. 35:15). “The field of Edom”

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 32:3" id="e-p48.4" parsed="|Gen|32|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.32.3">Gen. 32:3</scripRef>), “the land of Edom” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 36:16" id="e-p48.5" parsed="|Gen|36|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36.16">Gen. 36:16</scripRef>), was mountainous
(Obad. 1:8, 9, 19, 21). It was called the land, or “the mountain
of Seir,” the rough hills on the east side of the Arabah. It
extended from the head of the Gulf of Akabah, the Elanitic gulf,
to the foot of the Dead Sea (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 9:26" id="e-p48.6" parsed="|1Kgs|9|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.9.26">1 Kings 9:26</scripRef>), and contained, among
other cities, the rock-hewn Sela (q.v.), generally known by the
Greek name Petra (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 14:7" id="e-p48.7" parsed="|2Kgs|14|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.14.7">2 Kings 14:7</scripRef>). It is a wild and rugged region,

traversed by fruitful valleys. Its old capital was Bozrah (<scripRef passage="Isa. 63:1" id="e-p48.8" parsed="|Isa|63|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.63.1">Isa. 63:1</scripRef>). The early inhabitants of the land were Horites. They were
destroyed by the Edomites (<scripRef passage="Deut. 2:12" id="e-p48.9" parsed="|Deut|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.2.12">Deut. 2:12</scripRef>), between whom and the
kings of Israel and Judah there was frequent war (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 8:20" id="e-p48.10" parsed="|2Kgs|8|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.8.20">2 Kings 8:20</scripRef>;
2 Chr. 28:17).
At the time of the Exodus they churlishly refused permission
to the Israelites to pass through their land (<scripRef passage="Num. 20:14-21" id="e-p49.1" parsed="|Num|20|14|20|21" osisRef="Bible:Num.20.14-Num.20.21">Num. 20:14-21</scripRef>),
and ever afterwards maintained an attitude of hostility toward

them. They were conquered by David (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 8:14" id="e-p49.2" parsed="|2Sam|8|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.8.14">2 Sam. 8:14</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="1 Kings 9:26" id="e-p49.3" parsed="|1Kgs|9|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.9.26">1 Kings 9:26</scripRef>), and afterwards by Amaziah (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 25:11" id="e-p49.4" parsed="|2Chr|25|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.25.11">2 Chr. 25:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 25:12" id="e-p49.5" parsed="|2Chr|25|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.25.12">12</scripRef>). But they
regained again their independence, and in later years, during
the decline of the Jewish kingdom (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 16:6" id="e-p49.6" parsed="|2Kgs|16|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.16.6">2 Kings 16:6</scripRef>; R.V. marg.,
“Edomites”), made war against Israel. They took part with the
Chaldeans when Nebuchadnezzar captured Jerusalem, and afterwards
they invaded and held possession of the south of Palestine as
far as Hebron. At length, however, Edom fell under the growing
Chaldean power (Jer. 27:3, 6).
There are many prophecies concerning Edom (Isa. 34:5, 6; Jer. 49:7-18; Ezek. 25:13; 35:1-15; Joel 3:19; Amos 1:11; Obad.; Mal. 1:3, 4) which have been remarkably fulfilled. The present
desolate condition of that land is a standing testimony to the
inspiration of these prophecies. After an existence as a people
for above seventeen hundred years, they have utterly
disappeared, and their language even is forgotten for ever. In
Petra, “where kings kept their court, and where nobles
assembled, there no man dwells; it is given by lot to birds, and
beasts, and reptiles.”
The Edomites were Semites, closely related in blood and in
language to the Israelites. They dispossessed the Horites of
Mount Seir; though it is clear, from <scripRef passage="Gen. 36" id="e-p51.1" parsed="|Gen|36|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36">Gen. 36</scripRef>, that they
afterwards intermarried with the conquered population. Edomite
tribes settled also in the south of Judah, like the Kenizzites

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 36:11" id="e-p51.2" parsed="|Gen|36|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36.11">Gen. 36:11</scripRef>), to whom Caleb and Othniel belonged (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:17" id="e-p51.3" parsed="|Josh|15|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.17">Josh. 15:17</scripRef>).
The southern part of Edom was known as Teman.
</def>
<term id="e-p51.4">Edrei</term>
<def id="e-p51.5">
Mighty; strength. (1.) One of the chief towns of the kingdom of

Bashan (<scripRef passage="Josh. 12:4" id="e-p52.1" parsed="|Josh|12|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.12.4">Josh. 12:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 12:5" id="e-p52.2" parsed="|Josh|12|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.12.5">5</scripRef>). Here Og was defeated by the Israelites,
and the strength of the Amorites broken (<scripRef passage="Num. 21:33-35" id="e-p52.3" parsed="|Num|21|33|21|35" osisRef="Bible:Num.21.33-Num.21.35">Num. 21:33-35</scripRef>). It
subsequently belonged to Manasseh, for a short time apparently,

and afterwards became the abode of banditti and outlaws (<scripRef passage="Josh. 13:31" id="e-p52.4" parsed="|Josh|13|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.31">Josh. 13:31</scripRef>). It has been identified with the modern Edr’a, which
stands on a rocky promontory on the south-west edge of the Lejah
(the Argob of the Hebrews, and Trachonitis of the Greeks). The
ruins of Edr’a are the most extensive in the Hauran. They are 3
miles in circumference. A number of the ancient houses still
remain; the walls, roofs, and doors being all of stone. The wild
region of which Edrei was the capital is thus described in its
modern aspect: “Elevated about 20 feet above the plain, it is a
labyrinth of clefts and crevasses in the rock, formed by
volcanic action; and owing to its impenetrable condition, it has
become a refuge for outlaws and turbulent characters, who make
it a sort of Cave of Adullam...It is, in fact, an impregnable
natural fortress, about 20 miles in length and 15 in breadth”
(Porter’s Syria, etc.). Beneath this wonderful city there is
also a subterranean city, hollowed out probably as a refuge for
the population of the upper city in times of danger. (See BASHAN.)
(2.) A town of Naphtali (Josh. 19:37).
</def>
<term id="e-p53.2">Effectual call</term>
<def id="e-p53.3">
See CALL.
</def>
<term id="e-p54.2">Effectual prayer</term>
<def id="e-p54.3">
Occurs in Authorized Version, James 5:16. The Revised Version
renders appropriately: “The supplication of a righteous man
availeth much in its working”, i.e., “it moves the hand of Him
who moves the world.”
</def>
<term id="e-p55.2">Egg</term>
<def id="e-p55.3">
(Heb. beytsah, “whiteness”). Eggs deserted (Isa. 10:14), of a

bird (<scripRef passage="Deut. 22:6" id="e-p56.2" parsed="|Deut|22|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.22.6">Deut. 22:6</scripRef>), an ostrich (<scripRef passage="Job 39:14" id="e-p56.3" parsed="|Job|39|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.39.14">Job 39:14</scripRef>), the cockatrice (<scripRef passage="Isa. 59:5" id="e-p56.4" parsed="|Isa|59|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.59.5">Isa. 59:5</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="Luke 11:12" id="e-p56.5" parsed="|Luke|11|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.11.12">Luke 11:12</scripRef>, an egg is contrasted with a scorpion,
which is said to be very like an egg in its appearance, so much
so as to be with difficulty at times distinguished from it. In
<scripRef passage="Job 6:6" id="e-p56.6" parsed="|Job|6|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.6.6">Job 6:6</scripRef> (“the white of an egg”) the word for egg (hallamuth’)
occurs nowhere else. It has been translated “purslain” (R.V.
marg.), and the whole phrase “purslain-broth”, i.e., broth made
of that herb, proverbial for its insipidity; and hence an
insipid discourse. Job applies this expression to the speech of
Eliphaz as being insipid and dull. But the common rendering,
“the white of an egg”, may be satisfactorily maintained.
</def>
<term id="e-p56.7">Eglah</term>
<def id="e-p56.8">
A heifer, one of David’s wives, and mother of Ithream (2 Sam. 3:5; 1 Chr. 3:3). According to a Jewish tradition she was
Michal.
</def>
<term id="e-p57.3">Eglaim</term>
<def id="e-p57.4">
Two ponds, (Isa. 15:8), probably En-eglaim of Ezek. 47:10.
</def>
<term id="e-p58.3">Eglon</term>
<def id="e-p58.4">
The bullock; place of heifers. (1.) Chieftain or king of one of
the Moabite tribes (<scripRef passage="Judg. 3:12-14" id="e-p59.1" parsed="|Judg|3|12|3|14" osisRef="Bible:Judg.3.12-Judg.3.14">Judg. 3:12-14</scripRef>). Having entered into an
alliance with Ammon and Amalek, he overran the trans-Jordanic
region, and then crossing the Jordan, seized on Jericho, the
“city of palm trees,” which had been by this time rebuilt, but
not as a fortress. He made this city his capital, and kept
Israel in subjection for eighteen years. The people at length
“cried unto the Lord” in their distress, and he “raised them up
a deliverer” in Ehud (q.v.), the son of Gera, a Benjamite.
(2.) A city in Judah, near Lachish (Josh. 15:39). It was
destroyed by Joshua (10:5, 6). It has been identified with Tell
Nejileh, 6 miles south of Tell Hesy or Ajlan, north-west of
Lachish. (See LACHISH.)
</def>
<term id="e-p60.3">Egypt</term>
<def id="e-p60.4">
The land of the Nile and the pyramids, the oldest kingdom of
which we have any record, holds a place of great significance in
Scripture.
The Egyptians belonged to the white race, and their original
home is still a matter of dispute. Many scholars believe that it
was in Southern Arabia, and recent excavations have shown that
the valley of the Nile was originally inhabited by a low-class
population, perhaps belonging to the Nigritian stock, before the
Egyptians of history entered it. The ancient Egyptian language,
of which the latest form is Coptic, is distantly connected with
the Semitic family of speech.
Egypt consists geographically of two halves, the northern
being the Delta, and the southern Upper Egypt, between Cairo and
the First Cataract. In the Old Testament, Northern or Lower

Egypt is called Mazor, “the fortified land” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 19:6" id="e-p63.1" parsed="|Isa|19|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.19.6">Isa. 19:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 37" id="e-p63.2" parsed="|Isa|37|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.37">37</scripRef>: 25,
where the A.V. mistranslates “defence” and “besieged places”);
while Southern or Upper Egypt is Pathros, the Egyptian
Pa-to-Res, or “the land of the south” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 11:11" id="e-p63.3" parsed="|Isa|11|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.11.11">Isa. 11:11</scripRef>). But the
whole country is generally mentioned under the dual name of
Mizraim, “the two Mazors.”
The civilization of Egypt goes back to a very remote
antiquity. The two kingdoms of the north and south were united
by Menes, the founder of the first historical dynasty of kings.
The first six dynasties constitute what is known as the Old
Empire, which had its capital at Memphis, south of Cairo, called
in the Old Testament Moph (<scripRef passage="Hos. 9:6" id="e-p64.1" parsed="|Hos|9|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.9.6">Hos. 9:6</scripRef>) and Noph. The native name
was Mennofer, “the good place.”
The Pyramids were tombs of the monarchs of the Old Empire,
those of Gizeh being erected in the time of the Fourth Dynasty.
After the fall of the Old Empire came a period of decline and
obscurity. This was followed by the Middle Empire, the most
powerful dynasty of which was the Twelfth. The Fayyum was
rescued for agriculture by the kings of the Twelfth Dynasty; and
two obelisks were erected in front of the temple of the sun-god
at On or Heliopolis (near Cairo), one of which is still
standing. The capital of the Middle Empire was Thebes, in Upper
Egypt.
The Middle Empire was overthrown by the invasion of the
Hyksos, or shepherd princes from Asia, who ruled over Egypt,
more especially in the north, for several centuries, and of whom
there were three dynasties of kings. They had their capital at
Zoan or Tanis (now San), in the north-eastern part of the Delta.
It was in the time of the Hyksos that Abraham, Jacob, and Joseph
