at length came to denote one of the armed bodyguard of the
emperor. Herod Antipas, in imitation of the emperor, had in
attendance on him a company of speculatores. They were sometimes
employed as executioners, but this was a mere accident of their
office. (See MARK, GOSPEL OF.)
</def>
<term id="e-p351.3">Exercise, bodily</term>
(1 Tim. 4:8). An ascetic mortification of the flesh and denial
of personal gratification (comp. <scripRef passage="Col. 2:23" id="e-p352.2" parsed="|Col|2|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.2.23">Col. 2:23</scripRef>) to which some sects
of the Jews, especially the Essenes, attached importance.
</def>
<term id="e-p352.3">Exile</term>
(1.) Of the kingdom of Israel. In the time of Pekah,

Tiglath-pileser II. carried away captive into Assyria (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 15:29" id="e-p353.1" parsed="|2Kgs|15|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.29">2 Kings 15:29</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Isa. 10:5" id="e-p353.2" parsed="|Isa|10|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.5">Isa. 10:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 10:6" id="e-p353.3" parsed="|Isa|10|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.6">6</scripRef>) a part of the inhabitants of Galilee
and of Gilead (B.C. 741).
After the destruction of Samaria (B.C. 720) by Shalmaneser and
Sargon (q.v.), there was a general deportation of the Israelites

into Mesopotamia and Media (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:6" id="e-p354.1" parsed="|2Kgs|17|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.6">2 Kings 17:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:9" id="e-p354.2" parsed="|2Kgs|18|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.9">18:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 5:26" id="e-p354.3" parsed="|1Chr|5|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5.26">1 Chr. 5:26</scripRef>).
(See ISRAEL, KINGDOM OF.)
(2.) Of the kingdom of the two tribes, the kingdom of Judah.
Nebuchadnezzar, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim (<scripRef passage="Jer. 25:1" id="e-p355.1" parsed="|Jer|25|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.25.1">Jer. 25:1</scripRef>),
invaded Judah, and carried away some royal youths, including
Daniel and his companions (B.C. 606), together with the sacred

vessels of the temple (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 36:7" id="e-p355.2" parsed="|2Chr|36|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.36.7">2 Chr. 36:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Dan. 1:2" id="e-p355.3" parsed="|Dan|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.1.2">Dan. 1:2</scripRef>). In B.C. 598 (<scripRef passage="Jer. 52:28" id="e-p355.4" parsed="|Jer|52|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.52.28">Jer. 52:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 24:12" id="e-p355.5" parsed="|2Kgs|24|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.24.12">2 Kings 24:12</scripRef>), in the beginning of Jehoiachin’s reign (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 24:8" id="e-p355.6" parsed="|2Kgs|24|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.24.8">2 Kings 24:8</scripRef>), Nebuchadnezzar carried away captive 3,023 eminent
Jews, including the king (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 36:10" id="e-p355.7" parsed="|2Chr|36|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.36.10">2 Chr. 36:10</scripRef>), with his family and
officers (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 24:12" id="e-p355.8" parsed="|2Kgs|24|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.24.12">2 Kings 24:12</scripRef>), and a large number of warriors (16),
with very many persons of note (14), and artisans (16), leaving
behind only those who were poor and helpless. This was the first
general deportation to Babylon.
In B.C. 588, after the revolt of Zedekiah (q.v.), there was a

second general deportation of Jews by Nebuchadnezzar (<scripRef passage="Jer. 52:29" id="e-p356.1" parsed="|Jer|52|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.52.29">Jer. 52:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 25:8" id="e-p356.2" parsed="|2Kgs|25|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.25.8">2 Kings 25:8</scripRef>), including 832 more of the principal men of
the kingdom. He carried away also the rest of the sacred vessels
(<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 36:18" id="e-p356.3" parsed="|2Chr|36|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.36.18">2 Chr. 36:18</scripRef>). From this period, when the temple was destroyed
(2 Kings 25:9), to the complete restoration, B.C. 517 (Ezra 6:15), is the period of the “seventy years.”
In B.C. 582 occurred the last and final deportation. The
entire number Nebuchadnezzar carried captive was 4,600 heads of

families with their wives and children and dependants (<scripRef passage="Jer. 52:30" id="e-p357.1" parsed="|Jer|52|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.52.30">Jer. 52:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 43:5-7" id="e-p357.2" parsed="|Jer|43|5|43|7" osisRef="Bible:Jer.43.5-Jer.43.7">43:5-7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 36:20" id="e-p357.3" parsed="|2Chr|36|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.36.20">2 Chr. 36:20</scripRef>, etc.). Thus the exiles formed a
very considerable community in Babylon.
When Cyrus granted permission to the Jews to return to their

own land (<scripRef passage="Ezra 1:5" id="e-p358.1" parsed="|Ezra|1|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.1.5">Ezra 1:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezra 7:13" id="e-p358.2" parsed="|Ezra|7|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.7.13">7:13</scripRef>), only a comparatively small number at
first availed themselves of the privilege. It cannot be
questioned that many belonging to the kingdom of Israel
ultimately joined the Jews under Ezra, Zerubbabel, and Nehemiah,

and returned along with them to Jerusalem (<scripRef passage="Jer. 50:4" id="e-p358.3" parsed="|Jer|50|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.50.4">Jer. 50:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer. 50:5" id="e-p358.4" parsed="|Jer|50|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.50.5">5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer. 50:17" id="e-p358.5" parsed="|Jer|50|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.50.17">17</scripRef>-20,
Large numbers had, however, settled in the land of Babylon,
and formed numerous colonies in different parts of the kingdom.
Their descendants very probably have spread far into Eastern
lands and become absorbed in the general population. (See JUDAH,
KINGDOM OF; CAPTIVITY.)
</def>
<term id="e-p359.3">Exodus</term>
The great deliverance wrought for the children of Isreal when
they were brought out of the land of Egypt with “a mighty hand

and with an outstretched arm” (<scripRef passage="Ex 12:51" id="e-p360.1" parsed="|Exod|12|51|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.51">Ex 12:51</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 26:8" id="e-p360.2" parsed="|Deut|26|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.26.8">Deut. 26:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 114" id="e-p360.3" parsed="|Ps|114|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.114">Ps 114</scripRef>;
136), about B.C. 1490, and four hundred and eighty years (1 Kings 6:1) before the building of Solomon’s temple.
The time of their sojourning in Egypt was, according to Ex. 12:40, the space of four hundred and thirty years. In the LXX.,
the words are, “The sojourning of the children of Israel which
they sojourned in Egypt and in the land of Canaan was four
hundred and thirty years;” and the Samaritan version reads, “The
sojourning of the children of Israel and of their fathers which
they sojourned in the land of Canaan and in the land of Egypt
was four hundred and thirty years.” In <scripRef passage="Gen. 15:13-16" id="e-p361.2" parsed="|Gen|15|13|15|16" osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.13-Gen.15.16">Gen. 15:13-16</scripRef>, the period
is prophetically given (in round numbers) as four hundred years.
This passage is quoted by Stephen in his defence before the
council (Acts 7:6).
The chronology of the “sojourning” is variously estimated.
Those who adopt the longer term reckon thus:
| Years
|    From the descent of Jacob into Egypt to the
|     death of Joseph               71
|    From the death of Joseph to the birth of
|     Moses                    278
|    From the birth of Moses to his flight into
|     Midian                    40
|    From the flight of Moses to his return into
|     Egypt                    40
|    From the return of Moses to the <scripRef passage="Exodus 1" id="e-p363.1" parsed="|Exod|1|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.1">Exodus     1</scripRef>
Others contend for the shorter period of two hundred and
fifteen years, holding that the period of four hundred and
thirty years comprehends the years from the entrance of Abraham
into Canaan (see LXX. and Samaritan) to the descent of Jacob
into Egypt. They reckon thus:
| Years
|    From Abraham’s arrival in Canaan to Isaac’s
|     birth                    25
|    From Isaac’s birth to that of his twin sons
|     Esau and Jacob                60
|    From Jacob’s birth to the going down into
|     Egypt                    130
|    From Jacob’s going down into Egypt to the
|     death of Joseph               71
|    From death of Joseph to the birth of Moses   64
|    From birth of Moses to the <scripRef passage="Exodus 80" id="e-p365.1" parsed="|Exod|80|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.80">Exodus       80</scripRef>
During the forty years of Moses’ sojourn in the land of
Midian, the Hebrews in Egypt were being gradually prepared for
the great national crisis which was approaching. The plagues
that successively fell upon the land loosened the bonds by which
Pharaoh held them in slavery, and at length he was eager that
they should depart. But the Hebrews must now also be ready to
go. They were poor; for generations they had laboured for the
Egyptians without wages. They asked gifts from their neighbours
around them (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:35" id="e-p366.1" parsed="|Exod|12|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.35">Ex. 12:35</scripRef>), and these were readily bestowed. And
then, as the first step towards their independent national
organization, they observed the feast of the Passover, which was
now instituted as a perpetual memorial. The blood of the paschal
lamb was duly sprinkled on the door-posts and lintels of all
their houses, and they were all within, waiting the next
movement in the working out of God’s plan. At length the last
stroke fell on the land of Egypt. “It came to pass, that at
midnight Jehovah smote all the firstborn in the land of Egypt.”
Pharaoh rose up in the night, and called for Moses and Aaron by
night, and said, “Rise up, and get you forth from among my
people, both ye and the children of Israel; and go, serve
Jehovah, as ye have said. Also take your flocks and your herds,
as ye have said, and be gone; and bless me also.” Thus was
Pharaoh (q.v.) completely humbled and broken down. These words
he spoke to Moses and Aaron “seem to gleam through the tears of
the humbled king, as he lamented his son snatched from him by so
sudden a death, and tremble with a sense of the helplessness
which his proud soul at last felt when the avenging hand of God
had visited even his palace.”
The terror-stricken Egyptians now urged the instant departure
of the Hebrews. In the midst of the Passover feast, before the
dawn of the 15th day of the month Abib (our April nearly), which
was to be to them henceforth the beginning of the year, as it
was the commencement of a new epoch in their history, every
family, with all that appertained to it, was ready for the
march, which instantly began under the leadership of the heads
of tribes with their various sub-divisions. They moved onward,
increasing as they went forward from all the districts of
Goshen, over the whole of which they were scattered, to the
common centre. Three or four days perhaps elapsed before the
whole body of the people were assembled at Rameses, and ready to

set out under their leader Moses (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:37" id="e-p367.1" parsed="|Exod|12|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.37">Ex. 12:37</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 33:3" id="e-p367.2" parsed="|Num|33|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.3">Num. 33:3</scripRef>). This
city was at that time the residence of the Egyptian court, and
here the interviews between Moses and Pharaoh had taken place.
From Rameses they journeyed to Succoth (Ex. 12:37), identified
with Tel-el-Maskhuta, about 12 miles west of Ismailia. (See PITHOM.) Their third station was Etham (q.v.), 13:20,
“in the edge of the wilderness,” and was probably a little to
the west of the modern town of Ismailia, on the Suez Canal. Here
they were commanded “to turn and encamp before Pi-hahiroth,
between Migdol and the sea”, i.e., to change their route from
east to due south. The Lord now assumed the direction of their
march in the pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night. They
were then led along the west shore of the Red Sea till they came
to an extensive camping-ground “before Pi-hahiroth,” about 40
miles from Etham. This distance from Etham may have taken three
days to traverse, for the number of camping-places by no means
indicates the number of days spent on the journey: e.g., it took
fully a month to travel from Rameses to the wilderness of Sin
(<scripRef passage="Ex. 16:1" id="e-p368.3" parsed="|Exod|16|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.16.1">Ex. 16:1</scripRef>), yet reference is made to only six camping-places
during all that time. The exact spot of their encampment before
they crossed the Red Sea cannot be determined. It was probably
somewhere near the present site of Suez.
Under the direction of God the children of Israel went
“forward” from the camp “before Pi-hahiroth,” and the sea opened
a pathway for them, so that they crossed to the farther shore in
safety. The Egyptian host pursued after them, and, attempting to
follow through the sea, were overwhelmed in its returning
waters, and thus the whole military force of the Egyptians
perished. They “sank as lead in the mighty waters” (<scripRef passage="Ex. 15:1-9" id="e-p369.1" parsed="|Exod|15|1|15|9" osisRef="Bible:Exod.15.1-Exod.15.9">Ex. 15:1-9</scripRef>;
comp. Ps. 77:16-19).
Having reached the eastern shore of the sea, perhaps a little
way to the north of ‘Ayun Musa (“the springs of Moses”), there
they encamped and rested probably for a day. Here Miriam and the
other women sang the triumphal song recorded in Ex. 15:1-21.
From ‘Ayun Musa they went on for three days through a part of
the barren “wilderness of Shur” (22), called also the

“wilderness of Etham” (<scripRef passage="Num. 33:8" id="e-p371.1" parsed="|Num|33|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.8">Num. 33:8</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Ex. 13:20" id="e-p371.2" parsed="|Exod|13|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.13.20">Ex. 13:20</scripRef>), without
finding water. On the last of these days they came to Marah
(q.v.), where the “bitter” water was by a miracle made
drinkable.
Their next camping-place was Elim (q.v.), where were twelve
springs of water and a grove of “threescore and ten” palm trees
(Ex. 15:27).
After a time the children of Israel “took their journey from
Elim,” and encamped by the Red Sea (<scripRef passage="Num. 33:10" id="e-p373.1" parsed="|Num|33|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.10">Num. 33:10</scripRef>), and thence
removed to the “wilderness of Sin” (to be distinguished from the
wilderness of Zin, 20:1), where they again encamped. Here,
probably the modern el-Markha, the supply of bread they had
brought with them out of Egypt failed. They began to “murmur”
for want of bread. God “heard their murmurings” and gave them
quails and manna, “bread from heaven” (<scripRef passage="Ex. 16:4-36" id="e-p373.2" parsed="|Exod|16|4|16|36" osisRef="Bible:Exod.16.4-Exod.16.36">Ex. 16:4-36</scripRef>). Moses
directed that an omer of manna should be put aside and preserved
as a perpetual memorial of God’s goodness. They now turned
inland, and after three encampments came to the rich and fertile
valley of Rephidim, in the Wady Feiran. Here they found no
water, and again murmured against Moses. Directed by God, Moses
procured a miraculous supply of water from the “rock in Horeb,”
one of the hills of the Sinai group (17:1-7); and shortly
afterwards the children of Israel here fought their first battle
with the Amalekites, whom they smote with the edge of the sword.
From the eastern extremity of the Wady Feiran the line of
march now probably led through the Wady esh-Sheikh and the Wady
Solaf, meeting in the Wady er-Rahah, “the enclosed plain in
front of the magnificient cliffs of Ras Sufsafeh.” Here they

encamped for more than a year (<scripRef passage="Num. 1:1" id="e-p374.1" parsed="|Num|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.1.1">Num. 1:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 10:11" id="e-p374.2" parsed="|Num|10|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.10.11">10:11</scripRef>) before Sinai
The different encampments of the children of Israel, from the
time of their leaving Egypt till they reached the Promised Land,
are mentioned in Ex. 12:37-19; Num. 10-21; 33; Deut. 1, 2, 10.
It is worthy of notice that there are unmistakable evidences
that the Egyptians had a tradition of a great exodus from their
country, which could be none other than the exodus of the
Hebrews.
</def>
<term id="e-p376.1">Exodus, Book of</term>
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="e-p376.3" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="Exod 0" id="e-p376.4" parsed="|Exod|0|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod" />
Exodus is the name given in the LXX. to the second book of the
Pentateuch (q.v.). It means “departure” or “outgoing.” This name
was adopted in the Latin translation, and thence passed into
other languages. The Hebrews called it by the first words,
according to their custom, Ve-eleh shemoth (i.e., “and these are
the names”).
It contains, (1.) An account of the increase and growth of the
Israelites in Egypt (ch. 1) (2.) Preparations for their
departure out of Egypt (2-12:36). (3.) Their journeyings from
Egypt to Sinai (12:37-19:2). (4.) The giving of the law and the
establishment of the institutions by which the organization of
the people was completed, the theocracy, “a kingdom of priest
and an holy nation” (19:3-ch. 40).
The time comprised in this book, from the death of Joseph to
the erection of the tabernacle in the wilderness, is about one
hundred and forty-five years, on the supposition that the four
hundred and thirty years (12:40) are to be computed from the
time of the promises made to Abraham (Gal. 3:17).
The authorship of this book, as well as of that of the other
books of the Pentateuch, is to be ascribed to Moses. The
unanimous voice of tradition and all internal evidences
abundantly support this opinion.
</def>
<term id="e-p380.1">Exorcist</term>
(Acts 19:13). “In that sceptical and therefore superstitious age
professional exorcist abounded. Many of these professional
exorcists were disreputable Jews, like Simon in Samaria and
Elymas in Cyprus (8:9; 13:6).” Other references to exorcism as

practised by the Jews are found in <scripRef passage="Matt. 12:27" id="e-p381.2" parsed="|Matt|12|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.12.27">Matt. 12:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 9:38" id="e-p381.3" parsed="|Mark|9|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.9.38">Mark 9:38</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 9:49" id="e-p381.4" parsed="|Luke|9|49|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.9.49">Luke 9:49</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Luke 9:50" id="e-p381.5" parsed="|Luke|9|50|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.9.50">50</scripRef>. It would seem that it was an opinion among the Jews
that miracles might be wrought by invoking the divine name. Thus
also these “vagabond Jews” pretended that they could expel
daemons.
The power of casting out devils was conferred by Christ on his

apostles (<scripRef passage="Matt. 10:8" id="e-p382.1" parsed="|Matt|10|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.10.8">Matt. 10:8</scripRef>), and on the seventy (<scripRef passage="Luke 10:17-19" id="e-p382.2" parsed="|Luke|10|17|10|19" osisRef="Bible:Luke.10.17-Luke.10.19">Luke 10:17-19</scripRef>), and
was exercised by believers after his ascension (Mark 16:17; Acts 16:18); but this power was never spoken of as exorcism.
</def>
<term id="e-p382.5">Expiation</term>
Guilt is said to be expiated when it is visited with punishment
falling on a substitute. Expiation is made for our sins when
they are punished not in ourselves but in another who consents
to stand in our room. It is that by which reconciliation is
effected. Sin is thus said to be “covered” by vicarious
satisfaction.
The cover or lid of the ark is termed in the LXX. hilasterion,
that which covered or shut out the claims and demands of the law
against the sins of God’s people, whereby he became “propitious”
to them.
The idea of vicarious expiation runs through the whole Old
Testament system of sacrifices. (See PROPITIATION.)
</def>
<term id="e-p385.2">Eye</term>
(Heb. ‘ain, meaning “flowing”), applied (1) to a fountain,
frequently; (2) to colour (<scripRef passage="Num. 11:7" id="e-p386.1" parsed="|Num|11|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.11.7">Num. 11:7</scripRef>; R.V., “appearance,” marg.

“eye”); (3) the face (<scripRef passage="Ex. 10:5" id="e-p386.2" parsed="|Exod|10|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.10.5">Ex. 10:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 10:15" id="e-p386.3" parsed="|Exod|10|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.10.15">15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 22:5" id="e-p386.4" parsed="|Num|22|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.22.5">Num. 22:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 22:11" id="e-p386.5" parsed="|Num|22|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.22.11">11</scripRef>), in <scripRef passage="Num. 14:14" id="e-p386.6" parsed="|Num|14|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.14.14">Num. 14:14</scripRef>, “face to face” (R.V. marg., “eye to eye”). “Between the
eyes”, i.e., the forehead (Ex. 13:9, 16).
The expression (Prov. 23:31), “when it giveth his colour in
the cup,” is literally, “when it giveth out [or showeth] its
eye.” The beads or bubbles of wine are thus spoken of. “To set

the eyes” on any one is to view him with favour (<scripRef passage="Gen. 44:21" id="e-p387.2" parsed="|Gen|44|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.44.21">Gen. 44:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 24:23" id="e-p387.3" parsed="|Job|24|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.24.23">Job 24:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 39:12" id="e-p387.4" parsed="|Jer|39|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.39.12">Jer. 39:12</scripRef>). This word is used figuratively in the
expressions an “evil eye” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 20:15" id="e-p387.5" parsed="|Matt|20|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.20.15">Matt. 20:15</scripRef>), a “bountiful eye”

(<scripRef passage="Prov. 22:9" id="e-p387.6" parsed="|Prov|22|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.22.9">Prov. 22:9</scripRef>), “haughty eyes” (6:17 marg.), “wanton eyes” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 3:16" id="e-p387.7" parsed="|Isa|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.16">Isa. 3:16</scripRef>), “eyes full of adultery” (2 Pet. 2:14), “the lust of the
eyes” (<scripRef passage="1 John 2:16" id="e-p387.8" parsed="|1John|2|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.2.16">1 John 2:16</scripRef>). Christians are warned against “eye-service”

(<scripRef passage="Eph. 6:6" id="e-p387.9" parsed="|Eph|6|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.6.6">Eph. 6:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Col. 3:22" id="e-p387.10" parsed="|Col|3|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.3.22">Col. 3:22</scripRef>). Men were sometimes punished by having

their eyes put out (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 11:2" id="e-p387.11" parsed="|1Sam|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.11.2">1 Sam. 11:2</scripRef>; Samson, <scripRef passage="Judg. 16:21" id="e-p387.12" parsed="|Judg|16|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.16.21">Judg. 16:21</scripRef>; Zedekiah,
2 Kings 25:7).
The custom of painting the eyes is alluded to in 2 Kings 9:30,

R.V.; <scripRef passage="Jer. 4:30" id="e-p388.2" parsed="|Jer|4|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.4.30">Jer. 4:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 23:40" id="e-p388.3" parsed="|Ezek|23|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.23.40">Ezek. 23:40</scripRef>, a custom which still prevails
extensively among Eastern women.
</def>
<term id="e-p388.4">Ezekias</term>
Grecized form of Hezekiah (Matt. 1:9, 10).
</def>
<term id="e-p389.3">Ezekiel</term>
God will strengthen. (1.) 1 Chr. 24:16, “Jehezekel.”
(2.) One of the great prophets, the son of Buzi the priest
(<scripRef passage="Ezek. 1:3" id="e-p391.1" parsed="|Ezek|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.1.3">Ezek. 1:3</scripRef>). He was one of the Jewish exiles who settled at
Tel-Abib, on the banks of the Chebar, “in the land of the
Chaldeans.” He was probably carried away captive with Jehoiachin
(1:2; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 24:14-16" id="e-p391.2" parsed="|2Kgs|24|14|24|16" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.24.14-2Kgs.24.16">2 Kings 24:14-16</scripRef>) about B.C. 597. His prophetic call came
to him “in the fifth year of Jehoiachin’s captivity” (B.C. 594).
He had a house in the place of his exile, where he lost his
wife, in the ninth year of his exile, by some sudden and

unforeseen stroke (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 8:1" id="e-p391.3" parsed="|Ezek|8|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.8.1">Ezek. 8:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek 24:18" id="e-p391.4" parsed="|Ezek|24|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.24.18">24:18</scripRef>). He held a prominent place
among the exiles, and was frequently consulted by the elders
(8:1; 11:25; 14:1; 20:1). His ministry extended over
twenty-three years (29:17), B.C. 595-573, during part of which
he was contemporary with Daniel (14:14; 28:3) and Jeremiah, and
probably also with Obadiah. The time and manner of his death are
unknown. His reputed tomb is pointed out in the neighbourhood of
Bagdad, at a place called Keffil.
</def>
<term id="e-p391.5">Ezekiel, Book of</term>
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="e-p391.7" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="Ezek 0" id="e-p391.8" parsed="|Ezek|0|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek" />
Consists mainly of three groups of prophecies. After an account
of his call to the prophetical office (1-3:21), Ezekiel (1)
utters words of denunciation against the Jews (3:22-24), warning
them of the certain destruction of Jerusalem, in opposition to
the words of the false prophets (4:1-3). The symbolical acts, by
which the extremities to which Jerusalem would be reduced are
described in ch. 4, 5, show his intimate acquaintance with the

Levitical legislation. (See <scripRef passage="Ex. 22:30" id="e-p392.1" parsed="|Exod|22|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.22.30">Ex. 22:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 14:21" id="e-p392.2" parsed="|Deut|14|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.14.21">Deut. 14:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 5:2" id="e-p392.3" parsed="|Lev|5|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.5.2">Lev. 5:2</scripRef>;
7:18, 24; 17:15; 19:7; 22:8, etc.)
(2.) Prophecies against various surrounding nations: against
the Ammonites (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 25:1-7" id="e-p393.1" parsed="|Ezek|25|1|25|7" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.25.1-Ezek.25.7">Ezek. 25:1-7</scripRef>), the Moabites (8-11), the Edomites
(12-14), the Philistines (15-17), Tyre and Sidon (26-28), and
against Egypt (29-32).
(3.) Prophecies delivered after the destruction of Jerusalem
by Nebuchadnezzar: the triumphs of Israel and of the kingdom of
God on earth (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 33" id="e-p394.1" parsed="|Ezek|33|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.33">Ezek. 33</scripRef>-39); Messianic times, and the
establishment and prosperity of the kingdom of God (40;48).
The closing visions of this book are referred to in the book

of Revelation (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 38" id="e-p395.1" parsed="|Ezek|38|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.38">Ezek. 38</scripRef>=<scripRef passage="Rev. 20:8" id="e-p395.2" parsed="|Rev|20|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.20.8">Rev. 20:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 47:1-8" id="e-p395.3" parsed="|Ezek|47|1|47|8" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.47.1-Ezek.47.8">Ezek. 47:1-8</scripRef>=<scripRef passage="Rev. 22:1" id="e-p395.4" parsed="|Rev|22|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.22.1">Rev. 22:1</scripRef>,<scripRef passage="Rev 22:2" id="e-p395.5" parsed="|Rev|22|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.22.2">2</scripRef>).
Other references to this book are also found in the New
Testament. (Comp. Rom. 2:24 with Ezek. 36:2; Rom. 10:5, Gal. 3:12 with Ezek. 20:11; 2 Pet. 3:4 with Ezek. 12:22.)
It may be noted that Daniel, fourteen years after his
deportation from Jerusalem, is mentioned by Ezekiel (14:14)
along with Noah and Job as distinguished for his righteousness,
and some five years later he is spoken of as pre-eminent for his
wisdom (28:3).
Ezekiel’s prophecies are characterized by symbolical and
allegorical representations, “unfolding a rich series of
majestic visions and of colossal symbols.” There are a great
many also of “symbolcal actions embodying vivid conceptions on
etc.) “The mode of representation, in which symbols and
allegories occupy a prominent place, gives a dark, mysterious
character to the prophecies of Ezekiel. They are obscure and
enigmatical. A cloudy mystery overhangs them which it is almost
impossible to penetrate. Jerome calls the book ‘a labyrith of
the mysteries of God.’ It was because of this obscurity that the
Jews forbade any one to read it till he had attained the age of
thirty.”
Ezekiel is singular in the frequency with which he refers to

the Pentateuch (e.g., <scripRef passage="Ezek. 27" id="e-p398.1" parsed="|Ezek|27|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27">Ezek. 27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek 28:13" id="e-p398.2" parsed="|Ezek|28|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.28.13">28:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek 31:8" id="e-p398.3" parsed="|Ezek|31|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.31.8">31:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek 36:11" id="e-p398.4" parsed="|Ezek|36|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.36.11">36:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek 36:34" id="e-p398.5" parsed="|Ezek|36|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.36.34">34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek 47:13" id="e-p398.6" parsed="|Ezek|47|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.47.13">47:13</scripRef>,
etc.). He shows also an acquaintance with the writings of Hosea

(<scripRef passage="Ezek. 37:22" id="e-p398.7" parsed="|Ezek|37|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.37.22">Ezek. 37:22</scripRef>), Isaiah (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 8:12" id="e-p398.8" parsed="|Ezek|8|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.8.12">Ezek. 8:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek 29:6" id="e-p398.9" parsed="|Ezek|29|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.29.6">29:6</scripRef>), and especially with
those of Jeremiah, his older contemporary (Jer. 24:7, 9; 48:37).
</def>
<term id="e-p398.12">Ezel</term>
A separation, (1 Sam. 20:19), a stone, or heap of stones, in the
neighbourhood of Saul’s residence, the scene of the parting of
David and Jonathan (42). The margin of the Authorized Version
reads, “The stone that sheweth the way,” in this rendering
following the Targum.
</def>
<term id="e-p399.2">Ezer</term>
Treasure. (1.) One of the sons of Seir, the native princes,

“dukes,” of Mount Hor (<scripRef passage="Gen. 36:21" id="e-p400.1" parsed="|Gen|36|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36.21">Gen. 36:21</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 36:27" id="e-p400.2" parsed="|Gen|36|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36.27">27</scripRef>). (2.) <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 7:21" id="e-p400.3" parsed="|1Chr|7|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.7.21">1 Chr. 7:21</scripRef>; (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 3" id="e-p400.4" parsed="|1Chr|3|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.3">3</scripRef>.)
4:4. (4.) One of the Gadite champions who repaired to David at
Ziklag (12:9). (5.) A Levite (Neh. 3:19). (6.) A priest (12:42).
</def>
<term id="e-p400.6">Ezion-geber</term>
The giant’s backbone (so called from the head of a mountain
which runs out into the sea), an ancient city and harbour at the
north-east end of the Elanitic branch of the Red Sea, the Gulf

of Akabah, near Elath or Eloth (<scripRef passage="Num. 33:35" id="e-p401.1" parsed="|Num|33|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.35">Num. 33:35</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 2:8" id="e-p401.2" parsed="|Deut|2|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.2.8">Deut. 2:8</scripRef>). Here
Solomon built ships, “Tarshish ships,” like those trading from

Tyre to Tarshish and the west, which traded with Ophir (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 9:26" id="e-p401.3" parsed="|1Kgs|9|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.9.26">1 Kings 9:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 8:17" id="e-p401.4" parsed="|2Chr|8|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.8.17">2 Chr. 8:17</scripRef>); and here also Jehoshaphat’s fleet was

shipwrecked (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 22:48" id="e-p401.5" parsed="|1Kgs|22|48|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.22.48">1 Kings 22:48</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 20:36" id="e-p401.6" parsed="|2Chr|20|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.20.36">2 Chr. 20:36</scripRef>). It became a populous
town, many of the Jews settling in it (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 16:6" id="e-p401.7" parsed="|2Kgs|16|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.16.6">2 Kings 16:6</scripRef>, “Elath”).
It is supposed that anciently the north end of the gulf flowed
further into the country than now, as far as ‘Ain el-Ghudyan,
which is 10 miles up the dry bed of the Arabah, and that
Ezion-geber may have been there.
</def>
<term id="e-p401.8">Ezra</term>
Help. (1.) A priest among those that returned to Jerusalem under
Zerubabel (Neh. 12:1).
(2.) The “scribe” who led the second body of exiles that
returned from Babylon to Jerusalem B.C. 459, and author of the
book of Scripture which bears his name. He was the son, or
perhaps grandson, of Seraiah (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 25:18-21" id="e-p403.1" parsed="|2Kgs|25|18|25|21" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.25.18-2Kgs.25.21">2 Kings 25:18-21</scripRef>), and a lineal
descendant of Phinehas, the son of Aaron (<scripRef passage="Ezra 7:1-5" id="e-p403.2" parsed="|Ezra|7|1|7|5" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.7.1-Ezra.7.5">Ezra 7:1-5</scripRef>). All we
know of his personal history is contained in the last four
chapters of his book, and in Neh. 8 and 12:26.
In the seventh year of the reign of Artaxerxes Longimanus (see
DARIUS), he obtained leave to go up to Jerusalem and
to take with him a company of Israelites (<scripRef passage="Ezra 8" id="e-p404.2" parsed="|Ezra|8|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.8">Ezra 8</scripRef>). Artaxerxes
manifested great interest in Ezra’s undertaking, granting him
“all his request,” and loading him with gifts for the house of
God. Ezra assembled the band of exiles, probably about 5,000 in
all, who were prepared to go up with him to Jerusalem, on the
banks of the Ahava, where they rested for three days, and were
put into order for their march across the desert, which was
completed in four months. His proceedings at Jerusalem on his
arrival there are recorded in his book.
He was “a ready scribe in the law of Moses,” who “had prepared
his heart to seek the law of the Lord and to do it, and to teach
in Israel statutes and judgments.” “He is,” says Professor
Binnie, “the first well-defined example of an order of men who
have never since ceased in the church; men of sacred erudition,
who devote their lives to the study of the Holy Scriptures, in
order that they may be in a condition to interpret them for the
instruction and edification of the church. It is significant
that the earliest mention of the pulpit occurs in the history of
Ezra’s ministry (<scripRef passage="Neh. 8:4" id="e-p405.1" parsed="|Neh|8|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.8.4">Neh. 8:4</scripRef>). He was much more of a teacher than a
priest. We learn from the account of his labours in the book of
Nehemiah that he was careful to have the whole people instructed
in the law of Moses; and there is no reason to reject the
constant tradition of the Jews which connects his name with the
collecting and editing of the Old Testament canon. The final
completion of the canon may have been, and probably was, the
work of a later generation; but Ezra seems to have put it much
into the shape in which it is still found in the Hebrew Bible.
When it is added that the complete organization of the synagogue
dates from this period, it will be seen that the age was
emphatically one of Biblical study” (The Psalms: their History,
etc.).
For about fourteen years, i.e., till B.C. 445, we have no
record of what went on in Jerusalem after Ezra had set in order
the ecclesiastical and civil affairs of the nation. In that year
another distinguished personage, Nehemiah, appears on the scene.
After the ruined wall of the city had been built by Nehemiah,
there was a great gathering of the people at Jerusalem
preparatory to the dedication of the wall. On the appointed day
the whole population assembled, and the law was read aloud to
them by Ezra and his assistants (<scripRef passage="Neh. 8:3" id="e-p406.1" parsed="|Neh|8|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.8.3">Neh. 8:3</scripRef>). The remarkable scene
is described in detail. There was a great religious awakening.
For successive days they held solemn assemblies, confessing
their sins and offering up solemn sacrifices. They kept also the
feast of Tabernacles with great solemnity and joyous enthusiasm,
and then renewed their national covenant to be the Lord’s.
Abuses were rectified, and arrangements for the temple service
completed, and now nothing remained but the dedication of the
walls of the city (Neh. 12).
</def>
<term id="e-p406.3">Ezra, Book of</term>
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="e-p406.5" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="Ezra 0" id="e-p406.6" parsed="|Ezra|0|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra" />
This book is the record of events occurring at the close of the
Babylonian exile. It was at one time included in Nehemiah, the
Jews regarding them as one volume. The two are still
distinguished in the Vulgate version as I. and II. Esdras. It
consists of two principal divisions:
(1.) The history of the first return of exiles, in the first
year of Cyrus (B.C. 536), till the completion and dedication of
the new temple, in the sixth year of Darius Hystapes (B.C. 515),
ch. 1-6. From the close of the sixth to the opening of the
seventh chapter there is a blank in the history of about sixty
years.
(2.) The history of the second return under Ezra, in the
seventh year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, and of the events that
took place at Jerusalem after Ezra’s arrival there (7-10).
The book thus contains memorabilia connected with the Jews,
from the decree of Cyrus (B.C. 536) to the reformation by Ezra
(B.C. 456), extending over a period of about eighty years.
There is no quotation from this book in the New Testament, but
there never has been any doubt about its being canonical. Ezra
was probably the author of this book, at least of the greater
part of it (comp. 7:27, 28; 8:1, etc.), as he was also of the
Books of Chronicles, the close of which forms the opening
passage of Ezra.
</def>
<term id="e-p411.1">Ezrahite</term>
A title given to Ethan (1 Kings 4:31; Ps. 89, title) and Heman
(Ps. 88, title). They were both sons of Zerah (1 Chr. 2:6).
</def>
<term id="e-p412.5">Ezri</term>
Help of Jehovah, the son of Chelub. He superintended, under
David, those who “did the work of the field for tillage” (1 Chr. 27:26).
</def>
</glossary>

<glossary id="f-p0.1">
<term id="f-p0.2">Fable</term>
<def id="f-p0.3">
Applied in the New Testament to the traditions and speculations,
“cunningly devised fables”, of the Jews on religious questions

(<scripRef passage="1 Tim. 1:4" id="f-p1.1" parsed="|1Tim|1|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.1.4">1 Tim. 1:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Tim. 4:7" id="f-p1.2" parsed="|1Tim|4|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.4.7">4:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Tim. 4:4" id="f-p1.3" parsed="|2Tim|4|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.4.4">2 Tim. 4:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Titus 1:14" id="f-p1.4" parsed="|Titus|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Titus.1.14">Titus 1:14</scripRef>; 2 Pet. 1:16). In such
passages the word means anything false and unreal. But the word
is used as almost equivalent to parable. Thus we have (1) the
fable of Jotham, in which the trees are spoken of as choosing a
king (<scripRef passage="Judg. 9:8-15" id="f-p1.5" parsed="|Judg|9|8|9|15" osisRef="Bible:Judg.9.8-Judg.9.15">Judg. 9:8-15</scripRef>); and (2) that of the cedars of Lebanon and
the thistle as Jehoash’s answer to Amaziah (2 Kings 14:9).
</def>
<term id="f-p1.7">Face</term>
<def id="f-p1.8">
Means simply presence, as when it is recorded that Adam and Eve
hid themselves from the “face [R.V., ‘presence’] of the Lord

God” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 3:8" id="f-p2.1" parsed="|Gen|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.3.8">Gen. 3:8</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Ex. 33:14" id="f-p2.2" parsed="|Exod|33|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.33.14">Ex. 33:14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 33:15" id="f-p2.3" parsed="|Exod|33|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.33.15">15</scripRef>, where the same Hebrew word
is rendered “presence”). The “light of God’s countenance” is his

favour (<scripRef passage="Ps. 44:3" id="f-p2.4" parsed="|Ps|44|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.44.3">Ps. 44:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Dan. 9:17" id="f-p2.5" parsed="|Dan|9|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.9.17">Dan. 9:17</scripRef>). “Face” signifies also anger,

justice, severity (<scripRef passage="Gen. 16:6" id="f-p2.6" parsed="|Gen|16|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.16.6">Gen. 16:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 16:8" id="f-p2.7" parsed="|Gen|16|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.16.8">8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex. 2:15" id="f-p2.8" parsed="|Exod|2|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.2.15">Ex. 2:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 68:1" id="f-p2.9" parsed="|Ps|68|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.68.1">Ps. 68:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 6:16" id="f-p2.10" parsed="|Rev|6|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.6.16">Rev. 6:16</scripRef>).
To “provoke God to his face” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 65:3" id="f-p2.11" parsed="|Isa|65|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.65.3">Isa. 65:3</scripRef>) is to sin against him
openly.
The Jews prayed with their faces toward the temple and

Jerusalem (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 8:38" id="f-p3.1" parsed="|1Kgs|8|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.8.38">1 Kings 8:38</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 8:44" id="f-p3.2" parsed="|1Kgs|8|44|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.8.44">44</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 8:48" id="f-p3.3" parsed="|1Kgs|8|48|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.8.48">48</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Dan. 6:10" id="f-p3.4" parsed="|Dan|6|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.6.10">Dan. 6:10</scripRef>). To “see God’s face”
is to have access to him and to enjoy his favour (<scripRef passage="Ps. 17:15" id="f-p3.5" parsed="|Ps|17|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.17.15">Ps. 17:15</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Ps 27:8" id="f-p3.6" parsed="|Ps|27|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.27.8">27:8</scripRef>). This is the privilege of holy angels (<scripRef passage="Matt. 18:10" id="f-p3.7" parsed="|Matt|18|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.18.10">Matt. 18:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 1:19" id="f-p3.8" parsed="|Luke|1|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.19">Luke 1:19</scripRef>). The “face of Jesus Christ” (<scripRef passage="2 Cor. 4:6" id="f-p3.9" parsed="|2Cor|4|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.4.6">2 Cor. 4:6</scripRef>) is the office and
person of Christ, the revealer of the glory of God (John 1:14, 18).
</def>
<term id="f-p3.12">Fair Havens</term>
<def id="f-p3.13">
A harbour in the south of Crete, some 5 miles to the east of
which was the town of Lasea (<scripRef passage="Acts 27:8" id="f-p4.1" parsed="|Acts|27|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.27.8">Acts 27:8</scripRef>). Here the ship of
Alexandria in which Paul and his companions sailed was detained
a considerable time waiting for a favourable wind. Contrary to
Paul’s advice, the master of the ship determined to prosecute
the voyage, as the harbour was deemed incommodious for wintering
in (9-12). The result was that, after a stormy voyage, the
vessel was finally wrecked on the coast of Malta (27:40-44).
</def>
<term id="f-p4.2">Fairs</term>
<def id="f-p4.3">
(Heb. ‘izabhonim), found seven times in Ezek. 27, and nowhere
else. The Authorized Version renders the word thus in all these
instances, except in verse 33, where “wares” is used. The
Revised Version uniformly renders by “wares,” which is the
correct rendering of the Hebrew word. It never means “fairs” in
the modern sense of the word.
</def>
<term id="f-p5.2">Faith</term>
<def id="f-p5.3">
Faith is in general the persuasion of the mind that a certain

statement is true (<scripRef passage="Phil. 1:27" id="f-p6.1" parsed="|Phil|1|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Phil.1.27">Phil. 1:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Thess. 2:13" id="f-p6.2" parsed="|2Thess|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Thess.2.13">2 Thess. 2:13</scripRef>). Its primary idea
is trust. A thing is true, and therefore worthy of trust. It
admits of many degrees up to full assurance of faith, in
accordance with the evidence on which it rests.
Faith is the result of teaching (Rom. 10:14-17). Knowledge is
an essential element in all faith, and is sometimes spoken of as

an equivalent to faith (<scripRef passage="John 10:38" id="f-p7.2" parsed="|John|10|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.10.38">John 10:38</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 John 2:3" id="f-p7.3" parsed="|1John|2|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.2.3">1 John 2:3</scripRef>). Yet the two are
distinguished in this respect, that faith includes in it assent,
which is an act of the will in addition to the act of the
understanding. Assent to the truth is of the essence of faith,
and the ultimate ground on which our assent to any revealed
truth rests is the veracity of God.
Historical faith is the apprehension of and assent to certain
statements which are regarded as mere facts of history.
Temporary faith is that state of mind which is awakened in men
(e.g., Felix) by the exhibition of the truth and by the
influence of religious sympathy, or by what is sometimes styled
the common operation of the Holy Spirit.
Saving faith is so called because it has eternal life
inseparably connected with it. It cannot be better defined than
in the words of the Assembly’s Shorter Catechism: “Faith in
Jesus Christ is a saving grace, whereby we receive and rest upon
him alone for salvation, as he is offered to us in the gospel.”
The object of saving faith is the whole revealed Word of God.
Faith accepts and believes it as the very truth most sure. But
the special act of faith which unites to Christ has as its

object the person and the work of the Lord Jesus Christ (<scripRef passage="John 7:38" id="f-p11.1" parsed="|John|7|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.7.38">John 7:38</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 16:31" id="f-p11.2" parsed="|Acts|16|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.16.31">Acts 16:31</scripRef>). This is the specific act of faith by which a

sinner is justified before God (<scripRef passage="Rom. 3:22" id="f-p11.3" parsed="|Rom|3|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.3.22">Rom. 3:22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Rom. 3:25" id="f-p11.4" parsed="|Rom|3|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.3.25">25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal. 2:16" id="f-p11.5" parsed="|Gal|2|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.2.16">Gal. 2:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Phil. 3:9" id="f-p11.6" parsed="|Phil|3|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Phil.3.9">Phil. 3:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 3:16-36" id="f-p11.7" parsed="|John|3|16|3|36" osisRef="Bible:John.3.16-John.3.36">John 3:16-36</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 10:43" id="f-p11.8" parsed="|Acts|10|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.10.43">Acts 10:43</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 16:31" id="f-p11.9" parsed="|Acts|16|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.16.31">16:31</scripRef>). In this act of faith the
believer appropriates and rests on Christ alone as Mediator in
all his offices.
This assent to or belief in the truth received upon the divine
testimony has always associated with it a deep sense of sin, a
distinct view of Christ, a consenting will, and a loving heart,
together with a reliance on, a trusting in, or resting in
Christ. It is that state of mind in which a poor sinner,
conscious of his sin, flees from his guilty self to Christ his
Saviour, and rolls over the burden of all his sins on him. It
consists chiefly, not in the assent given to the testimony of
God in his Word, but in embracing with fiducial reliance and
trust the one and only Saviour whom God reveals. This trust and
reliance is of the essence of faith. By faith the believer
directly and immediately appropriates Christ as his own. Faith
in its direct act makes Christ ours. It is not a work which God
graciously accepts instead of perfect obedience, but is only the
hand by which we take hold of the person and work of our
Redeemer as the only ground of our salvation.
Saving faith is a moral act, as it proceeds from a renewed
will, and a renewed will is necessary to believing assent to the

truth of God (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 2:14" id="f-p13.1" parsed="|1Cor|2|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.2.14">1 Cor. 2:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 4:4" id="f-p13.2" parsed="|2Cor|4|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.4.4">2 Cor. 4:4</scripRef>). Faith, therefore, has
its seat in the moral part of our nature fully as much as in the
intellectual. The mind must first be enlightened by divine

teaching (<scripRef passage="John 6:44" id="f-p13.3" parsed="|John|6|44|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.6.44">John 6:44</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 13:48" id="f-p13.4" parsed="|Acts|13|48|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.13.48">Acts 13:48</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 4:6" id="f-p13.5" parsed="|2Cor|4|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.4.6">2 Cor. 4:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 1:17" id="f-p13.6" parsed="|Eph|1|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.1.17">Eph. 1:17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Eph. 1:18" id="f-p13.7" parsed="|Eph|1|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.1.18">18</scripRef>)
before it can discern the things of the Spirit.
Faith is necessary to our salvation (Mark 16:16), not because
there is any merit in it, but simply because it is the sinner’s
taking the place assigned him by God, his falling in with what
God is doing.
The warrant or ground of faith is the divine testimony, not
the reasonableness of what God says, but the simple fact that he
says it. Faith rests immediately on, “Thus saith the Lord.” But
in order to this faith the veracity, sincerity, and truth of God
must be owned and appreciated, together with his
unchangeableness. God’s word encourages and emboldens the sinner
personally to transact with Christ as God’s gift, to close with
him, embrace him, give himself to Christ, and take Christ as
his. That word comes with power, for it is the word of God who
has revealed himself in his works, and especially in the cross.
God is to be believed for his word’s sake, but also for his
name’s sake.
Faith in Christ secures for the believer freedom from
condemnation, or justification before God; a participation in

the life that is in Christ, the divine life (<scripRef passage="John 14:19" id="f-p16.1" parsed="|John|14|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.14.19">John 14:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 6:4-10" id="f-p16.2" parsed="|Rom|6|4|6|10" osisRef="Bible:Rom.6.4-Rom.6.10">Rom. 6:4-10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 4:15" id="f-p16.3" parsed="|Eph|4|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.4.15">Eph. 4:15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Eph. 4:16" id="f-p16.4" parsed="|Eph|4|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.4.16">16</scripRef>, etc.); “peace with God” (<scripRef passage="Rom. 5:1" id="f-p16.5" parsed="|Rom|5|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.5.1">Rom. 5:1</scripRef>); and
sanctification (Acts 26:18; Gal. 5:6; Acts 15:9).
All who thus believe in Christ will certainly be saved (John 6:37, 40; 10:27, 28; Rom. 8:1).
The faith=the gospel (Acts 6:7; Rom. 1:5; Gal. 1:23; 1 Tim. 3:9; Jude 1:3).
</def>
<term id="f-p18.6">Faithful</term>
<def id="f-p18.7">
As a designation of Christians, means full of faith, trustful,
and not simply trustworthy (Acts 10:45; 16:1; 2 Cor. 6:15; Col. 1:2; 1 Tim. 4:3, 12; 5:16; 6:2; Titus 1:6; Eph. 1:1; 1 Cor. 4:17, etc.).
It is used also of God’s word or covenant as true and to be

trusted (<scripRef passage="Ps. 119:86" id="f-p20.1" parsed="|Ps|119|86|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.119.86">Ps. 119:86</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps. 119:138" id="f-p20.2" parsed="|Ps|119|138|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.119.138">138</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 25:1" id="f-p20.3" parsed="|Isa|25|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.25.1">Isa. 25:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Tim. 1:15" id="f-p20.4" parsed="|1Tim|1|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.1.15">1 Tim. 1:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 21:5" id="f-p20.5" parsed="|Rev|21|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.21.5">Rev. 21:5</scripRef>;
22:6, etc.).
</def>
<term id="f-p20.7">Fall of man</term>
<def id="f-p20.8">
An expression probably borrowed from the Apocryphal Book of
Wisdom, to express the fact of the revolt of our first parents
from God, and the consequent sin and misery in which they and
all their posterity were involved.
The history of the Fall is recorded in Gen. 2 and 3. That
history is to be literally interpreted. It records facts which
underlie the whole system of revealed truth. It is referred to
by our Lord and his apostles not only as being true, but as
furnishing the ground of all God’s subsequent dispensations and
dealings with the children of men. The record of Adam’s
temptation and fall must be taken as a true historical account,
if we are to understand the Bible at all as a revelation of
God’s purpose of mercy.
The effects of this first sin upon our first parents
themselves were (1) “shame, a sense of degradation and
pollution; (2) dread of the displeasure of God, or a sense of
guilt, and the consequent desire to hide from his presence.
These effects were unavoidable. They prove the loss not only of
innocence but of original righteousness, and, with it, of the
favour and fellowship of God. The state therefore to which Adam
was reduced by his disobedience, so far as his subjective
condition is concerned, was analogous to that of the fallen
angels. He was entirely and absolutely ruined” (Hodge’s
Theology).
But the unbelief and disobedience of our first parents brought
not only on themselves this misery and ruin, it entailed also
the same sad consequences on all their descendants. (1.) The
guilt, i.e., liability to punishment, of that sin comes by
imputation upon all men, because all were represented by Adam in
the covenant of works (q.v.). (See IMPUTATION.)
(2.) Hence, also, all his descendants inherit a corrupt
nature. In all by nature there is an inherent and prevailing
tendency to sin. This universal depravity is taught by universal
experience. All men sin as soon as they are capable of moral
actions. The testimony of the Scriptures to the same effect is
most abundant (Rom. 1; 2; 3:1-19, etc.).
(3.) This innate depravity is total: we are by nature “dead in
trespasses and sins,” and must be “born again” before we can
enter into the kingdom (John 3:7, etc.).
(4.) Resulting from this “corruption of our whole nature” is
our absolute moral inability to change our nature or to obey the
law of God.
Commenting on John 9:3, Ryle well remarks: “A deep and
instructive principle lies in these words. They surely throw
some light on that great question, the origin of evil. God has
thought fit to allow evil to exist in order that he may have a
platform for showing his mercy, grace, and compassion. If man
had never fallen there would have been no opportunity of showing
divine mercy. But by permitting evil, mysterious as it seems,
God’s works of grace, mercy, and wisdom in saving sinners have
been wonderfully manifested to all his creatures. The redeeming
of the church of elect sinners is the means of ‘showing to

principalities and powers the manifold wisdom of God’ (<scripRef passage="Eph. 3:10" id="f-p28.2" parsed="|Eph|3|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.3.10">Eph. 3:10</scripRef>). Without the Fall we should have known nothing of the
Cross and the Gospel.”
On the monuments of Egypt are found representations of a deity
in human form, piercing with a spear the head of a serpent. This
is regarded as an illustration of the wide dissemination of the
tradition of the Fall. The story of the “golden age,” which
gives place to the “iron age”, the age of purity and innocence,
which is followed by a time when man becomes a prey to sin and
misery, as represented in the mythology of Greece and Rome, has
also been regarded as a tradition of the Fall.
</def>
<term id="f-p29.1">Fallow-deer</term>
<def id="f-p29.2">
Deut. 14:5 (R.V., “Wild goat”); 1 Kings 4:23 (R.V., “roebucks”).
This animal, called in Hebrew yahmur, from a word meaning “to
be red,” is regarded by some as the common fallow-deer, the
Cervus dama, which is said to be found very generally over
Western and Southern Asia. It is called “fallow” from its
pale-red or yellow colour. Some interpreters, however, regard
the name as designating the bubale, Antelope bubale, the “wild
cow” of North Africa, which is about the size of a stag, like
the hartebeest of South Africa. A species of deer has been found
at Mount Carmel which is called yahmur by the Arabs. It is
said to be similar to the European roebuck.
</def>
<term id="f-p30.3">Fallow-ground</term>
<def id="f-p30.4">
The expression, “Break up your fallow ground” (Hos. 10:12; Jer. 4:3) means, “Do not sow your seed among thorns”, i.e., break off
all your evil habits; clear your hearts of weeds, in order that
they may be prepared for the seed of righteousness. Land was
allowed to lie fallow that it might become more fruitful; but
when in this condition, it soon became overgrown with thorns and
weeds. The cultivator of the soil was careful to “break up” his
fallow ground, i.e., to clear the field of weeds, before sowing
seed in it. So says the prophet, “Break off your evil ways,
repent of your sins, cease to do evil, and then the good seed of
the word will have room to grow and bear fruit.”
</def>
<term id="f-p31.3">Familiar spirit</term>
<def id="f-p31.4">
Sorcerers or necormancers, who professed to call up the dead to

answer questions, were said to have a “familiar spirit” (<scripRef passage="Deut. 18:11" id="f-p32.1" parsed="|Deut|18|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.18.11">Deut. 18:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 21:6" id="f-p32.2" parsed="|2Kgs|21|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.21.6">2 Kings 21:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 33:6" id="f-p32.3" parsed="|2Chr|33|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.33.6">2 Chr. 33:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 19:31" id="f-p32.4" parsed="|Lev|19|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.31">Lev. 19:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 20:6" id="f-p32.5" parsed="|Lev|20|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.20.6">20:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 8:19" id="f-p32.6" parsed="|Isa|8|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.8.19">Isa. 8:19</scripRef>;
29:4). Such a person was called by the Hebrews an ’ob, which
properly means a leathern bottle; for sorcerers were regarded as
vessels containing the inspiring demon. This Hebrew word was
equivalent to the pytho of the Greeks, and was used to denote
both the person and the spirit which possessed him (<scripRef passage="Lev. 20:27" id="f-p32.8" parsed="|Lev|20|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.20.27">Lev. 20:27</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 28:8" id="f-p32.9" parsed="|1Sam|28|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.28.8">1 Sam. 28:8</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Acts 16:16" id="f-p32.10" parsed="|Acts|16|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.16.16">Acts 16:16</scripRef>). The word “familiar” is from the
Latin familiaris, meaning a “household servant,” and was
intended to express the idea that sorcerers had spirits as their
servants ready to obey their commands.
</def>
<term id="f-p32.11">Famine</term>
The first mentioned in Scripture was so grievous as to compel
Abraham to go down to the land of Egypt (<scripRef passage="Gen. 26:1" id="f-p33.1" parsed="|Gen|26|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.26.1">Gen. 26:1</scripRef>). Another is
mentioned as having occurred in the days of Isaac, causing him

to go to Gerar (<scripRef passage="Gen. 26:1" id="f-p33.2" parsed="|Gen|26|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.26.1">Gen. 26:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 26:17" id="f-p33.3" parsed="|Gen|26|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.26.17">17</scripRef>). But the most remarkable of all
was that which arose in Egypt in the days of Joseph, which
lasted for seven years (Gen. 41-45).
Famines were sent as an effect of God’s anger against a guilty

people (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 8:1" id="f-p34.1" parsed="|2Kgs|8|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.8.1">2 Kings 8:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 8:2" id="f-p34.2" parsed="|2Kgs|8|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.8.2">2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Amos 8:11" id="f-p34.3" parsed="|Amos|8|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.8.11">Amos 8:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 28:22-42" id="f-p34.4" parsed="|Deut|28|22|28|42" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.22-Deut.28.42">Deut. 28:22-42</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:1" id="f-p34.5" parsed="|2Sam|21|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.1">2 Sam. 21:1</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="2 Kings 6:25-28" id="f-p34.6" parsed="|2Kgs|6|25|6|28" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.6.25-2Kgs.6.28">2 Kings 6:25-28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 25:3" id="f-p34.7" parsed="|2Kgs|25|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.25.3">25:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 14:15" id="f-p34.8" parsed="|Jer|14|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.14.15">Jer. 14:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 19:9" id="f-p34.9" parsed="|Jer|19|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.19.9">19:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 42:17" id="f-p34.10" parsed="|Jer|42|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.42.17">42:17</scripRef>, etc.). A famine
was predicted by Agabus (<scripRef passage="Acts 11:28" id="f-p34.11" parsed="|Acts|11|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.11.28">Acts 11:28</scripRef>). Josephus makes mention of
the famine which occurred A.D. 45. Helena, queen of Adiabene,
being at Jerusalem at that time, procured corn from Alexandria
and figs from Cyprus for its poor inhabitants.
</def>
<term id="f-p34.12">Fan</term>
A winnowing shovel by which grain was thrown up against the wind
that it might be cleansed from broken straw and chaff (Isa. 30:24; Jer. 15:7; Matt. 3:12). (See AGRICULTURE.)
</def>
<term id="f-p35.5">Farm</term>
<def id="f-p35.6">
(Matt. 22:5). Every Hebrew had a certain portion of land
assigned to him as a possession (<scripRef passage="Num. 26:33-56" id="f-p36.2" parsed="|Num|26|33|26|56" osisRef="Bible:Num.26.33-Num.26.56">Num. 26:33-56</scripRef>). In Egypt the
lands all belonged to the king, and the husbandmen were obliged
to give him a fifth part of the produce; so in Palestine Jehovah
was the sole possessor of the soil, and the people held it by
direct tenure from him. By the enactment of Moses, the Hebrews
paid a tithe of the produce to Jehovah, which was assigned to
the priesthood. Military service when required was also to be
rendered by every Hebrew at his own expense. The occuptaion of a
husbandman was held in high honour (1 Sam. 11:5-7; 1 Kings 19:19; 2 Chr. 26:10). (See LAND LAWS; TITHE.)
</def>
<term id="f-p36.7">Farthing</term>
<def id="f-p36.8">
(1.) Matt. 10:29; Luke 12:6. Greek assarion, i.e., a small as,
which was a Roman coin equal to a tenth of a denarius or
drachma, nearly equal to a halfpenny of our money.
(2.) Matt. 5:26; Mark 12:42 (Gr. kodrantes), the quadrant, the
fourth of an as, equal to two lepta, mites. The lepton (mite)
was the very smallest copper coin.
</def>
<term id="f-p38.3">Fast</term>
<def id="f-p38.4">
The sole fast required by the law of Moses was that of the great
Day of Atonement (q.v.), <scripRef passage="Lev. 23:26-32" id="f-p39.1" parsed="|Lev|23|26|23|32" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.26-Lev.23.32">Lev. 23:26-32</scripRef>. It is called “the fast”
(Acts 27:9).
The only other mention of a periodical fast in the Old

Testament is in <scripRef passage="Zech. 7:1-7" id="f-p40.1" parsed="|Zech|7|1|7|7" osisRef="Bible:Zech.7.1-Zech.7.7">Zech. 7:1-7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech 8:19" id="f-p40.2" parsed="|Zech|8|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.8.19">8:19</scripRef>, from which it appears that
during their captivity the Jews observed four annual fasts.
(1.) The fast of the fourth month, kept on the seventeenth day
of Tammuz, the anniversary of the capture of Jerusalem by the
Chaldeans; to commemorate also the incident recorded <scripRef passage="Ex. 32:19" id="f-p41.1" parsed="|Exod|32|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.32.19">Ex. 32:19</scripRef>.
(Comp. Jer. 52:6, 7.)
(2.) The fast of the fifth month, kept on the ninth of Ab
(comp. <scripRef passage="Num. 14:27" id="f-p42.1" parsed="|Num|14|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.14.27">Num. 14:27</scripRef>), to commemorate the burning of the city and
temple (Jer. 52:12, 13).
(3.) The fast of the seventh month, kept on the third of Tisri
(comp. <scripRef passage="2 Kings 25" id="f-p43.1" parsed="|2Kgs|25|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.25">2 Kings 25</scripRef>), the anniversary of the murder of Gedaliah
(Jer. 41:1, 2).
(4.) The fast of the tenth month (comp. Jer. 52:4; Ezek. 33:21; 2 Kings 25:1), to commemorate the beginning of the siege
of the holy city by Nebuchadnezzar.
There was in addition to these the fast appointed by Esther
Public national fasts on account of sin or to supplicate
divine favour were sometimes held. (1.) 1 Sam. 7:6; (2.) 2 Chr. 20:3; (3.) Jer. 36:6-10; (4.) Neh. 9:1.
There were also local fasts. (1.) Judg. 20:26; (2.) 2 Sam. 1:12; (3.) 1 Sam. 31:13; (4.) 1 Kings 21:9-12; (5.) Ezra 8:21-23: (6.) Jonah 3:5-9.
There are many instances of private occasional fasting (1 Sam. 1:7: 20:34; 2 Sam. 3:35; 12:16; 1 Kings 21:27; Ezra 10:6; Neh. 1:4; Dan. 10:2, 3). Moses fasted forty days (Ex. 24:18; 34:28),
and so also did Elijah (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 19:8" id="f-p48.11" parsed="|1Kgs|19|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.19.8">1 Kings 19:8</scripRef>). Our Lord fasted forty
days in the wilderness (Matt. 4:2).
In the lapse of time the practice of fasting was lamentably

abused (<scripRef passage="Isa. 58:4" id="f-p49.1" parsed="|Isa|58|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.58.4">Isa. 58:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 14:12" id="f-p49.2" parsed="|Jer|14|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.14.12">Jer. 14:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 7:5" id="f-p49.3" parsed="|Zech|7|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.7.5">Zech. 7:5</scripRef>). Our Lord rebuked the

Pharisees for their hypocritical pretences in fasting (<scripRef passage="Matt. 6:16" id="f-p49.4" parsed="|Matt|6|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.16">Matt. 6:16</scripRef>). He himself appointed no fast. The early Christians,
however, observed the ordinary fasts according to the law of
their fathers (Acts 13:3; 14:23; 2 Cor. 6:5).
</def>
<term id="f-p49.8">Fat</term>
<def id="f-p49.9">
(Heb. heleb) denotes the richest part of the animal, or the

fattest of the flock, in the account of Abel’s sacrifice (<scripRef passage="Gen. 4:4" id="f-p50.1" parsed="|Gen|4|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.4.4">Gen. 4:4</scripRef>). It sometimes denotes the best of any production (<scripRef passage="Gen. 45:18" id="f-p50.2" parsed="|Gen|45|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.45.18">Gen. 45:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 18:12" id="f-p50.3" parsed="|Num|18|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.18.12">Num. 18:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 81:16" id="f-p50.4" parsed="|Ps|81|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.81.16">Ps. 81:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 147:47" id="f-p50.5" parsed="|Ps|147|47|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.147.47">147:47</scripRef>). The fat of sacrifices was
to be burned (Lev. 3:9-11; 4:8; 7:3; 8:25; Num. 18:17. Comp. Ex. 29:13-22; Lev. 3:3-5).
It is used figuratively for a dull, stupid state of mind (Ps 17:10).
In Joel 2:24 the word is equivalent to “vat,” a vessel. The
hebrew word here thus rendered is elsewhere rendered “wine-fat”
and “press-fat” (Hag. 2:16; Isa. 63:2).
</def>
<term id="f-p52.4">Father</term>
<def id="f-p52.5">
A name applied (1) to any ancestor (Deut. 1:11; 1 Kings 15:11;

<scripRef passage="Matt. 3:9" id="f-p53.3" parsed="|Matt|3|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.9">Matt. 3:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 23:30" id="f-p53.4" parsed="|Matt|23|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.23.30">23:30</scripRef>, etc.); and (2) as a title of respect to a

chief, ruler, or elder, etc. (<scripRef passage="Judg. 17:10" id="f-p53.5" parsed="|Judg|17|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.17.10">Judg. 17:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg 18:19" id="f-p53.6" parsed="|Judg|18|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.18.19">18:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 10:12" id="f-p53.7" parsed="|1Sam|10|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.10.12">1 Sam. 10:12</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="2 Kings 2:12" id="f-p53.8" parsed="|2Kgs|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.2.12">2 Kings 2:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 23:9" id="f-p53.9" parsed="|Matt|23|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.23.9">Matt. 23:9</scripRef>, etc.). (3) The author or beginner of
anything is also so called; e.g., Jabal and Jubal (Gen. 4:20, 21; comp. Job 38:28).
Applied to God (Ex. 4:22; Deut. 32:6; 2 Sam. 7:14; Ps. 89:27, 28, etc.). (1.) As denoting his covenant relation to the Jews
(Jer. 31:9; Isa. 63:16; 64:8; John 8:41, etc.).
(2.) Believers are called God’s “sons” (John 1:12; Rom. 8:16;

<scripRef passage="Matt. 6:4" id="f-p55.3" parsed="|Matt|6|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.4">Matt. 6:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 6:8" id="f-p55.4" parsed="|Matt|6|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.8">8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 6:15" id="f-p55.5" parsed="|Matt|6|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.15">15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 6:18" id="f-p55.6" parsed="|Matt|6|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.18">18</scripRef>; 10:20, 29). They also call him “Father”
(Rom. 1:7; 1 Cor. 1:3; 2 Cor. 1:2; Gal. 1:4)
</def>
<term id="f-p55.11">Fathom</term>
(Old A.S. faethm, “bosom,” or the outstretched arms), a span of
six feet (<scripRef passage="Acts 27:28" id="f-p56.1" parsed="|Acts|27|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.27.28">Acts 27:28</scripRef>). Gr. orguia (from orego, “I stretch”), the
distance between the extremities of both arms fully stretched
out.
</def>
<term id="f-p56.2">Fatling</term>
<def id="f-p56.3">
(1.) A fatted animal for slaughter (2 Sam. 6:13; Isa. 11:6;

<scripRef passage="Ezek. 39:18" id="f-p57.3" parsed="|Ezek|39|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.39.18">Ezek. 39:18</scripRef>. Comp. <scripRef passage="Matt. 22:4" id="f-p57.4" parsed="|Matt|22|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.22.4">Matt. 22:4</scripRef>, where the word used in the
original, sitistos, means literally “corn-fed;” i.e., installed,
fat). (2.) <scripRef passage="Ps. 66:15" id="f-p57.5" parsed="|Ps|66|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.66.15">Ps. 66:15</scripRef> (Heb. meah, meaning “marrowy,” “fat,” a
species of sheep). (3.) <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 15:9" id="f-p57.6" parsed="|1Sam|15|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.15.9">1 Sam. 15:9</scripRef> (Heb. mishneh, meaning “the
second,” and hence probably “cattle of a second quality,” or
lambs of the second birth, i.e., autmnal lambs, and therfore of
less value).
</def>
<term id="f-p57.7">Fear of the Lord the</term>
<def id="f-p57.8">
Is in the Old Testament used as a designation of true piety

(<scripRef passage="Prov. 1:7" id="f-p58.1" parsed="|Prov|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.1.7">Prov. 1:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 28:28" id="f-p58.2" parsed="|Job|28|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.28.28">Job 28:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 19:9" id="f-p58.3" parsed="|Ps|19|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.19.9">Ps. 19:9</scripRef>). It is a fear conjoined with
love and hope, and is therefore not a slavish dread, but rather

filial reverence. (Comp. <scripRef passage="Deut. 32:6" id="f-p58.4" parsed="|Deut|32|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.6">Deut. 32:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos. 11:1" id="f-p58.5" parsed="|Hos|11|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.11.1">Hos. 11:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 1:2" id="f-p58.6" parsed="|Isa|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.2">Isa. 1:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 63:16" id="f-p58.7" parsed="|Isa|63|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.63.16">63:16</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Isa 64:8" id="f-p58.8" parsed="|Isa|64|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.64.8">64:8</scripRef>.) God is called “the Fear of Isaac” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 31:42" id="f-p58.9" parsed="|Gen|31|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.42">Gen. 31:42</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 31:53" id="f-p58.10" parsed="|Gen|31|53|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.53">53</scripRef>), i.e.,
the God whom Isaac feared.
A holy fear is enjoined also in the New Testament as a
preventive of carelessness in religion, and as an incentive to

penitence (<scripRef passage="Matt. 10:28" id="f-p59.1" parsed="|Matt|10|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.10.28">Matt. 10:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 5:11" id="f-p59.2" parsed="|2Cor|5|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.5.11">2 Cor. 5:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 7:1" id="f-p59.3" parsed="|2Cor|7|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.7.1">7:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Phil. 2:12" id="f-p59.4" parsed="|Phil|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Phil.2.12">Phil. 2:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 5:21" id="f-p59.5" parsed="|Eph|5|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.5.21">Eph. 5:21</scripRef>;
Heb. 12:28, 29).
</def>
<term id="f-p59.8">Feast</term>
<def id="f-p59.9">
As a mark of hospitality (Gen. 19:3; 2 Sam. 3:20; 2 Kings 6:23);

on occasions of domestic joy (<scripRef passage="Luke 15:23" id="f-p60.4" parsed="|Luke|15|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.15.23">Luke 15:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen. 21:8" id="f-p60.5" parsed="|Gen|21|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.8">Gen. 21:8</scripRef>); on

birthdays (<scripRef passage="Gen. 40:20" id="f-p60.6" parsed="|Gen|40|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.40.20">Gen. 40:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 1:4" id="f-p60.7" parsed="|Job|1|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.1.4">Job 1:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 14:6" id="f-p60.8" parsed="|Matt|14|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.14.6">Matt. 14:6</scripRef>); and on the occasion
of a marriage (Judg. 14:10; Gen. 29:22).
Feasting was a part of the observances connected with the

offering up of sacrifices (<scripRef passage="Deut. 12:6" id="f-p61.1" parsed="|Deut|12|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.12.6">Deut. 12:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 12:7" id="f-p61.2" parsed="|Deut|12|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.12.7">7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 9:19" id="f-p61.3" parsed="|1Sam|9|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.9.19">1 Sam. 9:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 16:3" id="f-p61.4" parsed="|1Sam|16|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.16.3">16:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 16:5" id="f-p61.5" parsed="|1Sam|16|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.16.5">5</scripRef>),
and with the annual festivals (<scripRef passage="Deut. 16:11" id="f-p61.6" parsed="|Deut|16|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.16.11">Deut. 16:11</scripRef>). “It was one of the
designs of the greater solemnities, which required the
attendance of the people at the sacred tent, that the oneness of
the nation might be maintained and cemented together, by
statedly congregating in one place, and with one soul taking
part in the same religious services. But that oneness was
primarily and chiefly a religious and not merely a political
one; the people were not merely to meet as among themselves, but
with Jehovah, and to present themselves before him as one body;
the meeting was in its own nature a binding of themselves in
fellowship with Jehovah; so that it was not politics and
commerce that had here to do, but the soul of the Mosaic
dispensation, the foundation of the religious and political
existence of Israel, the covenant with Jehovah. To keep the
people’s consciousness alive to this, to revive, strengthen, and
perpetuate it, nothing could be so well adapated as these annual
feasts.” (See FESTIVALS.)
</def>
<term id="f-p61.8">Felix</term>
<def id="f-p61.9">
Happy, the Roman procurator of Judea before whom Paul “reasoned”
(<scripRef passage="Acts 24:25" id="f-p62.1" parsed="|Acts|24|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.24.25">Acts 24:25</scripRef>). He appears to have expected a bribe from Paul, and
therefore had several interviews with him. The “worthy deeds”
referred to in 24:2 was his clearing the country of banditti and
impostors.
At the end of a two years’ term, Porcius Festus was appointed
in the room of Felix (A.D. 60), who proceeded to Rome, and was
there accused of cruelty and malversation of office by the Jews
of Caesarea. The accusation was rendered nugatory by the
influence of his brother Pallas with Nero. (See Josephus, Ant.
Drusilla, the daughter of Herod Agrippa, having been induced
by Felix to desert her husband, the king of Emesa, became his
adulterous companion. She was seated beside him when Paul
“reasoned” before the judge. When Felix gave place to Festus,
being “willing to do the Jews a pleasure,” he left Paul bound.
</def>
<term id="f-p64.1">Fellowship</term>
<def id="f-p64.2">
(1.) With God, consisting in the knowledge of his will (Job 22:21; John 17:3); agreement with his designs (Amos 3:2); mutual

affection (<scripRef passage="Rom. 8" id="f-p65.4" parsed="|Rom|8|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.8">Rom. 8</scripRef>: 38, 39); enjoyment of his presence (<scripRef passage="Ps. 4:6" id="f-p65.5" parsed="|Ps|4|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.4.6">Ps. 4:6</scripRef>);

conformity to his image (<scripRef passage="1 John 2:6" id="f-p65.6" parsed="|1John|2|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.2.6">1 John 2:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 John 1:6" id="f-p65.7" parsed="|1John|1|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.1.6">1:6</scripRef>); and participation of
his felicity (1 John 1:3, 4; Eph. 3:14-21).
(2.) Of saints with one another, in duties (Rom. 12:5; 1 Cor. 12:1; 1 Thess. 5:17, 18); in ordinances (Heb. 10:25; Acts 2:46);

in grace, love, joy, etc. (<scripRef passage="Mal. 3:16" id="f-p66.7" parsed="|Mal|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mal.3.16">Mal. 3:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 8:4" id="f-p66.8" parsed="|2Cor|8|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.8.4">2 Cor. 8:4</scripRef>); mutual

interest, spiritual and temporal (<scripRef passage="Rom. 12:4" id="f-p66.9" parsed="|Rom|12|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.12.4">Rom. 12:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Rom. 12:13" id="f-p66.10" parsed="|Rom|12|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.12.13">13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 13:16" id="f-p66.11" parsed="|Heb|13|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.13.16">Heb. 13:16</scripRef>); in

sufferings (<scripRef passage="Rom. 15:1" id="f-p66.12" parsed="|Rom|15|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.15.1">Rom. 15:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Rom 15:2" id="f-p66.13" parsed="|Rom|15|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.15.2">2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal. 6:1" id="f-p66.14" parsed="|Gal|6|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.6.1">Gal. 6:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gal 6:2" id="f-p66.15" parsed="|Gal|6|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.6.2">2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 12:15" id="f-p66.16" parsed="|Rom|12|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.12.15">Rom. 12:15</scripRef>; and in glory
(Rev. 7:9).
</def>
<term id="f-p66.18">Fence</term>
(Heb. gader), Num. 22:24 (R.V.). Fences were constructions of
unmortared stones, to protect gardens, vineyards, sheepfolds,
etc. From various causes they were apt to bulge out and fall

(<scripRef passage="Ps. 62:3" id="f-p67.2" parsed="|Ps|62|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.62.3">Ps. 62:3</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="Ps. 80:12" id="f-p67.3" parsed="|Ps|80|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.80.12">Ps. 80:12</scripRef>, R.V. (see <scripRef passage="Isa. 5:5" id="f-p67.4" parsed="|Isa|5|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.5.5">Isa. 5:5</scripRef>), the psalmist
says, “Why hast thou broken down her fences?” Serpents delight
to lurk in the crevices of such fences (Eccl. 10:8; comp. Amos 5:19).
</def>
<term id="f-p67.7">Fenced cities</term>
<def id="f-p67.8">
There were in Palestine (1) cities, (2) unwalled villages, and
(3) villages with castles or towers (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 27:25" id="f-p68.1" parsed="|1Chr|27|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.27.25">1 Chr. 27:25</scripRef>). Cities, so
called, had walls, and were thus fenced. The fortifications
consisted of one or two walls, on which were towers or parapets

at regular intervals (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 32:5" id="f-p68.2" parsed="|2Chr|32|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.32.5">2 Chr. 32:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 31:38" id="f-p68.3" parsed="|Jer|31|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.31.38">Jer. 31:38</scripRef>). Around ancient
Jerusalem were three walls, on one of which were ninety towers,
on the second fourteen, and on the third sixty. The tower of
Hananeel, near the north-east corner of the city wall, is

frequently referred to (<scripRef passage="Neh. 3:1" id="f-p68.4" parsed="|Neh|3|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.3.1">Neh. 3:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh 12:39" id="f-p68.5" parsed="|Neh|12|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.12.39">12:39</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 14:10" id="f-p68.6" parsed="|Zech|14|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.14.10">Zech. 14:10</scripRef>). The
