gateways of such cities were also fortified (<scripRef passage="Neh. 2:8" id="f-p68.7" parsed="|Neh|2|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.2.8">Neh. 2:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh 3:3" id="f-p68.8" parsed="|Neh|3|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.3.3">3:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Neh 3:6" id="f-p68.9" parsed="|Neh|3|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.3.6">6</scripRef>;
Judg. 16:2, 3; 1 Sam. 23:7).
The Hebrews found many fenced cities when they entered the

Promised Land (<scripRef passage="Num. 13:28" id="f-p69.1" parsed="|Num|13|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.13.28">Num. 13:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 32:17" id="f-p69.2" parsed="|Num|32|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.32.17">32:17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num 32:34-42" id="f-p69.3" parsed="|Num|32|34|32|42" osisRef="Bible:Num.32.34-Num.32.42">34-42</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 11:12" id="f-p69.4" parsed="|Josh|11|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.12">Josh. 11:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 11:13" id="f-p69.5" parsed="|Josh|11|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.13">13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 1:27-33" id="f-p69.6" parsed="|Judg|1|27|1|33" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.27-Judg.1.33">Judg. 1:27-33</scripRef>), and we may estimate the strength of some of these
cities from the fact that they were long held in possession by
the Canaanites. The Jebusites, e.g., were enabled to hold
possession of Jerusalem till the time of David (2 Sam. 5:6, 7; 1 Chr. 11:5).
Several of the kings of Israel and Judah distinguished
themselves as fortifiers or “builders” of cities.
</def>
<term id="f-p70.1">Ferret</term>
<def id="f-p70.2">
Lev. 11:30 (R.V., “gecko”), one of the unclean creeping things.
It was perhaps the Lacerta gecko which was intended by the
Hebrew word (anakah, a cry, “mourning,” the creature which
groans) here used, i.e., the “fan-footed” lizard, the gecko
which makes a mournful wail. The LXX. translate it by a word
meaning “shrew-mouse,” of which there are three species in
Palestine. The Rabbinical writers regard it as the hedgehog. The
translation of the Revised Version is to be preferred.
</def>
<term id="f-p71.2">Ferry boat</term>
<def id="f-p71.3">
(2 Sam. 19:18), some kind of boat for crossing the river which
the men of Judah placed at the service of the king. Floats or
rafts for this purpose were in use from remote times (Isa. 18:2).
</def>
<term id="f-p72.3">Festivals, Religious</term>
<def id="f-p72.4">
There were daily (Lev. 23), weekly, monthly, and yearly
festivals, and great stress was laid on the regular observance
of them in every particular (Num. 28:1-8; Ex. 29:38-42; Lev. 6:8-23; Ex. 30:7-9; 27:20).
(1.) The septenary festivals were,
(a) The weekly Sabbath (Lev. 23:1-3; Ex. 19:3-30; 20:8-11;
31:12, etc.).
(b) The seventh new moon, or the feast of Trumpets (Num. 28:11-15; 29:1-6).
(c) The Sabbatical year (Ex. 23:10, 11; Lev. 25:2-7).
(d) The year of jubilee (Lev. 23-35; 25: 8-16; 27:16-25).
(2.) The great feasts were,
(a) The Passover. (b) The feast of Pentecost, or of weeks. (c)
The feast of Tabernacles, or of ingathering.
On each of these occasions every male Israelite was commanded

“to appear before the Lord” (<scripRef passage="Deut. 27:7" id="f-p81.1" parsed="|Deut|27|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.27.7">Deut. 27:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh. 8:9-12" id="f-p81.2" parsed="|Neh|8|9|8|12" osisRef="Bible:Neh.8.9-Neh.8.12">Neh. 8:9-12</scripRef>). The

attendance of women was voluntary. (Comp. <scripRef passage="Luke 2:41" id="f-p81.3" parsed="|Luke|2|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.41">Luke 2:41</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 1:7" id="f-p81.4" parsed="|1Sam|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.1.7">1 Sam. 1:7</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 2:19" id="f-p81.5" parsed="|1Sam|2|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.2.19">2:19</scripRef>.) The promise that God would protect their homes (<scripRef passage="Ex. 34:23" id="f-p81.6" parsed="|Exod|34|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.34.23">Ex. 34:23</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex 34:24" id="f-p81.7" parsed="|Exod|34|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.34.24">24</scripRef>) while all the males were absent in Jerusalem at these
feasts was always fulfilled. “During the whole period between
Moses and Christ we never read of an enemy invading the land at
the time of the three festivals. The first instance on record is
thirty-three years after they had withdrawn from themselves the
divine protection by imbruing their hands in the Saviour’s
blood, when Cestius, the Roman general, slew fifty of the people
of Lydda while all the rest had gone up to the feast of
Tabernacles, A.D. 66.”
These festivals, besides their religious purpose, had an
important bearing on the maintenance among the people of the
feeling of a national unity. The times fixed for their
observance were arranged so as to interfere as little as
possible with the industry of the people. The Passover was kept
just before the harvest commenced, Pentecost at the conclusion
of the corn harvest and before the vintage, the feast of
Tabernacles after all the fruits of the ground had been gathered
in.
(3.) The Day of Atonement, the tenth day of the seventh month
(Lev. 16:1, 34; 23:26-32; Num. 29:7-11). (See ATONEMENT, DAY OF.)
Of the post-Exilian festivals reference is made to the feast
of Dedication (<scripRef passage="John 10:22" id="f-p84.1" parsed="|John|10|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.10.22">John 10:22</scripRef>). This feast was appointed by Judas
Maccabaeus in commemoration of the purification of the temple
after it had been polluted by Antiochus Epiphanes. The “feast of
Purim” (q.v.), <scripRef passage="Esther 9:24-32" id="f-p84.2" parsed="|Esth|9|24|9|32" osisRef="Bible:Esth.9.24-Esth.9.32">Esther 9:24-32</scripRef>, was also instituted after the
Exile. (Cf. John 5:1.)
</def>
<term id="f-p84.4">Festus, Porcius</term>
<def id="f-p84.5">
The successor of Felix (A.D. 60) as procurator of Judea (Acts 24:27). A few weeks after he had entered on his office the case
of Paul, then a prisoner at Caesarea, was reported to him. The
“next day,” after he had gone down to Caesarea, he heard Paul
defend himself in the presence of Herod Agrippa II. and his
sister Bernice, and not finding in him anything worthy of death
or of bonds, would have set him free had he not appealed unto

Caesar (<scripRef passage="Acts 25:11" id="f-p85.2" parsed="|Acts|25|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.25.11">Acts 25:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 25:12" id="f-p85.3" parsed="|Acts|25|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.25.12">12</scripRef>). In consequence of this appeal Paul was
sent to Rome. Festus, after being in office less than two years,
died in Judea. (See AGRIPPA.)
</def>
<term id="f-p85.5">Fever</term>
<def id="f-p85.6">
(Deut. 28:22; Matt. 8:14; Mark 1:30; John 4:52; Acts 28:8), a
burning heat, as the word so rendered denotes, which attends all
febrile attacks. In all Eastern countries such diseases are very
common. Peter’s wife’s mother is said to have suffered from a
“great fever” (<scripRef passage="Luke 4:38" id="f-p86.6" parsed="|Luke|4|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.4.38">Luke 4:38</scripRef>), an instance of Luke’s professional
exactitude in describing disease. He adopts here the technical
medical distinction, as in those times fevers were divided into
the “great” and the “less.”
</def>
<term id="f-p86.7">Field</term>
<def id="f-p86.8">
(Heb. sadeh), a cultivated field, but unenclosed. It is applied

to any cultivated ground or pasture (<scripRef passage="Gen. 29:2" id="f-p87.1" parsed="|Gen|29|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.29.2">Gen. 29:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 31:4" id="f-p87.2" parsed="|Gen|31|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.4">31:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 34:7" id="f-p87.3" parsed="|Gen|34|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.34.7">34:7</scripRef>), or

tillage (<scripRef passage="Gen. 37:7" id="f-p87.4" parsed="|Gen|37|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.7">Gen. 37:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 47:24" id="f-p87.5" parsed="|Gen|47|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.47.24">47:24</scripRef>). It is also applied to woodland (<scripRef passage="Ps. 132:6" id="f-p87.6" parsed="|Ps|132|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.132.6">Ps. 132:6</scripRef>) or mountain top (<scripRef passage="Judg. 9:32" id="f-p87.7" parsed="|Judg|9|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.9.32">Judg. 9:32</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Judg. 9:36" id="f-p87.8" parsed="|Judg|9|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.9.36">36</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 1:21" id="f-p87.9" parsed="|2Sam|1|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.1.21">2 Sam. 1:21</scripRef>). It denotes

sometimes a cultivated region as opposed to the wilderness (<scripRef passage="Gen. 33:19" id="f-p87.10" parsed="|Gen|33|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.33.19">Gen. 33:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 36:35" id="f-p87.11" parsed="|Gen|36|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36.35">36:35</scripRef>). Unwalled villages or scattered houses are spoken

of as “in the fields” (<scripRef passage="Deut. 28:3" id="f-p87.12" parsed="|Deut|28|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.3">Deut. 28:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 28:16" id="f-p87.13" parsed="|Deut|28|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.16">16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 25:31" id="f-p87.14" parsed="|Lev|25|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.25.31">Lev. 25:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 6:36" id="f-p87.15" parsed="|Mark|6|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.6.36">Mark 6:36</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Mark 6:56" id="f-p87.16" parsed="|Mark|6|56|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.6.56">56</scripRef>). The “open field” is a place remote from a house (<scripRef passage="Gen. 4:8" id="f-p87.17" parsed="|Gen|4|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.4.8">Gen. 4:8</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Lev. 14:7" id="f-p87.18" parsed="|Lev|14|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.14.7">Lev. 14:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 14:53" id="f-p87.19" parsed="|Lev|14|53|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.14.53">53</scripRef>; 17:5). Cultivated land of any extent was called a
field (Gen. 23:13, 17; 41:8; Lev. 27:16; Ruth 4:5; Neh. 12:29).
</def>
<term id="f-p87.25">Fig</term>
First mentioned in Gen. 3:7. The fig-tree is mentioned (Deut. 8:8) as one of the valuable products of Palestine. It was a sign

of peace and prosperity (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:25" id="f-p88.3" parsed="|1Kgs|4|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.25">1 Kings 4:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Micah 4:4" id="f-p88.4" parsed="|Mic|4|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.4.4">Micah 4:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zech. 3:10" id="f-p88.5" parsed="|Zech|3|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.3.10">Zech. 3:10</scripRef>).
Figs were used medicinally (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 20:7" id="f-p88.6" parsed="|2Kgs|20|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.20.7">2 Kings 20:7</scripRef>), and pressed together
and formed into “cakes” as articles of diet (1 Sam. 30:12; Jer. 24:2).
Our Lord’s cursing the fig-tree near Bethany (Mark 11:13) has
occasioned much perplexity from the circumstance, as mentioned
by the evangelist, that “the time of figs was not yet.” The
explanation of the words, however, lies in the simple fact that
the fruit of the fig-tree appears before the leaves, and hence
that if the tree produced leaves it ought also to have had
fruit. It ought to have had fruit if it had been true to its
“pretensions,” in showing its leaves at this particular season.
“This tree, so to speak, vaunted itself to be in advance of all
the other trees, challenged the passer-by that he should come
and refresh himself with its fruit. Yet when the Lord accepted
its challenge and drew near, it proved to be but as the others,
without fruit as they; for indeed, as the evangelist observes,
the time of figs had not yet arrived. Its fault, if one may use
the word, lay in its pretensions, in its making a show to run
before the rest when it did not so indeed” (Trench, Miracles).
The fig-tree of Palestine (Ficus carica) produces two and
sometimes three crops of figs in a year, (1) the bikkurah, or

“early-ripe fig” (<scripRef passage="Micah 7:1" id="f-p90.1" parsed="|Mic|7|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.7.1">Micah 7:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 28:4" id="f-p90.2" parsed="|Isa|28|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.28.4">Isa. 28:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos. 9:10" id="f-p90.3" parsed="|Hos|9|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.9.10">Hos. 9:10</scripRef>, R.V.), which
is ripe about the end of June, dropping off as soon as it is
ripe (<scripRef passage="Nah. 3:12" id="f-p90.4" parsed="|Nah|3|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Nah.3.12">Nah. 3:12</scripRef>); (2) the kermus, or “summer fig,” then begins
to be formed, and is ripe about August; and (3) the pag (plural

“green figs,” <scripRef passage="Cant. 2:13" id="f-p90.5" parsed="|Song|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.2.13">Cant. 2:13</scripRef>; Gr. olynthos, <scripRef passage="Rev. 6:13" id="f-p90.6" parsed="|Rev|6|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.6.13">Rev. 6:13</scripRef>, “the untimely
fig”), or “winter fig,” which ripens in sheltered spots in
spring.
</def>
<term id="f-p90.7">Fillets</term>
<def id="f-p90.8">
Heb. hashukum, plur., joinings (Ex. 27:17; 38:17, 28), the rods
by which the tops of the columns around the tabernacle court
were joined together, and from which the curtains were suspended
(Ex. 27:10, 11; 36:38).
In Jer. 52:21 the rendering of a different word, hut,
meaning a “thread,” and designating a measuring-line of 12
cubits in length for the circumference of the copper pillars of
Solomon’s temple.
</def>
<term id="f-p92.2">Finer</term>
<def id="f-p92.3">
A worker in silver and gold (Prov. 25:4). In Judg. 17:4 the word
(tsoreph) is rendered “founder,” and in Isa. 41:7 “goldsmith.”
</def>
<term id="f-p93.4">Fining pot</term>
<def id="f-p93.5">
A crucible, melting-pot (Prov. 17:3; 27:21).
</def>
<term id="f-p94.3">Fir</term>
<def id="f-p94.4">
The uniform rendering in the Authorized Version (marg. R.V.,
“cypress”) of berosh (2 Sam. 6:5; 1 Kings 5:8, 10; 6:15, 34;
9:11, etc.), a lofty tree (<scripRef passage="Isa. 55:13" id="f-p95.4" parsed="|Isa|55|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.55.13">Isa. 55:13</scripRef>) growing on Lebanon
(37:24). Its wood was used in making musical instruments and
doors of houses, and for ceilings (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 3:5" id="f-p95.5" parsed="|2Chr|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.3.5">2 Chr. 3:5</scripRef>), the decks of

ships (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:5" id="f-p95.6" parsed="|Ezek|27|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.5">Ezek. 27:5</scripRef>), floorings and spear-shafts (<scripRef passage="Nah. 2:3" id="f-p95.7" parsed="|Nah|2|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Nah.2.3">Nah. 2:3</scripRef>, R.V.).
The true fir (abies) is not found in Palestine, but the pine
tree, of which there are four species, is common.
The precise kind of tree meant by the “green fir tree” (Hos. 14:8) is uncertain. Some regard it as the sherbin tree, a
cypress resembling the cedar; others, the Aleppo or maritime
pine (Pinus halepensis), which resembles the Scotch fir; while
others think that the “stone-pine” (Pinus pinea) is probably
meant. (See PINE.)
</def>
<term id="f-p96.3">Fire</term>
<def id="f-p96.4">
(1.) For sacred purposes. The sacrifices were consumed by fire
(<scripRef passage="Gen. 8:20" id="f-p97.1" parsed="|Gen|8|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.8.20">Gen. 8:20</scripRef>). The ever-burning fire on the altar was first

kindled from heaven (<scripRef passage="Lev. 6:9" id="f-p97.2" parsed="|Lev|6|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.6.9">Lev. 6:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 6:13" id="f-p97.3" parsed="|Lev|6|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.6.13">13</scripRef>; 9:24), and afterwards

rekindled at the dedication of Solomon’s temple (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 7:1" id="f-p97.4" parsed="|2Chr|7|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.7.1">2 Chr. 7:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 7:3" id="f-p97.5" parsed="|2Chr|7|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.7.3">3</scripRef>).
The expressions “fire from heaven” and “fire of the Lord”
generally denote lightning, but sometimes also the fire of the
altar was so called (Ex. 29:18; Lev. 1:9; 2:3; 3:5, 9).
Fire for a sacred purpose obtained otherwise than from the
altar was called “strange fire” (Lev. 10:1, 2; Num. 3:4).
The victims slain for sin offerings were afterwards consumed
by fire outside the camp (Lev. 4:12, 21; 6:30; 16:27; Heb. 13:11).
(2.) For domestic purposes, such as baking, cooking, warmth,

etc. (<scripRef passage="Jer. 36:22" id="f-p100.1" parsed="|Jer|36|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.36.22">Jer. 36:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 14:54" id="f-p100.2" parsed="|Mark|14|54|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.14.54">Mark 14:54</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 18:18" id="f-p100.3" parsed="|John|18|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.18.18">John 18:18</scripRef>). But on Sabbath no
fire for any domestic purpose was to be kindled (Ex. 35:3; Num. 15:32-36).
(3.) Punishment of death by fire was inflicted on such as were
guilty of certain forms of unchastity and incest (<scripRef passage="Lev. 20:14" id="f-p101.1" parsed="|Lev|20|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.20.14">Lev. 20:14</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Lev 21:9" id="f-p101.2" parsed="|Lev|21|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.21.9">21:9</scripRef>). The burning of captives in war was not unknown among the

Jews (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 12:31" id="f-p101.3" parsed="|2Sam|12|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.12.31">2 Sam. 12:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 29:22" id="f-p101.4" parsed="|Jer|29|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.29.22">Jer. 29:22</scripRef>). The bodies of infamous persons
who were executed were also sometimes burned (Josh. 7:25; 2 Kings 23:16).
(4.) In war, fire was used in the destruction of cities, as

Jericho (<scripRef passage="Josh. 6:24" id="f-p102.1" parsed="|Josh|6|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.6.24">Josh. 6:24</scripRef>), Ai (8:19), Hazor (11:11), Laish (<scripRef passage="Judg. 18:27" id="f-p102.2" parsed="|Judg|18|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.18.27">Judg. 18:27</scripRef>), etc. The war-chariots of the Canaanites were burnt

(<scripRef passage="Josh. 11:6" id="f-p102.3" parsed="|Josh|11|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.6">Josh. 11:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 11:9" id="f-p102.4" parsed="|Josh|11|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.9">9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 11:13" id="f-p102.5" parsed="|Josh|11|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.13">13</scripRef>). The Israelites burned the images (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 10:26" id="f-p102.6" parsed="|2Kgs|10|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.10.26">2 Kings 10:26</scripRef>; R.V., “pillars”) of the house of Baal. These objects of
worship seem to have been of the nature of obelisks, and were
sometimes evidently made of wood.
Torches were sometimes carried by the soldiers in battle
(Judg. 7:16).
(5.) Figuratively, fire is a symbol of Jehovah’s presence and
the instrument of his power (Ex. 14:19; Num. 11:1, 3; Judg. 13:20; 1 Kings 18:38; 2 Kings 1:10, 12; 2:11; Isa. 6:4; Ezek. 1:4; Rev. 1:14, etc.).
God’s word is also likened unto fire (Jer. 23:29). It is

referred to as an emblem of severe trials or misfortunes (<scripRef passage="Zech. 12:6" id="f-p105.2" parsed="|Zech|12|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.12.6">Zech. 12:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 12:49" id="f-p105.3" parsed="|Luke|12|49|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.12.49">Luke 12:49</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 3:13" id="f-p105.4" parsed="|1Cor|3|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.3.13">1 Cor. 3:13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 3:15" id="f-p105.5" parsed="|1Cor|3|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.3.15">15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Pet. 1:7" id="f-p105.6" parsed="|1Pet|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.1.7">1 Pet. 1:7</scripRef>), and of eternal
punishment (Matt. 5:22; Mark 9:44; Rev. 14:10; 21:8).
The influence of the Holy Ghost is likened unto fire (Matt. 3:11). His descent was denoted by the appearance of tongues as
of fire (Acts 2:3).
</def>
<term id="f-p106.3">Firebrand</term>
Isa. 7:4, Amos 4:11, Zech. 3:2, denotes the burnt end of a stick
(Heb. ‘ud); in <scripRef passage="Judg. 15:4" id="f-p107.4" parsed="|Judg|15|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.15.4">Judg. 15:4</scripRef>, a lamp or torch, a flambeau (Heb.

lappid); in <scripRef passage="Prov. 26:18" id="f-p107.5" parsed="|Prov|26|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.26.18">Prov. 26:18</scripRef> (comp. <scripRef passage="Eph. 6:16" id="f-p107.6" parsed="|Eph|6|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.6.16">Eph. 6:16</scripRef>), burning darts or
arrows (Heb. zikkim).
</def>
<term id="f-p107.7">Firepan</term>
(Ex. 27:3; 38:3), one of the vessels of the temple service

(rendered “snuff-dish” <scripRef passage="Ex. 25:38" id="f-p108.3" parsed="|Exod|25|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.25.38">Ex. 25:38</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 37:23" id="f-p108.4" parsed="|Exod|37|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.37.23">37:23</scripRef>; and “censer” <scripRef passage="Lev. 10:1" id="f-p108.5" parsed="|Lev|10|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.10.1">Lev. 10:1</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Lev 16:12" id="f-p108.6" parsed="|Lev|16|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.16.12">16:12</scripRef>). It was probably a metallic cinder-basin used for the
purpose of carrying live coal for burning incense, and of
carrying away the snuff in trimming the lamps.
</def>
<term id="f-p108.7">Firkin</term>
Used only in John 2:6; the Attic amphora, equivalent to the
Hebrew bath (q.v.), a measure for liquids containing about 8 7/8
gallons.
</def>
<term id="f-p109.2">Firmament</term>
From the Vulgate firmamentum, which is used as the translation
of the Hebrew raki’a. This word means simply “expansion.” It
denotes the space or expanse like an arch appearing immediately
above us. They who rendered raki’a by firmamentum regarded it
as a solid body. The language of Scripture is not scientific but
popular, and hence we read of the sun rising and setting, and
also here the use of this particular word. It is plain that it
was used to denote solidity as well as expansion. It formed a
division between the waters above and the waters below (Gen. 1:7). The raki’a supported the upper reservoir (Ps. 148:4). It
was the support also of the heavenly bodies (<scripRef passage="Gen. 1:14" id="f-p110.3" parsed="|Gen|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.1.14">Gen. 1:14</scripRef>), and is
spoken of as having “windows” and “doors” (Gen. 7:11; Isa. 24:18; Mal. 3:10) through which the rain and snow might descend.
</def>
<term id="f-p110.7">First-born</term>
Sons enjoyed certain special privileges (Deut. 21:17; Gen. 25:23, 31, 34; 49:3; 1 Chr. 5:1; Heb. 12:16; Ps. 89:27). (See BIRTHRIGHT.)
The “first-born of the poor” signifies the most miserable of
the poor (<scripRef passage="Isa. 14:30" id="f-p112.1" parsed="|Isa|14|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.14.30">Isa. 14:30</scripRef>). The “church of the first-born” signifies
the church of the redeemed.
The destruction of the first-born was the last of the ten
plagues inflicted on the Egyptians (Ex. 11:1-8; 12:29, 30).
Menephtah is probably the Pharaoh whose first-born was slain.
His son did not succeed or survive his father, but died early.
The son’s tomb has been found at Thebes unfinished, showing it
was needed earlier than was expected. Some of the records on the
tomb are as follows: “The son whom Menephtah loves; who draws
towards him his father’s heart, the singer, the prince of
archers, who governed Egypt on behalf of his father. Dead.”
</def>
<term id="f-p114.1">First-born, Redemption of</term>
From the beginning the office of the priesthood in each family
belonged to the eldest son. But when the extensive plan of
sacrificial worship was introduced, requiring a company of men
to be exclusively devoted to this ministry, the primitive office

of the first-born was superseded by that of the Levites (<scripRef passage="Num. 3:11-13" id="f-p115.1" parsed="|Num|3|11|3|13" osisRef="Bible:Num.3.11-Num.3.13">Num. 3:11-13</scripRef>), and it was ordained that the first-born of man and of
unclean animals should henceforth be redeemed (18:15).
The laws concerning this redemption of the first-born of man

are recorded in <scripRef passage="Ex. 13:12-15" id="f-p116.1" parsed="|Exod|13|12|13|15" osisRef="Bible:Exod.13.12-Exod.13.15">Ex. 13:12-15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 22:29" id="f-p116.2" parsed="|Exod|22|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.22.29">22:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 34:20" id="f-p116.3" parsed="|Exod|34|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.34.20">34:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 3:45" id="f-p116.4" parsed="|Num|3|45|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.3.45">Num. 3:45</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 8:17" id="f-p116.5" parsed="|Num|8|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.8.17">8:17</scripRef>;
18:16; Lev. 12:2, 4.
The first-born male of every clean animal was to be given up
to the priest for sacrifice (Deut. 12:6; Ex. 13:12; 34:20; Num. 18:15-17).
But the first-born of unclean animals was either to be

redeemed or sold and the price given to the priest (<scripRef passage="Lev. 27:11-13" id="f-p118.1" parsed="|Lev|27|11|27|13" osisRef="Bible:Lev.27.11-Lev.27.13">Lev. 27:11-13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev 27:27" id="f-p118.2" parsed="|Lev|27|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.27.27">27</scripRef>). The first-born of an ass, if not redeemed, was to
be put to death (Ex. 13:13; 34:20).
</def>
<term id="f-p118.5">First-born, Sanctification of the</term>
A peculiar sanctity was attached to the first-born both of man
and of cattle. God claimed that the first-born males of man and
of animals should be consecrated to him, the one as a priest

(<scripRef passage="Ex. 19:22" id="f-p119.1" parsed="|Exod|19|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.19.22">Ex. 19:22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 19:24" id="f-p119.2" parsed="|Exod|19|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.19.24">24</scripRef>), representing the family to which he belonged,
and the other to be offered up in sacrifice (Gen. 4:4).
</def>
<term id="f-p119.4">First-fruits</term>
The first-fruits of the ground were offered unto God just as the
first-born of man and animals.
The law required, (1.) That on the morrow after the Passover
Sabbath a sheaf of new corn should be waved by the priest before
the altar (Lev. 23:5, 6, 10, 12; 2:12).
(2.) That at the feast of Pentecost two loaves of leavened
bread, made from the new flour, were to be waved in like manner
(Lev. 23:15, 17; Num. 28:26).
(3.) The feast of Tabernacles was an acknowledgement that the
fruits of the harvest were from the Lord (Ex. 23:16; 34:22).
(4.) Every individual, besides, was required to consecrate to

God a portion of the first-fruits of the land (<scripRef passage="Ex. 22:29" id="f-p124.1" parsed="|Exod|22|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.22.29">Ex. 22:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 23:19" id="f-p124.2" parsed="|Exod|23|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.19">23:19</scripRef>;
34:26; Num. 15:20, 21).
(5.) The law enjoined that no fruit was to be gathered from
newly-planted fruit-trees for the first three years, and that
the first-fruits of the fourth year were to be consecrated to
the Lord (<scripRef passage="Lev. 19:23-25" id="f-p125.1" parsed="|Lev|19|23|19|25" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.23-Lev.19.25">Lev. 19:23-25</scripRef>). Jeremiah (2:3) alludes to the
ordinance of “first-fruits,” and hence he must have been
acquainted with the books of Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers,
where the laws regarding it are recorded.
</def>
<term id="f-p125.2">Fish</term>
Called dag by the Hebrews, a word denoting great fecundity

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 9:2" id="f-p126.1" parsed="|Gen|9|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.9.2">Gen. 9:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 11:22" id="f-p126.2" parsed="|Num|11|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.11.22">Num. 11:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jonah 2:1" id="f-p126.3" parsed="|Jonah|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jonah.2.1">Jonah 2:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jonah 2:10" id="f-p126.4" parsed="|Jonah|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jonah.2.10">10</scripRef>). No fish is mentioned by
name either in the Old or in the New Testament. Fish abounded in
the Mediterranean and in the lakes of the Jordan, so that the
Hebrews were no doubt acquainted with many species. Two of the
villages on the shores of the Sea of Galilee derived their names
from their fisheries, Bethsaida (the “house of fish”) on the
east and on the west. There is probably no other sheet of water
in the world of equal dimensions that contains such a variety
and profusion of fish. About thirty-seven different kinds have
been found. Some of the fishes are of a European type, such as
the roach, the barbel, and the blenny; others are markedly
African and tropical, such as the eel-like silurus. There was a

regular fish-market apparently in Jerusalem (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 33:14" id="f-p126.5" parsed="|2Chr|33|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.33.14">2 Chr. 33:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh. 3:3" id="f-p126.6" parsed="|Neh|3|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.3.3">Neh. 3:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh 12:39" id="f-p126.7" parsed="|Neh|12|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.12.39">12:39</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zeph. 1:10" id="f-p126.8" parsed="|Zeph|1|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zeph.1.10">Zeph. 1:10</scripRef>), as there was a fish-gate which was
probably contiguous to it.
Sidon is the oldest fishing establishment known in history.
</def>
<term id="f-p127.1">Fisher</term>
Besides its literal sense (Luke 5:2), this word is also applied
by our Lord to his disciples in a figurative sense (<scripRef passage="Matt. 4:19" id="f-p128.2" parsed="|Matt|4|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.4.19">Matt. 4:19</scripRef>;
Mark 1:17).
</def>
<term id="f-p128.4">Fish-hooks</term>
Were used for catching fish (Amos 4:2; comp. Isa. 37:29; Jer. 16:16; Ezek. 29:4; Job. 41:1, 2; Matt. 17:27).
</def>
<term id="f-p129.8">Fishing, the art of</term>
Was prosecuted with great industry in the waters of Palestine.
It was from the fishing-nets that Jesus called his disciples
(<scripRef passage="Mark 1:16-20" id="f-p130.1" parsed="|Mark|1|16|1|20" osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.16-Mark.1.20">Mark 1:16-20</scripRef>), and it was in a fishing-boat he rebuked the
winds and the waves (<scripRef passage="Matt. 8:26" id="f-p130.2" parsed="|Matt|8|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.8.26">Matt. 8:26</scripRef>) and delivered that remarkable
series of prophecies recorded in <scripRef passage="Matt. 13" id="f-p130.3" parsed="|Matt|13|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.13">Matt. 13</scripRef>. He twice miraculously

fed multitudes with fish and bread (<scripRef passage="Matt. 14:19" id="f-p130.4" parsed="|Matt|14|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.14.19">Matt. 14:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 15:36" id="f-p130.5" parsed="|Matt|15|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.15.36">15:36</scripRef>). It was

in the mouth of a fish that the tribute-money was found (<scripRef passage="Matt. 17:27" id="f-p130.6" parsed="|Matt|17|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.17.27">Matt. 17:27</scripRef>). And he “ate a piece of broiled fish” with his disciples

after his resurrection (<scripRef passage="Luke 24:42" id="f-p130.7" parsed="|Luke|24|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.24.42">Luke 24:42</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Luke 24:43" id="f-p130.8" parsed="|Luke|24|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.24.43">43</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Acts 1:3" id="f-p130.9" parsed="|Acts|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.3">Acts 1:3</scripRef>). At the
Sea of Tiberias (<scripRef passage="John 21:1-14" id="f-p130.10" parsed="|John|21|1|21|14" osisRef="Bible:John.21.1-John.21.14">John 21:1-14</scripRef>), in obedience to his direction,
the disciples cast their net “on the right side of the ship,”
and enclosed so many that “they were not able to draw it for the
multitude of fishes.”
Two kinds of fishing-nets are mentioned in the New Testament:
(1.) The casting-net (Matt. 4:18; Mark 1:16).
(2.) The drag-net or seine (Matt. 13:48).
Fish were also caught by the fishing-hook (Matt. 17:27). (See NET.)
</def>
<term id="f-p134.3">Fish-pools</term>
(Cant. 7:4) should be simply “pools,” as in the Revised Version.
The reservoirs near Heshbon (q.v.) were probably stocked with
fish (2 Sam. 2:13; 4:12; Isa. 7:3; 22:9, 11).
</def>
<term id="f-p135.7">Fitches</term>
(Isa. 28:25, 27), the rendering of the Hebrew ketsah, “without
doubt the Nigella sativa, a small annual of the order
Ranunculacece, which grows wild in the Mediterranean countries,
and is cultivated in Egypt and Syria for its seed.” It is
rendered in margin of the Revised Version “black cummin.” The
seeds are used as a condiment.
In Ezek. 4:9 this word is the rendering of the Hebrew
kussemeth (incorrectly rendered “rye” in the Authorized

Version of <scripRef passage="Ex. 9:32" id="f-p137.2" parsed="|Exod|9|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.9.32">Ex. 9:32</scripRef> and <scripRef passage="Isa. 28:25" id="f-p137.3" parsed="|Isa|28|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.28.25">Isa. 28:25</scripRef>, but “spelt” in the Revised
Version). The reading “fitches” here is an error; it should be
“spelt.”
</def>
<term id="f-p137.4">Flag</term>
(Heb., or rather Egyptian, ahu, Job 8:11), rendered “meadow” in

<scripRef passage="Gen. 41:2" id="f-p138.2" parsed="|Gen|41|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.41.2">Gen. 41:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 41:18" id="f-p138.3" parsed="|Gen|41|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.41.18">18</scripRef>; probably the Cyperus esculentus, a species of
rush eaten by cattle, the Nile reed. It also grows in Palestine.
In Ex. 2:3, 5, Isa. 19:6, it is the rendering of the Hebrew
suph_, a word which occurs frequently in connection with _yam;
as yam suph, to denote the “Red Sea” (q.v.) or the sea of
weeds (as this word is rendered, <scripRef passage="Jonah 2:5" id="f-p139.4" parsed="|Jonah|2|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jonah.2.5">Jonah 2:5</scripRef>). It denotes some
kind of sedge or reed which grows in marshy places. (See
PAPER, REED.)
</def>
<term id="f-p139.7">Flagon</term>
Heb. ashishah, (2 Sam. 6:19; 1 Chr. 16:3; Cant. 2:5; Hos. 3:1),
meaning properly “a cake of pressed raisins.” “Flagons of wine”
of the Authorized Version should be, as in the Revised Version,
“cakes of raisins” in all these passages. In <scripRef passage="Isa. 22:24" id="f-p140.5" parsed="|Isa|22|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.22.24">Isa. 22:24</scripRef> it is
the rendering of the Hebrew nebel, which properly means a
bottle or vessel of skin. (Comp. 1 Sam. 1:24; 10:3; 25:18; 2 Sam. 16:1, where the same Hebrew word is used.)
</def>
<term id="f-p140.10">Flame of fire</term>
Is the chosen symbol of the holiness of God (Ex. 3:2; Rev. 2:18), as indicating “the intense, all-consuming operation of
his holiness in relation to sin.”
</def>
<term id="f-p141.3">Flax</term>
(Heb. pishtah, i.e., “peeled”, in allusion to the fact that the
stalks of flax when dried were first split or peeled before
being steeped in water for the purpose of destroying the pulp).
This plant was cultivated from earliest times. The flax of Egypt
was destroyed by the plague of hail when it “was bolled”, i.e.,
was forming pods for seed (<scripRef passage="Ex. 9:31" id="f-p142.1" parsed="|Exod|9|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.9.31">Ex. 9:31</scripRef>). It was extensively
cultivated both in Egypt and Palestine. Reference is made in
<scripRef passage="Josh. 2:6" id="f-p142.2" parsed="|Josh|2|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.2.6">Josh. 2:6</scripRef> to the custom of drying flax-stalks by exposing them
to the sun on the flat roofs of houses. It was much used in
forming articles of clothing such as girdles, also cords and
bands (Lev. 13:48, 52, 59; Deut. 22:11). (See LINEN.)
</def>
<term id="f-p142.8">Flea</term>
David at the cave of Adullam thus addressed his persecutor Saul
(<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 24:14" id="f-p143.1" parsed="|1Sam|24|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.24.14">1 Sam. 24:14</scripRef>): “After whom is the king of Israel come out?
after whom dost thou pursue? after a dead dog, after a flea?” He
thus speaks of himself as the poor, contemptible object of the
monarch’s pursuit, a “worthy object truly for an expedition of
the king of Israel with his picked troops!” This insect is in

Eastern language the popular emblem of insignificance. In <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 26:20" id="f-p143.2" parsed="|1Sam|26|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.26.20">1 Sam. 26:20</scripRef> the LXX. read “come out to seek my life” instead of “to
seek a flea.”
</def>
<term id="f-p143.3">Fleece</term>
The wool of a sheep, whether shorn off or still attached to the

skin (<scripRef passage="Deut. 18:4" id="f-p144.1" parsed="|Deut|18|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.18.4">Deut. 18:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 31:20" id="f-p144.2" parsed="|Job|31|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.31.20">Job 31:20</scripRef>). The miracle of Gideon’s fleece
(<scripRef passage="Judg. 6:37-40" id="f-p144.3" parsed="|Judg|6|37|6|40" osisRef="Bible:Judg.6.37-Judg.6.40">Judg. 6:37-40</scripRef>) consisted in the dew having fallen at one time
on the fleece without any on the floor, and at another time in
the fleece remaining dry while the ground was wet with dew.
</def>
<term id="f-p144.4">Flesh</term>
In the Old Testament denotes (1) a particular part of the body

of man and animals (<scripRef passage="Gen. 2:21" id="f-p145.1" parsed="|Gen|2|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.2.21">Gen. 2:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 41:2" id="f-p145.2" parsed="|Gen|41|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.41.2">41:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 102:5" id="f-p145.3" parsed="|Ps|102|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.102.5">Ps. 102:5</scripRef>, marg.); (2) the
whole body (<scripRef passage="Ps. 16:9" id="f-p145.4" parsed="|Ps|16|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.16.9">Ps. 16:9</scripRef>); (3) all living things having flesh, and

particularly humanity as a whole (<scripRef passage="Gen. 6:12" id="f-p145.5" parsed="|Gen|6|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.6.12">Gen. 6:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 6:13" id="f-p145.6" parsed="|Gen|6|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.6.13">13</scripRef>); (4) mutability

and weakness (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 32:8" id="f-p145.7" parsed="|2Chr|32|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.32.8">2 Chr. 32:8</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Isa. 31:3" id="f-p145.8" parsed="|Isa|31|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.31.3">Isa. 31:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 78:39" id="f-p145.9" parsed="|Ps|78|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.78.39">Ps. 78:39</scripRef>). As
suggesting the idea of softness it is used in the expression
“heart of flesh” (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 11:19" id="f-p145.10" parsed="|Ezek|11|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.11.19">Ezek. 11:19</scripRef>). The expression “my flesh and
bone” (Judg. 9:2; Isa. 58:7) denotes relationship.
In the New Testament, besides these it is also used to denote
the sinful element of human nature as opposed to the “Spirit”

(<scripRef passage="Rom. 6:19" id="f-p146.1" parsed="|Rom|6|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.6.19">Rom. 6:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 16:17" id="f-p146.2" parsed="|Matt|16|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.16.17">Matt. 16:17</scripRef>). Being “in the flesh” means being

unrenewed (<scripRef passage="Rom. 7:5" id="f-p146.3" parsed="|Rom|7|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.7.5">Rom. 7:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom 8:8" id="f-p146.4" parsed="|Rom|8|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.8">8:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Rom 8:9" id="f-p146.5" parsed="|Rom|8|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.9">9</scripRef>), and to live “according to the
flesh” is to live and act sinfully (Rom. 8:4, 5, 7, 12).
This word also denotes the human nature of Christ (John 1:14,
“The Word was made flesh.” Comp. also 1 Tim. 3:16; Rom. 1:3).
</def>
<term id="f-p147.4">Flesh-hook</term>
A many-pronged fork used in the sacrificial services (1 Sam. 2:13, 14; Ex. 27:3; 38:3) by the priest in drawing away the
flesh. The fat of the sacrifice, together with the breast and
shoulder (<scripRef passage="Lev. 7:29-34" id="f-p148.5" parsed="|Lev|7|29|7|34" osisRef="Bible:Lev.7.29-Lev.7.34">Lev. 7:29-34</scripRef>), were presented by the worshipper to the
priest. The fat was burned on the alter (3:3-5), and the breast
and shoulder became the portion of the priests. But Hophni and
Phinehas, not content with this, sent a servant to seize with a
flesh-hook a further portion.
</def>
<term id="f-p148.6">Flint</term>
Abounds in all the plains and valleys of the wilderness of the

forty years’ wanderings. In <scripRef passage="Isa. 50:7" id="f-p149.1" parsed="|Isa|50|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.50.7">Isa. 50:7</scripRef> and <scripRef passage="Ezek. 3:9" id="f-p149.2" parsed="|Ezek|3|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.3.9">Ezek. 3:9</scripRef> the
expressions, where the word is used, means that the “Messiah
would be firm and resolute amidst all contempt and scorn which
he would meet; that he had made up his mind to endure it, and
would not shrink from any kind or degree of suffering which
would be necessary to accomplish the great work in which he was

engaged.” (Comp. <scripRef passage="Ezek. 3:8" id="f-p149.3" parsed="|Ezek|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.3.8">Ezek. 3:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 3:9" id="f-p149.4" parsed="|Ezek|3|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.3.9">9</scripRef>.) The words “like a flint” are
used with reference to the hoofs of horses (Isa. 5:28).
</def>
<term id="f-p149.6">Flood</term>
An event recorded in Gen. 7 and 8. (See DELUGE.) In

<scripRef passage="Josh. 24:2" id="f-p150.3" parsed="|Josh|24|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.24.2">Josh. 24:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 24:3" id="f-p150.4" parsed="|Josh|24|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.24.3">3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 24:14" id="f-p150.5" parsed="|Josh|24|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.24.14">14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 24:15" id="f-p150.6" parsed="|Josh|24|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.24.15">15</scripRef>, the word “flood” (R.V., “river”) means
the river Euphrates. In <scripRef passage="Ps. 66:6" id="f-p150.7" parsed="|Ps|66|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.66.6">Ps. 66:6</scripRef>, this word refers to the river
Jordan.
</def>
<term id="f-p150.8">Flour</term>
Grain reduced to the form of meal is spoken of in the time of
Abraham (<scripRef passage="Gen. 18:6" id="f-p151.1" parsed="|Gen|18|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.18.6">Gen. 18:6</scripRef>). As baking was a daily necessity, grain was
also ground daily at the mills (<scripRef passage="Jer. 25:10" id="f-p151.2" parsed="|Jer|25|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.25.10">Jer. 25:10</scripRef>). The flour mingled
with water was kneaded in kneading-troughs, and sometimes leaven

(<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:34" id="f-p151.3" parsed="|Exod|12|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.34">Ex. 12:34</scripRef>) was added and sometimes omitted (<scripRef passage="Gen. 19:3" id="f-p151.4" parsed="|Gen|19|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.19.3">Gen. 19:3</scripRef>). The
dough was then formed into thin cakes nine or ten inches in
diameter and baked in the oven.
Fine flour was offered by the poor as a sin-offering (Lev. 5:11-13), and also in connection with other sacrifices (Num. 15:3-12; 28:7-29).
</def>
<term id="f-p152.4">Flowers</term>
Very few species of flowers are mentioned in the Bible although
they abounded in Palestine. It has been calculated that in
Western Syria and Palestine from two thousand to two thousand
five hundred plants are found, of which about five hundred
probably are British wild-flowers. Their beauty is often alluded

to (<scripRef passage="Cant. 2:12" id="f-p153.1" parsed="|Song|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.2.12">Cant. 2:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 6:28" id="f-p153.2" parsed="|Matt|6|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.28">Matt. 6:28</scripRef>). They are referred to as affording

an emblem of the transitory nature of human life (<scripRef passage="Job 14:2" id="f-p153.3" parsed="|Job|14|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.14.2">Job 14:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 103:15" id="f-p153.4" parsed="|Ps|103|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.103.15">Ps. 103:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 28:1" id="f-p153.5" parsed="|Isa|28|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.28.1">Isa. 28:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 40:6" id="f-p153.6" parsed="|Isa|40|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.40.6">40:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="James 1:10" id="f-p153.7" parsed="|Jas|1|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jas.1.10">James 1:10</scripRef>). Gardens containing flowers
and fragrant herbs are spoken of (Cant. 4:16; 6:2).
</def>
<term id="f-p153.10">Flute</term>
A musical instrument, probably composed of a number of pipes,
mentioned Dan. 3:5, 7, 10, 15.
In Matt. 9:23, 24, notice is taken of players on the flute,
here called “minstrels” (but in R.V. “flute-players”).
Flutes were in common use among the ancient Egyptians.
</def>
<term id="f-p156.1">Fly</term>
Heb. zebub, (Eccl. 10:1; Isa. 7:18). This fly was so grievous a
pest that the Phoenicians invoked against it the aid of their
god Baal-zebub (q.v.). The prophet Isaiah (7:18) alludes to some
poisonous fly which was believed to be found on the confines of
Egypt, and which would be called by the Lord. Poisonous flies
exist in many parts of Africa, for instance, the different kinds
of tsetse.
Heb. ‘arob, the name given to the insects sent as a plague on

the land of Egypt (<scripRef passage="Ex. 8:21-31" id="f-p158.1" parsed="|Exod|8|21|8|31" osisRef="Bible:Exod.8.21-Exod.8.31">Ex. 8:21-31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 78:45" id="f-p158.2" parsed="|Ps|78|45|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.78.45">Ps. 78:45</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 105:31" id="f-p158.3" parsed="|Ps|105|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.105.31">105:31</scripRef>). The LXX.
render this by a word which means the “dog-fly,” the cynomuia.
The Jewish commentators regarded the Hebrew word here as
connected with the word ’arab, which means “mingled;” and they
accordingly supposed the plague to consist of a mixed multitude
of animals, beasts, reptiles, and insects. But there is no doubt
that “the ’arab“ denotes a single definite species. Some
interpreters regard it as the Blatta orientalis, the cockroach,
a species of beetle. These insects “inflict very painful bites
with their jaws; gnaw and destroy clothes, household furniture,
leather, and articles of every kind, and either consume or
render unavailable all eatables.”
</def>
<term id="f-p158.4">Foam</term>
(Hos. 10:7), the rendering of ketseph, which properly means
twigs or splinters (as rendered in the LXX. and marg. R.V.). The
expression in Hosea may therefore be read, “as a chip on the
face of the water,” denoting the helplessness of the piece of
wood as compared with the irresistable current.
</def>
<term id="f-p159.2">Fodder</term>
Heb. belil, (Job 6:5), meaning properly a mixture or medley
(Lat. farrago), “made up of various kinds of grain, as wheat,
barley, vetches, and the like, all mixed together, and then sown
or given to cattle” (<scripRef passage="Job 24:6" id="f-p160.2" parsed="|Job|24|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.24.6">Job 24:6</scripRef>, A.V. “corn,” R.V. “provender;”
Isa. 30:24, provender”).
</def>
<term id="f-p160.4">Fold</term>
An enclosure for flocks to rest together (Isa. 13:20).

Sheep-folds are mentioned <scripRef passage="Num. 32:16" id="f-p161.2" parsed="|Num|32|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.32.16">Num. 32:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 32:24" id="f-p161.3" parsed="|Num|32|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.32.24">24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 32:36" id="f-p161.4" parsed="|Num|32|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.32.36">36</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 7:8" id="f-p161.5" parsed="|2Sam|7|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.7.8">2 Sam. 7:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zeph. 2:6" id="f-p161.6" parsed="|Zeph|2|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zeph.2.6">Zeph. 2:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 10:1" id="f-p161.7" parsed="|John|10|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.10.1">John 10:1</scripRef>, etc. It was prophesied of the cities of Ammon

(<scripRef passage="Ezek. 25:5" id="f-p161.8" parsed="|Ezek|25|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.25.5">Ezek. 25:5</scripRef>), Aroer (<scripRef passage="Isa. 17:2" id="f-p161.9" parsed="|Isa|17|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.17.2">Isa. 17:2</scripRef>), and Judaea, that they would be
folds or couching-places for flocks. “Among the pots,” of the
Authorized Version (<scripRef passage="Ps. 68:13" id="f-p161.10" parsed="|Ps|68|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.68.13">Ps. 68:13</scripRef>), is rightly in the Revised
Version, “among the sheepfolds.”
</def>
<term id="f-p161.11">Food</term>
Originally the Creator granted the use of the vegetable world
for food to man (<scripRef passage="Gen. 1:29" id="f-p162.1" parsed="|Gen|1|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.1.29">Gen. 1:29</scripRef>), with the exception mentioned
(2:17). The use of animal food was probably not unknown to the
antediluvians. There is, however, a distinct law on the subject
given to Noah after the Deluge (<scripRef passage="Gen. 9:2-5" id="f-p162.2" parsed="|Gen|9|2|9|5" osisRef="Bible:Gen.9.2-Gen.9.5">Gen. 9:2-5</scripRef>). Various articles of
food used in the patriarchal age are mentioned in <scripRef passage="Gen. 18:6-8" id="f-p162.3" parsed="|Gen|18|6|18|8" osisRef="Bible:Gen.18.6-Gen.18.8">Gen. 18:6-8</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Gen 25:34" id="f-p162.4" parsed="|Gen|25|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.34">25:34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 27:3" id="f-p162.5" parsed="|Gen|27|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.3">27:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 27:4" id="f-p162.6" parsed="|Gen|27|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.4">4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 43:11" id="f-p162.7" parsed="|Gen|43|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.43.11">43:11</scripRef>. Regarding the food of the Israelites in

Egypt, see <scripRef passage="Ex. 16:3" id="f-p162.8" parsed="|Exod|16|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.16.3">Ex. 16:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 11:5" id="f-p162.9" parsed="|Num|11|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.11.5">Num. 11:5</scripRef>. In the wilderness their ordinary
food was miraculously supplied in the manna. They had also
quails (Ex. 16:11-13; Num. 11:31).
In the law of Moses there are special regulations as to the

animals to be used for food (<scripRef passage="Lev. 11" id="f-p163.1" parsed="|Lev|11|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.11">Lev. 11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 14:3-21" id="f-p163.2" parsed="|Deut|14|3|14|21" osisRef="Bible:Deut.14.3-Deut.14.21">Deut. 14:3-21</scripRef>). The Jews
were also forbidden to use as food anything that had been
consecrated to idols (<scripRef passage="Ex. 34:15" id="f-p163.3" parsed="|Exod|34|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.34.15">Ex. 34:15</scripRef>), or animals that had died of

disease or had been torn by wild beasts (<scripRef passage="Ex. 22:31" id="f-p163.4" parsed="|Exod|22|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.22.31">Ex. 22:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 22:8" id="f-p163.5" parsed="|Lev|22|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.22.8">Lev. 22:8</scripRef>).

(See also for other restrictions <scripRef passage="Ex. 23:19" id="f-p163.6" parsed="|Exod|23|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.19">Ex. 23:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 29:13-22" id="f-p163.7" parsed="|Exod|29|13|29|22" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.13-Exod.29.22">29:13-22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 3:4-9" id="f-p163.8" parsed="|Lev|3|4|3|9" osisRef="Bible:Lev.3.4-Lev.3.9">Lev. 3:4-9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 9:18" id="f-p163.9" parsed="|Lev|9|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.9.18">9:18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev 9:19" id="f-p163.10" parsed="|Lev|9|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.9.19">19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 22:8" id="f-p163.11" parsed="|Lev|22|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.22.8">22:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 14:21" id="f-p163.12" parsed="|Deut|14|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.14.21">Deut. 14:21</scripRef>.) But beyond these
restrictions they had a large grant from God (<scripRef passage="Deut. 14:26" id="f-p163.13" parsed="|Deut|14|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.14.26">Deut. 14:26</scripRef>;
32:13, 14).
Food was prepared for use in various ways. The cereals were

sometimes eaten without any preparation (<scripRef passage="Lev. 23:14" id="f-p164.1" parsed="|Lev|23|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.14">Lev. 23:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 23:25" id="f-p164.2" parsed="|Deut|23|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.23.25">Deut. 23:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 4:42" id="f-p164.3" parsed="|2Kgs|4|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.4.42">2 Kings 4:42</scripRef>). Vegetables were cooked by boiling (<scripRef passage="Gen. 25:30" id="f-p164.4" parsed="|Gen|25|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.30">Gen. 25:30</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 25:34" id="f-p164.5" parsed="|Gen|25|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.34">34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 4:38" id="f-p164.6" parsed="|2Kgs|4|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.4.38">2 Kings 4:38</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 4:39" id="f-p164.7" parsed="|2Kgs|4|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.4.39">39</scripRef>), and thus also other articles of

food were prepared for use (<scripRef passage="Gen. 27:4" id="f-p164.8" parsed="|Gen|27|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.4">Gen. 27:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 23:3" id="f-p164.9" parsed="|Prov|23|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.23.3">Prov. 23:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 24:10" id="f-p164.10" parsed="|Ezek|24|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.24.10">Ezek. 24:10</scripRef>;
Luke 24:42; John 21:9). Food was also prepared by roasting (Ex. 12:8; Lev. 2:14). (See COOK.)
</def>
<term id="f-p164.16">Footstool</term>
Connected with a throne (2 Chr. 9:18). Jehovah symbolically
dwelt in the holy place between the cherubim above the ark of

the covenant. The ark was his footstool (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 28:2" id="f-p165.2" parsed="|1Chr|28|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.28.2">1 Chr. 28:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 99:5" id="f-p165.3" parsed="|Ps|99|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.99.5">Ps. 99:5</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Ps 132:7" id="f-p165.4" parsed="|Ps|132|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.132.7">132:7</scripRef>). And as heaven is God’s throne, so the earth is his
footstool (Ps. 110:1; Isa. 66:1; Matt. 5:35).
</def>
<term id="f-p165.8">Forces</term>
Of the Gentiles (Isa. 60:5, 11; R.V., “the wealth of the
nations”) denotes the wealth of the heathen. The whole passage
means that the wealth of the Gentile world should be consecrated
to the service of the church.
</def>
<term id="f-p166.3">Ford</term>
Mention is frequently made of the fords of the Jordan (Josh. 2:7; Judg. 3:28; 12:5, 6), which must have been very numerous;
about fifty perhaps. The most notable was that of Bethabara.
Mention is also made of the ford of the Jabbok (<scripRef passage="Gen. 32:22" id="f-p167.5" parsed="|Gen|32|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.32.22">Gen. 32:22</scripRef>), and
of the fords of Arnon (Isa. 16:2) and of the Euphrates (Jer. 51:32).
</def>
<term id="f-p167.8">Forehead</term>
The practice common among Oriental nations of colouring the
forehead or impressing on it some distinctive mark as a sign of

devotion to some deity is alluded to in <scripRef passage="Rev. 13:16" id="f-p168.1" parsed="|Rev|13|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.13.16">Rev. 13:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Rev. 13:17" id="f-p168.2" parsed="|Rev|13|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.13.17">17</scripRef>; 14:9;
The “jewel on thy forehead” mentioned in Ezek. 16:12 (R.V., “a
ring upon thy nose”) was in all probability the “nose-ring”
(Isa. 3:21).
In Ezek. 3:7 the word “impudent” is rightly rendered in the
Revised Version “an hard forehead.” (See also ver. 8, 9.)
</def>
<term id="f-p170.2">Foreigner</term>
A Gentile. Such as resided among the Hebrews were required by

the law to be treated with kindness (<scripRef passage="Ex. 22:21" id="f-p171.1" parsed="|Exod|22|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.22.21">Ex. 22:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 23:9" id="f-p171.2" parsed="|Exod|23|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.9">23:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 19:33" id="f-p171.3" parsed="|Lev|19|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.33">Lev. 19:33</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev 19:34" id="f-p171.4" parsed="|Lev|19|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.34">34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 23:22" id="f-p171.5" parsed="|Lev|23|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.22">23:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 14:28" id="f-p171.6" parsed="|Deut|14|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.14.28">Deut. 14:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut 16:10" id="f-p171.7" parsed="|Deut|16|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.16.10">16:10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut 16:11" id="f-p171.8" parsed="|Deut|16|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.16.11">11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut 24:19" id="f-p171.9" parsed="|Deut|24|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.24.19">24:19</scripRef>). They enjoyed

in many things equal rights with the native-born residents (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:49" id="f-p171.10" parsed="|Exod|12|49|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.49">Ex. 12:49</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 24:22" id="f-p171.11" parsed="|Lev|24|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.24.22">Lev. 24:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 15:15" id="f-p171.12" parsed="|Num|15|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.15.15">Num. 15:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 35:15" id="f-p171.13" parsed="|Num|35|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.35.15">35:15</scripRef>), but were not allowed to
do anything which was an abomination according to the Jewish law
(Ex. 20:10; Lev. 17:15, 16; 18:26; 20:2; 24:16, etc.).
</def>
<term id="f-p171.17">Foreknowledge of God</term>
Acts 2:23; Rom. 8:29; 11:2; 1 Pet. 1:2), one of those high
attributes essentially appertaining to him the full import of
which we cannot comprehend. In the most absolute sense his

knowledge is infinite (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 23:9-13" id="f-p172.5" parsed="|1Sam|23|9|23|13" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.23.9-1Sam.23.13">1 Sam. 23:9-13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 38:17-23" id="f-p172.6" parsed="|Jer|38|17|38|23" osisRef="Bible:Jer.38.17-Jer.38.23">Jer. 38:17-23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 42:9-22" id="f-p172.7" parsed="|Jer|42|9|42|22" osisRef="Bible:Jer.42.9-Jer.42.22">42:9-22</scripRef>,
Matt. 11:21, 23; Acts 15:18).
</def>
<term id="f-p172.11">Forerunner</term>
John the Baptist went before our Lord in this character (Mark 1:2, 3). Christ so called (Heb. 6:20) as entering before his
people into the holy place as their head and guide.
</def>
<term id="f-p173.4">Forest</term>
Heb. ya’ar, meaning a dense wood, from its luxuriance. Thus all

the great primeval forests of Syria (<scripRef passage="Eccl. 2:6" id="f-p174.1" parsed="|Eccl|2|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eccl.2.6">Eccl. 2:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 44:14" id="f-p174.2" parsed="|Isa|44|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.44.14">Isa. 44:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 5:6" id="f-p174.3" parsed="|Jer|5|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.5.6">Jer. 5:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Micah 5:8" id="f-p174.4" parsed="|Mic|5|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.5.8">Micah 5:8</scripRef>). The most extensive was the trans-Jordanic

forest of Ephraim (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 18:6" id="f-p174.5" parsed="|2Sam|18|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.18.6">2 Sam. 18:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 18:8" id="f-p174.6" parsed="|2Sam|18|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.18.8">8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 17:15" id="f-p174.7" parsed="|Josh|17|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.17.15">Josh. 17:15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 17:18" id="f-p174.8" parsed="|Josh|17|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.17.18">18</scripRef>), which is
probably the same as the wood of Ephratah (<scripRef passage="Ps. 132:6" id="f-p174.9" parsed="|Ps|132|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.132.6">Ps. 132:6</scripRef>), some part
of the great forest of Gilead. It was in this forest that
Absalom was slain by Joab. David withdrew to the forest of

Hareth in the mountains of Judah to avoid the fury of Saul (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 22:5" id="f-p174.10" parsed="|1Sam|22|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.22.5">1 Sam. 22:5</scripRef>). We read also of the forest of Bethel (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 2:23" id="f-p174.11" parsed="|2Kgs|2|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.2.23">2 Kings 2:23</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 2:24" id="f-p174.12" parsed="|2Kgs|2|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.2.24">24</scripRef>), and of that which the Israelites passed in their pursuit of
the Philistines (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 14:25" id="f-p174.13" parsed="|1Sam|14|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.14.25">1 Sam. 14:25</scripRef>), and of the forest of the cedars
of Lebanon (1 Kings 4:33; 2 Kings 19:23; Hos. 14:5, 6).
“The house of the forest of Lebanon (1 Kings 7:2; 10:17; 2 Chr. 9:16) was probably Solomon’s armoury, and was so called
because the wood of its many pillars came from Lebanon, and they
had the appearance of a forest. (See BAALBEC.)
Heb. horesh, denoting a thicket of trees, underwood, jungle,
bushes, or trees entangled, and therefore affording a safe

hiding-place. place. This word is rendered “forest” only in <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 27:4" id="f-p176.1" parsed="|2Chr|27|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.27.4">2 Chr. 27:4</scripRef>. It is also rendered “wood”, the “wood” in the

“wilderness of Ziph,” in which david concealed himself (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 23:15" id="f-p176.2" parsed="|1Sam|23|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.23.15">1 Sam. 23:15</scripRef>), which lay south-east of Hebron. In <scripRef passage="Isa. 17:19" id="f-p176.3" parsed="|Isa|17|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.17.19">Isa. 17:19</scripRef> this word
is in Authorized Version rendered incorrectly “bough.”
Heb. pardes, meaning an enclosed garden or plantation. Asaph
is (<scripRef passage="Neh. 2:8" id="f-p177.1" parsed="|Neh|2|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.2.8">Neh. 2:8</scripRef>) called the “keeper of the king’s forest.” The same
Hebrew word is used <scripRef passage="Eccl. 2:5" id="f-p177.2" parsed="|Eccl|2|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eccl.2.5">Eccl. 2:5</scripRef>, where it is rendered in the
plural “orchards” (R.V., “parks”), and <scripRef passage="Cant. 4" id="f-p177.3" parsed="|Song|4|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.4">Cant. 4</scripRef>: 13, rendered
“orchard” (R.V. marg., “a paradise”).
“The forest of the vintage” (Zech. 11:2, “inaccessible
forest,” or R.V. “strong forest”) is probably a figurative
allusion to Jerusalem, or the verse may simply point to the
devastation of the region referred to.
The forest is an image of unfruitfulness as contrasted with a

cultivated field (<scripRef passage="Isa. 29:17" id="f-p179.1" parsed="|Isa|29|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.29.17">Isa. 29:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 32:15" id="f-p179.2" parsed="|Isa|32|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.32.15">32:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 26:18" id="f-p179.3" parsed="|Jer|26|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.26.18">Jer. 26:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos. 2:12" id="f-p179.4" parsed="|Hos|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.2.12">Hos. 2:12</scripRef>).
Isaiah (10:19, 33, 34) likens the Assyrian host under
Sennacherib (q.v.) to the trees of some huge forest, to be
suddenly cut down by an unseen stroke.
</def>
<term id="f-p179.5">Forgiveness of sin</term>
One of the constituent parts of justification. In pardoning sin,
God absolves the sinner from the condemnation of the law, and
that on account of the work of Christ, i.e., he removes the
guilt of sin, or the sinner’s actual liability to eternal wrath
on account of it. All sins are forgiven freely (<scripRef passage="Acts 5:31" id="f-p180.1" parsed="|Acts|5|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.5.31">Acts 5:31</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Acts 13:38" id="f-p180.2" parsed="|Acts|13|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.13.38">13:38</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 John 1:6-9" id="f-p180.3" parsed="|1John|1|6|1|9" osisRef="Bible:1John.1.6-1John.1.9">1 John 1:6-9</scripRef>). The sinner is by this act of grace for
ever freed from the guilt and penalty of his sins. This is the

peculiar prerogative of God (<scripRef passage="Ps. 130:4" id="f-p180.4" parsed="|Ps|130|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.130.4">Ps. 130:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 2:5" id="f-p180.5" parsed="|Mark|2|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.2.5">Mark 2:5</scripRef>). It is offered
to all in the gospel. (See JUSTIFICATION.)
</def>
<term id="f-p180.7">Fornication</term>
In every form of it was sternly condemned by the Mosaic law

(<scripRef passage="Lev. 21:9" id="f-p181.1" parsed="|Lev|21|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.21.9">Lev. 21:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 19:29" id="f-p181.2" parsed="|Lev|19|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.29">19:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 22:20" id="f-p181.3" parsed="|Deut|22|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.22.20">Deut. 22:20</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 22:21" id="f-p181.4" parsed="|Deut|22|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.22.21">21</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 22:23" id="f-p181.5" parsed="|Deut|22|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.22.23">23</scripRef>-29; 23:18; <scripRef passage="Ex. 22:16" id="f-p181.6" parsed="|Exod|22|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.22.16">Ex. 22:16</scripRef>).
(See ADULTERY.)
But this word is more frequently used in a symbolical than in
its ordinary sense. It frequently means a forsaking of God or a

following after idols (<scripRef passage="Isa. 1:2" id="f-p182.1" parsed="|Isa|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.2">Isa. 1:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 2:20" id="f-p182.2" parsed="|Jer|2|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.2.20">Jer. 2:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 16" id="f-p182.3" parsed="|Ezek|16|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.16">Ezek. 16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos. 1:2" id="f-p182.4" parsed="|Hos|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.1.2">Hos. 1:2</scripRef>;
2:1-5; Jer. 3:8, 9).
</def>
<term id="f-p182.8">Fortunatus</term>
Fortunate, a disciple of Corinth who visited Paul at Ephesus,
and returned with Stephanas and Achaicus, the bearers of the
apostle’s first letter to the Corinthians (1 Cor. 16:17).
</def>
<term id="f-p183.2">Fountain</term>
(Heb. ‘ain; i.e., “eye” of the water desert), a natural source
of living water. Palestine was a “land of brooks of water, of
fountains, and depths that spring out of valleys and hills”
(Deut. 8:7; 11:11).
These fountains, bright sparkling “eyes” of the desert, are
remarkable for their abundance and their beauty, especially on
the west of Jordan. All the perennial rivers and streams of the
country are supplied from fountains, and depend comparatively
little on surface water. “Palestine is a country of mountains
and hills, and it abounds in fountains of water. The murmur of
these waters is heard in every dell, and the luxuriant foliage
which surrounds them is seen in every plain.” Besides its
rain-water, its cisterns and fountains, Jerusalem had also an
abundant supply of water in the magnificent reservoir called
“Solomon’s Pools” (q.v.), at the head of the Urtas valley,
whence it was conveyed to the city by subterrean channels some
10 miles in length. These have all been long ago destroyed, so
that no water from the “Pools” now reaches Jerusalem. Only one
fountain has been discovered at Jerusalem, the so-called
“Virgins’s Fountains,” in the valley of Kidron; and only one
well (Heb. beer), the Bir Eyub, also in the valley of Kidron,
south of the King’s Gardens, which has been dug through the
solid rock. The inhabitants of Jerusalem are now mainly
dependent on the winter rains, which they store in cisterns.
(See WELL.)
</def>
<term id="f-p185.2">Fountain of the Virgin</term>
The perennial source from which the Pool of Siloam (q.v.) is
supplied, the waters flowing in a copious stream to it through a
tunnel cut through the rock, the actual length of which is 1,750
feet. The spring rises in a cave 20 feet by 7. A serpentine
tunnel 67 feet long runs from it toward the left, off which the
tunnel to the Pool of Siloam branches. It is the only unfailing
fountain in Jerusalem.
The fountain received its name from the “fantastic legend”
that here the virgin washed the swaddling-clothes of our Lord.
This spring has the singular characteristic of being
intermittent, flowing from three to five times daily in winter,
twice daily in summer, and only once daily in autumn. This
peculiarity is accounted for by the supposition that the outlet
from the reservoir is by a passage in the form of a siphon.
</def>
<term id="f-p188.1">Fowler</term>
The arts of, referred to Ps. 91:3; 124:7; Prov. 6:5; Jer. 5:26;

<scripRef passage="Hos. 9:8" id="f-p189.5" parsed="|Hos|9|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.9.8">Hos. 9:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 17:20" id="f-p189.6" parsed="|Ezek|17|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.17.20">Ezek. 17:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eccl. 9:12" id="f-p189.7" parsed="|Eccl|9|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eccl.9.12">Eccl. 9:12</scripRef>. Birds of all kinds abound in
Palestine, and the capture of these for the table and for other
uses formed the employment of many persons. The traps and snares

used for this purpose are mentioned <scripRef passage="Hos. 5:1" id="f-p189.8" parsed="|Hos|5|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.5.1">Hos. 5:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 7:23" id="f-p189.9" parsed="|Prov|7|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.7.23">Prov. 7:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov 22:5" id="f-p189.10" parsed="|Prov|22|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.22.5">22:5</scripRef>;
Amos 3:5; Ps. 69:22; comp. Deut. 22:6, 7.
</def>
<term id="f-p189.15">Fox</term>
(Heb. shu’al, a name derived from its digging or burrowing under
ground), the Vulpes thaleb, or Syrian fox, the only species of
this animal indigenous to Palestine. It burrows, is silent and
solitary in its habits, is destructive to vineyards, being a
plunderer of ripe grapes (<scripRef passage="Cant. 2:15" id="f-p190.1" parsed="|Song|2|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.2.15">Cant. 2:15</scripRef>). The Vulpes Niloticus, or
Egyptian dog-fox, and the Vulpes vulgaris, or common fox, are
also found in Palestine.
The proverbial cunning of the fox is alluded to in Ezek. 13:4,
and in <scripRef passage="Luke 13:32" id="f-p191.2" parsed="|Luke|13|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.13.32">Luke 13:32</scripRef>, where our Lord calls Herod “that fox.” In

<scripRef passage="Judg. 15:4" id="f-p191.3" parsed="|Judg|15|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.15.4">Judg. 15:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Judg. 15:5" id="f-p191.4" parsed="|Judg|15|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.15.5">5</scripRef>, the reference is in all probability to the
jackal. The Hebrew word shu’al_ through the Persian _schagal
becomes our jackal (Canis aureus), so that the word may bear
that signification here. The reasons for preferring the
rendering “jackal” are (1) that it is more easily caught than
the fox; (2) that the fox is shy and suspicious, and flies
mankind, while the jackal does not; and (3) that foxes are
difficult, jackals comparatively easy, to treat in the way here
described. Jackals hunt in large numbers, and are still very
numerous in Southern Palestine.
</def>
<term id="f-p191.5">Frankincense</term>
(Heb. lebonah; Gr. libanos, i.e., “white”), an odorous resin

imported from Arabia (<scripRef passage="Isa. 60:6" id="f-p192.1" parsed="|Isa|60|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.60.6">Isa. 60:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 6:20" id="f-p192.2" parsed="|Jer|6|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.6.20">Jer. 6:20</scripRef>), yet also growing in
Palestine (<scripRef passage="Cant. 4:14" id="f-p192.3" parsed="|Song|4|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.4.14">Cant. 4:14</scripRef>). It was one of the ingredients in the
perfume of the sanctuary (<scripRef passage="Ex. 30:34" id="f-p192.4" parsed="|Exod|30|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.30.34">Ex. 30:34</scripRef>), and was used as an

accompaniment of the meat-offering (<scripRef passage="Lev. 2:1" id="f-p192.5" parsed="|Lev|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.2.1">Lev. 2:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 2:16" id="f-p192.6" parsed="|Lev|2|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.2.16">16</scripRef>; 6:15; 24:7).
When burnt it emitted a fragrant odour, and hence the incense

became a symbol of the Divine name (<scripRef passage="Mal. 1:11" id="f-p192.7" parsed="|Mal|1|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mal.1.11">Mal. 1:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Cant. 1:3" id="f-p192.8" parsed="|Song|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.1.3">Cant. 1:3</scripRef>) and an
emblem of prayer (Ps. 141:2; Luke 1:10; Rev. 5:8; 8:3).
This frankincense, or olibanum, used by the Jews in the temple
services is not to be confounded with the frankincense of modern
commerce, which is an exudation of the Norway spruce fir, the
Pinus abies. It was probably a resin from the Indian tree known
to botanists by the name of Boswellia serrata or thurifera,
which grows to the height of forty feet.
</def>
<term id="f-p193.1">Freedom</term>
The law of Moses pointed out the cases in which the servants of

the Hebrews were to receive their freedom (<scripRef passage="Ex. 21:2-4" id="f-p194.1" parsed="|Exod|21|2|21|4" osisRef="Bible:Exod.21.2-Exod.21.4">Ex. 21:2-4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex 21:7" id="f-p194.2" parsed="|Exod|21|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.21.7">7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex 21:8" id="f-p194.3" parsed="|Exod|21|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.21.8">8</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Lev. 25:39-42" id="f-p194.4" parsed="|Lev|25|39|25|42" osisRef="Bible:Lev.25.39-Lev.25.42">Lev. 25:39-42</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev 25:47-55" id="f-p194.5" parsed="|Lev|25|47|25|55" osisRef="Bible:Lev.25.47-Lev.25.55">47-55</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 15:12-18" id="f-p194.6" parsed="|Deut|15|12|15|18" osisRef="Bible:Deut.15.12-Deut.15.18">Deut. 15:12-18</scripRef>). Under the Roman law the
“freeman” (ingenuus) was one born free; the “freedman”
(libertinus) was a manumitted slave, and had not equal rights

with the freeman (<scripRef passage="Acts 22:28" id="f-p194.7" parsed="|Acts|22|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.22.28">Acts 22:28</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Acts 16:37-39" id="f-p194.8" parsed="|Acts|16|37|16|39" osisRef="Bible:Acts.16.37-Acts.16.39">Acts 16:37-39</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 21:39" id="f-p194.9" parsed="|Acts|21|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.21.39">21:39</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 22:25" id="f-p194.10" parsed="|Acts|22|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.22.25">22:25</scripRef>;
25:11, 12).
</def>
<term id="f-p194.13">Free-will offering</term>
A spontaneous gift (Ex. 35:29), a voluntary sacrifice (Lev. 22:23; Ezra 3:5), as opposed to one in consequence of a vow, or
in expiation of some offence.
</def>
<term id="f-p195.4">Frog</term>
(Heb. tsepharde’a, meaning a “marsh-leaper”). This reptile is
mentioned in the Old Testament only in connection with one of
the plagues which fell on the land of Egypt (Ex. 8:2-14; Ps. 78:45; 105:30).
In the New Testament this word occurs only in Rev. 16:13,
where it is referred to as a symbol of uncleanness. The only
species of frog existing in Palestine is the green frog (Rana
esculenta), the well-known edible frog of the Continent.
</def>
<term id="f-p197.2">Frontlets</term>
Occurs only in Ex. 13:16; Deut. 6:8, and 11:18. The meaning of
the injunction to the Israelites, with regard to the statues and
precepts given them, that they should “bind them for a sign upon
their hand, and have them as frontlets between their eyes,” was
that they should keep them distinctly in view and carefully
attend to them. But soon after their return from Babylon they
began to interpret this injunction literally, and had
accordingly portions of the law written out and worn about their
person. These they called tephillin, i.e., “prayers.” The

passages so written out on strips of parchment were these, <scripRef passage="Ex. 12:2-10" id="f-p198.3" parsed="|Exod|12|2|12|10" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.2-Exod.12.10">Ex. 12:2-10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 13:11-21" id="f-p198.4" parsed="|Exod|13|11|13|21" osisRef="Bible:Exod.13.11-Exod.13.21">13:11-21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 6:4-9" id="f-p198.5" parsed="|Deut|6|4|6|9" osisRef="Bible:Deut.6.4-Deut.6.9">Deut. 6:4-9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut 11:18-21" id="f-p198.6" parsed="|Deut|11|18|11|21" osisRef="Bible:Deut.11.18-Deut.11.21">11:18-21</scripRef>. They were then “rolled
up in a case of black calfskin, which was attached to a stiffer
piece of leather, having a thong one finger broad and one cubit
and a half long. Those worn on the forehead were written on four
strips of parchment, and put into four little cells within a
square case, which had on it the Hebrew letter called shin, the
three points of which were regarded as an emblem of God.” This
case tied around the forehead in a particular way was called
“the tephillah on the head.” (See PHYLACTERY.)
</def>
<term id="f-p198.8">Frost</term>
(Heb. kerah, from its smoothness) Job 37:10 (R.V., “ice”); Gen. 31:40; Jer. 36:30; rendered “ice” in Job 6:16, 38:29; and
“crystal” in <scripRef passage="Ezek. 1:22" id="f-p199.6" parsed="|Ezek|1|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.1.22">Ezek. 1:22</scripRef>. “At the present day frost is entirely
unknown in the lower portions of the valley of the Jordan, but
slight frosts are sometimes felt on the sea-coast and near
Lebanon.” Throughout Western Asia cold frosty nights are
frequently succeeded by warm days.
“Hoar frost” (Heb. kephor, so called from its covering the
ground) is mentioned in Ex. 16:14; Job 38:29; Ps. 147:16.
In Ps. 78:47 the word rendered “frost” (R.V. marg., “great
hail-stones”), hanamal, occurs only there. It is rendered by
Gesenius, the Hebrew lexicographer, “ant,” and so also by
others, but the usual interpretation derived from the ancient
versions may be maintained.
</def>
<term id="f-p201.2">Fruit</term>
A word as used in Scripture denoting produce in general, whether
vegetable or animal. The Hebrews divided the fruits of the land
into three classes:,
(1.) The fruit of the field, “corn-fruit” (Heb. dagan); all
kinds of grain and pulse.
(2.) The fruit of the vine, “vintage-fruit” (Heb. tirosh);
grapes, whether moist or dried.
(3.) “Orchard-fruits” (Heb. yitshar), as dates, figs, citrons,
etc.
Injunctions concerning offerings and tithes were expressed by

these Hebrew terms alone (<scripRef passage="Num. 18:12" id="f-p206.1" parsed="|Num|18|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.18.12">Num. 18:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 14:23" id="f-p206.2" parsed="|Deut|14|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.14.23">Deut. 14:23</scripRef>). This word

“fruit” is also used of children or offspring (<scripRef passage="Gen. 30:2" id="f-p206.3" parsed="|Gen|30|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.30.2">Gen. 30:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 7:13" id="f-p206.4" parsed="|Deut|7|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.7.13">Deut. 7:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 1:42" id="f-p206.5" parsed="|Luke|1|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.42">Luke 1:42</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 21:10" id="f-p206.6" parsed="|Ps|21|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.21.10">Ps. 21:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 132:11" id="f-p206.7" parsed="|Ps|132|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.132.11">132:11</scripRef>); also of the progeny of
beasts (Deut. 28:51; Isa. 14:29).
It is used metaphorically in a variety of forms (Ps. 104:13;

<scripRef passage="Prov. 1:31" id="f-p207.2" parsed="|Prov|1|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.1.31">Prov. 1:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov 11:30" id="f-p207.3" parsed="|Prov|11|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.11.30">11:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov 31:16" id="f-p207.4" parsed="|Prov|31|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.31.16">31:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 3:10" id="f-p207.5" parsed="|Isa|3|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.10">Isa. 3:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 10:12" id="f-p207.6" parsed="|Isa|10|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.12">10:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 3:8" id="f-p207.7" parsed="|Matt|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.8">Matt. 3:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 21:41" id="f-p207.8" parsed="|Matt|21|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.21.41">21:41</scripRef>;
26:29; Heb. 13:15; Rom. 7:4, 5; 15:28).
The fruits of the Spirit (Gal. 5:22, 23; Eph. 5:9; James 3:17, 18) are those gracious dispositions and habits which the Spirit
produces in those in whom he dwells and works.
</def>
<term id="f-p208.6">Frying-pan</term>
(Heb. marhesheth, a “boiler”), a pot for boiling meat (Lev. 2:7;
7:9).
</def>
<term id="f-p209.3">Fuel</term>
Almost every kind of combustible matter was used for fuel, such

as the withered stalks of herbs (<scripRef passage="Matt. 6:30" id="f-p210.1" parsed="|Matt|6|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.30">Matt. 6:30</scripRef>), thorns (<scripRef passage="Ps. 58:9" id="f-p210.2" parsed="|Ps|58|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.58.9">Ps. 58:9</scripRef>;
