<scripRef passage="Eccl. 7:6" id="f-p210.3" parsed="|Eccl|7|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eccl.7.6">Eccl. 7:6</scripRef>), animal excrements (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 4:12-15" id="f-p210.4" parsed="|Ezek|4|12|4|15" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.4.12-Ezek.4.15">Ezek. 4:12-15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek 15:4" id="f-p210.5" parsed="|Ezek|15|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.15.4">15:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek 15:6" id="f-p210.6" parsed="|Ezek|15|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.15.6">6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek 21:32" id="f-p210.7" parsed="|Ezek|21|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.21.32">21:32</scripRef>).
Wood or charcoal is much used still in all the towns of Syria
and Egypt. It is largely brought from the region of Hebron to
Jerusalem. (See COAL.)
</def>
<term id="f-p210.9">Fugitive</term>
Gen. 4:12, 14, a rover or wanderer (Heb. n’a); Judg. 12:4, a
refugee, one who has escaped (Heb. palit); <scripRef passage="2 Kings 25:11" id="f-p211.4" parsed="|2Kgs|25|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.25.11">2 Kings 25:11</scripRef>, a
deserter, one who has fallen away to the enemy (Heb. nophel);
<scripRef passage="Ezek. 17:21" id="f-p211.5" parsed="|Ezek|17|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.17.21">Ezek. 17:21</scripRef>, one who has broken away in flight (Heb. mibrah);

<scripRef passage="Isa. 15:5" id="f-p211.6" parsed="|Isa|15|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.15.5">Isa. 15:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 43:14" id="f-p211.7" parsed="|Isa|43|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.43.14">43:14</scripRef>, a breaker away, a fugitive (Heb. beriah), one
who flees away.
</def>
<term id="f-p211.8">Fuller</term>
The word “full” is from the Anglo-Saxon fullian, meaning “to
whiten.” To full is to press or scour cloth in a mill. This art
is one of great antiquity. Mention is made of “fuller’s soap”

(<scripRef passage="Mal. 3:2" id="f-p212.1" parsed="|Mal|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mal.3.2">Mal. 3:2</scripRef>), and of “the fuller’s field” (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:17" id="f-p212.2" parsed="|2Kgs|18|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.17">2 Kings 18:17</scripRef>). At his
transfiguration our Lord’s rainment is said to have been white
“so as no fuller on earth could white them” (<scripRef passage="Mark 9:3" id="f-p212.3" parsed="|Mark|9|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.9.3">Mark 9:3</scripRef>). En-rogel
(q.v.), meaning literally “foot-fountain,” has been interpreted
as the “fuller’s fountain,” because there the fullers trod the
cloth with their feet.
</def>
<term id="f-p212.4">Fuller’s field</term>
A spot near Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:17; Isa. 36:2; 7:3), on the
side of the highway west of the city, not far distant from the
“upper pool” at the head of the valley of Hinnom. Here the
fullers pursued their occupation.
</def>
<term id="f-p213.4">Fuller’s soap</term>
(Heb. borith mekabbeshim, i.e., “alkali of those treading

cloth”). Mention is made (<scripRef passage="Prov. 25:20" id="f-p214.1" parsed="|Prov|25|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.25.20">Prov. 25:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 2:22" id="f-p214.2" parsed="|Jer|2|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.2.22">Jer. 2:22</scripRef>) of nitre and
also (<scripRef passage="Mal. 3:2" id="f-p214.3" parsed="|Mal|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mal.3.2">Mal. 3:2</scripRef>) of soap (Heb. borith) used by the fuller in his
operations. Nitre is found in Syria, and vegetable alkali was
obtained from the ashes of certain plants. (See SOAP.)
</def>
<term id="f-p214.5">Fulness</term>
(1.) Of time (Gal. 4:4), the time appointed by God, and foretold
by the prophets, when Messiah should appear. (2.) Of Christ
(<scripRef passage="John 1:16" id="f-p215.2" parsed="|John|1|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.1.16">John 1:16</scripRef>), the superabundance of grace with which he was

filled. (3.) Of the Godhead bodily dwelling in Christ (<scripRef passage="Col. 2:9" id="f-p215.3" parsed="|Col|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.2.9">Col. 2:9</scripRef>), i.e., the whole nature and attributes of God are in
Christ. (4.) <scripRef passage="Eph. 1:23" id="f-p215.4" parsed="|Eph|1|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.1.23">Eph. 1:23</scripRef>, the church as the fulness of Christ,
i.e., the church makes Christ a complete and perfect head.
</def>
<term id="f-p215.5">Funeral</term>
Burying was among the Jews the only mode of disposing of corpses
(Gen. 23:19; 25:9; 35:8, 9, etc.).
The first traces of burning the dead are found in 1 Sam. 31:12. The burning of the body was affixed by the law of Moses
as a penalty to certain crimes (Lev. 20:14; 21:9).
To leave the dead unburied was regarded with horror (1 Kings 13:22; 14:11; 16:4; 21:24, etc.).
In the earliest times of which we have record kinsmen carried

their dead to the grave (<scripRef passage="Gen. 25:9" id="f-p219.1" parsed="|Gen|25|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.9">Gen. 25:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 35:29" id="f-p219.2" parsed="|Gen|35|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.35.29">35:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 16:31" id="f-p219.3" parsed="|Judg|16|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.16.31">Judg. 16:31</scripRef>), but in
later times this was done by others (Amos 6:16).
Immediately after decease the body was washed, and then

wrapped in a large cloth (<scripRef passage="Acts 9:37" id="f-p220.1" parsed="|Acts|9|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.9.37">Acts 9:37</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 27:59" id="f-p220.2" parsed="|Matt|27|59|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.59">Matt. 27:59</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 15:46" id="f-p220.3" parsed="|Mark|15|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.15.46">Mark 15:46</scripRef>).
In the case of persons of distinction, aromatics were laid on
the folds of the cloth (John 19:39; comp. John 12:7).
As a rule the burial (q.v.) took place on the very day of the

death (<scripRef passage="Acts 5:6" id="f-p221.1" parsed="|Acts|5|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.5.6">Acts 5:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 5:10" id="f-p221.2" parsed="|Acts|5|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.5.10">10</scripRef>), and the body was removed to the grave in
an open coffin or on a bier (<scripRef passage="Luke 7:14" id="f-p221.3" parsed="|Luke|7|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.7.14">Luke 7:14</scripRef>). After the burial a
funeral meal was usually given (2 Sam. 3:35; Jer. 16:5, 7; Hos. 9:4).
</def>
<term id="f-p221.8">Furlong</term>
A stadium, a Greek measure of distance equal to 606 feet and 9
inches (Luke 24:13; John 6:19; 11:18; Rev. 14:20; 21:16).
</def>
<term id="f-p222.6">Furnace</term>
(1.) Chald. attun, a large furnace with a wide open mouth, at

the top of which materials were cast in (<scripRef passage="Dan. 3:22" id="f-p223.1" parsed="|Dan|3|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.3.22">Dan. 3:22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan. 3:23" id="f-p223.2" parsed="|Dan|3|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.3.23">23</scripRef>; comp.
<scripRef passage="Jer. 29:22" id="f-p223.3" parsed="|Jer|29|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.29.22">Jer. 29:22</scripRef>). This furnace would be in constant requisition, for
the Babylonians disposed of their dead by cremation, as did also
the Accadians who invaded Mesopotamia.
(2.) Heb. kibshan, a smelting furnace (Gen. 19:28), also a
lime-kiln (Isa. 33:12; Amos 2:1).
(3.) Heb. kur, a refining furnace (Prov. 17:3; 27:21; Ezek. 22:18).
(4.) Heb. alil, a crucible; only used in Ps. 12:6.
(5.) Heb. tannur, oven for baking bread (Gen. 15:17; Isa. 31:9; Neh. 3:11). It was a large pot, narrowing towards the top.
When it was heated by a fire made within, the dough was spread
over the heated surface, and thus was baked. “A smoking furnace
and a burning lamp” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 15:17" id="f-p227.4" parsed="|Gen|15|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.17">Gen. 15:17</scripRef>), the symbol of the presence of
the Almighty, passed between the divided pieces of Abraham’s
sacrifice in ratification of the covenant God made with him.
(See OVEN.)
(6.) Gr. kamnos, a furnace, kiln, or oven (Matt. 13:42, 50;
Rev. 1:15; 9:2).
</def>
<term id="f-p228.5">Furrow</term>
An opening in the ground made by the plough (Ps. 65:10; Hos. 10:4, 10).
</def>
<term id="f-p229.4">Fury</term>
As attributed to God, is a figurative expression for dispensing
afflictive judgments (Lev. 26:28; Job 20:23; Isa. 63:3; Jer. 4:4; Ezek. 5:13; Dan. 9:16; Zech. 8:2).
</def>
</glossary>
</div2>
<div2 title="G" prev="f" next="h" id="g">
<glossary id="g-p0.1">
<term id="g-p0.2">Gaal</term>
<def id="g-p0.3">
Loathing, the son of Ebed, in whom the Shechemites “placed their
confidence” when they became discontented with Abimelech. He
headed the revolution, and led out the men of Shechem against
Abimelech; but was defeated, and fled to his own home (Judg. 9:26-46). We hear no more of him after this battle.
</def>
<term id="g-p1.2">Gaash</term>
<def id="g-p1.3">
A shaking, a hill, on the north side of which Joshua was buried

(<scripRef passage="Josh. 24:30" id="g-p2.1" parsed="|Josh|24|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.24.30">Josh. 24:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 2:9" id="g-p2.2" parsed="|Judg|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.2.9">Judg. 2:9</scripRef>), in the territory of Ephraim. (See
TIMNATH-SERAH.)
</def>
<term id="g-p2.4">Gabbatha</term>
<def id="g-p2.5">
Gab Baitha, i.e., “the ridge of the house” = “the temple-mound,”
on a part of which the fortress of Antonia was built. This
“temple-mound” was covered with a tesselated “pavement” (Gr.
lithostroton, i.e., “stone-paved”). A judgement-seat (bema) was
placed on this “pavement” outside the hall of the “praetorium”
(q.v.), the judgment-hall (John 18:28; 19:13).
</def>
<term id="g-p3.3">Gabriel</term>
<def id="g-p3.4">
Champion of God, used as a proper name to designate the angel
who was sent to Daniel (8:16) to explain the vision of the ram
and the he-goat, and to communicate the prediction of the
seventy weeks (Dan. 9:21-27).
He announced also the birth of John the Baptist (Luke 1:11),
and of the Messiah (26). He describes himself in the words, “I
am Gabriel, who stand in the presence of God” (1:19).
</def>
<term id="g-p5.2">Gad</term>
<def id="g-p5.3">
Fortune; luck. (1.) Jacob’s seventh son, by Zilpah, Leah’s

handmaid, and the brother of Asher (<scripRef passage="Gen. 30:11-13" id="g-p6.1" parsed="|Gen|30|11|30|13" osisRef="Bible:Gen.30.11-Gen.30.13">Gen. 30:11-13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 46:16" id="g-p6.2" parsed="|Gen|46|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.46.16">46:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 46:18" id="g-p6.3" parsed="|Gen|46|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.46.18">18</scripRef>).
In the Authorized Version of 30:11 the words, “A troop cometh:
and she called,” etc., should rather be rendered, “In fortune
[R.V., ‘Fortunate’]: and she called,” etc., or “Fortune cometh,”
etc.
The tribe of Gad during the march through the wilderness had
their place with Simeon and Reuben on the south side of the
tabernacle (<scripRef passage="Num. 2:14" id="g-p7.1" parsed="|Num|2|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.2.14">Num. 2:14</scripRef>). The tribes of Reuben and Gad continued
all through their history to follow the pastoral pursuits of the
patriarchs (Num. 32:1-5).
The portion allotted to the tribe of Gad was on the east of
Jordan, and comprehended the half of Gilead, a region of great
beauty and fertility (<scripRef passage="Deut. 3:12" id="g-p8.1" parsed="|Deut|3|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.12">Deut. 3:12</scripRef>), bounded on the east by the
Arabian desert, on the west by the Jordan (<scripRef passage="Josh. 13:27" id="g-p8.2" parsed="|Josh|13|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.27">Josh. 13:27</scripRef>), and on
the north by the river Jabbok. It thus included the whole of the
Jordan valley as far north as to the Sea of Galilee, where it
narrowed almost to a point.
This tribe was fierce and warlike; they were “strong men of
might, men of war for the battle, that could handle shield and
buckler, their faces the faces of lions, and like roes upon the

mountains for swiftness” (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 12:8" id="g-p9.1" parsed="|1Chr|12|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.12.8">1 Chr. 12:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 5:19-22" id="g-p9.2" parsed="|1Chr|5|19|5|22" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5.19-1Chr.5.22">5:19-22</scripRef>). Barzillai (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 17:27" id="g-p9.3" parsed="|2Sam|17|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.17.27">2 Sam. 17:27</scripRef>) and Elijah (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 17:1" id="g-p9.4" parsed="|1Kgs|17|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.17.1">1 Kings 17:1</scripRef>) were of this tribe. It was
carried into captivity at the same time as the other tribes of
the northern kingdom by Tiglath-pileser (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 5:26" id="g-p9.5" parsed="|1Chr|5|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5.26">1 Chr. 5:26</scripRef>), and in
the time of Jeremiah (49:1) their cities were inhabited by the
Ammonites.
(2.) A prophet who joined David in the “hold,” and at whose

advice he quitted it for the forest of Hareth (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 29:29" id="g-p10.1" parsed="|1Chr|29|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.29.29">1 Chr. 29:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 29:25" id="g-p10.2" parsed="|2Chr|29|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.29.25">2 Chr. 29:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 22:5" id="g-p10.3" parsed="|1Sam|22|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.22.5">1 Sam. 22:5</scripRef>). Many years after we find mention made
of him in connection with the punishment inflicted for numbering

the people (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 24:11-19" id="g-p10.4" parsed="|2Sam|24|11|24|19" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.24.11-2Sam.24.19">2 Sam. 24:11-19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 21:9-19" id="g-p10.5" parsed="|1Chr|21|9|21|19" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.21.9-1Chr.21.19">1 Chr. 21:9-19</scripRef>). He wrote a book
called the “Acts of David” (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 29:29" id="g-p10.6" parsed="|1Chr|29|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.29.29">1 Chr. 29:29</scripRef>), and assisted in the
arrangements for the musical services of the “house of God” (2 Chr. 29:25). He bore the title of “the king’s seer” (2 Sam. 24:11, 13; 1 Chr. 21:9).
</def>
<term id="g-p10.11">Gadara</term>
The capital of the Roman province of Peraea. It stood on the
summit of a mountain about 6 miles south-east of the Sea of
Galilee. Mark (5:1) and Luke (8:26-39) describe the miracle of
the healing of the demoniac (Matthew [8:28-34] says two
demoniacs) as having been wrought “in the country of the
Gadarenes,” thus describing the scene generally. The miracle
could not have been wrought at Gadara itself, for between the
lake and this town there is the deep, almost impassable ravine
of the Hieromax (Jarmuk). It is identified with the modern
village of Um-Keis, which is surrounded by very extensive ruins,
all bearing testimony to the splendour of ancient Gadara.
“The most interesting remains of Gadara are its tombs, which
dot the cliffs for a considerable distance round the city,
chiefly on the north-east declivity; but many beautifully
sculptured sarcophagi are scattered over the surrounding
heights. They are excavated in the limestone rock, and consist
of chambers of various dimensions, some more than 20 feet
square, with recesses in the sides for bodies...The present
inhabitants of Um-Keis are all troglodytes, ‘dwelling in tombs,’
like the poor maniacs of old, and occasionally they are almost
as dangerous to unprotected travellers.”
</def>
<term id="g-p12.1">Gadarenes</term>
<def id="g-p12.2">
The inhabitants of Gadara, in Revised Version “Gerasenes” (Mark 5:1; Luke 8:26, 37). In Matt. 8:28 they are called Gergesenes,
Revised Version “Gadarenes.”
</def>
<term id="g-p13.5">Gaddi</term>
<def id="g-p13.6">
Fortunate, the representative of the tribe of Manasseh among the
twelve “spies” sent by Moses to spy the land (Num. 13:11).
</def>
<term id="g-p14.2">Gaddiel</term>
<def id="g-p14.3">
Fortune (i.e., sent) of God, the representative of the tribe of
Zebulum among the twelve spies (Num. 13:10).
</def>
<term id="g-p15.2">Gahar</term>
<def id="g-p15.3">
Lurking-place, one of the chief of the Nethinim, whose
descendants returned to Jerusalem under Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:47).
</def>
<term id="g-p16.2">Gaius</term>
<def id="g-p16.3">
(1.) A Macedonian, Paul’s fellow-traveller, and his host at
Corinth when he wrote his Epistle to the Romans (16:23). He with
his household were baptized by Paul (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 1:14" id="g-p17.1" parsed="|1Cor|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.1.14">1 Cor. 1:14</scripRef>). During a
heathen outbreak against Paul at Ephesus the mob seized Gaius
and Aristarchus because they could not find Paul, and rushed
with them into the theatre. Some have identified this Gaius with
(2.) A man of Derbe who accompanied Paul into Asia on his last
journey to Jerusalem
(3.) A Christain of Asia Minor to whom John addressed his
third epistle (3 John 1:1).
</def>
<term id="g-p19.2">Galatia</term>
<def id="g-p19.3">
Has been called the “Gallia” of the East, Roman writers calling
its inhabitants Galli. They were an intermixture of Gauls and
Greeks, and hence were called Gallo-Graeci, and the country
Gallo-Graecia. The Galatians were in their origin a part of that
great Celtic migration which invaded Macedonia about B.C. 280.
They were invited by the king of Bithynia to cross over into
Asia Minor to assist him in his wars. There they ultimately
settled, and being strengthened by fresh accessions of the same
clan from Europe, they overran Bithynia, and supported
themselves by plundering neighbouring countries. They were great
warriors, and hired themselves out as mercenary soldiers,
sometimes fighting on both sides in the great battles of the
times. They were at length brought under the power of Rome in
B.C. 189, and Galatia became a Roman province B.C. 25.
This province of Galatia, within the limits of which these
Celtic tribes were confined, was the central region of Asia
Minor.
During his second missionary journey Paul, accompanied by
Silas and Timothy (<scripRef passage="Acts 16:6" id="g-p22.1" parsed="|Acts|16|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.16.6">Acts 16:6</scripRef>), visited the “region of Galatia,”
where he was detained by sickness (<scripRef passage="Gal. 4:13" id="g-p22.2" parsed="|Gal|4|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.4.13">Gal. 4:13</scripRef>), and had thus the
longer opportunity of preaching to them the gospel. On his third
journey he went over “all the country of Galatia and Phrygia in
order” (<scripRef passage="Acts 18:23" id="g-p22.3" parsed="|Acts|18|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.23">Acts 18:23</scripRef>). Crescens was sent thither by Paul toward
the close of his life (2 Tim. 4:10).
</def>
<term id="g-p22.5">Galatians, Epistle to</term>
<def id="g-p22.6">
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="g-p22.7" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="Gal 0" id="g-p22.8" parsed="|Gal|0|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal" />
The genuineness of this epistle is not called in question. Its
Pauline origin is universally acknowledged.
Occasion of. The churches of Galatia were founded by Paul

himself (<scripRef passage="Acts 16:6" id="g-p24.1" parsed="|Acts|16|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.16.6">Acts 16:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal. 1:8" id="g-p24.2" parsed="|Gal|1|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.1.8">Gal. 1:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal 4:13" id="g-p24.3" parsed="|Gal|4|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.4.13">4:13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gal 4:19" id="g-p24.4" parsed="|Gal|4|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.4.19">19</scripRef>). They seem to have been
composed mainly of converts from heathenism (4:8), but partly
also of Jewish converts, who probably, under the influence of
Judaizing teachers, sought to incorporate the rites of Judaism
with Christianity, and by their active zeal had succeeded in
inducing the majority of the churches to adopt their views (1:6;
3:1). This epistle was written for the purpose of counteracting
this Judaizing tendency, and of recalling the Galatians to the
simplicity of the gospel, and at the same time also of
vindicating Paul’s claim to be a divinely-commissioned apostle.
Time and place of writing. The epistle was probably written
very soon after Paul’s second visit to Galatia (<scripRef passage="Acts 18:23" id="g-p25.1" parsed="|Acts|18|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.23">Acts 18:23</scripRef>). The
references of the epistle appear to agree with this conclusion.
The visit to Jerusalem, mentioned in <scripRef passage="Gal. 2:1-10" id="g-p25.2" parsed="|Gal|2|1|2|10" osisRef="Bible:Gal.2.1-Gal.2.10">Gal. 2:1-10</scripRef>, was identical
with that of <scripRef passage="Acts 15" id="g-p25.3" parsed="|Acts|15|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.15">Acts 15</scripRef>, and it is spoken of as a thing of the
past, and consequently the epistle was written subsequently to
the council of Jerusalem. The similarity between this epistle
and that to the Romans has led to the conclusion that they were
both written at the same time, namely, in the winter of A.D.

57-8, during Paul’s stay in Corinth (<scripRef passage="Acts 20:2" id="g-p25.4" parsed="|Acts|20|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.2">Acts 20:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 20:3" id="g-p25.5" parsed="|Acts|20|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.3">3</scripRef>). This to the
Galatians is written on the urgency of the occasion, tidings
having reached him of the state of matters; and that to the
Romans in a more deliberate and systematic way, in exposition of
the same great doctrines of the gospel.
Contents of. The great question discussed is, Was the Jewish
law binding on Christians? The epistle is designed to prove
against the Jews that men are justified by faith without the

works of the law of Moses. After an introductory address (<scripRef passage="Gal. 1:1-10" id="g-p26.1" parsed="|Gal|1|1|1|10" osisRef="Bible:Gal.1.1-Gal.1.10">Gal. 1:1-10</scripRef>) the apostle discusses the subjects which had occasioned
the epistle. (1) He defends his apostolic authority (1:11-19;
2:1-14); (2) shows the evil influence of the Judaizers in
destroying the very essence of the gospel (3 and 4); (3) exhorts
the Galatian believers to stand fast in the faith as it is in
Jesus, and to abound in the fruits of the Spirit, and in a right
use of their Christian freedom (5-6:1-10); (4) and then
concludes with a summary of the topics discussed, and with the
benediction.
The Epistle to the Galatians and that to the Romans taken
together “form a complete proof that justification is not to be
obtained meritoriously either by works of morality or by rites
and ceremonies, though of divine appointment; but that it is a
free gift, proceeding entirely from the mercy of God, to those
who receive it by faith in Jesus our Lord.”
In the conclusion of the epistle (6:11) Paul says, “Ye see how
large a letter I have written with mine own hand.” It is implied
that this was different from his ordinary usage, which was
simply to write the concluding salutation with his own hand,
indicating that the rest of the epistle was written by another
hand. Regarding this conclusion, Lightfoot, in his Commentary on
the epistle, says: “At this point the apostle takes the pen from
his amanuensis, and the concluding paragraph is written with his
own hand. From the time when letters began to be forged in his

name (<scripRef passage="2 Thess. 2:2" id="g-p28.1" parsed="|2Thess|2|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Thess.2.2">2 Thess. 2:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Thess. 3:17" id="g-p28.2" parsed="|2Thess|3|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Thess.3.17">3:17</scripRef>) it seems to have been his practice to
close with a few words in his own handwriting, as a precaution
against such forgeries...In the present case he writes a whole
paragraph, summing up the main lessons of the epistle in terse,
eager, disjointed sentences. He writes it, too, in large, bold
characters (Gr. pelikois grammasin), that his hand-writing may
reflect the energy and determination of his soul.” (See JUSTIFICATION.)
</def>
<term id="g-p28.4">Galbanum</term>
<def id="g-p28.5">
Heb. helbenah, (Ex. 30:34), one of the ingredients in the holy
incense. It is a gum, probably from the Galbanum officinale.
</def>
<term id="g-p29.2">Galeed</term>
<def id="g-p29.3">
Heap of witness, the name of the pile of stones erected by Jacob
and Laban to mark the league of friendship into which they

entered with each other (<scripRef passage="Gen. 31:47" id="g-p30.1" parsed="|Gen|31|47|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.47">Gen. 31:47</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 31:48" id="g-p30.2" parsed="|Gen|31|48|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.48">48</scripRef>). This was the name
given to the “heap” by Jacob. It is Hebrew, while the name
Jegar-sahadutha, given to it by Laban, is Aramaic (Chaldee or
Syriac). Probably Nahor’s family originally spoke Aramaic, and
Abraham and his descendants learned Hebrew, a kindred dialect,
in the land of Canaan.
</def>
<term id="g-p30.3">Galilean</term>
<def id="g-p30.4">
An inhabitant or native of Galilee. This word was used as a name

of contempt as applied to our Lord’s disciples (<scripRef passage="Luke 22:59" id="g-p31.1" parsed="|Luke|22|59|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.22.59">Luke 22:59</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 2:7" id="g-p31.2" parsed="|Acts|2|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.2.7">Acts 2:7</scripRef>). All the apostles, with the exception of Judas Iscariot
(<scripRef passage="Acts 1:11" id="g-p31.3" parsed="|Acts|1|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.11">Acts 1:11</scripRef>), were Galileans. Peter was detected by his Galilean
accent (Matt. 26:69; Mark 14:70).
This was also one of the names of reproach given to the early
Christians. Julian the Apostate, as he is called, not only used
the epithet himself when referring to Christ and his apostles,
but he made it a law that no one should ever call the Christians
by any other name.
</def>
<term id="g-p32.1">Galilee</term>
<def id="g-p32.2">
Circuit. Solomon rewarded Hiram for certain services rendered
him by the gift of an upland plain among the mountains of
Naphtali. Hiram was dissatisfied with the gift, and called it
“the land of Cabul” (q.v.). The Jews called it Galil. It
continued long to be occupied by the original inhabitants, and
hence came to be called “Galilee of the Gentiles” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 4:15" id="g-p33.1" parsed="|Matt|4|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.4.15">Matt. 4:15</scripRef>),
and also “Upper Galilee,” to distinguish it from the extensive
addition afterwards made to it toward the south, which was
usually called “Lower Galilee.” In the time of our Lord, Galilee
embraced more than one-third of Western Palestine, extending
“from Dan on the north, at the base of Mount Hermon, to the
ridges of Carmel and Gilboa on the south, and from the Jordan
valley on the east away across the splendid plains of Jezreel
and Acre to the shores of the Mediterranean on the west.”
Palestine was divided into three provinces, Judea, Samaria, and
Galilee, which comprehended the whole northern section of the
country (Acts 9:31), and was the largest of the three.
It was the scene of some of the most memorable events of
Jewish history. Galilee also was the home of our Lord during at
least thirty years of his life. The first three Gospels are
chiefly taken up with our Lord’s public ministry in this
province. “The entire province is encircled with a halo of holy
associations connected with the life, works, and teachings of
Jesus of Nazareth.” “It is noteworthy that of his thirty-two
beautiful parables, no less than ninteen were spoken in Galilee.
And it is no less remarkable that of his entire thirty-three
great miracles, twenty-five were wrought in this province. His
first miracle was wrought at the wedding in Cana of Galilee, and
his last, after his resurrection, on the shore of Galilee’s sea.
In Galilee our Lord delivered the Sermon on The Mount, and the
discourses on ‘The Bread of Life,’ on ‘Purity,’ on
’Forgiveness,’ and on ‘Humility.’ In Galilee he called his first
disciples; and there occurred the sublime scene of the
Transfiguration” (Porter’s Through Samaria).
When the Sanhedrin were about to proceed with some plan for
the condemnation of our Lord (<scripRef passage="John 7:45-52" id="g-p35.1" parsed="|John|7|45|7|52" osisRef="Bible:John.7.45-John.7.52">John 7:45-52</scripRef>), Nicodemus

interposed in his behalf. (Comp. <scripRef passage="Deut. 1:16" id="g-p35.2" parsed="|Deut|1|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.1.16">Deut. 1:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut. 1:17" id="g-p35.3" parsed="|Deut|1|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.1.17">17</scripRef>; 17:8.) They
replied, “Art thou also of Galilee?.... Out of Galilee ariseth
no prophet.” This saying of theirs was “not historically true,
for two prophets at least had arisen from Galilee, Jonah of
Gath-hepher, and the greatest of all the prophets, Elijah of
Thisbe, and perhaps also Nahum and Hosea. Their contempt for
Galilee made them lose sight of historical accuracy” (Alford,
Com.).
The Galilean accent differed from that of Jerusalem in being
broader and more guttural (Mark 14:70).
</def>
<term id="g-p36.2">Galilee, Sea of</term>
<def id="g-p36.3">
(Matt. 4:18; 15:29), is mentioned in the Bible under three other
names. (1.) In the Old Testament it is called the “sea of

Chinnereth” (<scripRef passage="Num. 34:11" id="g-p37.3" parsed="|Num|34|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.34.11">Num. 34:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 12:3" id="g-p37.4" parsed="|Josh|12|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.12.3">Josh. 12:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 13:27" id="g-p37.5" parsed="|Josh|13|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.27">13:27</scripRef>), as is supposed from
its harp-like shape. (2). The “lake of Gennesareth” once by Luke
(5:1), from the flat district lying on its west coast. (3.) John
(6:1; 21:1) calls it the “sea of Tiberias” (q.v.). The modern
Arabs retain this name, Bahr Tabariyeh.
This lake is 12 1/2 miles long, and from 4 to 7 1/2 broad. Its
surface is 682 feet below the level of the Mediterranean. Its
depth is from 80 to 160 feet. The Jordan enters it 10 1/2 miles
below the southern extremity of the Huleh Lake, or about 26 1/2
miles from its source. In this distance of 26 1/2 miles there is
a fall in the river of 1,682 feet, or of more than 60 feet to
the mile. It is 27 miles east of the Mediterranean, and about 60
miles north-east of Jerusalem. It is of an oval shape, and
abounds in fish.
Its present appearance is thus described: “The utter
loneliness and absolute stillness of the scene are exceedingly
impressive. It seems as if all nature had gone to rest,
languishing under the scorching heat. How different it was in
the days of our Lord! Then all was life and bustle along the
shores; the cities and villages that thickly studded them
resounded with the hum of a busy population; while from
hill-side and corn-field came the cheerful cry of shepherd and
ploughman. The lake, too, was dotted with dark fishing-boats and
spangled with white sails. Now a mournful, solitary silence
reigns over sea and shore. The cities are in ruins!”
This sea is chiefly of interest as associated with the public
ministry of our Lord. Capernaum, “his own city” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 9:1" id="g-p40.1" parsed="|Matt|9|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.9.1">Matt. 9:1</scripRef>),
stood on its shores. From among the fishermen who plied their
calling on its waters he chose Peter and his brother Andrew, and
James and John, to be disciples, and sent them forth to be

“fishers of men” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 4:18" id="g-p40.2" parsed="|Matt|4|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.4.18">Matt. 4:18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 4:22" id="g-p40.3" parsed="|Matt|4|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.4.22">22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 1:16-20" id="g-p40.4" parsed="|Mark|1|16|1|20" osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.16-Mark.1.20">Mark 1:16-20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 5" id="g-p40.5" parsed="|Luke|5|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.5">Luke 5</scripRef>: 1-11). He
stilled its tempest, saying to the storm that swept over it,

“Peace, be still” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 8:23-27" id="g-p40.6" parsed="|Matt|8|23|8|27" osisRef="Bible:Matt.8.23-Matt.8.27">Matt. 8:23-27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 7:31-35" id="g-p40.7" parsed="|Mark|7|31|7|35" osisRef="Bible:Mark.7.31-Mark.7.35">Mark 7:31-35</scripRef>); and here also
he showed himself after his resurrection to his disciples (John 21).
“The Sea of Galilee is indeed the cradle of the gospel. The
subterranean fires of nature prepared a lake basin, through
which a river afterwards ran, keeping its waters always fresh.
In this basin a vast quantity of shell-fish swarmed, and
multiplied to such an extent that they formed the food of an
extraordinary profusion of fish. The great variety and abundance
of the fish in the lake attracted to its shores a larger and
more varied population than existed elsewhere in Palestine,
whereby this secluded district was brought into contact with all
parts of the world. And this large and varied population, with
access to all nations and countries, attracted the Lord Jesus,
and induced him to make this spot the centre of his public
ministry.”
</def>
<term id="g-p41.1">Gall</term>
<def id="g-p41.2">
(1) Heb. mererah, meaning “bitterness” (Job 16:13); i.e., the
bile secreted in the liver. This word is also used of the poison
of asps (20:14), and of the vitals, the seat of life (25).
(2.) Heb. rosh. In Deut. 32:33 and Job 20:16 it denotes the
poison of serpents. In <scripRef passage="Hos. 10:4" id="g-p43.3" parsed="|Hos|10|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.10.4">Hos. 10:4</scripRef> the Hebrew word is rendered
“hemlock.” The original probably denotes some bitter, poisonous
plant, most probably the poppy, which grows up quickly, and is

therefore coupled with wormwood (<scripRef passage="Deut. 29:18" id="g-p43.4" parsed="|Deut|29|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.29.18">Deut. 29:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 9:15" id="g-p43.5" parsed="|Jer|9|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.9.15">Jer. 9:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lam. 3:19" id="g-p43.6" parsed="|Lam|3|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lam.3.19">Lam. 3:19</scripRef>). Comp. <scripRef passage="Jer. 8:14" id="g-p43.7" parsed="|Jer|8|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.8.14">Jer. 8:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 23:15" id="g-p43.8" parsed="|Jer|23|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.23.15">23:15</scripRef>, “water of gall,” Gesenius, “poppy
juice;” others, “water of hemlock,” “bitter water.”
(3.) Gr. chole (Matt. 27:34), the LXX. translation of the
Hebrew rosh in Ps. 69; 21, which foretells our Lord’s
sufferings. The drink offered to our Lord was vinegar (made of
light wine rendered acid, the common drink of Roman soldiers)
“mingled with gall,” or, according to Mark (15:23), “mingled
with myrrh;” both expressions meaning the same thing, namely,
that the vinegar was made bitter by the infusion of wormwood or
some other bitter substance, usually given, according to a
merciful custom, as an anodyne to those who were crucified, to
render them insensible to pain. Our Lord, knowing this, refuses
to drink it. He would take nothing to cloud his faculties or
blunt the pain of dying. He chooses to suffer every element of
woe in the bitter cup of agony given him by the Father (John 18:11).
</def>
<term id="g-p44.5">Gallery</term>
<def id="g-p44.6">
(1.) Heb. ‘attik (Ezek. 41:15, 16), a terrace; a projection;
ledge.
(2.) Heb. rahit (Cant. 1:17), translated “rafters,” marg.
“galleries;” probably panel-work or fretted ceiling.
</def>
<term id="g-p46.2">Gallim</term>
<def id="g-p46.3">
Heaps, (1 Sam. 25:44; Isa. 10:30). The native place of Phalti,
to whom Michal was given by Saul. It was probably in Benjamin,
to the north of Jerusalem.
</def>
<term id="g-p47.3">Gallio</term>
<def id="g-p47.4">
The elder brother of Seneca the philosopher, who was tutor and
for some time minister of the emperor Nero. He was “deputy”,
i.e., proconsul, as in Revised Version, of Achaia, under the
emperor Claudius, when Paul visited Corinth (<scripRef passage="Acts 18:12" id="g-p48.1" parsed="|Acts|18|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.12">Acts 18:12</scripRef>). The
word used here by Luke in describing the rank of Gallio shows
his accuracy. Achaia was a senatorial province under Claudius,
and the governor of such a province was called a “proconsul.” He
is spoken of by his contemporaries as “sweet Gallio,” and is
described as a most popular and affectionate man. When the Jews
brought Paul before his tribunal on the charge of persuading
“men to worship God contrary to the law” (18:13), he refused to
listen to them, and “drave them from the judgment seat” (18:16).
</def>
<term id="g-p48.2">Gallows</term>
<def id="g-p48.3">
Heb. ‘ets, meaning “a tree” (Esther 6:4), a post or gibbet. In
Gen. 40:19 and Deut. 21:22 the word is rendered “tree.”
</def>
<term id="g-p49.4">Gamaliel</term>
<def id="g-p49.5">
Reward of God. (1.) A chief of the tribe of Manasseh at the
census at Sinai (Num. 1:10; 2:20; 7:54, 59).
(2.) The son of rabbi Simeon, and grandson of the famous rabbi
Hillel. He was a Pharisse, and therefore the opponent of the
party of the Sadducees. He was noted for his learning, and was
president of the Sanhedrim during the regins of Tiberius,
Caligula, and Claudius, and died, it is said, about eighteen
years before the destruction of Jerusalem.
When the apostles were brought before the council, charged
with preaching the resurrection of Jesus, as a zealous Pharisee
Gamaliel councelled moderation and calmness. By a reference to
well-known events, he advised them to “refrain from these men.”
If their work or counsel was of man, it would come to nothing;
but if it was of God, they could not destroy it, and therefore
ought to be on their guard lest they should be “found fighting
against God” (<scripRef passage="Acts 5:34-40" id="g-p52.1" parsed="|Acts|5|34|5|40" osisRef="Bible:Acts.5.34-Acts.5.40">Acts 5:34-40</scripRef>). Paul was one of his disciples
</def>
<term id="g-p52.2">Games</term>
<def id="g-p52.3">
(1.) Of children (Zech. 8:5; Matt. 11:16). The Jewish youth were
also apparently instructed in the use of the bow and the sling
(Judg. 20:16; 1 Chr. 12:2).
(2.) Public games, such as were common among the Greeks and
Romans, were foreign to the Jewish institutions and customs.
Reference, however, is made to such games in two passages (Ps. 19:5; Eccl. 9:11).
(3.) Among the Greeks and Romans games entered largely into
their social life.
(a) Reference in the New Testament is made to gladiatorial
shows and fights with wild beasts (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 15:32" id="g-p56.1" parsed="|1Cor|15|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.15.32">1 Cor. 15:32</scripRef>). These were
common among the Romans, and sometimes on a large scale.
(b) Allusion is frequently made to the Grecian gymnastic

contests (<scripRef passage="Gal. 2:2" id="g-p57.1" parsed="|Gal|2|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.2.2">Gal. 2:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal 5:7" id="g-p57.2" parsed="|Gal|5|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.5.7">5:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Phil. 2:16" id="g-p57.3" parsed="|Phil|2|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Phil.2.16">Phil. 2:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Phil 3:14" id="g-p57.4" parsed="|Phil|3|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Phil.3.14">3:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Tim. 6:12" id="g-p57.5" parsed="|1Tim|6|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.6.12">1 Tim. 6:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Tim. 2:5" id="g-p57.6" parsed="|2Tim|2|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.2.5">2 Tim. 2:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 12:1" id="g-p57.7" parsed="|Heb|12|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.12.1">Heb. 12:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Heb. 12:4" id="g-p57.8" parsed="|Heb|12|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.12.4">4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Heb. 12:12" id="g-p57.9" parsed="|Heb|12|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.12.12">12</scripRef>). These were very numerous. The Olympic,
Pythian, Nemean, and Isthmian games were esteemed as of great
national importance, and the victors at any of these games of
wrestling, racing, etc., were esteemed as the noblest and the
happiest of mortals.
</def>
<term id="g-p57.10">Gammadim</term>
(Ezek. 27:11) brave warriors; R.V. marg., “valorous men;” others
interpret this word as meaning “short-swordsmen,” or “daring
ones”, the name of a class of men who were defenders of the
towers of Tyre.
</def>
<term id="g-p58.2">Gamul</term>
<def id="g-p58.3">
Weaned the leader of one of the priestly courses (1 Chr. 24:17).
</def>
<term id="g-p59.2">Gap</term>
<def id="g-p59.3">
A rent or opening in a wall (Ezek. 13:5; comp. Amos 4:3). The
false prophets did not stand in the gap (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 22" id="g-p60.3" parsed="|Ezek|22|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.22">Ezek. 22</scripRef>: 30), i.e.,
they did nothing to stop the outbreak of wickedness.
</def>
<term id="g-p60.4">Gardens</term>
<def id="g-p60.5">
Mentioned in Scripture, of Eden (Gen. 2:8, 9); Ahab’s garden of

herbs (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 21:2" id="g-p61.3" parsed="|1Kgs|21|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.21.2">1 Kings 21:2</scripRef>); the royal garden (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 21:18" id="g-p61.4" parsed="|2Kgs|21|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.21.18">2 Kings 21:18</scripRef>); the
royal garden at Susa (<scripRef passage="Esther 1:5" id="g-p61.5" parsed="|Esth|1|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.1.5">Esther 1:5</scripRef>); the garden of Joseph of
Arimathea (John 19:41); of Gethsemane (John 18:1).
The “king’s garden” mentioned 2 Kings 25:4, Neh. 3:15, was
near the Pool of Siloam.
Gardens were surrounded by hedges of thorns (Isa. 5:5) or by
walls of stone (<scripRef passage="Prov. 24:31" id="g-p63.2" parsed="|Prov|24|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.24.31">Prov. 24:31</scripRef>). “Watch-towers” or “lodges” were

also built in them (<scripRef passage="Isa. 1:8" id="g-p63.3" parsed="|Isa|1|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.8">Isa. 1:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 12:1" id="g-p63.4" parsed="|Mark|12|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.12.1">Mark 12:1</scripRef>), in which their keepers
sat. On account of their retirement they were frequently used as
places for secret prayer and communion with God (<scripRef passage="Gen. 24:63" id="g-p63.5" parsed="|Gen|24|63|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.63">Gen. 24:63</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Matt. 26:30-36" id="g-p63.6" parsed="|Matt|26|30|26|36" osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.30-Matt.26.36">Matt. 26:30-36</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 1:48" id="g-p63.7" parsed="|John|1|48|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.1.48">John 1:48</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 18:1" id="g-p63.8" parsed="|John|18|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.18.1">18:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="John 18:2" id="g-p63.9" parsed="|John|18|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.18.2">2</scripRef>). The dead were sometimes
buried in gardens (Gen. 23:19, 20; 2 Kings 21:18, 26; 1 Sam. 25:1; Mark 15:46; John 19:41). (See PARADISE.)
</def>
<term id="g-p63.18">Gareb</term>
Scabby; itch. (1.) One of David’s warriors (2 Sam. 23:38), an
Ithrite.
(2.) A hill near Jerusalem (Jer. 31:39), probably the hill of
lepers, and consequently a place outside the boundary of the
city.
</def>
<term id="g-p65.2">Garlands</term>
<def id="g-p65.3">
(Acts 14:13). In heathen sacrifices the victims were adorned
with fillets and garlands made of wool, with leaves and flowers
interwoven. The altar and the priests and attendants were also
in like manner adorned.
</def>
<term id="g-p66.2">Garlic</term>
<def id="g-p66.3">
(Heb. shum, from its strong odour), mentioned only once (Num. 11:5). The garlic common in Eastern countries is the Allium
sativum or Allium Ascalonicum, so called from its having been
brought into Europe from Ascalon by the Crusaders. It is now
known by the name of “shallot” or “eschalot.”
</def>
<term id="g-p67.2">Garner</term>
<def id="g-p67.3">
(1.) Heb. ‘otsar, a treasure; a store of goods laid up, and
hence also the place where they are deposited (Joel 1:17; 2 Chr. 32:27, rendered “treasury”).
(2.) Heb. mezev, a cell, storeroom (Ps. 144:13); Gr. apotheke,
a place for storing anything, a granary (Matt. 3:12; Luke 3:17).
</def>
<term id="g-p69.4">Garnish</term>
<def id="g-p69.5">
Overlay with stones (2 Chr. 3:6), adorn (Rev. 21:19), deck with
garlands (Matt. 23:29), furnish (12:44).
In Job 26:13 (Heb. shiphrah, meaning “brightness”), “By his
spirit the heavens are brightness” i.e., are bright, splendid,
beautiful.
</def>
<term id="g-p71.2">Garrison</term>
<def id="g-p71.3">
(1.) Heb. matstsab, a station; a place where one stands (1 Sam. 14:12); a military or fortified post (1 Sam. 13:23; 14:1, 4, 6,
etc.).
(2.) Heb. netsib, a prefect, superintendent; hence a military

post (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 10:5" id="g-p73.1" parsed="|1Sam|10|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.10.5">1 Sam. 10:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 13:3" id="g-p73.2" parsed="|1Sam|13|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.13.3">13:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 13:4" id="g-p73.3" parsed="|1Sam|13|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.13.4">4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 8:6" id="g-p73.4" parsed="|2Sam|8|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.8.6">2 Sam. 8:6</scripRef>). This word has also been
explained to denote a pillar set up to mark the Philistine
conquest, or an officer appointed to collect taxes; but the idea
of a military post seems to be the correct one.
(3.) Heb. matstsebah, properly a monumental column; improperly
rendered pl. “garrisons” in <scripRef passage="Ezek. 26:11" id="g-p74.1" parsed="|Ezek|26|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.26.11">Ezek. 26:11</scripRef>; correctly in Revised
Version “pillars,” marg. “obelisks,” probably an idolatrous
image.
</def>
<term id="g-p74.2">Gate</term>
<def id="g-p74.3">
(1.) Of cities, as of Jerusalem (Jer. 37:13; Neh. 1:3; 2:3;
3:3), of Sodom (Gen. 19:1), of Gaza (Judg. 16:3).
(2.) Of royal palaces (Neh. 2:8).
(3.) Of the temple of Solomon (1 Kings 6:34, 35; 2 Kings 18:16); of the holy place (1 Kings 6:31, 32; Ezek. 41:23, 24);
of the outer courts of the temple, the beautiful gate (Acts 3:2).
(4.) Tombs (Matt. 27:60).
(5.) Prisons (Acts 12:10; 16:27).
(6.) Caverns (1 Kings 19:13).
(7.) Camps (Ex. 32:26, 27; Heb. 13:12).
The materials of which gates were made were,
(1.) Iron and brass (Ps. 107:16; Isa. 45:2; Acts 12:10).
(2.) Stones and pearls (Isa. 54:12; Rev. 21:21).
(3.) Wood (Judg. 16:3) probably.
At the gates of cities courts of justice were frequently held,

and hence “judges of the gate” are spoken of (<scripRef passage="Deut. 16:18" id="g-p86.1" parsed="|Deut|16|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.16.18">Deut. 16:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut 17:8" id="g-p86.2" parsed="|Deut|17|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.17.8">17:8</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Deut 21:19" id="g-p86.3" parsed="|Deut|21|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.21.19">21:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut 25:6" id="g-p86.4" parsed="|Deut|25|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.25.6">25:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut 25:7" id="g-p86.5" parsed="|Deut|25|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.25.7">7</scripRef>, etc.). At the gates prophets also frequently

delivered their messages (<scripRef passage="Prov. 1:21" id="g-p86.6" parsed="|Prov|1|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.1.21">Prov. 1:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov 8:3" id="g-p86.7" parsed="|Prov|8|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.8.3">8:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 29:21" id="g-p86.8" parsed="|Isa|29|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.29.21">Isa. 29:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 17:19" id="g-p86.9" parsed="|Jer|17|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.17.19">Jer. 17:19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer 17:20" id="g-p86.10" parsed="|Jer|17|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.17.20">20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 26:10" id="g-p86.11" parsed="|Jer|26|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.26.10">26:10</scripRef>). Criminals were punished without the gates (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 21:13" id="g-p86.12" parsed="|1Kgs|21|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.21.13">1 Kings 21:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 7:59" id="g-p86.13" parsed="|Acts|7|59|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.7.59">Acts 7:59</scripRef>). By the “gates of righteousness” we are
probably to understand those of the temple (<scripRef passage="Ps. 118:19" id="g-p86.14" parsed="|Ps|118|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.118.19">Ps. 118:19</scripRef>). “The
gates of hell” (R.V., “gates of Hades”) <scripRef passage="Matt. 16:18" id="g-p86.15" parsed="|Matt|16|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.16.18">Matt. 16:18</scripRef>, are
generally interpreted as meaning the power of Satan, but
probably they may mean the power of death, denoting that the
Church of Christ shall never die.
</def>
<term id="g-p86.16">Gath</term>
A wine-vat, one of the five royal cities of the Philistines

(<scripRef passage="Josh. 13:3" id="g-p87.1" parsed="|Josh|13|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.3">Josh. 13:3</scripRef>) on which the ark brought calamity (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 5:8" id="g-p87.2" parsed="|1Sam|5|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.5.8">1 Sam. 5:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 5:9" id="g-p87.3" parsed="|1Sam|5|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.5.9">9</scripRef>;
6:17). It was famous also as being the birthplace or residence
of Goliath (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:4" id="g-p87.4" parsed="|1Sam|17|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.4">1 Sam. 17:4</scripRef>). David fled from Saul to Achish, king

of Gath (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 21:10" id="g-p87.5" parsed="|1Sam|21|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.21.10">1 Sam. 21:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 27:2-4" id="g-p87.6" parsed="|1Sam|27|2|27|4" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.27.2-1Sam.27.4">27:2-4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 56" id="g-p87.7" parsed="|Ps|56|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.56">Ps. 56</scripRef>), and his connection with
it will account for the words in <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 1:20" id="g-p87.8" parsed="|2Sam|1|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.1.20">2 Sam. 1:20</scripRef>. It was afterwards
conquered by David (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 8:1" id="g-p87.9" parsed="|2Sam|8|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.8.1">2 Sam. 8:1</scripRef>). It occupied a strong position

on the borders of Judah and Philistia (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 21:10" id="g-p87.10" parsed="|1Sam|21|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.21.10">1 Sam. 21:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 18:1" id="g-p87.11" parsed="|1Chr|18|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.18.1">1 Chr. 18:1</scripRef>). Its site has been identified with the hill called Tell
esSafieh, the Alba Specula of the Middle Ages, which rises 695
feet above the plain on its east edge. It is noticed on
monuments about B.C. 1500. (See METHEGAMMAH.)
</def>
<term id="g-p87.13">Gath-hepher</term>
Wine-press of the well, a town of Lower Galilee, about 5 miles
from Nazareth; the birthplace of Jonah (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 14:25" id="g-p88.1" parsed="|2Kgs|14|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.14.25">2 Kings 14:25</scripRef>); the same
as Gittah-hepher (<scripRef passage="Josh. 19:13" id="g-p88.2" parsed="|Josh|19|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.13">Josh. 19:13</scripRef>). It has been identified with the
modern el-Meshed, a village on the top of a rocky hill. Here the
supposed tomb of Jonah, Neby Yunas, is still pointed out.
</def>
<term id="g-p88.3">Gath-rimmon</term>
<def id="g-p88.4">
Press of the pomegranate. (1.) A Levitical city in the tribe of
Dan (Josh. 19:45; 21:24; 1 Chr. 6:69).
(2.) Another city of the same name in Manasseh, west of the
Jordan (Josh. 21:25), called also Bileam (1 Chr. 6:70).
</def>
<term id="g-p90.3">Gaulanitis</term>
<def id="g-p90.4">
A name derived from “Golan” (q.v.), one of the cities of refuge

in the territory of Manasseh (<scripRef passage="Josh. 20:8" id="g-p91.1" parsed="|Josh|20|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.20.8">Josh. 20:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 21:27" id="g-p91.2" parsed="|Josh|21|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.21.27">21:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 4:43" id="g-p91.3" parsed="|Deut|4|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.4.43">Deut. 4:43</scripRef>).
This was one of the provinces ruled by Herod Antipas. It lay to
the east of the Lake of Galilee, and included among its towns
Bethsaida-Julias (Mark 8:22) and Seleucia.
</def>
<term id="g-p91.5">Gaza</term>
<def id="g-p91.6">
Called also Azzah, which is its Hebrew name (Deut. 2:23; 1 Kings 4:24; Jer. 25:20), strong, a city on the Mediterranean shore,
remarkable for its early importance as the chief centre of a
great commercial traffic with Egypt. It is one of the oldest

cities of the world (<scripRef passage="Gen. 10:19" id="g-p92.4" parsed="|Gen|10|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.19">Gen. 10:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 15:47" id="g-p92.5" parsed="|Josh|15|47|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.47">Josh. 15:47</scripRef>). Its earliest
inhabitants were the Avims, who were conquered and displaced by

the Caphtorims (<scripRef passage="Deut. 2:23" id="g-p92.6" parsed="|Deut|2|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.2.23">Deut. 2:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 13:2" id="g-p92.7" parsed="|Josh|13|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.2">Josh. 13:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 13:3" id="g-p92.8" parsed="|Josh|13|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.3">3</scripRef>), a Philistine tribe.

In the division of the land it fell to the lot of Judah (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:47" id="g-p92.9" parsed="|Josh|15|47|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.47">Josh. 15:47</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 1:18" id="g-p92.10" parsed="|Judg|1|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.18">Judg. 1:18</scripRef>). It was the southernmost of the five great
Philistine cities which gave each a golden emerod as a
trespass-offering unto the Lord (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 6:17" id="g-p92.11" parsed="|1Sam|6|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.6.17">1 Sam. 6:17</scripRef>). Its gates were
carried away by Samson (<scripRef passage="Judg. 16:1-3" id="g-p92.12" parsed="|Judg|16|1|16|3" osisRef="Bible:Judg.16.1-Judg.16.3">Judg. 16:1-3</scripRef>). Here he was afterwards a
prisoner, and “did grind in the prison house.” Here he also
pulled down the temple of Dagon, and slew “all the lords of the

Philistines,” himself also perishing in the ruin (<scripRef passage="Judg. 16:21-30" id="g-p92.13" parsed="|Judg|16|21|16|30" osisRef="Bible:Judg.16.21-Judg.16.30">Judg. 16:21-30</scripRef>). The prophets denounce the judgments of God against it

(<scripRef passage="Jer. 25:20" id="g-p92.14" parsed="|Jer|25|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.25.20">Jer. 25:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 47:5" id="g-p92.15" parsed="|Jer|47|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.47.5">47:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Amos 1:6" id="g-p92.16" parsed="|Amos|1|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.1.6">Amos 1:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Amos 1:7" id="g-p92.17" parsed="|Amos|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.1.7">7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Zeph. 2:4" id="g-p92.18" parsed="|Zeph|2|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zeph.2.4">Zeph. 2:4</scripRef>). It is referred to in
<scripRef passage="Acts 8:26" id="g-p92.19" parsed="|Acts|8|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.8.26">Acts 8:26</scripRef>. Philip is here told to take the road from Jerusalem
to Gaza (about 6 miles south-west of Jerusalem), “which is
desert”, i.e., the “desert road,” probably by Hebron, through
the desert hills of Southern Judea. (See SAMSON.)
It is noticed on monuments as early as B.C. 1600. Its small
port is now called el-Mineh.
</def>
<term id="g-p93.1">Geba</term>
<def id="g-p93.2">
The hill, (2 Sam. 5:25 [1 Chr. 14:16, “Gibeon”]; 2 Kings 23:8;

<scripRef passage="Neh. 11:31" id="g-p94.4" parsed="|Neh|11|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.11.31">Neh. 11:31</scripRef>), a Levitical city of Benjamin (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 15:22" id="g-p94.5" parsed="|1Kgs|15|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.15.22">1 Kings 15:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 13:16" id="g-p94.6" parsed="|1Sam|13|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.13.16">1 Sam. 13:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 14:5" id="g-p94.7" parsed="|1Sam|14|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.14.5">14:5</scripRef>, wrongly “Gibeah” in the A.V.), on the north border

of Judah near Gibeah (<scripRef passage="Isa. 10:29" id="g-p94.8" parsed="|Isa|10|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.29">Isa. 10:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 18:24" id="g-p94.9" parsed="|Josh|18|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.18.24">Josh. 18:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 18:28" id="g-p94.10" parsed="|Josh|18|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.18.28">28</scripRef>). “From Geba
to Beersheba” expressed the whole extent of the kingdom of
Judah, just as “from Dan to Beersheba” described the whole
length of Palestine (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 23:8" id="g-p94.11" parsed="|2Kgs|23|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.8">2 Kings 23:8</scripRef>). It has been identified with

Gaba (<scripRef passage="Josh. 18:24" id="g-p94.12" parsed="|Josh|18|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.18.24">Josh. 18:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezra 2:26" id="g-p94.13" parsed="|Ezra|2|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2.26">Ezra 2:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh. 7:30" id="g-p94.14" parsed="|Neh|7|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.7.30">Neh. 7:30</scripRef>), now Jeb’a, about 5 1/2
miles north of Jerusalem.
</def>
<term id="g-p94.15">Gebal</term>
A line (or natural boundary, as a mountain range). (1.) A tract
in the land of Edom south of the Dead Sea (<scripRef passage="Ps. 83:7" id="g-p95.1" parsed="|Ps|83|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.83.7">Ps. 83:7</scripRef>); now called
Djebal.
(2.) A Phoenician city, not far from the sea coast, to the
north of Beyrout (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:9" id="g-p96.1" parsed="|Ezek|27|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.9">Ezek. 27:9</scripRef>); called by the Greeks Byblos. Now
Jibeil. Mentioned in the Amarna tablets.
An important Phoenician text, referring to the temple of
Baalath, on a monument of Yehu-melek, its king (probably B.C.
600), has been discovered.
</def>
<term id="g-p97.1">Gebalites</term>
<def id="g-p97.2">
(1 Kings 5:18 R.V., in A.V. incorrectly rendered, after the
Targum, “stone-squarers,” but marg. “Giblites”), the inhabitants
of Gebal (2).
</def>
<term id="g-p98.2">Geber</term>
<def id="g-p98.3">
A valiant man, (1 Kings 4:19), one of Solomon’s purveyors,
having jurisdiction over a part of Gilead, comprising all the
kingdom of Sihon and part of the kingdom of Og (Deut. 2; 31).
</def>
<term id="g-p99.4">Gebim</term>
<def id="g-p99.5">
Cisterns, (rendered “pits,” Jer. 14:3; “locusts,” Isa. 33:4), a
small place north of Jerusalem, whose inhabitants fled at the
approach of the Assyrian army (<scripRef passage="Isa. 10:31" id="g-p100.3" parsed="|Isa|10|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.31">Isa. 10:31</scripRef>). It is probably the
modern el-Isawiyeh.
</def>
<term id="g-p100.4">Gedaliah</term>
Made great by Jehovah. (1.) the son of Jeduthum (1 Chr. 25:3, 9). (2.) The grandfather of the prophet Zephaniah, and the
father of Cushi (<scripRef passage="Zeph. 1:1" id="g-p101.3" parsed="|Zeph|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zeph.1.1">Zeph. 1:1</scripRef>). (3.) One of the Jewish nobles who
conspired against Jeremiah (<scripRef passage="Jer. 38:1" id="g-p101.4" parsed="|Jer|38|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.38.1">Jer. 38:1</scripRef>). (4.) The son of Ahikam,
and grandson of Shaphan, secretary of king Josiah (<scripRef passage="Jer. 26:24" id="g-p101.5" parsed="|Jer|26|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.26.24">Jer. 26:24</scripRef>).
After the destruction of Jerusalem (see ZEDEKIAH),
Nebuchadnezzar left him to govern the country as tributary to

him (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 25:22" id="g-p101.7" parsed="|2Kgs|25|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.25.22">2 Kings 25:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 40:5" id="g-p101.8" parsed="|Jer|40|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.40.5">Jer. 40:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 52:16" id="g-p101.9" parsed="|Jer|52|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.52.16">52:16</scripRef>). Ishmael, however, at the
head of a party of the royal family, “Jewish irreconcilables”,
rose against him, and slew him and “all the Jews that were with

him” (<scripRef passage="Jer. 41:2" id="g-p101.10" parsed="|Jer|41|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.41.2">Jer. 41:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer. 41:3" id="g-p101.11" parsed="|Jer|41|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.41.3">3</scripRef>) at Mizpah about three months after the
destruction of Jerusalem. He and his band also plundered the
town of Mizpah, and carried off many captives. He was, however,
overtaken by Johanan and routed. He fled with such of his
followers as escaped to the Ammonites (41:15). The little
remnant of the Jews now fled to Egypt.
</def>
<term id="g-p101.12">Geder</term>
A walled place, (Josh. 12:13), perhaps the same as Gederah or
</def>
<term id="g-p102.2">Gederah</term>
The fortress; a fortified place, a town in the plain (shephelah)
of Judah (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:36" id="g-p103.1" parsed="|Josh|15|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.36">Josh. 15:36</scripRef>). This is a very common Canaanite and
Phoenician name. It is the feminine form of Geder (12:13); the
plural form is Gederoth (15:41). This place has by some been
identified with Jedireh, a ruin 9 miles from Lydda, toward
Eleutheropolis, and 4 miles north of Sur’ah (Zorah), in the
valley of Elah.
</def>
<term id="g-p103.2">Gederathite</term>
An epithet applied to Josabad, one of David’s warriors at Ziklag
(1 Chr. 12:4), a native of Gederah.
</def>
<term id="g-p104.2">Gedor</term>
A wall. (1.) A city in the mountains or hill country of Judah
(<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:58" id="g-p105.1" parsed="|Josh|15|58|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.58">Josh. 15:58</scripRef>), identified with Jedar, between Jerusalem and
Hebron.
(2.) 1 Chr. 4:39, the Gederah of Josh. 15:36, or the
well-known Gerar, as the LXX. read, where the patriarchs of old

had sojourned and fed their flocks (<scripRef passage="Gen. 20:1" id="g-p106.3" parsed="|Gen|20|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.20.1">Gen. 20:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 20:14" id="g-p106.4" parsed="|Gen|20|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.20.14">14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 20:15" id="g-p106.5" parsed="|Gen|20|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.20.15">15</scripRef>; 26:1, 6,
(3.) A town apparently in Benjamin (1 Chr. 12:7), the same
probably as Geder (Josh. 12:13).
</def>
<term id="g-p107.3">Gehazi</term>
Valley of vision, Elisha’s trusted servant (2 Kings 4:31; 5:25;

<scripRef passage="2 Kings 8:4" id="g-p108.3" parsed="|2Kgs|8|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.8.4">8:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 8:5" id="g-p108.4" parsed="|2Kgs|8|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.8.5">5</scripRef>). He appears in connection with the history of the

Shunammite (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 4:14" id="g-p108.5" parsed="|2Kgs|4|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.4.14">2 Kings 4:14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 4:31" id="g-p108.6" parsed="|2Kgs|4|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.4.31">31</scripRef>) and of Naaman the Syrian. On this
latter occasion he was guilty of duplicity and dishonesty of
conduct, causing Elisha to denounce his crime with righteous
sternness, and pass on him the terrible doom that the leprosy of
Naaman would cleave to him and his for ever (5:20-27).
He afterwards appeared before king Joram, to whom he recounted
the great deeds of his master (2 Kings 8:1-6).
</def>
<term id="g-p109.2">Gehenna</term>
(originally Ge bene Hinnom; i.e., “the valley of the sons of
Hinnom”), a deep, narrow glen to the south of Jerusalem, where
the idolatrous Jews offered their children in sacrifice to

Molech (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 28:3" id="g-p110.1" parsed="|2Chr|28|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.28.3">2 Chr. 28:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 33:6" id="g-p110.2" parsed="|2Chr|33|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.33.6">33:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 7:31" id="g-p110.3" parsed="|Jer|7|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.7.31">Jer. 7:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 19:2-6" id="g-p110.4" parsed="|Jer|19|2|19|6" osisRef="Bible:Jer.19.2-Jer.19.6">19:2-6</scripRef>). This valley
afterwards became the common receptacle for all the refuse of
the city. Here the dead bodies of animals and of criminals, and
all kinds of filth, were cast and consumed by fire kept always
burning. It thus in process of time became the image of the
place of everlasting destruction. In this sense it is used by

our Lord in <scripRef passage="Matt. 5:22" id="g-p110.5" parsed="|Matt|5|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.22">Matt. 5:22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 5:29" id="g-p110.6" parsed="|Matt|5|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.29">29</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 5:30" id="g-p110.7" parsed="|Matt|5|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.30">30</scripRef>; 10:28; 18:9; 23:15, 33; <scripRef passage="Mark 9:43" id="g-p110.8" parsed="|Mark|9|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.9.43">Mark 9:43</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Mark 9:45" id="g-p110.9" parsed="|Mark|9|45|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.9.45">45</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Mark 9:47" id="g-p110.10" parsed="|Mark|9|47|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.9.47">47</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 12:5" id="g-p110.11" parsed="|Luke|12|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.12.5">Luke 12:5</scripRef>. In these passages, and also in <scripRef passage="James 3:6" id="g-p110.12" parsed="|Jas|3|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jas.3.6">James 3:6</scripRef>, the word is uniformly rendered “hell,” the Revised Version
placing “Gehenna” in the margin. (See HELL; HINNOM.)
</def>
<term id="g-p110.15">Geliloth</term>
Circles; regions, a place in the border of Benjamin (Josh. 18:17); called Gilgal in 15:7.
</def>
<term id="g-p111.2">Gemariah</term>
Jehovah has made perfect. (1.) The son of Shaphan, and one of
the Levites of the temple in the time of Jehoiakim (<scripRef passage="Jer. 36:10" id="g-p112.1" parsed="|Jer|36|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.36.10">Jer. 36:10</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="2 Kings 22:12" id="g-p112.2" parsed="|2Kgs|22|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.22.12">2 Kings 22:12</scripRef>). Baruch read aloud to the people from Gemariah’s
chamber, and again in the hearing of Gemariah and other scribes,
the prophecies of Jeremiah (<scripRef passage="Jer. 36:11-20" id="g-p112.3" parsed="|Jer|36|11|36|20" osisRef="Bible:Jer.36.11-Jer.36.20">Jer. 36:11-20</scripRef>), which filled him
with terror. He joined with others in entreating the king not to
destroy the roll of the prophecies which Baruch had read
(2.) The son of Hilkiah, who accompanied Shaphan with the
tribute-money from Zedekiah to Nebuchadnezzar, and was the
bearer at the same time of a letter from Jeremiah to the Jewish
captives at Babylon (Jer. 29:3, 4).
</def>
<term id="g-p113.3">Generation</term>
Gen. 2:4, “These are the generations,” means the “history.” 5:1,
“The book of the generations,” means a family register, or
history of Adam. 37:2, “The generations of Jacob” = the history
of Jacob and his descendants. 7:1, “In this generation” = in
this age. <scripRef passage="Ps. 49:19" id="g-p114.2" parsed="|Ps|49|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.49.19">Ps. 49:19</scripRef>, “The generation of his fathers” = the
dwelling of his fathers, i.e., the grave. <scripRef passage="Ps. 73:15" id="g-p114.3" parsed="|Ps|73|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.73.15">Ps. 73:15</scripRef>, “The
generation of thy children” = the contemporary race. <scripRef passage="Isa. 53:8" id="g-p114.4" parsed="|Isa|53|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.53.8">Isa. 53:8</scripRef>,
“Who shall declare his generation?” = His manner of life who
shall declare? or rather = His race, posterity, shall be so
numerous that no one shall be able to declare it.
In Matt. 1:17, the word means a succession or series of
persons from the same stock. <scripRef passage="Matt. 3:7" id="g-p115.2" parsed="|Matt|3|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.7">Matt. 3:7</scripRef>, “Generation of vipers” =
brood of vipers. 24:34, “This generation” = the persons then
living contemporary with Christ. <scripRef passage="1 Pet. 2:9" id="g-p115.3" parsed="|1Pet|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.2.9">1 Pet. 2:9</scripRef>, “A chosen
generation” = a chosen people.
The Hebrews seem to have reckoned time by the generation. In
the time of Abraham a generation was an hundred years, thus:
<scripRef passage="Gen. 15:16" id="g-p116.1" parsed="|Gen|15|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.16">Gen. 15:16</scripRef>, “In the fourth generation” = in four hundred years

(comp. verse 13 and <scripRef passage="Ex. 12:40" id="g-p116.2" parsed="|Exod|12|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.40">Ex. 12:40</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="Deut. 1:35" id="g-p116.3" parsed="|Deut|1|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.1.35">Deut. 1:35</scripRef> and 2:14 a
generation is a period of thirty-eight years.
</def>
<term id="g-p116.4">Genesis</term>
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="g-p116.6" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="Gen 0" id="g-p116.7" parsed="|Gen|0|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen" />
The five books of Moses were collectively called the Pentateuch,
a word of Greek origin meaning “the five-fold book.” The Jews
called them the Torah, i.e., “the law.” It is probable that the
division of the Torah into five books proceeded from the Greek
translators of the Old Testament. The names by which these
several books are generally known are Greek.
The first book of the Pentateuch (q.v.) is called by the Jews
Bereshith, i.e., “in the beginning”, because this is the first
word of the book. It is generally known among Christians by the
name of Genesis, i.e., “creation” or “generation,” being the
name given to it in the LXX. as designating its character,
because it gives an account of the origin of all things. It
contains, according to the usual computation, the history of
about two thousand three hundred and sixty-nine years.
Genesis is divided into two principal parts. The first part
(1-11) gives a general history of mankind down to the time of
the Dispersion. The second part presents the early history of
Israel down to the death and burial of Joseph (12-50).
There are five principal persons brought in succession under
our notice in this book, and around these persons the history of
the successive periods is grouped, viz., Adam (1-3), Noah (4-9),
In this book we have several prophecies concerning Christ
this book was Moses. Under divine guidance he may indeed have
been led to make use of materials already existing in primeval
documents, or even of traditions in a trustworthy form that had
come down to his time, purifying them from all that was
unworthy; but the hand of Moses is clearly seen throughout in
its composition.
</def>
<term id="g-p121.1">Gennesaret</term>
A garden of riches. (1.) A town of Naphtali, called Chinnereth
(<scripRef passage="Josh. 19:35" id="g-p122.1" parsed="|Josh|19|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.35">Josh. 19:35</scripRef>), sometimes in the plural form Chinneroth (11:2).
In later times the name was gradually changed to Genezar and
Gennesaret (<scripRef passage="Luke 5:1" id="g-p122.2" parsed="|Luke|5|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.5.1">Luke 5:1</scripRef>). This city stood on the western shore of
the lake to which it gave its name. No trace of it remains. The
plain of Gennesaret has been called, from its fertility and
beauty, “the Paradise of Galilee.” It is now called el-Ghuweir.
(2.) The Lake of Gennesaret, the Grecized form of CHINNERETH
(q.v.). (See GALILEE, SEA OF.)
</def>
<term id="g-p123.2">Gentiles</term>
(Heb., usually in plural, goyim), meaning in general all nations
except the Jews. In course of time, as the Jews began more and
more to pride themselves on their peculiar privileges, it
acquired unpleasant associations, and was used as a term of
contempt.
In the New Testament the Greek word Hellenes, meaning

literally Greek (as in <scripRef passage="Acts 16:1" id="g-p125.1" parsed="|Acts|16|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.16.1">Acts 16:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 16:3" id="g-p125.2" parsed="|Acts|16|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.16.3">3</scripRef>; 18:17; <scripRef passage="Rom. 1:14" id="g-p125.3" parsed="|Rom|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.14">Rom. 1:14</scripRef>),
generally denotes any non-Jewish nation.
</def>
<term id="g-p125.4">Genubath</term>
Theft, the son of Hadad, of the Edomitish royal family. He was
brought up in Pharaoh’s household. His mother was a sister of
Tahpenes, the king of Egypt’s wife, mentioned in 1 Kings 11:20.
</def>
<term id="g-p126.2">Gera</term>
Grain. (1.) The son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin (1 Chr. 8:3, 5, 7).
(2.) The father of Ehud the judge (Judg. 3:15).
(3.) The father of Shimei, who so grossly abused David (2 Sam. 16:5; 19:16, 18).
</def>
<term id="g-p129.4">Gerah</term>
A bean, probably of the carob tree, the smallest weight, and
also the smallest piece of money, among the Hebrews, equal to

the twentieth part of a shekel (<scripRef passage="Ex. 30:13" id="g-p130.1" parsed="|Exod|30|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.30.13">Ex. 30:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 27:25" id="g-p130.2" parsed="|Lev|27|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.27.25">Lev. 27:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 3:47" id="g-p130.3" parsed="|Num|3|47|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.3.47">Num. 3:47</scripRef>). This word came into use in the same way as our word
“grain,” from a grain of wheat.
</def>
<term id="g-p130.4">Gerar</term>
A region; lodging-place, a very ancient town and district in the
south border of Palestine, which was ruled over by a king named

Abimelech (<scripRef passage="Gen. 10:19" id="g-p131.1" parsed="|Gen|10|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.19">Gen. 10:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 20:1" id="g-p131.2" parsed="|Gen|20|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.20.1">20:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 20:2" id="g-p131.3" parsed="|Gen|20|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.20.2">2</scripRef>). Abraham sojourned here, and
perhaps Isaac was born in this place. Both of these patriarchs
were guilty of the sin of here denying their wives, and both of
them entered into a treaty with the king before they departed to
Beersheba (21:23-34; 26). It seems to have been a rich pastoral
country (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 14:12-18" id="g-p131.4" parsed="|2Chr|14|12|14|18" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.14.12-2Chr.14.18">2 Chr. 14:12-18</scripRef>). Isaac here reaped an hundred-fold,
and was blessed of God (Gen. 26:12). The “valley of Gerar” (Gen. 26:17) was probably the modern Wady el-Jerdr.
</def>
<term id="g-p131.7">Gergesa</term>
=Gerasa, identified with the modern Khersa, “over against
Galilee,” close to the lake. This was probably the scene of the
miracle, <scripRef passage="Mark 5:1-20" id="g-p132.1" parsed="|Mark|5|1|5|20" osisRef="Bible:Mark.5.1-Mark.5.20">Mark 5:1-20</scripRef>, etc. “From the base of the great plateau
of Bashan, 2,000 feet or more overhead, the ground slopes down
steeply, in places precipitously, to the shore. And at the foot
of the declivity a bold spur runs out to the water’s edge. By it
the frantic swine would rush on headlong into the lake and
perish.” Porter’s Through Samaria. (See GADARA.)
</def>
<term id="g-p132.3">Gerizim</term>
A mountain of Samaria, about 3,000 feet above the Mediterranean.
It was on the left of the valley containing the ancient town of
Shechem (q.v.), on the way to Jerusalem. It stood over against
Mount Ebal, the summits of these mountains being distant from

each other about 2 miles (<scripRef passage="Deut. 27" id="g-p133.1" parsed="|Deut|27|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.27">Deut. 27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 8:30-35" id="g-p133.2" parsed="|Josh|8|30|8|35" osisRef="Bible:Josh.8.30-Josh.8.35">Josh. 8:30-35</scripRef>). On the
slopes of this mountain the tribes descended from the handmaids
of Leah and Rachel, together with the tribe of Reuben, were
gathered together, and gave the responses to the blessing
pronounced as the reward of obedience, when Joshua in the valley
below read the whole law in the hearing of all the people; as
those gathered on Ebal responded with a loud Amen to the
rehearsal of the curses pronounced on the disobedient. It was
probably at this time that the coffin containing the embalmed
body of Joseph was laid in the “parcel of ground which Jacob
bought of the sons of Hamor” (Gen. 33:19; 50:25).
Josephus relates (Ant. 11:8, 2-4) that Sanballat built a
temple for the Samaritans on this mountain, and instituted a
priesthood, as rivals to those of the Jews at Jerusalem. This
temple was destroyed after it had stood two hundred years. It
was afterwards rebuilt by Herod the Great. There is a Samaritan

tradition that it was the scene of the incident recorded in <scripRef passage="Gen. 22" id="g-p134.1" parsed="|Gen|22|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.22">Gen. 22</scripRef>. There are many ruins on this mountain, some of which are
evidently of Christian buildings. To this mountain the woman of
Sychar referred in <scripRef passage="John 4:20" id="g-p134.2" parsed="|John|4|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.4.20">John 4:20</scripRef>. For centuries Gerizim was the
centre of political outbreaks. The Samaritans (q.v.), a small
but united body, still linger here, and keep up their ancient
ceremonial worship.
</def>
<term id="g-p134.3">Gershom</term>
Expulsion. (1.) The eldest son of Levi (1 Chr. 6:16, 17, 20, 43, 62, 71; 15:7)=GERSHON (q.v.).
(2.) The elder of the two sons of Moses born to him in Midian

(<scripRef passage="Ex. 2:22" id="g-p136.1" parsed="|Exod|2|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.2.22">Ex. 2:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 18:3" id="g-p136.2" parsed="|Exod|18|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.18.3">18:3</scripRef>). On his way to Egypt with his family, in
obedience to the command of the Lord, Moses was attacked by a
sudden and dangerous illness (4:24-26), which Zipporah his wife
believed to have been sent because he had neglected to
circumcise his son. She accordingly took a “sharp stone” and
circumcised her son Gershom, saying, “Surely a bloody husband
art thou to me”, i.e., by the blood of her child she had, as it
were, purchased her husband, had won him back again.
(3.) A descendant of Phinehas who returned with Ezra from
Babylon (Ezra 8:2).
(4.) The son of Manasseh (Judg. 18:30), in R.V. “of Moses.”
</def>
<term id="g-p138.2">Gershon</term>
=Ger’shom expulsion, the eldest of Levi’s three sons (Gen. 46:11; Ex. 6:16).
In the wilderness the sons of Gershon had charge of the
fabrics of the tabernacle when it was moved from place to place,
the curtains, veils, tent-hangings (<scripRef passage="Num. 3" id="g-p140.1" parsed="|Num|3|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.3">Num. 3</scripRef>: 21-26). Thirteen
Levitical cities fell to the lot of the Gershonites (Josh. 21:27-33).
</def>
<term id="g-p140.3">Geshem</term>
Or Gashmu, firmness, probably chief of the Arabs south of
Palestine, one of the enemies of the Jews after the return from

Babylon (<scripRef passage="Neh. 2:19" id="g-p141.1" parsed="|Neh|2|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.2.19">Neh. 2:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh 6:1" id="g-p141.2" parsed="|Neh|6|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.6.1">6:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Neh 6:2" id="g-p141.3" parsed="|Neh|6|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.6.2">2</scripRef>). He united with Sanballat and Tobiah
in opposing the rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem.
</def>
<term id="g-p141.4">Geshur</term>
Bridge, the name of a district or principality of Syria near

Gilead, between Mount Hermon and the Lake of Tiberias (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 15:8" id="g-p142.1" parsed="|2Sam|15|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.15.8">2 Sam. 15:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 2:23" id="g-p142.2" parsed="|1Chr|2|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.2.23">1 Chr. 2:23</scripRef>). The Geshurites probably inhabited the rocky
fastness of Argob, the modern Lejah, in the north-east corner of
Bashan. In the time of David it was ruled by Talmai, whose
daughter he married, and who was the mother of Absalom, who fled
to Geshur after the murder of Amnon (2 Sam. 13:37).
</def>
<term id="g-p142.4">Geshurites</term>
(1.) The inhabitants of Geshur. They maintained friendly
relations with the Israelites on the east of Jordan (<scripRef passage="Josh. 12:5" id="g-p143.1" parsed="|Josh|12|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.12.5">Josh. 12:5</scripRef>;
13:11, 13).
(2.) Another aboriginal people of Palestine who inhabited the
south-west border of the land. Geshuri in <scripRef passage="Josh. 13:2" id="g-p144.1" parsed="|Josh|13|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.2">Josh. 13:2</scripRef> should be
“the Geshurite,” not the Geshurites mentioned in ver. 11, 13,
but the tribe mentioned in 1 Sam. 27:8.
</def>
<term id="g-p144.3">Gethsemane</term>
Oil-press, the name of an olive-yard at the foot of the Mount of
Olives, to which Jesus was wont to retire (<scripRef passage="Luke 22:39" id="g-p145.1" parsed="|Luke|22|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.22.39">Luke 22:39</scripRef>) with his
disciples, and which is specially memorable as being the scene
