of his agony (<scripRef passage="Mark 14:32" id="g-p145.2" parsed="|Mark|14|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.14.32">Mark 14:32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 18:1" id="g-p145.3" parsed="|John|18|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.18.1">John 18:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 22:44" id="g-p145.4" parsed="|Luke|22|44|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.22.44">Luke 22:44</scripRef>). The plot of
ground pointed out as Gethsemane is now surrounded by a wall,
and is laid out as a modern European flower-garden. It contains
eight venerable olive-trees, the age of which cannot, however,
be determined. The exact site of Gethsemane is still in
question. Dr. Thomson (The Land and the Book) says: “When I
first came to Jerusalem, and for many years afterward, this plot
of ground was open to all whenever they chose to come and
meditate beneath its very old olivetrees. The Latins, however,
have within the last few years succeeded in gaining sole
possession, and have built a high wall around it...The Greeks
have invented another site a little to the north of it...My own
impression is that both are wrong. The position is too near the
city, and so close to what must have always been the great
thoroughfare eastward, that our Lord would scarcely have
selected it for retirement on that dangerous and dismal
night...I am inclined to place the garden in the secluded vale
several hundred yards to the north-east of the present
Gethsemane.”
</def>
<term id="g-p145.5">Gezer</term>
A precipice, an ancient royal Canaanitish city (Josh. 10:33;
<scripRef passage="Josh 12:12" id="g-p146.2" parsed="|Josh|12|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.12.12">12:12</scripRef>). It was allotted with its suburbs to the Kohathite
Levites (21:21; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 6:67" id="g-p146.3" parsed="|1Chr|6|67|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.6.67">1 Chr. 6:67</scripRef>). It stood between the lower

Beth-horon and the sea (<scripRef passage="Josh. 16:3" id="g-p146.4" parsed="|Josh|16|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.16.3">Josh. 16:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 9:17" id="g-p146.5" parsed="|1Kgs|9|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.9.17">1 Kings 9:17</scripRef>). It was the
last point to which David pursued the Philistines (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 5:25" id="g-p146.6" parsed="|2Sam|5|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.5.25">2 Sam. 5:25</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 14:16" id="g-p146.7" parsed="|1Chr|14|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.14.16">1 Chr. 14:16</scripRef>) after the battle of Baal-perazim. The Canaanites
retained possession of it till the time of Solomon, when the
king of Egypt took it and gave it to Solomon as a part of the

dowry of the Egyptian princess whom he married (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 9:15-17" id="g-p146.8" parsed="|1Kgs|9|15|9|17" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.9.15-1Kgs.9.17">1 Kings 9:15-17</scripRef>). It is identified with Tell el-Jezer, about 10 miles
south-west of Beth-horon. It is mentioned in the Amarna tablets.
</def>
<term id="g-p146.9">Ghost</term>
An old Saxon word equivalent to soul or spirit. It is the
translation of the Hebrew nephesh_ and the Greek _pneuma, both

meaning “breath,” “life,” “spirit,” the “living principle” (<scripRef passage="Job 11:20" id="g-p147.1" parsed="|Job|11|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.11.20">Job 11:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 15:9" id="g-p147.2" parsed="|Jer|15|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.15.9">Jer. 15:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 27:50" id="g-p147.3" parsed="|Matt|27|50|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.50">Matt. 27:50</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 19:30" id="g-p147.4" parsed="|John|19|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.30">John 19:30</scripRef>). The expression “to

give up the ghost” means to die (<scripRef passage="Lam. 1:19" id="g-p147.5" parsed="|Lam|1|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lam.1.19">Lam. 1:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen. 25:17" id="g-p147.6" parsed="|Gen|25|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.17">Gen. 25:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 35:29" id="g-p147.7" parsed="|Gen|35|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.35.29">35:29</scripRef>;
49:33; Job 3:11). (See HOLY GHOST.)
</def>
<term id="g-p147.11">Giants</term>
(1.) Heb. nephilim, meaning “violent” or “causing to fall” (Gen. 6:4). These were the violent tyrants of those days, those who
fell upon others. The word may also be derived from a root
signifying “wonder,” and hence “monsters” or “prodigies.” In
<scripRef passage="Num. 13:33" id="g-p148.2" parsed="|Num|13|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.13.33">Num. 13:33</scripRef> this name is given to a Canaanitish tribe, a race of
large stature, “the sons of Anak.” The Revised Version, in these
passages, simply transliterates the original, and reads
“Nephilim.”
(2.) Heb. rephaim, a race of giants (Deut. 3:11) who lived on
the east of Jordan, from whom Og was descended. They were
probably the original inhabitants of the land before the
immigration of the Canaanites. They were conquered by
Chedorlaomer (<scripRef passage="Gen. 14:5" id="g-p149.2" parsed="|Gen|14|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.5">Gen. 14:5</scripRef>), and their territories were promised as
a possession to Abraham (15:20). The Anakim, Zuzim, and Emim
were branches of this stock.
In Job 26:5 (R.V., “they that are deceased;” marg., “the
shades,” the “Rephaim”) and <scripRef passage="Isa. 14:9" id="g-p150.2" parsed="|Isa|14|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.14.9">Isa. 14:9</scripRef> this Hebrew word is
rendered (A.V.) “dead.” It means here “the shades,” the departed
spirits in Sheol. In Sam. 21:16, 18, 20, 33, “the giant” is
(A.V.) the rendering of the singular form ha raphah, which may
possibly be the name of the father of the four giants referred
to here, or of the founder of the Rephaim. The Vulgate here
reads “Arapha,” whence Milton (in Samson Agonistes) has borrowed

the name “Harapha.” (See also <scripRef passage="1 Chron. 20:5" id="g-p150.3" parsed="|1Chr|20|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.20.5">1 Chron. 20:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Chron. 20:6" id="g-p150.4" parsed="|1Chr|20|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.20.6">6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Chron. 20:8" id="g-p150.5" parsed="|1Chr|20|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.20.8">8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 2:11" id="g-p150.6" parsed="|Deut|2|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.2.11">Deut. 2:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut 2:20" id="g-p150.7" parsed="|Deut|2|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.2.20">20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut 3:13" id="g-p150.8" parsed="|Deut|3|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.13">3:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 15:8" id="g-p150.9" parsed="|Josh|15|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.8">Josh. 15:8</scripRef>, etc., where the word is similarly rendered

“giant.”) It is rendered “dead” in (A.V.) <scripRef passage="Ps. 88:10" id="g-p150.10" parsed="|Ps|88|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.88.10">Ps. 88:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 2:18" id="g-p150.11" parsed="|Prov|2|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.2.18">Prov. 2:18</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Prov 9:18" id="g-p150.12" parsed="|Prov|9|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.9.18">9:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov 21:16" id="g-p150.13" parsed="|Prov|21|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.21.16">21:16</scripRef>: in all these places the Revised Version marg. has
“the shades.” (See also Isa. 26:14.)
(3.) Heb. ‘Anakim (Deut. 2:10, 11, 21; Josh. 11:21, 22; 14:12,
15; called “sons of Anak,” <scripRef passage="Num. 13:33" id="g-p151.6" parsed="|Num|13|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.13.33">Num. 13:33</scripRef>; “children of Anak,”
13:22; <scripRef passage="Josh. 15:14" id="g-p151.7" parsed="|Josh|15|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.14">Josh. 15:14</scripRef>), a nomad race of giants descended from Arba
(<scripRef passage="Josh. 14:15" id="g-p151.8" parsed="|Josh|14|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.14.15">Josh. 14:15</scripRef>), the father of Anak, that dwelt in the south of

Palestine near Hebron (<scripRef passage="Gen. 23:2" id="g-p151.9" parsed="|Gen|23|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.23.2">Gen. 23:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 15:13" id="g-p151.10" parsed="|Josh|15|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.13">Josh. 15:13</scripRef>). They were a
Cushite tribe of the same race as the Philistines and the
Egyptian shepherd kings. David on several occasions encountered
them (2 Sam. 21:15-22). From this race sprung Goliath (1 Sam. 17:4).
(4.) Heb. ‘emin, a warlike tribe of the ancient Canaanites.
They were “great, and many, and tall, as the Anakims” (Gen. 14:5; Deut. 2:10, 11).
(5.) Heb. Zamzummim (q.v.), Deut. 2:20 so called by the
Amorites.
(6.) Heb. gibbor (Job 16:14), a mighty one, i.e., a champion
or hero. In its plural form (gibborim) it is rendered “mighty

men” (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 23:8-39" id="g-p154.2" parsed="|2Sam|23|8|23|39" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.23.8-2Sam.23.39">2 Sam. 23:8-39</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 1:8" id="g-p154.3" parsed="|1Kgs|1|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.1.8">1 Kings 1:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 11:9-47" id="g-p154.4" parsed="|1Chr|11|9|11|47" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.11.9-1Chr.11.47">1 Chr. 11:9-47</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 29:24" id="g-p154.5" parsed="|1Chr|29|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.29.24">29:24</scripRef>.) The
band of six hundred whom David gathered around him when he was a
fugitive were so designated. They were divided into three
divisions of two hundred each, and thirty divisions of twenty
each. The captians of the thirty divisions were called “the
thirty,” the captains of the two hundred “the three,” and the

captain over the whole was called “chief among the captains” (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 23:8" id="g-p154.6" parsed="|2Sam|23|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.23.8">2 Sam. 23:8</scripRef>). The sons born of the marriages mentioned in <scripRef passage="Gen. 6:4" id="g-p154.7" parsed="|Gen|6|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.6.4">Gen. 6:4</scripRef>
are also called by this Hebrew name.
</def>
<term id="g-p154.8">Gibbethon</term>
A height, a city of the Philistines in the territory of Dan,

given to the Kohathites (<scripRef passage="Josh. 19:44" id="g-p155.1" parsed="|Josh|19|44|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.44">Josh. 19:44</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 21:23" id="g-p155.2" parsed="|Josh|21|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.21.23">21:23</scripRef>). Nadab the king of
Israel, while besieging it, was slain under its walls by Baasha,
one of his own officers (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 15:27" id="g-p155.3" parsed="|1Kgs|15|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.15.27">1 Kings 15:27</scripRef>). It was in the
possession of the Philistines after the secession of the ten
tribes (2 Chr. 11:13, 14).
</def>
<term id="g-p155.6">Gibeah</term>
A hill or hill-town, “of Benjamin” (1 Sam. 13:15), better known
as “Gibeah of Saul” (11:4; <scripRef passage="Isa. 10:29" id="g-p156.2" parsed="|Isa|10|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.29">Isa. 10:29</scripRef>). It was here that the
terrible outrage was committed on the Levite’s concubine which
led to the almost utter extirpation of the tribe of Benjamin

(<scripRef passage="Judg. 19" id="g-p156.3" parsed="|Judg|19|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.19">Judg. 19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg 20" id="g-p156.4" parsed="|Judg|20|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.20">20</scripRef>), only six hundred men surviving after a
succession of disastrous battles. This was the birthplace of

Saul, and continued to be his residence after he became king (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 10:26" id="g-p156.5" parsed="|1Sam|10|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.10.26">1 Sam. 10:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 11:4" id="g-p156.6" parsed="|1Sam|11|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.11.4">11:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 15:34" id="g-p156.7" parsed="|1Sam|15|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.15.34">15:34</scripRef>). It was reckoned among the ancient

sanctuaries of Palestine (10:26; 15:34; 23:19; 26:1; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:6-10" id="g-p156.8" parsed="|2Sam|21|6|21|10" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.6-2Sam.21.10">2 Sam. 21:6-10</scripRef>), and hence it is called “Gibeah of God” (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 10:5" id="g-p156.9" parsed="|1Sam|10|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.10.5">1 Sam. 10:5</scripRef>,
R.V. marg.). It has been identified with the modern Tell el-Ful
(i.e., “hill of the bean”), about 3 miles north of Jerusalem.
</def>
<term id="g-p156.10">Gibeah-haaraloth</term>
(Josh. 5:3, marg.), hill of the foreskins, a place at Gilgal
where those who had been born in the wilderness were
circumcised. All the others, i.e., those who were under twenty
years old at the time of the sentence at Kadesh, had already
been circumcised.
</def>
<term id="g-p157.2">Gibeah of Judah</term>
(Josh. 15:57), a city in the mountains of Judah, the modern
Jeba, on a hill in the Wady Musurr, about 7 1/2 miles
west-south-west of Bethlehem.
</def>
<term id="g-p158.2">Gibeah of Phinehas</term>
(Josh. 15:57, R.V. marg.), a city on Mount Ephraim which had
been given to Phinehas (24:33 “hill,” A.V.; R.V. marg. and Heb.,
“Gibeah.”). Here Eleazar the son of Aaron was buried. It has
been identified with the modern Khurbet Jibia, 5 miles north of
Guphna towards Shechem.
</def>
<term id="g-p159.2">Gibeon</term>
Hill-city, “one of the royal cities, greater than Ai, and all
the men thereof were mighty” (<scripRef passage="Josh. 10:2" id="g-p160.1" parsed="|Josh|10|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.2">Josh. 10:2</scripRef>). Its inhabitants were
Hivites (11:19). It lay within the territory of Benjamin, and
became a priest-city (18:25; 21:17). Here the tabernacle was set
up after the destruction of Nob, and here it remained many years
till the temple was built by Solomon. It is represented by the
modern el-Jib, to the south-west of Ai, and about 5 1/2 miles
north-north-west of Jerusalem.
A deputation of the Gibeonites, with their allies from three

other cities (<scripRef passage="Josh. 9" id="g-p161.1" parsed="|Josh|9|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.9">Josh. 9</scripRef>;<scripRef passage="Josh 17" id="g-p161.2" parsed="|Josh|17|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.17">17</scripRef>), visited the camp at Gilgal, and by
false representations induced Joshua to enter into a league with
them, although the Israelites had been specially warned against

any league with the inhabitants of Canaan (<scripRef passage="Ex. 23:32" id="g-p161.3" parsed="|Exod|23|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.32">Ex. 23:32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 34:12" id="g-p161.4" parsed="|Exod|34|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.34.12">34:12</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Num. 33:55" id="g-p161.5" parsed="|Num|33|55|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.55">Num. 33:55</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 7:2" id="g-p161.6" parsed="|Deut|7|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.7.2">Deut. 7:2</scripRef>). The deception practised on Joshua was
detected three days later; but the oath rashly sworn “by Jehovah
God of Israel” was kept, and the lives of the Gibeonites were
spared. They were, however, made “bondmen” to the sanctuary
(Josh. 9:23).
The most remarkable incident connected with this city was the

victory Joshua gained over the kings of Palestine (<scripRef passage="Josh. 10:16-27" id="g-p162.1" parsed="|Josh|10|16|10|27" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.16-Josh.10.27">Josh. 10:16-27</scripRef>). The battle here fought has been regarded as “one of
the most important in the history of the world.” The kings of
southern Canaan entered into a confederacy against Gibeon
(because it had entered into a league with Joshua) under the
leadership of Adoni-zedec, king of Jerusalem, and marched upon
Gibeon with the view of taking possession of it. The Gibeonites
entreated Joshua to come to their aid with the utmost speed. His
army came suddenly upon that of the Amorite kings as it lay
encamped before the city. It was completely routed, and only
broken remnants of their great host found refuge in the fenced
cities. The five confederate kings who led the army were taken
prisoners, and put to death at Makkedah (q.v.). This eventful
battle of Beth-horon sealed the fate of all the cities of
Southern Palestine. Among the Amarna tablets is a letter from
Adoni-zedec (q.v.) to the king of Egypt, written probably at
Makkedah after the defeat, showing that the kings contemplated
flight into Egypt.
This place is again brought into notice as the scene of a
battle between the army of Ish-bosheth under Abner and that of
David led by Joab. At the suggestion of Abner, to spare the
effusion of blood twelve men on either side were chosen to
decide the battle. The issue was unexpected; for each of the men
slew his fellow, and thus they all perished. The two armies then
engaged in battle, in which Abner and his host were routed and
put to flight (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 2:12-17" id="g-p163.1" parsed="|2Sam|2|12|2|17" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.2.12-2Sam.2.17">2 Sam. 2:12-17</scripRef>). This battle led to a virtual
truce between Judah and Israel, Judah, under David, increasing
in power; and Israel, under Ish-bosheth, continually losing
ground.
Soon after the death of Absalom and David’s restoration to his
throne his kingdom was visited by a grievous famine, which was

found to be a punishment for Saul’s violation (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:2" id="g-p164.1" parsed="|2Sam|21|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.2">2 Sam. 21:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:5" id="g-p164.2" parsed="|2Sam|21|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.5">5</scripRef>)
of the covenant with the Gibeonites (<scripRef passage="Josh. 9:3-27" id="g-p164.3" parsed="|Josh|9|3|9|27" osisRef="Bible:Josh.9.3-Josh.9.27">Josh. 9:3-27</scripRef>). The
Gibeonites demanded blood for the wrong that had been done to
them, and accordingly David gave up to them the two sons of
Rizpah (q.v.) and the five sons of Michal, and these the
Gibeonites took and hanged or crucified “in the hill before the
Lord” (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:9" id="g-p164.4" parsed="|2Sam|21|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.9">2 Sam. 21:9</scripRef>); and there the bodies hung for six months
(21:10), and all the while Rizpah watched over the blackening
corpses and “suffered neither the birds of the air to rest on
them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night.” David
afterwards removed the bones of Saul and Jonathan at
Jabeshgilead (21:12, 13).
Here, “at the great stone,” Amasa was put to death by Joab (2 Sam. 20:5-10). To the altar of burnt-offering which was at
Gibeon, Joab (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 2:28-34" id="g-p165.2" parsed="|1Kgs|2|28|2|34" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.2.28-1Kgs.2.34">1 Kings 2:28-34</scripRef>), who had taken the side of
Adonijah, fled for sanctuary in the beginning of Solomon’s
reign, and was there also slain by the hand of Benaiah.
Soon after he came to the throne, Solomon paid a visit of

state to Gibeon, there to offer sacrifices (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 3:4" id="g-p166.1" parsed="|1Kgs|3|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.3.4">1 Kings 3:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 1:3" id="g-p166.2" parsed="|2Chr|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.1.3">2 Chr. 1:3</scripRef>). On this occasion the Lord appeared to him in a memorable

dream, recorded in <scripRef passage="1 Kings 3:5-15" id="g-p166.3" parsed="|1Kgs|3|5|3|15" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.3.5-1Kgs.3.15">1 Kings 3:5-15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 1:7-12" id="g-p166.4" parsed="|2Chr|1|7|1|12" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.1.7-2Chr.1.12">2 Chr. 1:7-12</scripRef>. When the
temple was built “all the men of Israel assembled themselves” to
king Solomon, and brought up from Gibeon the tabernacle and “all
the holy vessels that were in the tabernacle” to Jerusalem,
where they remained till they were carried away by
Nebuchadnezzar (2 Kings 24:13).
</def>
<term id="g-p166.6">Gideon</term>
Called also Jerubbaal (Judg. 6:29, 32), was the first of the
judges whose history is circumstantially narrated (<scripRef passage="Judg. 6" id="g-p167.3" parsed="|Judg|6|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.6">Judg. 6</scripRef>-8).
His calling is the commencement of the second period in the
history of the judges. After the victory gained by Deborah and
Barak over Jabin, Israel once more sank into idolatry, and the
Midianites (q.v.) and Amalekites, with other “children of the
east,” crossed the Jordan each year for seven successive years
for the purpose of plundering and desolating the land. Gideon
received a direct call from God to undertake the task of
delivering the land from these warlike invaders. He was of the

family of Abiezer (<scripRef passage="Josh. 17:2" id="g-p167.4" parsed="|Josh|17|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.17.2">Josh. 17:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 7:18" id="g-p167.5" parsed="|1Chr|7|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.7.18">1 Chr. 7:18</scripRef>), and of the little
township of Ophrah (<scripRef passage="Judg. 6:11" id="g-p167.6" parsed="|Judg|6|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.6.11">Judg. 6:11</scripRef>). First, with ten of his
servants, he overthrew the altars of Baal and cut down the
asherah which was upon it, and then blew the trumpet of alarm,
and the people flocked to his standard on the crest of Mount
Gilboa to the number of twenty-two thousand men. These were,
however, reduced to only three hundred. These, strangely armed
with torches and pitchers and trumpets, rushed in from three
different points on the camp of Midian at midnight, in the
valley to the north of Moreh, with the terrible war-cry, “For
the Lord and for Gideon” (<scripRef passage="Judg. 7:18" id="g-p167.7" parsed="|Judg|7|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.7.18">Judg. 7:18</scripRef>, R.V.). Terror-stricken,
the Midianites were put into dire confusion, and in the darkness
slew one another, so that only fifteen thousand out of the great
army of one hundred and twenty thousand escaped alive. The
memory of this great deliverance impressed itself deeply on the

mind of the nation (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 12:11" id="g-p167.8" parsed="|1Sam|12|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.12.11">1 Sam. 12:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 83:11" id="g-p167.9" parsed="|Ps|83|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.83.11">Ps. 83:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 9:4" id="g-p167.10" parsed="|Isa|9|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.9.4">Isa. 9:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 10:26" id="g-p167.11" parsed="|Isa|10|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.26">10:26</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Heb. 11:32" id="g-p167.12" parsed="|Heb|11|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.11.32">Heb. 11:32</scripRef>). The land had now rest for forty years. Gideon died
in a good old age, and was buried in the sepulchre of his
fathers. Soon after his death a change came over the people.
They again forgot Jehovah, and turned to the worship of Baalim,

“neither shewed they kindness to the house of Jerubbaal” (<scripRef passage="Judg. 8:35" id="g-p167.13" parsed="|Judg|8|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.8.35">Judg. 8:35</scripRef>). Gideon left behind him seventy sons, a feeble, sadly
degenerated race, with one exception, that of Abimelech, who
seems to have had much of the courage and energy of his father,
yet of restless and unscrupulous ambition. He gathered around
him a band who slaughtered all Gideon’s sons, except Jotham,
upon one stone. (See OPHRAH.)
</def>
<term id="g-p167.15">Gier eagle</term>
Heb. raham = “parental affection,” Lev. 11:18; Deut. 14:17;
R.V., “vulture”), a species of vulture living entirely on
carrion. “It is about the size of a raven; has an almost
triangular, bald, and wrinkled head, a strong pointed beak,
black at the tip, large eyes and ears, the latter entirely on
the outside, and long feet.” It is common in Egypt, where it is
popularly called “Pharaoh’s chicken” (the Neophron
percnopterus), and is found in Palestine only during summer.
Tristram thinks that the Hebrew name, which is derived from a
root meaning “to love,” is given to it from the fact that the
male and female bird never part company.
</def>
<term id="g-p168.3">Gift</term>
(1.) An gratuity (Prov. 19:6) to secure favour (18:16; 21:14), a
thank-offering (Num. 18:11), or a dowry (Gen. 34:12).
(2.) An oblation or proppitatory gift (2Sa 8:2, 6; 1Ch 18:2, 6;
2Ch 26:8; Ps. 45:12; 72:10).
(3.) A bribe to a judge to obtain a favourable verdict (Ex. 23:8; Deut. 16:19).
(4.) Simply a thing given (Matt. 7:11; Luke 11:13; Eph. 4:8);

sacrifical (<scripRef passage="Matt. 5:23" id="g-p172.4" parsed="|Matt|5|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.23">Matt. 5:23</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 5:24" id="g-p172.5" parsed="|Matt|5|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.24">24</scripRef>; 8:4); eleemosynary (<scripRef passage="Luke 21:1" id="g-p172.6" parsed="|Luke|21|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.21.1">Luke 21:1</scripRef>); a

gratuity (<scripRef passage="John 4:10" id="g-p172.7" parsed="|John|4|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.4.10">John 4:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 8:20" id="g-p172.8" parsed="|Acts|8|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.8.20">Acts 8:20</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="Acts 2:38" id="g-p172.9" parsed="|Acts|2|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.2.38">Acts 2:38</scripRef> the generic word

dorea is rendered “gift.” It differs from the charisma (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 12:4" id="g-p172.10" parsed="|1Cor|12|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.12.4">1 Cor. 12:4</scripRef>) as denoting not miraculous powers but the working of a new
spirit in men, and that spirit from God.
The giving of presents entered largely into the affairs of
common life in the East. The nature of the presents was as

various as were the occasions: food (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 9:7" id="g-p173.1" parsed="|1Sam|9|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.9.7">1 Sam. 9:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 16:20" id="g-p173.2" parsed="|1Sam|16|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.16.20">16:20</scripRef>), sheep

and cattle (<scripRef passage="Gen. 32:13-15" id="g-p173.3" parsed="|Gen|32|13|32|15" osisRef="Bible:Gen.32.13-Gen.32.15">Gen. 32:13-15</scripRef>), gold (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 18:11" id="g-p173.4" parsed="|2Sam|18|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.18.11">2 Sam. 18:11</scripRef>), jewels (<scripRef passage="Gen. 24:53" id="g-p173.5" parsed="|Gen|24|53|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.53">Gen. 24:53</scripRef>), furniture, and vessels for eating and drinking (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 17:28" id="g-p173.6" parsed="|2Sam|17|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.17.28">2 Sam. 17:28</scripRef>); delicacies, as spices, honey, etc. (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:25" id="g-p173.7" parsed="|1Kgs|10|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.25">1 Kings 10:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 5" id="g-p173.8" parsed="|2Kgs|5|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.5">2 Kings 5</scripRef>: 22). The mode of presentation was with as much parade
as possible: the presents were conveyed by the hands of servants
(<scripRef passage="Judg. 3:18" id="g-p173.9" parsed="|Judg|3|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.3.18">Judg. 3:18</scripRef>), or still better, on the backs of beasts of burden
(<scripRef passage="2 Kings 8:9" id="g-p173.10" parsed="|2Kgs|8|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.8.9">2 Kings 8:9</scripRef>). The refusal of a present was regarded as a high
indignity; and this constituted the aggravated insult noticed in
Matt. 22:11, the marriage robe having been offered and refused.
</def>
<term id="g-p173.12">Gifts, spiritual</term>
(Gr. charismata), gifts supernaturally bestowed on the early
Christians, each having his own proper gift or gifts for the
edification of the body of Christ. These were the result of the
extraordinary operation of the Spirit, as on the day of
Pentecost. They were the gifts of speaking with tongues, casting

out devils, healing, etc. (<scripRef passage="Mark 16:17" id="g-p174.1" parsed="|Mark|16|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.16.17">Mark 16:17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Mark 16:18" id="g-p174.2" parsed="|Mark|16|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.16.18">18</scripRef>), usually communicated
by the medium of the laying on of the hands of the apostles

(<scripRef passage="Acts 8:17" id="g-p174.3" parsed="|Acts|8|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.8.17">Acts 8:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 19:6" id="g-p174.4" parsed="|Acts|19|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.19.6">19:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Tim. 4:14" id="g-p174.5" parsed="|1Tim|4|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.4.14">1 Tim. 4:14</scripRef>). These charismata were enjoyed
only for a time. They could not continue always in the Church.
They were suited to its infancy and to the necessities of those
times.
</def>
<term id="g-p174.6">Gihon</term>
A stream. (1.) One of the four rivers of Eden (Gen. 2:13). It
has been identified with the Nile. Others regard it as the Oxus,
or the Araxes, or the Ganges. But as, according to the sacred
narrative, all these rivers of Eden took their origin from the
head-waters of the Euphrates and the Trigris, it is probable
that the Gihon is the ancient Araxes, which, under the modern
name of the Arras, discharges itself into the Caspian Sea. It
was the Asiatic and not the African “Cush” which the Gihon
compassed (Gen. 10:7-10). (See EDEN.)
(2.) The only natural spring of water in or near Jerusalem is
the “Fountain of the Virgin” (q.v.), which rises outside the
city walls on the west bank of the Kidron valley. On the
occasion of the approach of the Assyrian army under Sennacherib,
Hezekiah, in order to prevent the besiegers from finding water,
“stopped the upper water course of Gihon, and brought it

straight down to the west side of the city of David” (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 32:30" id="g-p176.1" parsed="|2Chr|32|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.32.30">2 Chr. 32:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 33:14" id="g-p176.2" parsed="|2Chr|33|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.33.14">33:14</scripRef>). This “fountain” or spring is therefore to be
regarded as the “upper water course of Gihon.” From this
“fountain” a tunnel cut through the ridge which forms the south
part of the temple hill conveys the water to the Pool of Siloam,
which lies on the opposite side of this ridge at the head of the
Tyropoeon (“cheesemakers’”) valley, or valley of the son of
Hinnom, now filled up by rubbish. The length of this tunnel is
about 1,750 feet. In 1880 an inscription was accidentally
discovered on the wall of the tunnel about nineteen feet from
where it opens into the Pool of Siloam. This inscription was
executed in all probability by Hezekiah’s workmen. It briefly
narrates the history of the excavation. It may, however, be
possible that this tunnel was executed in the time of Solomon.
If the “waters of Shiloah that go softly” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 8:6" id="g-p176.3" parsed="|Isa|8|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.8.6">Isa. 8:6</scripRef>) refers to
the gentle stream that still flows through the tunnel into the
Pool of Siloam, then this excavation must have existed before
the time of Hezekiah.
In the upper part of the Tyropoeoan valley there are two pools
still existing, the first, called Birket el-Mamilla, to the west
of the Jaffa gate; the second, to the south of the first, called
Birket es-Sultan. It is the opinion of some that the former was
the “upper” and the latter the “lower” Pool of Gihon (2 Kings 18:17; Isa. 7:3; 36:2; 22:9). (See CONDUIT; SILOAM.)
</def>
<term id="g-p177.7">Gilboa</term>
Boiling spring, a mountain range, now Jebel Fukua’, memorable as
the scene of Saul’s disastrous defeat by the Philistines. Here
also his three sons were slain, and he himself died by his own

hand (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 28:4" id="g-p178.1" parsed="|1Sam|28|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.28.4">1 Sam. 28:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 31:1-8" id="g-p178.2" parsed="|1Sam|31|1|31|8" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.31.1-1Sam.31.8">31:1-8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 1:6-21" id="g-p178.3" parsed="|2Sam|1|6|1|21" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.1.6-2Sam.1.21">2 Sam. 1:6-21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:12" id="g-p178.4" parsed="|2Sam|21|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.12">21:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 10:1" id="g-p178.5" parsed="|1Chr|10|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.10.1">1 Chr. 10:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 10:8" id="g-p178.6" parsed="|1Chr|10|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.10.8">8</scripRef>). It was a low barren range of mountains bounding the valley
of Esdraelon (Jezreel) on the east, between it and the Jordan
valley. When the tidings of this defeat were conveyed to David,
he gave utterance to those pathetic words in the “Song of the
Bow” (2 Sam. 1:19-27).
</def>
<term id="g-p178.8">Gilead</term>
Hill of testimony, (Gen. 31:21), a mountainous region east of
Jordan. From its mountainous character it is called “the mount
of Gilead” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 31:25" id="g-p179.2" parsed="|Gen|31|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.25">Gen. 31:25</scripRef>). It is called also “the land of Gilead”

(<scripRef passage="Num. 32:1" id="g-p179.3" parsed="|Num|32|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.32.1">Num. 32:1</scripRef>), and sometimes simply “Gilead” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 60:7" id="g-p179.4" parsed="|Ps|60|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.60.7">Ps. 60:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen. 37:25" id="g-p179.5" parsed="|Gen|37|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.25">Gen. 37:25</scripRef>). It comprised the possessions of the tribes of Gad and

Reuben and the south part of Manasseh (<scripRef passage="Deut. 3:13" id="g-p179.6" parsed="|Deut|3|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.13">Deut. 3:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 32:40" id="g-p179.7" parsed="|Num|32|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.32.40">Num. 32:40</scripRef>).
It was bounded on the north by Bashan, and on the south by Moab

and Ammon (<scripRef passage="Gen. 31:21" id="g-p179.8" parsed="|Gen|31|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.21">Gen. 31:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 3:12-17" id="g-p179.9" parsed="|Deut|3|12|3|17" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.12-Deut.3.17">Deut. 3:12-17</scripRef>). “Half Gilead” was
possessed by Sihon, and the other half, separated from it by the
river Jabbok, by Og, king of Bashan. The deep ravine of the
river Hieromax (the modern Sheriat el-Mandhur) separated Bashan
from Gilead, which was about 60 miles in length and 20 in
breadth, extending from near the south end of the Lake of
Gennesaret to the north end of the Dead Sea. Abarim, Pisgah,
Nebo, and Peor are its mountains mentioned in Scripture.
</def>
<term id="g-p179.10">Gilead, Balm of</term>
The region of Gilead abounded in spices and aromatic gums, which

were exported to Egypt and Tyre (<scripRef passage="Gen. 37:25" id="g-p180.1" parsed="|Gen|37|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.25">Gen. 37:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 8:22" id="g-p180.2" parsed="|Jer|8|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.8.22">Jer. 8:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 46:11" id="g-p180.3" parsed="|Jer|46|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.46.11">46:11</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:17" id="g-p180.4" parsed="|Ezek|27|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.17">Ezek. 27:17</scripRef>). The word “balm” is a contracted form of “balsam,”
a word derived from the Greek balsamon, which was adopted as
the representative of the Hebrew words baal shemen, meaning
“lord” or “chief of oils.”
The Hebrew name of this balm was tsori. The tree yielding
this medicinal oil was probably the Balsamodendron opobalsamum
of botanists, and the Amyris opobalsamum of Linnaeus. It is an
evergreen, rising to the height of about 14 feet. The oil or
resin, exuding through an orifice made in its bark in very small
quantities, is esteemed of great value for its supposed
medicinal qualities. (See BALM.) It may be noted that
Coverdale’s version reads in <scripRef passage="Jer. 8:22" id="g-p181.2" parsed="|Jer|8|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.8.22">Jer. 8:22</scripRef>, “There is no triacle in
Galaad.” The word “triacle” = “treacle” is used in the sense of
ointment.
</def>
<term id="g-p181.3">Gilgal</term>
Rolling. (1.) From the solemn transaction of the reading of the
law in the valley of Shechem between Ebal and Gerizim the
Israelites moved forward to Gilgal, and there made a permanent

camp (<scripRef passage="Josh. 9:6" id="g-p182.1" parsed="|Josh|9|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.9.6">Josh. 9:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 10:6" id="g-p182.2" parsed="|Josh|10|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.6">10:6</scripRef>). It was “beside the oaks of Moreh,” near

which Abraham erected his first altar (<scripRef passage="Gen. 12:6" id="g-p182.3" parsed="|Gen|12|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.12.6">Gen. 12:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 12:7" id="g-p182.4" parsed="|Gen|12|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.12.7">7</scripRef>). This was
one of the three towns to which Samuel resorted for the
administration of justice (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 7:16" id="g-p182.5" parsed="|1Sam|7|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.7.16">1 Sam. 7:16</scripRef>), and here also he
offered sacrifices when the ark was no longer in the tabernacle

at Shiloh (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 10:8" id="g-p182.6" parsed="|1Sam|10|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.10.8">1 Sam. 10:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 13:7-9" id="g-p182.7" parsed="|1Sam|13|7|13|9" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.13.7-1Sam.13.9">13:7-9</scripRef>). To this place, as to a central
sanctuary, all Israel gathered to renew their allegiance to Saul
(11:14). At a later period it became the scene of idolatrous

worship (<scripRef passage="Hos. 4:15" id="g-p182.8" parsed="|Hos|4|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.4.15">Hos. 4:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos 9:15" id="g-p182.9" parsed="|Hos|9|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.9.15">9:15</scripRef>). It has been identified with the ruins
of Jiljilieh, about 5 miles south-west of Shiloh and about the
same distance from Bethel.
(2.) The place in “the plains of Jericho,” “in the east border
of Jericho,” where the Israelites first encamped after crossing

the Jordan (<scripRef passage="Josh. 4:19" id="g-p183.1" parsed="|Josh|4|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.4.19">Josh. 4:19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 4:20" id="g-p183.2" parsed="|Josh|4|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.4.20">20</scripRef>). Here they kept their first Passover
in the land of Canaan (5:10) and renewed the rite of
circumcision, and so “rolled away the reproach” of their
Egyptian slavery. Here the twelve memorial stones, taken from
the bed of the Jordan, were set up; and here also the tabernacle
remained till it was removed to Shiloh (18:1). It has been
identified with Tell Jiljulieh, about 5 miles from Jordan.
(3.) A place, probably in the hill country of Ephraim, where
there was a school of the prophets (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 4:38" id="g-p184.1" parsed="|2Kgs|4|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.4.38">2 Kings 4:38</scripRef>), and whence
Elijah and Elisha, who resided here, “went down” to Bethel
(2:1, 2). It is mentioned also in <scripRef passage="Deut. 11:30" id="g-p184.2" parsed="|Deut|11|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.11.30">Deut. 11:30</scripRef>. It is now known as
Jiljilia, a place 8 miles north of Bethel.
</def>
<term id="g-p184.3">Giloh</term>
Exile, a city in the south-west part of the hill-country of
Judah (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:51" id="g-p185.1" parsed="|Josh|15|51|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.51">Josh. 15:51</scripRef>). It was the native place or residence of the

traitor Ahithophel “the Gilonite” (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:51" id="g-p185.2" parsed="|Josh|15|51|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.51">Josh. 15:51</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 15:12" id="g-p185.3" parsed="|2Sam|15|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.15.12">2 Sam. 15:12</scripRef>),
and where he committed suicide (17:23). It has been identified
with Kurbet Jala, about 7 miles north of Hebron.
</def>
<term id="g-p185.4">Gimzo</term>
A place fertile in sycamores, a city in the plain of Judah, the
villages of which were seized by the Philistines (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 28:18" id="g-p186.1" parsed="|2Chr|28|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.28.18">2 Chr. 28:18</scripRef>).
It is now called Jimzu, about 3 miles south-east of Ludd, i.e.,
Lydda.
</def>
<term id="g-p186.2">Gin</term>
A trap. (1.) Ps. 140:5, 141:9, Amos 3:5, the Hebrew word used,
mokesh, means a noose or “snare,” as it is elsewhere rendered
(Ps. 18:5; Prov. 13:14, etc.).
(2.) Job 18:9, Isa. 8:14, Heb. pah, a plate or thin layer; and
hence a net, a snare, trap, especially of a fowler (<scripRef passage="Ps. 69" id="g-p188.3" parsed="|Ps|69|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.69">Ps. 69</scripRef>: 22,
“Let their table before them become a net;” <scripRef passage="Amos 3:5" id="g-p188.4" parsed="|Amos|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.3.5">Amos 3:5</scripRef>, “Doth a
bird fall into a net [pah] upon the ground where there is no
trap-stick [mokesh] for her? doth the net [pah] spring up from
the ground and take nothing at all?”, Gesenius.)
</def>
<term id="g-p188.5">Girdle</term>
(1.) Heb. hagor, a girdle of any kind worn by soldiers (1 Sam. 18:4; 2 Sam. 20:8; 1 Kings 2:5; 2 Kings 3:21) or women (Isa. 3:24).
(2.) Heb. ‘ezor, something “bound,” worn by prophets (2 Kings 1:8; Jer. 13:1), soldiers (Isa. 5:27; 2 Sam. 20:8; Ezek. 23:15),
Kings (Job 12:18).
(3.) Heb. mezah, a “band,” a girdle worn by men alone (Ps. 109:19; Isa. 22:21).
(4.) Heb. ‘abnet, the girdle of sacerdotal and state officers
(Ex. 28:4, 39, 40; 29:9; 39:29).
(5.) Heb. hesheb, the “curious girdle” (Ex. 28:8; R.V.,
“cunningly woven band”) was attached to the ephod, and was made
of the same material.
The common girdle was made of leather (2 Kings 1:8; Matt. 3:4); a finer sort of linen (Jer. 13:1; Ezek. 16:10; Dan. 10:5).
Girdles of sackcloth were worn in token of sorrow (<scripRef passage="Isa. 3:24" id="g-p194.6" parsed="|Isa|3|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.24">Isa. 3:24</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Isa 22:12" id="g-p194.7" parsed="|Isa|22|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.22.12">22:12</scripRef>). They were variously fastened to the wearer (<scripRef passage="Mark 1:6" id="g-p194.8" parsed="|Mark|1|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.6">Mark 1:6</scripRef>;
Jer. 13:1; Ezek. 16:10).
The girdle was a symbol of strength and power (Job 12:18, 21;

30:11; <scripRef passage="Isa. 22:21" id="g-p195.3" parsed="|Isa|22|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.22.21">Isa. 22:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 45:5" id="g-p195.4" parsed="|Isa|45|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.45.5">45:5</scripRef>). “Righteousness and faithfulness” are
the girdle of the Messiah (Isa. 11:5).
Girdles were used as purses or pockets (Matt. 10:9. A. V.,
“purses;” R.V., marg., “girdles.” Also Mark 6:8).
</def>
<term id="g-p196.3">Girgashite</term>
Dwelling in clayey soil, the descendants of the fifth son of
Canaan (<scripRef passage="Gen. 10:16" id="g-p197.1" parsed="|Gen|10|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.16">Gen. 10:16</scripRef>), one of the original tribes inhabiting the
land of Canaan before the time of the Israelites (<scripRef passage="Gen. 15:21" id="g-p197.2" parsed="|Gen|15|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.21">Gen. 15:21</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Deut. 7:1" id="g-p197.3" parsed="|Deut|7|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.7.1">Deut. 7:1</scripRef>). They were a branch of the great family of the
Hivites. Of their geographical position nothing is certainly
known. Probably they lived somewhere in the central part of
Western Palestine.
</def>
<term id="g-p197.4">Gittah-hepher</term>
(Josh. 19:13). See GATH-HEPHER.
</def>
<term id="g-p198.3">Gittaim</term>
Two wine-presses, (2 Sam. 4:3; Neh. 11:33), a town probably in
Benjamin to which the Beerothites fled.
</def>
<term id="g-p199.3">Gittite</term>
A native of the Philistine city of Gath (Josh. 13:3). Obed-edom,

in whose house the ark was placed, is so designated (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 6:10" id="g-p200.2" parsed="|2Sam|6|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.6.10">2 Sam. 6:10</scripRef>). Six hundred Gittites came with David from Gath into
</def>
<term id="g-p200.3">Gittith</term>
A stringed instrument of music. This word is found in the titles

of <scripRef passage="Ps. 8" id="g-p201.1" parsed="|Ps|8|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.8">Ps. 8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps. 81" id="g-p201.2" parsed="|Ps|81|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.81">81</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps. 84" id="g-p201.3" parsed="|Ps|84|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.84">84</scripRef>. In these places the LXX. render the word by
“on the wine-fats.” The Targum explains by “on the harp which
David brought from Gath.” It is the only stringed instrument
named in the titles of the Psalms.
</def>
<term id="g-p201.4">Gizonite</term>
A name given to Hashem, an inhabitant of Gizoh, a place
somewhere in the mountains of Judah (1 Chr. 11:34; 2 Sam. 23:32, 34).
</def>
<term id="g-p202.4">Glass</term>
Was known to the Egyptians at a very early period of their
national history, at least B.C. 1500. Various articles both
useful and ornamental were made of it, as bottles, vases, etc. A
glass bottle with the name of Sargon on it was found among the
ruins of the north-west palace of Nimroud. The Hebrew word
zekukith (Job 28:17), rendered in the Authorized Version
“crystal,” is rightly rendered in the Revised Version “glass.”
This is the only allusion to glass found in the Old Testament.

It is referred to in the New Testament in <scripRef passage="Rev. 4:6" id="g-p203.2" parsed="|Rev|4|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.4.6">Rev. 4:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev 15:2" id="g-p203.3" parsed="|Rev|15|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.15.2">15:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev 21:18" id="g-p203.4" parsed="|Rev|21|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.21.18">21:18</scripRef>,

<scripRef passage="Rev 21:21" id="g-p203.5" parsed="|Rev|21|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.21.21">21</scripRef>. In <scripRef passage="Job 37:18" id="g-p203.6" parsed="|Job|37|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.37.18">Job 37:18</scripRef>, the word rendered “looking-glass” is in the
Revised Version properly rendered “mirror,” formed, i.e., of
some metal. (Comp. <scripRef passage="Ex. 38:8" id="g-p203.7" parsed="|Exod|38|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.38.8">Ex. 38:8</scripRef>: “looking-glasses” are brazen
mirrors, R.V.). A mirror is referred to also in James 1:23.
</def>
<term id="g-p203.9">Glean</term>
The corners of fields were not to be reaped, and the sheaf
accidentally left behind was not to be fetched away, according

to the law of Moses (<scripRef passage="Lev. 19:9" id="g-p204.1" parsed="|Lev|19|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.9">Lev. 19:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev 23:22" id="g-p204.2" parsed="|Lev|23|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.22">23:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 24:21" id="g-p204.3" parsed="|Deut|24|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.24.21">Deut. 24:21</scripRef>). They were
to be left for the poor to glean. Similar laws were given
regarding vineyards and oliveyards. (Comp. Ruth 2:2.)
</def>
<term id="g-p204.5">Glede</term>
An Old English name for the common kite, mentioned only in Deut. 14:13 (Heb. ra’ah), the Milvus ater or black kite. The Hebrew
word does not occur in the parallel passage in Leviticus (11:14,
da’ah, rendered “vulture;” in R.V., “kite”). It was an unclean
bird. The Hebrew name is from a root meaning “to see,” “to
look,” thus designating a bird with a keen sight. The bird
intended is probably the buzzard, of which there are three
species found in Palestine. (See VULTURE.)
</def>
<term id="g-p205.3">Glorify</term>
(1.) To make glorious, or cause so to appear (John 12:28; 13:31,
32; 17:4, 5).
(2.) Spoken of God to “shew forth his praise” (1 Cor. 6:20;
10:31).
</def>
<term id="g-p207.3">Glory</term>
(Heb. kabhod; Gr. doxa). (1.) Abundance, wealth, treasure, and
hence honour (Ps. 49:12); glory (Gen. 31:1; Matt. 4:8; Rev. 21:24, 26).
(2.) Honour, dignity (1 Kings 3:13; Heb. 2:7 1 Pet. 1:24); of

God (<scripRef passage="Ps. 19:1" id="g-p209.4" parsed="|Ps|19|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.19.1">Ps. 19:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 29:1" id="g-p209.5" parsed="|Ps|29|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.29.1">29:1</scripRef>); of the mind or heart (<scripRef passage="Gen. 49:6" id="g-p209.6" parsed="|Gen|49|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.6">Gen. 49:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 7:5" id="g-p209.7" parsed="|Ps|7|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.7.5">Ps. 7:5</scripRef>;
Acts 2:46).
(3.) Splendour, brightness, majesty (Gen. 45:13; Isa. 4:5;
Acts 22:11; 2 Cor. 3:7); of Jehovah (Isa. 59:19; 60:1; 2 Thess. 1:9).
(4.) The glorious moral attributes, the infinite perfections

of God (<scripRef passage="Isa. 40:5" id="g-p211.1" parsed="|Isa|40|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.40.5">Isa. 40:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 7:2" id="g-p211.2" parsed="|Acts|7|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.7.2">Acts 7:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 1:23" id="g-p211.3" parsed="|Rom|1|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.23">Rom. 1:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom 9:23" id="g-p211.4" parsed="|Rom|9|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.9.23">9:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 1:12" id="g-p211.5" parsed="|Eph|1|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.1.12">Eph. 1:12</scripRef>). Jesus

is the “brightness of the Father’s glory” (<scripRef passage="Heb. 1:3" id="g-p211.6" parsed="|Heb|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.1.3">Heb. 1:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 1:14" id="g-p211.7" parsed="|John|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.1.14">John 1:14</scripRef>;
2:11).
(5.) The bliss of heaven (Rom. 2:7, 10; 5:2; 8:18; Heb. 2:10;
1 Pet. 5:1, 10).
(6.) The phrase “Give glory to God” (Josh. 7:19; Jer. 13:16)
is a Hebrew idiom meaning, “Confess your sins.” The words of the
Jews to the blind man, “Give God the praise” (<scripRef passage="John 9:24" id="g-p213.3" parsed="|John|9|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.9.24">John 9:24</scripRef>), are an
adjuration to confess. They are equivalent to, “Confess that you
are an impostor,” “Give God the glory by speaking the truth;”
for they denied that a miracle had been wrought.
</def>
<term id="g-p213.4">Glutton</term>
(Deut. 21:20), Heb. zolel, from a word meaning “to shake out,”
“to squander;” and hence one who is prodigal, who wastes his
means by indulgence. In <scripRef passage="Prov. 23:21" id="g-p214.2" parsed="|Prov|23|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.23.21">Prov. 23:21</scripRef>, the word means debauchees
or wasters of their own body. In <scripRef passage="Prov. 28:7" id="g-p214.3" parsed="|Prov|28|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.28.7">Prov. 28:7</scripRef>, the word (pl.) is
rendered Authorized Version “riotous men;” Revised Version,

“gluttonous.” <scripRef passage="Matt. 11:19" id="g-p214.4" parsed="|Matt|11|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.11.19">Matt. 11:19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Luke 7:34" id="g-p214.5" parsed="|Luke|7|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.7.34">Luke 7:34</scripRef>, Greek phagos, given to
eating, gluttonous.
</def>
<term id="g-p214.6">Gnash</term>
Heb. harak, meaning “to grate the teeth”, (Job 16:9; Ps. 112:10;
Lam. 2:16), denotes rage or sorrow. (See also Acts 7:54; Mark 9:18.)
</def>
<term id="g-p215.6">Gnat</term>
Only in Matt. 23:24, a small two-winged stinging fly of the
genus Culex, which includes mosquitoes. Our Lord alludes here to
the gnat in a proverbial expression probably in common use, “who
strain out the gnat;” the words in the Authorized Version,
“strain at a gnat,” being a mere typographical error, which has
been corrected in the Revised Version. The custom of filtering
wine for this purpose was common among the Jews. It was founded

on <scripRef passage="Lev. 11:23" id="g-p216.2" parsed="|Lev|11|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.11.23">Lev. 11:23</scripRef>. It is supposed that the “lice,” <scripRef passage="Ex. 8:16" id="g-p216.3" parsed="|Exod|8|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.8.16">Ex. 8:16</scripRef> (marg.
R.V., “sand-flies”), were a species of gnat.
</def>
<term id="g-p216.4">Goad</term>
(Heb. malmad, only in Judg. 3: 31), an instrument used by
ploughmen for guiding their oxen. Shamgar slew six hundred
Philistines with an ox-goad. “The goad is a formidable weapon.
It is sometimes ten feet long, and has a sharp point. We could
now see that the feat of Shamgar was not so very wonderful as
some have been accustomed to think.”
In 1 Sam. 13:21, a different Hebrew word is used, dorban,
meaning something pointed. The expression (<scripRef passage="Acts 9:5" id="g-p218.2" parsed="|Acts|9|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.9.5">Acts 9:5</scripRef>, omitted in
the R.V.), “It is hard for thee to kick against the pricks”,
i.e., against the goad, was proverbial for unavailing resistance
to superior power.
</def>
<term id="g-p218.3">Goat</term>
(1.) Heb. ‘ez, the she-goat (Gen. 15:9; 30:35; 31:38). This

Hebrew word is also used for the he-goat (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:5" id="g-p219.4" parsed="|Exod|12|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.5">Ex. 12:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 4:23" id="g-p219.5" parsed="|Lev|4|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.4.23">Lev. 4:23</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Num. 28:15" id="g-p219.6" parsed="|Num|28|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.28.15">Num. 28:15</scripRef>), and to denote a kid (<scripRef passage="Gen. 38:17" id="g-p219.7" parsed="|Gen|38|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.38.17">Gen. 38:17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 38:20" id="g-p219.8" parsed="|Gen|38|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.38.20">20</scripRef>). Hence it may
be regarded as the generic name of the animal as domesticated.
It literally means “strength,” and points to the superior
strength of the goat as compared with the sheep.
(2.) Heb. ‘attud, only in plural; rendered “rams” (Gen. 31:10, 12); he-goats (Num. 7:17-88; Isa. 1:11); goats (Deut. 32:14; Ps. 50:13). They were used in sacrifice (Ps. 66:15). This
word is used metaphorically for princes or chiefs in <scripRef passage="Isa. 14:9" id="g-p220.8" parsed="|Isa|14|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.14.9">Isa. 14:9</scripRef>,
and in Zech. 10:3 as leaders. (Comp. Jer. 50:8.)
(3.) Heb. gedi, properly a kid. Its flesh was a delicacy among
the Hebrews (Gen. 27:9, 14, 17; Judg. 6:19).
(4.) Heb. sa’ir, meaning the “shaggy,” a hairy goat, a he-goat

(<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 29:23" id="g-p222.1" parsed="|2Chr|29|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.29.23">2 Chr. 29:23</scripRef>); “a goat” (<scripRef passage="Lev. 4:24" id="g-p222.2" parsed="|Lev|4|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.4.24">Lev. 4:24</scripRef>); “satyr” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 13:21" id="g-p222.3" parsed="|Isa|13|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.13.21">Isa. 13:21</scripRef>);
“devils” (Lev. 17:7). It is the goat of the sin-offering (Lev. 9:3, 15; 10:16).
(5.) Heb. tsaphir, a he-goat of the goats (2 Chr. 29:21). In
Dan. 8:5, 8 it is used as a symbol of the Macedonian empire.
(6.) Heb. tayish, a “striker” or “butter,” rendered “he-goat”
(Gen. 30:35; 32:14).
(7.) Heb. ‘azazel (q.v.), the “scapegoat” (Lev. 16:8, 10, 26).
(8.) There are two Hebrew words used to denote the
undomesticated goat:, Yael, only in plural mountain goats (1 Sam. 24:2; Job 39:1; Ps. 104:18). It is derived from a word
meaning “to climb.” It is the ibex, which abounded in the
mountainous parts of Moab. And ’akko, only in Deut. 14:5, the
wild goat.
Goats are mentioned in the New Testament in Matt. 25:32, 33;

<scripRef passage="Heb. 9:12" id="g-p227.3" parsed="|Heb|9|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.12">Heb. 9:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Heb. 9:13" id="g-p227.4" parsed="|Heb|9|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.13">13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Heb. 9:19" id="g-p227.5" parsed="|Heb|9|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.19">19</scripRef>; 10:4. They represent oppressors and wicked men
(Ezek. 34:17; 39:18; Matt. 25:33).
Several varieties of the goat were familiar to the Hebrews.
They had an important place in their rural economy on account of
the milk they afforded and the excellency of the flesh of the
kid. They formed an important part of pastoral wealth (Gen. 31:10, 12;32:14; 1 Sam. 25:2).
</def>
<term id="g-p228.5">Goath</term>
A lowing, a place near Jerusalem, mentioned only in Jer. 31:39.
</def>
<term id="g-p229.2">Gob</term>
A pit, a place mentioned in 2 Sam. 21:18, 19; called also Gezer,
in 1 Chr. 20:4.
</def>
<term id="g-p230.4">Goblet</term>
A laver or trough for washing garments. In Cant. 7:2, a bowl or
drinking vessel, a bowl for mixing wine; in <scripRef passage="Ex. 24:6" id="g-p231.2" parsed="|Exod|24|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.24.6">Ex. 24:6</scripRef>, a
sacrificial basin. (See CUP.)
</def>
<term id="g-p231.4">God</term>
(A.S. and Dutch God; Dan. Gud; Ger. Gott), the name of the
Divine Being. It is the rendering (1) of the Hebrew ’El, from
a word meaning to be strong; (2) of ’Eloah_, plural _’Elohim.
The singular form, Eloah, is used only in poetry. The plural
form is more commonly used in all parts of the Bible, The Hebrew
word Jehovah (q.v.), the only other word generally employed to
denote the Supreme Being, is uniformly rendered in the
Authorized Version by “LORD,” printed in small capitals. The
existence of God is taken for granted in the Bible. There is
nowhere any argument to prove it. He who disbelieves this truth
is spoken of as one devoid of understanding (Ps. 14:1).
The arguments generally adduced by theologians in proof of the
being of God are:
(1.) The a priori argument, which is the testimony afforded by
reason.
(2.) The a posteriori argument, by which we proceed logically
from the facts of experience to causes. These arguments are,
(a) The cosmological, by which it is proved that there must be
a First Cause of all things, for every effect must have a cause.
(b) The teleological, or the argument from design. We see
everywhere the operations of an intelligent Cause in nature.
(c) The moral argument, called also the anthropological
argument, based on the moral consciousness and the history of
mankind, which exhibits a moral order and purpose which can only
be explained on the supposition of the existence of God.
Conscience and human history testify that “verily there is a God
that judgeth in the earth.”
The attributes of God are set forth in order by Moses in Ex. 34:6, 7. (see also Deut. 6:4; 10:17; Num. 16:22; Ex. 15:11;

<scripRef passage="Ex 33:19" id="g-p239.7" parsed="|Exod|33|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.33.19">33:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 44:6" id="g-p239.8" parsed="|Isa|44|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.44.6">Isa. 44:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hab. 3:6" id="g-p239.9" parsed="|Hab|3|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hab.3.6">Hab. 3:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 102:26" id="g-p239.10" parsed="|Ps|102|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.102.26">Ps. 102:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 34:12" id="g-p239.11" parsed="|Job|34|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.34.12">Job 34:12</scripRef>.) They are
also systematically classified in Rev. 5:12 and 7:12.
God’s attributes are spoken of by some as absolute, i.e., such
as belong to his essence as Jehovah, Jah, etc.; and relative,
i.e., such as are ascribed to him with relation to his
creatures. Others distinguish them into communicable, i.e.,
those which can be imparted in degree to his creatures:
goodness, holiness, wisdom, etc.; and incommunicable, which
cannot be so imparted: independence, immutability, immensity,
and eternity. They are by some also divided into natural
attributes, eternity, immensity, etc.; and moral, holiness,
goodness, etc.
</def>
<term id="g-p240.1">Godhead</term>
(Acts 17:29; Rom. 1:20; Col. 2:9), the essential being or the
nature of God.
</def>
<term id="g-p241.4">Godliness</term>
The whole of practical piety (1 Tim. 4:8; 2 Pet. 1:6). “It
supposes knowledge, veneration, affection, dependence,
submission, gratitude, and obedience.” In <scripRef passage="1 Tim. 3:16" id="g-p242.2" parsed="|1Tim|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.3.16">1 Tim. 3:16</scripRef> it denotes
the substance of revealed religion.
</def>
<term id="g-p242.3">Goel</term>
In Hebrew the participle of the verb gaal, “to redeem.” It is

rendered in the Authorized Version “kinsman,” <scripRef passage="Num. 5:8" id="g-p243.1" parsed="|Num|5|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.5.8">Num. 5:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ruth 3:12" id="g-p243.2" parsed="|Ruth|3|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.3.12">Ruth 3:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ruth 4:1" id="g-p243.3" parsed="|Ruth|4|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.4.1">4:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ruth 4:6" id="g-p243.4" parsed="|Ruth|4|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.4.6">6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ruth 4:8" id="g-p243.5" parsed="|Ruth|4|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.4.8">8</scripRef>; “redeemer,” <scripRef passage="Job 19:25" id="g-p243.6" parsed="|Job|19|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.19.25">Job 19:25</scripRef>; “avenger,” <scripRef passage="Num. 35:12" id="g-p243.7" parsed="|Num|35|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.35.12">Num. 35:12</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Deut. 19:6" id="g-p243.8" parsed="|Deut|19|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.19.6">Deut. 19:6</scripRef>, etc. The Jewish law gave the right of redeeming and
repurchasing, as well as of avenging blood, to the next
relative, who was accordingly called by this name. (See REDEEMER.)
</def>
<term id="g-p243.10">Gog</term>
(1.) A Reubenite (1 Chr. 5:4), the father of Shimei.
(2.) The name of the leader of the hostile party described in

<scripRef passage="Ezek. 38" id="g-p245.1" parsed="|Ezek|38|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.38">Ezek. 38</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 39" id="g-p245.2" parsed="|Ezek|39|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.39">39</scripRef>, as coming from the “north country” and assailing
the people of Israel to their own destruction. This prophecy has
been regarded as fulfilled in the conflicts of the Maccabees
with Antiochus, the invasion and overthrow of the Chaldeans, and
the temporary successes and destined overthrow of the Turks. But
“all these interpretations are unsatisfactory and inadequate.

The vision respecting Gog and Magog in the Apocalypse (<scripRef passage="Rev. 20:8" id="g-p245.3" parsed="|Rev|20|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.20.8">Rev. 20:8</scripRef>) is in substance a reannouncement of this prophecy of
Ezekiel. But while Ezekiel contemplates the great conflict in a
more general light as what was certainly to be connected with
the times of the Messiah, and should come then to its last
decisive issues, John, on the other hand, writing from the
commencement of the Messiah’s times, describes there the last
struggles and victories of the cause of Christ. In both cases
alike the vision describes the final workings of the world’s
evil and its results in connection with the kingdom of God, only
the starting-point is placed further in advance in the one case
than in the other.”
It has been supposed to be the name of a district in the wild
north-east steppes of Central Asia, north of the Hindu-Kush, now
a part of Turkestan, a region about 2,000 miles north-east of
Nineveh.
</def>
<term id="g-p246.1">Golan</term>
Exile, a city of Bashan (Deut. 4:43), one of the three cities of
refuge east of Jordan, about 12 miles north-east of the Sea of
Galilee (<scripRef passage="Josh. 20:8" id="g-p247.2" parsed="|Josh|20|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.20.8">Josh. 20:8</scripRef>). There are no further notices of it in
Scripture. It became the head of the province of Gaulanitis, one
of the four provinces into which Bashan was divided after the
Babylonish captivity, and almost identical with the modern
Jaulan, in Western Hauran, about 39 miles in length and 18 in
breath.
</def>
<term id="g-p247.3">Gold</term>
(1.) Heb. zahab, so called from its yellow colour (Ex. 25:11; 1 Chr. 28:18; 2 Chr. 3:5).
(2.) Heb. segor, from its compactness, or as being enclosed or
treasured up; thus precious or “fine gold” (1 Kings 6:20; 7:49).
(3.) Heb. paz, native or pure gold (Job 28:17; Ps. 19:10;
21:3, etc.).
(4.) Heb. betzer, “ore of gold or silver” as dug out of the
mine (Job 36:19, where it means simply riches).
(5.) Heb. kethem, i.e., something concealed or separated (Job 28:16, 19; Ps. 45:9; Prov. 25:12). Rendered “golden wedge” in
Isa. 13:12.
(6.) Heb. haruts, i.e., dug out; poetic for gold (Prov. 8:10;
16:16; Zech. 9:3).
Gold was known from the earliest times (Gen. 2:11). It was
principally used for ornaments (<scripRef passage="Gen. 24:22" id="g-p254.2" parsed="|Gen|24|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.22">Gen. 24:22</scripRef>). It was very

abundant (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 22:14" id="g-p254.3" parsed="|1Chr|22|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.22.14">1 Chr. 22:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Nah. 2:9" id="g-p254.4" parsed="|Nah|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Nah.2.9">Nah. 2:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Dan. 3:1" id="g-p254.5" parsed="|Dan|3|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.3.1">Dan. 3:1</scripRef>). Many tons of it
were used in connection with the temple (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 1:15" id="g-p254.6" parsed="|2Chr|1|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.1.15">2 Chr. 1:15</scripRef>). It was
found in Arabia, Sheba, and Ophir (1 Kings 9:28; 10:1; Job 28:16), but not in Palestine.
In Dan. 2:38, the Babylonian Empire is spoken of as a “head of
gold” because of its great riches; and Babylon was called by
Isaiah (14:4) the “golden city” (R.V. marg., “exactress,”
adopting the reading marhebah, instead of the usual word
madhebah).
</def>
<term id="g-p255.2">Golden calf</term>
(Ex. 32:4, 8; Deut. 9:16; Neh. 9:18). This was a molten image of
a calf which the idolatrous Israelites formed at Sinai. This
symbol was borrowed from the custom of the Egyptians. It was
destroyed at the command of Moses (<scripRef passage="Ex. 32:20" id="g-p256.5" parsed="|Exod|32|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.32.20">Ex. 32:20</scripRef>). (See
AARON; MOSES.)
</def>
<term id="g-p256.8">Goldsmith</term>
(Neh. 3:8, 32; Isa. 40:19; 41:7; 46:6). The word so rendered
means properly a founder or finer.
</def>
<term id="g-p257.6">Golgotha</term>
The common name of the spot where Jesus was crucified. It is
interpreted by the evangelists as meaning “the place of a skull”

(<scripRef passage="Matt. 27:33" id="g-p258.1" parsed="|Matt|27|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.33">Matt. 27:33</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 15:22" id="g-p258.2" parsed="|Mark|15|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.15.22">Mark 15:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 19:17" id="g-p258.3" parsed="|John|19|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.17">John 19:17</scripRef>). This name represents in
Greek letters the Aramaic word Gulgaltha, which is the Hebrew

Gulgoleth (<scripRef passage="Num. 1:2" id="g-p258.4" parsed="|Num|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.1.2">Num. 1:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 23:3" id="g-p258.5" parsed="|1Chr|23|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.23.3">1 Chr. 23:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 23:24" id="g-p258.6" parsed="|1Chr|23|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.23.24">24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 9:35" id="g-p258.7" parsed="|2Kgs|9|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.9.35">2 Kings 9:35</scripRef>), meaning “a
skull.” It is identical with the word Calvary (q.v.). It was a
little knoll rounded like a bare skull. It is obvious from the
evangelists that it was some well-known spot outside the gate

(comp. <scripRef passage="Heb. 13:12" id="g-p258.8" parsed="|Heb|13|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.13.12">Heb. 13:12</scripRef>), and near the city (<scripRef passage="Luke 23:26" id="g-p258.9" parsed="|Luke|23|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.23.26">Luke 23:26</scripRef>), containing a
“garden” (<scripRef passage="John 19:41" id="g-p258.10" parsed="|John|19|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19.41">John 19:41</scripRef>), and on a thoroughfare leading into the
country. Hence it is an untenable idea that it is embraced
within the present “Church of the Holy Sepulchre.” The hillock
above Jeremiah’s Grotto, to the north of the city, is in all
probability the true site of Calvary. The skull-like appearance
of the rock in the southern precipice of the hillock is very
remarkable.
</def>
<term id="g-p258.11">Goliath</term>
Great. (1.) A famous giant of Gath, who for forty days openly
defied the armies of Israel, but was at length slain by David
with a stone from a sling (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:4" id="g-p259.1" parsed="|1Sam|17|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.4">1 Sam. 17:4</scripRef>). He was probably
descended from the Rephaim who found refuge among the

Philistines after they were dispersed by the Ammonites (<scripRef passage="Deut. 2:20" id="g-p259.2" parsed="|Deut|2|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.2.20">Deut. 2:20</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut 2:21" id="g-p259.3" parsed="|Deut|2|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.2.21">21</scripRef>). His height was “six cubits and a span,” which, taking
the cubit at 21 inches, is equal to 10 1/2 feet. David cut off
his head (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:51" id="g-p259.4" parsed="|1Sam|17|51|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.51">1 Sam. 17:51</scripRef>) and brought it to Jerusalem, while he
hung the armour which he took from him in his tent. His sword
was preserved at Nob as a religious trophy (21:9). David’s
victory over Goliath was the turning point in his life. He came
into public notice now as the deliverer of Israel and the chief
among Saul’s men of war (18:5), and the devoted friend of
Jonathan.
(2.) In 2 Sam. 21:19 there is another giant of the same name
mentioned as slain by Elhanan. The staff of his apear “was like
a weaver’s beam.” The Authorized Version interpolates the words
“the brother of” from <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 20:5" id="g-p260.2" parsed="|1Chr|20|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.20.5">1 Chr. 20:5</scripRef>, where this giant is called
Lahmi.
</def>
<term id="g-p260.3">Gomer</term>
Complete; vanishing. (1.) The daughter of Diblaim, who (probably
in vision only) became the wife of Hosea (1:3).
(2.) The eldest son of Japheth, and father of Ashkenaz,

Riphath, and Togarmah (<scripRef passage="Gen. 10:2" id="g-p262.1" parsed="|Gen|10|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.2">Gen. 10:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 10:3" id="g-p262.2" parsed="|Gen|10|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.3">3</scripRef>), whose descendants formed
the principal branch of the population of South-eastern Europe.
He is generally regarded as the ancestor of the Celtae and the
Cimmerii, who in early times settled to the north of the Black
Sea, and gave their name to the Crimea, the ancient Chersonesus
Taurica. Traces of their presence are found in the names
Cimmerian Bosphorus, Cimmerian Isthmus, etc. In the seventh
century B.C. they were driven out of their original seat by the
Scythians, and overran western Asia Minor, whence they were
afterwards expelled. They subsequently reappear in the times of
the Romans as the Cimbri of the north and west of Europe, whence
they crossed to the British Isles, where their descendants are
still found in the Gaels and Cymry. Thus the whole Celtic race
may be regarded as descended from Gomer.
</def>
<term id="g-p262.3">Gomorrah</term>
Submersion, one of the five cities of the plain of Siddim (q.v.)

which were destroyed by fire (<scripRef passage="Gen. 10:19" id="g-p263.1" parsed="|Gen|10|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.19">Gen. 10:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 13:10" id="g-p263.2" parsed="|Gen|13|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.13.10">13:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 19:24" id="g-p263.3" parsed="|Gen|19|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.19.24">19:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 19:28" id="g-p263.4" parsed="|Gen|19|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.19.28">28</scripRef>).
These cities probably stood close together, and were near the
northern extremity of what is now the Dead Sea. This city is
always mentioned next after Sodom, both of which were types of

impiety and wickedness (<scripRef passage="Gen. 18:20" id="g-p263.5" parsed="|Gen|18|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.18.20">Gen. 18:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 9:29" id="g-p263.6" parsed="|Rom|9|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.9.29">Rom. 9:29</scripRef>). Their
destruction is mentioned as an “ensample unto those that after
should live ungodly” (2 Pet. 2:6; <scripRef passage="Jude 1" id="g-p263.7" parsed="|Jude|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jude.1.1">Jude 1</scripRef>:4-7). Their wickedness

became proverbial (<scripRef passage="Deut. 32:32" id="g-p263.8" parsed="|Deut|32|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.32">Deut. 32:32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 1:9" id="g-p263.9" parsed="|Isa|1|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.9">Isa. 1:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 1:10" id="g-p263.10" parsed="|Isa|1|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.10">10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 23:14" id="g-p263.11" parsed="|Jer|23|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.23.14">Jer. 23:14</scripRef>). But

that wickedness may be exceeded (<scripRef passage="Matt. 10:15" id="g-p263.12" parsed="|Matt|10|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.10.15">Matt. 10:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 6:11" id="g-p263.13" parsed="|Mark|6|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.6.11">Mark 6:11</scripRef>). (See
DEAD SEA).
</def>
<term id="g-p263.15">Goodly trees</term>
Boughs of, were to be carried in festive procession on the first
day of the feast of Tabernacles (<scripRef passage="Lev. 23:40" id="g-p264.1" parsed="|Lev|23|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.40">Lev. 23:40</scripRef>). This was probably
the olive tree (<scripRef passage="Neh. 8:15" id="g-p264.2" parsed="|Neh|8|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.8.15">Neh. 8:15</scripRef>), although no special tree is
mentioned.
</def>
<term id="g-p264.3">Goodness</term>
In man is not a mere passive quality, but the deliberate
preference of right to wrong, the firm and persistent resistance
of all moral evil, and the choosing and following of all moral
good.
</def>
<term id="g-p265.1">Goodness of God</term>
A perfection of his character which he exercises towards his
creatures according to their various circumstances and relations

(<scripRef passage="Ps. 145:8" id="g-p266.1" parsed="|Ps|145|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.145.8">Ps. 145:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps. 145:9" id="g-p266.2" parsed="|Ps|145|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.145.9">9</scripRef>; 103:8; <scripRef passage="1 John 4:8" id="g-p266.3" parsed="|1John|4|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.4.8">1 John 4:8</scripRef>). Viewed generally, it is
benevolence; as exercised with respect to the miseries of his
creatures it is mercy, pity, compassion, and in the case of
impenitent sinners, long-suffering patience; as exercised in
communicating favour on the unworthy it is grace. “Goodness and
justice are the several aspects of one unchangeable, infinitely
wise, and sovereign moral perfection. God is not sometimes
merciful and sometimes just, but he is eternally infinitely just

and merciful.” God is infinitely and unchangeably good (<scripRef passage="Zeph. 3:17" id="g-p266.4" parsed="|Zeph|3|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zeph.3.17">Zeph. 3:17</scripRef>), and his goodness is incomprehensible by the finite mind
(<scripRef passage="Rom. 11" id="g-p266.5" parsed="|Rom|11|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.11">Rom. 11</scripRef>: 35, 36). “God’s goodness appears in two things, giving
and forgiving.”
</def>
<term id="g-p266.6">Gopher</term>
A tree from the wood of which Noah was directed to build the ark
(<scripRef passage="Gen. 6:14" id="g-p267.1" parsed="|Gen|6|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.6.14">Gen. 6:14</scripRef>). It is mentioned only there. The LXX. render this
word by “squared beams,” and the Vulgate by “planed wood.” Other
versions have rendered it “pine” and “cedar;” but the weight of
authority is in favour of understanding by it the cypress tree,
which grows abundantly in Chaldea and Armenia.
</def>
<term id="g-p267.2">Goshen</term>
(1.) A district in Egypt where Jacob and his family settled, and

in which they remained till the Exodus (<scripRef passage="Gen. 45:10" id="g-p268.1" parsed="|Gen|45|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.45.10">Gen. 45:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 46:28" id="g-p268.2" parsed="|Gen|46|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.46.28">46:28</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 46:29" id="g-p268.3" parsed="|Gen|46|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.46.29">29</scripRef>,
<scripRef passage="Gen 46:31" id="g-p268.4" parsed="|Gen|46|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.46.31">31</scripRef>, etc.). It is called “the land of Goshen” (47:27), and also

simply “Goshen” (46:28), and “the land of Rameses” (47:11; <scripRef passage="Ex. 12:37" id="g-p268.5" parsed="|Exod|12|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.37">Ex. 12:37</scripRef>), for the towns Pithom and Rameses lay within its borders;
also Zoan or Tanis (<scripRef passage="Ps. 78:12" id="g-p268.6" parsed="|Ps|78|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.78.12">Ps. 78:12</scripRef>). It lay on the east of the Nile,
and apparently not far from the royal residence. It was “the

best of the land” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 47:6" id="g-p268.7" parsed="|Gen|47|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.47.6">Gen. 47:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 47:11" id="g-p268.8" parsed="|Gen|47|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.47.11">11</scripRef>), but is now a desert. It is
first mentioned in Joseph’s message to his father. It has been
identified with the modern Wady Tumilat, lying between the
eastern part of the Delta and the west border of Palestine. It
was a pastoral district, where some of the king’s cattle were
kept (<scripRef passage="Gen. 47:6" id="g-p268.9" parsed="|Gen|47|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.47.6">Gen. 47:6</scripRef>). The inhabitants were not exclusively
Israelites (Ex. 3:22; 11:2; 12:35, 36).
(2.) A district in Palestine (Josh. 10:41; 11:16). It was a
part of the maritime plain of Judah, and lay between Gaza and
Gibeon.
(3.) A town in the mountains of Judah (Josh. 15:51).
</def>
<term id="g-p270.2">Gospel</term>
A word of Anglo-Saxon origin, and meaning “God’s spell”, i.e.,
word of God, or rather, according to others, “good spell”, i.e.,
good news. It is the rendering of the Greek evangelion, i.e.,
“good message.” It denotes (1) “the welcome intelligence of
salvation to man as preached by our Lord and his followers. (2.)
It was afterwards transitively applied to each of the four
histories of our Lord’s life, published by those who are
therefore called ‘Evangelists’, writers of the history of the
gospel (the evangelion). (3.) The term is often used to express
collectively the gospel doctrines; and ‘preaching the gospel’ is
often used to include not only the proclaiming of the good
tidings, but the teaching men how to avail themselves of the
offer of salvation, the declaring of all the truths, precepts,
promises, and threatenings of Christianity.” It is termed “the
gospel of the grace of God” (<scripRef passage="Acts 20:24" id="g-p271.1" parsed="|Acts|20|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.24">Acts 20:24</scripRef>), “the gospel of the

kingdom” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 4:23" id="g-p271.2" parsed="|Matt|4|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.4.23">Matt. 4:23</scripRef>), “the gospel of Christ” (<scripRef passage="Rom. 1:16" id="g-p271.3" parsed="|Rom|1|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.16">Rom. 1:16</scripRef>), “the
gospel of peace (<scripRef passage="Eph. 6:15" id="g-p271.4" parsed="|Eph|6|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.6.15">Eph. 6:15</scripRef>), “the glorious gospel,” “the
everlasting gospel,” “the gospel of salvation” (Eph. 1:13).
</def>
<term id="g-p271.6">Gospels</term>
The central fact of Christian preaching was the intelligence

that the Saviour had come into the world (<scripRef passage="Matt. 4:23" id="g-p272.1" parsed="|Matt|4|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.4.23">Matt. 4:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 10:15" id="g-p272.2" parsed="|Rom|10|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.10.15">Rom. 10:15</scripRef>); and the first Christian preachers who called their
account of the person and mission of Christ by the term
evangelion_ (= good message) were called _evangelistai (=
evangelists) (Eph. 4:11; Acts 21:8).
There are four historical accounts of the person and work of
Christ: “the first by Matthew, announcing the Redeemer as the
promised King of the kingdom of God; the second by Mark,
declaring him ‘a prophet, mighty in deed and word’; the third by
Luke, of whom it might be said that he represents Christ in the

special character of the Saviour of sinners (<scripRef passage="Luke 7:36" id="g-p273.1" parsed="|Luke|7|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.7.36">Luke 7:36</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 15:18" id="g-p273.2" parsed="|Luke|15|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.15.18">15:18</scripRef>);
the fourth by John, who represents Christ as the Son of God, in
whom deity and humanity become one. The ancient Church gave to
Matthew the symbol of the lion, to Mark that of a man, to Luke
that of the ox, and to John that of the eagle: these were the
four faces of the cherubim” (Ezek. 1:10).
Date. The Gospels were all composed during the latter part of
the first century, and there is distinct historical evidence to
show that they were used and accepted as authentic before the
end of the second century.
Mutual relation. “If the extent of all the coincidences be
represented by 100, their proportionate distribution will be:
Matthew, Mark, and Luke, 53; Matthew and Luke, 21; Matthew and
Mark, 20; Mark and Luke, 6. Looking only at the general result,
it may be said that of the contents of the synoptic Gospels
[i.e., the first three Gospels] about two-fifths are common to
the three, and that the parts peculiar to one or other of them
are little more than one-third of the whole.”
