Origin. Did the evangelists copy from one another? The opinion
is well founded that the Gospels were published by the apostles
orally before they were committed to writing, and that each had
an independent origin. (See MATTHEW, GOSPEL OF.)
</def>
<term id="g-p276.2">Gourd</term>
(1.) Jonah’s gourd (Jonah 4:6-10), bearing the Hebrew name
kikayon (found only here), was probably the kiki of the
Egyptians, the croton. This is the castor-oil plant, a species
of ricinus, the palma Christi, so called from the palmate
division of its leaves. Others with more probability regard it
as the cucurbita the el-keroa of the Arabs, a kind of pumpkin
peculiar to the East. “It is grown in great abundance on the
alluvial banks of the Tigris and on the plain between the river
and the ruins of Nineveh.” At the present day it is trained to
run over structures of mud and brush to form boots to protect
the gardeners from the heat of the noon-day sun. It grows with
extraordinary rapidity, and when cut or injured withers away
also with great rapidity.
(2.) Wild gourds (2 Kings 4:38-40), Heb. pakkuoth, belong to
the family of the cucumber-like plants, some of which are
poisonous. The species here referred to is probably the
colocynth (Cucumis colocynthus). The LXX. render the word by
“wild pumpkin.” It abounds in the desert parts of Syria, Egypt,
and Arabia. There is, however, another species, called the
Cucumis prophetarum, from the idea that it afforded the gourd
which “the sons of the prophets” shred by mistake into their
pottage.
</def>
<term id="g-p278.2">Government of God</term>
See PROVIDENCE.
</def>
<term id="g-p279.2">Governments</term>
(1 Cor. 12:28), the powers which fit a man for a place of
influence in the church; “the steersman’s art; the art of
guiding aright the vessel of church or state.”
</def>
<term id="g-p280.2">Governor</term>
(1.) Heb. nagid, a prominent, conspicuous person, whatever his

capacity: as, chief of the royal palace (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 28:7" id="g-p281.1" parsed="|2Chr|28|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.28.7">2 Chr. 28:7</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:6" id="g-p281.2" parsed="|1Kgs|4|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.6">1 Kings 4:6</scripRef>), chief of the temple (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 9:11" id="g-p281.3" parsed="|1Chr|9|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.9.11">1 Chr. 9:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 20:1" id="g-p281.4" parsed="|Jer|20|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.20.1">Jer. 20:1</scripRef>), the
leader of the Aaronites (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 12:27" id="g-p281.5" parsed="|1Chr|12|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.12.27">1 Chr. 12:27</scripRef>), keeper of the sacred
treasury (26:24), captain of the army (13:1), the king (1 Sam. 9:16), the Messiah (Dan. 9:25).
(2.) Heb. nasi, raised; exalted. Used to denote the chiefs of

families (<scripRef passage="Num. 3:24" id="g-p282.1" parsed="|Num|3|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.3.24">Num. 3:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 3:30" id="g-p282.2" parsed="|Num|3|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.3.30">30</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 3:32" id="g-p282.3" parsed="|Num|3|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.3.32">32</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 3:35" id="g-p282.4" parsed="|Num|3|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.3.35">35</scripRef>); also of tribes (2:3; 7:2;
3:32). These dignities appear to have been elective, not
hereditary.
(3.) Heb. pakid, an officer or magistrate. It is used of the

delegate of the high priest (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 24:11" id="g-p283.1" parsed="|2Chr|24|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.24.11">2 Chr. 24:11</scripRef>), the Levites (<scripRef passage="Neh. 11:22" id="g-p283.2" parsed="|Neh|11|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.11.22">Neh. 11:22</scripRef>), a military commander (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 25:19" id="g-p283.3" parsed="|2Kgs|25|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.25.19">2 Kings 25:19</scripRef>), Joseph’s officers
in Egypt (Gen. 41:34).
(4.) Heb. shallit, one who has power, who rules (Gen. 42:6;
Ezra 4:20; Eccl. 8:8; Dan. 2:15; 5:29).
(5.) Heb. aluph, literally one put over a thousand, i.e., a
clan or a subdivision of a tribe. Used of the “dukes” of Edom
(Gen. 36), and of the Jewish chiefs (Zech. 9:7).
(6.) Heb. moshel, one who rules, holds dominion. Used of many

classes of rulers (<scripRef passage="Gen. 3:16" id="g-p286.1" parsed="|Gen|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.3.16">Gen. 3:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 24:2" id="g-p286.2" parsed="|Gen|24|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.2">24:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 45:8" id="g-p286.3" parsed="|Gen|45|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.45.8">45:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 105:20" id="g-p286.4" parsed="|Ps|105|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.105.20">Ps. 105:20</scripRef>); of the
Messiah (Micah 5:2); of God (1 Chr. 29:12; Ps. 103:19).
(7.) Heb. sar, a ruler or chief; a word of very general use.
It is used of the chief baker of Pharaoh (<scripRef passage="Gen. 40:16" id="g-p287.1" parsed="|Gen|40|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.40.16">Gen. 40:16</scripRef>); of the

chief butler (40:2, etc. See also <scripRef passage="Gen. 47:6" id="g-p287.2" parsed="|Gen|47|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.47.6">Gen. 47:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex. 1:11" id="g-p287.3" parsed="|Exod|1|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.1.11">Ex. 1:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Dan. 1:7" id="g-p287.4" parsed="|Dan|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.1.7">Dan. 1:7</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Judg. 10:18" id="g-p287.5" parsed="|Judg|10|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.10.18">Judg. 10:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 22:26" id="g-p287.6" parsed="|1Kgs|22|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.22.26">1 Kings 22:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 20:15" id="g-p287.7" parsed="|1Kgs|20|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.20.15">20:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 1:9" id="g-p287.8" parsed="|2Kgs|1|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.1.9">2 Kings 1:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 24:2" id="g-p287.9" parsed="|2Sam|24|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.24.2">2 Sam. 24:2</scripRef>). It

is used also of angels, guardian angels (<scripRef passage="Dan. 10:13" id="g-p287.10" parsed="|Dan|10|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.10.13">Dan. 10:13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan. 10:20" id="g-p287.11" parsed="|Dan|10|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.10.20">20</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan. 10:21" id="g-p287.12" parsed="|Dan|10|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.10.21">21</scripRef>;
(8.) Pehah, whence pasha, i.e., friend of the king;

adjutant; governor of a province (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:24" id="g-p288.1" parsed="|2Kgs|18|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.24">2 Kings 18:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 36:9" id="g-p288.2" parsed="|Isa|36|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.36.9">Isa. 36:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 51" id="g-p288.3" parsed="|Jer|51|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.51">Jer. 51</scripRef>: 57; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 23:6" id="g-p288.4" parsed="|Ezek|23|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.23.6">Ezek. 23:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 23:23" id="g-p288.5" parsed="|Ezek|23|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.23.23">23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Dan. 3:2" id="g-p288.6" parsed="|Dan|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.3.2">Dan. 3:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Esther 3" id="g-p288.7" parsed="|Esth|3|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.3">Esther 3</scripRef>: 12), or a perfect

(<scripRef passage="Neh. 3:7" id="g-p288.8" parsed="|Neh|3|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.3.7">Neh. 3:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh 5:14" id="g-p288.9" parsed="|Neh|5|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.5.14">5:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezra 5:3" id="g-p288.10" parsed="|Ezra|5|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.5.3">Ezra 5:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hag. 1:1" id="g-p288.11" parsed="|Hag|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hag.1.1">Hag. 1:1</scripRef>). This is a foreign word,
Assyrian, which was early adopted into the Hebrew idiom (1 Kings 10:15).
(9.) The Chaldean word segan is applied to the governors of

the Babylonian satrapies (<scripRef passage="Dan. 3:2" id="g-p289.1" parsed="|Dan|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.3.2">Dan. 3:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan. 3:27" id="g-p289.2" parsed="|Dan|3|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.3.27">27</scripRef>; 6:7); the prefects over
the Magi (2:48). The corresponding Hebrew word segan is used

of provincial rulers (<scripRef passage="Jer. 51:23" id="g-p289.3" parsed="|Jer|51|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.51.23">Jer. 51:23</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer. 51:28" id="g-p289.4" parsed="|Jer|51|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.51.28">28</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer. 51:57" id="g-p289.5" parsed="|Jer|51|57|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.51.57">57</scripRef>); also of chiefs and

rulers of the people of Jerusalem (<scripRef passage="Ezra 9:2" id="g-p289.6" parsed="|Ezra|9|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.9.2">Ezra 9:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh. 2:16" id="g-p289.7" parsed="|Neh|2|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.2.16">Neh. 2:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh 4:14" id="g-p289.8" parsed="|Neh|4|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.4.14">4:14</scripRef>,
19; 5:7, 17; 7:5; 12:40).
In the New Testament there are also different Greek words
rendered thus.
(1.) Meaning an ethnarch (2 Cor. 11:32), which was an office
distinct from military command, with considerable latitude of
application.
(2.) The procurator of Judea under the Romans (Matt. 27:2).
(Comp. <scripRef passage="Luke 2:2" id="g-p292.2" parsed="|Luke|2|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.2">Luke 2:2</scripRef>, where the verb from which the Greek word so
rendered is derived is used.)
(3.) Steward (Gal. 4:2).
(4.) Governor of the feast (John 2:9), who appears here to
have been merely an intimate friend of the bridegroom, and to
have presided at the marriage banquet in his stead.
(5.) A director, i.e., helmsman; Lat. gubernator, (James 3:4).
</def>
<term id="g-p295.2">Gozan</term>
A region in Central Asia to which the Israelites were carried

away captive (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:6" id="g-p296.1" parsed="|2Kgs|17|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.6">2 Kings 17:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 5:26" id="g-p296.2" parsed="|1Chr|5|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5.26">1 Chr. 5:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 19:12" id="g-p296.3" parsed="|2Kgs|19|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.19.12">2 Kings 19:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 37:12" id="g-p296.4" parsed="|Isa|37|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.37.12">Isa. 37:12</scripRef>). It was situated in Mesopotamia, on the river Habor (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:6" id="g-p296.5" parsed="|2Kgs|17|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.6">2 Kings 17:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:11" id="g-p296.6" parsed="|2Kgs|18|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.11">18:11</scripRef>), the Khabur, a tributary of the Euphrates.
The “river of Gozan” (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 5:26" id="g-p296.7" parsed="|1Chr|5|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5.26">1 Chr. 5:26</scripRef>) is probably the upper part of
the river flowing through the province of Gozan, now
Kizzel-Ozan.
</def>
<term id="g-p296.8">Grace</term>
(1.) Of form or person (Prov. 1:9; 3:22; Ps. 45:2). (2.) Favour,

kindness, friendship (<scripRef passage="Gen. 6:8" id="g-p297.4" parsed="|Gen|6|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.6.8">Gen. 6:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 18:3" id="g-p297.5" parsed="|Gen|18|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.18.3">18:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 19:19" id="g-p297.6" parsed="|Gen|19|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.19.19">19:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Tim. 1:9" id="g-p297.7" parsed="|2Tim|1|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.1.9">2 Tim. 1:9</scripRef>). (3.)

God’s forgiving mercy (<scripRef passage="Rom. 11:6" id="g-p297.8" parsed="|Rom|11|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.11.6">Rom. 11:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 2:5" id="g-p297.9" parsed="|Eph|2|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.5">Eph. 2:5</scripRef>). (4.) The gospel as

distinguished from the law (<scripRef passage="John 1:17" id="g-p297.10" parsed="|John|1|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.1.17">John 1:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 6:14" id="g-p297.11" parsed="|Rom|6|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.6.14">Rom. 6:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Pet. 5:12" id="g-p297.12" parsed="|1Pet|5|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.5.12">1 Pet. 5:12</scripRef>).
(5.) Gifts freely bestowed by God; as miracles, prophecy,

tongues (<scripRef passage="Rom. 15:15" id="g-p297.13" parsed="|Rom|15|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.15.15">Rom. 15:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 15:10" id="g-p297.14" parsed="|1Cor|15|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.15.10">1 Cor. 15:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 3:8" id="g-p297.15" parsed="|Eph|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.3.8">Eph. 3:8</scripRef>). (6.) Christian
virtues (<scripRef passage="2 Cor. 8:7" id="g-p297.16" parsed="|2Cor|8|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.8.7">2 Cor. 8:7</scripRef>; 2 Pet. 3:18). (7.) The glory hereafter to
be revealed (1 Pet. 1:13).
</def>
<term id="g-p297.18">Grace, means of</term>
An expression not used in Scripture, but employed (1) to denote
those institutions ordained by God to be the ordinary channels
of grace to the souls of men. These are the Word, Sacraments,
and Prayer.
(2.) But in popular language the expression is used in a wider
sense to denote those exercises in which we engage for the
purpose of obtaining spiritual blessing; as hearing the gospel,
reading the Word, meditation, self-examination, Christian
conversation, etc.
</def>
<term id="g-p299.1">Graft</term>
The process of inoculating fruit-trees (Rom. 11:17-24). It is
peculiarly appropriate to olive-trees. The union thus of
branches to a stem is used to illustrate the union of true
believers to the true Church.
</def>
<term id="g-p300.2">Grain</term>
Used, in Amos 9:9, of a small stone or kernel; in Matt. 13:31,

of an individual seed of mustard; in <scripRef passage="John 12:24" id="g-p301.3" parsed="|John|12|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.12.24">John 12:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="John 12:1" id="g-p301.4" parsed="|John|12|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.12.1">1</scripRef> Cor. 15:37,
of wheat. The Hebrews sowed only wheat, barley, and spelt; rye
and oats are not mentioned in Scripture.
</def>
<term id="g-p301.5">Grape</term>
The fruit of the vine, which was extensively cultivated in

Palestine. Grapes are spoken of as “tender” (<scripRef passage="Cant. 2:13" id="g-p302.1" parsed="|Song|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.2.13">Cant. 2:13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Cant. 2:15" id="g-p302.2" parsed="|Song|2|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.2.15">15</scripRef>),

“unripe” (<scripRef passage="Job 15:33" id="g-p302.3" parsed="|Job|15|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.15.33">Job 15:33</scripRef>), “sour” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 18:5" id="g-p302.4" parsed="|Isa|18|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.18.5">Isa. 18:5</scripRef>), “wild” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 5:2" id="g-p302.5" parsed="|Isa|5|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.5.2">Isa. 5:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 5:4" id="g-p302.6" parsed="|Isa|5|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.5.4">4</scripRef>).

(See <scripRef passage="Rev. 14:18" id="g-p302.7" parsed="|Rev|14|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.14.18">Rev. 14:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Micah 7:1" id="g-p302.8" parsed="|Mic|7|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mic.7.1">Micah 7:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 6:9" id="g-p302.9" parsed="|Jer|6|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.6.9">Jer. 6:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 18:2" id="g-p302.10" parsed="|Ezek|18|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.18.2">Ezek. 18:2</scripRef>, for figurative
use of the word.) (See VINE.)
</def>
<term id="g-p302.12">Grass</term>
(1.) Heb. hatsir, ripe grass fit for mowing (1 Kings 18:5; Job 40:15; Ps. 104:14). As the herbage rapidly fades under the
scorching sun, it is used as an image of the brevity of human

life (<scripRef passage="Isa. 40:6" id="g-p303.4" parsed="|Isa|40|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.40.6">Isa. 40:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 40:7" id="g-p303.5" parsed="|Isa|40|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.40.7">7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 90:5" id="g-p303.6" parsed="|Ps|90|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.90.5">Ps. 90:5</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="Num. 11:5" id="g-p303.7" parsed="|Num|11|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.11.5">Num. 11:5</scripRef> this word is
rendered “leeks.”
(2.) Heb. deshe’, green grass (Gen. 1:11, 12; Isa. 66:14;
<scripRef passage="Deut. 32:2" id="g-p304.4" parsed="|Deut|32|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.2">Deut. 32:2</scripRef>). “The sickly and forced blades of grass which spring
up on the flat plastered roofs of houses in the East are used as
an emblem of speedy destruction, because they are small and
weak, and because, under the scorching rays of the sun, they
soon wither away” (2 Kings 19:26; Ps. 129:6; Isa. 37:27).
The dry stalks of grass were often used as fuel for the oven
(Matt. 6:30; 13:30; Luke 12:28).
</def>
<term id="g-p305.4">Grasshopper</term>
Belongs to the class of neuropterous insects called Gryllidae.
This insect is not unknown in Palestine.
In Judg. 6:5; 7:12; Job 39:30; Jer. 46:23, where the
Authorized Version has “grasshopper,” the Revised Version more
correctly renders the Hebrew word (‘arbeh) by “locust.” This is

the case also in <scripRef passage="Amos 7:1" id="g-p307.5" parsed="|Amos|7|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.7.1">Amos 7:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Nah. 3:17" id="g-p307.6" parsed="|Nah|3|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Nah.3.17">Nah. 3:17</scripRef>, where the Hebrew word
gob is used; and in Lev. 11:22; Num. 13:33; Eccl. 12:5; Isa. 40:22, where hagab is used. In all these instances the proper
rendering is probably “locust” (q.v.).
</def>
<term id="g-p307.11">Grate</term>
A network of brass for the bottom of the great altar of
sacrifice (Ex. 27:4; 35:16; 38:4, 5, 30).
</def>
<term id="g-p308.6">Grave</term>
Among the ancient Hebrews graves were outside of cities in the

open field (<scripRef passage="Luke 7:12" id="g-p309.1" parsed="|Luke|7|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.7.12">Luke 7:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 11:30" id="g-p309.2" parsed="|John|11|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.11.30">John 11:30</scripRef>). Kings (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 2:10" id="g-p309.3" parsed="|1Kgs|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.2.10">1 Kings 2:10</scripRef>) and
prophets (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 25:1" id="g-p309.4" parsed="|1Sam|25|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.25.1">1 Sam. 25:1</scripRef>) were generally buried within cities.
Graves were generally grottoes or caves, natural or hewn out in

rocks (<scripRef passage="Isa. 22:16" id="g-p309.5" parsed="|Isa|22|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.22.16">Isa. 22:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 27:60" id="g-p309.6" parsed="|Matt|27|60|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.60">Matt. 27:60</scripRef>). There were family cemeteries

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 47:29" id="g-p309.7" parsed="|Gen|47|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.47.29">Gen. 47:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 50:5" id="g-p309.8" parsed="|Gen|50|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.50.5">50:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 19:37" id="g-p309.9" parsed="|2Sam|19|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.19.37">2 Sam. 19:37</scripRef>). Public burial-places were

assigned to the poor (<scripRef passage="Jer. 26:23" id="g-p309.10" parsed="|Jer|26|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.26.23">Jer. 26:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 23:6" id="g-p309.11" parsed="|2Kgs|23|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.6">2 Kings 23:6</scripRef>). Graves were
usually closed with stones, which were whitewashed, to warn
strangers against contact with them (<scripRef passage="Matt. 23:27" id="g-p309.12" parsed="|Matt|23|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.23.27">Matt. 23:27</scripRef>), which caused
ceremonial pollution (Num. 19:16).
There were no graves in Jerusalem except those of the kings,
and according to tradition that of the prophetess Huldah.
</def>
<term id="g-p310.1">Graven image</term>
Deut. 27:15; Ps. 97:7 (Heb. pesel), refers to the household gods
of idolaters. “Every nation and city had its own gods...Yet
every family had its separate household or tutelary god.”
</def>
<term id="g-p311.3">Graving</term>
(1.) Heb. hatsabh. Job 19:24, rendered “graven,” but generally
means hewn stone or wood, in quarry or forest.
(2.) Heb. harush. Jer. 17:1, rendered “graven,” and indicates
generally artistic work in metal, wood, and stone, effected by
fine instruments.
(3.) Heb. haqaq. Ezek. 4:1, engraving a plan or map, rendered
“pourtray;” Job 19:23, “written.”
(4.) Heb. pasal points rather to the sculptor’s or the
carver’s art (Isa. 30:22; 40:19; 41:7; 44:12-15).
(5.) Pathah refers to intaglio work, the cutting and engraving
of precious stones (Ex. 28:9-11, 21; Zech. 3:9; Cant. 1:10, 11).
(6.) Heret. In Ex. 32:4 rendered “graving tool;” and in Isa. 8:1, “a pen.”
</def>
<term id="g-p317.3">Greaves</term>
Only in 1 Sam. 17:6, a piece of defensive armour (q.v.) reaching
from the foot to the knee; from French greve, “the shin.” They
were the Roman cothurni.
</def>
<term id="g-p318.2">Grecians</term>
Hellenists, Greek-Jews; Jews born in a foreign country, and thus

did not speak Hebrew (<scripRef passage="Acts 6:1" id="g-p319.1" parsed="|Acts|6|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.6.1">Acts 6:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 9:29" id="g-p319.2" parsed="|Acts|9|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.9.29">9:29</scripRef>), nor join in the Hebrew
services of the Jews in Palestine, but had synagogues of their
own in Jerusalem. Joel 3:6 =Greeks.
</def>
<term id="g-p319.4">Greece</term>
Orginally consisted of the four provinces of Macedonia, Epirus,
Achaia, and Peleponnesus. In <scripRef passage="Acts 20:2" id="g-p320.1" parsed="|Acts|20|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.2">Acts 20:2</scripRef> it designates only the
Roman province of Macedonia. Greece was conquered by the Romans
B.C. 146. After passing through various changes it was erected
into an independent monarchy in 1831.
Moses makes mention of Greece under the name of Javan (Gen. 10:2-5); and this name does not again occur in the Old Testament
till the time of Joel (3:6). Then the Greeks and Hebrews first
came into contact in the Tyrian slave-market. Prophetic notice
is taken of Greece in Dan. 8:21.
The cities of Greece were the special scenes of the labours of
the apostle Paul.
</def>
<term id="g-p322.1">Greek</term>
Found only in the New Testament, where a distinction is observed
between “Greek” and “Grecian” (q.v.). The former is (1) a Greek

by race (<scripRef passage="Acts 16:1-3" id="g-p323.1" parsed="|Acts|16|1|16|3" osisRef="Bible:Acts.16.1-Acts.16.3">Acts 16:1-3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 18:17" id="g-p323.2" parsed="|Acts|18|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.18.17">18:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 1:14" id="g-p323.3" parsed="|Rom|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.14">Rom. 1:14</scripRef>), or (2) a Gentile as

opposed to a Jew (<scripRef passage="Rom. 2:9" id="g-p323.4" parsed="|Rom|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.2.9">Rom. 2:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Rom. 2:10" id="g-p323.5" parsed="|Rom|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.2.10">10</scripRef>). The latter, meaning properly
“one who speaks Greek,” is a foreign Jew opposed to a home Jew
who dwelt in Palestine.
The word “Grecians” in Acts 11:20 should be “Greeks,” denoting
the heathen Greeks of that city, as rendered in the Revised
Version according to the reading of the best manuscripts
(“Hellenes”).
</def>
<term id="g-p324.2">Greyhound</term>
(Prov. 30:31), the rendering of the Hebrew zarzir mothnayim,
meaning literally “girded as to the lions.” Some (Gesen.; R.V.
marg.) render it “war-horse.” The LXX. and Vulgate versions
render it “cock.” It has been by some interpreters rendered also
“stag” and “warrior,” as being girded about or panoplied, and
“wrestler.” The greyhound, however, was evidently known in
ancient times, as appears from Egyptian monuments.
</def>
<term id="g-p325.2">Grind</term>
(Ex. 32:20; Deut. 9:21; Judg. 16:21), to crush small (Heb.
tahan); to oppress the poor (<scripRef passage="Isa. 3:5" id="g-p326.4" parsed="|Isa|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.5">Isa. 3:5</scripRef>). The hand-mill was early
used by the Hebrews (<scripRef passage="Num. 11:8" id="g-p326.5" parsed="|Num|11|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.11.8">Num. 11:8</scripRef>). It consisted of two stones, the

upper (<scripRef passage="Deut. 24:6" id="g-p326.6" parsed="|Deut|24|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.24.6">Deut. 24:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 11:21" id="g-p326.7" parsed="|2Sam|11|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.11.21">2 Sam. 11:21</scripRef>) being movable and slightly
concave, the lower being stationary. The grinders mentioned
Eccl. 12:3 are the teeth. (See MILL.)
</def>
<term id="g-p326.10">Grizzled</term>
Party-coloured, as goats (Gen. 31:10, 12), horses (Zech. 6:3, 6).
</def>
<term id="g-p327.5">Grove</term>
(1.) Heb. ‘asherah, properly a wooden image, or a pillar
representing Ashtoreth, a sensual Canaanitish goddess, probably

usually set up in a grove (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 21:7" id="g-p328.1" parsed="|2Kgs|21|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.21.7">2 Kings 21:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 23:4" id="g-p328.2" parsed="|2Kgs|23|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.4">23:4</scripRef>). In the Revised
Version the word “Asherah” (q.v.) is introduced as a proper
noun, the name of the wooden symbol of a goddess, with the
plurals Asherim (Ex. 34:13) and Asheroth (Judg. 3:13).
The LXX. have rendered asherah in 2 Chr. 15:16 by “Astarte.”
The Vulgate has done this also in Judg. 3:7.
(2.) Heb. ‘eshel (Gen. 21:33). In 1 Sam. 22:6 and 31:13 the
Authorized Version renders this word by “tree.” In all these
passages the Revised Version renders by “tamarisk tree.” It has
been identified with the Tamariscus orientalis, five species of
which are found in Palestine.
(3.) The Heb. word ‘elon, uniformly rendered in the Authorized
Version by “plain,” properly signifies a grove or plantation. In
the Revised Version it is rendered, pl., “oaks” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 13:18" id="g-p331.1" parsed="|Gen|13|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.13.18">Gen. 13:18</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Gen 14:13" id="g-p331.2" parsed="|Gen|14|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.13">14:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 18:1" id="g-p331.3" parsed="|Gen|18|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.18.1">18:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 12:6" id="g-p331.4" parsed="|Gen|12|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.12.6">12:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 11:30" id="g-p331.5" parsed="|Deut|11|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.11.30">Deut. 11:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 19:33" id="g-p331.6" parsed="|Josh|19|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.33">Josh. 19:33</scripRef>). In the earliest
times groves are mentioned in connection with religious worship.
The heathen consecrated groves to particular gods, and for this
reason they were forbidden to the Jews (Jer. 17:3; Ezek. 20:28).
</def>
<term id="g-p331.9">Guard</term>
(1.) Heb. tabbah (properly a “cook,” and in a secondary sense
“executioner,” because this office fell to the lot of the cook
in Eastern countries), the bodyguard of the kings of Egypt (Gen. 37:36) and Babylon (2 Kings 25:8; Jer. 40:1; Dan. 2:14).
(2.) Heb. rats, properly a “courier,” one whose office was to

run before the king’s chariot (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 15:1" id="g-p333.1" parsed="|2Sam|15|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.15.1">2 Sam. 15:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 1:5" id="g-p333.2" parsed="|1Kgs|1|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.1.5">1 Kings 1:5</scripRef>). The

couriers were also military guards (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 22:17" id="g-p333.3" parsed="|1Sam|22|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.22.17">1 Sam. 22:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 10:25" id="g-p333.4" parsed="|2Kgs|10|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.10.25">2 Kings 10:25</scripRef>). They were probably the same who under David were called
Pelethites (1 Kings 14:27; 2 Sam. 15:1).
(3.) Heb. mishmereth, one who watches (Neh. 4:22), or a
watch-station (7:3; 12:9; Job 7:12).
In the New Testament (Mark 6:27) the Authorized Version
renders the Greek spekulator by “executioner,” earlier English
versions by “hangman,” the Revised Version by “soldier of his
guard.” The word properly means a “pikeman” or “halberdier,” of

whom the bodyguard of kings and princes was composed. In <scripRef passage="Matt. 27:65" id="g-p335.2" parsed="|Matt|27|65|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.65">Matt. 27:65</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt 27:66" id="g-p335.3" parsed="|Matt|27|66|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.66">66</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 28:11" id="g-p335.4" parsed="|Matt|28|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.28.11">28:11</scripRef>, the Authorized Version renders the Greek
kustodia by “watch,” and the Revised Version by “guard,” the
Roman guard, which consisted of four soldiers, who were relieved
every three hours (<scripRef passage="Acts 12:4" id="g-p335.5" parsed="|Acts|12|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.12.4">Acts 12:4</scripRef>). The “captain of the guard”
mentioned <scripRef passage="Acts 28:16" id="g-p335.6" parsed="|Acts|28|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.28.16">Acts 28:16</scripRef> was the commander of the Praetorian troops,
whose duty it was to receive and take charge of all prisoners
from the provinces.
</def>
<term id="g-p335.7">Guest-chamber</term>
The spare room on the upper floor of an Eastern dwelling (Mark 14:14; Luke 22:11). In Luke 2:7 the word is translated “inn”
</def>
<term id="g-p336.4">Gur</term>
A whelp, a place near Ibleam where Jehu’s servants overtook and
mortally wounded king Ahaziah (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 9:27" id="g-p337.1" parsed="|2Kgs|9|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.9.27">2 Kings 9:27</scripRef>); an ascent from the
plain of Jezreel.
</def>
<term id="g-p337.2">Gur-baal</term>
Sojourn of Baal, a place in Arabia (2 Chr. 26:7) where there was
probably a temple of Baal.
</def>
<term id="g-p338.2">Gutter</term>
Heb. tsinnor, (2 Sam. 5:8). This Hebrew word occurs only
elsewhere in <scripRef passage="Ps. 42:7" id="g-p339.2" parsed="|Ps|42|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.42.7">Ps. 42:7</scripRef> in the plural, where it is rendered
“waterspouts.” It denotes some passage through which water
passed; a water-course.
In Gen. 30:38, 41 the Hebrew word rendered “gutters” is
rahat, and denotes vessels overflowing with water for cattle
(Ex. 2:16); drinking-troughs.
</def>
</glossary>
</div2>
<div2 title="H" prev="g" next="i" id="h">
<glossary id="h-p0.1">
<term id="h-p0.2">Habakkuk</term>
<def id="h-p0.3">
Embrace, the eighth of the twelve minor prophets. Of his
personal history we have no reliable information. He was
probably a member of the Levitical choir. He was contemporary
with Jeremiah and Zephaniah.
</def>
<term id="h-p1.1">Habakkuk, Prophecies of</term>
<def id="h-p1.2">
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="h-p1.3" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="Hab 0" id="h-p1.4" parsed="|Hab|0|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hab" />
Were probably written about B.C. 650-627, or, as some think, a
few years later. This book consists of three chapters, the
contents of which are thus comprehensively described: “When the
prophet in spirit saw the formidable power of the Chaldeans
approaching and menacing his land, and saw the great evils they
would cause in Judea, he bore his complaints and doubts before
Jehovah, the just and the pure (1:2-17). And on this occasion
the future punishment of the Chaldeans was revealed to him (2).
In the third chapter a presentiment of the destruction of his
country, in the inspired heart of the prophet, contends with his
hope that the enemy would be chastised.” The third chapter is a
sublime song dedicated “to the chief musician,” and therefore
intended apparently to be used in the worship of God. It is
“unequalled in majesty and splendour of language and imagery.”
The passage in 2:4, “The just shall live by his faith,” is
quoted by the apostle in Rom. 1:17. (Comp. Gal. 3:12; Heb. 10:37, 38.)
</def>
<term id="h-p3.5">Habergeon</term>
<def id="h-p3.6">
An Old English word for breastplate. In Job 41:26 (Heb. shiryah)
it is properly a “coat of mail;” the Revised Version has

“pointed shaft.” In <scripRef passage="Ex. 28:32" id="h-p4.2" parsed="|Exod|28|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.32">Ex. 28:32</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 28:39" id="h-p4.3" parsed="|Exod|28|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.39">39</scripRef>:23, it denotes a military
garment strongly and thickly woven and covered with mail round
the neck and breast. Such linen corselets have been found in
Egypt. The word used in these verses is tahra, which is of
Egyptian origin. The Revised Version, however, renders it by
“coat of mail.” (See ARMOUR.)
</def>
<term id="h-p4.5">Habitation</term>
<def id="h-p4.6">
God is the habitation of his people, who find rest and safety in

him (<scripRef passage="Ps. 71:3" id="h-p5.1" parsed="|Ps|71|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.71.3">Ps. 71:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 91:9" id="h-p5.2" parsed="|Ps|91|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.91.9">91:9</scripRef>). Justice and judgment are the habitation of
God’s throne (<scripRef passage="Ps. 89:14" id="h-p5.3" parsed="|Ps|89|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.89.14">Ps. 89:14</scripRef>, Heb. mekhon, “foundation”), because all

his acts are founded on justice and judgment. (See <scripRef passage="Ps. 132:5" id="h-p5.4" parsed="|Ps|132|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.132.5">Ps. 132:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps 132:13" id="h-p5.5" parsed="|Ps|132|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.132.13">13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 2:22" id="h-p5.6" parsed="|Eph|2|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.22">Eph. 2:22</scripRef>, of Canaan, Jerusalem, and the temple as God’s
habitation.) God inhabits eternity (<scripRef passage="Isa. 57:15" id="h-p5.7" parsed="|Isa|57|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.57.15">Isa. 57:15</scripRef>), i.e., dwells
not only among men, but in eternity, where time is unknown; and
“the praises of Israel” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 22:3" id="h-p5.8" parsed="|Ps|22|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.22.3">Ps. 22:3</scripRef>), i.e., he dwells among those
praises and is continually surrounded by them.
</def>
<term id="h-p5.9">Habor</term>
<def id="h-p5.10">
The united stream, or, according to others, with beautiful
banks, the name of a river in Assyria, and also of the district
through which it flowed (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 5:26" id="h-p6.1" parsed="|1Chr|5|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5.26">1 Chr. 5:26</scripRef>). There is a river called
Khabur which rises in the central highlands of Kurdistan, and
flows south-west till it falls into the Tigris, about 70 miles
above Mosul. This was not, however, the Habor of Scripture.
There is another river of the same name (the Chaboras) which,
after a course of about 200 miles, flows into the Euphrates at
Karkesia, the ancient Circesium. This was, there can be little
doubt, the ancient Habor.
</def>
<term id="h-p7.1">Hachilah</term>
<def id="h-p7.2">
The darksome hill, one of the peaks of the long ridge of
el-Kolah, running out of the Ziph plateau, “on the south of
Jeshimon” (i.e., of the “waste”), the district to which one
looks down from the plateau of Ziph (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 23:19" id="h-p8.1" parsed="|1Sam|23|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.23.19">1 Sam. 23:19</scripRef>). After his
reconciliation with Saul at Engedi (24:1-8), David returned to
Hachilah, where he had fixed his quarters. The Ziphites
treacherously informed Saul of this, and he immediately (26:1-4)
renewed his pursuit of David, and “pitched in the hill of
Hachilah.” David and his nephew Abishai stole at night into the
midst of Saul’s camp, when they were all asleep, and noiselessly
removed the royal spear and the cruse from the side of the king,
and then, crossing the intervening valley to the height on the
other side, David cried to the people, and thus awoke the
sleepers. He then addressed Saul, who recognized his voice, and
expostulated with him. Saul professed to be penitent; but David
could not put confidence in him, and he now sought refuge at
Ziklag. David and Saul never afterwards met. (1 Sam. 26:13-25).
</def>
<term id="h-p8.3">Hadad</term>
<def id="h-p8.4">
Adod, brave(?), the name of a Syrian god. (1.) An Edomite king
who defeated the Midianites (Gen. 36:35; 1 Chr. 1:46).
(2.) Another Edomite king (1 Chr. 1:50, 51), called also Hadar
(Gen. 36:39; 1 Chr. 1:51).
(3.) One of “the king’s seed in Edom.” He fled into Egypt,
where he married the sister of Pharaoh’s wife (1 Kings 11:14-22). He became one of Solomon’s adversaries.
Hadad, sharp, (a different name in Hebrew from the preceding),
one of the sons of Ishmael (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 1:30" id="h-p12.1" parsed="|1Chr|1|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.1.30">1 Chr. 1:30</scripRef>). Called also Hadar
(Gen. 25:15).
</def>
<term id="h-p12.3">Hadadezer</term>
<def id="h-p12.4">
Hadad is help; called also Hadarezer, Adod is his help, the king
of Zobah. Hanun, the king of the Ammonites, hired among others
the army of Hadadezer to assist him in his war against David.
Joab, who was sent against this confederate host, found them in
double battle array, the Ammonities toward their capital of
Rabbah, and the Syrian mercenaries near Medeba. In the battle
which was fought the Syrians were scattered, and the Ammonites
in alarm fled into their capital. After this Hadadezer went
north “to recover his border” (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 8:3" id="h-p13.1" parsed="|2Sam|8|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.8.3">2 Sam. 8:3</scripRef>, A.V.); but rather, as
the Revised Version renders, “to recover his dominion”, i.e., to
recruit his forces. Then followed another battle with the Syrian
army thus recruited, which resulted in its being totally routed
at Helam (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 10:17" id="h-p13.2" parsed="|2Sam|10|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.10.17">2 Sam. 10:17</scripRef>). Shobach, the leader of the Syrian army,
died on the field of battle. The Syrians of Damascus, who had
come to help Hadadezer, were also routed, and Damascus was made
tributary to David. All the spoils taken in this war, “shields
of gold” and “very much brass,” from which afterwards the
“brasen sea, and the pillars, and the vessels of brass” for the
temple were made (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 18:8" id="h-p13.3" parsed="|1Chr|18|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.18.8">1 Chr. 18:8</scripRef>), were brought to Jerusalem and
dedicated to Jehovah. Thus the power of the Ammonites and the
Syrians was finally broken, and David’s empire extended to the
Euphrates (2 Sam. 10:15-19; 1 Chr. 19:15-19).
</def>
<term id="h-p13.6">Hadad-rimmon</term>
<def id="h-p13.7">
(composed of the names of two Syrian idols), the name of a place
in the valley of Megiddo. It is alluded to by the prophet
Zechariah (12:11) in a proverbial expression derived from the
lamentation for Josiah, who was mortally wounded near this place
(<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 35:22-25" id="h-p14.1" parsed="|2Chr|35|22|35|25" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.35.22-2Chr.35.25">2 Chr. 35:22-25</scripRef>). It has been identified with the modern
Rummaneh, a village “at the foot of the Megiddo hills, in a
notch or valley about an hour and a half south of Tell
Metzellim.”
</def>
<term id="h-p14.2">Hadar</term>
<def id="h-p14.3">
Adod, brave(?). (1.) A son of Ishmael (Gen. 25:15); in 1 Chr. 1:30 written Hadad.
(2.) One of the Edomitish kings (Gen. 36:39) about the time of
Saul. Called also Hadad (1 Chr. 1:50, 51).
It is probable that in these cases Hadar may be an error
simply of transcription for Hadad.
</def>
<term id="h-p17.1">Hadarezer</term>
<def id="h-p17.2">
Adod is his help, the name given to Hadadezer (2 Sam. 8:3-12) in
2 Sam. 10.
</def>
<term id="h-p18.3">Hadashah</term>
<def id="h-p18.4">
New, a city in the valley of Judah (Josh. 15:37).
</def>
<term id="h-p19.2">Hadassah</term>
<def id="h-p19.3">
Myrtle, the Jewish name of Esther (q.v.), Esther 2:7.
</def>
<term id="h-p20.2">Hadattah</term>
<def id="h-p20.3">
New, one of the towns in the extreme south of Judah (Josh. 15:25).
</def>
<term id="h-p21.2">Hades</term>
<def id="h-p21.3">
That which is out of sight, a Greek word used to denote the
state or place of the dead. All the dead alike go into this
place. To be buried, to go down to the grave, to descend into
hades, are equivalent expressions. In the LXX. this word is the
usual rendering of the Hebrew sheol, the common receptacle of

the departed (<scripRef passage="Gen. 42:38" id="h-p22.1" parsed="|Gen|42|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.42.38">Gen. 42:38</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 139:8" id="h-p22.2" parsed="|Ps|139|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.139.8">Ps. 139:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos. 13:14" id="h-p22.3" parsed="|Hos|13|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.13.14">Hos. 13:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 14:9" id="h-p22.4" parsed="|Isa|14|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.14.9">Isa. 14:9</scripRef>).
This term is of comparatively rare occurrence in the Greek New
Testament. Our Lord speaks of Capernaum as being “brought down

to hell” (hades), i.e., simply to the lowest debasement, (<scripRef passage="Matt. 11:23" id="h-p22.5" parsed="|Matt|11|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.11.23">Matt. 11:23</scripRef>). It is contemplated as a kind of kingdom which could
never overturn the foundation of Christ’s kingdom (16:18), i.e.,
Christ’s church can never die.
In Luke 16:23 it is most distinctly associated with the doom
and misery of the lost.
In Acts 2:27-31 Peter quotes the LXX. version of Ps. 16:8-11,
plainly for the purpose of proving our Lord’s resurrection from
the dead. David was left in the place of the dead, and his body
saw corruption. Not so with Christ. According to ancient
prophecy (Ps. 30:3) he was recalled to life.
</def>
<term id="h-p24.4">Hadid</term>
<def id="h-p24.5">
Pointed, a place in the tribe of Benjamin near Lydda, or Lod,

and Ono (<scripRef passage="Ezra 2:33" id="h-p25.1" parsed="|Ezra|2|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2.33">Ezra 2:33</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh. 7:37" id="h-p25.2" parsed="|Neh|7|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.7.37">Neh. 7:37</scripRef>). It is identified with the modern
el-Haditheh, 3 miles east of Lydda.
</def>
<term id="h-p25.3">Hadlai</term>
<def id="h-p25.4">
Resting, an Ephraimite; the father of Amasa, mentioned in 2 Chr. 28:12.
</def>
<term id="h-p26.2">Hadoram</term>
<def id="h-p26.3">
Is exalted. (1.) The son of Tou, king of Hamath, sent by his
father to congratulate David on his victory over Hadarezer, king
of Syria (1 Chr. 18:10; called Joram 2 Sam. 8:10).
(2.) The fifth son of Joktan, the founder of an Arab tribe
(Gen. 10:27; 1 Chr. 1:21).
(3.) One who was “over the tribute;” i.e., “over the levy.” He
was stoned by the Israelites after they had revolted from

Rehoboam (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 10:18" id="h-p29.1" parsed="|2Chr|10|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.10.18">2 Chr. 10:18</scripRef>). Called also Adoram (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 20:24" id="h-p29.2" parsed="|2Sam|20|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.20.24">2 Sam. 20:24</scripRef>) and
Adoniram (1 Kings 4:6).
</def>
<term id="h-p29.4">Hadrach</term>
<def id="h-p29.5">
The name of a country (Zech. 9:1) which cannot be identified.
Rawlinson would identify it with Edessa. He mentions that in the
Assyrian inscriptions it is recorded that “Shalmanezer III. made
two expeditions, the first against Damascus B.C. 773, and the
second against Hadrach B.C. 772; and again that Asshurdanin-il
II. made expeditions against Hadrach in B.C. 765 and 755.”
</def>
<term id="h-p30.2">Haemorrhoids</term>
<def id="h-p30.3">
Or Emerods, bleeding piles known to the ancient Romans as
mariscae, but more probably malignant boils of an infectious and
fatal character. With this loathsome and infectious disease the
men of Ashdod were smitten by the hand of the Lord. This
calamity they attributed to the presence of the ark in their
midst, and therefore they removed it to Gath (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 5:6-8" id="h-p31.1" parsed="|1Sam|5|6|5|8" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.5.6-1Sam.5.8">1 Sam. 5:6-8</scripRef>). But
the same consequences followed from its presence in Gath, and
therefore they had it removed to Ekron, 11 miles distant. The
Ekronites were afflicted with the same dreadful malady, but more
severely; and a panic seizing the people, they demanded that the
ark should be sent back to the land of Israel (9-12; 6:1-9).
</def>
<term id="h-p31.2">Haft</term>
<def id="h-p31.3">
A handle as of a dagger (Judg. 3:22).
</def>
<term id="h-p32.2">Hagar</term>
<def id="h-p32.3">
Flight, or, according to others, stranger, an Egyptian, Sarah’s

handmaid (<scripRef passage="Gen. 16:1" id="h-p33.1" parsed="|Gen|16|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.16.1">Gen. 16:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 21:9" id="h-p33.2" parsed="|Gen|21|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.9">21:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 21:10" id="h-p33.3" parsed="|Gen|21|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.10">10</scripRef>), whom she gave to Abraham (q.v.)
as a secondary wife (16:2). When she was about to become a
mother she fled from the cruelty of her mistress, intending
apparently to return to her relatives in Egypt, through the
desert of Shur, which lay between. Wearied and worn she had
reached the place she distinguished by the name of
Beer-lahai-roi (“the well of the visible God”), where the angel
of the Lord appeared to her. In obedience to the heavenly
visitor she returned to the tent of Abraham, where her son
Ishmael was born, and where she remained (16) till after the
birth of Isaac, the space of fourteen years. Sarah after this
began to vent her dissatisfaction both on Hagar and her child.
Ishmael’s conduct was insulting to Sarah, and she insisted that
he and his mother should be dismissed. This was accordingly

done, although with reluctance on the part of Abraham (<scripRef passage="Gen. 21:14" id="h-p33.4" parsed="|Gen|21|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.14">Gen. 21:14</scripRef>). They wandered out into the wilderness, where Ishmael,
exhausted with his journey and faint from thirst, seemed about
to die. Hagar “lifted up her voice and wept,” and the angel of
the Lord, as before, appeared unto her, and she was comforted
and delivered out of her distresses (Gen. 21:18, 19).
Ishmael afterwards established himself in the wilderness of
Paran, where he married an Egyptian (Gen. 21:20, 21).
“Hagar” allegorically represents the Jewish church (Gal. 4:24), in bondage to the ceremonial law; while “Sarah”
represents the Christian church, which is free.
</def>
<term id="h-p35.2">Hagarene</term>
<def id="h-p35.3">
Or Hagarite. (1.) One of David’s mighty men (1 Chr. 11:38), the
son of a foreigner.
(2.) Used of Jaziz (1 Chr. 27:31), who was over David’s
flocks. “A Hagarite had charge of David’s flocks, and an
Ishmaelite of his herds, because the animals were pastured in
districts where these nomadic people were accustomed to feed
their cattle.”
(3.) In the reign of Saul a great war was waged between the
trans-Jordanic tribes and the Hagarites (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 5" id="h-p38.1" parsed="|1Chr|5|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5">1 Chr. 5</scripRef>), who were
overcome in battle. A great booty was captured by the two tribes
and a half, and they took possession of the land of the
Hagarites.
Subsequently the “Hagarenes,” still residing in the land on
the east of Jordan, entered into a conspiracy against Israel
(comp. Ps. 83:6). They are distinguished from the Ishmaelites.
</def>
<term id="h-p39.2">Haggai</term>
<def id="h-p39.3">
Festive, one of the twelve so-called minor prophets. He was the
first of the three (Zechariah, his contemporary, and Malachi,
who was about one hundred years later, being the other two)
whose ministry belonged to the period of Jewish history which
began after the return from captivity in Babylon. Scarcely
anything is known of his personal history. He may have been one
of the captives taken to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar. He began his
ministry about sixteen years after the Return. The work of
rebuilding the temple had been put a stop to through the
intrigues of the Samaritans. After having been suspended for
fifteen years, the work was resumed through the efforts of
Haggai and Zechariah (<scripRef passage="Ezra 6:14" id="h-p40.1" parsed="|Ezra|6|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.6.14">Ezra 6:14</scripRef>), who by their exhortations
roused the people from their lethargy, and induced them to take
advantage of the favourable opportunity that had arisen in a
change in the policy of the Persian government. (See
DARIUS [2].) Haggai’s prophecies have thus been
characterized:, “There is a ponderous and simple dignity in the
emphatic reiteration addressed alike to every class of the
community, prince, priest, and people, ‘Be strong, be strong, be
strong’ (2:4). ‘Cleave, stick fast, to the work you have to do;’
or again, ‘Consider your ways, consider, consider, consider’
(1:5, 7;2:15, 18). It is the Hebrew phrase for the endeavour,
characteristic of the gifted seers of all times, to compel their
hearers to turn the inside of their hearts outwards to their own
view, to take the mask from off their consciences, to ‘see life
steadily, and to see it wholly.’”, Stanley’s Jewish Church. (See SIGNET.)
</def>
<term id="h-p40.4">Haggai, Book of</term>
<def id="h-p40.5">
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="h-p40.6" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="Hag 0" id="h-p40.7" parsed="|Hag|0|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hag" />
Consists of two brief, comprehensive chapters. The object of the
prophet was generally to urge the people to proceed with the
rebuilding of the temple.
Chapter first comprehends the first address (2-11) and its
effects (12-15). Chapter second contains,
(1.) The second prophecy (1-9), which was delivered a month
after the first.
(2.) The third prophecy (10-19), delivered two months and
three days after the second; and
(3.) The fourth prophecy (20-23), delivered on the same day as
the third.
These discourses are referred to in Ezra 5:1; 6:14; Heb. 12:26. (Comp. Hag. 2:7, 8, 22.)
</def>
<term id="h-p46.7">Haggith</term>
<def id="h-p46.8">
Festive; the dancer, a wife of David and the mother of Adonijah

(<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 3:4" id="h-p47.1" parsed="|2Sam|3|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.3.4">2 Sam. 3:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 1:5" id="h-p47.2" parsed="|1Kgs|1|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.1.5">1 Kings 1:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 1:11" id="h-p47.3" parsed="|1Kgs|1|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.1.11">11</scripRef>; 2:13; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 3:2" id="h-p47.4" parsed="|1Chr|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.3.2">1 Chr. 3:2</scripRef>), who, like
Absalom, was famed for his beauty.
</def>
<term id="h-p47.5">Hagiographa</term>
<def id="h-p47.6">
The holy writings, a term which came early into use in the
Christian church to denote the third division of the Old
Testament scriptures, called by the Jews Kethubim, i.e.,
“Writings.” It consisted of five books, viz., Job, Proverbs, and
Psalms, and the two books of Chronicles. The ancient Jews
classified their sacred books as the Law, the Prophets, and the
Kethubim, or Writings. (See BIBLE.)
In the New Testament (Luke 24:44) we find three corresponding
divisions, viz., the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms.
</def>
<term id="h-p49.2">Hail!</term>
<def id="h-p49.3">
A salutation expressive of a wish for the welfare of the person
addressed; the translation of the Greek Chaire, “Rejoice”
(Luke 1:8). Used in mockery in Matt. 27:29.
</def>
<term id="h-p50.3">Hail</term>
<def id="h-p50.4">
Frozen rain-drops; one of the plagues of Egypt (Ex. 9:23). It is
mentioned by Haggai as a divine judgment (<scripRef passage="Hag. 2:17" id="h-p51.2" parsed="|Hag|2|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hag.2.17">Hag. 2:17</scripRef>). A
hail-storm destroyed the army of the Amorites when they fought
against Joshua (<scripRef passage="Josh. 10:11" id="h-p51.3" parsed="|Josh|10|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.11">Josh. 10:11</scripRef>). Ezekiel represents the wall daubed
with untempered mortar as destroyed by great hail-stones (Ezek. 13:11). (See also 38:22; Rev. 8:7; 11:19; 16:21.)
</def>
<term id="h-p51.8">Hair</term>
<def id="h-p51.9">
(1.) The Egyptians let the hair of their head and beard grow
only when they were in mourning, shaving it off at other times.
“So particular were they on this point that to have neglected it
was a subject of reproach and ridicule; and whenever they
intended to convey the idea of a man of low condition, or a
slovenly person, the artists represented him with a beard.”
Joseph shaved himself before going in to Pharoah (<scripRef passage="Gen. 41:14" id="h-p52.1" parsed="|Gen|41|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.41.14">Gen. 41:14</scripRef>).
The women of Egypt wore their hair long and plaited. Wigs were
worn by priests and laymen to cover the shaven skull, and false
beards were common. The great masses of hair seen in the
portraits and statues of kings and priests are thus altogether
artificial.
(2.) A precisely opposite practice, as regards men, prevailed
among the Assyrians. In Assyrian sculptures the hair always
appears long, and combed closely down upon the head. The beard
also was allowed to grow to its full length.
(3.) Among the Greeks the custom in this respect varied at
different times, as it did also among the Romans. In the time of
the apostle, among the Greeks the men wore short hair, while

that of the women was long (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 11:14" id="h-p54.1" parsed="|1Cor|11|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.11.14">1 Cor. 11:14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 11:15" id="h-p54.2" parsed="|1Cor|11|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.11.15">15</scripRef>). Paul reproves the
Corinthians for falling in with a style of manners which so far
confounded the distinction of the sexes and was hurtful to good

morals. (See, however, <scripRef passage="1 Tim. 2:9" id="h-p54.3" parsed="|1Tim|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.2.9">1 Tim. 2:9</scripRef>, and <scripRef passage="1 Pet. 3:3" id="h-p54.4" parsed="|1Pet|3|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.3.3">1 Pet. 3:3</scripRef>, as regards
women.)
(4.) Among the Hebrews the natural distinction between the
sexes was preserved by the women wearing long hair (<scripRef passage="Luke 7:38" id="h-p55.1" parsed="|Luke|7|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.7.38">Luke 7:38</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="John 11:2" id="h-p55.2" parsed="|John|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.11.2">John 11:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 11:6" id="h-p55.3" parsed="|1Cor|11|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.11.6">1 Cor. 11:6</scripRef>), while the men preserved theirs as a
rule at a moderate length by frequent clipping.
Baldness disqualified any one for the priest’s office (Lev. 21).
Elijah is called a “hairy man” (2 Kings 1:8) from his flowing
locks, or more probably from the shaggy cloak of hair which he
wore. His raiment was of camel’s hair.
Long hair is especially noticed in the description of
Absalom’s person (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 14:26" id="h-p58.1" parsed="|2Sam|14|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.14.26">2 Sam. 14:26</scripRef>); but the wearing of long hair
was unusual, and was only practised as an act of religious

observance by Nazarites (<scripRef passage="Num. 6:5" id="h-p58.2" parsed="|Num|6|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.6.5">Num. 6:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 13:5" id="h-p58.3" parsed="|Judg|13|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.13.5">Judg. 13:5</scripRef>) and others in
token of special mercies (Acts 18:18).
In times of affliction the hair was cut off (Isa. 3:17, 24;

15:2; 22:12; <scripRef passage="Jer. 7:29" id="h-p59.3" parsed="|Jer|7|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.7.29">Jer. 7:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Amos 8:10" id="h-p59.4" parsed="|Amos|8|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.8.10">Amos 8:10</scripRef>). Tearing the hair and letting
it go dishevelled were also tokens of grief (<scripRef passage="Ezra 9:3" id="h-p59.5" parsed="|Ezra|9|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.9.3">Ezra 9:3</scripRef>). “Cutting
off the hair” is a figure of the entire destruction of a people
(<scripRef passage="Isa. 7:20" id="h-p59.6" parsed="|Isa|7|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.7.20">Isa. 7:20</scripRef>). The Hebrews anointed the hair profusely with

fragrant ointments (<scripRef passage="Ruth 3:3" id="h-p59.7" parsed="|Ruth|3|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.3.3">Ruth 3:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 14:2" id="h-p59.8" parsed="|2Sam|14|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.14.2">2 Sam. 14:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 23:5" id="h-p59.9" parsed="|Ps|23|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.23.5">Ps. 23:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 45:7" id="h-p59.10" parsed="|Ps|45|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.45.7">45:7</scripRef>,
etc.), especially in seasons of rejoicing (Matt. 6:17; Luke 7:46).
</def>
<term id="h-p59.13">Hakkoz</term>
The thorn, the head of one of the courses of the priests (1 Chr. 24:10).
</def>
<term id="h-p60.2">Halah</term>
<def id="h-p60.3">
A district of Media to which captive Israelites were transported

by the Assyrian kings (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:6" id="h-p61.1" parsed="|2Kgs|17|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.6">2 Kings 17:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:11" id="h-p61.2" parsed="|2Kgs|18|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.11">18:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 5:26" id="h-p61.3" parsed="|1Chr|5|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5.26">1 Chr. 5:26</scripRef>). It lay
along the banks of the upper Khabur, from its source to its
junction with the Jerujer. Probably the district called by
Ptolemy Chalcitis.
</def>
<term id="h-p61.4">Halak</term>
<def id="h-p61.5">
Smooth; bald, a hill at the southern extremity of Canaan (Josh. 11:17). It is referred to as if it were a landmark in that
direction, being prominent and conspicuous from a distance. It
has by some been identified with the modern Jebel el-Madura, on
the south frontier of Judah, between the south end of the Dead
Sea and the Wady Gaian.
</def>
<term id="h-p62.2">Halhul</term>
<def id="h-p62.3">
Full of hollows, a town in the highlands of Judah (Josh. 15:58).
It is now a small village of the same name, and is situated
about 5 miles north-east of Hebron on the way to Jerusalem.
There is an old Jewish tradition that Gad, David’s seer (2 Sam. 24:11), was buried here.
</def>
<term id="h-p63.3">Hall</term>
<def id="h-p63.4">
(Gr. aule, Luke 22:55; R.V., “court”), the open court or
quadrangle belonging to the high priest’s house. In <scripRef passage="Matt. 26:69" id="h-p64.2" parsed="|Matt|26|69|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.69">Matt. 26:69</scripRef>
and <scripRef passage="Mark 14:66" id="h-p64.3" parsed="|Mark|14|66|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.14.66">Mark 14:66</scripRef> this word is incorrectly rendered “palace” in the
Authorized Version, but correctly “court” in the Revised

Version. In <scripRef passage="John 10:1" id="h-p64.4" parsed="|John|10|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.10.1">John 10:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="John 10:16" id="h-p64.5" parsed="|John|10|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.10.16">16</scripRef> it means a “sheep-fold.” In <scripRef passage="Matt. 27:27" id="h-p64.6" parsed="|Matt|27|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.27">Matt. 27:27</scripRef>
and <scripRef passage="Mark 15:16" id="h-p64.7" parsed="|Mark|15|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.15.16">Mark 15:16</scripRef> (A.V., “common hall;” R.V., “palace”) it refers
to the proetorium or residence of the Roman governor at
Jerusalem. The “porch” in <scripRef passage="Matt. 26:71" id="h-p64.8" parsed="|Matt|26|71|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.71">Matt. 26:71</scripRef> is the entrance-hall or
passage leading into the central court, which is open to the
sky.
</def>
<term id="h-p64.9">Hallel</term>
Praise, the name given to the group of Psalms 113-118, which are
preeminently psalms of praise. It is called “The Egyptian
Hallel,” because it was chanted in the temple whilst the
Passover lambs were being slain. It was chanted also on other
festival occasions, as at Pentecost, the feast of Tabernacles,
and the feast of Dedication. The Levites, standing before the
altar, chanted it verse by verse, the people responding by
repeating the verses or by intoned hallelujahs. It was also
chanted in private families at the feast of Passover. This was
probably the hymn which our Saviour and his disciples sung at
the conclusion of the Passover supper kept by them in the upper
room at Jerusalem (Matt. 26:30; Mark 14:26).
There is also another group called “The Great Hallel,”
comprehending <scripRef passage="Psalms 118" id="h-p66.1" parsed="|Ps|118|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.118">Psalms 118</scripRef>-136, which was recited on the first
evening at the Passover supper and on occasions of great joy.
</def>
<term id="h-p66.2">Hallelujah</term>
<def id="h-p66.3">
Praise ye Jehovah, frequently rendered “Praise ye the LORD,”
stands at the beginning of ten of the psalms (106, 111-113, 135,
146-150), hence called “hallelujah psalms.” From its frequent
occurrence it grew into a formula of praise. The Greek form of
the word (alleluia) is found in Rev. 19:1, 3, 4, 6.
</def>
<term id="h-p67.5">Hallow</term>
<def id="h-p67.6">
To render sacred, to consecrate (Ex. 28:38; 29:1). This word is
from the Saxon, and properly means “to make holy.” The name of
God is “hallowed”, i.e., is reverenced as holy (Matt. 6:9).
</def>
<term id="h-p68.4">Halt</term>
<def id="h-p68.5">
Lame on the feet (Gen. 32:31; Ps. 38:17). To “halt between two
opinions” (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 18:21" id="h-p69.3" parsed="|1Kgs|18|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.18.21">1 Kings 18:21</scripRef>) is supposed by some to be an
expression used in “allusion to birds, which hop from spray to
spray, forwards and backwards.” The LXX. render the expression
“How long go ye lame on both knees?” The Hebrew verb rendered
“halt” is used of the irregular dance (“leaped upon”) around the
altar (ver. 26). It indicates a lame, uncertain gait, going now
in one direction, now in another, in the frenzy of wild leaping.
</def>
<term id="h-p69.4">Ham</term>
<def id="h-p69.5">
Warm, hot, and hence the south; also an Egyptian word meaning
“black”, the youngest son of Noah (<scripRef passage="Gen. 5:32" id="h-p70.1" parsed="|Gen|5|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.5.32">Gen. 5:32</scripRef>; comp. 9:22, 24).
The curse pronounced by Noah against Ham, properly against
Canaan his fourth son, was accomplished when the Jews
subsequently exterminated the Canaanites.
One of the most important facts recorded in Gen. 10 is the
foundation of the earliest monarchy in Babylonia by Nimrod the
grandson of Ham (6, 8, 10). The primitive Babylonian empire was
thus Hamitic, and of a cognate race with the primitive
inhabitants of Arabia and of Ethiopia. (See ACCAD.)
The race of Ham were the most energetic of all the descendants
of Noah in the early times of the post-diluvian world.
</def>
<term id="h-p72.1">Haman</term>
<def id="h-p72.2">
(of Persian origin), magnificent, the name of the vizier (i.e.,
the prime minister) of the Persian king Ahasuerus (<scripRef passage="Esther 3:1" id="h-p73.1" parsed="|Esth|3|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Esth.3.1">Esther 3:1</scripRef>,
etc.). He is called an “Agagite,” which seems to denote that he
was descended from the royal family of the Amalekites, the
bitterest enemies of the Jews, as Agag was one of the titles of
the Amalekite kings. He or his parents were brought to Persia as
captives taken in war. He was hanged on the gallows which he had
erected for Mordecai the Jew (Esther 7:10). (See ESTHER.)
</def>
<term id="h-p73.4">Hamath</term>
<def id="h-p73.5">
Fortress, the capital of one of the kingdoms of Upper Syria of
the same name, on the Orontes, in the valley of Lebanon, at the

northern boundary of Palestine (<scripRef passage="Num. 13:21" id="h-p74.1" parsed="|Num|13|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.13.21">Num. 13:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 34:8" id="h-p74.2" parsed="|Num|34|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.34.8">34:8</scripRef>), at the foot

of Hermon (<scripRef passage="Josh. 13:5" id="h-p74.3" parsed="|Josh|13|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.5">Josh. 13:5</scripRef>) towards Damascus (<scripRef passage="Zech. 9:2" id="h-p74.4" parsed="|Zech|9|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Zech.9.2">Zech. 9:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 49:23" id="h-p74.5" parsed="|Jer|49|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.49.23">Jer. 49:23</scripRef>).
It is called “Hamath the great” in <scripRef passage="Amos 6:2" id="h-p74.6" parsed="|Amos|6|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.6.2">Amos 6:2</scripRef>, and “Hamath-zobah”
in 2 Chr. 8:3.
Hamath, now Hamah, had an Aramaean population, but Hittite
monuments discovered there show that it must have been at one
time occupied by the Hittites. It was among the conquests of the
Pharaoh Thothmes III. Its king, Tou or Toi, made alliance with
David (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 8:10" id="h-p75.1" parsed="|2Sam|8|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.8.10">2 Sam. 8:10</scripRef>), and in B.C. 740 Azariah formed a league
with it against Assyria. It was, however, conquered by the
Assyrians, and its nineteen districts placed under Assyrian
governors. In B.C. 720 it revolted under a certain Yahu-bihdi,
whose name, compounded with that of the God of Israel (Yahu),
perhaps shows that he was of Jewish origin. But the revolt was
suppressed, and the people of Hamath were transported to Samaria

(<scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:24" id="h-p75.2" parsed="|2Kgs|17|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.24">2 Kings 17:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:30" id="h-p75.3" parsed="|2Kgs|17|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.30">30</scripRef>), where they continued to worship their god
Ashima. Hamah is beautifully situated on the Orontes, 32 miles
north of Emesa, and 36 south of the ruins of Assamea.
The kingdom of Hamath comprehended the great plain lying on
both banks of the Orontes from the fountain near Riblah to
Assamea on the north, and from Lebanon on the west to the desert
on the east. The “entrance of Hamath” (<scripRef passage="Num. 34:8" id="h-p76.1" parsed="|Num|34|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.34.8">Num. 34:8</scripRef>), which was the
north boundary of Palestine, led from the west between the north
end of Lebanon and the Nusairiyeh mountains.
</def>
<term id="h-p76.2">Hamath-zobah</term>
<def id="h-p76.3">
Fortress of Zobah, (2 Chr. 8:3) is supposed by some to be a
different place from the foregoing; but this is quite uncertain.
</def>
<term id="h-p77.2">Hammath</term>
<def id="h-p77.3">
Warm springs, one of the “fenced cities” of Naphtali (Josh. 19:35). It is identified with the warm baths (the heat of the
water ranging from 136 degrees to 144 degrees) still found on
the shore a little to the south of Tiberias under the name of
Hummam Tabariyeh (“Bath of Tiberias”).
</def>
<term id="h-p78.2">Hammedatha</term>
<def id="h-p78.3">
Father of Haman, designated usually “the Agagite” (Esther 3:1, 10; 8:5).
</def>
<term id="h-p79.4">Hammelech</term>
<def id="h-p79.5">
The king’s, the father of Jerahmeel, mentioned in Jer. 36:26.
Some take this word as a common noun, “the king”, and understand
that Jerahmeel was Jehoiakim’s son. Probably, however, it is to
be taken as a proper name.
</def>
<term id="h-p80.2">Hammer</term>
<def id="h-p80.3">
(1.) Heb. pattish, used by gold-beaters (Isa. 41:7) and by

quarry-men (<scripRef passage="Jer. 23:29" id="h-p81.2" parsed="|Jer|23|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.23.29">Jer. 23:29</scripRef>). Metaphorically of Babylon (<scripRef passage="Jer. 50:23" id="h-p81.3" parsed="|Jer|50|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.50.23">Jer. 50:23</scripRef>)
or Nebuchadnezzar.
(2.) Heb. makabah, a stone-cutter’s mallet (1 Kings 6:7), or
of any workman (Judg. 4:21; Isa. 44:12).
(3.) Heb. halmuth, a poetical word for a workman’s hammer,
found only in <scripRef passage="Judg. 5:26" id="h-p83.1" parsed="|Judg|5|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.5.26">Judg. 5:26</scripRef>, where it denotes the mallet with which
the pins of the tent of the nomad are driven into the ground.
(4.) Heb. mappets, rendered “battle-axe” in Jer. 51:20. This
was properly a “mace,” which is thus described by Rawlinson:
“The Assyrian mace was a short, thin weapon, and must either
have been made of a very tough wood or (and this is more
probable) of metal. It had an ornamented head, which was
sometimes very beautifully modelled, and generally a strap or
string at the lower end by which it could be grasped with
greater firmness.”
</def>
<term id="h-p84.2">Hammoleketh</term>
<def id="h-p84.3">
The queen, the daughter of Machir and sister of Gilead (1 Chr. 7:17, 18). Abiezer was one of her three children.
</def>
<term id="h-p85.3">Hammon</term>
<def id="h-p85.4">
Warm springs. (1.) A town in the tribe of Asher, near Zidon
(Josh. 19:28), identified with ‘Ain Hamul.
(2.) A Levitical city of Naphtali (1 Chr. 6:76).
</def>
<term id="h-p87.2">Hammoth-dor</term>
<def id="h-p87.3">
Warm springs, a Levitical city of Naphtali (Josh. 21:32);
probably Hammath in 19:35.
</def>
<term id="h-p88.2">Hamon</term>
<def id="h-p88.3">
See BAAL-HAMON.
</def>
<term id="h-p89.2">Hamonah</term>
<def id="h-p89.3">
Multitude, a name figuratively assigned to the place in which
the slaughter and burial of the forces of Gog were to take place
(Ezek. 39:16).
</def>
<term id="h-p90.2">Hamon-gog</term>
<def id="h-p90.3">
Multitude of Gog, the name of the valley in which the

slaughtered forces of Gog are to be buried (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 39:11" id="h-p91.1" parsed="|Ezek|39|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.39.11">Ezek. 39:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 39:15" id="h-p91.2" parsed="|Ezek|39|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.39.15">15</scripRef>),
“the valley of the passengers on the east of the sea.”
</def>
<term id="h-p91.3">Hamor</term>
<def id="h-p91.4">
He-ass, a Hivite from whom Jacob purchased the plot of ground in
which Joseph was afterwards buried (<scripRef passage="Gen. 33:19" id="h-p92.1" parsed="|Gen|33|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.33.19">Gen. 33:19</scripRef>). He is called
“Emmor” in <scripRef passage="Acts 7:16" id="h-p92.2" parsed="|Acts|7|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.7.16">Acts 7:16</scripRef>. His son Shechem founded the city of that
name which Simeon and Levi destroyed because of his crime in the
matter of Dinah, Jacob’s daughter (<scripRef passage="Gen. 34:20" id="h-p92.3" parsed="|Gen|34|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.34.20">Gen. 34:20</scripRef>). Hamor and
Shechem were also slain (ver. 26).
</def>
<term id="h-p92.4">Hamul</term>
<def id="h-p92.5">
Spared, one of the sons of Pharez, son of Judah (1 Chr. 2:5).
His descendants are called Hamulites (Num. 26:21).
</def>
<term id="h-p93.3">Hamutal</term>
<def id="h-p93.4">
Kinsman of the dew, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah, wife of
king Josiah, and mother of king Jehoahaz (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 23:31" id="h-p94.1" parsed="|2Kgs|23|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.23.31">2 Kings 23:31</scripRef>), also
of king Zedekiah (2 Kings 24:18).
</def>
<term id="h-p94.3">Hanameel</term>
<def id="h-p94.4">
Whom God has graciously given, the cousin of Jeremiah, to whom
he sold the field he possessed in Anathoth, before the siege of
Jerusalem (Jer. 32:6-12).
</def>
<term id="h-p95.2">Hanan</term>
<def id="h-p95.3">
Merciful. (1.) A Benjamite (1 Chr. 8:23). (2.) One of David’s

heroes (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 11:43" id="h-p96.2" parsed="|1Chr|11|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.11.43">1 Chr. 11:43</scripRef>). (3.) <scripRef passage="Jer. 35:4" id="h-p96.3" parsed="|Jer|35|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.35.4">Jer. 35:4</scripRef>. (4.) A descendant of Saul

(<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 8:38" id="h-p96.4" parsed="|1Chr|8|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.8.38">1 Chr. 8:38</scripRef>). (5.) One of the Nethinim (<scripRef passage="Ezra 2:46" id="h-p96.5" parsed="|Ezra|2|46|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.2.46">Ezra 2:46</scripRef>). (6.) One of
the Levites who assisted Ezra (<scripRef passage="Neh. 8:7" id="h-p96.6" parsed="|Neh|8|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.8.7">Neh. 8:7</scripRef>). (7.) One of the chiefs
who subscribed the covenant (Neh. 10:22).
</def>
<term id="h-p96.8">Hananeel</term>
<def id="h-p96.9">
God has graciously given, a tower in the wall of Jerusalem (Neh. 3:1; 12:39). It is mentioned also in Jer. 31:38; Zech. 14:10.
</def>
<term id="h-p97.5">Hanani</term>
<def id="h-p97.6">
God has gratified me, or is gracious. (1.) One of the sons of

Heman (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 25:4" id="h-p98.1" parsed="|1Chr|25|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.25.4">1 Chr. 25:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 25:25" id="h-p98.2" parsed="|1Chr|25|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.25.25">25</scripRef>). (2.) A prophet who was sent to rebuke
king Asa for entering into a league with Benhadad I., king of
Syria, against Judah (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 16:1-10" id="h-p98.3" parsed="|2Chr|16|1|16|10" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.16.1-2Chr.16.10">2 Chr. 16:1-10</scripRef>). He was probably the
father of the prophet Jehu (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 16:7" id="h-p98.4" parsed="|1Kgs|16|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.16.7">1 Kings 16:7</scripRef>). (3.) Probably a

brother of Nehemiah (<scripRef passage="Neh. 1:2" id="h-p98.5" parsed="|Neh|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.1.2">Neh. 1:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh 7:2" id="h-p98.6" parsed="|Neh|7|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.7.2">7:2</scripRef>), who reported to him the
melancholy condition of Jerusalem. Nehemiah afterwards appointed
him to have charge of the city gates.
</def>
<term id="h-p98.7">Hananiah</term>
<def id="h-p98.8">
Jehovah has given. (1.) A chief of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chr. 8:24). (2.) One of the sons of Heman (1 Chr. 25:4, 23). (3.) One
of Uzziah’s military officers (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 26:11" id="h-p99.4" parsed="|2Chr|26|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.26.11">2 Chr. 26:11</scripRef>). (4.) Grandfather

of the captain who arrested Jeremiah (<scripRef passage="Jer. 37:13" id="h-p99.5" parsed="|Jer|37|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.37.13">Jer. 37:13</scripRef>). (5.) <scripRef passage="Jer. 36:12" id="h-p99.6" parsed="|Jer|36|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.36.12">Jer. 36:12</scripRef>. (6.) <scripRef passage="Neh. 10:23" id="h-p99.7" parsed="|Neh|10|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.10.23">Neh. 10:23</scripRef>. (7.) Shadrach, one of the “three Hebrew

children” (<scripRef passage="Dan. 1" id="h-p99.8" parsed="|Dan|1|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.1">Dan. 1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Dan 6:7" id="h-p99.9" parsed="|Dan|6|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.6.7">6:7</scripRef>). (8.) Son of Zerubbabel (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 3:19" id="h-p99.10" parsed="|1Chr|3|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.3.19">1 Chr. 3:19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 3:21" id="h-p99.11" parsed="|1Chr|3|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.3.21">21</scripRef>). (9.) <scripRef passage="Ezra 10:28" id="h-p99.12" parsed="|Ezra|10|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.10.28">Ezra 10:28</scripRef>. (10.) The “ruler of the palace; he was a

faithful man, and feared God above many” (<scripRef passage="Neh. 7:2" id="h-p99.13" parsed="|Neh|7|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.7.2">Neh. 7:2</scripRef>). (11.) <scripRef passage="Neh. 3:8" id="h-p99.14" parsed="|Neh|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.3.8">Neh. 3:8</scripRef>. (12.) <scripRef passage="Neh. 3:30" id="h-p99.15" parsed="|Neh|3|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.3.30">Neh. 3:30</scripRef> (13.) A priest, son of Jeremiah (<scripRef passage="Neh. 12:12" id="h-p99.16" parsed="|Neh|12|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.12.12">Neh. 12:12</scripRef>). (14.) A false prophet contemporary with Jeremiah (28:3,
</def>
<term id="h-p99.17">Hand</term>
Called by Galen “the instrument of instruments.” It is the

symbol of human action (<scripRef passage="Ps. 9:16" id="h-p100.1" parsed="|Ps|9|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.9.16">Ps. 9:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 9:30" id="h-p100.2" parsed="|Job|9|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.9.30">Job 9:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 1:15" id="h-p100.3" parsed="|Isa|1|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.15">Isa. 1:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Tim. 2:8" id="h-p100.4" parsed="|1Tim|2|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.2.8">1 Tim. 2:8</scripRef>). Washing the hands was a symbol of innocence (<scripRef passage="Ps. 26:6" id="h-p100.5" parsed="|Ps|26|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.26.6">Ps. 26:6</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Ps 73:13" id="h-p100.6" parsed="|Ps|73|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.73.13">73:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 27:24" id="h-p100.7" parsed="|Matt|27|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.24">Matt. 27:24</scripRef>), also of sanctification (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 6:11" id="h-p100.8" parsed="|1Cor|6|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.6.11">1 Cor. 6:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 51:16" id="h-p100.9" parsed="|Isa|51|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.51.16">Isa. 51:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 24:3" id="h-p100.10" parsed="|Ps|24|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.24.3">Ps. 24:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps. 24:4" id="h-p100.11" parsed="|Ps|24|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.24.4">4</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="Ps. 77:2" id="h-p100.12" parsed="|Ps|77|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.77.2">Ps. 77:2</scripRef> the correct rendering is, as in
the Revised Version, “My hand was stretched out,” etc., instead
of, as in the Authorized Version, “My sore ran in the night,”
etc.
The right hand denoted the south, and the left the north (Job 23:9; 1 Sam. 23:19). To give the right hand was a pledge of

fidelity (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 10:15" id="h-p101.3" parsed="|2Kgs|10|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.10.15">2 Kings 10:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezra 10:19" id="h-p101.4" parsed="|Ezra|10|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.10.19">Ezra 10:19</scripRef>); also of submission to the

victors (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 17:18" id="h-p101.5" parsed="|Ezek|17|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.17.18">Ezek. 17:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 50:15" id="h-p101.6" parsed="|Jer|50|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.50.15">Jer. 50:15</scripRef>). The right hand was lifted up
in taking an oath (<scripRef passage="Gen. 14:22" id="h-p101.7" parsed="|Gen|14|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.22">Gen. 14:22</scripRef>, etc.). The hand is frequently
mentioned, particularly the right hand, as a symbol of power and

strength (<scripRef passage="Ps. 60:5" id="h-p101.8" parsed="|Ps|60|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.60.5">Ps. 60:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 28:2" id="h-p101.9" parsed="|Isa|28|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.28.2">Isa. 28:2</scripRef>). To kiss the hand is an act of

homage (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 19:18" id="h-p101.10" parsed="|1Kgs|19|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.19.18">1 Kings 19:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 31:27" id="h-p101.11" parsed="|Job|31|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.31.27">Job 31:27</scripRef>), and to pour water on one’s
hands is to serve him (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 3:11" id="h-p101.12" parsed="|2Kgs|3|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.3.11">2 Kings 3:11</scripRef>). The hand of God is the

symbol of his power: its being upon one denotes favour (<scripRef passage="Ezra 7:6" id="h-p101.13" parsed="|Ezra|7|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.7.6">Ezra 7:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezra 7:28" id="h-p101.14" parsed="|Ezra|7|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.7.28">28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 1:25" id="h-p101.15" parsed="|Isa|1|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.25">Isa. 1:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 1:66" id="h-p101.16" parsed="|Luke|1|66|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.66">Luke 1:66</scripRef>, etc.) or punishment (<scripRef passage="Ex. 9:3" id="h-p101.17" parsed="|Exod|9|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.9.3">Ex. 9:3</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Judg. 2:15" id="h-p101.18" parsed="|Judg|2|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.2.15">Judg. 2:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 13:11" id="h-p101.19" parsed="|Acts|13|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.13.11">Acts 13:11</scripRef>, etc.). A position at the right hand was
regarded as the chief place of honour and power (<scripRef passage="Ps. 45:9" id="h-p101.20" parsed="|Ps|45|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.45.9">Ps. 45:9</scripRef>;
80:17; 110:1; Matt. 26:64).
</def>
<term id="h-p101.24">Handbreadth</term>
A measure of four fingers, equal to about four inches (Ex. 25:25; 37:12; Ps. 39:5, etc.).
</def>
<term id="h-p102.4">Handkerchief</term>
Only once in Authorized Version (Acts 19:12). The Greek word
(sudarion) so rendered means properly “a sweat-cloth.” It is
rendered “napkin” in John 11:44; 20:7; Luke 19:20.
</def>
<term id="h-p103.5">Handmaid</term>
Servant (Gen. 16:1; Ruth 3:9; Luke 1:48). It is probable that
Hagar was Sarah’s personal attendant while she was in the house
of Pharaoh, and was among those maid-servants whom Abram had
brought from Egypt.
</def>
<term id="h-p104.4">Handwriting</term>
(Col. 2:14). The “blotting out the handwriting” is the removal
by the grace of the gospel of the condemnation of the law which
we had broken.
</def>
<term id="h-p105.2">Hanes</term>
A place in Egypt mentioned only in Isa. 30:4 in connection with
