a reproof given to the Jews for trusting in Egypt. It was
considered the same as Tahpanhes, a fortified town on the
eastern frontier, but has been also identified as
Ahnas-el-Medeeneh, 70 miles from Cairo.
</def>
<term id="h-p106.2">Hanging</term>
(as a punishment), a mark of infamy inflicted on the dead bodies
of criminals (<scripRef passage="Deut. 21:23" id="h-p107.1" parsed="|Deut|21|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.21.23">Deut. 21:23</scripRef>) rather than our modern mode of

punishment. Criminals were first strangled and then hanged (<scripRef passage="Nu. 25:4" id="h-p107.2" parsed="|Num|25|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.25.4">Nu. 25:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 21:22" id="h-p107.3" parsed="|Deut|21|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.21.22">Deut. 21:22</scripRef>). (See <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:6" id="h-p107.4" parsed="|2Sam|21|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.6">2 Sam. 21:6</scripRef> for the practice of the
Gibeonites.)
Hanging (as a curtain). (1.) Heb. masak, (a) before the
entrance to the court of the tabernacle (<scripRef passage="Ex. 35:17" id="h-p108.1" parsed="|Exod|35|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.35.17">Ex. 35:17</scripRef>); (b) before
the door of the tabernacle (26:36, 37); (c) before the entrance
to the most holy place, called “the veil of the covering”
(35:12; 39:34), as the word properly means.
(2.) Heb. kelaim, tapestry covering the walls of the

tabernacle (<scripRef passage="Ex. 27:9" id="h-p109.1" parsed="|Exod|27|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.27.9">Ex. 27:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 35:17" id="h-p109.2" parsed="|Exod|35|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.35.17">35:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 3:26" id="h-p109.3" parsed="|Num|3|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.3.26">Num. 3:26</scripRef>) to the half of the
height of the wall (<scripRef passage="Ex. 27:18" id="h-p109.4" parsed="|Exod|27|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.27.18">Ex. 27:18</scripRef>; comp. 26:16). These hangings were
fastened to pillars.
(3.) Heb. bottim (2 Kings 23:7), “hangings for the grove”
(R.V., “for the Asherah”); marg., instead of “hangings,” has
“tents” or “houses.” Such curtained structures for idolatrous
worship are also alluded to in Ezek. 16:16.
</def>
<term id="h-p110.3">Hannah</term>
Favour, grace, one of the wives of Elkanah the Levite, and the

mother of Samuel (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 1" id="h-p111.1" parsed="|1Sam|1|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.1">1 Sam. 1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 2" id="h-p111.2" parsed="|1Sam|2|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.2">2</scripRef>). Her home was at
Ramathaim-zophim, whence she was wont every year to go to
Shiloh, where the tabernacle had been pitched by Joshua, to
attend the offering of sacrifices there according to the law

(<scripRef passage="Ex. 23:15" id="h-p111.3" parsed="|Exod|23|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.15">Ex. 23:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 34:18" id="h-p111.4" parsed="|Exod|34|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.34.18">34:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 16:16" id="h-p111.5" parsed="|Deut|16|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.16.16">Deut. 16:16</scripRef>), probably at the feast of the
Passover (comp. <scripRef passage="Ex. 13:10" id="h-p111.6" parsed="|Exod|13|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.13.10">Ex. 13:10</scripRef>). On occasion of one of these “yearly”
visits, being grieved by reason of Peninnah’s conduct toward
her, she went forth alone, and kneeling before the Lord at the
sanctuary she prayed inaudibly. Eli the high priest, who sat at
the entrance to the holy place, observed her, and
misunderstanding her character he harshly condemned her conduct
(<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 1:14-16" id="h-p111.7" parsed="|1Sam|1|14|1|16" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.1.14-1Sam.1.16">1 Sam. 1:14-16</scripRef>). After hearing her explanation he retracted his
injurious charge and said to her, “Go in peace: and the God of
Israel grant thee thy petition.” Perhaps the story of the wife
of Manoah was not unknown to her. Thereafter Elkanah and his
family retired to their quiet home, and there, before another
Passover, Hannah gave birth to a son, whom, in grateful memory
of the Lord’s goodness, she called Samuel, i.e., “heard of God.”
After the child was weaned (probably in his third year) she
brought him to Shiloh into the house of the Lord, and said to
Eli the aged priest, “Oh my lord, I am the woman that stood by
thee here, praying unto the Lord. For this child I prayed; and
the Lord hath given me my petition which I asked of him:
therefore I also have granted him to the Lord; as long as he

liveth he is granted to the Lord” (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 1:27" id="h-p111.8" parsed="|1Sam|1|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.1.27">1 Sam. 1:27</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 1:28" id="h-p111.9" parsed="|1Sam|1|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.1.28">28</scripRef>, R.V.). Her
gladness of heart then found vent in that remarkable prophetic
song (2:1-10; comp. <scripRef passage="Luke 1:46-55" id="h-p111.10" parsed="|Luke|1|46|1|55" osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.46-Luke.1.55">Luke 1:46-55</scripRef>) which contains the first
designation of the Messiah under that name (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 2:10" id="h-p111.11" parsed="|1Sam|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.2.10">1 Sam. 2:10</scripRef>,
“Annointed” = “Messiah”). And so Samuel and his parents parted.
He was left at Shiloh to minister “before the Lord.” And each
year, when they came up to Shiloh, Hannah brought to her absent
child “a little coat” (Heb. meil, a term used to denote the
“robe” of the ephod worn by the high priest, <scripRef passage="Ex. 28:31" id="h-p111.12" parsed="|Exod|28|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.31">Ex. 28:31</scripRef>), a
priestly robe, a long upper tunic (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 15:27" id="h-p111.13" parsed="|1Chr|15|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.15.27">1 Chr. 15:27</scripRef>), in which to

minister in the tabernacle (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 2:19" id="h-p111.14" parsed="|1Sam|2|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.2.19">1 Sam. 2:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 15:27" id="h-p111.15" parsed="|1Sam|15|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.15.27">15:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 2:12" id="h-p111.16" parsed="|Job|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.2.12">Job 2:12</scripRef>). “And
the child Samuel grew before the Lord.” After Samuel, Hannah had
three sons and two daughters.
</def>
<term id="h-p111.17">Hanniel</term>
Grace of God. (1.) A chief of the tribe of Manasseh (Num. 34:23). (2.) A chief of the tribe of Asher (1 Chr. 7:39).
</def>
<term id="h-p112.3">Hanun</term>
Graciously given. (1.) The son and successor of Nahash, king of
Moab. David’s messengers, sent on an embassy of condolence to
him to Rabbah Ammon, his capital, were so grossly insulted that
he proclaimed war against Hanun. David’s army, under the command
of Joab, forthwith crossed the Jordan, and gained a complete
victory over the Moabites and their allies (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 10:1-14" id="h-p113.1" parsed="|2Sam|10|1|10|14" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.10.1-2Sam.10.14">2 Sam. 10:1-14</scripRef>) at
Medeba (q.v.).
(2.) Neh. 3:13. (3.) 3:30.
</def>
<term id="h-p114.2">Hara</term>
Mountainous land, a province of Assyria (1 Chr. 5:26), between
the Tigris and the Euphrates, along the banks of the Khabur, to
which some of the Israelite captives were carried. It has not
been identified. Some think the word a variation of Haran.
</def>
<term id="h-p115.2">Haradah</term>
Fright; fear, the twenty-fifth station of the Israelites in
their wanderings (Num. 33:24).
</def>
<term id="h-p116.2">Haran</term>
(1.) Heb. haran; i.e., “mountaineer.” The eldest son of Terah,
brother of Abraham and Nahor, and father of Lot, Milcah, and
Iscah. He died before his father (<scripRef passage="Gen. 11:27" id="h-p117.1" parsed="|Gen|11|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.11.27">Gen. 11:27</scripRef>), in Ur of the
Chaldees.
(2.) Heb. haran, i.e., “parched;” or probably from the
Accadian charana, meaning “a road.” A celebrated city of Western
Asia, now Harran, where Abram remained, after he left Ur of the

Chaldees, till his father Terah died (<scripRef passage="Gen. 11:31" id="h-p118.1" parsed="|Gen|11|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.11.31">Gen. 11:31</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 11:32" id="h-p118.2" parsed="|Gen|11|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.11.32">32</scripRef>), when he
continued his journey into the land of Canaan. It is called
“Charran” in the LXX. and in <scripRef passage="Acts 7:2" id="h-p118.3" parsed="|Acts|7|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.7.2">Acts 7:2</scripRef>. It is called the “city of
Nahor” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 24:10" id="h-p118.4" parsed="|Gen|24|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.10">Gen. 24:10</scripRef>), and Jacob resided here with Laban (30:43).
It stood on the river Belik, an affluent of the Euphrates, about
70 miles above where it joins that river in Upper Mesopotamia or
Padan-aram, and about 600 miles northwest of Ur in a direct
line. It was on the caravan route between the east and west. It
is afterwards mentioned among the towns taken by the king of

Assyria (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 19:12" id="h-p118.5" parsed="|2Kgs|19|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.19.12">2 Kings 19:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 37:12" id="h-p118.6" parsed="|Isa|37|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.37.12">Isa. 37:12</scripRef>). It was known to the Greeks
and Romans under the name Carrhae.
(3.) The son of Caleb of Judah (1 Chr. 2:46) by his concubine
Ephah.
</def>
<term id="h-p119.2">Harbona</term>
(a Persian word meaning “ass-driver”), one of the seven eunuchs
or chamberlains of king Ahasuerus (Esther 1:10; 7:9).
</def>
<term id="h-p120.3">Hare</term>
(Heb. ‘arnebeth) was prohibited as food according to the Mosaic

law (<scripRef passage="Lev. 11:6" id="h-p121.1" parsed="|Lev|11|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.11.6">Lev. 11:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 14:7" id="h-p121.2" parsed="|Deut|14|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.14.7">Deut. 14:7</scripRef>), “because he cheweth the cud, but
divideth not the hoof.” The habit of this animal is to grind its
teeth and move its jaw as if it actually chewed the cud. But,
like the cony (q.v.), it is not a ruminant with four stomachs,
but a rodent like the squirrel, rat, etc. Moses speaks of it
according to appearance. It is interdicted because, though
apparently chewing the cud, it did not divide the hoof.
There are two species in Syria, (1) the Lepus Syriacus or
Syrian hare, which is like the English hare; and (2) the Lepus
Sinaiticus, or hare of the desert. No rabbits are found in
Syria.
</def>
<term id="h-p122.1">Hareth</term>
Thicket, a wood in the mountains of Judah where David hid when
pursued by Saul (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 22:5" id="h-p123.1" parsed="|1Sam|22|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.22.5">1 Sam. 22:5</scripRef>). It was possibly while he was here

that the memorable incident narrated in <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 23:14-17" id="h-p123.2" parsed="|2Sam|23|14|23|17" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.23.14-2Sam.23.17">2 Sam. 23:14-17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 11:16-19" id="h-p123.3" parsed="|1Chr|11|16|11|19" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.11.16-1Chr.11.19">1 Chr. 11:16-19</scripRef> occurred. This place has not been identified, but
perhaps it may be the modern Kharas, on the borders of the chain
of mountains some 3 miles east of Keilah.
</def>
<term id="h-p123.4">Harhaiah</term>
Zeal of Jehovah, (Neh. 3:8) “of the goldsmiths,” one whose son
helped to repair the wall of Jerusalem.
</def>
<term id="h-p124.2">Harhur</term>
Fever, one of the Nethinim (Ezra 2:51).
</def>
<term id="h-p125.2">Harim</term>
Flat-nosed. (1.) The head of the second course of priests (1 Chr. 24:8). (2.) Ezra 2:32, 39; Neh. 7:35, 42. (3.) Neh. 3:11.
</def>
<term id="h-p126.7">Hariph</term>
Autumnal rain. (1.) Neh. 7:24. (2.) 10:19.
</def>
<term id="h-p127.2">Harlot</term>
(1.) Heb. zonah (Gen. 34:31; 38:15). In verses 21, 22 the Hebrew
word used in kedeshah, i.e., a woman consecrated or devoted to
prostitution in connection with the abominable worship of
Asherah or Astarte, the Syrian Venus. This word is also used in

<scripRef passage="Deut. 23:17" id="h-p128.3" parsed="|Deut|23|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.23.17">Deut. 23:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hos. 4:14" id="h-p128.4" parsed="|Hos|4|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.4.14">Hos. 4:14</scripRef>. Thus Tamar sat by the wayside as a
consecrated kedeshah.
It has been attempted to show that Rahab, usually called a

“harlot” (<scripRef passage="Josh. 2:1" id="h-p129.1" parsed="|Josh|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.2.1">Josh. 2:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 6:17" id="h-p129.2" parsed="|Josh|6|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.6.17">6:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 11:31" id="h-p129.3" parsed="|Heb|11|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.11.31">Heb. 11:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="James 2:25" id="h-p129.4" parsed="|Jas|2|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jas.2.25">James 2:25</scripRef>), was only an
innkeeper. This interpretation, however, cannot be maintained.
Jephthah’s mother is called a “strange woman” (Judg. 11:2).
This, however, merely denotes that she was of foreign
extraction.
In the time of Solomon harlots appeared openly in the streets,
and he solemnly warns against association with them (<scripRef passage="Prov. 7:12" id="h-p131.1" parsed="|Prov|7|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.7.12">Prov. 7:12</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Prov 9:14" id="h-p131.2" parsed="|Prov|9|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.9.14">9:14</scripRef>. See also <scripRef passage="Jer. 3:2" id="h-p131.3" parsed="|Jer|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.3.2">Jer. 3:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 16:24" id="h-p131.4" parsed="|Ezek|16|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.16.24">Ezek. 16:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 16:25" id="h-p131.5" parsed="|Ezek|16|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.16.25">25</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 16:31" id="h-p131.6" parsed="|Ezek|16|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.16.31">31</scripRef>). The Revised
Version, following the LXX., has “and the harlots washed,” etc.,
instead of the rendering of the Authorized Version, “now they
washed,” of 1 Kings 22:38.
To commit fornication is metaphorically used for to practice

idolatry (<scripRef passage="Jer. 3:1" id="h-p132.1" parsed="|Jer|3|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.3.1">Jer. 3:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 16:15" id="h-p132.2" parsed="|Ezek|16|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.16.15">Ezek. 16:15</scripRef>; Hos. throughout); hence
Jerusalem is spoken of as a harlot (Isa. 1:21).
(2.) Heb. nokriyah, the “strange woman” (1 Kings 11:1; Prov. 5:20; 7:5; 23:27). Those so designated were Canaanites and other
Gentiles (<scripRef passage="Josh. 23:13" id="h-p133.5" parsed="|Josh|23|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.23.13">Josh. 23:13</scripRef>). To the same class belonged the
“foolish”, i.e., the sinful, “woman.”
In the New Testament the Greek pornai, plural, “harlots,”

occurs in <scripRef passage="Matt. 21:31" id="h-p134.1" parsed="|Matt|21|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.21.31">Matt. 21:31</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 21:32" id="h-p134.2" parsed="|Matt|21|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.21.32">32</scripRef>, where they are classed with publicans;

<scripRef passage="Luke 15:30" id="h-p134.3" parsed="|Luke|15|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.15.30">Luke 15:30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 6:15" id="h-p134.4" parsed="|1Cor|6|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.6.15">1 Cor. 6:15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 6:16" id="h-p134.5" parsed="|1Cor|6|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.6.16">16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 11:31" id="h-p134.6" parsed="|Heb|11|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.11.31">Heb. 11:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="James 2:25" id="h-p134.7" parsed="|Jas|2|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jas.2.25">James 2:25</scripRef>. It is used
symbolically in Rev. 17:1, 5, 15, 16; 19:2.
</def>
<term id="h-p134.12">Harnepher</term>
A chief of the tribe of Asher (1 Chr. 7:36).
</def>
<term id="h-p135.2">Harness</term>
(1.) Heb. ‘asar, “to bind;” hence the act of fastening animals
to a cart (1 Sam. 6:7, 10; Jer. 46:4, etc.).
(2.) An Old English word for “armour;” Heb. neshek (2 Chr. 9:24).
(3.) Heb. shiryan, a coat of mail (1 Kings 22:34; 2 Chr. 18:33; rendered “breastplate” in Isa. 59:17).
(4.) The children of Israel passed out of Egypt “harnessed”
(<scripRef passage="Ex. 13:18" id="h-p139.1" parsed="|Exod|13|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.13.18">Ex. 13:18</scripRef>), i.e., in an orderly manner, and as if to meet a
foe. The word so rendered is probably a derivative from Hebrew
hamesh (i.e., “five”), and may denote that they went up in
five divisions, viz., the van, centre, two wings, and
rear-guard.
</def>
<term id="h-p139.2">Harod</term>
Palpitation, a fountain near which Gideon and his army encamped
on the morning of the day when they encountered and routed the
Midianites (<scripRef passage="Judg. 7" id="h-p140.1" parsed="|Judg|7|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.7">Judg. 7</scripRef>). It was south of the hill Moreh. The
present ‘Ain Jalud (“Goliath’s Fountain”), south of Jezreel and
nearly opposite Shunem, is probably the fountain here referred
</def>
<term id="h-p140.2">Harodite</term>
An epithet applied to two of David’s heroes (2 Sam. 23:25).
(Comp. 1 Chr. 11:27.)
</def>
<term id="h-p141.3">Harosheth of the Gentiles</term>
(Judg. 4:2) or nations, a city near Hazor in Galilee of the
Gentiles, or Upper Galilee, in the north of Palestine. It was
here that Jabin’s great army was marshalled before it went forth
into the great battlefield of Esdraelon to encounter the army of
Israel, by which it was routed and put to flight (<scripRef passage="Judg. 4" id="h-p142.2" parsed="|Judg|4|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.4">Judg. 4</scripRef>). It
was situated “at the entrance of the pass to Esdraelon from the
plain of Acre” at the base of Carmel. The name in the Hebrew is
Harosheth ha Gojim, i.e., “the smithy of the nations;”
probably, as is supposed, so called because here Jabin’s iron
war-chariots, armed with scythes, were made. It is identified
with el-Harithiyeh.
</def>
<term id="h-p142.3">Harp</term>
(Heb. kinnor), the national instrument of the Hebrews. It was
invented by Jubal (Gen. 4:21). Some think the word kinnor
denotes the whole class of stringed instruments. It was used as
an accompaniment to songs of cheerfulness as well as of praise

to God (<scripRef passage="Gen. 31:27" id="h-p143.2" parsed="|Gen|31|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.27">Gen. 31:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 16:23" id="h-p143.3" parsed="|1Sam|16|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.16.23">1 Sam. 16:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 20:28" id="h-p143.4" parsed="|2Chr|20|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.20.28">2 Chr. 20:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 33:2" id="h-p143.5" parsed="|Ps|33|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.33.2">Ps. 33:2</scripRef>;
137:2).
In Solomon’s time harps were made of almug-trees (1 Kings 10:11, 12). In 1 Chr. 15:21 mention is made of “harps on the
Sheminith;” Revised Version, “harps set to the Sheminith;”
better perhaps “harps of eight strings.” The soothing effect of

the music of the harp is referred to <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 16:16" id="h-p144.4" parsed="|1Sam|16|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.16.16">1 Sam. 16:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 16:23" id="h-p144.5" parsed="|1Sam|16|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.16.23">23</scripRef>; 18:10;
19:9. The church in heaven is represented as celebrating the
triumphs of the Redeemer “harping with their harps” (Rev. 14:2).
</def>
<term id="h-p144.7">Harrow</term>
(Heb. harits), a tribulum or sharp threshing sledge; a frame
armed on the under side with rollers or sharp spikes (2 Sam. 12:31; 1 Chr. 20:3).
Heb. verb sadad, to harrow a field, break its clods (Job 39:10; Isa. 28:4; Hos. 10: 11). Its form is unknown. It may have
resembled the instrument still in use in Egypt.
</def>
<term id="h-p146.4">Harsha</term>
Worker or enchanter, one of the Nethinim (Ezra 2:52; Neh. 7:54).
</def>
<term id="h-p147.3">Hart</term>
(Heb. ‘ayal), a stag or male deer. It is ranked among the clean

animals (<scripRef passage="Deut. 12:15" id="h-p148.1" parsed="|Deut|12|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.12.15">Deut. 12:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut 14:5" id="h-p148.2" parsed="|Deut|14|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.14.5">14:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut 15:22" id="h-p148.3" parsed="|Deut|15|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.15.22">15:22</scripRef>), and was commonly killed for
food (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:23" id="h-p148.4" parsed="|1Kgs|4|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.23">1 Kings 4:23</scripRef>). The hart is frequently alluded to in the
poetical and prophetical books (Isa. 35:6; Cant. 2:8, 9; Lam. 1:6; Ps. 42:1).
</def>
<term id="h-p148.10">Harum</term>
Elevated, (1 Chr. 4:8), a descendant of Judah.
</def>
<term id="h-p149.2">Haruphite</term>
A native of Hariph; an epithet given to Shephatiah, one of those
who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr. 12:5).
</def>
<term id="h-p150.2">Haruz</term>
Eager, the father of Meshullemeth, the wife of king Manasseh (2 Kings 21:19) and mother of king Amon.
</def>
<term id="h-p151.2">Harvest</term>
The season for gathering grain or fruit. On the 16th day of Abib
(or April) a handful of ripe ears of corn was offered as a
first-fruit before the Lord, and immediately after this the

harvest commenced (<scripRef passage="Lev. 23:9-14" id="h-p152.1" parsed="|Lev|23|9|23|14" osisRef="Bible:Lev.23.9-Lev.23.14">Lev. 23:9-14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:9" id="h-p152.2" parsed="|2Sam|21|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.9">2 Sam. 21:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 21:10" id="h-p152.3" parsed="|2Sam|21|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.21.10">10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ruth 2:23" id="h-p152.4" parsed="|Ruth|2|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.2.23">Ruth 2:23</scripRef>). It
began with the feast of Passover and ended with Pentecost, thus
lasting for seven weeks (<scripRef passage="Ex. 23:16" id="h-p152.5" parsed="|Exod|23|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.16">Ex. 23:16</scripRef>). The harvest was a season of

joy (<scripRef passage="Ps. 126:1-6" id="h-p152.6" parsed="|Ps|126|1|126|6" osisRef="Bible:Ps.126.1-Ps.126.6">Ps. 126:1-6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 9:3" id="h-p152.7" parsed="|Isa|9|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.9.3">Isa. 9:3</scripRef>). This word is used figuratively
Matt. 9:37; 13:30; Luke 10:2; John 4:35. (See AGRICULTURE.)
</def>
<term id="h-p152.13">Hasadiah</term>
Favoured by Jehovah, one of the sons of Pedaiah (1 Chr. 3:20),
of the royal line of David.
</def>
<term id="h-p153.2">Hasenuah</term>
Bristling or hated, a Benjamite (1 Chr. 9:7).
</def>
<term id="h-p154.2">Hashabiah</term>
Regarded by Jehovah. (1.) Merarite Levite (1 Chr. 6:45; 9:14).
(2.) A son of Jeduthun (25:3, 19). (3.) Son of Kemuel (26:30).

(4.) One of the chief Levites (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 35:9" id="h-p155.3" parsed="|2Chr|35|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.35.9">2 Chr. 35:9</scripRef>). (5.) A Levite (<scripRef passage="Neh. 11:22" id="h-p155.4" parsed="|Neh|11|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.11.22">Neh. 11:22</scripRef>). (6.) One of the chief priests in the time of Ezra (<scripRef passage="Ezra 8:24" id="h-p155.5" parsed="|Ezra|8|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.8.24">Ezra 8:24</scripRef>). (7.) A chief of the Levites (<scripRef passage="Neh. 12:24" id="h-p155.6" parsed="|Neh|12|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.12.24">Neh. 12:24</scripRef>). (8.) <scripRef passage="Ezra 8:19" id="h-p155.7" parsed="|Ezra|8|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.8.19">Ezra 8:19</scripRef>.
(9.) Neh. 3:17.
</def>
<term id="h-p155.9">Hashabniah</term>
(1.) Neh. 3:10. (2.) One of the Levites whom Ezra appointed to
interpret the law to the people (Neh. 9:5).
</def>
<term id="h-p156.3">Hashbadana</term>
Consideration in judging, stood at Ezra’s left hand when he read
the law (Neh. 8:4).
</def>
<term id="h-p157.2">Hashmonah</term>
Fatness, the thirtieth halting-place of the Israelites during
their wanderings in the wilderness, not far from Mount Hor (Num. 33:29, 30).
</def>
<term id="h-p158.3">Hashub</term>
Intelligent. (1.) A Levite of the family of Merari (Neh. 11:15;
1 Chr. 9:14). (2.) Neh. 3:23. 3:11.
</def>
<term id="h-p159.4">Hashubah</term>
Ibid., a descendant of David (1 Chr. 3:20).
</def>
<term id="h-p160.2">Hashum</term>
Opulent. (1.) Ezra 2:19; Neh. 7:22. (2.) Stood on Ezra’s left
hand while he read the law (Neh. 8:4).
</def>
<term id="h-p161.4">Hasrah</term>
Poverty, “keeper of the wardrobe,” i.e., of the sacerdotal

vestments (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 34:22" id="h-p162.1" parsed="|2Chr|34|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.34.22">2 Chr. 34:22</scripRef>); called Harhas <scripRef passage="2 Kings 22:14" id="h-p162.2" parsed="|2Kgs|22|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.22.14">2 Kings 22:14</scripRef>. He was
husband of the prophetess Huldah.
</def>
<term id="h-p162.3">Hasupha</term>
Uncovered, one of the Nethinim (Ezra 2:43; Neh. 7:46).
</def>
<term id="h-p163.3">Hat</term>
Chald. karb’ela, (Dan. 3:21), properly mantle or pallium. The
Revised Version renders it “tunic.”
</def>
<term id="h-p164.2">Hatach</term>
Verity, one of the eunuchs or chamberlains in the palace of
Ahasuerus (Esther 4:5, 6, 9, 10).
</def>
<term id="h-p165.5">Hathath</term>
Terror, son of Othniel (1 Chr. 4:13).
</def>
<term id="h-p166.2">Hatipha</term>
Captured, one of the Nethinim (Ezra 2:54).
</def>
<term id="h-p167.2">Hatita</term>
Exploration, one of the temple porters or janitors (Ezra 2:42).
He returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel.
</def>
<term id="h-p168.2">Hatred</term>
Among the works of the flesh (Gal. 5:20). Altogether different
is the meaning of the word in Deut. 21:15; Matt. 6:24; Luke 14:26; Rom. 9:13, where it denotes only a less degree of love.
</def>
<term id="h-p169.6">Hattush</term>
Assembled. (1.) A priest who returned with Zerubbabel (Neh. 12:2). (2.) Ezra 8:2. (3.) Neh. 3:10. (4.) Neh. 10:4. (5.) 1 Chr. 3:22.
</def>
<term id="h-p170.6">Hauran</term>
Cave-land, mentioned only in Ezek. 47:16, 18. It was one of the
ancient divisions of Bashan (q.v.), and lay on the south-east of
Gaulanitis or the Jaulan, and on the south of Lejah, extending
from the Arnon to the Hieromax. It was the most fertile region
in Syria, and to this day abounds in the ruins of towns, many of
which have stone doors and massive walls. It retains its ancient
name. It was known by the Greeks and Romans as “Auranitis.”
</def>
<term id="h-p171.3">Haven</term>
A harbour (Ps. 107:30; Acts 27: 12). The most famous on the
coast of Palestine was that of Tyre (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:3" id="h-p172.3" parsed="|Ezek|27|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.3">Ezek. 27:3</scripRef>). That of Crete,
called “Fair Havens,” is mentioned Acts 27:8.
</def>
<term id="h-p172.5">Havilah</term>
The sand region. (1.) A land mentioned in Gen. 2:11 rich in gold
and bdellium and onyx stone. The question as to the locality of
this region has given rise to a great diversity of opinion. It
may perhaps be identified with the sandy tract which skirts
Babylonia along the whole of its western border, stretching from
the lower Euphrates to the mountains of Edom.
(2.) A district in Arabia-Felix. It is uncertain whether the
tribe gave its name to this region or derived its name from it,
and whether it was originally a Cushite (<scripRef passage="Gen. 10:7" id="h-p174.1" parsed="|Gen|10|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.7">Gen. 10:7</scripRef>) or a
Joktanite tribe (10:29; comp. 25:18), or whether there were both
a Cushite and a Joktanite Havilah. It is the opinion of Kalisch,
however, that Havilah “in both instances designates the same
country, extending at least from the Persian to the Arabian
Gulf, and on account of its vast extent easily divided into two
distinct parts.” This opinion may be well vindicated.
(3.) One of the sons of Cush (Gen. 10:7).
(4.) A son of Joktan (Gen. 10:29; 1 Chr. 1:23).
</def>
<term id="h-p176.3">Havoth-jair</term>
Hamlets of the enlightener a district in the east of Jordan.
(1.) Jair, the son of Manasseh, took some villages of Gilead and
called them by this name (Num. 32:41).
(2.) Again, it is said that Jair “took all the tract of
Argob,” and called it Bashanhavoth-jair (<scripRef passage="Deut. 3:14" id="h-p178.1" parsed="|Deut|3|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.14">Deut. 3:14</scripRef>). (See also
Josh. 13:30; 1 Kings 4:13; 1 Chr. 2:22, 23.)
</def>
<term id="h-p178.6">Hawk</term>
(Heb. netz, a word expressive of strong and rapid flight, and

hence appropriate to the hawk). It is an unclean bird (<scripRef passage="Lev. 11:16" id="h-p179.1" parsed="|Lev|11|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.11.16">Lev. 11:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 14:15" id="h-p179.2" parsed="|Deut|14|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.14.15">Deut. 14:15</scripRef>). It is common in Syria and surrounding
countries. The Hebrew word includes various species of
Falconidae, with special reference perhaps to the kestrel (Falco
tinnunculus), the hobby (Hypotriorchis subbuteo), and the lesser
kestrel (Tin, Cenchris). The kestrel remains all the year in
Palestine, but some ten or twelve other species are all migrants
from the south. Of those summer visitors to Palestine special
mention may be made of the Falco sacer and the Falco lanarius.
(See NIGHT-HAWK.)
</def>
<term id="h-p179.4">Hay</term>
Properly so called, was not in use among the Hebrews; straw was
used instead. They cut the grass green as it was needed. The
word rendered “hay” in <scripRef passage="Prov. 27:25" id="h-p180.1" parsed="|Prov|27|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.27.25">Prov. 27:25</scripRef> means the first shoots of the
grass. In <scripRef passage="Isa. 15:6" id="h-p180.2" parsed="|Isa|15|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.15.6">Isa. 15:6</scripRef> the Revised Version has correctly “grass,”
where the Authorized Version has “hay.”
</def>
<term id="h-p180.3">Hazael</term>
Whom God beholds, an officer of Ben-hadad II., king of Syria,
who ultimately came to the throne, according to the word of the
Lord to Elijah (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 19:15" id="h-p181.1" parsed="|1Kgs|19|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.19.15">1 Kings 19:15</scripRef>), after he had put the king to
death (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 8:15" id="h-p181.2" parsed="|2Kgs|8|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.8.15">2 Kings 8:15</scripRef>). His interview with Elisha is mentioned in
<scripRef passage="2 Kings 8" id="h-p181.3" parsed="|2Kgs|8|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.8">2 Kings 8</scripRef>. The Assyrians soon after his accession to the throne
came against him and defeated him with very great loss; and
three years afterwards again invaded Syria, but on this occasion
Hazael submitted to them. He then turned his arms against

Israel, and ravaged “all the land of Gilead,” etc. (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 10:33" id="h-p181.4" parsed="|2Kgs|10|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.10.33">2 Kings 10:33</scripRef>), which he held in a degree of subjection to him (13:3-7,
22). He aimed at the subjugation also of the kingdom of Judah,
when Joash obtained peace by giving him “all the gold that was
found in the treasures of the house of the Lord, and in the

king’s house” (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 12:18" id="h-p181.5" parsed="|2Kgs|12|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.12.18">2 Kings 12:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 24:24" id="h-p181.6" parsed="|2Chr|24|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.24.24">2 Chr. 24:24</scripRef>). He reigned about
forty-six years (B.C. 886-840), and was succeeded on the throne
by his son Ben-hadad (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 13:22-25" id="h-p181.7" parsed="|2Kgs|13|22|13|25" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.13.22-2Kgs.13.25">2 Kings 13:22-25</scripRef>), who on several
occasions was defeated by Jehoash, the king of Israel, and
compelled to restore all the land of Israel his father had
taken.
</def>
<term id="h-p181.8">Hazar-addar</term>
Village of Addar, a place in the southern boundary of Palestine
(<scripRef passage="Num. 34:4" id="h-p182.1" parsed="|Num|34|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.34.4">Num. 34:4</scripRef>), in the desert to the west of Kadesh-barnea. It is
called Adar in Josh. 15:3.
</def>
<term id="h-p182.3">Hazar-enan</term>
Village of fountains, a place on the north-east frontier of

Palestine (<scripRef passage="Num. 34:9" id="h-p183.1" parsed="|Num|34|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.34.9">Num. 34:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 34:10" id="h-p183.2" parsed="|Num|34|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.34.10">10</scripRef>). Some have identified it with Ayan
ed-Dara in the heart of the central chain of Anti-Libanus. More
probably, however, it has been identified with Kuryetein, about
60 miles east-north-east of Damascus. (Comp. Ezek. 47:17; 48:1.)
</def>
<term id="h-p183.5">Hazar-gaddah</term>
Village of fortune, a city on the south border of Judah (Josh. 15:27), midway between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea.
</def>
<term id="h-p184.2">Hazar-hatticon</term>
Village of the midway, a place near Hamath in the confines of
Hauran (Ezek. 47:16), probably on the north brow of Hermon.
</def>
<term id="h-p185.2">Hazar-maveth</term>
Court of death, the third son of Joktan, and a region in

Arabia-Felix settled by him (<scripRef passage="Gen. 10:26" id="h-p186.1" parsed="|Gen|10|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.26">Gen. 10:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 1:20" id="h-p186.2" parsed="|1Chr|1|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.1.20">1 Chr. 1:20</scripRef>). It is
probably the modern province of Hadramaut, situated on the
Indian Ocean east of the modern Yemen.
</def>
<term id="h-p186.3">Hazar-shual</term>
Village or enclosure of the jackal, a city on the south border

of Judah (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:28" id="h-p187.1" parsed="|Josh|15|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.28">Josh. 15:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh. 11:27" id="h-p187.2" parsed="|Neh|11|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.11.27">Neh. 11:27</scripRef>). It has been identified with
the ruins of Saweh, half-way between Beersheba and Moladah.
</def>
<term id="h-p187.3">Hazar-susah</term>
Village of the horse, the same as Sansannah, one of Solomon’s

“chariot cities” (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:31" id="h-p188.1" parsed="|Josh|15|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.31">Josh. 15:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 1:14" id="h-p188.2" parsed="|2Chr|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.1.14">2 Chr. 1:14</scripRef>), a depot in the
south border of Judah.
</def>
<term id="h-p188.3">Hazel</term>
Heb. luz, (Gen. 30:37), a nutbearing tree. The Hebrew word is
rendered in the Vulgate by amygdalinus, “the almond-tree,” which
is probably correct. That tree flourishes in Syria.
</def>
<term id="h-p189.2">Hazerim</term>
Villages, probably the name of the temporary villages in which
the nomad Avites resided (Deut. 2:23).
</def>
<term id="h-p190.2">Hazeroth</term>
Fenced enclosures consisting of “a low wall of stones in which
thick bundles of thorny acacia are inserted, the tangled
branches and long needle-like spikes forming a perfectly
impenetrable hedge around the encampment” of tents and cattle
which they sheltered. Such like enclosures abound in the
wilderness of Paran, which the Israelites entered after leaving

Sinai (<scripRef passage="Num. 11:35" id="h-p191.1" parsed="|Num|11|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.11.35">Num. 11:35</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 12:16" id="h-p191.2" parsed="|Num|12|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.12.16">12:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 33:17" id="h-p191.3" parsed="|Num|33|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.17">33:17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num 33:18" id="h-p191.4" parsed="|Num|33|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.18">18</scripRef>). This third encampment of
the Israelites has been identified with the modern ‘Ain
el-Hudhera, some 40 miles north-east of Sinai. Here Miriam
(q.v.), being displeased that Moses had married a Cushite wife
(<scripRef passage="Num. 12:1" id="h-p191.5" parsed="|Num|12|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.12.1">Num. 12:1</scripRef>), induced Aaron to join with her in rebelling against
Moses. God vindicated the authority of his “servant Moses,” and
Miriam was smitten with leprosy. Moses interceded for her, and
she was healed (<scripRef passage="Num. 12:4-16" id="h-p191.6" parsed="|Num|12|4|12|16" osisRef="Bible:Num.12.4-Num.12.16">Num. 12:4-16</scripRef>). From this encampment the
Israelites marched northward across the plateau of et-Tih, and
at length reached KADESH.
</def>
<term id="h-p191.7">Hazezon-tamar</term>
Pruning of the palm, the original name of the place afterwards
called ENGEDI (q.v.), Gen. 14:7; called also HAZAZON-TAMAR (2 Chr. 20:2).
</def>
<term id="h-p192.3">Hazo</term>
Vision, one of the sons of Nahor (Gen. 22:22).
</def>
<term id="h-p193.2">Hazor</term>
Enclosed; fortified. (1.) A stronghold of the Canaanites in the
mountains north of Lake Merom (<scripRef passage="Josh. 11:1-5" id="h-p194.1" parsed="|Josh|11|1|11|5" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.1-Josh.11.5">Josh. 11:1-5</scripRef>). Jabin the king
with his allied tribes here encountered Joshua in a great
battle. Joshua gained a signal victory, which virtually
completed his conquest of Canaan (11:10-13). This city was,
however, afterwards rebuilt by the Canaanites, and was ruled by
a king with the same hereditary name of Jabin. His army, under a
noted leader of the name of Sisera, swept down upon the south,
aiming at the complete subjugation of the country. This powerful
army was met by the Israelites under Barak, who went forth by
the advice of the prophetess Deborah. The result was one of the
most remarkable victories for Israel recorded in the Old

Testament (<scripRef passage="Josh. 19:36" id="h-p194.2" parsed="|Josh|19|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.36">Josh. 19:36</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 4:2" id="h-p194.3" parsed="|Judg|4|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.4.2">Judg. 4:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 12:9" id="h-p194.4" parsed="|1Sam|12|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.12.9">1 Sam. 12:9</scripRef>). The city of
Hazor was taken and occupied by the Israelites. It was fortified
by Solomon to defend the entrance into the kingdom from Syria
and Assyria. When Tiglath-pileser, the Assyrian king, invaded
the land, this was one of the first cities he captured, carrying
its inhabitants captive into Assyria (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 15:29" id="h-p194.5" parsed="|2Kgs|15|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.29">2 Kings 15:29</scripRef>). It has
been identified with Khurbet Harrah, 2 1/2 miles south-east of
Kedesh.
(2.) A city in the south of Judah (Josh. 15:23). The name here
should probably be connected with the word following, Ithnan,
HAZOR-ITHNAN instead of “Hazor and Ithnan.”
(3.) A district in Arabia (Jer. 49:28-33), supposed by some to
be Jetor, i.e., Ituraea.
(4.) “Kerioth and Hezron” (Josh. 15: 25) should be
“Kerioth-hezron” (as in the R.V.), the two names being joined
together as the name of one place (e.g., like Kirjath-jearim),
“the same is Hazor” (R.V.). This place has been identified with
el-Kuryetein, and has been supposed to be the home of Judas
Iscariot. (See KERIOTH.)
</def>
<term id="h-p197.3">Hazor-hadattah</term>
New Hazor, a city in the south of Judah (Josh. 15:25). It is
probably identified with the ruins of el-Hazzarah, near Beit
Jebrin.
</def>
<term id="h-p198.2">Head-bands</term>
(Heb. kishshurim), properly girdles or belts for the waist (Isa. 3:20, R.V., “sashes;” Jer. 2:32, rendered “attire”, i.e., a
girdle round the waist).
</def>
<term id="h-p199.3">Head-dress</term>
Not in common use among the Hebrews. It is first mentioned in
<scripRef passage="Ex. 28:40" id="h-p200.1" parsed="|Exod|28|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.28.40">Ex. 28:40</scripRef> (A.V., “bonnets;” R.V., “head-tires”). It was used

especially for purposes of ornament (<scripRef passage="Job 29:14" id="h-p200.2" parsed="|Job|29|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.29.14">Job 29:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 3:23" id="h-p200.3" parsed="|Isa|3|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.23">Isa. 3:23</scripRef>;
62:3). The Hebrew word here used, tsaniph, properly means a
turban, folds of linen wound round the head. The Hebrew word
peer, used in Isa. 61:3, there rendered “beauty” (A.V.) and
“garland” (R.V.), is a head-dress or turban worn by females

(<scripRef passage="Isa. 3" id="h-p200.6" parsed="|Isa|3|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3">Isa. 3</scripRef>: 20, “bonnets”), priests (<scripRef passage="Ex. 39:28" id="h-p200.7" parsed="|Exod|39|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.39.28">Ex. 39:28</scripRef>), a bridegroom (<scripRef passage="Isa. 61:10" id="h-p200.8" parsed="|Isa|61|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.61.10">Isa. 61:10</scripRef>, “ornament;” R.V., “garland”). <scripRef passage="Ezek. 16:10" id="h-p200.9" parsed="|Ezek|16|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.16.10">Ezek. 16:10</scripRef> and <scripRef passage="Jonah 2:5" id="h-p200.10" parsed="|Jonah|2|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jonah.2.5">Jonah 2:5</scripRef>
are to be understood of the turban wrapped round the head. The
Hebrew shebisim (Isa. 3:18), in the Authorized Version
rendered “cauls,” and marg. “networks,” denotes probably a kind

of netted head-dress. The “horn” (Heb. keren) mentioned in <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 2:1" id="h-p200.12" parsed="|1Sam|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.2.1">1 Sam. 2:1</scripRef> is the head-dress called by the Druses of Mount Lebanon
the tantura.
</def>
<term id="h-p200.13">Heap</term>
When Joshua took the city of Ai (Josh. 8), he burned it and
“made it an heap [Heb. tel] for ever” (8:28). The ruins of this
city were for a long time sought for in vain. It has been at
length, however, identified with the mound which simply bears
the name of “Tel.” “There are many Tels in modern Palestine,
that land of Tels, each Tel with some other name attached to it
to mark the former site. But the site of Ai has no other name
’unto this day.’ It is simply et-Tel, ‘the heap’ par
excellence.”
</def>
<term id="h-p201.2">Heart</term>
According to the Bible, the heart is the centre not only of
spiritual activity, but of all the operations of human life.
“Heart” and “soul” are often used interchangeably (<scripRef passage="Deut. 6:5" id="h-p202.1" parsed="|Deut|6|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.6.5">Deut. 6:5</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Deut 26:16" id="h-p202.2" parsed="|Deut|26|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.26.16">26:16</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Matt. 22:37" id="h-p202.3" parsed="|Matt|22|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.22.37">Matt. 22:37</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 12:30" id="h-p202.4" parsed="|Mark|12|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.12.30">Mark 12:30</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Mark 12:33" id="h-p202.5" parsed="|Mark|12|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.12.33">33</scripRef>), but this is not
generally the case.
The heart is the “home of the personal life,” and hence a man
is designated, according to his heart, wise (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 3:12" id="h-p203.1" parsed="|1Kgs|3|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.3.12">1 Kings 3:12</scripRef>,

etc.), pure (<scripRef passage="Ps. 24:4" id="h-p203.2" parsed="|Ps|24|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.24.4">Ps. 24:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 5:8" id="h-p203.3" parsed="|Matt|5|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.8">Matt. 5:8</scripRef>, etc.), upright and righteous

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 20:5" id="h-p203.4" parsed="|Gen|20|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.20.5">Gen. 20:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 20:6" id="h-p203.5" parsed="|Gen|20|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.20.6">6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 11:2" id="h-p203.6" parsed="|Ps|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.11.2">Ps. 11:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 78:72" id="h-p203.7" parsed="|Ps|78|72|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.78.72">78:72</scripRef>), pious and good (<scripRef passage="Luke 8:15" id="h-p203.8" parsed="|Luke|8|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.8.15">Luke 8:15</scripRef>),
etc. In these and such passages the word “soul” could not be
substituted for “heart.”
The heart is also the seat of the conscience (Rom. 2:15). It
is naturally wicked (<scripRef passage="Gen. 8:21" id="h-p204.2" parsed="|Gen|8|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.8.21">Gen. 8:21</scripRef>), and hence it contaminates the

whole life and character (<scripRef passage="Matt. 12:34" id="h-p204.3" parsed="|Matt|12|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.12.34">Matt. 12:34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 15:18" id="h-p204.4" parsed="|Matt|15|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.15.18">15:18</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Eccl. 8:11" id="h-p204.5" parsed="|Eccl|8|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eccl.8.11">Eccl. 8:11</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Ps. 73:7" id="h-p204.6" parsed="|Ps|73|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.73.7">Ps. 73:7</scripRef>). Hence the heart must be changed, regenerated (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 36:26" id="h-p204.7" parsed="|Ezek|36|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.36.26">Ezek. 36:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek 11:19" id="h-p204.8" parsed="|Ezek|11|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.11.19">11:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 51:10-14" id="h-p204.9" parsed="|Ps|51|10|51|14" osisRef="Bible:Ps.51.10-Ps.51.14">Ps. 51:10-14</scripRef>), before a man can willingly obey
God.
The process of salvation begins in the heart by the believing
reception of the testimony of God, while the rejection of that

testimony hardens the heart (<scripRef passage="Ps. 95:8" id="h-p205.1" parsed="|Ps|95|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.95.8">Ps. 95:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 28:14" id="h-p205.2" parsed="|Prov|28|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.28.14">Prov. 28:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 36:13" id="h-p205.3" parsed="|2Chr|36|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.36.13">2 Chr. 36:13</scripRef>). “Hardness of heart evidences itself by light views of
sin; partial acknowledgment and confession of it; pride and
conceit; ingratitude; unconcern about the word and ordinances of
God; inattention to divine providences; stifling convictions of
conscience; shunning reproof; presumption, and general ignorance
of divine things.”
</def>
<term id="h-p205.4">Hearth</term>
Heb. ah (Jer. 36:22, 23; R.V., “brazier”), meaning a large pot
like a brazier, a portable furnace in which fire was kept in the
king’s winter apartment.
Heb. kiyor (Zech. 12:6; R.V., “pan”), a fire-pan.
Heb. moqed (Ps. 102:3; R.V., “fire-brand”), properly a fagot.
Heb. yaqud (Isa. 30:14), a burning mass on a hearth.
</def>
<term id="h-p209.2">He-ass</term>
Heb. hamor, (Gen. 12:16), the general designation of the donkey
used for carrying burdens (Gen. 42:26) and for ploughing (Isa. 30:24). It is described in Gen. 49:14, 2 Sam. 19:26. (See ASS.)
</def>
<term id="h-p210.7">Heath</term>
Heb. ‘arar, (Jer. 17:6; 48:6), a species of juniper called by
the Arabs by the same name (‘arar), the Juniperus sabina or
savin. “Its gloomy, stunted appearance, with its scale-like
leaves pressed close to its gnarled stem, and cropped close by
the wild goats, as it clings to the rocks about Petra, gives
great force to the contrast suggested by the prophet, between
him that trusteth in man, naked and destitute, and the man that
trusteth in the Lord, flourishing as a tree planted by the
waters” (Tristram, Natural History of the Bible).
</def>
<term id="h-p211.3">Heathen</term>
(Heb. plural goyum). At first the word goyim denoted generally

all the nations of the world (<scripRef passage="Gen. 18:18" id="h-p212.1" parsed="|Gen|18|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.18.18">Gen. 18:18</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Gal. 3:8" id="h-p212.2" parsed="|Gal|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.3.8">Gal. 3:8</scripRef>). The
Jews afterwards became a people distinguished in a marked manner
from the other goyim. They were a separate people (Lev. 20:23;

<scripRef passage="Lev 26:14-45" id="h-p212.4" parsed="|Lev|26|14|26|45" osisRef="Bible:Lev.26.14-Lev.26.45">26:14-45</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 28" id="h-p212.5" parsed="|Deut|28|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.28">Deut. 28</scripRef>), and the other nations, the Amorites,
Hittites, etc., were the goyim, the heathen, with whom the

Jews were forbidden to be associated in any way (<scripRef passage="Josh. 23:7" id="h-p212.6" parsed="|Josh|23|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.23.7">Josh. 23:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 11:2" id="h-p212.7" parsed="|1Kgs|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.11.2">1 Kings 11:2</scripRef>). The practice of idolatry was the characteristic of
these nations, and hence the word came to designate idolaters
(Ps. 106:47; Jer. 46:28; Lam. 1:3; Isa. 36:18), the wicked (Ps. 9:5, 15, 17).
The corresponding Greek word in the New Testament, ethne,

has similar shades of meaning. In <scripRef passage="Acts 22:21" id="h-p213.1" parsed="|Acts|22|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.22.21">Acts 22:21</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gal. 3:14" id="h-p213.2" parsed="|Gal|3|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.3.14">Gal. 3:14</scripRef>, it
denotes the people of the earth generally; and in <scripRef passage="Matt. 6:7" id="h-p213.3" parsed="|Matt|6|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.7">Matt. 6:7</scripRef>, an
idolater. In modern usage the word denotes all nations that are
strangers to revealed religion.
</def>
<term id="h-p213.4">Heaven</term>
(1.) Definitions. The phrase “heaven and earth” is used to

indicate the whole universe (<scripRef passage="Gen. 1:1" id="h-p214.1" parsed="|Gen|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.1.1">Gen. 1:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 23:24" id="h-p214.2" parsed="|Jer|23|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.23.24">Jer. 23:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 17:24" id="h-p214.3" parsed="|Acts|17|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.17.24">Acts 17:24</scripRef>).
According to the Jewish notion there were three heavens,
(a) The firmament, as “fowls of the heaven” (Gen. 2:19; 7:3,
23; Ps. 8:8, etc.), “the eagles of heaven” (Lam. 4:19), etc.
(b) The starry heavens (Deut. 17:3; Jer. 8:2; Matt. 24:29).
(c) “The heaven of heavens,” or “the third heaven” (Deut. 10:14; 1 Kings 8:27; Ps. 115:16; 148:4; 2 Cor. 12:2).
(2.) Meaning of words in the original,
(a) The usual Hebrew word for “heavens” is shamayim, a
plural form meaning “heights,” “elevations” (Gen. 1:1; 2:1).
(b) The Hebrew word marom is also used (Ps. 68:18; 93:4;
102:19, etc.) as equivalent to shamayim, “high places,”
“heights.”
(c) Heb. galgal, literally a “wheel,” is rendered “heaven” in
Ps. 77:18 (R.V., “whirlwind”).
(d) Heb. shahak, rendered “sky” (Deut. 33:26; Job 37:18; Ps. 18:11), plural “clouds” (Job 35:5; 36:28; Ps. 68:34, marg.
“heavens”), means probably the firmament.
(e) Heb. rakia is closely connected with (d), and is rendered
“firmamentum” in the Vulgate, whence our “firmament” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 1:6" id="h-p223.1" parsed="|Gen|1|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.1.6">Gen. 1:6</scripRef>;
Deut. 33:26, etc.), regarded as a solid expanse.
(3.) Metaphorical meaning of term. Isa. 14:13, 14; “doors of

heaven” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 78:23" id="h-p224.3" parsed="|Ps|78|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.78.23">Ps. 78:23</scripRef>); heaven “shut” (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 8:35" id="h-p224.4" parsed="|1Kgs|8|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.8.35">1 Kings 8:35</scripRef>); “opened”
(Ezek. 1:1). (See 1 Chr. 21:16.)
(4.) Spiritual meaning. The place of the everlasting
blessedness of the righteous; the abode of departed spirits.
(a) Christ calls it his “Father’s house” (John 14:2).
(b) It is called “paradise” (Luke 23:43; 2 Cor. 12:4; Rev. 2:7).
(c) “The heavenly Jerusalem” (Gal. 4: 26; Heb. 12:22; Rev. 3:12).
(d) The “kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 25:1; James 2:5).
(e) The “eternal kingdom” (2 Pet. 1:11).
(f) The “eternal inheritance” (1 Pet. 1:4; Heb. 9:15).
(g) The “better country” (Heb. 11:14, 16).
(h) The blessed are said to “sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and

Jacob,” and to be “in Abraham’s bosom” (<scripRef passage="Luke 16:22" id="h-p233.1" parsed="|Luke|16|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.16.22">Luke 16:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 8:11" id="h-p233.2" parsed="|Matt|8|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.8.11">Matt. 8:11</scripRef>);
to “reign with Christ” (2 Tim. 2:12); and to enjoy “rest” (Heb. 4:10, 11).
In heaven the blessedness of the righteous consists in the
possession of “life everlasting,” “an eternal weight of glory”
(<scripRef passage="2 Cor. 4:17" id="h-p234.1" parsed="|2Cor|4|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.4.17">2 Cor. 4:17</scripRef>), an exemption from all sufferings for ever, a

deliverance from all evils (<scripRef passage="2 Cor. 5:1" id="h-p234.2" parsed="|2Cor|5|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.5.1">2 Cor. 5:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 5:2" id="h-p234.3" parsed="|2Cor|5|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.5.2">2</scripRef>) and from the society
of the wicked (<scripRef passage="2 Tim. 4:18" id="h-p234.4" parsed="|2Tim|4|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.4.18">2 Tim. 4:18</scripRef>), bliss without termination, the

“fulness of joy” for ever (<scripRef passage="Luke 20:36" id="h-p234.5" parsed="|Luke|20|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.20.36">Luke 20:36</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 4:16" id="h-p234.6" parsed="|2Cor|4|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.4.16">2 Cor. 4:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Cor. 4:18" id="h-p234.7" parsed="|2Cor|4|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.4.18">18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Pet. 1:4" id="h-p234.8" parsed="|1Pet|1|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.1.4">1 Pet. 1:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Pet. 5:10" id="h-p234.9" parsed="|1Pet|5|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.5.10">5:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 John 3:2" id="h-p234.10" parsed="|1John|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.3.2">1 John 3:2</scripRef>). The believer’s heaven is not only a
state of everlasting blessedness, but also a “place”, a place
“prepared” for them (John 14:2).
</def>
<term id="h-p234.12">Heave offering</term>
Heb. terumah, (Ex. 29:27) means simply an offering, a present,
including all the offerings made by the Israelites as a present.
This Hebrew word is frequently employed. Some of the rabbis
attach to the word the meaning of elevation, and refer it to the
heave offering, which consisted in presenting the offering by a
motion up and down, distinguished from the wave offering, which
consisted in a repeated movement in a horizontal direction, a
“wave offering to the Lord as ruler of earth, a heave offering
to the Lord as ruler of heaven.” The right shoulder, which fell
to the priests in presenting thank offerings, was called the

heave shoulder (<scripRef passage="Lev. 7:34" id="h-p235.2" parsed="|Lev|7|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.7.34">Lev. 7:34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 6:20" id="h-p235.3" parsed="|Num|6|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.6.20">Num. 6:20</scripRef>). The first fruits offered
in harvest-time (Num. 15:20, 21) were heave offerings.
</def>
<term id="h-p235.6">Heber</term>
Passing over. (1.) Son of Beriah and grandson of Asher (Gen. 46:17; 1 Chr. 7:31, 32).
(2.) The Kenite (Judg. 4:11, 17; 5:24), a descendant of Hobab.
His wife Jael received Sisera (q.v.) into her tent and then
killed him.
(3.) 1 Chr. 4:18.
(4.) A Benjamite (1 Chr. 8:17).
(5.) A Gadite (5:13). (See EBER.)
</def>
<term id="h-p240.2">Hebrew</term>
A name applied to the Israelites in Scripture only by one who is

a foreigner (<scripRef passage="Gen. 39:14" id="h-p241.1" parsed="|Gen|39|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.39.14">Gen. 39:14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 39:17" id="h-p241.2" parsed="|Gen|39|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.39.17">17</scripRef>; 41:12, etc.), or by the Israelites
when they speak of themselves to foreigners (40:15; <scripRef passage="Ex. 1:19" id="h-p241.3" parsed="|Exod|1|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.1.19">Ex. 1:19</scripRef>),
or when spoken of an contrasted with other peoples (<scripRef passage="Gen. 43:32" id="h-p241.4" parsed="|Gen|43|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.43.32">Gen. 43:32</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Ex. 1:3" id="h-p241.5" parsed="|Exod|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.1.3">Ex. 1:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 1:7" id="h-p241.6" parsed="|Exod|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.1.7">7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 1:15" id="h-p241.7" parsed="|Exod|1|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.1.15">15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 15:12" id="h-p241.8" parsed="|Deut|15|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.15.12">Deut. 15:12</scripRef>). In the New Testament there is the
same contrast between Hebrews and foreigners (Acts 6:1; Phil. 3:5).
Derivation. (1.) The name is derived, according to some, from
Eber (<scripRef passage="Gen. 10:24" id="h-p242.1" parsed="|Gen|10|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.24">Gen. 10:24</scripRef>), the ancestor of Abraham. The Hebrews are
“sons of Eber” (10:21).
(2.) Others trace the name of a Hebrew root-word signifying
“to pass over,” and hence regard it as meaning “the man who
passed over,” viz., the Euphrates; or to the Hebrew word meaning
“the region” or “country beyond,” viz., the land of Chaldea.
This latter view is preferred. It is the more probable origin of
the designation given to Abraham coming among the Canaanites as
a man from beyond the Euphrates (Gen. 14:13).
(3.) A third derivation of the word has been suggested, viz.,
that it is from the Hebrew word ’abhar, “to pass over,” whence
’ebher, in the sense of a “sojourner” or “passer through” as
distinct from a “settler” in the land, and thus applies to the
condition of Abraham (Heb. 11:13).
</def>
<term id="h-p244.2">Hebrew language</term>
The language of the Hebrew nation, and that in which the Old
Testament is written, with the exception of a few portions in
Chaldee. In the Old Testament it is only spoken of as “Jewish”

(<scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:26" id="h-p245.1" parsed="|2Kgs|18|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.26">2 Kings 18:26</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:28" id="h-p245.2" parsed="|2Kgs|18|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.28">28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 36:11" id="h-p245.3" parsed="|Isa|36|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.36.11">Isa. 36:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 36:13" id="h-p245.4" parsed="|Isa|36|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.36.13">13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr 32:18" id="h-p245.5" parsed="|2Chr|32|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.32.18">2 Chr 32:18</scripRef>). This name is
first used by the Jews in times subsequent to the close of the
Old Testament.
It is one of the class of languages called Semitic, because
they were chiefly spoken among the descendants of Shem.
When Abraham entered Canaan it is obvious that he found the
language of its inhabitants closely allied to his own. Isaiah
(19:18) calls it “the language of Canaan.” Whether this
language, as seen in the earliest books of the Old Testament,
was the very dialect which Abraham brought with him into Canaan,
or whether it was the common tongue of the Canaanitish nations
which he only adopted, is uncertain; probably the latter opinion
is the correct one. For the thousand years between Moses and the
Babylonian exile the Hebrew language underwent little or no
modification. It preserves all through a remarkable uniformity
of structure. From the first it appears in its full maturity of
development. But through intercourse with Damascus, Assyria, and
Babylon, from the time of David, and more particularly from the
period of the Exile, it comes under the influence of the Aramaic
idiom, and this is seen in the writings which date from this
period. It was never spoken in its purity by the Jews after
their return from Babylon. They now spoke Hebrew with a large
admixture of Aramaic or Chaldee, which latterly became the
predominant element in the national language.
The Hebrew of the Old Testament has only about six thousand
words, all derived from about five hundred roots. Hence the same
word has sometimes a great variety of meanings. So long as it
was a living language, and for ages after, only the consonants
of the words were written. This also has been a source of
difficulty in interpreting certain words, for the meaning varies
according to the vowels which may be supplied. The Hebrew is one
of the oldest languages of which we have any knowledge. It is
essentially identical with the Phoenician language. (See MOABITE STONE.) The Semitic languages, to which class the
Hebrew and Phoenician belonged, were spoken over a very wide
area: in Babylonia, Mesopotamia, Syria, Palestine and Arabia, in
all the countries from the Mediterranean to the borders of
Assyria, and from the mountains of Armenia to the Indian Ocean.
The rounded form of the letters, as seen in the Moabite stone,
was probably that in which the ancient Hebrew was written down
to the time of the Exile, when the present square or Chaldean
form was adopted.
</def>
<term id="h-p248.2">Hebrew of the Hebrews</term>
One whose parents are both Hebrews (Phil. 3:5; 2 Cor. 11:22); a
genuine Hebrew.
</def>
<term id="h-p249.3">Hebrews</term>
(Acts 6:1) were the Hebrew-speaking Jews, as distinguished from
those who spoke Greek. (See GREEKS.)
</def>
<term id="h-p250.3">Hebrews, Epistle to</term>
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="h-p250.5" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="Heb 0" id="h-p250.6" parsed="|Heb|0|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb" />
(1.) Its canonicity. All the results of critical and historical
research to which this epistle has been specially subjected
abundantly vindicate its right to a place in the New Testament
canon among the other inspired books.
(2.) Its authorship. A considerable variety of opinions on
this subject has at different times been advanced. Some have
maintained that its author was Silas, Paul’s companion. Others
have attributed it to Clement of Rome, or Luke, or Barnabas, or
some unknown Alexandrian Christian, or Apollos; but the
conclusion which we think is best supported, both from internal
and external evidence, is that Paul was its author. There are,
no doubt, many difficulties in the way of accepting it as
Paul’s; but we may at least argue with Calvin that there can be
no difficulty in the way of “embracing it without controversy as
one of the apostolical epistles.”
(3.) Date and place of writing. It was in all probability
written at Rome, near the close of Paul’s two years’

imprisonment (<scripRef passage="Heb. 13:19" id="h-p253.1" parsed="|Heb|13|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.13.19">Heb. 13:19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Heb. 13:24" id="h-p253.2" parsed="|Heb|13|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.13.24">24</scripRef>). It was certainly written before
the destruction of Jerusalem (13:10).
(4.) To whom addressed. Plainly it was intended for Jewish
converts to the faith of the gospel, probably for the church at
Jerusalem. The subscription of this epistle is, of course,
without authority. In this case it is incorrect, for obviously
Timothy could not be the bearer of it (13:23).
(5.) Its design was to show the true end and meaning of the
Mosaic system, and its symbolical and transient character. It
proves that the Levitical priesthood was a “shadow” of that of
Christ, and that the legal sacrifices prefigured the great and
all-perfect sacrifice he offered for us. It explains that the
gospel was designed, not to modify the law of Moses, but to
supersede and abolish it. Its teaching was fitted, as it was
designed, to check that tendency to apostatize from Christianity
and to return to Judaism which now showed itself among certain
Jewish Christians. The supreme authority and the transcendent
glory of the gospel are clearly set forth, and in such a way as
to strengthen and confirm their allegiance to Christ.
(6.) It consists of two parts: (a) doctrinal (1-10:18), (b)
and practical (10:19-ch. 13). There are found in it many
references to portions of the Old Testament. It may be regarded
as a treatise supplementary to the Epistles to the Romans and
Galatians, and as an inspired commentary on the book of
Leviticus.
</def>
<term id="h-p256.1">Hebron</term>
A community; alliance. (1.) A city in the south end of the
valley of Eshcol, about midway between Jerusalem and Beersheba,
from which it is distant about 20 miles in a straight line. It

was built “seven years before Zoan in Egypt” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 13:18" id="h-p257.1" parsed="|Gen|13|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.13.18">Gen. 13:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 13:22" id="h-p257.2" parsed="|Num|13|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.13.22">Num. 13:22</scripRef>). It still exists under the same name, and is one of the
most ancient cities in the world. Its earlier name was

Kirjath-arba (<scripRef passage="Gen. 23:2" id="h-p257.3" parsed="|Gen|23|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.23.2">Gen. 23:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 14:15" id="h-p257.4" parsed="|Josh|14|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.14.15">Josh. 14:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 15:3" id="h-p257.5" parsed="|Josh|15|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.3">15:3</scripRef>). But “Hebron would
appear to have been the original name of the city, and it was
not till after Abraham’s stay there that it received the name
Kirjath-arba, who [i.e., Arba] was not the founder but the
conqueror of the city, having led thither the tribe of the
Anakim, to which he belonged. It retained this name till it came
into the possession of Caleb, when the Israelites restored the
original name Hebron” (Keil, Com.). The name of this city does
not occur in any of the prophets or in the New Testament. It is
found about forty times in the Old. It was the favorite home of
Abraham. Here he pitched his tent under the oaks of Mamre, by
which name it came afterwards to be known; and here Sarah died,
and was buried in the cave of Machpelah (<scripRef passage="Gen. 23:17-20" id="h-p257.6" parsed="|Gen|23|17|23|20" osisRef="Bible:Gen.23.17-Gen.23.20">Gen. 23:17-20</scripRef>), which
he bought from Ephron the Hittite. From this place the patriarch
departed for Egypt by way of Beersheba (37:14; 46:1). It was

taken by Joshua and given to Caleb (<scripRef passage="Josh. 10:36" id="h-p257.7" parsed="|Josh|10|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.36">Josh. 10:36</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 10:37" id="h-p257.8" parsed="|Josh|10|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.37">37</scripRef>; 12:10;
14:13). It became a Levitical city and a city of refuge (20:7;
21:11). When David became king of Judah this was his royal

residence, and he resided here for seven and a half years (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 5:5" id="h-p257.9" parsed="|2Sam|5|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.5.5">2 Sam. 5:5</scripRef>); and here he was anointed as king over all Israel (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 2:1-4" id="h-p257.10" parsed="|2Sam|2|1|2|4" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.2.1-2Sam.2.4">2 Sam. 2:1-4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 2:11" id="h-p257.11" parsed="|2Sam|2|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.2.11">11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 2:11" id="h-p257.12" parsed="|1Kgs|2|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.2.11">1 Kings 2:11</scripRef>). It became the residence also of
the rebellious Absalom (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 15:10" id="h-p257.13" parsed="|2Sam|15|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.15.10">2 Sam. 15:10</scripRef>), who probably expected to
find his chief support in the tribe of Judah, now called
el-Khulil.
In one part of the modern city is a great mosque, which is
built over the grave of Machpelah. The first European who was
permitted to enter this mosque was the Prince of Wales in 1862.
It was also visited by the Marquis of Bute in 1866, and by the
late Emperor Frederick of Germany (then Crown-Prince of Prussia)
One of the largest oaks in Palestine is found in the valley of
Eshcol, about 3 miles north of the town. It is supposed by some
to be the tree under which Abraham pitched his tent, and is
called “Abraham’s oak.” (See OAK.)
(2.) The third son of Kohath the Levite (Ex. 6:18; 1 Chr. 6:2, 18).
(3.) 1 Chr. 2:42, 43.
(4.) A town in the north border of Asher (Josh. 19:28).
</def>
<term id="h-p262.2">Hegai</term>
Eunuch, had charge of the harem of Ahasuerus (Esther 2:8).
</def>
<term id="h-p263.2">Heifer</term>
Heb. ‘eglah, (Deut. 21:4, 6; Jer. 46:20). Untrained to the yoke

(<scripRef passage="Hos. 10:11" id="h-p264.4" parsed="|Hos|10|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.10.11">Hos. 10:11</scripRef>); giving milk (<scripRef passage="Isa. 7:21" id="h-p264.5" parsed="|Isa|7|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.7.21">Isa. 7:21</scripRef>); ploughing (<scripRef passage="Judg. 14:18" id="h-p264.6" parsed="|Judg|14|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.14.18">Judg. 14:18</scripRef>);
treading out grain (<scripRef passage="Jer. 50:11" id="h-p264.7" parsed="|Jer|50|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.50.11">Jer. 50:11</scripRef>); unsubdued to the yoke an emblem
of Judah (Isa. 15:5; Jer. 48:34).
Heb. parah (Gen. 41:2; Num. 19:2). Bearing the yoke (Hos. 4:16); “heifers of Bashan” (Amos 4:1), metaphorical for the
voluptuous females of Samaria. The ordinance of sacrifice of the
“red heifer” described in Num. 19:1-10; comp. Heb. 9:13.
</def>
<term id="h-p265.7">Heir</term>
Under the patriarchs the property of a father was divided among

the sons of his legitimate wives (<scripRef passage="Gen. 21:10" id="h-p266.1" parsed="|Gen|21|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.10">Gen. 21:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 24:36" id="h-p266.2" parsed="|Gen|24|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24.36">24:36</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 25:5" id="h-p266.3" parsed="|Gen|25|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.5">25:5</scripRef>), the
eldest son getting a larger portion than the rest. The Mosaic
law made specific regulations regarding the transmission of real

property, which are given in detail in <scripRef passage="Deut. 21:17" id="h-p266.4" parsed="|Deut|21|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.21.17">Deut. 21:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 27:8" id="h-p266.5" parsed="|Num|27|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.27.8">Num. 27:8</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Num 36:6" id="h-p266.6" parsed="|Num|36|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.36.6">36:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 27:9-11" id="h-p266.7" parsed="|Num|27|9|27|11" osisRef="Bible:Num.27.9-Num.27.11">27:9-11</scripRef>. Succession to property was a matter of right and
not of favour. Christ is the “heir of all things” (<scripRef passage="Heb. 1:2" id="h-p266.8" parsed="|Heb|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.1.2">Heb. 1:2</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Col. 1:15" id="h-p266.9" parsed="|Col|1|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.1.15">Col. 1:15</scripRef>). Believers are heirs of the “promise,” “of
righteousness,” “of the kingdom,” “of the world,” “of God,”

“joint heirs” with Christ (<scripRef passage="Gal 3:29" id="h-p266.10" parsed="|Gal|3|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.3.29">Gal 3:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 6:17" id="h-p266.11" parsed="|Heb|6|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.6.17">Heb. 6:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb 11:7" id="h-p266.12" parsed="|Heb|11|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.11.7">11:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="James 2:5" id="h-p266.13" parsed="|Jas|2|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jas.2.5">James 2:5</scripRef>;
Rom. 4:13; 8:17).
</def>
<term id="h-p266.16">Helah</term>
Rust, (1 Chr. 4:5, 7), one of the wives of Ashur.
</def>
<term id="h-p267.3">Helam</term>
Place of abundance, a place on the east of Jordan and west of
the Euphrates where David gained a great victory over the Syrian
army (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 10:16" id="h-p268.1" parsed="|2Sam|10|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.10.16">2 Sam. 10:16</scripRef>), which was under the command of Shobach.
Some would identify it with Alamatta, near Nicephorium.
</def>
<term id="h-p268.2">Helbah</term>
Fatness, a town of the tribe of Asher (Judg. 1:31), in the plain
of Phoenicia.
</def>
<term id="h-p269.2">Helbon</term>
Fat; i.e., “fertile”, (Ezek. 27: 18 only), a place whence wine
was brought to the great market of Tyre. It has been usually
identified with the modern Aleppo, called Haleb by the native
Arabs, but is more probably to be found in one of the villages
in the Wady Helbon, which is celebrated for its grapes, on the
east slope of Anti-Lebanon, north of the river Barada (Abana).
</def>
<term id="h-p270.2">Heldai</term>
Wordly. (1.) 1 Chr. 27:15; called also Heleb (2 Sam. 23:29); one
of David’s captains.
(2.) Zech. 6:10, one who returned from Babylon.
</def>
<term id="h-p272.2">Heleb</term>
Fatness, one of David’s warriors (2 Sam. 23:29).
</def>
<term id="h-p273.2">Heled</term>
This world, (1 Chr. 11:30); called Heleb (2 Sam. 23:29).
</def>
<term id="h-p274.3">Helek</term>
A portion, (Josh. 17:2), descended from Manasseh.
</def>
<term id="h-p275.2">Helem</term>
A stroke, great-grandson of Asher (1 Chr. 7:35).
</def>
<term id="h-p276.2">Heleph</term>
Exchange, a city on the north border of Naphtali (Josh. 19:33).
</def>
<term id="h-p277.2">Helez</term>
Strong, or loin (?) (1.) One of Judah’s posterity (1 Chr. 2:39).
(2.) One of David’s warriors (2 Sam. 23:26).
</def>
<term id="h-p279.2">Heli</term>
Elevation, father of Joseph in the line of our Lord’s ancestry
(Luke 3:23).
</def>
<term id="h-p280.2">Helkai</term>
Smooth-tongued, one of the chief priests in the time of Joiakim
(Neh. 12:15).
</def>
<term id="h-p281.2">Helkath</term>
Smoothness, a town of Asher, on the east border (Josh. 19:25;
21:31); called also Hukok (1 Chr. 6:75).
</def>
<term id="h-p282.4">Helkath-hazzurim</term>
Plot of the sharp blades, or the field of heroes, (2 Sam. 2:16).
After the battle of Gilboa, so fatal to Saul and his house,
David, as divinely directed, took up his residence in Hebron,
and was there anointed king over Judah. Among the fugitives from
Gilboa was Ish-bosheth, the only surviving son of Saul, whom
Abner, Saul’s uncle, took across the Jordan to Mahanaim, and
there had him proclaimed king. Abner gathered all the forces at
his command and marched to Gibeon, with the object of wresting
Judah from David. Joab had the command of David’s army of
trained men, who encamped on the south of the pool, which was on
the east of the hill on which the town of Gibeon was built,
while Abner’s army lay on the north of the pool. Abner proposed
that the conflict should be decided by twelve young men engaging
in personal combat on either side. So fiercely did they
encounter each other that “they caught every man his fellow by
the head, and thrust his sword in his fellow’s side; so they
fell down together: wherefore that place was called
Helkath-hazzurim.” The combat of the champions was thus
indecisive, and there followed a severe general engagement
between the two armies, ending in the total rout of the
Israelites under Abner. The general result of this battle was
that “David waxed stronger and stronger, and the house of Saul
waxed weaker and weaker” (2 Sam. 3:1). (See GIBEON.)
</def>
<term id="h-p283.4">Hell</term>
Derived from the Saxon helan, to cover; hence the covered or the
invisible place. In Scripture there are three words so rendered:
(1.) Sheol, occurring in the Old Testament sixty-five times.
This word sheol is derived from a root-word meaning “to ask,”

“demand;” hence insatiableness (<scripRef passage="Prov. 30:15" id="h-p285.1" parsed="|Prov|30|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.30.15">Prov. 30:15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Prov. 30:16" id="h-p285.2" parsed="|Prov|30|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.30.16">16</scripRef>). It is rendered

“grave” thirty-one times (<scripRef passage="Gen. 37:35" id="h-p285.3" parsed="|Gen|37|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.35">Gen. 37:35</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 42:38" id="h-p285.4" parsed="|Gen|42|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.42.38">42:38</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 44:29" id="h-p285.5" parsed="|Gen|44|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.44.29">44:29</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 44:31" id="h-p285.6" parsed="|Gen|44|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.44.31">31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 2:6" id="h-p285.7" parsed="|1Sam|2|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.2.6">1 Sam. 2:6</scripRef>, etc.). The Revisers have retained this rendering in the
historical books with the original word in the margin, while in
the poetical books they have reversed this rule.
In thirty-one cases in the Authorized Version this word is
rendered “hell,” the place of disembodied spirits. The

inhabitants of sheol are “the congregation of the dead” (<scripRef passage="Prov. 21:16" id="h-p286.1" parsed="|Prov|21|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.21.16">Prov. 21:16</scripRef>). It is (a) the abode of the wicked (<scripRef passage="Num. 16:33" id="h-p286.2" parsed="|Num|16|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.16.33">Num. 16:33</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 24:19" id="h-p286.3" parsed="|Job|24|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.24.19">Job 24:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 9:17" id="h-p286.4" parsed="|Ps|9|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.9.17">Ps. 9:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 31:17" id="h-p286.5" parsed="|Ps|31|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.31.17">31:17</scripRef>, etc.); (b) of the good (<scripRef passage="Ps. 16:10" id="h-p286.6" parsed="|Ps|16|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.16.10">Ps. 16:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 30:3" id="h-p286.7" parsed="|Ps|30|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.30.3">30:3</scripRef>;
49:15; 86:13, etc.).
Sheol is described as deep (Job 11:8), dark (10:21, 22), with
bars (17:16). The dead “go down” to it (Num. 16:30, 33; Ezek. 31:15, 16, 17).
(2.) The Greek word hades of the New Testament has the same
scope of signification as sheol of the Old Testament. It is a
prison (1 Pet. 3:19), with gates and bars and locks (Matt. 16:18; Rev. 1:18), and it is downward (Matt. 11:23; Luke 10:15).
The righteous and the wicked are separated. The blessed dead
are in that part of hades called paradise (<scripRef passage="Luke 23:43" id="h-p289.1" parsed="|Luke|23|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.23.43">Luke 23:43</scripRef>). They are
also said to be in Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:22).
(3.) Gehenna, in most of its occurrences in the Greek New
Testament, designates the place of the lost (<scripRef passage="Matt. 23:33" id="h-p290.1" parsed="|Matt|23|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.23.33">Matt. 23:33</scripRef>). The
fearful nature of their condition there is described in various
figurative expressions (Matt. 8:12; 13:42; 22:13; 25:30; Luke 16:24, etc.). (See HINNOM.)
</def>
<term id="h-p290.8">Helmet</term>
(Heb. kob’a), a cap for the defence of the head (1 Sam. 17:5, 38). In the New Testament the Greek equivalent is used (Eph. 6:17; 1 Thess. 5:8). (See ARMS.)
</def>
<term id="h-p291.6">Helon</term>
Strong, father of Eliab, who was “captain of the children of
Zebulun” (Num. 1:9; 2:7).
</def>
<term id="h-p292.3">Help-meet</term>
(Heb. ‘ezer ke-negdo; i.e., “a help as his counterpart” = a help
suitable to him), a wife (Gen. 2:18-20).
</def>
<term id="h-p293.2">Helps</term>
(1 Cor. 12:28) may refer to help (i.e., by interpretation) given
to him who speaks with tongues, or more probably simply help
which Christians can render to one another, such as caring for
the poor and needy, etc.
</def>
<term id="h-p294.2">Hem</term>
Of a garment, the fringe of a garment. The Jews attached much

importance to these, because of the regulations in <scripRef passage="Num. 15:38" id="h-p295.1" parsed="|Num|15|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.15.38">Num. 15:38</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num 15:39" id="h-p295.2" parsed="|Num|15|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.15.39">39</scripRef>. These borders or fringes were in process of time enlarged so
as to attract special notice (<scripRef passage="Matt. 23:5" id="h-p295.3" parsed="|Matt|23|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.23.5">Matt. 23:5</scripRef>). The hem of Christ’s
garment touched (9:20; 14:36; Luke 8:44).
</def>
<term id="h-p295.5">Heman</term>
Faithful. (1.) 1 Kings 4:31; 1 Chr. 2:6, a son of Zerah, noted

for his wisdom. (2.) Grandson of Samuel (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 6:33" id="h-p296.3" parsed="|1Chr|6|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.6.33">1 Chr. 6:33</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 15:17" id="h-p296.4" parsed="|1Chr|15|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.15.17">15:17</scripRef>), to
whom the 88th Psalm probably was inscribed. He was one of the

“seers” named in <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 29:14" id="h-p296.5" parsed="|2Chr|29|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.29.14">2 Chr. 29:14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 29:30" id="h-p296.6" parsed="|2Chr|29|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.29.30">30</scripRef>, and took a leading part in
the administration of the sacred services.
</def>
<term id="h-p296.7">Hemath</term>
A Kenite (1 Chr. 2:55), the father of the house of Rechab.
</def>
<term id="h-p297.2">Hemlock</term>
(1.) Heb. rosh (Hos. 10:4; rendered “gall” in Deut. 29:18;

<scripRef passage="Deut 32:32" id="h-p298.3" parsed="|Deut|32|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.32">32:32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 69:21" id="h-p298.4" parsed="|Ps|69|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.69.21">Ps. 69:21</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 9:15" id="h-p298.5" parsed="|Jer|9|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.9.15">Jer. 9:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer 23:15" id="h-p298.6" parsed="|Jer|23|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.23.15">23:15</scripRef>; “poison,” <scripRef passage="Job 20:16" id="h-p298.7" parsed="|Job|20|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.20.16">Job 20:16</scripRef>;
