“venom,” <scripRef passage="Deut. 32:33" id="h-p298.8" parsed="|Deut|32|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.32.33">Deut. 32:33</scripRef>). “Rosh is the name of some poisonous plant
which grows quickly and luxuriantly; of a bitter taste, and

therefore coupled with wormwood (<scripRef passage="Deut. 29:18" id="h-p298.9" parsed="|Deut|29|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.29.18">Deut. 29:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lam. 3:19" id="h-p298.10" parsed="|Lam|3|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lam.3.19">Lam. 3:19</scripRef>). Hence
it would seem to be not the hemlock cicuta, nor the colocynth or
wild gourd, nor lolium darnel, but the poppy so called from its
heads” (Gesenius, Lex.).
(2.) Heb. la’anah, generally rendered “wormwood” (q.v.), Deut. 29:18, Text 17; Prov. 5:4; Jer. 9:15; 23:15. Once it is rendered
“hemlock” (<scripRef passage="Amos 6:12" id="h-p299.5" parsed="|Amos|6|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Amos.6.12">Amos 6:12</scripRef>; R.V., “wormwood”). This Hebrew word is
from a root meaning “to curse,” hence the accursed.
</def>
<term id="h-p299.6">Hen</term>
Common in later times among the Jews in Palestine (Matt. 23:37;
<scripRef passage="Luke 13:34" id="h-p300.2" parsed="|Luke|13|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.13.34">Luke 13:34</scripRef>). It is noticeable that this familiar bird is only
mentioned in these passages in connection with our Lord’s
lamentation over the impenitence of Jerusalem.
</def>
<term id="h-p300.3">Hena</term>
One of the cities of Mesopotamia destroyed by sennacherib (2 Kings 18:34; 19:13). It is identified with the modern Anah,
lying on the right bank of the Euphrates, not far from
Sepharvaim.
</def>
<term id="h-p301.3">Henadad</term>
Favour of Hadad, the name of a Levite after the Captivity (Ezra 3:9).
</def>
<term id="h-p302.2">Henoch</term>
See ENOCH.
</def>
<term id="h-p303.2">Hepher</term>
A well or stream. (1.) A royal city of the Canaanites taken by
(2.) The youngest son of Gilead (Num. 26:32; 27:1).
(3.) The second son of Asher (1 Chr. 4:6).
(4.) One of David’s heroes (1 Chr. 11:36).
</def>
<term id="h-p307.2">Hephzibah</term>
My delight is in her. (1.) The wife of Hezekiah and mother of
king Manasseh (2 Kings 21:1).
(2.) A symbolical name of Zion, as representing the Lord’s
favour toward her (Isa. 62:4).
</def>
<term id="h-p309.2">Herb</term>
(1.) Heb. ‘eseb, any green plant; herbage (Gen. 1:11, 12, 29, 30; 2:5; 3:18, etc.); comprehending vegetables and all green
herbage (Amos 7:1, 2).
(2.) Yarak, green; any green thing; foliage of trees (2 Kings 19:26; Ps. 37:2); a plant; herb (Deut. 11:10).
(3.) Or, meaning “light” In Isa. 26:19 it means “green
herbs;” in 2 Kings 4:39 probably the fruit of some plant.
(4.) Merorim, plural, “bitter herbs,” eaten by the

Israelites at the Passover (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:8" id="h-p313.1" parsed="|Exod|12|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.8">Ex. 12:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 9:11" id="h-p313.2" parsed="|Num|9|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.9.11">Num. 9:11</scripRef>). They were
bitter plants of various sorts, and referred symbolically to the
oppression in Egypt.
</def>
<term id="h-p313.3">Herd</term>
Gen. 13:5; Deut. 7:14. (See CATTLE.)
</def>
<term id="h-p314.4">Herdsman</term>
In Egypt herdsmen were probably of the lowest caste. Some of

Joseph’s brethren were made rulers over Pharaoh’s cattle (<scripRef passage="Gen. 47:6" id="h-p315.1" parsed="|Gen|47|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.47.6">Gen. 47:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 47:17" id="h-p315.2" parsed="|Gen|47|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.47.17">17</scripRef>). The Israelites were known in Egypt as “keepers of
cattle;” and when they left it they took their flocks and herds
with them (<scripRef passage="Ex. 12:38" id="h-p315.3" parsed="|Exod|12|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.38">Ex. 12:38</scripRef>). Both David and Saul came from “following

the herd” to occupy the throne (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 9" id="h-p315.4" parsed="|1Sam|9|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.9">1 Sam. 9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 11:5" id="h-p315.5" parsed="|1Sam|11|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.11.5">11:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 78:70" id="h-p315.6" parsed="|Ps|78|70|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.78.70">Ps. 78:70</scripRef>).
David’s herd-masters were among his chief officers of state. The
daughters also of wealthy chiefs were wont to tend the flocks of

the family (<scripRef passage="Gen. 29:9" id="h-p315.7" parsed="|Gen|29|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.29.9">Gen. 29:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex. 2:16" id="h-p315.8" parsed="|Exod|2|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.2.16">Ex. 2:16</scripRef>). The “chief of the herdsmen”

was in the time of the monarchy an officer of high rank (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 21:7" id="h-p315.9" parsed="|1Sam|21|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.21.7">1 Sam. 21:7</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 27:29" id="h-p315.10" parsed="|1Chr|27|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.27.29">1 Chr. 27:29</scripRef>). The herdsmen lived in tents (<scripRef passage="Isa. 38:12" id="h-p315.11" parsed="|Isa|38|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.38.12">Isa. 38:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 6:3" id="h-p315.12" parsed="|Jer|6|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.6.3">Jer. 6:3</scripRef>); and there were folds for the cattle (<scripRef passage="Num. 32:16" id="h-p315.13" parsed="|Num|32|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.32.16">Num. 32:16</scripRef>), and watch-towers for the herdsmen, that he might
therefrom observe any coming danger (Micah 4:8; Nah. 3:8).
</def>
<term id="h-p315.16">Heres</term>
Sun. (1.) “Mount Heres” (Judg. 1:35), Heb. Har-heres, i.e.,
“sun-mountain;” probably identical with Irshemesh in Josh. 19:41.
(2.) Isa. 19:18, marg. (See ON.)
</def>
<term id="h-p317.3">Heresy</term>
From a Greek word signifying (1) a choice, (2) the opinion
chosen, and (3) the sect holding the opinion. In the Acts of the
Apostles (5:17; 15:5; 24:5, 14; 26:5) it denotes a sect, without
reference to its character. Elsewhere, however, in the New
Testament it has a different meaning attached to it. Paul ranks
“heresies” with crimes and seditions (<scripRef passage="Gal. 5:20" id="h-p318.1" parsed="|Gal|5|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.5.20">Gal. 5:20</scripRef>). This word also
denotes divisions or schisms in the church (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 11:19" id="h-p318.2" parsed="|1Cor|11|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.11.19">1 Cor. 11:19</scripRef>). In
<scripRef passage="Titus 3:10" id="h-p318.3" parsed="|Titus|3|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Titus.3.10">Titus 3:10</scripRef> a “heretical person” is one who follows his own
self-willed “questions,” and who is to be avoided. Heresies thus
came to signify self-chosen doctrines not emanating from God (2 Pet. 2:1).
</def>
<term id="h-p318.4">Hermas</term>
Mercury, a Roman Christian to whom Paul sends greetings (Rom. 16: 14). Some suppose him to have been the author of the
celebrated religious romance called The Shepherd, but it is very
probable that that work is the production of a later generation.
</def>
<term id="h-p319.2">Hermes</term>
Mercury, a Roman Christian (Rom. 16:14).
</def>
<term id="h-p320.2">Hermogenes</term>
Mercury-born, at one time Paul’s fellow-labourer in Asia Minor,
who, however, afterwards abandoned him, along with one
Phygellus, probably on account of the perils by which they were
beset (2 Tim. 1:15).
</def>
<term id="h-p321.2">Hermon</term>
A peak, the eastern prolongation of the Anti-Lebanon range,
reaching to the height of about 9,200 feet above the

Mediterranean. It marks the north boundary of Palestine (<scripRef passage="Deut. 3:8" id="h-p322.1" parsed="|Deut|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.8">Deut. 3:8</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut 3:4" id="h-p322.2" parsed="|Deut|3|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.4">4</scripRef>:48; <scripRef passage="Josh. 11:3" id="h-p322.3" parsed="|Josh|11|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.3">Josh. 11:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 11:17" id="h-p322.4" parsed="|Josh|11|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.17">17</scripRef>; 13:11; 12:1), and is seen from a
great distance. It is about 40 miles north of the Sea of
Galilee. It is called “the Hermonites” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 42:6" id="h-p322.5" parsed="|Ps|42|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.42.6">Ps. 42:6</scripRef>) because it has
more than one summit. The Sidonians called it Sirion, and the

Amorites Shenir (<scripRef passage="Deut. 3:9" id="h-p322.6" parsed="|Deut|3|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.3.9">Deut. 3:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Cant. 4:8" id="h-p322.7" parsed="|Song|4|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.4.8">Cant. 4:8</scripRef>). It is also called

Baal-hermon (<scripRef passage="Judg. 3:3" id="h-p322.8" parsed="|Judg|3|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.3.3">Judg. 3:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 5:23" id="h-p322.9" parsed="|1Chr|5|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5.23">1 Chr. 5:23</scripRef>) and Sion (<scripRef passage="Deut. 4:48" id="h-p322.10" parsed="|Deut|4|48|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.4.48">Deut. 4:48</scripRef>).
There is every probability that one of its three summits was the
scene of the transfiguration (q.v.). The “dew of Hermon” is
referred to (<scripRef passage="Ps. 89" id="h-p322.11" parsed="|Ps|89|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.89">Ps. 89</scripRef>: 12). Its modern name is Jebel-esh-Sheikh,
“the chief mountain.” It is one of the most conspicuous
mountains in Palestine or Syria. “In whatever part of Palestine
the Israelite turned his eye northward, Hermon was there,
terminating the view. From the plain along the coast, from the
Jordan valley, from the heights of Moab and Gilead, from the
plateau of Bashan, the pale, blue, snow-capped cone forms the
one feature in the northern horizon.”
Our Lord and his disciples climbed this “high mountain apart”
one day, and remained on its summit all night, “weary after
their long and toilsome ascent.” During the night “he was
transfigured before them; and his face did shine as the sun.”
The next day they descended to Caesarea Philippi.
</def>
<term id="h-p323.1">Hermonites, the</term>
(Ps. 42:6, 7) = “the Hermons”, i.e., the three peaks or summits
of Hermon, which are about a quarter of a mile apart.
</def>
<term id="h-p324.3">Herod Agrippa I.</term>
Son of Aristobulus and Bernice, and grandson of Herod the Great.
He was made tetrarch of the provinces formerly held by Lysanias
II., and ultimately possessed the entire kingdom of his
grandfather, Herod the Great, with the title of king. He put the
apostle James the elder to death, and cast Peter into prison

(<scripRef passage="Luke 3:1" id="h-p325.1" parsed="|Luke|3|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.1">Luke 3:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 12:1-19" id="h-p325.2" parsed="|Acts|12|1|12|19" osisRef="Bible:Acts.12.1-Acts.12.19">Acts 12:1-19</scripRef>). On the second day of a festival held
in honour of the emperor Claudius, he appeared in the great
theatre of Caesarea. “The king came in clothed in magnificent
robes, of which silver was the costly brilliant material. It was
early in the day, and the sun’s rays fell on the king, so that
the eyes of the beholders were dazzled with the brightness which
surrounded him. Voices here and there from the crowd exclaimed
that it was the apparition of something divine. And when he
spoke and made an oration to them, they gave a shout, saying,
’It is the voice of a god, and not of a man.’ But in the midst
of this idolatrous ostentation an angel of God suddenly smote
him. He was carried out of the theatre a dying man.” He died
(A.D. 44) of the same loathsome malady which slew his
grandfather (<scripRef passage="Acts. 12:21-23" id="h-p325.3" parsed="|Acts|12|21|12|23" osisRef="Bible:Acts.12.21-Acts.12.23">Acts. 12:21-23</scripRef>), in the fifty-fourth year of his
age, having reigned four years as tetrarch and three as king
over the whole of Palestine. After his death his kingdom came
under the control of the prefect of Syria, and Palestine was now
fully incorporated with the empire.
</def>
<term id="h-p325.4">Herod Antipas</term>
Herod’s son by Malthace (Matt. 14:1; Luke 3:1, 19; 9:7; Acts 13:1). (See ANTIPAS.)
</def>
<term id="h-p326.6">Herod Archelaus</term>
(Matt. 2:22), the brother of Antipas (q.v.).
</def>
<term id="h-p327.2">Herod Arippa II.</term>
The son of Herod Agrippa I. and Cypros. The emperor Claudius
made him tetrarch of the provinces of Philip and Lysanias, with

the title of king (<scripRef passage="Acts 25:13" id="h-p328.1" parsed="|Acts|25|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.25.13">Acts 25:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 26:2" id="h-p328.2" parsed="|Acts|26|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.26.2">26:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 26:7" id="h-p328.3" parsed="|Acts|26|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.26.7">7</scripRef>). He enlarged the city of
Caesarea Philippi, and called it Neronias, in honour of Nero. It
was before him and his sister that Paul made his defence at
Caesarea (<scripRef passage="Acts 25:12-27" id="h-p328.4" parsed="|Acts|25|12|25|27" osisRef="Bible:Acts.25.12-Acts.25.27">Acts 25:12-27</scripRef>). He died at Rome A.D. 100, in the third
year of the emperor Trajan.
</def>
<term id="h-p328.5">Herodians</term>
A Jewish political party who sympathized with (Mark 3:6; 12:13;
Matt, 22:16; <scripRef passage="Luke 20:20" id="h-p329.3" parsed="|Luke|20|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.20.20">Luke 20:20</scripRef>) the Herodian rulers in their general
policy of government, and in the social customs which they
introduced from Rome. They were at one with the Sadducees in
holding the duty of submission to Rome, and of supporting the
Herods on the throne. (Comp. Mark 8:15; Matt. 16:6.)
</def>
<term id="h-p329.6">Herodias</term>
(Matt. 14:3-11; Mark 6:17-28; Luke 3:19), the daughter of
Aristobulus and Bernice. While residing at Rome with her husband
Herod Philip I. and her daughter, Herod Antipas fell in with her
during one of his journeys to that city. She consented to leave
her husband and become his wife. Some time after, Herod met John
the Baptist, who boldly declared the marriage to be unlawful.
For this he was “cast into prison,” in the castle probably of
Machaerus (q.v.), and was there subsequently beheaded.
</def>
<term id="h-p330.4">Herodion</term>
A Christian at Rome whom Paul salutes and calls his “kinsman”
(Rom. 16:11).
</def>
<term id="h-p331.2">Herod Philip I.</term>
(Mark 6:17), the son of Herod the Great by Mariamne, the
daughter of Simon, the high priest. He is distinguished from
another Philip called “the tetrarch.” He lived at Rome as a
private person with his wife Herodias and his daughter Salome.
</def>
<term id="h-p332.2">Herod Philip II.</term>
The son of Herod the Great and Cleopatra of Jerusalem. He was
“tetrarch” of Batanea, Iturea, Trachonitis, and Auranitis. He
rebuilt the city of Caesarea Philippi, calling it by his own
name to distinguish it from the Caesarea on the sea-coast which
was the seat of the Roman government. He married Salome, the
daughter of Herodias (Matt. 16:13; Mark 8:27; Luke 3:1).
</def>
<term id="h-p333.4">Herod the Great</term>
(Matt. 2:1-22; Luke 1:5; Acts 23:35), the son of Antipater, an
Idumaean, and Cypros, an Arabian of noble descent. In the year
B.C. 47 Julius Caesar made Antipater, a “wily Idumaean,”
procurator of Judea, who divided his territories between his
four sons, Galilee falling to the lot of Herod, who was
afterwards appointed tetrarch of Judea by Mark Antony (B.C. 40),
and also king of Judea by the Roman senate.
He was of a stern and cruel disposition. “He was brutish and a
stranger to all humanity.” Alarmed by the tidings of one “born
King of the Jews,” he sent forth and “slew all the children that
were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years
old and under” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 2:16" id="h-p335.1" parsed="|Matt|2|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.2.16">Matt. 2:16</scripRef>). He was fond of splendour, and
lavished great sums in rebuilding and adorning the cities of his
empire. He rebuilt the city of Caesarea (q.v.) on the coast, and
also the city of Samaria (q.v.), which he called Sebaste, in
honour of Augustus. He restored the ruined temple of Jerusalem,
a work which was begun B.C. 20, but was not finished till after
Herod’s death, probably not till about A.D. 50 (<scripRef passage="John 2:20" id="h-p335.2" parsed="|John|2|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.2.20">John 2:20</scripRef>).
After a troubled reign of thirty-seven years, he died at Jericho
amid great agonies both of body and mind, B.C. 4, i.e.,
according to the common chronology, in the year in which Jesus
was born.
After his death his kingdom was divided among three of his
sons. Of these, Philip had the land east of Jordan, between
Caesarea Philippi and Bethabara, Antipas had Galilee and Peraea,
while Archelaus had Judea and Samaria.
</def>
<term id="h-p336.1">Heron</term>
(Lev. 11:19; Deut. 14:18), ranked among the unclean birds. The
Hebrew name is ’anaphah, and indicates that the bird so named
is remarkable for its angry disposition. “The herons are
wading-birds, peculiarly irritable, remarkable for their
voracity, frequenting marshes and oozy rivers, and spread over
the regions of the East.” The Ardea russeta, or little golden
egret, is the commonest species in Asia.
</def>
<term id="h-p337.3">Heshbon</term>
Intelligence, a city ruled over by Sihon, king of the Amorites

(<scripRef passage="Josh. 3:10" id="h-p338.1" parsed="|Josh|3|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.3.10">Josh. 3:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 13:17" id="h-p338.2" parsed="|Josh|13|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.17">13:17</scripRef>). It was taken by Moses (<scripRef passage="Num. 21:23-26" id="h-p338.3" parsed="|Num|21|23|21|26" osisRef="Bible:Num.21.23-Num.21.26">Num. 21:23-26</scripRef>), and
became afterwards a Levitical city (<scripRef passage="Josh. 21:39" id="h-p338.4" parsed="|Josh|21|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.21.39">Josh. 21:39</scripRef>) in the tribe of
Reuben (<scripRef passage="Num. 32:37" id="h-p338.5" parsed="|Num|32|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.32.37">Num. 32:37</scripRef>). After the Exile it was taken possession of

by the Moabites (<scripRef passage="Isa. 15:4" id="h-p338.6" parsed="|Isa|15|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.15.4">Isa. 15:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 48:2" id="h-p338.7" parsed="|Jer|48|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.2">Jer. 48:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer. 48:34" id="h-p338.8" parsed="|Jer|48|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.34">34</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Jer. 48:45" id="h-p338.9" parsed="|Jer|48|45|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.45">45</scripRef>). The ruins of
this town are still seen about 20 miles east of Jordan from the
north end of the Dead Sea. There are reservoirs in this
district, which are probably the “fishpools” referred to in
Cant. 7:4.
</def>
<term id="h-p338.11">Heshmon</term>
Fatness, a town in the south of Judah (Josh. 15:27).
</def>
<term id="h-p339.2">Heth</term>
Dread, a descendant of Canaan, and the ancestor of the Hittites

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 10:18" id="h-p340.1" parsed="|Gen|10|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.18">Gen. 10:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 7:1" id="h-p340.2" parsed="|Deut|7|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.7.1">Deut. 7:1</scripRef>), who dwelt in the vicinity of Hebron

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 23:3" id="h-p340.3" parsed="|Gen|23|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.23.3">Gen. 23:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 23:7" id="h-p340.4" parsed="|Gen|23|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.23.7">7</scripRef>). The Hittites were a Hamitic race. They are
called “the sons of Heth” (Gen. 23:3, 5, 7, 10, 16, 18, 20).
</def>
<term id="h-p340.12">Hethlon</term>
Wrapped up, a place on the north border of Palestine. The “way

of Hethlon” (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 47:15" id="h-p341.1" parsed="|Ezek|47|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.47.15">Ezek. 47:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek 48:1" id="h-p341.2" parsed="|Ezek|48|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.48.1">48:1</scripRef>) is probably the pass at the end
of Lebanon from the Mediterranean to the great plain of Hamath
(q.v.), or the “entrance of Hamath.”
</def>
<term id="h-p341.3">Hezekiah</term>
Whom Jehovah has strengthened. (1.) Son of Ahaz (2 Kings 18:1; 2 Chr. 29:1), whom he succeeded on the throne of the kingdom of
Judah. He reigned twenty-nine years (B.C. 726-697). The history

of this king is contained in <scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:20" id="h-p342.3" parsed="|2Kgs|18|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.20">2 Kings 18:20</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 36" id="h-p342.4" parsed="|Isa|36|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.36">Isa. 36</scripRef>-39, and <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 29" id="h-p342.5" parsed="|2Chr|29|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.29">2 Chr. 29</scripRef>-32. He is spoken of as a great and good king. In public
life he followed the example of his great-granfather Uzziah. He
set himself to abolish idolatry from his kingdom, and among
other things which he did for this end, he destroyed the “brazen
serpent,” which had been removed to Jerusalem, and had become an
object of idolatrous worship (<scripRef passage="Num. 21:9" id="h-p342.6" parsed="|Num|21|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.21.9">Num. 21:9</scripRef>). A great reformation
was wrought in the kingdom of Judah in his day (2 Kings 18:4; 2 Chr. 29:3-36).
On the death of Sargon and the accession of his son
Sennacherib to the throne of Assyria, Hezekiah refused to pay
the tribute which his father had paid, and “rebelled against the
king of Assyria, and served him not,” but entered into a league

with Egypt (<scripRef passage="Isa. 30" id="h-p343.1" parsed="|Isa|30|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.30">Isa. 30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 31" id="h-p343.2" parsed="|Isa|31|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.31">31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 36:6-9" id="h-p343.3" parsed="|Isa|36|6|36|9" osisRef="Bible:Isa.36.6-Isa.36.9">36:6-9</scripRef>). This led to the invasion of
Judah by Sennacherib (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:13-16" id="h-p343.4" parsed="|2Kgs|18|13|18|16" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.13-2Kgs.18.16">2 Kings 18:13-16</scripRef>), who took forty cities,
and besieged Jerusalem with mounds. Hezekiah yielded to the
demands of the Assyrian king, and agreed to pay him three
hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold (18:14).
But Sennacherib dealt treacherously with Hezekiah (Isa. 33:1),

and a second time within two years invaded his kingdom (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:17" id="h-p344.2" parsed="|2Kgs|18|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.17">2 Kings 18:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 32:9" id="h-p344.3" parsed="|2Chr|32|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.32.9">2 Chr. 32:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 36" id="h-p344.4" parsed="|Isa|36|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.36">Isa. 36</scripRef>). This invasion issued in the
destruction of Sennacherib’s army. Hezekiah prayed to God, and
“that night the angel of the Lord went out, and smote in the
camp of the Assyrians 185,000 men.” Sennacherib fled with the
shattered remnant of his forces to Nineveh, where, seventeen
years after, he was assassinated by his sons Adrammelech and
Sharezer (2 Kings 19:37). (See SENNACHERIB.)
The narrative of Hezekiah’s sickness and miraculous recovery

is found in <scripRef passage="2 Kings 20:1" id="h-p345.1" parsed="|2Kgs|20|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.20.1">2 Kings 20:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 20:2" id="h-p345.2" parsed="|2Kgs|20|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.20.2">2</scripRef> Chr. 32:24, <scripRef passage="Isa. 38:1" id="h-p345.3" parsed="|Isa|38|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.38.1">Isa. 38:1</scripRef>. Various
ambassadors came to congratulate him on his recovery, and among

them Merodach-baladan, the viceroy of Babylon (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 32:23" id="h-p345.4" parsed="|2Chr|32|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.32.23">2 Chr. 32:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 20:12" id="h-p345.5" parsed="|2Kgs|20|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.20.12">2 Kings 20:12</scripRef>). He closed his days in peace and prosperity, and
was succeeded by his son Manasseh. He was buried in the

“chiefest of the sepulchres of the sons of David” (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 32:27-33" id="h-p345.6" parsed="|2Chr|32|27|32|33" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.32.27-2Chr.32.33">2 Chr. 32:27-33</scripRef>). He had “after him none like him among all the kings
of Judah, nor any that were before him” (2 Kings 18:5). (See ISAIAH.)
</def>
<term id="h-p345.9">Hezion</term>
Vision, the father of Tabrimon, and grandfather of Ben-hadad,
king of Syria (1 Kings 15:18).
</def>
<term id="h-p346.2">Hezir</term>
Swine or strong. (1.) The head of the seventeenth course of the

priests (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 24:15" id="h-p347.1" parsed="|1Chr|24|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.24.15">1 Chr. 24:15</scripRef>). (2.) <scripRef passage="Neh. 10:20" id="h-p347.2" parsed="|Neh|10|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.10.20">Neh. 10:20</scripRef>, one who sealed
Nehemiah’s covenant.
</def>
<term id="h-p347.3">Hezro</term>
A Carmelite, one of David’s warriors (1 Chr. 11:37).
</def>
<term id="h-p348.2">Hezron</term>
Enclosed. (1.) One of the sons of Reuben (Gen. 46:9; Ex. 6:14).
(2.) The older of the two sons of Pharez (<scripRef passage="Gen. 46:12" id="h-p349.3" parsed="|Gen|46|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.46.12">Gen. 46:12</scripRef>). (3.) A
plain in the south of Judah, west of Kadesh-barnea (Josh. 15:3).
</def>
<term id="h-p349.5">Hiddai</term>
Rejoicing of Jehovah, one of David’s thirty-seven guards (2 Sam. 23:30).
</def>
<term id="h-p350.2">Hiddekel</term>
Called by the Accadians id Idikla; i.e., “the river of Idikla”,
the third of the four rivers of Paradise (<scripRef passage="Gen. 2:14" id="h-p351.1" parsed="|Gen|2|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.2.14">Gen. 2:14</scripRef>). Gesenius
interprets the word as meaning “the rapid Tigris.” The Tigris
rises in the mountains of Armenia, 15 miles south of the source
of the Euphrates, which, after pursuing a south-east course, it
joins at Kurnah, about 50 miles above Bassorah. Its whole length
is about 1,150 miles.
</def>
<term id="h-p351.2">Hiel</term>
Life of (i.e., from) God, a native of Bethel, who built (i.e.,
fortified) Jericho some seven hundred years after its
destruction by the Israelites. There fell on him for such an act
the imprecation of Joshua (6:26). He laid the foundation in his

first-born, and set up the gates in his youngest son (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 16:34" id="h-p352.1" parsed="|1Kgs|16|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.16.34">1 Kings 16:34</scripRef>), i.e., during the progress of the work all his children
died.
</def>
<term id="h-p352.2">Hierapolis</term>
Sacred city, a city of Phrygia, where was a Christian church

under the care of Epaphras (<scripRef passage="Col. 4:12" id="h-p353.1" parsed="|Col|4|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.4.12">Col. 4:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Col. 4:13" id="h-p353.2" parsed="|Col|4|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.4.13">13</scripRef>). This church was
founded at the same time as that of Colosse. It now bears the
name of Pambuk-Kalek, i.e., “Cotton Castle”, from the white
appearance of the cliffs at the base of which the ruins are
found.
</def>
<term id="h-p353.3">Higgaion</term>
In Ps. 92:3 means the murmuring tone of the harp. In Ps. 9:16 it
is a musical sign, denoting probably a pause in the instrumental
interlude. In <scripRef passage="Ps. 19:14" id="h-p354.3" parsed="|Ps|19|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.19.14">Ps. 19:14</scripRef> the word is rendered “meditation;” and
in Lam. 3:62, “device” (R.V., “imagination”).
</def>
<term id="h-p354.5">High place</term>
An eminence, natural or artificial, where worship by sacrifice

or offerings was made (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 13:32" id="h-p355.1" parsed="|1Kgs|13|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.13.32">1 Kings 13:32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:29" id="h-p355.2" parsed="|2Kgs|17|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.29">2 Kings 17:29</scripRef>). The first
altar after the Flood was built on a mountain (<scripRef passage="Gen. 8:20" id="h-p355.3" parsed="|Gen|8|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.8.20">Gen. 8:20</scripRef>).
Abraham also built an altar on a mountain (12:7, 8). It was on a
mountain in Gilead that Laban and Jacob offered sacrifices
(31:54). After the Israelites entered the Promised Land they
were strictly enjoined to overthrow the high places of the

Canaanites (<scripRef passage="Ex. 34:13" id="h-p355.4" parsed="|Exod|34|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.34.13">Ex. 34:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 7:5" id="h-p355.5" parsed="|Deut|7|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.7.5">Deut. 7:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut 12:2" id="h-p355.6" parsed="|Deut|12|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.12.2">12:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Deut 12:3" id="h-p355.7" parsed="|Deut|12|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.12.3">3</scripRef>), and they were
forbidden to worship the Lord on high places (<scripRef passage="Deut. 12:11-14" id="h-p355.8" parsed="|Deut|12|11|12|14" osisRef="Bible:Deut.12.11-Deut.12.14">Deut. 12:11-14</scripRef>),

and were enjoined to use but one altar for sacrifices (<scripRef passage="Lev. 17:3" id="h-p355.9" parsed="|Lev|17|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.17.3">Lev. 17:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev 17:4" id="h-p355.10" parsed="|Lev|17|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.17.4">4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 12" id="h-p355.11" parsed="|Deut|12|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.12">Deut. 12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut 16:21" id="h-p355.12" parsed="|Deut|16|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.16.21">16:21</scripRef>). The injunction against high places
was, however, very imperfectly obeyed, and we find again and

again mention made of them (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 14:4" id="h-p355.13" parsed="|2Kgs|14|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.14.4">2 Kings 14:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 15:4" id="h-p355.14" parsed="|2Kgs|15|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.4">15:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 15:35" id="h-p355.15" parsed="|2Kgs|15|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.35">35</scripRef>:<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 15:17" id="h-p355.16" parsed="|2Chr|15|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.15.17">2 Chr. 15:17</scripRef>,
etc.).
</def>
<term id="h-p355.17">High priest</term>
Aaron was the first who was solemnly set apart to this office

(<scripRef passage="Ex. 29:7" id="h-p356.1" parsed="|Exod|29|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.7">Ex. 29:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 30:23" id="h-p356.2" parsed="|Exod|30|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.30.23">30:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Lev. 8:12" id="h-p356.3" parsed="|Lev|8|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.8.12">Lev. 8:12</scripRef>). He wore a peculiar dress, which on

his death passed to his successor in office (<scripRef passage="Ex. 29:29" id="h-p356.4" parsed="|Exod|29|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.29">Ex. 29:29</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 29:30" id="h-p356.5" parsed="|Exod|29|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.29.30">30</scripRef>).
Besides those garments which he wore in common with all priests,
there were four that were peculiar to himself as high priest:
(1.) The “robe” of the ephod, all of blue, of “woven work,”
worn immediately under the ephod. It was without seam or
sleeves. The hem or skirt was ornamented with pomegranates and
golden bells, seventy-two of each in alternate order. The
sounding of the bells intimated to the people in the outer court
the time when the high priest entered into the holy place to
burn incense before the Lord (Ex. 28).
(2.) The “ephod” consisted of two parts, one of which covered
the back and the other the breast, which were united by the
“curious girdle.” It was made of fine twined linen, and
ornamented with gold and purple. Each of the shoulder-straps was
adorned with a precious stone, on which the names of the twelve
tribes were engraved. This was the high priest’s distinctive
vestment (1 Sam. 2:28; 14:3; 21:9; 23:6, 9; 30:7).
(3.) The “breastplate of judgment” (Ex. 28:6-12, 25-28;
<scripRef passage="Ex 39:2-7" id="h-p359.3" parsed="|Exod|39|2|39|7" osisRef="Bible:Exod.39.2-Exod.39.7">39:2-7</scripRef>) of “cunning work.” It was a piece of cloth doubled, of
one span square. It bore twelve precious stones, set in four
rows of three in a row, which constituted the Urim and Thummim
(q.v.). These stones had the names of the twelve tribes engraved
on them. When the high priest, clothed with the ephod and the
breastplate, inquired of the Lord, answers were given in some

mysterious way by the Urim and Thummim (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 14:3" id="h-p359.4" parsed="|1Sam|14|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.14.3">1 Sam. 14:3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 14:18" id="h-p359.5" parsed="|1Sam|14|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.14.18">18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 14:19" id="h-p359.6" parsed="|1Sam|14|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.14.19">19</scripRef>;
23:2, 4, 9, 11, 12; 28:6; 2 Sam. 5:23).
(4.) The “mitre,” or upper turban, a twisted band of eight
yards of fine linen coiled into a cap, with a gold plate in
front, engraved with “Holiness to the Lord,” fastened to it by a
ribbon of blue.
To the high priest alone it was permitted to enter the holy of
holies, which he did only once a year, on the great Day of
Atonement, for “the way into the holiest of all was not yet made

manifest” (<scripRef passage="Heb. 9" id="h-p361.1" parsed="|Heb|9|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9">Heb. 9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb 10" id="h-p361.2" parsed="|Heb|10|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.10">10</scripRef>). Wearing his gorgeous priestly vestments,
he entered the temple before all the people, and then, laying
them aside and assuming only his linen garments in secret, he
entered the holy of holies alone, and made expiation, sprinkling
the blood of the sin offering on the mercy seat, and offering up
incense. Then resuming his splendid robes, he reappeared before
the people (<scripRef passage="Lev. 16" id="h-p361.3" parsed="|Lev|16|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.16">Lev. 16</scripRef>). Thus the wearing of these robes came to be
identified with the Day of Atonement.
The office, dress, and ministration of the high priest were

typical of the priesthood of our Lord (<scripRef passage="Heb. 4:14" id="h-p362.1" parsed="|Heb|4|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.4.14">Heb. 4:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb 7:25" id="h-p362.2" parsed="|Heb|7|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.7.25">7:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb 9:12" id="h-p362.3" parsed="|Heb|9|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.12">9:12</scripRef>,
etc.).
It is supposed that there were in all eighty-three high
priests, beginning with Aaron (B.C. 1657) and ending with
Phannias (A.D. 70). At its first institution the office of high
priest was held for life (but comp. <scripRef passage="1 Kings 2:27" id="h-p363.1" parsed="|1Kgs|2|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.2.27">1 Kings 2:27</scripRef>), and was
hereditary in the family of Aaron (<scripRef passage="Num. 3:10" id="h-p363.2" parsed="|Num|3|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.3.10">Num. 3:10</scripRef>). The office
continued in the line of Eleazar, Aaron’s eldest son, for two
hundred and ninety-six years, when it passed to Eli, the first
of the line of Ithamar, who was the fourth son of Aaron. In this
line it continued to Abiathar, whom Solomon deposed, and

appointed Zadok, of the family of Eleazar, in his stead (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 2:35" id="h-p363.3" parsed="|1Kgs|2|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.2.35">1 Kings 2:35</scripRef>), in which it remained till the time of the Captivity.
After the Return, Joshua, the son of Josedek, of the family of
Eleazar, was appointed to this office. After him the succession
was changed from time to time under priestly or political
influences.
</def>
<term id="h-p363.4">Highway</term>
A raised road for public use. Such roads were not found in
Palestine; hence the force of the language used to describe the

return of the captives and the advent of the Messiah (<scripRef passage="Isa. 11:16" id="h-p364.1" parsed="|Isa|11|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.11.16">Isa. 11:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 35:8" id="h-p364.2" parsed="|Isa|35|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.35.8">35:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 40:3" id="h-p364.3" parsed="|Isa|40|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.40.3">40:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 62:10" id="h-p364.4" parsed="|Isa|62|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.62.10">62:10</scripRef>) under the figure of the preparation of
a grand thoroughfare for their march.
During their possession of Palestine the Romans constructed
several important highways, as they did in all countries which
they ruled.
</def>
<term id="h-p365.1">Hilkiah</term>
Portion of Jehovah. (1.) 1 Chr. 6:54. (2.) 1 Chr. 26:11. (3.)

The father of Eliakim (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:18" id="h-p366.3" parsed="|2Kgs|18|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.18">2 Kings 18:18</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:26" id="h-p366.4" parsed="|2Kgs|18|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.26">26</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:37" id="h-p366.5" parsed="|2Kgs|18|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.37">37</scripRef>). (4.) The father
of Gemariah (<scripRef passage="Jer. 29:3" id="h-p366.6" parsed="|Jer|29|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.29.3">Jer. 29:3</scripRef>). (5.) The father of the prophet Jeremiah
(6.) The high priest in the reign of Josiah (1 Chr. 6:13; Ezra 7:1). To him and his deputy (2 Kings 23:5), along with the
ordinary priests and the Levites who had charge of the gates,
was entrusted the purification of the temple in Jerusalem. While
this was in progress, he discovered in some hidden corner of the
building a book called the “book of the law” (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 22:8" id="h-p367.4" parsed="|2Kgs|22|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.22.8">2 Kings 22:8</scripRef>) and
the “book of the covenant” (23:2). Some have supposed that this
“book” was nothing else than the original autograph copy of the
Pentateuch written by Moses (<scripRef passage="Deut. 31:9-26" id="h-p367.5" parsed="|Deut|31|9|31|26" osisRef="Bible:Deut.31.9-Deut.31.26">Deut. 31:9-26</scripRef>). This remarkable
discovery occurred in the eighteenth year of Josiah’s reign
(B.C. 624), a discovery which permanently affected the whole
subsequent history of Israel. (See JOSIAH; SHAPHAN.)
(7.) Neh. 12:7. (8.) Neh. 8:4.
</def>
<term id="h-p368.3">Hill</term>
(1.) Heb. gib’eah, a curved or rounded hill, such as are common
to Palestine (Ps. 65:12; 72:3; 114:4, 6).
(2.) Heb. har, properly a mountain range rather than an

individual eminence (<scripRef passage="Ex. 24:4" id="h-p370.1" parsed="|Exod|24|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.24.4">Ex. 24:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 24:12" id="h-p370.2" parsed="|Exod|24|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.24.12">12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 24:13" id="h-p370.3" parsed="|Exod|24|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.24.13">13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 24:18" id="h-p370.4" parsed="|Exod|24|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.24.18">18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 14:40" id="h-p370.5" parsed="|Num|14|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.14.40">Num. 14:40</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 14:44" id="h-p370.6" parsed="|Num|14|44|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.14.44">44</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 14:45" id="h-p370.7" parsed="|Num|14|45|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.14.45">45</scripRef>).

In <scripRef passage="Deut. 1:7" id="h-p370.8" parsed="|Deut|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.1.7">Deut. 1:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 9:1" id="h-p370.9" parsed="|Josh|9|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.9.1">Josh. 9:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 10:40" id="h-p370.10" parsed="|Josh|10|40|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.10.40">10:40</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 11:16" id="h-p370.11" parsed="|Josh|11|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.16">11:16</scripRef>, it denotes the elevated
district of Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim, which forms the
watershed between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea.
(3.) Heb. ma’aleh in 1 Sam. 9:11. Authorized Version “hill” is
correctly rendered in the Revised Version “ascent.”
(4.) In Luke 9:37 the “hill” is the Mount of Transfiguration.
</def>
<term id="h-p372.2">Hillel</term>
Praising, a Pirathonite, father of the judge Abdon (Judg. 12:13, 15).
</def>
<term id="h-p373.3">Hill of Evil Counsel</term>
On the south of the Valley of Hinnom. It is so called from a
tradition that the house of the high priest Caiaphas, when the
rulers of the Jews resolved to put Christ to death, stood here.
</def>
<term id="h-p374.1">Hind</term>
Heb. ‘ayalah (2 Sam. 22:34; Ps. 18:33, etc.) and ‘ayeleth (Ps. 22, title), the female of the hart or stag. It is referred to as

an emblem of activity (<scripRef passage="Gen. 49:21" id="h-p375.4" parsed="|Gen|49|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.49.21">Gen. 49:21</scripRef>), gentleness (<scripRef passage="Prov. 5:19" id="h-p375.5" parsed="|Prov|5|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.5.19">Prov. 5:19</scripRef>),

feminine modesty (<scripRef passage="Cant. 2:7" id="h-p375.6" parsed="|Song|2|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.2.7">Cant. 2:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Cant 3:5" id="h-p375.7" parsed="|Song|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.3.5">3:5</scripRef>), earnest longing (<scripRef passage="Ps. 42:1" id="h-p375.8" parsed="|Ps|42|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.42.1">Ps. 42:1</scripRef>),

timidity (<scripRef passage="Ps. 29:9" id="h-p375.9" parsed="|Ps|29|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.29.9">Ps. 29:9</scripRef>). In the title of <scripRef passage="Ps. 22" id="h-p375.10" parsed="|Ps|22|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.22">Ps. 22</scripRef>, the word probably
refers to some tune bearing that name.
</def>
<term id="h-p375.11">Hinge</term>
(Heb. tsir), that on which a door revolves. “Doors in the East
turn rather on pivots than on what we term hinges. In Syria, and
especially in the Hauran, there are many ancient doors,
consisting of stone slabs with pivots carved out of the same
piece inserted in sockets above and below, and fixed during the
building of the house” (Prov. 26:14).
</def>
<term id="h-p376.2">Hinnom</term>
A deep, narrow ravine separating Mount Zion from the so-called
“Hill of Evil Counsel.” It took its name from “some ancient
hero, the son of Hinnom.” It is first mentioned in <scripRef passage="Josh. 15:8" id="h-p377.1" parsed="|Josh|15|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.8">Josh. 15:8</scripRef>.
It had been the place where the idolatrous Jews burned their
children alive to Moloch and Baal. A particular part of the
valley was called Tophet, or the “fire-stove,” where the
children were burned. After the Exile, in order to show their
abhorrence of the locality, the Jews made this valley the
receptacle of the offal of the city, for the destruction of
which a fire was, as is supposed, kept constantly burning there.
The Jews associated with this valley these two ideas, (1) that
of the sufferings of the victims that had there been sacrificed;
and (2) that of filth and corruption. It became thus to the
popular mind a symbol of the abode of the wicked hereafter. It
came to signify hell as the place of the wicked. “It might be
shown by infinite examples that the Jews expressed hell, or the
place of the damned, by this word. The word Gehenna [the Greek
contraction of Hinnom] was never used in the time of Christ in
any other sense than to denote the place of future punishment.”
About this fact there can be no question. In this sense the word
is used eleven times in our Lord’s discourses (Matt. 23:33; Luke 12:5; Matt. 5:22, etc.).
</def>
<term id="h-p378.4">Hiram</term>
High-born. (1.) Generally “Huram,” one of the sons of Bela (1 Chr. 8:5).
(2.) Also “Huram” and “Horam,” king of Tyre. He entered into
an alliance with David, and assisted him in building his palace
by sending him able workmen, and also cedar-trees and fir-trees

from Lebanon (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 5:11" id="h-p380.1" parsed="|2Sam|5|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.5.11">2 Sam. 5:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 14:1" id="h-p380.2" parsed="|1Chr|14|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.14.1">1 Chr. 14:1</scripRef>). After the death of
David he entered into a similar alliance with Solomon, and

assisted him greatly in building the temple (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 5:1" id="h-p380.3" parsed="|1Kgs|5|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.5.1">1 Kings 5:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 9:11" id="h-p380.4" parsed="|1Kgs|9|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.9.11">9:11</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 2:3" id="h-p380.5" parsed="|2Chr|2|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.2.3">2 Chr. 2:3</scripRef>). He also took part in Solomon’s traffic to the
Eastern Seas (1 Kings 9:27; 10:11; 2 Chr. 8:18; 9:10).
(3.) The “master workman” whom Hiram sent to Solomon. He was

the son of a widow of Dan, and of a Tyrian father. In <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 2:13" id="h-p381.1" parsed="|2Chr|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.2.13">2 Chr. 2:13</scripRef> “Huram my father” should be Huram Abi, the word “Abi”
(rendered here “my father”) being regarded as a proper name, or
it may perhaps be a title of distinction given to Huram, and

equivalent to “master.” (Comp. <scripRef passage="1 Kings 7:14" id="h-p381.2" parsed="|1Kgs|7|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.7.14">1 Kings 7:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 4:16" id="h-p381.3" parsed="|2Chr|4|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.4.16">2 Chr. 4:16</scripRef>.) He
cast the magnificent brazen works for Solomon’s temple in
clay-beds in the valley of Jordan, between Succoth and Zarthan.
</def>
<term id="h-p381.4">Hireling</term>
A labourer employed on hire for a limited time (Job 7:1; 14:6;
<scripRef passage="Mark 1:20" id="h-p382.3" parsed="|Mark|1|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.20">Mark 1:20</scripRef>). His wages were paid as soon as his work was over
(<scripRef passage="Lev. 19:13" id="h-p382.4" parsed="|Lev|19|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.19.13">Lev. 19:13</scripRef>). In the time of our Lord a day’s wage was a “penny”
(q.v.) i.e., a Roman denarius (Matt. 20:1-14).
</def>
<term id="h-p382.6">Hiss</term>
To express contempt (Job 27:23). The destruction of the temple
is thus spoken of (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 9:8" id="h-p383.2" parsed="|1Kgs|9|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.9.8">1 Kings 9:8</scripRef>). Zechariah (10:8) speaks of the
Lord gathering the house of Judah as it were with a hiss: “I
will hiss for them.” This expression may be “derived from the
noise made to attract bees in hiving, or from the sound
naturally made to attract a person’s attention.”
</def>
<term id="h-p383.3">Hittites</term>
Palestine and Syria appear to have been originally inhabited by
three different tribes. (1.) The Semites, living on the east of
the isthmus of Suez. They were nomadic and pastoral tribes. (2.)
The Phoenicians, who were merchants and traders; and (3.) the
Hittites, who were the warlike element of this confederation of
tribes. They inhabited the whole region between the Euphrates
and Damascus, their chief cities being Carchemish on the
Euphrates, and Kadesh, now Tell Neby Mendeh, in the Orontes
valley, about six miles south of the Lake of Homs. These
Hittites seem to have risen to great power as a nation, as for a
long time they were formidable rivals of the Egyptian and
Assyrian empires. In the book of Joshua they always appear as
the dominant race to the north of Galilee.
Somewhere about the twenty-third century B.C. the Syrian
confederation, led probably by the Hittites, arched against
Lower Egypt, which they took possession of, making Zoan their
capital. Their rulers were the Hyksos, or shepherd kings. They
were at length finally driven out of Egypt. Rameses II. sought
vengeance against the “vile Kheta,” as he called them, and
encountered and defeated them in the great battle of Kadesh,
four centuries after Abraham. (See JOSHUA.)
They are first referred to in Scripture in the history of
Abraham, who bought from Ephron the Hittite the field and the
cave of Machpelah (<scripRef passage="Gen. 15:20" id="h-p386.1" parsed="|Gen|15|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.20">Gen. 15:20</scripRef>: 23:3-18). They were then settled
at Kirjath-arba. From this tribe Esau took his first two wives
They are afterwards mentioned in the usual way among the
inhabitants of the Promised Land (<scripRef passage="Ex. 23:28" id="h-p387.1" parsed="|Exod|23|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.28">Ex. 23:28</scripRef>). They were closely
allied to the Amorites, and are frequently mentioned along with
them as inhabiting the mountains of Palestine. When the spies
entered the land they seem to have occupied with the Amorites
the mountain region of Judah (<scripRef passage="Num. 13:29" id="h-p387.2" parsed="|Num|13|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.13.29">Num. 13:29</scripRef>). They took part with
the other Canaanites against the Israelites (Josh. 9:1; 11:3).
After this there are few references to them in Scripture.
Mention is made of “Ahimelech the Hittite” (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 26:6" id="h-p388.1" parsed="|1Sam|26|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.26.6">1 Sam. 26:6</scripRef>), and of

“Uriah the Hittite,” one of David’s chief officers (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 23:39" id="h-p388.2" parsed="|2Sam|23|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.23.39">2 Sam. 23:39</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 11:41" id="h-p388.3" parsed="|1Chr|11|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.11.41">1 Chr. 11:41</scripRef>). In the days of Solomon they were a
powerful confederation in the north of Syria, and were ruled by
“kings.” They are met with after the Exile still a distinct
people (Ezra 9:1; comp. Neh. 13:23-28).
The Hebrew merchants exported horses from Egypt not only for

the kings of Israel, but also for the Hittites (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:28" id="h-p389.1" parsed="|1Kgs|10|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.28">1 Kings 10:28</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:29" id="h-p389.2" parsed="|1Kgs|10|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.29">29</scripRef>). From the Egyptian monuments we learn that “the Hittites
were a people with yellow skins and ‘Mongoloid’ features, whose
receding foreheads, oblique eyes, and protruding upper jaws are
represented as faithfully on their own monuments as they are on
those of Egypt, so that we cannot accuse the Egyptian artists of
caricaturing their enemies. The Amorites, on the contrary, were
a tall and handsome people. They are depicted with white skins,
blue eyes, and reddish hair, all the characteristics, in fact,
of the white race” (Sayce’s The Hittites). The original seat of
the Hittite tribes was the mountain ranges of Taurus. They
belonged to Asia Minor, and not to Syria.
</def>
<term id="h-p389.3">Hivites</term>
One of the original tribes scattered over Palestine, from Hermon
to Gibeon in the south. The name is interpreted as “midlanders”

or “villagers” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 10:17" id="h-p390.1" parsed="|Gen|10|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.10.17">Gen. 10:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 1:15" id="h-p390.2" parsed="|1Chr|1|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.1.15">1 Chr. 1:15</scripRef>). They were probably a
branch of the Hittites. At the time of Jacob’s return to Canaan,
Hamor the Hivite was the “prince of the land” (Gen. 24:2-28).
They are next mentioned during the Conquest (Josh. 9:7;
<scripRef passage="Josh 11:19" id="h-p391.2" parsed="|Josh|11|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.19">11:19</scripRef>). They principally inhabited the northern confines of

Western Palestine (<scripRef passage="Josh. 11:3" id="h-p391.3" parsed="|Josh|11|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.3">Josh. 11:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 3:3" id="h-p391.4" parsed="|Judg|3|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.3.3">Judg. 3:3</scripRef>). A remnant of them
still existed in the time of Solomon (1 Kings 9:20).
</def>
<term id="h-p391.6">Hizkiah</term>
An ancestor of the prophet Zephaniah (1:1).
</def>
<term id="h-p392.1">Hizkijah</term>
(Neh. 10:17), one who sealed the covenant.
</def>
<term id="h-p393.2">Hobab</term>
Beloved, the Kenite, has been usually identified with Jethro

(q.v.), <scripRef passage="Ex. 18:5" id="h-p394.1" parsed="|Exod|18|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.18.5">Ex. 18:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 18:27" id="h-p394.2" parsed="|Exod|18|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.18.27">27</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Num. 10:29" id="h-p394.3" parsed="|Num|10|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.10.29">Num. 10:29</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 10:30" id="h-p394.4" parsed="|Num|10|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.10.30">30</scripRef>. In <scripRef passage="Judg. 4:11" id="h-p394.5" parsed="|Judg|4|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.4.11">Judg. 4:11</scripRef>, the
word rendered “father-in-law” means properly any male relative
by marriage (comp. <scripRef passage="Gen. 19:14" id="h-p394.6" parsed="|Gen|19|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.19.14">Gen. 19:14</scripRef>, “son-in-law,” A.V.), and should
be rendered “brother-in-law,” as in the R.V. His descendants
followed Israel to Canaan (<scripRef passage="Num. 10:29" id="h-p394.7" parsed="|Num|10|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.10.29">Num. 10:29</scripRef>), and at first pitched
their tents near Jericho, but afterwards settled in the south in
the borders of Arad (Judg. 1:8-11, 16).
</def>
<term id="h-p394.10">Hobah</term>
Hiding-place, a place to the north of Damascus, to which Abraham
pursued Chedorlaomer and his confederates (Gen. 14:15).
</def>
<term id="h-p395.2">Hodijah</term>
Majesty of Jehovah. (1.) One of the Levites who assisted Ezra in

expounding the law (<scripRef passage="Neh. 8:7" id="h-p396.1" parsed="|Neh|8|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.8.7">Neh. 8:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Neh 9:5" id="h-p396.2" parsed="|Neh|9|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.9.5">9:5</scripRef>). (2.) <scripRef passage="Neh. 10:18" id="h-p396.3" parsed="|Neh|10|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Neh.10.18">Neh. 10:18</scripRef>, a Levite
who sealed the covenant.
</def>
<term id="h-p396.4">Hoglah</term>
Partridge, one of the daughters of Zelophehad the Gileadite, to
whom portions were assigned by Moses (Num. 26:33; 27:1; 36:11).
</def>
<term id="h-p397.4">Hoham</term>
Jehovah impels, the king of Hebron who joined the league against
Gibeon. He and his allies were defeated (Josh. 10:3, 5, 16-27).
</def>
<term id="h-p398.4">Hold</term>
A fortress, the name given to David’s lurking-places (1 Sam. 22:4, 5; 24:22).
</def>
<term id="h-p399.4">Holiness</term>
In the highest sense belongs to God (Isa. 6:3; Rev. 15:4), and
to Christians as consecrated to God’s service, and in so far as

they are conformed in all things to the will of God (<scripRef passage="Rom. 6:19" id="h-p400.3" parsed="|Rom|6|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.6.19">Rom. 6:19</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Rom 6:22" id="h-p400.4" parsed="|Rom|6|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.6.22">22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 1:4" id="h-p400.5" parsed="|Eph|1|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.1.4">Eph. 1:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Titus 1:8" id="h-p400.6" parsed="|Titus|1|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Titus.1.8">Titus 1:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Pet. 1:15" id="h-p400.7" parsed="|1Pet|1|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.1.15">1 Pet. 1:15</scripRef>). Personal holiness is a
work of gradual development. It is carried on under many
hindrances, hence the frequent admonitions to watchfulness,
prayer, and perseverance (1 Cor. 1:30; 2 Cor. 7:1; Eph. 4:23, 24). (See SANCTIFICATION.)
</def>
<term id="h-p400.13">Holy Ghost</term>
The third Person of the adorable Trinity.
His personality is proved (1) from the fact that the
attributes of personality, as intelligence and volition, are

ascribed to him (<scripRef passage="John 14:17" id="h-p402.1" parsed="|John|14|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.14.17">John 14:17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="John 14:26" id="h-p402.2" parsed="|John|14|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.14.26">26</scripRef>; 15:26; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 2:10" id="h-p402.3" parsed="|1Cor|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.2.10">1 Cor. 2:10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 2:11" id="h-p402.4" parsed="|1Cor|2|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.2.11">11</scripRef>; 12:11).

He reproves, helps, glorifies, intercedes (<scripRef passage="John 16:7-13" id="h-p402.5" parsed="|John|16|7|16|13" osisRef="Bible:John.16.7-John.16.13">John 16:7-13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 8:26" id="h-p402.6" parsed="|Rom|8|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.26">Rom. 8:26</scripRef>). (2) He executes the offices peculiar only to a person.
The very nature of these offices involves personal distinction
(Luke 12:12; Acts 5:32; 15:28; 16:6; 28:25; 1 Cor. 2:13; Heb. 2:4; 3:7; 2 Pet. 1:21).
His divinity is established (1) from the fact that the names

of God are ascribed to him (<scripRef passage="Ex. 17:7" id="h-p403.1" parsed="|Exod|17|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.17.7">Ex. 17:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 95:7" id="h-p403.2" parsed="|Ps|95|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.95.7">Ps. 95:7</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Heb. 3:7-11" id="h-p403.3" parsed="|Heb|3|7|3|11" osisRef="Bible:Heb.3.7-Heb.3.11">Heb. 3:7-11</scripRef>); and (2) that divine attributes are also ascribed to

him, omnipresence (<scripRef passage="Ps. 139:7" id="h-p403.4" parsed="|Ps|139|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.139.7">Ps. 139:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 2:17" id="h-p403.5" parsed="|Eph|2|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.17">Eph. 2:17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Eph. 2:18" id="h-p403.6" parsed="|Eph|2|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.18">18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 12:13" id="h-p403.7" parsed="|1Cor|12|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.12.13">1 Cor. 12:13</scripRef>);

omniscience (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 2:10" id="h-p403.8" parsed="|1Cor|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.2.10">1 Cor. 2:10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 2:11" id="h-p403.9" parsed="|1Cor|2|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.2.11">11</scripRef>); omnipotence (<scripRef passage="Luke 1:35" id="h-p403.10" parsed="|Luke|1|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.35">Luke 1:35</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 8:11" id="h-p403.11" parsed="|Rom|8|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.11">Rom. 8:11</scripRef>); eternity (<scripRef passage="Heb. 9:4" id="h-p403.12" parsed="|Heb|9|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.4">Heb. 9:4</scripRef>). (3) Creation is ascribed to him

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 1:2" id="h-p403.13" parsed="|Gen|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.1.2">Gen. 1:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 26:13" id="h-p403.14" parsed="|Job|26|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.26.13">Job 26:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 104:30" id="h-p403.15" parsed="|Ps|104|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.104.30">Ps. 104:30</scripRef>), and the working of miracles

(<scripRef passage="Matt. 12:28" id="h-p403.16" parsed="|Matt|12|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.12.28">Matt. 12:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 12:9-11" id="h-p403.17" parsed="|1Cor|12|9|12|11" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.12.9-1Cor.12.11">1 Cor. 12:9-11</scripRef>). (4) Worship is required and
ascribed to him (Isa. 6:3; Acts 28:25; Rom. 9:1; Rev. 1:4; Matt. 28:19).
</def>
<term id="h-p403.23">Holy of holies</term>
The second or interior portion of the tabernacle. It was left in
total darkness. No one was permitted to enter it except the high
priest, and that only once a year. It contained the ark of the
covenant only (<scripRef passage="Ex. 25:10-16" id="h-p404.1" parsed="|Exod|25|10|25|16" osisRef="Bible:Exod.25.10-Exod.25.16">Ex. 25:10-16</scripRef>). It was in the form of a perfect
cube of 20 cubits. (See TABERNACLE.)
</def>
<term id="h-p404.3">Holy place</term>
One of the two portions into which the tabernacle was divided

(<scripRef passage="Ex. 26:31" id="h-p405.1" parsed="|Exod|26|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.26.31">Ex. 26:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 37:17-25" id="h-p405.2" parsed="|Exod|37|17|37|25" osisRef="Bible:Exod.37.17-Exod.37.25">37:17-25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 9:2" id="h-p405.3" parsed="|Heb|9|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.2">Heb. 9:2</scripRef>). It was 20 cubits long and 10 in
height and breadth. It was illuminated by the golden
candlestick, as it had no opening to admit the light. It
contained the table of showbread (<scripRef passage="Ex. 25:23-29" id="h-p405.4" parsed="|Exod|25|23|25|29" osisRef="Bible:Exod.25.23-Exod.25.29">Ex. 25:23-29</scripRef>) and the golden
altar of incense (30:1-11). It was divided from the holy of
holies by a veil of the most costly materials and the brightest
colours.
The arrangement of the temple (q.v.) was the same in this
respect. In it the walls of hewn stone were wainscotted with
cedar and overlaid with gold, and adorned with beautiful
carvings. It was entered from the porch by folding doors
overlaid with gold and richly embossed. Outside the holy place
stood the great tank or “sea” of molten brass, supported by
twelve oxen, three turned each way, capable of containing two
thousand baths of water. Besides this there were ten lavers and
the brazen altar of burnt sacrifice.
</def>
<term id="h-p406.1">Homer</term>
Heap, the largest of dry measures, containing about 8 bushels or

1 quarter English = 10 ephahs (<scripRef passage="Lev. 27:16" id="h-p407.1" parsed="|Lev|27|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.27.16">Lev. 27:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 11:32" id="h-p407.2" parsed="|Num|11|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.11.32">Num. 11:32</scripRef>) = a COR.
(See OMER.)
“Half a homer,” a grain measure mentioned only in Hos. 3:2.
</def>
<term id="h-p408.2">Honey</term>
(1.) Heb. ya’ar, occurs only 1 Sam. 14:25, 27, 29; Cant. 5:1,
where it denotes the honey of bees. Properly the word signifies
a forest or copse, and refers to honey found in woods.
(2.) Nopheth, honey that drops (Ps. 19:10; Prov. 5:3; Cant. 4:11).
(3.) Debash denotes bee-honey (Judg. 14:8); but also
frequently a vegetable honey distilled from trees (<scripRef passage="Gen. 43:11" id="h-p411.2" parsed="|Gen|43|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.43.11">Gen. 43:11</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:17" id="h-p411.3" parsed="|Ezek|27|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.17">Ezek. 27:17</scripRef>). In these passages it may probably mean “dibs,” or
syrup of grapes, i.e., the juice of ripe grapes boiled down to
one-third of its bulk.
(4.) Tsuph, the cells of the honey-comb full of honey (Prov. 16:24; Ps. 19:10).
(5.) “Wild honey” (Matt. 3:4) may have been the vegetable
honey distilled from trees, but rather was honey stored by bees
in rocks or in trees (Deut. 32:13; Ps. 81:16; 1 Sam. 14:25-29).
Canaan was a “land flowing with milk and honey” (Ex. 3:8).
Milk and honey were among the chief dainties in the earlier
ages, as they are now among the Bedawin; and butter and honey
are also mentioned among articles of food (<scripRef passage="Isa. 7:15" id="h-p414.2" parsed="|Isa|7|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.7.15">Isa. 7:15</scripRef>). The

ancients used honey instead of sugar (<scripRef passage="Ps. 119:103" id="h-p414.3" parsed="|Ps|119|103|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.119.103">Ps. 119:103</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 24:13" id="h-p414.4" parsed="|Prov|24|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.24.13">Prov. 24:13</scripRef>);
but when taken in great quantities it caused nausea, a fact

referred to in <scripRef passage="Prov. 25:16" id="h-p414.5" parsed="|Prov|25|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.25.16">Prov. 25:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Prov. 25:17" id="h-p414.6" parsed="|Prov|25|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.25.17">17</scripRef> to inculcate moderation in
pleasures. Honey and milk also are put for sweet discourse
(Cant. 4:11).
</def>
<term id="h-p414.8">Hood</term>
(Heb. tsaniph) a tiara round the head (Isa. 3:23; R.V., pl.,
“turbans”). Rendered “diadem,” <scripRef passage="Job 29:14" id="h-p415.2" parsed="|Job|29|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.29.14">Job 29:14</scripRef>; high priest’s “mitre,”
Zech. 3:5; “royal diadem,” Isa. 62:3.
</def>
<term id="h-p415.5">Hoof</term>
A cleft hoof as of neat cattle (Ex. 10:26; Ezek. 32:13); hence
also of the horse, though not cloven (<scripRef passage="Isa. 5:28" id="h-p416.3" parsed="|Isa|5|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.5.28">Isa. 5:28</scripRef>). The “parting
of the hoof” is one of the distinctions between clean and
unclean animals (Lev. 11:3; Deut. 14:7).
</def>
<term id="h-p416.6">Hook</term>
(1.) Heb. hah, a “ring” inserted in the nostrils of animals to

which a cord was fastened for the purpose of restraining them (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 19:28" id="h-p417.1" parsed="|2Kgs|19|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.19.28">2 Kings 19:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 37:28" id="h-p417.2" parsed="|Isa|37|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.37.28">Isa. 37:28</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 37:29" id="h-p417.3" parsed="|Isa|37|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.37.29">29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 29:4" id="h-p417.4" parsed="|Ezek|29|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.29.4">Ezek. 29:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek 38:4" id="h-p417.5" parsed="|Ezek|38|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.38.4">38:4</scripRef>). “The Orientals
make use of this contrivance for curbing their
work-beasts...When a beast becomes unruly they have only to draw
the cord on one side, which, by stopping his breath, punishes
him so effectually that after a few repetitions he fails not to
become quite tractable whenever he begins to feel it”
(Michaelis). So God’s agents are never beyond his control.
(2.) Hakkah, a fish “hook” (Job 41:2, Heb. Text, 40:25; Isa. 19:8; Hab. 1:15).
(3.) Vav, a “peg” on which the curtains of the tabernacle were
hung (Ex. 26:32).
(4.) Tsinnah, a fish-hooks (Amos 4:2).
(5.) Mazleg, flesh-hooks (1 Sam. 2:13, 14), a kind of fork
with three teeth for turning the sacrifices on the fire, etc.
(6.) Mazmeroth, pruning-hooks (Isa. 2:4; Joel 3:10).
(7.) ‘Agmon (Job 41:2, Heb. Text 40:26), incorrectly rendered
in the Authorized Version. Properly a rush-rope for binding
animals, as in Revised Version margin.
</def>
<term id="h-p423.2">Hope</term>
One of the three main elements of Christian character (1 Cor. 13:13). It is joined to faith and love, and is opposed to seeing

or possessing (<scripRef passage="Rom. 8:24" id="h-p424.2" parsed="|Rom|8|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.24">Rom. 8:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 John 3:2" id="h-p424.3" parsed="|1John|3|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.3.2">1 John 3:2</scripRef>). “Hope is an essential and
fundamental element of Christian life, so essential indeed,
that, like faith and love, it can itself designate the essence

of Christianity (<scripRef passage="1 Pet. 3:15" id="h-p424.4" parsed="|1Pet|3|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.3.15">1 Pet. 3:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 10:23" id="h-p424.5" parsed="|Heb|10|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.10.23">Heb. 10:23</scripRef>). In it the whole glory

of the Christian vocation is centred (<scripRef passage="Eph. 1:18" id="h-p424.6" parsed="|Eph|1|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.1.18">Eph. 1:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph 4:4" id="h-p424.7" parsed="|Eph|4|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.4.4">4:4</scripRef>).”

Unbelievers are without this hope (<scripRef passage="Eph. 2:12" id="h-p424.8" parsed="|Eph|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.12">Eph. 2:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Thess. 4:13" id="h-p424.9" parsed="|1Thess|4|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Thess.4.13">1 Thess. 4:13</scripRef>).
Christ is the actual object of the believer’s hope, because it
is in his second coming that the hope of glory will be fulfilled

(<scripRef passage="1 Tim. 1:1" id="h-p424.10" parsed="|1Tim|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.1.1">1 Tim. 1:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Col. 1:27" id="h-p424.11" parsed="|Col|1|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Col.1.27">Col. 1:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Titus 2:13" id="h-p424.12" parsed="|Titus|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Titus.2.13">Titus 2:13</scripRef>). It is spoken of as
“lively”, i.e., a living, hope, a hope not frail and perishable,

but having a perennial life (<scripRef passage="1 Pet. 1:3" id="h-p424.13" parsed="|1Pet|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.1.3">1 Pet. 1:3</scripRef>). In <scripRef passage="Rom. 5:2" id="h-p424.14" parsed="|Rom|5|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.5.2">Rom. 5:2</scripRef> the “hope”
spoken of is probably objective, i.e., “the hope set before us,”
namely, eternal life (comp. 12:12). In <scripRef passage="1 John 3:3" id="h-p424.15" parsed="|1John|3|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.3.3">1 John 3:3</scripRef> the expression
“hope in him” ought rather to be, as in the Revised Version,
“hope on him,” i.e., a hope based on God.
</def>
<term id="h-p424.16">Hophni</term>
Pugilist or client, one of the two sons of Eli, the high priest

(<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 1:3" id="h-p425.1" parsed="|1Sam|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.1.3">1 Sam. 1:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 2:34" id="h-p425.2" parsed="|1Sam|2|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.2.34">2:34</scripRef>), who, because he was “very old,” resigned to
them the active duties of his office. By their scandalous
conduct they brought down a curse on their father’s house (2:22,
12-27, 27-36; 3:11-14). For their wickedness they were called
“sons of Belial,” i.e., worthless men (2:12). They both perished
in the disastrous battle with the Philistines at Aphek (4:11).
(See PHINEHAS.)
</def>
<term id="h-p425.4">Hophra</term>
I.e., PHARAOH-HOPHRA (called Apries by the Greek historian
Herodotus) king of Egypt (B.C. 591-572) in the time of Zedekiah,
king of Judah (Jer. 37:5 44:30; Ezek. 29:6, 7).
</def>
<term id="h-p426.4">Hor</term>
Mountain. (1.) One of the mountains of the chain of Seir or

Edom, on the confines of Idumea (<scripRef passage="Num. 20:22-29" id="h-p427.1" parsed="|Num|20|22|20|29" osisRef="Bible:Num.20.22-Num.20.29">Num. 20:22-29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 33:37" id="h-p427.2" parsed="|Num|33|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.33.37">33:37</scripRef>). It was
one of the stations of the Israelites in the wilderness (33:37),
which they reached in the circuitous route they were obliged to
take because the Edomites refused them a passage through their
territory. It was during the encampment here that Aaron died
(Num. 33:37-41). (See AARON.) The Israelites passed
this mountain several times in their wanderings. It bears the
modern name of Jebel Harun, and is the highest and most
conspicious of the whole range. It stands about midway between
the Dead Sea and the Elanitic gulf. It has two summits, in the
hallow between which it is supposed that Aaron died. Others,
however, suppose that this mountain is the modern Jebel Madurah,
on the opposite, i.e., the western, side of the Arabah.
(2.) One of the marks of the northern boundary of Palestine

(<scripRef passage="Num. 34:7" id="h-p428.1" parsed="|Num|34|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.34.7">Num. 34:7</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 34:8" id="h-p428.2" parsed="|Num|34|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.34.8">8</scripRef>). Nowhere else mentioned. Perhaps it is one of the
peaks of Lebanon.
</def>
<term id="h-p428.3">Horeb</term>
Desert or mountain of the dried-up ground, a general name for
the whole mountain range of which Sinai was one of the summits

(<scripRef passage="Ex. 3:1" id="h-p429.1" parsed="|Exod|3|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.3.1">Ex. 3:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 17:6" id="h-p429.2" parsed="|Exod|17|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.17.6">17:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 33:6" id="h-p429.3" parsed="|Exod|33|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.33.6">33:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 106:19" id="h-p429.4" parsed="|Ps|106|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.106.19">Ps. 106:19</scripRef>, etc.). The modern name of the
whole range is Jebel Musa. It is a huge mountain block, about 2
miles long by about 1 in breadth, with a very spacious plain at
its north-east end, called the Er Rahah, in which the Israelites
encamped for nearly a whole year. (See SINAI.)
</def>
<term id="h-p429.6">Horem</term>
Consecrated, one of the fenced cities of Naphtali (Josh. 19:38).
</def>
<term id="h-p430.2">Horites</term>
Cave-men, a race of Troglodytes who dwelt in the limestone caves
which abounded in Edom. Their ancestor was “Seir,” who probably
gave his name to the district where he lived. They were a branch

of the Hivites (<scripRef passage="Gen. 14:6" id="h-p431.1" parsed="|Gen|14|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.6">Gen. 14:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 36:20-30" id="h-p431.2" parsed="|Gen|36|20|36|30" osisRef="Bible:Gen.36.20-Gen.36.30">36:20-30</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 1:38" id="h-p431.3" parsed="|1Chr|1|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.1.38">1 Chr. 1:38</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 1:39" id="h-p431.4" parsed="|1Chr|1|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.1.39">39</scripRef>). They were
dispossessed by the descendants of Esau, and as a people
gradually became extinct (Deut. 2:12-22).
</def>
<term id="h-p431.6">Hormah</term>
Banning; i.e., placing under a “ban,” or devoting to utter
destruction. After the manifestation of God’s anger against the
Israelites, on account of their rebellion and their murmurings
when the spies returned to the camp at Kadesh, in the wilderness
of Paran, with an evil report of the land, they quickly repented
of their conduct, and presumed to go up “to the head of the
mountain,” seeking to enter the Promised Land, but without the
presence of the Lord, without the ark of the convenant, and
without Moses. The Amalekites and the Canaanites came down and
“smote and discomfited them even unto Hormah” (<scripRef passage="Num. 14:45" id="h-p432.1" parsed="|Num|14|45|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.14.45">Num. 14:45</scripRef>). This
place, or perhaps the watch-tower commanding it, was originally
called Zephath (<scripRef passage="Judg. 1:17" id="h-p432.2" parsed="|Judg|1|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.17">Judg. 1:17</scripRef>), the modern Sebaiteh. Afterwards
(<scripRef passage="Num. 21:1-3" id="h-p432.3" parsed="|Num|21|1|21|3" osisRef="Bible:Num.21.1-Num.21.3">Num. 21:1-3</scripRef>) Arad, the king of the Canaanites, at the close of
the wanderings, when the Israelites were a second time encamped
at Kadesh, “fought against them, and took some of them
prisoners.” But Israel vowed a vow unto the Lord utterly to
destroy the cities of the Canaanites; they “banned” them, and
hence the place was now called Hormah. But this “ban” was not
fully executed till the time of Joshua, who finally conquered
the king of this district, so that the ancient name Zephath
became “Hormah” (Josh. 12:14; Judg. 1:17).
</def>
<term id="h-p432.6">Horn</term>
Trumpets were at first horns perforated at the tip, used for
various purposes (Josh. 6:4, 5).
Flasks or vessels were made of horn (1 Sam. 16:1, 13; 1 Kings 1:39).
But the word is used also metaphorically to denote the
projecting corners of the altar of burnt offerings (<scripRef passage="Ex. 27:2" id="h-p435.1" parsed="|Exod|27|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.27.2">Ex. 27:2</scripRef>)
and of incense (30:2). The horns of the altar of burnt offerings
were to be smeared with the blood of the slain bullock (29:12;
<scripRef passage="Lev. 4:7-18" id="h-p435.2" parsed="|Lev|4|7|4|18" osisRef="Bible:Lev.4.7-Lev.4.18">Lev. 4:7-18</scripRef>). The criminal, when his crime was accidental, found
an asylum by laying hold of the horns of the altar (1 Kings 1:50; 2:28).
The word also denotes the peak or summit of a hill (Isa. 5:1,
where the word “hill” is the rendering of the same Hebrew word).
This word is used metaphorically also for strength (Deut. 33:17) and honour (Job 16:15; Lam. 2:3). Horns are emblems of
power, dominion, glory, and fierceness, as they are the chief
means of attack and defence with the animals endowed with them

(<scripRef passage="Dan. 8:5" id="h-p437.4" parsed="|Dan|8|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.8.5">Dan. 8:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan. 8:9" id="h-p437.5" parsed="|Dan|8|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.8.9">9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 2:1" id="h-p437.6" parsed="|1Sam|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.2.1">1 Sam. 2:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 16:1" id="h-p437.7" parsed="|1Sam|16|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.16.1">16:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 16:13" id="h-p437.8" parsed="|1Sam|16|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.16.13">13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 1:39" id="h-p437.9" parsed="|1Kgs|1|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.1.39">1 Kings 1:39</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 22:11" id="h-p437.10" parsed="|1Kgs|22|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.22.11">22:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 6:4" id="h-p437.11" parsed="|Josh|6|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.6.4">Josh. 6:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh 6:5" id="h-p437.12" parsed="|Josh|6|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.6.5">5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 75:5" id="h-p437.13" parsed="|Ps|75|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.75.5">Ps. 75:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps. 75:10" id="h-p437.14" parsed="|Ps|75|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.75.10">10</scripRef>; 132:17; <scripRef passage="Luke 1:69" id="h-p437.15" parsed="|Luke|1|69|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.69">Luke 1:69</scripRef>, etc.). The expression
“horn of salvation,” applied to Christ, means a salvation of
strength, or a strong Saviour (<scripRef passage="Luke 1:69" id="h-p437.16" parsed="|Luke|1|69|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.69">Luke 1:69</scripRef>). To have the horn

“exalted” denotes prosperity and triumph (<scripRef passage="Ps. 89:17" id="h-p437.17" parsed="|Ps|89|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.89.17">Ps. 89:17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps. 89:24" id="h-p437.18" parsed="|Ps|89|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.89.24">24</scripRef>). To
“lift up” the horn is to act proudly (Zech. 1:21).
Horns are also the symbol of royal dignity and power (Jer. 48:25; Zech. 1:18; Dan. 8:24).
</def>
<term id="h-p438.4">Hornet</term>
Heb. tsir’ah, “stinging”, (Ex. 23:28; Deut. 7:20; Josh. 24:12).
The word is used in these passages as referring to some means by
which the Canaanites were to be driven out from before the
Israelites. Some have supposed that the word is used in a
metaphorical sense as the symbol of some panic which would seize
the people as a “terror of God” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 35:5" id="h-p439.4" parsed="|Gen|35|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.35.5">Gen. 35:5</scripRef>), the consternation
with which God would inspire the Canaanites. In Palestine there
are four species of hornets, differing from our hornets, being
larger in size, and they are very abundant. They “attack human
beings in a very furious manner.” “The furious attack of a swarm
of hornets drives cattle and horses to madness, and has even
caused the death of the animals.”
</def>
<term id="h-p439.5">Horonaim</term>
Two caverns, a city of Moab to the south of the Arnon, built,
apparently, upon an eminence, and a place of some importance
(Isa. 15:5; Jer. 48:3, 5, 34).
</def>
<term id="h-p440.5">Horonite</term>
The designation of Sanballat (Neh. 2:10, 19), a native of
Horonaim, or of one of the two Beth-horons, the “upper” or the
“nether,” mentioned in Josh. 16:3, 5.
</def>
<term id="h-p441.5">Horse</term>
Always referred to in the Bible in connection with warlike

operations, except <scripRef passage="Isa. 28:28" id="h-p442.1" parsed="|Isa|28|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.28.28">Isa. 28:28</scripRef>. The war-horse is described <scripRef passage="Job 39:19-25" id="h-p442.2" parsed="|Job|39|19|39|25" osisRef="Bible:Job.39.19-Job.39.25">Job 39:19-25</scripRef>. For a long period after their settlement in Canaan the
Israelites made no use of horses, according to the prohibition,

<scripRef passage="Deut. 17:16" id="h-p442.3" parsed="|Deut|17|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.17.16">Deut. 17:16</scripRef>. David was the first to form a force of cavalry (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 8:4" id="h-p442.4" parsed="|2Sam|8|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.8.4">2 Sam. 8:4</scripRef>). But Solomon, from his connection with Egypt, greatly

multiplied their number (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:26" id="h-p442.5" parsed="|1Kgs|4|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.26">1 Kings 4:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:26" id="h-p442.6" parsed="|1Kgs|10|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.26">10:26</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:29" id="h-p442.7" parsed="|1Kgs|10|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.29">29</scripRef>). After this,

horses were freely used in Israel (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 22:4" id="h-p442.8" parsed="|1Kgs|22|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.22.4">1 Kings 22:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 3:7" id="h-p442.9" parsed="|2Kgs|3|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.3.7">2 Kings 3:7</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="2 Kings 9:21" id="h-p442.10" parsed="|2Kgs|9|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.9.21">9:21</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 9:33" id="h-p442.11" parsed="|2Kgs|9|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.9.33">33</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 11:16" id="h-p442.12" parsed="|2Kgs|11|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.11.16">11:16</scripRef>). The furniture of the horse consisted simply of
a bridle (Isa. 30:28) and a curb (Ps. 32:9).
</def>
<term id="h-p442.15">Horse-gate</term>
A gate in the wall of Jerusalem, at the west end of the bridge,
leading from Zion to the temple (Neh. 3:28; Jer. 31:40).
</def>
<term id="h-p443.3">Horse-leech</term>
