Occurs only in Prov. 30:15 (Heb. ‘alukah); the generic name for
any blood-sucking annelid. There are various species in the
marshes and pools of Palestine. That here referred to, the
Hoemopis, is remarkable for the coarseness of its bite, and is
therefore not used for medical purposes. They are spoken of in
the East with feelings of aversion and horror, because of their
propensity to fasten on the tongue and nostrils of horses when
they come to drink out of the pools. The medicinal leech (Hirudo
medicinalis), besides other species of leeches, are common in
the waters of Syria.
</def>
<term id="h-p444.2">Horseman</term>
Heb. ba’al parash, “master of a horse.” The “horsemen” mentioned
<scripRef passage="Ex. 14:9" id="h-p445.1" parsed="|Exod|14|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.14.9">Ex. 14:9</scripRef> were “mounted men”, i.e., men who rode in chariots. The
army of Pharaoh consisted of a chariot and infantry force. We
find that at a later period, however, the Egyptians had cavalry
(2 Chr. 12:3). (See HORSE.)
</def>
<term id="h-p445.4">Hosah</term>
Refuge. (1.) A place on the border of the tribe of Asher (Josh. 19:29), a little to the south of Zidon.
(2.) A Levite of the family of Merari (1 Chr. 16:38).
</def>
<term id="h-p447.2">Hosanna</term>
Save now! or Save, we beseech, (Matt. 21:9). This was a
customary form of acclamation at the feast of Tabernacles.
(Comp. Ps. 118:25.)
</def>
<term id="h-p448.3">Hose</term>
(Dan. 3:21), a tunic or undergarment.
</def>
<term id="h-p449.2">Hosea</term>
Salvation, the son of Beeri, and author of the book of
prophecies bearing his name. He belonged to the kingdom of
Israel. “His Israelitish origin is attested by the peculiar,
rough, Aramaizing diction, pointing to the northern part of
Palestine; by the intimate acquaintance he evinces with the
localities of Ephraim (5:1; 6:8, 9; 12:12; 14:6, etc.); by
passages like 1:2, where the kingdom is styled ‘the land’, and
7:5, where the Israelitish king is designated as ‘our’ king.”
The period of his ministry (extending to some sixty years) is

indicated in the superscription (<scripRef passage="Hos. 1:1" id="h-p450.1" parsed="|Hos|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.1.1">Hos. 1:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Hos 1:2" id="h-p450.2" parsed="|Hos|1|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.1.2">2</scripRef>). He is the only
prophet of Israel who has left any written prophecy.
</def>
<term id="h-p450.3">Hosea, Prophecies of</term>
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="h-p450.5" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="Hos 0" id="h-p450.6" parsed="|Hos|0|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos" />
This book stands first in order among the “Minor Prophets.” “The
probable cause of the location of Hosea may be the thoroughly
national character of his oracles, their length, their earnest
tone, and vivid representations.” This was the longest of the
prophetic books written before the Captivity. Hosea prophesied
in a dark and melancholy period of Israel’s history, the period
of Israel’s decline and fall. Their sins had brought upon them
great national disasters. “Their homicides and fornication,
their perjury and theft, their idolatry and impiety, are
censured and satirized with a faithful severity.” He was a
contemporary of Isaiah. The book may be divided into two parts,
the first containing chapters 1-3, and symbolically representing
the idolatry of Israel under imagery borrowed from the
matrimonial relation. The figures of marriage and adultery are
common in the Old Testament writings to represent the spiritual
relations between Jehovah and the people of Israel. Here we see
the apostasy of Israel and their punishment, with their future
repentance, forgiveness, and restoration.
The second part, containing 4-14, is a summary of Hosea’s
discourses, filled with denunciations, threatenings,
exhortations, promises, and revelations of mercy.
Quotations from Hosea are found in Matt. 2:15; 9:15; 12:7;

<scripRef passage="Rom. 9:25" id="h-p453.4" parsed="|Rom|9|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.9.25">Rom. 9:25</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Rom. 9:26" id="h-p453.5" parsed="|Rom|9|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.9.26">26</scripRef>. There are, in addition, various allusions to it
in other places (Luke 23:30; Rev. 6:16, comp. Hos. 10:8; Rom. 9:25, 26; 1 Pet. 2:10, comp. Hos. 1:10, etc.).
As regards the style of this writer, it has been said that
“each verse forms a whole for itself, like one heavy toll in a
funeral knell.” “Inversions (7:8; 9:11, 13; 12: 8), anacolutha
(9:6; 12:8, etc.), ellipses (9:4; 13:9, etc.), paranomasias, and
plays upon words, are very characteristic of Hosea (8:7; 9:15;
</def>
<term id="h-p454.1">Hoshea</term>
Salvation. (1.) The original name of the son of Nun, afterwards
called Joshua (Num. 13:8, 16; Deut. 32:44).
(2.) 1 Chr. 27:20. The ruler of Ephraim in David’s time.
(3.) The last king of Israel. He conspired against and slew
his predecessor, Pekah (<scripRef passage="Isa. 7:16" id="h-p457.1" parsed="|Isa|7|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.7.16">Isa. 7:16</scripRef>), but did not ascend the

throne till after an interregnum of warfare of eight years (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:1" id="h-p457.2" parsed="|2Kgs|17|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.1">2 Kings 17:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:2" id="h-p457.3" parsed="|2Kgs|17|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.2">2</scripRef>). Soon after this he submitted to Shalmaneser, the
Assyrian king, who a second time invaded the land to punish
Hoshea, because of his withholding tribute which he had promised
to pay. A second revolt brought back the Assyrian king Sargon,
who besieged Samaria, and carried the ten tribes away beyond the

Euphrates, B.C. 720 (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:5" id="h-p457.4" parsed="|2Kgs|17|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.5">2 Kings 17:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Kings 17:6" id="h-p457.5" parsed="|2Kgs|17|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.17.6">6</scripRef>; 18:9-12). No more is heard
of Hoshea. He disappeared like “foam upon the water” (<scripRef passage="Hos. 10:7" id="h-p457.6" parsed="|Hos|10|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hos.10.7">Hos. 10:7</scripRef>;
13:11).
</def>
<term id="h-p457.8">Host</term>
An entertainer (Rom. 16:23); a tavern-keeper, the keeper of a
caravansary (Luke 10:35).
In warfare, a troop or military force. This consisted at first

only of infantry. Solomon afterwards added cavalry (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:26" id="h-p459.1" parsed="|1Kgs|4|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.26">1 Kings 4:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:26" id="h-p459.2" parsed="|1Kgs|10|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.26">10:26</scripRef>). Every male Israelite from twenty to fifty years of
age was bound by the law to bear arms when necessary (<scripRef passage="Num. 1:3" id="h-p459.3" parsed="|Num|1|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.1.3">Num. 1:3</scripRef>;
26:2; 2 Chr. 25:5).
Saul was the first to form a standing army (1 Sam. 13:2;

<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 24:2" id="h-p460.2" parsed="|1Sam|24|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.24.2">24:2</scripRef>). This example was followed by David (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 27:1" id="h-p460.3" parsed="|1Chr|27|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.27.1">1 Chr. 27:1</scripRef>), and
Solomon (1 Kings 4:26), and by the kings of Israel and Judah (2 Chr. 17:14; 26:11; 2 Kings 11:4, etc.).
</def>
<term id="h-p460.8">Hostage</term>
A person delivered into the hands of another as a security for
the performance of some promise, etc. (2 Kings 14:14; 2 Chr. 25:24).
</def>
<term id="h-p461.3">Host of heaven</term>
The sun, moon, and stars are so designated (Gen. 2:1). When the
Jews fell into idolatry they worshipped these (Deut. 4:19; 2 Kings 17:16; 21:3, 5; 23:5; Jer. 19:13; Zeph. 1:5; Acts 7:42).
</def>
<term id="h-p462.10">Hough</term>
To hamstring, i.e., sever the “tendon of Achilles” of the hinder

legs of captured horses (<scripRef passage="Josh. 11:6" id="h-p463.1" parsed="|Josh|11|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.11.6">Josh. 11:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 8:4" id="h-p463.2" parsed="|2Sam|8|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.8.4">2 Sam. 8:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 18:4" id="h-p463.3" parsed="|1Chr|18|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.18.4">1 Chr. 18:4</scripRef>),
so as to render them useless.
</def>
<term id="h-p463.4">Hour</term>
First found in Dan. 3:6; 4:19, 33;5:5. It is the rendering of
the Chaldee shaah, meaning a “moment,” a “look.” It is used in
the New Testament frequently to denote some determinate season
(Matt. 8:13; Luke 12:39).
With the ancient Hebrews the divisions of the day were
“morning, evening, and noon-day” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 55:17" id="h-p465.1" parsed="|Ps|55|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.55.17">Ps. 55:17</scripRef>, etc.). The Greeks,
following the Babylonians, divided the day into twelve hours.
The Jews, during the Captivity, learned also from the
Babylonians this method of dividing time. When Judea became
subject to the Romans, the Jews adopted the Roman mode of

reckoning time. The night was divided into four watches (<scripRef passage="Luke 12:38" id="h-p465.2" parsed="|Luke|12|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.12.38">Luke 12:38</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 14:25" id="h-p465.3" parsed="|Matt|14|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.14.25">Matt. 14:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 13:25" id="h-p465.4" parsed="|Matt|13|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.13.25">13:25</scripRef>). Frequent allusion is also made to
hours (Matt. 25:13; 26:40, etc.). (See DAY.)
An hour was the twelfth part of the day, reckoning from
sunrise to sunset, and consequently it perpetually varied in
length.
</def>
<term id="h-p466.1">House</term>
Till their sojourn in Egypt the Hebrews dwelt in tents. They

then for the first time inhabited cities (<scripRef passage="Gen. 47:3" id="h-p467.1" parsed="|Gen|47|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.47.3">Gen. 47:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex. 12:7" id="h-p467.2" parsed="|Exod|12|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.7">Ex. 12:7</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Heb. 11:9" id="h-p467.3" parsed="|Heb|11|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.11.9">Heb. 11:9</scripRef>). From the earliest times the Assyrians and the
Canaanites were builders of cities. The Hebrews after the
Conquest took possession of the captured cities, and seem to
have followed the methods of building that had been pursued by
the Canaanites. Reference is made to the stone (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 7:9" id="h-p467.4" parsed="|1Kgs|7|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.7.9">1 Kings 7:9</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Isa. 9:10" id="h-p467.5" parsed="|Isa|9|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.9.10">Isa. 9:10</scripRef>) and marble (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 29:2" id="h-p467.6" parsed="|1Chr|29|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.29.2">1 Chr. 29:2</scripRef>) used in building, and to the

internal wood-work of the houses (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 6:15" id="h-p467.7" parsed="|1Kgs|6|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.6.15">1 Kings 6:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 7:2" id="h-p467.8" parsed="|1Kgs|7|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.7.2">7:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:11" id="h-p467.9" parsed="|1Kgs|10|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.11">10:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 10:12" id="h-p467.10" parsed="|1Kgs|10|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.10.12">12</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 3:5" id="h-p467.11" parsed="|2Chr|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.3.5">2 Chr. 3:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 22:14" id="h-p467.12" parsed="|Jer|22|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.22.14">Jer. 22:14</scripRef>). “Ceiled houses” were such as had beams

inlaid in the walls to which wainscotting was fastened (<scripRef passage="Ezra 6:4" id="h-p467.13" parsed="|Ezra|6|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.6.4">Ezra 6:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 22:14" id="h-p467.14" parsed="|Jer|22|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.22.14">Jer. 22:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Hag. 1:4" id="h-p467.15" parsed="|Hag|1|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hag.1.4">Hag. 1:4</scripRef>). “Ivory houses” had the upper parts
of the walls adorned with figures in stucco with gold and ivory
(1 Kings 22:39; 2 Chr. 3:6; Ps. 45:8).
The roofs of the dwelling-houses were flat, and are often

alluded to in Scripture (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 11:2" id="h-p468.1" parsed="|2Sam|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.11.2">2 Sam. 11:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 22:1" id="h-p468.2" parsed="|Isa|22|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.22.1">Isa. 22:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 24:17" id="h-p468.3" parsed="|Matt|24|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.24.17">Matt. 24:17</scripRef>).
Sometimes tents or booths were erected on them (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 16:22" id="h-p468.4" parsed="|2Sam|16|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.16.22">2 Sam. 16:22</scripRef>).
They were protected by parapets or low walls (<scripRef passage="Deut. 22:8" id="h-p468.5" parsed="|Deut|22|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.22.8">Deut. 22:8</scripRef>). On

the house-tops grass sometimes grew (<scripRef passage="Prov. 19:13" id="h-p468.6" parsed="|Prov|19|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.19.13">Prov. 19:13</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov 27:15" id="h-p468.7" parsed="|Prov|27|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.27.15">27:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 129:6" id="h-p468.8" parsed="|Ps|129|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.129.6">Ps. 129:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps 129:7" id="h-p468.9" parsed="|Ps|129|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.129.7">7</scripRef>). They were used, not only as places of recreation in
the evening, but also sometimes as sleeping-places at night (1 Sam. 9:25, 26; 2 Sam. 11:2; 16:22; Dan. 4:29; Job 27:18; Prov. 21:9), and as places of devotion (Jer. 32:29; 19:13).
</def>
<term id="h-p468.19">Hukkok</term>
Decreed, a town near Zebulun, not far from Jordan, on the border
of Naphtali (Josh. 19:34). (See HELKATH.)
</def>
<term id="h-p469.3">Hul</term>
Circle, the second son of Aram (Gen. 10:23), and grandson of
Shem.
</def>
<term id="h-p470.2">Huldah</term>
Weasel, a prophetess; the wife of Shallum. She was consulted
regarding the “book of the law” discovered by the high priest

Hilkiah (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 22:14-20" id="h-p471.1" parsed="|2Kgs|22|14|22|20" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.22.14-2Kgs.22.20">2 Kings 22:14-20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 34:22-28" id="h-p471.2" parsed="|2Chr|34|22|34|28" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.34.22-2Chr.34.28">2 Chr. 34:22-28</scripRef>). She resided in that
part of Jerusalem called the Mishneh (A.V., “the college;” R.V.,
“the second quarter”), supposed by some to be the suburb between
the inner and the outer wall, the second or lower city, Akra.

Miriam (<scripRef passage="Ex. 15:20" id="h-p471.3" parsed="|Exod|15|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.15.20">Ex. 15:20</scripRef>) and Deborah (<scripRef passage="Judg. 4:4" id="h-p471.4" parsed="|Judg|4|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.4.4">Judg. 4:4</scripRef>) are the only others
who bear the title of “prophetess,” for the word in <scripRef passage="Isa. 8:3" id="h-p471.5" parsed="|Isa|8|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.8.3">Isa. 8:3</scripRef>
means only the prophet’s wife.
</def>
<term id="h-p471.6">Humiliation of Christ</term>

(Phil. 2:8), seen in (1) his birth (Gal. 4:4; Luke 2:7; John 1:46; Heb. 2:9), (2) his circumstances, (3) his reputation (Isa. 53; Matt. 26:59, 67; Ps. 22:6; Matt. 26:68), (4) his soul (Ps. 22:1; Matt. 4:1-11; Luke 22:44; Heb. 2:17, 18; 4:15), (5) his

death (<scripRef passage="Luke 23" id="h-p472.16" parsed="|Luke|23|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.23">Luke 23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 19" id="h-p472.17" parsed="|John|19|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.19">John 19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 15:24" id="h-p472.18" parsed="|Mark|15|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.15.24">Mark 15:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Mark 15:25" id="h-p472.19" parsed="|Mark|15|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.15.25">25</scripRef>), (6) and his burial
(Isa. 53:9; Matt. 27:57, 58, 60).
His humiliation was necessary (1) to execute the purpose of

God (<scripRef passage="Acts 2:23" id="h-p473.1" parsed="|Acts|2|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.2.23">Acts 2:23</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 2:24" id="h-p473.2" parsed="|Acts|2|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.2.24">24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 40:6-8" id="h-p473.3" parsed="|Ps|40|6|40|8" osisRef="Bible:Ps.40.6-Ps.40.8">Ps. 40:6-8</scripRef>), (2) fulfil the Old Testament
types and prophecies, (3) satisfy the law in the room of the

guilty (<scripRef passage="Isa. 53" id="h-p473.4" parsed="|Isa|53|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.53">Isa. 53</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 9:12" id="h-p473.5" parsed="|Heb|9|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.12">Heb. 9:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Heb. 9:15" id="h-p473.6" parsed="|Heb|9|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.15">15</scripRef>), procure for them eternal
redemption, (4) and to show us an example.
</def>
<term id="h-p473.7">Humility</term>
A prominent Christian grace (Rom. 12:3; 15:17, 18; 1 Cor. 3:5-7;

<scripRef passage="2 Cor. 3:5" id="h-p474.5" parsed="|2Cor|3|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.3.5">2 Cor. 3:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Phil. 4:11-13" id="h-p474.6" parsed="|Phil|4|11|4|13" osisRef="Bible:Phil.4.11-Phil.4.13">Phil. 4:11-13</scripRef>). It is a state of mind well pleasing
to God (1 Pet. 3:4); it preserves the soul in tranquillity (Ps. 69:32, 33), and makes us patient under trials (Job 1:22).
Christ has set us an example of humility (Phil. 2:6-8). We
should be led thereto by a remembrance of our sins (<scripRef passage="Lam. 3:39" id="h-p475.2" parsed="|Lam|3|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lam.3.39">Lam. 3:39</scripRef>),
and by the thought that it is the way to honour (<scripRef passage="Prov. 16:18" id="h-p475.3" parsed="|Prov|16|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.16.18">Prov. 16:18</scripRef>),

and that the greatest promises are made to the humble (<scripRef passage="Ps. 147:6" id="h-p475.4" parsed="|Ps|147|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.147.6">Ps. 147:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 57:15" id="h-p475.5" parsed="|Isa|57|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.57.15">Isa. 57:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 66:2" id="h-p475.6" parsed="|Isa|66|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.66.2">66:2</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Pet. 5:5" id="h-p475.7" parsed="|1Pet|5|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.5.5">1 Pet. 5:5</scripRef>). It is a “great paradox in
Christianity that it makes humility the avenue to glory.”
</def>
<term id="h-p475.8">Hunting</term>
Mentioned first in Gen. 10:9 in connection with Nimrod. Esau was
“a cunning hunter” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 25:27" id="h-p476.2" parsed="|Gen|25|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.27">Gen. 25:27</scripRef>). Hunting was practised by the

Hebrews after their settlement in the “Land of Promise” (<scripRef passage="Lev. 17:15" id="h-p476.3" parsed="|Lev|17|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.17.15">Lev. 17:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Prov. 12:27" id="h-p476.4" parsed="|Prov|12|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Prov.12.27">Prov. 12:27</scripRef>). The lion and other ravenous beasts were

found in Palestine (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:34" id="h-p476.5" parsed="|1Sam|17|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.34">1 Sam. 17:34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 23:20" id="h-p476.6" parsed="|2Sam|23|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.23.20">2 Sam. 23:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 13:24" id="h-p476.7" parsed="|1Kgs|13|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.13.24">1 Kings 13:24</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Ezek. 19:3-8" id="h-p476.8" parsed="|Ezek|19|3|19|8" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.19.3-Ezek.19.8">Ezek. 19:3-8</scripRef>), and it must have been necessary to hunt and
destroy them. Various snares and gins were used in hunting (Ps. 91:3; Amos 3:5; 2 Sam. 23:20).
War is referred to under the idea of hunting (Jer. 16:16;
Ezek. 32:30).
</def>
<term id="h-p477.3">Hur</term>
A hole, as of a viper, etc. (1.) A son of Caleb (1 Chr. 2:19, 50; 4:1, 4; comp. 2 Chr. 1:5).
(2.) The husband of Miriam, Moses’ sister (Ex. 17:10-12). He
was associated with Aaron in charge of the people when Moses was
absent on Sinai (<scripRef passage="Ex. 24:14" id="h-p479.2" parsed="|Exod|24|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.24.14">Ex. 24:14</scripRef>). He was probably of the tribe of
Judah, and grandfather of Bezaleel (Ex. 31:2; 35:30; 1 Chr. 2:19).
(3.) One of the five princes of Midian who were defeated and
slain by the Israelites under the command of Phinehas (Num. 31:8).
</def>
<term id="h-p480.2">Hurai</term>
Linen-worker, one of David’s heroes, a native of the valley of
Mount Gaash (1 Chr. 11:32).
</def>
<term id="h-p481.2">Husband</term>
I.e., the “house-band,” connecting and keeping together the
whole family. A man when betrothed was esteemed from that time a

husband (<scripRef passage="Matt. 1:16" id="h-p482.1" parsed="|Matt|1|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.1.16">Matt. 1:16</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 1:20" id="h-p482.2" parsed="|Matt|1|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.1.20">20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 2:5" id="h-p482.3" parsed="|Luke|2|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.5">Luke 2:5</scripRef>). A recently married man was
exempt from going to war for “one year” (Deut. 20:7; 24:5).
</def>
<term id="h-p482.6">Husbandman</term>
One whose business it is to cultivate the ground. It was one of

the first occupations, and was esteemed most honourable (<scripRef passage="Gen. 9:20" id="h-p483.1" parsed="|Gen|9|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.9.20">Gen. 9:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 26:12" id="h-p483.2" parsed="|Gen|26|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.26.12">26:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 26:14" id="h-p483.3" parsed="|Gen|26|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.26.14">14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 37:7" id="h-p483.4" parsed="|Gen|37|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.7">37:7</scripRef>, etc.). All the Hebrews, except those
engaged in religious services, were husbandmen. (See AGRICULTURE.)
</def>
<term id="h-p483.6">Hushai</term>
Quick, “the Archite,” “the king’s friend” (1 Chr. 27:33). When
David fled from Jerusalem, on account of the rebellion of
Absalom, and had reached the summit of Olivet, he there met
Hushai, whom he sent back to Jerusalem for the purpose of
counteracting the influence of Ahithophel, who had joined the

ranks of Absalom (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 15:32" id="h-p484.2" parsed="|2Sam|15|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.15.32">2 Sam. 15:32</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 15:37" id="h-p484.3" parsed="|2Sam|15|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.15.37">37</scripRef>; 16:16-18). It was by his
advice that Absalom refrained from immediately pursuing after
David. By this delay the cause of Absalom was ruined, for it
gave David time to muster his forces.
</def>
<term id="h-p484.4">Husk</term>
In Num. 6:4 (Heb. zag) it means the “skin” of a grape. In 2 Kings 4:42 (Heb. tsiqlon) it means a “sack” for grain, as
rendered in the Revised Version. In <scripRef passage="Luke 15:16" id="h-p485.3" parsed="|Luke|15|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.15.16">Luke 15:16</scripRef>, in the parable
of the Prodigal Son, it designates the beans of the carob tree,
or Ceratonia siliqua. From the supposition, mistaken, however,
that it was on the husks of this tree that John the Baptist fed,
it is called “St. John’s bread” and “locust tree.” This tree is
in “February covered with innumerable purple-red pendent
blossoms, which ripen in April and May into large crops of pods
from 6 to 10 inches long, flat, brown, narrow, and bent like a
horn (whence the Greek name keratia, meaning ‘little horns’),
with a sweetish taste when still unripe. Enormous quantities of
these are gathered for sale in various towns and for
exportation.” “They were eaten as food, though only by the
poorest of the poor, in the time of our Lord.” The bean is
called a “gerah,” which is used as the name of the smallest
Hebrew weight, twenty of these making a shekel.
</def>
<term id="h-p485.4">Hymn</term>
Occurs only Eph. 5:19 and Col. 3:16. The verb to “sing an hymn”

occurs <scripRef passage="Matt. 26:30" id="h-p486.3" parsed="|Matt|26|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.30">Matt. 26:30</scripRef> and <scripRef passage="Mark 14:26" id="h-p486.4" parsed="|Mark|14|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.14.26">Mark 14:26</scripRef>. The same Greek word is
rendered to “sing praises” <scripRef passage="Acts 16:25" id="h-p486.5" parsed="|Acts|16|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.16.25">Acts 16:25</scripRef> (R.V., “sing hymns”) and
<scripRef passage="Heb. 2:12" id="h-p486.6" parsed="|Heb|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.2.12">Heb. 2:12</scripRef>. The “hymn” which our Lord sang with his disciples at
the last Supper is generally supposed to have been the latter
part of the Hallel, comprehending <scripRef passage="Ps. 113" id="h-p486.7" parsed="|Ps|113|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.113">Ps. 113</scripRef>-118. It was thus a
name given to a number of psalms taken together and forming a
devotional exercise.
The noun hymn is used only with reference to the services of
the Greeks, and was distinguished from the psalm. The Greek
tunes required Greek hymns. Our information regarding the
hymnology of the early Christians is very limited.
</def>
<term id="h-p487.1">Hypocrite</term>
One who puts on a mask and feigns himself to be what he is not;
a dissembler in religion. Our Lord severely rebuked the scribes

and Pharisees for their hypocrisy (<scripRef passage="Matt. 6:2" id="h-p488.1" parsed="|Matt|6|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.2">Matt. 6:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 6:5" id="h-p488.2" parsed="|Matt|6|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.5">5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 6:16" id="h-p488.3" parsed="|Matt|6|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.6.16">16</scripRef>). “The
hypocrite’s hope shall perish” (<scripRef passage="Job 8:13" id="h-p488.4" parsed="|Job|8|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.8.13">Job 8:13</scripRef>). The Hebrew word here
rendered “hypocrite” rather means the “godless” or “profane,” as
it is rendered in Jer. 23:11, i.e., polluted with crimes.
</def>
<term id="h-p488.6">Hyssop</term>
(Heb. ‘ezob; LXX. hyssopos), first mentioned in Ex. 12:22 in
connection with the institution of the Passover. We find it

afterwards mentioned in <scripRef passage="Lev. 14:4" id="h-p489.2" parsed="|Lev|14|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.14.4">Lev. 14:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 14:6" id="h-p489.3" parsed="|Lev|14|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.14.6">6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Lev. 14:52" id="h-p489.4" parsed="|Lev|14|52|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Lev.14.52">52</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num. 19:6" id="h-p489.5" parsed="|Num|19|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.19.6">Num. 19:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 19:18" id="h-p489.6" parsed="|Num|19|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.19.18">18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 9:19" id="h-p489.7" parsed="|Heb|9|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.9.19">Heb. 9:19</scripRef>. It is spoken of as a plant “springing out of the wall” (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:33" id="h-p489.8" parsed="|1Kgs|4|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.33">1 Kings 4:33</scripRef>). Many conjectures have been formed as to what this
plant really was. Some contend that it was a species of marjoram
(origanum), six species of which are found in Palestine. Others
with more probability think that it was the caper plant, the
Capparis spinosa of Linnaeus. This plant grew in Egypt, in the
desert of Sinai, and in Palestine. It was capable of producing a

stem three or four feet in length (<scripRef passage="Matt. 27:48" id="h-p489.9" parsed="|Matt|27|48|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.48">Matt. 27:48</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 15:36" id="h-p489.10" parsed="|Mark|15|36|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.15.36">Mark 15:36</scripRef>.
Comp. John 19:29).
</def>
</glossary>
</div2>
<div2 title="I" prev="h" next="j" id="i">
<glossary id="i-p0.1">
<term id="i-p0.2">Ibhar</term>
<def id="i-p0.3">
Chosen, one of David’s sons (1 Chr. 3:6; 2 Sam. 5:15).
</def>
<term id="i-p1.3">Ibleam</term>
<def id="i-p1.4">
People-waster, a city assigned to Manasseh (Josh. 17:11), from
which the Israelites, however, could not expel the Canaanites

(<scripRef passage="Judg. 1:27" id="i-p2.2" parsed="|Judg|1|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.27">Judg. 1:27</scripRef>). It is also called Bileam (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 6:70" id="i-p2.3" parsed="|1Chr|6|70|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.6.70">1 Chr. 6:70</scripRef>). It was
probably the modern Jelamah, a village 2 1/2 miles north of
Jenin.
</def>
<term id="i-p2.4">Ibzan</term>
<def id="i-p2.5">
Illustrious, the tenth judge of Israel (Judg. 12:8-10). He ruled
seven years.
</def>
<term id="i-p3.2">Ice</term>
<def id="i-p3.3">
Frequently mentioned (Job 6:16; 38:29; Ps. 147:17, etc.). (See CRYSTAL.)
</def>
<term id="i-p4.5">Ichabod</term>
<def id="i-p4.6">
When the tidings of the disastrous defeat of the Israelites in
the battle against the Philistines near to Mizpeh were carried
to Shiloh, the wife of Phinehas “was near to be delivered. And
when she heard the tidings that the ark of God was taken, and
that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she bowed
herself and travailed” (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 4:19-22" id="i-p5.1" parsed="|1Sam|4|19|4|22" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.4.19-1Sam.4.22">1 Sam. 4:19-22</scripRef>). In her great distress
she regarded not “the women that stood by her,” but named the
child that was born “Ichabod” i.e., no glory, saying, “The glory
is departed from Isreal;” and with that word on her lips she
expired.
</def>
<term id="i-p5.2">Iconium</term>
<def id="i-p5.3">
The capital of ancient Lycaonia. It was first visited by Paul
and Barnabas from Antioch-in-Pisidia during the apostle’s first

missionary journey (<scripRef passage="Acts 13:50" id="i-p6.1" parsed="|Acts|13|50|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.13.50">Acts 13:50</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 13:51" id="i-p6.2" parsed="|Acts|13|51|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.13.51">51</scripRef>). Here they were persecuted
by the Jews, and being driven from the city, they fled to
Lystra. They afterwards returned to Iconium, and encouraged the
church which had been founded there (14:21, 22). It was probably
again visited by Paul during his third missionary journey along
with Silas (18:23). It is the modern Konieh, at the foot of
Mount Taurus, about 120 miles inland from the Mediterranean.
</def>
<term id="i-p6.3">Idalah</term>
<def id="i-p6.4">
Snares(?), a city near the west border of Zebulun (Josh. 19:15).
It has been identified with the modern Jeida, in the valley of
Kishon.
</def>
<term id="i-p7.2">Iddo</term>
<def id="i-p7.3">
(1.) Timely (1 Chr. 6:21). A Gershonite Levite.
(2.) Lovely. The son of Zechariah (1 Chr. 27:21), the ruler of
Manasseh in David’s time.
(3.) Timely. The father of Ahinadab, who was one of Solomon’s
purveyors (1 Kings 4:14).
(4.) Lovely. A prophet of Judah who wrote the history of
Rehoboam and Abijah (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 12:15" id="i-p11.1" parsed="|2Chr|12|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.12.15">2 Chr. 12:15</scripRef>). He has been identified with
Oded (2 Chr. 15:1).
(5.) Lovely. The father of Berachiah, and grandfather of the
prophet Zechariah (Zech. 1:1, 7). He returned from Babylon (Neh. 12:4).
</def>
<term id="i-p12.4">Idol</term>
<def id="i-p12.5">
(1.) Heb. aven, “nothingness;” “vanity” (Isa. 66:3; 41:29; Deut. 32:21; 1 Kings 16:13; Ps. 31:6; Jer. 8:19, etc.).
(2.) ‘Elil, “a thing of naught” (Ps. 97:7; Isa. 19:3); a word
of contempt, used of the gods of Noph (Ezek. 30:13).
(3.) ‘Emah, “terror,” in allusion to the hideous form of idols
(Jer. 50:38).
(4.) Miphletzeth, “a fright;” “horror” (1 Kings 15:13; 2 Chr. 15:16).
(5.) Bosheth, “shame;” “shameful thing” (Jer. 11:13; Hos. 9:10); as characterizing the obscenity of the worship of Baal.
(6.) Gillulim, also a word of contempt, “dung;” “refuse”
(Ezek. 16:36; 20:8; Deut. 29:17, marg.).
(7.) Shikkuts, “filth;” “impurity” (Ezek. 37:23; Nah. 3:6).
(8.) Semel, “likeness;” “a carved image” (Deut. 4:16).
(9.) Tselem, “a shadow” (Dan. 3:1; 1 Sam. 6:5), as
distinguished from the “likeness,” or the exact counterpart.
(10.) Temunah, “similitude” (Deut. 4:12-19). Here Moses
forbids the several forms of Gentile idolatry.
(11.) ‘Atsab, “a figure;” from the root “to fashion,” “to
labour;” denoting that idols are the result of man’s labour

(<scripRef passage="Isa. 48:5" id="i-p23.1" parsed="|Isa|48|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.48.5">Isa. 48:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 139:24" id="i-p23.2" parsed="|Ps|139|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.139.24">Ps. 139:24</scripRef>, “wicked way;” literally, as some
translate, “way of an idol”).
(12.) Tsir, “a form;” “shape” (Isa. 45:16).
(13.) Matztzebah, a “statue” set up (Jer. 43:13); a memorial

stone like that erected by Jacob (<scripRef passage="Gen. 28:18" id="i-p25.2" parsed="|Gen|28|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.28.18">Gen. 28:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 31:45" id="i-p25.3" parsed="|Gen|31|45|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.45">31:45</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 35:14" id="i-p25.4" parsed="|Gen|35|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.35.14">35:14</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen 35:20" id="i-p25.5" parsed="|Gen|35|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.35.20">20</scripRef>),
by Joshua (4:9), and by Samuel (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 7:12" id="i-p25.6" parsed="|1Sam|7|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.7.12">1 Sam. 7:12</scripRef>). It is the name
given to the statues of Baal (2 Kings 3:2; 10:27).
(14.) Hammanim, “sun-images.” Hamman is a synonym of Baal, the
sun-god of the Phoenicians (2 Chr. 34:4, 7; 14:3, 5; Isa. 17:8).
(15.) Maskith, “device” (Lev. 26:1; Num. 33:52). In Lev. 26:1,
the words “image of stone” (A.V.) denote “a stone or cippus with
the image of an idol, as Baal, Astarte, etc.” In <scripRef passage="Ezek. 8:12" id="i-p27.4" parsed="|Ezek|8|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.8.12">Ezek. 8:12</scripRef>,
“chambers of imagery” (maskith), are “chambers of which the
walls are painted with the figures of idols;” comp. ver. 10, 11.
(16.) Pesel, “a graven” or “carved image” (Isa. 44:10-20). It
denotes also a figure cast in metal (Deut. 7:25; 27:15; Isa. 40:19; 44:10).
(17.) Massekah, “a molten image” (Deut. 9:12; Judg. 17:3, 4).
(18.) Teraphim, pl., “images,” family gods (penates)
worshipped by Abram’s kindred (<scripRef passage="Josh. 24:14" id="i-p30.1" parsed="|Josh|24|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.24.14">Josh. 24:14</scripRef>). Put by Michal in
David’s bed (Judg. 17:5; 18:14, 17, 18, 20; 1 Sam. 19:13).
“Nothing can be more instructive and significant than this
multiplicity and variety of words designating the instruments
and inventions of idolatry.”
</def>
<term id="i-p31.1">Idolatry</term>
<def id="i-p31.2">
Image-worship or divine honour paid to any created object. Paul
describes the origin of idolatry in <scripRef passage="Rom. 1:21-25" id="i-p32.1" parsed="|Rom|1|21|1|25" osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.21-Rom.1.25">Rom. 1:21-25</scripRef>: men forsook
God, and sank into ignorance and moral corruption (1:28).
The forms of idolatry are, (1.) Fetishism, or the worship of
trees, rivers, hills, stones, etc.
(2.) Nature worship, the worship of the sun, moon, and stars,
as the supposed powers of nature.
(3.) Hero worship, the worship of deceased ancestors, or of
heroes.
In Scripture, idolatry is regarded as of heathen origin, and
as being imported among the Hebrews through contact with heathen
nations. The first allusion to idolatry is in the account of
Rachel stealing her father’s teraphim (<scripRef passage="Gen. 31:19" id="i-p36.1" parsed="|Gen|31|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.31.19">Gen. 31:19</scripRef>), which were
the relics of the worship of other gods by Laban’s progenitors
“on the other side of the river in old time” (<scripRef passage="Josh. 24:2" id="i-p36.2" parsed="|Josh|24|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.24.2">Josh. 24:2</scripRef>).
During their long residence in Egypt the Hebrews fell into
idolatry, and it was long before they were delivered from it

(<scripRef passage="Josh. 24:14" id="i-p36.3" parsed="|Josh|24|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.24.14">Josh. 24:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 20:7" id="i-p36.4" parsed="|Ezek|20|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.20.7">Ezek. 20:7</scripRef>). Many a token of God’s displeasure
fell upon them because of this sin.
The idolatry learned in Egypt was probably rooted out from
among the people during the forty years’ wanderings; but when
the Jews entered Palestine, they came into contact with the
monuments and associations of the idolatry of the old
Canaanitish races, and showed a constant tendency to depart from
the living God and follow the idolatrous practices of those
heathen nations. It was their great national sin, which was only
effectually rebuked by the Babylonian exile. That exile finally
purified the Jews of all idolatrous tendencies.
The first and second commandments are directed against
idolatry of every form. Individuals and communities were equally
amenable to the rigorous code. The individual offender was
devoted to destruction (<scripRef passage="Ex. 22:20" id="i-p38.1" parsed="|Exod|22|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.22.20">Ex. 22:20</scripRef>). His nearest relatives were
not only bound to denounce him and deliver him up to punishment
(<scripRef passage="Deut. 13:20-10" id="i-p38.2" parsed="|Deut|13|20|13|10" osisRef="Bible:Deut.13.20-Deut.13.10">Deut. 13:20-10</scripRef>), but their hands were to strike the first blow
when, on the evidence of two witnesses at least, he was stoned
(<scripRef passage="Deut. 17:2-7" id="i-p38.3" parsed="|Deut|17|2|17|7" osisRef="Bible:Deut.17.2-Deut.17.7">Deut. 17:2-7</scripRef>). To attempt to seduce others to false worship was
a crime of equal enormity (13:6-10). An idolatrous nation shared
the same fate. No facts are more strongly declared in the Old
Testament than that the extermination of the Canaanites was the

punishment of their idolatry (<scripRef passage="Ex. 34:15" id="i-p38.4" parsed="|Exod|34|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.34.15">Ex. 34:15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 34:16" id="i-p38.5" parsed="|Exod|34|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.34.16">16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 7" id="i-p38.6" parsed="|Deut|7|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.7">Deut. 7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut 12:29-31" id="i-p38.7" parsed="|Deut|12|29|12|31" osisRef="Bible:Deut.12.29-Deut.12.31">12:29-31</scripRef>;
<scripRef passage="Deut 20:17" id="i-p38.8" parsed="|Deut|20|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.20.17">20:17</scripRef>), and that the calamities of the Israelites were due to
the same cause (<scripRef passage="Jer. 2:17" id="i-p38.9" parsed="|Jer|2|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.2.17">Jer. 2:17</scripRef>). “A city guilty of idolatry was
looked upon as a cancer in the state; it was considered to be in
rebellion, and treated according to the laws of war. Its
inhabitants and all their cattle were put to death.” Jehovah was
the theocratic King of Israel, the civil Head of the
commonwealth, and therefore to an Israelite idolatry was a state
offence (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 15:23" id="i-p38.10" parsed="|1Sam|15|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.15.23">1 Sam. 15:23</scripRef>), high treason. On taking possession of
the land, the Jews were commanded to destroy all traces of every

kind of the existing idolatry of the Canaanites (<scripRef passage="Ex. 23:24" id="i-p38.11" parsed="|Exod|23|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.24">Ex. 23:24</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ex. 23:32" id="i-p38.12" parsed="|Exod|23|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.32">32</scripRef>;
34:13; Deut. 7:5, 25; 12:1-3).
In the New Testament the term idolatry is used to designate
covetousness (Matt. 6:24; Luke 16:13; Col. 3:5; Eph. 5:5).
</def>
<term id="i-p39.5">Idumaea</term>
<def id="i-p39.6">
The Greek form of Edom (Isa. 34:5, 6; Ezek. 35:15; 36:5, but in
R.V. “Edom”). (See EDOM).
</def>
<term id="i-p40.6">Igal</term>
<def id="i-p40.7">
Avengers. (1.) Num. 13:7, one of the spies of the tribe of
Issachar. (2.) Son of Nathan of Zobah, and one of David’s
warriors (2 Sam. 23:36). (3.) 1 Chr. 3:22.
</def>
<term id="i-p41.4">Iim</term>
<def id="i-p41.5">
Ruins. (1.) A city in the south of Judah (Josh. 15:29).
(2.) One of the stations of the Israelites in the wilderness
(Num. 33:45).
</def>
<term id="i-p43.2">Ije-abarim</term>
<def id="i-p43.3">
Ruins of Abarim, the forty-seventh station of the Israelites in
the wilderness, “in the border of Moab” (Num. 33:44).
</def>
<term id="i-p44.2">Ijon</term>
<def id="i-p44.3">
A ruin, a city of Naphtali, captured by Ben-hadad of Syria at
the instance of Asa (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 15:20" id="i-p45.1" parsed="|1Kgs|15|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.15.20">1 Kings 15:20</scripRef>), and afterwards by
Tiglath-pileser of Assyria (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 15:29" id="i-p45.2" parsed="|2Kgs|15|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.29">2 Kings 15:29</scripRef>) in the reign of
Pekah; now el-Khiam.
</def>
<term id="i-p45.3">Ilai</term>
<def id="i-p45.4">
An Ahohite, one of David’s chief warriors (1 Chr. 11:29); called
also Zalmon (2 Sam. 23:28).
</def>
<term id="i-p46.3">Illyricum</term>
<def id="i-p46.4">
A country to the north-west of Macedonia, on the eastern shores
of the Adriatic, now almost wholly comprehended in Dalmatia, a

name formerly given to the southern part of Illyricum (<scripRef passage="2 Tim. 4:10" id="i-p47.1" parsed="|2Tim|4|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.4.10">2 Tim. 4:10</scripRef>). It was traversed by Paul in his third missionary journey
(<scripRef passage="Rom. 15:19" id="i-p47.2" parsed="|Rom|15|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.15.19">Rom. 15:19</scripRef>). It was the farthest district he had reached in
preaching the gospel of Christ. This reference to Illyricum is
in harmony with <scripRef passage="Acts 20:2" id="i-p47.3" parsed="|Acts|20|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.2">Acts 20:2</scripRef>, inasmuch as the apostle’s journey
over the parts of Macedonia would bring him to the borders of
Illyricum.
</def>
<term id="i-p47.4">Imagery</term>
<def id="i-p47.5">
Only in the phrase “chambers of his imagery” (Ezek. 8:12). (See CHAMBER.)
</def>
<term id="i-p48.3">Imla</term>
<def id="i-p48.4">
Replenisher, the father of Micaiah the prophet (2 Chr. 18:7, 8).
</def>
<term id="i-p49.3">Immanuel</term>
<def id="i-p49.4">
God with us. In the Old Testament it occurs only in Isa. 7:14
and 8:8. Most Christian interpreters have regarded these words
as directly and exclusively a prophecy of our Saviour, an
interpretation borne out by the words of the evangelist Matthew
</def>
<term id="i-p50.2">Immer</term>
<def id="i-p50.3">
Talkative. (1.) The head of the sixteenth priestly order (1 Chr. 24:14). (2.) Jer. 20:1. (3.) Ezra 2:37; Neh. 7:40. (4.) Ezra 2:59; Neh. 7:61. (5.) The father of Zadok (Neh. 3:29).
</def>
<term id="i-p51.8">Immortality</term>
<def id="i-p51.9">
Perpetuity of existence. The doctrine of immortality is taught
in the Old Testament. It is plainly implied in the writings of

Moses (<scripRef passage="Gen. 5:22" id="i-p52.1" parsed="|Gen|5|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.5.22">Gen. 5:22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 5:24" id="i-p52.2" parsed="|Gen|5|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.5.24">24</scripRef>; 25:8; 37:35; 47:9; 49:29, comp. <scripRef passage="Heb. 11:13-16" id="i-p52.3" parsed="|Heb|11|13|11|16" osisRef="Bible:Heb.11.13-Heb.11.16">Heb. 11:13-16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex. 3:6" id="i-p52.4" parsed="|Exod|3|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.3.6">Ex. 3:6</scripRef>, comp. <scripRef passage="Matt. 22:23" id="i-p52.5" parsed="|Matt|22|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.22.23">Matt. 22:23</scripRef>). It is more clearly and

fully taught in the later books (<scripRef passage="Isa. 14:9" id="i-p52.6" parsed="|Isa|14|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.14.9">Isa. 14:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 17:15" id="i-p52.7" parsed="|Ps|17|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.17.15">Ps. 17:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps 49:15" id="i-p52.8" parsed="|Ps|49|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.49.15">49:15</scripRef>;
73:24). It was thus a doctrine obviously well known to the Jews.
With the full revelation of the gospel this doctrine was
“brought to light” (2 Tim. 1:10; 1 Cor. 15; 2 Cor. 5:1-6; 1 Thess. 4:13-18).
</def>
<term id="i-p53.5">Imputation</term>
<def id="i-p53.6">
Is used to designate any action or word or thing as reckoned to
a person. Thus in doctrinal language (1) the sin of Adam is
imputed to all his descendants, i.e., it is reckoned as theirs,
and they are dealt with therefore as guilty; (2) the
righteousness of Christ is imputed to them that believe in him,
or so attributed to them as to be considered their own; and (3)
our sins are imputed to Christ, i.e., he assumed our
“law-place,” undertook to answer the demands of justice for our
sins. In all these cases the nature of imputation is the same
(Rom. 5:12-19; comp. Philemon 1:18, 19).
</def>
<term id="i-p54.3">Incarnation</term>
<def id="i-p54.4">
That act of grace whereby Christ took our human nature into
union with his Divine Person, became man. Christ is both God and
man. Human attributes and actions are predicated of him, and he
of whom they are predicated is God. A Divine Person was united

to a human nature (<scripRef passage="Acts 20:28" id="i-p55.1" parsed="|Acts|20|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.20.28">Acts 20:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 8:32" id="i-p55.2" parsed="|Rom|8|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.32">Rom. 8:32</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 2:8" id="i-p55.3" parsed="|1Cor|2|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.2.8">1 Cor. 2:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 2:11-14" id="i-p55.4" parsed="|Heb|2|11|2|14" osisRef="Bible:Heb.2.11-Heb.2.14">Heb. 2:11-14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Tim. 3:16" id="i-p55.5" parsed="|1Tim|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.3.16">1 Tim. 3:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gal. 4:4" id="i-p55.6" parsed="|Gal|4|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gal.4.4">Gal. 4:4</scripRef>, etc.). The union is
hypostatical, i.e., is personal; the two natures are not mixed
or confounded, and it is perpetual.
</def>
<term id="i-p55.7">Incense</term>
<def id="i-p55.8">
A fragrant composition prepared by the “art of the apothecary.”
It consisted of four ingredients “beaten small” (<scripRef passage="Ex. 30:34-36" id="i-p56.1" parsed="|Exod|30|34|30|36" osisRef="Bible:Exod.30.34-Exod.30.36">Ex. 30:34-36</scripRef>).
That which was not thus prepared was called “strange incense”
(30:9). It was offered along with every meat-offering; and
besides was daily offered on the golden altar in the holy place,
and on the great day of atonement was burnt by the high priest
in the holy of holies (30:7, 8). It was the symbol of prayer
(Ps. 141:1, 2; Rev. 5:8; 8:3, 4).
</def>
<term id="i-p56.7">India</term>
<def id="i-p56.8">
Occurs only in Esther 1:1 and 8:9, where the extent of the
dominion of the Persian king is described. The country so
designated here is not the peninsula of Hindustan, but the
country surrounding the Indus, the Punjab. The people and the
products of India were well known to the Jews, who seem to have
carried on an active trade with that country (Ezek. 27:15, 24).
</def>
<term id="i-p57.4">Inkhorn</term>
<def id="i-p57.5">
The Hebrew word so rendered means simply a round vessel or cup
for containing ink, which was generally worn by writers in the

girdle (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 9:2" id="i-p58.1" parsed="|Ezek|9|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.9.2">Ezek. 9:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 9:3" id="i-p58.2" parsed="|Ezek|9|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.9.3">3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 9:11" id="i-p58.3" parsed="|Ezek|9|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.9.11">11</scripRef>). The word “inkhorn” was used by the
translators, because in former times in this country horns were
used for containing ink.
</def>
<term id="i-p58.4">Inn</term>
<def id="i-p58.5">
In the modern sense, unknown in the East. The khans or
caravanserais, which correspond to the European inn, are not
alluded to in the Old Testament. The “inn” mentioned in <scripRef passage="Ex. 4:24" id="i-p59.1" parsed="|Exod|4|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.4.24">Ex. 4:24</scripRef>
was just the halting-place of the caravan. In later times khans
were erected for the accommodation of travellers. In <scripRef passage="Luke 2:7" id="i-p59.2" parsed="|Luke|2|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.7">Luke 2:7</scripRef>
the word there so rendered denotes a place for loosing the

beasts of their burdens. It is rendered “guest-chamber” in <scripRef passage="Mark 14:14" id="i-p59.3" parsed="|Mark|14|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.14.14">Mark 14:14</scripRef> and <scripRef passage="Luke 22:11" id="i-p59.4" parsed="|Luke|22|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.22.11">Luke 22:11</scripRef>. In <scripRef passage="Luke 10:34" id="i-p59.5" parsed="|Luke|10|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.10.34">Luke 10:34</scripRef> the word so rendered is
different. That inn had an “inn-keeper,” who attended to the
wants of travellers.
</def>
<term id="i-p59.6">Inspiration</term>
<def id="i-p59.7">
That extraordinary or supernatural divine influence vouchsafed
to those who wrote the Holy Scriptures, rendering their writings
infallible. “All scripture is given by inspiration of God”
(R.V., “Every scripture inspired of God”), <scripRef passage="2 Tim. 3:16" id="i-p60.1" parsed="|2Tim|3|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.3.16">2 Tim. 3:16</scripRef>. This is
true of all the “sacred writings,” not in the sense of their
being works of genius or of supernatural insight, but as
“theopneustic,” i.e., “breathed into by God” in such a sense
that the writers were supernaturally guided to express exactly
what God intended them to express as a revelation of his mind
and will. The testimony of the sacred writers themselves
abundantly demonstrates this truth; and if they are infallible
as teachers of doctrine, then the doctrine of plenary
inspiration must be accepted. There are no errors in the Bible
as it came from God, none have been proved to exist.
Difficulties and phenomena we cannot explain are not errors. All
these books of the Old and New Testaments are inspired. We do
not say that they contain, but that they are, the Word of God.
The gift of inspiration rendered the writers the organs of God,
for the infallible communication of his mind and will, in the
very manner and words in which it was originally given.
As to the nature of inspiration we have no information. This
only we know, it rendered the writers infallible. They were all
equally inspired, and are all equally infallible. The
inspiration of the sacred writers did not change their
characters. They retained all their individual peculiarities as
thinkers or writers. (See BIBLE; WORD OF GOD.)
</def>
<term id="i-p61.3">Intercession of Christ</term>
<def id="i-p61.4">
Christ’s priestly office consists of these two parts, (1) the
offering up of himself as a sacrifice, and (2) making continual
intercession for us.
When on earth he made intercession for his people (Luke 23:34;

<scripRef passage="John 17:20" id="i-p63.2" parsed="|John|17|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.17.20">John 17:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 5:7" id="i-p63.3" parsed="|Heb|5|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.5.7">Heb. 5:7</scripRef>); but now he exercises this function of his
priesthood in heaven, where he is said to appear in the presence
of God for us (Heb. 9:12, 24).
His advocacy with the Father for his people rests on the basis
of his own all-perfect sacrifice. Thus he pleads for and obtains
the fulfilment of all the promises of the everlasting covenant

(<scripRef passage="1 John 2:1" id="i-p64.1" parsed="|1John|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1John.2.1">1 John 2:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 17:24" id="i-p64.2" parsed="|John|17|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.17.24">John 17:24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Heb. 7:25" id="i-p64.3" parsed="|Heb|7|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.7.25">Heb. 7:25</scripRef>). He can be “touched with the
feeling of our infirmities,” and is both a merciful and a

faithful high priest (<scripRef passage="Heb. 2:17" id="i-p64.4" parsed="|Heb|2|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.2.17">Heb. 2:17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Heb. 2:18" id="i-p64.5" parsed="|Heb|2|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.2.18">18</scripRef>; 4:15, 16). This
intercession is an essential part of his mediatorial work.

Through him we have “access” to the Father (<scripRef passage="John 14:6" id="i-p64.6" parsed="|John|14|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.14.6">John 14:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph. 2:18" id="i-p64.7" parsed="|Eph|2|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.2.18">Eph. 2:18</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Eph 3:12" id="i-p64.8" parsed="|Eph|3|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.3.12">3:12</scripRef>). “The communion of his people with the Father will
ever be sustained through him as mediatorial Priest” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 110:4" id="i-p64.9" parsed="|Ps|110|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.110.4">Ps. 110:4</scripRef>;
Rev. 7:17).
</def>
<term id="i-p64.11">Intercession of the Spirit</term>
(Rom. 8:26, 27; John 14:26). “Christ is a royal Priest (Zech. 6:13). From the same throne, as King, he dispenses his Spirit to
all the objects of his care, while as Priest he intercedes for
them. The Spirit acts for him, taking only of his things. They
both act with one consent, Christ as principal, the Spirit as
his agent. Christ intercedes for us, without us, as our advocate
in heaven, according to the provisions of the everlasting
covenant. The Holy Spirit works upon our minds and hearts,
enlightening and quickening, and thus determining our desires
’according to the will of God,’ as our advocate within us. The
work of the one is complementary to that of the other, and
together they form a complete whole.”, Hodge’s Outlines of
Theology.
</def>
<term id="i-p65.5">Iphedeiah</term>
<def id="i-p65.6">
Set free by Jehovah, a chief of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chr. 8:25).
</def>
<term id="i-p66.2">Ira</term>
<def id="i-p66.3">
Citizen; wakeful. (1.) A Tekoite, one of David’s thirty warriors
(2 Sam. 23:26).
(2.) An Ithrite, also one of David’s heroes (2 Sam. 23:38).
(3.) A Jairite and priest, a royal chaplain (2 Sam. 20:26) or
confidential adviser (comp. 2 Sam. 8:18; 1 Chr. 18:17).
</def>
<term id="i-p69.4">Irad</term>
<def id="i-p69.5">
Runner; wild ass, one of the antediluvian patriarchs, the father
of Mehujael (Gen. 4:18), and grandson of Cain.
</def>
<term id="i-p70.2">Iram</term>
<def id="i-p70.3">
Citizen, chief of an Edomite tribe in Mount Seir (Gen. 36:43).
</def>
<term id="i-p71.2">Irha-heres</term>
<def id="i-p71.3">
According to some MSS., meaning “city of destruction.” Other
MSS. read ’Irhahares; rendered “city of the sun”, Isa. 19:18,
where alone the word occurs. This name may probably refer to
Heliopolis. The prophecy here points to a time when the Jews
would so increase in number there as that the city would fall
under their influence. This might be in the time of the
Ptolemies. (See ON.)
</def>
<term id="i-p72.3">Iron</term>
<def id="i-p72.4">
Tubal-Cain is the first-mentioned worker in iron (Gen. 4:22).
The Egyptians wrought it at Sinai before the Exodus. David
prepared it in great abundance for the temple (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 22:3" id="i-p73.2" parsed="|1Chr|22|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.22.3">1 Chr. 22:3</scripRef>:
29:7). The merchants of Dan and Javan brought it to the market
of Tyre (<scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:19" id="i-p73.3" parsed="|Ezek|27|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.19">Ezek. 27:19</scripRef>). Various instruments are mentioned as made
of iron (Deut. 27:5; 19:5; Josh. 17:16, 18; 1 Sam. 17:7; 2 Sam. 12:31; 2 Kings 6:5, 6; 1 Chr. 22:3; Isa. 10:34).
Figuratively, a yoke of iron (Deut. 28:48) denotes hard
service; a rod of iron (<scripRef passage="Ps. 2:9" id="i-p74.2" parsed="|Ps|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.2.9">Ps. 2:9</scripRef>), a stern government; a pillar

of iron (<scripRef passage="Jer. 1:18" id="i-p74.3" parsed="|Jer|1|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.1.18">Jer. 1:18</scripRef>), a strong support; a furnace of iron (<scripRef passage="Deut. 4:20" id="i-p74.4" parsed="|Deut|4|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.4.20">Deut. 4:20</scripRef>), severe labour; a bar of iron (<scripRef passage="Job 40:18" id="i-p74.5" parsed="|Job|40|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.40.18">Job 40:18</scripRef>), strength;
fetters of iron (<scripRef passage="Ps. 107:10" id="i-p74.6" parsed="|Ps|107|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.107.10">Ps. 107:10</scripRef>), affliction; giving silver for iron
(Isa. 60:17), prosperity.
</def>
<term id="i-p74.8">Irrigation</term>
<def id="i-p74.9">
As streams were few in Palestine, water was generally stored up
in winter in reservoirs, and distributed through gardens in
numerous rills, which could easily be turned or diverted by the
foot (Deut. 11:10).
For purposes of irrigation, water was raised from streams or
pools by water-wheels, or by a shaduf, commonly used on the
banks of the Nile to the present day.
</def>
<term id="i-p76.1">Isaac</term>
<def id="i-p76.2">
Laughter. (1) Israel, or the kingdom of the ten tribes (Amos 7:9, 16).
(2.) The only son of Abraham by Sarah. He was the longest
lived of the three patriarchs (<scripRef passage="Gen. 21:1-3" id="i-p78.1" parsed="|Gen|21|1|21|3" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.1-Gen.21.3">Gen. 21:1-3</scripRef>). He was circumcised
when eight days old (4-7); and when he was probably two years
old a great feast was held in connection with his being weaned.
The next memorable event in his life is that connected with
the command of God given to Abraham to offer him up as a
sacrifice on a mountain in the land of Moriah (Gen. 22). (See ABRAHAM.) When he was forty years of age Rebekah was
chosen for his wife (<scripRef passage="Gen. 24" id="i-p79.3" parsed="|Gen|24|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.24">Gen. 24</scripRef>). After the death and burial of his
father he took up his residence at Beer-lahai-roi (25:7-11),
where his two sons, Esau and Jacob, were born (21-26), the
former of whom seems to have been his favourite son (27, 28).
In consequence of a famine (Gen. 26:1) Isaac went to Gerar,
where he practised deception as to his relation to Rebekah,
imitating the conduct of his father in Egypt (12:12-20) and in
Gerar (20:2). The Philistine king rebuked him for his
prevarication.
After sojourning for some time in the land of the Philistines,
he returned to Beersheba, where God gave him fresh assurance of
covenant blessing, and where Abimelech entered into a covenant
of peace with him.
The next chief event in his life was the blessing of his sons
(<scripRef passage="Gen. 27:1" id="i-p82.1" parsed="|Gen|27|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.27.1">Gen. 27:1</scripRef>). He died at Mamre, “being old and full of days”
(35:27-29), one hundred and eighty years old, and was buried in
the cave of Machpelah.
In the New Testament reference is made to his having been

“offered up” by his father (<scripRef passage="Heb. 11:17" id="i-p83.1" parsed="|Heb|11|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.11.17">Heb. 11:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="James 2:21" id="i-p83.2" parsed="|Jas|2|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jas.2.21">James 2:21</scripRef>), and to his
blessing his sons (<scripRef passage="Heb. 11:20" id="i-p83.3" parsed="|Heb|11|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.11.20">Heb. 11:20</scripRef>). As the child of promise, he is
contrasted with Ishmael (Rom. 9:7, 10; Gal. 4:28; Heb. 11:18).
Isaac is “at once a counterpart of his father in simple
devoutness and purity of life, and a contrast in his passive
weakness of character, which in part, at least, may have sprung
from his relations to his mother and wife. After the expulsion
of Ishmael and Hagar, Isaac had no competitor, and grew up in
the shade of Sarah’s tent, moulded into feminine softness by
habitual submission to her strong, loving will.” His life was so
quiet and uneventful that it was spent “within the circle of a
few miles; so guileless that he let Jacob overreach him rather
than disbelieve his assurance; so tender that his mother’s death
was the poignant sorrow of years; so patient and gentle that
peace with his neighbours was dearer than even such a coveted
possession as a well of living water dug by his own men; so
grandly obedient that he put his life at his father’s disposal;
so firm in his reliance on God that his greatest concern through
life was to honour the divine promise given to his race.”,
Geikie’s Hours, etc.
</def>
<term id="i-p84.1">Isaiah</term>
<def id="i-p84.2">
(Heb. Yesh’yahu, i.e., “the salvation of Jehovah”). (1.) The son

of Amoz (<scripRef passage="Isa. 1:1" id="i-p85.1" parsed="|Isa|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.1.1">Isa. 1:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 2:1" id="i-p85.2" parsed="|Isa|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.2.1">2:1</scripRef>), who was apparently a man of humble
rank. His wife was called “the prophetess” (8:3), either because

she was endowed with the prophetic gift, like Deborah (<scripRef passage="Judg. 4:4" id="i-p85.3" parsed="|Judg|4|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.4.4">Judg. 4:4</scripRef>) and Huldah (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 22:14-20" id="i-p85.4" parsed="|2Kgs|22|14|22|20" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.22.14-2Kgs.22.20">2 Kings 22:14-20</scripRef>), or simply because she was
the wife of “the prophet” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 38:1" id="i-p85.5" parsed="|Isa|38|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.38.1">Isa. 38:1</scripRef>). He had two sons, who bore
symbolical names.
He exercised the functions of his office during the reigns of
Uzziah (or Azariah), Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (1:1). Uzziah
reigned fifty-two years (B.C. 810-759), and Isaiah must have
begun his career a few years before Uzziah’s death, probably
B.C. 762. He lived till the fourteenth year of Hezekiah, and in
all likelihood outlived that monarch (who died B.C. 698), and
may have been contemporary for some years with Manasseh. Thus
Isaiah may have prophesied for the long period of at least
sixty-four years.
His first call to the prophetical office is not recorded. A
second call came to him “in the year that King Uzziah died”
(<scripRef passage="Isa. 6:1" id="i-p87.1" parsed="|Isa|6|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.6.1">Isa. 6:1</scripRef>). He exercised his ministry in a spirit of
uncompromising firmness and boldness in regard to all that bore
on the interests of religion. He conceals nothing and keeps
nothing back from fear of man. He was also noted for his
spirituality and for his deep-toned reverence toward “the holy
One of Israel.”
In early youth Isaiah must have been moved by the invasion of
Israel by the Assyrian monarch Pul (q.v.), <scripRef passage="2 Kings 15:19" id="i-p88.1" parsed="|2Kgs|15|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.19">2 Kings 15:19</scripRef>; and
again, twenty years later, when he had already entered on his
office, by the invasion of Tiglath-pileser and his career of
conquest. Ahaz, king of Judah, at this crisis refused to
co-operate with the kings of Israel and Syria in opposition to
the Assyrians, and was on that account attacked and defeated by

Rezin of Damascus and Pekah of Samaria (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 16:5" id="i-p88.2" parsed="|2Kgs|16|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.16.5">2 Kings 16:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 28:5" id="i-p88.3" parsed="|2Chr|28|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.28.5">2 Chr. 28:5</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 28:6" id="i-p88.4" parsed="|2Chr|28|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.28.6">6</scripRef>). Ahaz, thus humbled, sided with Assyria, and sought the
aid of Tiglath-pileser against Israel and Syria. The consequence
was that Rezin and Pekah were conquered and many of the people

carried captive to Assyria (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 15:29" id="i-p88.5" parsed="|2Kgs|15|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.29">2 Kings 15:29</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Kings 16:9" id="i-p88.6" parsed="|2Kgs|16|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.16.9">16:9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 5:26" id="i-p88.7" parsed="|1Chr|5|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.5.26">1 Chr. 5:26</scripRef>).
Soon after this Shalmaneser determined wholly to subdue the
kingdom of Israel. Samaria was taken and destroyed (B.C. 722).
So long as Ahaz reigned, the kingdom of Judah was unmolested by
the Assyrian power; but on his accession to the throne, Hezekiah

(B.C. 726), who “rebelled against the king of Assyria” (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:7" id="i-p88.8" parsed="|2Kgs|18|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.7">2 Kings 18:7</scripRef>), in which he was encouraged by Isaiah, who exhorted the
people to place all their dependence on Jehovah (<scripRef passage="Isa. 10:24" id="i-p88.9" parsed="|Isa|10|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.10.24">Isa. 10:24</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Isa 37:6" id="i-p88.10" parsed="|Isa|37|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.37.6">37:6</scripRef>), entered into an alliance with the king of Egypt (<scripRef passage="Isa. 30:2-4" id="i-p88.11" parsed="|Isa|30|2|30|4" osisRef="Bible:Isa.30.2-Isa.30.4">Isa. 30:2-4</scripRef>). This led the king of Assyria to threaten the king of
Judah, and at length to invade the land. Sennacherib (B.C. 701)
led a powerful army into Palestine. Hezekiah was reduced to
despair, and submitted to the Assyrians (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 18:14-16" id="i-p88.12" parsed="|2Kgs|18|14|18|16" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.18.14-2Kgs.18.16">2 Kings 18:14-16</scripRef>). But
after a brief interval war broke out again, and again
Sennacherib (q.v.) led an army into Palestine, one detachment of

which threatened Jerusalem (<scripRef passage="Isa. 36:2-22" id="i-p88.13" parsed="|Isa|36|2|36|22" osisRef="Bible:Isa.36.2-Isa.36.22">Isa. 36:2-22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 37:8" id="i-p88.14" parsed="|Isa|37|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.37.8">37:8</scripRef>). Isaiah on that
occasion encouraged Hezekiah to resist the Assyrians (37:1-7),
whereupon Sennacherib sent a threatening letter to Hezekiah,
which he “spread before the Lord” (37:14). The judgement of God
now fell on the Assyrian host. “Like Xerxes in Greece,
Sennacherib never recovered from the shock of the disaster in
Judah. He made no more expeditions against either Southern
Palestine or Egypt.” The remaining years of Hezekiah’s reign

were peaceful (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 32:23" id="i-p88.15" parsed="|2Chr|32|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.32.23">2 Chr. 32:23</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 32:27" id="i-p88.16" parsed="|2Chr|32|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.32.27">27</scripRef>-29). Isaiah probably lived to
its close, and possibly into the reign of Manasseh, but the time
and manner of his death are unknown. There is a tradition that
he suffered martyrdom in the heathen reaction in the time of
Manasseh (q.v.).
(2.) One of the heads of the singers in the time of David (1 Chr. 25:3, 15, “Jeshaiah”).
(3.) A Levite (1 Chr. 26:25).
(4.) <scripRef passage="Ezra 8:7" id="i-p90.2" parsed="|Ezra|8|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezra.8.7">Ezra 8:7</scripRef>.
(5.) Neh. 11:7.
</def>
<term id="i-p90.4">Isaiah, The Book of</term>
<def id="i-p90.5">
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="i-p90.6" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="Isa 0" id="i-p90.7" parsed="|Isa|0|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa" />
Consists of prophecies delivered (Isa. 1) in the reign of Uzziah
(1-5), (2) of Jotham (6), (3) Ahaz (7-14:28), (4) the first half
of Hezekiah’s reign (14:28-35), (5) the second half of
Hezekiah’s reign (36-66). Thus, counting from the fourth year
before Uzziah’s death (B.C. 762) to the last year of Hezekiah
(B.C. 698), Isaiah’s ministry extended over a period of
sixty-four years. He may, however, have survived Hezekiah, and
may have perished in the way indicated above.
The book, as a whole, has been divided into three main parts:
(1.) The first thirty-five chapters, almost wholly prophetic,
Israel’s enemy Assyria, present the Messiah as a mighty Ruler
and King. (2.) Four chapters are historical (36-39), relating to
the times of Hezekiah. (3.) Prophetical (40-66), Israel’s enemy
Babylon, describing the Messiah as a suffering victim, meek and
lowly.
The genuineness of the section Isa. 40-66 has been keenly
opposed by able critics. They assert that it must be the
production of a deutero-Isaiah, who lived toward the close of
the Babylonian captivity. This theory was originated by Koppe, a
German writer at the close of the last century. There are other
portions of the book also (e.g., ch. 13; 24-27; and certain
verses in ch. 14 and 21) which they attribute to some other
prophet than Isaiah. Thus they say that some five or seven, or
even more, unknown prophets had a hand in the production of this
book. The considerations which have led to such a result are
various: (1.) They cannot, as some say, conceive it possible
that Isaiah, living in B.C. 700, could foretell the appearance
and the exploits of a prince called Cyrus, who would set the
Jews free from captivity one hundred and seventy years after.
(2.) It is alleged that the prophet takes the time of the
Captivity as his standpoint, and speaks of it as then present;
and (3) that there is such a difference between the style and
language of the closing section (40-66) and those of the
preceding chapters as to necessitate a different authorship, and
lead to the conclusion that there were at least two Isaiahs. But
even granting the fact of a great diversity of style and
language, this will not necessitate the conclusion attempted to
be drawn from it. The diversity of subjects treated of and the
peculiarities of the prophet’s position at the time the
prophecies were uttered will sufficiently account for this.
The arguments in favour of the unity of the book are quite
conclusive. When the LXX. version was made (about B.C. 250) the
entire contents of the book were ascribed to Isaiah, the son of
Amoz. It is not called in question, moreover, that in the time
of our Lord the book existed in the form in which we now have
it. Many prophecies in the disputed portions are quoted in the

New Testament as the words of Isaiah (<scripRef passage="Matt. 3:3" id="i-p94.1" parsed="|Matt|3|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.3">Matt. 3:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 3:4-6" id="i-p94.2" parsed="|Luke|3|4|3|6" osisRef="Bible:Luke.3.4-Luke.3.6">Luke 3:4-6</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Luke 4:16-41" id="i-p94.3" parsed="|Luke|4|16|4|41" osisRef="Bible:Luke.4.16-Luke.4.41">4:16-41</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 12:38" id="i-p94.4" parsed="|John|12|38|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.12.38">John 12:38</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 8:28" id="i-p94.5" parsed="|Acts|8|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.8.28">Acts 8:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 10:16-21" id="i-p94.6" parsed="|Rom|10|16|10|21" osisRef="Bible:Rom.10.16-Rom.10.21">Rom. 10:16-21</scripRef>). Universal and
persistent tradition has ascribed the whole book to one author.
Besides this, the internal evidence, the similarity in the
language and style, in the thoughts and images and rhetorical
ornaments, all points to the same conclusion; and its local
colouring and allusions show that it is obviously of Palestinian
origin. The theory therefore of a double authorship of the book,
much less of a manifold authorship, cannot be maintained. The
book, with all the diversity of its contents, is one, and is, we
believe, the production of the great prophet whose name it
bears.
</def>
<term id="i-p95.1">Iscah</term>
<def id="i-p95.2">
Spy, the daughter of Haran and sister of Milcah and Lot (Gen. 11:29, 31).
</def>
<term id="i-p96.3">Iscariot</term>
<def id="i-p96.4">
(See JUDAS.)
</def>
<term id="i-p97.2">Ishbak</term>
<def id="i-p97.3">
Leaving, one of Abraham’s sons by Keturah (Gen. 25:2).
</def>
<term id="i-p98.2">Ishbi-benob</term>
<def id="i-p98.3">
My seat at Nob, one of the Rephaim, whose spear was three
hundred shekels in weight. He was slain by Abishai (2 Sam. 21:16, 17).
</def>
<term id="i-p99.3">Ish-bosheth</term>
<def id="i-p99.4">
Man of shame or humiliation, the youngest of Saul’s four sons,
and the only one who survived him (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 2" id="i-p100.1" parsed="|2Sam|2|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.2">2 Sam. 2</scripRef>-4). His name was

originally Eshbaal (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 8:33" id="i-p100.2" parsed="|1Chr|8|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.8.33">1 Chr. 8:33</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 9:39" id="i-p100.3" parsed="|1Chr|9|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.9.39">9:39</scripRef>). He was about forty years
of age when his father and three brothers fell at the battle of
Gilboa. Through the influence of Abner, Saul’s cousin, he was
acknowledged as successor to the throne of Saul, and ruled over
all Israel, except the tribe of Judah (over whom David was
king), for two years, having Mahanaim, on the east of Jordan, as
his capital (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 2:9" id="i-p100.4" parsed="|2Sam|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.2.9">2 Sam. 2:9</scripRef>). After a troubled and uncertain reign
he was murdered by his guard, who stabbed him while he was
asleep on his couch at mid-day (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 4:5-7" id="i-p100.5" parsed="|2Sam|4|5|4|7" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.4.5-2Sam.4.7">2 Sam. 4:5-7</scripRef>); and having cut
off his head, presented it to David, who sternly rebuked them
for this cold-blooded murder, and ordered them to be immediately
executed (9-12).
</def>
<term id="i-p100.6">Ishi</term>
My husband, a symbolical name used in Hos. 2:16 (See BAALI.)
</def>
<term id="i-p101.3">Ishmael</term>
God hears. (1.) Abraham’s eldest son, by Hagar the concubine

(<scripRef passage="Gen. 16:15" id="i-p102.1" parsed="|Gen|16|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.16.15">Gen. 16:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Gen 17:23" id="i-p102.2" parsed="|Gen|17|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.17.23">17:23</scripRef>). He was born at Mamre, when Abraham was
eighty-six years of age, eleven years after his arrival in
Canaan (16:3; 21:5). At the age of thirteen he was circumcised
(17:25). He grew up a true child of the desert, wild and
wayward. On the occasion of the weaning of Isaac his rude and
wayward spirit broke out in expressions of insult and mockery
(21:9, 10); and Sarah, discovering this, said to Abraham, “Expel
this slave and her son.” Influenced by a divine admonition,
Abraham dismissed Hagar and her son with no more than a skin of
water and some bread. The narrative describing this act is one
of the most beautiful and touching incidents of patriarchal life
(Gen. 21:14-16). (See HAGAR.)
Ishmael settled in the land of Paran, a region lying between
Canaan and the mountains of Sinai; and “God was with him, and he
became a great archer” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 21:9-21" id="i-p103.1" parsed="|Gen|21|9|21|21" osisRef="Bible:Gen.21.9-Gen.21.21">Gen. 21:9-21</scripRef>). He became a great desert
chief, but of his history little is recorded. He was about
ninety years of age when his father Abraham died, in connection
with whose burial he once more for a moment reappears. On this
occasion the two brothers met after being long separated. “Isaac
with his hundreds of household slaves, Ishmael with his troops
of wild retainers and half-savage allies, in all the state of a
Bedouin prince, gathered before the cave of Machpelah, in the
midst of the men of Heth, to pay the last duties to the ‘father
of the faithful,’ would make a notable subject for an artist”
(<scripRef passage="Gen. 25:9" id="i-p103.2" parsed="|Gen|25|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.9">Gen. 25:9</scripRef>). Of the after events of his life but little is
known. He died at the age of one hundred and thirty-seven years,
but where and when are unknown (25:17). He had twelve sons, who
became the founders of so many Arab tribes or colonies, the
Ishmaelites, who spread over the wide desert spaces of Northern

Arabia from the Red Sea to the Euphrates (<scripRef passage="Gen. 37:25" id="i-p103.3" parsed="|Gen|37|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.25">Gen. 37:25</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 37:27" id="i-p103.4" parsed="|Gen|37|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.27">27</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Gen. 37:28" id="i-p103.5" parsed="|Gen|37|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.37.28">28</scripRef>;
39:1), “their hand against every man, and every man’s hand
against them.”
(2.) The son of Nethaniah, “of the seed royal” (Jer. 40:8, 15). He plotted against Gedaliah, and treacherously put him and
others to death. He carried off many captives, “and departed to
go over to the Ammonites.”
</def>
<term id="i-p104.3">Ishmaiah</term>
Heard by Jehovah. (1.) A Gibeonite who joined David at Ziklag,
“a hero among the thirty and over the thirty” (1 Chr. 12:4).
(2.) Son of Obadiah, and viceroy of Zebulun under David and
Solomon (1 Chr. 27:19).
</def>
<term id="i-p106.2">Ishmeelites</term>
(Gen. 37:28; 39:1, A.V.) should be “Ishmaelites,” as in the
Revised Version.
</def>
<term id="i-p107.3">Ishtob</term>
Man of Tob, one of the small Syrian kingdoms which together
constituted Aram (2 Sam. 10:6, 8).
</def>
<term id="i-p108.3">Island</term>
(Heb. ‘i, “dry land,” as opposed to water) occurs in its usual

signification (<scripRef passage="Isa. 42:4" id="i-p109.1" parsed="|Isa|42|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.42.4">Isa. 42:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 42:10" id="i-p109.2" parsed="|Isa|42|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.42.10">10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 42:12" id="i-p109.3" parsed="|Isa|42|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.42.12">12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Isa. 42:15" id="i-p109.4" parsed="|Isa|42|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.42.15">15</scripRef>, comp. <scripRef passage="Jer. 47:4" id="i-p109.5" parsed="|Jer|47|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.47.4">Jer. 47:4</scripRef>), but more

frequently simply denotes a maritime region or sea-coast (<scripRef passage="Isa. 20:6" id="i-p109.6" parsed="|Isa|20|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.20.6">Isa. 20:6</scripRef>, R.V.,” coastland;” 23:2, 6; <scripRef passage="Jer. 2:10" id="i-p109.7" parsed="|Jer|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.2.10">Jer. 2:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:6" id="i-p109.8" parsed="|Ezek|27|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.6">Ezek. 27:6</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:7" id="i-p109.9" parsed="|Ezek|27|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.7">7</scripRef>).
(See CHITTIM.) The shores of the Mediterranean are
called the “islands of the sea” (<scripRef passage="Isa. 11:11" id="i-p109.11" parsed="|Isa|11|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.11.11">Isa. 11:11</scripRef>), or the “isles of
the Gentiles” (Gen. 10:5), and sometimes simply “isles” (Ps. 72:10); Ezek. 26:15, 18; 27:3, 35; Dan. 11:18).
</def>
<term id="i-p109.17">Israel</term>
The name conferred on Jacob after the great prayer-struggle at
Peniel (<scripRef passage="Gen. 32:28" id="i-p110.1" parsed="|Gen|32|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.32.28">Gen. 32:28</scripRef>), because “as a prince he had power with God
and prevailed.” (See JACOB.) This is the common name
given to Jacob’s descendants. The whole people of the twelve

tribes are called “Israelites,” the “children of Israel” (<scripRef passage="Josh. 3:17" id="i-p110.3" parsed="|Josh|3|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.3.17">Josh. 3:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 7:25" id="i-p110.4" parsed="|Josh|7|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.7.25">7:25</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 8:27" id="i-p110.5" parsed="|Judg|8|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.8.27">Judg. 8:27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 3:21" id="i-p110.6" parsed="|Jer|3|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.3.21">Jer. 3:21</scripRef>), and the “house of Israel”
(Ex. 16:31; 40:38).
This name Israel is sometimes used emphatically for the true
Israel (Ps. 73:1: Isa. 45:17; 49:3; John 1:47; Rom. 9:6; 11:26).
After the death of Saul the ten tribes arrogated to themselves

this name, as if they were the whole nation (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 2:9" id="i-p112.1" parsed="|2Sam|2|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.2.9">2 Sam. 2:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 2:10" id="i-p112.2" parsed="|2Sam|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.2.10">10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 2:17" id="i-p112.3" parsed="|2Sam|2|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.2.17">17</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 2:28" id="i-p112.4" parsed="|2Sam|2|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.2.28">28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 3:10" id="i-p112.5" parsed="|2Sam|3|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.3.10">3:10</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 3:17" id="i-p112.6" parsed="|2Sam|3|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.3.17">17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 19:40-43" id="i-p112.7" parsed="|2Sam|19|40|19|43" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.19.40-2Sam.19.43">19:40-43</scripRef>), and the kings of the ten tribes were
called “kings of Israel,” while the kings of the two tribes were
called “kings of Judah.”
After the Exile the name Israel was assumed as designating the
entire nation.
</def>
<term id="i-p113.1">Israel, Kingdom of</term>
(B.C. 975-B.C. 722). Soon after the death of Solomon, Ahijah’s
prophecy (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 11:31-35" id="i-p114.1" parsed="|1Kgs|11|31|11|35" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.11.31-1Kgs.11.35">1 Kings 11:31-35</scripRef>) was fulfilled, and the kingdom was
