at the van on the east of the tabernacle (<scripRef passage="Num. 2:3-9" id="j-p498.5" parsed="|Num|2|3|2|9" osisRef="Bible:Num.2.3-Num.2.9">Num. 2:3-9</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 10:14" id="j-p498.6" parsed="|Num|10|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.10.14">10:14</scripRef>),
its standard, as is supposed, being a lion’s whelp. Under Caleb,
during the wars of conquest, they conquered that portion of the
country which was afterwards assigned to them as their
inheritance. This was the only case in which any tribe had its
inheritance thus determined (Josh. 14:6-15; 15:13-19).
The inheritance of the tribe of Judah was at first fully
one-third of the whole country west of Jordan, in all about
2,300 square miles (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15" id="j-p499.1" parsed="|Josh|15|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15">Josh. 15</scripRef>). But there was a second
distribution, when Simeon received an allotment, about 1,000
square miles, out of the portion of Judah (<scripRef passage="Josh. 19:9" id="j-p499.2" parsed="|Josh|19|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.9">Josh. 19:9</scripRef>). That
which remained to Judah was still very large in proportion to
the inheritance of the other tribes. The boundaries of the
territory are described in Josh. 15:20-63.
This territory given to Judah was divided into four sections.
(1.) The south (Heb. negeb), the undulating pasture-ground
between the hills and the desert to the south (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:21" id="j-p500.1" parsed="|Josh|15|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.21">Josh. 15:21</scripRef>.)
This extent of pasture-land became famous as the favourite
camping-ground of the old patriarchs. (2.) The “valley” (15:33)
or lowland (Heb. shephelah), a broad strip lying between the
central highlands and the Mediterranean. This tract was the
garden as well as the granary of the tribe. (3.) The
“hill-country,” or the mountains of Judah, an elevated plateau
stretching from below Hebron northward to Jerusalem. “The towns
and villages were generally perched on the tops of hills or on
rocky slopes. The resources of the soil were great. The country
was rich in corn, wine, oil, and fruit; and the daring shepherds
were able to lead their flocks far out over the neighbouring
plains and through the mountains.” The number of towns in this
district was thirty-eight (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:48-60" id="j-p500.2" parsed="|Josh|15|48|15|60" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.48-Josh.15.60">Josh. 15:48-60</scripRef>). (4.) The

“wilderness,” the sunken district next the Dead Sea (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:61" id="j-p500.3" parsed="|Josh|15|61|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.61">Josh. 15:61</scripRef>), “averaging 10 miles in breadth, a wild, barren,
uninhabitable region, fit only to afford scanty pasturage for
sheep and goats, and a secure home for leopards, bears, wild

goats, and outlaws” (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 17:34" id="j-p500.4" parsed="|1Sam|17|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.17.34">1 Sam. 17:34</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 22:1" id="j-p500.5" parsed="|1Sam|22|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.22.1">22:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 1:13" id="j-p500.6" parsed="|Mark|1|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.13">Mark 1:13</scripRef>). It was
divided into the “wilderness of En-gedi” (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 24:1" id="j-p500.7" parsed="|1Sam|24|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.24.1">1 Sam. 24:1</scripRef>), the

“wilderness of Judah” (<scripRef passage="Judg. 1:16" id="j-p500.8" parsed="|Judg|1|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.16">Judg. 1:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 3:1" id="j-p500.9" parsed="|Matt|3|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.3.1">Matt. 3:1</scripRef>), between the
Hebron mountain range and the Dead Sea, the “wilderness of Maon”
(1 Sam. 23:24). It contained only six cities.
Nine of the cities of Judah were assigned to the priests
(Josh. 21:9-19).
</def>
<term id="j-p501.2">Judah upon Jordan</term>
The Authorized Version, following the Vulgate, has this
rendering in <scripRef passage="Josh. 19:34" id="j-p502.1" parsed="|Josh|19|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.34">Josh. 19:34</scripRef>. It has been suggested that, following
the Masoretic punctuation, the expression should read thus, “and
Judah; the Jordan was toward the sun-rising.” The sixty cities
(Havoth-jair, <scripRef passage="Num. 32:41" id="j-p502.2" parsed="|Num|32|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.32.41">Num. 32:41</scripRef>) on the east of Jordan were reckoned as
belonging to Judah, because Jair, their founder, was a Manassite
only on his mother’s side, but on his father’s side of the tribe
of Judah (1 Chr. 2:5, 21-23).
</def>
<term id="j-p502.5">Judas</term>
The Graecized form of Judah. (1.) The patriarch (Matt. 1:2, 3).
(2.) Son of Simon (John 6:71; 13:2, 26), surnamed Iscariot,
i.e., a man of Kerioth (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:25" id="j-p504.4" parsed="|Josh|15|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.25">Josh. 15:25</scripRef>). His name is uniformly the
last in the list of the apostles, as given in the synoptic
(i.e., the first three) Gospels. The evil of his nature probably

gradually unfolded itself till “Satan entered into him” (<scripRef passage="John 13:27" id="j-p504.5" parsed="|John|13|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.13.27">John 13:27</scripRef>), and he betrayed our Lord (18:3). Afterwards he owned his
sin with “an exceeding bitter cry,” and cast the money he had
received as the wages of his iniquity down on the floor of the

sanctuary, and “departed and went and hanged himself” (<scripRef passage="Matt. 27:5" id="j-p504.6" parsed="|Matt|27|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.5">Matt. 27:5</scripRef>). He perished in his guilt, and “went unto his own place”

(<scripRef passage="Acts 1:25" id="j-p504.7" parsed="|Acts|1|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.25">Acts 1:25</scripRef>). The statement in <scripRef passage="Acts 1:18" id="j-p504.8" parsed="|Acts|1|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.18">Acts 1:18</scripRef> that he “fell headlong
and burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out,”
is in no way contrary to that in <scripRef passage="Matt. 27:5" id="j-p504.9" parsed="|Matt|27|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.5">Matt. 27:5</scripRef>. The sucide first
hanged himself, perhaps over the valley of Hinnom, “and the rope
giving way, or the branch to which he hung breaking, he fell
down headlong on his face, and was crushed and mangled on the
rocky pavement below.”
Why such a man was chosen to be an apostle we know not, but it
is written that “Jesus knew from the beginning who should betray
him” (<scripRef passage="John 6:64" id="j-p505.1" parsed="|John|6|64|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.6.64">John 6:64</scripRef>). Nor can any answer be satisfactorily given to
the question as to the motives that led Judas to betray his
Master. “Of the motives that have been assigned we need not care
to fix on any one as that which simply led him on. Crime is, for
the most part, the result of a hundred motives rushing with
bewildering fury through the mind of the criminal.”
(3.) A Jew of Damascus (Acts 9:11), to whose house Ananias was
sent. The street called “Straight” in which it was situated is
identified with the modern “street of bazaars,” where is still
pointed out the so-called “house of Judas.”
(4.) A Christian teacher, surnamed Barsabas. He was sent from
Jerusalem to Antioch along with Paul and Barnabas with the

decision of the council (<scripRef passage="Acts 15:22" id="j-p507.1" parsed="|Acts|15|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.15.22">Acts 15:22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 15:27" id="j-p507.2" parsed="|Acts|15|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.15.27">27</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 15:32" id="j-p507.3" parsed="|Acts|15|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.15.32">32</scripRef>). He was a “prophet”
and a “chief man among the brethren.”
</def>
<term id="j-p507.4">Jude</term>
= Judas. Among the apostles there were two who bore this name,

(1) Judas (<scripRef passage="Jude 1" id="j-p508.1" parsed="|Jude|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jude.1.1">Jude 1</scripRef>:1; <scripRef passage="Matt. 13:55" id="j-p508.2" parsed="|Matt|13|55|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.13.55">Matt. 13:55</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 14:22" id="j-p508.3" parsed="|John|14|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.14.22">John 14:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Acts 1:13" id="j-p508.4" parsed="|Acts|1|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.13">Acts 1:13</scripRef>), called

also Lebbaeus or Thaddaeus (<scripRef passage="Matt. 10:3" id="j-p508.5" parsed="|Matt|10|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.10.3">Matt. 10:3</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 3:18" id="j-p508.6" parsed="|Mark|3|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.3.18">Mark 3:18</scripRef>); and (2)

Judas Iscariot (<scripRef passage="Matt. 10:4" id="j-p508.7" parsed="|Matt|10|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.10.4">Matt. 10:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Mark 3:19" id="j-p508.8" parsed="|Mark|3|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.3.19">Mark 3:19</scripRef>). He who is called “the
brother of James” (<scripRef passage="Luke 6:16" id="j-p508.9" parsed="|Luke|6|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.6.16">Luke 6:16</scripRef>), may be the same with the Judas
surnamed Lebbaeus. The only thing recorded regarding him is in
John 14:22.
</def>
<term id="j-p508.11">Judea</term>
After the Captivity this name was applied to the whole of the

country west of the Jordan (<scripRef passage="Hag. 1:1" id="j-p509.1" parsed="|Hag|1|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hag.1.1">Hag. 1:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Hag. 1:14" id="j-p509.2" parsed="|Hag|1|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Hag.1.14">14</scripRef>; 2:2). But under the
Romans, in the time of Christ, it denoted the southernmost of

the three divisions of Palestine (<scripRef passage="Matt. 2:1" id="j-p509.3" parsed="|Matt|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.2.1">Matt. 2:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Matt. 2:5" id="j-p509.4" parsed="|Matt|2|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.2.5">5</scripRef>; 3:1; 4:25),
although it was also sometimes used for Palestine generally
(Acts 28:21).
The province of Judea, as distinguished from Galilee and
Samaria, included the territories of the tribes of Judah,
Benjamin, Dan, Simeon, and part of Ephraim. Under the Romans it
was a part of the province of Syria, and was governed by a
procurator.
</def>
<term id="j-p510.1">Jude, Epistle of</term>
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="j-p510.3" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="Jude 0" id="j-p510.4" parsed="|Jude|1|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jude.1" />
The author was “Judas, the brother of James” the Less (Jude 1:1), called also Lebbaeus (Matt. 10:3) and Thaddaeus (Mark 3:18). The genuineness of this epistle was early questioned, and
doubts regarding it were revived at the time of the Reformation;
but the evidences in support of its claims are complete. It has
all the marks of having proceeded from the writer whose name it
bears.
There is nothing very definite to determine the time and place
at which it was written. It was apparently written in the later
period of the apostolic age, for when it was written there were
persons still alive who had heard the apostles preach (ver. 17).
It may thus have been written about A.D. 66 or 70, and
apparently in Palestine.
The epistle is addressed to Christians in general (ver. 1),
and its design is to put them on their guard against the
misleading efforts of a certain class of errorists to which they
were exposed. The style of the epistle is that of an
“impassioned invective, in the impetuous whirlwind of which the
writer is hurried along, collecting example after example of
divine vengeance on the ungodly; heaping epithet upon epithet,
and piling image upon image, and, as it were, labouring for
words and images strong enough to depict the polluted character
of the licentious apostates against whom he is warning the
Church; returning again and again to the subject, as though all
language was insufficient to give an adequate idea of their
profligacy, and to express his burning hatred of their
perversion of the doctrines of the gospel.”
The striking resemblance this epistle bears to 2 Peter
suggests the idea that the author of the one had seen the
epistle of the other.
The doxology with which the epistle concludes is regarded as
the finest in the New Testament.
</def>
<term id="j-p515.1">Judge</term>
(Heb. shophet, pl. shophetim), properly a magistrate or ruler,
rather than one who judges in the sense of trying a cause. This
is the name given to those rulers who presided over the affairs
of the Israelites during the interval between the death of
Joshua and the accession of Saul (<scripRef passage="Judg. 2:18" id="j-p516.1" parsed="|Judg|2|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.2.18">Judg. 2:18</scripRef>), a period of
general anarchy and confusion. “The office of judges or regents
was held during life, but it was not hereditary, neither could
they appoint their successors. Their authority was limited by
the law alone, and in doubtful cases they were directed to
consult the divine King through the priest by Urim and Thummim
(<scripRef passage="Num. 27:21" id="j-p516.2" parsed="|Num|27|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.27.21">Num. 27:21</scripRef>). Their authority extended only over those tribes by
whom they had been elected or acknowledged. There was no income
attached to their office, and they bore no external marks of
dignity. The only cases of direct divine appointment are those
of Gideon and Samson, and the latter stood in the peculiar
position of having been from before his birth ordained ‘to begin
to deliver Israel.’ Deborah was called to deliver Israel, but
was already a judge. Samuel was called by the Lord to be a
prophet but not a judge, which ensued from the high gifts the
people recognized as dwelling in him; and as to Eli, the office
of judge seems to have devolved naturally or rather ex officio
upon him.” Of five of the judges, Tola (<scripRef passage="Judg. 10:1" id="j-p516.3" parsed="|Judg|10|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.10.1">Judg. 10:1</scripRef>), Jair (3),
Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon (12:8-15), we have no record at all
beyond the bare fact that they were judges. Sacred history is
not the history of individuals but of the kingdom of God in its
onward progress.
In Ex. 2:14 Moses is so styled. This fact may indicate that
while for revenue purposes the “taskmasters” were over the
people, they were yet, just as at a later time when under the
Romans, governed by their own rulers.
</def>
<term id="j-p517.2">Judges, Book of</term>
<scripCom type="About" target="/ccel/easton/ebd2.html?term=" id="j-p517.4" />
<scripCom type="About" passage="Judg 0" id="j-p517.5" parsed="|Judg|0|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg" />
Is so called because it contains the history of the deliverance
and government of Israel by the men who bore the title of the
“judges.” The book of Ruth originally formed part of this book,
but about A.D. 450 it was separated from it and placed in the
Hebrew scriptures immediately after the Song of Solomon.
The book contains, (1.) An introduction (1-3:6), connecting it
with the previous narrative in Joshua, as a “link in the chain
of books.” (2.) The history of the thirteen judges (3:7-16:31)
in the following order:
| FIRST PERIOD (3:7-ch. 5)
|                       Years
| I. Servitude under Chushan-rishathaim of
|  Mesopotamia                8
|  1. OTHNIEL delivers Israel, rest      40
| II. Servitude under Eglon of Moab:
|  Ammon, Amalek               18
|  2. EHUD’S deliverance, rest        80
|  3. SHAMGAR Unknown.
| III. Servitude under Jabin of Hazor in
|  Canaan                  20
|  4. DEBORAH and,
|  5. BARAK                  40
|       SECOND PERIOD (6-10:5)
| IV. Servitude under Midian, Amalek, and
|  children of the east            7
|  6. GIDEON                 40
|   ABIMELECH, Gideon’s son, reigns as
|    king over Israel            3
|  7. TOLA                  23
|  8. JAIR                  22
|     THIRD PERIOD (10:6-ch. 12)
| V. Servitude under Ammonites with the
|  Philistines                18
|  9. JEPHTHAH                 6
| 10. IBZAN                  7
| 11. ELON                  10
| 12. ABDON                  8
|      FOURTH PERIOD (13-16)
| VI. Seritude under Philistines        40
| 13. SAMSON                 20
| In all 410
Samson’s exploits probably synchronize with the period
immediately preceding the national repentance and reformation
under Samuel (1 Sam. 7:2-6).
After Samson came Eli, who was both high priest and judge. He
directed the civil and religious affairs of the people for forty
years, at the close of which the Philistines again invaded the
land and oppressed it for twenty years. Samuel was raised up to
deliver the people from this oppression, and he judged Israel
for some twelve years, when the direction of affairs fell into
the hands of Saul, who was anointed king. If Eli and Samuel are
included, there were then fifteen judges. But the chronology of
this whole period is uncertain.
(3.) The historic section of the book is followed by an
appendix (17-21), which has no formal connection with that which
goes before. It records (a) the conquest (17, 18) of Laish by a
portion of the tribe of Dan; and (b) the almost total extinction
of the tribe of Benjamin by the other tribes, in consequence of
their assisting the men of Gibeah (19-21). This section properly
belongs to the period only a few years after the death of
Joshua. It shows the religious and moral degeneracy of the
people.
The author of this book was most probably Samuel. The internal
evidence both of the first sixteen chapters and of the appendix
warrants this conclusion. It was probably composed during Saul’s
reign, or at the very beginning of David’s. The words in
18:30, 31, imply that it was written after the taking of the ark
by the Philistines, and after it was set up at Nob (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 21" id="j-p524.1" parsed="|1Sam|21|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.21">1 Sam. 21</scripRef>).
In David’s reign the ark was at Gibeon (1 Chr. 16:39)
</def>
<term id="j-p524.3">Judgment hall</term>
Gr. praitorion (John 18:28, 33; 19:9; Matt. 27:27), “common
hall.” In all these passages the Revised Version renders
“palace.” In <scripRef passage="Mark 15:16" id="j-p525.4" parsed="|Mark|15|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Mark.15.16">Mark 15:16</scripRef> the word is rendered “Praetorium”
(q.v.), which is a Latin word, meaning literally the residence
of the praetor, and then the governor’s residence in general,
though not a praetor. Throughout the Gospels the word
“praitorion” has this meaning (comp. <scripRef passage="Acts 23:35" id="j-p525.5" parsed="|Acts|23|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.23.35">Acts 23:35</scripRef>). Pilate’s
official residence when he was in Jerusalem was probably a part
of the fortress of Antonia.
The trial of our Lord was carried on in a room or office of
the palace. The “whole band” spoken of by Mark were gathered
together in the palace court.
</def>
<term id="j-p526.1">Judgment seat</term>
(Matt. 27:19), a portable tribunal (Gr. bema) which was placed
according as the magistrate might direct, and from which
judgment was pronounced. In this case it was placed on a
tesselated pavement, probably in front of the procurator’s
residence. (See GABBATHA.)
</def>
<term id="j-p527.3">Judgments of God</term>
(1.) The secret decisions of God’s will (Ps. 110:5; 36:6). (2.)

The revelations of his will (<scripRef passage="Ex. 21:1" id="j-p528.3" parsed="|Exod|21|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.21.1">Ex. 21:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 6:20" id="j-p528.4" parsed="|Deut|6|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.6.20">Deut. 6:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 119:7-175" id="j-p528.5" parsed="|Ps|119|7|119|175" osisRef="Bible:Ps.119.7-Ps.119.175">Ps. 119:7-175</scripRef>). (3.) The infliction of punishment on the wicked (<scripRef passage="Ex. 6:6" id="j-p528.6" parsed="|Exod|6|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.6.6">Ex. 6:6</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 12:12" id="j-p528.7" parsed="|Exod|12|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.12.12">12:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 25:11" id="j-p528.8" parsed="|Ezek|25|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.25.11">Ezek. 25:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 16:7" id="j-p528.9" parsed="|Rev|16|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.16.7">Rev. 16:7</scripRef>), such as is mentioned in
Gen. 7; 19:24, 25; Judg. 1:6, 7; Acts 5:1-10, etc.
</def>
<term id="j-p528.16">Judgment, The final</term>
The sentence that will be passed on our actions at the last day
(Matt. 25; Rom. 14:10, 11; 2 Cor. 5:10; 2 Thess. 1:7-10).
The judge is Jesus Christ, as mediator. All judgment is

committed to him (<scripRef passage="Acts 17:31" id="j-p530.1" parsed="|Acts|17|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.17.31">Acts 17:31</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 5:22" id="j-p530.2" parsed="|John|5|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.5.22">John 5:22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="John 5:27" id="j-p530.3" parsed="|John|5|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.5.27">27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 1:7" id="j-p530.4" parsed="|Rev|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.1.7">Rev. 1:7</scripRef>). “It
pertains to him as mediator to complete and publicly manifest
the salvation of his people and the overthrow of his enemies,
together with the glorious righteousness of his work in both
respects.”
The persons to be judged are, (1) the whole race of Adam

without a single exception (<scripRef passage="Matt. 25:31-46" id="j-p531.1" parsed="|Matt|25|31|25|46" osisRef="Bible:Matt.25.31-Matt.25.46">Matt. 25:31-46</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 15:51" id="j-p531.2" parsed="|1Cor|15|51|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.15.51">1 Cor. 15:51</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Cor. 15:52" id="j-p531.3" parsed="|1Cor|15|52|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.15.52">52</scripRef>;
Rev. 20:11-15); and (2) the fallen angels (2 Pet. 2:4; Jude 1:6).
The rule of judgment is the standard of God’s law as revealed

to men, the heathen by the law as written on their hearts (<scripRef passage="Luke 12:47" id="j-p532.1" parsed="|Luke|12|47|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.12.47">Luke 12:47</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Luke 12:48" id="j-p532.2" parsed="|Luke|12|48|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.12.48">48</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rom. 2:12-16" id="j-p532.3" parsed="|Rom|2|12|2|16" osisRef="Bible:Rom.2.12-Rom.2.16">Rom. 2:12-16</scripRef>); the Jew who “sinned in the law shall be
judged by the law” (<scripRef passage="Rom. 2:12" id="j-p532.4" parsed="|Rom|2|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.2.12">Rom. 2:12</scripRef>); the Christian enjoying the light

of revelation, by the will of God as made known to him (<scripRef passage="Matt. 11:20-24" id="j-p532.5" parsed="|Matt|11|20|11|24" osisRef="Bible:Matt.11.20-Matt.11.24">Matt. 11:20-24</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="John 3:19" id="j-p532.6" parsed="|John|3|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.3.19">John 3:19</scripRef>). Then the secrets of all hearts will be

brought to light (<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 4:5" id="j-p532.7" parsed="|1Cor|4|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.4.5">1 Cor. 4:5</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 8:17" id="j-p532.8" parsed="|Luke|8|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.8.17">Luke 8:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Luke 12:2" id="j-p532.9" parsed="|Luke|12|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.12.2">12:2</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Luke 12:3" id="j-p532.10" parsed="|Luke|12|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.12.3">3</scripRef>) to vindicate
the justice of the sentence pronounced.
The time of the judgment will be after the resurrection (Heb. 9:27; Acts 17:31).
As the Scriptures represent the final judgment “as certain

[<scripRef passage="Eccl. 11:9" id="j-p534.1" parsed="|Eccl|11|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eccl.11.9">Eccl. 11:9</scripRef>], universal [<scripRef passage="2 Cor. 5:10" id="j-p534.2" parsed="|2Cor|5|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Cor.5.10">2 Cor. 5:10</scripRef>], righteous [<scripRef passage="Rom. 2:5" id="j-p534.3" parsed="|Rom|2|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rom.2.5">Rom. 2:5</scripRef>],
decisive [<scripRef passage="1 Cor. 15:52" id="j-p534.4" parsed="|1Cor|15|52|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Cor.15.52">1 Cor. 15:52</scripRef>], and eternal as to its consequences
[<scripRef passage="Heb. 6:2" id="j-p534.5" parsed="|Heb|6|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Heb.6.2">Heb. 6:2</scripRef>], let us be concerned for the welfare of our immortal
interests, flee to the refuge set before us, improve our
precious time, depend on the merits of the Redeemer, and adhere
to the dictates of the divine word, that we may be found of him
in peace.”
</def>
<term id="j-p534.6">Judith</term>
Jewess, the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and one of Esau’s
wives (Gen. 26:34), elsewhere called Aholibamah (36:2-14).
</def>
<term id="j-p535.2">Julia</term>
A Christian woman at Rome to whom Paul sent his salutations
(Rom. 16:15), supposed to be the wife of Philologus.
</def>
<term id="j-p536.2">Julius</term>
The centurion of the Augustan cohort, or the emperor’s

body-guard, in whose charge Paul was sent prisoner to Rome (<scripRef passage="Acts 27:1" id="j-p537.1" parsed="|Acts|27|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.27.1">Acts 27:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 27:3" id="j-p537.2" parsed="|Acts|27|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.27.3">3</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Acts 27:43" id="j-p537.3" parsed="|Acts|27|43|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.27.43">43</scripRef>). He entreated Paul “courteously,” showing in many
ways a friendly regard for him.
</def>
<term id="j-p537.4">Junia</term>
(Rom. 16:7), a Christian at Rome to whom Paul sends salutations
along with Andronicus.
</def>
<term id="j-p538.2">Juniper</term>
(Heb. rothem), called by the Arabs retem, and known as Spanish
broom; ranked under the genus genista. It is a desert shrub, and
abounds in many parts of Palestine. In the account of his
journey from Akabah to Jerusalem, Dr. Robinson says: “This is
the largest and most conspicuous shrub of these deserts, growing
thickly in the water-courses and valleys. Our Arabs always
selected the place of encampment, if possible, in a spot where
it grew, in order to be sheltered by it at night from the wind;
and during the day, when they often went on in advance of the
camels, we found them not unfrequently sitting or sleeping under
a bush of retem to shelter them from the sun. It was in this
very desert, a day’s journey from Beersheba, that the prophet

Elijah lay down and slept beneath the same shrub” (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 19:4" id="j-p539.1" parsed="|1Kgs|19|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.19.4">1 Kings 19:4</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Kings 19:5" id="j-p539.2" parsed="|1Kgs|19|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.19.5">5</scripRef>). It afforded material for fuel, and also in cases of

extremity for human food (<scripRef passage="Ps. 120:4" id="j-p539.3" parsed="|Ps|120|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.120.4">Ps. 120:4</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Job 30:4" id="j-p539.4" parsed="|Job|30|4|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.30.4">Job 30:4</scripRef>). One of the
encampments in the wilderness of Paran is called Rithmah, i.e.,
“place of broom” (Num. 33:18).
“The Bedawin of Sinai still burn this very plant into a
charcoal which throws out the most intense heat.”
</def>
<term id="j-p540.1">Jupiter</term>
The principal deity of the ancient Greeks and Romans. He was
worshipped by them under various epithets. Barnabas was
identified with this god by the Lycaonians (<scripRef passage="Acts 14:12" id="j-p541.1" parsed="|Acts|14|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.14.12">Acts 14:12</scripRef>), because
he was of stately and commanding presence, as they supposed
Jupiter to be. There was a temple dedicated to this god outside
the gates of Lystra (14:13).
</def>
<term id="j-p541.2">Justice</term>
Is rendering to every one that which is his due. It has been
distinguished from equity in this respect, that while justice
means merely the doing what positive law demands, equity means
the doing of what is fair and right in every separate case.
</def>
<term id="j-p542.1">Justice of God</term>
That perfection of his nature whereby he is infinitely righteous
in himself and in all he does, the righteousness of the divine
nature exercised in his moral government. At first God imposes
righteous laws on his creatures and executes them righteously.
Justice is not an optional product of his will, but an
unchangeable principle of his very nature. His legislative
justice is his requiring of his rational creatures conformity in
all respects to the moral law. His rectoral or distributive
justice is his dealing with his accountable creatures according
to the requirements of the law in rewarding or punishing them
(<scripRef passage="Ps. 89:14" id="j-p543.1" parsed="|Ps|89|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.89.14">Ps. 89:14</scripRef>). In remunerative justice he distributes rewards

(<scripRef passage="James 1:12" id="j-p543.2" parsed="|Jas|1|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jas.1.12">James 1:12</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Tim. 4:8" id="j-p543.3" parsed="|2Tim|4|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.4.8">2 Tim. 4:8</scripRef>); in vindictive or punitive justice he
inflicts punishment on account of transgression (<scripRef passage="2 Thess. 1:6" id="j-p543.4" parsed="|2Thess|1|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Thess.1.6">2 Thess. 1:6</scripRef>).
He cannot, as being infinitely righteous, do otherwise than
regard and hate sin as intrinsically hateful and deserving of
punishment. “He cannot deny himself” (<scripRef passage="2 Tim. 2:13" id="j-p543.5" parsed="|2Tim|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Tim.2.13">2 Tim. 2:13</scripRef>). His
essential and eternal righteousness immutably determines him to
visit every sin as such with merited punishment.
</def>
<term id="j-p543.6">Justification</term>
A forensic term, opposed to condemnation. As regards its nature,
it is the judicial act of God, by which he pardons all the sins
of those who believe in Christ, and accounts, accepts, and
treats them as righteous in the eye of the law, i.e., as
conformed to all its demands. In addition to the pardon (q.v.)
of sin, justification declares that all the claims of the law
are satisfied in respect of the justified. It is the act of a
judge and not of a sovereign. The law is not relaxed or set
aside, but is declared to be fulfilled in the strictest sense;
and so the person justified is declared to be entitled to all
the advantages and rewards arising from perfect obedience to the
law (Rom. 5:1-10).
It proceeds on the imputing or crediting to the believer by
God himself of the perfect righteousness, active and passive, of
his Representative and Surety, Jesus Christ (<scripRef passage="Rom. 10:3-9" id="j-p545.1" parsed="|Rom|10|3|10|9" osisRef="Bible:Rom.10.3-Rom.10.9">Rom. 10:3-9</scripRef>).
Justification is not the forgiveness of a man without
righteousness, but a declaration that he possesses a
righteousness which perfectly and for ever satisfies the law,
namely, Christ’s righteousness (2 Cor. 5:21; Rom. 4:6-8).
The sole condition on which this righteousness is imputed or
credited to the believer is faith in or on the Lord Jesus
Christ. Faith is called a “condition,” not because it possesses
any merit, but only because it is the instrument, the only
instrument by which the soul appropriates or apprehends Christ
and his righteousness (Rom. 1:17; 3:25, 26; 4:20, 22; Phil. 3:8-11; Gal. 2:16).
The act of faith which thus secures our justification secures
also at the same time our sanctification (q.v.); and thus the
doctrine of justification by faith does not lead to
licentiousness (<scripRef passage="Rom. 6:2-7" id="j-p547.1" parsed="|Rom|6|2|6|7" osisRef="Bible:Rom.6.2-Rom.6.7">Rom. 6:2-7</scripRef>). Good works, while not the ground,
are the certain consequence of justification (6:14; 7:6). (See
GALATIANS, EPISTLE TO.)
</def>
<term id="j-p547.3">Justus</term>
(1.) Another name for Joseph, surnamed Barsabas. He and Matthias
are mentioned only in <scripRef passage="Acts 1:23" id="j-p548.1" parsed="|Acts|1|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Acts.1.23">Acts 1:23</scripRef>. “They must have been among the
earliest disciples of Jesus, and must have been faithful to the
end; they must have been well known and esteemed among the
brethren. What became of them afterwards, and what work they
did, are entirely unknown” (Lindsay’s Acts of the Apostles).
(2.) A Jewish proselyte at Corinth, in whose house, next door
to the synagogue, Paul held meetings and preached after he left
the synagogue (Acts 18:7).
(3.) A Jewish Christian, called Jesus, Paul’s only
fellow-labourer at Rome, where he wrote his Epistle to the
Colossians (Col. 4:11).
</def>
<term id="j-p550.2">Juttah</term>
Extended, a Levitical city in the mountains or hill-country of

Judah (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:55" id="j-p551.1" parsed="|Josh|15|55|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.55">Josh. 15:55</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh 21:16" id="j-p551.2" parsed="|Josh|21|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.21.16">21:16</scripRef>). Its modern name is Yutta, a place
about 5 1/2 miles south of Hebron. It is supposed to have been
the residence of Zacharias and Elisabeth, and the birthplace of
John the Baptist, and on this account is annually visited by
thousands of pilgrims belonging to the Greek Church (<scripRef passage="Luke 1:39" id="j-p551.3" parsed="|Luke|1|39|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.39">Luke 1:39</scripRef>).
(See MARY.)
</def>
</glossary>
</div2>
<div2 title="K" prev="j" next="l" id="k">
<glossary id="k-p0.1">
<term id="k-p0.2">Kabzeel</term>
<def id="k-p0.3">
Gathering of God, a city in the extreme south of Judah, near to
Idumaea (<scripRef passage="Josh. 15:21" id="k-p1.1" parsed="|Josh|15|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.15.21">Josh. 15:21</scripRef>), the birthplace of Benaiah, one of David’s

chief warriors (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 23:20" id="k-p1.2" parsed="|2Sam|23|20|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.23.20">2 Sam. 23:20</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Chr. 11:22" id="k-p1.3" parsed="|1Chr|11|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.11.22">1 Chr. 11:22</scripRef>). It was called also
Jekabzeel (Neh. 11:25), after the Captivity.
</def>
<term id="k-p1.5">Kadesh</term>
<def id="k-p1.6">
Holy, or Kadesh-Barnea, sacred desert of wandering, a place on
the south-eastern border of Palestine, about 165 miles from
Horeb. It lay in the “wilderness” or “desert of Zin” (<scripRef passage="Gen. 14:7" id="k-p2.1" parsed="|Gen|14|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.14.7">Gen. 14:7</scripRef>;

<scripRef passage="Num. 13:3-26" id="k-p2.2" parsed="|Num|13|3|13|26" osisRef="Bible:Num.13.3-Num.13.26">Num. 13:3-26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 14:29-33" id="k-p2.3" parsed="|Num|14|29|14|33" osisRef="Bible:Num.14.29-Num.14.33">14:29-33</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 20:1" id="k-p2.4" parsed="|Num|20|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.20.1">20:1</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Num 27:14" id="k-p2.5" parsed="|Num|27|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.27.14">27:14</scripRef>), on the border of Edom
(20:16). From this place, in compliance with the desire of the
people, Moses sent forth “twelve spies” to spy the land. After
examining it in all its districts, the spies brought back an
evil report, Joshua and Caleb alone giving a good report of the
land (13:18-31). Influenced by the discouraging report, the
people abandoned all hope of entering into the Promised Land.
They remained a considerable time at Kadesh. (See
HORMAH; KORAH.) Because of their unbelief, they
were condemned by God to wander for thirty-eight years in the
wilderness. They took their journey from Kadesh into the deserts
of Paran, “by way of the Red Sea” (<scripRef passage="Deut. 2:1" id="k-p2.8" parsed="|Deut|2|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.2.1">Deut. 2:1</scripRef>). (One theory is
that during these thirty-eight years they remained in and about
Kadesh.)
At the end of these years of wanderings, the tribes were a
second time gathered together at Kadesh. During their stay here
at this time Miriam died and was buried. Here the people
murmured for want of water, as their forefathers had done
formerly at Rephidim; and Moses, irritated by their chidings,
“with his rod smote the rock twice,” instead of “speaking to the
rock before their eyes,” as the Lord had commanded him (comp.

<scripRef passage="Num. 27:14" id="k-p3.1" parsed="|Num|27|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.27.14">Num. 27:14</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 9:23" id="k-p3.2" parsed="|Deut|9|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.9.23">Deut. 9:23</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ps. 106:32" id="k-p3.3" parsed="|Ps|106|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.106.32">Ps. 106:32</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps. 106:33" id="k-p3.4" parsed="|Ps|106|33|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.106.33">33</scripRef>). Because of this act of
his, in which Aaron too was involved, neither of them was to be

permitted to set foot within the Promised Land (<scripRef passage="Num. 20:12" id="k-p3.5" parsed="|Num|20|12|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.20.12">Num. 20:12</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 20:24" id="k-p3.6" parsed="|Num|20|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.20.24">24</scripRef>).
The king of Edom would not permit them to pass on through his
territory, and therefore they commenced an eastward march, and
“came unto Mount Hor” (20:22).
This place has been identified with ‘Ain el-Kadeis, about 12
miles east-south-east of Beersheba. (See SPIES.)
</def>
<term id="k-p4.2">Kadesh</term>
<def id="k-p4.3">
The sacred city of the Hittites, on the left bank of the
Orontes, about 4 miles south of the Lake of Homs. It is
identified with the great mound Tell Neby Mendeh, some 50 to 100
feet high, and 400 yards long. On the ruins of the temple of
Karnak, in Egypt, has been found an inscription recording the
capture of this city by Rameses II. (See PHARAOH.)
Here the sculptor “has chiselled in deep work on the stone, with
a bold execution of the several parts, the procession of the
warriors, the battle before Kadesh, the storming of the
fortress, the overthrow of the enemy, and the camp life of the
Egyptians.” (See HITTITES.)
</def>
<term id="k-p5.3">Kadmiel</term>
<def id="k-p5.4">
Before God; i.e., his servant, one of the Levites who returned
with Zerubbabel from the Captivity (Neh. 9:4; 10:9; 12:8).
</def>
<term id="k-p6.4">Kadmonites</term>
<def id="k-p6.5">
Orientals, the name of a Canaanitish tribe which inhabited the

north-eastern part of Palestine in the time of Abraham (<scripRef passage="Gen. 15:19" id="k-p7.1" parsed="|Gen|15|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.19">Gen. 15:19</scripRef>). Probably they were identical with the “children of the
east,” who inhabited the country between Palestine and the
Euphrates.
</def>
<term id="k-p7.2">Kanah</term>
<def id="k-p7.3">
Reedy; brook of reeds. (1.) A stream forming the boundary
between Ephraim and Manasseh, from the Mediterranean eastward to
Tappuah (<scripRef passage="Josh. 16:8" id="k-p8.1" parsed="|Josh|16|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.16.8">Josh. 16:8</scripRef>). It has been identified with the sedgy
streams that constitute the Wady Talaik, which enters the sea
between Joppa and Caesarea. Others identify it with the river’
Aujeh.
(2.) A town in the north of Asher (Josh. 19:28). It has been
identified with ‘Ain-Kana, a village on the brow of a valley
some 7 miles south-east of Tyre. About a mile north of this
place are many colossal ruins strown about. And in the side of a
neighbouring ravine are figures of men, women, and children cut
in the face of the rock. These are supposed to be of Phoenician
origin.
</def>
<term id="k-p9.2">Kareah</term>
<def id="k-p9.3">
Bald, the father of Johanan and Jonathan, who for a time were
loyal to Gedaliah, the Babylonian governor of Jerusalem (Jer. 40:8, 13, 15, 16).
</def>
<term id="k-p10.5">Karkaa</term>
<def id="k-p10.6">
A floor; bottom, a place between Adar and Azmon, about midway
between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea (Josh. 15:3).
</def>
<term id="k-p11.2">Karkor</term>
<def id="k-p11.3">
Foundation, a place in the open desert wastes on the east of
Jordan (<scripRef passage="Judg. 8:10" id="k-p12.1" parsed="|Judg|8|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.8.10">Judg. 8:10</scripRef>), not far beyond Succoth and Penuel, to the
south. Here Gideon overtook and routed a fugitive band of
Midianites under Zeba and Zalmunna, whom he took captive.
</def>
<term id="k-p12.2">Kartah</term>
<def id="k-p12.3">
City, a town in the tribe of Zebulun assigned to the Levites of
the family of Merari (<scripRef passage="Josh. 21:34" id="k-p13.1" parsed="|Josh|21|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.21.34">Josh. 21:34</scripRef>). It is identical with Kattath
(19:15), and perhaps also with Kitron (Judg. 1:30).
</def>
<term id="k-p13.3">Kartan</term>
<def id="k-p13.4">
Double city, a town of Naphali, assigned to the Gershonite
Levites, and one of the cities of refuge (<scripRef passage="Josh. 21:32" id="k-p14.1" parsed="|Josh|21|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.21.32">Josh. 21:32</scripRef>). It was
probably near the north-western shore of the Sea of Tiberias,
identical with the ruined village el-Katanah.
</def>
<term id="k-p14.2">Kattath</term>
<def id="k-p14.3">
(Josh. 19:15), a town of Asher, has been identified with Kana el
Jelil. (See CANA.)
</def>
<term id="k-p15.3">Kedar</term>
<def id="k-p15.4">
Dark-skinned, the second son of Ishmael (Gen. 25:13).
It is the name for the nomadic tribes of Arabs, the Bedouins

generally (<scripRef passage="Isa. 21:16" id="k-p17.1" parsed="|Isa|21|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.21.16">Isa. 21:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 42:11" id="k-p17.2" parsed="|Isa|42|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.42.11">42:11</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa 60:7" id="k-p17.3" parsed="|Isa|60|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.60.7">60:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Jer. 2:10" id="k-p17.4" parsed="|Jer|2|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.2.10">Jer. 2:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ezek. 27:21" id="k-p17.5" parsed="|Ezek|27|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ezek.27.21">Ezek. 27:21</scripRef>), who
dwelt in the north-west of Arabia. They lived in black
hair-tents (<scripRef passage="Cant. 1:5" id="k-p17.6" parsed="|Song|1|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Song.1.5">Cant. 1:5</scripRef>). To “dwell in the tents of Kedar” was to
be cut off from the worship of the true God (<scripRef passage="Ps. 120:5" id="k-p17.7" parsed="|Ps|120|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.120.5">Ps. 120:5</scripRef>). The
Kedarites suffered at the hands of Nebuchadnezzar (Jer. 49:28, 29).
</def>
<term id="k-p17.10">Kedemah</term>
Eastward, the last-named of the sons of Ishmael (Gen. 25:15).
</def>
<term id="k-p18.2">Kedemoth</term>
<def id="k-p18.3">
Beginnings; easternmost, a city of Reuben, assigned to the
Levites of the family of Merari (<scripRef passage="Josh. 13:18" id="k-p19.1" parsed="|Josh|13|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.13.18">Josh. 13:18</scripRef>). It lay not far
north-east of Dibon-gad, east of the Dead Sea.
</def>
<term id="k-p19.2">Kedesh</term>
<def id="k-p19.3">
Sanctuary. (1.) A place in the extreme south of Judah (Josh. 15:23). Probably the same as Kadesh-barnea (q.v.).
(2.) A city of Issachar (1 Chr. 6:72). Possibly Tell Abu
Kadeis, near Lejjun.
(3.) A “fenced city” of Naphtali, one of the cities of refuge

(<scripRef passage="Josh. 19:37" id="k-p22.1" parsed="|Josh|19|37|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.19.37">Josh. 19:37</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 4:6" id="k-p22.2" parsed="|Judg|4|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.4.6">Judg. 4:6</scripRef>). It was assigned to the Gershonite
Levites (<scripRef passage="Josh. 21:32" id="k-p22.3" parsed="|Josh|21|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.21.32">Josh. 21:32</scripRef>). It was originally a Canaanite royal city

(<scripRef passage="Josh. 12:22" id="k-p22.4" parsed="|Josh|12|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.12.22">Josh. 12:22</scripRef>), and was the residence of Barak (<scripRef passage="Judg. 4:6" id="k-p22.5" parsed="|Judg|4|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.4.6">Judg. 4:6</scripRef>); and
here he and Deborah assembled the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali
before the commencement of the conflict with Sisera in the plain
of Esdraelon, “for Jehovah among the mighty” (9, 10). In the
reign of Pekah it was taken by Tiglath-Pileser (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 15:29" id="k-p22.6" parsed="|2Kgs|15|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.15.29">2 Kings 15:29</scripRef>).
It was situated near the “plain” (rather “the oak”) of Zaanaim,
and has been identified with the modern Kedes, on the hills
fully four miles north-west of Lake El Huleh.
It has been supposed by some that the Kedesh of the narrative,
where Barak assembled his troops, was not the place in Upper
Galilee so named, which was 30 miles distant from the plain of
Esdraelon, but Kedish, on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, 12
miles from Tabor.
</def>
<term id="k-p23.1">Kedron</term>
<def id="k-p23.2">
The valley, now quite narrow, between the Mount of Olives and
Mount Moriah. The upper part of it is called the Valley of
Jehoshaphat. The LXX., in <scripRef passage="1 Kings 15:13" id="k-p24.1" parsed="|1Kgs|15|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.15.13">1 Kings 15:13</scripRef>, translate “of the
cedar.” The word means “black,” and may refer to the colour of
the water or the gloom of the ravine, or the black green of the
cedars which grew there. <scripRef passage="John 18:1" id="k-p24.2" parsed="|John|18|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.18.1">John 18:1</scripRef>, “Cedron,” only here in New
Testament. (See KIDRON.)
</def>
<term id="k-p24.4">Kehelathah</term>
<def id="k-p24.5">
Assembly, one of the stations of the Israelites in the desert
(Num. 33:22, 23).
</def>
<term id="k-p25.3">Keilah</term>
<def id="k-p25.4">
Citadel, a city in the lowlands of Judah (Josh. 15:44). David
rescued it from the attack of the Philistines (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 23:1-8" id="k-p26.2" parsed="|1Sam|23|1|23|8" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.23.1-1Sam.23.8">1 Sam. 23:1-8</scripRef>);
but the inhabitants proving unfaithful to him, in that they
sought to deliver him up to Saul (13), he and his men “departed
from Keilah, and went whithersoever they could go.” They fled to
the hill Hareth, about 3 miles to the east, and thence through
Hebron to Ziph (q.v.). “And David was in the wilderness of Ziph,
in a wood” (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 23:15" id="k-p26.3" parsed="|1Sam|23|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.23.15">1 Sam. 23:15</scripRef>). Here Jonathan sought him out, “and
strengthened his hand in God.” This was the last interview
between David and Jonathan (23:16-18). It is the modern Khurbet
Kila. Others identify it with Khuweilfeh, between Beit Jibrin
(Eleutheropolis) and Beersheba, mentioned in the Amarna tablets.
</def>
<term id="k-p26.4">Kelita</term>
<def id="k-p26.5">
Dwarf, a Levite who assisted Ezra in expounding the law to the
people (Neh. 8:7; 10:10).
</def>
<term id="k-p27.3">Kemuel</term>
<def id="k-p27.4">
Helper of God, or assembly of God. (1.) The third son of Nahor
(Gen. 22:21).
(2.) Son of Shiphtan, appointed on behalf of the tribe of
Ephraim to partition the land of Canaan (Num. 34:24).
(3.) A Levite (1 Chr. 27:17).
</def>
<term id="k-p30.2">Kenath</term>
<def id="k-p30.3">
Possession, a city of Gilead. It was captured by Nobah, who
called it by his own name (<scripRef passage="Num. 32:42" id="k-p31.1" parsed="|Num|32|42|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.32.42">Num. 32:42</scripRef>). It has been identified
with Kunawat, on the slopes of Jebel Hauran (Mount Bashan), 60
miles east from the south end of the Sea of Galilee.
</def>
<term id="k-p31.2">Kenaz</term>
<def id="k-p31.3">
Hunter. (1.) One of the sons of Eliphaz, the son of Esau. He
became the chief of an Edomitish tribe (Gen. 36:11, 15, 42).
(2.) Caleb’s younger brother, and father of Othniel (Josh. 15:17), whose family was of importance in Israel down to the
time of David (1 Chr. 27:15). Some think that Othniel (Judg. 1:13), and not Kenaz, was Caleb’s brother.
(3.) Caleb’s grandson (1 Chr. 4:15).
</def>
<term id="k-p34.2">Kenites</term>
<def id="k-p34.3">
Smiths, the name of a tribe inhabiting the desert lying between
southern Palestine and the mountains of Sinai. Jethro was of

this tribe (<scripRef passage="Judg. 1:16" id="k-p35.1" parsed="|Judg|1|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.16">Judg. 1:16</scripRef>). He is called a “Midianite” (<scripRef passage="Num. 10:29" id="k-p35.2" parsed="|Num|10|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.10.29">Num. 10:29</scripRef>), and hence it is concluded that the Midianites and the
Kenites were the same tribe. They were wandering smiths, “the
gipsies and travelling tinkers of the old Oriental world. They
formed an important guild in an age when the art of metallurgy
was confined to a few” (Sayce’s Races, etc.). They showed
kindness to Israel in their journey through the wilderness. They
accompanied them in their march as far as Jericho (<scripRef passage="Judg. 1:16" id="k-p35.3" parsed="|Judg|1|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.16">Judg. 1:16</scripRef>),
and then returned to their old haunts among the Amalekites, in
the desert to the south of Judah. They sustained afterwards
friendly relations with the Israelites when settled in Canaan

(<scripRef passage="Judg. 4:11" id="k-p35.4" parsed="|Judg|4|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.4.11">Judg. 4:11</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Judg. 4:17" id="k-p35.5" parsed="|Judg|4|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.4.17">17</scripRef>-21; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 27:10" id="k-p35.6" parsed="|1Sam|27|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.27.10">1 Sam. 27:10</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Sam. 30:29" id="k-p35.7" parsed="|1Sam|30|29|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.30.29">30:29</scripRef>). The Rechabites
belonged to this tribe (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 2:55" id="k-p35.8" parsed="|1Chr|2|55|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.2.55">1 Chr. 2:55</scripRef>) and in the days of Jeremiah
(35:7-10) are referred to as following their nomad habits. Saul
bade them depart from the Amalekites (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 15:6" id="k-p35.9" parsed="|1Sam|15|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.15.6">1 Sam. 15:6</scripRef>) when, in
obedience to the divine commission, he was about to “smite
Amalek.” And his reason is, “for ye showed kindness to all the
children of Israel when they came up out of Egypt.” Thus “God is
not unrighteous to forget the kindnesses shown to his people;
but they shall be remembered another day, at the farthest in the
great day, and recompensed in the resurrection of the just” (M.
Henry’s Commentary). They are mentioned for the last time in
Scripture in 1 Sam. 27:10; comp. 30:20.
</def>
<term id="k-p35.11">Kenizzite</term>
(1.) The name of a tribe referred to in the covenant God made
with Abraham (<scripRef passage="Gen. 15:19" id="k-p36.1" parsed="|Gen|15|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.15.19">Gen. 15:19</scripRef>). They are not mentioned among the

original inhabitants of Canaan (<scripRef passage="Ex. 3:8" id="k-p36.2" parsed="|Exod|3|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.3.8">Ex. 3:8</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Josh. 3:10" id="k-p36.3" parsed="|Josh|3|10|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.3.10">Josh. 3:10</scripRef>), and
probably they inhabited some part of Arabia, in the confines of
Syria.
(2.) A designation given to Caleb (R.V., Num. 32:12; A.V.,
Kenezite).
</def>
<term id="k-p37.2">Kerchief</term>
<def id="k-p37.3">
Mentioned only Ezek. 13:18, 21, as an article of apparel or
ornament applied to the head of the idolatrous women of Israel.
The precise meaning of the word is uncertain. It appears to have
been a long loose shawl, such as Oriental women wrap themselves

in (<scripRef passage="Ruth 3:15" id="k-p38.3" parsed="|Ruth|3|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ruth.3.15">Ruth 3:15</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Isa. 3:22" id="k-p38.4" parsed="|Isa|3|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.3.22">Isa. 3:22</scripRef>). Some think that it was a long veil or
head-dress, denoting by its form the position of those who wore
it.
</def>
<term id="k-p38.5">Keren-happuch</term>
<def id="k-p38.6">
Horn of the face-paint = cosmetic-box, the name of Job’s third
daughter (<scripRef passage="Job. 42:14" id="k-p39.1" parsed="|Job|42|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.42.14">Job. 42:14</scripRef>), born after prosperity had returned to
him.
</def>
<term id="k-p39.2">Kerioth</term>
<def id="k-p39.3">
Cities. (1.) A town in the south of Judah (Josh. 15:25). Judas
the traitor was probably a native of this place, and hence his
name Iscariot. It has been identified with the ruins of
el-Kureitein, about 10 miles south of Hebron. (See
HAZOR [4]).
(2.) A city of Moab (Jer. 48:24, 41), called Kirioth (Amos 2:2).
</def>
<term id="k-p41.4">Kesitah</term>
<def id="k-p41.5">
(Gen. 33:19, R.V., marg., a Hebrew word, rendered, A.V., pl.
“pieces of money,” marg., “lambs;” <scripRef passage="Josh. 24:32" id="k-p42.2" parsed="|Josh|24|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.24.32">Josh. 24:32</scripRef>, “pieces of
silver;” <scripRef passage="Job 42:11" id="k-p42.3" parsed="|Job|42|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Job.42.11">Job 42:11</scripRef>, “piece of money”). The kesitah was probably
a piece of money of a particular weight, cast in the form of a
lamb. The monuments of Egypt show that such weights were used.
(See PIECES.)
</def>
<term id="k-p42.5">Kettle</term>
<def id="k-p42.6">
A large pot for cooking. The same Hebrew word (dud, “boiling”)

is rendered also “pot” (<scripRef passage="Ps. 81:6" id="k-p43.1" parsed="|Ps|81|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.81.6">Ps. 81:6</scripRef>), “caldron” (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 35:13" id="k-p43.2" parsed="|2Chr|35|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.35.13">2 Chr. 35:13</scripRef>),
“basket” (<scripRef passage="Jer. 24:2" id="k-p43.3" parsed="|Jer|24|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Jer.24.2">Jer. 24:2</scripRef>). It was used for preparing the
peace-offerings (1 Sam. 2:13, 14).
</def>
<term id="k-p43.6">Keturah</term>
<def id="k-p43.7">
Incense, the wife of Abraham, whom he married probably after
Sarah’s death (<scripRef passage="Gen. 25:1-6" id="k-p44.1" parsed="|Gen|25|1|25|6" osisRef="Bible:Gen.25.1-Gen.25.6">Gen. 25:1-6</scripRef>), by whom he had six sons, whom he
sent away into the east country. Her nationality is unknown. She
is styled “Abraham’s concubine” (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 1:32" id="k-p44.2" parsed="|1Chr|1|32|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.1.32">1 Chr. 1:32</scripRef>). Through the
offshoots of the Keturah line Abraham became the “father of many
nations.”
</def>
<term id="k-p44.3">Key</term>
<def id="k-p44.4">
Frequently mentioned in Scripture. It is called in Hebrew
maphteah, i.e., the opener (Judg. 3:25); and in the Greek New
Testament kleis, from its use in shutting (Matt. 16:19; Luke 11:52; Rev. 1:18, etc.). Figures of ancient Egyptian keys are
frequently found on the monuments, also of Assyrian locks and
keys of wood, and of a large size (comp. Isa. 22:22).
The word is used figuratively of power or authority or office

(<scripRef passage="Isa. 22:22" id="k-p46.1" parsed="|Isa|22|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.22.22">Isa. 22:22</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 3:7" id="k-p46.2" parsed="|Rev|3|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.3.7">Rev. 3:7</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 1:8" id="k-p46.3" parsed="|Rev|1|8|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.1.8">Rev. 1:8</scripRef>; comp. 9:1; 20:1; comp. also

<scripRef passage="Matt. 16:19" id="k-p46.4" parsed="|Matt|16|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.16.19">Matt. 16:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 18:18" id="k-p46.5" parsed="|Matt|18|18|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.18.18">18:18</scripRef>). The “key of knowledge” (<scripRef passage="Luke 11:52" id="k-p46.6" parsed="|Luke|11|52|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Luke.11.52">Luke 11:52</scripRef>; comp.
<scripRef passage="Matt. 23:13" id="k-p46.7" parsed="|Matt|23|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.23.13">Matt. 23:13</scripRef>) is the means of attaining the knowledge regarding
the kingdom of God. The “power of the keys” is a phrase in
general use to denote the extent of ecclesiastical authority.
</def>
<term id="k-p46.8">Kezia</term>
<def id="k-p46.9">
Cassia, the name of Job’s second daughter (42:14), born after
prosperity had returned to him.
</def>
<term id="k-p47.1">Keziz</term>
<def id="k-p47.2">
Abrupt; cut off, a city of the tribe of Benjamin (Josh. 18:21).
</def>
<term id="k-p48.2">Kibroth-hattaavah</term>
<def id="k-p48.3">
The graves of the longing or of lust, one of the stations of the
Israelites in the wilderness. It was probably in the Wady
Murrah, and has been identified with the Erweis el-Ebeirig,
where the remains of an ancient encampment have been found,
about 30 miles north-east of Sinai, and exactly a day’s journey
from ‘Ain Hudherah.
“Here began the troubles of the journey. First, complaints
broke out among the people, probably at the heat, the toil, and
the privations of the march; and then God at once punished them
by lightning, which fell on the hinder part of the camp, and
killed many persons, but ceased at the intercession of Moses

(<scripRef passage="Num. 11:1" id="k-p50.1" parsed="|Num|11|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.11.1">Num. 11:1</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num 11:2" id="k-p50.2" parsed="|Num|11|2|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.11.2">2</scripRef>). Then a disgust fell on the multitude at having
nothing to eat but the manna day after day, no change, no flesh,
no fish, no high-flavoured vegetables, no luscious fruits...The
people loathed the ‘light food,’ and cried out to Moses, ‘Give
us flesh, give us flesh, that we may eat.’” In this emergency
Moses, in despair, cried unto God. An answer came. God sent “a
prodigious flight of quails, on which the people satiated their
gluttonous appetite for a full month. Then punishment fell on
them: they loathed the food which they had desired; it bred
disease in them; the divine anger aggravated the disease into a
plague, and a heavy mortality was the consequence. The dead were
buried without the camp; and in memory of man’s sin and of the
divine wrath this name, Kibroth-hattaavah, the Graves of Lust,

was given to the place of their sepulchre” (<scripRef passage="Num. 11:34" id="k-p50.3" parsed="|Num|11|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.11.34">Num. 11:34</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Num. 11:35" id="k-p50.4" parsed="|Num|11|35|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Num.11.35">35</scripRef>;

33:16, 17; <scripRef passage="Deut. 9:22" id="k-p50.5" parsed="|Deut|9|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.9.22">Deut. 9:22</scripRef>; comp. <scripRef passage="Ps. 78:30" id="k-p50.6" parsed="|Ps|78|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.78.30">Ps. 78:30</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Ps. 78:31" id="k-p50.7" parsed="|Ps|78|31|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Ps.78.31">31</scripRef>)., Rawlinson’s Moses,
p. 175. From this encampment they journeyed in a north-eastern
direction to Hazeroth.
</def>
<term id="k-p50.8">Kibzaim</term>
<def id="k-p50.9">
Two heaps, a city of Ephraim, assigned to the Kohathite Levites,
and appointed as a city of refuge (<scripRef passage="Josh. 21" id="k-p51.1" parsed="|Josh|21|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.21">Josh. 21</scripRef>: 22). It is also
called Jokmeam (1 Chr. 6:68).
</def>
<term id="k-p51.3">Kid</term>
<def id="k-p51.4">
The young of the goat. It was much used for food (Gen. 27:9;

<scripRef passage="Gen 38:17" id="k-p52.2" parsed="|Gen|38|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.38.17">38:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg. 6:19" id="k-p52.3" parsed="|Judg|6|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.6.19">Judg. 6:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Judg 14:6" id="k-p52.4" parsed="|Judg|14|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.14.6">14:6</scripRef>). The Mosaic law forbade to dress a kid

in the milk of its dam, a law which is thrice repeated (<scripRef passage="Ex. 23:19" id="k-p52.5" parsed="|Exod|23|19|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.23.19">Ex. 23:19</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Ex 34:26" id="k-p52.6" parsed="|Exod|34|26|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Exod.34.26">34:26</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Deut. 14:21" id="k-p52.7" parsed="|Deut|14|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Deut.14.21">Deut. 14:21</scripRef>). Among the various reasons assigned
for this law, that appears to be the most satisfactory which
regards it as “a protest against cruelty and outraging the order
of nature.” A kid cooked in its mother’s milk is “a gross,
unwholesome dish, and calculated to kindle animal and ferocious
passions, and on this account Moses may have forbidden it.
Besides, it is even yet associated with immoderate feasting; and
originally, I suspect,” says Dr. Thomson (Land and the Book),
“was connected with idolatrous sacrifices.”
</def>
<term id="k-p52.8">Kidron</term>
<def id="k-p52.9">
= Kedron = Cedron, turbid, the winter torrent which flows
through the Valley of Jehoshaphat, on the eastern side of
Jerusalem, between the city and the Mount of Olives. This valley
is known in Scripture only by the name “the brook Kidron.” David
crossed this brook bare-foot and weeping, when fleeing from

Absalom (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 15:23" id="k-p53.1" parsed="|2Sam|15|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.15.23">2 Sam. 15:23</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 15:30" id="k-p53.2" parsed="|2Sam|15|30|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.15.30">30</scripRef>), and it was frequently crossed by our
Lord in his journeyings to and fro (<scripRef passage="John 18:1" id="k-p53.3" parsed="|John|18|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:John.18.1">John 18:1</scripRef>). Here Asa burned
the obscene idols of his mother (<scripRef passage="1 Kings 15:13" id="k-p53.4" parsed="|1Kgs|15|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.15.13">1 Kings 15:13</scripRef>), and here
Athaliah was executed (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 11:16" id="k-p53.5" parsed="|2Kgs|11|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.11.16">2 Kings 11:16</scripRef>). It afterwards became the

receptacle for all manner of impurities (<scripRef passage="2 Chr. 29:16" id="k-p53.6" parsed="|2Chr|29|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.29.16">2 Chr. 29:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Chr. 30:14" id="k-p53.7" parsed="|2Chr|30|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Chr.30.14">30:14</scripRef>);
and in the time of Josiah this valley was the common cemetery of
the city (2 Kings 23:6; comp. Jer. 26:23).
Through this mountain ravine no water runs, except after heavy
rains in the mountains round about Jerusalem. Its length from
its head to en-Rogel is 2 3/4 miles. Its precipitous, rocky
banks are filled with ancient tombs, especially the left bank
opposite the temple area. The greatest desire of the Jews is to
be buried there, from the idea that the Kidron is the “valley of
Jehoshaphat” mentioned in Joel 3:2.
Below en-Rogel the Kidron has no historical or sacred
interest. It runs in a winding course through the wilderness of
Judea to the north-western shore of the Dead Sea. Its whole
length, in a straight line, is only some 20 miles, but in this
space its descent is about 3,912 feet. (See KEDRON.)
Recent excavations have brought to light the fact that the old
bed of the Kidron is about 40 feet lower than its present bed,
and about 70 feet nearer the sanctuary wall.
</def>
<term id="k-p56.1">Kinah</term>
<def id="k-p56.2">
An elegy, a city in the extreme south of Judah (Josh. 15:22). It
was probably not far from the Dead Sea, in the Wady Fikreh.
</def>
<term id="k-p57.2">Kine</term>
<def id="k-p57.3">
(Heb. sing. parah, i.e., “fruitful”), mentioned in Pharaoh’s
dream (<scripRef passage="Gen. 41" id="k-p58.1" parsed="|Gen|41|0|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Gen.41">Gen. 41</scripRef>: 18). Here the word denotes “buffaloes,” which
fed on the reeds and sedge by the river’s brink.
</def>
<term id="k-p58.2">King</term>
<def id="k-p58.3">
Is in Scripture very generally used to denote one invested with
authority, whether extensive or limited. There were thirty-one

kings in Canaan (<scripRef passage="Josh. 12:9" id="k-p59.1" parsed="|Josh|12|9|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.12.9">Josh. 12:9</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Josh. 12:24" id="k-p59.2" parsed="|Josh|12|24|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Josh.12.24">24</scripRef>), whom Joshua subdued.
Adonibezek subdued seventy kings (<scripRef passage="Judg. 1:7" id="k-p59.3" parsed="|Judg|1|7|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Judg.1.7">Judg. 1:7</scripRef>). In the New

Testament the Roman emperor is spoken of as a king (<scripRef passage="1 Pet. 2:13" id="k-p59.4" parsed="|1Pet|2|13|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.2.13">1 Pet. 2:13</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Pet. 2:17" id="k-p59.5" parsed="|1Pet|2|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Pet.2.17">17</scripRef>); and Herod Antipas, who was only a tetrarch, is also called
a king (Matt. 14:9; Mark 6:22).
This title is applied to God (1 Tim. 1:17), and to Christ, the

Son of God (<scripRef passage="1 Tim. 6:15" id="k-p60.2" parsed="|1Tim|6|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.6.15">1 Tim. 6:15</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="1 Tim. 6:16" id="k-p60.3" parsed="|1Tim|6|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Tim.6.16">16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 27:11" id="k-p60.4" parsed="|Matt|27|11|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.11">Matt. 27:11</scripRef>). The people of God are

also called “kings” (<scripRef passage="Dan. 7:22" id="k-p60.5" parsed="|Dan|7|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.7.22">Dan. 7:22</scripRef>, <scripRef passage="Dan. 7:27" id="k-p60.6" parsed="|Dan|7|27|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Dan.7.27">27</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt. 19:28" id="k-p60.7" parsed="|Matt|19|28|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.19.28">Matt. 19:28</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Rev. 1:6" id="k-p60.8" parsed="|Rev|1|6|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Rev.1.6">Rev. 1:6</scripRef>,
etc.). Death is called the “king of terrors” (Job 18:14).
Jehovah was the sole King of the Jewish nation (1 Sam. 8:7;
<scripRef passage="Isa. 33:22" id="k-p61.2" parsed="|Isa|33|22|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.33.22">Isa. 33:22</scripRef>). But there came a time in the history of that people
when a king was demanded, that they might be like other nations
(<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 8:5" id="k-p61.3" parsed="|1Sam|8|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.8.5">1 Sam. 8:5</scripRef>). The prophet Samuel remonstrated with them, but the
people cried out, “Nay, but we will have a king over us.” The
misconduct of Samuel’s sons was the immediate cause of this
demand.
The Hebrew kings did not rule in their own right, nor in name
of the people who had chosen them, but partly as servants and

partly as representatives of Jehovah, the true King of Israel (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 10:1" id="k-p62.1" parsed="|1Sam|10|1|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.10.1">1 Sam. 10:1</scripRef>). The limits of the king’s power were prescribed (<scripRef passage="1 Sam. 10:25" id="k-p62.2" parsed="|1Sam|10|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Sam.10.25">1 Sam. 10:25</scripRef>). The officers of his court were, (1) the recorder or

remembrancer (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 8:16" id="k-p62.3" parsed="|2Sam|8|16|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.8.16">2 Sam. 8:16</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:3" id="k-p62.4" parsed="|1Kgs|4|3|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.3">1 Kings 4:3</scripRef>); (2) the scribe (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 8:17" id="k-p62.5" parsed="|2Sam|8|17|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.8.17">2 Sam. 8:17</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="2 Sam. 20:25" id="k-p62.6" parsed="|2Sam|20|25|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.20.25">20:25</scripRef>); (3) the officer over the house, the chief steward
(<scripRef passage="Isa. 22:15" id="k-p62.7" parsed="|Isa|22|15|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Isa.22.15">Isa. 22:15</scripRef>); (4) the “king’s friend,” a confidential companion

(<scripRef passage="1 Kings 4:5" id="k-p62.8" parsed="|1Kgs|4|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.4.5">1 Kings 4:5</scripRef>); (5) the keeper of the wardrobe (<scripRef passage="2 Kings 22:14" id="k-p62.9" parsed="|2Kgs|22|14|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.22.14">2 Kings 22:14</scripRef>);
(6) captain of the bodyguard (<scripRef passage="2 Sam. 20:23" id="k-p62.10" parsed="|2Sam|20|23|0|0" osisRef="Bible:2Sam.20.23">2 Sam. 20:23</scripRef>); (7) officers over
the king’s treasures, etc. (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 27:25-31" id="k-p62.11" parsed="|1Chr|27|25|27|31" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.27.25-1Chr.27.31">1 Chr. 27:25-31</scripRef>); (8)
commander-in-chief of the army (<scripRef passage="1 Chr. 27:34" id="k-p62.12" parsed="|1Chr|27|34|0|0" osisRef="Bible:1Chr.27.34">1 Chr. 27:34</scripRef>); (9) the royal
counsellor (1 Chr. 27:32; 2 Sam. 16:20-23).
(For catalogue of kings of Israel and Judah see chronological
table in Appendix.)
</def>
<term id="k-p63.1">Kingdom of God</term>
<def id="k-p63.2">
(Matt. 6:33; Mark 1:14, 15; Luke 4:43) = “kingdom of Christ”

(<scripRef passage="Matt. 13:41" id="k-p64.5" parsed="|Matt|13|41|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.13.41">Matt. 13:41</scripRef>; <scripRef passage="Matt 20:21" id="k-p64.6" parsed="|Matt|20|21|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Matt.20.21">20:21</scripRef>) = “kingdom of Christ and of God” (<scripRef passage="Eph. 5:5" id="k-p64.7" parsed="|Eph|5|5|0|0" osisRef="Bible:Eph.5.5">Eph. 5:5</scripRef>)
